experiment_title: Retrospective Evaluation of Incidence and Severity of Adverse Health Effects Due to Host-Microorganism Interactions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Previous research has demonstrated that the spaceflight environment corresponds with several changes in microorganisms and the human immune system which could potentially increase the risk of infectious disease or an microbial-associated allergic response among crewmembers. However, the nature of the spaceflight environment’s contribution to these changes and the larger risk remains understudied.

In this investigation, the researchers sought to adapt the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) approach to understanding the relationship between human health risk with plants, animals, and their shared environment using a collaborative, multisectoral, and transdisciplinary framework. To leverage this approach for spaceflight health risks, the investigator team combined clinical data from astronauts and environmental microbiological monitoring data from the International Space Station (ISS) to better understand the actual risk of infectious disease in crew and potential impacts to crew performance.

The original scope of this study analyzed disease events based on symptomology or other event descriptions and/or documentation of pharmaceutical use (e.g., antibiotics, antivirals, antihistamines, corticosteroids). In 2025, an augmentation was added to this study to incorporate a new list of clinical events describing the incidence of infectious disease aboard ISS over a ten-year period. This new list was presented to the Human System Risk Board (HSRB) in December 2024 and constrained the included health events to those where crew symptomology resulting in the prescription of antibiotics and did not include events where the disease event could have been caused by multiple factors (e.g., skin rash).

Specific Aims:
  1. Conduct retrospective data mining of available clinical incidence reports before, during, and after ISS spaceflight missions to model microbial changes relative to adverse health events (infections and/or allergies) and to capture potentially missed data that could improve low resolution implications of infectious disease.
  2. Identify and compare contributing factors of infectious disease on clinical incidence reports and health from Aim 1 by assessing questionnaires, diary inputs, environmental microbiological monitoring and other relevant operational and research data.
  3. Input data into a machine learning-based model of clinically relevant microbe presence on ISS that is currently in development as a TRISH-sponsored project to establish a foundation for improvement of future studies and potential operational use.
  4. Based on identification of knowledge gaps during this study, develop requirements recommendations to support future tracking of preflight, inflight, and postflight infectious disease events.
An additional aim was added as part of the augmentation to this study:
5. Model microbial changes relative to adverse infectious disease events based on the updated ten-year clinical incidence based on the prescription of antibiotics.

APPROACH:
During the original study, the investigators mined retrospective data of available clinical incidence of infectious disease before, during, and after ISS spaceflight missions to model microbial changes relative to adverse health events. The investigators then used the following approaches to evaluate the resulting dataset:
  1. Assess health events recorded up to L-45 and R+30, including all inflight data available.
  2. Assess health events with no definitive diagnoses, subtle clinical manifestations, and/or subclinical manifestation to capture potentially missed infectious disease events (for example: allergies, rash, headache, congestion, etc.).
  3. Evaluate photos of problems like skin rashes, descriptions of clinical signs, length of time affected, progression/resolution descriptions, anything that was recommended/used to help resolve (not just antibiotic treatment).
  4. Preflight, inflight, and postflight environmental monitoring data, focusing on microbiological analyses of air, surface, water, and food;
  5. Preflight, inflight, and postflight samples for culture diagnostics as well as clinical events reported (e.g., upper respiratory, GI, skin, etc.);
  6. Preflight, inflight, and postflight immune changes, including antibody titers, cell counts, etc.
An augmentation to this study added that this effort would specifically focus on the updated approach for determining 10-year (2010-2020) clinical incidence for incidence of adverse infectious disease events based on the prescription of antibiotics. The investigator team used a random forest approach, a supervised machine learning algorithm which generates decision trees for classification and regression tasks, to analyze the microbial and crew health datasets.

RESULTS:
The investigators expected that leveraging the CDC’s transdisciplinary approach to understanding human health risk for a spaceflight context would identify additional factors that could be incorporated into prospective studies in the future, such as crew immunological status, spaceflight-induced alterations in microbial virulence, and the impact of plants and rodents on the environment. If successful, this integrative approach would help to improve future decision making on countermeasures to prevent loss of crew or loss of performance due to adverse health events.

Due to the restrictions on the 10-year infectious disease incidence dataset aboard ISS (requiring (1) flight surgeon diagnosis and (2) the prescription of antibiotics), the resulting dataset suffered from a small sample size (n=11).

As the conclusion of this study, the investigators were able to provide a list of recommendations for future efforts to collect data that will have a high likelihood of generating predictive relationships in random forest analysis and creating a forecasting model which would improve risk assessment and response to infectious disease during long-duration spaceflight:
  • Time-match longitudinal crew health monitoring and microbiome and environmental surveillance.
  • Enable point-of-care pathogen diagnostics to deploy rapid molecular diagnostics and enable real-time identification of pathogens and guide immediate interventions to lessen the impacts of disease to crewmembers and the mission.
  • Enable immunologic monitoring to measure immune system markers such as cytokines, leukocyte activity, and stress hormones.
  • Use standardized electronic health records and real-time symptom reporting, and leverage machine learning approaches to detect emerging disease patterns.
  • Conduct retrospective analysis of stored samples and crew health data after conclusion of the mission. This would help to identify delayed infections and refine surveillance strategies.

Due to the low number of disease events captured by the analyzed dataset, it was not possible to identify statistical significance when attempting to model the relationship between microbial populations and clinical outcomes. The investigators suggested that larger, multidimensional datasets would be required to fully leverage machine learning techniques to better understand the microbial ecology impact on astronaut health outcomes during spaceflight.

experiment_title: Combined Effects of Space Radiation and Microgravity on the Function of Human Capillaries and the Endothelial Barrier:  Implications for Degenerative Disorders
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This investigation is aimed at determining the effects of space radiation combined with microgravity on the function of human blood vessels and capillaries. The average human body contains tens of thousands of miles of vessels that permeate every tissue down to the microscopic level. The vascular system is crucial to healthy functioning of the tissues. Its dysfunction is not only a primary event in a range of degenerative diseases, but also an important influencing factor in many others. Two functions of the human vascular system that greatly affect human health and disease are: 1. the growth of new vessels to replace damaged vessels (angiogenesis), and 2. the process that allows nutritious molecules to cross from the blood to tissues and waste molecules to be cleared out from tissues (endothelial barrier function). Disruption of these processes is known to cause degenerative disease.
Previous studies have shown that the human vasculature is an important target for radiation and it is also influenced by gravitational forces. Specifically, by using human endothelial cells in 2 and 3-dimensional human tissue models, it has been shown that space radiation inhibits angiogenesis and disrupts endothelial barrier function. Because the doses and time course for radiation-induced events are now known, it possible to assay for joint effects with other environmental influences. Since angiogenesis and barrier function are also affected by microgravity, there is a potential for further dysfunction of the human vasculature when applied in combination with radiation.
The objectives of this study are to use simulated microgravity to:
  1. Determine the combined effects of space radiation and microgravity on human blood vessel models.
  2. Determine the impact of the combination of space radiation and microgravity on degeneration by testing for angiogenesis and endothelial barrier function using previously established assays.

experiment_title: Self-Guided Multimedia Stress Management and Resilience Training
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Stress and anxiety-related problems are some of the most common and costly behavioral health problems in society. For those working in operational environments (i.e., astronauts, flight controllers, military), stress and anxiety-related problems before, during, or after missions can seriously compromise efficiency, safety, and performance. To address behavioral health issues like stress, it is important to maximize the privacy, validity, and acceptability of the training and countermeasures used. Technology-based behavioral health programs (e.g., computer or web-based programs) are effective for treating behavioral health problems. These programs increase availability of evidence-based interventions to individuals who are not able or willing to receive such in-person treatments. Prior research validated the autonomous multimedia resilience training program the investigators created (i.e., Stress Management and Resilience Training for Optimal Performance; SMART-OP). SMART-OP interactively trains users to manage stress and build resilience over six weekly training sessions lastly approximately 45 minutes each. Results from a randomized controlled trial with a stressed but otherwise healthy sample (N=66) indicated that SMART-OP decreased perceived stress, improved perceived control over stress, and was rated as significantly more useful than an attention control group that received marketed videos and published material on stress management. SMART-OP was also rated as “excellent” in terms of user-friendliness, acceptability, and had low dropout, and high homework adherence.
APPROACH:
The investigators propose to evaluate the effectiveness, usefulness, and usability of SMART-OP with a sample of flight controllers and instructors (including those in training flow) at Johnson Space Center (JSC) by comparing it to an attention control group. Additionally, they will examine the effects of self-guided stress management and resilience training on biomarkers for stress (i.e., cortisol, a-amylase), heart rate, and cognitive and behavioral performance. Based on several meetings with the Space Flight Resource Management (SFRM) Working Group, investigators learned that trainees are not progressing through the training flow satisfactorily and that they identified stress as a potential contributor to poor trainee performance. Additionally, stress was identified as an area of concern to address with flight controller and instructors. Since SMART-OP significantly reduced perceived stress, increased perceived control over stressors, and was rated as highly useful, SMART-OP could provide helpful stress management training for flight controllers. Also, since SMART-OP is evidence-based, confidential, and self-directed, it may be more acceptable to flight controller trainees than other programs.
RESULTS:
This experiment is in progress. However, preliminary results are available.
Study Implementation: The majority of work during 2013-2014 was spent on various aspects of implementing the study at JSC. The study is designed to be conducted in a self-guided fashion where possible which means the study participant needs to conduct much of the assessment and all of the stress management training independently (i.e., without research coordinators). IRB protocols and approvals were obtained at JSC and UCLA to conduct the study. Biweekly teleconferences with NASA BHP personnel addressed various areas of study implementation and maintained regular communication. Progress during this period covered several areas including reserving and setting up a study room on site to conduct the study including assessments. Study computers and iPads were programmed and authenticated for use in the study. Additional study materials were purchased including heart rate monitors. There were several logistical/technical issues/hurdles that were addressed to give the UCLA research team required access to conduct the study from afar. Accomplishing this involved regular communication with JSC BHP and IT staff and personnel. The UCLA research team made two trips to JSC to address various aspects of study implementation including giving several informational session presentations for study recruitment; adding software and other information to JSC computers for assessments and stress management training sessions; testing computers for functionality and reliability; and testing the downloading of training session and assessment data for functionality.
Assessment Procedures: The UCLA research team created several assessment tasks required for the study. The tasks involved computer programming so that study participants could conduct much of the assessments in a self-guided fashion. These involved creating online questionnaires, programming for computerized tasks designed to frustrate/stress users, modification of the neuropsychological battery for use in current study, creation of study protocols instructing the user how to conduct assessments and stress management training sessions on their own. The JSC Nutritional Biochemistry Lab (NBL) is leading a portion of the assessment procedures which involve collection of saliva and urine to measure stress biomarkers (cortisol and alpha amylase). This part of the assessment procedures was developed jointly between the UCLA and NBL teams, protocols formulated, and then the procedures were tested during the visits of the UCLA team to JSC.

experiment_title: Occupational Risk Surveillance for Bone: Pilot Study-Effects of In-flight Countermeasures on Sub-regions of the Hip Bone
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Measurement of areal bone mineral density (BMDa, g/cm2) by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is required by NASA for assessing skeletal integrity in astronauts. Advantages of DXA include the facts that BMDa is a widely applied predictor of fractures in the aging population and that there are BMDa-based guidelines for identifying persons at high risk for osteoporotic fractures. In contrast to the 2-d imaging by DXA, quantitative computed tomography (QCT) is a 3D bone imaging technology that is used typically to scan the hip and spine. QCT is capable of measuring, volumetric BMD (BMD, mg/cm3) of separate cortical and trabecular sub-regions as well as of total (integral) bone. QCT is limited to research applications at this time because there is not enough medical evidence to determine how QCT data should be used in clinical practice. QCT however provides additional information on bone structure and increases the understanding of how bones respond to effectors of bone loss or gain. NASA recently convened a panel of clinical bone experts to review available medical and research information from astronauts who flew on long-duration space missions. As part of its charge, the panel identified a clinical trigger upon which the flight surgeon should have the astronaut evaluated further by a bone endocrinologist. Specifically, the Panel recommended that if restoration to preflight BMD is not observed for the hip trabecular compartment at two years after return to earth, then that astronaut should be evaluated for possible therapeutic intervention to prevent premature osteoporotic fractures.
This pilot study used preflight and postflight QCT scanning of the hips in International Space Station (ISS) astronauts to evaluate the ability of in-flight countermeasures to prevent the occurrence of this clinical trigger. This study furthered hypothesized that QCT scanning could distinguish the effects of different categories of in-flight countermeasures/activities on distinct sub-regions of the hip bone. For example, this pilot study demonstrated that biochemically based countermeasures (e.g., dietary manipulation of acidic to basic amino acid intake or bisphosphonates medication) have a detectable prevention of BMD loss in the hip trabecular compartment while biomechanically based countermeasures (exercise regimens) have detectable expansion of cortical bone apposition -- increasing both bone cross-sectional area and integral BMD consequently. These different effects on hip morphology have subsequently translated to an effect on hip bone strength of the ISS astronaut. The combination of countermeasures that impact both compartments resulted in greater hip bone strength -- as estimated by analyzing QCT data by Finite Element Modeling (FEM) -- than of any singly applied countermeasure. This assertion was approached in this pilot study by addressing the following objectives in each ISS astronaut:
 
1) Characterize the response of i) trabecular and cortical BMDs of the hip and ii) cross-sectional areas of cortical bone, trabecular bone and integral bone, to countermeasures that are either based upon biochemistry or mechanical-loading – with QCT measures.
2) Translate the QCT-measured changes in hip bone morphology to hip bone fracture loads (aka, “hip bone strength”) using FEM.

3) Characterize QCT-measured changes in hip bone morphology following a 12-month postflight period on earth and, in addition, translate these changes to the percentage recovery of preflight hip bone strength determined by FEM.
 
APPROACH:

QCT scanning of the hip was performed at a local hospital (e.g., Christus St. John Hospital, GE VCT 64-slice scanner) on approximately L-45, R+5, R+360 and R+720.  Cotton medical scrubs were provided for the crewmember to wear during scans. The technician was positioning the crewmember in the CT scanner prior to scanning.  The QCT scan were performed at the scanning facility as close as possible to the final departure to Russia.  QCT scanning of the hip were performed in the same hospital facility as the postflight scans to ensure that the same scanning QCT protocol would be performed on the same CT machine.  In addition, crewmembers were asked to keep an exercise and medication log pre, in, and postflight. 

RESULTS:

In this study, utility of data acquired by hip QCT scans has been demonstrated by the following: i) its delineation of concurrent mechanical and biochemical countermeasures both of which can attenuate or prevent previously-observed declines in hip aBMD after spaceflight and ii) its ability to be transformed to a functional index “bone fracture load” - which could enable NASA to assess the probability of overloading bones with physical activities (especially under atypical and possibly hazardous conditions) or to establish engineering requirements to prevent astronauts from hazardous loads. Finally, researchers conclude that QCT is an important adjunct technology to DXA testing which cannot detect the novel effects of spaceflight on the 3-dimensional measures of trabecular and cortical bones of the hip. In the end, a fuller and more accurate documentation of spaceflight effects on hip bones would be obtained to evaluate risk/benefit of various countermeasures, to inform the feasibility of in-flight mitigation strategies and to refine decision-making for the selection/deselection of countermeasures for specific spaceflight missions.

experiment_title: AR/VR and Hybrid Reality for Verification Assessments: Phase 1
experiment_description:
Objective:

NASA has a growing interest in using extended reality (XR) technologies (virtual reality, augmented reality, and hybrid reality) verification and validation activities for the Spaceflight Program. To meet NASA minimum specifications, hardware systems are required to be verified human rated. Analysis, inspection, demonstration, and testing are several methods by which verification activities can be completed. Method determination depends on the requirement type, form factors of products, and test facility availability where verification activities can take place. Verification activities can be costly, as developers must often build high-fidelity physical mockups for certain verification tests. Leveraging XR technologies in human-in-the-loop testing requires little to no hardware, construction costs, or storage facilities, which is significant in cost savings. XR allows NASA systems to be replicated by a high-fidelity virtual reality simulation which approximates the appearance, size, and functionality of a real-world experience.

The validity of verification outcomes from XR methodologies are currently unclear. The researchers for this investigation will communicate directly with NASA subject matter experts (SMEs) on using XR for activities that can help this study. The biggest concern is that verification data collected with XR technology would not be comparable to data collected in a physical mockup using traditional methods. This could result in additional risk when used for flight readiness decisions. Taking this into consideration, NASA currently limits use of XR technologies for developmental test activities only. NASA needs data and theoretical knowledge to develop guidelines for how XR technology can be applied without increasing human health and performance risk for the future. This research will help NASA understand XR technologies strengths, limitations, and gaps.

This project has the following aim:
1.           To gather and synthesize available knowledge and generate new data that will help stakeholders make informed decisions regarding the use of XR technologies for verification-related activities.

Approach:
The literature review was carried out by the project team, an overview was created of how XR technology was used for verification and related activities, such as operational testing, examining evaluations, and training. Gathered information on XR training was the start towards understanding the strengths and weaknesses of XR for different tasks. The researchers interviewed experts and stakeholders, that allowed the researchers an understanding on XR technologies success. It also helped pinpoint the strengths, weaknesses, and barriers to implementation, while giving lessons on verification. This study included a pilot study to replicate verification activities using “equivalent” virtual and physical mockups. Results of the virtual and physical mockups are compared and provide validation for XR Verification Framework. The deliverables of Phase I are used for a separate Phase II investigation. Phase II will consist of a more comprehensive study to replicate and build upon the pilot study results.
The research was conducted according to the timeline and major milestones presented below: The projected duration of the project was 12 months.
·       Literature Review – ATP + 3 months
·       Interviews – ATP + 3 months
·       Requirements Framework – ATP + 5 months
·       Pilot study protocol peer review – ATP + 5 months
·       Pilot study – ATP + 7 months
·       Research report summarizing results of the pilot test, lessons learned, – ATP + 12months.


Results:
The results from the literature review, interviews, and the pilot study generated a report that helped future developers and researchers better understand when and how XR technologies are applied and when they should be avoided in hardware system verification and validation. Results from the literature review and SME interviews produced XR Verification Decision Framework. It is the first draft for NASA to make decisions on program requirements regarding XR technologies. The framework is the foundation for identifying gaps in research. The PI team created a VR duplicate of a high-fidelity physical mockup, the Habitable Airlock. Outcomes were observed to be about the same for both mockups with two exceptions. The appropriateness of VR mockups relative to a PR mockup was evaluated, but it is both resource intensive and impractical for NASA partners. PR and VR mockup for two verification-like tasks were compared, Hand Signal Identification and Field of View. These results support the cautious conclusion from phase 1, that VR might be best suited for demonstrations.

experiment_title: Crew Population Characteristics: Perspectives for Spacesuit Fit
experiment_description:
Objective:

Interactions between the spacesuit and the body are crucial for crew performance, mobility, and injury, particularly during demanding jobs or dynamic impact events. One of the main objectives of spacesuit design is to create suits whose size and shape correspond to the population of crew members. It is nevertheless recognized that some population subgroups are not as well accommodated as others, such as petite females or people with uncommon body ratios. Therefore, a structural evaluation of the crew population's characteristics is necessary to mitigate issues with suit fit. By identifying the geometric aspects that may be able to alleviate fit concerns, this evaluation can also aid in the development of recommendations for new suit designs. This work hypothesizes that spacesuit-to-body contact is closely correlated with the suit fit of the crew population, as the contact patterns can more sensitively and accurately measure the physical constraints and subjective perception of the wearer.
The investigative team will accomplish this objective using the following specific aims:
1. Conduct suit-to-body contact pattern assessments with a focus on the hard upper torso assembly (HUT). 2. Build a probability model to predict specific HUT sizes likely to be chosen by a given crewmember as a function of the suit-to-body contact pattern. 3. Build a generative model for suit design that can yield the targeted level of fit. 4. Evaluate a crew-like population to assess the proportion of the population that can be accommodated from the available suit sizes and identify segments of the population that require additional accommodations for adequate suit fit.

Approach:

The PI team will focus on 4 criteria as they approach the hypothesis in this study. Researchers will examine the Shuttle extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) suit, paying particular attention to the hard upper torso assembly (HUT), which is crucial for crew movement and fit. The resulting suit-to-body contact patterns for each crew member or test subject who took part in EVA training will be calculated by superimposing their 3D body scan with the suit computer-aided design (CAD). The researchers will then use the data of previously selected suit sizes to train the model and validate it on human participants wearing 3D-printed replica suits that are all uniquely made to mimic variances in contact patterns. Subjective opinions and mobility data from various designs will be collected. These will be used to compare discernibility and individual tolerance to off-optimal fit. The model will be projected onto the crew-like population consisting of approximately 4,000 body scans that have been screened for the EVA Suit System Requirements from the US Army Survey. These data will be used to determine what percentage of the population can fit into the suit sizes that are available, and which demographic groups (body sizes or shapes) were not accommodated (too small or large in uncommon body ratios). The researchers will then test "what-if" scenarios, such as how the Shuttle EMU's small size HUT should have been designed and how much better crew population accommodations could have been achieved despite it not being built for the Shuttle. Moreover, the researchers will describe a "perfect world" scenario in which there are an ideal number of suit sizes and shapes that can accommodate every member of the crew.

Results:

The results of this study will improve the characterization of the body size and ratios of the astronaut crew and ultimately improve the ability of the crew to perform during EVAs as suit-to-body interactions are better understood and issues relating to fit can be mitigated. The research team will produce a report and peer-reviewed publications, a summarized suit fit prediction model, a suit development and validation methodology, assessment results, and case studies.

experiment_title: Bed Rest Standard Measures: Lactulose Test
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Gastrointestinal (GI) function plays a critical role in the absorption and bioavailability of orally administered drugs. Further, the GI tract plays a pivotal role in the bioavailability of nutrients. The availability of energy depends on intake, absorption, storage, and utilization. The absorption and bioavailability of ingested compounds depend on physiological factors such as GI motility, splanchnic blood flow, and pH of gastric secretions.
Lactulose (Lac) and acetaminophen (APAP) are commonly used in research and clinical settings to measure gastrointestinal (GI) motility and absorption; similarly, Lac is used to measure GI Transit Time (GITT) and APAP to measure GI absorption as a function of GI motility. These measures are important as they influence absorption and bioavailability of orally administered drugs which in turn influence drug efficacy. These measures are also important because the effectiveness of orally administered drugs is affected by their rate of transit in the GI tract. GI motility has been shown to be slowed in flight and with certain orally administered drugs, astronauts report reduced efficacy and absence of common side effects elicited with the administered dose on the ground. Once validated, GITT and bioavailability measurements using Lac and APAP can serve as standard measures for estimating physiological and functional changes of the GI tract in microgravity and analog environments. These standard measures help understand and estimate risk of failure to treat due to ineffectiveness of medications.
APPROACH:
Lactulose Breath Hydrogen Test (LBHT) – Serial breath samples were collected after administration of 10 g of Lac. Samples were analyzed for hydrogen concentrations using the Quintron MicrolyzerTM. GITT was determined as the time after ingestion until the time of the first sustained increase in breath hydrogen levels greater than 10ppm.
Functional and pathologic changes in the GI tract, a site for absorption and extra-hepatic metabolism of drugs, were characterized by three tests: 1) the Lactulose/ Acetaminophen Test, 2) the Glucose Breath Test and 3) the Urea Breath Test. The characterization of GI function and pharmacokinetic changes involved the collection of pre-dose biologic (breath, saliva and urine) samples followed by the ingestion of oral acetaminophen as a pharmaceutical probe, and Lac, a non-digestible sugar.
RESULTS:
This experiment was performed during Bed Rest Campaigns 3A, 3B, 3C, 3D, 3E, 3F, 5A, 5B, and 5C.
GITT increased from pre-bed rest on all days during bed rest while no difference was observed post bed rest. These results were in close agreement with those from space flight. Longer GITT values were recorded in some of the subjects. Twelve subjects had GI transit times over 2 hours during bed rest.

experiment_title: Varicella Zoster Virus Shedding After Antiviral Drug (Valacyclovir) Treatment in Antarctic Expeditioners
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Previous spaceflight studies indicate that reactivation of varicella zoster virus (VZV), particularly during longer duration spaceflights, can potentially lead to clinical disease including zoster, chronic neuropathic pain, vision loss, stroke, and cognitive impairment. Continued viral shedding after spaceflight may cause clinical disease in crew contacts including uninfected or immunocompromised individuals, as well as newborn infants. It is essential to develop countermeasures to prevent VZV reactivation during spaceflight to ensure the health of the crew, as well as the health of their contacts upon return.

In this investigation, VZV shedding in Antarctic expeditioners having patterns of VZV DNA shedding in saliva similar to patterns in astronauts will be studied. Investigators hypothesize that prophylactic administration of 1 gram daily of the antiviral drug valacyclovir to the Antarctic expeditioners will significantly reduce salivary shedding of VZV compared to placebo controls. Measures of stress and immune dysregulation should remain unaltered.

Countermeasure efficacy of valacyclovir will be determined by measuring VZV reactivation and shedding in saliva as well as measuring the physiological stress biomarkers (cortisol, DHEA, and salivary amylase) and immune markers (inflammatory cytokines) before, during, and after the winter-over period.

Specific aims are to:

  1. Study the effect of antiviral drugs on the reactivation and shedding of VZV in the saliva of Antarctic expeditioners before, during, and after winter-over.
  2. Study the effect of antiviral drugs on stress hormones and immune biomarkers (inflammatory cytokines, etc.) in the saliva of Antarctic expeditioners before, during, and after winter-over

APPROACH:
Forty subjects will be selected to participate in the study. Potential subjects with a history of renal dysfunction, chronic headaches, or allergies to valacyclovir or similar drugs will be excluded from the study as will those over 65 years of age with declining renal function, those with known renal dysfunction, and those on other potentially nephrotoxic medications.

Twenty subjects will be randomly placed in the treatment group and twenty subjects in the control group.

The treatment group will receive valacyclovir treatment, (1 gram daily), during the Antarctic winter-over period. The control group will receive a daily placebo. VZV DNA, as well as other herpesviruses including herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV1) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), will be measured before, during, and after the expedition.

Samples, consisting of 2.0 ml of passive drool saliva, will be collected once in the two months preceding winter-over (baseline), monthly (twelve times) during winter-over (deployment), and once in the two months after winter-over (return). Sampling will be done on five consecutive days at each time point. Then, samples will be frozen until processed.

Assays will be performed to monitor viral DNA, salivary stress hormones and salivary cytokines.

RESULTS:
This investigation is in progress and results are not yet available. However, this experiment is expected to determine if prophylactic administration of valacyclovir is an effective countermeasure for reactivation and shedding of VZV during long-duration spaceflight missions.

experiment_title: NSCOR for Evaluating Risk Factors and Biomarkers for Adaptation and Resilience to Spaceflight: Emotional Valence and Social Processes in ICC/ICE Environments
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA’s future long-duration exploration missions (LDEMs) will involve four to six individuals living and working in the environment of deep space for unprecedented durations. The focus of this study is on using the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) areas of positive valence (e.g., patience, tolerance), negative valence (e.g., irritability, anger), and social processes (e.g., affiliation, attachment, sensitivity to self and other teammates) in response to stressors associated with space flight. This study seeks to relate individual adaptation and resiliency on confined and extreme environments to identify behavioral and biological factors to predict/identify a crew that can successfully perform under extreme conditions in space.

Investigators will use four analogs which will define resilience to space conditions which will be used in selecting crew most likely to maintain human health and performance during prolonged exploration missions. This NASA Specialized Center of Research (NSCOR) aims to use the NASA Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) as one of four analog facilities (3 human, 1 animal), in which to discover markers of vulnerability to individual behavioral health risks and team social processes in space flight. The other two human analogs used in the NSCOR are the University of Pennsylvania Isolation and Confinement Analog Research Unit for Spaceflight (ICARUS), an isolated, confined, extreme environment (ICC/ICE) and the Antarctic Neumayer Station III, which is a German research station of the Alfred-Wegener-Institute.

The fourth NSCOR analog involves animal research at Harvard Boston Children’s Hospital. This laboratory will provide a rodent model of the effects of confinement that will be used to inform human neuroimaging studies. This allows the research team to safely and ethically investigate the more specific molecular, cellular, and neural circuitry changes associated with living in ICC versus enriched sensory environments for “rodent- human equivalent” time-periods matching each of the two human ICC analog sites and the 14-month ICE analog.

This study has the following specific aims:


  1. Identify and quantify individual differences in adaptation and resilience, key threats to and promoters of mission relevant behavioral health and performance.
    Aim 1a. Perform a comprehensive literature review of the RDoC framework to identify the units of analysis (e.g., cells, etc.) of the individual risk factors most related to LDEMs and positive valence, negative valence, and social processes domains.
    Aim 1b. Identify how the risk factors within those three RDoC domains relate to performance outcomes, resiliency, and adaptation in LDEMs.
  2. Identify neural circuits and molecular/cellular mechanisms underlying adaptation and resilience in a rodent model using cross-species equivalency (i.e., mice exposed for “human” equivalent time).
  3. Encompasses the biological basis of social support to assess individual sociability and the neurobehavioral contributions to resiliency and/or adaptability of engaging positively in social interactions, tolerance, and awareness (e.g., affiliation, attachment).
  4. Identify how meaningful work mediates the relationship between risk factors, the valence and social process domains, and operational outcomes, as well as direct effects of meaningful work on performance.
  5. Encompasses the need to identify how positive and negative valence systems impact on psychological well-being and performance when confronted with the adverse conditions found in prolonged space flight.

APPROACH:
Over the course of the study, 90 volunteers are expected to participate. The NSCOR human analogs will include participants from different cultural backgrounds. German scientists, engineers, and other professionals will be the subjects at the Neumayer Antarctic Station, while Americans will be the subjects in the ICARUS and HERA analogs. All subjects will be thoroughly characterized across the RDoC domains at baseline before entering the analog. Potential biomarkers will be collected twice during the isolation period to determine whether their secular trend is associated with resilience in the positive/negative affect and social processing domains. Importantly, an identical set of candidate biomarkers will be sampled across all environments. Additionally, self-report measures of resilience and adaptability, well-being, social support, meaningfulness of work, and emotion regulation will be collected pre-, during, and post-mission in each of these environments to characterize patterns over time in each of these areas, as well as to allow for comparisons with trends identified in biomarkers hypothesized to be related.

During the first six months of the study investigators will undertake psychometric development to generate a more comprehensive scale of well-being that captures the essential characteristics of positive valence, adaptability, sociability and performance. This will be accomplished by evaluating a number of relevant questionnaires. Several well-validated surveys will be used to determine self-assessments of resilience, emotional regulation, well-being, work orientation, and social support. Throughout the period of confinement and isolation, study participants in the three analogs will complete visual analog scales (VAS) that include a stress scale, and validated brief surveys. Additionally, subjects will complete a written journal (Neumayer) or an audio/video journal (ICARUS, HERA). Content analysis of the journals will be conducted to determine changes in positive/negative valence and social processing. Investigators will also perform structured debriefs with study participants to elucidate how they perceived their experiences in the ICC/ICE environments relative to positive/negative valence and social processing.

During the HERA campaigns 32 subjects will undergo 45 day isolation studies in groups of four to assess sociability, resiliency, and psychological well-being. Subjects will complete tasks, questionnaires, and journal entries to determine changes in positive/negative valence and social processing.

In the Penn ICARUS ICC facility, 40 subjects will undergo seven-day isolation studies in groups of four in the specially designed study for confinement and isolation with frequent acute stressors—many like those that can occur during LDEMs as reported by astronauts. Subjects will be presented throughout the week in a sequence/time unknown to them. Mission control will ensure each crew undergoes a fully scripted sequence of mission stressors and non-stressors such as habitable volume, unpredictable work demands, changing environmental conditions, variable workload, work difficulty, and meaningfulness of work.

Structural and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) will be performed in all participants at baseline and immediately post-mission for obtaining reliable estimates of brain structure and function, including measures of anatomic and functional connectivity and circuitry. Blood and saliva will be analyzed for biomarkers associated with stress, emotional, or immune responses once at baseline, twice during isolation and once post-isolation in the three ICC/ICE environments. On the same days as blood draws from human subjects, 24 hour ECG data will be collected to derive heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV) measures as a peripheral index of emotion regulatory processes regulated via prefrontal mechanisms.

Lastly, the investigators will assess performance outcomes to determine ICC/ICE stress resilience. Participants will perform spatial navigation (radial arm maze and route learning) tests specifically targeting the hippocampal formation, striatum, and precuneus. These tasks are not only critical in terms of the requirements for long-duration exploratory missions (e.g. navigating on Mars), but they also provide precise behavioral information of the underlying circuitry that is expected to be affected by the social support system.

RESULTS:
This study is in progress. Results will be available at a later date.

experiment_title: Does Intermittent or Continuous Artificial Gravity Counteract Long Duration Bed Rest Induced Neurocognitive Declines?
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

There are numerous untoward effects of space flight on human physiology, which stem directly from the absence of gravity. These include sensorimotor effects such as postflight impairments in posture control and locomotion, as well as inflight spatial disorientation, reduced mass discrimination, and manual tracking errors under cognitive load. Crewmembers gradually adapt their sensorimotor processing inflight in response to body unloading and altered vestibular inputs. This adapted sensorimotor state is then inappropriate upon return to Earth’s gravitational environment, with crewmembers exhibiting slow re-adaptation over days to weeks postflight. Extensive deconditioning of the cardiovascular, muscular, and skeletal systems also occurs as a direct result of microgravity. Compounding the situation for potential deep space exploration to Mars is the fact that many of these declines show dose-dependent effects.
This research opportunity was specifically targeted to compare the protective effects of one single daily bout of intermittent artificial gravity (AG) versus multiple daily bouts of intermittent AG. While it was expected that both protocols would mitigate bed rest-induced cardiovascular deconditioning such as orthostatic intolerance and aerobic power, it would be important to contrast both exposures for both efficacy and tolerance.
There are multiple potential countermeasures in use and under investigation for all of these issues. Artificial gravity, by contrast, could provide a single integrated countermeasure by “replacing” Earth’s gravitational effects on the body. It remains unclear what impact this centrifugation might have on sensorimotor control, particularly vestibular function, however. Constant centrifugation is also not well tolerated by subjects, but a recent study found that intermittent delivery of six, five minute bursts of AG were more effective and better tolerated than a single, thirty minute bout for maintaining cardiovascular function after head down tilt bed rest. However, this and previous bed rest studies on the effectiveness of AG as a countermeasure have examined only short-duration bed rest (on the order of days to three weeks) and have not looked at the impact on functional or cognitive behaviors.
The investigators recently completed a 70 day 6° head down tilt bed rest study in which they examined a large range of brain structural, brain functional, sensorimotor, and cognitive metrics as outcome measures. Investigators selected those that are sensitive to this space flight analog environment as outcome metrics for the following aims:
  1. Determine whether 30 minutes per day of supine centrifugation +1Gz at the heart is effective at mitigating declines in brain structure, brain function, sensorimotor and cognitive performance induced by 60 days of 6° head down tilt bed rest in comparison to a control group that is not exposed to AG.
  2. Determine whether centrifugation is more effective and better tolerated as a countermeasure when it is delivered continuously for 30 minutes or in six, five minute sessions separated by breaks of five minutes each.
  3. Identify predictors of individual differences in bed rest and AG responses.
APPROACH:
Investigators examined whether pre-bed rest measures of brain structure and brain function are predictive of changes in sensory, motor, and cognitive function occurring in association with bed rest, and whether they also predicted AG tolerance. The investigators combined data collected during this study with those they acquired in two predictors studies, Developing Personalized Countermeasures for Sensorimotor Adaptability: A Bedrest Study (NCC958SA03801) and Developing Predictive Measures of Sensorimotor Adaptability to Produce Customized Countermeasure Prescriptions (NCC958SA02801) to increase their predictive power.
Investigators aimed to assess changes in brain structure, function, and network integrity prior to, during, and following 30 days of head down tilt bed rest in three groups: control (no AG), continuous AG (30 minutes per day continuous) and intermittent AG (30 minutes per day in five minute bursts). To this end, they acquired a high-resolution structural MRI scan, which allowed them to conduct volumetric measurements of structures, such as the cerebellum, that are likely to exhibit changes. Resting state functional connectivity MRI (fcMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) were used to assess brain functional (fcMRI) and structural (DTI) network connectivity, allowing for more integrative assessments of distributed neural systems than in the past. Data acquisition for both techniques was rapid and non-invasive. Moreover, because participants were not performing a task, there were no confounds of the effects of fatigue, attention, or task difficulty that often complicate interpretation of task-driven fMRI studies. The investigators acquired both types of scans as part of their outcome metrics.

Twenty-four participants were distributed across three groups for 60 days of head down tilt bed rest (HDBR). The three groups (n = 8 each) comprised of: control (HDBR with no AG), continuous AG (supine centrifugation at +1Gz at the heart for 30 minutes per day) and intermittent AG (supine centrifugation at +1Gz at the heart for 6 bouts of 5 minutes per day, each session separated by 5 minutes rest).
Neuroimaging assessments took place at the :envihab MRI facility. Investigators acquired a high-resolution structural MRI scan, allowing them to conduct volumetric measurements of brain structures such as the cerebellum and the motor cortex that are likely to exhibit body unloading-related changes. The investigators also conducted functional MRI while participants performed a variety of cognitive and sensorimotor tasks.
Investigators performed several laboratory tests of behavior outside of the MRI scanner to supplement those conducted during neuroimaging. Balance and mobility tests were performed at the pre- and post-bed rest time points. That is, investigators would not ask subjects to stand for the interim bed rest assessments; participants could perform the other behavioral tests in the supine position. These assessments would include measures of cognitive abilities such as spatial working memory capacity and processing speed; measures of hand motor function such as unimanual dexterity and bimanual coordination; measures of posture and locomotor control which has shown to be sensitive to both space flight and bed rest changes; and measures of vestibular function.

RESULTS:

This project was conducted as part of the ‘’AGREBSA’’ campaign at envihab in Cologne, Germany. This was a 60-day head down tilt bed rest study with daily centrifugation as a potential countermeasure. One group did not participate in centrifugation, one received 30 minutes per day of continuous centrifugation, and one received 30 minutes per day of intermittent centrifugation in 5-minute sessions.
In summary, the results revealed that daily centrifugation migrated some of the behavioral changes that occurred with long duration head down tilt bed rest. The results also showed that the intermittent artificial gravity group was less susceptible to post-rotation illusory motion. In some cases, effect sizes were moderate, but the results were not statistically significant. This could be due to the small sample sizes per group. It could also be because several of the measures relied on vestibular inputs, and the centrifugation only amounted to 0.3g at the level of the head. Several cases of group x time differences in brain functionality were noted during the performance of a range of tasks. These changes suggest greater neural efficiency in the artificial gravity groups, and/or differential sensory re-weighting between the artificial gravity and control groups.

experiment_title: Gender Differences in Bedrest: Autonomic and Neuroendocrine Changes and Vascular Responses in Lower and Upper Extremities
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Female astronauts are more susceptible to orthostatic hypotension and presyncope after space flight than are male astronauts. However, most space flight and bed rest studies that have sought to understand the mechanisms contributing to this increased incidence of orthostatic hypotension have not included women. Consequently, many conclusions about the effects of microgravity or simulated microgravity on humans are seriously flawed in that they fail to describe mechanisms in the very people who have the most serious problems.
Before flight, low vascular resistance in female astronauts is not associated with lower sympathetic responsiveness, as their supine and standing norepinephrine levels are similar to those of men. This suggests that the gender differences may lie in the responsiveness of the vasculature itself. Premenopausal women appear to have greater endothelium-dependent venodilatory as well as vasodilatory responses than those of men. This suggests that their lower resistance and lower venous return may be nitric oxide-mediated. Many studies have documented hemodynamic changes that occur during and after space flight or bed rest; very few have examined directly vascular responses, fewer still have compared vascular responses in men versus women before and after bed rest, and none has examined both arteries and veins. Therefore, the first purpose of this study was to examine vascular responsiveness in arteries and veins, in women versus men, before and after bed rest.
Important new information emerged in the animal literature that shows that different vascular beds respond differently to simulated microgravity. After male rats are hindlimb-suspended, vessels in their forelimbs undergo hypertrophic remodeling while vessels in their hindlimbs undergo atrophic remodeling. This is thought to occur as a result of the differential changes in transmural pressures and wall shear stress in the fore- and hindlimbs during the suspension. These studies have not been repeated in female rats. Upright humans have more than a 140 mmHg pressure gradient from head to foot. Elimination of this gradient would change the mechanical forces acting on the vasculature in the legs to an even greater extent than in the suspended rats. It is likely that humans in bed rest or space flight would show similar differential regional changes. Since humans are bipedal, both space flight and bed rest would greatly reduce pressures and wall shear stress in the vessels in the legs, but not the arms. Thus atrophic changes would be expected in the vasculature of the legs but not of the arms. This idea has not been pursued in humans, but such changes certainly could contribute to orthostatic hypotension. Therefore, the second purpose of this study was to compare changes in vascular responsiveness in the upper and lower extremities before and after bed rest and relate the findings to the occurrence of orthostatic hypotension.
Female astronauts, as well as a small subset of male astronauts, develop autonomic dysfunction during space flight. In these astronauts, sympathetic responsiveness to orthostatic stress is compromised after flight. Furthermore, both bed rest and space flight studies have shown decreased vagal activity and baroreflex sensitivity, yet these studies have primarily examined male subjects. Therefore, the third purpose of this study was to compare both autonomic and endocrine responses to arterial baroreceptor input in men and women before and after bed rest.
Specific Aim 1:
Compare arterial function in men and women before and after bed rest. It was hypothesized that woman, compared to men, would have greater flow-mediated vasodilation in the brachial and anterior tibial artery and that this gender difference would be exaggerated after bed rest. It was also hypothesized that brachial and anterior tibial artery vasodilation in response to sublingual nitroglycerin will not be different between women and men.
Specific Aim 2:
Compare venous function in men and women before and after bed rest. It was hypothesized that dorsal hand and foot veins of women would dilate more in response to acetylcholine; and constrict more in response to L-NMMA than men, and leg compliance will be greater in women. These gender differences will be exaggerated after bed rest.
Specific Aim 3:
Compare responses in the lower extremity before and after bed rest. Investigators tested the hypothesis that, after bed rest: anterior tibial artery diameter increases will be smaller following ischemia and larger following sublingual nitroglycerin; dorsal foot vein responses to phenylephrine, isoproterenol, acetylcholine and L-NMMA will be smaller after bed rest, and leg compliance will be greater after bed rest.
Specific Aim 4:
Compare responses in the upper extremity before and after bed rest. Investigators tested the hypothesis that, after bed rest: brachial artery diameter increases will be greater following ischemia and smaller following sublingual nitroglycerin; and that dorsal hand vein responses to phenylephrine, isoproterenol, acetylcholine and L-NMMA will be increased after bed rest.
Specific Aim 5:
Tested the hypothesis that women will have a greater loss of neuroendocrine responses to arterial baroreceptor input after bed rest than men. APPROACH:
Thirty-one subjects participated in 60 or 90 day 6 degree head-down bed rest (not all subjects completed all days due to two hurricane evacuations and others left early for personal reasons) conducted at the General Clinical Research Center (GCRC) Satellite Flight Analogs Research Unit at the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston, Texas (UTMB). All protocols were reviewed and approved by the NASA Johnson Space Center Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects, UTMB Institutional Review Board and UTMB GCRC Advisory Committee. Informed consent forms were signed prior to participation in the study.
Subjects were healthy, normotensive, non-smokers, not obese, taking no medications, and had passed a psychological examination. Female subjects were premenopausal, with regular menses lasting 28 ± 2 days and were studied across the menstrual cycle, starting at menses. Because hormonal changes affect the cardiovascular responses in women, the bed rest study was arranged so that all measurements were taken at the same time in the menstrual cycle (during menses).
The dorsal hand and foot vein and phenylephrine/sodium nitroprusside protocols were performed once during the pre-bed rest period after approximately 8-12 days of diet stabilization, and around bed rest days 30, 60 and 90 days, if applicable. These three protocols were performed on consecutive days. Female subjects were admitted to bed rest such that these test days would fall at the beginning of menstrual cycle. The reactive hyperemia and sublingual nitroglycerin protocols were performed once during pre-bed rest after 6-8 days of diet stabilization, and around bed rest days 7, 21, 31, 49, 60, 75, and during the post-bed rest period on day 0 and 3.
RESULTS:
Dorsal vein size in response to bed rest baseline foot vein size was significantly smaller in women compared to men pre-bed rest. By day 60 however, there were no differences in foot vein size such that vein size decreased in the men and women over the course of bed rest. Baseline hand vein size was similar between men and women pre-bed rest and did not change in response to bed rest.
The absolute change in artery diameter from resting to peak diameter following sublingual nitroglycerin administration was greater in the arm than in the leg, changed across bed rest days, and the change across bed rest days was different between the arm and the leg. Similar to previous findings, there was no effect of gender.
Parasympathetic modulation and baroreflex sensitivity decreased with bed rest, with women experiencing a larger decrease in baroreflex sensitivity by day 30 than men. The sympathetic activation of men and parasympathetic responsiveness of women in blood pressure control during physiological stress were preserved throughout bed rest. During PE infusions, women experienced saturation of the R-R interval at high frequency, whereas men did not, revealing a sex difference in the parabolic relationship between high-frequency R-R interval, a measurement of respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and R-R interval. These sex differences in blood pressure control during simulated microgravity reveal the need to study sex differences in long-duration space flight to ensure the health and safety of the entire astronaut corps.

experiment_title: Clinical Nutritional Assessment (Flight Analog)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this test was to assess nutrient intake and status during bed rest and to assure correction of nutritional status following bed rest.
APPROACH:
Assessment of body composition was required to determine changes in muscle and bone compartments. The nutritional assessment measured dietary intake and determined nutritional status through blood samples and 48-hour void-by-void urine samples.
Nutritional assessment is required to determine adequacy of nutrient stores prior to bed rest, to assess nutrient intake and status during bed rest, and to assure correction of nutritional status following bed rest. Assessment of body composition is required to determine changes in muscle and bone compartments during space flight.
Nutritional status was expected to decline/remain unchanged during bed rest. A decrease in bone mineral density and an increase in markers of bone resorption were expected.
The biological samples collected were used for determination of nutritional status, which included the following:
  • Protein status
  • Calcium and bone status
  • Mineral status
  • Antioxidant status
  • General blood chemistry
  • Water-soluble vitamin status
  • Fat-soluble vitamin status
  • Iron status
  • Renal stone risk
  • General urine chemistry

experiment_title: Validation of Fitness for Duty Standards Using Pre- and Post-Flight Capsule Egress and Suited Functional Performance Tasks in Simulated Reduced Gravity (Internal Research)
experiment_description:
Objective:
Physiological adaptations to long-duration microgravity environments and deficits in perceptual and motor function during gravitational transitions are likely to result in reduced functional capacity after landing either on Earth or at an exploration destination, such as water-based Orion landings or Mars surface landings. All astronauts experience significant decrements in functional performance upon return from a microgravity environment. The losses in functional performance can largely be attributed to neurovestibular/sensorimotor deficits that can take days or weeks to recover from. Currently, there are no operational countermeasures, but crewmembers need to be capable of egressing their landing vehicle unassisted. This study aims to accelerate the operational planning and implementation of how to execute this testing in the dynamic, operational environments of Soyuz, Boeing, and SpaceX landing zones. Similar testing is planned for the CIPHER study on various missions. The primary aim of this study is to allow the feasibility of the R+0/1 Egress Fitness CIPHER study tasks to be established before collecting data on the first CIPHER crew member. The investigators hypothesize that reductions in unassisted capsule egress and planetary EVA task performance will be observed after all mission durations. They also hypothesize that individual variability in planetary EVA task performance will depend on the task type and will be related to pre-flight fitness parameters, maintenance of in-flight muscle function, cardiorespiratory fitness, and sensorimotor function. The overall objectives of the Egress Fitness study are twofold. The investigators seek to: 1.) Quantify post-landing time course changes in unassisted capsule egress and planetary EVA task performance, and 2.) Characterize the recovery to acceptable planetary EVA task performance as a function of EVA task type, time in space, time post-landing, and other potential determinants of performance (e.g., sleep, nutrition, exercise, sensorimotor performance).

Approach:
Data will be collected for spaceflight missions ranging from two months, six months, and up to one year in duration. Six subjects, ideally two crew from each landing vehicle, will undergo three pre-flight sessions: EVA Suit Fit Check, Partial Planetary EVA & Familiarization activities (EVAs), and Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress & Familiarization to quantify performance parameters in an operationally relevant environment. Postflight sessions include the Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress on R+0 and Partial Planetary EVA on R+1. Prior to the Partial Planetary EVA Circuit, crew members will be measured for proper fit and size in a MKIII or xEMU EVA suit. After the suit check there is no preferred order for the remaining sessions, unless they are scheduled on the same day. In such case, the Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress and Familiarization should be scheduled first. The Partial Planetary EVA Circuit consists of actions, movements, and component tasks sequenced to provide realistic post-landing EVA scenarios. The tasks are sequenced to allow individual evaluation on the performance of each specific sub-element on the overall EVA timeline. Tasks include translation tasks necessary for crew members to move from a lander to a habitat upon landing on Mars, as well as tasks that may be particularly influenced by spaceflight deconditioning. Prior to the start of the egress tasks, the crew member will don a heart rate monitor and lay in a recumbent position on a yoga mat. During the timed egress, the crew member will attain an upright position, deploy and secure the top hatch ladder, lift a backpackstyle survival pack out of the capsule, walk up the ladder (simulating a top hatch egress) until the hip clears the hatch, then come back down. The crew member will then walk to a safe waypoint and doff the Heart Rate Monitor. When crew return in a Boeing or SpaceX vehicle, the Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress will be performed on R+0 at the rally airport. When crew return on a Soyuz vehicle, a partial Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress will be at the rally airport on R+0, and the full Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress will be conducted at the refueling airport on R+0. The Partial Planetary EVA Circuit will be on R+1 at JSC, as this requires the use of the Active Response Gravity Offload System (ARGOS), a permanent facility at JSC. The EVA tasks and gravity environment will be the same for both pre- and post-flight sessions.

Results:
It is critical to understand what crews are capable of, and at which time points they will be able to perform which tasks. The research product will be a temporal profile of unassisted capsule egress and planetary EVA task performance pre-flight and at multiple post-landing intervals, the timing of which will be determined based on post-landing logistics and coordination with other investigations. By having participants perform unassisted capsule egress task and a partial planetary EVA soon after landing, the data from this study will verify methods of execution of these egress tests in the operational environment of Soyuz, and Boeing and SpaceX landings.

experiment_title: Testosterone Supplementation as a Countermeasure against Musculoskeletal Losses during Space Exploration
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The long-term goal of this study was to determine the therapeutic efficacy of testosterone at preserving lean muscle mass, muscle strength, and bone mineral density in healthy humans during space flight. Investigators examined the interactive or additive effects of the combination of testosterone and exercise on lean body mass, muscle strength, and bone health.
To achieve these goals investigators tested the following hypotheses before, during, and after 70 days of bed rest:
  1. Cycled testosterone replacement (weekly testosterone injections for two weeks, followed by two weeks off) in conjunction with exercise will have an additive effect in preventing loss of muscle mass and muscle strength in men representative of the astronaut population compared to exercise with placebo testosterone.
  2. Cycled testosterone replacement (weekly testosterone injections for two weeks, followed by two weeks off) in conjunction with exercise will have an additive effect in preventing loss of bone mass and alterations in markers of bone metabolism in men representative of the astronaut population compared to exercise with placebo testosterone.
To address these hypotheses investigators studied the following specific aims before, during, and after 70 days of bed rest:
  1. To determine the effect of cycled testosterone replacement in conjunction with resistance exercise during bed rest on muscle mass, muscle strength, and fatigue in men aged 24-55 years.
  2. To determine the effect of cycled testosterone replacement in conjunction with resistance exercise during bed rest on markers of bone metabolism and bone mass in men aged 24-55 years.
APPROACH:
Male volunteers were randomly assigned to one of three bed rest groups 1) non-exercising + placebo (control group), 2) exercise + placebo (exercise A group) , and exercise + testosterone (exercise B group) using a standard of care approach with NASA space flight nutritional requirements and standard exercise protocols as the control condition. A total of 24 subjects completed the study. Eight subjects were in each bed rest group.
RESULTS:
Results suggest that exercise groups A and B appear protected against the bed rest-induced loss of lean body mass (LBM, total and legs). The exercise B group, but not A, significantly increased LBM and prevented increases in fat mass during bed rest. Effects on bone for both exercise groups was not significant.

experiment_title: Spaceflight Standard Measures: Personality Questionnaire
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Personality Questionnaire is one of nine Spaceflight Standard Measures conducted on International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers. Spaceflight Standard Measures are a set of core measurements, representative of many of the risks experienced by astronauts before, during, and after spaceflight. The purpose of this project is to populate a repository with data that enables high-level monitoring of countermeasure effectiveness and meaningful interpretation of health and performance outcomes. These standard measures will support future, hypothesis-driven research that enables planetary missions by providing an optimized minimal set of measures captured from all ISS crewmembers until the end of the ISS program. These measures will be available to other studies under data sharing agreements as well as undergo analysis for trends in the astronaut population.

The purpose of the Personality Questionnaire is to help with the interpretation of Behavioral Health and Human Factors data.

APPROACH:
The subject will complete a 120-question personality survey/questionnaire on paper or via secure, browser-based survey software.
The session to complete this standard measure will be performed anytime pre-flight for three mission scenarios: short duration (up to 105 days flight days), standard duration (between 105 to 240 flight days), and long duration (greater than 240 days).

RESULTS:
The Spaceflight Standard Measures project is not a hypothesis-driven study, but rather a project to create a collection of ISS data made available to future researchers and for trend analysis. As such, there are no specific hypotheses, outcome measures, or statistical analyses associated with the skeleton of the project. The project will capture a "snapshot" of optimized data that can be investigated by researchers in the future

experiment_title: Detecting Pilot Spatial Disorientation to Trigger Active Countermeasures during Lunar Landing
experiment_description:
Objective:

Neurovestibular adaptations that occur while in microgravity induce performance decrements in astronauts when re-exposed to a gravitational environment. This includes spatial disorientation, motion sickness, postural and locomotion impairment, ataxia, and manual control decrements These deficits are expected to occur upon initial exposure to another gravity environment, such as descending to the surface of the moon or Mars. Due to the sensorimotor impairment occurring during gravity transitions, these adaptations have the potential to be catastrophic, impacting mission critical tasks such as piloted vehicle landing with the acute risk of loss-of-crew from an accident or loss of mission through forced abort scenarios. This study proposes to develop, validate, and assess a system for detecting when astronauts may become disoriented in real-time, such that it can be used to trigger active countermeasures for piloted planetary landings. The investigative team will accomplish this objective using the following specific aims: 1. Validate the computational model’s predictions of pilot spatial disorientation, specifically for lunar landing. 2. Characterize manual control decrements without a countermeasure. 3. Demonstrate the benefits of triggering an active countermeasure in real-time using the computational model to predict spatial disorientation (SD).

Approach:

Astronauts landing on the moon will be faced with a gravity transition that will challenge their sensorimotor systems. Specifically, during 3+ days of transit, they will reinterpret sensory cues to appropriate for the microgravity environment. Then, during the critical landing phase, they will first be exposed to a lunar gravity. While orientation perception within lunar gravity has been studied well, much less is known about how astronauts perceive their vehicle’s orientation during lunar landing following sensorimotor adaptation to microgravity. In order to test their hypothesis, two experiments (Experiment A and Experiment B) will be performed by the PI team. In Experiment A, the PI team will revalidate their computational tool for the unique lunar landing-like motions following an analog for the gravity transition. This experiment aims to quantify pilot SD during simulated lunar landings following the analog microgravity transition. During this experiment, as subjects are experiencing lunar landing like motions, at various points, the motion will freeze. At this instant, subjects will be shown veridical vehicle orientation information and mentally compare their perceived orientation at the freeze to the veridical information in order to gain a sense of their own disorientation. Subjects will report their SD severity, using a visual analog scale. Once their SD severity is reported that trial is terminated. This will capture the magnitude of SD experienced at the SD freeze. In Experiment B, the validated computational tool, that detects pilot SD in real-time to trigger and active countermeasure, the team will assess the pilot aiding system’s efficacy versus a control group. To assess the efficacy of the triggering system, the team will use an adaptive display which will alert the pilot and draw their attention towards a display of the vehicle’s attitude and motion to actively help them reorient. In the team’s initial implementation, the countermeasure will remain active for a fixed period to help reorient the pilot and then will deactivate. Two subject cohorts will be tested in a between-subject design. A control group will perform the lunar landing manual control piloting task but receive no countermeasure. Computational tools will be used in the control group to predict when the pilot is likely disoriented, however it will not activate any countermeasure. This will allow the PI team to identify whether the trials in which their performance was most degraded where indeed those the computational tool predicted SD. In a second cohort of subjects, the PI team will assess the potential benefits of the computational tool triggering the active countermeasure described above. The subject will continue to fly the DRD simulation until landing, abort, or crash. There will be 12 subjects in Experiment B’s control group and another 12 subjects in the cohort of subjects with the countermeasure, for a total of N=24 subjects. The PI team expects that the countermeasure approach will help to avoid increasing the pilots’ workload and the tool will be able to identify when the pilot if suffering from SD, including Type I SD. This will likely help reduce workload by removing the burden from the pilot of always having to assess whether they are becoming disoriented, as well as trying to prevent the pilot from having to “fly through’’ severe SD. When the active countermeasure is triggered, it will aid the pilot, likely improving manual control performance, increasing SA of vehicle orientation, and resulting in fewer failed landings, compared to the control group.

Results:

The investigators aim to develop an approach to actively trigger countermeasures, so it may be integrated with other potential countermeasures (e.g., a vibrotactile vest, HUDs), potentially including those being proposed by other investigator teams. The PI team expects pilot aiding countermeasure system to mitigate manual control performance decrements, as compared to the control group, which performs the lunar landing piloting task without a countermeasure. It is expected that the countermeasure system will reduce pilot mental workload and increase situational awareness.
