experiment_title: Effects of Exposure to Heavy Particles
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Future missions in space may involve long-term travel beyond the magnetic field of the earth, subjecting astronauts to radiation hazards posed by solar flares and galactic cosmic rays. The objectives of this research project were to describe and characterize heavy particle-induced behavioral and neurochemical deficits, determine their underlying causes, and develop approaches to minimize such deficits. To achieve these objectives, behavioral and neurochemical models were used that have been previously shown to be sensitive to radiation exposure, and which may provide a basis for defining the risks of exposure to heavy particles on brain functioning and related behavior. An understanding of this risk may be vital to the effective performance and possibly the survival of astronauts during future missions in space.

Project Aims
The general objectives of the experiments reviewed in this report were to determine the effects of exposure to heavy particles on dopaminergic neurons in the brain, the neurochemical processes that mediate the effects of exposure, and on the behaviors that depend upon the integrity of the dopaminergic system.

More specifically, the aims of the research program were to:
1. Further characterize the neurochemical effects and the mechanisms that mediate the effects of exposure to 56Fe particles.
2. Further characterize both acute and late behavioral/cognitive effects of exposure to 56Fe and other particles.
3. Characterize organismic variables, such as age, as mediators of the effects of exposure to HZE particles.
4. Further characterize the effects of exposure to high-energy protons on neurochemical and behavioral functioning.
5. Evaluate the effects of diet on the neurochemical and behavioral effects of exposure to 56Fe particles.

APPROACH:
Behavioral Measures
Measurement of behaviors within 3-7 days following exposure to heavy particles or protons utilized the facilities available at the site of irradiation. For the measurement of behaviors that require specialized equipment, or which can take repeated trials for the acquisition (e.g., conditioned place preference, water maze performance or operant conditioning procedures) the animals were shipped to University of Maryland Baltimore County (UMBC) or Human Nutrition Research Center on Aging at Tufts University (HNRCA) for testing. In each case, both irradiated and non-irradiated controls were shipped to provide a control for any possible effects of the shipping. The basis for the selection of the behavioral tests is: (a) the behaviors are dopamine mediated (CPP, amphetamine-induced CTA, variable interval operant responding, upper body strength); and (b) they are behaviors that show deterioration as a function of age (water maze, radial arm maze).

Conditioned Taste Aversions:
The conditioned taste aversion (CTA) is a procedure by which rats are placed on a 23.5-hr water deprivation schedule for 7 days. On the conditioning day, they are presented with a calibrated drinking tube containing 10% sucrose solution instead of water, and intake recorded. Immediately following the drinking period, the rats are presented with the unconditioned stimulus (amphetamine, 3 mg/kg, ip). On the test day the rats are again given the 10% sucrose solution for 30 min. The acquisition of a CTA is shown by reduced sucrose intake on the test day compared to the conditioning day.

Conditioned Place Preference:
This procedure, which is used to evaluate the reinforcing qualities of a specific stimulus, utilizes an apparatus with three distinct compartments (black and white compartments which are separated by a gray compartment). The rat is given a reinforcing stimulus (e.g., amphetamine, 2 mg/kg) in one compartment and, on alternate days, a neutral stimulus (e.g., saline) in the other. An “unbiased” procedure is used, in which the compartment associated with injection of amphetamine is randomly assigned - some rats are given the amphetamine in the black compartment and some in the white compartment. After three pairings of each compound with a specific compartment, the rat is allowed to move freely about the apparatus and the amount of time spent in each compartment is measured. A Conditioned Place Preference (CPP) is shown when the organism spends significantly more time in the compartment paired with the presumptive reinforcing stimulus (amphetamine) than in the compartment paired with the neutral stimulus.

Operant Conditioning: The proposed procedure is a standard one in which rats are rewarded for making an instrumental response on a fixed ratio schedule. In a fixed-ratio design, the animal is rewarded after n number of responses, such that on an FR-5 schedule, the rat is rewarded after 5 responses (bar presses) and on an FR-10 schedule, after 10 responses. Rats are first trained to press a lever using an FR1 schedule by placing them in an operant chamber for 12 hrs. After the response has been learned, the rats are trained to respond on a fixed-ratio schedule by providing several trials using an FR-5 schedule. During testing the rats are then given 30-min sessions in which they are rewarded using FR-1, FR-5, FR-10, FR-15, FR-20, FR- 25, FR-30 and FR-35 reinforcement schedules. If exposure to 56Fe particles disrupts operant performance, then the irradiated animals should make fewer responses than the sham-irradiated controls and the discrepancy between the irradiated and control rats should increase as the number of responses required for the delivery of a food pellet increases.

Water Maze and Radial-Arm Maze:
These procedures are the standard ones used to evaluate changes in spatial learning and memory. Performance on these tasks were sensitive to hippocampal damage and show decreased performance in aged organisms.

Morris water maze: The Morris water maze consists of a circular black fiberglass pool (134 cm in diameter x 50 cm in height), filled to a depth of 30 cm with water maintained at 23oC. The pool is divided into four equal-size quadrants. A circular escape platform (10 cm in diameter) is colored black and therefore hidden from sight. The platform is submerged 2 cm below the surface of the water in the center of one of the quadrants; its location is changed to a different quadrant for each session of testing. The maze is placed in a room with the lights dimmed, and there are numerous extramaze cues on the walls. Performance on each test is videotaped and analyzed with image tracking software (HVS Image, Hampton, England). The task requires an animal to use spatial learning and memory to find a hidden platform just below the surface of the water, and to remember its location from the previous trial. The rat must acquire a cognitive representation of location in space and have the ability to effectively navigate the environment; therefore, the animal must use distal cues to effectively locate the hidden platform. Accurate navigation is rewarded by escape from the pool. Several dependent measures are used to estimate the efficiency of the rat's performance: directionality, latency of finding the hidden platform on each trial, length of swim path as well as the distribution of swimming time and swim path in the four quadrants of the pool during transfer or probe trials (in which the platform is removed from the pool) or during reversal trials (in which the platform is moved to another quadrant of the pool), number of crossings and latency to cross a previous platform location, and swim speed. Several experimental procedures have been developed to measure different aspects of cognitive performance, including reference (long-term) and working (short-term) memory.

Radial Arm Maze: The radial arm maze consists of eight equally spaced plexiglass arms (70 cm long, 12 cm wide) radiating from an octagonal central area 30 cm in diameter. Various extra-maze cues are present in the testing room. Each maze arm contains a small dish at its end that can be baited with 0.25 ml of 0.30% saccharine solution or a small food pellet (45 mg pellet). The task involves the successive selection of arms, radiating from the center of the maze, in order to obtain a water or food reward. Rats are water or food deprived to 85% of their body weight to ensure motivation. An optimal strategy involves using spatial memory to visit each arm only once, since the arms are not rebaited. Working memory is required while the rat is selecting the next arm to visit, apparently "keeping track of" which arms were previously selected. Various control experiments strongly suggest that the rat performs the radial arm maze test by utilizing extra-maze cues. One possibility is that the rat builds a cognitive map of the environment to learn the maze, and utilizes its working memory to monitor which arms have been visited.

Motor Behavior
Motor behavior is assessed using a wire suspension task. Each rat's forepaws are placed on a taut horizontal wire placed 10 cm above a foam cushion. The length of time that the animal can remain suspended is measured. This test measures muscle strength and prehensile reflex of the forepaws. Each animal serves as its control, with suspension time measured before, and following irradiation.

Neurochemical Measures

Dopamine Release:
Dopamine release was determined by preparing 300: m slices of striata using a McIlwain tissue chopper. Slices of one caudate nucleus from each animal were placed in glass vials containing a modified Krebs-Ringer buffer that has been bubbled for 30 min with 95% O2/5% CO2. The buffer consists of 21 mM NaHCO3, 3.4 mM glucose, 1.3 mM NaH2PO4, 1 mM EGTA, 0.93 mM MgCl2, 127 mM NaCl and 2.5 mM KCl (pH 7.4). The slices were washed in this medium and 150: l aliquots are placed into two chambers of a superfusion apparatus containing 16 chambers, the perfusion of the slices from eight animals in the same experimental "run". The tissue and buffer media are maintained at 37oC throughout the course of the experiment. The tissue is then allowed to equilibrate for 30 min while being perfused with the oxygenated basal release medium at the rate of 124: l/min. After equilibration, a 5 min baseline fraction is collected and the medium is switched to one containing (in mM) KCl 30, CaCl2.H2O 1.26, (in place of EGTA) and NaCl 57, as well as the other components listed above. Following the switch, 5-min fractions continue to be collected for 30 min into vials containing 0.4 perchloric acid (to prevent the autoxidation of the dopamine). To assess cholinergic effects on dopamine release, oxotremorine (500: M) is added to the release medium perfusing alternate chambers. Dopamine release is assessed by HPLC coupled to electrochemical detection.

Oxidative Stress
Aliquots of tissue were prepared the same as the dopamine release. To evaluate oxidative stress the aliquots of tissue were loaded with 2',7'-dichlorofluorescin diacetate which oxidizes to 2',7'-dichlorofluorescein in the presence of reactive oxygen species. The level of brain-associated fluorescence was monitored using a Cyto Fluor Multi-Well Plate Reader (perSeptive Biosystem, Framingham, MA).

Neurogenesis
Assessment of neurogenesis in the rat brains is determined by bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation into the nuclei of dividing cells. BrdU is a thymidine analog used as a mutagen in genetic research, which is selectively incorporated into cellular DNA during the S-phase of cell division. Each rat receives 1 daily intraperitoneal injection of BrdU (50mg/kg) for 6 consecutive days. Rats are sacrificed and perfused one day after the last BrdU injection in order to study the proliferation of newly divided cells. Additional rats are sacrificed 28 days following the last injection to study the differentiation into cell types. Every sixth section of a series through the hippocampus (approx. 240um apart) will be selected and BrdU-positive cells were counted using a modified version of the optical fractionator method. Stereological estimates are made of the total number of BrdUpositive cells located throughout the entire extent of the granular cell layer, subgranular zone and the hilus.

RESULTS:
Neurochemical Mechanisms
Oxidative Stress: Different brain regions (striatum, hippocampus, frontal cortex) were evaluated for oxidative stress using 2',7'- dichlorofluorescin diacetate 1-2 months following exposure to 1.5 Gy 56Fe particles. In the presence of reactive oxygen species, the compound oxidizes and becomes highly fluorescent. Results indicated that there were significant increases in reactive oxygen species in the hippocampus and frontal cortex, but not in the striatum of rats exposed to 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles. These results suggest that exposure to 56Fe particles cause oxidative stress, although irradiation may not produce equivalent effects throughout the entire brain.

Cellular Signaling in the Brain: Calcium homeostasis and calcium-dependent signaling (e.g. calcium dependent protein kinases (PKs) and calcium-mediated neurotransmitter release) are essential for memory formation, particularly spatial memory. Changes in calcium-dependent PKC, PKA, were observed during the experiment, suggesting altered cellular signaling. Furthermore, these changes in brain responses significantly correlated with reference and working memory errors in the radial arm maze. These results show differential brain-region-specific sensitivity induced by exposure to 56Fe particles.

Neurogenesis: Recent research has indicated that, neurogenesis occurs in mature, as well as developing organisms. One way of determining whether or not neurogenesis is occurring is to evaluate cells in specific brain regions for bromo-deoxy-uridine (BrdU) staining. Preliminary combined counts of the subgranular zone and granular cell layer of the hippocampus suggest that the subjects irradiated with 2.5Gy of 56Fe radiation have significantly less BrDU-stained cells in this region than do control subjects.

Behavioral Studies of Exposure to 56Fe and Other HZE Particles
Conditioned Taste Aversion Learning: Previous research had shown that the motor deficits in dopaminergic function were still observed up to 180 days following exposure to 1 Gy of 600 MeV/n 56Fe particles. The amphetamine-induced CTA, which depends upon the integrity of the dopaminergic system was utilized to evaluate whether or not there is recovery of behavioral function 4 months following exposure to 1 Gy of 56Fe particles (1 GeV/n). These results compared to the control animals revealed that radiated animals showed a significantly greater decrease in sucrose intake, indicating an enhanced aversion to the normally preferred sucrose solution. Although more research is needed to evaluate the mechanisms that may have been responsible for this change in behavior, it is possible that the loss of dopamine may have resulted in the up regulation of these receptors.

Morris Water Maze: The effects of exposure to 56Fe particles on cognitive performance were analyzed by using the Morris water maze to evaluate possible heavy particle induced deficits in spatial learning and memory. Rats exposed to 1.5 Gy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe particles demonstrated cognitive impairment compared to a control group, as shown by increased latency to find the hidden platform, particularly when the location of the platform was moved 180° from its previous location or when the platform was removed from the pool to test for the use of spatial strategies. These results provided the first indication that exposure to non-lethal levels of 56Fe particles could affect the cognitive ability of an organism.

Radial Arm Maze: The radial arm maze consists of 8 arms radiating from a central area. The arms can be baited with food and the rat enters each arm to obtain food. The most efficient procedure is to enter each arm once, and only once, to obtain the food. When all arms are baited, rats exposed to 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles show somewhat better performance than control rats by entering each arm in turn. However, when only half the arms contain food, the performance of the radiated rats is poorer than that of controls. It appears that under these conditions, the radiated rats are not able to use spatial cues to guide their behavior, so they repeatedly enter the unbaited arms or arms which they have previously entered. These results support previous research, which indicates deficits in spatial learning and memory following exposure to 56Fe particles.

Operant Responding: Groups of rats were exposed to 0, 1.0, 1.5, or 2.0 Gy of 56Fe particles and trained to press a lever in order to obtain food reinforcement. Once the response was acquired the rats were placed on an ascending fixed-ratio (FR) schedule starting with FR-1 (every lever press rewarded with a food pellet) and extending to FR-35 (35 lever presses are required to produce 1 food pellet). In general, as the ratio increases, rats increase their rate of responding. However, the results showed that at ratios greater than FR-20, rats exposed to 2.0 Gy failed to increase their rate responding. These results indicate that rats exposed to 2.0 Gy of 56Fe particles cannot respond appropriately to increasing work requirements.

The rats that had been trained on the operant response tested on the ascending fixed ratio reinforcement schedule at 7, 10 and 15 months following irradiation. The results showed that the rats exposed to 1.0 or 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles and which showed no differences from control animals (0 Gy) when tested at 3 months post-irradiation, showed significant decreases in performance compared to the control rats when tested at these later time intervals. In addition, the rats exposed to 2.0 Gy continued to show a significant reduction in performance. These results indicate that, not only is there no recovery of function over time following exposure to heavy particles, there is a further decrease in performance which may be related to the increased age of the rats at the time of testing.

Conditioned Place Preference (CPP): CPP, a standard procedure for evaluating the capacity of a stimulus to reinforce behavior, is produced by pairing a rewarding stimulus (e.g., amphetamine) with specific environmental cues. The first experiment in this series showed that 2-4 weeks following exposure to 1.0 Gy of 56Fe particles, radiated rats fail to acquire an amphetamine-induced place preference. This indicates a disruption of the dopaminergic mechanisms that mediate reinforcement. Follow-up experiments evaluated place preference learning 2 months and 4 months following irradiation to determine if there was any recovery of function. The results showed that the irradiated rats failed to acquire an amphetamine-induced place preference when trained 2 or 4 months following exposure to 56Fe particles. These results indicate that the effects of irradiation on reinforcement show no recovery as a function of time following exposure to 1.0 Gy of 56Fe particles.

Because the results of the initial experiment showed a high degree of variability in terms of the amount of time spent in the amphetamine-paired compartment, it was decided to use a higher dose of 56Fe particles (1.5 Gy) to determine if the higher dose could eliminate the variability in the behavioral effects of exposure. Although the higher dose did eliminate the variability, it also eliminated the effect of irradiation on behavior: there was no effect of exposure on the acquisition of an amphetamine-induced place preference. Currently available data do not permit a determination of the factors that might be responsible for the dose-dependent effects of exposure to 56Fe particles on behavior.

Environmental Responsiveness: As shown with operant responding, rats exposed to 56Fe particles have difficulty in responding to changes in environmental contingencies, including adjusting work requirements to reinforcement contingencies. An alternate approach determining the effects of irradiation on the responsiveness of the organism to the environment is to evaluate the open field activity of irradiated rats and their reaction to spatial and non-spatial changes. Animals irradiated with 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles took longer to enter, visited less and spent significantly less time in the middle and the center portions of the open-field than did controls independently of total frequency and duration of activity of both groups. Likewise, irradiated subjects reacted significantly more to novel objects placed in the open-field than did controls. However, irradiated subjects did not vary from controls in their exploration patterns when objects in the open-field were spatially rearranged. Thus, irradiation with a dose of 1.5 Gy of 56Fe high-energy particle radiation elicited age-like effects during the spatial and non-spatial rearrangement tasks.

Taste Aversion Learning 28Si: Because astronauts will be exposed to other types of heavy particles in addition to 56Fe on long-duration missions outside the magnetosphere, it is necessary to evaluate the neurochemical and behavioral toxicity of other types of heavy particles. The initial experiments evaluated the effects of exposure to 28Si particles on amphetamine-induced CTA learning. This endpoint was selected because it has been shown to be very sensitive to irradiation with 56Fe particles and because there is a significant amount of data from 56Fe experiments to provide comparisons. Rats were exposed to 2.0, 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of silicon particles. These doses were selected to take into account the lower LET of 600 MeV 28Si compared to that of 1GeV and 600 MeV 56Fe particles which have thresholds for behavioral and neurochemical effects of .8 and .1 Gy, respectively. Doses of 28Si particles produced an enhanced aversion compared to the non-irradiated controls. Because similar results have been observed following exposure to higher doses of 56Fe particles, these results suggest that the tested doses were too high, despite the lower LET of 600 MeV/n 28Si particles.

Operant Responding Following Exposure to 5 GeV/n 56Fe: Most of the research reviewed in this report has utilized 1 GeV/n 56Fe, which has an LET = 148keV/?m. For one run we had access to 5 GeV/n 56Fe, which has an LET = 142keV/?m. Rats were exposed to doses ranging between 1.5 to 2.5 Gy. When tested on an ascending fixed-ratio task 3 months following exposure, there were no significant differences between any irradiated group and the non-irradiated controls.

Organismic Variables (Aging)
Two approaches have been utilized to evaluate the effects of age on neurochemical and behavioral endpoints following exposure to HZE particles. First, rats have been maintained up to 1 year post irradiation and performance on specific tasks measured at intervals during the is time period. This approach using operant responding on a fixed-ratio reinforcement schedule shows that performance decreases as age increases: doses of 56Fe particles that were ineffective in altering performance in young animals had deleterious effects on aged animals.

The second approach studied the effects of exposure to HZE particles in older organisms. Exposure to HZE particles produces a series of neurochemical changes and motor deficits that are similar, but not identical, to those seen in older animals. To begin an evaluation of the possibility of an interaction between age and heavy particle irradiation, a preliminary experiment was run to determine oxotremorine-enhanced dopamine release in young and middle-aged F-344 rats following exposure to 1 Gy of 56Fe particles. The results showed a greater deficit in dopaminergic function in the older animals than in the younger animals. Statistical analysis of the results showed that there was a significant decrease in dopamine released in the aged, non-irradaiated rats. The difference between the middle-aged control rats and the irradiated young animals was not significant. These results suggest that dopamine release in a young rat exposed to 1 Gy of 56Fe particles is similar to that in old rats that have not been irradiated.

Neurochemistry: Exposing rats to 1.5, 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of 250 MeV protons produced no significant alterations in dopamine release. Comparted to control animals, all groups of irradiated animals, particularly those exposed to 1.5 and 3.0 Gy, showed a slight increase in dopamine release, but this was not significant. These results indicate that exposure to up to 4.0 Gy of high energy protons does not affect the functioning of the dopaminergic system.

Conditioned Place Preference: Rats were tested for the acquisition of a CPP following exposure to 4 Gy of protons or following control procedures. Both the irradiated and the control rats showed a similar preference for the amphetamine-paired compartment. The amount of time spent in each compartment was not significantly different for the proton-exposed and control rats.

Spatial Learning and Memory: Exposing rats to protons produced no consistent alteration in water maze performance. Rats irradiated with 4.0 Gy showed increase latency to find the hidden platform on Day 1, but by Day 2 were identical to controls. Rats irradiated with 1.5 Gy demonstrated impairments in re-learning compared to the control group as shown by increased latencies on the reversal day (Day 4), when the platform was moved to the opposite quadrant. However, spatial memory and learning were not disrupted as all groups performed equally well on the probe trials, showing that all groups utilized spatial strategies to find the platform.

CTA Learning: Two sets of experiments were conducted. In the first experiment, rats were exposed to 1.5, 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of protons. There were no significant differences between the irradiated or the control rats; both groups of rats showed equivalent test day sucrose intakes following injection of amphetamine. In contrast to the results obtained with rats exposed to 56Fe particles, exposing rats to up to 4.0 Gy of 250 MeV protons did not disrupt the acquisition of the dopamine-mediated CTA produced by injection of amphetamine.

In the second experiment, the rats were placed behind 6 gm/cm2 aluminum to see whether the fragmentation characteristics produced by protons passing through aluminum shielding would affect the behavioral response to administration of a dopamine agonist. The acquisition of a CTA following exposure to 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of protons was not affected by shielding. There were no differences in the intensity of the amphetamine-induced CTA between the control rats and the radiated rats.

Operant Responding: Proton-irradiated and control animals were trained to press a lever for food reinforcement using a fixed-ratio schedule. In contrast to the results obtained following exposure to 56Fe particles exposure to 4 Gy of high-energy protons had no effect on fixed-ratio responding for food reinforcement. Both irradiated and control animals showed increased levels of responding as the ratio was increased from FR-1 to FR-35. Exposing rats to high-energy protons does not affect the capacity of the organism to respond appropriately to changes in reinforcement contingencies.

Effects of Antioxidant Diets
Dopamine Release: Previous research had shown that exposing rats to 1.5 Gy 56Fe particles produces a significant decrease in potassium-enhanced striatal dopamine release. Because similar effects are observed in aged animals, and because diets rich in antioxidant phytochemicals can prevent the neurochemical change, the first experiment in this series was designed to evaluate whether or not these diets are equally effective in preventing heavy particle-induced neurochemical changes. Rats maintained on the control diet continued to show a 56Fe-induced reduction in dopamine release. In contrast, the rats maintained on either the strawberry or blueberry diets did not show the radiation-induced reduction in dopamine release. Compared to their respective controls, the radiated animals maintained on the antioxidant diets apparently showed an enhanced dopamine release.

Dopamine-Mediated Taste Aversion Learning: Rats were maintained on the control diet or on the diets containing 2% blueberry of strawberry extract. Two days following irradiation with 1.5 Gy of articles failed to develop a CTA to amphetamine. The rats fed either the blueberry or strawberry diet did show an amphetamine-induced CTA. These results indicate that antioxidant diets that have been shown to ameliorate the effects of normal aging are equally effective in preventing the disruption of amphetamine-induced CTA learning by exposure to 6Fe particles.

Tumorigenesis: Among other effects on the health and functioning of the organism, oxidative stress and the production of reactive oxygen species have been linked to carcinogenesis. As part of another study, rats that had been given either antioxidant or control diets prior to 56Fe exposure were evaluated for tumor development for 1 year after irradiation. Rats were sacrificed when a tumor developed or when there was some obvious health problem. The rats that were maintained on the blueberry or strawberry diets prior to irradiation with 56Fe particles showed a significantly greater survival time and developed significantly fewer tumors than rats maintained on the control diet.

Effects of Diet on Operant Responding: Rats were maintained on control or antioxidant diets for 2 months prior to exposure to 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles. When tested on an ascending fixed-ratio schedule 7 months post-irradiation, there were no significant differences in response rate as a function of irradiation status or diet. When tested 12 months post-irradiation, the irradiated rats fed control or blueberry diets showed significantly poorer performance than the non-irradiated rats or the radiated rats fed the strawberry diet.

experiment_title: Effect of Space Travel on Skeletal Myofibers
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The physiological mechanisms that lead to a loss of skeletal muscle mass during space flight are not understood. This study utilized engineered 3-dimensional skeletal muscle tissues composed of several thousand aligned post-mitotic myofibers. These bioartificial muscles (BAMs) were used to study the effects of microgravity upon skeletal muscle tissues.

Approach:

Pre-launch experimental procedures were identical to NIH.C5 (STS-72). On STS-77, 24 BAMs were flown on the Shuttle and another 24 were used as ground controls. Inflight, lactate production and glucose metabolism were measured by removing culture medium samples (1-3 ml), storing them in the Space Tissue Loss (STL) Module, and analyzing the aliquots with a YSI Glucose/Lactate Model 2000 analyzer. On the last day of flight, selected bioreactors were infused with 50% (w/v) trichloroacetic acid (TCA) to a concentration of 10% (w/v) and left for 12-24 hours. Postflight, the BAMs were removed from their culture wells and sonicated in 1 ml of sucrose buffer. DNA and total noncollagenous protein content were then determined. [3H] phenylalanine (Phe) was used to determine protein synthesis rates both during and postflight. Quantitative polyacrylamide gels (PAGE) were used to determine muscle contractile protein MHC, fibronectin, and beta-1 collagen synthesis rates. BAMs were fixed postflight, embedded in Epon, thin sectioned, stained, and randomly selected cross-sections were analyzed to determine cross-sectional area.

Results:

The tissue-cultured myofibers' reaction to space flight was analogous to that of humans and animals in space. These results suggest that BAMs may be used to test possible countermeasures to the effects of microgravity. However, caution must be taken when comparing neonatal-like avian muscle cells with adult mammalian muscle cells. Alterations in protein synthesis rates in microgravity could possibly be due to the coupling of muscle cells tension and protein synthesis via the cytoskeleton. The effects of space flight on the BAMs were most likely caused by alterations in the cytoskeletal/sarcomeric network of fibrils, although it is likely that there are numerous secondary effects. Further analysis suggests that anabolic factors such as GH or IGF-1 could be used to counteract muscle atrophy in space. Overall, a combination of exercise and delivery of anabolic factors might be the most effective countermeasure to muscle wasting in microgravity.

experiment_title: Astronaut's Energy Requirement for Long-Term Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Loss of body mass commonly occurs during long-duration space flight. One explanation for the loss in body mass is the decrease of skeletal muscle use. It is also expected that the systematic ongoing negative energy balance observed in flight contributes significantly to such a loss. However, the reason for the imbalance between energy intake and energy output is not clear.

Additional knowledge of energy intake requirements during space flight is needed to maintain the health of long-duration crewmembers, to ensure high performances and the overall success of a mission, but also to ensure adequate, but not excessive cargo allotments for food. In this regard, the determination of energy requirements as a function of exercise load is a clear pre-requisite to any planed long-term manned space flight.

Astronaut's Energy Requirements for Long-Term Space Flight (Energy) will measure changes in energy balance after long term spaceflight, adaptations in the components of the total energy expenditure and derive an equation for the energy requirements of astronauts.

APPROACH:
Preflight data collection consists of one active measurement day, and a follow up void collection ten days later. The subject is wearing an activity monitor during the entire 10 day time period. After an overnight fast, the measurement day starts with a body weight measurement to calculate the Doubly Labeled Water (DLW) dosage given to each subject. A baseline urine collection is collected prior to the DLW ingestion. Approximately 45 minutes after DLW ingestion, the first oxygen uptake (OU) measurement is scheduled for 45 minutes, followed by a special breakfast. Over the next five hours, the crewmember is asked to perform a total of seven more OU measurements of 20 minutes each, which alternate with resting periods. After the second, fifth, and seventh OU void samples are collected.

Ten days after the measurement day, two additional void samples are requested from the subject, preferably from two consecutive voids.

The Baseline Data Collection (BDC) can be scheduled anytime between L-4 months and launch. The subjects should not have large deviations in their body mass (±5%) in the period from BDC to launch. The BDC data are valid for 6 months. It is preferable during the 11 days of the BDC to stay within the same geographical region (continent).

Energy in-flight data collection should be scheduled with crewmembers staying in orbit for four months or longer. The data collection should be scheduled no earlier than three months into the mission, and at least three weeks prior to landing. This 4-week limit is chosen to avoid confounding effects of the increased countermeasure programs at the end before landing.

The astronauts total energy expenditure will be measured by the DLW method, and by indirect calorimetry. In addition, body composition will be measured through hydrometry. The in-flight and preflight protocols will be conducted over a 10-day period, starting with the main measurement day. The day before the measurement day the experiment hardware is set up and the standardized meals will be consumed. Those meals will be of similar macronutrient composition and energy content and will be based on individual’s body mass.

At the start of the measurement day, intake of the DLW and a urine sampling are performed. During the measurement day, two sessions of 45 min and 4 hours of physical rest will be required during which OU is measured using the Pulmonary Function System (PFS). The 45-minute measurement period is scheduled approximately 45 minutes after the DLW intake. Then a standardized breakfast is consumed and the 4 hour session starts. This session contains continuous online OU measurements by the PFS, paused only by void samplings and 10 minute breaks for comfort. Over the following nine days, a series of void and water samplings are scheduled for every other day and the activity monitor is worn continuously.

RESULTS:
Results for this investigation are unavailable. This is an international experiment. NASA does not currently have an agreement with international space partners to archive their data in the LSDA.

experiment_title: Blood and Oxidative Stress
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
On Earth, the body constantly produces natural substances that can cause damage to cells and also tissues, the so-called prooxidants and/or free radicals. These can be caused by smoking or exposure to sunlight, drugs etc.

However, the body has an antioxidant system made up of enzymes and molecules that protects against the damage caused by prooxidants by converting them into safe compounds. Examples of antioxidants are vitamins E, A, C and beta-carotene. These are available through diet or in nutritional supplements. Oxidative stress, a pronounced prooxidant state, is caused by the excessive production of free radicals or from the weakening of the antioxidant defense system, and is the cause of many pathologies, aging processes and is believed to be a possible cause of cancer. The space environment is obviously very different to that of Earth. The body has to adapt to weightlessness and the effect of background radiation. Nowadays, around six months is considered a safe amount of time to spend in space, allowing astronauts to carry out their functions as normal and allowing their bodies to readapt on return to Earth. Loss of red blood cell mass, volume of blood plasma, and hemoglobin has been continuously observed in astronauts during space missions. This phenomenon has been termed "spatial anemia" and the underlying mechanisms causing this are still not clear. This could be due to suppressed production of red blood cells or increased destruction of red blood cells. Many studies have demonstrated that red blood cells exposed to weightlessness have a modified flow and undergo damage to the cell membrane causing the release of hemoglobin to a greater degree. This experiment aims to determine the degree of "stress" that the red blood cells have undergone to bring about cell damage, the quantity of substances in blood serum that would prevent this damage (antioxidants), the damage that the red blood cell membranes have undergone, and the time it takes to recover. This will be done by measuring the antioxidant status of astronauts prior to and after space flight, and the time it takes to recover from oxidative stress occurring during space radiation exposure. Moreover red blood cells will be analyzed to evaluate their membrane composition and the activities of the enzymes involved in antioxidant defenses. This experiment will provide results that will help in finding methods to reduce the current effects of oxidative space anemia by, for example integrating appropriate dietary elements and natural compounds that act as antioxidants. These results will also impact on future longer-term space missions to, for example, Mars. APPROACH:
Relevant comparisons were made from blood samples taken from the astronaut before and after the mission. Blood samples were taken one time prior to launch and three times after landing. They were stored under refrigerated conditions in special tubes to avoid clotting and freezing. As soon as a sample was taken, it was shipped for analysis. The first sample was taken as close as possible to the launch date. A sample was also taken as soon as possible after landing. Hereafter, one sample was drawn 15 days after landing and the last sample was drawn 30 days after landing. Total blood was analyzed to quantify oxidative stress of the subject and to measure levels of antioxidants, which help to prevent cell damage. Blood plasma was analyzed to determine fatty acid composition and levels of molecules that cause cell damage such as free radicals and oxidized compounds. Red blood cells were analyzed for enzymatic proteins, which help to break down elements that cause cell damage and injury.

RESULTS:
Space anemia is a 15-day ailment. Blood becomes more concentrated because of water loss during space flight and the amount of hemoglobin in red blood cells decreases by as much as 20 percent. Space flight also significantly reduces total antioxidant status of blood, blood enzyme activity, and cholesterol and phospholipid content. All these effects disappear within 15 days after a crew member has returned to Earth. This “space anemia” may be caused by accelerated cell aging due to increased exposure to oxidative stress in space. These observations may help to develop appropriate medical supplements for astronauts.

experiment_title: Choroid Plexus, Brain and Heart Natriuretic Peptide Development in Space
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The aims of the studies were 1) to investigate by electron microscopy and immunocytochemistry, the choroidal alterations induced by 11-days of development in space in developing rats and pups, and to compare results obtained in adult rats flown during the SLS-2 experiments with the ultrastructural and immunocytochemical observations obtained from dams dissected 2 days after landing from an 11-day spaceflight and, 2) to evaluate by immunocytochemistry and radioimmunoassays, in situ hybridization and/or competitive RT-PCR qualitative or quantitative changes in storage and biosynthesis of natriuretic peptides in cardiac tissues, in rats that developed for 11 days in space and in the dams, which delivered 2 days after landing.

Approach:

Brains from dams, fetuses and pups were removed after decapitation. Choroid plexuses were carefully dissected either 3-4 hours or 2 days after landing. Samples were fixed by immersion in 2.5% glutaraldehyde in cacodylate buffer 0.1M, pH 7.4, post-fixed in 1% osmium tetroxide in sodium barbital-acetate buffer 0.05M, pH 7.4 and embedded in LX-112 epoxy resin, or in 3% paraformaldehyde in PBS. The hypothalamus and remaining brain with brainstem from the same brains were removed and directly frozen on dry ice, before storage at -80°C. and shipping on dry ice to the lab, where they were stored at -80°C, until sectioning and observation. Whole brains from 2 additional animals in each group were immersed in Bouinï¿½s fixative for 16 h, washed in water and dehydrated in ethanol, before embedding in Paraplast. Four other whole brains were directly frozen on dry ice, frozen and stored at -80°C. Hearts were similarly processed for electron microscopy and immunocytochemistry. Atrial and ventricle samples were frozen to be studied by radioimmunoassay, in situ hybridization and competitive RT-PCR.

Results:

Ultrastructural observations showed that, in dams, there was a strong restoration of the cell polarity and a restored choroidal protein expression. These results suggested that, after 2 days of readaptation to earth gravity, choroidal functions were restored, indicating that secretory processes were re-established early after landing. In fetuses and pups, maturation of choroid plexuses appeared slightly delayed, in comparison with fetuses and pups developed on earth. Results on the expression of natriuretic peptides in the heart showed that cardiac ANP biosynthesis of rat dams flown in space for 11 days and readapted for 2 days to Earthï¿½s gravity, was increased approximately two-fold, when compared to synchronous and vivarium control rats. More obviously, rat fetuses developed in space displayed an altered maturation of cardiac ANP, evidenced by an increased mRNA biosynthesis (p<0.05), whereas the cardiac ANP storage was slightly reduced (p<0.05) in both flight and synchronous control groups, compared to vivarium control rats. This suggests that ANP metabolism during development is impacted by both the microgravitational environment and the housing conditions.

experiment_title: Adaptive Stress Training for Hazardous Conditions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Acute stress has the potential to significantly debilitate human performance, both physically and cognitively. For long-duration space flight, the results of such reduced cognitive performance could be life-threatening, and therefore warrants the creation of behavioral countermeasures for mitigating crew health and performance risks. Currently most emergency training focuses on performance outcomes, but new research should be centered on preventing negative performance outcomes through acute stress management techniques. Traditional training can be effective under predictable conditions, but performance can degrade rapidly if unexpected stressors are introduced. Additionally, the proposed system could serve as a preflight screening measure to help identify individuals who are more likely to perform better in high stress situations. The goal of this experiment, using Virtual Reality (VR) simulated situations, was to reduce acute stress response during space flight using an adaptive inoculation approach. Exposure was administered gradually and used a biofeedback system to respond and adapt to individual stress response in a way that promotes learning voluntary physiological control without overwhelming the subject.

Specific aims of this research included:

  1. Identifying stressors in a microgravity environment;
  2. Evaluating formal objective methods to measure baseline chronic and acute stress, in-training performance, psychological stress response, physiological stress response, and procedural errors;
  3. Developing a prototype for graduated stress training;
  4. Conducting a proof-of-concept of the training program based on NASA’s emergency protocols for the International Space Station (ISS); and
  5. Establishing guidelines for implementation of the graduated stress training.

APPROACH:

The research team and panel of experts reviewed and identified the stressors associated with emergency spaceflight situations of fire on the International Space Station (ISS) with respect to task and effect on users. Procedural information for virtual reality (VR) training was detailed, including the events likely to occur in the environment, the types of stressors encountered, NASA emergency procedures, resources to respond during the event, and the performance effects the stressors may have. Stress training requires procedural information to be included in the scenarios and conveyed to the user, so the stressors do not interfere with skill/knowledge acquisition. The stressors were categorized by manipulation type (environment or task manipulation), which indicates if a stressor may affect the task and deviate from the selected emergency procedure. From the environmental stressors, a simplified fire procedure was created based on the existing NASA ISS emergency procedures to develop adaptation and Training Module logic. The adaptations used implicit biofeedback, consisting of physiological signals exceeding a threshold “zone” and triggering a change in simulated stressors. The Training Module design was informed by past research on Stress Inoculation Training and Graduated Stress Exposure to implement a stress inoculation training strategy over five training sessions. The adaptation and training module rules taken together were used to produce a training pedagogy for use within the system.

To implement a Prototype Training System, the research team designed and implemented the system architecture for a VR-ISS with a emergency fire simulation. The VR environment was developed for the stressors and emergency procedure selected in the Training Module design. This environment was designed so that users can complete a NASA emergency fire procedure and locate the source of a fire. The procedure requires emergency equipment including a portable breathing apparatus (PBA), portable fire extinguisher (PFE), and Compound Specific Analyzer–Combustion Products (CSA-CP). Three different stressor levels were created in the simulation, involving a combination of stressors of varying intensity, including smoke density, fire alarms, and module power-outages that flickered the lights. The stressor levels were validated through objective physiological measures and subjective stress questionnaires as participants conducted the emergency procedure to locate the fire source. Results showed that the three-stressor levels implemented in a VR environment result in significantly different participant stress, workload, and distress. The adaptive nature of the VR training system required that the trainee’s stress level be measured in real-time, and a stress detection system was created with machine learning methods. Physiological signals were calculated from sensors which include electrocardiogram (ECG), respiration (RSP), electrodermal activity (EDA), and non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP). The physiological signals were streamed in real-time to apply preprocessing, high-dimensional feature extraction, feature selection, and classification using supervised machine learning approaches. Current limitations with supervised machine learning approaches propelled the development of a statistical classification method by our research team, known as Approximate Bayes (ABayes). ABayes uses kernel density probability estimates to find conditional class probabilities for three stress states: low, medium, high. The advantage of ABayes is the direct and transparent calculation of the class probabilities. ABayes was evaluated on its accuracy of predicting stress using cross-validation and hold-out on unseen data.

Three human-in-the-loop experiments were performed to test the components of the Adaptive VR turning system in isolation and as a system. The first experiment assessed the ability to manipulate a person’s stress level in a virtual environment. Specifically, an evaluation was preformed to determine the extent to which operationally relevant VR stressor levels (i.e., low, medium, high) derived from existing emergency spaceflight procedures could evoke a reliable stress response. The second experiment evaluated the ability to reliably detect the stress level of a person in VR using a combination of biophysical sensors and machine learning to correctly classify low, medium, or high stress. The third experiment was conducted to determine if the closed-loop VR training system could successfully inoculate participant’s stress over a series of training trials with graduated stress exposure. 

RESULTS:

A physiological-based stress detection system for classifying multiple levels of acute stress was developed with a novel classifier, ABayes, using a personalized time-series interval approach. The approach was evaluated against common machine learning classification systems in their ability to classify stress for two different tasks: a fire response task aboard a VR International Space Station (VR-ISS) or a computer-based (N-back) task. The current findings suggest that three levels of stress can be classified by means of the ABayes approach, providing promising accuracy when compared to past research on multi-class stress detection. Stress was accurately predicted for both the simplified lab task, N-back, and the more complex VR-ISS task. Analysis on the window sizes gave insight into which sensors/features were useful for varying time-intervals. Future work will further investigate these personalized stress detection systems with the aim of implementing real-time stress monitoring.

experiment_title: Technological Support for Crew/MCC Communication and Collaboration During Space Exploration Operations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES

As space exploration missions journey further from Low-Earth orbit, crewmembers will be confronted with
longer communication delays with ground support. This lag time can be up to 20 minutes one way for Mars
missions. These delays degrade the space-ground communication process and make it more difficult for Mission
Control Center (MCC) to establish a common understanding with space crewmembers during their interactions.
Deep space exploration missions will necessitate increased crewmember autonomy however, MCC will still need
to collaborate with the crew to ensure their safety and address unforeseen problems that may arise during
missions that may jeopardize the success of the mission. Transmission speed is fixed by the laws of physics and,
therefore, it is necessary to explore solutions that focus on the communication process.
Previously, the investigators identified three critical features of asynchronous communication: Timing (when to
expect a response), Thread (tracking and maintaining conversational threads), and Transmission Efficiency
(‘chunking’ relevant information in a single message). This study builds upon the medium-specific
communication protocols and a training module that the investigators created to help space crews and MCC
personnel communicate and collaborate during time delay. Braiding is a novel, text-based software that was
developed to arrange communication sessions into threads, or ‘braids’ along a carousel. Remote team members
communicate with each other by viewing opposite sides of the carousel and interacting with the braid directly in
front of them. As each team member responds to the content on their braid, the carousel will rotate one step and
bring new content waiting for a response. Braiding is expected to help space crewmembers and MCC to organize
and track their time delayed communications, and thus to prevent topics from getting ‘tangled.’
In order to provide a comprehensive proof-of-concept, the investigators will explore two aims. During Aim 1, the
investigators will attempt to demonstrate the feasibility and benefits of the Braiding support system. In Aim 2, the
goal is to identify refinements and features required for use in space operations.

APPROACH

The investigators plan to recruit 8 to 12 volunteers to participate in a human-in-the loop (HITL) evaluation of
Braiding. Four to six volunteers will be assigned the role of crewmember and the remaining volunteers will act
as MCC personnel (flight surgeon or capcom, dependent on test scenario). Pairs of volunteers will collaborate
remotely on four scenarios, communicating under delayed condition, first via a traditional texting tool
(comparable to the one currently used in NASA analog missions) and subsequently via Braiding. During the first
two scenarios, volunteers will use the traditional texting tool to get accustomed to delayed communication and
have a standard against which to compare Braiding, the tool they will use in the remaining scenarios.
Communication between remote team members during the test scenarios will be delayed by up to five minutes
one-way. Test scenarios and communication tool will be counterbalanced across pairs of volunteers. A short
survey comparing Braiding to the standard texting tool with respect to communication quality, ease of task
accomplishment and associated workload will be administered at the end of the HITL evaluation. The
communication between remote team members during the scenarios will be examined in terms of length, level of
detail and completeness of information provided, and communication efficiency. Individual semi-structured
interviews with volunteers will be conducted following the study to assess the value of Braiding and its features.

RESULTS

The results of this HITL evaluation are expected to demonstrate the feasibility, acceptability, and benefits of
Braiding to facilitate crew/MCC communication under time delay. Improving communication between members
of the crew/MCC Multi-Team system will enhance efficiency and joint task success during future long duration
space missions.

experiment_title: Glucose Kinetics and Muscle Atrophy
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In response to decreased usage, skeletal muscle undergoes a reductive remodeling due to the decrease in tension on the weight bearing components of the musculoskeletal system. Accompanying this reductive remodeling of skeletal muscle in all of these situations is a decreased ability to oxidize fatty acids. The reason is not known. Possible mechanisms for the fuel shift are: 1) a shift in fuel utilization pattern involving the up regulation of glycolysis and the down regulation of fatty acid oxidation, 2) a change at a specific locus leading to a decreased ability to oxidize fat (e.g. reduction in the carnitine acyltransferase cycle, 3) a general decrease in metabolic activity since energy needs of inactive muscle are necessarily less and so excess fuel substrates (triglycerides, glycogen) are stored rather than used, and 4) no effect at the enzyme level.

The objectives of this project were to distinguish between these three using a combination of human bed test study of glucose kinetics during bed rest and rodent hind limb unloading (HLS) studies. Work involved using the miroarray gene expression analysis with the Affymetrix gene chip system to investigate the effect of HLS on fuel pathways in metabolism in rodent soleus muscle and liver.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
The muscle study has been completed. The principle finding was disuse atrophy is associated with a down regulation of the total fatty acid oxidation pathway and upregulation of the glycolytic pathway.

experiment_title: The effect of weightlessness on the tendon-to-bone insertion
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The overall objective of this proposal is to examine the effect of prolonged weightlessness on the biology of tendons and their insertions into bone. Samples from STS135 will allow us to verify our results from STS131. These specimens will also allow us to perform additional assays to verify our hypotheses. Raman microprobe spectroscopy will be performed at the tendon-to-bone insertion to determine the mineral gradient across the insertion.

APPROACH:

Experiment animals: 15 mice flew on this mission and 30 mice were housed at KSC to serve as ground controls. Left and right shoulders (humerus-rotator cuff-scapula units) and ankles (Achilles tendon-calcaneous bone) were removed from each mouse approximately two hours after landing, processed, and shipped to our laboratory. Ongoing studies analyzing specimens from this mission include: biochemistry and proteomics on rotator cuff mouse muscles, micro-computed tomography on the humeral head bone, biomechanics on the supraspinatus tendon-to-bone insertion, and histology on supraspinatus tendon-humeral head and Achilles tendon-calcaneous samples.

RESULTS:

The effect of microgravity on the rotator cuff tendons and their bony insertions: Microgravity led to significant increases in MMP-3 and MMP-13 mRNA expression and significant decreases in tendon cross-sectional area. These changes led to a surprising increase in the modulus and strength of the tendon-to-bone insertion. The stiffer tendon-to-bone insertion may be indicative of early tissue pathology.

The effect of microgravity on the humeral head bone: Preliminary data from STS-131 and STS-135 demonstrate that bone resorption is increased (as indicated by increases in the ratio of RANK-L to OPG gene expression) and osteoblast differentiation is decreased (as indicated by decreases in osterix and Runx-2 gene expression). Bone mineral density (BMD) and trabecular thickness (Tb.Th.) were decreased due to microgravity.

The effect of microgravity on the rotator cuff muscles: Microgravity significantly downregulated the expression of myogenic genes indicating atrophy/degeneration of the muscles due to microgravity. Downregulation of adipogenic genes indicated that degeneration due to microgravity may occur through different pathways than degeneration due to tendon and/or nerve injury in gravity conditions. An increase in collagen type III indicates muscle fibrosis. Preliminary proteomics results indicated that the expression of a large number of proteins was changed due to microgravity conditions. These changes included proteins related to muscle metabolism, muscle type, and fatty acid/glucose metabolism.

experiment_title: In-flight Evaluation of a Portable Clinical Blood Analyzer
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Research on human adaptation to microgravity often involves storing blood samples for later analysis on Earth. Immediate, inflight analysis would make results available during a mission and would avoid the need for refrigeration or freezing and the possibility of deterioration of the samples. The objective of this hardware study was to test a portable device for inflight analysis of blood samples.

APPROACH:
The Portable Clinical Blood Analyzer (PCBA) is a hand-held, battery-powered device that measures electrolytes by ion-selective electrode potentiometry, glucose by amperometry, hematocrit by conductometrics, and pH by direct potentiometry. It does not measure hemoglobin. The analyzer was tested on the ground against traditional laboratory methods, using capillary blood, venous blood and control solutions. It was then tested for inflight use on 5 Shuttle missions. Control solutions were analyzed before and during the flights. Twice during flight, 21 astronauts performed finger sticks on each other, collected capillary blood using heparinized capillary tubes, and transferred the blood to the analyzer. Blood samples were also collected and analyzed before and after flights.

RESULTS:
The performance of the analyzer in microgravity was similar to its performance on the ground for all the control solutions except sodium, and the small difference in sodium levels was within clinical laboratory performance standards. The astronauts were able to collect and analyze blood samples in flight. Some changes were noted in pH and levels of potassium and ionized calcium during flight or on landing day, but the values returned to preflight levels within 3 to 6 days. The analyzer was found to be very reliable for immediate analysis of sodium, potassium, ionized calcium, pH and glucose on the ground and during space flight. It is being flown routinely to help flight surgeons evaluate the health of the astronauts, and it will be especially useful for following calcium levels and evaluating bone changes during long spaceflights. The device may also prove useful in remote areas on Earth.

experiment_title: Gravitropic Threshold (GTHRES)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The widespread occurrence of statocytes with sedimenting statoliths in higher plants is compelling evidence that they are involved in some way with the process of detection of the g-force vector direction. Whether the same process serves to detect the intensity of that force is not well established. The transduction mechanism by which positional information is translated into meaningful biological changes is also not understood. Determination of the smallest stimulus capable of eliciting a response, referred to as threshold, was an important experiment objective. Other objectives were to determine the maximum response to laterally directed g-acceleration between zero and one g, to determine the sensitivity of the plant's response parameter and to determine whether the plant's response is proportional to the intensity of the stimulation.

APPROACH:
The test organism was Avena sativa. Nine seeds were planted in 5 groups of 4 cubes. The seedlings were raised in darkness. Prior to testing, the seedlings were in space under centrifugation at 1 g. Tropistic stimulations were produced by laterally directed centripetal accelerations on variable speed centrifuges that were programmed to apply stimulus doses where both centrifuge speed and duration of stimulation were varied. Stimulus doses were defined as g x t in which g and t were independent variables. In different tests, centripetal accelerations were varied between 0.1 and 1.0 g and t was varied from 2 to 130 min. Stimulus doses were varied from 1.8 to 25.2 min. Temperatures were controlled and recorded continuously. The nominal temperature was 22.5 degrees C. Tropistic response was measured before and after stimulation with time lapse images using infrared light. Gas samples were taken from 3 cubes and analyzed for oxygen, carbon dioxide and ethylene content.

RESULTS:
To determine threshold stimulation times, logarithmic curve fitting was used. Characteristic qualitative features of the Avena coleoptile's tropistic response pattern in weightlessness were not greatly different from ground based studies. For flight data, logarithmic plots extrapolated to positive threshold values in the range 0.9 to 7.8 min. The shortest stimulation time to cause a response at 1.0 g was 2.0 min., and by extrapolation, the threshold was less than 1 min. The least g-value used to stimulate coleoptiles in flight was 0.1 g. In that experiment, a significant response of 19.6 plus or minus 2.2 degrees was observed, which demonstrated that if there is an absolute g-threshold for gravitropic response, it must be below 0.1 g. Qualitatively, autotropic counterreactions after initial tropistic bending were evident from visual inspection of time series of response images. As a general trend, autotropic responses were more prominent the greater the stimulus and the tropistic response.

experiment_title: Mechanisms for Plant Adaptation to Space Environment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The molecular study of human health conditions that develop in response to long term habitation in spaceflight conditions is inherently limited by the necessity to insure safety of study participants. As such, the cellular and molecular pathology of these disease states and potential remediations are unknown. Comparative biology, or the study of similar situations in different types of organisms, presents a unique opportunity to explore these human conditions with minimal associated risks. The study of conserved cellular stress responsive pathways between humans and plants provides this benefit and many others. In particular, plants are the primary production source for metabolic energy and oxygen in our terrestrial environment, and proper application in extraterrestrial and spaceflight conditions could potentially reduce the cost of recreating human habitable environments in extremely harsh conditions. Plants, like animals, suffer from stress linked to a variety of challenges. For example, certain adverse environmental conditions, such as changes in temperature, reduced nutrients, and disease, as well as physiological situations, such as growth, are known to generate an imbalance between demand and capacity of protein synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), a condition that is also known as ER stress (1, 2). The ER, a conserved structure in human and plant cells, initiates the production of all secretory proteins. Secretory proteins constitute one third of the cellular proteome and allow cells to communicate with the external environment. The ER can sense stress due to accumulation of unfolded proteins in its lumen, and restores homeostasis by invoking a largely conserved cytoprotective signaling pathway, called the unfolded protein response (UPR). Compromised UPR leads to serious conditions and even death in animals and plants (3-5). In spaceflight conditions a number of factors including microgravity, radiations, vibration, limited exchange of gases, and suboptimal growth conditions (temperature, light, nutrients) reduces overall plant growth, impairs development and reduces yield. In animals and plants, several sensors and transducers initiate the UPR; however, IRE1, an ER-associated protein kinase and ribonuclease, functions as a major ER stress sensor and plays a key role in the UPR signaling by controlling UPR gene expression (4, 6, 7). Activities in our lab and others have demonstrated that plant IRE1 is needed to respond to a diversified portfolio of stimuli linked to abiotic and biotic stress and cell growth and differentiation, as well as to modulate responsive outputs (4, 5). In all eukaryotes, IRE1 activates the UPR by an unconventional splicing of a bZIP transcription factor, namely Hac1 in yeast8-10 and Xbp1 in metazoans (11, 12). Recent efforts in our lab and others have shown that in the model species Arabidopsis thaliana, the functional equivalent of Hac1 and Xbp1 is bZIP60 (5, 13, 14). The bZIP60 mRNA splicing is followed by the synthesis of the mature form of bZIP60, which can modulate transcription of UPR genes in the nucleus. Thus, synthesis of the transcriptionally active bZIP60 occurs only in conditions of stress. In our research we will adopt the stress-dependent activation of bZIP60 to generate plants that can function as real-time stress bioreporters that can be easily used to report on the onset of stress in plants. We believe that we will learn the mechanisms that enable plants to respond to ER stress. This is highly significant for the understanding of basic defense mechanisms in plants, and for engineering plants that can cope with stress on Earth. We also expect that our research will have an important impact in biology with implications well beyond plants. Because the signaling pathways between plant and mammalian UPR are largely conserved, it is likely that understanding the UPR in a tractable multicellular model system, such as Arabidopsis, will allow building approaches with a strong potential to contribute to the solution of the problems in humans confronting cellular stress. We also expect that we will be able to develop transplantable bioindicators of stress without the need of sophisticated instrumentation. These reporters will potentially facilitate the optimization of plant cultivation in hostile environments, such as marginal lands. In addition, because of the conservation of UPR mechanisms in plants and humans, real-time stress bioindicators will likely reflect the perception of stress in other organisms besides plants and thus they may be useful to develop practices to improve quality of life for humans. In conclusion, not only will our research improve our nation's scientific competitiveness, it will also benefit education and the quality of life on Earth. Life on Earth depends on plants. With sharply growing environmental concerns (global warming, pollution, necessity to expand agriculture to marginal lands, etc.), understanding how plants can resist stress in hostile environments and adopting bioindicators help research to expand agriculture practices and thus ensure continued survival of the ever-growing human population.

APPROACH:
Successful plant growth in closed-loop life support conditions is a difficult challenge for the realization of long-term habitation of spacecraft and other extraterrestrial environments. In such environments, plants can undergo stress induced by a number of factors including changes in gravity, radiations, vibration, limited exchange of gases, and suboptimal growth conditions (temperature, light, nutrients). These sources of stress are often associated with reprogramming of gene expression and can cause limited plant growth, development, and yield. To facilitate plant life in space, it is crucial to acquire a better understanding of the genetic changes that enable plant cells to respond to spaceflight stress. To do so, one goal of this proposal is to define the underlying mechanisms of plant adaptation to the spaceflight environment at a transcriptional level. Through research supported by NASA, we have successfully identified a protein named AtIRE1 as a master regulator of transcription in conditions of stress responses to abiotic, biotic stress and to gravity changes in plants. However, the downstream signaling pathways controlled by AtIRE1 are not well defined, especially in conditions of altered gravity. A better understanding of the signaling pathways controlled by AtIRE1 is important to understand how plants can grow in conditions of stress. We propose to use in-flight and ground resources along with genomics and transcriptomics analyses in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana to understand the regulatory role of AtIRE1 in adaptation to spaceflight stress. Development of our research will continue to contribute to the understanding of basic signaling pathways that are in place to ensure stress survival in hostile environments, thus making possible the design and growth of plants that are resistant to space stress. To contribute further to the successful realization of habitation in space, we also aim to develop plants that can function as bioindicators of stress during in-flight situations. To do so, we will engineer plants with an AtIre1 substrate that is activated specifically in conditions of stress and that we will adapt to function as a visual stress reporter. The availability of real-time stress bioindicators will provide scientists and astronauts with direct read-outs of stress in the space environment. The results gathered in our research will contribute to NASA's strategic plans for the realization of long-term habitation of space and planetary surfaces. Because of the conservation of stress sensing and response mechanisms across multicellular organisms, we expect that our results will also have important implications for the general knowledge of stress and in the design of solutions for space stress management in multicellular organisms, including humans.

RESULTS: In the previous BRIC-18-2 (Biological Research in Canisters) experiment, we have established differential gene regulation in wild type but also in mutant Arabidopsis with defects in pro-survival management strategies. These findings open new areas of research on plant management of the different stresses that are found in space; a manuscript regarding these findings is currently in preparation.

experiment_title: Quantum Multiple Scattering Model of Heavy Ion Fragmentation (QMSFRG)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The quantum multiple scattering model of heavy ion fragmentation (QMSFRG) is an important input to risk evaluation and radiation shielding calculations. Several areas of development in nuclear data base development and output deliverables with the QMSFRG model will be the focus of this directed research as guided by previous results.

Applications include biophysical models of biological damage as ions pass through complex tissue structures, radiation transport code applications including shielding evaluations and comparisons of models to flight experiments, and space radiation risk assessments. It is important to note that although measurements of nuclear fragmentation cross sections are a step in code development for biophysical, shielding, and risk analysis, only theoretical models can provide a complete data base for such studies.

Past nuclear fragmentation models have relied on parameterizations of experiments or semi-classical physics models. These approaches have been shown to fail badly in heavy ion radiation transport code comparisons to experiments. Typical fragmentation measurements do not measure all secondary products and are usually restricted to fragments from ZP-1 to ZP/2 where ZP is the projectile charge. Lower charged fragments make important contributions to the GCR transport. Parametric models include no underlying physical description and thus fail outside the range of measurements. This failure is amplified when consideration is given to the large number of projectiles, target, and energies of interest and the lack of measurements for most of these reaction partners. Important aspects of nuclear reactions are not reproduced in Monte-Carlo models of heavy ion reactions and indicate the need for a quantum description that is capable of being implemented for GCR data bases. These features include the role of the nuclear surface, and nuclear structure effects such as shell structure and clustering. This investigation will develop the quantum mechanical models of nuclear fragmentation based in multiple scattering theory (QMSFRG) that will substantially advance the nuclear data bases for space radiation transport applications and the ability to extrapolate away from existing experimental data sets. The QMSFRG theory has been shown to be a robust and accurate approach to multiple types of galactic cosmic ray (GCR) computational evaluations.

Specific Aims for this study are:

1: To develop computer subroutines from the QMSFRG model that will generate require cross section data for application within the HZETRN code. A 190-ion grid for 9 projectile energies on arbitrary target materials (Hydrogen to Lead) applicable to GCR shielding problems will be generated with appropriate interpolation schemes for other materials and energies. A data base generator for Monte-Carlo transport code applications will be prepared and tested in the Geant4 code.

2: To report on the extension of the light ion production cross sections in the QMSFRG model for nuclear coalescence formation of light particles (d, t, h, a), and the resulting losses to n and p production. Also, data bases of light-particle production multiplicities will be generated. Comparisons to experimental data will be reported.

3: To improve the model energy density formalisms used in the nuclear de-excitation process in QMSFRG Master decay-solutions. Cross-comparisons of different models and to experimental data will be reported.

4: To implement the JSC Selected Core formalism for the description of pre-fragment excitation functions in nuclear abrasion for selected GCR nuclei (12C, 16O, 20Ne, and 28Si) and to extend the formalism for alpha-clusters. Fragmentation cross section calculations will be compared to experimental data.

Future work will extend the quantum multiple scattering theory to explicit pion channels, to consider other light particle clusters, and to produce data bases of light and heavy particle energy spectra.
