experiment_title: Lunar EVA Dosimetry: Design of a Radiation Dosimeter for Astronauts during Lunar Extravehicular Activities
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Task 1: Design, Fabrication and Testing TEPC detectors
The purpose of this task was to design, build and assemble a prototype Tissue Equivalent Proportional Counters (TEPC) that would satisfy the basic specifications outlined by NASA for a dosimeter for astronauts during lunar EVAs and as area monitors in space craft and habitats. The spherical TEPC is based on a single-wire anode with recessed guard ring insulators to shape the electric field near the poles. The diameter of the gas cavity is 18mm and the wall thickness is 3mm for a total diameter of 24mm (~ 1 inch). Aluminum vacuum chambers with a shell thickness of 0.5mm were designed and gold plated to maintain electrical conductivity. A system using a high sensitivity mass spectrometer was assembled to measure vacuum leaks for the assembled detectors with high special specificity.

Task 2: Modeling Detector Response
The objective of this task was to determine the response of the TEPC under ambient conditions and during SPE events on the lunar surface. Computations using the Monte Carlo Code PHITS have been made to determine the energy deposition in the TEPC using protons with an energy spectrum from a SPE in October 2003. These data were compared with the dose that would be delivered to the skin beneath a space suit with an areal density of 0.4 g/cm2. It is clear that a stainless steel vacuum chamber in Mod 1 needs to be replaced with lighter and thinner materials. These results will be important in determining what additional modifications will be necessary to achieve the design goal for real time measurements to the skin and BFO.

Task 3 Modeling the Variance-Covariance Method
The original proposal for the Extravehicular Activity (EVA) dosimeter was based on the concept of having two independent proportional counters that would be used to obtain estimates of dose, D, and a quality factor, Q, based on estimating using the variance-covariance method. It was recognized that because of size limitations, the proportional counters would have to be located too close to one another to satisfy the condition that a single particle could not intercept both detectors. The additional constraint that one of the detectors must measure the dose at the skin surface and the other at a depth corresponding to the blood forming organs makes the original variance-covariance method with paired detectors impractical. Investigators have developed a method using a single detector in a variance-covariance scheme. The concepts are based on collecting the charge, q(i), in a single TEPC for n successive time intervals, i. The method proposed by Borak at CSU separates the data set into two groups of n/2 entries of values for q(i) based on odd and even indices. The n/2 pairs of data (odd and even) are used to obtain the covariance and each of the two sets of n/2 values (odd or even) to estimate a variance. Monte Carlo codes have been written to test the algorithmic using microdosimetric spectra obtained from measurements in Task 1. The tests indicated that if the change in dose rate between successive intervals was less than 1%, the single detector scheme provided reliable estimated of dose rate and dose averaged lineal energy for estimating quality factors. The analysis also indicated that the estimate of dose mean lineal energy for high energy heavy ions (HZE) and recoil protons from PuBe neutrons converged to the correct value when the number of intervals exceeded 100 and the width of each interval was selected such that the mean number of events in each time interval (i) was less than 30.

APPROACH:
The method was tested using Monte Carlo simulations based on single event distributions measured with spherical tissue equivalent proportional counters where the event sizes spanned more than two orders of magnitude. The evaluation included testing at various mean numbers of events per interval (i.e., dose rate) and numbers of intervals (i.e., total duration).

RESULTS:
Results of the expectation analysis and Monte Carlo simulation showed that the algorithm corrects for the excess dispersion due to the random number of events in each time interval when the underlying dose rate is constant. It also converges to the correct value when there is a linear trend in dose rate of the duration of the measurement process.

experiment_title: Genotypic and phenotypic changes in yeast related to selective growth pressures unique to microgravity (Micro-4)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Micro-4 study investigates how yeast cells adapt to the unique aspects of the space environment by using the yeast deletion series; a collection of yeast strains where every gene has been individually knocked out. In this manner, the selective growth of every strain in the yeast deletion series can be assayed. The goal of the study is to understand the different responses and physical effects of microgravity on yeast cells by examining which specific deletion strains best survive. Direct assessment of selective pressures on cell populations through generations using the yeast deletion series is a critical experiment to directly address risks to biological integrity and life-based support systems for long-term occupation of space. Results from this study allow researchers to gain a global perspective on the genes that play a role in survival under microgravity conditions and will allow for a more thorough understanding of the effects of microgravity on a model organism.

APPROACH:
Eight OptiCell Processing Modules and four Plate Habitats will be loaded with liquid and solid cultures of the yeast deletion series. Cultures will be stored in cold stowage using a CGBA until after launch. Once in orbit half of the cultures will be activated by a temperature shift by transferring to a second CGBA. Liquid cultures will be subcultured twice during their growth to ensure sufficient generations. Growth will be terminated by a temperature shift via transfer back to the cold CGBA.

RESULTS:
Scanning electron microscopy (10,000X) demonstrated differences in shape, surface texture and budding pattern when grown in YPD in Opticells as suspension cultures. Static ground controls had egg to barrel shaped cells, with single pole budding, and an undulated surface. Rotating wall vessel grown yeast were round to barrel shaped, with multiple, bi-polar budding, and greatly undulated surface. Space flown cultured yeast were round to egg shaped, with multiple budding > ground Identification of genetic - environmental interactions in the flown and grown samples versus flown-not grown controls. In this analysis the normalized sizes of each of 4 replicates for each single mutant deletion strain was compared to the flown not-grown samples that were grown upon their return.

Pathway analysis: The 50 strains with the greatest space-related fitness defects were imported into the meta-analytical tool, GeneMANIA. GeneMANIA comprises a series of algorithms that search large, publicly available biological datasets to find related genes. We then prepared a visual representation of the output from this analysis where each gene is a node in the network, and the links between each node represents one type of interaction between these 50 genes. This preliminary analysis reveals several clusters of functionally interconnected genes, including clusters of genes involved in DNA repair and metabolism, transcription, chromatin remodeling, mitochondrial function, polarity, ribosome assembly, and stress.

Yeast deletion series are a powerful tool to study pathways mediating evolution fitness for life. These studies have allowed us to define the genes which convey survival advantage and disadvantage during space flight, the pathways which the genes populate, and the control mechanisms which determine the changes.

experiment_title: The Effects of Long Duration Space Flight on Gaze Control
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A number of investigators have assessed the role of vestibular-based subsystems both during and immediately following exposure to microgravity. While providing information specific to one or more sensorimotor subsystems there is little documentation of changes in the strategies used for coordination among subsystems or for those strategies supporting performance of natural, goal-directed behaviors. In particular, there may be several strategies selected for use during the process of adaptation to microgravity. These strategies may become more reliable for missions of increasing duration. Prime among these strategies are: (1) the reduced use of head movements during the early phases of the mission, (2) the reliance on either an internal coordinate system (intrinsic) or environmental coordinates (extrinsic) during different phases of space flight for spatial orientation, and (3) compensation for the changing role of proprioceptive information during flight. The investigators believed these strategies could be evaluated using goal-directed head and eye coordination tasks. Therefore, the primary objective of this study was to investigate the emergence or alteration of goal-oriented strategies required to maintain effective gaze when the interactive sensorimotor systems required for this function have been modified following extended exposure to the stimulus rearrangement of space flight.

APPROACH:
A cruciform target arrangement was used to provide the visual stimulation for target acquisition, pursuit tracking, memorized head rotations, and sinusoidal head oscillations (as a spacecraft fixed target). The target arrangement, placed approximately 75 cm from the subject's retinal plane, was used to provide a variety of static, time optimal, and dynamic visual stimuli to the subject in both the horizontal and vertical planes. Each axis of the cross was approximately 1.25 m long and contained a line of 495 miniature LEDs with a spacing between LEDs of 2.54 mm. Illumination of the LEDs were under microprocessor control, and multiple LEDs could be illuminated at any given time. Software drivers were developed to enable concurrent or sequential illumination of “special” standard target positions in the horizontal (0°, ±20°, ±30°) and vertical (0°, ±15°, ±20°, ±30°) planes, as well as to present both sinusoidal and non-predictable,constant-velocity ramp-type target motion along either axis. The device was also equipped with the capability of controlling remote or eccentric LEDs beyond the effective ocular-motor range (EOM range). For these experiments at least one set of these targets was located at ±60° horizontal and ±50° vertical. Targets within the EOM range are defined as those that can be acquired with the eyes alone and do not require a head movement to foveate the target.

RESULTS:
Preliminary results suggest that the gaze holding mechanism responsible for maintaining the eye on target may be affected by prolonged exposure to microgravity.

experiment_title: Modeling and Control of Bio-systems
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In 1964, NASA discovered that sufficient cooling of an astronaut could not be accomplished via air convection in the suit due to ventilation. Thus, NASA upgraded to the liquid cooling garment (LCG) to provide better thermal comfort. The astronaut controls the temperature of the water flowing through the LCG by manually adjusting the temperature control valve (TCV) located on the front of the space suit. However, manually manipulating the TCV setting can dramatically reduce the productivity of the astronaut, distracting them from the extra-vehicular activity (EVA) mission at hand. In general, humans are poor judges of their thermal state and since an astronaut’s attention is focused on other things during EVA, there are time lags in the application of temperature control. This can cause overheating or overcooling; placing unneeded thermal stress on the astronaut, and possibly degrading EVA performance. An attractive solution to this problem is the use of automatic control for thermal comfort. Before an automatic controller can be designed, human thermal models are needed to accurately describe the transient heat transfer processes and predict the thermal response within an acceptable band of accuracy. Such human thermal models can also be extended to predict thermal stress for various applications involving fire fighters, combat pilots, hazardous waste workers, and other relevant industries.

Hysterical paralysis is a conversion disorder characterized by some lack of motor functioning brought about by psychological mechanisms without the presence of organic injury in the central nervous system. In conversion disorders, it is assumed that the victim when presented with distressing mental conflict, which seem insurmountable, converts this anxiety into a somatic symptom to resolve or alleviate the tension. It is important to note that these physical symptoms are not intentionally produced to malinger. In many instances, the victim is unaware of the stressor that might have caused the symptoms. An assumption can be made that there must be some neurobiological dysfunction that can explain hysterical paralysis. So, mathematical modeling could be the first step to elucidate the neurobiology involved with conversion motor paralysis. In turn, identifying the specific location of brain lesions that produce hysterical paralysis can aid in the diagnosis of this disorder.

The first goal of this research was to develop a more complete model of the human's thermoregulation to handle various applications involving astronauts in space, warfighters, fire fighters, combat pilots, hazardous waste workers, and other industries where comfort in thermally stressful environments needs to be insured. Specifically, the model includes: the arteriovenous anastomoses (AVAs), an accurate model of the human digits, and cold induced vasodilation (CIVD). Future work will be needed to 'individualize' the model to investigate the effect of physiological variations (gender, age, race, body composition, body type, etc.). In addition, the effect of microgravity on human thermal physiology will need to be quantified.

The second part of this research was to develop a preliminary computational model for hysterical paralysis using neuro-circuitry information and systems biology principles. The model captures the salient features of the neuro-psychiatric disorder reported in the literature. Studies are on-going to model in more detail both the intra-cellular and extra-cellular features of the model, within the framework proposed.

The third part of this research was to develop a computational model of a pyramidal cell in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to better understand its role in the reinstatement of cocaine-seeking behavior. Studies have shown that the BLA and nucleus accumbens (NAcc) play a key role in cue-primed reinstatement. Therefore, once the BLA model is complete, a network level model involving the BLA and NAcc will be developed.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the Results below.

RESULTS:
In the human thermal modeling front, a comparison in cold-induced vasoilation response (CIVD) response between predicted and measured finger temperatures was conducted and it was shown that there is a fairly good agreement, indicating that the model is capable of showing CIVD responses in the fingers. As anticipated, the predicted response of finger temperature without CIVD is lower than the finger temperature response with CIVD during the oscillatory stage. The obvious conclusion is that the CIVD mechanism reduces extremity discomfort and prevents injuries due to cold exposure.

A study was conducted by the author and colleagues for the purpose of determining tolerance limits for subjects experiencing extreme heat stress. Participants (7 males, 7 females, 19 – 26 years old) exercised (200 and 425 W) at three different environments (normal – 23.9ºC, 45% RH; jungle – 35ºC, 75% RH; and desert – 43.3ºC, 20% RH) while wearing heavy clothing. A neural network predictive model based on the experimental data was developed. In addition, another objective was to determine whether previously developed heat strain models like the Givoni-Goldman prediction can accurately predict tolerance limits in comparison to experimental data obtained by the author and colleagues. Both models predict the response of the ‘average’ individual, thus correction factors based on individual characteristics (i.e. fitness, body type, acclimation status, etc) were incorporated to improve the prediction of heat strain. In addition, past heat strain predictive models and individual characteristics that effect tolerance limits were extensively reviewed by the author.

experiment_title: Novel Microstructures for Vascular Tissue Engineering
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The major goal of this research project was to tissue-engineer small diameter blood vessel substitutes. Such tissue-engineered blood vessels can also serve as tissue models for studying the effects of microgravity environmental changes on tissue adaptation and to assess potential therapeutic strategies. Requirements for a blood vessel substitute include sufficient burst pressure, viscoelastic mechanical properties, vasoactivity, and nonthrombogenicity. Native blood vessels have evolved a sophisticated structure and hierarchical organization of cell types and matrix molecules in order to satisfy these requirements.

The central hypothesis is that the physiological spatial arrangement of cells and extracellular matrix in an engineered blood vessel will affect the viscoelastic mechanical properties, which in turn, will affect vascular smooth muscle and endothelial cell response. This hypothesis will be tested by answering questions directly posed in Specific Aims 1 and 2 in which the effects of two main biomaterial scaffold properties on tissue function will be explored: (1) microstructure and (2) mechanics.

APPROACH:
The strategy of fabricating novel scaffolds with defined microstructure and mechanical properties will help to reveal the effects of specific ultrastructural and mechanical factors on cell response and tissue development. Investigators used this approach to develop a new generation of biomaterials for vascular tissue engineering that will provide an in vitro model tissue in which parameters can be varied systematically to investigate cell mechanics, tissue development, cell-substrate and cell-cell interactions in controlled microgravity environments in order to attain a better understanding of effects of microgravity on human physiology. Furthermore, the investigators recognize that these tissues may also be used as potential blood vessel replacements that are in high demand and are an integral part of more complex organs and tissues.

RESULTS:
Investigators have made significant progress in investigating the role of microstructure on vascular smooth muscle cells, specifically studying the role of substrate microtopography combined with mechanical cyclic strain on cell orientation. They also developed novel methodologies to self-assemble biomacromolecules such as collagen that are critical components of blood vessels. They also showed that they could stack several layers of microtopographically patterned thin scaffold films and keep the cells viable in this configuration, a critical step in forming the blood vessels.

experiment_title: Psychosocial Performance Factors in Space Dwelling Groups
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The aims of this project focused upon the development of an experimental test bed for modeling performance effectiveness and psychosocial adaptation in support of exploratory space flight missions beyond Earth's atmosphere. The physical, hardware, and software environment which serves as the experimental platform is referred to as the Planetary Exploration Simulation (PES), and provides an automated means for analyzing space crew performance as well as monitoring electronically the interactive effects of simulated communication modality constraints, mission management systems, and other stressful conditions. Within this context, the objectives of this project were to provide risk assessment and countermeasure evaluation of the following fundamental behavioral interaction operations that would most likely affect crew performance effectiveness and psychosocial adaptation: 1) the structure and function of communication channels within and between simulated space-dwelling and Earth-based groups; 2) factors associated with variations in the behavioral management systems between space-dwelling and Earth-based groups; 3) factors associated with variations in workloads, stressful time pressure, and conflict conditions; and 4) behavioral and psychosocial interaction systems between spaceflight crews and Earth-centered mission support operations that are most likely to influence individual and group performance during long-duration missions.

APPROACH:
Newly-initiated studies on management system variations consisted of developing methodologies for assessing crew performance effectiveness under rigid schedule-based management of crew activities by Mission Control versus more flexible, contingency-based, autonomous management of crew activities by themselves. Autonomous management consisted of having a crew arranging all aspects of their exploratory activities. Schedule-based management was simulated by Mission Control-defined performance requirements with regard to ordering and time spent in each geographic region and surface vehicle task assignments, and requiring that this schedule be strictly adhered to. Tests of this methodology have shown clear adverse effects of mission control-defined schedule limitations that resulted in both decrements in crew performance effectiveness and increases in negative psychosocial adaptation self-report measures.

RESULTS:
In a follow-up study to the first investigation of what is now known as "bounded autonomy," the psychosocial and performance effects of autonomous mission management were robust to communications constraints despite a physiological stress reaction to the unexpected loss of audio and text-messaging abilities. A subsequent experiment further supported the performance and psychosocial benefits of autonomy as assessed in longer-duration, 12-hour simulation missions conducted during different phases of the 24-hour circadian cycle (Early: 9am-9pm versus Late: 9pm-9am). As with previous work, crew performance was higher and physiological stress reactivity lower under autonomous conditions; however, overnight workloads produced significant decrements in individual performances that included reaction time deficits, attentional lapses, psychosocial communication reductions, and decreases in voluntary cooperation. Importantly, despite these decrements, crew performance efficiency remained normal. Lapses in individual performances thus appeared to be compensated for in the overall crew performance, indicating the utility of multi-person crews as a countermeasure to individual performance lapses under heavy workload and circadian disruption. Nevertheless, the dramatic decrease in psychosocial communication during late missions could be an early warning sign of crew fragmentation that could hinder cohesion and adaptability to malfunctions, environmental disruptions, or schedule demands.

The newly-developed Team Performance Task (TPT) has moved from initial software development into an early application phase as a simple, rapid, and objective measure of voluntary cooperative behavior as an assay of group cohesion. Extensive laboratory tests have established the basic parameters and novel behavioral economic analysis methods for TPT data, and preliminary TPT tests in intact work-groups show that the task is easily learned and remarkably sensitive to task duration, external incentives, and stable inter-crew differences. The results of this work are now being prepared for peer-reviewed publication. Additional larger-scale validation efforts are now ongoing both domestically and with ESA-supported international partners, and reveal the TPT's ability to objectively discriminate between 3-person groups composed of friends versus groups composed of strangers.

experiment_title: Lunar EVA Dosimetry: Microdosimeter-Dosimeter Instrument
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
To determine the risk from currently used radiation dosimeters requires knowledge of the species, energies, and frequencies of the radiation types or the frequency distributions as a function of linear energy transfer. The more frequently used passive dosimeters are also processed after the exposure and are not real-time instruments so the risk is inferred only after exposure. Microdosimeters are unique in that they can be used to directly determine the regulatory risk from radiation in real time when neither the species nor energies of the radiation are known. Thus it is a superior instrument for use in situations when the radiation environment is unknown and perhaps time varying.

Specific Aims:

  1. Develop a benchtop system to advance the state-of-the-art of solid-state microdosimeters (SSDM) incorporating proven advancements into the flight engineering model.
  2. Develop a flight engineering model suitable as a personal SSDM.
  3. evelop improved SSDM sensors.
  4. Utilize computer modeling to support instrument development and compare with observations.
  5. Explore opportunities to transition to a flight program.

APPROACH:
Benchtop System - Having established the feasibility of particle identification with the SSMDs investigators aimed to:
A. build a new prototype with smaller DE detectors with lower noise characteristics to reduce the number of random events.
B. obtain data with protons and iron to investigate contributions from low-energy delta rays, typically responsible for 20-30% of the physical dose not seen by typical TEPCs.
C. compare new sensor with the previous and with silicon sensors of the same thicknesses of a few microns but with larger cross-sectional areas.

Flight Engineering Model - Complete development of the flight engineering model, MIDN-III, and carry out radiation tests at the U.S. Naval Academy (USNA) and at NSRL. The remote command capability will be expanded. Further the optical calibration technique.

Sensor Development - Carry out detailed testing of 3rd generation SSMD sensors anticipating additional improved sensors from our collaborators.

Modeling - Add to the radiation transport codes by integrating the newly available GRAS (generally recognized as safe) module into the transport code suite.

Flight Opportunity - Continue to work with the DoD Space Test Program Office to obtain a future flight opportunity.

RESULTS:
Key Findings
1. Benchtop System - Obtained and analyzed SSMD spectra for NSRL beams (protons and heavy ions) to identify particle types, energies, and mass-to-charge ratios in the beams and produced by intervening materials. Reduced instrument noise levels near a factor of 10 during the NSBRI funding period. Best noise measurements at NSRL with 200 feet of cable is ~0.3keV/micron (~0.2 keV/micron-tissue). Compared SSMD spectra from the first generation sensors with silicon surface barrier detectors and also obtained spectra for neutrons, the most damaging particles.

2. Flight Engineering Model - The instrument developed in year 1 is MIDN-II. Investigators have designed an improved version, MIDN-III, reducing size and mass with an expanded set of remote commands that should be available by the end of 2010. MIDN-II tests showed good agreement with the benchtop system observations, radiation codes, and TEPC results used as references. Its noise cutoffs is approximately 1keV/micron. Continued development of this unique optical calibration system and applied for a patent in Sept 2010. This provides a continuous end-to-end test and confirms the calibration or recalibrates the SSMD while in operation accomplished without a problematic radiation source.

3. Sensor Development - Prior observations were with the first generation SSMD sensors. A second generation SSMD sensor was produced and tests confirmed performance using the benchtop and flight engineering instruments. A third generation sensor has been designed and fabricated, preliminary tests look promising with more testing to continue in year 3.

4. Modeling - Several versions of the Geant4 radiation code are employed to compare to the SSMD observations. Collaboration has produced detailed SSMD distributions for each particle type and energy, critical for interpreting observations, especially since individual components can be measured with the DE coincidence system. Investigators obtained acceptable agreement between their observations and radiation transport codes. They also employ the SolidWorks tool to develop test fixtures and housings and Electronic Workbench tool to model electrical circuits.

5. Flight Opportunity - Completed a conceptual design to fit a NanoRacks configuration for the ISS through the auspices of the DoD Space Test Program. The system has been approved annually for several years for inclusion on DoD space missions. The investigators declined a flight opportunity for a potential launch in 2012 due to insufficient funds and impact to the MIDN project.

experiment_title: Optimizing Light Spectrum for Long Duration Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this study is to determine the optimal wavelengths of light for use as a countermeasure to sleep and circadian disruption for astronauts. Sleep deficits are a risk factor during space missions. The resulting physiological and behavioral changes from sleep and circadian disruption can threaten the success of a mission by diminishing alertness, cognitive ability, and psychomotor performance. Currently, over 45 percent of all medications taken in space are sleep aids.

Ambient light is the primary stimulus for human circadian regulation. While on Earth, humans have a 24-hour day/night cycle to maintain healthy circadian entrainment. In space, astronauts must contend with either a rapidly changing or severely disrupted day/night cycle, and must work in a dimly lit spacecraft interior with few or no windows. Bright white light has already been implemented as a pre-launch countermeasure, but has yet to be used during space flight. Providing sufficient light intensities to work areas in the International Space Station (ISS), the planned Crew Exploration Vehicle (CEV), and future lunar habitats raises several concerns, among which are heat production, energy consumption, and upmass. Mitigating these factors requires a better understanding of how different wavelengths of light regulate the human circadian system. From this data it may be possible to optimize the light spectrum both as a countermeasure for sleep and circadian disturbances before or during space exploration. Listed below are the specific aims of this study. Given changes in NASA priorities and a budget cut to this project, the third specific aim was re-aligned mid-project.

1) Test the hypothesis that the white polychromatic fluorescent lamps currently used by NASA as a pre-launch countermeasure for circadian and sleep disruption will have increased efficacy for melatonin suppression when they are enriched in the blue portion of the spectrum.
2) Test the hypothesis that the white polychromatic fluorescent lamps currently used by NASA as a pre-launch countermeasure for circadian and sleep disruption have increased efficacy for circadian phase-shifting when they are enriched in the blue part of the spectrum. For this aim, investigators are comparing the magnitude of circadian phase-shifts in healthy subjects following exposure to equal photon densities of blue-enriched fluorescent lights versus the white lamps currently used by NASA. Each subject went through a seven day, 24 hour a day, inpatient trial with assessment of multiple biological and behavioral endpoints. A total of 21 subjects were entered into the protocol and of these, 20 completed the full study.
3) Test the hypothesis that three ambient extraterrestrial light environments (skylight during low earth orbit for ISS and the CEV, ambient light on the lunar surface, and ambient light on the surface of Mars) differ in their capacity to regulate melatonin. Since circadian and sleep regulation depends on an astronaut’s total exposure to both artificial and passive ambient illumination through windows or space suit visors, it is essential to determine the circadian effects of non-terrestrial light exposures.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study is embedded in the Objectives above and Results below.

RESULTS:
Aim 1: Test the hypothesis that the white fluorescent lamps currently used by NASA as a pre-launch countermeasure for circadian and sleep disruption will have increased efficacy for melatonin suppression when they are enriched in the blue portion of the spectrum. Philips Lighting B.V., an NSBRI industry partner, donated the prototype blue-enriched lamps and exposure systems used in this study. Since the start of the project, 25 human subjects have completed a total of 248 nighttime melatonin suppression trials. Three full fluence response curves have been completed. Ultimately, the results from healthy men and women will determine if white-appearing, blue enriched fluorescent light (17, 000 Kelvin) is significantly stronger for melatonin suppression than the white-appearing fluorescent light (4,000 Kelvin) currently used by NASA as a pre-launch countermeasure for astronauts.

Aim 2: Test the hypothesis that the white fluorescent lamps currently used by NASA have increased efficacy for circadian phase-shifting when they are enriched in the blue portion of the spectrum. For this aim, investigators were comparing the magnitude of circadian phase-shifts in healthy subjects following exposure to blue-enriched fluorescent lights versus equal photon densities of the white lamps currently used by NASA. Each subject went through a seven day, inpatient trial with assessment of multiple biological and behavioral endpoints. Over 300 subjects were screened, with 21 meeting all study requirements and enrolling in the study. As proposed, 20 healthy men and women completed the full study.

Aim 3: Test the hypothesis that ambient extraterrestrial light environments (low Earth orbit skylight, light on the lunar surface, and light on the surface of Mars) differ in their capacity to regulate melatonin. Since circadian and sleep regulation depends on an astronaut’s total exposure to both artificial light and passive ambient illumination through windows or space suit visors, it is essential to determine the circadian effects of non-terrestrial light exposures. To test this hypothesis, we collaborated with LPL optical engineers at the University of Arizona. Nine human subjects have completed over 80 nighttime melatonin suppression trials with simulated lunar light and nine other subjects have completed over 60 nighttime trials with simulated martian light.

experiment_title: New Automated System for Real-Time Bio-Imaging of a Vascular Cell Function in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It is critical to NASA's mission for human exploration and development of space to understand the influence of the space environment, specifically microgravity, on human physiology. Previous work has shown that microgravity can modify host cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, and thereby exert potentially deleterious effects on human vascular and immune functions and regeneration processes. For simulated microgravity, such as in a rotating wall vessel (RWV), adhesion assays as currently conducted have important limitations. First, to remove a cell sample from the RWV, rotation must be stopped, interrupting the simulated microgravity, not just for the sample, but for all cells in the chamber. Second, adhesion assays can take over an hour to perform when one considers cell preparation, transfer of cells from the microgravity chamber to the assay, and incubation periods. While these delays may be acceptable for general adhesion research, it is important to minimize elapsed time when studying gravitational effects, so that the cells won’t have time to recover from microgravity. In this project, investigators developed a novel human tissue bio-imaging technology applicable to microgravity research to overcome these shortcomings. Lessons learned from development of this Earth-based system can form the basis for a future space-flight culture and assay system to allow NASA to monitor microgravity-inducible physiological events during space flights.

The purpose of this project was to develop a novel human tissue bioimaging technology applicable to microgravity research. This system was to integrate automated bioreactor sampling and real-time bioimaging. This will enable researchers to monitor, for the first time, effects of simulated microgravity on an important vascular function--adhesion between white blood cells and the blood vessel wall, without interruption of the culture conditions and with essentially no delay between sample extraction and cell-function assay. Technology developed in this project ultimately has potential applications for monitoring astronaut immune system function on long-term space flights. Task Objective: To develop a new, automated system for real-time bio-imaging of effects of microgravity on cell-cell adhesion through completion of the following objectives:

1. Design and develop a system to automatically extract and deliver cell samples from a rotating wall vessel to an assay system at predetermined intervals.
2.Design and develop a small, integrated, real-time digital bio-imaging system to produce digital images of cell samples.
3.Integrate into the bio-imaging system an assay of vascular cell function that utilizes the unique Amgel matrix system and sensitive real-time computer tracking of adhesive cell interactions.
The system developed for this purpose can be adapted to assay other effects of simulated microgravity on cultured cells. It can also be useful as a compact, portable flow-cell based adhesion assay to measure adhesion of leukocytes or other cells under shear-stress conditions similar to those found in the blood stream.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Objective 1: Development of the cell extraction and delivery system
Even though extraction of fluid from a rotating RWV was a relatively straightforward engineering project, extraction of the cells from a rotating system is not trivial. Beyond the technical issue of a leak-free rotating interface between the chamber and external tubing, there is the issue that cells are often not uniformly distributed within the chamber. Although various models have been proposed to describe the location of cells in such a system, models do not always agree. Investigators determined the best sample points empirically. Their current system reliably delivers cells at a uniform concentration from two separate locations (after an initial mixing period of approx. 10 minutes.) without interrupting rotation.

In the first year, feasibility was confirmed with a largely manual system of valves and a syringe pump system that used a command line interface for each action of the pump. However, entering of individual commands made experimentation cumbersome and time consuming. The control process was improved by transitioning to a graphical control program where embedded script files are created and programmed into the syringe pump. These pre-programmed script files are executed directly from the laptop graphical control program. This software configuration for control of the syringe pump streamlines the control process and also increases the reliability of the commands. In addition, a system of several manual valves in various locations has been replaced by one central multivalve that controls the entire system. These advances represent major improvements in efficient extraction of cells, optimization of valves and control points, miniaturization, and automation of the system.

Objective 2: Development of the real-time bio-imaging system
One of the problems with previous adhesion assay systems for cells undergoing shear stress is that a research microscope is required for imaging of the process. This necessarily requires relatively long tubing between the RWV and the assay chamber, which increases the time between rotation and assay. The research microscope also costs more than all of the other components of the system the system combined. Therefore, a completely new, low cost, custom-designed optical system was developed to reliably image cell adhesion under flow conditions in our adhesion assay system. The mini-microscope was tested extensively in real experiments, and has provided video image data of sufficient quality for the high-speed motion analysis necessary for flow-chamber cell adhesion data. In addition, the investigators have converted from a tape-storage system to direct digitization, streamlining data analysis and improving fidelity of motion tracking.

Objective 3: Integration of the bio-imaging system and the cell adhesion assay
In preparation for biological experiments, a new flow chamber was developed, with an improved sealing mechanism, to provide a more portable and robust flow chamber. Although beyond the scope of the current project, these modifications are an important step in development of a space flight system. In order to accommodate budget cuts and shortened time frame, however, it was necessary to focus on developing a basic flow-chamber-based adhesion assay, setting aside the work on the Amgel matrix system and the real-time computer tracking. This has resulted in a complete system for assay of the microgravity effect on leukocyte adhesion that, although lacking the real-time computer analysis system originally planned, will permit state-of-the-art analysis as good as current systems in use for conventional adhesion studies.

experiment_title: Influence of Sensory Integration on the Neural Processing of Gravito-Inertial Cues
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Our sense of spatial orientation results from a complex set of neural processes of sensory integration; these processes utilize information from many different physiological systems. Evidence suggests that extended exposure to microgravity yields adaptive changes in these neural processes. For the most part, these adaptive changes appear functionally relevant for space flight but yield significant transient problems when astronauts return to gravitational environments (Earth, Mars, Moon, etc.). In-flight countermeasures that reinforce the normal sensory interactions encountered in a gravitational environment (e.g., rotations about any axis not aligned with gravity are accompanied by changes in the relative orientation of gravity) will almost certainly help astronauts function adequately when they transition to a gravitational environment. This will be important to pilot astronauts landing spacecraft as well as to crewmembers trying to rapidly exit a spacecraft. Furthermore, artificial gravity has been proposed as a countermeasure for numerous problems associated with space flight (including cardiovascular deconditioning, bone decalcification, etc.). One undesired side effect of artificial gravity will be additional alterations in these processes of sensory integration. For all of these reasons, it is essential that we understand the predominant sensory interactions that are altered by exposure to microgravity. Specifically, investigators proposed to investigate how rotational signals from the semicircular canals influence how humans process the ambiguous gravito-inertial force measured by the otolith 0rgans. Investigators performed a series of ground experiments that sought a better understanding of sensory interactions between the semicircular canals and graviceptors. They proposed to perform these investigations using several different measurement techniques including measures of reflexive eye responses as well as psychophysical measures of human perception.

This project was originally a flight experiment that was scaled back to be a ground study shortly after the space shuttle accident. After this change in plans, our project goals were altered. Our new goal was to use psychophysics and eye movement measurements to investigate how humans utilize semicircular canal cues to help estimate the relative orientation of gravity here on Earth. Investigators proposed a ground study to measure human responses (perceptual and eye movement) during combined canal-otolith stimulation on Earth. Their goal was to develop new tests that will allow them to investigate how canalotolith interactions adapt to micro-gravity exposure.

APPROACH:
Subjects were tested using protocols in which the subjects a) tilted, b) translated, or c) tilted and translated simultaneously. Investigators expected the human responses to be consistent with those previously measured in monkeys, with canal cues essential for accurate estimation of gravity and linear acceleration.

RESULTS:
1. Investigators developed a new hypothesis designed to explain space flight adaptation, the disorientation experienced in microgravity, and the motion sickness that sometimes occurs.
2. The team successfully developed a new testing paradigm that allowed them to investigate human tilt and translation responses. The new testing paradigm is ready to be used as part of a preflight/postflight investigation to study how astronauts adapt to the micro-gravity environment.
3. The team successfully completed an extensive set of human studies in which they found that the mechanism used to evoke human translational VOR responses is different than the mechanism used to evoke monkey translational VOR responses.
4. These same studies showed that human perception and human action (i.e., the VOR) employ qualitatively different neural mechanisms, which emphasizes the importance of studying perception to complement our existing extensive understanding of the VOR.

experiment_title: Cellular Homeostasis in Microgravity: Energy and Structure
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Analysis of previously reported biochemical parameters of spaceflight have shown that an animal's metabolic status is greatly affected when it undergoes a transition from 0 to 1 g. The importance of this study was the opportunity to examine biosamples isolated and fixed in space. This allows a better understanding of metabolic balance in microgravity and its qualitative and quantitative changes upon return to the Earth's gravitational field. For this purpose, enzyme activities were measured in plasma as well as subcellular fractions, isolated by differential centrifugation of liver homogenates.

APPROACH:
Samples were taken from three groups of rats decapitated on flight day 13, on landing day (four hours after landing), or 14 days after landing. The liver was removed and a mitochondrial supernatant was prepared and analyzed using commercial Boehringer Mannheim test kits. Blood samples were taken and studies were performed on isolated erythrocytes. Metabolic parameters were measured using a spectrophotometer. The results were calculated per one gram hemoglobin, measured by means of the cyan methemoglobin procedure. Membrane lipids and phospholipids were determined by thin-layer chromatography. Mitochondrial enzymes were evaluated by quantitative cytochemistry.

RESULTS:
Glucose and ICDH levels were decreased while glycolysis and ATP synthesis were increased in flight rats. Immediately after recovery, hypoglycemia was replaced with hyperglycemia. Some enzymes (AST, LDH, CPK) returned to preflight levels, while alkaline phosphatase decreased and acid phosphatase increased. Nitrogen metabolism changes occurred during flight and persisted immediately after flight, leading to a higher level of creatine in the blood and lower activity in the Krebs cycle. Study of activity of hepatic subcellular fractions gave evidence that the recovery of metabolic balance in blood challenges biochemical processes in the liver: at R+14 aminotransferases in the cytoplasm were in the hypercompensation state. Changes in basic metabolic parameters in erythrocytes and lymphocytes were evidently produced by changes in the structure and function of their membranes. This was shown by the lipid and phospholipid composition of membranes.

experiment_title: Noninvasive Biosensor Algorithms for Continuous Metabolic Rate Determination--SMS01302
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA is designing new spacesuits to meet the needs of future space exploration. Real-time measurement of metabolic rate during astronaut activity is a key function of the biosensor suite which is planned for the new spacesuit. This project developed novel near infrared spectroscopic (NIRS) algorithms and sensors for real-time assessment of metabolic rate (measured as the rate of oxygen consumption, VO2). This capability was intended to be incorporated into a smart system advising astronauts on their use of consumables during Extravehicular Activity (EVA). The specific aims of this project include the development of algorithms to calculate VO2 from NIRS spectra and validation of the algorithms during exercise in ground-based protocols which simulate plasma volume reduction during spaceflight. An additional aim of this project is to support the EVA suit testing program by developing small, lightweight, and robust sensors which can be used within the spacesuit to evaluate metabolic cost of the suit itself, on individual muscles.

APPROACH:
Data collection in the first year of this study was shown to provide an early indication of patients who had significant plasma leakage and were at risk for shock. The company formed to commercialize the sensor, Reflectance Medical, has received substantial funding from the US Army Medical Research and Materiel Command. The company received clearance from the FDA to sell the CareGuide Oximeter 1100, a hospital-based system to noninvasively and continuously determine SmO2. The company has submitted its second 510(k) application for the mobile CareGuide 2100 Oximeter, which is a battery powered SmO2 sensor that displays results on an Android tablet or the Sotera ViSi mobile wrist worn vital sign monitor. The CareGuide 3100 development is complete. The 3100 updates the CareGuide 2100 software to calculate pHm and hematocrit (Hct) from the same spectra.

RESULTS:
Investigators completed the development of an algorithm for calculating VO2 during cycling using data from the Near Infrared Spectroscopic Sensor to determine muscle oxygen saturation (SmO2) and heart rate. This algorithm was demonstrated to be accurate for 11 subjects who completed a cycling protocol in both a normovolemic and hypovolemic state. Reflectance Medical, with synergistic funding from the US Army Medical Research and Materiel Command, completed the development of a wearable, lightweight solid state NIRS sensor which is small and lightweight enough to be worn under the spacesuit. The system has been shown to reliably determine SmO2, pH, and blood hematocrit for both light and dark skin individuals with a range of fat thicknesses over the muscle. Reflectance Medical has received clearance from the FDA to market the SmO2 sensor, and will soon submit an application to add pH and hematocrit capability to the sensor. This sensor is slated to be included in a newly approved NASA flight study to examine the effects of fluid shifts in space.

experiment_title: Does Spaceflight Alter the Virulence of a Natural Parasite of Drosophila?
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The seminal discovery of Toll and Toll-NF-#B signaling as a central mediator of innate immune responses in the model insect Drosophila catalyzed similar discoveries in other organisms including innate immunity in humans. These findings led to an appreciation of the fundamental roles of innate immunity in human immune deficiency on the one hand, and immune health of insects on the other. In Drosophila larvae, primed, but quiescent hematopoietic progenitors are called into action from an organ with functional similarities to mammalian bone marrow. Blood cells signal the fat body (equivalent to the mammalian liver) to activate the expression of antimicrobial peptide genes (humoral immunity). Antimicrobial peptides efficiently combat deadly bacteria and fungi. The Leptopilina wasps are natural metazoan enemies of Drosophila and their attack kills fruit flies. Wasp attack (e.g., L. boulardi) activates both the humoral and cellular immune arms of larval hosts, each being dependent on Toll-NF-#B signaling. Previous NASA-funded studies of Drosophila have shown that stresses in the space environment compromise hematopoietic development and modulate larval and adult innate immunity. We hypothesize that stimuli from the space environment will also alter the virulence of the parasitic wasps, and therefore their success on the fly hosts cultured in space.

APPROACH:
In Drosophila-wasp co-culture experiments using the NASA Fruit Fly Lab hardware over 30-days, we propose to (1) examine whether the fly or the wasp partner wins the arms race in space; (2) examine the effects of spaceflight on the anti-parasite response in fruit fly hosts; and (3) examine if virulence of “space-cultured” wasps is different from counterparts grown on Earth. While both L. boulardi and L. heterotoma parasites always succeed on the wild type, only the latter wasp species produces unique cell-killing activities residing in its virus-like particles. It also suppresses humoral immunity completely. We will examine if changes in the expression of VLP genes underlies changes in parasite virulence affected by spaceflight. Host defense and virulence will be inferred from a suite of other well-established assays of fly/host survival and measures of immune response.

RESULTS:
Experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) after Exposure to Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In microgravity, bones and muscles are not used as they are on Earth. As many studies have shown, this altered use results in calcium loss, degeneration of the skeleton, lengthening of the spine by expansion of the intervertebral discs, change in spinal bone marrow composition and muscle atrophy. Bedrest patients on earth show this same musculo-skeletal response with the exception of bone marrow alterations.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is one method that can be used to measure the resulting muscular and skeletal changes. MRI is a safe, non-invasive scanning technique that uses a large magnet and low frequency radio waves to form an image by reading the amount of hydrogen in an area of the body. These images can be used to examine soft tissues in the body, as well as determine muscle volume, spinal bone marrow mass and cross-sectional area of intervertebral discs.

The objectives of this investigation were to use MRI procedures (1) to measure the muscle volumes of the calf, thigh, back and neck of the Mir astronauts and cosmonauts before and after flight; (2) to determine and compare muscle volume changes on the day of landing and four days after landing; (3) to determine the change in intervertebral disc size in the lumbar spine after flight, and determine the rate of recovery after return to gravity; and (4) to determine the bone marrow cellularity of the third lumbar vertebra (L3) before and after flight.

Findings from this investigation will lead to improved therapies that will facilitate the recovery of patients on Earth who have been bedridden for extended periods and will aid in the development of countermeasures allowing longer duration space flights.

APPROACH:
All crewmembers of the NASA 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 missions, as well as the Mir 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25 missions participated as subjects in this study. MRI scans were performed 30 and 60 days before launch, on the day of landing (U.S. crewmembers only), and 4, 14 and 30 days after landing on all crewmembers.

Imaging was performed using a 1.5 Tesla Siemens Magnetom MRI system (1.5 Tesla denotes the strength of the magnet used for the test) with various coils, including spine, Helmholz neck and whole body coils. These coils are the antenna of the MRI system that broadcast the radio frequency signal to the patient and/or receive the return signal to form an image. Specific coils are used to image different parts of the body; for example, Helmholz coils are used to image the cervical spine and muscles in the neck.

To begin the test, crewmembers were to lie down on a padded table, which would enter the magnet. Crewmembers were recumbent for approximately 10-15 minutes before beginning the test to minimize the effects of fluid shifts caused by lying down after standing. The order in which the measurements were made was kept the same for each crewmember from one imaging session to the next. The normal order was L3 spectroscopy, and then imaging of the intervertebral discs, then differential muscle volume measurements of the back muscles, neck muscles, thigh muscles and calf muscles.

A number of variables are used to acquire MRI images, including echo time, echo sequence, repetition time and matrix size. The echo time is the amount of time between magnetic pulses. Echo sequences are the number of magnetic pulses used to create an image. The repetition time is the amount of time between repetitions of the echo sequence, and the matrix size determines the resolution quality, or clearness, of the image.

Muscle volume of calf, thigh, lower back and neck:
For imaging of the calf and thigh muscles, the feet of the subject were positioned in a holder during the test to minimize movement and insure repositioning. The portion of the leg being imaged was suspended, while the non-imaged portion was supported with foam supports. A radio frequency (RF) shield was positioned caudally to the imaged portion of the leg to remove artifacts in the image, which arise from parts of the body outside the imaging region but near the edge of the gradient coils.

For the thigh and calf muscles of NASA 2, 3, 4 and 7 and Mir 21, 22, and 23 crewmembers, 32, 1 centimeter slices (0.8 centimeter slices for NASA 5, NASA 6, Mir 24, and Mir 25) with a 0.2 millimeter gap between slices were obtained using an echo time equal to 10 milliseconds (msec), a repetition time of 800 msec and a 256 x 512 matrix.

Every tissue in the human body has its own spin-spin relaxation time (T2) value. Therefore, it can be used to differentiate between different tissue types (e.g. fat and muscle) and changes due to tissue changes (e.g. edema in sore muscles). Calf muscle spin-spin relaxation time (T2) was measured by rescanning the calf region using the same receiver gain at an echo time of 50 msec. Spin-spin relaxation times for each muscle pixel were calculated by comparing the image intensity between the echo times of 10 msec and 50 msec. T2 for a particular muscle was obtained by averaging the T2 for all pixels within that muscle.

For the back muscles, 20, 0.5 centimeter slices centered on the third lumbar vertebra were obtained using a spine coil and a 10 msec echo time, an 800 msec repetition time and a 256 x 512 matrix. For the neck muscles, a similar protocol was used with 32, 3 millimeter thick slices, and a Helmholtz neck coil in place of the spine coil.

Lumbar spine disc size and lumbar spine length:
To measure lumbar spine intervertebral disc size and lumbar spine length, subjects were positioned within the MRI machine so that the imaging area was centered within the third lumbar vertebra, determined from a sagittal scout view. A coronal scout image was used to position a 1 centimeter slice of interest down the center of the spinal column.

Imaging sequences of the lumbar spine varied between missions. During NASA 2 and 3 and Mir 21 and 22, two acquisitions of a four echo, spin echo sequence were obtained using echo times of 20, 45, 72 and 106 msec and a repetition time of 1 second.

For NASA 4, 5, 6 and 7 and Mir 23, 24 and 25, two different sequences were performed. First, one gradient echo sequence was obtained with an echo time of 7 msec and a repetition time of 400 msec. Second, two single echo, spin echo sequences were obtained using echo times of 10 and 25 msec and a repetition time of 400 msec. The matrix size for spinal images of all NASA-Mir crewmembers was 256 x 256.

Disc area was obtained for intervertebral discs in the lower back (T12-L1, L1-2, L2-3, L3-4 and L4-5) from the number of pixels in each image. A phantom was also imaged during each imaging session to correct for any changes in pixel size.

To measure spine length, templates (small sub-images) were taken from the first preflight images, each containing a spinal disc. Each of these was registered (a mathematical best fit of position) for each subsequent measurement. The change in separation from the preflight positions to postflight positions was the change in spine length.

Bone marrow content (L3 spectroscopy):
To measure the fat to water ratio in vertebral bone marrow, volume selective proton spectroscopy was performed on a 15mm x 15mm cubic volume of interest in the third lumbar vertebra (L3) using a surface receive coil. Spectroscopy uses absorption, emission or scattering of electromagnetic radiation by atoms or molecules to qualitatively or quantitatively study the atoms or molecules. The Gradient Inversion Spectroscopy (GIS) technique was used to acquire spectra at echo times equal to 12, 18, 24 and 30 msec with a repetition time of 2 sec. Images were corrected for T2 weighting by exponential extrapolation of the spectra obtained at various echo times. Non-linear peak fitting was performed on the final spectrum to separate the water peak and different fat peaks from the background and to calculate their relative intensities. Bone marrow cellularity was determined from the fat to water ratio. T2 of the fat and water component was determined by fitting the decay of fat and water peaks with an exponential function.

Back pain questionnaire:
The crew also filled out questionnaires to document the frequency, severity and location of back pain or discomfort during the first 10 days of flight and the first 10 days after flight.

RESULTS:
Muscle volume:
The muscle volume changes as a percentage of the mean baseline volume in 16 crewmembers after long-duration flight were determined. To calculate percent change from baseline, the first postflight measurement at 0 to 4 days after landing was used. These flights ranged from 115 to197 days in duration. Paired t-tests of the average preflight volume to the first postflight measurement showed significant decreases for all regions except the neck muscles. The values, expressed as a percent of baseline (%±SD), for the 16 subjects were: anterior leg, 85.5±2.9%; gastrocnemius, 83.1±4.4%; soleus, 83.2±4.4%; quadriceps, 89.9±4.4%; hamstrings, 87.3±3.4%; intrinsic back, 84.1±5.8%; psoas, 95.6±6.1%; neck, 100.9±8.3%. A linear regression of the percent loss against flight duration showed no significant slope for any of the regions suggesting that the volume changes reached a new steady state by or before about four months of flight.

After landing, each of the flight crew were measured at multiple time points. Results indicate that muscle volume recovers at variable rates depending on the region, but generally have returned to baseline by 30-60 days postflight.

A comparison of percent change in muscle volume versus the size of the muscle before flight showed poor or no correlation for any of the muscle groups except the hamstrings, r=0.71. This was also true for when change in muscle volume was correlated with total weight or total body lean mass. This indicates that the suggestion that the percentage loss might be greater in those individuals with greatest mass before flight is not supported by the results in this study.

There was no significant correlation between the percentage loss in spinal bone mineral content and intrinsic back muscle volume during flight (n=12). However, when 12 bed rest subjects, half who performed an exercise countermeasure and the remaining who served as controls, were added to the flight data, the correlation was significant (r=0.61, p<0.0009). This may indicate that muscle atrophy might provide an early indicator for the extent of bone loss.

Comparison of flight results with bed rest data shows that the changes in the leg muscles during flight were generally less than bed rest. This is likely a consequence of the exercise countermeasure employed during flight since the bed rest data did not include exercise. The back muscles, however, showed greater loss during flight compared to bed rest, which may be reasonable, considering that the back muscles are active to a substantial degree in bed rest.

Muscle T2:
No muscle T2 measurements were possible on landing day. Therefore, the initial postflight measurements were obtained several days after landing which would obviously include significant ambulation prior to the first T2 measurement. The general pattern, however, is that T2 tends to be increased relative to baseline at the first postflight measurement and was almost always elevated at R+14 compared to the initial postflight measurement or baseline. By 30-70 days postflight the T2 decreased toward baseline in all cases where these measurements were available. The general response pattern is consistent with postflight muscle swelling associated with muscle damage.

Muscle Swelling:
Results show that muscle swelling can occur during the early reambulation period after landing. A similar pattern is seen following reambulation after bed rest. The largest changes were in the calf, particularly the gastrocnemius. The explanation for this swelling could represent rehydration of the muscle following dehydration of the muscle in microgravity. However, the muscle T2 postflight were invariably elevated above baseline, increased further for several weeks after flight and then returned toward the original baseline. These changes along with the reported sore muscles postflight would suggest muscle damage. The large change in the intrinsic back muscles of one crewmember has not been seen previously and may represent postflight swelling.

Intervertebral Disc:
Data indicate only minor spine lengthening and disc expansion by the time measurements were obtained on landing day. Measurements were made within 2-4 hours after landing with some walking and sitting up on a stretcher by the crewmember before testing. By 2-4 days postflight, slight residual expansion remained which by 2 weeks was back to baseline. Importantly, no long-term residual changes in disc size were found following these flights.

Proton Spectroscopy:
Comparison of NASA-Mir data to the LMS 17-day mission suggests that although the postflight T2 tends to increase as in the shorter LMS flight followed by a gradual return to baseline levels, there appears to be some differences. The first postflight T2 values were significantly reduced relative to preflight values; this was not detected after the shorter LMS flight. There is some evidence that the degree of decrease in the cellular bone marrow T2 is correlated with the percent change in spinal bone mineral density. Two distinct patterns exist. Postflight, some individuals begin below baseline and simply return to values close to baseline, while others like the LMS crew increase above baseline and gradually return to baseline over a period of several months.

Back Pain:
Out of 17 crewmembers (including one German guest cosmonaut on the Mir 97 mission), 9 (53%) indicated that they experienced back pain or discomfort during the flight. Generally, this occurred in the lower lumbar region during the first week or two of flight. The pain was typically described as "can be ignored," lasted a few hours to several days in duration and was most noticeable during or after resting. In one crewmember, it was most noticeable during exercise or applying bungies. Some crewmembers indicated that bending or application of massage seemed to relieve the pain. Postflight 8 of 17 (47%) crewmembers reported significant discomfort for some or all 10 days that monitoring was reported following flight. There were a number of cases where written reports were not available or were not filled out. Whenever possible, the crew were asked about their experience during and after flight. When no information was available these were treated as being negative reports and therefore, the incidence rates above may underestimate actual rates.

Conclusion:
There are measurable decreases in muscle volume during flight, which presumably represents muscle atrophy. These changes appear to be maximized within the first 4 months of flight. This degree of atrophy may indicate that bone loss may also reach a maximum probably at or around this same point, i.e., the rates of loss are different, but it seems reasonable that the degree of loss may be similar at the equilibrium point. If this turns out to be the case, muscle atrophy might be used as an early indicator of bone loss. Compared to bed rest without exercise, the inflight muscle changes are less, except in the back muscles. Recovery in all muscle groups is complete within the first 30-60 days after return to Earth, similar to recovery after bed rest. There are muscle volume and T2 changes during the first days and weeks after return from space flight compatible with muscle damage. We did observe small, but no long-term changes in disc size following these flights. There was a significant decrease in the T2 of the cellular component of the bone marrow of L3 which either increases to baseline during the first few weeks after landing or increases above baseline and subsequently returns to baseline over several months. No significant changes in the T2 of the lipid fraction of the same bone marrow or in the cellular to lipid fraction was seen. About 50% of the crewmembers reported some back pain during flight, however, the duration and magnitude of this problem seems not to be of major concern for long-duration flight. A more important consideration may be the potential for significant injury/pain after flight since about 47% reported significant postflight discomfort lasting for a number of days to weeks. This may be an important consideration after lengthy flights in microgravity followed by a visit to a planet that has significant gravity.

experiment_title: The Role of Microgravity and Stress-related Humoral Factors in Dysregulated NK-cell Function during Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Before astronauts can be sent ethically to distant locations in space, such as Mars or asteroids, it is critical that it is understand how space flight affects the human immune system. For years, postflight data has suggested that space flight has a negative impact on the immune system. Unfortunately, the majority of this data was obtained following short-duration missions after the astronauts had returned to Earth, meaning that no in-flight data was collected. The recent ‘Integrated Immune’ study filled many of these knowledge gaps by analyzing blood obtained from astronauts on the Space Shuttle or the International Space Station (ISS) while they were still in space. Of particular interest were the findings that anti-viral immune responses were compromised during space flight. Consequently, latent viral reactivation can result in many negative consequences including shingles, reduced vaccine efficacy, and increased susceptibility to infection. While the ‘Integrated Immune’ study focused primarily on the adaptive immune system, the ‘Salivary Markers’ flight experiment has focused on the innate immune system.

The current proposal focuses on Natural Killer (NK)-cells, which are able to kill virally-infected and malignant cells without prior exposure. This experiment team's in-flight data shows that NK-cell anti-tumor activity is greatly reduced during space flight, while cytomegalovirus driven responses are amplified. This current proposal will explore two plausible mechanisms for these observations-microgravity and stress. It is hypothesized that treatment with simulated microgravity and space flight derived serum will mimic the deleterious effects of space flight on NK-cells. Once the mechanisms underpinning the adverse effects of space flight on NK-cells are determined, countermeasures can be developed that will protect future space explorers from becoming immunocompromised during long-duration missions.

APPROACH:
The effects of microgravity can be simulated with a rotating wall vessel that keeps the cells in a constant state of free fall, while stress can be simulated using serum (with natural stress hormones) from astronauts on the ISS.

experiment_title: Integrated Radiation Analysis and Design Tools
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Integrated Radiation Analysis and Design Tools (IRADT) Project develops and maintains an integrated tool set that collects the current best practices, databases, and state-of-the-art methodologies to evaluate and optimize human systems such as spacecraft, spacesuits, rovers, and habitats. IRADT integrates design models and methodologies in support of evaluation/verification of design limits and design solutions to meet As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA) requirements (NASA STD 3001, Vol 2). IRADT provides the radiation community access to physics and transport capabilities and research improvements. The capabilities are developed under strict version control and are independently verified and validated to the extent possible. Current customers include NASA Exploration Systems Mission Directorate's (ESMD) Directorate Integration Office studies (i.e. LAT, MAT, LSOS), Lunar Surface Systems as well as Constellation's Orion and Vehicle Integration Office, universities, industry, and Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR). IRADT is designed for utilization by future commercial customers concerned about transfer of proprietary data and results.

APPROACH:
IRADT specifically addressed the limitations associated with simplified geometry description (equivalent aluminum, three-layer transport interpolation, random orientation) and straight ahead transport. The design tools increases fidelity by incorporating common spacecraft and user specified materials in the geometry description with ray-by-ray transport to minimize the uncertainties due to range-scaling of material thicknesses and material ordering. Ray-by ray transport also establishes the basis to calculate the forward/backward neutron generation within vehicle/lunar surface geometries. The back-scattered neutron environment was calculated from the opposite sides of the vehicle for a crewmember’s specific orientation at specific tissue locations. This increases the ability to evaluate the effectiveness of shielding systems. In supporting the closure of these gaps, the Design Tool Project tools and models supported specification, implementation, verification, and monitoring of Spaceflight Human Systems Standard, Vol. 2 (NASA STD 3001, Vol. 2) radiation design and operational requirements with improved uncertainty quantification.

RESULTS:
The model can be defined one of three ways, by selecting an historic solar minimum/maximum, by entering specific dates, or by entering a fitting parameter. A comprehensive comparison of the various GCR models shown that the Matthia model was on par with the Badhwar-O'Neill 2010 model in terms of uncertainty for space radiation calculations. The Badhwar-O'Neill 2010 and 2004 models are also still available. The linear energy transfer (LET) response has been activated for all geometry and project types. It was previously only available for interpolation-based, thickness distribution jobs for free-space environments. Both the integral and differential flux/fluence versus LET is computed and the target material can be specified as either tissue or silicon.

A new atmosphere model has been added for Mars surface environments. The Mars Climate Database (MCD, http://www-mars.lmd.jussieu.fr/ ) is a database of atmospheric statistics compiled from state-of-the-art simulations of the Martian atmosphere. It is a much more refined model than MarsGRAM and takes into account the surface location (latitude and longitude), the Martian seasons (Solar longitude) and the time of day (Local solar time).

OLTARIS ( https://oltaris.nasa.gov/ ) currently has 223 active accounts. Eighty one accounts are government (including NASA, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Air Force Research Laboratory, and Federal Aviation Administration), eighty six are university professors/researchers/students, and fifty six are industry (including Boeing, Space X, Lockheed-Martin, Alliant Techsystems Inc., Northrup Grumman, and Bigelow Aerospace). There have been nearly 4000 jobs run through OLTARIS during the last reporting period and 14,500 since counting began in November 2009.

No datasets are available for this study. A final report was archived.
