experiment_title: Autonomous Behavioral Health Countermeasures for Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this study is to enhance the NSBRI-developed suite of behavioral health countermeasures tailored for astronauts (the Virtual Space Station or VSS), by evaluating them in an Antarctic space analog setting, improving the conflict management content, incorporating an integrated behavioral health assessment, and developing an immersive virtual reality component. This study brings together a team with experience in: (a) computer-based psychological training and treatment programs, (b) evaluation and assessment of depression treatments, (c) conflict management training, (d) digital communication, and (d) space psychology. Members of the investigator team have been involved for over 10 years in the development of a suite of space-relevant behavioral health countermeasures (the VSS). The VSS programs include conflict management training, a depression treatment, and stress management modules.

The aims of the proposed project are to: 1) Customize the Virtual Space Station program for use by astronauts by evaluating the program in an isolated environment (i.e., Antarctica) and collecting detailed information on program use, including user choices, ease of navigation, usability, and acceptability. 2) Modify the existing VSS program to add enhanced conflict resolution content and an integrated behavioral health assessment. 3) Enhance the VSS program to include a mood enhancement system that allows users to experience immersive relaxing situations using virtual reality.

Components of the VSS have been validated in different settings. The conflict content has been tested for usability and acceptability with astronauts, the depression content has been evaluated in an efficacy trial in depressed individuals, and the stress program has been tested in a randomized trial with business and law students. To fully customize the VSS for astronaut use, the program needs additional conflict management content, enhanced content for maintaining psychosocial well-being (immersive virtual reality (VR)) and testing in a space-analog environment (Antarctica). This project directly addresses the goal outlined in the research announcement to “Modify and customize for astronaut use a clinically validated suite of products that will determine the need for, and autonomously administer, behavioral health countermeasures. In particular these modules should facilitate conflict resolution and promote psychosocial well-being.”

The project impact would be reducing the risk of mission failure due to psychological and interpersonal problems. The use of VR also has the potential to strengthen the conflict content, and to expand the stress management offerings. Currently, the conflict management conflict includes a simulated interaction with another crewmember. Interactions like these could be more immersive, and potentially more effective, by using VR. Additionally, VR offers the ability to provide immersive, natural environments that could be useful for relaxation, stress reduction, and attention restoration.

experiment_title: The Effect of Microgravity on the Morphology and Function of the Nervous System, Skeleton and Endocrine Organs of the Gecko
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

To perform histological examinations of the central nervous system, peripheral organs of senses (visual, auditory, vestibular, olfactory and vomero-nasal systems), musculo-skeletal system (bones, tendons, ligaments), endocrine and reproductive systems of geckos in order to detect cell growth and morphological tissue changes.

APPROACH:

The gecko Pachydactylus turneri was used as a spaceflight model organsim due to its robustness in adapting to long periods of fasting and xeric conditions with limited water and its ability to adhere to wall surfaces in spacefight habitat.The animals are poikilothermic, have tissue regenerative ability and are adapted to moderate periods of fasting and can survive prolonged periods without water. One male and four females were housed in each Gecko housing unit. One unit with 5 animals was flown. A second unit with 5 animals was used as a basal control and a third unit with 5 geckos served as a 48 hour delayed control. Approximately 30 hours after the 16 day flight, without food or water, the geckos were recovered, examined and euthanized for histological and other analyses.

RESULTS:

The Geckos showed no apparent negative health effects. Detailed analysis of bone mass and architecture showed that both synchronous controls and spaceflight animals lost significant amounts of cancellous bone in the distal femur and humerus. In addition cell cycle analysis of 30h post-flight liver tissue revealed a shift of DNA content from G2 and S to G1, both in spaceflight and synchronous controls. These results suggest that housing conditions alone induce rapid catabolism of cancellous bone and reduced normal tissue regeneration. (See results for Geckos on Foton-M3).

experiment_title: The Effects of Spaceflight on Some Liver Enzymes Concerned with Carbohydrate and Lipid Metabolism in the Rat
experiment_description:
Objectives:

During early manned space flights, a specific physiological enigma concerning caloric requirements was noted. While theoretically in the absence of gravitational force less energy should be required for life-sustaining functions, on the initial flights where caloric intake was restricted, a marked inflight loss in body weight resulted. It is important to study a key organ like the liver in order to determine whether any regulative enzymes of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism might have been affected; that is, whether the capabilities of the organ to produce these cellular constituents is, in fact, altered in space flight.

Approach:

In the rat liver, the activities of about thirty enzymes concerned with carbohydrate and lipid metabolism were examined according to well-established methods or modifications of currently used techniques. In addition, the levels of glycogen and of the individual fatty acids in hepatic lipids were determined. The livers from rats subjected to near weightlessness space flight and rats subjected to a 1 g force via an onboard centrifuge were compared to appropriate ground-based controls. Several key enzymes of lipid biosynthesis, many of which are known to be regulative, were studied in this experiment, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase, fatty acid synthetase, palmitoyl-CoA synthetase, and stearoyl-CoA desaturase.

Results:

In rats sacrificed at recovery, statistically significant decreases in the activity levels of a-glycerol-phosphate acyltransferase, diglyceride acyltransferase, aconitase, and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase were noted in the flight-weightless group versus flight-centrifuged animals. The flight-weightless group also contained, on average, more than twice the amount of glycogen than did flight- centrifuged livers, and a remarkable shift in the ratio of palmitate to palmitoleate was noted. As a possible explanation, it was observed that although glycogen synthetase activity was about the same in all groups, its glycogen phosphorylase activity was significantly less. The observed alterations, particularly those that involved increased glycogen levels and decreased activities of the acyl transferases concerned with lipid synthesis, appear unique to the weightless condition. Most of the enzyme activities, though, did not show any significant differences between weightless and centrifuged rats, and all parameters had returned to normal by 25 days postflight.

experiment_title: Molecular Biology of Plant Development in the Space Flight Environment (CARA)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
The space flight environment addresses key gravity-related biological issues using a simple, robust operational approach that has been successfully demonstrated with previous Space Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS) flights. Plants experiencing space flight mount an adaptive response that can be measured in terms of patterns of gene expression and morphological (shape) changes in growth and development. During previous space flight experiments a remarkable number of gene expression changes during space flight that are associated with cell wall restructuring and altered root growth were observed. Differences in the way two distinct ecotypes (genetically distinct population) of Arabidopsis responded to the space flight environment, particularly with respect to inherent root-growth patterns were also observed. This project is designed to tie these observations together.

The Characterizing Arabidopsis Root Attractions (CARA) experiment looks at mechanisms at the molecular and genetic level that influence the growth of a plant’s roots in the absence of gravity, and how those change with or without light. Researchers expose one set of seedlings to light, keep another set in the dark, and then examine how each environment influences the patterns of root growth. Some of the plants are also imaged with the Light Microscopy Module on orbit, and at the end of the experiment, all plants are harvested by the astronaut, and preserved for their return to Earth in order to evaluate genes associated with plant responses on orbit.

Characterizing Arabidopsis Root Attractions (CARA) advances the fundamental understanding of the molecular biological responses to extraterrestrial environments. This understanding further defines the impacts of space flight on biological systems to better enable the United States’ future space exploration goals.

The hypothesis to be tested is that the differences between the WS and Col-0 will reveal key genes involved in the morphology of root growth on orbit. Further, it is hypothesized that phyD contributes to the light-mediated signal transduction that influences the tropic direction of root growth on orbit, and that Col-0 plants deficient in this gene will mimic the negatively phototrophic patterns of WS roots on orbit. Two tools are used for analyses: whole genome transcriptome analyses and morphometric analysis. The results anticipated include the identification of a number of differentially expressed genes that help define gravity-independent responses unique to each ecotype, and insight into the role of the phyD gene in root growth. The fundamental scientific relevance of this experiment is that it provides insight into the signal transduction pathways that control tropism and adaptive physiology in plants. The experiment also showcases how the unique research environment of the ISS provides insight into fundamental and widely applicable biological questions that cannot be answered on earth where gravity would mask many of the underlying phenomena.

APPROACH:

Twenty petri plates, ten KFTs and one Harvest Kit are transferred from ambient stowage on the ascent vehicle to ISS. To activate the experiment, blackout cloths wrapped around each petri plate are removed and petri plates are attached to a wall (using Velcro) to be exposed to ambient light. After 1 to 12 hours of light exposure, ten petri plates are re-wrapped in blackout cloth and returned to ambient stowage. The remaining ten petri plates remain attached to a wall for the duration of the experiment run. After an experiment duration of 11 days, all of the petri plates, KFTs and the Harvest Kit are transferred to the Maintenance Work Area for the harvest activity. The ABRS Photogrid, currently on ISS, is the preferred method to secure the petri plate during harvest and to provide a black background for photography. Each petri plate is photographed, one photo with the lid on and one with the lid off, and harvested. The KFTs have a mesh divider so that one dark grown and one light grown petri plate can be harvested into a single KFT. The harvest activity requires the crewmember to use forceps from the Harvest Kit to pull the plants from the agar surface of the petri plate. Once the plants are in a KFT, the KFT are actuated to deliver the RNALater chemical preservative to the plants. The harvest procedure is completed for all twenty petri plates. Upon completion of the harvest, the petri plates and Harvest Kit are trashed. Eight to twenty-four hours following the harvest, the ten KFTs are transferred to MELFI at -80°C. The KFTs return in a Cold Bag at -20°C.

RESULTS:
Plants physiologically adapt to a changing environment by regulating patterns of gene expression. This “transcriptome” (the segments of DNA copied into RNA) creates a map of the response, which can then be compared among varieties, and between treatments – like between plants grown in space, and those grown on the ground. Plants did not evolve in an environment without gravity, so they do not have an evolutionary history of how to metabolically deal with such a stimulus. Because plants have not developed adaptive strategies to cope with microgravity, it raises the possibility that signals in this novel environment inappropriately activate non-adaptive responses. This study investigated whether inappropriate, or non-adaptive responses to microgravity could be identified by comparing the spaceflight transcriptomes of genetically similar cultivars of Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis), and also by comparing the spaceflight transcriptomes of plants differing by only a single gene. RNA sequencing (RNAseq) was used to identify the differentially expressed genes in root tips of plants grown on the ISS in microgravity, and in comparable plants on the ground. RNAseq provided a quantitative measure of how variations in genetic background and lighting impacted the expression of genes in the spaceflight environment. Results showed that all plants grown in microgravity in this study expressed genes differently relative to their ground controls, indicating that changes in gene expression are required for physiological adaptation to spaceflight. The relative impact of the spaceflight environment was inferred by the number of genes that were differentially expressed. In other words, a plant genotype that required the differential expression of a large number of genes was thought to struggle more to adjust to spaceflight than a genotype that expressed fewer genes. The genotype of the cultivar WS required far fewer genes to physiologically adapt to spaceflight than the genotype of cultivar Col-0. This study then asked whether manipulating the genotype of the Col-0 plant could alter the plant’s response to microgravity. It was found that disabling just one gene in Col-0 could reduce the number of genes needed by Col-0 to physiologically adapt to spaceflight. These results suggest that a strategy of genome manipulation could be used to improve the adaptability of plants to spaceflight by reducing the transcriptome cost of physiological adaptation. In addition, the observation that of the hundreds of genes that are differentially expressed in each genotype, only about a dozen are held in common to all three, thus hundreds of differentially expressed genes are likely not to be truly necessary for physiological adaptation to spaceflight. Taken together, these results suggest that responses to truly novel environments may include responses from signals that are incorrectly activated, and further suggests that these incorrect responses can be genetically removed to lighten the metabolic load on the adaptive process. In conclusion, these data suggest that genetic manipulation can produce varieties that are better adapted for growth in microgravity through the elimination of unnecessary environmental responses (Paul, 2017)

experiment_title: Non-Invasive Assessment of Intracranial Pressure for Space Flight and Related Visual Impairment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary objective of this study is to non-invasively estimate the changes in intracranial pressure and cerebral circulation induced by long-duration spaceflights by analyzing the arterial blood pressure (ABP) and the cerebral blood flow velocity (CBFV) waveforms before and after long-duration spaceflight. In addition, it will be confirmed that abnormal visual function and/or ocular structure (e.g. optic disc edema) occurs among the subjects whose intracranial pressure has increased.

Currently, this is the only study that relates to optic disc edema looking at “intracranial pressure”, by using non-invasively obtained multiple indexes. It is expected that the non-invasive methods developed and validated during space flight of six months will be found appropriate for the monitoring of space-related intracranial alterations. This study method may also lead to development of a screening examination.

APPROACH:
The Principal Investigator and Co-Investigator have reported changes in cerebral auto-regulation by analyzing ABP and CBFV in middle cerebral artery by non-invasive ABP monitor and transcranial Doppler sonography during variety of environment including spaceflight. Recently, an analysis method has been developed which uses high resolution waveforms with increased sampling frequency to estimate intracranial pressure. Intracranial pressure can be estimated non-invasively by this method.

Before and after flight, ABP and CBFV waveforms will be recorded simultaneously in a supine/sitting position at rest, and/or while doing a 15 sec Valsalva maneuver. Two preflight data collections are planned. The first will be at Launch - 3 months (L-3 months) and the second at L-2 months. Postflight data collections will take place at Return to Earth + 0 (R+0) and R+1.5 months. During flight, 4 months after launch, facial photographs will be taken to document facial edema. The analysis of changes in intracranial pressure and cerebral circulation will be performed offline.

experiment_title: Effects of Spaceflight on Ocular Oxidative Stress and the Blood-Retinal Barrier
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Although humans have been flying in space for over fifty years, a relatively new medical phenomenon has been found to occur with longer duration flights, and that is the degradation of visual acuity. Approximately 29% of astronauts on short-term (~2 wk) space shuttle flights and 60% on long-duration (~6 mo) missions to the International Space Station (ISS) are reported to have experienced some impairment in distant or near visual acuity, and with the long-term flights the visual degradation in several astronauts has not resolved over time upon return to Earth (1). Though data are limited, overall findings from 10 long-duration astronauts who experienced in-flight and post-flight complications demonstrate symptoms of optic disc edema, globe flattening, choroidal folds, cotton wool spots, nerve fiber layer thickening, and elevated intracranial pressure. These visual disturbances have been hypothesized to be related to increases in intracranial pressure (ICP) (1-3). Various factors have been suggested to account for the elevations in ICP during spaceflight, including alterations in cerebral artery structure, mechanics and function. In addition, modeling studies have shown that a compromise in the integrity of the vascular blood-brain barrier would serve to elevate ICP. While much attention has been directed toward the role of the cerebral vasculature in elevating ICP, little work has been done to examine conditions of the vasculature in the eye and the potential role of microgravity in altering the blood-retinal barrier, which maintains a similar function in the eye for regulating intraocular pressure as the blood-brain barrier does in the cranium. One condition known to compromise the blood-retinal barrier is oxidative stress. For example, in diabetic retinopathy, the leading cause of blindness in Western society, elevations in oxidative stress compromise the blood-retinal barrier and increase vascular permeability in the eye. Therefore, the purpose of this biospecimen request is to address the following specific aims:

Aim 1. To determine whether spaceflight on the ISS increases levels of 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) in the retina, a marker of lipid peroxidation due to oxidative stress, and up-regulates genes involved in the vascular endothelial cell response to oxidative stress and extracellular matrix remodeling in the eye. Like that found in the eyes from mice flown for 13 d on the STS-135 Space Shuttle mission, it is hypothesized that long-term spaceflight will increase levels of 4-HNE in the retina and that multiple genes involved in the regulation of oxidative stress will likewise be up-regulated.

Aim 2. To determine whether markers of oxidative stress in the eye differ in RR-1 mice that are euthanized and frozen on the ISS versus mice where the eyes are harvested and frozen following live return from the ISS via splashdown in the Pacific Ocean and naval transport to the California coast. Levels of retinal 4-HNE and expression of genes involved in vascular endothelial cell response to oxidative stress and extracellular matrix remodeling will be compared in the eyes obtained from the RR-1 mice and eyes obtained from mice as part of the JAXA-NASA Tissue Sharing for Rodent Research agreement. This latter research project, entitled, “Mouse Epigenetics,” with Satoru Takahashi, M.D., Ph.D., and Michael Delp, Ph.D., serving as the JAXA and NASA Principal Investigators, respectively, will provide Michael Delp with the eyes from these live return mice after spending 30 days on the ISS. Comparison of the responses in the eyes from these two groups of ISS mice will allow investigators to estimate the impact of the live return on oxidative stress in the eyes. It is hypothesized that the live return and the conditions associated with obtaining live animals back on Earth will exacerbate markers of oxidative stress in the eyes. APPROACH:

Change in expression of genes involved in cellular functions of mitochondrial biology, endothelial cell biology and oxidative stress will be examined in the eyes from each of the four groups. RNA extraction from whole eye and quantitative reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) array services will be performed at Qiagen service core (Frederick, MD).

PCR reactions will be performed to evaluate expression of 84 genes/array using RT2 ProliferTM PCR array PAMM-15A (Mouse Endothelial Cell Biology PCR Array), and PAMM-065 (Mouse Oxidative Stress PCR Array). Data analysis will be performed using Qiagen’ PCR array data analysis software. Relative changes in gene expression will be calculated using the comparative threshold cycle (Delta Delta Ct, DDCt) method. This method first subtracts the Ct (threshold cycle number) of the gene-average Ct of the 5 housekeeping genes on the array (Gusb, Hprt, Hsp90ab1, Gapdh and Actb) to normalize for the amount of RNA per sample. Finally the DDCt will be calculated: normalized average Ct of the flight group – normalized average Ct of the AEM control group. This DDCt value will be raised to the power of 2 to calculate the degree of change. Whole eyes from five mice in each group will be evaluated individually.

experiment_title: Cognitive Performance and Stress in a Simulated Space Environment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project involved neurobehavioral and physiological assessments in two NASA analog environments: N=8 participants in NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO 14, which was 14 days) in May 2010, and N=6 participants in Desert Research and Technology Study (DRATS, which was 14 days) in August-September 2009. The purpose of this study was twofold: (1) Identify fatigue and stress in relation to performance during analog missions, and (2) further develop normative databases on astronauts in analog environments.

APPROACH:
The goals of the study were accomplished by making the following assessments in each analog mission. (1) Cognitive performance was assessed with three brief validated software-based cognitive performance tests (PVT Self Test, Digit Symbol Substitution Test [DSST]) and the Descending Subtraction Test [DST]), which collectively formed the Penn Neurobehavioral Test Battery (PennNTB). (2) Behavioral ratings of fatigue and stress were assessed using visual analog scale ratings of stress and fatigue (part of the PennNTB). (3) Physiological stress was assessed using salivary cortisol. (4) Feasibility of optical computer recognition (OCR) using facial videos acquired during the cognitive performance testing was assessed with computer webcams that recorded facial videos, which were subsequently evaluated by human scorers for OCR feasibility. (5) Sleep-wake patterns were assessed using wrist actigraphy and sleep logs (in NEEMO 14 only, as comparable data in DRATS was obtained by a different project and principal investigator).

RESULTS:
Data acquisition in both analogs and for all measurement domains ranged from 84% to 89% (grand average was 86%). Penn NTB cognitive performance tests were completed on 497 test bouts out of 580 planned (86%). Visual analog scale ratings of fatigue and stress were completed for 497 assessments out of 580 planned (86%). Salivary cortisol was assayed on 410 samples out of 476 planned (86%). Facial videos for OCR feasibility were acquired in 414 test bouts out of 476 planned (87%). Days of wrist actigraphy and sleep log data were acquired on 135 out of 150 days (90.0%) in NEEMO 14.

experiment_title: Adaptation in Artificial Gravity Environments
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this study was to provide a technical base for evaluating the feasibility of a rotating "artificial gravity" environment for long-duration space missions. The investigators previously demonstrated that Coriolis forces generated during rotation at 10 rpm disrupt head and arm movements but adaptation is possible. Specific goals were to study 1) the rotation rates up to which adaptation is possible, 2) whether measurements of disruptions caused by rotation and subsequent adaptation in 1-G underestimate or overestimate the effects to be expected during rotation in environments with a background force level less than 1-G, and 3) how the magnitude and orientation of the background force affect retention and transfer of adaptation to rotation.

APPROACH:
Twelve subjects stood in a heel-to-toe stance in the rotating room. Each test session involved three phases: 1) pre-rotation, 2) per-rotation, and 3) post-rotation. In each phase, subjects were tested in both eyes open and eyes closed conditions. Four measures were used to characterize center of mass movement and head movement: mean sway amplitude, total power, mean power frequency, and frequency of maximum power. Each measure was computed for anterior-posterior and medial-lateral sway.

RESULTS:
Both anterior-posterior and medial-lateral head and center of mass sway during rotation had significantly greater mean sway amplitude and total power compared with pre- and post-rotation values. Mean power frequency and frequency of maximum power were little affected. Eyes open conditions were significantly more stable in all test phases than eyes-closed, but vision did not completely suppress the effects of rotation. The greatest effect of rotation was in the eyes-closed condition with mean sway amplitude and total power increasing more than twofold. Inverted pendulum sway was maintained in all phases of both test conditions. No aftereffects of rotation were present after the four 25-s exposures each subject received.

experiment_title: Effects of Age and Activity Level on Tibia Mass and Distribution
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this study is to gain a better understanding of the relationship between age, activity level (runners vs non-runners) and site specific bone mass and long bone structure.

APPROACH:
Three studies were performed because nonbone soft issue in the path of the x-ray beam bone is comprised of materials that have different attenuation properties than mineralized bone. The first accuracy study involved the construction of a large plexiglass tube with a bladder filled with saline to emulate soft tissues for the leg. An aluminum phantom was used to estimate in vivo setup accuracy at 3 different angles and two energies by two sets of three scans. The second study determined the in vivo precision of cross-sectional structural parameters in the long bones of 15 female human non-runners on the same day repeated measures for 60o and 90o. The third study compared the parameters in the legs of 14 25-35 year old women with the same in 12 women >age 60 and at two activity levels (recreational runners and non-runners). Scans were taken of the middle third of the lower right leg; structural parameters for the tibia and fibula were determined on each scan line, averaged over the section and adjusted by factors accounting for body size variations.

RESULTS:
Study one: Parameters for the eight rectangular sections of the aluminum phantom were averaged over four lines per section and errors computed as differences from expected values. Principal moments were estimated within 2.3% and principal angles were estimated within 2.3o. Study two: Low energy yielded slightly better precision than high with the area measurement the highest precision (CV <1%). Principal and polar moment CV were 2-6% and the precision of the principal angle was 3-6o. Study three: Low loaders had higher body weights than high loaders, emphasizing the need to account for body size in estimates of bone structure. All differences in the tibia were related to load level, not age. Imax was higher by 46%, Imin by 30%, J by 41% and A by 27% and along the midshaft, the principle angle for runners was consistently aligned closer to the AP direction than in nonrunners. Fibula results did not show the same pattern of results as in the tibia. There was no dependence on age or load group in any parameter for the fibula. Conclusions: A three-scan densitometric method for measuring cross-sectional structural parameters in long bones in vivo was validated; accuracy and precision measurements established confidence limits. Structural parameters related to bone stiffness and strength are increased in female recreational runners compared with nonrunners and these increases are maintained with age. These measures that incorporate bone mass distribution all had larger percent differences than area (A) and were therefore more sensitive measures in detecting differences between runners and nonrunners than simple bone mass measurements (A) alone or I in a single, nonprincipal plane. From the activity study results, it is postulated that higher loads associated with running lead to increased cross-sectional parameters to support axial loads, bending and torsion in the tibia.

experiment_title: Biological Rhythm and Temperature Regulation: I. Biological Rhythms and Temperature Regulation
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This study examined the influence of microgravity on temperature regulation and circadian timekeeping systems in two Rhesus monkeys. Animals were exposed to fourteen days of microgravity while constantly monitoring the circadian patterns, temperature regulation, heart rate and activity. This experiment extended results from Cosmos 1514, as well as providing insights into the physiological mechanisms that produce these changes.

Approach:

Four monkeys (3.5-4.0 kg), two serving as ground controls, were implanted with auxiliary temperature/ECG transmitters. The ECG was hardwired; the CR/T equipment received pulses corresponding to R-waves which were sensed and converted to heart rate within the CR/T signal processor. Motor activity rhythms were monitored via piezoelectric sensors attached to the monkey's restraint jacket. Skin sensors recorded temperatures from the ankle, proximal leg, and head. Ambient temperatures at the top and bottom of the primate restraint system were recorded. Data were collected at five-minute intervals and stored on a battery operated logger. Experiment data were transferred to a microcomputer for waveform and period analysis, and storage.

Results:

It is clear that circadian rhythms in the various parameters studied persisted in the subjects. However, data indicate that the microgravity environment has a significant influence on both temperature regulation and circadian timing. In general, there is a tendency for a reduction in skin temperatures, and a possible reduction in metabolism and a concomitant reduction in deep body temperature. The circadian timing system appears to be more liable in the microgravity environment, even in the presence of a 24-hour light/dark cycle. Activity-related rhythms appear to be maintained with a 24-hour period, while thermoregulatory rhythms are more variable in the periodic responses and tend to show a greater variability in phase. Observations suggest that the two or more central pacemakers, which compose the circadian timing system, show differential responses to the micro- gravity environment. Heart rate and motor activity evidence appropriate 24-hour rhythms in a 24-hour light/dark cycle, while the pacemaker for body temperature does not show such stability.

experiment_title: Cancer Induction by Repeated Doses of High-LET Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Past research has shown that radiation is a strong carcinogen. Vitamin A, a retinoid, can reduce the cancers caused by radiation in rat skin. This ground-based study focused on identifying genes whose expression is either induced or blocked by radiation and on the counteraction of retinyl acetate on those changes in gene expression.

Although retinoids, which are chemical derivatives of vitamin A, have been shown to counteract carcinogenic effects in several animal models, the molecular mechanisms behind the retinoid inhibition of radiation-induced cancer are not established. To better understand the mechanisms, this project focused on how a non-toxic naturally occurring retinoid in the diet called retinyl acetate, or vitamin A acetate, alters gene expression upon exposure of rat skin to radiation. This study may apply to the identification of genes involved in the broad mechanism of the retinoid role in skin cancer, such as its influence on cell proliferation, cell differentiation and apoptosis, which is also known as programmed cell death. Although these and other cellular responses to ionizing radiation are protective, if the responses are insufficient or overwhelmed, genetic errors may accumulate in cells. Those cells then divide, and cancer could eventually occur.

Preliminary findings with low Linear Energy Transfer (LET) radiation showed that dietary retinyl acetate counteracts radiation-induced expression in hundreds of genes. The most prominently affected genes were markers of cell proliferation in keratinocytes suggesting that the retinoid prevented radiation-induced increases of cell proliferation genes. No information is available on the effect of high LET radiation such as ƒ56/ƒFe on gene expression in skin keratinocytes. It is of interest to obtain information on gene expression patterns following skin exposure to the ƒ56/ƒFe beam in rats on normal diet and diet with retinyl acetate supplement. Similarities and differences between high and low LET radiation could then be analyzed. Earlier results suggested that the vitamin A retinoid is almost as effective against induction of skin tumors induced by ƒ56/ƒFe as by those induced by low LET electron radiation, thus gene expression studies are of interest.

One approach to study genes of interest is to find the genes that are altered by radiation and vitamin A in opposite ways. The expression of such genes may change in response to radiation exposure. These same genes may be expressed in the opposite manner upon vitamin A exposure without the radiation. In addition, some genes may not be affected by the vitamin A treatment without the radiation, but, if radiation is given and it causes changes, the vitamin A may be able to reverse those changes even though an effect of vitamin A alone is not observed. Organization of the genes into groups with similar functions in the cell can enable researchers to glean insight on whether certain functions of the cell are affected by radiation and, possibly, the counteraction of vitamin A.

APPROACH:
Eight rats that were 23 days old were divided into two dietary groups of four rats each. One dietary group was fed the regular food while the second group received the same food mixed with 250 ppm vitamin A acetate supplement. After one week, all of the rats received nine Gray and eighteen Gray of low LET electron radiation on two different dorsal skin patches about the size of 1.5 cm by 2 cm. A separate dorsal patch that was not exposed to the radiation was analyzed as a control. Each rat then had three patches of skin that were evaluated. One patch received zero radiation, one received nine Gray and the other received eighteen Gray. Twenty-four hours or seven days after the irradiation, the rats were euthanized, and the irradiated skin and non-irradiated skin sections were excised and pooled according to the radiation dose and vitamin A condition.

Total ribonucleic acid (RNA) was extracted from the skin samples and reverse transcribed to synthesize a special type of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). This particular DNA, called cDNA, was comprised only of the genes that were expressed at the time of analysis. The reverse transcription utilized a primer, a short segment of nucleic acid, which hybridized adjacent to the RNA polymerase promoter region. Double stranded cDNAs were then transcribed into a cRNA probe that was labeled with biotin through in vitro transcription as suggested by the gene chip manufacturer.

The cRNAs were differentially displayed using a rat genome gene chip. Each chip contained 8740 specific probes for rat genes. They represented every known functional category of genes. With this chip, expression all 8740 genes and gene groups were examined in one hybridization. The function of the chip was to recognize the genes that were expressed under the radiation and retinyl acid conditions. The gene chip identified by name those genes that were expressed and recognized. Northern blotting and reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) confirmed the genes that were differentially displayed, those that were identified when the probe bound to the specific genes on the rat genome gene chip. Finally, the patterns of the gene expression alterations from the radiation and vitamin A were categorized. Affected genes were grouped by their cellular functions to focus on pathways that are involved in the process of carcinogenesis by radiation and its reversal by retinyl acetate.

The gene chip analysis was not used for the eighteen Gray plus vitamin A treatment. Thus, five skin samples were analyzed for gene expression under low LET radiation. The five samples were from rats with normal diet and zero Gray radiation, normal diet with nine Gray radiation, normal diet with eighteen Gray radiation, vitamin A diet with zero Gray radiation and vitamin A diet with nine Gray radiation exposure.

For a study of carcinogenesis, the skin of approximately 200 rats was exposed to high LET radiation, a ƒ56/ƒFe beam. The rats were observed weekly for four weeks, then at six-week intervals thereafter. All skin abnormalities were noted, photographed and identified for histological diagnosis. The effects of multiple doses of high-LET ƒ56/ƒFe radiation in comparison to single doses of argon ion radiation were examined.

A different experiment utilizing the high LET radiation was to obtain information on gene expression patterns in a manner similar to that of the low LET electron radiation experiment. Rats were grouped into groups of three, with only twelve rats irradiated. One group of rats, the control group, received no treatment. Another group received vitamin A dietary retinoid and no radiation. Of the twelve irradiated rats, one group received vitamin A and three Gray of ƒ56/ƒFe high LET radiation. Another group received vitamin A plus 1.5 Gy ƒ56/ƒFe. Two groups of irradiated rats had no vitamin A supplement; one of these received three Gray of ƒ56/ƒFe and the other 1.5 Gy. At 24 hours or seven days after radiation exposure, the rats were euthanized, and the irradiated tissue was excised and frozen in liquid nitrogen for future analysis of RNA expression patterns with the gene chip technology.

RESULTS:
Retinol concentration in the skin was measured in rats with both diets. By seven days after the retinyl acid diet was begun, the retinol had accumulated in the skin but not in the blood of the rats that were given the supplement. The skin concentration of retinol in rats on that diet was 4.5-fold higher than in the rats that did not consume the retinyl acid diet. Plasma retinol levels were steady with or without the retinyl acid diet.

Gene expression signals ranged from zero to 278,710, with an average of 4217. Signal strength above 1000 was considered significant. For the five experimental groups, normal diet at zero, nine and eighteen Gray and vitamin A diet at zero and nine Gray, 50.4% of the genes were considered positive in at least one of the groups and the remaining 49.6% were considered as not significantly expressed in any of the five gene chips. Thus, 4402 of the 8740 genes were altered in expression for at least one of the five conditions, and 4338 of the genes did not show an alteration in expression in any of the five conditions.

Genes with induction or inhibition were compared among experimental conditions. Normal diet with nine Gray radiation versus normal diet with no radiation showed 188 altered genes. Eighteen Gray radiation versus normal diet with no radiation gave 92 altered genes, with 54 of those genes also altered under the nine Gray of radiation versus zero Gray, showing a radiation response dependent on dose. Eighteen Gray versus nine Gray of radiation with a normal diet showed 77 altered genes. For vitamin A supplemented diet, the vitamin A with no radiation compared to normal diet with no radiation showed 231 altered genes. Nine Gray of radiation on normal diet versus nine Gray of radiation with the vitamin A diet showed 58 altered genes.

There were 56 genes that showed at least 2.5 fold change between nine Gray and nine Gray with the vitamin A diet gene chips, and also had consistency in the other chips. In one group, genes were repressed by vitamin A alone and were induced by radiation, and the radiation induction was reduced by the vitamin A retinoid. In a different group, vitamin A alone did not change the expression in comparison to control but the combination of vitamin A and radiation reverted the radiation back to control levels. Other genes were inhibited by radiation, but were reversed to control level by vitamin A. The genes that showed the greatest reversal of radiation effects by vitamin A were a keratin gene, ornithine decarboxylase, an intracellular calcium-binding protein and a gene that is similar to an intracellular calcium-binding protein.

Genes that share similar functions were grouped together to learn if any groups were more susceptible to the radiation or the mitigating effects of vitamin A. The genes were checked to see if a significant change of greater than two-fold in expression levels were observed. Several functional groups did not show any genes with significant changes after radiation with or without vitamin A treatments. Tumor suppressor genes and genes related to apoptosis were two of the functional gene groups of interest that showed no changes in expression. The gene chips contained 16 cytokines and only one, Cyclin G, showed a greater than two-fold change between nine Gray with normal diet and nine Gray with vitamin A supplement.

The top one hundred genes with the greatest alteration in expression between nine Gray versus zero Gray normal diet and between vitamin A with no radiation versus zero Gray normal diet were grouped into one category. As a control, one hundred random genes from the expressed control sample were assigned into different functional categories. The genes affected most by the radiation or the vitamin A belonged to the categories of differentiation, stress response, inflammation or immune related and nucleic acid metabolism.

Northern blots, which analyzed RNA, showed a similar trend of expression as the gene chip for the keratin gene, a putative marker of proliferating basal cells. Although the Northern blot supports the gene chip results, the expression ratios differed between the two techniques for expression analysis. On the gene chip, the keratin gene showed 11.7-fold increase in expression with radiation versus the zero radiation. The vitamin A treatment (vitamin A with radiation) reversed the expression back to the control level. On the Northern blot, the increase in the radiation over control was only 4.9-fold rather than 11.7-fold, and the vitamin A reduced the expression to 2.2-fold above the control level rather than control level. The increase in gene expression from radiation that was reversible by vitamin A suggested that the vitamin A may have inhibited the dedifferentiating effects of radiation, and restored the normal differentiation status of the rat skin. Another laboratory technique, PCR, was also used to confirm gene chip results, and the gene chip expression pattern of the involucrin gene was confirmed by RT-PCR.

For the carcinogenesis study in which rat skin was exposed to radiation and the rats observed for tumors, a strong tendency was observed for the tumors to be inhibited by the presence of 250 ppm retinyl acetate in the food. Multiple doses of high LET ƒ56/ƒFe ion radiation in comparison to single doses of argon ion radiation were examined and indications were that multiple exposures produced more carcinomas than expected from the summation of single dose responses. Cancer induced by high LET radiation was indicated to be possibly as preventable by retinyl acetate in the diet as low LET radiation was in previous experiments.

Most tumors found in rats that had been irradiated with the ƒ56/ƒFe beam appeared to be fibromas. Single doses of ƒ56/ƒFe ions were somewhat more effective than argon in producing tumors at 4.5 Gy but not at three Gray or nine Gray. The 250 ppm of dietary retinyl acetate reduced the incidence of tumors to approximately 30% of the incidence found in groups that did not have the supplement in the diet.

Beneficial effects of vitamin A have been observed upon exposure to both high LET radiation and low LET electron radiation. Vitamin A reduced tumor incidence in rats exposed to high LET radiation. Under low LET radiation exposure, vitamin A blocked the expression of genes associated with increased proliferation and inflammation, and accelerated the expression of genes associated with epidermal differentiation. Some fibroblast or macrophage migration or invasion responses may have been inhibited as well. Vitamin A promoted epidermal differentiation on top of the abnormal differentiation from the radiation. Thus, it possibly protected the skin from cancer by preventing damaged cells from producing more cells and by promoting their death. Inhibition of epidermal cell proliferation and stimulation of differentiation limited the number of irradiated cells that could pass the genetic damage to future cells.

experiment_title: Skeletal Muscle Response to Bed Rest and Cortisol Induced Stress
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Prolonged inactivity is inherent to trauma, serious injury, or major surgery. These events represent a significant stress to the patient such that the resultant muscle loss and weakness impairs subsequent rehabilitation. Studies reveal that the requirement for hospital intensive care often entails hypocaloric intake in the patient, thus further exacerbating the deleterious results of stress. This project was designed to investigate countermeasures which would maintain muscle mass during periods of prolonged inactivity, hypocaloric intake, and stress. The proposed interventions are primarily nutritional, and are of unique design and composition so as to have a maximal benefit on a gram per gram basis. Thus, these investigations were directly applicable and translatable to a patient population.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
The investigators examined muscle amino acid and protein kinetics over 24 hour periods, with and without accompanying hypercortisolemia, before and at the end of bed rest and demonstrated that: An amino acid/carbohydrate supplement stimulates net muscle protein synthesis during the two-hour period immediately following ingestion. The normal anabolic effect of meals was not be affected by prior ingestion of an amino acid and carbohydrate supplement. The post-absorptive nadir in net muscle protein synthesis was no greater in subjects receiving supplementation than in control subjects. In response to these findings, they investigated the effects of 28days of hypercortisolemia alone and demonstrated a much greater loss in lean body mass and a dramatic decline in muscle insulin sensitivity.

Investigators completed the study in which seven subjects received an essential amino acid/carbohydrate supplement (EAA group) and six subjects received a placebo (Placebo group). The findings indicate that supplementation with EAA maintained lean body mass (LBM) throughout 28 days of bed rest, while a placebo group experienced a loss of LBM. The EAA supplement maintained LBM by stimulating net muscle protein synthesis to a much greater extent than meal ingestion alone. Although this stimulation is diminished with increased inactivity, the net gain in muscle protein is still significantly greater than that produced by meals alone. In other words, even though the anabolic response to the EAA supplement decreases after 28days of bed rest, it is still capable of producing a significant increase in net muscle protein synthesis.

Though EAA supplementation is capable of maintaining LBM, it does not fully maintain muscle strength. While the loss of muscle strength was twice as great in the placebo group, the EAA group also lost leg muscle strength after 28days of bed rest despite the preservation of leg lean mass. These findings demonstrate that the maintenance of LBM alone is insufficient to fully maintain muscle function. In a concurrent investigation they also demonstrated that ingestion of an amino acid and carbohydrate supplement does not results in a subsequent compensatory nadir in net phenylalanine balance and does not affect the normal anabolic response to ingestion of a nutritionally mixed meal.

These findings also demonstrate that an EAA supplement is capable of stimulating net protein synthesis during an acute and chronic periods of hypercortisolemia; a model mimicking the stress response to space flight. Investigators noted that hypercortisolemia amplifies the loss of muscle protein during the post-absorptive state both before and after 28 days of bed rest. Though the EAA supplement can slow this loss, it only does so temporarily, such that within one to two hours after the supplement, the muscle protein balance is again negative. After 28 days of inactivity, the response to a meal during elevated cortisol is further diminished, such that the muscle is dramatically catabolic. The EAA supplement is not capable of eliciting an anabolic response in the muscle after 28 of bed rest. On the contrary, when the supplement is given without the presence of cortisol, the net effect is muscle anabolism over the study time period.

Investigators studied the effects of 28 days of bed rest and hypercortisolemia, on lean mass and skeletal muscle protein metabolism. Findings indicate that with elevated cortisol, the loss in muscle mass is almost three-fold greater than with inactivity alone. In addition, the presence of elevated cortisol induces insulin resistance. After 28 days of inactivity and elevated cortisol, the effectiveness of insulin on skeletal muscle glucose uptake and protein metabolism is greatly diminished.

Findings demonstrate that the anabolic response to a meal diminishes with prolonged inactivity and a stress challenge. The stimulation of net muscle protein synthesis immediately following each EAA supplement translates to maintenance of muscle protein over a 24 hour period, and in turn, over the 28 days of bed rest. However, the maintenance of LBM does not translate to maintenance of muscle strength. The interaction of inactivity and stress exacerbates the ineffectiveness of ordinary meals. Though the EAA supplement can offset muscle catabolism during the stress state, the response is transient and incapable of ameliorating the overall loss of muscle protein. Taken together, these findings indicate that a nutritional supplement alone can reduce the muscle atrophy associated with space flight. However, whereas muscle mass can be maintained with a specified nutritional intervention, other modalities are required to preserve muscle function.

The catabolic interaction of inactivity and hypercortisolemia is particularly applicable to a patient population where trauma or major surgery results in prolonged inactivity and a stress response. This combination is particularly deleterious to skeletal muscle resulting in a dramatic loss of muscle mass and function, in great part due to the accompanying insulin resistance.

experiment_title: Enhanced Labeling Techniques to Study the Cytoskeleton During Root Growth and Gravitropism
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this research is to investigate the role of the cytoskeleton in root responses to gravity. Results from the proposed research will extend our understanding of how plants tell their correct orientation (i.e. know up from down). The ability of plants to respond to gravity is important for agriculture since crop productivity depends largely on plant form so it can more efficiently explore the soil for nutrients and water as well as optimize light absorption for photosynthesis. The cytoskeleton is critical to achieving the correct orientation of the plant thus the basic knowledge gained from this research should be helpful for optimizing strategies for crop production on Earth.

APPROACH:
This proposal will use roots to study the dynamic behavior of the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton during gravity-induced differential growth in plants. Roots are ideal subjects for studies on the mechanisms of growth control because of the clear distinctions between developmental zones along the longitudinal axis (e.g. meristem, elongation and maturation zones) and because roots have a predictable growth response to gravity (i.e. curvature). The ability to observe these developmental stages in a single root and the predictable gravity-induced growth responses has allowed correlative studies between a specific type of cytoskeletal structure and the stage of cellular development. The proposed research will re-examine the actin cytoskeleton in gravistimulated roots using improved labeling methods that include green fluorescent protein (GFP)-cytoskeletal constructs for live cell imaging and an MBS crosslinking/glycerol permeabilization method for fixed roots.

RESULTS:
We have shown that the actin cytoskeleton is likely to have a role in regulating plant gravitropism that is different from the predictions of current models. For instance, a popular explanation for actin's involvement in plant gravity sensing and signaling is that sedimenting amyloplasts (statoliths) pull on actin filaments that are linked to mechanosensitive ion channels in the plasma membrane. To probe further into the cellular mechanisms underlying the enhanced gravity response of roots induced by actin disruption, we conducted studies with seedling roots of Arabidopsis so we could exploit the molecular tools available in this model plant. We studied cellular events that are well known to be associated with root gravity responses including the development of asymmetric auxin gradients across opposite flanks of the root, cytoplasmic pH signaling in the gravity sensing columella cells of the root cap, and amyloplast dynamics and sedimentation in the columella cells. Our results show that all three of these events were modified by Lat B-treatment indicating that the actin cytoskeleton is involved in modulating these events. The amplification of the above signals when actin was disrupted with Lat B is consistent with actin's role as a down regulator of gravity signaling in roots.

experiment_title: Effects of Microgravity on Ocular Vascular Hydrodynamics
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) is reported to affect ~40% of astronauts completing long-duration spaceflights (as of May 2017) and has been characterized as the development of one or more findings: optic disc edema, hyperopic shifts, globe flattening, cotton-wool spots, or choroidal folds. The leading hypothesis for the development of ocular changes is that prolonged exposure to the headward fluid shift that occurs in weightlessness is the primary instigating factor, and additional factors such as genetic disposition, ambient CO2 on the International Space Station, or on-orbit exercise countermeasures may augment or diminish the development of ocular symptoms. However, the pathophysiology of SANS remains unclear. Evidence for the contribution of intracranial pressure alone in SANS is controversial. Therefore, studies of ocular vascular hydrodynamics are required to clarify if chronic mild elevations of ocular pressure variables compromise ocular structure and function. Since all blood and lymph vessels are compliant, fluid-filled structures whose pressures are strongly influenced by gravity, we propose to focus our studies on the potential changes directly to the ocular vasculature caused by microgravity. Perfusion of the optic nerve and inner retina for sufficient delivery of oxygen and nutrients is dependent on retinal blood flow. The pressure gradient for driving blood flow through the inner retina begins with the arterial pressure in the feed artery, which is the central retinal artery in humans. Changes in retinal blood flow or pressure may contribute to the formation of cotton wool spots and optic disc edema. Optic disc edema, choroidal folds, and optic nerve thickening may also result from ocular venous congestion and/or elevated venous compliance, disruption of the blood-retinal barrier, and/or reduction in ocular lymph flow. There has been no systematic analysis of the ocular vascular changes in microgravity. We have assembled a team of experts in SANS and all 3 main vascular types (arteries, veins, and lymphatics) to address this information gap. Thus, the objective of this application is to determine whether microgravity alters the structure and function of the ocular vasculature at the level of feed arteries, venous exchange and capacitance vessels, and lymph vessels. This provides a novel comprehensive evaluation of the ocular vascular elements. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that microgravity/spaceflight-induced changes in the structure/function of the ocular vasculature lead to alterations in ocular hydrodynamics and promote symptoms of SANS. We will accomplish this objective using in vivo measures of vascular function (retinal artery blood flow, retinal arteriole and venular diameter measurements, and retinal venular permeability measures) and in vitro studies of freshly isolated vascular structure and function (vessel/tissue histology, arterial vasomotor regulation, venous compliance measures, and lymphatic transport characteristics). These studies will be conducted in mice flown in space and the corresponding ground controls to address the following specific aims:1: Evaluate the effects of microgravity on ocular artery structure/function.2: Evaluate the effects of microgravity on ocular vein structure/function.3: Evaluate the effects of microgravity on ocular lymphatic structure/function.

APPROACH:
To examine the Specific Aims 1-3 outlined in the research proposal, Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) will be used. The in vivo assessments of blood flow velocity (Doppler ultrasound) and permeability (intravital microscopy) between eyes (left and right) from flight and ground animals will be analyzed using two-way ANOVA without repeated measures. For in vitro assessment of vascular reactivity to pharmacological agonists at different concentrations between eyes (left and right) from flight and ground animals, two-way ANOVA with repeated measures will be used. All statistical tests will be two-sided and a test resulting in a p-value of less than or equal to 0.05 will be considered statistically significant. The post hoc unpaired least significant difference tests will be performed and interpreted with the Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons. All the p values will be based on two-sided tests.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Evaluation of the Space Therapeutics Assessment Recorder (STARx) and the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric (ANAM) Readiness Evaluation System (ARES) on the Palm PDA Platform:  A Device for Real-Time Monitoring of Drug Effectiveness
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of the STARx study performed during the NEEMO missions was three-fold. First, the relative efficacies of medications taken by each NEEMO 4 and 5 crewmember were evaluated. Second, the effect of medications on NEEMO 5 crewmembers' neuro-cognitive performance was evaluated. The third objective was to evaluate the functionality of the device used to collect drug effectiveness and neuro-cognitive data during both NEEMO 4 and 5 missions.

APPROACH:
A hand-held Palm Personal Data Assistant (PDA) preloaded with both the Space Therapeutics Assessment Recorder (STARx) application and the ANAM (Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics) Readiness Evaluation System (ARES) was provided to each crewmember.

The STARx software application allowed crewmembers to record drug effectiveness data in real time using a severity of symptoms scale specific for each class of medications, as well as information about the clinical status. Each time a crewmember took a medication, they entered that information into the Palm PDA. The crewmember then decided when to be notified by the PDA to enter in data regarding the drug’s effectiveness. At the specified time, an alarm sounded on the PDA, and the crewmember entered in the requested data. In addition to the effectiveness data, crewmembers completed a sleepiness score loaded as part of the STARx application, which recorded the ability of medications to induce drowsiness. Any additional information was entered as notes using the "Memo Pad" application also loaded on the Palm PDA.

The ARES software application consisted of two short-term memory tests known as the Match to Sample (MTS) and Continuous Processing Task (CPT) for neuro-cognitive analysis. The crew completed the ARES test two times a day, once in the morning and once before retiring to bed.

RESULTS:
The STARx software application was not used during the mission due to the fact that no medications were taken during the 14-day NEEMO 5 mission.

All four NEEMO 5 aquanauts completed the pre-mission training sessions and daily ARES data collection during the 14-day mission. A total of 26 sessions were completed in the Aquarius habitat. However, changes in cognitive performance could not be correlated with medication use, because no medications were taken.

A comparison between early morning and late evening ARES scores was performed with the following results:

  1. Evening MTS response times were 10 to 22% less than morning response times. The decrease in two of the four aquanauts was statistically significant (p<0.01).
  2. Evening CPT response times were 2 to 8% less than morning response times. The decrease in one of the four aquanauts was statistically significant (p<0.05).
  3. Aquanaut accuracy scores during all test sessions for the MTS and CPT tests were very high regardless of morning or evening conditions, i.e., greater than 80% and 88%, respectively.

experiment_title: Preflight and Postflight Parallel Swing Tests
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
An otolith is a structure in the inner ear, specifically in the vestibular labyrinth. They are sensitive to gravity and linear acceleration. The vestibular otolith receptors respond to linear motion and gravity. If motion cues from visual and skin receptors were reduced or eliminated, responses to roll and linear translation attributable primarily to the otolith receptors could be examined. The Miami University Parallel Swing and its associated restraint system made this examination possible. This investigation examined two types of responses associated with roll and linear translation stimulation: perceived self-motion path and eye movements. These responses were examined before and after orbital flight. Because the otoliths are gravity receptors, it was hypothesized that adaptation to the loss of stimulation due to gravity during flight would alter responses to which the otoliths contribute.

This investigation assessed changes in responses associated with otolith receptor activity following prolonged space flight. The results led to the development of an otolith tilt translation reinterpretation hypothesis which, in conjunction with the sensory conflict hypothesis, provides a conceptual framework for comprehending space motion sickness.

APPROACH:
On STS-8, a subject performed head tilts (roll and pitch) and followed a self-motion reporting procedure. On STS-41B (a.k.a. STS-11), two subjects repeated the STS-8 protocol, and examined the hypothesis that the brain's reinterpretation of otolith information would affect eye movement reflexes. The STS-41B subjects were exposed to the same motion stimuli as on STS-8 and reported their self-motion in the same manner. In addition, their eye movements were recorded in the dark using an infrared-sensitive video camera.

A second purpose of DSO 433 was to examine possible changes in linear self-motion detection thresholds following weightlessness. Ocular counterrolling during static head tilt was recorded preflight and immediately postflight.

RESULTS:
STS-8: This investigation obtained data from one subject. The results indicated that prolonged exposure to weightlessness resulted in reinterpretation by the brain of signals from the otolith organs. The subject was exposed to roll around the head (X axis) and linear translation along the head (Y axis). The subject reported self-motion perception following exposure to the two types of motion. Preflight, the subject's self-motion reports corresponded with the actual motion; roll was perceived as roll and translation as translation. Immediately postflight, the self-motion sensation associated with roll differed dramatically from that reported preflight. At R+2.5 hours, roll motion was perceived primarily as linear translation along the Y axis. At R+36 hours, self-motion sensations were approximately the same as those observed preflight.

The STS-8 observations led to the following hypothesis: During prolonged weightlessness, the adaptive brain learns to interpret all signals from the otolith linear accelerometer as linear translation. In weightlessness, the otoliths do not produce a signal indicating head tilt (roll or pitch) because linear acceleration due to gravity is absent. Following return to earth, and before the brain re-adapts, the interpretation that all otolith signals indicate is that linear motion persists. However, the otoliths produce a signal during head tilt (roll) because gravity is present. Consequently, the observer reports that roll motion is perceived as linear translation plus a roll component due to the semicircular canals. Following re-adaptation to normal gravity, true perception of roll motion returns.

STS-41B (a.k.a. STS-11): Preflight and postflight self-motion reports following roll and linear translation were nearly the same as those reported on STS-8. Eye movements recorded preflight indicated that the linear translation stimulus produced nearly pure horizontal translation of the eyeball, and that roll stimuli produced nearly pure ocular counterrolling (eye torsion). Immediately postflight, the eye movements differed dramatically from those seen preflight. For one subject, who was seen at R+70 minutes, both roll and linear motion stimulation produced horizontal translation of the eyeball. For the second subject, seen at R+2 hours, roll stimulation produced horizontal eye movements in combination with a small amount of torsion. Self-motion reports indicated that roll was perceived as a combination of linear translation and roll. The roll component of the perceptual report was probably due to semicircular canal stimulation. At R+2 days, both subjects' self-motion reports had returned to the preflight state. However, some horizontal eye movement was still present. By R+3 days, both perceptual reports and eye movement were approximately the same as preflight.

In conclusion, the otolith reinterpretation hypothesis derived from STS-8 was supported by the results from STS-41B. The eye movement results were consistent with a hypothesis that the reinterpretation of the otolith signals occurs in the brain stem in the nuclei associated with vestibular-ocular reflexes (VOR). The results suggested ways in which an astronaut's performance might be disturbed during the immediate postflight period. The results imply that performance of tasks that require accurate perception of complex self-motion should be avoided. It was also suggested that SAS symptoms and orientation disturbances are related to the period in which the brain is learning to reinterpret the otolith signals in weightlessness. This suggestion is consistent with the reports indicating that head tilts, particularly in the pitch plane, are provocative. This suggestion can be evaluated by performing appropriate inflight observations and employing appropriate preflight countermeasures during future missions.

A second purpose of DSO 433 was to examine possible changes in linear self-motion detection thresholds following weightlessness. The large threshold elevation reported for STS-8 was not seen with the STS-41B subjects. Results for ocular counterrolling during static head tilt are not available.

DSO 433 was renamed to DSO 449 prior to the STS-51D flight, and additional subjects' data were obtained on DSO 449.

Information archived for this experiment was provided by the William E.Thornton collection.

experiment_title: Energy and Metabolic Requirements for Extended Duration Space Flight (Energy Utilization)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
An astronaut will lose lean body mass if energy balance is not maintained. This is especially true if energy expenditure exceeds energy intake. However, astronauts on Skylab lost lean body mass in spite of the apparent adequate intake of energy and protein. Energy requirements could be affected by microgravity and by the limits on physical activity in the close confines of the spacecraft. Before this study, energy requirements during space flight had only been estimated from metabolic balance studies and food intake records. The objectives of this study were to measure total energy expenditure (TEE) during space flight and to compare the results with calculated energy intake.

APPROACH:
Two five-day test sessions (one before and 1 during flight) were completed by each of 13 astronauts on six Shuttle flights lasting eight to 14 days. The astronauts consumed doubly labeled water (labeled with the heavy isotopes 2H and 18O) and periodically provided urine and saliva samples. It was necessary to account for baseline differences in the isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen in the Shuttle's drinking water, which is made by fuel cells from liquid oxygen and hydrogen. Total energy expenditure was determined by indirect calorimetry and was corrected for body weight and fat-free mass. Energy intake was calculated from records of food and fluid intake. One-way repeated-measures ANOVA identified differences in energy intake and expenditure between the preflight and postflight periods. The Student-Newman-Keuls test was used for post-hoc comparisons. Paired t-tests were used to detect any differences between preflight and inflight dietary intake.

RESULTS:
Energy expenditures were similar before and during flight. However, energy and fluid intake were lower during flight (energy intake was 23% less; fluid intake was 19% less.) Weight changes ranged from a gain of 1.0 kilogram (kg) to a loss of 3.9 kg, with a mean weight loss of 1.5 kg. In flight energy expenditures were similar to estimates published by the World Health Organization (WHO) of energy requirements for healthy adults. The results indicated that energy expenditure was not changed during space flight and that the WHO estimates of energy requirements were appropriate for estimating the dietary needs of space crews. However, most of the 13 astronauts were in negative energy balance because they had reduced their caloric intake. This is undesirable because the loss of lean body mass reduces work capacity and promotes the loss of electrolytes that are important to muscle function and cardiovascular function. The astronauts also consumed inadequate fluid. The importance of maintaining adequate food and fluid intake should be emphasized in future flights.

experiment_title: Charged Particle Effects on Neuronal Injury, Plasticity and Neurodegeneration
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The space radiation environment poses unique hazards to astronauts since a range of potential complications can result from exposure of the central nervous system (CNS) to these dangerous radiation fields. Damage caused by the traversal of charged particles in space through the brain is likely to elicit alterations to the structure and function of neurons and perturb the critical interactions between multiple cell types in the CNS. Irradiation also elicits a persistent increase in free radicals or “oxidative stress” that will complicate further the recovery of the CNS after exposure. Thus, investigators believe that exposure to the charged particles in space will cause acute and chronic alterations to the cell types in the brain that are critical for learning and memory, thereby having an adverse effect on the functionality of the CNS.

APPROACH:
To address the foregoing problems investigators will measure the impact of charged particle irradiation on neuronal anatomy and function using cultures of human neurons grown in the presence and absence of additional cell types known to be critical for proper neuronal function. Studies will also be performed in the presence of antioxidants that can minimize damage from reactive species, providing a useful strategy for gauging the importance of radiation-induced oxidative stress. These cell-based studies will be complemented by animal studies in which similar endpoints will be measured in brain tissue isolated from irradiated mice. One animal model genetically modified to express a neuronal fluorescent marker will be used to measure the subtle structural changes to neurons after irradiation. Another animal model genetically modified to exhibit early onset dementia will be used to gauge how exposure to charged particles found in space might impact the onset and/or severity of neurodegenerative phenotypes. Collectively, these studies will provide new data regarding the consequences of charged particle irradiation in the CNS, data that will be useful in estimating the uncertainties and risks associated with space travel.

RESULTS:
Investigators have made considerable progress in defining the extent and temporal progression of charged particle induced cognitive dysfunction in mice. Mice (6 months of age) have now been subjected to an extensive series of cognitive testing 6, 12, and 24 weeks following low dose exposure (5, 30 cGy) to 16O and 48Ti HZE ions. Behavioral tasks administered at these times reveal marked if not stunning decrements in behavior that persist six months following a single acute dose. Temporally coincident with these decrements are significant reductions in dendritic complexity and spine density along the very neurons that mediate neurotransmission important for the selected behavioral tasks. These measurements have also facilitated efforts at defining the relationship between individual performance and specific alterations in structural and/or synaptic integrity. When performance is calculated as a discrimination index and plotted versus spine density or synaptic puncta one can evaluate at what level these parameters translate to impaired cognition, thereby providing a quantitative criterion for risk. Thus, it appears as if HZE ion irradiation elicits significant structural deterioration of neurons that persists and contributes to the progressive dementia found long after exposure. Investigators have also made progress in the analysis of the neurovascular niche as multiple cell types grown in conjunction in either 96-well plates or in pre-vascularized microfluidic chambers. As multiple cells types (endothelial, pericytes, mesenchymal, and neural stem) are cultured under these conditions, radiation has been found to elicit oxidative stress, and a tropism of neural stem cells migrating away from the vascularized network. These studies will be expanded in upcoming BNL campaigns to elucidate the impact of HZE ion irradiation on the interaction between neurons and the perfused vasculature.
