experiment_title: Influence of Gender and Age on Renal and Cardio-Endocrine Responses to Simulated Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Orthostatic intolerance remains an operational problem following space flight. In the last six years, investigators have addressed the subject of renal, endocrine and volume- regulating function during head-down tilt bed rest. They have found that simulated microgravity induces changes in the volume-regulating systems and electrolyte excretion, and leads to changes in cardiac electrical stability. They have also found that using their tilt-test protocol, pre-bed rest tilt-test tolerance was predictive of post-bed rest tilt-test tolerance.

APPROACH:
Investigators proposed to conduct a double-blinded randomized trial 1) to investigate the use of a pre-bed rest tilt-test as a means to screen countermeasures against orthostatic intolerance, and investigate the influence of these countermeasures on the renal and endocrine responses to orthostatic stress and 2) to investigate the effectiveness of individualized countermeasures identified during a pre-bed rest tilt-test in reducing post-bed rest orthostatic intolerance, as well as their influence on the renal and endocrine responses to orthostatic stress.

RESULTS:
During the past several years, investigators have addressed the subject of renal, cardiovascular and endocrine volume-regulating factors using a simulated microgravity protocol (sixteen day-head-down tilt bed rest) in a rigorously controlled environment (in-patient General Clinical Research Center with constant dietary intake, controlled activity, and regulated temperature, light exposure and sleep/wake cycles). Among the several observations that they have made on the forty individuals studied to date, the followings are key for the present proposal:
- Initial loss of urinary volume and sodium followed by reestablishment of sodium balance through activation of the renin-angio system;
- Continuous potassium loss;
- A dissociation between renin and aldosterone responses to simulated microgravity and up-right tilt;
- A decrease in autonomic function with a change towards a sympathetic-dominated system;
- Cardiac electrical instability;
- Subjects intolerant to head-up tilt pre-bed rest are intolerant post-bed rest, but the reverse is not true, suggesting individual susceptibility to orthostatic intolerance independent of simulated microgravity;
- Finally, in a randomized double-blinded trial, investigators observed that midodrine was an efficient intervention for the treatment of orthostatic intolerance following simulated microgravity.

experiment_title: Synergistic Effect of Zero-g and Radiation on White Blood Cells
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Biological effects, such as genetic mutation, chromosome aberrations and cell lysis, were seen in both ballistic and orbital space flights that occurred before Gemini 3. In some cases, these effects were of magnitudes many times greater than would have been predicted from the expected radiation exposure received during flight. These magnitudes were thought to occur for two reasons: (1) it was thought that the components (particles) of radiation above the Earth’s atmosphere might have unexpected biological effects that could not be predicted in Earth-based laboratories and (2) it was thought that radiation and zero-g acted synergistically to produce unexpectedly large effects. This experiment was conducted to test these two possibilities.

APPROACH:
A series of human whole blood samples was irradiated during the mission with radioactive phosphorus (32P) beta-rays, with a known quantity and quality of radiation. Inflight control samples were also used, and were not irradiated with the experiment source, but just flew to encounter the normal radiation of the space flight. An identical series of blood samples was irradiated on the ground and used as a control. Increased aberrations in the inflight samples, including the control, would be evidence of an effect of some space flight parameter. Any effect not seen in the inflight control would be attributed to a synergism between radiation and some space flight parameter.

Because induction of chromosome aberrations is a non-linear function of radiation dose, a graded series of four different radiation exposures was used. Two complete sets of blood samples were flown to protect against loss of data; each sample set was from a different blood donor. In total, ten 3 ml blood samples were flown; eight were irradiated with each of the four doses, and two were not irradiated and served as the inflight controls. The simultaneous ground control experiment consisted of ten 3 ml samples drawn from the same donors at the same time as the inflight samples. As an additional control, blood samples were obtained from the flight crew before and after the flight, and short-term leukocyte cultures were prepared. Preflight, on Gemini 3, the samples were obtained as close to the mission as possible (2 days prior to launch) from both the flight and backup crews, so that the samples would remain viable. On Gemini 11, the samples were obtained 9 days prior to launch. On both flights, the leukocyte cultures were prepared and incubated at 37 degrees C, treated with colchicine, fixed and then chromosome preparations were made.

Irradiation was accomplished by identical experimental devices, one on the ground at the launch site, and the other on the righthand hatch of the Gemini 3 spacecraft. Each device contained 22 fluoroglass dosimeters. Approximately 9 hours before launch the two identical experiment devices were assembled and tested, then at 210 minutes before launch (for Gemini 3) and 150 minutes before launch (for Gemini 11), the flight unit was mounted into the spacecraft. On Gemini 3, the ground-control unit was placed inside a temperature-controlled cabinet, in which the temperature was periodically adjusted to correspond to the temperature readout from the spacecraft. The longer duration of Gemini 11 meant that the samples were in the weightless period much longer before they were irradiated. Samples were refrigerated inflight to ensure the survival of the leukocytes. Therefore, the ground control unit was placed inside a refrigerator that matched the refrigerator temperature of the inflight samples (2 to 4 degrees Celsius). Furthermore, the device provided a telemetry signal for monitoring the temperature on the ground, an improvement over the Gemini 3 mission.

Irradiation was initiated by the pilot 50 minutes and 18 seconds after launch, and continued for 20 minutes. Correspondingly, the ground unit was activated and deactivated at 52 and 72 minutes, respectively. Except for minor accelerations caused by maneuvering “burns” of the spacecraft, the flight device remained weightless for nearly 3.5 hours.

Ideally, the team wanted to use X- or gamma-rays to irradiate the blood samples, but could not for two reasons: (1) the small mass allotted to them for the experiment excluded it and (2) too much shielding would have been required to protect the flight crew. Therefore, beta-rays were chosen. Radioactive phosphorus (32P) was chosen as the radiation source for three reasons: (1)it emits only a single beta-particle, (2) the particle energy was suitable and (3) it had been used extensively in radiobiology studies to date. On Gemini 11, the amount of 32P in the device was decreased, since the samples would be subjected to increased beta-ray leakage and Bremsstrahlung radiation within the device.

After the mission, blood samples were obtained as soon as possible from the flight crew (6.5 hours after landing). By 10 hours after launch, all blood samples had been put into culture, and all cultures were fixed between 72 and 77 hours after launch. A cytogenetic analysis was made of each sample; the frequencies of chromosome aberrations were determined. Yields of both single-break and multiple-break aberrations were calculated, both for the flight samples as well as the ground samples.

Production of chromosomal aberrations is one of the best known effects of radiation, so it was selected as the parameter to measure for this study. Human leukocytes were chosen as the cell to be studied, since the cells would all be in a uniformly sensitive stage in the cell cycle and because the investigator team had extensive experience working with leukoctyes.

RESULTS:
Gemini 3 postflight analysis of the fluoroglass dosimeters in the experiment device showed that the doses, start/stop times of irradiation, and temperatures for the ground and flight units all agreed well. For Gemini 3, the flight device temperature stayed between 14 and 38 degrees Celsius, whereas the ground device stayed within a 2 to 29 degree Celsius range. For Gemini 11, the temperature of the flight device increased, starting at approximately 14 minutes after launch, to between 6 to 10 degrees Celsius and remained in that range for the first 24 hours of the mission. The device temperature decreased when the spacecraft was depressurized for the first extravehicular activity (EVA). The device operated within the normal 2 to 4 degree range until switched off simultaneously with the ground unit after approximately 65 hours inflight. The ground unit always remained within the normal temperature range. Later, it was discovered that an unusually high hatch temperature caused the inflight high refrigerator temperature. The higher temperatures did not affect the blood samples nor the results.

The dosimeters also confirmed that the radiation exposures were of the required duration. The inflight readings of the 22 dosimeters in the flight device compared well with the readings of the 22 dosimeters in the ground device. Doses were estimated for preflight and postflight by means of fluoroglass or Fricke-solution dosimetry. As a result, there was a 2 rad dose on the ground samples, with a large portion (about one-third) of that being Bremsstrahlung with a peak energy of about 65 keV. The inflight package registered somewhat higher exposures than 2 rad.

All of the blood sample cultures were successful and yielded satisfactory chromosome preparations. Very little hemolysis was noted. A total of 4600 cells were analyzed.

Results showed that the occurrence of single-break aberrations was much higher in the flight samples. There was no significant difference between the yields of multiple-break aberrations in the flight and ground control samples. The flight crew chromosome aberration analyses showed no increase in aberration frequency due to space flight. However, the small positive effect seen in the differences of single-break aberrations did stimulate further scientific interest in this topic. It appeared that some space flight factor did interact synergistically with radiation to affect the chromosome rejoining system (i.e. the cell’s ability to repair damage), thus producing the single breaks.

On Gemini 11, a parallel test was also conducted on the bread mold Neurospora crassa. Those results are reported in another experiment record in this archive.

experiment_title: Effect of Spaceflight on Herpesvirus Genome Stability and Diversity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Viral reactivation, especially of the Herpesviruses, is known to increase during space flight. At least four (Epstein Barr virus- EBV, Varicella zoster virus- VZV, Cytomegalovirus– CMV, and Herpes simplex virus 1 -HSV1) of the eight known human Herpesviruses are common life-long infections humans have shown to reactivated due to space flight. The fact that space flight is known to increase the frequency and duration of Herpesvirus reactivation sets up a biological environment for these reactivating and replicating viruses to mutate. Recently it has been shown that environmental factors such as diet and medications can alter the mutation rate and pathogenesis of human viruses, so it seems likely that effects of microgravity, radiation, and other physiological aspects of space flight may have a profound effect on the evolution of mutations and adaptations of the Herpesviruses during space flight.

APPROACH:
The goal of this study will be to determine the changes in the genomic and mutational diversity that is present in the Herpesvirus virome present in astronaut saliva and urine samples collected before, during, and after space flight. Ground subjects will serve as the control group providing saliva and urine samples preflight and postflight during the same schedule as the astronauts. In order to determine the effect of space flight on the generation of mutations and diversity of the Herpesviruses investigators will: 1) Collect and analyze astronaut saliva and urine samples for Herpesvirus shedding, 2) Perform deep sequence analysis of the Herpesviruses present in the saliva and urine of astronauts before, during, and after space flight, and 3) Analyze these data to determine the overall diversity of the viruses present in the samples before, during, and after space flight and the mutation frequency present in the samples before, during, and after space flight. In summary, the proposed study is a unique opportunity to examine the influence of space flight on the mutation rate and diversity of human persistent viruses and to assess the potential risk of virus mutations accumulating during long-duration missions.

experiment_title: HZE Radiation: Modulation Of Genetic Effects By RNA Interference Of NHEJ
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
For extended missions in space, astronauts will be exposed to a radiation environment unlike any on the earth's surface. Galactic cosmic rays include a particularly worrisome component of energetic iron nuclei which are high atomic number, high energy (HZE) charged particles with linear energy transfer (LET) similar to alpha particles but with very different track structures. While the relative biological effectiveness (RBE) of a particular radiation roughly depends on the LET, the very different track structures for these two radiations may well modulate this RBE even if they have identical average LETs. Further, this "radiation quality" for the exposures actually relevant for astronauts will be modified by interactions with materials in the spacecraft, including their own bodies.

Basic to virtually all relevant biological effects of ionizing radiation is the underlying damage produced in DNA, and the subsequent cellular processing of such damage. The damage can be qualitatively different for different kinds of radiations, and the genetics of the biological systems exposed can greatly affect damage processing and ultimate outcome the biological effect of concern. The accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) is critical for the maintenance of genomic integrity and function. Incorrect repair of such lesions results in chromosome rearrangements and mutations that can lead to cancer and heritable defects in the progeny of irradiated parents. It is important, therefore, to understand cellular responses to DNA damage and to elucidate the mechanisms and phenotypic consequences of DSB misrepair.

APPROACH:
The general aim in this proposal is to examine connections between cellular radiosensitivity phenotypes relevant for carcinogenesis, namely chromosome aberration formation, mutagenesis and telomere fusions, and deficiencies in various components of the non-homologous end joining system, using RNA interference to systematically knockdown gene products known to be involved, either singly or in combination.

RESULTS:
This project utilized the powerful technique of RNA interference (RNAi) to deplete levels of various components of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) double-strand break (DSB) repair system, then to study the effects on HZE radiation-induced chromosomal rearrangements, gene mutation and telomere dysfunction.

The accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) is critical for the maintenance of genomic integrity and function. Incorrect repair of such lesions results in chromosomal rearrangements and mutations that can lead to cancer and heritable defects in the progeny of irradiated parents. Focus was on the consequent phenotypic effects of faulty repair by examining connections between cellular radiosensitivity phenotypes relevant for carcinogenesis after exposure to IR, and deficiencies in various components of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) system. In the past year, the deficiency of a protein, called Apollo, was produced using RNAi in a human lymphoblastoid cell line. Exposure of cells exhibiting reduced protein expression to either gamma-rays or 1GeV/nu Fe particles demonstrated differential effects on telomere dysfunction and mutation frequency, as well as differential effects between radiation qualities.

Apollo is a nuclease required for DNA interstrand cross-link repair, and in fact it appears to interact with FANCD2, also involved in that repair pathway. In addition, Apollo may be involved in a more generalized response to DNA damage, in that it may stimulate the activation of ATM, and it seems to interact with the MRN complex, which is a focal point for several modes of repair.

The Apollo nuclease is also implicated in the protection of telomeres; it interacts with TRF2 in S-phase, and actually is an attractive candidate for the processing of telomere ends to generate 3’ single strand overhangs, a critical event and integral part of proper telomere formation. Knockdown of Apollo produced an increase in radiation mutagenesis, both for gamma-ray exposures and for 1 GeV/n Fe particles. The increases were of the same order as those caused by inhibition of DNA-PKcs, and furthermore there were no interactions, synergistic or antagonistic, of Apollo knockdown and DNA-PKcs inhibition. These results suggest that Apollo may be involved in the same pathway as DNA-PKcs, namely repair of DSB by NHEJ.

Telomere instability was also examine following siRNA knockdown of Apollo. Telomere uncapping was found with knockdown of Apollo that was similar to that seen with inhibition of DNA-PKcs and similar between radiation types. These results suggest possible Apollo involvement in repair of IR-induced damage, as well as support a telomeric role for Apollo.

Most recently, a collaborative effort with Dr. Sandy Chang at M.D. Anderson, TX in which SNMIB/Apollo knockout mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) were generated, resulted in data implicating SNMIB/Apollo as a key 5’-3’ exonuclease required for generation of 3’ single-stranded overhangs at newly replicated leading-strand telomeres to protect them from engaging the non-homologous end joining pathway. Results and informtion on this can be found in the EMBO Journal citation listed below.

These experiments have resulted in valuable information regarding CPR question 10.12, “What are the effects of inter-individual diversity?” It was hypothesized that NHEJ repair components are major genetic determinants controlling individual susceptibility to radiation-induced cancer, as well as heritable effects of exposure. Therefore, naturally occurring deficiencies of these proteins within the population will put these individuals at increased risk. Our RNAi approach of experimentally mimicking highly relevant human deficiencies has shed light of this important issue. Our results support the relevance of deficiencies/hypomorphic mutations in NHEJ factors in that they can deregulate rejoining reactions sufficiently to increase incidence of oncogenic rearrangements (misrepair).

This work supports the concept that inherited or acquired mutations in NHEJ factors represent important risk factors for developing cancer, an especially relevant consideration following exposure to ionizing radiations (increased complexity the damage and its repair), and so also impact on CPR question 10.07, “What are the cancer risks in humans from spaceflight?” Our characterizations of telomere dysfunction, chromosome aberration formation and gene mutation serve as important and informative surrogate endpoints for predicting cancer risks.

experiment_title: Countermeasures to Neurobehavioral Deficits from Cumulative Sleep Deprivation during Space Flight: Dose-Response Effects of Recovery Sleep Opportunities
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The optimal performance of astronauts during extended-duration space flight depends heavily on achieving recovery through adequate sleep. There is now extensive evidence that astronaut sleep in space averages 4 to 6.5 hours per day, and when critical operations (e.g., nighttime docking) are scheduled, very little sleep may be obtained during a day prior to the critical event. Ground-based experiments on healthy adults have demonstrated that limiting daily sleep duration to less than 7 hours leads to cumulative deficits in neurocognitive performance and alertness. Within 1-2 weeks of sleep restriction at levels experienced by astronauts, performance deficits were serious; impairments on tasks requiring sustained attention, working memory, and cognitive throughput reached levels equivalent to those found after 1-2 nights of total sleep loss.

The primary aim is to determine the sleep dose-response effects of an acute change in sleep duration that occurs between two periods of chronic sleep restriction, on neurocognitive performance functions, subjective states, and waking and sleep physiology. The objective of the experiment was to determine the countermeasure benefits for performance (during critical operations and subsequent days of sleep restriction) from an acute increase in sleep duration (i.e., single night of recovery sleep). The knowledge gained has the potential to change work scheduling and further understand the effect of sleep lose and recovery on neurobehavioral function in many Earth-based safety-sensitive occupations, such as transportation workers (e.g., truck drivers, train conductors, airline pilots); operators in safety-sensitive industries (e.g., power plant control rooms); and military personnel.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this experiment isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Seventy-two subjects completed the 16 day in-laboratory study protocol (for a total of 1152 laboratory days). Preliminary data suggests that a single sleep period of 8 hours, 10 hours or 12 hours after five nights of 4 hours sleep, provides substantial acute recovery, but not protection against the immediate reappearance of performance deficits when it is followed by five additional nights of sleep restriction.

experiment_title: Role of Visual Cues in Spatial Orientation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Role of Visual Cues in Spatial Orientation experiment was one of three sensory motor and performance experiments performed during the 1998 Neurolab mission. This experiment focused on how the balance between visual and vestibular cues shifts toward the visual system in microgravity.

Using virtual reality, this investigation was designed to study how visual scene content and symmetry influenced the astronauts perception of up and down, to determine how quickly a moving visual scene would produce the illusion of self-motion, and to explore how the direction of perceived "down" altered the ability to recognize shapes and interpret curvature from shading.

Information gained from this experiment will help investigators understand why, in the absence of gravity, astronauts become dependent on visual stimuli. This information is also of potential value to medical researchers seeking insight into inner ear impairments and other balance disorders in Earth-bound patients, as well as related rehabilitative testing and training methods for those individuals. As an added value, portable head-mounted displays similar to the one developed for use in this experiment may prove useful for patients, perhaps someday even providing visual prostheses for the vestibularly impaired.

APPROACH:
The Role of Visual Cues in Spatial Orientation experiment was performed using NASA's Virtual Environment Generator (VEG), a head-mounted display, which allowed the subjects to view a succession of visual scenes rendered by the VEG graphic computer. The VEG also tracked the motion of the head, so scenes that were displayed appeared stable when the head moved. The astronauts participated in three types of spatial orientation experiments:
1) the Virtual Tilting Room Test (ROOM)
2) the Linear Vection Test (VECTION)
3) the Object Recognition Test (OBJECT). Tests were performed with the astronaut free-floating and, alternately, wearing a constant force spring harness that provided artificial "down" cues to the shoulders and hips. Preflight ROOM, OBJECT and VECTION tests were performed 1 year before launch in NASA's training airplane, the KC-135, and in the laboratory at 90, 89, 60 and 59 days before launch. The OBJECT test was performed on flight day 3, and the ROOM and VECTION tests were performed on flight day 4, with an additional session performed by one subject on flight day 16. Postflight, all three tests were performed on the day of landing and 1, 2, 4 and 6 days after landing.

The ROOM test allowed investigators to study the influence of visual scene symmetry, scene rotation, orientation expectation, and tactile/proprioceptive cues on perceived self-tilt. Subjects wearing the VEG head mounted display viewed the interior of a virtual room. Two presentation types were used, static and continuously rotating at constant angular velocity. The VEG joystick, also called the Subject Interface Device (SID), recorded subject responses. The subject made comments using a microphone and entered notes after testing using the IBM Thinkpad laptop computer.

During both the ROOM and VECTION tests, subjects wore the Subject Restraint System for testing under free-floating and simulated "standing upright" conditions. When free-floating, the subject's body was not in contact with the Spacelab; loose cloth tethers clipped between the restraint harness, D-rings on the center aisle, and rack handrails prevented the subject from drifting. When the subject was "standing," constraint force springs connecting the harness to the floor allowed the subject to stand erect with his feet on the floor, with proprioceptive and tactile compressive loading on the trunk and lower extremities.

Several hypotheses were tested during the ROOM sessions, including:
1) Visual reorientation illusions could be created in the frontal (roll) plane using a VEG-controlled, visual stimulus. Inversion illusions could be elicited in subjects susceptible to them, because the visual cues for static self-tilt perception are usually derived from the ambiguous underlying horizontal and vertical visual symmetries in conventional room interiors
2) A subject's indication of the subjective vertical can be predicted in rooms with differing degrees of visual symmetry (dotted, walled, or furnished rooms). A subject's self-tilt report in static and rotating virtual rooms depends (in a predictable way) not only on scene symmetry, but on expectation, which is determined by internal sensory cues associated with 0-g fluid shift and saccular unloading. The latter will be manipulated using preconditioning visual and haptic stimuli
3) As subjects adapt to weightlessness, their self-orientation becomes less biased by internal sensory cues and increasingly veridical.

The VECTION test was used with and without haptic cues to determine how quickly a moving visual scene would produce the illusion of self-motion. Haptic cues are clues that allow orientation by providing input from the restraint system that, for example, forces the feet against the floor, thereby giving the feeling of standing. The VEG was programmed to present a binocular "looming vection" display to the subject in successive 30-second tests. The stimulus velocity and subject orientation were manipulated across tests. Objects in the scene moved radially on the display, simulating subject movement along a path parallel to the visual axis.

Previous research on the role of visual cues in 0-g spatial orientation has addressed the phenomenon of rotational vection about the roll axis of the head (roll circular vection). The results suggested an increasing dependence on visual and haptic cues and indicated that less weight was given to otolithic cues (probably because their response to head tilt seems initially unfamiliar in 0-g). Otolith organs physically responded equally well to linear acceleration and head tilt. Therefore, it is important to know whether otolith responses to linear acceleration were also given less weight. If so, the linear, as well as angular, component of visually induced self-motion should show changes in 0-g. If all otolith cues are discounted in 0-g, the following was hypothesized for the VECTION test: 1) the latency of linear vection onset to constant velocity visual stimulation would be shorter; and 2) vection magnitude would increase faster and with fewer dropouts than on Earth.

The OBJECT test used two types of stimuli to study the influence of perceived "down" on the visual recognition of complex figures and interpretation of shading gradients. Whether an item was determined to be concave or convex depended on how the visual system interpreted the shading. Hypotheses for the OBJECT test included:
1) For complex figure recognition and shading gradient interpretation, the critical factor would be subjective orientation of the "perceptual down," the exocentric frame of reference cognitively adopted by the subject, not gravity
2) Because subjects can voluntarily change their exocentric reference frame, the experiment should show that this change results in object recognition and concavity/convexity interpretation.

RESULTS:
Eight of 8 nominally scheduled sessions were performed early in flight. One additional session was performed on flight day 16 before a hardware failure that prevented further additional sessions. Data appear to be of good quality based on the initial evaluation. Results from this experiment are expected to add insight into how the nervous system establishes a new balance between information gathered from the eyes, inner ear, and joints. This could help in the design of the next generation spacecraft, in the testing of patients with neurological diseases, and in understanding the relative role of vision in human spatial orientation not only in space, but also in our lives on Earth.

experiment_title: Development of an Objective Behavioral Assay of Cohesion to Enhance Composition, Task Performance, and Psychosocial Adaptation in Long-Term Work Groups
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The overarching goal of this study was to generate experimentally-derived insights on how crew composition and trait-like cooperative motivation predict task cohesion, social cohesion, and biopsychosocial adaptation in long-term work groups through systematic ground-based research and development of a simple, rapid, and objective behavioral assay of implicit propensity toward cooperation, productivity, and fairness.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Investigate effects of group composition on voluntary cooperation.
  2. Investigate effects of crew composition on performance, task cohesion, social cohesion, and psychosocial adaptation in long-term work groups.
  3. Develop next-generation Task Performance Task (TPT) software.
  4. Extended long-term research of group cohesion, team performance, and biopsychosocial adaptation to several space analog environments; the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facility, NASA's Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) laboratory, and the investigator's laboratory using Planetary Exploration Simulation (PES).

APPROACH:
Investigators conducted ground-based experiments to systematically investigate the effects of group composition (gender and personality) on voluntary cooperative propensity in three-person teams. They also assessed the predictive validity of pre-mission TPT "social personality profiles" and the effects of group composition on performance, task cohesion, social cohesion, and biopsychosocial adaptation in mixed-gender "crews" participating in a long-term simulated space exploration task. In addition, investigators also developed next-generation software to advance the technology beyond their current prototype used for proof-of-concept/validation research into a broadly applicable tool with cross-platform networking and connectivity, enhanced usability/human factors features, extensive parameter manipulation/flexibility to maximize sensitivity, and integrated data collection and processing capabilities.

RESULTS:
Results indicate that the TPT/COHESION objective social behavioral assay approach is sensitive to team composition factors and temporal dynamics in both laboratory and field settings. Laboratory experiments reveal a potential risk of decreased cooperation and reduced cooperative resilience in majority female teams and teams with whose members are all high in conscientiousness. The TPT/COHESION tool quantifies "individual differences" in social behavioral processes over time at both the person and team levels, which correlate with subjective ratings of team cohesion. A single pre-mission TPT/COHESION session can predict several objective in-mission team performance outcomes.

experiment_title: Effect of Microgravity on Afferent Innervation
experiment_description:
Objectives:

To determine the effects of microgravity on connectivity of afferent neurons and inner ear hair cells and vestibular nuclei neurons, and characterize changes in innervation patterns of inner ear afferent and efferent neurons.

Approach:

This experiment was performed twice, once during Mir 18 (returning on STS-71) and once during Mir 19 (returning on STS-74). Fertilized eggs were carried to the Mir space station aboard a Russian Progress (227) supply vessel, and placed in an incubator supplied by the Institute for Biomedical Problems. On days 7, 10, 14 and 17, eight eggs were fixed and stored for return to Earth. The branching pattern and morphology of the afferent terminals in one ear was analyzed under light and electron microsopy. The brainstem and opposite ear were sectioned and analyzed immunohistochemically for neurofilament (NF) content, the S100§ protein, and synthesizing and degrading enzymes for neurotransmitters gamma-amino-butyric acid (GABA), and acetylcholine (ACh). The branching patterns of afferents inside the epithelia will be observed with NF staining. Changes in GABA and ACh staining will suggest changes in the afferent and efferent system respectively. The utricle-lateral canal ampulla (ULC) was dissected and observed with electron microscopy in order to evaluate synaptic density.

Results:

During both runs of the experiment, internal incubator temperature was higher than nominal throughout the experiment, and most of the quail embryos failed to develop as expected, resulting in low science return. During Mir 18, only one embryo developed to an appropriate age, and preliminary assessment indicated that most embryos did not survive past 4-5 days of incubation. After sharing viable specimens with other researchers, this experiment received only three partially intact flight specimens, preventing statistically significant analysis. However, analysis of ground control embryos was conducted, providing normative data for future flight experiments.

experiment_title: Optimizing Crew Performance in Long Duration Space Exploration: Best Practices for Team Training and Cohesion Measurement
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project addressed questions regarding methods and technologies for training crews to maintain crew cohesion and optimal performance during exploration missions Specific aims of this project were threefold: (1) identify evidence-based guidelines/best practices for training to maximize team cohesion, and team performance; (2) design, develop, and validate evidence-based instructional strategies to mitigate performance failures from cohesion decrements among space flight crews and coordinating ground crews; and (3) design, develop, and validate an evidence-based index measuring and diagnosing cohesion over the course of a mission. These specific project aims meet NASA goals and objectives by capturing cohesion levels shown to be integral to long-duration space flight mission success as well as developing countermeasures designed to mitigate the negative impact of cohesion issues. Organized as a multi-year project, primary tasks for the first year included the development of recommendations for training crews to optimize cohesion and team performance, mitigate negative impacts of long-duration missions, and measuring crew cohesion over time. Second and third years of the project focused on applying recommendations derived from year one research by developing, implementing, and evaluating instructional strategies to maximize crew cohesion and mitigate negative psychosocial impacts of long-duration missions. Overarching project goals were to: (1) mitigate performance failures due to a lack of cohesion between space flight crews and coordinating ground crews, (2) diagnose cohesion decrements during exploration missions, and (3) provide just-in-time training to improve any noted cohesion decrements during space flight.

APPROACH:
Semistructured interviews centering on a recent complex problem were conducted with seven MCC professionals. In order to assess collaborative problem-solving processes in NASA's Mission Control Center (MCC) with those predicted by the Macrocognition in Teams Model, a coding scheme was developed to analyze the interview transcriptions.

RESULTS:
This research project was dedicated to providing valid, evidence based training recommendations for optimizing and maintaining crew cohesion and team performance during long-duration space flight (LDSF) missions. The specific objectives associated with Project PEGASUS included: (1) Identify evidence-based guidelines and best practices for training to maximize team cohesion and team performance; (2) Design, develop, and validate theoretically driven, evidence based instructional strategies to mitigate performance failures from cohesion decrements among spaceflight crews and coordinating ground crews; and (3) design, develop, and validate an evidence based toolkit for measuring and diagnosing cohesion over the course of LDSF missions.

The first phases of the project involved investigating the characteristics of the LDSF environment, by reviewing the literature of team performance in isolated, confined, and extreme (ICE) environments. The literature review was organized by investigating three constructs—categorized as thrusts—that are considered important for effective team performance in ICE environments: (1) cohesion, (2) stress, and (3) self-regulation.

The literature review helped in the development of inquiries for the structured interviews with subject matter experts. These subject matter experts were astronauts with NASA who had previous experience with LDSF mission in the International Space Station (ISS). These interviews involved astronauts to provide insight into their experiences of these missions, including stress that they experience during task work and in the work environment, preparing crewmembers for space flight missions, and working with fellow teammates before and during the mission. Additionally, investigators gained insight about what conditions of training interventions they deemed useful for preparing the team for their space flight mission. Based on the literature review and talking with the subject matter experts,investigators concluded that Team Dimensional Training (TDT), a structured debriefing strategy that is associated with team self-correction, can help personnel in the space flight context for learning and maintaining optimal collective performance.

The conduction and conclusion of the field study investigated TDT in a Mission Control setting. This involved data collection, analysis, and interpretation of results. Findings indicate that participants rate the TDT debriefing strategy to allow for more open and participative debriefing, and also rated the TDT strategy with higher levels of learning value than the baseline debriefing condition. Additionally, findings indicate that the TDT strategy has resulted in quicker certification times for trainees in comparison to the baseline condition.

experiment_title: Direct Measurement of the Initial Bone Response to Space Flight in Humans
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The human skeleton undergoes a continuous renewing process. Under normal conditions a balance exists between breakdown and reformation of the bone material. There is evidence that space flight upsets the system and causes an imbalance, even during short-duration missions. Furthermore, the cumulative effect of multiple short-term flights may be similar to that of extended exposure to microgravity. This is a major concern for the health of astronauts.

Scientists believe that reduced mechanical work loads on the body in space induce the skeleton to discard bone it no longer needs. It is believed that the process of bone resorption begins almost immediately upon reaching microgravity. Researchers feel that the temporal relationships in calcium/bone homeostatic and endocrine responses will serve to prove or disprove this hypothesis. The purpose of this investigation is to define the response of the human calcium/bone homeostatic system to microgravity and gather data that will allow prediction of consequences for the health of astronauts.

Previous investigations flown on the Spacelab Life Sciences 1 and 2 (SLS-1 and SLS-2) missions (see experiment titled Pathophysiology of Mineral Loss During Space Flight) verified that the human calcium regulatory hormone system functions normally in space. The increased calcium levels in the bloodstream, from increased bone breakdown, cause higher excretion of calcium in urine and a decrease in calcium absorption in the intestines. A higher calcium intake - the therapy for osteoporosis on Earth - is expected to cause further urinary calcium excretion and increases the risk of kidney stones for space travelers.

APPROACH:
From 10 days before launch until 7 days after landing, each participating astronaut ingested a nonradioactive, stable isotope of calcium (48Ca) with each meal. The labeling was done to distinguish between calcium coming from the diet and calcium being resorbed from bone material. Samples of blood, urine and feces were collected. The samples collected during the space flight were frozen at -20° Celsius. The ratios of calcium isotopes (48Ca/40Ca) were measured after landing. In addition, the astronauts kept a log book, tracking their food and drug intake as well as exercise sessions.

RESULTS:
Bone resorption increases relatively early in space flight (3-5 days). Serum ionized calcium is increased as a result and remains elevated throughout the duration of the flight. The normal adaptive responses of a decrease in serum PTH as ionized calcium is increased occur. The effect of a short term exposure to space flight is still manifest two months postflight with increased bone turnover and possibly elevated serum calcium.

experiment_title: Starch Metabolism in Space-Grown Soybean Seedlings
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

This was the second flight of this experiment, in which the hypothesis that starch concentration in plant tissue decreases due to the effects of the space/microgravity environment was tested and possible mechanistic causes for the changes in starch concentration were investigated. Measurements were made of starch and soluble sugar concentrations, critical biosynthetic and degradative enzyme activities, localization and visualization of the starch grains, structural and ultra structural make-up of different tissues within soybean (Glycine max) seedlings, along with growth and biomass partitioning, and canister atmospheric components.

APPROACH:

The BRIC-03 experiment flew on STS-63 in February 1995. This was an 8-day mission. Two canisters of twenty-six soybeans (Glycine max) each were flown. One was frozen in space after 5 days and the other returned unfrozen for postflight harvesting. Analyses for these experiments included measurements of growth, biomass partitioning, gas concentrations in the canisters, carbohydrate concentrations and related enzyme activity measurements in the cotyledons and ultrastructural analysis of cotyledon, hypocotyl and root tissue sections.

RESULTS:

While overall biomass accumulation by the growing seedling was diminished as a result of space flight, the mobilization of reserves for the cotyledons was not affected, suggesting an increase in respiration in the space-grown plants. Analysis of the cotyledons frozen in flight revealed lower starch concentration, lower activity of the starch synthetic enzyme adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-glucose pyrophosphorylase and higher activity of the sucrose synthetic enzyme sucrose phosphate synthase relative to the ground controls. Other starch and sucrose metabolic enzymes were unaffected by space flight. In seedlings returned to earth unfrozen, starch concentrations in the flight cotyledons were not significantly different from those in the ground controls. However, ultrastrucutural analysis revealed that both the number and total area of the starch grains were significantly greater in the cotyledons from the space-grown plants, suggesting a reduction in starch grain density. Ethylene concentrations were twice as high in the headspace of the space-flight canisters relative to the ground controls. Ethylene, often produced under conditions of plant stress, may play a role in the observed space-flight effects on growth and carbohydrate metabolism.

experiment_title: Biochemical and Morphological Evaluation of the Effects of Space Flight on Rat Salivary Glands
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Studying salivary gland biochemistry and morphology in experimental animals can yield information regarding general hormonal and environmental responses, specific reactions affecting the oral cavity, and comparative aspects of exocrine gland function. Environmental stimuli such as the action of catecholamines are known to result in altered cell morphology and in changes of cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase (cA-PK) activity and cellular localization. In this experiment, the biochemical and morphological changes in salivary glands of space-flown rats were examined.

Approach:

Tissues were fixed and processed for electron microscopy. Salivary glands were trimmed, homogenized, and separated into a soluble and particulate fraction by centrifugation. The fractions were assayed for protein kinase activity, and photoaffinity labeled to determine the distribution of protein kinase. A photoaffinity probe (32P-labeled azido analog of cAMP) was used to determine the compartmental distribution of the R subunits in salivary gland cells.

Results:

Several aspects of phosphorylative protein modification in rat salivary glands are apparently influenced by space flight conditions. Endogenous protein phosphorylation was increased in the parotid and in the sublingual glands of flight animals, while measurements of cA-PK activity using an exogenous substrate showed no significant difference in the flight animals. An increase in photoaffinity labeling of regulatory subunits in the parotid cell particulate fractions from flight animals was noted when compared to controls. Changes in cA-PK holoenzyme association and subcellular subunit distribution suggest alterations in reactions which are mediated via cyclic AMP, observations which are consistent with the reported decrease in circulating catecholamines during simulated weightlessness. Testing human saliva or salivary glands after space flight may yield useful indices of cellular reactions related to catecholamine metabolism and thus afford some insight into possible stress-associated responses.

experiment_title: The Effect of Bed Rest on Bone Histology and the Calcium Endocrine System in Adult Men
experiment_description:
Objectives:
It is known that small animals show decreases in bone formation when the skeleton is unloaded and that humans develop acute disuse osteoporosis (bone loss) after prolonged periods of unloading. The purpose of this experiment was to determine the response of human bone to a brief period of unloading in a bed rest model for space flight.

Approach:
Eight healthy men, similar in age to astronauts, were recruited for a 7-day bed rest study. Their bones were labeled with antibiotics that have an affinity for bone tissue 7 days before bed rest, the first day of bed rest and the last day of bed rest. An iliac crest bone biopsy was obtained 2-3 days after the last bed rest day and examined for rates of bone formation and resorption. Newer assays that serve as markers of bone metabolism (formation and resorption) were carried out on urine and serial blood specimens. Diets were controlled and a metabolic study was conducted for a few days before, during 7 days bed rest and for up to 5 days after bed rest. The urinary excretion of calcium, phosphorus, sodium and potassium was monitored and calcium regulating hormones in the circulation were monitored before, during and after bed rest. Statistical analyses estimated the changes in parameters measured by repeated measures ANOVA primarily and comparisons of bone histomorphometry with data from healthy normal volunteers the same age as the bed rest subjects. The concentration of calcium and phosphorus in sublingual cells before and after the bed rest period was measured.

Results:
The response of bone, as estimated by markers, revealed prompt increases in markers of bone resorption with significant increases by the 4th day of bed rest. A marker of bone turnover in blood, osteocalcin, showed an increase within one day of bed rest, remained high for the 7 days of bed rest and returned to pre-bed rest values within 5 days of reambulation. This non-collagenous protein originating in bone proved to be the most sensitive indicator of the bed rest response. We found average rates of bone formation were reduced in 6, unchanged in 1 and increased in 1. The decreased was greatest in the most active subjects and the increase occurred in a swimmer.

There was an increase in the urinary excretion of calcium and sodium evident the 2nd bed rest day and continuing for the entire week. Reduced excretion of phosphorus and 3', 5' cyclic adenosine monophosphate on the first and second bed rest days was followed by an increase in serum phosphorus on the 6th bed rest day. Serum ionized calcium; parathyroid hormone and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D were decreased by the 6th and 7th bed rest day. We concluded that the response of the bone and the calcium endocrine system of healthy men after only 7 days was similar to results in longer bed rest studies and emphasized the responsiveness of the adult human skeleton to the biomechanical stimuli induced by changes in activity and/or position.

The concentration of calcium and phosphorus in sublingual cells, representative of epithelial soft tissue, showed significant increases from 81±13 to 109±13 for calcium and 1180±98 to 1577±187 Exa units after 7 days bed rest, a phenomenon that was later shown to be prevented by exercise in a longer 30 day bed rest study.

experiment_title: An Integrated Low-Volume Nutritional Countermeasure to Maintain Muscle Mass and Function During Space Exploration
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Mechanical unloading, an inherent characteristic of space flight, results in a loss of muscle mass and muscle strength. These losses threaten the integrity of space missions and crew health upon return to Earth's gravity. Nutrition-based countermeasures represent one of the few viable intervention strategies available during long-duration space flight.

The long-term goal of this investigation was to identify, prevent, and remedy defects in the metabolic pathway that contribute to the loss of muscle mass and function during exposure to microgravity. Demographic data indicated that the average age of shuttle crewmembers had increased from 40.7 years in 1995 to 46.7 years in 2007 with an increasing number of astronauts over 50 years of age. The investigators contended that the loss of muscle mass and function during space flight was facilitated by an age-associated, progressive impairment in the ability to mount an anabolic response to standard mixed nutrient meals.

In this study it was proposed that enriching daily meals with a low-volume leucine supplement would reduce the deleterious effects of microgravity on skeletal muscle and facilitate recovery during rehabilitation. The skeletal muscle unloading that occurred during microgravity would be modeled using an established fourteen day bed rest (BR) protocol. Recovery of muscle mass and functional capacity during a seven day rehabilitation period would also be examined.

The objective of the investigation was to test the following hypotheses:

  1. Bed rest would blunt the anabolic response to a mixed nutrient meal, facilitating a loss of muscle mass and functional capacity that would only be partially restored during rehabilitation.
  2. Enriching daily meals with leucine would promote protein synthesis and maintain the anabolic response to mixed nutrient meal ingestion. This would preserve lean muscle mass and function during bed rest and facilitate the recovery of functional and metabolic capacity during rehabilitation.

APPROACH:
Subjects, aged 45 to 60 years (representative of long-duration crew members), were divided into two groups. Both groups underwent fourteen days of horizontal bed rest and a seven day recovery (rehabilitation) period following bed rest. The first group (CON) was administered a placebo. The second group (LEU) received .06 grams of leucine per kilogram of lean body mass per meal for three meals per day.

RESULTS:
Markers of translation initiation, muscle protein synthesis, muscle mass and body composition, and strength and aerobic capacity were assessed. Changes in muscle mass were assessed by DEXA; strength was evaluated with standard isokinetic dynamometry. Stable isotope tracer methodology was used to quantify muscle protein synthesis pre-BR, post-BR, and post-rehabilitation. Ongoing analysis of muscle samples for measures of protein metabolism and cell signaling was performed. All subjects tolerated the supplement (leucine or placebo) well, with no complaints.

Primary findings were:

  1. Leucine attenuated the loss of whole body lean mass during the first seven days of BR compared to control subjects (LEU: -0.6±0.2 kg versus CON: -1.1±0.2 kg, p<0.05) and reduced or prevented decrements in knee extensor strength (LEU: -8±3% versus CON: -15±3%, p<0.05), ankle extensor strength (LEU: -13±5% versus CON: -20±5%, p<0.05), and knee extensor endurance (LEU: -2±4% versus CON: -14±3%, p<0.05) during 14 days of BR.
  2. LEU maintained both post-absorptive and post-prandial muscle protein synthesis (MPS) during BR; in contrast, BR decreased post-absorptive MPS (pre-BR: 0.061% per hour versus post-BR: 0.043% per hour, p<0.05).
  3. The insulin area under the curve during an oral glucose tolerance test was unchanged in LEU after BR (21±8%) but elevated in CON (52±23%, p<0.05) and whole body insulin sensitivity in LEU was significantly increased above pre-BR values after 7 days of rehabilitation (17±10% versus CON: -9±9%, p<0.05).

experiment_title: Effects of Spaceflight on Morphology of the Rat Adenohypophysis
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Spaceflight has been shown to have a profound effect on homeostasis in both humans and rats. The endocrine system plays a significant role in homeostasis and is particularly sensitive to the effects of spaceflight. The function of the adenohypophysis may have a strong influence in these endocrine changes. Given that changes in adenohypophyseal functions may lead to endocrinological changes, the purpose of this study was to comprehensively examine the morphological response of adenohypophyseal cell types to spaceflight.

Approach:

Immunochemistry was performed on both flight and synchronous control rats. Antibodies for growth hormone (GH), prolactin (PRL), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) were used. Gonadotroph and corticotroph sizes were measured and corticotroph cells were counted. Semi-thin sections of pituitary tissue were stained, and the ultrastructure was examined using transmission electron microscopy. Cellular distribution of mRNAs for GH, PRL, and propiomelanocortin (POMC) was determined by in situ hybridization.

Results:

Significant enlargement of corticotrophs was seen in flight rats. Nuclear and cytoplasmic size increased in equal magnitudes. Corticotrophs showed ultrastructural evidence of enhanced secretory activity. The expression of POMC mRNA, the transcript for the precursor of ACTH, was also increased. Gonadotrophs also exhibited a significant increase in size, but did not show ultrastructural evidence of enhanced secretory activity. No changes were seen in the overall cell type of any singular adenohypophyseal cell type. No evidence of cell necrosis or injury was seen in adenohypophyseal secretory or vascular elements. In conclusion, changes were seen in only 2 of the 5 secretory cells of the anterior pituitary, indicating that the adenohypophysis is resistant to the effects of spaceflight. Changes in corticotrophs and gonadotrophs appear to be a result of compensatory changes in the endocrine system, rather than pathological damage to the anterior pituitary.

experiment_title: Morphological Investigations of Skeletal Muscles of SLS-2
experiment_description:
Objectives:

A large body of data available today gives an adequate idea about changes in skeletal muscles of mammals developing in the course of their adaptation to microgravity. The data indicate that the lack of static loads and a reduction of dynamic loads on the musculo-skeletal apparatus in microgravity causes muscle atrophy associated with loss of sarcoplasmic and myofibrillar proteins. Functionally different muscles underwent various changes. Red muscles, e.g., the soleus and adductor longus, showed more significant changes. Upon returning to earth, though, the two muscles developed hemodynamic disorders that led to interstitial edema and death of myofibers. It was difficult to identify microgravity-induced changes because of the modifications associated with recovery and gravitational stress. This experiment will examine the changes in muscles caused by microgravity through dissection of rat subjects mid-flight.

Approach:

The soleus and gastrocnemius muscles were dissected and fixed. For histological examination, muscles were sectioned and stained with hematoxyline-eosine, iron hematoxyline and nigrosine, and impregnated with silver. Additionally, gastrocnemium samples were stained to differentiate myofiber types. Morphometric measurement of the cross-sectional area (CSA) of myofibers of various types in the gastrocnemius sample was performed with an image analyzer. Morphometric analysis of myofibers of the soleus was conducted on hemotoxline-eosine sections, without reference to myofiber types. Nigrosine and iron hemotoxyline sections were used to count the total number of capillaries and the number of functioning capillaries per 100 fibers. Samples were also analyzed using electron microscopy.

Results:

Histological analysis of the soleus of rats dissected inflight (IF) and on recovery (F+0) revealed a small number of atrophied triangle-shaped, gigantic round-shaped, and split myofibers. Histological examination of the soleus of rats dissected 14 days after recovery (F+14) showed sites of repaired myofibers with clusters of small newly formed fibers and a host of splitting myofibers giving rise to new fibers. Histological analysis of the gastrocnemius muscle did not reveal any significant differences between flight and control groups. Morphometric analysis revealed that muscle fiber CSA in IF and F+0 rats were in the soleus approximately 50% that of controls, and in the gastrocnemius was reduced by 11-22%. Electron microscopic analysis of the soleus and gastrocnemius revealed changes indicating atrophy. Differences in the gastrocnemius were less expressed than in the soleus.

experiment_title: Electron Microscopic Analysis of Archived Tissues
experiment_description:
Objectives:

To determine whether selected archived tissues stored in primary fixative are adequately preserved to warrant further processing and morphological analysis of spaceflight-induced changes at the electron microscopic level.

Approach:

Small samples (1-8 mm3) of the primary specimens will be excised, rinsed, postfixed in osmium tetraoxide, dehydrated and embedded in plastic resin for ultramicrotomy. Because the organs were fixed by immersion, a gradient of preservation from good to poor is expected for the superficial to deep portions. To determine the quality of preservation rigorously, for each specimen a superficial region will be compared with a deep region. Thin sections (70 nm) will be cut, picked up on grids, poststained and examined by transmission electron microscopy.

A set of specimens for each time point consist of 10 organs sampled superficial and deep from 5 rats. Kidney and testis are good organs to study because the organs are sensitive to poor fixation.
Representative light and electron micrographs will be taken and evaluated for morphological integrity. A summary report, including appraisal of the quality of the specimen for further scientific study, will be prepared for each specimen.

experiment_title: Pulmonary Toxicity Studies of Lunar Dust in Mice and Rats
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA established the Lunar Airborne Dust Toxicity Advisory Group (LADTAG) to evaluate the risk of exposure to the dust and to establish safe exposure limits for astronauts working in the lunar habitat. Because the toxicity of lunar dust is not known, LADTAG has recommended investigating its toxicity in the lungs of laboratory animals.

APPROACH:
After receiving this recommendation, NASA directed the JSC Toxicology Laboratory to determine the pulmonary toxicity of lunar dust in exposed rodents. The rodent pulmonary toxicity studies proposed here are the same as those proposed by the LADTAG. Studies of the pulmonary toxicity of a dust are generally done first in rodents by intratracheal instillation (ITI). This toxicity screening test is then followed by an inhalation study, which requires much more of the test dust and is labor intensive. We succeeded in completing an ITI study on JSC-1 lunar dust simulant in mice and are now proposing to do a study with Apollo lunar dust samples. This study will be similar to the study with the lunar dust simulant.

RESULTS:
Toxicological Assessment of Lunar Dust
To evaluate toxicity of dust particles in human lungs, studies are generally carried out in rodents. In a toxicity study conducted by the DuPont toxicology laboratory to assess five mineral dusts in in vitro lung cell cultures (epithelial cells and macrophages) and in rats, the investigators concluded that the effects of dusts in cell cultures do not correlate with the pulmonary toxicity observed in rats. Generally, pulmonary toxicity investigation is first done in rats or mice by an intratracheal or intrapharyngeal instillation (ITI / IPI). In an ITI / IPI study, a test dust is suspended in saline solution or another nontoxic medium, and is instilled into the upper respiratory tract of a rodent, where the instillant is aspirated directly into the lungs. Such a study allows comparative toxicity testing of the dust of unknown toxicity with reference dusts of known toxicities at several doses and several time points. Relatively small amounts of test dusts will be needed. However, dust administration by ITI / IPI is an unnatural exposure route, and an ITI/IPI study is normally followed by an inhalation study.

In the ITI study in rats, a native (unground) and two ground lunar dust samples of respirable sizes, prepared by the geology team from the parent Apollo 14 regolith sample (14003,93), were tested simultaneously with two common reference dusts, TiO2 and crystalline silica (quartz). The pulmonary toxicities of these two reference dusts are well characterized: TiO2 is low in toxicity, whereas quartz is a fibrogenic dust that can produce a spectrum of lung lesions. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists have set occupational exposure limits on both dusts.

Toxicity of Lunar Dust Assessed in Rats Exposed by Intratracheal Instillation
If an irritative or toxic dust lands deep in the lung on the alveolar surface, it can irritate or injure the alveolar epithelial cells that line the alveolar surface. This will trigger the cells to produce cytokines or chemokines. Some of these cellular mediators (literally, SOS signals) reach the blood to recruit white blood cells (WBCs), while others induce dilation of capillary walls, making them porous and thus allowing the WBCs and serum proteins to enter the alveolar space. These events are similar to those observed in pulmonary infection. In an infection, the recruited WBCs, particularly the neutrophils, possess destructive oxidants that can kill the invading microorganisms. However, in the case of dust exposure, oxidants have no defensive roles. These harmful molecules could be released from the short-lived recruited WBCs, especially the neutrophils, when they die; the released oxidants can kill the lung cells and cause tissue injury. Injured or dead alveolar epithelial cells would release their cellular contents, including enzymes. The alveolar fluid can be obtained by lung lavage to assess these biomarkers (or indices) of toxicity. Persistent inflammation, characterized by continuous influx of neutrophils, can result in a spectrum of lesions, which can be revealed by microscopic examination of lung tissues. Investigators showed that all five of the respirable dusts they tested caused dose-dependent increases in levels of the biomarkers of toxicity that were assessed in bronchoalveolar lavage fluids and lesions in the lungs. The toxicity of lunar dust was moderate, greater than that of TiO2 but less than that of quartz. As pointed out above, the surface of lunar dust particles on the moon could be reactive. However, grinding lunar dust by zirconia ball mill, which increased surface reactivity of the dust as much as 14-fold, had no impact on its toxicity. Three lunar dusts, ground or not ground, were equally toxic. The comparative toxicity obtained in the ITI study in rats allows investigators to propose an exposure limit of airborne lunar dust for humans.

Toxicity of Lunar Dust Assessed in Rats Exposed by Inhalation
As pointed out above, an ITI study is generally followed by an inhalation study. The latter requires a greater amount of test dust and is technologically more difficult to perform. The results of the ITI study showed that the respirable lunar dusts isolated from ground (either by jet mill or ball mill) and unground lunar soil samples produced comparable pulmonary toxicity. Thus investigators concluded that the jet-milled lunar dust is a good surrogate for the unground parent sample. In the inhalation exposure study, they exposed rats to air only or to four different lunar dust (jet-milled) concentrations (roughly 2, 7, 20, and 60 mg/m3) for 4 weeks or 1 month (6 hours/day, 5 days/week). The rat lungs were assessed 1 day, 1 week, 4 weeks, and 13 weeks after the last inhalation exposure. Pulmonary toxicity was evaluated in a manner similar to that described above. The findings, that a dose of 7 mg/m3 produced no observable toxicity, allows investigators to propose exposure limits for different exposure durations.

Summary of the NASA Lunar Dust Toxicity Study
Humans will set foot on the moon again and be exposed to lunar dust, and information about the toxicity of lunar dust is essential for assessing the health risks of human exposure, setting permissible exposure limits, and designing appropriate dust decontamination systems for a lunar habitat or landing vehicle. The present studies were carried out to acquire toxicity information on airborne lunar dust for these purposes. The overall results from the rat studies showed that the toxicity of lunar dust was moderate, greater than that of TiO2 but less than that of quartz.

experiment_title: Genotypic and phenotypic responses of Candida albicans to spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Modeling the microgravity environment, using rotating suspension culture bioreactors, has allowed investigation of eukaryotic cellular responses in a ground-based model and has provided insights into the impact of spaceflight on cellular physiology. Extrapolation of results from modeled systems to that expected in space is useful and informative, but evaluating the impact of actual space exposure strengthens the validity and interpretation of data from both environments. Using the Candida albicans (C. albicans) yeast system, it is demonstrated that simulated microgravity affects differential expression of several groups of genes, including those related to morphogenic transformation, environmental sensing and ergosterol biosynthesis; induces morphologic changes such as filamentation, biofilm formation and colony morphology; and results in an increased resistance to the antimicrobial agent Amphotericin B. The constellation of these physiological responses is consistent with a potential increase in the virulence of this opportunistic yeast pathogen. The focus of the current proposal is to characterize physiological outcome measures of C. albicans following exposure to flight on the International Space Station (ISS). The overall objective of this experiment is to evaluate the response of C. albicans to spaceflight in order to 1) predict the potential health risk posed by this opportunistic pathogen in the spaceflight environment, and 2) to further characterize the phenotypic and genotypic response of a eukaryotic system to conditions of microgravity.

APPROACH:
The Micro-6 experiment will provide new insights into better management and treatment of Candida infections. Candida albicans was chosen since extensive studies have provided a broad set of benchmarks, including the sequence of the entire genome, against which results can be compared. By comparing the cells grown in microgravity to cells grown in normal gravity, the susceptibility of the yeast to an antimicrobial agent will be examined. The equipment consists of BioServe's flight certified hardware: Group Activation Packs (GAPs) stored in a Commercial Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus (CGBA), an incubator capable of controlling the temperature between 8ºC and 37ºC. Each GAP contains eight Fluid Processing Apparatus (FPA) inserts designed to meet the unique requirement of mixing fluids in microgravity. Each FPA contains an isolated amount of the microbial culture of Candida, a growth medium, and a termination reagent or fixative. The experiment will be initiated by increasing the incubator temperature to 30ºC and activating the FPAs by mixing the Candida with a growth medium. After 24 or 50 hours, depending on the sample, the experiment will be terminated by combining a fixative agent to effectively stop the growth of the yeast cultures. After the yeast return from the three-week flight aboard the space station, changes to the genetics within the organism will be examined.

RESULTS:
A primary concern was the survival of the yeast stored in water until experimental processing and then, for the appropriate experiments, survival during return to Earth. As predicted based on our ground-based assessment, the yeast survived the pre-experimental-processing storage in water as well as the post-experiment storage during the trip back to Earth. The next basic analysis was to assess whether yeast grow more quickly when exposed to the microgravity environment, as has been documented for some prokaryotes. Our data would suggest that there is not a significant difference in growth between ground and flight samples (data not shown) although design of appropriate ground control conditions is difficult due to sedimentation or employing a rotation device. Perhaps more interesting is the suggestive, but not significant data, that the longer cells are exposed to flight, the slower they are likely to grow relative to ground.

Our preliminary LSMMG studies demonstrated that cells acquired a complex and highly convoluted colony morphology following growth in the HARV. In the Micro-6 study, colonies with similar morphology as was observed during LSMMG where not observed in the live samples when plated upon return to the Montana laboratory. Actually, the colonies derived from flight cells were more normal than those derived from ground based samples. Either exposure to microgravity was not long enough to induce similar changes (phenotype takes 5-8 days of continuous culture in HARV to observe, whereas cells in flight only grew 1.5-2 days), the phenotype reverted during the 4 days of gravity exposure before the analysis could be performed (although the phenotype was relatively irreversible when induced by LSMMG), or the response to microgravity is different than the response to LSMMG.

Our ground-based studies demonstrated that yeast grown under LSMMG conditions were more resistant to the effects of the antifungal agent Amphotericin B. For this reason, we evaluated the ability of cells to grow in the presence of the antifungal agent while on the ISS. Cells were then fixed on station and cell growth was quantified upon sample return. In addition, viable cells were exposed to AB upon sample return and cell viability was analyzed by flow cytometry. Flight samples were significantly more resistant to the highest dose (2.4 mg/L) of drug, similar to the results obtained in our LSMMG studies. Although less conclusive, both in-flight and post-flight samples showed a trend toward increased resistance at lower concentrations of drug (1.2 mg/L) as compared to ground controls.
