experiment_title: Cognitive Process for 3-D Orientation Perception and Navigation in Weightlessness
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Cogni experiment consisted of two parts:

1.) The 3D Navigation protocol was geared towards understanding how the human brain represents motion, especially the issue as to whether all three dimensions are represented in the same way or whether the horizontal level is treated differently. This part of the experiment is to help better understand what spatial references the brain used to build a mental representation of the path of motion.

2.) The Visual Orientation protocol was to examine if the brain gives priority to the gravitational axis when perceiving visual scenes.

APPROACH:
Implementing the two experiment protocols involves performing psychophysical tasks. Astronauts look at computer-generated images and then indicate what they have seen. The same observations take place four times: once before the flight, twice on-orbit and once upon return to Earth. This allows for comparison of the errors made on the ground and in flight.

3D Navigation
For this experiment, the astronaut is immersed in a virtual world on a laptop computer screen. She/he looks at the display through a mask and a circular tube that eliminates any visual indicators. The astronaut moves around through a sequence of tunnels that run through a three-dimensional space. Virtual motion can take place in two ways. In terrestrial mode, the astronauts gaze remains vertical in relation to initial positioning. When a tunnel goes up or down, the astronaut goes through it as s/he would an elevator. In a weightless situation, the astronaut plunges into all of the tunnels, looking straight ahead, in alignment with the tunnel axis. The picture astronauts draw on screen transcribes their representation of the tunnels they have gone through. The picture allows the observer to see if preference for this type of motion is really linked to the presence or absence of gravity or if this preference stems from the human brains specialization in gravitational environments.

Visual Orientation
In the Visual Orientation protocol, a line is presented on screen. The astronaut must memorize the orientation of the line. The circular tube removes all visual markers. After a moment, the stimulus disappears and a second line, oriented differently, appears on screen. The astronaut spins the second stimulus around to put it in the same direction as the first. Several conclusions have already been drawn:
- on the ground, the adjustment takes place with less effort
- during earlier flights, astronauts have demonstrated a similar preference for horizontal and vertical orientations in weightless conditions.

Gravity appears to be a prerequisite for this process of perception. In earlier flights, however, astronauts were strapped into their seats. The experiment on the Andromede mission should complete these earlier observations by studying the subjects in free float. The astronauts will have virtually no contact with the stations internal walls.

RESULTS:
Previous experiments indicate that the subject's performance is better when in an "upright" position. Results from this experiment show that human subjects might adapt their ability to represent internally complex 3D displacements. Additional information from this experiment can be found in the publication cited below.

experiment_title: Synaptogenesis in Microgravity
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Gravity plays a key role in the development of many biological systems. This study uses the embryos and larvae of Drosophila melanogaster (fruit flies) to examine the effects of microgravity on the development and formation of neural connections between specific motorneurons and their target cells in muscle fibers. Specifically, the ability of neurons and their targets to maintain connectivity during development in a microgravity environment will be examined.

Approach:

Both embryos and larvae at different stages in development were prepared, examined with fluorescent microscopy, and stored at eleven degrees C in order to arrest development. Specimens were housed on petri plates containing a culture medium in the incubator containment module (ICM) and launched on the STS-93 mission. The petri dishes were housed in seven group activation packages (GAPs) within the ICM. At specific time points in-flight, each GAP was heated to twenty-five degrees to restart development for a set duration. Prior to landing and recovery, the GAPs were cooled to eleven degrees to halt development. Cell-specific Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) expression methodologies were used to analyze the data. This allows targeting errors and subtle defects to be detected in a large sample set.

Results:

Hardware malfunction during flight caused the results to be indeterminate. Specifically, significant problems occurred with the Bioserve incubators. This same experiment was reflown on space mission STS-106. Results of the STS-106 experiment are still being analyzed.

experiment_title: Magnetically Agitated Photocatalytic Reactor for Water Recovery
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Magnetically Agitated Photocatalytic Reactor (MAPR) under development at the University of Florida is well suited for many water purification applications including recovering water during missions in space, removing contaminants from water in the home, providing drinking water onboard ocean vessels, supplying troops with drinking water during military operations, and providing safe water for disaster response when water is desperately required but not available. Additionally, the technology has homeland security applications for decontamination of intentionally poisoned water supplies and a safe method disposal of the chemical weapons arsenal. As sunlight can be used as the light source, this technique offers a unique and affordable solution to water quality problems that face developing countries. In addition to water applications, the MAPR could be designed for air purification applications including use in the airline industry, underground mining, or automobiles. Traditionally water has been purified of harmful contaminants by activated carbon adsorption or photocatalytic oxidation. Although both are effective, activated carbon has a finite adsorption capacity and requires replacement or regeneration. Photocatalytic slurries may encounter problems such as separation of photocatalysts from recovered water. The advantage of using magnetic substrates is that they can be agitated by an external magnetic field to provide enhanced mixing of the photocatalyst particles with pollutants, and to enhance exposure to UV light. In addition, because the magnetic substrates are controlled by a magnetic field, the recovered water will be free of the composite particles. Faster destruction rates allow for compact treatment devices, which are critical to the applications listed above. Furthermore, this innovative technology is attractive because of its compactness and ability to function reliably without the extensive use of consumables (i.e., very infrequent replacement of UV lamps and media).

NASA has identified a number of water treatment options that have shown promise in space. The water recovery system on any particular mission will be a collection of individual treatment units, with each treatment unit focusing on a select group of contaminants. The goal of this research was to develop a post processor for the destruction of organic compounds and microbes that may not be removed in water subsystems prior to the MAPR. The overall objective was to develop a microgravity-compatible, compact reactor that is safe and reliable that provides product water that meets or exceeds NASA’s potable water quality requirements. Furthermore, this innovative technology has a reduced ESM because of its compactness and ability to function reliably without the extensive use of consumables (i.e., infrequent replacement of the UV lamps or use of solar UV). The technology proposed herein is applicable for implementation on board the International Space Station (ISS), in-flight, or for planetary (e.g., Lunar, Mars, etc.) missions. The assessment phase of the project will quantify the reactor removal efficiency with respect to pH, conductivity, total organic carbon (TOC), and trace organics. Optimize the MAPR with respect to particle design and loading, number of UV lamps, and UV wavelength. Post processing of water from prior subsystems is crucial to ensure crew health.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
The catalyst synthesis process has been improved. A barium ferrite core that is commercially available rather than ball milled lead to a greater consistency in the catalyst performance. Double coatings of silica and titania respectively produced further improvements in performance such that a 10 mg/L phenol solution can be mineralized without photolysis in 7 hours with 3-365 nm lamps and 100 mg of catalyst.

The magnetic field of the MAPR has been improved to increase the UV exposure of the catalyst. To accomplish this, a permanent magnet has been added above the reactor to counteract the force of gravity, which tends to cause the catalyst to remain near the bottom of the reactor. The result of this modification is that the reaction rate of mineralization is more than double that without the permanent magnet. In the context of long-term space missions, this is a highly advantageous modification as the field can be adapted to the gravitational requirements of the environment by using a DC electromagnet or changing permanent magnets. If a permanent magnet is used it will not contribute to increases in the power requirements for equivalent system mass calculation.

The MAPR with the permanent magnet addition was optimized for catalyst mass, solenoid operating frequency and current using phenol as a model pollutant. The optimal catalyst mass was 400 mg with steep declines in performance if the mass is either increased or decreased. The phenol mineralization was relatively consistent for solenoid frequencies between 20 and 80 Hz above which performance declined significantly. Phenol mineralization increased linearly with current up to 1 A. Further increases in current did not improve performance, but increased the heat and power requirements.

experiment_title: Constellation Program (CxP) EVA Systems Test 2 - Metabolic Costs and Biomechanics of Exploration Tasks in a Planetary Suit
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Constellation Program (CxP) extravehicular activity (EVA) Systems Project Office (ESPO), which is developing design requirements for the next-generation lunar EVA suit, initiated a series of tests, working with the EVA Physiology, Systems, and Performance (EPSP) Project and the Anthropometry and Biomechanics Facility (ABF) aimed at understanding human performance and suit kinematics under a variety of simulated lunar EVA conditions. These studies included matched unsuited controls in an attempt to identify the specific metabolic costs and biomechanics of the prototype Mark III Advanced Spacesuit Technology Demonstrator (MKIII). A primary goal of the overall test series is to provide evidence-based recommendations for suit mass, center of gravity (CG), pressure, and suit kinematic constraints that optimize human performance in partial gravity environments. Results of this test series will also be combined with studies in other lunar analogs to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of these environments.

This study, Integrated Suit Test-2 (IST-2), was conducted in the Space Vehicle Mock-up Facility (SVMF) at the Johnson Space Center (JSC) using the MKIII suit because the MKIII is the only planetary suit prototype in NASA’s inventory that is compatible with the partial-gravity simulator, nicknamed POGO. The MKIII also has the most variable operational pressure range of the available prototype suits. IST-2, the companion test to IST-1 (2), had identical objectives and similar test conditions but different test points. Whereas IST-1 focused on level-ground ambulation, IST-2 focused on exploration tasks and inclined ambulation.

The purpose of IST-2 was to move beyond level-ground locomotion and evaluate suited human performance during exploration-type tasks and inclined locomotion. Specifically, the primary objectives of this test were:

  1. Identify the individual contributions of weight, mass, pressure, and suit kinematics to the overall metabolic cost of the MKIII suit in its 121-kg (265-lb.) POGO configuration, including the mass of the Portable Life Support System (PLSS) mock-up and gimbal, which is 29.6 kPa (4.3 psi) during inclined ambulation and exploration tasks in 1/6-g.
  2. Quantify the effects of the following factors on suited and/or unsuited metabolic rate, biomechanics, and subjective ratings during exploration tasks and inclined ambulation:
    a. Suited – varied suit pressure at constant offload, mass, and CG
    b. Suited – varied suit offload (weight) at constant pressure, mass, and CG
    c. Unsuited – varied offload (weight) at constant mass and CG
    d. Unsuited – varied mass at constant offload and CG
  3. Compare the MKIII at POGO configuration to the MKIII at POGO configuration with the waist bearing locked.
  4. Develop predictive models of metabolic rate, subjective ratings, and suit kinematics based on measurable suit, task, and subject parameters.

The secondary objectives of IST-2 did not determine the test protocol. Rather, they are other expected ways for which these data could be applied. They include the following:

  1. Define standard measures and protocols for objectively evaluating future exploration suit candidates and requirements verification of the flight suit.
  2. Understand specific human performance limitations of the suit compared to matched shirtsleeve controls.
  3. Collect metabolic and ground-reaction force data to develop an EVA simulator for use on future prebreathe protocol verification tests.
  4. Provide data to estimate consumables usage for input to suit and PLSS design.
  5. Assess the cardiovascular and resistance exercise associated with partial-gravity EVA for planning appropriate exploration exercise countermeasures.

APPROACH:
Subjects were recruited from two different pools of personnel – those who typically perform EVA suited studies for the JSC Engineering Directorate and a group of astronauts, many of whom have previous in-space EVA experience, selected to support exploration EVA studies. Suit fit-checks in the MKIII suit were performed on a range of subjects, and only those who had good suit fit were considered for inclusion in this study due to potential medical and safety issues. From this list, six male astronaut subjects participated in the data collection phases of the study. All subjects had also participated in IST-1 and had significant experience with both the MKIII and the POGO. At this time, no available female astronauts properly fit in the MKIII suit.

For suited testing, the MKIII suit was used as it represents a suit concept that provides the dynamic ranges of motion considered necessary for a wide variety of planetary EVA tasks within today’s technology level given other constraints that must be considered in pressure garment design. The MKIII also had an existing method to integrate with the POGO and allowed for varied pressure testing. Thus, the MKIII provides a valid test bed from which attainable requirements for future suit development can be derived.

Each subject performed a battery of tasks representing typical activities expected during lunar EVA performance. Tasks included, in the order of performance, are small rock pickup, large rock pick up, shoveling (biomechanics emphasis), shoveling (metabolic emphasis), kneel and recover, rock transfer, hammering, ladder placement, and busy board. This testing protocol was performed during all suited and shirtsleeve configurations except for the two suited conditions at 34.5 kPa (5.0 psi) and 44.8 kPa (6.5 psi). These higher-pressure conditions were not tested because subjects used the Phase VI gloves with the MKIII suit, which were believed to provide better manual dexterity but were only rated to 29.6 kPa (4.3 psi).

Each subject walked on a level treadmill for three minutes at his lowest walking speed while carrying a weighted load in front of him. Each subject completed three different loads of 4.5, 9.1, and 13.6 kg (10, 20, and 30 lb) for three minutes each. The 4.5- and 13.6-kg loads were round rubber medicine balls, and the 9.1-kg load was a rectangular sandbag. This testing protocol was performed at the POGO suited configuration of 29.6 kPa (4.3 psi), 121-kg suit mass, and lunar gravity. It was also completed during the shirtsleeve configuration at lunar gravity.

RESULTS:
For inclined walking, shirtsleeve baseline costs and the cost of additional weight account for most of the energy cost; the percentage contribution from both of these factors increased as grade increased. For exploration tasks, the shirtsleeve baseline costs were also present, but weight actually had the opposite effect and acted to decrease metabolic rate.

Variation in suit pressure at simulated lunar gravity did not significantly affect metabolic rate with either exploration tasks or inclined walking. Task type and the walking grade primarily determined metabolic cost. Although there was little to no variation from changing suit pressure, it is important to note that exploration tasks did not test at the higher pressures of 34.5 or 44.8 kPa. In addition, while the tasks often involved gripping and hand use, no task was extremely hand-intensive for long periods of time.

experiment_title: Inflight Radiation Measurements
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Continuous exposure to radiation is one of the major health risks associated with long-term human space flight. When the International Space Station (ISS) receives its first crew in 2001 scientists would like to be able to accurately measure the amount of biologically important radiation the crew is receiving so that they know how long they can stay in orbit without endangering the crews health. Current models of determining radiation exposure don't take into account the fact that the primary radiation dose is much different than the dose received by human tissue after the radiation has passed through the spacecraft/human body. This modified dose is known as the biologically important dose equivalent and can only be obtained by accurately measuring the full linear energy transfer (LET) spectrum. Measurements of genetic risk can then be made using the total absorbed dose, dose rate, and the LET. The following objectives were outlined for this experiment.

1. To correlate independent simultaneous space radiation exposure measurements and independent radiation exposure calculations made by NASA/Johnson Space Center (JSC) with those made by Russian Space Alliance (RSA)/Institution of Biomedical Problems (IBMP).
2. Compare the absorbed dose measured throughout the Mir core module with calculated values and determine empirical correction factors for the currently used free space environment models.
3. Compare the measured LET spectra for the galactic cosmic radiation (GCR) and trapped particles with the calculated spectra using the most current radiation environment and transport models.

APPROACH:
To cover all aspects of this investigation, four different radiation measurement devices were flown:
1. Passive radiation dosimeters (PRD) were mounted at six preselected locations inside the Mir core module and at six locations inside the shuttle, during STS-74. The PRD's were lithium fluoride passive thermoluminescent detectors (TLD) and measured the total absorbed dose from charged particles.
2. Each of the Mir astronauts wore two crew passive dosimeters (CPDs), one dosimeter designed by the U.S., the other designed by the Russian Space Agency (RSA). The US dosimeter contained both LiF TLDs and CR-39 plastic nuclear track detectors (PNTDs), whereas the Russian dosimeters contained only TLDs.
3. A tissue equivalent proportional counter (TEPC), simulating a 2 micrometer diameter tissue was also flown on board the Mir Space Station (Mir core module). The TEPC measured the LET spectrum at one minute intervals from which the absorbed dose rates, and dose equivalent rates could be calculated. In addition, just the absorbed dose rate measured at 2 second intervals was recorded.
4. An area passive dosimeter (APD) that contained both LiF TLDs and PNTDs was also flown. The APD was mounted in the Mir core module next to the TEPC.

Although not part of this planned investigation, data from the Russian operation dosimeter, called R-16 and the French-Russian collaboration instrument, Nausicca, were also available for data comparison.

RESULTS:
Although this experiment was scheduled for both Mir 18 and 19 missions a technical problem with the Mir interface payloads system (MIPS) resulted in the loss of all TEPC data from the Mir 19 mission. Passive radiation dosimetry results show that the Russian measurements were 16% lower on Mir-18 and 8% higher on Mir-19 than the U.S results. Dose rates across the Mir core module vary by a factor of nearly two, due to the differences in shielding and spacecraft orientation. The dose rates measured by the US and Russian APDs that were mounted at the same location are in remarkable agreement. However, these rates are lower than the TEPC measured dose rate at the same location. The TEPC data is separated into two components, galactic cosmic radiation and trapped particles for calculation purposes.

Trapped Particles
The trapped particle dose rate was separated from the galactic cosmic radiation component using the one-minute TEPC dose rate data. The trapped dose rate varied by a factor of 1.7 with an average trapped absorbed dose rate of 153.4 µ Gy/day. AP8 MIN model calculations were within a reasonable limit for measurements of LET > 4 keV/µ m, but were increasingly inaccurate below 4 keV/µ m, the area where the majority of trapped particles are located.

Galactic Cosmic Radiation (GCR)
The GCR rate is modulated by changes in solar activity. The standard diffusion-convection theory describes the modulation of primary GCR differential energy spectra very well in terms of the deceleration potential. The dose rate is a monotonic non-linear function of the deceleration potential that depends on the orbit inclination. The calculated dose rate was 135 µ Gy/day with a quality factor of 3.25. Although the model provides good agreement between the dose and dose equivalent rates, there is room for considerable improvement in the model calculation of the LET spectrum.

The combined GCR plus trapped proton absorbed dose rate was 299.3 µ Gy/day, dose equivalent rate was 781 µ Sv/day, and average quality factor of 2.61. TLDs mounted next to the TEPC measured total dose rate of 241 µ Gy/day. Because TLDs are inefficient at detecting particles with LET > 10 keV/µ m PNTD data is used to estimate the additional dose. The adjusted absorbed dose rate is 272 µ Gy/day, which is only 9% lower than the TEPC measured dose rate. If the crew exposures measured with the TLDs were adjusted for this deficiency the U.S. crew skin exposure would be 1130 µ Sv/day.

The results of this experiment show: (1) our understanding of the GCR environment is fairly good in predicting the absorbed dose and dose equivalent. However, additional work is needed in the area of radiation transport models to better predict the LET spectrum; (2) the AP8 MIN model does not predict the absorbed dose, dose equivalent, or LET spectrum of trapped particles very well; (3) the average radiation quality factor, 2.6, is higher than model calculations. The major cause of this difference is due to errors in the AP8 MIN model. The effect of secondary neutrons that the TEPC measures but are not included in model calculations is also a contributing factor; (4) if the only radiation received by a crewmember is natural (GCR plus trapped particles) inside the spacecraft, crewmembers can stay in orbit for up to three years without exceeding their career limits (1000-4000 mSv); (5) there is a clear need to improve the trapped proton belt models. These static models are inadequate for predicting the exposure for long term stay in low earth orbit.

experiment_title: Interrogating the Unfolded Protein Response in Microgravity-Induced Osteoporosis and Sarcopenia
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Age-related sarcopenia lead to a significant degradation in quality of life in the elderly and are associated with a high economic burden. Thus, understanding of the mechanisms behind this loss of function is important with the large ageing population of the United States, which is expected to continue to increase. As sarcopenia occurs in microgravity, spaceflight is an excellent model to study these mechanisms, which may lead to therapeutic targets in the future.

Previous hindlimb-unloading models and simulated microgravity illustrate the involvement of the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR), specifically the PERK pathway, in the pathophysiology of muscle loss (1). More research needs to be done to look at the specifics of the UPR in muscle, especially for effector proteins such as CHAC1. CHAC1 degrades glutathione (2,3) and blocks Notch signaling (4,5), two functions that suggest a powerful role in cell fate regulation. Oxidative stress is a hypothesized player in the microgravity wasting disorders (6,7). However, little work has been done to explore the contribution that Notch signaling may play in microgravity-induced muscle wasting. Thus, this work looks to further refine the role of the UPR, glutathione, and Notch pathways in age-related and microgravity-induced muscle mass loss. APPROACH:

The overall experimental approach to address the specific aims will be qPCR based. Using a protocol and primers previously validated in the lab, RNA from gastrocnemius muscle will be extracted from flight, ground control, and vivarium control mice using TriZol reagent. RNA will be quantified using a NanoDrop, and reverse-transcribed into cDNA using a high-capacity cDNA kit. cDNA will then be quantified using the pooled standard curve method of qPCR with a Roche LightCycler 480. Primers to explore the UPR will be Ire1, Xbp1, spXbp1, Atf6, Bip, Perk, Atf4, Chop, Trib3, and Chac1. Classical Notch signaling genes, Hes1, Hey2, Herp1, and Nrarp, will also be analyzed. The glutathione pathway will be queried using primers for the glutathione anabolic enzymbes Gclc, Gclm, Gss, and the glutathione peroxidases, and glutathione transferases, which are required for the use of glutathione. Data will be analyzed using the Roche LightCycler 480 software and normalized to the housekeeping gene 36B4. Comparisons will be made using a two-tailed Student’s t-test between flight and ground control samples, a p-value less than 0.05 will be considered significant. This approach allows us to query a large number of genes with accuracy to further refine mechanisms of age-related muscle loss.

RESULTS:

experiment_title: Microgravity Induced Visual Alterations and Intracranial Pressure (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Humans have been traveling in space for more than 40 years without clear evidence of visual impairment in astronauts. However very recently, it has been identified that some astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS) seem to be at risk for visual changes that may be due to elevated pressure inside the head (intracranial pressure). It is well known that there is a relative shift in fluid towards the head in humans during space flight and therefore these changes may increase intracranial pressure to a greater degree than previously appreciated. Intracranial pressure may also be exacerbated or transiently elevated by small increases in the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the ISS’ atmosphere and during strength training exercise that is employed to try and maintain astronaut’s muscle mass.

APPROACH:
The primary aim of this study was to provide novel data about the impact of microgravity induced central fluid shifts on directly measured intracranial pressure, and the associated inflow and outflow of blood to the brain, accompanied by simultaneous assessment of structural changes in the eye. Furthermore, investigators examined the above factors during small changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide and during strength training exercise in microgravity.

RESULTS:
Our recent experiments show that the human brain and eye are subject to large habitual variations in intracranial pressure simply by moving from the supine to the upright posture. Removal of gravity (microgravity onboard parabolic flight) did not pathologically elevate pressure in the brain, but does prevent the normal lowering of ICP when standing. Thus, over twenty-four hours on the ISS, pressure in the brain is above that observed on earth, which may explain remodeling of the eye in astronauts. Clinically these data suggest that circadian cycles in intracranial pressure should be maintained in astronauts and in patients obligated to bed rest. Moreover, in contrast to contemporary thinking, these data imply that, if chronic, subtle deviations in pressure behind the eye may cause optic remodeling and visual impairment.

experiment_title: In-flight Countermeasures for SMS
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space adaptation syndrome (SAS) or space sickness is a condition experienced by most crewmembers during adaptation to microgravity. It is related to motion sickness as the vestibular system adapts to weightlessness. The objectives of this experiment were to evaluate ways of reducing symptoms of SAS. The methods included physical processes to reduce conflicting sensory inputs and medication intervention to reduce symptoms.

APPROACH:
Several physical devices to reduce conflict yet allow crew activity were devised. The devices included a cervical load device and improved pressure gradient devices for shifting fluids. Prototypes of two designs were evaluated. They were small in weight and volume and self-contained. A crewmember with symptoms of SAS donned and wore the devices with periods of monitoring. Electrooculograph (EOG) and/or audiometric evaluation before and after wearing the devices were required. Stowage space requirements for the devices were approximately 1 3/4 cubic feet under a mission specialist's seat. Preflight familiarization of all crewmembers with respect to monitor use required approximately one hour per crewmember. In flight use of the equipment required only one crewmember as a subject.

experiment_title: Microbiological Evaluation of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project Chambers and Crew
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As NASA prepares for long-term missions aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and spacecraft destined for Mars, self-contained/closed chambers on Earth have become important test beds for microbiological evaluations. The insight gained from these studies directly benefits NASA as this knowledge is incorporated into the development of monitoring systems and countermeasures against microbiological contamination problems unique to long-duration space missions.

The microbiological study of these chambers and their crew also addresses many Earth-based concerns. Many office buildings are semi-closed systems, which can develop air and surface contamination. Commonly referred to as "sick building syndrome," contamination in these facilities may affect up to 30% of new and remodeled buildings worldwide. The United States Navy has also investigated the problems associated with microbial growth in semi-closed systems to determine the potential health risks during long-term submarine missions. While studies of office buildings and submarines give some insight into changes in the microbial levels and diversity created by an artificial ecosystem, all terrestrial models eventually have access to fresh air and water and can be thoroughly disinfected. The NASA closed-chamber studies provided the unique opportunity to evaluate undisturbed changes in microbial ecology and its relationship to the crew.

During the chamber studies, the primary objective of microbiological evaluations was to ensure crew health by monitoring microbial levels and changes in microbial ecology.

APPROACH:
In every phase of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) studies, the scope of the analyses included the air, potable water, and surfaces that the crew directly contacted. The surfaces that were sampled included not only smooth surfaces, but also carpeting which builds high microbial levels and is difficult to disinfect. In addition, the ability of viral contaminants to survive the water treatment system was evaluated prior to the Phase II test using bacteriophages MS-2 and PDR-1. Monitoring microbial concentrations and diversity provided a way to assess other problems that could affect life support and other systems, such as microbial degradation of materials and the potential fouling of process lines. The use of in-line coupons provided a way to determine both the type of microorganism in the flow systems and the effect of these organisms on in-line materials.

Evaluations of the air, potable water, and surfaces were performed using standard culturing methodologies and biochemical identification. Physical techniques were applied to retrieve microbial samples from carpets, rugs, and biofilm evaluations of water lines from metal coupons that were then assayed for microbial concentration and identity. The viral challenge of the water reclamation system used standard culturing methodologies combined with plaque enumeration to determine phage survival.

To understand the risk of infectious disease among crewmembers during the chamber studies, microbial samples were also collected from the throat, nose, urine, and feces of each crewmember upon entering and exiting. A second throat swab was collected from each crewmember for a viral culture. This data also allowed the identification of microorganisms that may not be considered normal human flora.

RESULTS:
The microbial concentration and diversification in the air and surface samples varied dramatically over time at any given sampling site. Evidence suggested that these changes were directly related to crew activities. These activities range from obvious activities, such as cleaning, to innocuous activities, such as walking through the chamber. Microbial contamination of the air, especially fungal contamination, was maintained at minimal levels, possibly resulting from the complex air revitalization system. In general, the potable water system was successfully disinfected with iodine. The average bacterial concentration was generally kept below the NASA specification throughout the studies. After 60 days during Phase III, the unexpected emergence of various gram-positive Bacillus species as the dominant flora suggested potential long-term contamination problems.

Samples extracted from carpets and rugs indicated high levels of microorganisms; however, the concentration would on occasion drop dramatically, possibly due to housekeeping patterns. The evaluation of metal coupons in a heat exchanger line indicated bacterial biofilm formation. The coupons were coated with a biocide that limited biofilm buildup initially, but inevitably did not prevent bacterial colonization. Lipid analysis of the coupons suggested viable bacteria were not detectable, but did indicate a bacterial presence.

In conclusion, these studies confirm a generally accepted relationship between microorganisms and other living organisms in a closed ecosystem. Disinfection and cleaning patterns changed this equilibrium as displayed by shifts in both microbial concentration and identity. In a small ecosystem, such as the chambers, the relationship is more dramatically affected by the actions of participants and thus more difficult to control. This understanding applies not only to NASA spacecraft, but also other small confined areas such as office buildings. Further complicating the ecosystem is the microbial interrelationship. On surfaces, these studies suggest a competitive inhibition that limits bacterial diversity. This finding could be of great importance in decontamination as a sterile surface may be a more fertile breeding ground than expected for different, possibly pathogenic, microorganisms. The number of potential microorganisms at any given site is large, and thus continued sampling and analysis must continue to gain a better understanding of the diversity of microbial flora, their interrelationship, and the effect of human activities on the consortium.

These studies also showed the ability of advanced water recovery systems to microbially purify water to potable quality, including the removal of viruses. However, the purification process appears to be susceptible to bacterial biofilm formation and potential corrosion problems. The appearance of gram-positive bacteria after 60 days during Phase III suggests a major flora change. Future work should focus on the effect of recycling water on microbial flora after extended periods of time.

Perhaps the most intriguing need for future research may be the changes that occur in the microorganism in a confined environment. Both bacteria and fungi adapt to changes in their environment, and genotypic and phenotypic alterations should be expected. Environmental stresses such as the addition of disinfectants or possibly the proximity of several microbial populations to each other could cause eventual changes in phenotypic characteristics including antimicrobial resistance and virulence. As questions of this nature are answered in closed chambers, the safety and health of the astronauts will be ensured for future long-term missions.

experiment_title: The Space Environment Causes Acceleration of Vascular Aging: Roles of Hypogravity, Nutrition and Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Data indicate that many International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers experience an acceleration of changes to their veins and arteries that are similar to those of aging populations. Emerging research is pointing towards linkages among cardiovascular health risk, carotid artery aging, bone metabolism and blood biomarkers, insulin resistance and radiation. This study is expected to provide insights into the mechanisms of cardiovascular aging and diabetes development. Specific objectives are to:
  1. Identify the mechanism(s) of increased arterial stiffness
  2. Determine if insulin resistance develops during spaceflight and identify the cardio-metabolic consequences
  3. Identify the interactions between cardio-metabolic health and bone metabolism
  4. Identify the interactions between radiation and vascular health in spaceflight

APPROACH:
Testing for this experiment will include an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), blood sampling (two blood draws several days apart), 24-hr blood pressure monitoring, a 72 hour data collection using the Bio-Monitor Smart Shirt, and resting ultrasounds of the arteries.

Preflight, between 90 and 60 days (L-90 to L-60 days) prior to launch, each test will be performed once.

Inflight, each test will be performed twice, once early in the mission between 20 and 40 days (L+20 to L+40 days) after launch, and again later in the mission between 30 days and 1 day (R-30 to R-1 days) prior to return to Earth.

Postflight, the OGTT will be performed twice, once between 9 and 11 days (R+9 to R+11 days) after return to Earth and again at R+6 months. Blood sampling will be performed three times at R+0 days, between R+3 and R+4 days, and at R+6 months. 24 hour blood pressure monitoring will be done twice, once at R+5 days and again at R+6 months. Resting ultrasound will be performed twice, first at R+3 or R+4 days, and again at R+6 months.

Some sessions are identical to sessions included in the Vascular_Echo experiment. When a crewmember is enrolled in both this study and Vascular_Echo, the sessions will be performed once and shared between the two experiments.

Ultrasounds of the arteries will provide information on stiffness and aging. Blood samples will provide measurements of circulating bone biomarkers. The oral glucose tolerance test will provide information on early-onset insulin resistance. Wearable sensors will provide accompanying fitness and activity information. Data collected by other experiments and shared will include body mass, radiation, medications, and physical fitness evaluations.

RESULTS:
This experiment is in progress and results are not yet available. This is an international experiment. NASA does not currently have an agreement with international space partners to archive their data in the LSDA.

experiment_title: Biotechnology Water Treatment System (BWTS)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Numerous cell science biotechnology investigations are conducted on Space Shuttle missions. During in-flight biotechnology experiments, media solution from a concentrated liquid media must be mixed with ultra-pure water from the surface to support tissue growth. Presently, the Biotechnology Program must launch all water required for experiment use during a mission. This adds significant mass and volume to each payload and represents a significant logistics penalty.

The purpose of the Biotechnology Water Treatment System (BWTS) is to produce ultra-pure water from the Shuttle's fuel cell water. This water, when processed by BWTS, can replace manifested ultra-pure water supplies, and thus significantly decrease the mass and volume required to support Biotechnology payloads.

The objectives of this experiment were:
I. To evaluate the performance of the BWTS in a microgravity environment.
2. To evaluate the set-up and disassemble/stow procedure as well as the in-flight nominal operation procedures.
3. To evaluate the ability of the BWTS to produce ultra-pure grade water to be used in the Bioreactor Cell Science Experiments for support of cell and tissue growth.
4. To return water generated by the BWTS, in a microgravity environment for use in ground analysis science verification tests.

APPROACH:
Pre-flight: The crewmembers received a familiarization session and two training sessions with a laboratory version of the BWTS within the Shuttle middeck training facility containing the galley.

In-flight: The BWTS and stowage items were removed. The BWTS QD is attached to the Shuttle galley auxiliary port using aseptic techniques. The operator did not leave the system during the time of water processing and collection in the sample bags. Water from the galley was processed through the BWTS and samples collected in sample.bags from from the BWTS outlet port. Both start and stop collection times were recorded on each bag. After 11 samples were collected, one sample was collected at the BWTS port. Following collection of the influent water sample, the BWTS, sample bags, and all remaining items were stowed for return.

experiment_title: Foundational In Vivo Experiments on Osteocyte Biology in Space
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
Bone loss due to the weightlessness of space is a major health concern for astronauts that spend significant amounts of time in space. The development of effective countermeasures to bone loss in space requires a detailed understanding of the biological alterations among cells that control skeletal homeostasis. Those alterations can take on many forms, including chemical modifications to the genome (epigenetics), changes in the expression of certain genes (RNA transcription), and certain small nucleic acid chains that regulate protein production (microRNA), and changes in the physical properties of bone matrix, among others. This study will explore the changes in osteocyte biology and bone matrix properties that are associated with long-term space flight, with the goal of elucidating new mechanisms to target for maintaining bone health during space travel. These experiments will provide insight into the limitations of ground-based models, and identify the biological processes for which they exhibit high fidelity to space flight changes. Moreover, new mechanisms fostering bone loss will emerge, which will provide new targets to counteract space travel-induced bone loss.

APPROACH:
This experiment will involve mice that have spent 5 weeks or 4 months aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and investigate changes in tissue level properties (bone mass, turnover dynamics, and material properties). Using an “omics” approach, DNA, RNA, and protein will also be studied to capture all of the changes induced by spaceflight.

We propose to take a different approach to solving the problems of space-flight induced bone loss. Rather than proposing to send individual genetic mouse models up to the ISS (e.g., Wnt pathway mutants, osteoclast mutants), we propose in this application to take a step back, and dedicate some time and resources to really understand the biology that is altered in the normal “wildtype” osteocyte population in true microgravity. To this end, we propose to measure short- and long-term changes in the molecular biology of the osteocyte that are induced by space-flight. As the scientific community finds itself on the cusp of a revolution in genetic/genomic/proteomic technological advancement, we will be able to capitalize on these powerful techniques to capture the key changes—some of which will undoubtedly be novel, in light of the above discussion of models—to the osteocyte that will lead to improved strategies for bone loss in space.

experiment_title: Water Offset Nutrient Delivery Experimental Research
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
There is a need for microgravity-based plant culture nutrient delivery systems (NDS) for both bioregenerative Advanced Life Support and plant research functions. The provision of adequate levels of water and oxygen to the root zone are the most crucial components deterring major advancements in this area. The dominance of the surface tension of water under microgravity conditions has often been found to lead to either severe water-logging or excessive drying in the root zone. Consequently, differences in plant growth responses between spaceflight experiments and their ground controls are expected based merely upon differences in moisture distribution patterns between the two conditions. This project will address the questions of "comparability of environmental conditions" between the spaceflight and ground control experiments for both a porous tube plant NDS and a substrate-based NDS by employing three different wetness level treatments for each of these approaches. It is anticipated that different pre-set wetness levels than those used on Earth will be required to support optimal plant growth in space.

It is believed that the resulting nutrient delivery systems will have a dramatic impact on the success of future space-based plant growth efforts. This technology has the potential to reduce the amounts of power, volume, thermal control requirements, consumables, and crew-time needed for the reliable growth of plants in space. It may also provide NASA with an early benefit in terms of fulfilling the requirements for a space-based vegetable production unit. Spin-off applications in the areas of home-based and agricultural hydroponic units used to grow plants under conditions in which water conservation is critical in as the water and nutrient solution is fed directly to the roots of the plants, thereby minimizing excess water which would be lost through evaporation.

APPROACH:
WONDER utilizes the previously flown Plant Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus (PGBA) commercial hardware with an experiment unique Porous Tube Insert Module (PTIM) which will be flown for the first time and evaluated during the experiment. The PGBA will provide the appropriate environment (e.g., temperature, humidity and light intensity) in which to sustain wheat seedling growth in microgravity. The PTIM consists of three pairs of alternating porous tubes and substrate-based NDS. PTIM also has an array of cameras on two of its side walls to monitor and document plant growth over time. The PTIM hardware will deliver water and nutrients to the wheat plants via moisture sensor feedback. The Kennedy Space Center Fixation Tube Kit (KFT) and Nutrient Augmentation Syringe Kit are being reflown to demonstrate watering regimes within a porous tube system and a substrate/porous tube system. Moisture levels within both systems will be quantified via moisture sensors located in the vicinity of the wheat root zones, allowing maintenance of each of the specific water availability treatment set points throughout the flight.

The WONDER experiment is designed as a sortie payload and requires 2.5 Middeck Locker Equivalents (MLE) in either the middeck (preferred) or Spacehab, and requires continuous power from ascent through landing. In-flight operations are limited to daily status checks and one harvest session planned for late in the mission post-undocking from ISS. The PGBA requires late loading and early access, because the wheat plants (N=90) will be initiated 5-7 days prior to launch. The plants will then be grown under uniform conditions until reaching orbit, at which time the crew will initiate the experimental wetness level treatments for the duration of the 10-12 day flight. Time-lapsed video will monitor plant growth over time.

experiment_title: Portable Bone Quality Assessment Device
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The weakening of load-bearing bones due to resorption is one of the major concerns of prolonged exposure to microgravity. We lack both an understanding of and a way to measure the more specific biomechanical changes at work. Because of the limited medical capabilities on a spacecraft or at any remote landing site, there is clearly the need for additional diagnostic tools that are portable, reliable, and easy to use by a person with a minimal medical background. Vibrational analysis (structural dynamics) appears to be a very promising avenue for investigation. The frequency response of bone theoretically contains far more information about the structural properties than conventional imaging techniques, which can only examine the apparent properties of bone. Under laboratory conditions, a hand-held acoustic device has been developed at Rice University.

This award winning prototype, dubbed Osteosonic, won the 2003 "Create the Future" design contest sponsored by NASA Tech Briefs and Emhart Teknologies and is currently being tested on human subjects at Rice University. The objective of this experiment was to test the portable device for non-invasive evaluation of bone quality in the space flight analog provided by Aquarius.

APPROACH:
Prior to the mission, two crewmembers received training on how to operate the Osteosonic. During the mission, a team of two crewmembers used the Osteosonic to become familiar with the hardware and software every other day throughout the duration of the mission. At some time at the end of the mission, one crewmember was given simulated symptoms indicative of a bony fracture. A trained crewmember, following the instructions of the Principal Investigator (PI) in the Experimental Planning and Operations Center (ExPOC), attempted to manipulate the Osteosonic device in such a manner that allowed the PI to diagnose the bone condition. The quality of training received, the ease-of-use of the acoustic probe and its procedures, and the ability to communicate successfully with the PI from the remote environment were evaluated during this experiment.

RESULTS:
NEEMO 6 Crewmember feedback was positive and provided valuable information to the Rice University team. Rice University added wrist, elbow, and spine data to their baseline database collection.

experiment_title: Computational Models of the Cardiovascular System and Its Response to Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Experimental studies of the cardiovascular system in humans, and even in laboratory animals, are necessarily limited in scope because of restrictions on the types of measurements that can be made. Often, the true parameter of interest cannot be measured directly so it must be inferred from other measures. Even when appropriate measurements can be made, the cause of a particular observation may not be evident because of the complexity of the interactions between the numerous components of the system. These and other issues can often be addressed more effectively with the aid of a computational model that simulates the critical components and behaviors of the cardiovascular system. Models depend upon experiments for refinement and specification of their parameters, but also illuminate and enhance the interpretation of experimental results. Investigators view the experiments and computational models as highly synergistic in that the value of one is greatly enhanced by the existence of the other. It could be argued that these are not merely advantages, but essential aspects of a study of orthostatic intolerance.

The primary objectives of this project were to develop a general, modular model of cardiovascular function that contains the essential features associated with the effects of gravity, and to use this model to examine the short-term effects of changes in posture before and after exposure to the microgravity environment. The objective of the currently funded project was to extend a previously developed computational model of the cardiovascular system and to use this model to investigate the short-term (0--5 minutes) beat-to-beat hemodynamic response of the cardiovascular system to abrupt orthostatic stress, such as head-up tilt (HUT) or lower body negative pressure (LBNP). The project aimed at facilitating the understanding of the physiology and treatment (prevention) of orthostatic intolerance in post-flight astronauts.

Specific Aims:
1. Enhance the current version of the cardiovascular simulation to better represent the short-term effects of abrupt orthostatic stress.
2. Verify the model and use it to investigate and evaluate various hypotheses of orthostatic intolerance, and to predict the effects of countermeasures. This objective required extensive collection and archiving of experimental data from collaborators.
3. Complete, document, and disseminate to other investigators a form of the model implemented in JAVA. 4. Apply the cardiovascular model to the clinical problem of intelligent patient monitoring with particular emphasis on establishing an enhanced research database of multiparameter hemodynamic data from intensive care patients.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Transient Response: To understand better the transient hemodynamic events elicited during transitions from the supine to the head-up posture (or vice-versa), investigators previously conducted a small clinical study in which ten normal healthy volunteers underwent an active change in posture (stand-up), a slow head-up tilt (HUT to 75 degrees over 55 seconds), and a fast head-up tilt (HUT to 75 degrees over 2 seconds). Arterial blood pressure and heart rate were recorded continuously. Simulation results were obtained by matching the model's response to the changes in mean arterial pressure and heart rate at the onset of rapid tilt. Once matched to these two time series, the remaining six transient responses (HR and MAP response at the conclusion of rapid tilt, HR and MAP response at the beginning of slow tilt, and HR and MAP response at conclusion of slow tilt) were then predicted using the same parameter settings. The simulations are capable of reproducing all major features of the transient response within the limits of experimental observations. Furthermore, the simulations are consistent in that matching the model's response to one stress (rapid tilt) allows investigators to predict the outcome of a different stress (slow tilt).

Parameter Estimation: Major effort was allocated to implementing an algorithm that allows for parameter estimation by minimizing an error criterion between model output and hemodynamic time series from astronauts and bed rest subjects. While other error criteria can be envisioned and easily tested, investigators chose to use a least-squares error criterion to measure the distance between the time series. The model is quite non-linear with a large number of parameters that can be optimized in order to fit a given data set. In fact, when optimizing over all parameters it is very likely that the resultant parameter estimates are very sensitive to small perturbations of the data, a phenomenon that is typical of ill-conditioned problems. To circumvent this problem, investigators implemented a subset selection algorithm for gradient-based, non-linear least squares parameter estimation. Subset selection allows for partitioning of the model parameters into well-conditioned and ill-conditioned parameters. The former are likely to be estimated reliably from the given data streams whereas parameter estimates of the latter are likely to be unreliable, and their presence makes the parameter estimation problem very sensitive.

experiment_title: Plant Metabolism and Cell Wall Formation in Space (Microgravity) and on Earth
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The purpose of this experiment was to establish differences between Super Dwarf wheat (Triticum aestivum) plants grown in microgravity and at 1 G by examining changes in 1) rate and amount of photosynthesis and biomass production (e.g. roots, stems, etc.); 2) cytology and cytochemistry; 3) composition and amounts of plant cell wall polymers, cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, lignins and proteins; and 4) if possible, activity of key biosynthetic enzymes.

APPROACH:

Two Plant Growth Chambers (PGC) were used in positions 5 and 6. Each chamber held 12 Triticum aestivum (Super Dwarf wheat) plantlets that were 2 to 4 days old at planting (1 day prior to launch). The nutrient pack system was used for plant mechanical and nutrient support. Procedures to load these chambers began approximately 4 days prior to PGU closeout. Postflight analysis was conducted on leaf blade, stems, root tip and primary and lateral roots. Each tissue was sectioned into 2-mm segments and fixed in 3% glutaraldehyde solution. The new agar-bag nutrient system used for this part of the experiment was compared to Dr. Krikorian's foam cultivation system, which had flown twice previously as well as on this payload. The principal investigators shared tissues in an effort to compare the systems. The plants were flown for 10 days, and then recovered from the Shuttle for analysis.

RESULTS:

Results from this study seem to indicate that microgravity does not affect cell wall architecture, i.e., organization, to such an extent that microfibril architecture is interrupted. Shoot growth was excellent. Root growth was adequate, but indications of oxygen limitation due to the agar matrix were evident.

experiment_title: Morphologic and Metabolic Properties of Single Muscle Fibers in Hindlimb Muscles of the Rhesus
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous studies on rats have shown that within seven days of muscle unloading, there is considerable muscle atrophy and a small increase in the percentage of muscle fibers that express fast myosin isoforms mainly within slow muscles. These responses seem to be dependent on the function of the muscle and its original myosin composition. Two questions have arisen from these studies; 1) what are the physiological signals that trigger these changes and 2) how do these responses in rats compare to other animals? The purpose of this study was to further define the effects of spaceflight on selected morphology and metabolic properties of single muscle fibers from selected extensor and flexor muscles of the Rhesus monkey.

Approach:

Muscle biopsies were taken from 2 independent sites (one was taken 90-98 days prior to flight, the other was taken 2-5 days after flight) in the soleus (Sol), medial gastrocnemius (MG), tibialis anterior (TA) and the vastus lateralis (VL) muscles. Fiber cross-sectional area and succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) activity were determined for individual fibers (50-80 fibers) in a 10 micrometer cross section. Fibers were classified as type I (slow), type IIa (fast) or type IIb (fast) based on Properties, type specific for myosin heavy chains. To assess differences in fiber cross section area after flight, a sample of 200-500 fibers were measured from tissue cross section stained with an antibody specific for laminen, a protein in the basal lamina surrounding the muscle fiber.

Results:

The TA muscle showed significant atrophy in both flight monkeys (flight monkeys were numbered 151 and 906). In contrast, the Sol and MG of 906 showed a significant increase in size after flight whereas in 151, the muscles showed atrophy. In the Sol of 151 there was a decrease in SDH of all fiber types, however, the decrease in size was limited to type IIa and hybrid fibers. In contrast, the Sol of 906 exhibited an increase in SDH activity for all fiber types and a size increase for fast and hybrid fibers. The MG of 151 showed a decrease in size and SDH activity in all fiber types. The MG of 906 showed an increase in size and a decrease in SDH activity. The TA of 151 had a decrease in SDH activity in the type I and type IIa fibers and a decrease in size of the type IIb fibers. The TA of 906 had a decrease in SDH activity and size for all fiber types.

experiment_title: Intramuscular Pressure During Concentric and Eccentric Contraction in Isotonic and Isokinetic Exercise
experiment_description:
Objectives:
The purpose of this study was to determine whether electromyography (EMG) or intramuscular pressure (IMP) correlates better with ankle joint torque (force) during eccentric and concentric exercise of the tibialis anterior and soleus.

Approach:
Ten healthy male volunteers, aged 28 to 54 years, consented to the study after familiarization of the experimental exercise protocol. The foot was secured to a Lido active dynamometer (for force measurement) with the knee and hip joints flexed at 90o to prevent the gastrocnemius muscle from being activated during plantar and dorsiflexion of the ankle joint, the exercises used to test the muscles. Under local anaesthesia, a catheter, connected to a pressure transducer, was inserted into the anterior tibialis and a second into the soleus muscle. EMG recordings were obtained by both surface and intramuscular electrodes. The exercise protocol consisted of 5 maximum plantar flexion contractions (soleus) followed by 5 maximum dorsiflexions (tibialis anterior muscle). The contractions were performed at 25, 50, 75, and 100% of maximal voluntary contractions (MVC) for both plantarflexion and dorsiflexion. Five MVC were performed concentrically, and five, eccentrically with 3 minute rests between contractions.

Results:
Soleus and tibialis anterior IMP and EMG correlated with ankle joint torque, or muscle contraction force in all 9 subjects. For analysis, the IMP and EMG data were normalized to percent of maximum for each dynamic exercise.

Linear regression analysis of concentric contractions, normalized soleus plantarflexion against force revealed high correlations (r2=0.937 for IMP and r2=0.716 for EMG; and for the tibialis anterior, during dorsiflexion, r2=0.948 for IMP and r2=0.802 for EMG. During eccentric plantarflexion IMP correlated well with force (r2=0.883), but EMG did not (r2=0.489). Relationships of eccentric dorsiflexion and force were better with IMP, but good for both IMP and EMG (r2=0.904 and r2=. 702).

IMP values reflect joint forces during concentric and eccentric exercises while EMG did not appear to correlate as well as IMP with force output during eccentric contractions. IMP is theoretically dependent on the tension of muscle fibers at the site of measurement while EMG depends of the size and number of depolarized motor units that remain constant with changes in the length or tension of the muscle fibers. Although more invasive than EMG and also characterized by considerable intersubject variability, IMP provides a more direct and accurate index of muscle contraction force for both concentric and eccentric exercise. Soleus and tibialis anterior IMP and EMG correlated with ankle joint torque, or muscle contraction force in all 9 subjects. For analysis, the IMP and EMG data were normalized to percent of maximum for each dynamic exercise.

experiment_title: Study of Low Back Pain in Crewmembers During Space Flight
experiment_description:
The Study of Lower Back Pain in Crewmembers During Space Flight (Mus) studies the development of low back pain in astonauts during space flight, with the objective to assess the level of atrophy in the deep muscle corset in response to exposure to microgravity.

In the weightless conditions of space, crewmembers often experience some form of lower back pain. This is extraordinary since, on Earth, back pain is associated with heavy spinal load, mainly a consequence of gravity. Scientists have therefore developed a hypothesis that lower back pain may develop without compression of the vertebra. The explanation of the problem comes from the fact that the lower part of the vertebrae, the sacral bone, has to be kept in position in the pelvic girdle (hip bones). And a deep "muscle corset" plays an important role in this process, with the tonic postural muscles being activated when getting up in the morning and deactivated when resting.

It is hypothesized that this protective mechanism does not work in space. In space crewmember bones lose calcium and strength, their muscles lose mass: therefore, it is thought that the deep muscle corset atrophies during space flight, leading to strain in certain ligaments, in particular in the lower region in the back, which may contribute to low back pain in crewmembers.

experiment_title: Morphological and Biochemical Investigations of Microgravity-Induced Nerve and Muscle Breakdown: II. Biochemical Analysis of EDL and PLT Muscles
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Carbonic anhydrase III (CA III) is present in highest concentrations in slow oxidative muscle fibers whereas fast fibers have very low concentrations, and the levels of the enzyme can be affected by a number of physiological perturbations. Although the plantaris (PLT) and the extensor digitorum longus (EDL) are quite gravity insensitive, it was of interest to determine the influence of space flight on levels of CA III. Conversely, parvalbumin (PVA) is highest in concentration in the fast twitch muscle and functions as a relaxing factor facilitating the sequestration of calcium in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. In view of reports that unloading slows the 1/2 relaxation time, it was also of interest to measure possible concentration decreases of this protein.

Approach:

Measurements were made of two enzymes, the lysosomal tripeptidyl aminopeptidase (TAP) and CA III, and also the calcium binding protein, PVA, in PLT and EDL muscles.

Results:

The PLT muscle in flight rats showed a 30% decrease in TAP; the EDL did not show a decrease in flight activity. There was no difference in CA III content of these muscles, except for the PLT of the basal group. The PVA concentrations of the PLT were not significantly different in any of the groups. In the case of EDL, only the synchronous group showed a significant reduction in PVA, whereas the basal, vivarium and flight groups did not differ. Space flight showed significant perturbation only in the TAP concentration of the PLT; the concentrations of the CA III and the PVA were unaffected in either of the two muscles. Simulation of freezer failure holding the frozen muscle showed that a thawed condition for 24 hours using fresh muscles did not result in a reduction in TAP or CA III activities, whereas PVA was reduced by 24% in the EDL and unchanged in the PLT.

experiment_title: Physical Activity Profiles of LSAH Participants
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The physical activity profile of LSAH participants can be gleaned from their responses in the Lifestyle Questionnaire (LSQ).

APPROACH:
The questionnaire has been used to collect lifestyle data from each class of astronauts and comparison participants since 1993, with an update in 1997.

RESULTS:
Of 223 astronaut and 820 comparison participant respondents, the most recent data show that 58.8% of the former and 72.4% of the latter report 2 or fewer types of exercise (as defined in the LSQ) performed in their usual routine.

When broken down into exercise types, the data show that 69.8% of astronauts and 58.7% of comparison participants report running or jogging as their usual form of exercise (exercise types are not mutually exclusive). More astronauts report weight lifting as an activity than comparison participants, while fewer astronauts report walking as an activity than comparison participants (56.5% to 28.5%, and 29.2% to 48.9%, respectively). Note that the LSQ question on exercise type does not specify any flexibility exercise in its list of possible answers.

In terms of frequency, a higher percentage of astronauts reported more frequent exercise per week than comparison participants. Almost 29% of the astronauts reported exercising from five to seven days a week compared to 18% of comparison participants. Conversely, a higher percentage of comparison participants reported rarely exercising (occasionally to not at all) as compared to astronauts (31.8% to 11.2%, respectively).

These data suggest that both astronauts and comparison participants may benefit from incorporating additional modes of exercise into their usual routine, as well as varying activities. A well-rounded fitness program has three main components: cardiovascular exercise (e.g., running, walking, swimming), strength training (e.g., weight training, plyometrics), and flexibility (e.g., yoga, Pilates).

Objectives:

The major stimulus for secretion of atrial natriuretic factor is increased pressure in the cardiac atria. The responsiveness of the ANF-sensitive, guanylyl cyclase system was studied. Guanylyl cyclase activity was measured in the liver, and enzymatic activity was determined in response to various ANF analogs. Formed cyclic GMP was measured by radioimmunoassay.

The activity of ANF-sensitive guanylyl cyclase was unaltered. experiment_title: Impact of Age, Genetics Variants and High LET Track Structure on Mammary Cancer Risk Estimates
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A key NASA objective is to obtain quantitative data defining the risk of carcinogenesis following galactic cosmic ray (GCR) exposure. Current radiation quality factors used to determine cancer risk for space radiation do not provide the accuracy needed, and debate exists as to the relevance of the experimental studies they’re based upon. To formulate better risk estimates, key data is needed including how age, genetic susceptibility, and radiation quality affect carcinogenic potential in irradiation sensitive tissues. Towards this aim, investigators used a novel resource of a large collection of normal mammary epithelial cell strains, from women aged 16 to 80, including many in the age of astronauts, to address these important questions. They obtained quantitative data regarding radiation quality effects; ROS and DNA damage signaling, radiation-induced centrosome defects, and enrichment of stem cell populations using this cohort of strains from various aged individuals. In addition, they also investigated genetic susceptibility, including how loss of p16 expression, a sporadic event in individual cells of normal women in vivo and often observed in breast tumors, affects radiation quality effects and centrosome aberration frequency. Additionally they analyzed strains containing a BRCA1 or an ATM heterozygote genetic background, representing ~0.32 and ~1% of the normal population respectively, to determine how these genetic variants may make them more sensitive to high LET exposures. These studies provide critical data, which can be used to model how genetic susceptibility, age, and radiation quality interplay in defining the cancer risk of mammary cells to high LET radiation.

The intent of this study was to determine how age, genetic susceptibility, and radiation quality modify the risk of high LET radiation-induced cancer. A cohort of mammary epithelial cell strains isolated from women of various age groups was used for these studies. Centrosome studies were performed using both a novel flow cytometry based assay, which provided a less subjective and more rapid way to define centrosome defects, as well as a standard microscopy-based method. Previous studies have revealed that changes in stem cell numbers are associated with an increased risk of cancer. Thus these studies assessed how radiation exposure and radiation quality affect stem cell populations, and whether age plays a role in the differences observed.

APPROACH:
Frozen vials of primary cells from eighteen individuals were obtained from an HMEC Bank at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), generated by Dr. Martha Stampfer. Early passage (p=2) cells were expanded and used for subsequent experiments. Approximately seventy p4 vials were frozen down from each individual’s strain to have sufficient cell stocks to perform all experiments in the study. At Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) cells were exposed to three different doses (0, 0.05, and 0.5 Gy) of cesium, Si 93, and Ti 300 MeV/u in triplicate. Each strain was cultured in a T25 or a T75 flask at BNL, exposed to radiation, and then one day post exposure, cells were either sent back live to LBNL or trypsinized and frozen down for analysis after long term culture post radiation exposure. At LBNL, cells were plated at seeding densities to enable analysis at 85% confluency at different time points post radiation exposure (3, 9, and 14 days).

These studies required extremely labor-intensive tissue culture, scoring for centrosome defects using microscopy, and flow cytometry determination of stem cell population changes. As a majority of studies to date typically defined genomic instability at early times post exposure (3 days) post exposure, investigators assessed centrosome aberrations at two later time points as well, weeks post exposure; these are time points likely more relevant and useful in modeling cancer risk. Their aim was to compare early effects at day three to the persistent effects of radiation exposure at longer times. They examined how centrosome levels are affected by the age of the individual the strain was derived from and the radiation quality of the exposure. They also defined the percentage of stem/progenitor cells in these various exposed populations at long times post exposure to define if radiation influences the growth of this population and how age may impact this endpoint. Furthermore, to gain additional information from this cohort of samples, the investigators also performed assays using a smaller subset to assess the phosphorylation profile of select proteins involved in DNA damage response and miRNA expression from various age groups following high or low LET radiation exposure.

RESULTS:
Genetic instability was quantified based on levels of centrosome aberrations. This work sought to address whether age was an important defining characteristic in describing the effectiveness of the various radiation quality exposures to induce centrosome aberrations. These studies revealed a significant dose dependent increase in centrosome aberrations. In assessing age effects, the investigators noted that the percentage of cells with supernumerary centrosomes increases linearly with age particularly when exposed to Ti as compared to low LET. For Ti, the slopes for low dose (LD) and high dose (HD) appear parallel, with high dose exhibiting an approximately 2 fold increase in centrosome aberrations relative to low dose, for the same age. The baseline for centrosome aberrations in unexposed cells shows a slight increase with age that is not significant. In evaluating the distribution of the number of centrosomes in aberrant cells, results indicate a linear increase in the proportion of cells with >3 centrosomes with both low and high doses of Ti exposure. Time course studies with assessments at day 3, 9, and 12 post exposure revealed that, in comparison to day 3 and day 9, there is a significant age dependent linear increase in the frequency of centrosome aberration at day 12. Interestingly, the fraction of cells exhibiting aberrant pATF2 foci post Ti exposure at Day12 decreased with increasing age, suggesting that the pattern of repair signaling is opposite of what is seen with centrosome aberrations. In summary, this work suggests both age and radiation quality affects the levels of radiation induced-genomic instability.

No datasets exist for the study. A final report was archived.
