experiment_title: Physiological Mass Measurements in Skylab
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Body Mass Measurement experiment consisted of preflight and inflight calibrations, Special Tests, and Routine Mass Measurements of the crew. The BMMD was calibrated a number of times during the preflight period with calibration weights that were later used for inflight calibrations. The preflight and inflight calibration data were compared and then used to calculate a correction factor for the gravitational force that influenced the preflight measurements. The Special Tests were designed to verify the operation of the BMMD and the accuracy of the measurements. The tests included BMMD Repeatability, BMMD Mass Stability, BMMD Subject Repeatability, and the BMMD Subject Stability Test. The repeatability tests examined the accuracy of the BMMD by focusing on its ability to produce consecutive and equal measurements for the same object. The stability tests investigated how measurement accuracy was affected by excessive movement of the subject. The Routine Mass Measurements were the daily mass measurements of the crewmembers and these were recorded each morning immediately after urination. The same type of clothing of known mass was worn each day and any extra items were removed from the pockets.

APPROACH:
The physical data on astronauts returning from space flight consistently shows a notable loss in body mass. Scientists hypothesize that the weight loss may be due to factors such as fluid redistribution, metabolic deficiencies, and high physical activity. Exposure to microgravity causes redistribution of fluids from the lower body to the upper body where it is sensed by the circulatory system as an excess and then excreted by the kidneys. Metabolic deficiencies may result since food quantities and opportunities to eat are frequently minimal. In addition, food packaging methods for long-duration missions often adversely affects the taste of food items. Periods of high physical activity may cause weight loss because they are often accompanied by heat and other stresses. These results concerned medical researchers involved with the Skylab program because the planned missions were much longer than any previous mission flown. Their main concern was the possibility that weight loss may occur during the entire mission and therefore result in a significant loss in body mass by the end of the mission. A significant loss of body mass could seriously affect the astronauts’ health during the mission and after their return to Earth. In light of these concerns, the Body Mass Measurement experiments were designed to monitor the crews’ body mass and to support several other studies that focused on nutrition, energy metabolism, and musculoskeletal functions.

In order to validate the experiments, scientists first had to overcome the task of accurately measuring mass in a microgravity environment. The Body Mass Measurement Device (BMMD) was designed to meet this objective. Since the instrument was a prototype, several functional objectives were outlined in addition to the primary objective of obtaining accurate body mass measurements of the crew. The objectives of the Body Mass Measurement experiments were (1) to demonstrate mass measurement without gravity, (2) to verify the operation of the BMMD, and (3) to support the nutrition and energy metabolism experiments.

RESULTS:
The data from the 28 day Skylab 2 mission showed a consistent pattern of weight loss for each of the three crewmembers. Weight loss began with the initiation of the flight diet which was started 30 days preflight. The inflight loss pattern was characterized by a moderate decrease during the first few days of flight and an accelerated rate of loss during the remainder of the mission. Immediately postflight, there was a transient increase in weight followed by a plateau. Preflight and inflight weight loss amounts (lbs.) for the Commander, Pilot, and Scientist Pilot were 2.2, 3.6; 3.7, 8.3; and 2.7, 6.6, respectively. These data demonstrate a loss pattern that is consistent with a simple metabolic deficit.

Food intake and exercise were increased for the 59 day Skylab 3 mission and, therefore, a different pattern of weight loss was shown by these data. This pattern was characterized by a relatively stable preflight period during which only minimal weight loss was noted. The inflight data for the Commander and the Pilot show a sharp loss during the immediate inflight period and another loss near the end of the mission. The data for the Scientist Pilot also show a sharp immediate loss, however, a gradual loss was noted for the remainder of the mission. Upon recovery, all three crewmembers experienced an increase in weight followed by a plateau. Preflight and inflight weight losses (lbs.) for the Commander, Pilot, and Scientist Pilot were 1.8, 8.7; 1.4, 9.7; and 2.7, 8.2, respectively. The patterns observed on the Skylab 3 mission indicate that fluid shifts may be involved in body mass losses.

Further increases in food intake and exercise were implemented on the 84 day Skylab 4 mission and as a result, one crewmember, the Commander, did not show a loss in body mass. His data profile shows a preflight gain, a small initial inflight loss followed by a gradual increase, and a postflight gain. The other two crewmembers had loss patterns similar to the patterns observed for the Skylab 3 crew, however, the overall losses were smaller. The Commander had a preflight gain of 2 lbs. which stayed relatively constant throughout the mission. The preflight losses (lbs.) for the Scientist Pilot and the Pilot were 1.0 and 0.2, respectively. The Scientist Pilot and the Pilot had inflight losses of 3.0 lbs.

experiment_title: Standardized Pre-flight Exercise Tests to Predict Performance during Extravehicular Activities in a Lunar Environment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The original Apollo missions and more recent extravehicular activities on the International Space Station (ISS) have provided basic information that can be applied to activities that may occur during future long-duration lunar missions. However, despite these previous efforts, significant gaps remain in the understanding of the more complex physiological costs of different activities in a true lunar environment. Recently a ground-based simulation of a 10-kilometer Lunar Walkback was conducted to better understand the physical capabilities of a suited astronaut in partial gravity. Unfortunately, this study was limited because of the use of a stationary treadmill that did not accurately simulate the lunar environment (i.e. landscape and terrain). To date this overall lack of physiologic data collected during true lunar activities or their accurate simulation has limited the ability of NASA physicians and scientists to predict if an astronaut candidate is physically capable of completing the multiple lunar activities that may be required during long-duration missions.

APPROACH:
The goals of this study were to 1) develop a mobile test bed to accurately simulate partial-gravity lunar activities, and 2) determine subject performance and the concomitant physiological responses to these activities, which allowed investigators to 3) create a series of standardized tests that can be performed in a pre-flight setting to determine the readiness of the astronaut to perform physically demanding activities during a lunar mission.

RESULTS:
Project 1: The purpose was to evaluate the relationships between tests of fitness and several activities that simulate components of Lunar- and Martian-based extravehicular activities (EVA). Seventy-one subjects completed four field tests: 1) a physical abilities test which consisted of six stations - stair climbing, forward-backward zigzag, ladder climb and descent, horizontal rock wall, lifting heavy objects, and side step duck/step over; 2) a 10 km Walkback test; 3) material transport field test requiring the loading, transport, and unloading of geological samples; and 4) a device operations field test consisting of tasks associated with equipment set-up and the operations of controls and valves. The relationships between test times for each of these tests and the following parameters were determined: running: VO2max, gas exchange threshold (GET), speed at VO2max, highest sustainable rate of aerobic metabolism [critical speed (CS)]; arm cranking: VO2peak, GET, critical power (CP).

Important Findings:
A) Across the four tests, CS, running VO2max, s- VO2max, and arm cranking VO2peak had the highest correlations. CS and to a lesser extent VO2max are most strongly associated with tasks that simulate aspects of EVA performance, highlighting CS as a method for evaluating astronaut physical capacity.
B) Arm cranking tests are strongly associated with upper-body dependent tasks, highlighting that the nature of mission tasks needs to be considered when evaluating astronaut physical capacity.
C) When comparing arm to leg responses, as expected arm responses were lower than those seen with leg exercise. There was a significant correlation between arm-cranking and lower body VO2max, GET, and the O2 at LCS. Backward stepwise regression analyses revealed that arm-cranking physical fitness could explain 67%, 40%, and 49% of the variance in lower body VO2max, GET, and CS, respectively. Results suggest arm-cranking exercise can be used to obtain an approximation of lower body aerobic capacity.

Project 2: The purpose of the second project was to determine the physiological parameters associated with the ability to complete simulated exploration type tasks at metabolic rates which might be expected for Lunar and Martian ambulation. Two simulated EVA field tests were completed in 1-g at two intensities designed to elicit metabolic rates of ~20.0 and ~30.0 ml kg-1 min-1, which are similar to those previously reported for ambulation in simulated Lunar- and Martian-based environments, respectively.

Important Findings:
A) All subjects were able to complete the field test at the Lunar intensity, but 28% were unable to complete the field test at the Martian intensity (non-finishers).
B) During the Martian field test there were no differences in O2 between finishers and non-finishers, but the non-finishers were performing at a greater percent of VO2max compared to finishers.
C) Logistic regression analysis revealed fitness thresholds for a predicted probability of 0.5, at which finishing and non-finishing are equally likely, and 0.75, at which an individual has a 75% chance of finishing, to be a VO2max of 38 ml kg-1 min-1 and 40 ml kg-1 min-1 both significantly greater than the current minimum standard of ~32 ml kg-1 min-1 for the astronaut corps.
D) Logistic regression analysis also revealed that the expected percent of VO2max required to complete a field test could be used to successfully predict performance (X2=19.3).

Project 3: The purpose of the current project was to develop an offload hoist system that is able to simulate the gravitational environments of expected future mission destinations that may be used to determine insightful physiological variables and responses to monitor in an astronaut in order to assess mission readiness and EVA performance.

Important Findings:
A) The offload system was successfully designed, implemented, and tested.
B) Proof-of-concept data were collected for ambulatory activities in Earth (1-g), Martian (3/8-g), and Lunar (1/6-g) simulated gravitational environments. Metabolic and ventilatory measurements were collected during ambulation at constant-speeds in each of the gravitational environments.
C) Metabolic and cardiovascular responses were greatest in 1-g and least in Lunar microgravity. While responses for Martian gravity were lower than for 1-g Earth, they were substantially greater than for Lunar gravity. These data emphasize the need for careful consideration of critical mission tasks and the minimum fitness required for astronaut safety and mission success.

experiment_title: Virtual Reality Training: Prevention and Prediction of Space Motion Sickness and Disorientation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The overall goal of this research was to determine if variable training in multiple orientations in a virtual environment will decrease motion sickness and improve task performance upon exposure to a novel orientation at a later time, as compared to nonvariable training. This study proposed to: 1) determine the subjects' orientation rest frame type as either visual-spatial (VS) or internal z-axis (IZ), 2) determine if variable practice training in different initial orientations will result in reduced motion sickness and better task performance in subjects faced with a novel initial orientation, and 3) determine if and how orientation rest frame affects motion sickness and task performance. Specific responses that were examined included latency to the onset of vection (for classification of orientation rest frame), motion sickness symptoms and symptom severity, and task performance as measured by accuracy and time to task completion.

Space Motion Sickness (SMS) and vestibular disturbances can impact space flight crew productivity and safety. The potentially debilitating effects of SMS during the initial days of flight cause certain critical operations such as docking to the International Space Station (ISS) and extravehicular activity (EVA) to be delayed for several days. Research suggests that orientation rest frame, which can be determined by latency to vection (perceived self-motion) onset, may be a predictive factor for SMS. Subjects with shorter latencies have been classified as having a VS frame orientation of reference, while those with longer latencies have been classified as having a IZ frame of reference. Research also suggests that training devices, such as those using virtual reality, can partially simulate the sensory rearrangements present in microgravity. The plasticity of the human central nervous system makes it likely that subjects will eventually adapt to the novel sensory conditions present in a virtual environment. This study was designed to provide important information that will support the long range goal of developing preflight training procedures, (using virtual environments), that will allow astronauts to adapt to sensory conditions similar to microgravity before the flight occurs. Adaptation to these conditions is expected to reduce SMS, and sensorimotor and orientation disturbances on orbit.

APPROACH:
Subjects were assigned to either a variable training (VT) or nonvariable training (NVT) condition to perform a simple navigation and switch activation task in a virtual space station. VT subjects performed the task starting in several different orientations, whereas NVT subjects always performed the task starting in the same orientation. On a separate day, all subjects then performed the same task in a transfer of training session starting from a novel orientation.

RESULTS:
During the study, a number of important steps related to the research proposal have been accomplished. Most importantly, an experimental, titled “Virtual Reality Training for Spatial Orientation in Unfamiliar Environments” was completed using 40 subjects from the NASA JSC Human Test Subject Facility, to examine the ability to predict and prevent the occurrence of motion sickness and disorientation during exposure to a virtual environment similar to space flight. During the Spring of 2003, data collection was completed on 30 subjects, and upon subsequent data analysis, data from an additional 10 subjects was completed in November.

In addition to examining the feasibility of using virtual reality training for predicting and preventing SMS and disorientation, research into spacecraft design requirements to reduce vestibular disturbances upon return from a longer mission was completed. While SMS is the primary concern for short-duration missions, the effect of vestibular disturbances during landing may be particularly problematic following long-duration missions such as returning from the ISS, or on a Mars mission, where the vestibular system would likely have adapted from 1g, to 0g, to 0.38g, and then the reverse for the return trip. Due to the combination of the perceptual illusions inherent in flying, vestibular adaptation to different gravity environments, diminished muscle strength and proprioception, the many different directions of acceleration during reentry and landing, and the design of the spacecraft, vision, attitude, position, and motion perception will almost certainly be affected and could impair the astronaut’s ability to pilot the vehicle. Design aspects such as seat position and instrument and window location must be taken into account to provide a spacecraft environment to ensure a safe landing.

experiment_title: Exercise Countermeasures Demonstration Projects During The Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project Phases IIa and III
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The purpose of this demonstration project was to assess the compliance of crewmembers to perform exercise countermeasures similar to those planned for use during stays aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and to assess the outcome of performing these countermeasures.

The objectives of the Exercise Countermeasures Demonstration Projects were:

  • to assist in the development and evaluation of exercise testing and prescription methods being considered for ISS

  • to provide realistic perturbations of carbon dioxide production and oxygen utilization as anticipated during ISS to challenge the environmental control systems.

    Four crewmembers participated in each of two chamber tests. Phase IIa was a 60-day chamber test while the Phase III test had a duration of 91 days. Previous chamber studies were conducted in which exercise was performed, but these two projects were the first in which specific exercise prescriptions were developed for the crewmembers and the outcomes of the exercise protocols were measured. These two chamber studies served as ground-based test beds for exercise countermeasure procedure development in support of future activities for the crews of the International Space Station (ISS).

    APPROACH:

    In each project, eight crewmembers were selected for participation, four as prime and four as back-up. Crewmembers were screened for health status by means of a modified Air Force Class III Physical and a graded treadmill exercise test to volitional fatigue with 12-lead electrocardiogram. Subjects received written and verbal explanation of the procedures specific to the exercise countermeasures demonstration project and signed informed consent documents confirming their understanding and acceptance. All testing procedures and protocols were reviewed and approved by the NASA Johnson Space Center Institutional Review Board. All pre and postchamber testing, as well as prechamber training, were performed in the NASA Johnson Space Center Exercise Physiology Laboratory. Eventually, four crewmembers entered the chamber in each study and remained there for the duration of the test project. In Phase IIa, the crew consisted of three men and one woman. In Phase III, the crew consisted of two men and two women. Data presented here are from the four prime crewmembers only from each of the two chamber tests.

    For the 60-day Phase IIa test, the characteristics of the prime crewmembers, three males and one female, were: age - 31 ± 4 years; height - 175 ± 5 cm; and body mass - 70.4 ± 10.9 kg. Prior to entry into the chamber, crewmembers completed both a graded maximal cycle exercise test to volitional fatigue and a submaximal cycle ergometer exercise protocol. Crewmembers also received training on the aerobic and resistance exercise countermeasures prior to chamber entry. At the conclusion of the chamber test, the four crewmembers repeated the maximal cycle exercise test.

    The 91-day Phase III test provided an opportunity to evaluate potential exercise countermeasure and testing procedures during an even longer, 91-day chamber stay. In Phase III, two men and two women served as crewmembers with a mean (± standard deviation (SD)) age of 34 ± 6 years, height of 173.5 ± 11.9 cm, and body mass of 68.3 ± 10.4 kg.

    The testing and monitoring procedures were similar to those used in Phase IIa, except that isokinetic tests of muscle strength and endurance were added to the testing regime. Prechamber testing included maximal cycle and treadmill tests to volitional fatigue, two submaximal cycle ergometer exercise tests, training sessions for the cycle and treadmill aerobic exercise countermeasures, and two isokinetic muscular strength and endurance tests. Subjects also received two training sessions on the CES, the same resistance exercise training device used in Phase IIa. During the chamber stay, crewmembers performed the submaximal cycle exercise test biweekly on the seventh day of the week. After chamber stay, crewmembers returned to the laboratory for the maximal cycle and isokinetic strength and endurance tests.

    During the chamber test, on alternate days the crewmembers completed the aerobic and the resistive countermeasures three times per week. In several instances, exercise was delayed or cancelled due to malfunction of the environmental control systems. Three times during the 60-day period, on days 15, 30, and 58, crewmembers completed the submaximal exercise test in place of the aerobic exercise training to assess their training status.

    The aerobic exercise testing protocols chosen for this project are similar to those proposed for use in the Space Medicine Project (SMP) on the ISS as a means to monitor crew health. Similarly, the exercise countermeasures, both aerobic and resistive, were similar to those suggested for use on the ISS to maintain crew health. However, no pre to postchamber resistance exercise testing was performed during the Phase IIa test.

    During the 60-day Phase IIa project, crewmembers exercised for six consecutive days alternating between aerobic and resistive exercise, and rested on the seventh day. On the aerobic exercise days, subjects exercised for 30 minutes on an electronically braked cycle ergometer using an interval protocol. On the resistive exercise days, crewmembers performed five major multijoint resistive exercises (bench press, seated press, lat pull, squats, and heel raises) in a concentric-only mode, targeting those muscle groups and bones that are believed to be most severely affected by space flight.

    During the 91-day Phase III project, the frequency of the exercise countermeasures was increased to include both aerobic and resistive exercises each day for six days, with rest on the seventh day. For aerobic exercise, the cycle protocol was performed three days/week similar to the Phase IIa project. However a steady-state treadmill protocol was added on the remaining three exercise days. The same resistance exercise protocol was performed as in Phase IIa, except that the upper- and lower-body exercises were divided and performed on separate days.

    More information about these tests

    RESULTS:

    60-day Phase IIa project: subjects performed maximal efforts with each repetition. Both exercise protocols were well tolerated by the subjects, demonstrated by 98% compliance with the aerobic exercise prescription and 91% adherence to the resistive exercise prescription. After 60 days, the crewmembers improved their peak aerobic capacity by an average of 7%. Strength gains during all exercises were noted.

    91-day Phase III project: three of the four subjects tolerated the aerobic exercise training well. One crewmember developed knee pain in the final third of the chamber test and did not perform further cycle or lower-body resistive exercises for the remainder of the study. The three crewmembers who participated in all countermeasures and postchamber testing had an average increase in aerobic capacity of 14%. Of these remaining three crewmembers, one consistently refrained from resistive exercise one day per week. Strength gains were not consistently obtained during this study. These results, showing little or no change in muscle strength while demonstrating some improvement in aerobic capacity, may be consistent with an overtraining syndrome.

    Taken together, the results from these two studies suggest that the prescribed aerobic and resistive exercises generally were well tolerated. However, combining both resistive and aerobic exercises with only one day of rest each week may result in a decreased benefit of strength training. Periodization of exercise protocols and/or reduction of exercise intensity or frequency may be desired to obtain optimum increases in both aerobic and resistive exercise capacities.

    These LMLSTP studies have allowed preliminary evaluation of potential exercise testing and countermeasure procedures. Lessons learned from these projects may be applied to space flight with the important consideration that training responses in a 1-g environment may not be exactly representative of space flight; exercise in the chamber projects were intended to increase exercise capacity, while exercise countermeasures in a microgravity environment are intended to maintain overall conditioning. Additionally, exercise performed within the constraints imposed by microgravity (e.g., subject loading during treadmill exercise) or with the actual flight hardware may provide a different training stimulus. Further, thresholds for training and over training may differ between the two conditions and vary among the target organ systems. Data collected during actual space flights will be required to provide the final confirmation of our countermeasure programs.

    The data collected during these chamber studies also must be considered extremely preliminary due to the small number of subjects. In many cases, appropriate statistical analyses could not be performed due to the limited sample size.

    With these considerations, preliminary observations from these studies are:

    • The aerobic and resistive countermeasures tested in these projects provided a training stimulus when performed on separate days (Phase IIa). Further work is needed to explore a possible negative effect on strength training when aerobic exercise was performed on the same day as resistive training (Phase III).
    • Most crewmembers preferred treadmill exercise over cycle exercise. This has been reported also by long-duration space flight crews. However, due to effects of microgravity on treadmill exercise loading, exercise prescriptions and testing protocols can be more accurately applied on a cycle.
    • Compliance to our exercise prescriptions was very good, but some discontent was evident from the postchamber debriefs. Increasing the variety of exercise protocols, exercise devices and addition of virtual reality head gear or other forms of entertainment during exercise may improve exercise compliance. Almost all subjects reported a desire for more variety of exercise prescriptions.
    • The lack of strength increase may suggest that the rest periods between sets that were too long or that there was an overtraining response in the Phase III crew with the increased aerobic exercise volume. In future studies and during space flight, crew exercise time should be protected to optimize the effect of training. Also, the addition of muscle damage markers to future training studies may help to elucidate this issue.
    • The exercise logging materials used in this study and the feedback from these subjects has been used in developing the computer-based flight logs currently planned for the ISS.

experiment_title: A Novel Biodosimetry Method For Monitoring Radiation-Induced Genetic Damage
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
For extended space missions, exposure to hazardous radiation from galactic cosmic radiation and solar particle events poses a serious threat to the health of the astronauts. Dosimeters measure radiation dose received but not its biological effects or individual differences in radiation sensitivity. Accurate methods for measuring the extent of an individual’s genetic damage resulting from accumulated radiation exposure is critical for estimating personal health risks and need for countermeasures. The overall goal of this study was to investigate the efficacy of a novel biodosimetry method for monitoring mutational load resulting from radiation-induced mutations in repetitive DNA sequences. Repetitive sequences constitute nearly one third of the human genome and some have been shown to be extremely sensitive to radiation-induced mutations. Most repetitive sequences are in non-coding regions of the genome and, therefore, alterations in these loci are usually not deleterious to the survival of the host cell. Thus, mutations in non-coding repetitive sequences can accumulate, providing a stable molecular record of DNA damage from all past exposures. Progenitor stem cells are long lived and continually divide producing identical duplicate progeny cells. Mutations in repetitive DNA loci in progenitor stem cells will accumulate and through analysis of progeny blood or sperm cells can serve as biological sensors to monitor radiation-induced genetic damage.

APPROACH:
To test this hypothesis the investigators chose the following measures: (a) screen a broad range of highly mutable repetitive DNA sequences to identify genetic loci most sensitive to high-LET radiation-induced mutations, (b) show that radiation-induced mutations in progenitor stem cells are cumulative and that mutational load can be quantitatively measured by sampling a population of single or small pools of progeny blood or sperm cells for changes in repetitive DNA sequences, and (c) investigate possible mechanisms causing radiation-induced genomic instability in repetitive DNA loci. Knowledge obtained from completion of this proposal will determine the efficacy of a novel quantitative method for monitoring radiation-induced mutational load that would be applicable to both mouse models and humans. Mutational load profiling, through analysis of changes in repetitive DNA sequences, is a simple, non-invasive and generalized approach for monitoring an individual's cumulative record of radiation-induced mutations that would be useful in predicting and minimizing health risks.

RESULTS:
Microsatellite repeat markers were identified that exhibited a linear dose response up to 1 Gy of 1 GeV/nucleon 56Fe ions and 137Cs gamma rays in mouse and human cells. Short tandem repeats on the Y chromosome and mononucleotide repeats on autosomal chromosomes exhibited significant increases in mutations at =0.5 Gy of 56Fe ions with frequencies averaging 4.3-10.3 x 10-3 mutations/locus, high enough for direct observation of mutations in irradiated cells. The sensitivity of the PCR-based microsatellite mutation assay was 10-fold greater than that observed for the SupFG1 transgenic mouse mutation assay. A significant increase in radiation-induced mutations in extended mononucleotide repeats was detectible in vivo in mouse blood and cheek samples 10 and 26 weeks after radiation exposure and these mutations were additive over multiple exposures. This study demonstrates the feasibility of a novel method for biodosimetry that is applicable to humans and other species. This new approach should complement existing methods of biodosimetry and might be useful for measuring radiation exposure in circumstances that are not amenable to current methods.

experiment_title: Solar Particle Event Observations with MARIE and Correlations with Earth and Near-Earth Instruments
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Large solar particle events (SPEs) pose a significant radiation risk to astronauts’ health during long-duration missions, and they will be of critical concern during an interplanetary voyage. SPEs are created by fast coronal mass ejections (CMEs) from the sun accelerating out into space in a type of shock wave. The movement of these radioactive particles ejected from the sun during one of these events is difficult to observe due to its three-dimensional nature, lack of recorded observations, and the complex nature of other processes occurring near the sun during a CME.

The main objective of this experiment was to characterize the Martian radiation environment to better manage the radiation risk to crewmembers during future human missions to Mars. The Martian Radiation Environment Experiment (MARIE) instrument, designed to characterize the Martian radiation environment, was used to provide observations of SPEs in a critical region of the Mars heliosphere.

APPROACH:
Data collected by MARIE during SPEs was examined to extract critical information about acceleration of energetic radioactive particles, including timing and magnitude of event onset, peak, possible shock-enhanced peaks and subsequent delay.

RESULTS:
Initial work examined MARIE data collected during SPEs, extracted critical information including timing and magnitude of event onset, peak, possible shock-enhanced peaks, and subsequent decay. The data can be correlated with Earth and Near-Earth particle flux data (from GOES, ACE or other spacecraft) on the same event. The data can also be correlated with images from SOHO and other solar observatories of the solar source event. Because the separation of Earth and Mars varies over the nearly two-year orbital period of Mars, Odyssey observations help establish the heliospheric extent of SPEs (when do both Earth and Mars experience the same SPE, and when are SPEs noted at one, but not the other). These data can be used to impose constraints on SPE models, even when the observational information is limited to event onset, peak, and decay times.

Having a sensitive radiation sensor at Mars provides a unique opportunity to further our understanding of SPEs through the collection of distributed, multipoint observations. From March 2002 through October 2003 (the period during which MARIE was active) the Earth/Mars heliolongitude separation varies from zero to a full +/- 180 degrees. Heliolatitude separation varies from –46 to over 38 degrees. During the extended mission period, mid 2005 to mid 2007, the angle again varies from zero to a full +/- 180 degrees, while the Heliolatitude variation varies between +/- 45 degrees. This variation provides a natural laboratory to probe various geometries of interest. CMEs expand outward radially from the sun. They vary in extent from 10s of degrees to well over 180 degrees. The faster CMEs responsible for SPEs are generally the larger ones in extent. When Earth and Mars are within 90 degrees of one another, they are likely to both be affected by any shock wave associated with these larger CMEs. The extent, strength, and evolution of this shock enhanced peak, at the nose of the shock and along the leading and trailing edges of the shock, provides insight into the physics of the acceleration process and is of vital interest to astronaut safety.

The character of the SPE relative to the location of the center of the CME is one of the most important parameters for forecasting the evolution of the first few hours of the SPE (away from the shock enhanced peak). The accelerated particles that have escaped from the shock move out through the heliosphere “clockwise” along the “Archimedean spiral” of the interplanetary magnetic field line. The curvature of the spiral is a result of the Sun’s rotation and it depends on the solar wind speed. The solar wind typically varies from 300 to 500 km/sec. The ambient solar wind speed can be measured near Earth and estimated for Mars. The faster the wind, the lower the curvature.

Solar Particle Events are roughly correlated with the solar cycle, occurring more frequently during seven years of solar active years than the three or so years near solar minimum. The current solar cycle (Cycle 23) has produced several large solar particle events, many during the period MARIE was collecting data. Solar activity and SPEs decrease during Solar Minimum, and the period of the PS will overlap Solar Minimum. However, during the approach to Solar Minimum, there have been several significant SPEs and a few periods of minor events. Events during Solar Minimum are generally isolated events occurring in a simple solar wind background. These events are particularly good for testing models of event propagation. However, this requires multipoint observations. Continuing observations at Mars with the same data source used since 2002 (the GRS data) would continue to complement data collected at Earth by GOES and other spacecraft.

The MARIE instrument was optimized for high energy, low count rate GCR and secondary particles (including neutrons scattered up from the planetary atmosphere). The very high count rate experienced during large SPEs saturated the instrument. The PI prepared techniques to collect critical data as much as possible during SPEs as part of the core MARIE mission.

experiment_title: Bone Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The objective of this study is to perform high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the distal tibia before and after bed rest to detect subtle changes in trabecular pattern and consequent alterations in bone strength. These studies will require 15-20 minutes of imaging (not including scout images and set-up time). Investigators will implement newer software, thinner tissue slices, and a higher strength magnet than in previous studies. These changes will increase the detail of the bone structure images. Software and hardware will be provided by MicroMRI for use on the 1.5T scanner at UTMB. A protocol similar that described by Benito et al. (2003) will be used. The hardware consists of a custom made surface coil that fits over the distal tibia and a foot holder which uses vacuum bags to conform to the subject's foot and leg to ensure stability during the measurement. The software includes an axial 3D Fast Large-Angle Spin Echo (FLASE) acquisition sequence and navigator echoes to allow correction for subject motion in the transverse plane. The image voxel size will be 0.14 mm x 0.14mm x 0.4 mm.

Artificial gravity will protect against normal bone loss in bed rest. Normal bone loss is expected to be below the detectability in a 3 week time period, therefore there will be no measurable difference between treated and untreated subjects. Results from this study will also provide baseline data for longer duration studies.

APPROACH:
One pre-bed rest and one post-bed rest MRI scans were performed on each subject enrolled in this study. A system (either custom designed holder or commercial vacuum system) was used to immobilize the foot and leg during the scan. Images of the distal tibia and/or calcaneus was then obtained using UTMB’s 4.7 T scanner and a surface coil. Each session lasted about one hour. Image resolution was on the order 0.14 mm x 0.14 mm x 0.4 mm using a volume acquisition sequence (either spin-echo or gradient-echo) to chosen after the pilot study.

RESULTS:
This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during the Artificial Gravity Bed Rest Study. LSDA does not expect to receive results from this study.

experiment_title: Water Quality Monitor
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Water supplies on Earth are constantly monitored for any characteristics that could prove harmful to humans, animals and plants. This is no different in space. Water used in space must meet various standards (set by NASA, the Russian Space Agency and other government agencies), which are imposed to ensure the health of the crew. Therefore, the water supplies, whether originating from recycled humidity condensate or supplied from the ground via a Russian or U.S. spacecraft, need to be regularly monitored and analyzed.

The purpose of this investigation was to demonstrate functionality of the Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Analyzer in microgravity and to determine whether the design met analytical requirements for monitoring the quality of International Space Station (ISS) reclaimed water supplies. The experiment hardware was expected to provide real-time or near real-time feedback on the quality of the water available to the crew, instead of having to return samples to Earth for analysis.

APPROACH:
The Water Quality Monitor experiment was flown on STS-81 and operated on board the Shuttle only (not on Mir). Six water test samples of known composition were analyzed for total carbon, total organic carbon (TOC), total inorganic carbon (TIC), pH, and conductivity on flight days 2, 3, and 7. In addition, one Mir SVO-ZV (ground-supplied) water sample and one Mir hot water sample were analyzed on flight day 7.

In addition, six duplicate water test samples of known composition, as well as aliquots from the two Mir water samples were archived for analysis on Earth. Results were compared to on-orbit data, which helped to evaluate performance of the Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Analyzer in microgravity. These test samples were analyzed using commercial instruments, including the Sievers Model 800 for carbon, Orion Model SA720 for pH, and YSI Model 32 for conductivity. The difference between on-orbit and ground results was computed with percent errors, and the results were compared to accuracy specifications.

The Water Quality Monitor experiment hardware consisted of a Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Supply Kit and the Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Analyzer. The TOC Supply Kit contained water sample syringes (for two Mir water samples plus a spare), the ground prepared test sample syringes (six different test samples plus spares), spare fuses, RAM data card and other miscellaneous items. The Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Analyzer was a portable electronic box. Samples were inserted into a sample access door using a water sample syringe. The analysis took place automatically within the analyzer by pushing a button on the instrumen's front panel.

RESULTS:
All eight planned analyses were successfully completed on STS-81. Inflight test sample results met accuracy specifications with the exception of a few pH values and the Mir hot water TOC value. Inflight Mir sample results agreed with postflight archive sample results.

The experiment was successful in demonstrating the technology, and the hardware seemed to operate nominally on-orbit. However, after the hardware was disassembled upon return to Earth, several leaks were found inside the containment structure. The leakage problem will be corrected and minor packaging modifications will be made before utilization on the International Space Station (ISS).

Several inflight anomalies were encountered during the experiment. On flight day 3, a test sample analysis was prematurely halted due to a low-pressure error. The cause was determined to be insufficient tightening of the syringe connection. A backup test syringe was installed and analyzed without any loss of science. A locking syringe connector will be added to the hardware to prevent this from occurring during analysis on board the ISS.

On flight day 7, the first test sample syringe was initially analyzed without removing the syringe plunger spacer, causing a decrease in pressure within the system. An alarm should have sounded, indicating the low-pressure situation, and analysis shut down should have occurred. The plunger was subsequently removed, and the analysis was repeated successfully on a duplicate sample syringe. A device will be added to the hardware to prevent installation of the syringe with the spacer in place before use on the ISS.

Hardware changes for the International Space Station will include upgrading the pressure sensor to 200 PSIA instead of 100 PSIA, the waste container will be modified to eliminate leakage from the bags and housing, and the top of the housing will be designed to be removable with screws and an O-ring seal. Additional modifications will be made to enhance analytical performance, reliability, and reduce on-orbit crew time.

In conclusion, operation of the Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Analyzer in microgravity was demonstrated, and the technology was verified for use on the ISS. Hardware design changes for use on the ISS are in work based upon the STS-81 experience.

experiment_title: Monitoring the Cellular Immunity by In Vitro Delayed Type Hypersensitivity Assay on the ISS
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Assessing, monitoring and maintaining human health is a prerequisite for successful long-duration space flight. It has been observed that microgravity alters the ability of the immune system to defend against disease. As a result, latent viruses such as Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) are reactivating successively during space missions.

The Delayed Type Hypersensitive (DTH) skin test was previously used in space and on Earth as the common immune monitoring tool. Using the test, the dysfunction of Th1 cells and macrophages during space flight correlated with a decreased skin reaction compared to preflight results. However, this test has been phased out and removed from the market.

The objective of this study is to investigate the impact of space-flight stressors (µG, radiation etc.) on cellular immune functions ex vivo using a new in vitro DTH assay set-up, mirroring key properties of the Multitest CMI, but extending it by viral antigens and mitogens, and by analyzing the potential impact of stress hormones on the immune response.

APPROACH:
Blood and saliva samples will be collected and analyzed once preflight and three times postflight. A paper questionnaire (Current Stress Test) will also be completed.

Inflight, blood samples will be collected every thirty to forty-five days. After sample collection, the astronauts will process the samples and store them in a freezer for later analysis on the ground.

experiment_title: Information Presentation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Display and control user interfaces are the critical vehicle elements supporting crew performance for many, if not most, mission operations. Correctly defining, refining, and validating the requirements for the proper display and use of information for systems monitoring and vehicle control is critical for optimizing operational performance and minimizing operational risk. The goal of this Information Presentation Directed Research Project (DRP) is to address design questions related to the presentation of information to the crew. This includes not only the issues of information formatting, style, and layout, but also methods of interacting with the information, use of information under the extreme environments encountered in space travel, and refinement of human factors techniques, such as modeling, that will supplement traditional design techniques, and help ensure that optimal information design is accomplished in the most cost efficient manner. This DRP will result in the development of guidelines, requirements, and validation techniques for advanced information display solutions currently contemplated for the various spacecraft systems being designed and developed under the Constellation program.

The major areas of work, or subtasks, within this DRP are: 1) Displays, 2) Controls, 3) Electronic Procedures and Fault Management, and 4) Human Performance Modeling. The Displays subtask addresses label formatting, text color, auditory alarms, and navigation across and within display units. The effects of vibration on reading and speech communication are also investigated. The Controls subtask concentrates on cursor control functionality, design, and use under vibration and microgravity. The Electronic Procedures and Fault Management subtask focuses on information architecture issues for nominal and off-nominal electronic procedures, and their integration with advanced caution and warning systems. The Modeling subtask focuses on human performance modeling of user interfaces in the space environment.

The focus within each major subtask has been carefully selected to address either 1) a near-term identified need within ongoing Orion development work, or 2) a longer-term Exploration need that is sufficiently complex to warrant initiation of research. It is envisioned that activities within these subtasks will evolve and be modified for out-years, as additional research needs are identified.

experiment_title: Effect of Microgravity on Renal and Femoral Hemodynamics During Lower Body Negative Pressure and Intravenous Saline Load
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of adaptation to microgravity on the control of regional hemodynamics during acute changes in central blood volume and cardiac filling.

APPROACH:
Doppler ultrasound was used to examine renal and femoral hemodynamics in four payload crew members at rest and during progressive lower body negative pressure (LBNP) before and after the 10-day D-2 Spacelab flight and during intravenous saline loading (IVSL) before, during, and after flight. LBNP included 15 min at -11 mm Hg, 5 min at 30 mm Hg, and 15 min at -40 mm Hg and echocardiographic data collection was initiated at 5, 1, and 5 minutes, respectively. LBNP was performed preflight (L-60d and L- 20d), and Postflight (R+ 1 and R+9d). IVSL consisted of an infusion of 22 ml/kg isotonic saline over 20 min. IVSL was performed twice preflight, once with the subject sitting and once supine (L-270d and L-lS0d), inflight (+5d) and postflight (R+7d, supine). Renal vascular resistance (Rr) and femoral arterial flow (Qf) and vascular resistance (Rf) were measured before and during each procedure. Data are presented as per cent change relative to measurements obtained at rest shortly before each intervention. The peripheral circulatory measurements were evaluated in the context of central hemodynamic data obtained at rest before each test. Left ventricular end systolic and diastolic volumes, stroke volume, and cardiac output (LVDV, LVSV, SV, and CO) were measured by echocardiography.

RESULTS:
Renal vascular resistance at rest was reduced inflight (-10 % at +5d), and postflight (-5 % at + Id). Femoral vascular resistance was also lower inflight (-7 %), but had returned to preflight levels by postflight day R+ 1. LVDV and SV were lower inflight (-5 %) and postflight (-10 %) than preflight whereas CO was higher inflight (+ 15 %) due to heart rate increase, but had returned to baseline by postflight day R+1.

During preflight LBNP renal vascular resistance fell by approximately 10 % at -11 mm and IS % at -40 mm Hg. The magnitude of this decrease was similar during pre- and postflight LBNP.

Femoral flow decreased progressively from -28 % at -11 mm Hg to -40 % at -40 mm Hg according to the combined data from the two preflight LBNP sessions. The magnitude of this response was reduced during the postflight (R+ Id) to -15 % at -11 mm Hg and -25 % at -40 mm Hg.

The combined data from the two preflight LBNP sessions indicate that femoral vascular resistance increased progressively from +35 % at -11 mm Hg to +63 % at -40 mm Hg relative to the mean preflight resting level. Femoral vascular resistance increased significantly less during the postflight (R+ 1) LBNP session, + 15 % at -11 mm Hg and +25 % at -40 mm Hg. The heart rate increase was similar during all the pre- and postflight LBNP sessions.

During preflight IVSL, renal vascular resistance was approximately 5 % higher by the end of infusion than at rest. The magnitude of this increase was not significantly different inflight (+ 10 % at day 5) compared to preflight responses Sitting or supine. Femoral flow increased during the preflight test (+ 10 % sitting, +5 % supine), the magnitude of change was +5 % during the inflight test. Femoral vascular resistance decreased during the preflight saline load (-10 % sitting and -17 % supine). A similar decrease was recorded inflight (-16 %).

The changes in regional hemodynamics at rest conformed to the expected pattern. Systemic cardiovascular adaptation to microgravity may be viewed as a restoration of the hemodynamic conditions that normally prevail in the upright body position at Ig with central hypovolemia relative to supine rest at 1 g. Left ventricular end diastolic volume and stroke volume at rest inflight and early postflight were also below preflight supine levels, consistent with moderate hypovolemia. Renal vascular resistance at rest was reduced inflight on day 5 and early postflight (R+1). Femoral resistance at rest was also decreased inflight. The general features of adaptation of the renal circulation to changes of the central blood volume and cardiac filling have been well documented: renal resistance increases and decreases in parallel with changes in left ventricular end diastolic volume. A similar response pattern exists also in the cerebral circulation. Conversely the femoral resistance always decreases at rest during spaceflights and HDT, whatever countermeasures are used or not, whereas the femoral flow follows quite closely the cardiac output changes. This constant decrease of the lower limb resistances is in favor of a reduction of the vascular tone in the lower limb vascular network. On the other hand the passive changes of the femoral flow in relation with the cardiac output confirms that the femoral flow is poorly regulated in comparison to the cerebral one.

During the LBNP renal resistance decreased progressively as the pressure became more negative and caused a progressive decrease in central blood volume and cardiac filling, but the renal vascular response to LBNP was not significantly different pre- and postflight. The decreased resistance response in the femoral circulation during the postflight LBNP is consistent with a significant regulatory defect affecting lower limb postflight vascular response, and perhaps also the regulation of skeletal muscle blood flow in other regions. An attenuated femoral resistance response has previously been observed in subjects exhibiting orthostatic intolerance, e.g. in normal volunteers following prolonged head down tilt (HDT), and in two astronauts studied during and after 15 and 20 day spaceflights. The femoral vascular resistance index, (defined as the reflexion coefficient of the systolic velocity wave on the distal vascular resistance) has been found to be an accurate predictor of orthostatic intolerance during LBNP test. A decreased resistance index compared to the baseline level indicates a failure to produce increased vasoconstriction in the lower limb to compensate for a decrease in cardiac filling, stroke volume, and cardiac output, induced by actual or simulated microgravity. Recent studies including a detailed analysis of the systemic cardiovascular response to postflight orthostatic stress, based on studies in 14 astronauts following flights of 10 to 14 days (Blomqvist et al., to be published), clearly identified inadequate systemic vasoconstriction as the principal feature separating finishers from non-finishers of a stand test performed within 4 hours of landing.

In the present series of 3 subjects, pre- and inflight renal and femoral hemodynamic responses to IVSL were similar despite the reduced central blood volume and cardiac filling after 5 days at microgravity. The femoral flow increased as the volemia during the infusion period which confirms the absence of sensitive regulation in the lower limb vascular bed. The decreases in regional resistances paralleled the changes in total peripheral resistance observed before and during ground based simulations. This suggests that the regulatory defect induced by microgravity may primarily limit the maximal range of vasoconstriction.

Objectives:

This experiment will evaluate the effect of Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) on the immune and skeletal systems in microgravity. Both of these systems are impaired simultaneously during prolonged exposure to weightlessness. Simultaneous impairment of these two systems has also been observed in some diseases, suggesting that their physiological controls may be linked. This experiment will analyze BMP's effect on the bone, connective tissue, muscle, and lymphoid systems, to determine if BMP slows or prevents immune system impairment and bone demineralization.

Approach:

Before launch, rats were implanted with 6 subcutaneous pellets each, containing either the protein or a placebo, and injected with the bone marker calcein. Postflight, animals were euthanized and turned over to the commercial partner team for biosample processing and analysis.

experiment_title: The Effect of Spaceflight on Cartilage Cell Cycling and Differentiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Although space flight has long been known to induce loss of bone and muscle, the exact mechanism of loss is not understood. This experiment studied the effect of microgravity conditions on the cell differentiation process, which appears to be the physiological event most affected by space flight. Cartilage cells from chick limb buds flown in space were studied to determine the impacts on the differentiated cell, the cell cycle and differentiation process, and cell death.

APPROACH:

Mesenchymal cells from chick limb buds were grown for eight days preflight and then placed into WRAIR incubators. The incubators were divided into flight and Ground Control groups, and the flight group was flown for nine days. Cartilage samples were fixed with 70% ethyl alcohol and 2% sucrose at 2, 4, 7, and 9 days of flight. After flight, the samples were collected, divided and analyzed using either flow cytometry or immunocytochemistry.

RESULTS:

After performing flow cytometry, the flight cells showed significantly higher Cyclin E, PCNA and p27 protein content compared to Ground Controls, which indicates that the flight cells experienced more cell cycle activity. Flight cells metabolized glucose to lactate continuously throughout the flight and possibly at a reduced rate compared to Ground Controls, although this significance is still indeterminate. No significant differences were found when comparing number of cartilage nodules and cell cycling within the nodules in the flight and control groups. In conclusion, this experiment proved indeterminate due to significant variation in the flow cytometry and immunocytochemistry results. However, some of the collected data aided the understanding of how the cycling cells contribute to tissue growth.

experiment_title: Microorganisms in the Spacecraft Environment--NSBRI
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In order to better understand the microbial ecology of the spacecraft environment investigators are developing technology that can be used to characterize and monitor important microbial populations in the spacecraft environment with emphasis on early detection of increased levels of undesirable organisms. It is envisioned that such organisms might include some that are not normally pathogenic or problematic but become so as a result of unique characteristics of the space environment. Investigators previously developed the theoretical underpinnings for approaches that could characterize the phylogenetic position of any bacterium that is present in a sample regardless of prior expectations of what might be found. In particular it was found that a large number of "signature sequences" whose presence corresponds with important nodes in a phylogenetic tree exist and can be identified. Investigators tested prototype assay systems that rely on array hybridization, mass spectrometry, or homogenous (1-step) fluorescence to detect the presence of specific signatures of interest. So as to directly test the effects of the spacecraft environmental conditions on microbial physiology at the level of gene expression they are using array hybridization to monitor the expression of each gene product in E. coli growing both aerobically and anaerobically in a rotating wall vessel (RWV) under low shear modeled microgravity (LSMMG) conditions.

The specific hypothesis tested was that there are specific genes that are responsive to environmental perturbations associated with the space flight environment, some which may play a role in mediating the pathogenicity of microorganisms. In support of these activities, investigators were also seeking to develop improved spacecraft-compatible methodologies for use in microbial detection. It is anticipated that samples might be taken from surfaces, water, or air. This aspect of the project included identifying chemistries for nucleic acid isolation and detection suitable for implementation in space-borne monitoring systems. Investigators sought to further characterize and exploit their discovery of immobilized-metal affinity adsorption for RNA isolation and the removal of primers and dyes from samples to facilitate further analysis.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results below.

RESULTS:
Investigators completed the development of a set of 16S rRNA targeted probes that will indicate the presence of major problem and indicator bacteria in flight samples. These probes can be used with similar efficiency under a standard set of operating conditions. The utility of these probes was demonstrated on several samples isolated from various systems including Mars and Moon soil simulants. Investigators also completed the development of a computational algorithm that allows identification of short 16S rRNA subsequences that are highly characteristic of various phylogenetic groupings. In principle, an array of appropriately designed probes based on these signature sequences could be used to determine the genetic affinity (nearest known relatives) in the absence of any prior knowledge of what the problematic organism might be. In practice, the signature sequences themselves tend to be short (15 nucleotides or less) and hence not ideal for use in arrays.

An effective set of probes may have utility in a large variety of formats. It is likely that actual implementation in space flight will be driven by mission instrumentation capabilities. Although there is considerable interested in development of array-based instruments other approaches may be preferable, especially for International Space Station applications. Therefore, investigators have focused their attention on several alternative formats as well. In this regard, several probes for organisms of primary interest have been successfully implemented in a molecular beacon format. Homogenous solution assays of this type would require minimal sample processing and could be readily conducted by astronauts in flight with results signaled by the presence or absence of color changes. It was found that "red-shifted" beacons have minimal contributions from sample autofluorescence. In addition, the investigators demonstrated the potential utility of fluorescent nucleotides such as 2-aminopurine in molecular beacon applications.

Regardless of the assay system ultimately chosen, rapid and simplified systems for sample processing in space will be required. Investigators provided further evidence that RNA/DNA purification using compaction agents eliminates the need for preprocessing steps and that the same agents can be used to enhance the adsorption capacity of anion exchangers. Investigators also discovered evidence that immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC) which is widely used with proteins is also effective with nucleic acids. Most recently, they have begun to look at novel ways of obtaining rapid final purification of specific RNAs such as 16S rRNA.

experiment_title: Acoustic Noise During the Phase III Chamber Test
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP), four test subjects participated in the 91-day experiment. As part of the acoustic study, they measured sound decibels in different life support areas of the test chamber. The LMLSTP enclosed test chamber was divided into three levels. The first level contained general living quarters with a dining/work table, communications, test and video equipment. The first level also contained a kitchen, bathroom and laundry facilities. The second level contained the mechanical equipment for air revitalization, storage and stationary bicycle. This level was the noisiest, and due to the location of the stairs, the subjects had to pass through this level while traveling between the first and third levels. The third level contained primary living quarters with bedrooms, partial bath and entertainment equipment. This level was the quietest. The goal of the acoustic noise study was to monitor and describe the noise environment of the 20-foot chamber during its extended 91-day operation. Noise levels were measured at multiple locations and subjects performed hearing threshold tests called audiograms at various frequencies before and after the chamber experience. The hearing threshold is the softest sound a person is able to hear. It is not clear what level of hearing threshold shift is cause for concern, but it is certain that larger changes in threshold are more serious. Monitoring acoustic noise in the chamber enabled recommendations to be formulated for hearing protection, if necessary. These measurements also established a baseline measure of the noise environment for comparison with other Earth-bound analog test facilities.

In acoustic studies, noise is defined as undesirable sounds in the air in the hearing range of approximately 20 to 20,000 Hz. A certain level of noise can be tolerated over an eight-hour workday without long-term hearing detriment, but this same noise level may not be acceptable if it is continuous over a 24-hour period, such as in the closed environment of a space vehicle. During periods of loud noise, the blood vessels in the ear involuntarily constrict and reduce blood flow to protect the hair cells responsible for hearing. Outer hair cells respond to low intensity sound and become continuously stimulated or "saturated", by loud noise. The inner hair cells remain functional because they respond only to high intensity sounds. A temporary hearing threshold shift may thus occur due to chronic noise. An upward shift of hearing threshold can become permanent, since the outer hair cells that respond to low intensity sound would not have a chance to recover their normal function and would eventually die. Government regulations developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) set the maximum background noise level that an individual may be exposed to during an eight-hour day at 90 dB. Exposure to levels over 85 dB requires routine monitoring for hearing loss and the institution of hearing conservation programs. The EPA suggests that an eight-hour average noise level over 75 dB presents a reasonable risk for hearing loss.

APPROACH:
LMLSTP test subjects collected sound level measurements in various locations throughout the chamber module starting with entry day ceremonies, continuing regularly during the 91-day operation and ending with the welcome home celebrations. In total, 283 sample measurements of acoustic noise were collected from the chamber during the experiment.

Noise levels were measured using an audio dosimeter and a more accurate sound level meter to obtain an A-weighted overall sound pressure level measurement at each location. The A-weighting represents the ear sensitivity by combining all frequencies together and averaging them to give a decibel value. Sample measurement locations were determined using two methods. In one method, each subject was asked to subjectively identify the noise sources and noisier locations in the chamber. Following discussion, the subjects jointly decided upon 25 locations to measure noise, including quiet locations that served as controls. The other method of determining measurement locations was the use of predetermined, geographically-spaced areas on each chamber level. Four different heights above the floor were monitored based on locations where a hypothetical fiftieth-percentile person's ear would be located during various activities. Measurements were taken at 10 cm above the surface of the floor to represent a person lying down, at 75 cm above the floor to represent a person sitting on the floor, at 120 cm above the floor to monitor a person sitting in a chair, and at 150 cm above the floor to represent a person standing. The locations were spaced at 30-degree increments about 60 cm from the wall, space permitting, and at the center axis of each level. Locations where the subjects were likely to spend more time were also chosen, such as a computer workstation, bed, stove, table, exercise machine, etc. A measurement was taken within 60 to 100 cm of the middle of any large area not already measured by other methods. Since this was a screening procedure, most data were rounded off to the nearest unit.

Noise loudness is measured using sound level meters. Total noise exposure over a period of time is measured with a noise dosimeter. To determine how acoustic noise levels varied throughout a typical 24-hour day for each subject, an Ametek Audio Dosimeter (Model MK-3) was used in the dosimeter mode. An average was determined each minute as loudness equivalent (Leq 1 min) of a 24-hr period. This method produced 1440 samples each day. Data was downloaded to a desktop computer and graphed as noise level versus time, creating a histogram for each selected noise level interval.

Each test subject wore the dosimeter over two 24-hour periods. Additionally, one subject wore the dosimeter for approximately one hour before, and one hour after, entering the chamber on the first day and an hour before and after exiting the chamber on the last day. On each of three other days, the dosimeter was placed in a central location in a bedroom, left among equipment on the second level, and attached to the ceiling in the middle of the first level. The exact days that the subjects wore the dosimeter, and the exact days and locations that the dosimeter was placed in a room were up to the subjects' discretion.

Investigators wanted to know whether or not the noise levels inside the chamber would affect the threshold hearing levels of the subjects over the course of the 91-day stay in chamber. Hearing tests, called pure-tone air conduction audiometry, were conducted under standard conditions at the health clinic at NASA's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in a sound-insulated booth. A microprocessor-controlled audiometer presented pure tone stimuli to the subject and recorded his or her responses. The subject wore a headset through which the sounds were transmitted to each ear. When the subject heard a sound, he or she pushed a button, and the monitoring computer recorded the response. The computer presented sounds at predetermined frequencies and at incremental amplitudes, getting softer until there was no subject response, and then louder until there was a response, to double-check the person's threshold. Each ear was tested independently starting with frequencies of 1000 cycles per second (Hz). This first measurement at 1000 Hz was a training run. Then, the test was conducted at frequencies of 500 Hz, 1000 Hz, 2000 Hz, 3000 Hz, 4000 Hz, 6000 Hz and 8000 Hz for a total of seven data collection sessions and 42 audiogram measurements per subject.

In an audiometry test, the hearing level is quantified based on what the normal ear detects, and a score of zero indicates normal hearing. Scores above zero indicate hearing loss. A 100 dB hearing loss at any frequency is nearly equivalent to complete deafness at that particular frequency tested. The four chamber test subjects were each given three audiograms. The first, conducted at the time of medical examination for eligibility, established a baseline measure. The second audiogram was performed within two hours after the subject left the chamber to determine whether there was any shift in hearing threshold after 91 days in the chamber. The third audiogram occurred between six and fourteen weeks after chamber egress to determine whether the hearing threshold had returned to baseline. It was expected that there would be a hearing threshold shift on egress day, but that no permanent shift would occur.

RESULTS:
On the first chamber level, the acoustic noise from 105 measurements averaged 63.2 dB(A). The noisiest general area was the airlock, which averaged 63.7 dB(A), and where major noise contributors included exercise machines and ventilation fans. The only measurements that equaled or exceeded 70 dB(A) were from intermittent noise sources. The television was the loudest measured equipment noise source (average 75.2 dB(A)).

The second level was much noisier, and the subjects reportedly avoided the area. The average noise level over 94 measurements was 74.6 dB(A). Only two of the samples were measured at less than 70 dB(A). Twelve measurements were in excess of 80 dB(A).

On the third level, which was quieter than the others, noise levels were similar to those in a typical single-family residence. The average noise level over 84 measurements was 51.5 dB(A). Measurements in the immediate proximity of the beds averaged 42.4 dB(A). The noisiest area on the third level was in the hallway, averaging 59.8 dB(A), especially near the ladder that led to the noisier second level.

Data from the dosimeter attached to a subject for a 24-hour period was consistent with that obtained by the sound level meter. It was possible to discern where the subject was in the chamber by analyzing the readings from the dosimeter. The first level's background noise was measured in the mid-60 dB(A) range, with an occasional spike attributed to human voices during conversation. Periods of time where noise measured above 70 dB(A) represented transitions through, or short visits to, the louder second level. Rest or quiet work on the third level could be assumed from the periods of time that measured 60 dB(A). When the subjects exited the chamber at egress, the dosimeters measured above 90 dB(A) during the first 10 minutes and above 80 dB(A) for most of the first hour.

Audiogram measurements of the subjects on the pre-test ranged from 0 to 50 dB. A measure of 0 indicates that the threshold of hearing is the same as that for an average person without hearing loss, while larger numbers indicate hearing loss. Shifts of 5 dB or less are not considered problematic because they are within the range of expected test errors. On egress-day, audiogram measurements were 0 to 50 dB. Post-test measurements were 0 to 45 dB. For two subjects, all measurements were at or below 20 db; for another subject, all were at or below 25 dB. The final subject gave readings at or below 10 dB in one ear, while the other ear measured hearing loss in the 45 to 50 dB range for all three-test administrations. Audiometry data graphs indicate no clear distinction among pre-test, egress day and post-test audiometry measurements.

A modified sign test was performed on the data as an indication of the overall tendency of the measured hearing threshold. Arithmetic differences between the egress day and pre-test measures were obtained for each data pair. There was no significant difference between the two measurements for hearing loss or improvement. However, a similar comparison showed that the hearing threshold measured at the post-test was better than either the pre-test or egress day tests. Yet, of the 56 comparisons among the pre-test, egress day and post-test, there were five for which the egress day measurements suggested hearing threshold loss that did not return to pre-test baseline level.

Some interesting factors may explain the audiogram results. Upon egress, cheering crowds generated more noise than that found in the living areas of the chamber. This can be observed from the dosimeter readings. The loud celebration noise may have confounded the results of the egress day measures that were taken within two hours after egress. Another confounding factor may have been the subjects' environment during the pre-test baseline measures. During this timeframe, the subjects were involved in the development, assembly and testing of the mechanical equipment for the chamber. All pre-test hearing measurements were taken during the afternoon, after at least a half-day of work in a noisy environment. The subjects were also involved in the operation and maintenance of this equipment during the 91 days of the chamber test. About a week after egress day, the subjects took vacations, and the equipment was turned off. So the post-test measures were obtained after the subjects had been in a different noise environment, and under different stress conditions that were not monitored.

After the first data were analyzed and reported to the subjects in the chamber, steps were taken to reduce the noise. Noise insulation barriers were constructed and redundant equipment was turned off. Schedules were changed so that the noisiest equipment was not operated when the subjects were in that area. The results of this study will be used to provide motivation to reduce the noise levels of the air and water revitalization equipment. A continuing benefit for habitation study crews is an increased understanding and awareness of the noise levels in a closed environment.
