experiment_title: Effects of Angiotensin Converting Enzyme Inhibitors (ACEI) on Bone Turnover
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone loss during spaceflight remains a significant concern despite recent advances with resistance exercise, and the need for a countermeasure to help bone remodeling and maintain BMD remains unanswered. In ground-based studies, hypertension (HTN) is associated with bone loss due to activation of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) which affects bone turnover. Increased RAS activities were noted in humans during bed-rest and spaceflight, but whether an effect of RAS activation contributes to bone loss in these models has not been explored. Animal studies have shown decreased bone resorption (up to 19%) and increased bone mass (up to 2%) following treatment with RAS-targeted antihypertensive medications, e .g., Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEi) and angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB). ACEi and ARB render antihypertensive effects by blocking pathologic effects of Angiotensin II. Specifically, ACEi renders antihypertensive effects by blocking signaling in receptors AT1 and AT2 while ARB blocks signaling in AT1 only. Both AT1 and AT2 are expressed in osteoblasts and are associated with RANKL which lead to osteoclastogenic activity. While there is controversy about the effects of ACEi and ARB on bone, blocking signaling on both AT-I and AT-II by ACEi was linked to improved bone mass and bone turnover in animal studies. Human observational studies, including our preliminary data, established positive associations between ACEi use for HTN treatment and dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) acquired hip neck bone mineral density (BMD). However, the few available human studies are limited because of cross-sectional design and because they lack information on relevant biomarkers and mechanisms.

APPROACH:
We hypothesize that ACEI use for 3 months to treat hypertension (HTN) in older adults will decrease bone turnover by decreasing bone resorption, the primary factor in spaceflight induced bone loss. To investigate if ACEI prevents bone loss by decreasing bone turnover, we propose a proof of concept randomized controlled trial to evaluate if ACEi, as used for HTN control, decreases bone turnover through effects on resorption (serum CTX) and/or formation (serum P1NP) markers in 60 older adults (= 45 years of age; 30 men and 30 women; 15 treated with ACEI and 15 not treated with RAS related medications) randomized within each gender stratum to receive ACEi or a non-ACEi HTN control drug for 3-months. We will also measure serum levels of RANKL protein and the RANKL/OPG ratio before and after treatment.

Specific Aims: Among subjects (men and women = 45 years of age) with hypertension and no known history of osteoporosis attending outpatient clinics:
1) To compare changes in bone turnover markers (P1NP and CTX) between randomized groups with and without exposure to ACEi for 3 months
2) To compare changes in serum levels of RANKL protein between randomized groups with and without exposure to ACEi for 3 months.
For known differences in age-related bone loss and BMD ranges, separate analyses will be conducted for men and women. Descriptive statistics will provide patient characteristics by group (ACEi vs. non-ACEi). We will use a linear mixed model with group (ACEi, non-ACEi), time of assessment (baseline and 3 months) and age stratum as covariates and a random effect for subject to adjust for within subject correlation. Dependent variables will be bone markers, RANKL and RANKL/OPG levels. Each dependent variable will be evaluated separately. Estimates group differences at 3 months will be reported along with 95% confidence intervals for all outcomes. We will also describe outcome by patients with newly diagnosed or uncontrolled HTN in the treatment group.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Crewmember and Crew-Ground Interactions During NASA-Mir
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During future long duration missions, international crews will be engaged in complicated activities over long periods of time. A number of interpersonal issues likely to impact these missions must be addressed to ensure healthy crewmember interactions and optimal performance. The objectives of this study were to measure and characterize changes over time in a number of important interpersonal factors, such as tension, cohesion, leadership role, and the relationship between space crews and ground support personnel during the NASA/Mir missions.

The formal hypotheses addressed a number of aspects related to crew and ground control tension, cohesion, and leadership role. Over the course of long-term space missions, tension in the crew environment and crew cohesiveness were expected to change. Researchers expected an association between the level of tension in the crewmembers and their relationship with people on the ground, and between tension in mission control personnel and their relationship with management. Also, it was hypothesized that the perception of both the leadership role and outside monitoring support would change over time.

Although specific stressors that occur during the mission, there is evidence, can influence these issues, that time alone may be a factor. One approach, the biphasic model, proposes that significant psychological and interpersonal difficulties may occur after the halfway point of a mission. Hence, a sense of relief that half of the mission is over is outweighed by the realization that another half is yet to come, and this results in decrements in mood and interpersonal functioning of the crew. The triphasic model describes three phases of reaction for people working in isolating and confined conditions for long periods. The initial anxiety in the first few weeks are mainly due to the novelty of the situation; depression during the long middle period of the mission are mainly due to monotony and homesickness; and euphoria and adolescent behavior during the last few weeks due to anticipation of returning home.

When crews are composed of people from different countries or different ethnic backgrounds, language and cultural differences are important since they may lead to intra-crew tensions and disruptions in cohesion, and this in turn may negatively affect morale and interfere with the performance of mission tasks. Issues related to language and cultural differences have been reported in both simulation and space environments. Language and cultural issues also may adversely affect the interactions of mission control personnel on the ground, although these individuals have not been studied previously.

The relationship between the crewmembers and their mission control support personnel is important, since miscommunication or insensitivity between these two groups may lead to misaligned work schedules or inappropriate responses during times of danger. A phenomenon that may negatively influence crew ground communication is displacement, which occurs when tension and distressful dysphoric emotions (e.g., anger, depression) that arise within the crewmembers during the mission cannot be expressed openly and are instead transferred outside to ground personnel, who are perceived as unsupportive and negative. Interactions suggestive of displacement have been reported during space missions and during space simulation studies on Earth. In simulations, crewmember anger directed to outside monitors has been especially observed when overt anger and tension were not seen between the confined subjects, and vice versa.

Earlier work explored several of the above psychosocial issues in confined groups and included a questionnaire study of 54 astronauts and cosmonauts who had flown in space and a study of three male Russian subjects who were secluded in the Mir space station simulator in Moscow for 135 days. The study described in this paper involved a series of space missions in which two Russian cosmonauts and one American astronaut worked together on board the Mir space station for periods of four to seven months. The objectives of the study were to determine how tension, cohesion, and leader support affected the space crewmembers and mission control personnel on the ground and to determine how these factors changed over time.

Several of the hypotheses predicted decreases in crew behavior during the second half of the missions in accordance with the biphasic model. The value of the triphasic model was also explored and other time effects that might be present while the crewmembers were on orbit. As stated in the hypothesis, displacement of tension and dysphoria would occur from crewmembers to mission control personnel and from mission control personnel to management; differences in response between Russians and Americans and between crewmembers and mission control personnel, were explored. We made no predictions concerning these differences since little empirical evidence existed that would allow us to form hypotheses related to these socio-cultural factors.

APPROACH:
American astronauts, Russian cosmonauts, and American and Russian mission control personnel who were involved with the Shuttle/Mir space program were asked to participate in our study. The number of subjects who volunteered, gave informed consent, and participated in the study during the on orbit periods included 5 astronauts (in 5 U.S. missions), 8 cosmonauts (in 4 Russian missions), and 42 American and 16 Russian mission control personnel, who included flight surgeons, operations leads, engineers, mission scientists, spacecraft communicators, and psychological support staff.

To measure mood state and group interpersonal climate, standardized measures were used which have been shown to be valid and reliable in a number of studies on Earth. To assess emotions, we utilized the Profile of Mood States, or POMS, which consisted of 65 adjectives describing various affective states, such as "tense" and "cheerful", and were rated on a weekly basis by the subjects on 5 point Likert scales:

  • 0 = Not at all
  • 1 = A little
  • 2 = Moderately
  • 3 = Quite a bit
  • 4 = Extremely

    • To assess the interpersonal climate in the crew and mission control groups, subscales from two well-known instruments: the Group Environment Scale, or GES, and the Work Environment Scale, or WES. Both of these instruments measured dimensions of a group's interpersonal environment through subject endorsements of statements as being either "true" or "false" of their particular group during the previous week. An example of a question is: "There is a feeling of unity and cohesion in this group".

    Subscale scores were determined by summing the scores from related POMS, GES, or WES items. Examples of subscales were Tension-Anxiety (from the POMS), Cohesion (from the GES), and Supervisor Support (from the WES). Changes in subscale scores over time were regarded as alterations in the subjects' perception of mood and group climate. Descriptive analyses of the data suggested that the subjects considered the full range of responses when completing the measures. For example, on 63 of the 65 items from the Profile of Mood States, subjects gave all possible responses from 0-4 with exceptions for: "spiteful" and "forgetful", and on all 126 items from the GES and WES, subjects answered both true and false responses. For most items, however, the distributions were skewed in the direction of adaptive functioning (i.e., low values on negative subscales and high values on positive subscales).

    The above measures comprised our study questionnaire, which was available in both English and Russian computerized and hard copy formats. The questions took 15-20 minutes to complete. Both crew and ground subjects completed the questionnaire with reference to the preceding seven days Overall, 82% of the expected questionnaires were received from subjects participating during the on-orbit periods (70% from crewmembers and 85% from mission control personnel). This totaled 212 from crew subjects and 1,088 from ground subjects.

    Data analysis strategies

    One analyses examined the data for differences between U.S. and Russian subjects and between crewmembers and personnel in mission control personnel. Mean scores were calculated for each subject on each of the POMS, GES, and WES subscales. Subsequently, the number of observations that contributed to it weighted each mean, and a two-way repeated measure analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed. The model included main effects for country (American, Russian), group (crewmember, mission control personnel), and their interactions.

    A second set of previous analyses dealt with hypotheses related to the displacement of negative emotions for both crew and ground subjects. Displacement was operationalized as the negative association between measures of tension and dysphoria with WES Supervisor Support over the course of a mission. For the crewmembers, supervisors were defined as members of the outside monitoring staff in mission control, and for the mission control subjects, supervisors were defined as members of the American or Russian space agency management staff. A mixed model analysis was used to test the effects for each measure of tension or dysphoria. During weeks that there was high tension and dysphoria in the "in-group" (i.e., the crew or ground), we hypothesized that there would be a tendency to displace these feelings outwardly to the respective mission control or management "out-group" and to perceive these supervisors as not being supportive.

    A third set of analyses examined hypotheses related to the biphasic model, which predicted decrements in crewmember emotional state and interactions during the second half of the missions. Before analysis, the distribution of the raw data was examined for normality. Several subscales (dependent variables) had scores that were normally distributed. Others were successfully normalized using a logarithmic transformation. Still others had greatly skewed distributions and needed to be dichotomized. Cutoffs were made as close as possible to include 50% of the scores in the "high" category and 50% in the "low" category. These dichotomous variables were analyzed using Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) fixed effect models with logit link functions and binomial variance. All other variables were analyzed using a mixed model approach that modeled random intercepts and slopes and assumed a decreasing correlation as the lag interval increased. Both the GEE and the mixed model approaches accounted for the effects of autocorrelation and were not handicapped by missing values in our longitudinal data caused by random events that prevented the subjects from completing the measures during a given week.

    The bi-phasic analysis used a piecewise linear regression approach. The weekly subscale scores for each subject for each mission were arrayed around the midpoint of the mission (counted as week = 0) because the launches and mission periods of Americans and Russians were staggered in calendar time and were of differing lengths. The missions varied from 16 weeks (an American astronaut) to 28 weeks (two Russian cosmonauts). From the actual weekly subscale scores, overall estimates of the average slope in the first half and in the second half of the missions were calculated, with these slopes intercepting at the midpoint.

    Another analyses also tested for the effects of time during the on-orbit period but modeled the effects of triphasic rather than biphasic changes. A regression approach with a quadratic function was selected to test for a pattern indicative of the presence of three phases in all crewmembers and in the Americans and Russians taken separately. For example, the literatures have suggested that crew tension levels would be high initially, and then drop during the middle phase of the mission. Tension would then rise again at the end as the termination approaches. Since quadratic functions describe curves with one bend, this analytic procedure was a reasonable way for us to test for U-shaped patterns among the variables in the data. However, since other curvilinear patterns may give a significant quadratic result as well, we had to visually inspect the data to see if a U-shape or some other curve best defined it.

    Since the regression models with a quadratic function included tests for linear functions in the analysis, a comparison of the quadratic pattern with a linear pattern was explored for the subscales throughout the course of the mission. If both of these tests for a given subscale are significant, then it is appropriate to present only the quadratic results. It is important to realize that the pattern of change in the actual data for a given subscale variable may not in itself be linear. For example, for variables that were dichotomized and subject to a GEE analysis, what was being evaluated was the presence of a linear pattern in the logit transformed values, not in the actual data. The most one could infer from such a case was that there was an overall tendency for a variable to increase or decrease versus showing no change over time (e.g., the tension level rose or fell during the course of the total mission versus staying pretty much the same). Therefore, one needs to visually examine the plot to deduce what kind of pattern is evident.

    A second set of new analyses was conducted to determine whether crewmember subjects differed from normative samples on Earth. T-tests were used to compare mission means with normative scores from other groups on Earth, both in terms of all subjects pooled and in terms of American and Russian subjects taken separately.

    A third set of new analyses tested for differences in the subscale variables during the missions compared to pre- and post-mission. Mean scores were calculated for each subject on each of the POMS, GES, and WES subscales for the mission itself and for the pre- and post-mission periods. Subsequently, each mean was weighted by the number of observations that contributed to it, and a one-way repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed that compared crewmember subscale mean scores during the missions with pre- and post-mission means. Again, we looked at all crewmembers pooled and at Americans and Russians taken separately.

    All of the previously conducted and new regression analyses were performed using a SAS macro based to execute the GEE analysis and the SAS MIXED procedure for the mixed models. The t-tests were conducted using the SAS t-test procedure, and the ANOVAs were conducted using the SAS GLM procedure. To control for a possible inflated Type I error rate associated with multiple significance tests, the false discovery rate procedure was utilized to determine an adjusted significance threshold. This procedure controls the expected proportion of falsely rejected hypotheses (i.e., the false discovery rate). For each effect being evaluated, the actual p-values from each of the total number of N subscales being tested were rank ordered from smallest to largest. Multiplying .05 by the rank number of each subscale result and then dividing by N calculated a cutoff significance threshold. The p-value from each subscale result then was compared against the threshold p-value until a comparison was found that did not exceed the threshold. This p-value became the significance level threshold for that particular effect. The results reported below have been interpreted with reference to the appropriate calculated Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold.

    RESULTS:
    Interpersonal and cultural results

    To examine the potential impact of interpersonal and cultural factors, we used an analysis of variance to explore differences between Americans and Russians and between crew and ground subjects. Seven of the total of 21 subscale comparisons gave p-values lower than the adjusted significance threshold for the country main effect: Americans scored higher than Russians on POMS Vigor-Activity and WES Work Pressure, and lower on WES Managerial Control, GES Task Orientation, GES Self Discovery, WES Physical Comfort, and GES Leader Support. For the group main effect, four comparisons were significant, with mission control subjects scoring higher than crewmembers on four POMS measures of dysphoria (Tension-Anxiety, Fatigue-Inertia, Confusion-Bewilderment, and Total Mood Disturbance). There were significant country by group interactions for three GES subscales: Leader Support, Expressiveness, and Independence. American crewmembers scored lower than any other group on all three measures. Taken together, these findings suggested that Americans (especially U.S. crewmembers) experienced more emotional and work related problems than Russians, and that mission control personnel were more dysphoric than crewmembers.

    Displacement results

    Strong support was found in favor that displacement would occur for both crewmembers and mission control personnel using a mixed model analysis. Six subscales were picked to evaluate displacement (POMS: Tension-Anxiety, Depression-Dejection, Anger-Hostility, Total Mood Disturbance; GES Anger & Aggression; WES Work Pressure), and the phenomenon was indicated operationally when there was a significant negative association of each of these subscales with a measure of outside support (WES Supervisor Support). All six predicted associations were significant for the crewmembers, and five of the six were significant for the mission control subjects with the exception of WES Work Pressure. These results strongly suggested that crewmembers displaced tension and negative emotions to mission control personnel and that mission control personnel displaced tension and negative emotions to management.

    Biphasic model results

    According to the biphasic model, as hypothesized, there would be a significant rise in measures of crew tension, a drop in measures of crew cohesion and leader support, and a drop in measures of mission control leader support during the second half of the missions. The cohesion hypothesis was tested by examining six subscale variables: GES Cohesion, GES Task Orientation, GES Order and Organization, POMS Depression-Dejection, POMS Fatigue-Inertia, and POMS Vigor-Activity. We tested our tension hypothesis in terms of four variables: POMS Tension-Anxiety, POMS Anger-Hostility, GES Anger & Aggression, and WES Work Pressure. Finally, leader support was examined for both the crewmembers and the mission control personnel by exploring two variables: GES Leader Support and WES Supervisor Support. Using a piecewise linear regression approach with the appropriate mixed model or GEE analyses, only one of the, variables was significant when the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold was applied: there was a significant drop in GES Leader Support for crewmembers in the second half. Overall, the results did not indicate the presence of a moderate to strong biphasic time effect.

    The findings reported below deal with triphasic and linear time effects and with emotional and group climate responses reported by the crewmembers during their time on-orbit (the mission period). Unlike mission control personnel, the crewmembers were confined in space during the missions in an environment quite different from that on Earth. This isolation made them especially vulnerable to group and time pressures. Consequently, the results will have special relevance for the crew subjects.

    Quadratic (triphasic) model results

    The triphasic model was evaluated in terms of a regression approach with a quadratic function, since this gives a reasonable test of the U-shaped pattern one would expect to see in the subscales over the course of the missions if this pattern was in operation. However, since quadratic functions also describe non U-shaped curves, it is important to inspect the data visually to see just what kind of curve is depicted. A significant quadratic component in the model indicates that the quadratic function is a better representation of the data than a linear function.

    For the crewmembers, all of the 21 subscale variables from the POMS, GES, and WES were tested. After applying the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, the results indicated that none of tests for the quadratic function in these subscales met the adjusted significance threshold (p = .0024). Additional evaluations were made of the quadratic function in the 21 subscales for Russian and American crewmembers taken separately. For the Russians, none of the tests resulted in significant findings. For the American crewmembers, three of the subscales were significant for quadratic functions, with the p-value being less than the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold of p =.0024. These were: GES Order & Organization (beta = .007, p = .000); GES Task Orientation (beta = -.007, p = .000); and GES Self Discovery (beta = -.099, p = .000). Since all three of these variables had a skewed distribution and were dichotomized, they ~ere analyzed using a GEE model.

    Linear model results

    For all the crewmembers and for the Russians taken separately, regression analyses for the linear model were made on all 21 subscales. In both cases, none of the subscales resulted in p-values that were less than the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold (p = .0024).

    For the American crewmembers taken separately, only one subscale variable (other than GES Self Discovery) had a p-value that was less than the Benjamini and Hochberg threshold of p = .0048: GES Cohesion. A GEE analysis had been performed on GES Cohesion since the data were skewed and needed to be dichotomized, and this resulted in findings of beta = -.144 and p = .003. The negative beta meant that the probability of achieving a high score decreased in some manner from the beginning to the end of the mission. Although the shape of the logit curve was better described by a linear than a quadratic function, this did not imply that the actual data necessarily would plot as a straight line.

    Crewmember results versus scores from normative samples on Earth

    For nearly every subscale, the crewmember means were in the positive half of the subscale range. That is, where a high score defined a negative outcome (e.g., POMS Tension-Anxiety), the crew mean was below the scale midpoint (18 for this subscale), whereas where a high score defined a positive outcome (e.g., GES Cohesion), the crew mean was above the scale midpoint (4.5 for this subscale). This suggested that the crewmembers generally endorsed positive adaptive responses, especially for the POMS emotion variables.

    The normative means and standard deviations were determined from several thousand people participating in non-patient work and task groups. The POMS sample consisted of 1,130 adult males who participated in a smoking cessation program; the GES sample consisted of individuals who participated in 101 task-oriented groups in health care, correctional, and educational settings [41]; and the WES sample consisted of 8,146 individuals who participated in 116 general and health care work groups [42]. Using t-tests and the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, a total of 13 subscales resulted in p-values that were below the adjusted significance threshold of p = .033. For all six significant POMS variables, the crewmembers endorsed significantly less dysphoria than the POMS normative sample. They also scored lower on GES and WES measures of group expressiveness, independence, anger & aggression, and innovation; and higher on measures of cohesion, leader control, and managerial control.

    The subscale means and standard deviations for Russian and American crewmembers were taken separately, along with their respective comparisons with the normative samples; a given difference did not always reach significance (probably due to the smaller sample sizes). One notable new finding is GES Self Discovery, where the Russian mean is significantly greater than the norm, and the American mean is significantly smaller.

    Mission versus pre-and post-mission results

    Crewmember subjects were asked to complete the POMS, GES, and WES questions each week during the time they were on the Mir. They also were asked to complete these measures for four consecutive weeks pre-mission, ending at one month before launch (i.e., baseline data collection period), and for two consecutive weeks after they returned to Earth. However, it was discovered that during the post-mission period the American and Russian subjects were separated from each other, so there was no group environment to evaluate using the GES and WES items. Consequently, only POMS data were collected. To look for differences in subscale scores before, during, and after the missions, mean scores were calculated and compared using a repeated measures ANOVA (pre-mission versus on-orbit versus post-mission for the POMS subscales, and pre-mission versus on-orbit for the GES and WES subscales). After applying the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, none of these comparisons were significant in terms of all crewmembers, Russians alone, or Americans alone.

    CONCLUSION

    There was no support for the triphasic or linear models for all crewmembers or for Russian cosmonauts alone when the Benjamini and Hochberg criteria were applied to contol for Type I errors. Although there were three significant quadratic findings for American astronauts, only one variable, GES Order & Organization, showed a U-shaped pattern consistent with the triphasic model. This finding suggested that Americans in space felt that their interpersonal environment was comparatively more organized at the beginning and end of the on-orbit period than during the middle. This makes some sense because the new astronauts were formally oriented to the Mir shortly after arriving by the departing astronauts and by the continuing cosmonauts, and because the preparation for the return to Earth required the astronauts to undergo a number of specific procedures during the end of their on-orbit period.

    The other two significant quadratic functions for the Americans, GES Task Orientation and GES Self Discovery, gave a different pattern, with the probability of a high score being greater during the beginning weeks of the missions, then declining as time progressed. This pattem also was evident for the significant linear function finding for GES Cohesion. Taken together, the results from these three subscales suggested that the American crewmembers might have been impacted by the novelty of the situation during the first few weeks of their missions. They perceived the crew environment to be one where orientation to tasks was high, where they could grow individually, and where there was a strong bond among the crewmembers. Over time, there was a significant decrease in these areas. Perhaps the novelty of the situation simply disappeared. Alternatively, the decreases may have reflected an emotional change in the Americans due to homesickness or asthenia, although one would have expected to find some POMS changes as well if this explanation was valid.

    The above results were found only for American astronauts. The Russian estimated probabilities for high scores were in the .4 to .8 ranges for all four of the subscales shown in the figures, and they did not vary significantly over time. Thus, the cosmonauts were much more likely to endorse higher scores throughout the mission than their American counterparts. This difference may have reflected actual cultural differences or differences based on interpretations of the English and Russian versions of our measures. But it also might have reflected the specific interpersonal characteristics of the Shuttle/Mir missions, where there usually were two Russians and one American on-board, where the leader was always a Russian, where the Mir and its operation was in Russian control, and where the predominate language being spoken was Russian. Thus, an American astronaut was psychosocially isolated during these missions, and the U.S./Russian differences may have been more a reflection of the crew composition and operational situation than of characteristic cultural differences.

    First, although the estimated curves were significant, an inspection of the figures suggests that the estimates are not idea fits of the actual proportion data. The smooth estimated probability curves contradict the variation that is occurring in the mean weekly responses. Only biphasic, quadratic, and linear functions were tested, and perhaps some other function would give a better fit to the data. Second, for GES Order & Organization, GES Task Orientation, and GES Cohesion, the high/low splits were at 9/8. This means that about half of the total responses were the highest possible value of nine, and about half were eight and below. Therefore, in many cases, the indicated drop in scores was from a high of nine to a low of eight or seven, still in the upper part of the subscale range. In contrast, the high/low split for GES Self Discovery was 5/4, which gave more room at the top and bottom of the subscale range for the subjects to score. Little support was found for the presence of moderate to strong time effects in the crewmembers during the Shuttle/Mir missions.

    In comparison with other work and task groups on Earth, the crewmembers were significantly less dysphoric and perceived more cohesion and direction from their leaders and managers. They also felt that their group environment allowed them less opportunity to express themselves and to be independent and innovative, and they reported lower levels of group anger and aggression. American and Russian subjects taken separately generally echoed these overall findings. In addition, unlike many work environments on Earth, the Shuttle/Mir missions were busy and highly structured, with many timelines, procedures, and directions from the ground that needed to be followed. One interesting difference between Russian and American crewmembers pertained to GES Self Discovery, with the former scoring significantly higher than the normative sample and the latter Scoring significantly lower. Although the Russian crewmembers perceived their interpersonal environment as conducive to such discussion (compared with the normative group on Earth), the American crewmembers had an opposite perspective. Perhaps language differences and a sense of psychosocial isolation handicapped the latter and prevented them from learning about themselves through such informal group interactions. No significant differences were establish in crew response before, during, or after the missions in terms of all crewmembers or Americans and Russians taken separately.

    Significant pre/post seclusion differences using the same measures were found in our 135-day Mir simulator study, and we expected to replicate some of the findings. For example, POMS Tension-Anxiety levels were significantly lower, and GES Leader Support, Expressiveness, and Self Discovery levels were significantly higher during the Mir simulation seclusion period than before. However, the psychological meaning of this simulation was much different from the Shuttle/Mir missions in terms of anxiety and perceived danger, and one must be cautious in extrapolating the findings from earth-bound psychosocial simulation research into space.

    Crewmembers may be more comfortable with their work environment in space than mission control personnel are with their work environment on Earth, and it is possible that for astronauts and cosmonauts, the excitement of being in space offsets any negatives from living and working on earth. Thus, crewmembers perceived their work environment differently form people on Earth, and they demonstrated equanimity in mood and group perceptions, both in space and on the ground.

experiment_title: Regulation of Macrophage Migration and Satellite Cell Proliferation during Skeletal Muscle Regeneration: Role of Urokinase Plasminogen Activator
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Satellite cells (SC) appear necessary for skeletal muscle regeneration and recovery from atrophy. Urokinase plasminogen activator deficient (uPA-/-) mice display impaired muscle regeneration, potentially associated with decreased macrophage accumulation and SC proliferation. Hypothesis: uPA is required for macrophage migration and macrophage-induced proliferation of SCs following muscle injury. Specific aims: 1) determine whether accumulation of macrophages and proliferation of SCs following injury is impaired in uPA-/- mice, 2) determine whether macrophage and SC migration through a fibrin matrix is impaired in isolated uPA- /- cells and 3) determine whether macrophage induced proliferation of SCs is impaired in isolated uPA-/- cells. The goal of this study was to better understand the role of uPA and the function of macrophages and satellite cells in muscle remodeling, which may provide a target for therapeutic and medical interventions. Space flight is associated with muscle atrophy and return to weight bearing is associated with muscle injury. Urokinase plasminogen activator (uPA) is expressed by both macrophages and satellite cells, both of which are important for muscle remodeling. Mice deficient in urokinase demonstrate severely imparied skeletal muscle regeneration associated with decreased accumulation of macrophages.

APPROACH:
Repair of the extensor digitorum longus muscle was assessed after cardiotoxin injury in wild-type, uPA-/- and PAI-1-deficient (PAI-1/1) mice.

RESULTS:
As expected, there was no uPA activity in the injured muscles of uPA-/- mice, and muscles from these transgenic animals demonstrated impaired regeneration. On the other hand, uPA activity was increased in injured muscle from PAI-1/1 mice to a greater extent than in wild-type controls.

experiment_title: Radiation Dosimetry and Spectrometry: Passive Systems
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This experiment measured radiation under five conditions: 1) depth dose under very thin shielding on the outside of the spacecraft; 2) low energy, heavy particle LET spectra under very low shielding (outside the spacecraft); 3) the neutron spectra inside and outside the spacecraft; 4) high energy (> 1 MeV) neutron fluxes and dose equivalent rates averaged over mission duration ( 0.2 eV) and resonance (0.2 eV < E < 1 MeV) neutron fluxes and dose equivalent rates over mission duration.

Approach:

The Cosmos 2044 biosatellite mission offered the opportunity for radiation measurements under conditions which are seldom available (an inclination of 82.3 degrees and altitude of 294 x 216 km). Measurements were made on the outside of the spacecraft under near-zero shielding conditions. Also, this mission was the first in which temperature recorders (ATR-4) were flown to record the temperature profiles of detector stacks. As in previous experiments, plastic nuclear track detectors (PNTDs), thermoluminescent detectors (TLDs), and nuclear emulsion stacks were used. Also neutron monitors of 59Co activation foils, fission foil high energy detectors, and 6LiF low energy detectors were used.

Results:

The TLD depth dose results show a greater spread in dose rates as compared with Cosmos 1887, with a greater maximum (minimum shielding) and lesser minimum (maximum shielding). This is explained by the fact that the higher inclination, lower altitude orbit intersected greater electron fluxes at high latitudes in the horns of the electron belt, but lesser trapped proton fluxes in passing beneath the South Atlantic Anomaly. The PNTDs measured a smaller flux of particles with LET >4 keV*m-1 on Cosmos 2044, which is consistent with the TLD results. The measured neutron fluxes, outside the spacecraft, were smaller by factors of up to two from previous measurements made inside the Cosmos spacecraft. Total absorbed dose rates varied from 2.5 x 105 to 8.3 mrad d-1 under shielding of 0.0146 to 3.20 g/cm-2 LiF. For particles with LET >4 keV *m-1, dose rates varied from 7.01 mrad d-1 (53.8 mrem d-1) to 1.20 mrad d-1 (12.3 mrem d-1) under shielding of 0.164 to 1.95 g/cm-1 composite materials.

experiment_title: Virtual Reality-Based Pre-Flight Astronaut 3D Navigation Training
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this sensorimotor/human factors project was to develop a virtual reality (VR) based training method for astronauts aboard International Space Station (ISS) or a Mars mission vehicle as a countermeasure of inflight spatial disorientation and navigation. These problems have been frequently reported by crews of Space Shuttle, Mir, and ISS as complicating responses to emergencies. The three-dimensional (3D) architecture and inconsistency of the visual vertical of adjacent quarters and modules, combined with the limited visual experience of crewmembers is the major cause of the problem, identified as a significant risk by NASA. Astronauts normally see the interior of a spacecraft from a variety of body orientations and viewpoints that cannot be simulated on the ground. It requires cognitive skills to interrelate cues perceived in a body centered (egocentric) frame of reference built up directly through navigation and also in an overall (allocentric) frame of reference defined by the spacecraft. Astronauts can either learn this interrelationship inflight, or develop the required cognitive knowledge prior to flight via VR simulation.

APPROACH:
During training, subjects were each led on 12 tours through a space station by a virtual tour guide. Subjects wore a head-mounted display and controlled their motion with a game-pad. Each tour traversed multiple modules and involved up to three changes in visual vertical direction. Each subject was assigned to one of three groups that maintained different postures: visually upright relative to the "local" module; constant orientation relative to the "station" irrespective of local visual vertical; and "mixed.”

RESULTS:
Investigators have conducted a series of experiments of 3D spatial orientation and navigation performance in a virtual space station using simulated emergency egress tasks. In the first experiment in a fully immersive virtual environment with a head mounted display, they showed that individual 3D spatial abilities (e.g. mental rotation and perspective taking skills), relative orientation to the environment, and the configuration of the environment influence performance. Subjects trained locally visually upright developed landmark and route knowledge, whereas those who maintained a constant orientation with respect to the entire station during training enhanced sense of direction and 3D cognitive map, and therefore performance in low visibility in a simulated smoke condition. This result suggests that training initially should be performed locally upright, followed training in a constant station orientation, and then trainees should be challenged by trials in randomized orientation. This could be customized based on individual spatial ability and task performance.

In the second experiment, it was shown that most 3D navigation performance measures for this egress task were similar in the immersive and non-immersive VR systems. Subjects pointed out that this egress task was mainly "done in your head," and that vestibular cues were not critical. This finding is important, since it suggests that laptop trainers (analogous to DOUG for EVA training) could be used for preflight (or even inflight) emergency egress navigation training. Based on these results, this project intended to clarify whether VR training can help to develop cognitive skills and to learn retention, improvement, and limitation of 3D human spatial orientation and navigation for long-term training. In the experiment, investigators demonstrated that "see-through walls" and a miniature 3D model of the environment by VR technology features were useful. Subjects trained with those VR tools showed better performance than those without at the training day, but same in both groups in one month later. This result showed the effectiveness of preflight spatial orientation and navigation training, especially in early stage of learning. Taken together, these studies provide solid laboratory validation for a preflight VR based navigation training countermeasure at the CRL 7 level. The next step is CRL 8 validation with human subjects in space flight to demonstrate operational feasibility and efficacy.

experiment_title: Matroshka-1
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
An astronaut’s skin absorbs as much as 20 times more space radiation than do the organs deep inside the body. So what is the actual dose an individual receives? Based on a determination that radiation dose declines steeply in the first 8 mm of skin, researchers calculated an average dose rate for each critical organ. The calculated skin dose rate of the outermost 3 mm, about 1 mGy/day, is by far the highest, followed by that for the eye. Dose rates for other organs, with the exception of breast and salivary glands, range from 0.2 to 0.3 mGy/day. These depth-dose distribution characteristics can serve as benchmarks for future mission medical planning.

APPROACH:
The Matroshka-torso phantom facility was successfully mounted outside the ISS during the Extravehicular Activity (EVA) on February 26, 2004, and instrument activation was completed by the following April. The Matroshka-1 experiment spent 539 days outside the Russian Zvezda module and 77 days inside the International Space Station (ISS) for the total of 616 days in orbit between January 2004 and October 2005. The first phase of data collection provides detailed information about the depth of absorbed radiation dose for internal organs as well as skin dose in simulated EVA conditions. Temperature and pressure housekeeping data, and experimental data were frequently downloaded directly or brought back to earth stored on a memory card with Progress or Soyuz. The first memory card was delivered with the Soyuz Taxiflight at the end of April 2004.

RESULTS:
Data showed a thermally stable facility with temperatures between -20 and +20 degrees Celcius and pressure near one atmosphere inside the Matroshka container (Dettmann et al. 2007). First results from the active dosimetry telescope (DOSTEL) for April 2004 indicated a dose equivalent rate of 1.3 mSv (millisievert) per day during an EVA and revealed that the radiation exposure is about a factor of three higher than being inside the more protective environment of the ISS (people on Earth receive an average radiation dose of ~0.017 mSv per day). These results helped researchers understand the radiation risks for astronauts and cosmonauts working in space which is critical for efforts to expand space exploration (Reitz and Berger 2006).

Furthermore, the relationships between the skin and organ absorbed doses obtained from Matroshka phantom exposure showed a steep drop of about 20 times lower for the deep organs from the uppermost layer of the skin. This decrease due to the body self shielding and an associated increase of the radiation quality factor (biological damage factor) highlight the complexities of an adequate dosimetry determination for space radiation. Hence, the substantial increase in radiation exposure for an astronaut performing an EVA predominantly affects tissues and organs close to the body surface and, fortunately due to self shielding by the body, exposure of interior organs is only slightly enhanced over that inside the ISS. Organ dose rates calculated from TLD depth-dose distribution show that the surface organs (skin, eyes) receive the highest dose which decreases as it penetrates to the deeper organs (kidney, spleen) due to body shielding. Noteworthy, however, is the significant increase of the mean quality factor as the radiation quality changes upon its penetration into matter. It is also important to note that the exposure data of Matroshka during this time period was free of massive solar particle events (SPEs). As time changes with respect to the solar cycle, the orbit with respect to the radiation belts and the Earth’s magnetic shielding, or the material shielding around an astronaut, the internal dose distribution will change accordingly. A major purpose of the data gathered in the 3-dimensional dose distribution (and presently being further accumulated inside the ISS) is its application in the validation of radiation particle transport models that can calculate organ doses for the ISS orbit based on consolidated data regarding the external radiation field and on an accurate shielding model of the ISS, including the Earth’s shadow, and the self-shielding of Matroshka (Dettmann et al. 2007, Reitz et al., 2009.)

At present the best passive personal radiation dosimeters used for astronauts are thermoluminescence dosimeters (TLDs) and optically stimulated luminescence dosimeters (OSLDs) for low Linear Energy Transfer (LET), and Columbia Resin formula 39 (CR-39) plastic nuclear track detectors (PNTDs) for high LET ionizing particles detection. All three types were used in the Matroshka-torso phantom, however, following the postflight processing of the CR-39 detectors and analysis of the nuclear particle tracks, it was discovered that the doses observed were much less than expected, and the suspected cause was a sensitivity fading of CR-39 over the long period of exposure. Consequently, a method of “internal LET calibration using galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) iron peak” was used to develop the correction formula for the sensitivity fading which brings CR-39 PNTDs results, and those combined with TLDs results, in agreement with that measured by DOSTEL. The LET spectrum method and the combination CR-39 and TLDs correction method prove successful and reliable and will be used in current and future investigations (Zhou et al. 2006, 2010).

A related study compared the space radiation doses inside the Matroshka-Torso phantom with the doses in a cosmonaut body in Orlan-M spacesuit during an EVA and concluded that shielding properties of the spacesuit are essentially different from that of the Matroshka-Torso container. The calculated ratios of dose equivalents in critical organs of the Orlan-M spacesuit to those in Matroshka-Torso vary greatly dependent on the selected organ and solar cycle phase. In some practical cases considered in the analysis, Matroshka-Torso doses were well below or well above the doses in real spacesuit. The best agreement was observed for the eye lens when protected from solar light with extra screen. These results should be taken into account when transferring the data of the Matroshka-Torso experiment to the real EVA radiation conditions in Orlan-M spacesuit (Petrov et al. 2011).

experiment_title: Assessment of Pharmaceutical Stability in Space Using Ground-based Simulation of Spacecraft Environmental Factors
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Therapeutic efficacy and safety of pharmaceuticals flown on the space shuttle and International Space Station (ISS) remain critical issues for successful NASA medical operations. Stability of drugs on the ground is known to be dependent on a number of environmental factors including but not limited to exposure to heat, light, and humidity, as well as other storage conditions. Some medications used in space flight have been used in doses far higher than those used on the ground or have produced unusual side effects, both of which can be explained by alterations in drug stability. Drugs are stored in manners that are not conventional on the ground, and outside the normal stability-rated storage conditions manufacturers report to the FDA. In addition, objects in space are exposed to background cosmic radiation and to radiation from Solar Particle Events (SEPs) both of which contain ionizing radiation or heavy ions. The radiation dose inside spacecraft, however, is higher than without due to production of daughter ions and this increase can cause a reduction in the stability of drugs.

Preliminary studies indicated significant differences in potency of some pharmaceutical preparations flown on space flights compared to ground-based controls. It is hypothesized that space flight environment, especially radiation, affects stability of pharmaceuticals contained in the space shuttle and ISS medical kits. The objectives of this investigation are to 1) determine chemical and physical stability parameters of select pharmaceuticals contained in the shuttle and ISS medical kits along with matching ground-based controls; 2) characterize degradation profiles of the unstable formulations after exposure to particulate radiation using synchrotron light and radiation sources; and 3) develop mathematical models that can predict shelf life of pharmaceuticals during space flight.

APPROACH:
Select dosage forms from the medical kits returned to Earth after a space flight were analyzed and compared to matching formulations stored under controlled conditions on Earth. Disintegration, dissolution rates and concentrations of active drug and degradation products of these dosage forms were determined. Effects of high-energy radioactive particles on the stability of these pharmaceuticals were examined by exposing the formulations to synchrotron light and radiation sources at the National Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL). Predictive degradation models were constructed from these data to estimate the degree and magnitude of loss of pharmaceutical activity during space flights.

This experiment was divided into two separate but related parts, a flight payload experiment and a ground experiment conducted at the NSRL, both of which were initiated in 2006. In the flight portion of the experiment a payload of several identically packed medication kits containing 35 dosage forms comprised of 29 prescription or over the counter medications was launched onboard STS-121 on July 4, 2006, and transported to the ISS. Over a planned period of 18 months, individual packed medication kits were returned from the ISS and medications analyzed for total drug content and dissolution rate. On the ground, drugs are regulated by the FDA to deliver within five percent of the labelled claim of the dose for a predetermined time period which is not to exceed two years.

RESULTS:
The returned kits revealed stability decrements for several drugs. Several medications were found to have less than 95 percent of their label claim when flown on STS-121: clavulanate (in Augmentin), levothyroxin, and risedronate. Medications flown onboard STS-121 were also compared to identically packed kits which were left in controlled storage on the ground at Kennedy Space Center. Medications which showed a greater than five percent difference in active drug content compared to KSC controls were furosemide and cilastatin (in Primaxin). Similarly, in the ground-based study, researchers found decrements in overall drug content when exposed to iron (Fe) and proton (p+) beams ranging from 0.1 to 50 Gray, doses which although higher than terminal doses to humans, are suitable for accelerated stability testing as defined by the FDA. Some drugs failed to meet the expected 95% of dose in this scenario: acetaminophen, cavulanate (in Augmentin), ciprofloxacin (in ophthalmic solution), mupirocin, phenazopyridine, and promethazine. Compared to controls, two drugs had a greater than five percent reduction in content, clavulanate (in Augmentin) and phenazopyridine.

In addition to drug content delivered, other factors such as dissolution rate can be affected by environmental factors. Results from exposure to space flight on STS-121 indicates dissolution rates for several drugs were different from the rates of ground controls; the drugs with reduced release rates after exposure to space flight were azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, levothyroxin, folate (in a multivitamin), and niacin (in a multivitamin). Several drugs exposed to radiation exposures at NSRL also had reduced dissolution rates: amoxicillin and clavulanate, trimethoprim & sulfmethoxazole, ciprofloxacin tablets, and ibuprofen. Three drugs had reduced release rates when exposed to Fe beams but not p+ beams: levothyroxin, mupirocin, and riboflavin.

Analysis of drug content and dissolution rates in future payload returns, and in further exposures at NSRL, is required to ascertain the true effect of space flight on drugs.

experiment_title: Space Radiation Effects on the Central Nervous System
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment is aimed at: studying cosmic particles in the International Space Station (ISS) as revealed by an Advanced Silicon Telescope (AST) and studying the effects that such particles, and more in general the space environmental conditions, have on cerebral functions as monitored by an advanced electrophysiological recording system [ElectroEncephaloGrapher (EEG)]. In particular the study of Light Flashes (the visual phenomena originated by the interaction of cosmic radiation with the human visual apparatus) will be carried out. The scientific objectives of the program feature therefore two major aspects: radiobiological / Particle physics studies and electrophysiological studies. Alteino is the precursor of ALTEA , which will determine the risk factors linked to cerebral functions during long space missions.

APPROACH:
For the first part of the experiment, the cosmic particle detector (AST) is switched on for the whole duration of the mission to measure angle, charge and energy properties of heavy ions (nuclei) in cosmic radiation. The AST is composed of t wo scintillators and a series of 8 silicon strip detector planes. The two scintillators are located on top and bottom of the device and are used in coincidence to trigger the acquisition when the device is crossed by a cosmic ray. Each silicon detector plane is divided in 32 strips with a pitch of 0.25 mm to detect nature, energy, and angle of incidence of incoming particles. There are 4 planes with strips oriented in the X direction and 4 planes oriented in the Y direction to provide a stereoscopic view of the track. The acquisition system consists of a PC-104 based 486 CPU with a PCMCIA interface for data storage and download, coupled with an Analogue Devices DSP for the acquisition of the silicon planes. The second part of the experiment consists of the following operations: EEG monitoring of spontaneous or environment-induced changes in the brain functional state (e.g. level of vigilance), both in relation to and independent of the wakefulness/sleep pattern; EEG recording of changes in the brain functional state (e.g. level of vigilance) occurring in concomitance of the observation of phosphenes; identification of EEG functional patterns possibly related to phosphenes; EEG recording of the brain electrophysiological responses to the impact of particles, regardless of reports of subjective phosphenes will be executed. This part of the experiment consists of six Light Flash observations with real time EEG monitoring performed for a total astronaut time of 18 hours and 45 minutes (with an additional 3 hours and 30 minutes of assistance by the station commander). These sessions are selected in order to cover most of the area swept by the ISS to show latitudinal and longitudinal effects related to particle flux and nature.

RESULTS:
Official results have not yet been published. The PI speculates that they will aid in obtaining the data on the radiation safety of cosmonauts during long-duration and long-range missions, as well as the dynamics of their central nervous system functional state and changes in the level of their capacity as operators under these conditions. They will also determine the level of radiation protection in working compartments of ISS RS more precisely.

experiment_title: A Tool for the Automated Collection of Space Utilization Data
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this study was to develop and validate an automated data collection system that delivers useful data in the analysis of space utilization and vehicle habitability pertaining to crew activities on the International Space Station (ISS) as well as potential long duration space missions. The investigation utilized two independent technologies, 3D Radio Frequency Identification (RFID)-Real Time Location System (RTLS) and Microsoft Kinect 3D volumetric and anatomical scanning tools, integrating them into a single solution in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) platform. This comprehensive data collection provided data regarding: (a) the number of crew present in each area of the vehicle at any given time, (b) the quantity of time crew spend at each workstation in the performance of tasks, (c) the physical orientation of crew while utilizing the provided volume, (d) frequent or common translation paths and traffic flow patterns within the volume, (e) operational flow/volume required for mission tasks by single or multiple crew in the vehicle, and (f) 3D biomechanical and postural data related to individual and team based tasks.

APPROACH:
The first portion of this project focused on the integration of the 3D RFID-RTLS and Kinect hardware technologies involved and the initial development of software interfaces. The second portion included the development and refinement of the system and its software interfaces; and the third portion includes full validation of the completed system in the HERA analog environment.

RESULTS:
The Space Utilization Data System (SUDS) has been completed and with the full scope of functionality originally planned when it was first proposed. It provides a facile system for collection of 3D volumetric data, rough order of magnitude postural data, and time and motion tracking over time. It fully records and recreates the full 3D environment being assessed, and the volumes occupied by the occupants of the scene. It has been designed with future updates in mind through programming methods used, and the ability to support alternative devices for inclusion in the system. Laboratory testing has demonstrated its accuracy and functionality in various regards, and future work is recommended to further document its capabilities. The system is ready for use and implementation in analog testing environments and use in human-in-the-loop testing.

experiment_title: Cytogenetic Studies of Blood
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It has been established that increased frequency of chromosomal aberrations occurs in humans following exposure to ionizing radiation. Information has been obtained by studying persons exposed to a radiation source external to the body, such as by therapeutic dosage, or of those accidentally exposed. Others receiving radiation exposure from an internal source, such as the decay of radioisotopes administered for diagnosis or treatment, have also been studied. Concern regarding the development of cancer in irradiated human populations has been suggested by scientific studies. Therefore, cytogenetic studies were important in manned space flight with regard to the known health risks of radiation exposure. Skylab studies examined the effects of ionizing radiation exposure on human cells during long duration missions. The objective of this experiment was to determine whether the radiation exposure that crewmembers were subject to during the Skylab mission increased the frequency of chromosomal aberrations in human lymphocytes.

APPROACH:
A ground-based equivalent of the M111 study was also done; the Skylab Medical Experiments Altitude Test (SMEAT) provided an opportunity to study the effects of the Skylab environment (in a simulated chamber) without the weightlessness factor. Four pre-chamber and four post-chamber cultures were made on blood samples drawn from SMEAT crewmembers. In-chamber blood samples were also drawn. Unfortunately, control subjects were unavailable for this study. Cultures were prepared by adding blood to a medium containing phytohemagglutinin which stimulates leukocytes to undergo DNA synthesis and mitosis. Late in the incubation period, an inhibitor was used to stop cell division in metaphase. After centrifugation, cells were resuspended in sodium citrate, resulting in better chromosome spreading. Cells were then fixed in methyl alchohol and glacial acetic acid. Fixed specimens were then stained with Wright’s stain and mounted in Euparol.

For the inflight study, venous heparinized blood was drawn either at the Johnson Space Center or the Kennedy Space Center in one to two milliliter aliquots and was obtained at the time of drawing for other medical procedures. Each sample was allowed to settle, and five to seven drops of the buffy coat were placed in Chromosome Medium 1A. Four such cultures were initiated on each person from each blood drawing. The cultures were then incubated for a period of 60 to 70 hours at 37 degrees Celsius. The cells were treated with 0.1 micromilligrams per milliliter (micromg/ml) of Colcemid for two hours. Following the treatment with Colcemid, the cell suspensions were prepared for examination with light microscopy by fixation with methanol:acetic acid at a 3:1 ratio. The slides were prepared with Wright's stain for examination. Chromosomes were technically examined in the metaphase stage of cell division when the chromosomes are separated and paired together. Examiners studied from 100 to 150 cells from each specimen. When chromosome abnormalities were found, the cell was photographed. A karyotype analysis was performed to determine the type of chromosomal aberration. Blood samples were analyzed for chromosome breaks, fragments, deletions, translocation, and exchanges.

RESULTS:
Flight Study Results: A total of 79 specimens from the Skylab 2 mission and a total of 70 specimens from the Skylab 3 mission were completely analyzed. Only one specimen from each mission, that of a control subject, showed greater than 8.0% minor structural defects. Aberrations were noticed in 5.0 to 7.9 percent of the cells examined in 16 analyses from Skylab 2, and in 5.0 to 9.0 percent of the cells in six analyses from Skylab 3. One specimen from Skylab 2 showed an unusual rearrangement, not characteristic of the general population. However, the aberrations occurred sporadically throughout, and there was no difference between the crew and the control group with regard to such aberrations. The researchers expected to see 3 to 4 percent of cells with chromosomal aberrations, due to viral illness, after administration of viral vaccines, x-rays, and after exposure to chemicals.

Also, on Skylab 2, the structural rearrangements were more consistent in the postflight period than on Skylab 3. The observations were consistent with repeated exposures to radioactive tracer injections, and it was speculated that the post-flight structural rearrangements might be associated with exposures to radioactive tracers. Overall, the data did not seem to suggest that the external sources of radiation to which the crew were exposed in orbit resulted in an increase in chromosomal aberrations.

There were no individual studies from this mission that demonstrated greater than 8.0% minor structural defects except for one subject, a control. Only in 16 studies did such aberrations appear in 5.0 to 7.9 % of the cells examined. It is expected to see 3 to 4% of cells with chromosomal aberrations due to viral illness, after administration of viral vaccines, x-rays, and after exposure to chemicals. The appearance of one or more structural rearrangements in 250 cells is unusual, however, in this study there is no difference between the crew and the control group in regard to such aberrations, as they occur sporadically throughout. However, on Skylab 2, structural rearrangements were more consistent in the postflight period, which was consistent with the repeated exposure to the radioactive tracer injections. It was speculated that the structural rearrangements postflight were associated with exposure to the radioactive tracers. However, this observation was not found on Skylab 3. Overall, the data does not seem to suggest that the external sources of radiation to which the crew were exposed in orbit resulted in an aberration increase.

SMEAT results: (97) cells with suspected structural defects were photographed and karyotyped. Minor chromosome defects were noted, including both chromatid and isochromatid gaps and breaks, and fragments. The researchers noted that these defects are typically found in a small percentage of otherwise normal individuals; they increase temporarily under certain conditions including exposure to various drugs, viruses, isotope injections and ionizing radiation. The researchers also found a small number of more significant aberrations.

The results of this study seem to indicate that the chamber environment had no deleterious effect on the type of chromosomal aberrations studied in this investigation. The first post-chamber study showed values comparable to the first pre-chamber study. Following isotope injection, the aberrations increased to levels well above the normal range. The crews suffered no obvious illnesses, ingested no drugs, and had no unusual exposure to ionizing radiation during their stay in the chamber, so it appears likely that the aberrations were solely caused by the isotope injections.

Unusual structural rearrangements were noted in the pre-chamber cultures (done prior to any radioisotope injections), and in post-chamber cultures in two of the crewmembers. At the cytogenetic laboratory with which the investigators were affiliated (University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston), some 13,000 cells were examined annually, and translocations (chromosomes with extra chromatin attached) were rarely seen; chromatid exchanges and dicentrics were rarely seen except in a few expected conditions (none of the crewmembers had these conditions); and rings were rarely seen except in persons with multiple anomalies (the crewmembers did not fall under this category either).

While the number of aberrations found in the Skylab crews were small, they were nevertheless found in all crewmembers during all phases of these chamber studies, and were found both before and after radioisotope injection. It is interesting to note that these same investigators reported the same type of occasional defects in Gemini astronauts both before and after flight.

The conclusion of the Skylab SMEAT study was that the chamber environment itself had no bearing on these results. The findings were deemed less-than-clear-cut due to the confounding of the experiment design by the injection of isotopes for other experiments, and due to the lack of control subjects.

experiment_title: Effect of Spaceflight on Oxidative and Antioxidant Enzyme Activity in Rat Diaphragm and Intercostal Muscles
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous studies show oxidative marker enzymes respond to microgravity differently in different muscle fibers. In hindlimb suspension studies, oxidative enzyme levels have been shown to both increase and decrease in different experiments. The purpose of this experiment was to examine the effects of microgravity on oxidative and antioxidative enzyme levels in respiratory muscles.

Approach:

Diaphragm and intercostal muscles were taken from rats after 7 days of spaceflight. A portion of each tissue sample was homogenized and enzyme analysis was performed on the supernatent. Citrate synthase activity was measured using spectrophotometry. Superoxide dismutase levels were measured to indicate antioxidant activity. Lipid peroxidation was determined through levels of malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxyalkenal, by-products of lipid peroxidation.

Results:

An increase in citrate synthase activity (an oxidative activity) was seen in diaphragm muscles but not in intercostal muscles. A significant decrease was seen in lipid peroxidation activity of the diaphragm. Lipid peroxidation of the intercostals was not significantly affected. Antioxidant activity remained unchanged in the diaphragm. These results are inconsistent with previous hindlimb unloading studies in which citrate synthase activity decreased and peroxidation products increased in hindlimb muscles such as the soleus. This may be due to the fact that respiratory muscles do not experience unloading as a result of spaceflight; instead diaphragm muscles remains passively tense and tonic activity of intercostal muscles increases.

experiment_title: Scaling Body-Related Actions in the Absence of Gravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Recent experiments have shown that visual perception is modified in the absence of gravity. This experiment investigated how crewmembers perceive their visual environment in terms of the actions they can perform. This experiment provides important information on how a crewmember's workspace can be augmented with visual cues designed to avoid any errors in distance judgment that may occur during flight.

Main objectives:

  1. To demonstrate the possible decrease (disappearance) of the use of an “Eye-Height” strategy for estimating affordances after long exposure to weightlessness.
  2. To test the possibility of using a visual eye height (VEH) context to restore the Earth-adapted behavior in 0g.
  3. To test for effects of weightlessness on estimates of visual distance and perceived eye height (control measures).

APPROACH:
The laptop with light shield were firmly attached to the wall of the International Space Station (ISS) so that the laptop remained immobile. The crewmember explored a virtual environment on the screen through the tunnel by holding their face against the mask. A head strap was used to help the subject hold their head within the light shield. The crewmembers feet and body were free to float. While looking through the masks, crewmembers observed open doorways and estimated the “passability” by making decisions as to whether they could fit through the door opening. In addition, crewmembers adjusted a pointer up and down on the screen to indicate their perceived eye height within the visual field. Perceived distance from a doorway was indicated by changing positions on a rotary dial. A group of age-matched ground subjects performed the experiment on the same schedule as the crewmembers (pre-flight, inflight, post-flight).

RESULTS:
Investigators noted an effect of VEH influence on the critical aperture. When VEH decreased, the critical aperture decreased as well, indicating that widths relative to the body were perceived to be larger when VEH was smaller. This study demonstrates that the VEH approach appears to be very strong and can be used, if needed by the nature of the visual scene.
