experiment_title: Elucidating the Relationship Between the Effects of Various Radiation Qualities and Cancer Development Processes using Novel Flow-based Assays
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Current radiation quality factors used for determining cancer risk for space radiation do not provide the accuracy needed, and there is debate as to the relevance of the experimental studies they're based upon. Therefore, one of NASA's primary goals is to improve the understanding of the carcinogenic process related to high LET exposures to better define the risk. Recently the current understanding of carcinogenesis has improved, and a number of cancer hallmarks have been identified. Some hallmarks, or surrogate cancer endpoints include genetic instability, telomere length changes, and aberrant cellular signaling. Identifying relationships between early and late cell signaling profiles, later surrogate cancer endpoints, and radiation qualities will aid in determining a better risk assessment for cancer formation. In addition, using relevant cell types, such as human epithelial cells in which the majority of cancers develop is also key. In this proposal investigators will studied critical phosphorylation signaling at early and late time points as well as surrogate cancer endpoints of telomere length changes and genomic stability as measured by centrosome amplification, at these same late times post exposure. Epithelial and fibroblast cells from the same individuals were used to better understand the etiology of cancer, and why certain cell types more easily become carcinogenic. Investigators also performed studies to understand the heterogeneous nature of high LET radiation. Energy deposition from high LET ions is dense in the track cores, resulting in closely spaced and complex damages, and delta rays originating from cores provide additional exposures similar to X-rays. Using carefully chosen charge, energy, and LETs of particles to obtain differing populations of cells hit by tracks and delta rays alone they investigated how phosphorylation profiles change.

APPROACH:
Cells were set up in flasks or chamber slides prior to irradiation, irradiated at the various doses and then fixed at multiple time points thereafter. A methanol and a combination of paraformaldehyde and methanol fixation were used depending on what was optimal for the antibody. Fixed slides were sent back to our home institution from Brookhaven in PBS to stain with the appropriate primary and secondary antibodies. Cells exposed in flasks were trypsinized and fixed at various times after exposure, and then sent back on ice in methanol. Aliquots of fixed cells were then stained for various phospho-proteins and analyzed via flow cytometry. For analysis at longer timepoints after exposure (weeks) cells were grown to confluence while at Brookhaven, then frozen down before leaving (~ 1 week post exposure). Cells were then thawed back at the home institution, and expanded to then analyze for telomere length changes and centrosome defects. Cells were stained with pericentrin antibody, then fixed with a methanol fix for flow cytometry based analysis of centrosome dysfunction, and were hybridized to a telomere probe to allow detection of telomere length changes.

RESULTS:
SUMMARY OF RESEARCH ACCOMPLISHMENTS:
Track structure studies based on phospho-kinetics in normal hTERT immortalized fibroblast cells. Normal hTERT immortalized fibroblasts were exposed to a very comprehensive range of carefully chosen high LET ions and energies, to help identify the importance of track structure in defining biological effects. Various phospho-proteins known to be activated following radiation were analyzed for phospho-kinetics including gamma H2AX, pSMC1, and pATF2. Fibroblasts were exposed in triplicate independent experiments to: Fe 300, 600, and 1000 MeV/u; Ti 300, 326, and 386 MeV/u; Si 93, 173, 300, and 1000 MeV/u at timepoints between 0.5 and 24 h. Various comparisons for early and late timepoints were made between equal LET, energy, or Z2/beta2 (roughly equivalent to the number and intensity of delta rays). These studies revealed Z2/beta2 to be a primary determinant in the phosphorylation response. In addition, residual levels of foci (24 h post exposure) correlated well with the predicted energy deposition per nucleosome. This body of work was completed and submitted to Radiation Research recently and is currently in revision (no major revisions required). Conclusions from this work include that: 1) most high LET particles induce a greater induction of gamma H2AX and higher level of residual signaling as compared to equal doses of low LET; 2) at early timepoints ATM-mediated phospho-inductions are much lower following all high LET ion exposures as compared to low LET, indicating that the ATM protein is hampered in fully activating downstream proteins following high LET irradiation as compared to low LET exposures; 3) ions with high delta-ray component (Z2/b2) appear to show a greater persistent phosphorylation signal. Phospho-protein kinetics of primary isogenic mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells. To determine how phospho-kinetics may differ based on cell type and status (immortalized vs primary) we compared phosphorylation profiles of gamma H2AX, and pATF2 from primary isogenic (from same tissue biopsy) mammary fibroblasts and mammary epithelial cells. These genetically matched mammary cells where exposed to a variety of different radiation qualities: Fe 300 MeV/u, Ti 300 MeV/ u, Si93 MeV/u, cesium, and X-ray. Initial induction was assessed at 2h post exposure and the amount of residual signaling was assessed at 24 hour post exposure. We chose the 2 h timepoint as for most radiation qualities this timepoint either showed higher levels or the same levels as observed at 0.5 h. Our results indicate that gamma H2AX induction following high LET exposure is greater than following low LET exposure. For example, cells exposed to Si93 MeV/u exhibit a greater induction than following X-ray exposure. Comparing mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells, initial gamma H2AX inductions were similar for all high LET ions, although the Ti ion was uniquely higher for epithelial cells. At late times post exposure, epithelial cells revealed a much greater degree of residual gamma H2AX signal, indicative of a higher amount of unresolved damage in epithelial cells as compared to fibroblasts. This suggests that epithelial cells are more sensitive to high LET damage than fibroblast cells, since the genetic background of the lines cannot be the culprit of this difference as they are from the same individual and tissue section. A second phospho-protein that kinetics were studied in these lines post various radiation quality exposures was pATF2. ATF2 is known to have various functions within the cell however phosphorylation at this particular site (Ser490/498) has been documented to be specifically required for its role in DNA repair. As has been noted in past studies, pATF2 induction was lower than what was observed for gamma H2AX at early times, with levels saturating at about 0.5 Gy. Unexpectedly initial pATF2 induction in fibroblasts was greater than what was observed for epithelial cells for both high and low LET radiation, which is in contrast to the kinetics we observed for gamma H2AX. However, residual signaling for pATF2 was similar for both the fibroblasts and the epithelial cells. Also of interest was the fact that in general for fibroblast line pATF2 levels decreased with time; however, for epithelial cells in many cases the highest levels were observed at the latest timepoint (24h). This is very different from the findings with gamma H2AX, and suggests again that epithelial cells may have more difficulty responding to effects of high LET exposure. The difference observed between the phospho-protein results may also suggest that levels of pATF2 do not directly correlate with the level of double strand breaks (based on gamma H2AX levels), but instead might reflect others things such as perhaps the levels of oxidative stress present in cells. Similarly to the skin fibroblast study currently in revision, we had wanted to analyze data on a per cell basis on exported flow data. We are currently working with a statistician to finalize this work for publishing in next few months. High LET effects on telomere length of primary mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells. To better understand the relationship between radiation exposure and carcinogenesis we analyzed how the phospho-kinetic response following various radiation quality exposures corresponded to the surrogate cancer endpoint of telomere length shortening. The Flow cytometry-based telomere length assay, or flow FISH was used to determine how various qualities of radiation affected telomere lengths of cells differentially. A dose-dependent shortening of telomeres for both mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells following high LET exposures was observed. For low LET exposures, mammary fibroblasts were fairly resistant to shortening effects even at the highest doses, whereas mammary epithelial cells exhibited a dose-dependent shortening even with low LET exposure. The Fe ion irradiations appeared to show the least difference between cell types, in particular Fe 300 MeV/u, which revealed nearly the same change in telomere length over the majority of the doses. Fe 300 MeV/u has the highest delta ray component of all the radiation qualities tested and this may be one of the major drivers in terms of effects, given both cell types failed to show a resistance to the effects. Overall mammary epithelial cells were more sensitive to the effects of radiation and showed a greater decrease in telomere shortening per dose than did fibroblast cells, consistent with the fact that they reveal a greater sensitivity to radiation induced carcinogenesis. We have also exported individual cell flow cytometry data to define how telomere lengths change on an individual cell basis. Preliminary data has revealed that fibroblasts do not show an increase in cells with short telomeres with increasing X-ray dose, yet epithelial cells did reveal an increase in cells showing short telomeres with increasing dose. This additional analysis will allow us to understand in more detail the underlying reasons for the mean changes in telomere shortening for each cell type. Given that mean lengths can change, for example to show an overall longer length, yet the underlying reason for this mean change could be more cells containing shorter telomeres were lost. A finding of an increase in telomere length upon exposure to protons has been noted in the literature, thus detailing the underlying reason for the mean change in shortening should help us to better understand cell type differences and the mechanism involved in radiation-induced telomere shortening. This work is planned to be combined with phospho-kinetic data and as noted above should be submitted in next few months.

High LET effects on centrosome amplification in primary mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells. The second surrogate cancer endpoint, which investigators have studied in relationship to radiation quality, dose, and cell type, was centrosome amplifications. Again a flow-based assay was developed and used to identify increases in size or number of centrosomes as a function of dose and radiation quality, using the pericentrin antibody, which envelops the centrosome of the cell. Our preliminary study with mammary epithelial cells following levels days post X-ray exposure was performed to determine the temporal kinetics of centrosome formation and decline following radiation exposure. These studies revealed that at ~day 9 after exposure significant increases in centrosome aberrations were observed as denoted by the percent of cells showing higher pericentrin levels than the 80-90th percentile of controls. Further studies looking at dose and radiation quality effects were then initiated. We have also performed some studies to better understand how flow cytometry results may compare to the more common way of analysis, immunofluorescence and microscopic scoring of aberrant cells. These studies revealed based on Fe 1000MeV/u results, that similar results in terms of pattern of peak levels observed for both the microscopy and FACS assay were at 0.1 Gy. Why an intermediate dose may show higher levels of centrosome aberrations is uncertain; however, it may be that higher doses kill off cells with aberrant levels thus this is the dose where radiation induces damage, yet it is not enough to kill the exposed cells. Binned results for other ions and energies in assays looking at centrosome aberration frequencies were also performed. These studies revealed the greatest percentages of centrosome aberrations were obtained following Fe300 MeV/u exposures for mammary epithelial cells (far right bin for each radiation quality, showing percent of cells having pericentrin levels >80th percentile as compared to controls). Further statistical analysis was performed on individual centrosome cell data to more carefully define differences at lower doses. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (K-S test) was used for these studies; it provides a nonparametric test for the equality of a continuous, one-dimensional probability distribution. It was used to investigate how different doses and radiation qualities compared in terms of the level of pericentrin fluorescence (equal to aberrant centrosomes at high levels over controls) following exposure. The K-S test quantifies a distance between the empirical distribution function of the sample and the cumulative distribution function of the control distribution. Based on KS test investigators were able to note a significant difference from control levels with all radiation qualities and at all doses for mammary epithelial cells. Results with fibroblast cells from the same tissue (mammary) have shown that fibroblasts are much more resistant to forming centrosome aberrations and that levels in general were below detection using the flow-based assay. They went on to confirm this via the microscopy method following Fe1000 MeV/u exposure, and again found no increase in centrosome aberrations over control levels using this method as well. Thus it appears similarly to the telomere shortening, mammary epithelial cells are more sensitive to the formation of centrosome aberrations following radiation exposure as compared to mammary fibroblasts from the same individual. This again points to a heightened sensitivity for epithelial cells to radiation and potentially also carcinogenesis given these endpoints have been linked to cancer and a pre-malignant state.

Conclusions: The findings of this body of work point to the importance of radiation quality and cell type in determining the effectiveness of high LET exposure. Epithelial cells for the most part appear to show a greater sensitivity to high LET exposure and of particular importance also a greater induction in the two surrogate cancer endpoints investigated, telomere length shortening and centrosome aberration frequencies. Mammary cells, both fibroblast and epithelial cells, appear to show a less robust response to radiation in terms of phosphorylation of various DNA repair proteins after exposures as compared to a skin fibroblast line (82-6). However all lines revealed a greater response to high LET as compared to low LET radiation. These studies allowed investigators to study how well early phospho-protein profiles predict a cell’s response to other endpoints more closely aligned to cancer. They determined that there was not a direct correspondence between the ion/energy that showed the highest residual level of double-strand breaks (based on persistent gamma H2AX at 24 h) and the ion/energy that showed the highest level of centrosome defects and/or telomere shortening. For example, for phospho-protein signaling at 24 h Ti300 MeV/u reveals the greatest residual levels for mammary epithelial cells, whereas for centrosome aberrations, Fe 300 MeV/u generates the greatest number of aberrant cells weeks post exposure, and Si 93 MeV/u shows the greatest effect on telomere shortening, again weeks post exposure. However, studies in skin fibroblast cells, with a more comprehensive set of energies for each ion, suggest that the ions/energies that are the most effective when compared to other energies are Ti300, Si93, and Fe300 MeV/u. Thus in each case the ion/energy showing a more dramatic response for our mammary epithelial cells when compared to other energies of the same ion are the ones in which in the skin fibroblast study revealed more effectiveness. Thus, perhaps if additional energies had been used for surrogate cancer endpoints and phospho-kinetics for the mammary cell studies we would have seen a pattern similar to what was observed with the skin fibroblast cells, whereby the ions with the lowest energy, having the greatest delta ray component, were the most effective in each case. Why different types of ions show a preference for inducing greater levels for particular endpoints is uncertain and would require further investigation.

experiment_title: Molecular Mechanisms that Impact Transcription of Myosin Genes in Human Skeletal Muscle in Response to Unloading: Role of Resistance Exercise (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Unloading of skeletal muscle results in atrophy as well as alterations to the contractile properties and endurance capacities of muscle fibers. These deleterious alterations are largely attributed to modification to the expression of the myosin heavy chain (MHC) genes. In particular non-fatigable, or slow, skeletal muscle motor units which provide for postural support and sustained contractile activity, are remodeled to fatigable, or fast, muscle, involving shifts from type I/IIa to IIx MHC in humans. In earlier studies, resistance exercise has been shown to blunt these undesirable adaptations in both animals and humans.

Previous studies have also shown that both antisense ribonucleic acid (RNA) and histone modifications impact expression of the MHC genes in unloaded rat muscle. Specifically, it was shown that antisense RNA is implicated in transcriptional down-regulation of IIa MHC gene during muscle inactivity and that alterations to histone acetylation and methylation at specific MHC genes correspond with altered MHC gene transcription in response to muscle unloading.

Validation with humans of the mechanisms that regulate the genes of contractile and structural proteins in muscle may lead to strategies that most effectively ameliorate the effects of unloading on human skeletal muscle, as well as enhancing the understanding of these same processes that have significant impact on all humans with impaired muscle function.

The objectives of this investigation were to:

  1. Determine if antisense RNA plays a role in the transcriptional regulation of MHC genes in human skeletal muscle
  2. Determine if histone modifications are dynamically regulated at MHC genes during alterations to muscle loading state in human skeletal muscle
  3. Identify functional performance and cellular-level adaptations to unloading and exercise training and determine their relationship to the corresponding molecular-level responses

APPROACH:
The human exercise phase of research was completed with normally ambulating groups performing resistance and combined resistance and aerobic exercise. Fifteen subjects, eight male and seven female, completed resistance exercise-only training programs. Each program consisted of two training sessions per week for five weeks. Each training session consisted of squats (four sets of seven reps each) performed on the multi-mode exercise device (M-MED). Twenty subjects, twelve male and eight female, completed combined resistance plus aerobic exercise training programs. The aerobic portion of the training consisted of intervals of high and low intensity bouts for a total of 28 minutes, performed three times per week for five weeks, with the M-MED configured as a rowing ergometer. The resistance training portion was the same as for the resistance only group. Functional and morphological data was collected and muscle biopsies were obtained pre- and post- exercise.

Unloading in rats was studied in order to assess the degree that repressive histone modifications impact on the regulation of the MHC genes during muscle unloading and MHC gene expression shifts. Rat soleus muscle exposed to hind limb suspension was analyzed with the chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay and demonstrated altered methylation patterns to histones of the MHC genes.

Twenty six subjects completed the unilateral lower limb suspension (ULLS) studies. These subjects participated in ULLS for either 10 or 5 days, with or without concurrent exercise training. Soleus and vastus lateralis muscle biopsies were obtained, and RNA and protein analyses were initiated. RNA analyses were also completed on muscle biopsies obtained previously with subjects that completed different types of exercise. The proportion of individual myosin heavy chain (MHC) mRNAs and protein in human muscle samples was quantified. The proportions of protein isoforms of MHC were determined from SDS-PAGE. mRNA proportions were determined with inclusion of a control DNA fragment that includes sequence from each of six human MHC genes which is co-amplified during PCR of cDNA from muscle samples. mRNA, pre-mRNA, and antisense RNA from human muscle samples for the MHC genes were measured, as were mRNA levels of the genes of numerous other contractile and structural muscle proteins.

RESULTS:
The study showed that exercise with the M-MED gravity-independent exercise device was effective at increasing muscle size and strength, and improving work capacity. The volume of exercise that produced these results was relatively low, and no adverse injuries occurred. Thus, exercise with the M-MED produced improved muscle function in male and female subjects comparable to standard gravity-dependent exercise devices.

Aerobic capacity, or VO2 max, was found to have increased by 8%. Handgrip strength was improved by 72%. Leg press strength (3RM) was improved by 21% on average. Data are described as means of male and female combined. Muscle biopsies revealed a 10% increase in mean muscle fiber cross-sectional area. Total thigh muscle size increased by 11%, as measured by MRI. Fatigue, or torque produced after repeated contractions, was improved by 27% on average. Data were described as means of male and female combined.

An assay for quantification of the proportion of individual myosin heavy chain (MHC) mRNAs in a human muscle sample was developed. This involved development of a control DNA fragment that includes the sequence from each of six human MHC genes which is co-amplified during PCR of cDNA from muscle samples. This allows for the precise determination of the percent of each MHC mRNA as a proportion of the total MHC pool. New RNA extraction methods useful for detecting and measuring pre-mRNA and antisense RNA from human muscle samples were also developed.

Analysis of vastus lateralis biopsies obtained before and after five weeks of aerobic + resistance exercise showed the proportions of Type I and IIa MHC mRNA were both increased by 11%, while IIx was decreased by 38% after exercise training (all p < .05) in the vastus lateralis. As previously shown only in rats, lncRNA oriented antisense to the IIa MHC was detected and found to be down-regulated with exercise (-55%; p < .05). A regulatory role is inferred from an inverse correlation between the proportion of IIa MHC mRNA and its antisense pair (r = -0.66; p = .002). Low levels of IIb mRNA and pre-mRNA were detected, indicating that the IIb gene is not transcriptionally silent in human limb muscle, as previously thought. The finding of as-lncRNA to the IIb gene is also reported. These data reveal that insights to MHC regulatory mechanisms previously shown in rats and involving as-lncRNA are conserved in humans.

Soleus biopsies obtained from ULLS subjects were analyzed and gene expression of several large sarcomeric proteins that provide structural support to the myofilament (titin, nebulin and a-actin) and converge at the Z-disc were examined. Several signaling proteins that reside in this region (STARS, atrogin-1, and calcineurin via its modulator MCIP1) were studied. Nebulin, titin and a-actin RNA levels changed pre- to post- by -11%, +26% and +7% with ULLS, and by +25%*, +56%* and +16% with ULLS+T, respectively. In conclusion, these studies showed that a gravity-independent exercise device can induce alterations to key contractile and structural muscle genes, and can counteract some of the early alterations that occur with simulated microgravity.

experiment_title: Advanced, Multiple Projection, Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (AMPDXA) Scanning System
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of the advanced, multiple projection, dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (AMPDXA) scanner system project is to design, built, and test a precision scanner for monitoring the deleterious effects of weightlessness on the human musculoskeletal system during prolonged spaceflight. The instrument uses dual energy x-ray absorptiometry principles and is designed to measure bone mineral density (BMD), decompose soft tissue into fat and muscle, and derive bone structural properties (cross-sections, moments of inertia). Such data permits assessment of microgravity effects on bone and muscle and the associated fracture risk upon returning to planetary gravity levels. Ultimately designed for use on the space station or other long duration space missions, the AMPDXA will weigh less than 45 kg in its flight version and be capable of near real-time monitoring of bone loss as well as the effects of countermeasures. The AMPDXA will be able to detect changes of less than 1% in bone mass and geometry and less than 5% in muscle mass.

Specific tasks underway or planned for the near future include:
1. Human testing with the Clinical Test System to develop the final measurement parameters (e.g. dose, duration of X-ray pulses, final filters,operational screnarios, etc.)
2. Refinement of software algorithms for the extraction of soft tissue.
3. Developing a solution to the two-dimensional versus three-dimensional reconstruction problem.
4. Refinement of algorithms for relating bone strength and structure to the risk of fracture.
5. Software (and instrumentation) refinements to allow the collection of radiographs for diagnosis of injury and disease.
6. Design of a lightweight power supply.

experiment_title: Ocular Counter Rolling and Subjective Visual Vertical
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
To assess whether head down bed rest diminishes inner ear (otolith) sensitivity, the ocular counter-rolling response to postural tilting was measured before and after bed rest. Furthermore, to assess whether head down bed rest alters the perception of spatial orientation, the subjective visual vertical (SVV) was assessed before and after bed rest each using settings of a visual line to upright.

APPROACH:
Ocular Counter-Rolling (OCR) refers to the rotation of the eye about the line of sight. Measures of an otolith-mediated reflex was made using a Personnal Computer (PC)laptop-based head and eye tracker, developed by the investigators (MacDougall and Moore). Torsional eye movement (rotation about the line of sight) was calculated using images acquired from a miniature digital camera at a rate of 30 Hertz. Subjects were seated while wearing lightweight goggles with one digital video camera attached. Subjects looked straight ahead for 10 seconds and were then instructed to lie on their right side. After a period of 60 seconds, to allow semicircular canal input to diminish, the subjects looked straight ahead for 10 seconds. This process was repeated with the subject lying on their left side. The gain of OCR was calculated from the actual head roll position (i.e., upright, 90 degrees to the right or left) and the amount of roll eye movement.

Following removal of the video goggles, perception of the spatial upright was assessed using settings of a visual line to the Subjective Visual Vertical (SVV) using hardware and software developed for the Neurolab STS-90 vestibular experiment. Subjects were asked to adjust (using a handheld controller) the orientation of a luminous bar on a laptop display which is visible through a circular cut-out and shroud. The shroud was used to control for orientation cues from the computer itself. Subjects made 10 settings from start positions randomly offset of ±15° either side of the vertical meridian while seated with their head in the upright position. This sequence was repeated with the subject lying on their right side and left side. Subjects completed two pre-bed rest test sessions at approximately 2 sessions before bed rest and up to five post-bed rest test sessions.

It was expected that if bed rest induces deconditioning of otolith-ocular reflexes that this would not be reversed by Artificial Gravity (AG) exposure since the positioning of the subject on the centrifuge only allows for partial gravity stimulation of the otoliths during AG exposure. It is also expected that only a small decrease in OCR gain will be observed post bed rest, due to the partial unloading of the saccule.

RESULTS:

Results indicated that OCR was unaffected by bed rest and bed rest plus artificial gravity. Performance on the subjective visual vertical task was unaffected in the control group, but revealed a significant increase in error for 48 h after bed rest in the treatment (artificial gravity) group. Intermittent application of linear acceleration along the long body axis may have increased the weighting of the idiotropic vector, resulting in an increased of the SVV toward the long body axis during 90 degrees roll tilt.

This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during the Artificial Gravity Bed Rest Study. LSDA does not expect to receive results from this study however, more information can be found through the publication listed.

OBJECTIVES:
Techshot, Inc. proposes continued research and development of an on-orbit cell counter culminating in a deliverable hand-held blood cell counter in the form of a "Microfluidic Multichannel Flow Cytometer.” Crew health monitoring, the Human Research Program, and research in Fundamental Biology will all benefit from the availability of on-orbit cell counters that can provide immediate and repeated blood counts to assess potential anemia, neutropenia, neutrophila or possibility of infections, and signs of immune cell dysfunction. experiment_title: Musculoskeletal Effects of 16-Weeks of Training with the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (aRED)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Resistive exercise has been recommended as a means to ease musculoskeletal de-conditioning due to spaceflight. Currently, the interim Resistive Exercise Device (iRED) is used on-board the International Space Station (ISS) as a method of providing resistive exercise. The iRED may not provide an adequate stimulus to bring about changes in muscle strength and mass and bone mineral density (BMD) compared with free weights (FW). During a 16-week training study, conducted by the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Exercise Physiology laboratory, the rate of increase in muscle strength using iRED was slower compared to FW. In addition, iRED training resulted in no change in BMD, while FW training lead to an increase in lumbar BMD.

Differences in strength gains between iRED and FW training may be due to greater eccentric loads produced during FW training. Despite performing resistive exercise with the iRED, International Space Station (ISS) astronauts still experience losses in muscle strength and endurance and BMD following long-duration space missions (>4 months). The peak iRED load level may be inadequate to ease musculoskeletal losses in microgravity where the subject is not required to lift their body weight.

The aRED was developed to address the limitations of iRED. This new device was intended to mimic the force loading characteristics of FW exercise. In addition, aRED was designed to provide a more constant force throughout the range of motion with resistance generated by vacuum cylinders. The vacuum cylinders provide a concentric load up to 600 pounds with an eccentric load up to 90% of the concentric force. In addition, aRED is equipped with an inertial flywheel to mimic the inertial force characteristics of FW.

The purpose of this study was to compare the musculoskeletal adaptations to 16 weeks of resistive exercise training utilizing either aRED or FW in healthy, untrained men and women. Because the aRED was designed to be similar to FW, the investigators hypothesized increases in skeletal muscle strength, leg muscle volume, lean body mass, and BMD after 16 weeks of training with no differences between the groups.

APPROACH:
Twenty-four volunteers were recruited by the Human Test Subject Facility at NASA Johnson Space Center to participate in this study. All subjects were required to pass a modified Air Force Class III physical examination. Testing protocols were reviewed and approved by the NASA Johnson Space Center Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects. Subjects were instructed to maintain their pre-study exercise habits (intensity, frequency, and duration) and to not initiate any new exercise programs during the study. Additionally, subjects only performed the prescribed resistive exercise protocol, which did not include any upper body resistive exercise. Although diet was not controlled, subjects were instructed to maintain dietary habits for the duration of the study. Subjects were instructed not to take any nutritional supplements or similar products that may affect muscle performance, lean tissue mass, or bone metabolism.

Subjects participated in a 24-week study, comprised of six weeks of pre-training, sixteen weeks of training and two weeks of post-training testing. The volunteers were placed into one of two groups; one group worked with the aRED exercise device and the other with FW. The following tests were conducted during the pre- training, training, and/or post training:

Muscle Strength (1RM) - a one-repetition maximum (1RM) strength test was used as the criterion measure of muscle strength and was performed for each exercise, using both aRED and FW. Vertical Jump (VJ) test – is a measure of muscle power. Three counter-movement jumps were performed, and the VJ height determined was defined as the maximum height achieved over the three repetitions. This was performed on the same day but prior to 1RM testing to minimize the affect of fatigue on VJ performance.

Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA) and Quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT) scans – whole body and regional DXA scans were performed to determine area bone mineral density (aBMD) and volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) of the spine and hip.

Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) - used to measure whole body and leg lean tissue mass and thigh and lower leg muscle volume, respectively.

Blood and urine – collected for determination of markers of bone and muscle metabolism. All blood samples were collected fasting in the morning prior to performing any exercise. Following completion of the blood draw the 24-hour urine collection began, with the completion with the first void of the following day.

During the pre-training period, each subject had two DXA scans, one QCT scan, and one MRI scan. Urine and blood were collected at the end of pre-training. During this six week period subjects from both the aRED group and the FW group underwent weekly Muscle Strength (1RM) for each exercise and VJ training.

In the 16 weeks of training, each volunteer group (either aRED or FW) performed a set of lower body exercises prescribed during spaceflight (parallel squat, heel raise and dead lift). The training loads for the first half of this period was based on a percentage of the pre-training 1RM. Halfway through training, the muscle strength (1RM) for each exercise was re-measured. The training loads for the remainder of the training period were based on this 1RM value. Both group of subjects followed a periodized training protocol in which the resistance varied in a predetermined fashion within each week and incrementally increased every subsequent week. VJ, DXA, blood, and urine measurements were also determined.

Post-training, the VJ and 1RM on each exercise for both the aRED and FW groups were determined. QCT, MRI and DXA scans were conducted. Blood and urine samples were also taken.

RESULTS:
Total lumbar spine BMD significantly increased (p <0.05) after training in both the FW (Pre: 1.073 ± 0.140; Post: 1.091 ± 0.139 g·cm-2; + 2.6%) and ARED (Pre: 1.026 ± 0.071; Post: 1.053 ± 0.0732 g·cm-2; + 1.8%) groups with no difference between groups. Similarly, there was a main effect of training (p <0.05) on femoral neck BMD (FW, Pre: 0.870 ± 0.036, Post: 0.883 ± 0.057, + 1.6%; ARED, Pre: 0.846 ± 0.172, Post: 0.850 ± 0.176 g·cm-2, + 0.4%) with no between group differences. ARED exercise is not different than FW exercise with regard to stimulating increased BMD in the lumbar spine and femoral neck during 16 weeks of training in ambulatory subjects. The efficacy of ARED exercise to prevent space flight-induced BMD losses remains to be validated.

During Session 2, the SQ and DL 1RM (SQ: 90.2 ± 4.3, DL: 75.9 ± 3.3 kg) were less than Session 3 (SQ: 95.3 ± 4.1, DL: 81.5 ± 3.5 kg) and Session 4 (SQ: 96.6 ± 4.0, DL: 82.4 ± 3.9 kg), but there were no differences between Session 3 and Session 4. HR 1RM measured during Session 2 (150.1 ± 3.7 kg) and Session 3 (152.5 ± 3.9 kg) were not different from one another, but both were less than Session 4 (157.5 ± 3.8 kg). The reliability (ICC) of 1RM measures for Sessions 2-4 were 0.88, 0.83, and 0.87, for SQ, HR, and DL, respectively. When considering only Sessions 3 and 4, the reliability was 0.93, 0.91, and 0.86 for SQ, HR, and DL, respectively. One familiarization session and two test sessions (for SQ and DL) were required to obtain excellent reliability (ICC = 0.90) in 1RM values with novice subjects. The investigators were unable to attain this level of reliability following three HR testing sessions; additional sessions are required to obtain an ICC of =0.90. Resistive exercise training studies should consider the reliability of specific measures to ensure that reported strength changes are attributable to training and not to learning effects associated with 1RM testing.

SQ, HR, and DL 1RM increased in both FW (mean ± SE; SQ: 49 ± 6%, HR: 12 ±2 %, DL: 23 ±4 %) and ARED (SQ: 31 ± 4%, HR: 18 ± 2%, DL: 23 ± 3%) groups. Both groups increased muscle volume in the V (FW: 13 ± 2%, ARED: 10 ± 2%), H (FW: 3 ± 1%, ARED: 3 ± 1%), ADD (FW: 15 ± 2%, ARED: 10 ± 1%), LG (FW: 7 ± 2%, ARED: 4 ± 1%), MG (FW: 7 ± 2%, ARED: 5 ± 2%), and DP (FW: 2 ± 1%; ARED: 2 ± 1%) after training. There were no between-group differences in muscle strength or volume. The increase in muscle volume and strength following ARED training is not different than FW training. These findings indicate that ARED will likely protect against space flight-induced muscle atrophy and strength loss.

experiment_title: The Maturation of Bone and Dentin Matrices in Rats Flown on Cosmos 1887
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Maintaining musculoskeletal integrity in astronauts during prolonged space flight is important. This concern translates to questions about the role of gravity in calcium-mediated physiological mechanisms. The particular interest here in the skeletal status of rats flown in space focuses upon the normality of the matrix and mineral moieties deposited in the bones and teeth. This report deals with the analyses of various weight and non-weight bearing bones and incisor dentin from rats.

Approach:

The chemistry, hydroxyapatite crystal size, and maturation of bone and dentin (utilizing the mandible, skull cap or calvarium, and 5th lumbar vertebra) were characterized, including bone ash analysis, gradient density analysis, x-ray diffraction. Analyses for calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and zinc in bone and teeth were made on continuous traverses with a microprobe and appropriate crystal sensors.

Results:

Flight calvarial and vertebral bone ash were subnormal, but contained a normal percent composition of Ca, P, and Mg. These tissues varied from the norm by having lower Ca/P and higher Ca/Mg ratios than any of their age-matched controls (Vivarium and Synchronous). Gradient density analyses (calvaria) indicated a strong shift to the lower specific gravity fractions which was commensurate with impaired rates of matrix-mineral maturation. X-ray diffraction data were confirmatory. Bone hydroxyapatite crystal growth in flight rats was preferentially altered in a way to reduce the dimension of their C-axis. Flight rat dentin was normal with respect to age-matched control Ca, P, Mg, and Zn concentrations and Ca/P and Ca/Mg ratios. These observations affirm the concept that microgravity adversely affects the maturation of newly formed matrix and mineral moieties in bone.

experiment_title: Effect of Prolonged Space Flight on Human Skeletal Muscle
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
With humans currently occupying the International Space Station (ISS) for six months and space exploration missions of one to three years on the horizon, preservation of crewmember health and fitness is a major objective of the international space community. Exercise has been the primary utility used by the space agencies in an effort to protect cardiovascular, bone, and skeletal muscle health while in space for extended stays.

The aim of this study was to document the exercise program used by crewmembers aboard the ISS and examine its effectiveness for preserving skeletal muscle size and function. The focus of the study was on the calf muscles, since it has shown to atrophy more than other leg and upper body muscles with unloading. To obtain a comprehensive profile of skeletal muscle before and after flight, the investigators utilized magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to assess muscle volume, static and dynamic muscle testing to assess muscle performance, and muscle biopsies from the gastrocnemius and soleus to assess fiber type, contractile function, and microanatomy.

APPROACH:
Ten crewmembers participated in this investigation. The subject population consisted of American astronauts and Russian cosmonauts. During the six months the crewmembers were on the ISS, they had access to a treadmill (treadmill with vibration isolation system), two bicycle ergometers (cycle ergometer with vibration isolation system and a Velosiped, i.e., Russian bicycle exercise device), and an interim resistive exercise device (iRED). The crewmembers also had access to bungee cords, which they could use to provide resistance-type exercise for various muscle groups.

To determine muscle volume of the calf muscle, a MRI was performed on crewmembers 40 ± 3 (L - 40) days before launch and 4 ± 1 (R + 4) days after returning from the ISS. An additional MRI was obtained on each crewmember 19 ± 2 (R + 19) days after returning from space. All preflight MRI scans were conducted in Clear Lake, TX, and all postflight (R + 4) MRI scans were conducted in Moscow, Russia.

Maximal voluntary contraction and isokinetic strength of the left leg calf muscles was assessed using a torque velocity dynamometer. Each crewmember performed two familiarization sessions before preflight trials. Before launch, each crewmember performed four complete testing sessions over a four-month period (L - 127 ± 13, L - 87 ± 13, L - 40 ± 4, and L - 27 ± 1). Postflight, torque-velocity dynamometer measurements were obtained at R + 7 and R + 13 for all subjects.

A muscle biopsy was obtained from the lateral head of the gastrocnemius and soleus muscle of each crewmember before launch (L - 55 ± 2) and on landing day (R + 0). The landing day muscle biopsy was generally performed mid to late afternoon approximately six to eight hours after landing. Crewmembers were transported to the main medical operations facilities for observation. After a period of personal activities the crewmembers were brought to the data collection facility for the muscle biopsies. Crewmembers had performed very light ambulatory activities before the muscle biopsy procedure.

During flight, consumption of food and fluid was monitored according to the same schedule, but subjects used an automated bar code scanning system in which each individually packaged food item was labeled. The in-flight diet was designed to meet the nutritional requirements for ISS missions as established by NASA and the Russian Space Agency. Neither diet nor activity levels were restricted during any of the sampling periods. In-flight consumption data were stored in the bar code reader and downloaded to the ground.

RESULTS:
Exercise Training Profile
On average, subjects completed 138 ± 26 minutes per week of cycle exercise that generally ranged between 100 and 150 Watts (W). While in orbit, crewmembers used the cycle ergometer approximately 60% of mission days. Four of the crewmembers used the cycle ergometer approximately 81% or more of mission days, whereas four others averaged approximately 37% of mission days, and one crewmember did minimal cycling. For the treadmill exercise, subjects averaged 146 ± 34 minutes per week on a level grade at a speed ranging from 2.1 to 5.5 miles per hour. The treadmill appeared to be used less frequently compared with the cycle ergometer, accounting for less than 50% of total mission days. However, there was a wide range of treadmill use, with four crewmembers having a high volume (200 minutes per week) of walking/running activities. The other five crewmembers used the treadmill much less (85 minutes per week).

Muscle Volume
The gastrocnemius (medial and lateral) and soleus muscle were smaller (P < 0.05) after six months in space. Combined, the gastrocnemius and soleus atrophied (P < 0.05) - 13 ± 2% pre- to postflight. The soleus (- 15 ± 2%) atrophied more (P < 0.05) than the gastrocnemius (- 10 ± 2%) pre- to postflight. One crewmember had insignificant (- 1%) atrophy after the flight. Two of the crewmembers lost more than 20% of their calf muscle mass. Of the remaining six crewmembers, five lost more than 10% calf muscle mass. At R + 19 after landing, the gastrocnemius was still five to six percent atrophied, but this was not significant. Conversely, the soleus was still reduced (P < 0.05) compared with preflight, averaging - 9 ± 1% for all crewmembers. Although calf muscle volume was still reduced - 8 ± 2%, it represented a partial recovery from the more immediate (R + 4) flight measurement.

Muscle Performance
MVC was reduced (P < 0.05) -14 ± 2% at R + 7 and remained lower (- 13 ± 5%; P < 0.05) at R + 13. All nine crewmembers had a decline in MVC (range = - 7 to ± 22%) with flight. At R + 13, seven of the nine crewmembers were lower (range = -9 to ± 33%), with two crewmembers having a 5–10% increase compared with preflight. At the slow isokinetic speed (60° per second) there was a -20 ± 3% loss (P < 0.05), which was sustained (- 19 ± 4; P < 0.05) at R + 13. This pattern was also evident at the faster (180° per second) isokinetic speed with a 25 ± 10% reduction at R + 7 and R + 13. For both the slow and fast speeds, eight of the nine subjects had a decrease in muscle performance. On average, force-velocity characteristics were reduced - 20 to - 29% across the velocity spectrum (P < 0.05). Peak power was 134 ± 11, 91 ± 10, and 94 ± 13 W preflight, R + 7, and R + 13, respectively. On average, peak power declined 32% with spaceflight (P < 0.05).

Muscle Fiber Type
The investigators isolated and analyzed the MHC profile on a total of 4,328 single muscle fibers from the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles before and after flight. The breakdown was 1,960 muscle fibers for the gastrocnemius and 2,368 muscle fibers for the soleus. The gastrocnemius had a 12% decrease (P < 0.05) in MHC I fibers and an increase (P < 0.05) in MHC I/IIa (+ 4%) hybrid fibers and MHC IIa fibers (+ 9%). Seven of the eight subjects had a decrease in MHC I fibers (range = - 6 to - 31%). There were minimal MHC IIx and MHC I/IIa/IIx fibers detected in the pre- and postflight muscle samples. The four percent increase in hybrid muscle fibers appears to be the result of the MHC I/IIa hybrid fiber type. On average, the soleus had a 17% decrease (P < 0.05) in MHC I fibers. The shift away from MHC I fibers was distributed among the other fiber types (MHC I/IIa, IIa, IIa/IIx), with a non-significant increase of four to five percent within each MHC phenotype. Combined, the soleus had a 12% increase (P < 0.05) in hybrid MHC isoforms. Three of the crewmembers did not have any major alterations in fiber type of the soleus. Four of the crewmembers had a decrease in soleus MHC I fibers that ranged from - 20 to - 44%.

Nutrition
Crewmembers had a daily average caloric intake of 2,377 ± 118 kcal (range = 1,874 –2,902 kcal). The dietary percent breakdown of carbohydrate, fat, and protein was 48, 33, and 18%, respectively.

The average amount of muscle mass lost (- 13%) with space flight was slightly less than with previous long-duration stays on the Russian Space Station Mir (- 17%). The current ISS and previous Mir calf muscle volume loss is about one-half that of long-duration (60- to 120-day) bed rest studies showing a - 29% decrease among the control subjects without countermeasures. These data imply that the exercise in space is having a beneficial effect but is not complete, with the soleus being more difficult to protect than the gastrocnemius.

For more detailed results please refer to the PubMed article, Exercise In Space, which is freely available via PubMed's website or at the Journal of Applied Physiology's website, http://jap.physiology.org/.

experiment_title: Envihab Bed Rest Standard Measures: Psychological Testing
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Psychological Testing is one of eleven International Bedrest Standard Measures conducted on healthy subjects at the :envihab facility in Cologne, Germany. Psychological Testing will consist of Positive and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS) and the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ). The Positive and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS) Test Battery is a 20-item self-evaluation questionnaire that measures affects, or indicators of emotional stress. Emotional states are important to study during situations of isolation and confinement like bed rest experiments because they reflect the general state of the person at one step of the experiment. The PANAS separately assesses positive and negative effects. A positive affect reflects the extent to which a person feels enthusiastic, active, and alert. A person displaying high-positive affect has high energy, full concentration, and pleasurable engagement while a low-positive affect is characterized by sadness and lethargy. The separate measure of negative affect reflects the degree to which a person feels subjective distress and unpleasant engagement. A high-negative affect is described by anger, contempt, disgust, guilt, fear, and nervousness while a low-negative affect is described by a state of calmness and serenity.

GHQ is a self-evaluation questionnaire that measures the current mental health of the individual, utilizing the GHQ-12 and GHQ-28. For bed rest studies, GHQ is used to measure minor mental health problems and can be useful to prevent more important mental disorders during isolation and confinement situations. The GHQ-12 provides an overall total score for mental health, while the GHQ-28 provides an overall total score and scores on four subscales of somatic symptoms: anxiety, insomnia, social dysfunction and severe depression. The advantage of having four subscales makes the GHQ-28 a useful measure for bed rest studies. Each item on the GHQ is rated on a 4-point scale (0 to 3) indicating ‘less than usual’, ‘no more than usual’, rather more than usual’, ‘and much more than usual’.

The purpose of the standard measures project is to populate a repository with data that enables high-level monitoring of countermeasure effectiveness and meaningful interpretation of health and performance outcomes. These standard measures will support future, hypothesis-driven research that enables planetary missions by providing an optimized minimal set of measures captured from subjects. These measures will be available to other studies under data sharing agreements as well as undergo analysis to understand risk posture.

APPROACH:

Subjects are provided with the PANAS form and a pen or pencil. Subjects are asked to indicate to what extent they have felt each positive affect item and each negative affect item in the past week. Items are rates on a scale of 1 to 5, where 1 indicates not at all, and 5 indicates extremely. Scores for each affect are totaled and recorded. Positive and negative affect will be assessed once every two weeks throughout the study (pre-, in-, and post-bed rest). Each assessment will be completed about the same time of the day, within ±2 hours of the initial baseline assessment. PANAS should not be administered immediately after awakening or following maximal exercise.

Subjects are provided with the GHQ and asked to respond to questions inquiring about their health. GHQ is administered every two weeks throughout the study. Each assessment will be complete about the same time of the day, within ±2 hours of the initial baseline assessment. The GHQ-28 takes 10 minutes to complete and the GHQ-12 takes 5 minutes to complete. GHQ should not be administered immediately after awakening or following maximal exercise.

The scheduled days of collection are as follows:

  • 13 days and one day prior to mission
  • During the 14th and 28th day of the mission
  • One day and 13 days post mission
RESULTS:

The :envihab International Bedrest Standard Measures Test Battery is not a hypothesis-driven study, but rather a collection of data made available to future researchers and for trend analysis. As such, there are no specific hypotheses, outcome measures, or statistical analyses associated with the skeleton of the project. The questionnaire will capture a "snapshot" of optimized data that can be investigated by researchers in the future.

experiment_title: Mitigation of the Spacecraft Radiation Environment via Magnetic Shielding by an Array of Dispersed Superconducting Magnets
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Spacecraft are self-contained biospheres that must be designed to protect astronauts from harmful aspects of the interplanetary environment. Radiation encountered in deep space poses a significant threat to the health of astronauts and the success of future NASA missions beyond low-Earth orbit. Isotropic galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) and intermittent solar particle events (SPEs) threaten to cause acute radiation sickness and exceed NASA's permissible exposure limits for cancer risk for explorers in near-term space operations. Thus, effective methods of mitigating this radiation risk are high priorities for long-duration space flight. This experiment proposed to design a magnetic shielding architecture capable of reducing the amount of radiation by a factor of four to alleviate many biological uncertainties associated with this risk in the astronaut habitat. Through computational modeling, the spectra of harmful radiation was investigated and lead to the design of a “swarm-bot” type magnetic field configuration that deflected incoming radiation, thus forming a “safe-region” within the astronaut habitat. The novel method proposed here will work in concert with many aspects of existing superconductor technology. This system operates in parallel with the existing NASA Orion spacecraft infrastructure and in a continuous mode but without the need for continuous power.

APPROACH:
Investigators previously studied unexplored architecture for a radiation-protected deep space expedition. The Orion spacecraft itself will not be altered. Instead, a number of relatively small independent mobile satellites, each containing superconducting coils, will form a protective array around the spaceship. These satellites will act as magnetic lenses whose purpose is to reduce the radiation flux passing through the volume occupied by the spaceship, thus limiting crew exposure. The magnet array will be reconfigurable and its formation will exploit the principles of swarm-bot technology. Protection against both isotropic GCRs and late-phase SPEs require an evenly spherical magnetic shield which can be created by an array of magnets in a form of a regular polyhedron. The goal of the magnet array is to provide a safe region around the spacecraft in which the number density of the charged particles is lower than it would be in the absence of such a shield. Since magnetic fields do not change GCR and SPE particle energy, the dose of radiation absorbed by the biological tissue inside the protected region is reduced by the same proportion as the number density of the particles. This protection will also provide improved constraints for future models of biological responses to radiation and reduce uncertainties in studies of radiation effects.

RESULTS:
The investigators built an infrastructure of robust particle tracking simulations of 10^4-10^5 particles that create an isotropic flux of high order. This infrastructure can build evenly symmetric shields comprised of numerous dispersed magnetic dipoles. They have completed scaled-down, low energy (0.01 MeV) simulations showing that a dispersed 20-dipole shield at 50 m radius can successfully deflect significant isotropic radiation from a 10 m radius central volume (i.e., spacecraft). Despite the scaled-down energies and spatial scale, the code infrastructure is promising in showing that it is indeed feasible to shield a central volume from an isotropic particle flux using a dispersed magnetic shield.

experiment_title: Impact of Microgravity on Drug and Nutrient Absorption
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The long-term goal of this study was to identify gastrointestinal physiological alterations which are likely to occur in space flight and which will lead to profound alterations in drug and nutrient absorption. This study had three Specific Aims. (1) To utilize a pellet gastric emptying test to evaluate alterations in gastric emptying during antiorthosatatic bed rest conditions (ABR). (2) Determine the alterations in intestinal transit using the lactulose test during the ABR conditions simultaneously with the PGE test (Specific Aim 1) in order to discriminate gastric emptying changes from intestinal transit changes. (3) Identify alterations in the intestinal membrane permeability Peff of several model drugs and nutrients to determine the intestinal phenotype for absorption.

APPROACH:
The aims of the study were achieved through a protocol of normal subjects (under 3-day ambulatory) as well as a 5-day bed rest period. The study included gastric emptying and intestinal transit test prior to, during and following the ABR test.

RESULTS:
Drug absorption models were developed based on cyclical motility patterns in the gastrointestinal tract that lead to variable gastric emptying, intestinal transit, and drug absorption to allow more accurate monitoring of drug absorption variation and the correlation with gastrointestinal motility. The plasma concentration-time profiles following oral administration of drugs are often irregular and cannot be interpreted easily with conventional models based on first- or zero-order absorption kinetics and lag time. Six new models were developed using a time-dependent absorption rate coefficient, ka(t), wherein the time dependency was varied to account for the dynamic processes such as changes in fluid absorption or secretion, in absorption surface area, and in motility with time, in the gastrointestinal tract. In the present study, the plasma concentration profiles of propranolol obtained in human subjects following oral dosing were analyzed using the newly derived models based on mass balance and compared with the conventional models. Nonlinear regression analysis indicated that the conventional compartment model including lag time (CLAG model) could not predict the rapid initial increase in plasma concentration after dosing and the predicted Cmax values were much lower than that observed. On the other hand, all models with the time-dependent absorption rate coefficient, ka(t), were superior to the CLAG model in predicting plasma concentration profiles. Based on Akaike's Information Criterion (AIC), the fluid absorption model without lag time (FA model) exhibited the best overall fit to the data. The two-phase model including lag time, TPLAG model was also found to be a good model judging from the values of sum of squares. This model also described the irregular profiles of plasma concentration with time and frequently predicted Cmax values satisfactorily. A comparison of the absorption rate profiles also suggested that the TPLAG model is better at prediction of irregular absorption kinetics than the FA model. In conclusion, the incorporation of a time-dependent absorption rate coefficient ka(t) allows the prediction of nonlinear absorption characteristics in a more reliable manner.

The oral absorption model developed in the investigators’ laboratories has been applied to modeling a particularly complex absorption pattern observed for cimetidine which includes double peaks in the plasma level time curves Plasma cimetidine-time curves did not show the presence of double peaks in any subject following intravenous administration. The incidence of double peaks was 73% following oral administration and was independent of antral migrating motility complex phase. Further, it was found that oral administration of cimetidine in the quiescent phase resulted in significantly higher bioavailability and in other pharmacokinetic parameters compared to that obtained following administration in the active phase. Excellent linearity in plots of motility peaks versus plasma peaks with slopes close to unity were evident for both quiescent (r(2)=0.93) and active phase (r(2)=0.97) administration. A total of 14 peaks out of 22 (10 subjects, 64%) and 20 out of 27 peaks (11 subjects, 74%), were accounted for in quiescent and active phase oral administration, respectively. The proximal occurrence of plasma peaks to antral motility peaks typical of phase III contractions strongly implies that motility patterns may be responsible for secondary maxima following oral cimetidine administration in the fasted state.

The investigators further tested their pellet gastric emptying test to noninvasively measure changes in gastric emptying in the fasted-state in microgravity environment. This test is based on a salivary sampling and thus does not require blood withdrawal. To further validate the Pellet Gastric Emptying Test (PGET) as a marker of gastric emptying, a randomized, four-way crossover study was conducted with 12 healthy subjects. The study consisted of oral co-administration of enteric coated caffeine (CAFF) and acetaminophen (APAP) pellets in four treatment phases: Same Size (100 kcal), Fasted, Small Liquid Meal (100 kcal), and Standard Meal (847 kcal). The time of first appearance of measurable drug marker in plasma, t(initial), was taken as the emptying time for the markers. Co-administration of same size enteric coated pellets of CAFF and APAP (0.7 mm in diameter) revealed no statistically significant differences in t(initial) values indicating that emptying was dependent only on size and not on chemical make-up of the pellets. Co-administration of different size pellets indicated that the smaller 0.7-mm diameter (CAFF) pellets were emptied and absorbed significantly earlier than the larger 3.6-mm diameter (APAP) pellets with both the Small Liquid Meal (by 35 min) and the Standard Meal (by 33 min) (P<0.05). The differences in emptying of the pellets were not significant in the Fasted Phase. The results suggest that the pellet gastric emptying test could prove useful in monitoring changes in transit times in the fasted and fed states and their impact on drug absorption.”

In a previous study the investigators’ measured gene expression and correlated the gene expression with the absorption of a carrier-mediated antiviral drug, valacyclovir. The correlations observed in this study showed that the absorption of the carrier-mediated drug did indeed correlate with a transporter that has been reported to transport peptide compounds in vitro. The transport of valacyclovir, the l-valyl ester of acyclovir, has been suggested to be mediated by several carrier-mediated pathways in cell culture and animal models. The role and importance of these transporters in modulating valacyclovir absorption in humans has not been determined, however. Recent advances in genomic technology have facilitated the rapid and simultaneous determination of global mRNA expression profiles for thousands of genes in tissue biopsies directly associated with the absorption process, thereby dramatically increasing the value of studies in humans. Furthermore, there are correlations of pharmacokinetic parameters following oral valacyclovir or acyclovir administration with expression levels of intestinal genes in humans. Highly positive and significant correlations were observed with 4F2hc, an activator of cation-preferring amino acid transport systems, and human oligopeptide transporter (HPT1), an oligopeptide transporter expressed at higher levels in the human intestine compared with oligopeptide transporter (PEPT1). The validation of HPT1 microarray data with reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction and the enhanced valacyclovir uptake in HeLa/HPT1 cells suggest that the role of HPT1 in transport of peptides and peptidomimetics drugs needs to be examined in more detail. The interrelation of 4F2hc and HPT1 in transport may be of interest. No significant correlations of valacyclovir pharmacokinetic parameters with PEPT1 and with organic cation or anion transporter expression levels were observed. The highly negative correlations observed with known efflux pumps such as MDR1 (P-glycoprotein) and MRP2 (cMOAT), as well as with the CYP450 IIIA subfamily may indicate that these proteins may regulate the cellular accumulation and metabolism of acyclovir.

experiment_title: Quantitative Analysis of Selected Bone Parameters: Formation of Ectopic Bone in Implanted Matrices
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Undenatured bone matrix, demineralized and lyophilized, induces bone formation when implanted in muscle or fascia of host animals. This model was employed by Soviet scientists to evaluate the effects of space flight on bone formation in implanted matrices. Approximately half the implanted matrices recovered from basal, synchronous, vivarium control, and flight groups of rats were sent to the U.S. for independent evaluation. These were accompanied by samples of unimplanted bone matrix.

Approach:

Representative samples of ectopic bone recovered from each host rat were dried, weighed, and digested in 6N HCL. Calcium content was determined on an aliquot by atomic absorption spectrophotometry and µg Ca/mg dry weight of sample was calculated. Specimens were prepared by a method which has been developed to preserve enzyme activity in mineralized bone, thus permitting the identification of osteoclasts as well as osteoblasts. Specimens were cut into two to four segments and embedded for sagittal sectioning, producing 57 tissue blocks, each containing from one to three segments of the specimen. Sections were stained by the Goldner technique and a method intended to differentiate osteoblasts and osteoclasts by taking advantage of the high RNA content of the former and acid phosphatase activity of the latter, and examined microscopically.

Results:

A subjective study of slides suggests that the only areas stained green by the Goldner technique are mineralized bone, in contrast to what has been found in rat and human bone, and in unimplanted bone matrix. In these, all "mature," or once mineralized matrix stains green even after being completely demineralized, and only newly formed osteoid stains red. If that were the case in the implanted matrices, all the old, implanted matrix except its normal borders of osteoid would be stained green as well as the mineralized bone formed during the time the matrix was implanted in the host rat. One would then expect the red-stained area to be limited to the osteoid of the original matrix and the osteoid formed during the period of implantation which had not yet mineralized. Instead, it seems (but is not yet proven) that all the old matrix, whether once mineralized or not, is stained red. This suggests that a change occurred in the implanted matrix which could not be demonstrated in the specimens of the unimplanted matrix, reflected in a change of its tinctorial properties, and deserves further study.
