experiment_title: Multiplexed Colorimetric Solid Phase Extractions: Sensors for Monitoring Spacecraft Water Quality
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This three-year, ground-based project targeted the development, ground testing, and KC-135 flight-demonstration of chemical sensor systems and test kit methodologies for application to water quality monitoring in the life support systems used for space exploration. It focuses on the need for enabling analytical technologies that can function as a monitor of spacecraft water quality and as an alarm in the event of contamination.

This project sought to address both the near- and long-term needs of the space program for reliable easy-to-use methods to monitor the levels of key constituents in the drinking water storage distribution systems, including, iodine, silver, lead, cadmium, and nickel. Iodine and silver are the biocides used in the U.S. and Russian systems, respectively. Lead, cadmium, and nickel are contaminants detected in the potable water systems of the International Space Station (ISS) and must be monitored because of the potential threat to crew health. The unique feature of the proposed system, key components of which were successfully tested in recent KC-135 experiments, draws from the attributes of an innovative solid phase extraction (SPE) technique called colorimetric-SPE (C-SPE). C-SPE relies on the immobilization of selective optical reagents, high concentration factors, and the rapid readout of concentrated analytes via a hand held diffuse reflectance spectrophotometer. This work will take this innovation a step further by devising strategies for constructing multiple C-SPE addresses on the same disk. This extension will enhance the ability to rapidly determine several analytes in a set of operational steps, paralleling a multiplexed process. Investigators also planned to employ SPE for the development of a lightweight system that will concentrate organic alcohols (methanol, ethanol, and isopropyl alcohol), propylene glycol, formic acid, and a variety of semi-volatile organic compounds. This “microarchival” concept will dramatically reduce the down mass requirement for archival water quality monitoring. In all instances, efforts will focus on issues of crew health and safety, performance reliability, and minimization of consumables and stowage.

To carry out the above tasks, investigators assembled a team of scientists and engineers from the Microanalytical Instrumentation Center (MIC) at Iowa State University (ISU) and the Space Water Quality group at the Johnson Space Center (JSC). The ISU team was charged primarily with the first stage development of the chemical sensor systems and test kits. The lead tasks of the JSC team included methods development and validation as well as the design and development of flight compatible hardware for testing in microgravity environments. All stages of hardware design were guided by the extensive experience of the JSC team, and included considerations of system off-gassing, reagent toxicity, compatibility with operations in microgravity, and ease of use.

The results from our earlier project (NAG9 1191, “Rapid, Specific Chemical Sensors and Test Kit Methodologies for Spacecraft Water Quality Monitoring”) led to the development of a general procedure for the facile, low-level (mid-to-low part per billion) quantification of the biocides Ag+ and I2. The low detection limits largely reflect the high concentration factor (500-1000) obtained by the rapid extraction of an analyte onto a SPE membrane impregnated with an analyte-selective colorimetric reagent. This technology provides a generic platform that has the potential to be readily extended to a host of other analytes important to the space program. The current project takes this innovation a step further by devising strategies for constructing multiple C-SPE addresses on the same disk.

The goals of this project reflect the needs of the space program for analytical instruments and methodologies that: 1) meet the monitoring requirements of the ISS and ongoing Shuttle missions; 2) function as a platform for the development of the analytical methods and ancillary hardware for the projected monitoring requirements for the Mars and other visionary missions; and 3) enable the acquisition of the analytical data necessary for defining further the critical monitoring requirements for crew health and safety in such missions.

The integrated analytical method developed allows determination of low concentrations of iodine, iodide and silver ion. A high concentration factor is obtained by extraction of the selected analytes onto an impregnated membrane disk containing embedded polymer particles. No solvent elution or thermal desorption is required because the amount of the colored analyte complex is directly measured on the disk by DRS. The flow-through mode of SPE used here provides a much greater concentration effect and hence better sensitivity than methods in which a color species is measured in solution or on the surface of a probe that is merely dipped into the sample solution. The method is also very rapid. The concentration step requires about 40 seconds and the reflectance measurement only 2 seconds. The equipment is small, portable and battery operated so that analyses can be performed on spacecraft in a microgravity environment. The method also provides a generic platform with the potential for extension to the measurement of other analytes, either individually or more excitingly, through the development of a multiplexed C-SPE system for the simultaneous extraction of multiple analytes.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
1. KC-135 flight demonstrations of the efficacy of C-SPE for use in microgravity.
The major goal of the four KC-135 flights was to attain agreement between ground and flight data for this methodology. In this set of experiments, in flight water analyses were performed mostly without the added challenge of air bubbles in the test samples. In order to eliminate this difficulty, test solutions were prepared preflight that were devoid of air bubbles. This procedural change allowed investigators to address whether microgravity is the root cause of the past differences observed between flight and ground-based data. They also sought to test the microgravity compatibility of a method for the determination of nickel. The nickel analysis embodies a new sample manipulation platform and had yet to be tested in microgravity. As such, three of the four flights were aimed at assessing the zero-G performance of the C-SPE determinations of iodine, silver, and nickel.

Another goal was to better characterize the origin of experimental bias between ground and flight data observed in previous KC-135 experiments. Thus, the third flight used bubble-free solutions in syringes and bags would be analyzed along with samples (containing many bubbles) collected from a simulated water system. This comparison would indicate whether the error occurs in filling the Teflon bag from the sample port, from filling a syringe from that bag, or from some other source. The water samples used in these experiments were prepared as follows. Water containing iodine at various levels was obtained by diluting a volumetric iodine standard. These test solutions were analyzed by the LCV method for I2 content. Water containing silver at various trace levels was prepared by diluting a silver standard) with ultrapure water. These test solutions were analyzed by ICP-MS for total and dissolved silver. Dissolved silver was assayed by first filtering the sample or standard with a 0.45 micron nylon syringe filter. Buffered water samples containing nickel were prepared using a nickel standard and sodium borate (pH 9.0, 5% w/w). These test solutions were immediately analyzed by ICP-MS for total and dissolved nickel. Dissolved nickel was assayed by first filtering the sample or standard with a 0.45 micron nylon syringe filter.

All samples were concurrently analyzed by C-SPE both in flight and on the ground. These samples were also analyzed at the same time by the noted base-lined laboratory methods. To accurately compare ground and flight C-SPE findings, the following steps were taken: 1) ground analyses were conducted while the aircraft was flying the same experiment; 2) samples, reagents, and all other requisite materials for ground and flight testing came from the same preparative batches; 3) analyses were performed as close as possible to the same temperature; 4) analyses were performed on the ground in the same assembly line fashion as in flight by using a timer to keep each analytical step within the same time intervals as the zero-G intervals obtained in flight; and 5) flights #1, 2, and 4 were done using pre-loaded syringes containing bubble-free samples to eliminate sampling error from bubbles. Each C-SPE analysis required one parabola to expose the membrane, one to dry the membrane with 60 mL of air, and one to acquire the diffuse reflectance spectrum. The iodine tests were performed using 10.0-mL samples, while the silver and nickel tests both used 1.0-mL samples.

The iodine data showed that the C-SPE analysis is precise, linear, and gravity independent. Plots of both the ground and flight average diffuse reflectance values, expressed as F(R), the Kubelka-Munk function, verses iodine concentration as determined by LCV were linear, with R2 values of 0.999 and 0.997, respectively, with slopes differing by only 7.67%. This agreement is within experimental error. For silver experiments with syringes filled in one-G, both the ground and flight plots of F(R) verses silver concentration determined by ICP-MS were also linear, R2 values of 0.986 and 0.982, respectively, with slopes differing by only 0.63%. For both analyses, this agreement is a marked improvement over previous KC-135 flight experiments, and, more importantly, validates the general utility of C-SPE methodology for operation in microgravity.

For nickel, averaged F(R) for ground and flight measurements were also plotted using the ICP-MS results as the ordinate and the average diffuse reflectance values as the abscissa. Once again, linear regression was used to calculate the best-fit lines shown on the plots. The ground C-SPE data yielded an R2 value of 0.981. The flight C-SPE data, however, exhibited a marked decrease in linearity, having an R2 value of 0.901. The nickel C-SPE data obtained in flight had a slope that was half that of the ground C-SPE data, and relative standard deviations that were much higher than the ground data. By inspection, it was clear that the nickel flight membranes failed to develop a color intensity close to that observed on the ground. We also found that much more of the water sample remained upstream of the membrane upon disassembly of the cartridge. These discrepancies indicate an inability to effectively meter the 1-mL sample volume through the cartridge used in the nickel determinations, which had a much larger dead volume than that used in the silver and iodine analyses. We note that this shortcoming was revealed as a result of the microgravity simulation, demonstrating the importance of continued KC-135 testing.

In Flight #3, the C-SPE results obtained from the two preloaded syringes at each silver concentration produced a linear plot (R2 =0.992) with a slope that agrees with the results from the fourth flight. Five silver analyses each were done from a sample bag that had been degassed. Five additional samples were analyzed after collection from an identical bag that had been sampled from a water system simulating the space station water system, which allowed gas bubbles to enter the bag during sampling. Comparison of the precision and accuracy of these two sets of data was to indicate which step(s) of the procedure introduces the error caused by air bubbles. The bubble-free bag averaged an F(R) of 0.0641. Substituting this value into the linear equation derived from the silver standards analyzed during this flight gives 0.42 mg/L, or 84.7% recovery on this 0.50 mg/L standard. The bag sampled with bubbles present gave a value of 0.35 mg/L, also on a 0.50 mg/L standard. The relative standard deviation increased from 16% for pre-filled syringes to 29% with the addition of bubbles. This result clearly mandates the need for bubble removal, which is a key focus in the next phase of our research effort.

Another important change in the planning for the KC-135 flights should be noted. For this set of flights, investigators invoked a more rigorous preflight training program by extensively rehearsing each analysis on the ground the full week before the actual flights. With this change, all flyers repeatedly practiced all facets of each experiment. During this process, operational issues and details were carefully examined, with several improvements in each procedure identified and implemented. This procedural change clearly enhanced the effectiveness of the flight-testing, and will be adopted for all future simulations.

Conclusion- These KC-135 experiments have validated the effective operation of C-SPE as a method for the quantification of biocides in water samples in reduced gravity. The iodine C-SPE method was the most precise, showing close agreement between ground and flight results. The silver C-SPE method proved to be feasible with a drinking water sampling system almost identical to that currently used on the space station now. C-SPE was shown not to be effective in the analysis of nickel in its current configuration for in flight deployment. However, the dead volume shortcoming should be readily correctable through a redesign of fluid handling hardware. Overall, the results of these experiments show that, as a water quality monitoring system, C-SPE has the potential to provide a much-needed analytical capability for operation on the ISS.

2. Multiplexed Colorimetric Solid Phase Extraction (MC-SPE)
The creation of MC-SPE, which represents a new addition to parallel analysis systems, was driven in large part by the limited astronaut time available on ISS to conduct water testing. As such, the development of a multiplexed water analysis system has the potential to increase the collection of water quality data with a minimal investment of on-orbit crew time. In extending C-SPE to a multiplexed format (MC-SPE), a filter holder that incorporates discrete analysis channels and a jig that facilitates the concurrent operation of multiple syringes have been designed, enabling the simultaneous determination of three different measures of water quality. Separate, single parameter membranes, placed in a read-out cartridge create unique, parameter-specific addresses at the exit of each channel. Following sample exposure, the diffuse reflectance spectrum of each address is collected serially and the Kubelka-Munk function, F(R), is used to quantify each water quality parameter via calibration curves. Performance evaluations of the MC-SPE platform were conducted using sample pH, silver(I), and nickel(II). Determinations of silver(I) (0.05-0.5 ppm) and nickel(II) (1.8-5.0 ppm) follow established C-SPE methods on reversed phase extraction membranes using 5-(p-dimethylaminobenzylidene) rhodanine and dimethylglyoxime, respectively, as colorimetric reagents. Sample pH (2.5-5.0) is measured using an anion exchange membrane impregnated with fluorescein. These determinations require ~120 s to complete using a total sample volume of 3.0 mL.

A syringe jig was constructed that facilitates the concurrent operation of multiple syringes. The jig positions the syringes to allow all three plungers to be depressed simultaneously, introducing sample to the multiplexed filter holder. The multiplexed filter holder is composed of four sections, a syringe interface, a flow chamber, a read-out cartridge, and a base. Fabrication of each section is described below.

Syringe interface. The upper portion of the filter holder directs the sample flow from each syringe to one of the three analysis channels in the flow chamber. This piece was fabricated from 35-mm diameter white delrin. The bottom of the interface was machined to mate directly to the flow chamber, leaving no dead volume. Samples flow through the syringe interface into the flow chamber via three 1.6 mm-diameter ports lined with PEEK tubing. The PEEK port lining protrudes from the top of the interface and is connected to nylon Luer slip fittings with Silicone tubing. The Luer fittings were pressed into an acrylic brace to simplify connection to the sample syringes.

Flow Chamber. The center portion of the filter holder defines each analysis channel. The flow chamber was fabricated from 35-mm diameter white delrin cut to a length of 33.3 mm. Three equally spaced 7.0 mm-diameter holes were drilled along the axial direction of the cylinder to create the three analysis channels. The top of each channel was bored out to accept a 9.0-mm diameter support screen. These screens rest 12.0 mm above the channel outlets and facilitate the placement of the wool and paper used for the in-line addition of immobilized reagents (nickel(II) method) in the channels. The bottom of the flow chamber was machined to fit over the base of the filter holder. Base. The bottom portion of a 25-mm diameter Swinnex polypropylene filter holder was used as the filter holder base.

Read-out cartridge. Two 25-mm diameter circles were cut from 0.05-mm thick nitrile rubber. These circles were stacked and sealed together at one point on their circumference with double-sided tape. Three equally spaced 7-mm diameter holes were cut through the rubber circles to align with the analysis channels in the flow chamber and define the area of the read-out addresses. Loading individual, parameter-specific membrane disks between the two layers of nitrile rubber creates a single read-out cartridge with three separate 7.0-mm addresses.

Clamp. The entire multiplexed filter holder is held together with a brass screw clamp. The clamp consists of two brass rings machined to fit snugly around the syringe interface and base of the filter holder. Following assembly of the filter holder (described below), three screws are inserted through the ring at the syringe interface and threaded into the ring at the holder base. Tightening these screws secures the filter holder sections in place.

Three 10-mm diameter C-SPE membrane disks, one specific for each sample parameter, were loaded in the read-out cartridge. The read-out cartridge was placed on the filter holder base and the flow chamber was positioned such that the outlets of the analysis channels were aligned with the addresses on the read-out cartridge. Next, support screens were inserted in each flow channel. A DMG chad and a circle of buffer wool were added, in that order, to the support screen in the analysis channel above the nickel(II) membrane. The sample interface was positioned on top of the flow chamber ensuring that the PEEK-lined ports were oriented at the inlet of the analysis channels. Finally, the entire assembly was clamped together using the brass screw clamp.

A mask was used to match the aperture size of the spectrophotometer to the diameter of the addresses on the read-out cartridge. The mask was made by cutting a 7-mm diameter hole in a 100-µm thick polyester sheet and then painting the sheet flat black with spray paint. The mask was affixed to a BYK-Gardner sample locator using double sided tape.

Sampling procedure. Three 1.0-mL aliquots of a water sample were collected in 1.0-mL plastic syringes. These syringes were fitted into the syringe jig and connected to the syringe interface of the filter holder. The plungers of all three syringes were depressed simultaneously to meter 1.0 mL of sample solution through each analysis channel in the flow chamber. Following passage of these solutions, the syringes were removed and the membranes were dried by passing air through the filter holder with a 60-mL syringe and an adapter mated to the analysis channels. At this point, the filter holder was disassembled and the read-out cartridge was removed. The cartridge was placed under the sample locator so that one read-out address was visible through the aperture mask. The spectrum of that address was acquired and the cartridge was repositioned to sample the other two addresses in a serial fashion. This process entire process, beginning with syringe filling, requires ~120 s. Results-pH method development. There are three main reasons FL was chosen to demonstrate the ability to measure pH optically in MC-SPE. First, the biodegradability and low toxicity of FL make it an ideal reagent for use in spacecraft environments. Second, experiments have shown that the absorbance of aqueous FL at 490 nm changes with pH in the range 1.25 to 8.70. And third, most common metal ions do not interfere with the dye response.

The response of the FL membranes was assessed by running conventional C-SPE trials using 13-mm diameter membrane disks and 0.1 M buffer solutions with pH values between 2.17 and 6.23 as samples. The results of these experiments were compared to the published absorbance studies to determine if immobilization affected the reactivity of the dye. Because the diffuse reflectance spectrophotometer records relative reflectance in 20-nm intervals, the relative reflectance of the samples at 490 nm could not be recorded. Instead, the value of F(R) calculated from the relative reflectance at 480 nm was used to compare C-SPE results to absorbance experiments. When 1.0-mL buffer samples were tested, the trend in the plots of F(R) at 480 nm and the absorbance at 490 nm versus pH were very similar. However, because of the large absorbtivity of the FL dianion, the relative reflectance values above pH 4.5 are in the high error regime of spectrophotometric measurements. In order to reduce possible errors in pH measurements made by C-SPE, a detection wavelength where the pH membranes have a higher relative reflectance, and therefore a lower F(R) value, was used. Based on a visual inspection of the data, the F(R) value at 560 nm was selected. The F(R) values at this wavelength follow the same trend as the data at 480 nm, enabling determinations of sample pH between 2.17 and 6.23 with reduced error.

Multi-analyte experiments. To validate the performance of the MC-SPE system, calibration plots were constructed for silver(I), nickel(II), and pH using the three-channel filter holder. The collection of the silver(I) and nickel(II) data was accomplished by loading all three addresses in the read-out cartridge with C-SPE membrane disks specific for one analyte and running standard solutions containing only that analyte through the multiplexed holder. In the case of nickel(II), a DMG chad and a circle of buffer wool were loaded in each analysis channel before sampling. The F(R) values collected in these experiments were then averaged and plotted against the analyte concentration to obtain calibration plots. Data for the pH calibration were gathered using the silver(I) and nickel(II) standard solutions and a read-out cartridge loaded with three pH sensitive membrane disks. The F(R) values obtained from these trials were plotted against the pH values of these standards, as measured with a pH meter.

Silver(I) calibration. The same wavelength of detection used in the conventional C-SPE experiments, 580 nm, was employed for all silver(I) measurements with MC-SPE. These determinations exhibited an upper limit of the linear response range near 0.5 ppm. Above this concentration, the F(R) values at 580 nm begin to level off. The lower limit of detection, calculated as the blank signal plus three times the standard deviation of the blank was 0.05 ppm.

The observed leveling of the response is attributed to saturation of the DMABR. Conventional C-SPE measurements, which use a 13-mm diameter membrane disk to extract analytes also exhibit saturation, but at a higher level of silver(I) (i.e., ~1.0 ppm). The addresses on the read-out cartridge are only 7 mm in diameter, representing an active area that is approximately 70% smaller than that used in the conventional (single analyte) C-SPE system. Since both C-SPE platforms use 1.0-mL sample volumes, the multiplexed membrane disk saturates at a lower concentration than the conventional C-SPE disk. In the linear response region, between 0.05 ppm and 0.5 ppm, all measurements showed an uncertainty of less than 15%.

Nickel(II) calibration. The same wavelength of detection used in the conventional C-SPE experiments, 540 nm, was employed for all nickel(II) measurements with the multiplexed filter holder. Unlike the silver(I) experiments, the nickel(II) studies performed with the multiplexed holder demonstrated a smaller linear response range than the single analyte method. This decrease cannot be associated with membrane disk saturation, as the upper concentration limit of the analysis has been shown to be limited by the release of DMG from the reagent chad. Rather, the decreased range is a consequence of an increase in the concentration limit of detection from 0.5 ppm to 1.8 ppm.

The loss of membrane disk signal at low concentrations is ascribed to two factors: the proximity of the buffer wool to the reagent chad and the decrease in dead volume between the reagent chad and the collection disk. Both factors reduce the reaction time for the sample before passing through the membrane disk. In the conventional nickel(II) platform, the sample syringe is filled through a buffer wool cartridge. This step allows the sample to equilibrate at pH 9.0 in the syringe barrel while the buffer cartridge is detached from the syringe and the reagent chad/collection membrane assembly is attached to the syringe. In the multiplexed holder, the buffer wool sits directly on top of the reagent chad. As a consequence, solutions passing through the wool immediately encounter the reagent chad, which reduces the time available for equilibration of the buffer and sample before the sample encounters the reagent chad. Our earlier report on this method showed that if the sample does not reach the proper pH, the rate of reaction is severely diminished and the precipitate may not exhaustively form before the solution passes through the read-out address. This loss of precipitate will lower the F(R) at all concentrations, and have a negative effect on the limit of detection.

Decreasing the dead volume between the reagent chad and the collection address should have a similar effect on the measurement. In the conventional method, once the solution passes through the reagent chad, it fills the dead volume between the chad and the collection membrane disk. This dead volume is slightly less than the total sample volume (1.0 mL), so a small portion of the sample is passed through the membrane disk immediately. The remainder of the sample sits stationary above the collection disk until it is displaced by air during membrane drying. The time lapse associated with the removal of the sample syringe and connection of the drying syringe allows more time for the analyte and reagent to complex in solution. In the multiplexed holder, this dead volume is roughly half (~0.4 mL) that in the two cartridge assembly used for conventional experiments (~0.8 mL), but the sample volume is the same. As a result, more of the sample passes through the collection address without the benefit of extra residence time. At lower concentrations, samples may not form enough precipitate to be distinguished from the background. Despite the increased limit of detection, measurements made in the linear response region for nickel(II) in the multiplexed holder, 1.8 to 5.0 ppm, show an uncertainty similar to that of the silver(I) calibration, less than 15%.

pH calibration. In initial experiments with the silver(I) and nickel(II) standards, the response from the membrane disks was somewhat erratic, failing to follow the trend observed with the buffer solutions. This behavior was attributed to the varying ionic strengths of the standards, which has a known effect on the response of pH indicators, including immobilized forms of FL. The pH platform was tested again using silver(I) and nickel(II) standard solutions prepared in 0.05 M sodium nitrate to adjust the ionic strength of the standards. The response from these new solutions, which had measured pH values between 2.5 and 5.0, was more reproducible and showed an uncertainty less than 17%. Additionally, the demonstrated relation between F(R) at 560 nm and pH agreed closely with that observed using buffer samples. We note that the FL-impregnated membranes exhibited a response between pH 2.17 and 6.23, but our calibration run was restricted to the pH range encompassed by the silver(I) and nickel(II) standards.

The response of the pH membrane disks deviates from the sigmoidal behavior typically exhibited by pH indicators in absorbance studies. This same deviation is found in the solution absorbance studies with FL and has been attributed to the fact that all four forms of FL contribute to the solution absorbance at 490 nm. Because F(R) at 560 nm follows the same trend with pH as absorbance studies, multiple forms of FL are clearly contributing to the C-SPE response.

Multi-analyte trials. The sample solutions used in the performance evaluation of MC-SPE were prepared to contain levels of silver(I) and nickel(II) that spanned the linear response range of the two metals as defined by the calibration studies. Each sample was run in triplicate (N=3) and the average F(R) value at the wavelength of detection was used for quantification of all sample parameters.

Overall, there is strong agreement between the multiplexed determinations and the actual values of the sample parameters. All but one measurement showed a percent difference less than 14%, and all but three demonstrated a difference below 10%. Several measurements were discarded because of visible misalignment of the membrane disks with the addresses in the read-out cartridge. The cause of the misalignment is thought to be a shifting of the membrane disks between the layers of the read-out cartridge during assembly of the multiplexed filter holder. This created a small gap that allowed a portion of the sample to leak around the membrane in the read-out address. This issue will be addressed in future designs of the multiplexed platform by simplifying holder assembly and minimizing the need for manual alignment of platform components. Importantly, these results validate the performance of our MC-SPE platform for the concurrent analysis of several water quality parameters.

Conclusions - The ability of a MC-SPE to simultaneously determine three of NASA’s Priority 1 water quality parameters has been demonstrated. Methods encompassing two variations of C-SPE and requiring chemically different membranes were successfully combined to measure silver(I) levels ranging from 0.05 to 0.5 ppm, nickel(II) levels between 1.8 to 5.0 ppm, and sample pH between 2.5 and 5.0. All three parameters were determined in approximately 120 seconds using a total sample volume of 3.0 mL.

experiment_title: Foot Reaction Forces During Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The loss of bone mineral in the lower extremities is widely viewed as the critical factor that may limit long term human habitation of space. Decrements in muscle funciton as a result of prologned exposure to microgravity also have important implications for performance and safetly during space missions. Lower extremity loading during daily life in microgravity is thought to be markedly reduced compared to 1-G; although, no measurements have yet been made to quantify the load reduction. Recent studies have shown that as much as 1.58% per month of bone mineral is lost from the proximal femur during flights lasting from four to fourteen months and that more than 20% of knee extensor strength is lost in flights lasting 60 to 80 days. This study was performed in attempt to quantify mechanical load during periods of time that represent typical activities of daily life both on Earth and during a mission on the International Space Station (ISS).

The objective of the FOOT experiment was to quantify and explore the relationship between loading of the human body and changes in the homeostasis of the musculoskeletal system during space flight compared to Earth.

Another objective was to study the foot-ground reaction forces, electromyographic signals and joint movements at the hip, knee and ankle during twelve hour periods over several days of daily activities on Earth on ISS; and to examine postflight changes in strength, bone mineral density (BMD), and muscle volume.

APPROACH:
Hardware designed for ambulatory data collection on the Human Research Facility (HRF) was used to collect ground reaction force, electromyography (EMG), and three lower extremity joint angles (right hip, knee, and ankle) during full work days. Daily mechanical load stimulus was calculated using two competing theories and daily neural drive was estimated from the measurements obtained. Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA) scans of the proximal femur, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the leg muscles and maximum ankle, knee and hip joint torques were taken preflight and postflight to quantify any bone density, muscle volume and muscle strength changes that occurred during the mission.

The human body is designed to bear weight. Without the stimulation caused by placing weight on lower extremities, whether due to the microgravity environment or lack of use on Earth, bones lose mass and muscles lose strength. The Foot experiment characterized the load placed on lower extremities during daily activities on ISS and examined to what degree mechanical load stimulus, via an in-flight exercise routine, could prevent the muscle atrophy and bone loss associated with space flight.

To achieve this objective, Foot had several sensors mounted in a special pair of Lycra exercise pants known as the lower extremity monitoring suit (LEMS). The total force-foot ground interface (TF-FGI) served as an insole that, when placed inside a shoe, measures the amount of force placed on the bottom of the foot. Joint excursion sensors (JESs) record joint angles at the ankle, knee, and hip. Electromyography electrodes recorded muscle activity, including net neural drive, along the leg (the vastus medialis, rectus femoris, biceps femorics, gastrocnemius, and tibial anterior) and in the right arm (the biceps brachii and triceps brachii). Information was collected by an ambulatory data acquisition system (ADAS) and downloaded into the Human Research Facility (HRF) laptop on board ISS after each session.

A baseline for each participant was created preflight: a DXA image established bone mineral density; a muscle cross-sectional area was measured via Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI); and joint strength was determined using Cybex, an isokinetic dynamometer.

During their stay on ISS, the participants wore the LEMS and accompanying armband for approximately eight hours as they went about their daily activities, including exercise. Data was taken for four days evenly spaced throughout the Expedition. The FGI-FCU was used to calibrate the insoles; a nitrogen source kept a neoprene bladder inflated to maintain contact with the surface of the insole. The data was transferred from the ADAS1 to the HRF laptop after each session.

After flight, additional DEXA and MRI images and Cybex measurements were taken on each participant. The preflight, inflight, and postflight data are compared to create a complete dataset of activity, muscle strength, and bone density changes.

RESULTS:
Prior to the start of this experiment there was poor understanding about the negative effects of long-term exposure to microgravity on bone and muscle, and particularly the effectiveness of the exercise countermeasures in counteracting them. Previous studies have only reported bone and muscle loss in microgravity; whereas, the current experiment characterizes the movement environments that cause such atrophy from joint excursions, muscle activity and foot force data collected over entire typical working days. Comparison of data collected on the ISS with that on Earth gives a clear understanding of the amount of activity that still needs to be supplemented to compensate for weightlessness. The results provided insights on the improvements the exercise modalities and the exercise regimens themselves need, both qualitatively and quantitatively in order to provide the required stimulus that would preserve bone and muscle. The results have a direct impact and lessons to offer when planning for missions to the moon and Mars.

The findings from this experiment support the conclusion that the current exercise durations, combined with markedly reduced loading during ISS locomotor exercise compared to that on Earth, minimal loading from the cycle ergometer and the moderate loads from iRED exercise, may be insufficient to provide the loading stimulus required to prevent bone resorption. There is still high rate of bone and muscle loss in spite of the presence of exercise countermeasures. Muscles experienced a more dominant pattern of isometric action in microgravity at the expense of eccentric and concentric actions, with the hip, knee and ankle joints experiencing fewer, smaller amplitude, slower velocity movements.

It is recommended that approaches to using increased loads that are comfortable for crewmembers while they exercise on current ISS exercise devices be explored for future ISS missions. Future generations of exercise equipment should be designed to provide higher loads. Until increased loading is provided, it is too early to determine whether or not exercise can serve as an effective countermeasure to musculoskeletal deconditioning that occurs in long-duration exposure to microgravity. The possibility also exists; however, that even with improved exercise regimens, pharmacological or other mechanical intervention, perhaps in combination with exercise, will be required to maintain musculoskeletal health. Future experimental work is required to address these uncertainties.

experiment_title: Bed Rest Standard Measures: Psychological Stress Measures
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Prolonged exposure to reduced gravity, physiological stress or other factors associated with space flight may result in immune system dysregulation. Latent herpesvirus reactivation, a measurable result of dysregulated immunity, has been detected in crewmembers during and immediately following space missions.

In the investigator's previous studies of astronauts, investigators found altered peripheral leukocyte distribution, altered cytokine production profiles, elevated levels of latent viral reactivation and elevated levels of cortisol during or immediately following long and short duration space flight. In addition, significant increases in stress hormones (i.e., cortisol, catecholamines) were found after landing. Notably, investigators found increased shedding of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV), two medically important herpesviruses, during space flight along with evidence of decreased cellular immunity. These increases in stress hormones directly correlated with CMV and EBV reactivation. Thus, latent herpesvirus reactivation in these astronauts may have resulted from both direct (i.e., stress hormones) and indirect (i.e., decreased immune function) mechanisms stemming from launch and landing acceleration. These results underscore the need to determine the causes underlying immune suppression in space in order to develop countermeasures.

APPROACH:
A panel of assays was designed to monitor immune system dysregulation, viral reactivation, and physiological stress has been developed and validated at the Johnson Space Center (JSC). These assays will be applied to a future ISS/Shuttle Supplemental Medical Objective (SMO). This assay panel is also appropriate to monitor the status and function of the immune system, viral reactivation, and physiological stress during ground-based analog studies. These assays were included on all several bed rest campaigns for the purpose of monitoring the immune status of the participants. While bed rest is not the most appropriate model for space flight-associated immune dysregulation, it is possible that the various countermeasures proposed for evaluation during bed rest may affect immune function. For this reason, the immune function of the participants was monitored. Along with physiological stress, psychological stress will also be monitored for the bed rest studies.

The measurement of psychological stress was done using two standard questionnaires, the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) and the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS). Each subject was asked to complete both questionnaires prior to all saliva sample collections.

RESULTS:
This experiment was performed during Bed Rest Campaigns 3A, 3B, 3C, and 5A. In general, subjects did not display altered peripheral leukocyte subsets, constitutive immune activation, altered T cell function, or significant latent viral reactivation (EBV, VZV). Levels of constitutively activated T cells (CD8+/CD69+) and virus-specific T cells (CMV and EBV) decreased during the study. Cortisol levels (plasma and saliva) did not vary significantly during 90-day bed rest.

No significant difference was found in the Positive Assay score, the negative scores, or Perceived Stress Scores in the subjects during bed rest as compared to the pre-bed rest values.

Conclusions: These data demonstrate the absence of significant immune system alteration and physiological stress during 90-day bed rest, and establish control data against which future studies (including countermeasures) may be compared.

experiment_title: Non-pharmaceutical Motion Sickness Mitigation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES
Motion sickness represents one of the greatest clinical challenges impacting crew activities following G-transitions. This project seeks to validate a non-pharmaceutical tool using galvanic vestibular reduction (GVR) by transcutaneously delivering bilateral inhibitory signals to suppress vestibular sensitivity and reduce post-landing motion sickness. The first specific aim is to evaluate the effect of timing and magnitude on the administration of our non-pharmaceutical treatment to motion sickness.

While the researchers have previously demonstrated that their approach can mitigate motion sickness if introduced prior to provocative stimuli, one of the goals of this study is to determine the efficacy if they administer the treatment following the onset of symptoms. Validating the efficacy following symptom onset would greatly enhance flexibility to implement this treatment during recovery operations. Using a repeated measures counter-balanced design exposing subjects to provocative Coriolis cross-coupling stimuli on a rotating chair, the researchers will compare motion sickness severity across three treatment interventions: prior to stimulus (symptom) onset, following symptom onset, and placebo control. Symptom severity will be assessed using both subjective reports and objective autonomic measures (e.g., electrogastrography). They expect that the most effective administration will be GVR delivered prior to the onset of symptoms, but that it will continue to be more effective relative to placebo control even if delivered following symptom onset.

In order to leverage their non-pharmaceutical technique that allows continuous adjustments in “dosage” level throughout recovery, the researchers must map changes in GVR level with functional performance. The second specific aim is to characterize the dose response of GVR amplitude to functional fitness task performance. Investigators will measure performance on a sensorimotor and cognitive test battery in steps ranging from 0mA (control) to the level of GVR thought to provide maximal motion sickness protection. The advantages of their non-pharmaceutical countermeasure approach will be to provide rapid therapeutic effect while allowing continuous titration of GVR amplitude during recovery to minimize side effects while enhancing performance.

APPROACH
Twenty-nine healthy subjects (32.0 ±9.1 y mean ±std, 16 male/ 13 female) were recruited to participate in a repeated measures design involving four test sessions. Subjects completed a medical history questionnaire confirming they had no known history of vestibular pathology. Subjects completed a short version of a standardized motion sickness susceptibility questionnaire (MSSQ-short, Golding 2006), and recorded a simple 5 point self-rating of susceptibility from 0 = none to 4 = extreme. During the initial session all subjects were exposed to the galvanic vestibular reduction (GVR) stimulus and completed a battery of balance, mobility, and oculo-cognitive tests to evaluate the effect of GVR amplitude on functional fitness task performance. Two male subjects were unable to complete all of the testing. The remainder of the 27 subjects (32.2 ±9.4 y mean ±std, 14 male/ 13 female) completed three motion sickness sessions using a counter-balanced cross-over design to compare motion sickness severity across three treatment interventions: (1) Prevention: GVR on throughout stimulus testing, (2) Rescue: GVR on following symptom onset, and (3) Control: no GVR. The motion sickness sessions were scheduled several days apart (20 ± 40 d, mean ± std) to minimize carry-over (e.g., habituation) effects across sessions.

Galvanic vestibular reduction stimulation: Galvanic vestibular reduction was delivered using a proprietary system developed at the Mayo clinic laboratory. This utilizes a multi-channel commercial galvanic stimulator (Good Vibrations Engineering Ltd, King City, ON) with custom software. The stimulator bidirectionally delivered a sinusoidal profile (2.5 Hz) with variable amplitudes from ±1.75 to ±2.25 mA to provide matching cathodal or anodal currents simultaneously to each mastoid.

Motion sickness stressor: Each of the three sessions involved a series of trapezoid velocity profiles with acceleration (6 º/s2) up constant velocity of 60 º/s for 2.5 min during which 7 forward (chin to chest) and backward (return to upright) head movements were cued every 10 seconds. Although the head position was not measured, the typical range of motion for head flexion in young healthy adults is 60º. Subjects were tested in a dark room with their eyes closed and audio cueing over a chair-fixed speaker to pace the head movements and allow operator-subject communications throughout the protocol. Since the GVR stimulus was chair mounted and needed to be turned on manually, the 2 min pause between rotations was required to allow the operator to turn on the GVR during the rescue sessions. This pause also allowed time for symptom recovery and in part led to a higher-than-expected number of subjects who did not reach the symptom endpoint during the control session.

Symptom reporting: During the 2 min pause between head movement sets, symptom scoring was obtained using the Pensacola Diagnostic Index (PDI) and a Subjective Discomfort Rating (SDR). The PDI provides an acute score by obtaining the subjective intensity of eight different modalities of symptoms and signs reported on a “slight/moderate/severe” basis used to derive a weighted “malaise index”. The symptom endpoint for stopping the test was a PDI score of 8 pts, considered severe malaise. We also used the PDI to determine when to initiate the GVR during the Rescue session. During these sessions, the GVR was initiated with a moderate malaise (PDI = 3), or following 4 sets of head movements, whichever came first. The SDR used a subjective magnitude estimation scale of 0-20, with 20 indicating vomiting, similar to what has been used for Field Tests and Spaceflight Standard Measures. If GVR effectively suppresses vestibular sensitivity, it was hypothesized that subjects would experience lower symptom scores, and be able to perform more head movements before reaching the endpoint. An objective measure of sickness was also obtained using the physiological response of gastric myoelectric activity, known as the electrogastrogram (EGG). These EGG recordings were analyzed to derive the dominant power instability coefficient (DPIC) as an index for motion sickness. DPIC quantifies the stability of the power of the dominant frequency – higher DPIC values indicate higher gastric dysrhythmia, presumably in this case due to motion sickness.

Motion perception reporting: A chair-mounted joystick was used to obtain objective measures of motion perception in three-dimensions during the pitch head movements. During the head movements, subjects experienced a combination of yaw rotation from the persisting horizontal canal response to the angular acceleration of the chair rotation, pitch tilt from canal, otolith and cervical cues associated with alternating the head between upright and chin-to-chest positions, and Coriolis cross-coupled roll canal cues associated with aligning the roll plane of the head relative to plane of rotation. As the horizontal canal response decays, the conflicting cues from the cross-coupled roll canal cues and otolith cues of pitch head tilt give rise to the nauseogenic effects. Subjects were trained to indicate the direction and magnitude of perceived pitch and roll tilt using the joystick so that the maximum deflection represented the magnitude of the pitch forward and backward movement. If GVR effectively suppresses vestibular sensitivity, we hypothesized subjects would experience reduced pitch and roll tilt sensation during GVR versus the control condition without GVR.

Sensorimotor cognitive test battery: This test battery utilized both dynamic posturography as well as a modified timed up and go (TUG) locomotion task. A third test in the battery was designed to measure cognitive performance indicators during variable workload through eye movement features. The Oculo-Cognitive Addition Test (OCAT, Pradhan et al. 2022) tracks eye movements as the subject sums three consecutive single-digit numbers displayed at various positions around an infinity-loop pattern to elicit saccades in horizontal, vertical, and diagonal directions.


RESULTS
Fifteen of the 27 subjects were not susceptible to the motion stressor (i.e., did not reach an endpoint in the control condition). While the time to endpoint, or number of head movements, did not significantly vary across the three GVR conditions in the remaining subjects, the symptom levels were significantly delayed during the Prevention session when GVR was on throughout the testing. Initiating GVR following symptom onset did not appear to alter the symptom progression nor time to motion sickness endpoint. Based on the joystick measures, GVR significantly modified the perceived roll and pitch sensation during head movements, reducing the amplitude of tilt in most subjects. It is important to note that comparable levels of GVR did not impair performance on the functional test battery including mobility, balance, and oculometric tasks.

These findings suggest GVR may be useful in reducing disorienting roll and pitch illusions and delaying the onset of motion sickness. Further enhancements will be required to individualize the stimulation amplitude and optimize the waveform delivery. Adapting this non-pharmaceutical countermeasure approach to allow self-administered titration of current amplitude during recovery would enable transfer to post-flight treatment, perhaps combined with a pharmaceutical approach to mitigate G-transitional induced motion sickness.

experiment_title: Cardiovascular Conditioning
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The cardiovascular system was the first major body system to show physiologic change following space flight. As a result, it was extensively investigated by various means during the Gemini missions. The purpose of the Cardiovascular Conditioning (M001) experiment was to determine the effectiveness of the pneumatic cuff technique in preventing orthostatic intolerance to a 1-G stress after space flights lasting up to 14-days.

Water immersion studies in support of this experiment indicated that pneumatic leg cuffs alone, when inflated to 70 to 75 mm Hg for 2 out of every 6 minutes, provided protection against cardiovascular deconditioning. Four healthy, male subjects were immersed in water up to neck level for six hours on two separate occasions, two days apart. Before and after each period of water immersion, the heart rate of each subject was measured during a tilt table test. Data analysis indicated that the first water immersion period, during which the subjects' did not wear leg cuffs, resulted in cardiovascular deconditioning. This was evidenced by cardioacceleration in excess of that observed during the tilt-table test prior to water immersion. Also, syncope occurred in two of the four subjects. Tilt table responses following the second period of immersion, during which leg cuffs were utilized, revealed that a definite protective effect was achieved. Cardioacceleration was less pronounced, and no syncope occurred.

The physiological mechanisms responsible for the observed efficacy of the cuff technique were not completely understood. It was hypothesized that the cuffs prevented thoracic blood volume overload, thus resulting in the Henry-Gauer response with its resultant diuresis and decreased effective circulating blood volumes. It was also postulated that the cuffs induced an intermittent artificial hydrostatic gradient (by increasing venous pressure distal to the cuffs during inflation) across the walls of the leg veins, mimicking the deterioration of normal venomotor reflexes. It was theorized that this action would decrease the pooling of blood in the lower extremities and increase the effective circulating blood volume upon return to a 1-G environment following weightlessness or its simulation.

APPROACH:
One astronaut from each of the Gemini 5 (8-day) and Gemini 7 (14-day) missions participated as a test subject, described here as subjects A and B respectively. The remaining astronaut aboard each respective flight acted as a control subject (subjects C and D.) In-flight, the two test subjects wore cuff devices designed to maintain venous pressure in the lower extremities.

The experiment equipment consisted of a pneumatic cycling system and a pair of pneumatic cuffs. The cycling system alternately inflated and deflated the cuffs that were form-fitted to the proximal thigh region of the test subjects. The bladder portion of each cuff was positioned on the dorsomedial aspect of each thigh.

Upon reaching orbit, the cuffs were automatically pressurized to 80 mm Hg for 2 minutes out of every 6 minutes. The system was capable of continuous operation during flight, but could be switched off for sleep periods if required. The experiment imposed no operational requirement other than activation of the device after reaching orbit and deactivation prior to reentry.

The experiment lasted for the first 4 days of the Gemini 5 mission and for the first 13.5 days of the Gemini 7 mission. During the Gemini 5 mission, the cuffs were to operate continuously for the full 8-day mission. After 4 days, however, the pneumatic programmer stopped cycling when the oxygen pressure in the storage vessel dropped below operational levels.

Before and after flight, all Gemini Program astronauts, including the subjects of this experiment, were given a series of tilt table tests to measure orthostatic intolerance. Parameters measured included heart rate, blood pressure, pulse pressure, and leg volume. Leg volume was determined by the strain-gage technique. Changes in blood volume, plasma volume, and red cell mass were determined using radioactive isotope (125I, 51Cr) techniques. Body mass was also measured.

The tilt table test protocol was as follows: each subject lay supine for 5 minutes. The subject was then elevated into a +70 degree, head-up tilt position for 15 minutes. Leg volume was measured for the duration of the 15-minute tilt. After the tilt was completed, the subject was again supine for 5 minutes. Leg volume was measured for an additional 5 minutes after the tilt was completed. Heart rate and blood pressure were monitored continuously throughout the 25-minute test. All subjects completed three preflight tilt-table tests. The astronauts of Gemini 5 completed 6 post flight tilt table tests, while the astronauts of Gemini 7 completed 4 post flight tilt table tests. Post flight tests for the Gemini 5 astronauts were conducted between 2-104 hours after recovery. The Gemini 7 astronauts were measured between 2-56 hours after recovery.

RESULTS:
Post flight heart rates: All four Gemini 5 and 7 crewmembers had increased resting heart rates during the first 12 to 24 hours after recovery. Subjects A and C had a twofold greater increase in heart rate than did subjects B and D during the first two post flight tilts. Although subjects B and D had a smaller increase in heart rate during the tilt procedures, subject B had to be returned to the supine position after 12 minutes during the first tilt. This experience on the first tilt procedure may have accounted for his increased heart rate during the second and third tilts. The heart rates of all subjects decreased during succeeding tilts to approximately preflight values.

Post flight blood pressure: All four crewmembers had decreased resting systolic blood pressure 2 to 4 hours after recovery. Test subject B and control subject C maintained systolic pressures that were lower than the preflight values throughout the post flight test period. All four crewmembers had a decreased resting diastolic blood pressure during each post flight tilt test except during the first and last tilts of control subject C and during the second tilt of test subject B.

Post flight pulse pressure: All four Gemini 5 and Gemini 7 crewmembers had narrowed pulse pressures during the first post flight tilt (compared with the preflight tilt and the post flight resting values). Test subject A and control subject C also had a significant pulse pressure narrowing during the second (8 to 12 hours) post flight tilt. Control subject C maintained a low systolic pressure during the third and forth tilts, whereas the systolic pressure of test subject A returned to normal preflight levels after the second post flight tilt. Test subject B and control subject D had no significant pulse pressure narrowing during the second, third, or fourth post flight tilts.

Post flight leg volume changes: Leg volume changes during the post flight tilts indicated that test subjects A and B, who wore the pneumatic cuffs, pooled significantly less blood in their legs than did control subjects C and D. During the first post flight tilt table test, test subject B had signs of vasodepressor syncope. The tilt was interrupted and the subject was returned to the supine position. The episode occurred despite no evidence of increased pooling of blood in the lower extremities. During subsequent tilts, test subject B showed no signs of syncope or of impending syncope. It was significant that this episode of syncope occurred despite the fact that the measured blood volume of both test-subject B and control-subject D was unchanged from preflight values. Researchers concluded it was possible that the syncopal episode was the result of sudden vasodilation. The effects of which were a pooling of blood in the visceral region, a diminished venous return and cardiac output, and a decrease in cerebral blood flow.

Blood volume, plasma volume, and red cell mass variation: Subjects' B and D of Gemini 7 sustained a 4 and 15 percent increase respectively in plasma volume during the 14-day mission. Subjects' A and C of Gemini 5 lost 4 and 8 percent respectively of their plasma volume during the 8-day mission. All four subjects lost 7 to 20 percent of their red cell mass. The decrease in red cell mass and the increase in plasma volume of subjects B and D offset each other to result in a net zero percent change in blood volume. The reduction in plasma volume and red cell mass subjects A and C contributed to a 12 and 13 percent decrease in blood volume. These changes in blood volume may have reflected, in part, the extent of hydration of the Gemini 5 subjects, but this was not true for the Gemini 7 subjects.

Body mass changes: Test subject A and control subject C sustained a loss in body mass of 8.5 and 7.5 pounds, respectively. Test subject B and control subject D lost 6.5 and 10.0 pounds, respectively. These values were similar to those observed after other missions of shorter duration. Subjects' B and D regained less body weight during the first 24 hours post flight than did subjects A and C (25 percent and 40 percent compared with 50 percent.)

Flight conditions that were operative during the Gemini 7 mission were notably different from those that were operative during the Gemini 5 mission. These differences were of sufficient magnitude that a comparison of the experiment results from the two missions was difficult, if not impossible. The Gemini 7 mission was different from previous Gemini missions in that the Gemini 7 astronauts did not wear their suits during an extensive portion of the 14-day flight. Their food and water intake more closely approximated the optimum than it did on previous flights that assured better hydration and fluid electrolyte balance. Also, the Gemini 7 exercise regimen was more rigorous than that used on previous flights. These variables, in addition to the individual variability, precluded any direct comparison of results on the two missions. Further, the pneumatic cuffs were operative during only the first half of the Gemini 5 mission.

The post flight physiological responses of subjects B and D were different from, and generally improved in comparison with, those observed for subjects A and C. However, it was difficult to determine which variables were responsible for the observed improvement.

Researchers concluded that pneumatic cuffs were not effective in decreasing post flight orthostatic intolerance. This conclusion was not based on the occurrence of syncope during the first tilt of test subject B. It was based on the higher heart rates observed (as compared with the control subject) during subsequent tilts. (Syncope itself is a poor indicator of the extent of cardiovascular deconditioning.) Researchers did conclude, however, that the pneumatic cuffs did lessen the extent of post flight pooling of blood in the legs as determined by the strain-gage technique.

experiment_title: Improving Cardiovascular Risk Prediction - Biomarkers and Beyond; Implications for Astronaut Selection and Monitoring During Prolonged Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The most likely cause of a non-traumatic life- or mission-threatening medical events in astronauts are from acute cardiovascular disease (CVD). Current risk prediction models utilize only traditional atherosclerosis risk factors and focus narrowly on coronary heart disease events rather than global cardiovascular risk, ignoring outcomes such as heart failure or atrial fibrillation that could also be potentially mission-threatening. Numerous studies have evaluated novel risk markers in an attempt to improve CVD risk prediction, with several promising imaging and blood-based biomarkers identified. Most of these studies have investigated the incremental predictive value of a single biomarker added to a traditional risk factor model, with a few reporting combinations of biomarkers. Moreover, few studies have evaluated strategies for risk prediction that cross testing modalities. Such a multi-modality approach has the potential to markedly improve CVD risk prediction among potential and existing astronauts, and would have direct relevance to the general population.

The primary objective of this study was to develop a consortium of biomarker and aerospace medicine leaders, with expertise in multiple different testing modalities, and with access to robust existing databases, to identify and validate novel strategies to enhance global CVD risk prediction over two time windows: 1) 10-20 years, representing the full career of the astronaut and 2) 2-5 years, representing the planning and operational phase of a manned mission to Mars. The Biomarker Consortium aimed to provide “real time” advice to NASA on the design of existing screening programs, the status of new biomarkers, and the interpretation of test results.

APPROACH:
The team of collaborative investigators pooled data from multiple existing cohort studies to develop two distinct multi-modality risk prediction tools, one based on 10-year global CVD risk and one based on 3-year CVD risk. These models sequentially evaluated novel testing modalities on top of standard risk factors, including coronary calcium (a measure of the extent of coronary atherosclerosis), multiple blood based protein biomarkers that reflect inflammation, cardiac injury and cardiac stress, as well as imaging-based assessments of cardiac function. Finally, investigators worked directly with NASA researchers in the Human Research Program to explore the feasibility of transforming the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health into a prospective state-of-the-art cohort study of the astronaut corps. They utilized the expertise of the Biomarker Consortium to design a novel program for study of the effects of training and space flight on astronaut health.

RESULTS:
The investigators derived a multimodality risk prediction tool that led to marked improvement over traditional risk prediction algorithms both for predicting 10 year atherosclerotic risk as well as global and cause-specific CVD risk. Five screening tests - coronary calcium screening by CT, left ventricular hypertrophy by ECG, and elevated levels of N-terminal pro b-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), high-sensitive cardiac troponin (Ths-cTnT), and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) markedly improved global CVD risk prediction compared with standard risk assessment strategies. Investigators created a simple score, consisting of the number of abnormal CVD screening tests. In both MESA and DHS a > 25-fold gradient of risk for CVD was seen across the range of scores. Of particular relevance for NASA, participants with zero abnormal tests results have an extremely low risk for any CVD outcome over 10 years of follow-up. The findings replicate extremely well across the two distinct cohort studies.

experiment_title: Expression of Contractile Protein Isoforms in Microgravity
experiment_description:
Objectives:

To determine the effects of microgravity on developmentally programmed expression of Troponin T and I isoforms known to regulate cardiac and skeletal muscle contraction.

Approach:

This experiment was performed twice, once during Mir 18 (returning on STS-71) and once during Mir 19 (returning on STS-74). Fertilized eggs were carried to the Mir space station aboard a Russian Progress (227) supply vessel, and placed in an incubator supplied by the Institute for Biomedical Problems. On days 7, 10, 14 and 17, eight eggs were fixed and stored for return to Earth.

Results:

During both runs of the experiment, internal incubator temperature was higher than nominal throughout the experiment, and most of the quail embryos failed to develop as expected, resulting in low science return. During Mir 18, only one embryo developed to an appropriate age, and preliminary assessment indicated that most embryos did not survive past 4-5 days of incubation.

experiment_title: The Response of Single Human Cells to Zero Gravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Studies with centrifuges demonstrated that gravitational acceleration has a significant influence on cell biology systems. The purpose of this experiment was to determine the effects of zero-gravity on living human cells during and subsequent to the Skylab 3 mission. A strain of diploid human embryonic lung cells, WI-38, was chosen for this purpose. In general, this experiment was designed to detect the effects of zero-gravity on cell growth rates and on cell structure as observed by light microscopy, transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy, and histochemistry. Studies of the effects of zero-gravity on the cell function and the cell cycle were performed by time lapse motion picture photography and microspectrophotometry. Subsequent study of the returned living cells included karotyping, G- and C- banding, and analyses of the culture media. Some of the living cells returned were stored by deep freeze techniques for possible future experiments.

APPROACH:
The Woodlawn Wanderer 9 was used inflight to support the growth of human embryonic lung cells. Cell cultures were maintained with the proper replacement of media with new fresh media. The cells were kept at a constant temperature of 36 degrees Celsius and at a constant pressure of one atmosphere in a hermetically sealed compartment. Two phase-contrast time-lapse motion pictures of living cells for 28 days was used to collect data on the cell cycle and mitosis. An automated system fixed the cells at predetermined intervals for postflight examination under the light microscope, scanning electron microscope, and transmission electron microscope. Cultures were maintained at approximately 22 degrees Celsius after the first 12 days of the mission for the return of intact cells for subsequent subculture. The cell cultures brought back to ground for subculture were analyzed for chromosomal aberrations, and the cell culture media was analyzed to determine chemical composition.

Cellular growth rates were determined by cell counting procedures accomplished with the aid of a phase-contrast contrast microscope using a grid reticle in a 10X magnification eyepiece. Postflight, cell counting was performed with the 15X eyepiece due to the fact that the high density of the cell population made it difficult to determine single cells. Time lapse films were analyzed with a projector which permitted projection 1-8, 16, and 24 frames/second. Cells were counted every 3 hours. Cell multiplication was determined by adding the number of observed mitoses and mitotic activity, which was calculated from the average cell density. The rate of cell migration was determined by covering the projection screen with paper and tracing the location of the nucleus of individual cells every hour.

Whole coverslips with attached cell monolayers in 4 percent glutaraldehyde fixative with cacodylate buffer were processed for transmission electron microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and phase contrast microscopy. Scanning microspectrophotometry was performed on selected areas of the nuclei using a scanning microscope photometer having a 1-micron measuring at 1 micron intervals at 540 nanometers. Subcultures were incubated overnight with fresh growth medium, then harvested with standard colchimid arrest and hypotonic treatment procedures. Banding analysis was performed on air dried slides. Five cells from control cultures were analyzed for G-band pattern and 10 cells were analyzed for C-band pattern. At least 10 cells of the flight culture were analyzed for G-band pattern and 20 cells were analyzed for C-band pattern.

RESULTS:
Ten cultures were fixed during the first 12 days of flight. Growth curves, DNA microspectrophometery, phase microscopy, and ultrastructural studies of the fixed cells revealed no effects of a zero-gravity environment on the ten cultures. Two cultures were photographed by means of phase time-lapse cinematography during the first 27 days of the flight. Analysis of the films revealed no differences in mitotic index, cell cycle, and migration between the flight and control cells. No differences between the flight and control cell cultures were observed in the karotype and chromosome banding. Minor unexplained differences have been found in the biochemical constituents of the used flight and control media.

experiment_title: Gravity and Skeletal Growth: II. Morphological Studies of Bone and Tendon
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previously described results from Cosmos 1887 noted that drastic changes occurred in the vascular system within the diaphyseal bone, evidently in response to the microgravity experience. In addition to the study of the vascular supply to the periosteal region and the determination of osteoblast activity, this study also investigated the structural integrity of the rat foot. This tissue is sensitive to changes in mechanical stress, and it was thought that the reduced activity imposed by space flight might also cause structural changes in these tendons.

Approach:

Electron and light microscopy, histochemistry, and morphometric techniques were combined in this study to determine the effects of microgravity on bone cells and the vasculature within the diaphysis of the rat tibia. Silver staining of 3-5 µm sections was carried out to visualize collagen fibers. Osteoblasts were stained for acid phosphate activity to outline the Golgi complex. Cytoplasmic RNA was stained with pyronine so the Golgi complex free of RNA could be visualized by negative contrast. Measurements were made at 320x so that the Golgi presence could be easily determined.

Results:

Vasculature changes at the periosteal and sub-periosteal region were not apparent. Electron microscopy showed that vascular inclusions were present in flight rats; however, the blood vessels themselves appeared undamaged. Electron microscopy of the tendons of the foot showed some collagen fibril disorganization but this was not noticeable by light microscopy. Investigations of osteoblasts lining the endosteal surface indicated a reduction in activity, but morphometric measurements suggested that these alterations were not significantly different from controls. The general absence of vascular changes in this study is interesting since this flight was similar in many respects to Cosmos 1887, one notable difference being the almost 55-hour delay before recovery of 1887. This raises the possibility that vascular changes could have occurred when the animals became weight-bearing following reentry. Following a non-weight bearing period, the resumption of full weight bearing may be detrimental to the vascular system, especially at the periosteal surface of the bone.

experiment_title: Somatic Embryogenesis of Orchardgrass in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The overall objective of this research was to provide information on the influence of microgravity on embryo initiation, differentiation and development and the ultimate reproductive capacity of resultant plants, using an in vitro culture system in orchardgrass (Dactylis glomerata L.) in which the target cells remain in situ. The system was based on paired half-leaf segments, which provided a precise control and the opportunity to use paired statistics for analyses of the data.

APPROACH:

Somatic embryos form directly from mesophyll cells in cultured leaf segments and develop fully to a germinable stage. The basal 3 cm of the youngest two leaves were split down the midvein. Beginning at the base, these were cut transversely into six segments approximately 3 mm square. Segments from one half-leaf were used for the flight treatments and the corresponding sister segments served as controls. This provided a precise control for each treated leaf segment and the opportunity to use paired statistics for data analysis . Observations and data were collected on quality and quantity of embryo formation, axis determination and polarity. Embryo number was estimated using an already-developed formula and extensive histological data. Plants were established from somatic embryos and used for mitotic chromosome analyses. The same plants were transferred to the field and used for meiotic chromosome analyses and estimation of pollen fertility.

RESULTS:

In the flown samples somatic embryogenesis was only slightly reduced in leaf segments plated 21 days before launch, but significantly less in those plated 21 hours, 3 days and 7 days prior to liftoff. The greatest reduction (70%) occurred in the 21-hour treatment group. Histological examination of leaf tissues fixed immediately after landing indicated reduced cell-division activity, a higher ratio of anticlinal/periclinal divisions and a lower frequency of early embryogenic structures. Cells in the ground controls divided normally and produced numerous embryos. Chromosome analyses of somatic cells from 75 treatment and 20 control plants regenerated from the 21-hour plating period showed all control plants to be normal. One regenerate in the flight treatment group was mixploid and two others showed fragmented chromosomes. All field-established plants, controls and treated plants, showed normal pollen fertility. Meiotic analyses of the 21-hour plants showed a slightly higher frequency of laggards, bridges and fragments and 1.8 times more micronuclei in cells of treatment compared to control plants.
