experiment_title: Mechanisms of Gravity Sensing and Response in Hematopoietic Cells
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Data from 20 years of manned spaceflight consistently show reduced response of human T lymphocytes to mitogen-induced (mitogenic) challenge during and for several days after flight. Cells in vitro are also resistant to mitogen stimulation. Reasons are unclear. The objective of the study is to investigate the role of the cytoskeleton in gravity (microgravity) "sensing" and signal transduction in single cells (lymphocytes) using the human T lymphocyte cell line (Jurkat) and peripheral blood lymphocytes if crew time and hardware space is available. Specific aims are to evaluate 1) cytoskeletal morphology; 2) signal transduction mechanisms; and 3) expression of genes regulating cytoskeletal and related proteins. Membrane-cytoskeleton interactions leading to signal transduction and growth response require an intact cytoskeleton. New information on mechanisms relating the cytoskeleton to blunted human T cell responsiveness, thus immunity, during spaceflight is applicable to both space- and Earth-based medicine. This information may facilitate drug design and countermeasure development and may have ramifications for the treatment of cancer (Jurkat is a cell line derived from from acute human T-cell leukemia). The main objective of the experiment is to contribute to the database on the effect of spaceflight on single cells. Molecular and gene-level responses are studied in an attempt to explain depressed T lymphocyte growth activation during spaceflight compared to normal Earth-gravity and the 1g in-flight centrifuge controls.

APPROACH:
Cells, suspended in medium containing 2% fetal calf serum, are held at ambient temperature (20oC) for approximately twenty hours until activation of the experiment in microgravity. After the samples are incubated at 37°C for 1 hour, they are brought to the Biorack glovebox for growth activation by increasing the serum concentration to 10%. One sample set is placed in the 1g in-flight centrifuge; the other is held static. Both sets are incubated at 37oC for varying periods of time after which they are fixed with formalin or an RNA stabilizing solution.

Membrane-cytoskeletal interactions are involved in second messenger transduction by a signal amplification mechanism and intact microtubules are required: therefore, several specific scientific aims are defined to address the different steps of this complex process.

1) Evaluate the effects of spaceflight on the gross morphology of the cytoskeleton in human T cells (Jurkat).
2) Assess early signal transduction in growth-stimulated lymphocytes by evaluating protein kinase C (PKC) translocation in cells (an immediate response after mitogen binding and growth stimulation) and PKC gene expression after 24 hours. Cells from spaceflight are evaluated for PKC mRNA to determine if this gene is up-or down-regulated compared to the ground and in-flight 1-g control samples.
3) Investigate the turnover of inositol phosphate (IP, PIP2, IP3) at the cell membrane to evaluate very early signal transduction. (To be done if peripheral blood lymphocytes are flown).
4) Evaluate expression of selected cytoskeleton-associated genes including genes that encode for actin, tubulin, and the regulatory proteins, gelsolin and profilin since these cytoskeleton-associated proteins are involved in signal transduction.
5) To investigate the relationship and/or requirements for dendritic cells to facilitate lymphocyte activation in low gravity. The blunted response of lymphocytes in space may be a result of reduced secretion of interleukin-1 (IL-1) by monocytes. However, the influence of accessory cells(dendritics) has not been addressed. (This objective will only be met if hardward units and crew time are available to fly peripheral blood lymphocytes in addition to Jurkat cells).
6) To understand or rule-out stress s as a reason for failure of T cell populations to increase in number in micrograivty, mRNA for heat-shock proteins is evaluated by RT-PCR (Reverse Transcriptase - Polymerase Chain Reaction).
7) To determine if programmed cell death (apoptosis) is a factor in lympyhocyte population growth arrest during spaceflight, the percentage of cells showing nuclear apoptotic bodies are determined and nitric oxide (NO) levels in culture medium may be measured.
8) To address T lymphocyte responsiveness to growth stimulation, levels of secreted lympholines (IL-1ï¿½, IL-2, TNF-alpha and gamma interferon) are monitored using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA). (This aim depends on whether crew time and hardware is available to fly peripheral blood lymphocytes).

RESULTS:
Spaceflown Jurkat cells were metabolically active (using approximately 1.6 times more glucose at 48 hours than the ground controls in both static (P = 0.0046) and centrifuged (P = 0.0003) cultures) (002986) but cells did not grow in microgravity (002985). By comparison, ground control cells almost doubled within the same 48 hrs (hours). Because flown cells did not proliferate, the possibility of cell cycle arrest was evaluated by flow cytometry. Flown cells showed initial arrest in G2M (both static microgravity and 1g in-flight controls) at 4 hours. By 48 hrs, no significant differences in cell cycle distribution were found and cells appeared to be distributed across all cell cycle phases (002987).

The following results were obtained for each Scientific aim listed above:
1) Cytoskeletal morphology: (000738) Microtubule organizing centers (MTOC) were poorly organized in flown cells fixed at 4 hrs compared to ground controls. Microtubules appeared as randomly oriented, thickened cables of shortened filaments that terminated before reaching the cell membrane. These elements appeared to reorganize in flight by 48 hrs.

Though not an original aim, the effect of simulated shuttle launch vibration on microtubule morphology was evaluated (as ground-based test). Duplicate samples of vibrated and non-vibrated cells were fixed with formalin at 10 minutes, and 4, 24 and 48 hrs after vibration. In cells fixed at 10 minutes and 4 hrs after vibration the microtubules appeared coalesced, randomly distributed, and prematurely terminated (similar to flown cells). Many small, brightly stained dots, assumed to be depolymerized tubulin or disorganized MTOCs were observed. By 24 hrs, the microtubule cytoskeleton appeared to be re-established, and at 48 hrs cytoskeletal staining at the focal contacts between cells was restored. Vibration stress did not up-regulate the cell death factor, Fas/APO-1, nor increase glucose utilization as seen in the flown cells (see below).
2) Early Signal transduction: (000975) This aim was achieved through collaboration with Co-Investigators (Didier Schmitt and Jason Hatton). The experiment was flown on a different Biorack payload using peripheral blood lymphocytes and U937 cells. Protein Kinase C (PKC) translocation from the cytosol to the nucleus, membrane, and insoluble cytoskeleton occurred in cells in microgravity, the in-flight 1g control, and ground and 1.4g controls. Differences in translocation for several isoforms were related to T cell storage before activation in microgravity.
3, 5 & 8) IP3 trunover (001803), Dendritic cells, Secreted lymphokines (001898): These parameters would have been investigated if peripheral blood lymphocytes could have been flown in the TCELL experiment on STS-76. Due to the hardware availability and crew time limitations, experiments using peripheral blood lymphocytes were not flown and these objectives could not be achieved.
4) Cytoskeletal gene expression (001183, 001381, 001553), 001553, 002988): Gene expression analyses planned for the STS-76 Biorack flight were not achieved because of a technical problem in preserving RNA message. However, this objective was accomplished by use of residual Jurkat cells flown on STS-95 on a different payload. STS-76 Biorack funding was used to analyze gene expression by cDNA microarray and, for some genes, by RT-PCR. More than 4,324 genes (at 24 hrs) and 20,000 genes (at 48 hours) were evaluated by cDNA microarray in flown versus ground controls. (This is the first experiment to evaluate expression of thousands [>20,000]of genes by cDNA microarray in human lymphocytes). Though not a primary aim of the original Biorack proposal, Jurkat cells were also subjected to simulated shuttle launch vibration as a control to determine effect of vibration on gene expression. More than 4,324 genes were evaluated in vibrated cells at 4, 24, and 48 hrs. (The following URL address permits direct access to 53 pages of tabulated gene expression data for flown and vibrated cells: http://www.fasebj.org/cgi/content/abstract/00-
0820fjev1?ijkey=4kpP6Xbf7y/0o&keytype=ref&siteid=fasebj)
Expression levels of 10 cytoskeleton-related genes were up-regulated in space-flown compared to ground control cells (calponin, dynactin, tropomodulin, keratin 8, two myosins, an ankyrin EST, an actin-like protein, the cytoskeletal linker (plectin) and a centriole-associated protein (C-NAP1)). A gelsolin precursor gene (001553) was down-regulated. Message for actin (001183), tubulin (001381) profilin (001695), and PKC-related genes was unchanged. Up-regulation of plectin and C-NAP1 message in both spaceflown and vibrated cells is a novel finding and implies their role in vibration damage repair. Differential expression of genes that regulate growth, metabolism, signal transduction, adhesion, transcription, apoptosis, and tumor suppression was identified.

From these data we conclude that centriole-centriole, membrane-cytoskeletal, and cytoskeletal filament associations are altered in microgravity. Up-regulation in spaceflown cells of plectin, dynactin, C-NAP1, and tropomodulin and down-regulation of gelsolin precursor genes is of particular interest since these proteins are mediators of cytoskeletal organization.
6) Evaluation of Heat Shock proteins (002988): Spaceflight did not up-regulate mRNA levels for Heat Shock Protein (HSP) 70. The gene encoding HSP27 was up-regulated by spaceflight but not by ground-based simulated launch vibration. Up-regulation of HSP27 gene expression in microgravity is a new finding. In ground controls, the mRNA for HSP70 and HSP27 increased with cell density and time in culture. HSP70 gene expression is a useful indicator of stress related to culture density but does not appear to be an indicator of launch vibration stress or microgravity.
7) Apoptosis: (000227) A significantly higher number of apoptotic cells was found in cells fixed in microgravity at 4 hrs. Centrifugation (1g in space and 1.4g ground control) increased the number of apoptotic cells compared to non-centrifuged cultures. Identification of the time-dependent, microgravity-related cell death (apoptosis) factor (Fas/APO-1) suggests this as a possible mechanism mediating lymphocyte population dynamics during spaceflight.

experiment_title: Iron Overload and Oxidative Damage: Regulators of Bone Homeostasis in the Space Environment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Recent work in bone biology field has demonstrated that cellular damage due to molecules called reactive oxygen species (so-called oxidative damage) is a key mechanism contributing to aging-related bone loss, as well as to that occurring with the loss of estrogen after menopause. We know very little about whether the loss of gravity as experienced in the space environment modulates oxidative damage to bone. A newly recognized source of oxidative damage in bone is that due to iron overload, or an increase in body iron stores, as has now been demonstrated in both ISS crew members. Data published this month indicate that sub-pathological levels of serum ferritin (a marker for iron stores) contribute to accelerated bone loss and to incident vertebral fractures in healthy middle-aged men and women. We have preliminary data indicating that similar moderate elevations in body iron stores, as induced by a high iron diet, can result in loss of cancellous bone and diminished bone formation activity in rodents. The experiments in this proposal will utilize iron overload as an experimental intervention to exacerbate oxidative damage during a period of simulated microgravity (by hindlimb unloading in male and female mice) to define the gender-specific mechanistic role of oxidative damage as a key regulator of bone mass and, ultimately, fracture risk as modulated by the gravitational unloading of the space environment. In a final specific aim, we will test whether superimposing acute and continuous (over 42 days) radiation exposure exacerbates oxidative damage and bone decrements during hindlimb unloading. These experiments are deliberately designed to enable a rapid transition to flight experiments requiring minimal intervention during flight aboard ISS, should these ground-based simulations yield provocative findings to justify flight experiments. Iron overload can be maintained by dietary intake, and limiting the acute radiation exposure in Experiment 2 to just before the unloading period allows for testing of the same hypotheses in a flight experiment. The experiments outlined in this proposal addresses how microgravity affects key regulatory mechanisms governing alterations in bone (from OCB-2 in the Space Biology Plan) and also one of the NRC Decadal Survey's highest priority recommendations, to expand our understanding of gender differences in adaptation to the space environment, particularly in the area of bone and long-term radiation risks.

APPROACH:
The first specific aim of this project is to comprehensively define the impact of increasing iron stores (“iron overload”) on the bone response to microgravity, as simulated in a mouse model of hindlimb unloading (HU). We hypothesize that bone loss will be exacerbated and that the mechanism for this will be oxidative damage caused by iron overload. Further, we will be able to detect sex differences by completing these experiments in both male and female mice. Comprehensive testing of iron status and oxidative damage, both systemically and tissue-specific, will enable identification of mechanisms for the changes in bone integrity observed in all specific aims.

The second specific aim is to test our hypothesis that administration of n-acetylcysteine (NAC), a potent inhibitor of oxidative damage, will mitigate deleterious effects of iron overload on bone loss during HU. If it does, we then have evidence that a major mechanism for iron overload effect is due to exacerbation of oxidative damage. For this experiment we will use the one sex (male or female) that exhibited the largest response to iron overload in the first specific aim.

The third specific aim involves testing the added impact of very low-dose continuous radiation exposure during a period of HU in mice with normal and high iron stores. There is growing evidence that space-relevant levels of radiation initiate oxidative damage in the exposed tissues; hence we hypothesize that bone loss will be further exacerbated by the interactions of unweighting (HU), iron overload, and radiation exposure. We will use the one sex (male or female) for these experiments that exhibits the largest response to combined iron overload and HU in the initial specific aim.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Effects of High Versus Low Autonomy on Space Crewmember Performance (Autonomy)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In future space missions to an asteroid or Mars, crewmembers will be given more autonomy to plan and carry out their activities due to the long distances involved and the tasks that will be needed to explore a planetary surface. The impact of increased autonomy on crew performance has not been evaluated formally. In addition, while the evidence is largely anecdotal, strict adherence to timelines sent from mission control has been reported to be fatiguing and stressful for astronauts. Furthermore, such stressors can affect interpersonal interactions, resulting in increased team conflict and reduced morale and productivity.

The long-term goal of this experiment was to conduct a scientific hypotheses-testing study involving a series of on-orbit missions to the International Space Station (ISS) in which the investigators measured the effects on crewmember mood, team behavior, cohesion, task performance, and the crew-mission control interaction of “high” autonomy conditions (where crewmembers plan much of their work schedule and perhaps experience a “Mars-like” communication delay with family members and mission control personnel back on Earth). This was contrasted with “low” autonomy conditions (where mission control personnel communicate in real-time with the crew and develop the work schedule, much as happens now). The impact of high versus low crew autonomy on mission control personnel was also be studied.

Before engaging in the flight experiment, the investigators were asked by NASA/JSC management to test the feasibility and safety of their methods during pilot studies involving a series of ground-based space analog missions (e.g., NEEMO, Houghton-Mars Project, Mars-500 105-day Simulation), where key elements of the flight experiment can be evaluated. Thus, the short-term goal was to conduct such feasibility pilot studies involving such missions. This is the purpose of the current “Autonomy” pilot project, which deals with NEEMO and HMP simulations. Under separate funding from NASA and the NSBRI, the investigators also studied the Mars-500 105-day Simulation, but this will not be reported here.

APPROACH:
The investigators conducted a series of pilot studies in this project: NEEMO 12 and 13, and the Haughton-Mars Project in 2008 (HMP 2008). In the series of pilot studies reported below, crewmember and mission control subjects filled out a weekly Study Questionnaire, which included mood and interpersonal interactions questions from the Profile of Mood States, the Group Environment Scale, and the Work Environment Scale, as well as a critical incident log. Additionally, new measures were developed and tested in the Mars 500 105-day Simulation but not on any of the simulations described in this report. The investigators had planned to test these in the NEEMO 14 mission, but this mission was postponed due to operational reasons unrelated to the research done on this experiment.

The independent variable was low versus high autonomy, and the dependent variables were scores on the measures of crewmember mood, team behavior, cohesion, task performance, and the crew-mission control interaction. It was not expected that autonomy would adversely affect mood, group interactions, and performance. In fact, it was expected that mood, group interactions, and performance would be the same or better during high autonomy periods.

RESULTS:
NEEMO
One study involved the NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) program. The purpose of this program is to study human survival in the Aquarium underwater laboratory in preparation for future space missions. The Aquarius is located near Key Largo, Florida. Missions typically last 10 to 14 days and involve research and other activities conducted by 4 or more “aquanauts”, who are usually astronauts or other NASA personnel. These activities are conducted within the habitat or during simulated EVAs in the ocean. “Mission control” personnel located topside monitor crewmember progress and timeline the schedule.

The investigators studied two NEEMO missions: 12 and 13. NEEMO 12 consisted of two weeks of low autonomy, where the crewmember work schedules were timelined by the topside mission control. Subjects included three NASA crewmembers and 6 topside personnel. NEEMO 13 consisted of one week of low autonomy and one week of high autonomy (where the crew had more flexibility to plan their own work schedule). Subjects included four NASA crewmembers and eight topside personnel. At the end of each week, subjects completed a measure of mood [Profile of Mood States (PMS)], items from two measures of social climate [Group Environment Scale (GES), Work Environment Scale (WES)], and a critical incident log.

Due to the small number of data points, investigators could only analyze the data descriptively by examining change scores of the subscales of their measures from the first to the second week, separately for the two missions. Preliminary analyses suggested that the autonomy condition was successfully employed in NEEMO 13 with no adverse results. There seemed to be clear differences between the low and high autonomy weeks by the results, the crewmembers reported more direction from the mission commander (reflected by an increase in “Leader Control”) as well as a decrease in fatigue from the low to the high autonomy weeks during NEEMO 13 as compared to NEEMO 12, which only had low autonomy conditions. For the topside personnel, work pressure was stable in NEEMO 13, whereas it rose in the second week during NEEMO 12. However, confusion increased during the high autonomy second week of NEEMO 13 as compared to the second week of NEEMO 12 (where it declined), suggesting that the topside personnel were not as clear in their roles when the crew took over more of the schedule.

HMP 2008
A second pilot study involved some of the summer 2008 crewmembers working on the Haughton-Mars Project (HMP) on Devon Island in Canada. The location was an old, large impact crater which had similarities to the Martian surface in appearance and geological characteristics. People participating in this program dress up in space suits, travel in a Mars rover, and conduct tasks similar to those anticipated during an actual expedition to Mars. There is no formal “mission control” and the participants have great freedom to plan their activities each day. Hence, there is great autonomy in the work schedule.

Investigators studied the last three weeks of the 2008 mission. Eight non-NASA scientists and graduate students served as subjects. As in their previous work, they completed weekly POMS, GES, WES and critical incident log measures. Since they had no contrasting low autonomy period with which to compare their results, investigators decided to compare the subscale scores of the HMP subjects with those from published adult norms in the POMS, GES, and WES manuals, and with subscale scores from mission control subjects who participated in their previous on-orbit studies.

The HMP group reported greater levels of in-group leader direction and innovation and less need for outside direction as compared with other work groups on Earth, which presumably had more managerial control. These findings suggest that they were working under fairly high autonomous conditions. In addition, they reported being more cohesive than as compared with other work groups as well. They also reported being more tired than mission control groups, but this might have been an artifact of their working in the Canadian north in the summertime, when there is constant daylight and the work if more physically taxing than sitting in front of a mission control console. Taken together, these results suggest that people working under relatively high autonomous conditions are not adversely affected and may even bond together more cohesively than other work groups.

The results of these pilot studies suggest that in isolated and confined conditions that are meant to simulate those encountered during space missions, high autonomy is safe, well-received by crewmembers, and offers some potential advantages over low autonomy conditions. The crews have reported that they enjoy the high autonomy condition, and there have been no untoward effects to date. There have been some suggestions that high autonomy improves mood and cohesion, with more innovation and reliance on the crew leader. Outside mission monitors reported less work pressure but some confusion concerning their role. Clearly, these results are suggestive based on limited pilot data, but they point to the safety and possible advantages of high autonomy on crew functioning during actual space missions.

experiment_title: Kinematic and Electromyographic Evaluation of Locomotion on the enhanced-Zero Gravity Locomotion Simulator and in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Studying locomotion in actual microgravity is difficult and expensive. Data can be collected directly from astronauts during spaceflight, or during parabolic flight experiments. The drawbacks to spaceflight experiments include difficulty in using necessary data collection hardware, and in completing an experiment with adequate sample size. Parabolic flight offers a viable ground-based alternative, but periods of microgravity are limited to 20-30 seconds, which only allows for acute locomotion investigations. Measure variables such as comfort level and steady-state metabolic rate are difficult to impossible. Ground-based simulators such as the enhanced Zero-gravity Locomotion Simulator (eZLS) provide a relatively low-cost, longer duration simulation of locomotion in microgravity than parabolic flight.

The primary purpose of this investigation was to determine the similarities and differences between locomotion on the eZLS, in microgravity, and in normal gravity. The secondary purpose was to determine how the external load (EL) mechanism affected locomotion on the eZLS. The results of this investigation will help to determine how accurately locomotion in microgravity is replicated on the eZLS, and the important external loading mechanism characteristics that affect locomotion on the eZLS. Two hypotheses were tested during this investigation: (1) When walking and running (controlling for static external load magnitude), locomotion kinematics, ground reaction force (GRF), and lower extremity muscle activation patterns will differ between eZLS and microgravity environments. (2) When walking and running on the eZLS (controlling for static external load magnitude), locomotion kinematics, GRF, and lower extremity muscle activation patterns will differ between external load delivered by bungees and a linear motor subject loading device (LM-SLD).

APPROACH:
Eight subjects were tested on the eZLS and on a standard exercise treadmill while walking at 1.34 m*s-1 (3 mph) and running at 3.13 m*s-1 (7 mph). The EL was provided by either bungees or a linear motor subject loading device (LM-SLD) at approximately 55% and 90% of body weight during the eZLS exercise. Seven of the eight subjects completed locomotion in microgravity during parabolic flight while loaded with bungees at identical EL magnitudes as during the eZLS trials. Joint kinematics, GRF, and electromyographic (EMG) activity of lower body musculature were measured during each condition. All eZLS and normal gravity trials were conducted in the Exercise Countermeasures Laboratory at NASA-Glenn Research Center. All microgravity trials were collected during parabolic flight onboard the NASA DC-9 aircraft at NASA-Johnson Space Center. Repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) were used to test for differences between test locations within EL levels, and to test for differences between EL types within load levels on the eZLS (p<0.05).

RESULTS:
Subjects attained greater amounts of hip flexion during walking and running in microgravity. During running, subjects had greater hip range of motion. Trunk motion was significantly less on the eZLS than in microgravity. Peak impact forces, loading rate, and impulse were greater on the eZLS than in microgravity during walking with a low EL and running with a high EL. Activation timing differences existed between locations in all muscles except for the rectus femoris. The tibialis anterior and gluteus maximus were active for longer durations on the eZLS than in microgravity during walking. GRFs were greater with the LM-SLD than with bungees during eZLS locomotion.

Discussion and Operational Relevance:

  • Greater hip flexion during microgravity may be due to the decreased trunk motion on the eZLS. The greater hip range of motion coupled with greater thigh displacement in microgravity suggests that hip motion (flexion and extension) is greater in microgravity as compared to the eZLS. Therefore, extended exercise on the eZLS may not affect the hip musculature similar to long-term exercise in microgravity.
  • Greater contact time occurred at all speeds and EL levels on the eZLS compared to microgravity. Increases in contact time allows the body to experience ground reaction forces for a longer period, which is reflected by a larger impulse during running on the eZLS at a high EL as compared to microgravity. During longer durations of exercise, subjects may experience a greater total magnitude of GRF on the eZLS than in microgravity, suggesting that when prescribing exercise on the eZLS, a shorter period of exercise may be equivalent to a longer period in microgravity when increased total GRF is the primary aim.
  • Increased duration of tibialis anterior and gluteus maximus activity may be a result of the orientation of the subject relative to the treadmill on the eZLS, or due to the fact that the limbs still must work against gravity. Increased duration of activation on the eZLS may result in muscle soreness until subjects are conditioned.
  • Differences in activation times between eZLS, normal gravity, and microgravity locomotion suggest possible changes in the motor coordination required between conditions.
  • Greater GRF with a linear motor SLD than with bungees suggests that the use of a constant-force SLD may be of potential benefit during treadmill exercise, because locomotion patterns do not change but subjects experience increased force magnitude and loading rates applied at the feet.

experiment_title: Skylab Environmental and Crew Microbiology Studies
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Microbiology studies were performed during the Skylab missions to detect the presence of potentially pathogenic microorganisms on the crewmembers and their spacecraft, and to obtain data that would contribute to an understanding of the response of the crew's microbial flora to the space flight environment. These data were interpreted in light of theories of microbial simplification, the identification and transfer of medically important microorganisms between crewmembers, in-flight autoinfections, and postflight microbial shock.

APPROACH:
Before, during and after each Skylab flight, swab samples were collected from each astronaut from the following sample sites:

  • Neck - 13 cm2 below hairline at the base of the neck

  • Ears - Right and left external auditory canals with two revolutions of each swab in each ear canal

  • Axillae - 6.5 cm2 below hair area on each side

  • Hands - 6.5 cm2 on right and left palms

  • Navel - The internal area of the umbilicus, and a surrounding 13 cm2 area with at least two revolutions made with each swab

  • Groin - 5 cm strip from rear to front on right and left inguinal area between the legs

  • Toes - Area between the two smallest toes of each foot

  • Nares - Both nostrils

  • Throat swab - Surfaces of tonsils and posterior pharyngeal vault swabbed with each of two dry calcium alginate swabs

  • Gargle - 60 ml phosphate buffer used as gargle and washed through oral cavity three times

  • Urine - 60 ml midstream sample

  • Feces - Two samples of 100 mg each taken from center of the fecal specimen

    Two calcium alginate swabs, wetted in phosphate buffer, were used to sample the nostrils and each external body surface area. A single, dry alginate swab for virological analysis was used to sample the throat. Phosphate buffer was used to wash the oropharyngeal cavity. Additionally, a midstream urine sample was collected from the first void of the day and fecal specimens were collected at the convenience of the subject. In-flight crew samples were collected 16 days before the end of each Skylab mission and returned under chilled conditions for analysis on Earth.

    Spacecraft samples were collected before, during and after each Skylab mission from the command module, orbital workshop hardware and orbital workshop air. The orbital workshop was sampled up to 10 times, including one preflight sample set. In-flight air samples were collected two days before the end of each mission. The command module was sampled on launch and recovery days for each mission. In all cases, samples collected in-flight were stored differently, and for a longer time than were preflight and postflight samples. Therefore, direct correlation of the resulting data is not always applicable.

    In excess of ten thousand selected microbial isolates were analyzed by quantification, identification and characterization. For this study, the effects of space flight conditions on microbial populations was studied only to the first level of complexity. That is, only alterations affecting the total autoflora was evaluated. (More detailed analyses conducted at increasing degrees of complexity were published elsewhere).

    RESULTS:
    Crew Microbiology - A summary of the numerical means of recovered isolates of medically important microorganisms from all nine prime crewmembers indicated that the incidence of these species on the body decreased during the preflight quarantine period, establishing a low point the morning of launch. This event no doubt reflected decreased contact with these species during the quarantine period. The largest number of medically important microorganisms was recovered from the immediate postflight sample set after which the value returned to its near normal pre-quarantine value.

    Returning space travelers were feared to experience a microbial shock, responding negatively to renewed contact with potentially pathogenic microorganisms that were absent in the space flight environment. This fear was based on the assumption that contact with potential pathogens during space flight would be limited, resulting in a reduction of immunocompetence. Data collected during the Skylab 2, 3 and 4 missions showed an increase in the distribution of potential pathogens immediately following space flight. However, as with the Apollo missions, no clinical or microbiological evidence of any microbial shock was present following any of the Skylab missions.

    Transfer of pathogenic microorganisms between crewmembers during space flight has previously been documented in missions up to 18 days. During the Skylab series, in-flight cross-contamination, colonization, and infection with Staphylococcus aureus was demonstrated. Most strains of this species, which is one of the most infectious of the common inhabitants of man's autoflora, may be distinguished by their reaction with specific bacteriophages. Bacteriophage typing provides the ability to monitor the exchange of S. aureus with greater resolution. Data showed that the same S. aureus strain was recovered repeatedly from the nasal passages of one subject during Skylab 2, indicating that this crewmember was a carrier. Although spread to the orbital workshop was demonstrated, there was apparently no transfer to other crewmembers during the mission. Therefore, being restricted to a confined space for 28 days with an S. aureus carrier does not necessarily result in cross infection.

    Skylab 3 data indicated that two crewmembers were nasal carriers, carrying phage types 3A and 29/79, respectively. Prior to flight, S. aureus was not recovered from any samples from the third crewmember. Analysis of in-flight samples show that the workshop became contaminated with both phage types and that type 29/79 was temporarily transferred to the third crewmember. Postflight analysis indicated that type 3A had spread to the subject carrying 29/79 but, as could be expected, did not colonize as he was a carrier of another phage type. Phage type 3A was repeatedly isolated from the postflight samples of the third, previously uninfected, crewmember, indicating actual colonization. This was a clear demonstration of in-flight intercrew transfer of a pathogenic species where the contaminant could be shown to have established itself as a member of the autoflora of the new host.

    It was important to relate these observations to the incidence of in-flight crew illness during the Skylab 3 mission. The carrier of type 29/79 developed a sty that was successfully treated with Neosporin. The 3A carrier developed a boil that was treated with warm compresses. As neither of these infections was draining, in-flight contingency samples were not taken, so the causative agent could not be identified. However, S. aureus is the usual causative agent of both maladies, and both individuals were carriers. Therefore, the development of a pathogenic microorganism was traced from its preflight carrier state in two crewmembers through in-flight contamination of the orbital workshop, and colonization on the third crewmember. Also, this species was probably responsible for the active in-flight infections of the two S. aureus carriers.

    Environmental Microbiology -
    Air - Low levels of in-flight bacterial contamination were observed on the first two missions, whereas the recovery from Skylab 4 was considerable higher. These higher counts were due entirely to an influx of Serratia marcescens, a microorganism that has been shown to produce various infections in man. Whereas this species was not recovered from any preflight crew sample analysis, it was recovered from multiple sites from all three Skylab 4 astronauts upon recovery. Further, this species persisted in the nasal cavity of one Skylab 4 crewmember throughout the postflight quarantine period. Subsequent investigation demonstrated several potential sources of this microorganism in the Skylab environment. However, these potential sources could not be sampled in-flight and, therefore, a direct correlation could not be made. By active microbial monitoring, the release of this microbial contamination into the orbital workshop was traced from possible sources, detected in the Skylab air, subsequently recovered as a new species from all three crewmembers, and was ultimately shown to colonize the nasal passages of one astronaut.

    Spacecraft - In-flight samples were collected to evaluate the level of microbial contamination occurring in the orbital workshop. The results of analyses of samples collected prior to launch were typical of a clean (although obviously not sterile) environment. The reduction of aerobic bacteria recovered from the Skylab 2 in-flight samples was probably a reflection of the thermal problems experienced in the orbital workshop after launch. Although there was a simultaneous tenfold increase in the presence of anaerobic bacteria, the Skylab 2 crew apparently entered a very clean environment, which remained clean during the mission.

    The recovery of both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria from the Skylab 3 mission increased with no apparent reason except for increased length of habitation by the crewmembers. During the 84-day Skylab 4 mission, the total concentration of aerobic bacteria remained nearly constant although anaerobe recovery decreased significantly. This drop was due to the loss of Propionibacterium acnes, which contributed strongly to the anaerobe population of the other two Skylab missions. This loss of P. acnes reflected a similar loss of anaerobic bacteria from the skin surfaces of the astronauts. Therefore, this decrease in anaerobic bacterial contamination of the Skylab environment was shown to directly reflect a decrease in these same microbes in the skin of the astronauts.

    Sampled immediately before and after each Skylab mission, aerobic bacteria were recovered from 15 sites within the command modules. Whereas there was some variation in the contamination level of the different command modules, there were no major differences between preflight and postflight values for a particular command module. Therefore, the variations noted in the orbital workshop could not be shown to affect population levels of bacteria in the command modules.

    Suggestions have been made that molds would present problems on long-term space flights, especially if high humidity was experienced. Numbers of fungal isolations from the Skylab vehicle before and during launch were low until the Skylab 4 mission. Although overall humidity was low on the Skylab 4 mission, local areas of high humidity could not be entirely eliminated. The reasons for the large increase in fungal isolations on Skylab 4 have been well established. Early in the Skylab 4 mission, it was discovered that mildew was present on the liquid-cooled garments that had been previously stowed aboard. A sample was taken off this growth, and one liquid cooled garment was returned for additional sampling. In general, the species of fungi isolated from surface samples and air samples were the same species isolated from the liquid cooled garment. These same microorganisms also contaminated the Petri dishes of the ED31 experiment flown on Skylab 4. The liquid-cooled garments were apparently the source of spore contamination since some of these garments had not previously been removed from their original containers, but were subsequently found to harbor these microorganisms.

    This contamination was also reflected in the recovery of fungi from the crew samples collected 16 days before return from Skylab. For Skylab 2 and Skylab 3, a total of two and zero filamentous fungi, respectively, were isolated from the crew during flight. On Skylab 4, a total of 11 fungi were isolated, including a significant contamination to the astronauts. This contamination to the crew was demonstrated 62 days after the first exposure to the liquid-cooled garments, indicating either continued contamination from inanimate sources, abnormally slow return to normal levels, or both.

    Data show that the fungal contamination of the orbital workshop during Skylab 4 did not affect the command module samples collected on recovery day. Although the command module was attached to the orbital workshop during this period of contamination, it was a separate entity, out of the area of heavy use, and away from the contaminating space suits. This relatively clean command module probably contributed to the low level of fungal contamination of the crew postflight.

    In conclusion, microbiological data collected during the Skylab 2, 3, and 4 missions show that, while gross contamination of the Skylab environment was demonstrated and there were several in-flight disease events (presumably of microbial origin), such events were not shown to be limiting hazards for long-duration space flight. Evaluation of the major groups of microorganisms comprising the microbial populations tested, tended to support the theory of microbial simplification for anaerobic bacteria, but not for other microbes. Intercrew transfer of pathogens was demonstrated. The data mediate against the theory of postflight microbial shock. The question of in-flight autoinfection remains unanswered because none of the in-flight disease events were evaluated microbiologically.

experiment_title: A Low-Intensity Mechanical Countermeasure to Prohibit Osteoporosis in Astronauts During Long-Term Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The osteoporosis which develops in microgravity, is one of the greatest hurdles to an extended human presence in space. Earth-based animal and human studies have demonstrated that extremely low magnitude mechanical loading, if imposed at a high frequency, is strongly anabolic to the skeleton, and can serve to inhibit the bone loss, which typically parallels disuse. This experiment is designed to evaluate the efficacy of this unique biomechanical countermeasure to inhibit the microgravity-induced osteoporosis. To achieve this in a non-invasive, non-pharmacologic means would have tremendous impact not only in space, but would also address the bone loss which plagues over 20 million people world wide each year on Earth.

The specific objectives of this experiment are:
1. To establish the efficacy of a 10-minute daily in-flight dose of high frequency (30Hz), low magnitude (0.3-G, or 3m s-2) mechanical acceleration to inhibit the loss of bone density in the lower appendicular and axial skeleton.
2. To establish the efficacy of this same stimulus to inhibit the loss of muscle strength and postural stability in the lower appendicular skeleton.

APPROACH:
During extended missions International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers will receive ten-minute daily doses of high frequency (30Hz), low magnitude (0.3-G, or 3m s-2) mechanical accelerations. The subject will be secured to an oscillating plate by a shoulder harness, at 60% of their pre-launch body mass thus imparting sufficient force to allow the vibration of the platform to induce 0.3-G accelerations to the lower appendicular and axial skeleton. The experimental equipment is designed such that it will not transmit vibration to the vehicular structure. To determine efficacy, crewmembers not participating in the VIBE protocol will serve as prospective controls, as well as reference to previously collected Quantitative Computer Tomography (QCT) and Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) data from the astronaut corps. Comparison between control and treated crewmembers will allow for the efficacy of the treatment to be assessed in a dose dependent manner.

Following flight durations of at least three months, the bone quantity and quality will be evaluated by comparing postflight DXA, QCT and ultrasound measurements to baseline (preflight measurements). The principal areas of interest will be R&L femora, tibia, calcaneus, the spine (L1-4), and non-dominant radius. Assays will evaluate bone density, trabecular and cortical bone density, cortical thickness, apparent bone quality, and bone mineral density. Muscle strength and postural stability will also be evaluated, again comparing pre and post-launch data.

Differences from the baseline will be examined in terms of the ability of extremely low-level mechanical stimulation to inhibit the loss of bone quality and quantity. The preservation of muscle strength and postural stability, as based on these mechanical signals will provide a key to the regulatory stimulus in the maintenance of the musculoskeletal system.

Efficacy will be determined as based on the ability of the signal to inhibit bone loss, prevent loss of muscle power and loss of postural stability as compared to controls. Given the ground-based evidence, we anticipate that treated crewmembers will retain bone density and muscle strength regardless of the deleterious consequences of the absence of gravity. Further, it is anticipated that bone loss in the axial skeleton (spine) will be reduced through exposure to the low-level mechanical signal.

RESULTS:
Three clinical studies have been completed (post-menopausal women, children with cerebral palsy, young women w/ osteoporosis), each which supports the hypothesis that low-level mechanical signals can benefit the mass and morphology of the musculoskeletal system.

This investigation has been demanifested; therefore, there are no results available from this experiment.

experiment_title: Investigating the Physiology and Fitness of an Exoelectrogenic Microorganism Under Microgravity Conditions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary objective of this proposal is to gain fundamental understanding of the physiology of a microorganism (exoelectrogen) that is capable of respiring on solid electron acceptors such as metal oxides during spaceflight. These specialized organisms are used in bioelectrochemical systems, which have the potential to conduct life support processes such as wastewater treatment as well as yield a wide array of space-relevant products such as biofuels, food products, and therapeutics. The ability to respire on solid electron acceptors is dependent on a process called extracellular electron transport (EET) and is often biofilm-dependent. We hypothesize that the performance of exoelectrogens, particularly when respiring on solid electron acceptors, will be altered during spaceflight. The results of these experiments will not only help guide future research in strain development for bioelectrochemical systems but also provide further insight into the impact of microgravity and the space environment on microbial growth and physiology.

APPROACH:
The growth and biofilm development of a model exoelectrogen, Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 under EET-respiring spaceflight conditions will be characterized by comparing ground-based and microgravity experiments aboard the International Space Station. EET measurement experiments using the ferrozine assay will be conducted. Additionally, whole-genome expression and competitive mutant fitness (i.e., omic approaches) profiling will be used to identify genes that confer a selective advantage or disadvantage for cell growth and biofilm development under EET- respiring conditions during spaceflight. The flight definition phase is planned in 2016.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: A Study Of Dietary Retinoid for Prevention of 56Fe-Induced Cancers in Rat Skin
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Previous carcinogenesis experiments have shown that very high energy, high-Z, particulate radiation (56Fe) in either single dose or multiple dose format is about as carcinogenic in rat skin as low-Z particulate radiation with the same linear energy transfer (LET). An additional finding of these studies was that the cancers and benign tumors could be substantially (approximately 50%) prevented by a non-toxic (250 ppm) level of dietary vitamin A acetate. Preliminary gene expression microarray analysis demonstrated that the retinoid interfered with up-regulation of several radiation-induced genes associated with de-differentiation and increased cell proliferation. This study did a follow-up on these initial findings by testing the hypothesis that retinoids reduce the carcinogenic action of ionizing radiation by altering the DNA repair-related proliferative response of the pluripotent stem cells, which are considered to be plausible target cells for the carcinogenic action of radiation. Carcinogenesis experiments evaluate the efficacy of cancer prevention when the dietary retinoid is available during stem cell regeneration. Pluripotent stem cells were activated via radiation-induced epithelial denudation, and the action of a retinoid on epidermal gene expression was evaluated via commercial and custom gene expression arrays.

Microarray analysis was used to analyze in vivo transit amplifying keratinocytes, in vivo pluripotent stem cells and in vitro keratinocytes (which have stem-like properties). The cyclin D1-mediated proliferation pathway and the p53-dependent DNA repair pathways were studied in response to the 56Fe ion beam in the presence and absence of a dietary retinoid. The proposed study aimed to provide 1) better quantitative data than now exists on how cancer risk estimates are affected by short-term versus long-term treatments with a dietary retinoid; 2) a better definition of how closely gene expression changes in different types of keratinocytes are linked to the cancer preventive action of a dietary retinoid; 3) new data to evaluate if in vivo gene expression patterns, especially of cyclin D1 pathway and p53-dependent repair pathway, in pluripotent stem cells differ from than of transit amplifying keratinocytes; and 4) new data to establish whether keratinocyte cell lines in vitro exhibit gene expression patterns in response to radiation and/or retinoid that more closely mimic stem cells or ordinary keratinocytes in vivo.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
The results of the microarray work associated with this study suggest rather strongly that oxidative stress may be a significant pro-carcinogenic alteration produced by both low and high LET radiation and that vitamin A is about equally effective for preventing cancers induced by both types of radiation. This opens up a new and simple pathway whereby an anti-inflammatory inhibitor may be used to prevent cancer induction by space radiation. Gene expression patterns in rat skin exposed to a beam of 56Fe ions, a surrogate of the high-energy, heavy ion galactic radiation background, have been examined as a basis for obtaining a better understanding of the possible mechanism behind vitamin A’s radio-protective activity. At one day after 3.0 Gy of 56Fe ion irradiation, the expression of 110 genes were significantly up-regulated (p <= 0.05) in comparison to control, while no genes were altered by the vitamin A supplement alone. Combined with 56Fe ion radiation, the vitamin A supplement blocked the expression of 88 (80%) of the 110 genes and eliminated 16 of 18 gene categories that were significantly-altered (all increased) by the 56Fe ion radiation. Categories with large numbers of genes eliminated by the retinoid included ‘response to stress’ – 33 genes, ‘response to biotic stimulus’ – 38 genes, ‘signal transduction’ – 35 genes and ‘regulation of cellular/physiological process’ – 40 genes. Even for ‘immune response’ and ‘response to biotic stimulus’, the only two categories that remained significantly-altered in the presence of the vitamin, the combined number of altered genes was reduced from 74 to 13. No significant gene expression alterations were found at seven day relative to control. The results indicate that at one day dietary vitamin A strongly interfered with 56Fe ion-induced gene expression within broad categories of response-to-stimulus, immune-related and stress-related genes, implying that the latter gene categories likely have a role to play in the radioprotective action of the vitamin.

experiment_title: Effect of Simulated Solar Particle Events and Galactic Cosmic Rays on Crop Growth and Development
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
With the renewed goal of crewed Mars exploration, continuous fresh food production during long-term deep space missions may be a critical addition to the processed food system to meet astronauts’ nutritional requirements and to provide a psychological countermeasure for crew in the isolation and confinement of deep space. However, critical knowledge gaps, such as the impact of deep space radiation on plant crops, must be addressed prior to dependence on crop systems for any portion of a deep space food system. Although the biological impact of simulated space radiation on mammalian cells and rodents has been investigated extensively, the effects of long-term exposure to deep space radiation on crop seeds and plant growth has yet to be characterized. We must investigate the impact of deep space radiation on crop foods to either confirm that nutritious and high quality produce can be reliably grown in deep space or to provide a baseline to guide future radiation countermeasure development for crop foods.

APPROACH:
We propose to investigate the effect of simulated Solar Particle Events (SPEs) and Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs) on several model crops at different growing stages using the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) at Brookhaven National Lab (BNL). The selected crops have been grown successfully under spaceflight-like conditions (temperature, air, humidity, lighting, etc.) in ground analogs, and either have been or will be grown on International Space Station (ISS) for crew consumption. The additional knowledge of the response of each crop to deep space radiation will help identify candidate traits for successful growth on deep space vehicles. The effect of the simulated space radiation environment on crop seeds viability, seedling development, and the impact on nutritional value of fresh produce will be determined.

experiment_title: Cell and Molecular Biomechanics: Cardiac and Skeletal Muscle
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The major goal of this study was to produce a muscle cell model that will: explain biomechanical adaptations that occur with alterations in muscle protein isoforms due to changes in activity level, as in prolonged space travel; predict bioenergetic changes associated with changes in activity level; be integrated into computational models of human limb and heart. It was a collaborative project between Florida State University and the University of Washington. The original Aims of the project are: a. Identify contractile protein composition of skeletal and cardiac muscles from high-activity and low-activity rats. b. Characterize contractile properties (phenotype) of selected muscles containing unique mixtures of protein isoforms. c. Develop a “digital” cell biomechanical model.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Key Findings during the study period: a. Nano-mechanical model of the muscle sarcomere (a component of the Digital Astronaut): Presence of filament compliance could modulate the dependence of steady state isometric force and the rate of tension development on thin filament activation level that is determined by calcium in the living cell. Tuning of biomechanics through compliance at the protein level as demonstrated in the investigators’ studies may be as significant as biomechanical tuning at higher levels of organization as demonstrated by Professor Tom McMahon and colleagues’ ability to improve human runners’ performance through altering the characteristics of the track surface. The influence of compliance (or its inverse, elasticity) thus needs to be considered in biomechanical components at all levels of organization in physiological models to describe changes in muscle associated with exercise and microgravity. b. Signaling pathways in muscle plasticity: The immunosuppressant drug rapamycin has little or no effect on maximum calcium-activated force, but (at some concentrations) increases calcium-sensitivity of isometric force and inhibits the kinetics of tension redevelopment; this indicates that rapamycin affects calcium-regulatory proteins (troponin/tropomyosin) more than actomyosin. Attenuation of cardiac hypertrophy by rapamycin is not due to direct effects of rapamycin on myofilament contractility.

experiment_title: Metabolism and Heat Dissipation During Apollo EVA Periods
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During the zero-G extravehicular activities (EVAs) performed during the five Gemini missions, considerable difficulty was experienced by the crewmembers. In a space environment which imposed several life support requirements during EVA (the maintenance of a minimum oxygen pressure, the removal of expired carbon dioxide, the provision for useful mobility, and the maintenance of body temperature), the crewmen experienced high work rates and apparent overheating during the Gemini 4, 9, and 11 EVAs. The crewmen also encountered unexpected difficulty performing specific tasks on each of these missions.

Events such as these prompted several researchers to evaluate the effects of one-sixth (or lunar) gravity on the cost of work in a pressure suit. Results, however, were inconclusive. Predictions were made that metabolic costs would decrease with subgravity walking. Other researchers predicted metabolic increases would accompany low traction exercise. Other uncertainties arose from the considerations of lunar terrain and surface composition and their effect on mobility and metabolic rate. In response to these uncertainties, conservative biomedical estimates of the life support requirements were defined on the basis of available data. Although metabolic rates were not measured during the Gemini EVAs, it was clear in several instances that crewmen worked at levels above the heat removal capability of the gas cooled life support system. The Metabolism and Heat Dissipation experiment was therefore performed to determine life support requirements during Apollo EVAs.

APPROACH:
Since it was desirable to measure metabolic rate during EVA on the lunar surface and in free space, several measurement approaches were evaluated. Standard laboratory methods would have required breaking pressure suit integrity if used in space or during vacuum chamber training on the ground; this was undesirable. The operational data available from the crewman and from his life support system were assessed to determine their usefulness in approximating metabolic rate. This consisted of voice and electrocardiogram (ECG) data from each crewmember, oxygen bottle pressure, Liquid Cooling Garment (LCG) coolant-water entry and exit temperatures, and suit-gas entry temperature. In addition, the sublimator water usage data was available after the majority of the EVAs; sublimator water usage provided a measure of the total heat loss from the suit. All of the heat removed from the pressure suit was first transferred to a heat sink maintained by the sublimator which rejected heat by the change of state involved in sublimating ice to water vapor in the vacuum of space.

RESULTS:
Two types of task identification methods were used for separating the activities performed during EVA periods. For the first method, the metabolic rate monitors divided the operational tasks into four types of activities of importance to mission planners: overhead activities (those tasks required for each EVA, such as egressing and ingressing the vehicle), deploying the Apollo lunar surface experiment package (ALSEP), making geological surveys, and riding in the lunar roving vehicle. The oxygen and LCG measurement methods could be used to obtain accurate metabolic rates for these activities. The second method of task separation was based on a time and motion study which required dividing the tasks into as many definable activities as possible. However, this method resulted in some activities of such short duration that metabolic rates could only be assigned using the postflight heart rate method. Metabolic rate measurements were determined for both lunar surface EVAs (Apollo missions 11, 12, and 14 through 17) as well as zero-G EVAs (Apollo missions 9, 15, 16, 17).

Metabolic rates were lower than predicted before the Apollo missions for lunar surface EVAs. Overhead activities consumed the most energy, while driving or riding in the lunar roving vehicle consumed the least. This was comparable to shirt sleeve riding in an automobile. The highest average metabolic rate was experienced by one Apollo 11 subject who was very active in evaluating modes of locomotion. For discrete activities, the highest metabolic rates were associated with his transport of the ALSEP pallet, ingress to the Lunar Module (LM) with lunar samples, and drilling and removal of drill bits.

For the Apollo 14 mission, which included some of the most extensive walking traverses, a specific effort was made to correlate metabolic rate and traverse rate. However, data obtained showed poor correlation. The crewmen apparently maintained a comfortable walking effort and, to a large extent, the rate of traverse at this level of effort varied with the terrain and the operational requirements of each traverse. In general, both the speed and efficiency of lunar walking were greater than could be achieved while wearing a pressure suit in a 1-G environment, but neither speed nor efficiency was equivalent to that of a shirt sleeve operation in 1-G.

Operational film and kinescope were used in performing a time and motion study of Apollo 15 and 16 activities. Results from observations of Apollo 15 and 16 time and motion studies indicated that tasks were completed more rapidly at 1-G wearing space suits than at one-sixth-G, but at higher metabolic rates.

The zero-G EVA activities were measured using the heart rate method. This method tended to yield higher estimates of metabolic rates therefore results ranging from 150 to 500 kcal /hr were considered maximum values. Voice data did not indicate that the crewmen were performing strenuously. In some cases, the actual metabolic rates were much lower than the values obtained by means of heart rate calibration data. Excitement, rather than physical exertion, was considered the cause of elevation of heart rates.

The crewmen were able to perform planned EVAs and to extend them to the maximum time allowable without medical problems. The manually controlled Liquid Cooling Garment was effective in minimizing fatigue and water loss from sweating during EVA. Gas cooling was adequate during the short zero-G EVA performed from the Command Module. It was found that adequate body restraints, realistic zero-G preflight training in a water immersion simulator, and detailed planning of activities were essential to ensure completion of tasks and reduce fatigue.

experiment_title: Animal Enclosure Module Inflight Test
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The Animal Enclosure Module (AEM) was developed for an SSIP experiment flown on STS-41B. The purpose of this study was to test the ability of the AEM to maintain healthy rats in space with no dangers to crew safety, as this was the first time a cage of animals was flown in the crew compartment of the Shuttle. The major safety concerns involved microbial, particulate, and odor contamination of the crew atmosphere.

Approach:

The AEM was successfully flown for the first time with six specific pathogen free (SPF) male albino rats of the Lewis Wistar strain (the standard rodent research subject), 56 days old and an average of 275 grams at launch. Contamination was to be avoided by the use of germ-free (SPF) rats, microbial filters on the intake and exhaust areas of the AEM, and airtight seals around certain areas of the AEM. A control group of three rats was maintained on the ground for comparison purposes.

Results:

All six rats were healthy at the end of the flight. The flight rats consumed less food and did not gain weight at the expected rates, compared to the ground controls. This was due to the AEM food delivery system in which food was attached to the cage slides, while ground control cages had a more conventional food system. The water supply of half the flight rats was depleted before the end of the mission, and the water supply for the rest of the rats was nearly gone. As a result, minor changes in AEM food and water systems were recommended. In addition, it was determined that the air flow rate through the AEM needed to be increased in order to improve removal of the cage waste products.

experiment_title: Culture-based Environmental Monitoring of Crop-based Space Food Systems
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Crew members live and work in a closed-system environment that is monitored to ensure health and safety. The design and development of the International Space System (ISS) has incorporated lessons learned from microbial monitoring of previous spaceflight missions. The microbial control actions on the ISS include engineering designs, such as high efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filtering of the air, microbial monitoring of the air, surfaces, and water, and remediation procedures when necessary. The current spacecraft environmental microbial limits were evaluated based on the continual monitoring of the microbes in the spaceflight environment.

New systems, such as the Veggie plant growth system, are being introduced to enable mission success. Collecting measures on new systems is important to the development of spaceflight-grown produce requirements. Periodic sampling of the microbes will provide the data needed to assess the impact of the plant growth system on crewmembers’ safety. Since the Veggie system is open to the cabin environment, it is critical to understand what microbes are present in the plant growth system.

This investigation will focus on characterizing the microbial community of the Veggie plant growth system to assess the risk of adverse health effects due to host-microorganism interactions. The objective of this experiment is to characterize the microbial community of the Veggie plant growth system in order to identify a baseline of microorganisms. This experiment has the following specific aims:

experiment_title: Imaging and Serum Biomarkers to Predict and Identify Early Cardiac Injury from Radiation Exposure
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

As NASA moves toward long-duration missions, it is imperative that the adverse health effects of the space environment be understood. The cardiac effects of radiation from medical, occupational, and environmental exposures are of critical concern. This experiment aims to understand cardiac events from exposure to radiation therapy to develop tools for early identification of cardiac injury.

Human radiotherapy cohorts have not been utilized to identify adverse outcome pathways, progression rates and latency periods, and early surrogate markers for radiation-induced cardiovascular disease. The experiment will acquire data on cardiovascular impairments and associated biomarkers observed in patients undergoing cardiac exposure to ionizing radiation with emphasis on non-invasive imaging modalities to quantify predictive changes linked to late impairment. Identifying damage early on may prevent cardiac dysfunction though the use of interventions. Understanding cardiac functional changes that occur during and soon after radiation therapy may lead to the development of therapeutic interventions.

The objective of the experiment is to identify early markers of cardiac injury after radiation exposure in a timely manner so that steps can be taken to prevent irreversible cardiac dysfunction. In a short period after cardiac radiation exposure inflammation occurs and biomarkers are released. Without treatment radiation exposure progresses to reversible cardiac dysfunction and then irreversible cardiac dysfunction. Irreversible cardiac dysfunction can lead to coronary artery disease, valvular disease, myocardial damage, conduction defects, and diastolic dysfunction. This experiment has the following specific aims:

  1. Assess for cardiac toxicity in patients treated with radiation therapy to the chest.
  2. Assess for an association between 3D imaging findings suggestive of cardiac injury and radiation dosimetry.
  3. Explore the association of radiation exposure with serum biomarker levels
APPROACH:

Approximately 30 patients who are receiving standard radiation therapy with moderate cardiac exposure, which is an estimated mean heart dose 6-12 Gy, will be enrolled in the study. Investigators will gather preliminary data, provided initial estimates, and explore potential associations. Several tests will be utilized to assess for early cardiac effects of radiation exposure. For aim 1, patients will undergo an echocardiogram with global longitudinal strain measurements. The percentage of patients who experience a cardiac injury, which is a strain reduction of greater than 10 percent from pre-treatment/detection of serum ultrasensitive troponin, will be reported. Included in the report will be whether the cardiac injury was determined by strain, detectable troponin, or both. For aim 2, dosimetry and cardiac MRI photos will be used to visually identify possible relationships. Side-by-side comparisons of three-dimensional (3D) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and radiation treatment plans will be performed. For aim 3, the relationship between regions of early cardiac injury and biomarkers will measured repeatedly over time.

experiment_title: Quantifying selection for pathogenicity and antibiotic resistance in bacteria and fungi on the ISS – a microbial tracking study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bacteria, archaea and fungi inhabit virtually every realm of our planet, including our own bodies. Over their 4-billion-year evolutionary history, they have shown remarkable adaptation to the environment. However, these same microbes are now adapting to our built environments, such as our homes, hospitals, offices, and closed habitats like the International Space Station (ISS). Built environment-associated microbes originate predominantly from human occupants, and as such are often adapted to living on, or in, our bodies. Previously, we have shown that the microbes we shed into our buildings develop genetic mutations in order to survive in this dry, nutrient poor, hostile environment. These genetic changes often result in an increase in antibiotic resistance, immune evasion, and tissue invasion traits; as such, they can be a threat to human health. We hypothesize that if the built environment promotes microbial stress-survival we will see an increase in antibiotic resistance and virulence. To test our hypothesis, we will focus on the Microbiomes of the Built Environment of Spacecraft using existing data (GeneLab) and isolated microbial strains held at JPL/NASA. We will sequence the genome and quantify the antibiotic resistance and virulence of each microbe, and perform metagenomic analysis of ISS environments, to understand the potential human-health consequences of the genetic changes. We will also collect new microbes from the ISS to further develop our time series of observations, to improve our understanding of how microbes change in this unique environment. These studies will help us understand the impact of spaceflight stress on structural and functional changes in microbial communities and predict which microbes pose a threat to crew health.

Objective 1: To determine the distribution and selection of antimicrobial resistance and virulence genes in microbial and fungal genomes and metagenomes in the ISS environment.
Objective 2: To quantify antimicrobial resistance and virulence phenotypes in archived ISS microbial isolates. While there is substantial evidence to suggest increased antibiotic resistance and virulence in space-flown isolates when compared to ground-based organisms, the extent to which the presence of resistance or virulence genes associates with the phenotype in vivo is unclear. We will determine how microbial genotypes, identified in Aim 1, impact AMR and virulence.
Objective 3: To utilize live-dead cell characterization methods to determine the distribution and temporal dynamics of living microorganisms, as well as antimicrobial resistance and virulence phenotype in the ISS environment.

APPROACH:
Objective 1 Tasks: The goal of objective 1 is to understand genes and pathways that are under purifying selection in the ISS environment. All ISS culture collections, MT-1 and MT-2 flight project strains are currently at the co-PI institution, JPL, and will be available for this project to generate genomes from select isolates. To accomplish our goal, experiments are divided into 5 tasks, including: (Task 1) sequence the genomes of the existing ~1000 isolated strains of bacteria and fungi collected during ‘Microbial Tracking’ and previous ISS expeditions from over the past decade. These data will be used to determine the phylogenomic and phenotypic similarity of these isolates, and to build a picture of existing genetic compliment of these strains, especially, (Task 2) their antibiotic resistance profiles and (Task 3) genes associated with host-invasion potential. These data will also be combined with existing metagenomic data available through GeneLab to (Task 4) build assemblies of uncultured taxa, and examine the environmental genomic diversity of the sequenced strains. Using both genomic and metagenomic data we also intend to (Task 5) build ancestral genotype predictions of key bacterial species and quantify purifying selection of specific genes as a function of their non-synonymous to synonymous mutation ratio. All isolates will undergo AMR/virulence assays to validate findings (detailed in Objective 2). These predictions will enable us to examine the genetic elements that are under selection and determine mobile element acquisition events within each group.

Objective 2 Tasks: The goal of objective 2 is to determine how the microbial genomic profiles, identified in Aim 1, impact AMR and virulence. Objective 2 (UCSD and UCM) comprises 2 tasks, including (Task 6) whereby in vitro antibiotic resistance assays will be performed on 100 strains whose genomes maintain ARGs and 100 strains whose genomes do not, and (Task 7) virulence assays using nematodes as a model system on 50 organisms that show relevant virulence traits in their genomes. The results of these assays will be correlated with genetic evidence of antibiotic resistance genes and virulence pathways. As different isolates were also collected at different times over the last decade, we will also associate the results of these assays with time, especially for isolates within the same genus or species.

Objective 3 Tasks: In objective three, we propose a new flight series (MT-3) to further the application of PMA-based analysis of intact (potentially living) cells for metagenomic characterization. PMA-based metagenomics will be used to characterize phylogeny, AMR and virulence gene proportions (as in Objective 1), which will be compared to culture-based genomics, and validated by AMR and virulence assays (described in Objective 2). By combining PMA-based metagenomics with culture-based genomics and in vitro/in vivo assays, it will be possible to increase our understanding of the phylogenetic breadth of AMR and virulence genes in the ISS microbiome. Additionally, these data will complement our existing investigation, providing an ongoing record from the Microbial Tracking flight series of the longitudinal selection of genetic and phenotypic traits in microorganisms associated with the ISS built environment. Our third objective (JPL) comprises 3 tasks, including (Task 8) continuation of the previous “Microbial Tracking” efforts that enabled the first 2 objectives, through 3 consecutive flights as part of MT-3, comprising 5 consecutive days of sampling 8 surfaces each day towards the end of each flight. These 120 samples will be used to (Task 9) estimate culture-based CFU measurements, isolate ~250 new bacterial/fungal isolates for genome sequencing and characterization. In (Task 10) we will generate qPCR-based microbial burden analysis and PMA based shotgun metagenomic data to determine the unculturable phylogenetic, AMR and virulence gene diversity from intact cells. In (Task 11) we will determine the correlations between the microbiome data and the ISS surface and atmospheric data. Finally, in (Task 12) we will validate AMR and virulence genetic predictions, as in Objective 2.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.
