experiment_title: Therapeutic Modulation of Systemic Glucose-Dependent Insulintropic Peptide Levels to Counteract Microgravity-Induced Bone Loss
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Osteoporosis is a disease characterized by an imbalance between bone formation and breakdown leading to a decrease in bone mass, resulting in an increased risk of fractures. Osteoporosis is associated with significant morbidity and mortality due to fractures, in particular vertebral compression fractures and hip fractures. A number of epidemiological and clinical studies have linked abnormalities in nutrition to osteoporosis. Thus, although there is a considerable amount of clinical data to link abnormalities in nutritional intake with osteoporosis, very little research has delved into this phenomenon. Present therapy for osteoporosis is predominantly antiresorptive therapy, i.e. to prevent further bone breakdown and few medications (except for parathyroid hormone injection, perhaps estrogen in women and fluoride) are able to increase new bone formation. Our studies should shed further light on the mechanisms involved in the development of osteoporosis, and thus help in the development of new anabolic therapies. Our data demonstrates that GIP is a key hormone linking nutrient intake to bone formation. If GIP levels are elevated then increases in bone mass are observed. However if the elevation in GIP level is prolonged or excessive then this results in loss of the GIP effect and loss of bone mass.

Specific Aims:
(1) Determine whether elevations in endogenous Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) levels lead to an increase in bone formation by examining the bone phenotype in GIP-overexpressing transgenic mice.
(2) Determine whether endogenous elevations in GIP prevent bone loss in a model of weightlessness by measuring bone turnover rate in GIP-overexpressing transgenic mice with hindlimb suspension.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Major findings:
(1) Validation of our in vitro findings suggesting a role for GIP as a link between nutrient intake and bone formation. Investigators now have two animal models: (a) a GIP-overexpressing transgenic mouse which has a higher bone mass which, the indices demonstrate, have higher bone formation and decreased bone breakdown and (b) a functional GIP receptor knockout mouse, generated by chronically exposing them to high GIP levels. These mice have a lower bone mass, higher indices of bone breakdown and lower indices of bone formation. These mice are more prone to bone loss. These data suggest that GIP levels may be an important risk factor for development of osteoporosis and validates our original proposal that GIP might be a valuable countermeasure to microgravity-induced bone loss.
(2) Demonstration of GIP as a major nutritional “integrative” hormone capable to affect multiple tissues to maximize nutrient utilization. Thus, manipulation of GIP for bone maintenance in astronauts in space may have the additional benefit of increasing nutrient utilization and maximize nutritional health.
(3) Demonstration that GIP interactions with other anabolic hormones such as PTH on bone mass are complex with some indices (ex. alkaline phosphatase) rising more with the combination but not other parameters (ex. bone densitometry).

experiment_title: Alternative Compression Garment (Flight Analog)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The overall objective of this study was to improve upon existing suit designs by developing an elastic, gradient compression garment that would provide a continuous compression from the feet to the abdomen. Additionally, to develop a doffing protocol that enables the use of compression garments after simulated space flight to prevent hypotensive events without prolonging the recovery period.

Specific Aim I: To determine whether subjects wearing breast-high, graded compression garments developed symptoms of orthostatic intolerance after 14 days of head-down tilt bed rest (Groups 1 and 2).
Specific Aim II: To determine the time course of cardiovascular readaptation during the first three days of post-bed rest recovery after using compression garments for a short period of time on BR+0 (Group 1).
Specific Aim III: To determine the effect of wearing graded compression garments on BR+0, with reduced compression on subsequent days, on the time course of cardiovascular readaptation during the first three days of post-bed rest recovery (Group 2).

APPROACH:
All subjects participated in standard cardiovascular measures on BR–5, BR+0, BR+1, and BR+3, which included plasma volume, cardiac function, and head-up tilt tests. In addition, plasma volume was measured on BR+2. On days in which subjects wore compression garments, they were donned first thing in the morning. No compression garments were worn on BR+3.

The subjects were fitted with Jobst custom compression garments and a series of measurements were taken along the legs and torso. The circumference of each leg and of the torso was measured every 1.5 inches beginning at the foot and ending just below the breast-line. These measurements were used to construct the custom-made garments worn on BR+0. Approximately two weeks for construction of the garments were required between the time that these measurements were made and their delivery to the investigator. These procedures are the same as those employed for the Space Shuttle experiment “Evaluation of Commercial Compression Garments to Prevent Post-Spaceflight Orthostatic Intolerance” (Alternative Compression Garments) (ACG) (DSO 641). Additionally, measurements of the ankle, calf, thigh, and waist circumference were taken before and after bed rest (BR–5, BR+0, BR+1, BR+2, and BR+3) to track anthropometric changes as a result of and during recovery from bed rest. These measurements were not previously conducted during bed rest studies and mirrored the measurements made during the Space Shuttle investigation (DSO 641).

Data collected was used:

  • To ensure proper sizing of off-the-shelf thigh-high garments on BR+1 and BR+2
  • To compare to the flight study results
  • To refine the prescription of garment sizing for future studies

    • Group 1 donned the full compression, breast-high garment ensemble (shorts and thigh-high garments) upon waking and doffed the garment after BR+0 cardiovascular and orthostatic tolerance testing. This group did not wear any compression garment for the remainder of the study.

    Group 2 donned the full compression, breast-high garment ensemble upon waking and doffed the garment at the end of the day on BR+0. On BR+1, this group wore an off-the-shelf, thigh-high garment that provided 30-40 mmHg of compression at the ankle, and decreased up the leg following the Jobst gradient to approximately 10 mmHg at the top of the leg. On BR+2, this group wore an off-the-shelf, thigh-high garment that provided 10-20 mmHg of compression at the ankle, and decreased up the leg following the Jobst gradient to approximately 5 mmHg at the top of the leg. No group wore compression garments on BR+3.

    Plasma volume measurements were made on test days BR–5, BR+0, BR+1, BR+2, and BR+3 using the carbon monoxide rebreathing technique. Blood samples were analyzed for hemoglobin, carboxyhemoglobin, and hematocrit. Total blood volume, red blood cell volume, and plasma volume was calculated. Cardiac Function of the heart was also imaged using two- and three-dimensional echocardiography. Hemodynamic assessment was accomplished by the use of continuous, pulsed wave, and color flow doppler.

    The tilt test was performed as a standard measures tilt as previously described, but for up to 15 minutes only and without blood draws, on BR–5, BR+0, BR+1, and BR+3. Briefly, continuous finger blood pressure and electrocardiography (ECG) was acquired with a laboratory system. Images from at least three cardiac cycles were independently analyzed. Aortic annulus area, stroke volume, and cardiac output (stroke volume multiplied by heart rate) was calculated. Subjects were supine for five minutes for baseline data collection, followed by 15 space bar minutes of 80 degree head-up tilt or until symptoms of presyncope.

    RESULTS:
    This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division.

    These gradient compression garment's (GCG) prevented the orthostatic intolerance that is normally present after two weeks of head-down tilt bed rest. There were minimal differences between the control and treatment groups on BR+1, but both groups recovered to the same level by BR+3. Overall, these garments are effective in preventing immediate post-bed rest orthostatic intolerance, and the use of lower compression garments (thigh-high only) in the recovery period can provide additional protection without significantly impeding the recovery process. These results suggest that the GCG will be beneficial to protect long-duration astronauts and in commercial space flight applications during the immediate post-flight and recovery periods during re-adaptation to Earth gravity.

experiment_title: Time Course of Metabolic Adaptations during Loading and Unloading
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The alterations in skeletal muscle structure and function induced by space travel or endurance training are the result of a chronic mechanical stimulus (or lack of it) a series of metabolic interactions spanning from the cellular to the organism level. Reduced activation of the weight bearing muscles alters gene expression of myosin heavy chain isoforms to meet the functional demands of weightlessness and results in muscle atrophy, reduced capacity to process fatty acids, and reduced muscle endurance. On the other hand, endurance training induces an up-regulation of oxidative enzymes and results in increased fatty acid oxidation capacity and muscle endurance.

The few human and animal studies comparing skeletal muscle structure and function before and after unloading suggest that the adaptations are time and biological-level dependent. While some parameters may be altered within a week (muscle mass, insulin resistance), others may take longer to show changes (work efficiency, VO2max). Similar conclusions may be drawn from endurance training studies. Thus, to establish countermeasures aimed at restoring astronauts’ work capacity, it is critical to determine: (1) the time course of muscle atrophy, (2) the bioenergetic, metabolic, and fuel-processing factors that contribute to the reductions in endurance associated with muscle atrophy, and (3) the effects of skeletal muscle atrophy on whole-body metabolism. To answer these questions a multi-scale model of energy metabolism -linking cellular to whole organism processes is needed in combination with appropriate cellular to whole-body measurements collected during the period of adaptation. The objective of this study was to identify the time course of the adaptations to loading and unloading and to integrate them using a multi-scale model of skeletal muscle and whole body metabolism, in order to predict the system integrated response after periods of space travel or endurance training. Accordingly, a team of two computational modelers with expertise on scales ranging from cellular to whole body and three experimentalists with expertise in complementary methodologies in rodents were formed to reach the study’s objectives.

The specific aims of this study were:

  1. To identify and model the time course of the structural, metabolic and functional adaptations to loading and unloading,
  2. To develop and validate a multi-level (cell-muscle-whole body) computational model skeletal muscle metabolism in the context of the whole body.
  3. To predict the integrated response of muscle fibers, whole skeletal muscle, and whole body during periods of loading and unloading, in particular astronaut’s muscle energetics and function, as well as his/her whole body metabolism and performance.

APPROACH:
A novel top-down approach was applied to model whole-body metabolism and to bridge organism to cellular level. Thus, a minimal, but comprehensive, systems model of metabolism was developed which included: (a) brain, heart, liver, adipose tissue, and skeletal muscle, (b) a cardiorespiratory controller, (c) pancreas and liver, and (d) the cardiovascular system. Modeling transport processes across membranes constituted an essential feature of the integration process linking the various scales. For model validation, molecular and cellular measurements were used to assessed tissue and whole body metabolism. To maintain intact regulatory mechanisms, a novel methodological approach with emphasis on the use of in vivo measurements was applied, specifically, proteomics and metabolomics using state-of-the-art stable isotope techniques.

This multi-scale model of metabolism enabled testing of physiologically-feasible time profiles of the adaptations to loading/unloading in every organ/tissue, which would otherwise require collection of hundreds of samples in thousands of animals. Specifically, this model can be used to predict tissue metabolism (e.g., fuel efficiency, buffering capacity, and muscle endurance) as well as whole body metabolism (e.g., insulin resistance, lactate acidosis, work capacity).

RESULTS:
In this research, investigators documented and validated models to provide the desired simulations for integration into the Digital Astronaut program. In the model validation process, investigators compared simulations with experimental data from finished/published animal/human studies. The quantified validation of these models provides the Digital Astronaut project with defensible and credible evidence supporting the use of model simulations to predict muscle performance and atrophy.

Model M.1: Simulations were compared with experimental data to validate model predictions of a) cellular metabolic responses from muscle atrophy (by unloading) and training (by exercise loading) of rodents and b) gender differences and fiber types on oxygen uptake kinetics during exercise.

Model M.2: Simulations were compared with oxygenation data from skeletal muscle measurements of venous blood and muscle tissue data with various levels of arterial oxygen content and exercise. This validation procedure ensured model robustness under hypoxic stress so that whole-body metabolic function can be evaluated.

Model M.3: Simulations were compared with experimental data from skeletal muscle under ramp and constant load tests at different exercise intensities. This validation procedure identified model limitations in predicting metabolic responses to higher exercise intensities.

Model M.4: Simulations were compared with experimental data from cardio-respiratory and skeletal muscle responses to exercise in adults: (a) before and after training and (b) before and after bed rest.

Investigators provided the Digital Astronaut program with uniform and well-documented computer codes that were or can readily be converted to another format, e.g., MATLAB. The documentation includes:

1. Background theory, variable, derivations, conceptual model structure, fundamental assumptions and implementation documentation including developer’s notes.
2. Well-documented and commented code (FORTRAN and/or MATLAB) with references to all supporting documentation, including definition of all variables and units.
3. Users guides that explain the implementation of the stand-alone code.
4. Outcome of all verification and validation testing, including determination of model limitations.
5. Copies of all publications resulting from this work.

experiment_title: Effect of Spaceflight on TGF-Beta Expression by hFOB Cells
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The purpose of this study is to establish whether changes in gravitational loading have a direct effect on osteoblast ability to regulate TGF-beta expression. The effects of spaceflight and reloading on TGF-beta mRNA and peptide levels will be studied in a newly developed line of immortalized human fetal osteoblasts (hFOB) transfected with an SV40 temperature dependent mutant to generate proliferating, undifferentiated hFOB cells at 33-34 degrees Celsius and a non-proliferating, differentiated hFOB cells at 37-39 degrees Celsius. Unlike previous cell culture models, hFOB cells have unlimited proliferative capacity yet can be precisely regulated to differentiate into mature cells which express mature osteoblast function. If isolated osteoblasts respond to changes in mechanical loading in a manner similar to their response in animals, the cell system could provide a powerful model to investigate the signal transduction pathway for gravitational loading.

Approach:

Cell cultures were maintained in the cell culture module (CCM) at 37 degrees Celsius , the permissive temperature for SV40 large T-antigen in the FOB cell line. Fractions of culture media were collected on days 1, 4, 8, and 12 from both flight and ground cultures, and were analyzed for glucose content to measure glucose metabolism. At the appropriate time following recovery of the spacecraft, RNA was isolated from the FOB cultures and quantitated by UV spectrophotometry for Northern or RNase protection assays. Osteonectin, alkaline phosphates, and type I collagen were quantified with Northern Analysis. Cytosine gene expression was measured by RNase protection assay. The levels of carboxyterminal propertied of type I pro collagen (PCP) were measured by radioimmunoassay in order to evaluate matrix production rates. Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) levels were measured by enzyme immunoassay. The morphology of the cell cultures was also examined using electron microscopy.

Results:

Both flight and ground controls utilized glucose at a steady and nearly identical rate. High levels of collagen accumulation were detected in flight and ground cultures from flight day 4 increasing steadily to day 12 and stabilizing after day 12, suggesting a decrease in the rate of collagen synthesis, or increase in collagen breakdown occurring between day 12 and landing. The rates of collagen accumulation in flight and control cells were indistinguishable, consistent with similar rates of collagenous matrix production. No significant difference in PGE2 levels were detected between flight and ground cultures. The steady state level of osteonectin mRNA decreased dramatically, while alkaline phosphatase and collagen mRNA decreased slight from baseline. There was a trend toward lower levels of osteonectin (p<.06) and collagen (p<.09) mRNA in flight cultures. The level of TGF-beta2 (~30%) and TGF-beta1 mRNA (~20) decreased slight in flight cells compared to ground controls. Scanning electron microscopy demonstrated no qualitative morphological differences between flight and ground controls.

experiment_title: Regulation of Erythropoiesis During Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Experimental results from SLS-1 showed a decrease in the number of Epo-responsive total bone marrow progenitors in flight rats compared to the ground controls. SLS-2 allowed further investigations into this study with the addition of two features; the injection of recombinant human Epo (rhEpo) to examine its effect on progenitor cells in microgravity and the inflight collection of samples. The objective was to assess peripheral blood and bone marrow erythroid parameters.

APPROACH:
Flight animals were divided into four groups: group A (n=5) was used to collect blood, group B (n=5) was injected with recombinant human erythropoietin (rhEpo), group C (n=5) received saline as a control, and group D (n=5) was sacrificed in flight. Blood samples were taken at scheduled times from the tail vein. Automated blood cell counts were performed twice and results were averaged for each sample. Reticulocytes were counted both manually from slides and by flow cytometry. Erythroid cultures were assayed with various combinations of rhEpo and in the absence of rhEpo. A 200 cell differential count was performed on bone marrow smears. On dissection days, cardiocentesis was performed and serum was sampled. Epo was measured using commercial radioimmunoassay kits.

RESULTS:
No significant changes were seen in peripheral blood erythroid elements. Nonadherent bone marrow cells taken from rats on flight day 13 had a lower number of recombinant rat interleukin-3 (rrIL-3) - responsive cells and a lower number of (rrIL-3) plus rhEpo-responsive blast forming unit erythroid (BFU-e) colonies than ground controls. There was a slight increase in the number of rhEpo plus rrIL-3 responsive BFU-e colonies on landing day. Flight rats stimulated with rhEpo or rhEpo plus rrIL-3 showed an increase in the number of erythroid colony forming units and a decrease in BFU-e colonies nine days after flight. Results indicate that spaceflight affects rat bone marrow progenitor cells but has little effect on peripheral blood erythroid parameters. For additional experiment results, see Regulation of Erythropoiesis During Spaceflight, 178012 1_2.

experiment_title: Somatosensory Suppression and Prevention of Post-flight Re-entry Disturbances
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this experiment was to develop procedures for alleviating post-flight disturbances of posture and locomotion experienced by astronauts. The investigator’s team has shown that non-mechanically supportive contact of the hand with a stationary surface stabilizes postural and whole body movement control in 1) a normal 1g environment, 2) a rotating environment, and 3) parabolic flight. The team developed a hand-held sensory gyroscope that stabilizes posture in 1g. These observations provide the basis for four specific aims whose outcome will provide critical information for designing apparatus and procedures for suppressing re-entry disturbances after space flight and hastening sensory-motor readaptation to 1g.

The specific aims of the project were as follows:
• Measure how non-supportive contact with a surface and a hand held sensory gyroscope stabilize posture during exposure to different gravitoinertial force levels in parabolic flight maneuvers and in 1g after landing
• Evaluate the influence of non-supportive hand contact and of a sensory gyroscope on deep knee bends in the 1.8g portion of parabolic flight
• Determine how finger contact at non-supportive force levels and a sensory gyroscope attenuate body sway in a rotating environment
• Measure the influence of non-supportive finger contact and of a hand held sensory gyroscope on treadmill locomotion in a rotating environment

RESULTS:
Initial studies on student volunteers have indicated that a small lightweight device can be effective in reducing postural sway in a normal stationary environment. Future research is planned to devise an optimal lightweight hepatic aid to reduce re-entry disturbances of posture and locomotion.

experiment_title: Reactivation of Latent Viruses During the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Reactivation of latent viruses may pose an important health risk for people living and working in extreme environments, such as space and Antarctica. Risks associated with many infectious agents are reduced by the preventative measures of the health stabilization program before each mission. However, reactivation of latent viruses is unaffected by such actions. A variety of stess factors may cause reactivation of these viruses, such as psychosocial stress, trauma, sunlight, resiratory infection, and fever. Stress-induced changes in immune function under such conditions may also increase the incidence and duration of viral reactivation and shedding.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a DNA virus that infects more than 90% of the adult population worldwide and is the etiologic agent of infectious mononucleosis, is highly infectious. Normally, primary infection is a self-limiting disease leading to a lifelong persistence of EBV in the B-lymphocytes or epithelial cells of the oropharynx of infected individuals. EBV can be found in saliva after reactivation, which can be triggered by a variety of factors, perhaps including space flight. The physical and psychological stresses associated with the launch and landing of spacecraft, and living and working in the crowded, closed environment in microgravity, may result in viral reactivation and shedding.

The limited access to space requires the use of ground-based analogs of space flight. Environmental chambers have been used since the Skylab program (1973-1974) to simulate specific aspects of space flight. In the present study, the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was used to identify EBV DNA in saliva and CMV DNA in urine as a measure of viral shedding in response to 60-day (Phase IIa) and 91-day (Phase III) chamber studies of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) at NASA Johnson Space Center.

APPROACH:
Viral shedding and reactivation patterns were studied for eight subjects (five male and three female) participating in the 60-day (Phase IIa) and 91-day (Phase III) chamber studies of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) at NASA Johnson Space Center. Saliva samples were collected from the eight subjects before, during, and after chamber isolation. Blood and urine samples were collected once before entry and once after exit.

Samples from 11 healthy age-matched adults were collected as controls (ten males and one female). Saliva, urine, and blood samples (one of each) were collected from each of these subjects on day 1, day 7, and day 22 of the tests. This collection schedule closely approximates the pre- and postflight collection schedule of a 12-day Shuttle flight. One-time urine samples were also collected from 30 additional healthy age-matched subjects for CMV analysis.

Saliva samples were collected with Salivette kits, which consist of a cotton roll in a polypropylene vial. Subjects placed the roll in their mouth until it became saturated, and then returned the roll to the vial. Saliva samples were centrifuged immediately after collection and stored frozen at -70ºC. All samples collected from a given subject were analyzed simultaneously. Using a polymerase chain reaction assay, saliva samples were processed for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA and urine samples were analyzed for cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA detection. Saliva (2 to 3 ml) and urine (3 ml) specimens were concentrated with a 100-KD filtration unit. DNA was extracted by a nonorganic extraction method, and EBV DNA was detected as described here briefly. The PCR primers were directed at the EBV polymerase accessory protein gene (BMRF1): P1, 5-GTC CAA GAG CCACCACAC CTG and P2, 5-biotin CCC AGA AGT ATA CGT GGT GAC GTA GA. These primers were used at a concentrationof 200 µM with 10 µM deoxynucleic acid triphosphates. PCR was optimized using buffer II with 2.5 mM MgCl2. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was added to a final concentration of 5%. AmpliGold (2.5 units per 100 µl reaction mixture) was added, and 5 µl of the purified DNA was added to 20 µl of the reaction mixture. The cycle parameters were 95ºC for 9 min, followed by 40 cycles of 94ºC for 15 sec, 61ºC for 15 sec, and 72ºC for 15 sec, with a final extension step at 72ºC for 5 min.

CMV DNA was detected using primers that target the major immediate early gene (P1, 5-TGT CCT CCC GCT CCT C and P2, biotin 5-ATG AAG GTC TTT GCC CAG TA). All reactions were carried out using a Perkin-Elmer GenAmp system 9600. An initial denaturation step of 94ºC for 9 min was followed by 40 cycles of 94ºC for 30 sec, 69ºC for 15 sec, 72ºC for 30 sec, 72ºC for 7 min, and a 4ºC hold. The amplified product was analyzed for the presence of EBV or CMV using the Digene Sharp Signal System according to the manufacturer's instructions.

EBV and CMV antibody titers from blood samples were determined by indirect immunofluorescence assay. Commercially prepared substrate slides and control sera were used for determining antibody (IgG) titers for viral capsid antigen (VCA) and early antigen (EA) of EBV, CMV, and measles (Bion Enterprises, Park Ridge, IL). Four-fold dilutions of plasma were prepared with phosphate-buffered saline. The endpoint titer was determined as the highest dilution of serum in which immunofluorescent-positive cells could be detected. All specimens were batch analyzed and read blind-coded.

The frequency of viral shedding in saliva and viral antibody titers in plasma from chamber study subjects and controls were tested for normality. One-way analysis of variance was performed to study significant differences across different times during the study.

The method of generalized estimating equations with a logit link was used to find significant difference between the phases (pre-, in-, and postchamber). The differences between sampling periods were considered significant if P < 0.05.

RESULTS:
A total of 418 saliva samples were collected from the eight subjects participating in the two chamber studies. Overall, EBV DNA was detected in 35% of the 418 total saliva samples collected from these subjects. The subjects in the 60-day chamber study had EBV DNA in 13% (range 0 to 31%) of their samples, and the subjects in the 91-day study had EBV DNA in 51% (range 33 to 81%) of their samples. During both studies, all but one subject (in the 60-day chamber study) shed EBV.

Sixteen urine samples collected from the subjects of both chamber studies before and after the in-chamber phase were analyzed for CMV DNA. Interestingly, not a single sample showed evidence of CMV DNA. The presence of CMV DNA in urine from the control group was also rare (1/81 samples).

Viral antibody titers for EBV and CMV measured in samples from all 8 subjects before and after the study were not significantly different. Therefore, the data were pooled for further analysis. No significant differences in EBV VCA, EBV EA, or CMV IgG antibody titers were observed before and after either of the studies. Interestingly, EBV antibody titers did not differ significantly from the controls. However, CMV antibody titers of subjects were greater than those of the control group before and after the study.

Our current finding of increased viral reactivation in closed chamber study subjects agrees with our previous Space Shuttle and Antarctic data. These results support and extend our previous observations that latent viral reactivation increases during space flight, which is consistent with a stress-induced decrease in immune function.

experiment_title: Pilot Studies of Radiation Damage in Organ Tissues of Mice
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Low doses of radiation have been shown to protect against the biological effects of later exposure to toxic levels of radiation, a phenomenon known as the radioadaptive response. High dose whole body radiation is a common strategy in biomedical research to reduce or destroy bone marrow cells as an introduction to stem cell transplantation. Radiation treatments for cancer in humans or in biomedical research causes damage to other areas of the body, including the skeletal tissue.

APPROACH:
The pilot study involved a preliminary experiment with 12 mice and a comprehensive experiment with 36 mice. In the preliminary experiment, the mice were exposed to a low dose of 0.05 Gy, followed by a high dose of 6 Gy 24 hours later. The mice were sacrificed three days after the high dose exposure. The bone analysis included bone histomorphometry and microCT of tibia and lumbar vertebrae (L1 and L2) to evaluate the effects of bone marrow transplantation in mitigating whole body y-radiation-induced adverse skeletal effects.

RESULTS:
Radiation-induced death of marrow cells is associated with 1) a transient increase in bone formation due, at least in part, to activation of bone lining cells, and 2) an increase in bone resorption due to increased osteoclast perimeter. Bone marrow transplantation is effective in mitigating the detrimental effects of acute exposure to high dose whole body radiation on bone turnover. High dose whole-body gamma radiation results in a dramatic bone turnover response in which both formation and resorption are increased. The increased turnover is temporally associated with bone marrow failure and may result from disturbed regulation of osteoblast and osteoclast differentiation by hematopoietic cells. Bone marrow transplantation, by restoring normal bone marrow function, is effective in restoring normal bone turnover following lethal irradiation.

experiment_title: Spaceflight Resource Management Training
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Ground-based preflight training and in-space just-in-time training and task rehearsal will continue to be an important driver for exploration missions. On-board training systems will enhance the autonomy and effectiveness of exploration crews. Long-duration missions preclude the possibility of easily substituting new crew members from the ground who have been specially trained on specific emerging problems, new tasks and scientific or mission operations. We will continue to depend even more on the deep knowledge astronauts acquire of the idiosyncrasies of the flight systems they live with and the tasks they have to perform. However, given the nature of the missions, onboard training opportunities for individuals and teams will be necessary, such as in reconfigurable training and mission rehearsal systems. These systems will enable the crews to keep their skill levels up to par and to develop new skills or practice new procedures to resolve new challenges as they arise. Increasing communication delays between crews and ground support mean that astronauts need to be prepared to handle the unexpected on their own. As crews become more autonomous, their potential span of control and required expertise grow much greater than is needed today. It is not possible to train for every eventuality ahead of time on the ground or maintain such skills across long intervals of disuse. New training approaches must be skill-based rather than task-based, emphasizing the acquisition of general skills such as avionics trouble-shooting, or even broader skills such as creative problem solving. Furthermore, a team of experts is not necessarily an expert team. Thus, team training will be particularly important, and especially so for multicultural and international crews on long-duration missions. Research in many other highrisk domains (e.g., aviation, the military, nuclear power and medicine) shows that effective teamwork can provide resilience in the face of challenging problems. The same is true for the people of Launch and Mission Control, particularly as mission complexity increases and resources available for training decrease.

The current length of crew and flight controllers training has been identified as a major issue in various crew reports and debriefs, and it is predicted that future training will have to be more efficient. Leveraging from the investigation of existing training and the analysis of current training principles and approaches conducted during FY07 and FY08, a forward plan is proposed for FY09-FY11. Specifically, the proposal focuses on exploring some of the basics of learning and of skill acquisition and retention, as well as their practical implementation in two distinct target operations that provide a broad basis for principles and methodologies relevant for all aspects of NASA’s Exploration mission: mission control, and medical operations. Because validating training implementations and particularly those aimed at the long-term retention of skills takes time, this research must maintain its timeline so as to have finalized products in time to meet Constellation needs. What’s more, intermediate products from this research effort benefit current missions and allow for iterative improvement cycles with continuous feedback from key stakeholders.

The approach taken in the proposal and the particular products pursued are the result of close collaboration with MOD training organizations. Significant progress has been made in the past 2 years. MOD is very interested in the proposed work which they find very responsive to their current and future needs. The same is true for SD (Space Medicine Division) and its medical operations.

APPROACH:
The approach for this experiment is not available.

RESULTS:
Products from this study will include prototype MOD team training protocols and tools, as well as recommendations for the design of medical checklists incorporating training and decision support functions.

In an effort to streamline the way that International Space Station (ISS) flight controllers are trained, two new levels of flight controller have been developed – Operators and Specialists. Operators will be trained to have basic system knowledge at the level required for routine operations. Specialists will have a greater level of training and experience at the level required for dynamic and non-normal operations. Trainees at both levels will be expected to gain proficiency with far fewer lessons and far fewer training simulations than their predecessors. Thus, the training program will need to change, replacing much of the on-the-job learning-by-example and experience to directed instruction and practice. Providing trainees with an appropriate structure that they can begin to use immediately to organize their experiences can give them the “jump start” they need. To this end, in collaboration with the Space Flight Resource Management (SFRM) Working Group (WG), we constructed a model of Flight Controller’s problem solving and decision making process. In this paper we examined the utility of this model.

experiment_title: Rotating Membrane Water Purification for Long-Term Human Presence in Space
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The recovery of potable water from wastewater is critical for life support and the environmental health of crewmembers during long-term space missions. The wastewater stream is contaminated with particulates, microorganisms, detergents, salts, and organic compounds, all of which must be removed before the water is suitable for reuse. Standard terrestrial techniques for water treatment and recovery are not suitable for aboard spacecraft. However, rotating reverse osmosis (RO) systems, the focus of this research, show promise for water treatment and recovery. Rotating membrane systems in which a cylindrical filter rotates in a cylindrical shell setting up internal fluid flows have potential to greatly reduce the rate at which the filter loads with membrane foulants. This can substantially extend the life of water filtration systems requiring far less frequent change out of expendable components than standard filtration. Furthermore, because of their anti-fouling characteristics rotating membrane systems are applicable to ultrafiltration (UF) and RO to generate pure water. In their previous NASA-funded research, investigators studied the potential for combining rotating membrane filtration with RO to remove dissolved chemical species. Their initial measurements of rejection and flux for rotating RO membranes and their theoretical model indicate that rotating RO has higher flux and rejection than standard RO systems while simultaneously achieving a greater recovery. Their previous work established the concept of a low-pressure rotating RO membrane system. A mathematical model based on the film theory and the solution-diffusion model agreed well with the experimental results obtained using this first generation prototype. Based on the model, the filtrate flux and contaminant rejection depend more strongly on the transmembrane pressure than on the rotational speed. The first generation apparatus was built to provide proof of the concept for rotating RO and was not capable of operating at high pressures or for long time periods. Therefore, the goal of the current work has been to improve the flux of the device by increasing the transmembrane pressure up to 500 psi and enabling long term testing (7 to 60 days) of the device. To accomplish this, a second generation prototype of a rotating reverse osmosis filter and the accompanying flow circuit was designed and fabricated. The solution diffusion thin film modeling of the system was also continued. Due to the need for long-term testing with high pressures, the operational mode of the second generation apparatus was altered. The theoretical model was used to determine the optimal design geometry of the second generation prototype.

A separate supplemental study was conducted using ion exchange textiles as organic supports for urease immobilization with the aim of developing reactive fibrous materials able to promote urea removal. Investigators have shown that urease can be successfully immobilized on cation exchange textiles using various coupling agents. The urease immobilized onto cation exchange textile offers various advantages. First, the textile (nonwoven fabric) form offers high surface-to-volume ratio and packing density. Furthermore, ion exchange resins in the form of beads move around resulting in abrasion which produces fine particles and degrades the surface. Using an ion exchange textile can prevent such abrasion maintaining the active surface area and preventing plugging downstream. Second, the immobilization procedure used here is simple to carry out without the need for complicated immobilization methods or the use of electron beam or gamma irradiation. Third, the activation energy of the urease immobilized is nearly as low as that of free urease, suggesting that the enzymatic reaction of the immobilized urease is nearly as good as that of the free urease. Fourth, although the kinetic parameters are slightly less favorable than those of free urease, the good storage stability and operational stability of the immobilized enzyme suggest superior potential of the immobilized enzyme for practical application. Finally, a preliminary study of the performance of the biotextile in a continuous flow reactor indicates that the biotextile can convert over 80 % of the urea over a period of several days.

The objective of this project was to advance rotating membrane technology for practical application in wastewater recovery and water purification for long-term human space flight. The effective recovery of wastewater during long-term space missions is critical for life support and the environmental health of crewmembers. Standard terrestrial techniques for wastewater treatment are not suitable because of microgravity or limitations related to mass, volume, and power. Except for the problem of fouling, membrane technologies are quite promising because of their compactness, reliability, and energy-efficiency. The use of rotating membrane technology seems likely to overcome the problem of fouling. Rotating filters offer the potential for smaller size than comparable cartridge filters because of their anti-fouling character. As a result, the mass and volume penalties for rotating membrane systems are most likely less than for standard membrane systems. The results of this research will make available the design tools and technology that along with the understanding of the pertinent physical processes gained in previous research should allow rotating membrane technology to provide a significant, long-term impact in wastewater recovery and many spin-off applications.

APPROACH:
To further enhance the second generation prototype, the performance of commercially available reverse osmosis membranes was evaluated using a laboratory scale batch filtration method. The permeate flux and rejection of ionic solutes and dissolved organic carbon were measured experimentally to select best performing membranes among seven types of membranes (five RO and two nanofiltration) with three different ersatz wastewater solutions simulating transit mission wastewater, early planetary base wastewater, and biological water process effluent.

RESULTS:
Task 1 – Development of a Second Generation Prototype: A new rotating reverse osmosis filtration system was developed to accommodate an operating pressure of 500 psi for long-term tests.
Task 2 – Advanced Design Issues for the Relevant Environment on Board a Spacecraft: Investigators are working on minimizing mass, volume, and energy consumption of the rotating membrane unit, determining the scale-up factors, and extending the technology for the microgravity environment.
Task 3 – Integration of Rotating RO and Rotating MF with other Process Systems: Investigators have developed a rotating microfiltration system for pretreatment prior to the rotating RO system. In addition, the Equivalent System Mass (ESM) of the life support system using rotating membrane system has been preliminarily considered.

experiment_title: Variability in Flow Distribution within the Lung and Its Effects on Deposition and Clearance of Inhaled Particles in Normal and Reduced Gravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this project was to provide a better understanding of how variability in convective flow patterns in the lung affects aerosol deposition, and thus subsequent clearance between individuals. In order to achieve the goal, three specific aims need to be addressed: a) Map the spatial pattern of specific ventilation; b) Map deposition in the supine position at 1G; combine these with data on the spatial pattern of deposition of inhaled particles collected in low-gravity (µG) as part of existing NSBRI studies; c) The measured pattern of aerosol deposition will be compared with the Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) predictions, using uniform and the realistic boundary conditions. By comparing across a number of subjects, and different particles sizes, the mechanisms underlying the variability in deposition and regional ventilation can be elucidated. By comparing the data collected in 1G with data from µG, the magnitude of the gravitational effect can be assessed.

APPROACH:,
Using the magnetic resonance imaging method of arterial spin labeling (ASL) with subject-gated breathing, investigators produced a dynamic series of flow-weighted images in a single sagittal slice of the right lung. The mean flow pattern determined from a set of reference images was removed to produce a time series of blood flow fluctuations. The fluctuation dispersion (FD), defined as the spatial standard deviation of each flow fluctuation map, was used to quantify the changes in distribution of flow in six healthy subjects in response to 100 breaths of hypoxia (FiO2 = 0.125) or hyperoxia (FiO2 = 1.0). Two reference frames were used in calculation, one determined from the initial set of images (FDglobal), and one determined from the mean of each corresponding baseline or challenge period (FDlocal).

RESULTS:
In the first two years of the project investigators successfully developed a Magnetic Resonance Imaging technique for quantifying specific ventilation in the human lung - Specific Ventilation Imaging (SVI), completing point a) of the initial project aims. They have used SVI to quantify the vertical, gravitational induced, gradient in specific ventilation that is present in the human lung on Earth.

Aim 2 was completed by quantifying specific ventilation in 10 subjects, thus determining realistic boundary conditions required for addressing aim c) in an individualized subject by subject basis. Investigators have mapped the supine deposition of 5µm particles (1G supine) in the same 10 subjects. A subset of these (N=5) participated in a NASA parabolic flight campaign, where the first maps of particle deposition in low gravity were obtained, thus completing data acquisition for 5µm particles. A second parabolic flight opportunity to acquire the µG deposition maps for 1µm particles did not materialize, despite the continuous efforts. Investigators have completed the optimization of the analysis software and applied it to the µG and supine data. Additionally, they have completed a validation and reliability analysis of the MR-imaging technique, by comparing heterogeneity estimated using SVI and the spatial-insensitive Multiple Breath Nitrogen Washout technique. The analysis linking ventilation and deposition (aim c) is hampered by the missing 1µm particle deposition data.

experiment_title: Bed Rest and Neurovascular Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The long-range goal of this study was to examine the control of blood flow in humans after space flight. The goal of this project was to examine neurovascular function in individuals after two weeks of head-down-tilt bed rest (HDBR). HDBR serves as an earth-based model for the autonomic adjustments seen during space flight. The main hypothesis of this proposal was that peripheral vasoconstrictor responses are impaired with HDBR and this contributes to orthostatic intolerance (OI). Investigators noted that subjects with OI after HDBR do not effectively increase sympathetic nerve traffic directed to skeletal muscle. In this proposal investigators explored the implications of these observations on norepinephrine (NE) release in skeletal muscle. They utilized the microdialysis technique to measure skeletal muscle interstitial NE during tilt testing before and after HDBR. This state of the art method gave them previously unobtainable information regarding the release of NE from nerves that reside in the interstitial space and innervate the smooth muscle of blood vessels. In those subjects that are OI, they hypothesized that HDBR will result in an attenuated rise in interstitial NE during tilt. They blocked the local neuronal uptake of NE (desipramine) as well as measure indices of intraneuronal NE storage capacity. These experiments provided important data on NE release rates and how this release is influenced by tilt and HDBR. As a countermeasure investigators gave pyridostigmine (an oral dose of 60 mg) to half of the HDBR subjects.

experiment_title: RNA Binding Proteins as Evolutionarily Conserved Cellular Spaceflight Response Mechanisms
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Understanding infectious disease risks during spaceflight is critical to provide safe passage for human exploration to the moon and Mars. This issue is especially important given reports that the crew's immune system is dysfunctional during flight, and our recent discovery that spaceflight increased the disease-causing potential and globally altered the gene expression of the human food-borne pathogen Salmonella typhimurium. Our research also showed that many of the observed changes in Salmonella were associated with specific proteins in the cells, called RNA binding proteins, that bind to and regulate genetic material within the cell to control cellular characteristics in response to stress. In addition, our studies during spaceflight and using ground-based, spaceflight analogue culture systems have shown that increasing the concentration of certain ionic salts, like phosphates, in the growth media can prevent the increased disease causing potential observed for Salmonella during spaceflight. Interestingly, human cells also contain evolutionarily conserved RNA binding proteins that are very similar in structure and function to those found in bacteria. In human cells, these RNA binding proteins are critical for the cells proper function, including supporting a healthy immune system, maintaining tissue differentiation, and responding to cellular stress. We hypothesize that RNA binding regulatory proteins and their small RNA binding counterparts are key to a conserved, common cellular spaceflight response mechanism in both bacterial and human cells and that this response can be manipulated by environmental salt/ion levels. The implications of a universally conserved molecular response to spaceflight would affect NASA's approach to infectious disease risk assessment, development of biological processing systems for exploration, and changes in biodegradation during a mission. Indeed, if these responses are also observed in human cells, they may translate into knowledge of both the astronaut's response to infection and possibly larger physiological responses that are influenced by cellular changes.

The work performed for this ground experiment are directly related to and complement on-going work in our flight-based grant - NRA NNH08ZTT003N; “Space Tissue Loss Innate Mammalian Mechanisms Universal Novel Expressions ”

APPROACH:
Two different human epithelial cell lines representing model intestinal (HT-29) and lung (A549) epithelium were used in these studies and their molecular and phenotypic responses to the stress of spaceflight and microbial pathogen challenge were independently profiled. The Gram negative and Gram positive bacterial pathogens selected for use in the infection studies, S. typhimurium and S. aureus, respectively, have been shown by us to exhibit important changes during culture in spaceflight and/or spaceflight analogue conditions in ground-based simulation. All flight study results were compared to those obtained when the same experiments were performed with identical cells cultured as synchronous ground controls at the Kennedy Space Center in the same hardware used for flight (the Cell Culture Module/CCM), and as asynchronous controls under ground-based spaceflight analogue conditions in NASA-designed bioreactors.

This study was the first to use true spaceflight and spaceflight analogue culture to determine the effect of these environments on the host-pathogen interaction between S. typhimurium and human intestinal epithelium when both host and pathogen are simultaneously exposed to these conditions. In addition, this study was the first to profile the infectious disease process in human cells during spaceflight. By investigating the effect of spaceflight analogue culture on the interaction between S. typhimurium and human intestinal epithelium, insight will be gained into the ability of this environment to alter host resistance to infection, and thus the risk of infectious disease during space flight. This proposal focused on key questions that are pertinent to NASA goals for long duration manned spaceflight as well as the mitigation of risk to the crew of the International Space Station.

RESULTS:
Sample analysis is finalized for global alterations in both transcriptomic and proteomic profiling, cellular differentiation, immune function (inflammatory response mediators), and stress responses associated with space flight in the presence and absence of infection. All flight sample comparisons were made to identical synchronous ground controls housed in duplicate CCM hardware as that used for flight. Through iTRAQ analysis, we have identified 86 total unique human proteins (95% confidence, 1% FDR) that were expressed by the HT-29 intestinal epithelial cells cultured on orbit either before or after infection with Salmonella typhimurium. These proteins belonged to a range of different functional classes and categories, including those important for metabolism, apoptosis, cell communication, immune function, and others. Of the 89 proteins identified, a unique subset of these were found to be differentially regulated in response to space flight, and showed differences in response to infection between flight and ground cultures. Collectively, we found intriguing differences in how microgravity uniquely impacted the space flight infected intestinal cells as compared to the ground controls. We have also finalized global proteomic response profiling for the A549 lung epithelial cells as well. Moreover, immunohistochemical profiling has revealed differences in both distribution and expression patterns of targeted host cell proteins and alterations in cellular cytoarchitecture.

No data submitted. Summarized and analyzed data figures are available in Characterization of the invasive, multidrug resistant non-typhoidal Salmonella strain D23580 in a murine model of infection.

experiment_title: Advanced Trace Gas Monitoring Technology for NASA Human Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project was a joint Rice University- George Washington University-JPL research and development program of mid-infrared diode laser sources in the 3 to 4.4 micron region and their application to trace gas sensing in NASA applications relevant to spacecraft environmental monitoring and advanced life support. Presently, single frequency diode and quantum cascade lasers are not available in the proposed mid infrared spectral region that covers an important range where sensitive, selective and fast trace gas detection can now only be performed with complex spectroscopic sources, such as lead salt diode lasers and indirect laser sources based on difference frequency generation. Pulsed and continuous wave Type I quantum-cascade lasers, now commercially available cover the wavelength region from 4.4 - 24 microns. However, there is a significant need to access wavelengths from 3 to 4.4 microns, where a number of critical molecules (e.g. CH4, HCl, NO2, H2CO,SO2, and CO2) possess strong ro-vibrational lines. The Laser Science group at Rice University has accumulated a decade of experience in laser based trace gas detection in applications directly relevant to NASA as well as in other areas such as atmospheric chemistry, environmental monitoring, industrial process control and medical diagnostics. The group of Prof. Houston Miller provided expertise in spectroscopic strategy for detecting Code M molecular target gases as well as developing a cavity ringdown spectroscopy (CRDS) based sensor technology. JPL, with world-class semiconductor facilities and the expertise necessary, developed Sb-based diode and type II interband cascade lasers with distributed feedback structures for meeting the application needs. At Rice the primary emphasis was to demonstrate and emphasize a novel optical detection technique based on an ultracompact photoacoustic analyzer design that will significantly enhance the performance and robustness of near infrared and mid-infrared gas sensors.

APPROACH:
Investigators used a photoacoustic for the detection of trace gases utilizing a quartz tuning fork (TF) as a resonant acoustic transducer. Advantages of the technique called quartz-enhanced photoacoustic spectroscopy (QEPAS) compared to conventional resonant photoacoustic spectroscopy include QEPAS sensor immunity to environmental acoustic noise, a simple absorption detection module design, and its capability to analyze gas samples approximately 1 mm3 in volume.

RESULTS:
CRDS: Investigators have demonstrated the measurement of several air constituents at levels of detection required for indoor air pollution, medical diagnoses, or agricultural/industrial monitoring. Further, they have demonstrated that their sensors can be operated unattended for several days and provide reliable habitability data.
QEPAS: Demonstrated very compact robust sensors that can be used in industry-process streams, petrochemical and/or biomedical fields.
Investigators developed both technologies to the point where a select outside panel made a downselect and chose QEPAS for further development for deployment on the International Space Station (ISS) as a technology demonstration. QEPAS sensor and electronic is approximately 0.8 l total volume. Demonstrated approximately 60 ppb for formaldehyde but could go even lower. The downselection was made after an extensive system engineering study at JPL, using Team X resources to develop strawman instrument designs.

experiment_title: Bone Biochemistry and Mineral Distribution in the Femurs of Rats after Two Weeks in Space: Circulating Parathyroid Hormone, Calcitonin, and Osteocalcin
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The functional state of the parathyroid gland and the calcitonin cells of the thyroid is critical to the alterations in calcium and bone metabolism during space flight because of the major role each hormone has in their regulation. The purpose of this experiment was to document the early postflight levels of two calcium regulating hormones. Postflight evidence for impaired calcium homeostasis from exposure to space flight as well as the status of these hormones was reported.

Approach:

Blood was collected through a heparinized funnel after decapitation and the plasma separated. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) and calcitonin (CT) were measured by radioimmunoassay kits, modified for samples of 50 µl, and compared to appropriate controls. The parathyroid hormone assay uses an antibody raised to an N-terminal fragment of human hormone and human standard. The calcitonin assay used an antibody raised to synthetic human hormone, human standards and tracer. Analysis techniques included student's t-test, analysis of variance, and regression analysis computer programs.

Results:

Measurable differences in opposite directions for apparently unrelated reasons were found in plasma concentrations of both PTH and CT. Slight increases in flight PTH, compared to synchronous animals, were indicative of mild hyperparathyroidism, most likely related to impaired kidney function, supported by increases in serum magnesium, phosphorous, creatinine. Plasma CT, on the other hand, in fourteen-week-old rats, failed to show the normal increase with age after two weeks of tail suspension, similar to the postflight result. Postflight circulating levels of PTH appear to reflect disturbances in calcium homeostasis from impaired renal function and of CT in growth connected with the flight. Bone biochemistry revealed mineral deficits and changes in osteocalcin and reducible cross-links in the distal femoral diaphysis. Of interest were similar changes in cross links but not mineral composition in five controls.

experiment_title: Correlation of Disconjugate Eye Torsion with the Time Course of the Space Adaptation Syndrome
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space motion sickness (SMS) during space flight is very similar to motion sickness on Earth. SMS can be predicted during parabolic flights on Earth by observing characteristic eye movements. By identifying these same characteristic eye movements, particularly rotary eye movements during the course of space flight, researchers hope to obtain information on SMS, which will have a direct impact on Earth-based motion sickness. This study documented the correlation of eye torsional changes with the development and recovery over time of SMS.

APPROACH:
Three astronauts underwent preflight, inflight, and postflight testing of spontaneous ocular torsion and ocular counterrolling (OCR) reflexes governed by the gravity-responsive otolith organs in the inner ear. Subject A flew a 30-day space mission during Euromir '94 and was examined with a monocular video-oculography (VOG) system. Subjects B and C were studied with a binocular VOG during the 180-day Euromir '95 mission. VOG is a technique used to examine the function of the human balance system located in the inner ear (vestibular system) and the visuo-oculomotor interactions of the vestibular organ. The subjects’ eye movements were measured, recorded, and evaluated by state-of-the-art video techniques.

Preflight and postflight measurements were performed with the subject in a head-upright position. Inflight measurements required only that the subject remain stationary. To record images from both eyes simultaneously during Euromir ‘95, the monocular VOG used during Euromir '94 was augmented by one additional camera and recorder unit. The binocular system videotaped both eyes simultaneously providing 25 synchronized images of each per second. The torsional eye position was derived from surface landmarks of the iris. First, a circular ring segment or arc was selected and defined by its radius from the center of the pupil, the thickness of the ring segment, and the angle swept by the arc. A geometric assumption was made that the visible borders of the pupil were part of a circle or an ellipse. For each line of the video image that passed through the pupil, the threshold for entering and leaving the pupil was determined. If a line passing through the pupil was interrupted by reflections or other artifacts, that line was rejected. The accepted lines were calculated to form a circle. In this manner, reliable pupil center could be determined even though up to 50% of the pupil was not visible.

A reference iris profile was calculated and stored in computer memory. Using this reference, subsequent iris profiles could be compared to determine any changes in ocular torsion, e.g. the reference iris profile obtained preflight was compared with other profiles obtained preflight, during flight, and postflight.

In the preflight and postflight experiments, the astronauts were strapped into a special chair. An individual bitebar was made and fitted to a mask-headband assembly containing two small video cameras, one in front of each eye. The bitebar was also rigidly attached to the chair. The astronaut’s eyes were adjusted to Earth-horizontal. Once the bitebar-to-mask and bitebar-to-chair attachments were satisfactory, the joints were tightened and sealed in position. The bitebar could fit only one way to the mask and chair. This meant the relation of the mask and its cameras in front of the eyes could be precisely replicated for all other preflight and postflight experiments.

In the earth-based studies, subjects were seated in the special chair, the bitebar-mask-head apparatus donned, and the eye position verified to be Earth-horizontal. The subjects maintained their eyes in the primary position by gazing at a target one meter away. The heights of the cameras were adjusted so that the iris images were equidistant from the lower edge of the video monitor. In each of these Earth-based experiments, the eye positions were recorded for two minutes as the subject sat quietly upright. Following the upright position, eye positions were recorded for two minutes with the subject tilted and maintained at a 30º right-ear-down tilt and two minutes with the subject in a 30º left-ear-down tilt.

For space-flight experiments, an identical individual bitebar-to-camera apparatus was made for each subject and taken to the Mir Space Station. These masks maintained the same head-to-eye-to-camera relation as the ground experiments. The astronauts were adept at donning the apparatus and making sure the iris images were equidistant from the bottom of the video monitor. A two-minute videotape was made with the head “upright” in six to eight experiments during the six-month space flight.

As required, all three subjects had vestibular “deconditioning” training for several weeks before space flight and again toward the end of flight. This consisted of vigorous head rotation in the pitch and yaw modes. During each experimental session in flight, each subject marked a detailed questionnaire of SMS symptoms as being absent, mild, moderate, or severe.

RESULTS:
Five to six preflight baseline data collections (BDCs) were obtained for each subject. In the upright position while seated quietly, spontaneous torsional eye movements were approximately ±0.75º, consistent with earlier studies of normal subjects. The eyes were mostly conjugate. When held for two minutes in a static tipped position, mean ocular counterrolling (OCR) in the three subjects was –5.94º and +5.54º in response to the 30º right and left tilts, respectively.

All inflight and postflight analyses were based on a preflight external reference image enabling comparison of eye positions relative to the preflight baseline. In all three subjects, the torsional position of each eye was substantially changed from its preflight setting. A torsional reset was manifested during the entire inflight and postflight testing period, although each eye position might vary considerably throughout the study.

The SMS evaluation forms on two subjects indicated no SMS symptoms during space flight. One had moderate nausea in the Soyuz transport vehicle on the way to Mir and on flight day 4. This subject was symptom-free at all other times.

Upon return to Earth, two subjects were grossly ataxic immediately after landing. Seven hours after landing, both subjects could walk slowly with support. Turning caused them to lurch to one side. Both were pale and weak with marked atrophy of the legs. Both were nauseated and had headaches. One subject became nauseated by repeated head rotation, while the other felt too ill to be tested at all. The day after landing (R+1), both could slowly walk independently with no further nausea, even with head rotation maneuvers. After several more days, their overall behavior seemed normal. The leg atrophy was improved by R+10.

Postflight testing repeated the preflight protocol with two minutes in each upright position, 30º right and 30º left. In all three subjects, OCR amplitude differed from that observed preflight. Subject B showed increased OCR to both sides of tilt, especially to 30º left, even considering the torsional reset of the eyes in the upright position. Subject C also showed increased OCR to the left and approximately the same OCR to the right as preflight. Subject A had decreased OCR on the day of landing, increasing daily until postflight day 10 (R+10), at which time it exceeded the baseline OCR in both directions of tilt. At day 150, however, this subject’s torsional eye position had returned to its preflight baseline. No tests were performed between day 10 and 150, and therefore the time course of recovery cannot be ascertained. By R+10, subject B’s right eye had approached its preflight baseline; however, with the head in the upright position, the left eye remained about 2.5º torted counterclockwise. Subject C had likewise not returned to his baseline settings by R+10.

As two of the three subjects did not have SMS and the third had none or marginal SMS, none of the changes in ocular torsion found during this study can be related to SMS. However, analysis of parabolic flight disconjugacy in two of the present subjects correctly predicted absence of SMS.

experiment_title: Analysis of a novel sensory mechanism in root phototropism (TROPI)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objectives of this research are to understand the cellular mechanism of phototropism in plants and to determine the effects of gravity on light perception in plant roots. The objectives are relevant to the developmental and cell and molecular biology.

APPROACH:
Starchless mutant strains of Arabidopsis thaliana are used in this experiment. 24 experiment containers (EC) are flown in the European Modular Cultivation System (EMCS). Each EC contains five seedling cassettes. Approximately 1680 seedlings are grown in space during the experiment. Video recording of the plant growth is performed during flight. An initial dark and illumination period of 72 hours is performed then followed by the stimulation illumination phase which includes altered gravity and light (red or blue) environment. At the conclusion of the experiment during flight, seedling cassettes are removed from the ECs and placed into cryo-storage at -80 degrees C. Upon returning from flight, videotapes are analyzed for germination, growth and curvature of experimental samples. At the PI's laboratory, recovered frozen samples are also analyzed for gene expression effected by various light and gravity treatments.

RESULTS:
However, one problem encountered during TROPI-1 was low seed germination due to long storage periods (6-8 months) in flight hardware. Thus, the originally proposed fractional gravity studies were not performed. TROPI-2 provides an opportunity to regain the results from these important fractional gravity experiments.

experiment_title: Total System Approach
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA has established the goal of returning human expeditions to the moon and extending exploration to Mars. Extended manned missions of these types require massive quantities of food to be flown into space. This presents two challenges when dealing with a food system. These challenges are maintaining the quality of the food throughout its shelf life which may be in excess of five years, and to assure the mass and volume of the food system are minimized.

A Total System Approach is an operating system that considers each parameter of an overall process and seeks to optimize each of these parameters to maximize the output. In the case of the NASA food system, the output would be a food system with low mass packaging using high barrier packaging materials.

The purpose of this project was to evaluate the processes related to the packaging of the current NASA food system being used for the International Space Station (ISS) and the Shuttle (STS). The evaluation will define the current processing parameters and identify ways to improve the processes. These parameters include those related to sealing, internal atmosphere of the package, and materials. Parallel to this evaluation, a literature review will be conducted in an effort to identify available materials with high potential for long-duration missions, possible packaging defects, and ways to prevent them in the future, ways to improve oxygen elimination, and the impact of these on product shelf life.

Even though the current packaging system processing parameters have been documented, these parameters have not been evaluated from the perspective of improving packaging integrity and mass reduction. This is due largely to the success of the current packaging system using the current high payload vehicles such as the STS and Russian Progress vehicle. Payload for long-duration missions of years rather than months, like ISS missions, will require a greater quantity of food in proportion to other supplies than do the missions of today. Thus, the need for reduced packaging mass becomes critical in order to execute future missions.

APPROACH:
The outline below describes specific processing points that were evaluated. These processing points are parts of the Total Packaging System. Any improvements that can be made in each of these areas may benefit the overall packaging system.

1. Literature review - Identify high potential materials, minimize pinholes and critical defects, optimize Modified Atmosphere Packaging (MAP) flushing , and improve shelf life.
2. Define existing packaging system - food processing
3. Effects of Temperature on Materials - heat seal
4. Effects of temperature variation
5. Seal Width (possible area of mass reduction)
6. Quality - defects , seal Integrity, vacuum
7. Oxygen quantities - MAP flushing quality
8. Using current system
9. Modified system
10. Gases other than nitrogen - Material quality, film, septum, gases (i.e. ppm 02), Packaging design/configuration

RESULTS:
Optimal sealing parameters for each type of material currently being used by the space food system have already been incorporated into the packaging procedures. As new materials are added to the system, it is recommended that the procedure used in the heat seal evaluation be used to determine the optimal seal setting for each material.

Although the seal reduction evaluation showed considerable mass saving, it is not recommend that the seals be reduced below the 3/8” standard. The safety and health of the crew is more important than minimal mass savings when it comes to a mission’s success. Reducing the seals would increase the potential for package failure from contaminants in the seal leading to food spoilage and food borne illness.

The data that was gathered during the Modified Atmosphere Packaging (MAP) evaluation shows that the current methods used in the space food packaging system is inefficient and seals in a significant amount of air in some cases. It is highly recommended that the optimal equipment setting determined during the evaluation be incorporated as soon as possible to improve the quality of food in the space food system.

The gusseted pouch design yielded very good results in making the rehydratable packages easier to produce while minimizing mass, volume, and waste. It reduced the production process from using three pieces of packaging equipment to one. It reduced the packaging from two pouches to one and decreased the total amount of packaging mass by approximately 63%.

The literature review and MAP gas research stated that argon is a viable gas with great potential. Argon gas is more efficient, does not require a vacuum cycle, and can be used with liquid products, like the thermostabilized foods which currently have residual air in the headspace. More research and development is required for the use of argon gas for MAP applications because it is not widely used and requires equipment modifications. Also, it would need to be determined whether the levels of argon released from opened packages in an in enclosed environment would be hazardous to crew health.
