experiment_title: Molecular Characterization of Transmissible Chromosome Aberrations Produced by Ions of Intermediate and High Atomic Number
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Extremely low fluences of mixed-field galactic cosmic radiation (GCR) increase the risk of carcinogenesis following manned space flight. Additionally, the charged particles encountered in deep space vary enormously in terms of energy, ionization density, and the relative biological effects these particles produce. The cocktail of ions composing GCR cannot be produced to effectively duplicate a biologically meaningful, experimental setting on Earth. Instead, representative aspects of GCR, such as single charged particle tracks, can be used to simulate the deep space environment and its effects on human cells. Chromosome aberrations are used to estimate dose for individuals exposed to unknown magnitude and/or quality of radiation, and are considered the “gold standard” for biodosimetry.
Very little is known about the molecular biology of chromosome aberration formation by ionizing radiation and how these processes relate to changes in linear energy transfer (LET)/track structure. This experiment seeks to introduce an experimental model to sequence DNA at the breakpoint junctions of radiation-induced chromosome exchanges in human cells for the first time and investigate the role that track structure plays in the outcome of chromosome misrepair, particularly as it relates to microhomology-mediated nonhomologous end-joining (mmNHEJ). This will be accomplished using two specific aims.
1) Isolate and cytogenetically characterize human fibroblast cell clones that represent the survival and clonal expansion of single cells exposed to gamma rays, 56Fe and 7Li ions.
2) Characterize clones through the use of next-generation sequencing (NGS) in order to determine the nature of the breakpoint junctions identified in Specific Aim 1 and determine which major DNA repair pathways are involved.

APPROACH:
This experiment used subclones (K-1 lineage) of BJ-1 hTERT-immortalized human fibroblast cells, which are noted for their high plating efficiency, robust growth, and karyotypic stability. Confluent K-1 cultures were exposed to 1.5 MeV/amu 7Li and 630 MeV/amu 56Fe ions. Subsequently, single cell suspensions of irradiated cultures were plated at low density and allowed to form colonies. Clones exposed to 137Cs gamma rays were included as a low LET comparison.
To address Specific Aim 1, macroscopic colonies were randomly selected to isolate clonal descendants that stably carry radiation-induced translocations and/or inversions. Chromosome-type interchanges (translocations) were identified using 24-color multicolor fluorescent in situ hybridization (mFISH). The same clones were analyzed for intrachanges (inversions) by applying directional genomic hybridization (dGH) to chromosomes 1, 2, and 3. Analyzing these large chromosomes increased the probability of locating inversions compared to previous methods which applied dGH singly to either chromosome 3 or chromosome 10.
To meet Specific Aim 2, the researchers applied an NGS approach to DNA collected from the same colonies to generate genomic libraries that were used to further characterize radiation-induced structural variants (SVs), including translocations, inversions, and deletions, and their locations across the chromosomes. Small fragments (=400 bp) putatively containing chromosome breakpoints were identified using paired-end sequencing and bioinformatic techniques. Meerkat software was used to identify precise breakpoints using local alignment of the split reads that map to the breakpoint region for regions with split read support. To further investigate breakpoint regions without split read support, the researchers generated PCR fragments for the corresponding discordant reads identified by the software and sequenced fragments of anticipated size using Sanger methods. During the course of the experiment, it was found that long sequencing reads (~20 kb) with single-molecule, real-time (SMRT) sequencing would yield higher fidelity data for the identification of SVs. This method was used to sequence the DNA of six clones, including clones exposed to gamma radiation and 56Fe ions, and the parent (K-1) cell line.

RESULTS:
One important key step to understanding the process of chromosomal exchange aberration formation is molecular analysis of breakpoint junctions formed as the result of translocations and inversions. Further, investigating these chromosome aberrations and their related pathways will help to elucidate the mechanisms underlying cancer processes. As a result of this experiment, the researchers published the first sequence-level characterization of a known radiation-induced translocation in human cells using massively parallel sequencing. Further, a 4bp microhomology identified through this study supports the researchers’ hypothesis that such rearrangements are characteristic of mmNHEJ repair/misrepair pathways.
Analysis of the breakpoint junctions identified in chromosomes 3 and 4 revealed that both were located in regions of repetitive DNA. Repeat elements cause difficulties for NGS approaches, particularly methods utilizing short-read mate-pair approaches which can produce ambiguous alignments across repetitive sequences, resulting in a large number of false-positive calls to the reference genome. SMRT sequencing, however, allowed the researchers to identify all the translocations that were cytogenetically observed with only a few false-positive calls. One cytogenetically observed inversion on chromosome 3 was unable to be recovered by all three sequencing approaches (short-read paired end, mate pair, and SMRT), leading the researchers to conclude that a technical issue exists that likely either prevents (1) replication by DNA polymersases or (2) incorporation of nucleotides during sequencing and, subsequently, the identification of this breakpoint.

experiment_title: Evaluation of an On-Astronaut Wireless Sensor System to Support Crew Health Monitoring for Exploration Class Missions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Long-duration space flight requires a health monitoring system that is compact, interoperable with an integrated data management system, and requires limited consumables. Astroskin was the first prototype of this technology, consisting of a wired sensor system for continuous monitoring of electrocardiograph (ECG), heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, skin temperature, and body movement. NASA and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) began collaborating in 2014 to validate this system in controlled tests at both Ames Research Center (ARC) and Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facilities at Johnson Space Center (JSC). Lessons learned from these test activities led the CSA to develop the capabilities of a wireless version of the Astroskin that, unlike the current shirt-based version, would use small, unobtrusive, stand-alone patch sensors. Wireless sensor capabilities could enhance comfort, improve movement and fit, and minimize interference in crewmember performance of tasks. The proposed On-Astronaut Wireless Sensor System (OAWSS) included sensors on the upper body, as well as a Sensor Interface Unit (SIU) located on- or off-body that communicates via Bluetooth Low Energy with the body sensors. The SIU was developed to interface with NASA’s Medical Data Architecture (MDA) system to accurately monitor and manage crew health and performance data.

Monitoring multiple vital sign parameters over a prolonged period of time is not possible with other currently available wearable products. Compared to Astroskin, or other commercial products, the OAWSS offers a solution that allows exploration of a different operational mode. The dissemination, management and storage of data vary from other wearables created for space flight monitoring by: 1) the fully wireless nature of the technology; 2) the dynamic and flexible user interface; 3) the capability to acquire data continuously (up to one week without interruption); and 4) the possibility of adding additional sensors (plug-and-play) since there is no physical connection with the data acquisition module.

Specific aims of this experiment included:

  1. Determine the efficacy of OAWSS measures under lab and field test conditions;
  2. Evaluate OAWSS system performance relative to standard laboratory measures;
  3. Conduct participant surveys to assess usability and wearability of the OAWSS; and
  4. Integrate and demonstrate compatibility of the OAWSS with the NASA Medical Data Architecture (MDA).

APPROACH:
To develop OAWSS integration, a ground-based studie was conducted in 2 phases with a total of 16 participants between the ages of 25 and 45. Prior to study selection, participants underwent a complete Class II physical to ensure acceptable health and fitness levels.

Phase 1 of the research was carried out at ARC using 9 volunteer participants. These participants underwent 3 days of laboratory testing to assess the functionality of the OAWSS: submaximal ergometer and rowing exercise on days 1 and 2; and a standard rotating chair test designed to elicit motion sickness symptoms on day 3. Research subjects wore the OAWSS biosensors continuously for 48 hours off-site to collect biometric data and evaluate user comfort and functionality of the biosensors. In addition to OAWSS sensors, standard lab devices (Equivital harness and Empatica E4) were worn by participants to provide reference measures for comparison.

Phase 2 of the study was conducted at JSC using another 8 male and female research participants. For these tests, participants wore the OAWSS, Equivital harness and Empatica E4 while they performed a flight-like cycle ergometer protocol, followed by a self-pacing treadmill test with various inclines to simulate climbing up a hill to deploy a communication device and then descending. During this task participants wore a weighted suit with an additional 40% of their body weight to simulate interference experienced by the space suit. The purpose of the data collection in these conditions was to evaluate functionality and interference of the OAWSS in response to physical exercise and a simulated Lunar or Mars exploration task.

RESULTS:
This study evaluated the reliability and validity of the OAWSS for measuring heart rate (HR), respiration rate (RR), skin temperature (ST), and galvanic skin response (GSR) against criterion devices (e.g., EQ02 LifeMonitor, Equivital Inc. New York, NY and E4 wristband, Empatica, Boston, MA, respectively). In study 1, five male and four female volunteers (mean ± SD, 39.1 ± 5.1 yr) completed two days of testing in which HR, RR, ST, and GSR were collected from the OAWSS and criterion devices at the same time for approximately 90 minutes while engaged in low, medium, and high intensity activities which were repeated on two consecutive days. In study 2 four male and four female volunteers (mean ± SD, 35.1 ± 6.5 yr) completed one day of testing in which the above parameters were collected for approximately 3 hours while engaged in a flight-like aerobic exercise protocol and a simulated EVA task. Reliability was determined by calculating the change in measured parameters (i.e., error scores) between test activities on day 1 and day 2 (study 1 only). Validity was determined by calculating the change in measured parameters between OAWSS and criterion devices during test activities of both studies 1 and 2. Results demonstrated that only OAWSS ST was reliable during activities in study 1, and only OAWSS HR hill climb met the validity criteria in study 2. In conclusion, the OAWSS should not be evaluated further in its current configuration based on the poor reliability and validity of measurements from both studies. In addition, the low acceptability results strongly suggest the OAWSS will need a significant form factor improvement in order to be acceptable to flight crew as a health monitoring device. Future research should also examine other physiological variables such as body position, movement, SPO2, and blood pressure, to more accurately determine health status.

experiment_title: Development and Demonstration of an Integrated, Independent Human Factors Evaluation Process for Space Payloads and Equipment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
At NASA, and in everyday life experience, there are multiple examples of equipment that has passed through a rigorous requirements validation process, but which nevertheless is shown to have major usability difficulties upon implementation and actual use. At NASA, these usability difficulties can have a major impact on very precious resources—crew time on-orbit and the time of ground controllers. In extreme cases, such as responding to emergencies, usability difficulties can even threaten the physical well-being of the crew.

The project proposed here covers one way to improve the ultimate usability of fielded NASA equipment and systems, and thus enhance the productivity of crew and ground controllers—namely the use of an integrated, life-cycle human factors evaluation process. An integrated human factors evaluation process will be proposed that focuses on the unique NASA context and addresses NASA equipment and payloads, along with their associated procedures, user’s manuals, displays, labels and training.

APPROACH:
The draft Human Factors process document has been completed. The benefits of this process will then be demonstrated via pilot demonstrations (evaluations) with a NASA equipment or payload in the early design stage. The hardware will be selected such that physical and cognitive interfaces can be evaluated, along with related procedures, owner’s manuals and labeling. Human factors professionals, crew, and payload engineers and procedures writers will participate in the demonstration. Data from the pilot demonstration will be analyzed to determine the beneficial impacts from using the human factors process. Lessons learned from the pilot demonstration will be incorporated in the final version of the process document.

experiment_title: Brain Pituitary Axis Development in the CEBAS Minimodule
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Using the (CEBAS), which could lead to an aquatic CELSS to provide plant and animal biomass for nutrition on long duration flight, this study focused on the reproductive biology of animals in space. Information was gathered on microgravity-induced changes to the brain-pituitary axis and in the organs that receive information from the environment. Space flight conditions may affect the development and functioning of the neuroendocrine system that regulates the reproductive system.

Approach:

Xiphorous helleri, a freshwater teleost, was used to study the brain-pituitary axis in embryos, neonates, immature, and mature specimens. Two hundred juveniles and four gravid females were flown in the CEBAS. Histology, cytology, immunohistochemistry, morphometry, and in situ histochemistry were used to evaluate the synthesis, storage and release of neurotransmitters, neuroregulatory peptides, neurohormones, pituitary hormones, and the structure of the specimen's cells and organs. The olfactory system and the pineal organ were also studied in a similar fashion. Four living specimens were kept to monitor post flight growth and development.

Results:

The distributions of (Neuropeptide Y)NPY, (Neurotensin)NT, Androgen Receptor)AR, and (Dynorphin)DYN were found to be identical in both Flight specimens and ground-based laboratory module. Intense distribution of Immunoreactiv-Galanin (ir-GAL) in the cell bodies of the NOR was observed in all flight specimen while ir-GAL was absent in the laboratory module. The distribution of FMRF-amide fibers in the brains of the flight specimen appeared sparse and less intense when compared to laboratory controls. There was no significant difference in growth rate and maturity in both flight animals and laboratory control groups.

experiment_title: Real-Time Estimation of the Effects of a Simulated Long-Duration Exploration Mission on Flight Performance, Workload, and Situation Awareness
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Human space flight missions often requires long-term isolation of crewmembers in extreme environments. The space flight environment introduces stressors to both crewmember physiology and behavioral psychology. Specific human-factors stressors include long-duration isolation, sleep loss, circadian desynchronization, and high workload. These present a real, tangible risk of performance decrements, which could have significant negative impacts on the mission objectives. Research conducted in space flight analogs such as NASA’s Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) provide a unique opportunity to study these effects, in a larger sample size than International Space Station (ISS) crews, and develop essential metrics to identify and prevent performance decrements in an operationally-relevant setting.

In the field of human space flight, real-time performance metrics and the quantification of performance during operationally-relevant tasks and scenarios have the potential to make existing operations safer and more efficient, and improve the design of future vehicles. The identification of critical performance decrements, either in measures of task performance, workload, or situational awareness, may be used to alter the human-automation task allocation or suggest changes to crew resource management.

APPROACH:
An existing configurable and portable simulation platform was integrated into HERA for use during the HERA 45 day missions. The platform simulated two operationally-relevant scenarios—a piloted lunar landing task, and a Simplified Aid for EVA Rescue (SAFER) inspection of an ISS solar array. During Campaign 4 and 5, the simulation platform was used to characterize piloting metrics including flight performance, workload, and situation awareness during a simulated piloted lunar landing and ISS EVA SAFER solar array inspection tasks. The results from these two campaigns were correlated with mission timeline events and the NASA Behavioral Health and Performance (BHP) Standard Measures. 

RESULTS:
The final year of the project (Year 4) was comprised of tasks related to data analysis from Campaign 4 and Campaign 5. Extensive testing on the robustness continued to be conducted to ensure simulation stability and the data was properly and reliably logged. A set of data analysis routines was developed to support in the verification of the automatic speech recognition (ASR) algorithm. 

The Draper and UC Davis developed a configurable and portable simulation platform which was integrated with the HERA facility for the Campaign 4 and Campaign 5, 45- day, simulated long-duration space exploration missions (LDEMS). Lunar lander simulation flight performance data was collected every two days for the duration of each mission, for each of the four crewmembers, over the entirety of Campaign 4 Missions 1,3,4, 5; 20 days in Missions 2 (mission terminated early due to Hurricane Harvey), and the entirety of Campaign 5 Missions 1, 2, 3 and 4. 

Lunar lander metrics were assessed as a function of mission time in HERA, the presence of a Landing Point Redesignation (LPR), the landing site map orientation, and crew sleep duration derived from actigraphy data collected during Campaign 4. Analysis of trials that include the presence of a LPR, show an impact on most performance metrics consistent with past results. 

Assessment of performance and workload over time indicate crew improvement over mission time. The observed flight performance in Campaign 4 was assessed with crew sleep duration. Results indicated greater variation in Average Pitch RMSE for all subjects on days following reduced sleep (5 hours or less) than on days following unrestricted sleep, indicating performance was more consistent after unrestricted sleep.

experiment_title: Electronic Procedures for Crewed Missions beyond Low Earth Orbit (LEO)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In future missions, NASA plans to venture beyond Low Earth Orbit (LEO). Communication between the spacecraft and Earth will be subject to longer delays, and in some cases, will be unavailable. These spacecraft will require systems that will allow the crew to perform procedures without assistance from Mission Control. Crewmembers will rely much more heavily on the automated, computer-based tools available within their vehicle or habitat. Given the increased autonomy from the ground, missions will likely be even more dependent on procedures for day-to-day operations and survival. Crewmembers will need to be able to independently operate procedures without missing important steps, keep track of who is working each procedure (i.e., their crewmate, or the system automation), and maintain a view into the vehicle or habitat system’s health and status, along with the effects of their actions on those systems.

Two key questions addressed in this research were: 1) When incorporating automation into electronic procedures, how much automation should be provided? 2) What is the importance of a relevant graphical system display in the execution of electronic procedures, and how important is the visual integration of that display with electronic procedures? Of primary interest was the effect of these different procedure configurations on human performance, namely situational awareness (SA) and workload.

This study had the following specific aims:


  1. Determine the effect of level of automation of procedure step execution on SA, and other human-system performance metrics.
  2. In a complex, multiple-procedure scenario, determine the effect of procedure management aids (e.g., availability of task allocation information) on SA and other human-system performance metrics.
  3. Determine the effect of the level of integration of system and procedural information on SA and other human-system performance metrics.

APPROACH:
Two studies were completed as part of this research project. Study 1 addressed level of automation of electronic procedures (Aims 1 and 2), and Study 2 addressed procedure/display integration (Aim 3). One of the key measures of interest in both studies was Situation Awareness, which was measured using the Situation Presence Assessment Method (SPAM). SPAM uses time to answer a query about the system as a measure of SA. Accuracy, workload, trust, usability and subjective preferences were also measured in both studies.

Study 1 involved 27 crew-like subjects learning and performing tasks with PRocedure Integrated Development Environment (PRIDE) procedures and a habitat simulation system developed by TRACLabs. Subjects completed the scenario-based procedures while seated at a workstation intended to simulate a Habitat Control Station. The station consisted of two computers: the Procedures computer used to complete electronic procedures using PRIDE, and the Mission Control Center (MCC) computer where subjects answered computer-based questions from a mock MCC throughout the test session. MCC questions were SA queries or simple progress questions. For the within-subjects study, subjects completed the procedures under conditions of: 1) no automation, 2) mixed automation, and 3) high automation. Another experimental factor was the location of a procedure management aid (always visible or on request).

Study 2 involved 20 crew-like subjects learning and performing tasks with an electronic procedures system and a flight control simulation. Subjects completed the scenario-based procedures, which included responding to alarms, performing malfunction procedures, and monitoring spacecraft launches, while seated at a workstation intended to simulate a future space vehicle control station. The station consisted of two computers: the Procedures computer used to complete electronic procedures using Orion-like procedures developed by the Crew Interface Rapid Prototyping Laboratory, and a Mission Control Center (MCC) computer where the subjects answered computer-based questions from a mock MCC throughout the test session. MCC questions were SA queries or Bedford workload rating scales. For the within-subjects study, subjects completed the procedures under one of the following configurations: 1) procedures-only (no system display, telemetry only), 2) serial procedures (procedure was shown with an associated system display in toggle fashion, only for commands or on request), and 3) simultaneous procedures (procedure and related system display were shown on the same monitor). In addition to accuracy, workload, trust, usability and subjective preferences, performance data were collected from an eyetracker and a prototype functional Near Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS) sensor.

RESULTS:
The Electronic Procedures for Crewed Missions beyond Low Earth Orbit study was completed to determine: 1) the effect of level of procedure automation on performance, and 2) the effect of level procedure/display integration on performance. Two studies were performed using high-fidelity electronic procedures systems. Results from the first study indicate that a mixed level of automation is preferred because it keeps operators engaged in the task, while providing efficiencies. Results from the second study indicate that relevant graphical displays that are visible at the same time as electronic procedures provide important context. The simultaneous display of procedures and system information was highly preferred over designs that showed electronic procedural steps alone, or designs with only limited access to graphical displays.

experiment_title: Identification of Functional Metabolomic Alterations during the Simulated Spaceflight Environment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objectives of this experiment is to identify novel early biomarkers in plasma and urine to detect and monitor the progression of a number of physiological disturbances due to prolonged microgravity and CO2 exposure as experienced by crewmembers on long duration missions. These physiological manifestations include:
  1. Visual Impairment/Intracranial Pressure (VIIP);
  2. Sub-clinical or environmentally induced cardiovascular disease;
  3. Muscle atrophy and decreased muscle strength; and
  4. Bone loss

APPROACH:
Targeted and untargeted metabolomics will be applied to plasma and urine collected longitudinally rom study participants undergoing a 30 day six-degree head down bed rest combined with ambient 0.5% CO2. Metabolomics will be followed by a novel cell-based metabolic mammalian organ system assay to address how these metabolites affect physiological processes at the cellular and organ level.

RESULTS:
Results for this study are currently not available.

experiment_title: Motor Adaptation to Coriolis and Contact Forces
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A rotating space vehicle could be used to generate 'artificial gravity' during long-duration missions, however this would have side effects. Movements made during body rotation would generate transient Coriolis forces that act perpendicular to both the rotation axis and the movement direction. Such Coriolis forces initially deviate the trajectories and endpoints of reaching movements, but adaptation occurs to restore accuracy if exposure continues. The patterns of movement deviation generated by Coriolis forces differ from those observed when movements are perturbed by external, mechanical contact forces of comparable timing and magnitude. This implies that cutaneous contact cues are critical in the control and monitoring of movement endpoint, trajectory, and adaptation. The goal of this research was to investigate the conjoint influence on reaching and adaptation of cutaneous sensory signals, proprioceptors, and efferent commands. The effect on reaching movements of exposure to contact force perturbations, non-contact Coriolis forces, and combinations of the two were measured. Acquisition, retention, and transfer of adaptation was also studied.

APPROACH:
Experiments were conducted using the Slow Rotation Room Facility located at the Ashton Graybiel Spatial Orientation Laboratory, Brandeis University, Waltham, MA.

RESULTS:
The results of these experiments have shown the following: 1) reaching movements to targets are deviated by Coriolis forces and mechanical contact forces; 2) both contact and non-contact perturbations generate errors in reaching paths and endpoints in the direction of the perturbing forces; 3) adaptation of movement endpoint and movement path are dissociable; 4) endpoint adaptation occurs rapidly with additional movements even in the absence of visual error feedback so long as the hand makes contact with a surface at the end of the movement; 5) there are no aftereffects from adaptation to mechanically induced errors when the subjects' arms are no longer attached to the apparatus, however, after adaptation to Coriolis force perturbations when the slow rotation room was again at rest subjects showed large after-effects in pointing to targets; 6) there is partial cross-transfer between inertial Coriolis force perturbations and mechanical contact force perturbations, this indicates that adaptation to mechanical contact forces is context specific; and 7) If the hand is maintained in contact with a surface while moving to point to a target during rotation, adaptation to the Coriolis force will occur for movement trajectory but not movement endpoint if visual feedback is denied.

This research has enlightened the scientific community about the presence of Coriolis and other inertial accelerations on the arms and legs during self-generated, voluntary movements in a normal terrestrial environment. This research has also helped to provide a basis for anticipating and solving potential performance problems in a rotating artificial gravity environment.

experiment_title: Regulation and Biomechanics of Respiration in Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJJECTIVES:
The main objective of this study was the study of fundamental physiological mechanisms of external breathing function under long-duration orbital flight conditions.

Specific Aims:

  1. Study the dynamics of the relationship between thoracic (pectoral) and abdominal functional breathing reserves and their realization potential during spontaneous breathing.
  2. Assessment of functional state of respiratory system motility by dynamics of thoracic and abdominal components of forced inhalation and expiration rates.
  3. Study of coordinated spontaneous respiratory movements by dynamics of relationship between thoracic and abdominal components of volumetric, time and rate parameters of spontaneous respiratory cycle.
  4. Identified features of humoral-reflex regulation of breathing by dynamics of ventilation sensitivity of thoracic and abdominal components to chemoreceptor stimuli.
  5. Study of features of voluntary control of respiratory movements by dynamics of time-dependent and precision characteristics (spirokinography)

APPROACH:
The methodology isn’t available.

RESULTS:
This investigation looked at the mechanics of breathing in space. Data analysis showed no statistically significant changes in the volume or rate at which crew members breathe. However, the method by which breathing at rest is voluntarily controlled was affected by the transition from Earth to spaceflight and vice versa. The changes include increase in duration between breaths, decrease in variability of breathing pattern, and shifts in the voluntary control of respiratory movements. These are likely caused by changes in the body’s breathing regulation system and require further study.

experiment_title: Needs Assessment and Work Allocation Tools for Mission Operations and Procedures
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Increased system automation is critical for enabling more independent operation on long-duration and farther-distance space missions. Effective integration of human and automation elements is critical to success; this is demonstrated by the widespread involvement of poor Human-Automation Integration (HAI) design as a contributor to accidents and incidents in the sister application domain of aviation, where more data are available. While much is known about HAI design from research in aviation, long-duration space flight adds demands for robustness that are not well understood. HAI designs must be robust in supporting a variety of tasks playing out in circumstances that were impossible to fully anticipate, executed long after any training on these functions, by operators who must be competent in many types of work rather than specialists in any one.

The proposed research has an analytic and empirical strand. The purpose of the analytic strand is to provide methods and tools for measuring automation-to-work (ATW) alignment, for use guiding development and evaluation of HAI designs. The purpose of the empirical strand is to assess whether measured ATW alignment of HAI designs predicts the learnability of those designs, an important aspect of robustness. ATW alignment means the correspondence between the elements and structure of interaction with the elements and structure of the work. Needs analysis identifies elements and structure of the work. In the analytic strand investigators will develop a scoring method for measuring alignment. Their approach draws on and integrates a wide set of observations and proposals in HAI, Human Computer Interaction (HCI), Work Domain Analysis (WDA), and related disciplines. In the empirical strand they test the prediction that HAI designs that align with work more strongly will be easier to learn, particularly, easier to master using the automation for novel problem solving. They test this hypothesis by identifying and measuring designs that differ in ATW alignment and then comparing the designs with high versus low scores for how easily they are learned, how well retained, and how flexibly they can be used.

APPROACH:
The team developed a method that represents a work domain in terms of the required functions within that domain, and which enables evaluating technology with respect to how well and in what respects the technology supports that body of work.

1. Case Study. The team developed the method in concert with applying the analysis to a safety critical, highly automated work domain.
2. Tool Prototypes. The team developed initial prototype tools to aid application of the method.
3. Test environment. The team developed a medium fidelity test environment that was capable of performing the empirical assessment. The test environment (simulator is rapidly changeable and system design may be guided by those user preferences that are excessively shaped by familiarity and historical methods for accomplishing work rather than rigorous analysis of the current work needs).
4. Preliminary Empirical Assessment: The team conducted an empirical assessment, which produced supporting though preliminary data supporting our approach.

The Needs Analysis method represents work as a matrix, which identifies the work functions in the domain of interest and the variables that affect or are affected by those work functions. The work functions in a work domain specify a high-level task or goal to be accomplished, in terms of the variables that are needed as input (such as information or resources) and the variables, which are affected as output of the function. For example, checking a proposed route might be a work function in supervisory control of a robot; input variables might include the proposed route, data about characteristics of the route such as terrain and distance, characteristics about the robot such as its loads and power, and context information such as other tasks slated for the robot; output variables might include modifications to the route, setting time and approval for the robot to begin the trip, and setting check points for robot to verify continuing or human to monitor robot performance.

It is expected that for many complex domains there will be clusters of variables that support a set of work functions and conversely clusters of work functions related because they draw on a related set of variables. Input and output variables provide a common language that can be used to represent device affordances as well as the work domain. Technology components or devices can also be represented in terms of these same variables: the display variables provide input to the human (input needed by the work function) and the control variables enable action by the human (output the result of the work function). Because both work and technology components can be represented in the “common language” of these variables, this enables evaluating alternative technology designs or implemented systems with respect to how well it supports the work functions in the target work domain.

RESULTS:
The investigation team built a work representation of aircraft automation covering the domain of a nominal domestic passenger flight by a highly automated aircraft. Aircraft automation is an extremely useful test case for a new method because aviation allows control to range from highly automatic to highly human, is safety critical, and makes deep expertise available both from domain experts (pilots) and prior research. This domain provides a strong analog to space flight domains. The team built a medium fidelity flight simulator (a full cockpit, but it did have motion) a specific representation of work functions related to Air Traffic Control clearances, and alternative designs for mode control panels (MCPs), a critical part of the cockpit for auto-flight aircraft. The team compared how well aligned these MCP designs were to the work domain.

As the team developed the method and applied it to the case study, the simple template work matrices were built in a spreadsheet. However, the process was not well supported by using a spreadsheet. As a result, the team developed a tool using an SQL database with a custom browser interface, which was “above and beyond” the year one deliverable specified in the research plan. The tool is designed to enable a domain expert to enter the work functions, the work variables, and their mutual relevance more easily. A second tool “above and beyond” development project concerned identifying the clustering structure implicit in a work matrix to make that structure more systematically identified and more directly presented to a user. The team also extended the bi-clustering statistical methods developed in genomics and also recruited and extended visualization methods developed there. These above and beyond tool development projects were “bonuses,” drew heavily on contributed time, and greatly benefited from collaborators, and have not been validated at this date.

The investigation team predicted that technology that is better aligned with the work domain will provide performance benefits. For example, technology that is more closely aligned with work should show better performance (e.g., easier learning), than technology that is not well aligned with work. The team tested this hypothesis in a preliminary experiment comparing learning to use two alternative designs of MCP, by pilots who were knowledgeable about much of the work domain and selected to be unfamiliar with either design. Due to a reduction in budget, the team was only able to run six participants; however, the data from these users did seem to confirm the hypothesis by showing faster learning for the better aligned MCP, and better transfer to similar but new situations.

Assessing alignment of technology with the work it is intended to support, or its fitness-for-purpose is critical to ensure sound HARI (Risk of Inadequate Design of Human and Automation/Robotic Integration) design. The method developed in this task for representations in work matrices and device matrices, using a “common language” of input and output variables has promise. The approach can be applied early in the design process, e.g., in requirement specification, and carried through to evaluation. The preliminary results provide suggestive empirical support.

experiment_title: Protein Turnover During Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this experiment was to investigate the effects of space flight on whole-body protein metabolism by simultaneously assessing protein turnover and hormonal concentrations. Results from this experiment would provide crucial information for the establishment of a viable ground-based model for protein metabolism. Such a model would provide researchers the capability to test potential countermeasures and determine nutritional requirements for future extended-duration missions, as well as conferring benefits to healthy and metabolically stressed individuals on Earth.

APPROACH:
Whole-body protein turnover, including muscle protein breakdown, was assessed in two subjects before, during and after flight. Blood and urine samples were collected during all phases of the study. Hormonal and biochemical concentrations were measured to better understand neuroendocrine indices of protein metabolism during space flight. Food, fluid, drug intake, and amount and type of exercise were monitored. Body composition was assessed before and after flight. Preflight data were compared with inflight data to determine the effect of microgravity on each subject. Postflight data were used to monitor the readaptation process.

Blood: Blood samples were collected preflight, inflight and postflight during several 72-hour periods. These collection periods began 60 days before launch (L-60), L-35, on flight day 3 (FD3), FD6, 5 days after flight (R+5), and R+14. The protocol was similar for all collection sessions. Baseline specimens were drawn as soon as possible after awakening and before the first meal. Five milliliters (ml) of blood were drawn via butterfly into a serum separator (SST) VacutainerTM tube. An additional 2.7 ml blood sample was collected via monovette syringe for fasting glucose and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) determination with a commercial portable clinical blood analyzer (PCBA). After the fasting blood draw, each subject ingested 15N-alanine (approximately 333 micromole/kg) in capsule form.

Twelve hours after 15N-alanine ingestion, a second butterfly was inserted into the opposite arm from the initial blood draw. The subject was infused with 3-methyl-d3-histidine (1.3 micromole/kg to measure muscle protein breakdown. This was followed by a 5 ml flush of sterile saline to insure that all the tracer was delivered into the subject's circulatory system. Ten minutes later, a third butterfly was inserted in the contralateral arm and 5 ml of blood were drawn into a SST VacutainerTM. Additional blood draws (5 ml into SST) were collected 24, 48, and 72 hours after 15N-alanine ingestion. During these times, an additional 2.7 ml blood sample was collected via monovette syringe for fasting glucose and BUN determination by PCBA.

In flight, blood samples were centrifuged and stored frozen until returned for analysis. The time of inflight blood draws was recorded using a bar-code reader; relative time of day was also known (i.e., hours after awakening). After flight, specimens were analyzed for the 15N enrichments of urea and ammonia by gas chromatography / mass spectrometry. Muscle protein breakdown was determined by computer modeling of the concentration of 3-methyl-d3-histidine circulating in the blood. Serum cortisol and insulin were measured by radioimmunoassay to assess the endocrine regulation of protein metabolism and turnover.

Urine: Urine samples were collected as separate voids. Subjects were provided with small coolers and ice packs to store samples. Sample bottles were collected by the research team at least twice a day. Samples were logged and void volumes measured. Each sample was analyzed to determine protein turnover. Aliquots were removed from each sample and frozen. These frozen aliquots were used to construct 24-hour pools to determine total nitrogen excretion and nitrogen balance. Data collection took place over several 24-hour periods beginning with the first void prior to the 15N-alanine ingestion at L-60, L-35, R+5, and R+14.

During flight, urine voids were collected for 24-hour periods beginning on FD3 and on FD6 in specially configured urine collection bags. Each collection bag contained a known amount of lithium chloride (LiCl) as a volume marker. One aliquot was obtained from each void and stored frozen for processing after return to Earth. All urine aliquots were logged using a bar code reader. After flight, the urine volume per void was calculated via the LiCl marker and all samples were analyzed individually to determine protein turnover. The aliquots from FD3 and FD6 were used to construct separate 24-hour pools to determine total nitrogen excretion and nitrogen balance.

Urea and ammonia 15N enrichments were determined in all specimens by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry after flight. Although ammonia analysis depended on the ability to maintain frozen samples until return to Earth, it provided the added advantage of calculating protein turnover by averaging a rapid and smaller pool (ammonia) with a larger and slower (urea) pool. Total nitrogen (needed to determine body nitrogen balance) was determined from 24-hour urine pools by the Kjeldahl method.

Dietary Intake: Prepared and weighed meals were provided by certified dietitians during the 72 hour periods at L-60 to L-58, L-35 to L-33, R+5 to R+7, and R+14 to R+16 following the 15N-alanine ingestion. Three-day monitoring allowed any abrupt dietary changes that might affect protein turnover to be identified. In addition, subjects were asked to record any medications or supplements taken, duration and type of exercise, and phase of the menstrual cycle (if applicable).

During space flight, food/fluid/drug/exercise intakes were recorded and monitored by means of a bar-code reader during two 3-day periods: from awakening on FD3 to FD5 (inclusive) and, similarly, from FD6 to FD8 (inclusive). The bar code device had an integrated laser that allowed the user to scan items using only one hand. The bar-code reader logged the following information: subject ID, Mission Elapsed Time (MET), and food item (and lot number). This information was stored in the bar-code reader's internal memory to be retrieved after return to Earth.

Body Composition: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) was used to determine body composition (lean body mass) preflight and postflight. Whole-body scans were obtained on L-60 and L-35 and again on R+2, R+5, and R+14. Leg scans were subdivided at the knee into upper and lower regions to allow preflight-to-postflight comparisons of locomotor muscles.

RESULTS:
Space flight results in a down regulation of protein turnover; however, protein breakdown exceeds protein synthesis. In addition, hormonal changes which accompany space flight are conducive to a net loss of muscle and body protein. Nutritional, exercise or pharmacological interventions which promote net protein synthesis must be considered.

experiment_title: Torso Rotation Experiment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The neurological motor strategy of voluntarily keeping the head fixed on the torso as if wearing a rigid neck brace has been termed "torso rotation", since the upper body must turn to reposition the head. In most subjects, continuous torso rotation on the ground, or in 1-g, gradually leads to motion sickness, most likely because of excessive suppression of the vestibular system, which consists of the organs used for balance. A motor strategy similar to torso rotation is often adopted during weightlessness. While this can be a means of reducing head movements to combat motion sickness, it often precedes the onset of motion sickness symptoms. When experiencing motion sickness, an attempt to minimize head movements by moving in this manner might aggravate rather than alleviate the symptoms.

The main objective of this experiment was to determine if torso rotation in weightlessness leads to motion sickness. Should motor strategies similar to torso rotation be identified as a contributor to space motion sickness, it would then be relatively easy to train crewmembers to avoid such strategies, or to preadapt them by mimicking the provocative movements under controlled laboratory conditions. In addition, excessive vestibular suppression, similar to that caused by torso rotation, may be a major contributor to many kinds of motion sickness, including that experienced in cars, buses, planes, and boats. If so, this information may provide a new perspective on the problem and may suggest methods of preventing the disorder.

APPROACH:
The Torsion Rotation Experiment (TRE) is an experiment to monitor eye, head, and upper torso movements of space flight crew members during routine in-flight activities for evidence of egocentric motor strategies, that is, concentrating on a body frame of reference rather than on the external world. Data had to be obtained as early as possible before the onset of motion sickness to allow a correlation between the degree of suppression and the subsequent severity of motion sickness symptoms. Ideally, eye, head and torso rotation about all three axes (pitch, roll and yaw) should have been measured, but in reality, pitch and roll eye movements could not be determined with sufficient accuracy during space flight. As a result, off-line analysis will identify periods of activity dominated by yaw rotation, which will then be studied for evidence of unusual gaze slip during coordinated eye-head movements. At the same time, head rotation was compared to torso rotation to assess overall motor strategy. The hardware used for this experiment consisted of surface electrodes to record eye movements, a sensor package to monitor head rotations, and a second set of transducers mounted on the subject's back to detect upper body rotations. A microprocessor in the torso unit acquired all data and stored the information in removable modules.

RESULTS:
Preflight
Following periods during which the subject was performing pure yaw-axis head movements, with all calibration maneuvers, saccades, artifacts and periods of inactivity excluded. It was then possible to determine if the eyes were being stabilizing relative to the outside world or relative to the body during self-generated head rotations by plotting eye velocity relative to head velocity on a point by-point basis. If the subject's eyes were always stabilized relative to the outside world, eye velocity (relative to the head) and head velocity (relative to space) would be equal but in opposite directions. By contrast, if the eyes were always stabilized relative to the body, only head velocity would change. In real life, one might expect a tendency to move back and forth between the two strategies (arrows), with a change in weighting towards the latter in the presence of increased vestibular suppression.

Inflight
Maximum head and eye velocities are less than those seen pre-flight. One subject was no longer stabilizing his eyes relative to the outside world, as demonstrated by the fact that only 11 % of the 2419 data points now lie in sectors 3 and 4. However, 69% are now in sectors 1 and 2, indicating a great deal of suppression of the vestibular system in general and the vestibulo-ocular reflex in particular. These results are typical of all 4 subjects on Flight Day 1. Over a period of days, Subjects 2, 3 and 4 tended to return to a more ground-like eye stabilization strategy, but Subject 1 did not. All subjects increased their maximum head velocities after Flight Day 1.

Postflight
The data are similar in every respect to those obtained pre-flight from the same subject, indicating a rapid return to a normal pattern of eye stabilization. This was true of all subjects, although the strategy adopted by Subject 1 was still a hit unusual, as had been noted pre-flight.

experiment_title: Maturing Technology for Major Reductions in Energy, Mass, and Crew Time for Plant Lighting in Space
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
To develop and demonstrate proof of concept for two novel technologies that together will greatly advance the potential for growing food crops in space for crew life support at distant space destinations.

APPROACH:
The first technology is a “smart” LED-based sole-source lighting system for saving considerable energy for many reasons. The second technology is a crop-stand gas-exchange system consisting of a large cuvette, an open gas-exchange system, and computer controls for CO2, temperature, and atmosphere flow rate. Lighting parameters are controlled by a second computer. Using the smart lighting system in conjunction with the crop gas-exchange system will give real-time crop response of hydroponically grown crops to light (PPF, R/B ratio), temperature, and CO2 at all stages of crop production, which will define additional opportunities for significant energy savings during controlled-environment crop production.

RESULTS:
Due to the complex multiple components of the gas-exchange / cuvette / hydroponics / lighting system, plus the restrictions of a modest budget, it has been necessary to design, fabricate, build, test, troubleshoot, and refurbish components of the integrated plant-monitoring system using local resources and student projects rather than the services of a professional engineering corporation, which we wouldn’t have been able to afford. Other than HELIAC, which was developed in collaboration with ORBITEC, a (then) small business with strong interests in the space program, the rest of the crop-monitoring system has been developed locally. A design-build local engineer developed cuvette as a side job, and has been through several iterations of retrofit and refurbishment as our integration tests indicated. Purdue University Engineering and Engineering Technology students, both undergraduate as well as graduate, have contributed to development of the open air-flow system, to programming for control of CO2 concentration and air flow, data logging, calculating, and reporting of gas-exchange parameters, and to development of a uniform airflow and thermal-control environment within the cuvette per se. Life science undergraduates collaborate with engineering students to develop protocols for growing test crops hydroponically, to measure gas exchange, manage data, and perform routine system maintenance. At the end of the extended project all development tasks still were not completed because of limited student time, turnover, graduations, etc., but the effort to develop a fully integrated, operational crop-growth / multi-plant gas-exchange system continues using other funding sources. It is planned for a leak-free, thermally stabilized open gas-exchange system to be completed by the end of 2014, and for proof-of-concept crop-growth / gas-exchange studies to be conducted during the spring semester of 2015. That study will establish interactive dose-response curves for Pn vs. PPF at several different CO2 levels at each important phase of a crop-production cycle, and for those experiments to be replicated statistically. A key objective of that study will be to identify precisely when during the time course of a crop-production cycle that optimizing environments are needed, what the minimum inputs are, and when they no longer are needed. The outcome of that study is expected to identify additional times and ways in which significant resources (e.g., CO2) and energy (e.g., light, electricity) can be saved during crop production, and that is expected to additionally reduce costs of growing food in space. The current plan is to complete the proof-of-concept study by May, 2015, write up and internally review a manuscript for publication, and submit an article for publication to a peer-reviewed journal by fall, 2015. An army of past and present engineering, engineering technology, and life science students will be co-authors on that proof-of-concept article that will come out of this technology-development effort enabled by NASA grant NNX09AL99G. This NASA grant will be acknowledged as the main funding source supporting the new research technology proof-of-concept work. Once published and operational, this tool will be proposed for data gathering and further upgrade in future grant proposals. It is anticipated to provide incentive for future fund raising because of it’s powerful analytical capabilities.

experiment_title: Osteogenesis:  Tissue Factors of Regulation
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Bone physiological restructuring at a local level is regulated by short-distant factors which are synthesized by bone cells and released as a result of destruction of extracellular bone organic matrix. This experiment was to study osteogenic potentials and the activity of osteo-induction inhibitor in the bone of space flown rats, with special attention to bone morphogenetic protein (BMP).

Approach:

Osteo-inductive activity of bone matrix was determined and the biological activity of osteo-induction inhibitor in the bone was measured. The concentration of BMP was evaluated with respect to the degree of ectopic osteogenesis induced by its demineralized matrix, determined in relation to the inhibition, or degree of inhibition, of ectopic osteogenesis produced by a standard matrix. A method of induction of ectopic osteogenesis by femur demineralized matrix of flight and control rats (donors) was used; the concentration of elements in the mineral component was determined after implantation.

Results:

Results suggest that in space osteo-inductive activity of bone matrix increases, but remains unaltered in qualitative terms. The amount of de novo generated bone was not large in recipient rats (less than in the controls) but the level of its mineralization was significant. At R+9, osteo-inductive potentials of the matrix decreased and inhibitory activity increased; meaning, bone regenerative potentials declined, thus stimulating osteoporosis.

experiment_title: Sleep, Physical Inactivity, Circadian Rhythms, and Cardiovascular Vulnerability
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Round-the-clock work schedules aboard spaceships and in most industries on Earth leave people with an increased risk for developing cardiovascular diseases (CVD), in part due to the disruption of endogenous human clocks. Endogenous circadian rhythms, generated by these clocks form the basic framework of human physiology. In order to improve the understanding of the mechanisms leading to increased CVD, it is essential to understand the endogenous circadian rhythm in vascular endothelial function, which is an early and a robust marker of CVD. It will be determined if an endogenous circadian rhythm in endothelial function exists using a five day forced desynchrony protocol, and if standardized activities performed during the night shift impair endothelial function.

APPROACH:
Twelve healthy participants will live on four artificial 18 hour days consisting of six hour sleep and 12 hour wake periods. Participants will be isolated from all time cues and will remain in dim light during the wake periods and complete darkness during sleep. The dim light allows the human pacemaker to freely run. All behaviors including food and activity will be identical across all wake periods such that the effects of the behaviors and the endogenous circadian clocks can be separated out. Endothelial function will be measured as flow mediated dilation (FMD) every four hours during the wake periods. To understand mechanisms, blood will be drawn to measure physiological markers such as epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol, oxidative stress, and inflammatory cytokines. Biomarkers inform us about the mechanisms modulating vascular function at various circadian phases. Identification of a rhythm in endothelial function along with the mechanisms that control it will set the stage for developing chronotherapeutic countermeasures against vascular function impairment (such as timing antioxidants and exercise) in space and on Earth.

experiment_title: The Role of the p21/p53 Pathway in Spaceflight-Induced Tissue Degeneration
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Our objective for STS-135 was to confirm our results on p21 cell cycle arrest from the STS-131 experiment, and y expand our current findings to post-flight effects on bone health. We proposed to recover pelvis tissue from STS 135 because it would offer the best replication of STS 131 experimental results: the same mouse strain was used and the tissues were recovered immediately after landing, thus closely replicating the STS-131 experimental conditions, however these tissues were not provided by the BSP making direct comparisons impossible. Although the tissues we had requested were not provided, the metatarsals provided a good alternative model for a load-bearing set of bones for analysis. Metatarsal were used in organ culture assays to test some aspects of the original hypothesis in the proposal that spaceflight factors, such as radiation, affect the regenerative health of stem cells in bone.

APPROACH:

Following the STS-135 mouse BSP we dissected and collected bone samples at KSC and began analyzing the combined effects of microgravity and gamma irradiation on the p53 pathway in mouse metatarsals placed in organ culture immediately following spaceflight. Because of unfortunate errors in sample labeling and distribution, the number of replicate samples of the experimental tissues provided to BSP investigators was reduced. This impacted our ability to perform all of our planned analyses. However, due to the large number of metatarsal bones in the feet of each animal (10), we were able to conduct a slightly more limited but still statistically significant analysis of thickness, mineral content, and architectural differences in bones belonging to ground controls versus spaceflight, either non-irradiated or irradiated at 10 or 50 cGy.

RESULTS:

As a result we now know that cortical bone in metatarsals is sensitive to microgravity induced mineral loss, with significant decreases in cortical thickness. We also demineralized and sectioned additional metatarsal bones for immunohistochemical analysis of p53 pathway proteins, and recovered total RNA for gene expression studies, which are currently ongoing. Once those studies are concluded we expect to determine if osteoclast maturation and recruitment to endosteal bone surfaces is subject to synergistic or additive effects of low-dose gamma irradiation and microgravity, and if activation of the p53 pathway by irradiation is modulated by exposure to microgravity.

experiment_title: Regulation of Auxin Transport by Phosphorylation and Flavonoids during Gravitropism in Arabidopsis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this proposal will be to examine two potential mechanisms for regulation of auxin transport during gravitropism.

APPROACH:
The experimental approach will combine the use of Arabidopsis plants with mutations in genes that alter the regulation of auxin transport and gravity response and inhibitor treatments that mimic these mutant phenotypes; transgenic plants that provide information on changes in gene expression; and computer aided analysis of plant gravity response.

RESULTS:
We explored the role of flavonoids as endogenous regulators of auxin transport and asking if these molecules facilitate the redistribution of auxin in response to gravitropic stimulation. The tt4 mutant, which has a mutation in a gene encoding a flavonoid biosynthetic enzyme, makes no flavonoids. Auxin transport is elevated in multiple tissues in this mutant, consistent with flavonoids acting as endogenous negative regulators. Charles demonstrated that there is elevated movement of auxin from the root tip back in the flavonoid deficient mutant, consistent with flavonoids regulating this polarity of auxin transport, which has been linked to gravitropic responses (Buer and Muday, 2004). We characterized the gravity response in the tt4 mutant in detail. The roots of tt4 are much slower in initiating gravitropic bending. This defect in gravitropism can be reversed by feeding the tt4 plants naringenin, a flavonoid precursor that bypasses the step with the missing enzyme (Buer and Muday, 2004). Since the absence of flavonoids delays gravitropic bending, we asked whether gravitropic reorientation results in changes in accumulation or localization of flavonoids that may alter auxin transport at the root tip. This experiment is possible using a compound that becomes fluorescent in response to binding of flavonoids. We found that flavonoid localization does not change in response to gravity, but the concentration of flavonoids is increased in the root epidermal cells, in which gravitropic bending occurs (Buer and Muday, 2004). The model best supported by these combined results, is that flavonoids are locally induced at the root tip in response to gravity stimulation and that these compounds act to prevent polar auxin transport in the root, facilitating the formation of lateral gradients of auxin in response to the gravitropic signal.

experiment_title: Hepatic Function in Rats After Spaceflight: I. Analyses of Selected Parameters of Carbohydrate, Amino Acid, Lipid, and Xenobiotic Metabolism
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Since the liver is basically a central "clearing house" for the metabolism of most nutrients, drugs, and other foreign compounds, further studies of the effects of space flight on the organ appeared warranted. Previous findings suggest that the xenobiotic metabolism is altered by space flight. In attempts to further these findings, described in this report are additional data from analyses of liver samples and serum samples from space-flown rats.

Approach:

Liver and plasma samples were analyzed, with established methods, for hepatic protein (with bovine serum albumin as standard), glycogen (rabbit liver glycogen standard) and lipids, as well as the activities of a number of key enzymes involved in metabolism of these compounds and xenobiotics. DNA was quantified using calf thymus DNA as standard. Cytochrome P-450 was measured spectrophotometrically, and by the standard assays of testosterone metabolism and immunochemistry. Other enzyme and serum analyses were conducted using an analyzer.

Results:

The major differences between the flight group versus the synchronous control were: elevations in microsomal protein, liver glycogen content, tyrosine aminotransferase, and tryptophan oxygenase; and reductions in sphingolipids and the rate-limiting enzyme of heme biosynthesis, delta aminolevulinic acid synthase. These results support the hypothesis that space flight alters liver function; however, results with these samples differed notably from those of Skylab 3 and Cosmos 1887, presumably due to the conditions of space flight and/or the post- flight recovery period.

experiment_title: Evaluation of Muscle Size Measurement with Ultrasound and Magnetic Resonance Imaging – Pilot Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Crewmembers continue to experience muscle atrophy after space flight, particularly from long-duration missions on the International Space Station (ISS), which results in higher risk for injury upon their return to Earth. More robust exercise equipment is arriving on the ISS and new exercise prescriptions are planned to counteract the muscle losses. With these new exercise countermeasures; however, there currently are no methods to monitor muscle status in flight to assist in determining the efficacy of these countermeasures. Given that medical imaging with ultrasound is available on the ISS, it is feasible that ultrasound scanning could be performed before, during, and after space flight to assess muscle size changes. This ground-based pilot study evaluated and validated a technique of using ultrasound to measure leg muscle cross sectional area (CSA) and volume. These ultrasound measures were also compared with a magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the leg to determine the accuracy and repeatability of the ultrasound muscle measurements. This pilot study is part of the larger Integrated Resistive and Aerobic Training Study (SPRINT) conducted on the ISS. Ultrasound will ultimately be used to assess the effectiveness of the SPRINT exercise prescription on ISS crewmembers using the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED) and the second generation treadmill (T2) during their missions. This ultrasound technique could also be applicable for evaluating future exercise countermeasures both on ISS and Constellation missions.

APPROACH:
Subjects passed an Air Force Class III-equivalent physical examination and were cleared for exercise by the Human Test Subject Facility (HTSF) and by the HTSF Medical Monitor prior to entry into the study. Subjects completed a health history questionnaire each day prior to testing, which was reviewed by the test operators to ensure that their health status had not changed to the extent that testing was contraindicated. Potential issues were discussed with the Medical Monitor before testing commenced. Any subject with metal implants of any sort was excluded, since a MRI scan was required for participation.

Ten subjects were recruited for participation in this pilot study. Subjects were asked to participate in three separate data collection sessions, each with a duration of approximately 90 minutes or less. Two of the three sessions involved ultrasound scanning of the subject’s right leg muscles, calf (gastrocnemius, soleus) and thigh (vastus lateralis, rectus femoris). Panoramic ultrasound images were acquired by two sonographers using a customized template placed on the thigh and calf and analyzed by the same two sonographers (MyLab Gold, Biosound). MRI images of the leg were acquired while the subjects lay supine in a 1.5T scanner (Signa Horizon LX, General Electric) and analyzed by three trained investigators. The average of the two ultrasounds and three MRI values were used for validity analysis.

RESULTS:
A high inter-experimenter reliability was found using the ultrasound template. A significant correlation was found between ultrasound and MRI CSA measures. There were significant differences between absolute values of MRI and ultrasound for all muscles. The present results indicate that utilizing a customized ultrasound template along with panoramic imaging provides reliable measures of leg muscle CSA, and thus could be used to provide in-flight measures of changes in muscle CSA.

experiment_title: Bone Recovery Time Course Following Long Exposure to Microgravity

This experiment studies bone recovery at two different time intervals postflight; at “short term”, which is approximately 3 months postflight and at "long term" which is at a year and a half after landing. It is currently unknown what the biological basis of this phenomenon is, and it is therefore unclear whether PREBL may constitute a risk after space flight. experiment_title: Investigations of the Plant Cytoskeleton in Microgravity With Gene Profiling and Cytochemistry
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The major goal of this research is to study the effects of microgravity on the structure and organization of actin cytoskeleton in plants. This proposed project builds on our previous ground-based and spaceflight research using the model plant Arabidopsis. Thus, the specific aims of this proposed flight research using the BRIC-LED system are: (1) to investigate plastid position in statocytes (=gravity-perceiving cells) in microgravity; (2) to determine the effect of microgravity on the actin cytoskeletal organization in gravity-perceiving cells; (3) to study microgravity effects on actin cytoskeleton-related gene expression in plant cells. This project also will allow us to directly correlate results from cytological investigations and gene profiling in order to understand the nature of the actin cytoskeleton in mechanisms of gravity perception.

APROACH:
The NASA Biological Research in Canisters (BRIC) -16 project offered a unique opportunity to conduct a spaceflight experiment with minimal preparation time. Procedures were adapted from previous spaceflight studies conducted by our lab on the Space Shuttle and the ISS. Seedlings of Arabidopsis thaliana were grown from seed on the shuttle Discovery mission STS-131 in the BRIC- Petri Dish Fixation Unit (PDFU) flight hardware. After fourteen days of growth, samples were then stabilized by either an aldehyde-based fixative or RNAlater. We compared flight samples with a ground sample control, which was conducted in the flight hardware at 1g. Through additional studies, samples will be analyzed using molecular genetic techniques and three methods of microscopy including light (LM), transmission electron (TEM), and confocal. LM will be used to understand any overall anatomical differences and the placement of the statoliths. TEM will elucidate the interaction between statoliths and the sub-cellular structures such as cytoskeleton and organelles. Confocal microscopy will show us the structural differences in the development of the actin cytoskeleton between ground and flight.

OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this experiment was to develop a balanced traction to elongate the spine to the degree experienced by astronauts. The effects of traction on the spine exposed to the 6 degree head down tilt (HDT) model is compared to effects on the spine with traction and horizontal bed rest (HBR).  The second part of this study (ARCbedrest129) was designed to determine the electrical activity and intramuscular pressures of the muscles along the lumbar spine while upright and while in 6o HDT or HBR position.

APPROACH:
Healthy volunteers were tested in the MRI before and after 3 days exposure to a balanced traction device that placed a load on the spine by suspending a load corresponding to 5% of the body weight from each leg with a cable-pulley system.  The volunteer was at bed rest in the 6o HDT or in HBR position. Activity was not restricted. HDT with traction was compared with HBR with traction. The second part of the study conducted a few days after this one estimated the electrical activity of lumbar spine muscle through surface electrodes for specified hours of normal activity. Through a catheter inserted into the muscle on either side of the lumbar spine, the pressures were recorded during upright and then at three time intervals during of HDT or HBR.  Electrical activity was recorded concurrent with intramuscular pressure. Subjects were randomized into 2 groups of three. Group 1 underwent HBR followed by HDT in balanced traction. Group II underwent HDT in balanced traction followed by HBR. There was a two-week recovery period between the two forms of 3d-bed rest.

RESULTS:
Repeated measures ANOVA indicated that total body length increased more (mean±SE) during HDT with balanced traction (22±8 mm) than during HBR (16±4 mm). Spine length between L5 and C7 also increased more during HDT with traction (25±8 and 14±9 mm). Ultrasonography showed increases in lumbar disc height during HDT and HBR (2.9±0.8 mm vs. 3.3±0.6 mm), but there were no differences among groups. Seventy percent of the increase in disc height occurred during the first 5 hours of bed rest. Within the first hour of standing, there was a 10 mm decrease in body height, about 80% of the normal diurnal variation in our subjects. The intensity of pain in the back, abdomen and head was greater during HDT with traction than during HBR with traction. Reflexes were normal in both groups. Intramuscular pressure in erector spinae muscles that averaged 8.4±0.7 mm Hg did not change during the study and was similar in HBR and HDT. Ankle joint torque during plantar- and dorsi-flexion did not change during the study and was similar in HBR and HDT with balanced traction.

Conclusions: Results suggest that HDT with balanced traction may combine the advantages of both models to simulate total body and spinal lengthening, as well as back pain associated with microgravity. Note: Both studies were carried out on the same group of subjects. The measurements of intra muscular pressure in HR 129 were reported separately, but the protocols for each study were the same. Therefore, it is more complete to have both HR 117 and HR 129 reported together as the first part and the second part of the study as described.
