experiment_title: Clinical Trial of the Efficacy of Melatonin as a Countermeasure for Entrainment to the Sleep/Wake Schedules Required during Shuttle Missions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Shuttle astronauts are typically exposed to "sleep cycle shifting" due to mission-dependent orbital mechanics and mission requirements. This is equivalent to imposition of a non-24 hour 'day' and is likely to result in misalignment of the endogenous circadian timing system with respect to the desired sleep-wake cycle, even among crewmembers who begin the mission with their sleep-wake cycle well synchronized to mission elapsed time (MET) on the day of launch. Such misalignment is known to produce sleep disturbances, daytime sleepiness, reduced attention, negative mood, slower reaction times, gastrointestinal disorders and impaired daytime alertness. Although appropriately scheduled exposure to bright light has been shown to be capable of resetting the phase of the human circadian pacemaker, existing Shuttle technology precludes use of such bright light delivery systems aboard the Shuttle. Several lines of evidence, including the discovery of melatonin receptors on the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the human hypothalamus and the results of animal and human studies, indicate that melatonin administration may be effective in generating phase shifts of the circadian pacemaker. The current study evaluated the ability of melatonin to entrain the human circadian pacemaker in sighted humans to a shorter-than-24-hour day length.

The current research was designed to test the following hypotheses:

  1. the human circadian pacemaker will be unable to maintain synchronization with a sleep-wake cycle of 23.5 hours, typical of that required on Shuttle missions;
  2. that such loss of synchronization will result in sleep-onset insomnia, decreased sleep efficiency, and decreased daytime alertness and performance resulting from imposition of the 23.5-hour day; and
  3. that a daily dose of melatonin (5 mg), administered one hour before bedtime, will be sufficient to entrain the circadian pacemaker to a 23.5-hour scheduled sleep-wake cycle.

To test the hypotheses, researchers conducted long-term (50-day) inpatient trials utilizing methodologies that allowed direct measurement of endogenous circadian phase and amplitude before, during and after extended duration exposure to a shorter-than-24-hour day length (i.e., similar to that occurring on many space shuttle flights). Each trial took place in an environment with low light intensities similar to that measured aboard the space shuttle on STS-90. It was anticipated that when subjects were scheduled to a 23.5-hour day and room lighting conditions were maintained to 8 lux maximum, that the endogenous circadian pacemaker would oscillate with a period that was different (24.1 to 24.2 hours) from the period of the imposed sleep-wake/work cycle. Failure to entrain the human circadian pacemaker to the 23.5-hour day was expected to be associated with disturbed sleep, and impaired waking alertness and performance. It was also expected that a daily dose of 5 mg of melatonin, one hour prior to scheduled sleep, would entrain the human circadian pacemaker to the 23.5-hour day. The melatonin countermeasure was expected to maintain normal sleep and circadian patterns, and normal waking alertness and performance.

APPROACH:
Five healthy male subjects (age: mean ± SD, 34 ± 7.25; range, 26-44) were studied. All subjects were required to pass a rigorous health screening including medical history, physical and psychological exams, blood and urine chemistries and an electrocardiogram. Toxicology screens for drug use, including alcohol and caffeine verified that participants were drug-free upon admission to the laboratory.

Blood was sampled for melatonin and cortisol during circadian phase estimations (constant routines) and 28-hour sampling windows throughout the intervening study days between constant routines. (In general, during a constant routine protocol, subjects remain under constant conditions, awake, engaged in light, mainly sedentary activity, and consume identical food and fluid every hour.) Core body temperature, waking electroencephalogram (EEG) and polysomnography were recorded throughout most of the protocol. Subject's performance, alertness and mood were assessed every 2 hours during wakefulness using valid, reliable standardized measures, which are sensitive to circadian misalignment and homeostatic sleep drive.

Ceiling-mounted fluorescent lamps with a 4100 K color temperature produced a spectrum of white light. Clear polycarbonate lenses filtered 99.9% of the light in the UV range. Light-dark cycles during the 23.5-hour day were of very dim light (< 8 lux maximum at ~183 cm with the sensor aimed toward the light fixtures) during scheduled wakefulness and darkness during scheduled sleep. Light intensity was measured with a photometer. The < 8 lux maximum light intensity was very similar to the light intensity measured on the middeck of the Space Shuttle during research on the Neurolab STS-90 mission.

Subjects were assigned to one of two cells: A or B. The protocol was divided into 9 segments:

CELL A

Segment A1 (Ambulatory Baseline) consisted of a minimum of 7 days, during which wrist activity and light levels were recorded using ambulatory-recording devices while the subjects were at home on a normal routine maintaining a sleep log.

Segment A2 (Adaptation) began with admission to the Intensive Physiologic Monitoring (IPM) Unit of the Brigham & Women's Hospital on Experimental Day 1 and ended on the morning of Experimental Day 4. Physiologic and neurobehavioral monitoring commenced upon admission on Experimental Day 1 and continued throughout the duration of the study. Subjects continued to sleep and wake at their regularly scheduled times for three normal scheduled nights. A placebo, was administered (single blind) one hour prior to lights out on nights 2-3 to determine if .

Segment A3 (Endogenous Circadian Phase Assessment-ECPA) began on the morning of Experimental Day 4 and ended on the evening of Experimental Day 5. Upon waking on Experimental Day 4, the subjects were placed on a constant routine protocol for 40 hours after which time subjects underwent an 8-hour recovery sleep. The constant routine protocol, as is true with the rest of the protocol from this point forward, was conducted in dim room light. Blood was sampled for melatonin and cortisol until the morning of Experimental Day 5. The constant routine was used to assess the phase and amplitude of the endogenous circadian pacemaker under strictly controlled conditions.

Segment A4 consisted of eighteen successive 23.5-hour days, which began on the morning of Experimental Day 6 and ended on the evening of Experimental Day 23. Each day consisted of 15.67 hours of scheduled wakefulness and 7.83 hours of scheduled sleep. Melatonin (5.0 mg) was administered orally, double blind, one hour prior to lights out each night. Light exposure was maintained at < 8 lux maximum during scheduled wakefulness. In addition to the blood sampled during the constant routines, one 28-hour window of blood sampling took place during Experimental Days 14-15. During this window, blood was sampled for melatonin and for cortisol.

Segment A5 (ECPA Reassessment) consisted of a repetition of the constant routine and recovery sleep that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A3.

Segment A6 (Adaptation) consisted of a repetition of the adaptation that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A2.

Segment A7 (ECPA Reassessment) consisted of a repetition of the constant routine and recovery sleep that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segments A3 and A5. In addition, this segment was used to reestablish a normal phase relationship between sleep and the phase of the endogenous circadian pacemaker.

Segment A8 consisted of a repetition of the eighteen 23.5-hour-day segment that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A4. Placebo was administered, double blind, one hour prior to lights out each night.

Segment A9 (ECPA Reassessment) consisted of a repetition of the constant routine and recovery sleep that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A3, A5 and A7.

CELL B

The procedures for this cell were identical to that of Cell A except that in Segment B4 subjects received placebo instead of melatonin one hour prior to each sleep episode and in Segment B8 subjects received melatonin instead of a placebo one hour prior to each sleep episode.

In order to determine whether assessment of endogenous melatonin levels provided a method to assess the status of circadian phase and period, researchers assessed the potential impact of the sleep-wake cycle and associated light-dark cycle on the endogenous circadian rhythm of plasma melatonin. Researchers performed a detailed analysis of the melatonin phase during a 20-hour forced desynchrony protocol.

In this protocol, twelve young healthy subjects (5F, 7M) aged 24.1 ± 3.70 years (mean ± SD) were studied in an environment free of time cues for 18-27 days. Following three 24-hour baseline days (16 hour wake / 8 hour sleep), the subjects were scheduled to 24 cycles of a 20-hour flight day (FD) protocol (13.33 hour wake/6.67 hour sleep). Ambient light intensities were <15 lux during all scheduled wake times and <0.03 lux during all scheduled sleep episodes. Melatonin data were fitted with a non-orthogonal spectral analysis (NOSA) program, which simultaneously fit the imposed (20-hour, 2 harmonics) and endogenous (near 24-hour, 6 harmonics) components (and their interactions) of melatonin in order to calculate the subjects' intrinsic circadian periods t (tau). Each subject's melatonin data were then folded by their fitted t. For each circadian day researchers calculated: 1) duration of melatonin peak (DMP, time between upward and downward crossings of the mean); 2) circadian phase of melatonin peak (MIDPT, midpoint of upward and downward crossings of the mean); and 3) area under melatonin curve (AUC, estimated using the trapezoidal rule, z-scored for each subject). Linear regressions were fitted to the AUC and DMP data from the entire FD protocol to assess any overall change in the mean levels of melatonin secretion during the experiment. To determine whether the timing of the 20-hour sleep/wake schedule systematically modulated the phase or amount of melatonin secretion, each subject's AUC, DMP and MIDPT data were folded by the beat period (mean ± SD = 117.27 ± 0.13 hour) of their &964; (mean ± SD = 24.12 ± 3.10 hour) and the 20-hour FD protocol. For each variable, sine curves were then fitted to the data from all 10 subjects, and a Student's t-test was used to determine whether the fitted amplitude of the sinusoid was significantly different from 0.0.

RESULTS:
Hypothesis 1: Entrainment Studies of the Human Circadian Pacemaker to a 23.5 hour day.
Most subjects who received the placebo treatment failed to entrain to the scheduled 23.5-hour day, whereas most subjects given 5.0 mg of melatonin one hour prior to each bedtime maintained normal phase relationships between the timing of their core body temperature rhythms and the timing of the scheduled sleep-wake cycle. Two of three subjects in the melatonin condition maintained phase angles in the normal range with low levels during sleep suggesting that they entrained to the 23.5-hour day.

Hypothesis 2: Impaired Neurobehavioral Performance During Circadian Misalignment.
The neurobehavioral function during the entrainment studies to the 23.5-hour day with and without melatonin (n=3) was also examined. Daily performance averages were computed for subjects who completed both melatonin and placebo conditions. Researchers assessed vigilance performance every two hours during wakefulness using the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT). The primary outcome measures analyzed were median reaction time and lapses (response times > 500 ms). Results of these analyses showed that reaction time performance and lapses in attention were similar in the melatonin and placebo conditions. Researchers also assessed working memory, cognitive speed and accuracy trade-offs using the Addition Performance Task and the Digit Symbol Substitution Test. Both tasks showed significant interaction effects (P < 0.05) between Drug Condition and Day such that performance continued to improve (i.e., learning occurred) in the melatonin but not the placebo condition. Subjective Sleepiness on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale was significantly lower (less sleepiness) near the end of the protocol for the melatonin compared to the placebo condition (P < 0.05).

Hypothesis 3: Progress on the relationship between melatonin and circadian entrainment.
The AUC (p<0.20) and the DMP (p<0.15) did not show any significant changes in their mean levels over the course of the FD protocol. The DMP also showed no systematic alteration in relation to the 20-hour FD regimen. However, the AUC (p<0.0001) and the MIDPT (p<0.0001) manifested systematic modulations in relation to the 20-hour FD protocol. When sleep episodes were scheduled near circadian phase 240°, MIDPTs occurred approximately one hour later in the circadian day than when sleep was scheduled to occur near circadian phase 60°. When sleep episodes were scheduled near circadian phase 180°, the AUC was approximately 1.5 standard deviation larger than when sleep was scheduled to occur near circadian phase 0°.

These data demonstrated that the quantity of melatonin secreted and the phase of the midpoint of the melatonin curve are significantly affected by the timing of the sleep/wake, light/dark, upright/supine conditions during a 20-hour FD protocol. The data also demonstrated that the endogenous melatonin rhythm was robust and provided an accurate estimate of the period of the pacemaker under the current space-flight conditions of dim light.

The current results suggest that:

  1. additional research is necessary to evaluate the impact of non-24-hour sleep-wake/work schedules on circadian entrainment, sleep and performance during ground-based simulations and space-flight conditions;
  2. a dose of 5.0 mg of melatonin taken daily one hour prior to bedtime appears to be well tolerated and may be able to entrain the human circadian pacemaker to a shorter-than-24-hour day in some but not all individuals. Thus, additional research is needed to determine the effective dose necessary to entrain all individuals to non-24-hour day lengths. A flight-based test of daily administration of a larger dose of melatonin (=5.0 mg per day) as a countermeasure to circadian misalignment during space flight is warranted since melatonin appears to hold promise as an entraining agent at this higher dose;
  3. individual differences, likely due to differences in the intrinsic circadian period, make some individuals more vulnerable to circadian misalignment. These individual differences in vulnerability to circadian misalignment suggest that robust countermeasures need to be developed to ensure entrainment of all astronauts to a variety of imposed sleep-wake schedules during space flight.
  4. some sleep disturbances in space are likely related to a failure to maintain entrainment of the human circadian pacemaker to the imposed schedule, especially for missions with schedules that deviate from the 24-hour day; and
  5. measurement of the endogenous melatonin rhythm can be used to assess the status of the circadian time keeping system in humans under the current dim lighting conditions of space flight.

experiment_title: Environmental Radiation Measurements on Mir Station
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment attempted to expand the knowledge of environmental radiation at the 51.6 degree orbit, the location of the Mir station and future location of the International Space Station. Information on the shielding effects of the station and different methods of radiation dosimetry was also gathered. The data and associated analysis contributed to the establishment of a reliable database for the radiation environment in space.

APPROACH:
Two types of spectra were measured and compared: linear energy transfer (LET) and absorbed dose. The measurements for both spectra occurred inside six area passive dosimeters (APDs) that were flown to Mir via Shuttle mission STS-76 and placed at six different locations on Mir. LET spectra was measured using CR-39 PNTDs that were placed on the APDs. The CR-39 plates were etched with a NaOH solution and read out on an image digitizer system and analyzed. The absorbed spectra was measured using thermoluminescent detectors (TLDs) attached to the APDs. The flight data was compared with data read from background and calibration TLDs.

RESULTS:
By using identical APDs in the exact locations on Mir, changes in radiation levels over time were recorded and analyzed. The measured dose rates in the APDs ranged from 268 to 422 mGy/d, yielding an average of 324 mGy/d. The differences in the high and low values were most likely caused by shielding differences due to the individual APD placements on Mir. Also, secondary target fragments, generated by inelastic scattering of protons and alpha particles within the detector medium, contributed to the spread of values. The dose and dose equivalent rates were used to calculate the effective quality factor, which was determined to be about 9 for LETs 25 keV/mm. This value shows the significance of short-range high LET target fragments to dose equivalent. The shielding data is currently being used to model the APD measurements made in the Mir Core.

experiment_title: Project Mercury Ballistic and Orbital Chimpanzee Flights
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:

In April 1959, a chimpanzee test program with the following objectives was established for Project Mercury:

1. Animal verification of a successful space flight prior to manned space flight.

2. Collection of data on the physical and psychological demands, that would be encountered by the astronauts during space flight.

3. Completion of a dynamic test of operational procedures and training of support personnel in handling the biomedical program for manned flight.

4. Evaluation of the spacecraft environmental control system and bioinstrumentation under flight conditions.

Two chimpanzee flights were conducted in order to evaluate and accomplish the above objectives. Mercury-Redstone 2, the first of the two chimpanzee flights, was launched on January 31, 1961. This flight involved a chimpanzee, Ham, being placed through a ballistic trajectory flight. During the flight, Ham had to perform a continuous and discrete motor task that had been learned on the ground. Mercury-Atlas 5, the second chimpanzee flight, was launched on November 29, 1961. During this flight, a chimpanzee named Enos, performed a complex multiple operant task, while orbiting the earth twice.

Tests were performed during the Mercury animal flights to ascertain whether the restrained animal, retaining visual and kinesthetic references, could respond normally during weightlessness to a series of problems graded in difficulty and in motivation. The animal was trained to respond on a schedule that involved mild punishment for error. In addition, a reward system, in the form of food pellets and drinks of water, was provided. The purpose of the schedule was both to determine whether there was a loss of appetite for food or water and, to establish that eating and drinking could be carried out normally in the weightless state. The bioinstrumentation resembled, as closely as possible, that used in the human Mercury flights for which these animal flights were to be an introduction. One important addition for the Mercury-Atlas 5 flight was the use of a special instrumentation package by which onboard recordings would be made from both the low (venous) and high-pressure (arterial) systems of the circulation before and during flight.

The comprehensive series of operant tasks involving both reward and avoidance was based primarily on previously established conditioning techniques. Originally, the feasibility of applying such techniques--which had already been worked out for the pigeon, rat and monkey--to the chimpanzee was problematical since previous operant studies of these animals had not used avoidance conditioning. It is one of the accomplishments of the animal program that solutions to the various problems in comparative psychology were so rapidly found and that a highly effective and complex series of in-flight tasks were developed and successfully used in space.

APPROACH:

Mercury-Redstone 2 (MR-2)
Ham, the MR-2 flight subject, was a male chimpanzee weighing 37 pounds. On the basis of dental eruptions, his age was estimated at 44 months. Ham had received 219 hours of training in the behavioral task over a 15-month period; prior to the flight he had been subjected to simulated Redstone launch profiles in a centrifuge.

The following physiological parameters were measured before and during the MR-2 flight: electrocardiogram (ECG), respiration, and rectal temperature. The subject, along with all the physiological and performance hardware, was housed in a custom-made flight couch. During flight the subject was restrained in the flight couch using a specially fitted flight suit and harness inside the couch. Preflight physiological data were recorded on direct writing recorders; flight data were recorded on onboard tape and telemetered to ground stations and to recorders located on inflight aircraft. During the 18-month period prior to the MR-2 flight, Ham received six complete, quarterly physical examinations. After recovery of the MR-2 flight capsule, he was given another complete physical examination with blood, urine, and fecal analysis. Three more such examinations were conducted on Ham 2, 7, and 14 days after the MR-2 flight.

The performance tests were administered to Ham using a performance test panel developed specifically for the MR-2 flight. The performance test panel contained three lights and two levers, and was mounted perpendicular to the subject at waist level. The performance task for the MR-2 flight consisted of two components: a continuous-avoidance component and a discrete-avoidance component. Both components of the performance task were administered to the subject simultaneously. The continuous-avoidance component required the subject to depress the right-hand lever at least once every fifteen seconds, to avoid a shock. Each response by the subject on the right-hand lever postponed the occurrence of the next scheduled shock for 15 seconds and, as a consequence, a consistent and stable rate of responding was developed by which the subject could avoid shocks indefinitely. The discrete-avoidance component employed a signal as a warning of impending shock if the correct response was not made. The warning signal was the illumination of a blue light. This light came on once every 2 minutes. The subject had to press the left-hand lever within 5 seconds of the presentation of the blue light to avoid receiving a shock. The time between the appearance of the blue light and the pressing of the left lever was the subject's reaction time.

Because redundancy in data collection was desired, five digital counters were included in the programming unit of the flight couch. These counted the responses on the right-hand lever, the blue-light presentations, responses on the left-hand lever, the number of shocks for failure to perform continuous-avoidance task, and the number of shocks for failure to make discrete-avoidance responses. Readings from these counters after flight verified the information obtained via telemetry and the onboard tape recorders.

Mercury-Atlas 5 (MA-5)
Enos, the MA-5 flight subject, was a male chimpanzee weighing 42 pounds. His age was estimated at 63 months. Enos had received a total of approximately 1,263 hours of training over a 16-month period; 343 hours of this training was accomplished under restraint conditions in a laboratory model of the couch used during the flight.

The physiological parameters measured during the MA-5 flight were the same as for the MR-2 flight with the following two exceptions: venous and arterial catheters were used for blood pressure measurements, and Enos was catheterized for collection of urine during the flight. The subject, along with all the physiological and performance hardware, was housed in a custom-made flight couch. During flight the subject was restrained in the flight couch using a specially fitted flight suit and harness inside the couch. Physiological data were recorded using the same methods used during the MR-2 flight. Complete blood analysis was performed on Enos 1, 2, 5, 8, 20, and 50 days after the MA-5 flight.

The performance test panel used for the MA-5 flight was specifically designed for the orbital flight. The MA-5 performance test panel consisted of three miniature inline digital displays (IDD) and three levers. The performance test panel also controlled a pellet feeder that was incorporated into the panel, and a lip-lever activated drinking tube that was attached to the flight couch near the subject's head.

The performance task for the MA-5 flight consisted of a five-component, multiple-operant conditioning schedule. The first two components of the schedule, continuous-avoidance and discrete-avoidance, were the same as in the MR-2 flight. The third component of the schedule required the subject to perform on an operant conditioning schedule involving differential reinforcement of a low rate (DRL). Water was used as the reinforcer or reward. Performance of the DRL task was measured in terms of the time that the subject waited between reward lever presses. The fourth component was a fixed ratio (FR) reinforcement program for food reward. Performance on this component was measured in terms of the time required for the subject to make fifty lever presses (for every fifty lever presses a food pellet is dispensed). The final component of the schedule consisted of 18 oddity problems. The oddity problems required the subject to discriminate the odd symbol presented on the three IDDs, and press the corresponding lever within 15 seconds. The level of performance on this component was measured in terms of discrimination accuracy: number of oddity problems (18) was divided by the total number of discriminations.

Data was collected on the MA-5 flight using three data collection techniques simultaneously. Data were telemetered to ground receiving stations, continuously recorded on two sub-channels of the onboard recorder tape, and the total of all responses was recorded on a single digital counter mounted behind the performance test panel.

RESULTS:

Mercury-Redstone 2
During the MR-2 ballistic flight, Ham was subjected to the stresses of the prelauch operations, launch, flight, reentry, landing, and recovery from the ocean. Despite these various stresses, few measurable physiological and behavioral changes were noted. When compared with a photograph taken before the flight, the postflight picture of Ham indicates his good condition onboard the ship only a few hours after recovery. One measurable physiological change to Ham, was a significant lag after launch in the return of his heart rate to normal (preflight) values. Ham's heart rate rose to 158 beats per minute during the third and fourth minute following the launch, and required approximately 4 minutes of weightlessness for it to return to preflight values. A measurable increase in heart rate also occurred during the reentry acceleration following the period of weightlessness, and again the heart rate returned slowly to normal values. During this period, drogue parachute opening, main parachute opening, and impact may have deferred the return of the heart rate to normal. The subject's respiration rate was not greatly disturbed by the launch accelerations and returned to preflight values during weightlessness, varying from a low of 22 to a high of 72 breaths per minute with a mean throughout the flight of 44 breaths per minute. The environmental control system of the Mercury spacecraft performed so well that the subject's temperature was essentially unchanged throughout the flight.

A physiological change of particular interest was the neutrophile-lymphocyte ratio shift, which was believed to be a result of the exposure to the stresses of launch preparation, flight, and postlanding period in the ocean awaiting recovery. Upon recovery and release from the spacecraft, the white blood cell count showed a ratio of 94-percent neutrophiles to 4-percent lymphocytes with a total count of 16,000 white blood cells. Seventy-two hours later, there were 14-percent neutrophiles to 84-percent lymphocytes. By February 7, nine days after flight, the neutrophile-lymphocyte ratio had returned to the normal 35-percent of neutrophiles. The shift in the neutrophile-lymphocyte ratio, which is found during periods of stress, has previously been described in the analysis of blood samples obtained from chimpanzee subject studies exposing them to high temperature and humidity.

Ham's excellent performance on the two required tasks was gratifying. Of the two shocks received during the flight, only one was deserved. The reliability of the subject on the continuous-avoidance program, shows that this type of work can be monitored by a higher primate under space-flight conditions. In controlled laboratory experiments in a centrifuge, chimpanzee subjects have been exposed to acceleration of 6-G in simulating the launch of the Redstone vehicle. At that time, a decrement in performance on a continuous avoidance task was noted; therefore, the decrement observed following launch and reentry was to be expected. However, the decrement after launch was followed by recovery to preflight values within approximately 1 minute. There was also a performance decrement following reentry. Although the reentry decrement's significance has not been determined, it is possible that is was related to oscillation of the spacecraft prior to stabilization by the deployment of the drogue parachute.

Mercury-Atlas 5
Several inflight and postflight physiological events related to the MA-5 orbital flight warrant comment. The Zanzibar tracking station recorded premature ventricular contractions 26 minutes after launch. Since launch acceleration lasted for 5 minutes, the first premature ventricular contraction occurred after 21 minutes of weightlessness. The premature ventricular contractions continued singly, in pairs, and in runs until 3 hours 15 seconds after launch. At that time, the retrorockets were fired and the subject was subjected to increasing accelerations. Continuous data on the subject covers the period from 5 hours 30 minutes before launch until 3 hours 21 minutes after launch.

The chimpanzee's blood pressure was recorded onboard the spacecraft, but was not monitored via telemetry; therefore, no data were available until after the flight. Although the blood pressure was high, it was not inconsistent with the preflight values, which were also high, nor was it inconsistent with some of the data obtained previously on this subject.

It has not been possible to demonstrate any correlation with performance or shock being a factor in inducing the premature ventricular contractions, only that the premature ventricular contractions occurred during the weightless state. It may be speculated that they were associated with some changes in the position of the catheter in the heart during weightlessness. The physiological and psychomotor responses to the flight were as expected except for the sustained high blood pressure. This condition preceded the flight and was not due to the act of catheterization or to the presence of the catheters in the leg artery and vein. For example, subsequent studies have shown no increase in blood pressure, with values obtained being the same as those measured by sphygmomanometry.

The subject performed as desired throughout the launch and reentry acceleration and during the weightless state despite the unplanned stress caused by the failure of the center lever in the performance test panel, which resulted in numerous shocks during the oddity problem presentation. Subsequent to the oddity presentations, performance was within normal limits except during the peak acceleration of reentry. The data show no significant disturbance in the subject's behavior or physiology that could be attributed to the weightless state, to the other conditions accompanying the flight, or to the lever malfunction during the second orbital pass.

Nevertheless, the extra systoles and the high blood pressure do emphasize the importance of measuring the total subject response in terms of both behavior and physiology. Both approaches are required to evaluate the flight or any particular portion of it. That the physiological task recordings showed normal performance despite the cardiovascular irregularities was convincing evidence of the immediate value of the operant technique as a direct measure of the well being and performance capability of the subject.

From the results of the MR-2 and MA-5 flights, the following conclusions were drawn:

1. The numerous objectives of the Mercury animal test program were met. The MR-2 and MA-5 tests preceded the first ballistic and orbital manned flights, respectively, and provided valuable training in countdown procedures and range monitoring and recovery techniques. The bioinstrumentation was effectively tested and the adequacy of the environmental control system was demonstrated.

2. A 7-minute (MR-2) and a 3-hour (MA-5) exposure to weightlessness was experienced by the subjects in the context of an experiment design, which left visual and tactile references unimpaired. There was no significant change in the animal's physiological state or performance as measured during a series of tasks of graded motivation and difficulty.

3. The results met program objectives by answering questions concerning the physical and mental demands that the astronauts would encounter during space flight and by showing that these demands would not be excessive.

4. An incidental gain from the program was the demonstration that the young chimpanzee can be trained to be a highly reliable subject for space-flight studies.

experiment_title: Distributed Simulation of Integrated Human Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A synopsis of the four specific aims of the three-year project is as follows: 1. To develop, at Johns Hopkins University (JHU), an experimentally-based computational model of the human ventricular myocyte using cells isolated from tissue biopsies performed in patients; and to develop a finite-element model of the geometry and fiber structure of the human heart using diffusion-tensor imaging data to be collected at JHU, fit by a finite-element model to be developed at the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). 2. To develop a distributed simulation of human cardiac function, incorporating a simulation of the human cardiac ventricular cell resident at JHU based on the model discussed above and a simulation of coupled cardiac mechanical and electrical function resident at UCSD, with distributed simulation control based at JHU/APL; 3. Working with the NSBRI team, to select other appropriate cardiovascular system models that can be represented over time using simulations, and integrate them into a distributed simulation of cardiovascular function; and 4. Again working with the NSBRI team, to select other system (e.g., muscle) models that can be represented over time using simulations, and integrate them into a multi-function distributed simulation representative of the full IHF simulations that will be needed for long-duration space flight. The project is leveraging the significant body of research in constructing distributed interoperable simulations that has been performed in connection with the development of the High Level Architecture (HLA) for simulations developed by the U.S. Department of Defense.

experiment_title: Bioassays of Body Fluids
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Orthostatic hypotension and weight loss were observed in the crewmembers of Gemini 3, 4, 5, and 6 immediately after flight. Scientists were concerned that space flight might affect the balance of body fluid and electrolytes since fluid losses can contribute to both of these symptoms. This led to a series of ground-based studies to simulate some of the conditions of space flight. An attempt was made to define the physiological parameters that would be affected by the condition of microgravity. These studies utilized bed rest and water immersion as a means of simulating microgravity.

Both the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems experienced changes during the ground-based studies. Changes in body fluid chemistry were found to be reflective of the status of these systems. This experiment was designed to obtain objective data concerning the effects of space flight on the human body by examining alterations in the body fluid chemistry.

APPROACH:
Preflight plasma samples were collected from all crewmembers of Gemini 7, Gemini 8, and Gemini 9 approximately 10 days and 3 days before launch. Plasma samples were not collected in flight. Gemini 7 postflight plasma samples were collected immediately after recovery, and 6 hours, 24 hours and 72 hours after flight. Gemini 9 postflight plasma specimens were collected after recovery, and 6 hours and 72 hours after flight. The Gemini 8 mission was terminated after 11 hours and no postflight data was collected for this experiment.

Urine sampling was scheduled preflight, inflight, and postflight for Gemini 7, 8, and 9. Preflight, two 48-hour urine samples were collected approximately 10 days and 3 days before launch. Inflight urine collection on Gemini 7 and 9 was accomplished by utilizing a specially designed urine transport system. The urine transport system permitted researchers to calculate the total urine volume for each void by means of tritium dilution. A 75 ml aliquot of each void was collected into a plastic sample bag and stored for return to Earth. No refrigeration was used, but benzoic acid was added as a preservative. Urine was collected continuously for 48 hours after landing. Inflight and postflight urine samples were not collected for the Gemini 8 crewmembers.

Water and fluid electrolytes were examined to determine the mechanisms associated with weight loss during flight. The concentrations of plasma sodium, potassium, and chloride ions were measured preflight and postflight, and the rates of urinary excretion of these electrolytes were determined pre-, in-, and postflight. Total plasma protein concentrations, measured preflight and postflight, were used to indicate dehydration.

Fluid intake and output were measured to determine whether weight loss was caused by sweat and insensible losses or by changes in renal function. Fluid intake was ad lib, but the quantities ingested during the pre- and postflight phases were recorded. The majority of the fluid intake was obtained with the diet. Inflight intake was estimated from a water dispensing device on board the space craft. The information was not sufficiently precise to perform calculation of fluid balance data.

To complement the water measurements and electrolyte-balance measurements, both urinary antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and aldosterone were measured. The production of ADH is responsive to thoracic blood volume changes, and it was postulated that microgravity would decrease ADH secretion and result in an increase in urinary volume. Aldosterone was measured to study the mechanisms associated with sodium excretion. Increases in aldosterone secretion would result in decreased urinary excretion of sodium, and vice versa. Researchers hypothesized that aldosterone secretion would be decreased in space flight, resulting in an increased urinary excretion of sodium.

To measure the effects of stress in space, two groups of hormones were assayed. The first group assayed, 17-hydroxycorticosteroids, was indicative of long-term stress responses. The second group assayed, catecholamines, was indicative of short-term or emergency responses. These parameters provided an objective, long-term evaluation of the physiologic cost of space flight.

Bone demineralization was evaluated by measuring calcium, magnesium, phosphate, and hydroxyproline in plasma and urine both preflight and postflight and in urine collected in flight. Changes in bone mineralization were studied by calculating the ratio of bound to unbound calcium in the plasma. This ratio was approximated from an estimate of plasma protein and calcium. Hydroxyproline, an amino acid unique to collagen, was measured in urine to study bone and collagen breakdown. It was presumed that an increased excretion of hydroxyproline accompanying bone demineralization resulted from dissolution of bone matrix.

Urinary urea concentration was measured to study protein intake and tissue metabolism. Creatinine excretion was measured to study muscle protein metabolism. Decreases of creatinine excretion are associated with loss of muscle tone and activity.

RESULTS:
When the preflight and postflight plasma samples were analyzed for Gemini 7, by far the longest Gemini flight, electrophoretic patterns were normal. All values were in the normal range, except for an anticipated increase in 17-hydroxycorticosteroids in the first sample taken after recovery. These values decreased to preflight values within 6 hours following recovery. Hydroxyproline did not change significantly. Plasma uric acid was reduced. The cause of the reduction was unknown, but presumed to be dietary. Plasma ADH was significantly elevated in the first postflight plasma sample of one subject of Gemini 7, but returned within normal range as urine output returned to normal. It was concluded that 14 days of orbital space flight did not result in any gross aberrations of plasma electrolytes.

During the first 24-hours after Gemini 7, there was marked water retention for both subjects. The output for each subject was approximately 1 liter less than the preflight 24-hour volume. In addition, there was marked retention of chloride, sodium, and potassium. The water retention and the rapid weight gain after flight were consistent with the hypothesis that weight loss during flight was the result of fluid loss. Electrolyte and water retentions observed immediately postflight in the Gemini 7 subjects were consistent with bed rest studies that showed an increased ADH secretion contributed to decreased urinary volume.

During Gemini 9, inflight urine volumes based on the tritium dilution were as great as 12 liters per urination. This great variation in urine volumes was indicative of an anomaly. Therefore, no further attempt was made to analyze or interpret the urine samples collected in flight. The Gemini 9 subjects experienced significant postflight retention of water. This was accompanied by retention of sodium, potassium, and chloride. Urinary calcium decreased slightly immediately postflight. The excretion of 17-hydroxycorticosteroids was increased immediately postflight. This was probably caused by the stress of re-entry. Postflight, the increase of plasma protein and a slightly smaller increase of plasma electrolytes were consistent with an inflight water and electrolyte loss that resulted in dehydration followed by the retention of water and electrolytes. It was not known whether the losses resulted from diuresis during flight or from sweat.

experiment_title: Cellular Immune Response
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The functional capacity of lymphocytes (phytohemagglutinin (PHA) responsiveness only) was found to be depressed for studies conducted during Apollo missions 7 through 13 and Skylab missions 3 and 4. T-lymphocyte numbers were also suppressed in Skylab. The objective of this study was to examine the effects of space flight on the cellular immune response in Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) crewmembers.

APPROACH:
Samples of heparinized peripheral venous blood (10cc) were obtained preflight and postflight on days L-30 (30 days before liftoff), L-15, L-5, R+0 (day of recovery), R+1 (recovery +1 day), R+8 and R+13. Samples were processed within 1 to 24 hours of collection. Parameters measured for this study included: 1) white blood cell concentrations, 2) lymphocyte numbers, 3) B-lymphocyte and T-lymphocyte distributions in peripheral blood and 4) lymphocyte responsiveness to PHA, pokeweed mitogen (PWM), Concanavalin A (Con A) and influenza virus antigen. Before separation, total leukocyte counts were performed using a hemacytometer and/or a Coulter Counter. Differential counts were determined using slide preparations stained with Wright’s stain.

Lymphocytes were separated by Ficoll-Hypaque centrifugation, which uses a special liquid that provides a density gradient. Higher density blood cells are pulled far down into the liquid by centrifugal action, while the more buoyant lymphocytes remain near the center. The supernatant was removed by pipette, and the resulting mononuclear cells were washed three times in minimum essential medium (MEM).

B-lymphocyte distributions were determined by calculating the percentage of 200 mononuclear cells with surface immunoglobulins, which were detected by the immunofluorescent antibody technique. The presence of E-rosette-forming lymphocytes (T-cells) was determined using a concentration of one million lymphocytes in 0.25 ml of 0.5% sheep red blood cell (SRBC) suspension. After mixing, the tubes were incubated at 37 degrees Celsius for 5 minutes, and then placed in ice water for 2 hours. Approximately half of the supernatant was removed, and the top cell layer was gently resuspended. Two hundred lymphocytes were counted with 3 or more adhering SRBC’s, which were used as criteria for E-rosetted lymphocytes.

Purified lymphocytes (one million cells) in MEM containing 40% fetal calf serum were placed in culture plates. The antigens were diluted in MEM (containing Pen-Strep and L-glutamine) in the following concentrations: 0.01 ml PHA/ml MEM; 0.01 and 0.05 ml PWM/ml MEM; and 25 and 50 micrograms Con A/ml MEM. These diluted antigens were placed in the appropriate wells of the tissue culture plates in 0.1 ml aliquots (in duplicate). The cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide atmosphere at 37 degrees Celsius (3 days for PHA and 5 days for Con A and PWM). On the day of harvest, samples were treated as described in the following section for influenza virus antigen cultures.

An inactivated monovalent type A influenza virus vaccine containing 1600 chick cell agglutinating units/ml of a Hong Kong strain was dialyzed against phosphate-buffered saline and stored at -70 degrees Celsius until used for tests. Separated lymphocytes were added in 0.1 ml aliquots for each influenza antigen dilution, and the cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide incubator at 37 degrees Celsius for periods of either 2 or 3 days. On the day of harvest, cells were pulsed for 2 hours with 1 microcurie of methyl(tritium)-thymidine, a radioactive marker. Cells were then harvested with an automated harvester onto glass-fiber filter strips and counted in a liquid scintillation counter. Data were expressed as counts per minute (CPM)/one million lymphocytes, and the stimulation index (SI) was calculated by dividing the mean result for stimulated cultures by that for unstimulated cultures. Allantoic fluid was used separately as a control of each crewman’s reactivity to chick embryo proteins.

RESULTS:
Preflight (L-30) white blood cell (WBC) counts for ASTP and Skylab were 6640±1830 WBC/mm3 and 6013±254 WBC/ mm3, respectively. The ASTP crew had significant increases in WBC numbers noted on R+0 (11,110±4210 WBC/mm3) and R+1 (13,530±610 WBC/mm3). Individual variation in WBC values was noted among the three Skylab crewmembers at R+0 (8980±5560 WBC/mm3), which is reflected in the large standard deviation. However, all values were within clinically normal ranges (7110±2400 WBC/mm3). Less variation overall was noted for total lymphocyte values; however, values at R+0 for ASTP (1950±490 lymphocyte count/mm3) and Skylab 4 (1177±381 lymphocyte count/mm3) were decreased below their previous baseline values (ASTP L-30=2820±480 lymphocyte count/mm3 and Skylab L-30=1940±670 lymphocyte count/mm3). Fluctuations in the individual values of T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes and nonreactive lymphocytes of ASTP crewmembers were indicated, but values remain within one standard deviation for normal laboratory values. T-cell values ranged from 1.29 million +/- 490,000 to 2.53 million +/- 440,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=1.59 million +/- 630,000 lymphocytes/ml), B-lymphocytes from 470,000 +/- 20,000 to 710,000 +/- 40,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=510,000 +/- 300,000 lymphocytes/ml) and nonreactive lymphocytes from 120,000 +/- 120,000 to 710,000 +/- 370,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=850,000 +/- 560,000 lymphocytes/ml). In contrast, highly significant changes were noted in B and T cell distributions of the Skylab 4 crewmen.

Results from culture studies show a definite decrease in the ability of lymphocytes to react with PHA at R+0 (SI=20±15) and R+1 (SI=12±8) for all three Apollo astronauts. Baseline SI mean at L-30 was 36±4. By R+8, all were back within normal ranges (SI range=10 to 282). Crewmembers began and remained at low-level SI ranges for Con A (3 to 49) throughout the preflight and postflight periods, except for one subject, who had a strengthened Con A stimulation of 151 at splashdown. Considerable individual variation was noted in the PWM data and no consistent trend was obtained. Variation of antigen stimulation indexes may be expected, due to the rapid exchange of cells between different compartments in the body. The entire Apollo crew responded to influenza virus England strain preflight in cultures, and one of the three astronauts responded postflight to influenza virus Hong Kong strain. Total lack of reactivity may reflect influenza susceptibility.

ASTP crewmembers experienced contact with toxic gases upon splashdown. Depressions observed at R+0 were caused by either space flight or gas exposure a few hours prior to sample analysis. Similar depressions in lymphocytic responsiveness were observed in Skylab 3 and 4 data, although both of these missions were of much longer duration than ASTP. However, in comparable missions of similar lengths (i.e., the Apollo series) no changes in lymphocytic responsiveness were reported. The toxic gas exposure was severe enough to create concern for lung inflammation, which resulted in a corticosteroid treatment on R+1. Most cortisone preparations are known to cause a lymphocytic reaction. Consequently, it is likely that the increased immunosuppressions noted by cultural responses on R+1 for all mitogens and on R+8 for Con A were attributable to the steroid therapy.

experiment_title: The Effect of Spaceflight on Pituitary Oxytocin and Vasopressin Content
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Disturbances in fluid and electrolyte balance have been noted in humans exposed to space flight, as shown by a loss of plasma volume and increased excretion of sodium and potassium. Upon return to Earth these imbalances are quickly corrected with rehydration and increased renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activity. The purpose of these investigations was to measure levels of pituitary oxytocin (OT) and vasopressin (VP) as possible indicators of changes in fluid-electrolyte balance during flight.

Approach:

An aliquot of the pituitary homogenate (1 ml of 0.1 N HCL) was diluted 1:200,000 in a 0.05 m phosphate assay buffer for radioimmunoassay of OT and VP. To eliminate interassay variability, flight and control aliquots were measured within the same OT or VP radioimmunoassay. After hormone levels were determined, protein concentrations were measured by assay with bovine serum albumin as the standard. Hormone concentrations were then calculated as a function of total protein for each posterior pituitary homogenate.

Results:

The VP content of flight rats was 32%, 32%, and 20% lower than synchronous, vivarium, and tail-suspended animals, respectively, indicating that the animals may have been dehydrated during flight, or, alternatively, pituitary stores of the hormones may have been reduced due to decreased synthetic activities of the magnocellular neurons. However, increased hemotocritis in flight rats also raises the possibility that blood volume was reduced which would also be stimulus for VP secretion. Since it has been pointed out that OT may be released in response to "neurogenic" stress, whereas VP is released in response to "physical" stress, perhaps the observed decrease in pituitary OT may be attributed to a chronic neurogenic stress the rats experienced during flight in their efforts to adapt to microgravity.

experiment_title: The Impact of Objectively Measured Sleep Deficiency and Circadian Misalignment on Performance during Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Optimal cognitive performance requires that crewmembers’ circadian rhythms be synchronized with their sleep-wake cycle and that they obtain adequate uninterrupted sleep each night. Alertness and performance, which are critical to the success of space flight operations, are governed by four major physiological determinants: 1) circadian phase (time of day); 2) number of hours awake (acute sleep deprivation); 3) nightly sleep duration (chronic sleep deficiency); and 4) sleep inertia (impaired performance upon waking). Each of these four factors has been independently associated with decrements in neurobehavioral performance and an increased risk of accidents.

Ground-based studies show that chronic sleep deficiency produces safety-significant performance decrements. A previous ten year inflight study revealed that sleep deficiency and use of sleep-promoting medication was pervasive during both short and long-duration space flight. Specifically, astronauts attempted and obtained significantly less actigraphically-estimated sleep per night on space shuttle missions than they did upon their return to Earth. Astronauts on International Space Station (ISS) missions also obtained significantly less sleep during space flight, as compared to the first week post-mission. Neither study collected performance data. However, performance data (WinSCAT and PVT) was collected contemporaneously by other inflight experiments during the inflight study.

In this investigation, the associations among sleep, sleep-promoting medication use and performance were evaluated using the existing sleep and performance databases. This study had the following specific aims:

  1. During space flight, on days when crewmembers are estimated to have circadian misalignment, they will have greater performance decrements.
  2. During space flight, crewmembers with objectively measured acute sleep deficiency (e.g., awake for more than 16 hours) will have greater performance decrements.
  3. During space flight, crewmembers with objectively measured chronic sleep deficiency (i.e., less than six hours of sleep for four or more consecutive nights) will have greater performance decrements.

APPROACH:
The investigators teamed with other investigators and/or operational personnel who collected performance data on the WinSCAT and/or PVT self-test platforms. They evaluated the correlation among objective and subjective measures of sleep quantity and quality with cognitive performance variables. Specifically, they evaluated performance in relationship to 1) circadian phase, 2) acute sleep deficiency, and 3) chronic sleep deficiency. In addition, investigators evaluated performance with regards to reported sleep-promoting medication use.

experiment_title: Rodent Tissue Repair: II. Changes in Muscle Serine Proteases, Serpins, and Matrix Molecules
experiment_description:
Objectives:

In microgravity, type I muscle fibers atrophy and lose predominance, especially in slow-twitch muscles. No increase in mononuclear cells has been observed, as is the case with simple denervation, where both types I and II fibers atrophy, without infiltration of cells but with clear satellite cell proliferation. However, degradation of the extracellular matrix (ECM) takes place after denervation and, if reinnervation is encouraged, functional recovery to near control levels may be achieved. No information is available concerning the ECM milieu, the activation of serine proteases, their efficacy in degrading ECM, and the production of locally derived natural protease inhibitors (serpins) in effecting surface proteolytic control. This study was to examine the activation of these enzymes in microgravity and their response to muscle injury, both in space and on the ground.

Approach:

Gastrocnemius muscle was crushed by clamping down a hemostat for thirty seconds. Rat cells were grown in microcarrier cultures as a source of purified PNI, and affinity chromatography was used to obtain it. To determine if differences in previously injured gastrocnemius muscles could be detected, nitrocellulose or immobilon-bound samples were sequentially probed with antibodies to plasminogen activator (PA) and two serpins (PAI and PAI-I). PA activity was also determined by amidolytic assay; serpin activity by several synthetic chromogenic assays specific for the target protease. Immunologically stained slides were viewed under epifluorescence with a microscope. Protein determination was estimated using staining.

Results:

Although PNI increased in the flight group, levels were less than in the tail-suspended group, as compared to vivarium and synchronous controls. An increase in moles of active PAI-1 occurred after muscle crush, and in all cases PAI-1 was increased compared with basal extracts. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays for both serpins indicated that crush injury itself increased the amount of active plus complexed serpin, just significantly greater in injured flight muscles. In adult innervated muscle, uPA activity was barely detectable, uPA mRNA expression was second only to the kidney, suggesting that uPA message in kidney is in "ready reserve" awaiting some type of injury for rapid activation. This supports the theory that neutral, extracellular proteases are essential to degrade components of the old basement membrane/ECM in order to allow for a basement membrane to scaffold so that orderly regeneration can take place. Likewise, from the results it may be speculated that some interference with this "ready reserve" of uPA mRNA after injury characterizes zero gravity.

experiment_title: Skeletal Development in Embryonic Quail
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous studies of limb and musculoskeletal development in quail eggs incubated onboard the Mir space station showed that there was a developmental perturbation in the early embryo that seemed to be corrected during later embryogenesis. From these results, the following objectives were identified: 1) To determine if fibronectin influences the cellular differentiation process and the subsequent formation of a mineralizable matrix; 2) To investigate the effect of microgravity on cell cycle changes and/or cell death (apoptosis); 3) To localize and compare the distribution of BMP-2, PTHrP, and alkaline phosphatase activity in the developing bone and cartilage, as affected by microgravity; and 4) To analyze the early mineral deposition by FTIRM (Fourier transform infrared microscopy) to determine chemical changes or content of the mineralization process occurring during exposure to microgravity.

APPROACH:

Light and electron microscopy were used, coupled to morphometric analysis of bone and cartilage, to evaluate limb development during space flight. The ADF contained a 1 G centrifuge so that some embryos were exposed to 1 G during flight, whereas some were maintained at 0 G. Immunohistochemistry was used to determine cellular function of cartilage and bone and evaluate any matrix change. Edax and FTIR were used to analyze the mineral component of bone.

RESULTS:

Embryos at day 6 did not show any significant alteration in development among the four groups although the number of viable embryos was small. At day 12, the ADF Flight group maintained on the centrifuge at 1xG showed good embryo viability, increased body weight and longer limbs, compared to the ADF Flight group at 0xG. No effects of flight were seen in the cartilage as measured by Type X collagen, or proteoglycan content. The day-12 embryos also did not show any flight effect on osteocalcin staining in the bone matrix. Immunostaining for Type I procollagen, which is found in the osteoblast's cytoplasm, showed greater content in the 1 G (no spin) ground control than either one of the two flight groups. This result would suggest that application of 1 G during flight does not prevent a decrease in osteoblast activity and bone loss continues during flight due to reduced formation rates. The finding that the limbs were the same length among all groups would suggest that since the embryonic limbs are largely cartilage, space flight does not have an effect on the cartilage anlage formation. Thus, bone and cartilage may be differentially affected by space flight; a conclusion that requires supporting evidence from a longer duration space flight.

experiment_title: Mechanical and Gravitational Countermeasures to Ocular Changes during Strict Head-down Tilt Bedrest
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Spaceflight associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) is associated with structural and functional ocular and cerebral changes, including optic disc edema, and develops in approximately two-thirds of astronauts during long-duration space flight. Due to the potential of irreversible functional vision changes during exploration-class space flight missions, a countermeasure capable of preventing SANS is needed. Currently, the mechanisms underlying the development of SANS are unknown, however, exposure to a constant headward fluid shift during extended spaceflight is hypothesized to play a major role. Exposure to strict 6° head-down tilt (HDT) bed rest, a spaceflight analog, has been previously shown to induce optic disc edema in two-thirds of subjects. This study will implement 30 days of strict 6° HDT bed rest in healthy subjects to investigate various countermeasures to the development of optic disc edema and SANS.

This study has the following specific aims:

1. Determine if daily exposure to actual upright posture and simulated LBNP hydrostatic pressure gradients prevents ocular and cerebral structural changes during 30 days of strict 6° head-down tilt bed rest.

2. Determine if daily exposure to actual upright posture and simulated LBNP hydrostatic pressure gradients prevents ocular functional changes during 30 days of strict 6° head-down tilt bed rest.

3. Determine if daily exposure to actual upright posture and simulated LBNP hydrostatic pressure gradients prevents vascular and cerebrospinal fluid changes during 30 days of strict 6° head-down tilt bed rest.

APPROACH

This study will include 72 human subjects separated into 6 groups (12 subjects per group): two control groups defined by NASA and four countermeasure treatment groups. Control group 1 will be upright seated during the day (16 h) and supine at night (8 h). Control group 2 will remain in strict 6° HDT bedrest with no countermeasures (Group 2). Of the four countermeasure treatment groups, two will include countermeasures NASA previously selected to investigate: daily exposure to exercise with veno-occlusive thigh cuffs during HDT bedrest (Group 3) and daily B-vitamin supplement intake during HDT bedrest (Group 4). The remaining two treatment groups include strict HDT bed rest with six hours of 25 mmHg LBNP, daily, during strict HDT bedrest (Group 5), and six hours of upright (seated) posture, daily, during the strict HDT bedrest portion of the study (Group 6).

The six-hour exposures (Group 5 and Group 6) will be split into two sessions of three-hour exposures, once in the morning and once in the afternoon. All subjects will undergo baseline data collection for 14 days before the bedrest study (ambulatory), 30 days of bedrest, and 14 days of post-bedrest recovery data collection (ambulatory). This PI is responsible for groups 1, 2, 5 and 6. :

RESULTS:

This study will lay the groundwork to determine future countermeasure strategies that can prevent SANS during space flight. It is critical to determine if optic disc edema can be prevented or attenuated utilizing the most effective, currently available fluid shift countermeasures: LBNP and gravity. Overall, the quantification and comparison of physiological changes within the six groups included in this study will help to determine the necessary magnitude and duration of countermeasure needed to prevent SANS.

OBJECTIVES:
This was the first experiment to examine the effect of long-term exposure in space flight on human hair. Hair matrix cells actively divide in a hair follicle, and they sensitively reflect physical conditions. Investigators believed by examining human hair, they could determine stress levels and metabolic conditions of a human caused by the microgravity environment and cosmic radiation. Nucleic acids (RNA and mitochondrial DNA) were extracted from the collected hair root of ten crewmembers to assess gene expression changes in response to space flight adaptation. Investigators discovered that space flight changes human hair follicle gene expression. The degree of alterations in gene expression was found to vary among crewmembers.

experiment_title: Evaluation of the Kentavr as a Countermeasure to Orthostatic Intolerance
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
One of the most important physiological changes that negatively impact flight operations and crew safety is postflight orthostatic intolerance. Orthostatic intolerance is commonly experienced by astronauts when they return to Earth and can lead to hypotension and syncope (temporary loss of consciousness, fainting, or dizziness). This problem affects about 30% of crewmembers who fly short-duration missions (4-18 days), and 83% of astronauts who fly long-duration missions. This condition creates a potential hazard for the returning crew by impairing their ability to exit the vehicle after landing. A major driver for orthostatic intolerance is plasma volume loss. Despite the use of a mandatory fluid load before re-entry, astronauts return from space with plasma volume deficits ranging from 7-20%.

To provide additional protection against space flight induced orthostatic intolerance during re-entry and landing, both NASA and the Russian Federal Space Agency use compression garments, or antigravity suits. NASA astronauts use an inflatable antigravity suit (AGS) that is worn under the Advanced Crew Escape Suit. It has five interconnected air bladders that cover the abdomen, thighs, and calves. The AGS can be inflated to pressures ranging from 0.5 per square inch (psi), which is equivalent to 25.9 mmHg, to 2.5 psi (129.3 mmHg) in increments of 0.5 psi. When inflated, the AGS provides mechanical protection that reduces venous pooling and maintains arterial pressure.

Russian cosmonauts wear a non-inflatable compression garment, called the Kentavr, which is made of an elastic fabric. It is composed of shorts that extend from the waist to the knee and a pair of gaiters that cover the calves. Each component of the Kentavr has lacings to allow for an individualized fit. The nominal pressure provided by the Kentavr is 0.6 ± 0.1 psi (30 ± 5 mmHg).

The purpose of this study was to evaluate the ability of NASA’s AGS and the Russian Kentavr garment, to prevent hypovolemia-related orthostatic intolerance.

APPROACH:
Prior to participation, 19 healthy volunteers, ages 32 – 54 years, passed a modified Air Force Class III physical. Subjects were randomly assigned to one of two groups: AGS (six men and three women) or Kentavr (six men and four women). A separate group of 16 subjects (11 men and 5 women) from a related study participated in the same protocols and served as controls (no countermeasure group).

Data collection was completed in two visits to the cardiovascular laboratory. For the first session, subjects reported to the laboratory following voluntary reduction of their dietary salt intake for 24 hours. Subjects provided a urine sample to confirm that urinary sodium was less than 100 mEq/gm-1 creatinine. Those meeting the selection criteria participated in a carbon monoxide re-breathing protocol to measure plasma volume. Subjects then received a single dose of furosemide (a loop diuretic commonly marketed under the brand name Lasix) and consumed a low salt diet provided by the investigators.

Subjects returned to the laboratory 36 hours later, when the plasma volume measurement was repeated and subjects underwent a tilt test protocol to assess orthostatic tolerance with (AGS inflated to 1.5 per square inch or Kentavr) or without a compression garment (separate study). Subjects did not consume any caffeine, nicotine, or alcohol for 12 hours and did not participate in maximal exercise or take any medications for 24 hours prior to testing.

RESULTS:
Hypovolemia
Control subjects experienced a mean loss of plasma volume of 17.1 ± 1.7%. AGS and Kentavr groups had a plasma volume loss of 16.9 ± 4.0% and 18.4 ± 2.6%, respectively. There were no statistically significant differences in plasma volume loss between groups.

Incidence of Orthostatic Hypotension/Presyncope
The ability to complete the tilt test was significantly greater in both the AGS and Kentavr subjects compared to the controls. All subjects wearing a compression garment (either AGS or Kentavr) during the tilt test completed the test without symptoms of orthostatic hypotension or presyncope (0% incidence). In contrast, only nine control subjects (56%) were able to complete the tilt test without signs or symptoms of orthostatic hypotension or presyncope.

Hemodynamic Responses
Both compression garments prevented the decrease in systolic blood pressure at test termination which was observed in control subjects. The change in systolic blood pressure of control subjects was significantly greater than in the AGS and Kentavr subjects, but no differences were found between countermeasure groups. There were no differences in diastolic blood pressure between the groups.

The change in heart rate was greater in the control subjects than in the AGS and Kentavr subjects. The elevation of heart rate in AGS and Kentavr subjects due to tilt was not significantly different between treatment groups. The drop in stroke volume at the end of tilt was significantly less in the AGS compared to the control subjects but not different between the Kentavr and controls. However, the standing stroke volumes for the AGS and Kentavr subjects were significantly higher than the controls at the end of tilt, and there was not a significant difference between AGS and Kentavr subjects. Neither the change from supine to tilt nor the final cardiac output and total peripheral resistance at tilt termination were different between groups.

experiment_title: Changes in Endocrine Regulation of Orthostatic Tolerance Following Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In response to a drop in blood pressure, catecholamines (norepinephrine and epinephrine) are released from the sympathetic nerves and the adrenal gland to adjust the heart rate and peripheral resistance and thereby maintain normal blood pressure. Disruption of this response may be responsible, at least in part, for the orthostatic intolerance that astronauts frequently experience after space flight. The objective of this study was to evaluate orthostatic changes in plasma catecholamine levels and total peripheral resistance before and after space flight.

APPROACH:
Twenty-four astronauts who flew on missions of 5 to 14 days' duration participated in this study. Blood samples were drawn at the end of a 20-minute supine rest period, and after 5 minutes of standing, for measurement of plasma norepinephrine and epinephrine levels. The blood pressure and heart rate were recorded while the astronauts were lying supine and then standing. These assessments were done 10 days before launch, on landing day and 3 days after landing.

RESULTS:
Catecholamine levels were higher when the astronauts were standing than when they were lying supine, both before and after flight. Postflight catecholamine levels were higher than preflight levels in both the supine and the standing positions. From before the flight to landing day, supine plasma norepinephrine and epinephrine levels and standing norepinephrine and epinephrine levels increased by 34%, 65%, 65% and 91%, respectively. Standing catecholamine levels were reported for only 16 astronauts. Epinephrine levels had returned to preflight levels 3 days after landing, but norepinephrine levels remained elevated. Supine heart rate, supine systolic blood pressure, standing heart rate and standing diastolic blood pressure also increased between the preflight period and landing day. However, increases in peripheral vascular resistance per unit increase in circulating norepinephrine were reduced; sympathetic nervous system activity and peripheral resistance apparently became uncoupled.

experiment_title: Circadian Rhythms of Macaca Mulatta During Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Organisms coordinate physiological processes through their circadian system. Circadian rhythms ensure that activities occur at the most favorable time. Human health and performance can be adversely affected when the rhythm is desynchronized. Research has shown that alterations in gravitational forces, such as the exposure to microgravity that astronauts undergo, can affect circadian rhythms. This study attempts to analyze the effects that exposure to microgravity has upon the circadian rhythms of different individuals.

Approach:

Animals were flown on the fourteen day Bion 11 mission and housed in the BIOS-Primate capsules. While on a light-dark cycle of 16 hours of light followed by 8 hours of dark, the animals were offered food twice a day and given performance tests four times a day. Brain temperature (Tbr), head skin temperature (Thd), ankle skin temperature (Tank), motor activity (MA), heart rate (HR), and ambient temperature within the capsule (Tamb) were all recorded at ten second intervals and stored in a digital memory unit.

Results:

Analysis of the data supports the hypothesis that the gravitational environment affects circadian rhythms. The circadian rhythm of flight animals showed a significant phase delay when compared to the control animals. Tbr in the two flight monkeys, the best indicator of the circadian rhythm of the deep body temperature, showed a slower rise during the day than that of control animals. However, no free-running rhythms were detected, and each animal had an average period of about twenty-four hours. This suggests that the Zeitgebers mask the changes in circadian rhythm. This is also evidenced by the distinct peaks in Thd that correspond to meals and performance tests. The increase in the endogenous period that remains within the entrainment range is the most probable mechanism by which the circadian rhythm does not transform into a free-running one.
