experiment_title: Objective Monitoring of Crew Neurobehavioral Functions (105-day Russian Chamber Study)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project deployed two objective neurobehavioral monitoring techniques psychomotor vigilance test (PVT); facial video for optical computer recognition (OCR) and two mood scales (Beck Depression Inventory (BDI); Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) in the 105-day Russian chamber study at the Institute for Biomedical Problems (IBMP) in Moscow, Russia. The IBMP chamber consisted of interconnected sealed modules to simulate a space craft (analog) environment that included confinement, isolation, time delays, pressurization, dependence on and autonomy from mission control, and related behavioral factors. The 105-day isolation experiment in the chamber was the second of IBMP's three chamber studies (14-day study, 105-day study, and 520-day study), which collectively are referred to by IBMP as the Mars-500 project. IBMP indicated that the 105-day chamber study focused on obtaining and analyzing scientific-technical information for optimal organization of preparation and efficient conduct of the main (third) experiment (i.e., 520-day study) simulating all the stages of a manned flight to Mars. Consequently, the 105-day chamber experiment was a pilot study for the 520-day experiment. Lessons learned in the 105-day study were to be used to improve experimental techniques and the completeness and validity of the data acquired in the 520-day study.

This project on Objective Monitoring of Crew Neurobehavioral Functions in RCS-105 was one of 72 separate protocols conducted in the IBMP's 105-day chamber study. The overall goals of this project were to (1) determine the feasibility of acquiring neurobehavioral data (facial video, cognitive performance, psychological assessments) on the six-person crew during the 105-day simulated mission, using specially programmed computers (mission controllers were added to the data acquisition requirements after the study commenced); (2) determine the feasibility of monitoring mood and fatigue states in crew members throughout the 105-day mission; and (3) Determine the reliability of 3-minute PVT performance throughout the 105 days.

APPROACH:
A total of 1,104 10-minute Psychomotor Vigilance Tasks (PVT) and 1,104 3-minute PVTs (PVT Self test) were acquired from the 6 crewmembers over the course of the 105-day chamber confinement. All 2,208 PVT test bouts completed have been extracted and reduced to key outcome variables. The 18 mission controllers completed 978 10-minute and 978 3-minute PVT trials, which have been extracted and reduced to key outcome variables. A total of 1,129 facial videos (acquired from the six crewmembers during the 3-minute PVTs) were evaluated for feasibility of analysis by optical computer recognition (OCR). A total of 1,010 facial videos (acquired from the 18 mission controllers during the 3-minute PVTs) also were evaluated for feasibility of analysis by optical computer recognition (OCR).

RESULTS:
Acquisition of neurobehavioral data on the six crewmembers during the 105-day mission in the IBMP Mars-500 chamber was successfully completed using specially programmed notebook computers. During the simulated mission, crewmembers completed a total of 85 (94%) of scheduled Beck Depression Inventories (BDI-II); 78 (87%) of scheduled Positive and Negative Affect Schedules (PANAS); 1,104 (88%) Psychomotor Vigilance Tests (PVT) and visual analog scale (VAS) ratings; and 19 (63%) of the WinSCAT tests. Facial videos of crewmembers to assess feasibility of optical computer recognition (OCR) of emotional expressions and fatigue during the PVT tests yielded only 125 (11%) videos technically adequate for OCR evaluation, due to interference from facility lighting (i.e., face shadowed or too dark). Data from 19 mission controllers showed lower adherence on all measures than did the crewmembers. Controllers completed 63% of the PANAS and BDI-II assessments, and only 50% of PVT tests. Across time in mission, crewmembers' positive mood states tended to decline modestly, but negative moods states and depression were not evident and did not increase. Similarly, VAS ratings of stress and unhappiness did not change across the 105-day mission. In contrast, VAS mental fatigue declined and alertness improved significantly across time in mission. PVT performance on the standard 10-minute PVT task showed increasing errors across time in mission, but the optimized 3-minute PVT did not, nor did measures from the WinSCAT performance battery. Mission controllers showed no reliable changes in positive or negative mood states or performance across time in mission. Night shift work by crewmembers increased subjective (VAS) ratings of sleepiness, tiredness and physical exhaustion, and increased performance errors on the PVT, especially the 3-minute. PVT.

The 105-day project results identified the following changes to procedures that would be needed to ensure the success of such data in longer-duration analog studies (e.g., IBMP's 520-day Mars mission simulation).
1. Adherence to the neurobehavioral procedures in the special computer used need to be adjusted to reduce the evaluation time burden on crews.
2. Evaluation of data quality and quantity must occur regularly throughout the mission to reduce data loss by identifying and correcting problems.
3. Acquisition of facial video for OCR from the built-in computer camera is feasible in the chamber if environmental lighting is standardized, and if special portable lighting of the face in the plane of the computer screen is used during the testing, when video is acquired.
4. Acquisition of subjective reports should use brief rating scales, assess interpersonal conflicts, and by include a measure of social desirability bias at pre-mission.
5. Actigraphy should be used 24/7 during the mission to provide an objective measure of crew behavioral rest-activity cycles for interpretation of performance and subjective data.

experiment_title: Leg Muscle Volume by Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Muscle atrophy during space flight is known to result in postflight decrements, even after short duration missions (LeBlanc et al. 1995). The objective of this study was to use Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to determine leg muscle volumes in all subjects at the start and end of bed rest.

APPROACH:
Prior to the MRI session, subjects were positioned supine for at least 30 minutes. Proton magnetic resonance images were then collected (Adams et al 1993), using a 1.5 T G.E. imaging system. Ten mm-thick image "slices" were collected at 5 mm intervals along the entire length of the right and left lower limbs. To ensure that the images cover the same range of the limb, an invariant anatomical feature, the greater trochanter of the femur, was palpated and used to set the electronic land marking of the first image slice. Images were ported to a computer workstation, and the cross sectional area (CSA) of the individual thigh and leg muscles were determined using image analysis software. These data was used to calculate the volume of each muscle and also determined the degree of muscle atrophy elicited by the bed rest and Artificial Gravity (AG) protocols.

To accurately register the images from one session to the next, the marrow area (of either the tibia or femur) was measured for each slice. High contrast between the marrow and the surrounding bone was facilitated by semi-automatic analysis. In one of the central images, a region inside the marrow was selected, and a mask was created. A program was then used to expand this mask to cover the whole marrow region. The program was iteratively expanded and contracted the mask until a stable region was selected. A file containing all the marrow size values for a particular subject was then imported into a spreadsheet from which the position offset for each session was determined by plotting the position versus number of pixels for two sessions and visually determining the offset required for the two curves to coincide. The images were corrected for non-uniformity resulting from the coil sensitivity. The normalized images were windowed to select only muscle excluding the fat pixels. The windowing script also included procedures for excluding a ring around the marrow and around the outer edge of the leg.

Individual muscles were outlined. For the thighs, the adductors, quadriceps, hamstrings, and sartorius were separated and for the calves the gastrocnemius, soleus, and anterior muscles were separated. A Mask was created by selecting all the pixels having signal intensity in the appropriate muscle range. The number of pixels in each region was outputed to a text file along with the identification of the image. This file was imported into a spreadsheet where the position offset determined from the marrow size was added to the nominal position to allow aligning the images from different sessions. The maximum region present in every session was chosen to integrate the muscle volumes. To avoid changes associated with fluid shifts occurring during transition from bed rest (nightly or experimentally), all measures of muscle volume was scheduled before subject ambulation began for the day.

Results from this study were to provide baseline data for longer duration studies.

RESULTS

This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during the Artificial Gravity Bed Rest Study. LSDA does not expect to receive results from this study.

experiment_title: Investigation of Partial-g Effects on Ocular Alignment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES

During the g-level changes of parabolic flight there are changes in torsional eye position. These changes can be markedly asymmetric and are on the order of one degree. This change in torsional alignment may be due to loss of compensation for otolith asymmetry in unusual g environments. On earth, the nervous system presumably compensates for natural asymmetries (e.g., unequal otoconial mass) in otolith properties, but in other than 1 g this compensation is inappropriate and produces torsional misalignment. A similar disconjugate change has been found during space flight, persisting throughout flights up to 180 days and for many days after flight. Torsional offsets seen in parabolic flight have been proposed as a predictive test for space motion sickness.

Motion sickness in parabolic flight has likewise been correlated with differences in counterrolling with tilts to the right and left. This is intriguing because it implies a link between motion sickness susceptibility in parabolic flight and in space flight, while other studies have not been able to establish this connection. More recently, a connection between such vestibular asymmetry and terrestrial motion sickness has also been postulated. Central neural compensation for such asymmetry becomes inappropriate in gravity fields other than 1 g, leading to potentially disruptive changes in ocular alignment. A mathematical model of the central compensating mechanisms for otolith asymmetry has been developed based on the investigator’s team findings in parabolic flight.

This study has the following specific aims: 1) Evaluate modifications that permit use of the tablet-computer system in ambien lighting. 2) Assess binocular alignment (vertical and torsional skew) in different g levels of parabolic flight. 3) Determine the nature of the function that relates the sensorimotor response of binocular alignment to instantaneous g level: continuous (with what slope) or piecewise-linear (with a threshold).

APPROACH

During vertical alignment nulling (VAN) and torsional alignment nulling (TAN) testing, the subject views a red line and a blue line on the tablet screen through color-matched red and blue filters, one over each eye. This provides separate visual information to each eye. One line, designated as the stationary line, remains fixed on the screen, while the other line, the moving line, is repositioned by the subject: vertically (up and down) during VAN and torsionally (clockwise and counter-clockwise) during TAN. The subject’s objective during both VAN and TAN is to adjust the moving line until it appears perfectly in-line with the stationary line (i.e., to null any apparent vertical or rotational offset between the two lines). If there exists a small range for which the moving line appears aligned with the stationary line, meaning that the subject can perceptually fuse a slight physical offset in the two lines, the subject is instructed to find the middle of that range. The final amount by which the lines are separated from one another vertically or rotated relative to one another provides a measure of vertical and torsional ocular misalignment, respectively. For example, if a subject sets the right line above the left line during VAN, then researchers infer that this individual has a vertical misalignment such that the right eye is elevated relative to the left eye (i.e., the right fovea is elevated above the left fovea). If a subject orients the right line clockwise relative to the left line during TAN, then researchers infer that this subject has a torsional misalignment such that the right eye is extorted relative to the left eye. If a subject perfectly aligns the two lines during both VAN and TAN, then researchers infer that this individual has normal vertical and torsional binocular alignment.

RESULTS

Based on previous studies the researchers anticipate a threshold of about 0.3g between the response (binocular alignment) present in 1g and that present in 0g, for a given subject. A mathematical model suggests a slightly higher (not as abrupt) transition at about 0.6, so the researchers anticipate a switching threshold in the range of 0.3 to 0.6 g.

experiment_title: Morphology of End and Intermediate Brain
experiment_description:
Objectives:

One goal of spaceflight is to determine the neuronal mechanisms by which an organism adapts to microgravity in spaceflight. One structure that has shown changes in previous spaceflights is the cerebral cortex. However, in all previous studies, subjects had been exposed to reentry stresses, increasing the proprioceptive impulses to the brain. SLS-2 offered the first opportunity to examine the somatosensory and visual cortex of rats exposed to microgravity with out reentry effects.

Approach:

Three groups of rats were used, one group was decapitated on flight day 13, the others were decapitated five hours post flight and 14 days post flight. Brains were removed from skulls no more than three minutes after decapitation and sectioned in half along the midline. Sections were fixed in glutaraldehyde in 0.1M cacodylate buffer, pH 7.3 at 4 C. After fixation, cortical fragments were cut into 0.3-0.5 mm wide strips, dehydrated in ethanol of increasing concentrations and in acetone. They were then embedded in araldite oriented on such a way that all cortical sections were cut when making ultrathin frontal sections. Electron microscopy was performed on these sections by Russian specialists. Ultrathin sections of 3-5 blocks of each cortical area was examined with a JEM electron microscope.

Results:

Electron microscopic examinations of the somatosensory cortex of rats decapitated in flight revealed ultrastructural changes in the II-IV layers, which pointed to a lower number of signals entering the cortex in microgravty. This was seen as by an emergence of presynaptic axonal terminals with a low electron density of the matrix and an insignificant content of synaptic vessicles, termed "light" axonal terminals. The study of the ultrastructure of the somatosensory cortex of rats decapitated 14 days after recovery indicates that microgravity induced changes are reversible, but not complete after 14 days.

experiment_title: Neuroendocrine and Immune Responses in Humans during and After Long Term Stay at ISS
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Immuno will determine neuroendocrine and immunological changes during and after working and living on the International Space Station (ISS). A focus on cellular energy metabolism and cell signaling will provide additional information on the psycho-neuroendocrine and immunologic adaptation of human physiology to space and a better insight on how these processes are dependent on the cellular level of signal processing. The aim of this experiment was to determine changes in stress and immune responses, during and after a stay on the ISS. This included the sampling of saliva, blood and urine to check for hormones associated with stress response and for carrying out white blood cell analysis.

APPROACH:
Space flight effects on the immune system were studied in 30 cosmonauts flown onto the ISS for long- and short-term missions. Immunological investigations before launch and after landing were performed by using methods for quantitative and functional evaluation of the immunologically competent cells. Specific assays include: peripheral leukocyte distribution, natural killer (NK) cell cytotoxic activity, phagocytic activity of monocytes and granulocytes, proliferation of T-cells in response to a mitogen, levels of immunoglobulins IgA, IgM, IgG, virus-specific antibody and cytokine in serum.

RESULTS:
This investigation analyzed the immune system of 30 astronauts on short- and long-duration missions. Observations include: no notable changes in antiviral antibody levels, specific antibodies for Epstein-Barr viruses. There is a marked increase in white blood cells, however no change in overall population of T- and B-lymphocytes. Observed decreases in T-lymphocyte function, cytokines (cell-signaling agents), and in population and activity of natural killer cells (defenders against microbes and toxins) could mean more susceptibility to potential infections. Because such alterations could compromise the body's defenses against pathogens, in depth studies of the post-flight immune system in human space explorers are essential.

experiment_title: Speech Alarms Pilot Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Correct and fast detection, discrimination, and identification of alarms are crucial to crew safety, efficiency, and mission success. Speech alarms can reduce cognitive workload and may lead to faster and more accurate detection of anomalous conditions than tone-based alarms. Existing caution and warning systems on NASA spacecraft have used only non-speech auditory signals for the three categories of alerts: caution, warning, and emergency. Redundant alarms, such as the combination of speech and tone information can ensure that the alarms are detected faster and more accurately, even in conditions of noise or high workload, or when eyes are busy. Deconditioned crewmembers may also be aided by the supplemental information provided in a speech alarm. During missions beyond Low-Earth Orbit, it will be critically important for crew to be able to detect off-nominal situations so that they can put the vehicle/habitat in a safe configuration without ground coordination. This is highly relevant when considering missions with increasing crew autonomy.

Previous studies conducted in 2008-2010 evaluated auditory alerts currently in use with NASA flight deck displays along with proposed candidate alerts. In the 2009 study, non-crew and crew participants were asked to compare and rate in each category six candidate alerts relative to the current ones on their adequacy. One sound included a speech component after the alert tone, termed a “speech suffix” that gave additional information about the location of the event. The results showed that the inclusion of a speech suffix was preferred by both crew and non-crew subjects. In a follow-on 2010 study, various combinations of tone, speech, and speech suffix components were used with and without background conversation noise (voice loop). Overall, alerts starting with a speech component were identified faster than alerts starting with a tone. Listening to the alerts over the voice loop led to decreased identification speed, but speech alarms were still identified faster than tones. These results show that speech alarms lead to faster identification even in the presence of background noise. Due to advances in sound synthesis, investigators would like to replicate the study with higher quality sounds. They would also like to determine if in addition to identification time, response to the content of the alert is also improved. This work would provide the opportunity to begin establishing the feasibility and potential benefits of speech alarms. This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Replicate the 2010 study with new sound stimuli to validate results related to speech alarms.
  2. Conduct a pilot test in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA), potentially including crew participants, to demonstrate the feasibility of speech alarms in a realistic environment.

APPROACH:
The current study replicated the results from the previous study in a more rigorous experimental design to determine if the candidate speech alarms are ready for transition to operations or if more research is needed. Participants were instructed to complete items on a task list and respond to caution and warning alerts as they occurred. The HERA portion of this study was a feasibility assessment only.

RESULTS:
Four types of alarms (caution, warning, fire, and depressurization) were presented to participants in both tone and speech formats in laboratory settings and later in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA). In the laboratory study, the alerts were presented by software and participants were asked to identify the alert as quickly and as accurately as possible. Reaction time and accuracy were measured. Participants identified speech alerts significantly faster than tone alerts. The HERA study investigated the performance of participants in a flight-like environment. Participants were instructed to complete items on a task list and respond to C&W alerts as they occurred. Reaction time and accuracy were measured to determine if the benefits of speech alarms are still present in an applied setting.

experiment_title: Evaluation of Exercise Hardware for use in the Crew Exploration Vehicle
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During space flight, astronauts lose muscle mass, muscle strength, and muscle power. The decrease in muscle performance is concerning because it might impair the astronauts’ ability to perform various tasks that are critical to mission success and safety. There are currently exercise devices used on the International Space Station (ISS) to counteract the effects of zero gravity, but those are too large (weight and size) for use on the upcoming crew exploration vehicle, Orion. With this in mind, new more compact exercise devices are being designed and prototyped to evaluate their capabilities. The Exercise Physiology and Countermeasures (ExPC) Project was tasked with performing evaluations of these prototype devices in order to assess their potential for being included in an exploration vehicle. This evaluation was performed as an engineering checkout of two proposed exercise devices: an Inertia Wheel prototype exercise device and an Air Spring prototype exercise device. During the functional evaluation, a rowing exercise (aerobic and anaerobic) and a series of resistance exercises were performed at sub-maximal effort to ensure the devices were operating properly and to evaluate the performance of each device.

APPROACH:
Seven exercise subjects participated in this evaluation. All subjects were approved by the Human Test Subject Facility and provided informed consent. The evaluation was approved by the Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects. Subjects were in general good health with no recent sickness or injury, had no history of cardiovascular or musculoskeletal disease, and were free of significant muscle, joint, or bone injury for the last six months. Subjects were briefed on the protocol they performed and signed the consent form before proceeding with any testing.

Prior to any test sessions, subjects participated in a familiarization session during which they had the opportunity to practice exercising on each device, and received instruction on how to properly perform the resistance training exercises in the evaluation on each device. For each resistance exercise, subjects had the opportunity to perform at various loading levels. The resistance in the Inertial Wheel is created by a spinning flywheel, and was dependent upon how fast or slow the subject moved. The resistance in the Air Spring is created by air pressure inside a resistance cylinder, and can be lowered or raised by the user, just like a typical weight lifting machine. Because it was important that subjects lift approximately the same level of resistance with each device, they completed their practices on the Inertial Wheel first, and the loads that they developed during practice were measured and recorded. When subjects completed their practice on the Air Spring, the loads they developed with the Inertial Wheel were used to determine the Air Spring loads. Those loads were used on the Air Spring during the later data collection. After the familiarization session, subjects were scheduled for two exercise tests during which data was collected. There was at least 48 hours between scheduled sessions to ensure that subjects were fully recovered and free from fatigue.

During the exercise tests subjects participated in the following protocol:

Subjects reported to the specified test location in comfortable exercise shoes. They were provided with a spandex shirt and shorts to wear during the testing. They were given a chance to practice with the equipment and perform some simple muscle stretches. They then began the rowing exercise. They were instructed to row slowly and with a steady motion, and not to strain themselves or pull hard. While rowing, the test operators recorded force and speed data from the device. Subjects rowed for up to five minutes at a pace that they selected. Subjects were encouraged to row at a pace that made them feel like they’re moderately exercising, but that they could continue at for the entire five minutes. When the five minute session was complete, subjects were given a questionnaire asking about their experience exercising on the device. After they were rested, subjects completed a second rowing exercise trial. During this trial, subjects were asked to complete one minute of exercise, and to exercise at a pace they could sustain for one minute, but would have trouble continuing after a minute had passed. During space flight, the astronauts will need to perform high intensity exercise to stay healthy, and the investigators needed to understand if the devices are capable of allowing high intensity exercise to occur. After one minute, subjects stopped exercising, and were once again asked to complete a questionnaire detailing their experience with the device.

After completing the rowing exercise, subjects completed resistance exercises on the other device. Subjects had another opportunity to try the squat, dead lift, diagonal dead lift, heel raise, bench press, shoulder press, full body press, upright row, bicep curls, bent over rows, and triceps press. For each movement, subjects were asked to perform a light lift, medium lift, and a heavy lift at their self-selected intensity level. If a device was not capable of allowing a certain exercise, it was not attempted. Subjects completed a questionnaire during the rest periods. They rested from 30-90 seconds between each set. Subjects could request longer rest periods between tests if necessary. Load and speed data from the device were collected during each set.

During each exercise session, the motions of the subject’s arms, legs, and upper body were measured using a motion capture system with 12 cameras. Reflective markers were placed on the subjects with double-sided adhesive tape. The markers were attached to their clothing. If markers need to be attached to a body location that is not covered with clothing (knees), the marker was attached to fabric prewrap. A digital video camera recorded the subjects’ movements. They wore a chest strap heart rate monitor that was used to measure heart rate during all exercise.

RESULTS:
This experiment has concluded. Data will be used only to characterize capabilities of each device. No data will be published; this is an engineering evaluation only.

experiment_title: Detection and Prevention of Neurobehavioral Vulnerability to Space Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The critically-needed research on the effects of ionizing radiation on cognitive/behavioral functions will provide the basis for extrapolating the effects of the space radiation environment on human cognitive function and performance. Earth-based applications of this research will extend to comparing the effects of other types of radiation exposures (e.g., from the workplace, medical environment, home) on neurobehavioral functions. Knowledge of those neurobehavioral functions and related brain areas affected by acute exposure to space radiation is extremely important in not only the development of a biobehavioral risk assessment model of radiation-induced deficits that could compromise operational performance during long-duration space exploration missions, but also in the development of mitigation strategies, countermeasures, as well as appropriate self-administered tests that astronauts can use to gauge their performance readiness for critical tasks. In addition, the development of a comprehensive and experimentally flexible animal model of neurobehavioral performance provides a useful tool for preclinical research and development in other domains such as sleep/chronobiology, neuropsychiatric disorders, aging, and cognitive enhancement. Moreover, the human Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) is a standardized and widely validated objective measure of neurobehavioral status not only employed by NASA, but also utilized in a variety of settings such as clinical neuropsychiatric assessment, military, shiftwork, and aviation. As such, the present rodent analog of the PVT (rPVT) provides a direct translational link to performance capacity on Earth. Once validated, the rPVT model developed here may be used as a basic and translational research tool to predict performance deficits induced by radiation or other CNS insults while providing an innovative experimental platform for exploring the bases of individual vulnerability to performance impairments and evaluating potential prophylactics, countermeasures, and treatments.

Specific Aims:

  1. To assess the effects of space radiation across a range of neurobehavioral functions in rodents, including assessments of general motor function and speed, inhibitory control ( impulsivity ), timing, learning, selective attention, and motivation.
  2. To assess the long-term effects of radiation across a range of cognitive/behavioral functions via extended post-exposure testing for potential performance deficits.
  3. To assess both the acute and long-term effects of radiation on the neurochemical mechanisms underlying changes in neurobehavioral functions by examining the integrity of the neurotransmitter systems known to mediate those neurobehavioral functions found impaired.

APPROACH:
To evaluate the neurobehavioral performance risks during long-duration missions the effects of head-only proton irradiation at low levels were examined in adult rats while performing in the rPVT to follow neurobehavioral performance (decreased accuracy, increased impulsivity, and increased lapses in attention) and slow motor function.

RESULTS:
Results from the project have demonstrated the reliability and validity of the neurobehavioral procedures in detecting behavioral changes following radiation, and that such procedures can be used to effectively track changes in neurobehavioral function over extended intervals following radiation exposure. Using the rPVT, head-only exposure to radiation (including both protons and 56Fe particles) has been shown to significantly impair neurobehavioral function (e.g., decreased accuracy, increased impulsivity, increased lapses in attention) and slow motor function. These findings support the success of the rPVT as a rodent model for studying the risks of living in the space radiation environment due to changes in neurobehavioral function.

Specific findings from this study include:
1. Demonstrating that individual differences in susceptibility to the effects of radiation exist, with 56% of rats exposed to proton radiation showing a radiation sensitivity as indicated by marked neurobehavioral deficits, with these deficits being independent of dose (i.e., 25 cGy produced effects similar to 50 – 200 cGy). Importantly, only radiation-sensitive animals showed significant changes in proteins associated with the levels of dopamine (DA) D2 receptors as well as dopamine transporter (DAT) in the brain, suggesting that DA level differences may play an important role in how an organism responds to radiation neurobehaviorally, and have important implications for possible screening of radiation sensitivity and future development of radioprotectants.

2. Demonstrating that exposure to 56Fe ions at 10, 25, and 50 cGy produces highly specific effects on vigilance. Similar to the effects of proton radiation, 56Fe ion exposures produced an "individual differences" effect in that only a subset of irradiated animals showed neurobehavioral deficits (i.e., were "radiation sensitive"), with these deficits also being independent of dose. In contrast to proton radiation, 56Fe radiation did not produce deficits in inattention or motor function, and 56Fe radiation produced deficits in only 15% of the exposed animals.

3. Assessing the initial inflammatory response in the brain following proton irradiation by examining the expression of translocator protein 18 kDa (TSPO), a sensitive marker of reactive gliosis in proton-exposed rats. TSPO levels were significantly elevated in the forebrain, cerebellum, and whole brain tissue following proton exposure up to 14 days post-exposure, suggesting that proton radiation causes immediate damage to the brain via inflammation and reactive gliosis, and that the immediate inflammatory response and likely subsequent glial cell death and extended brain inflammation could underlie such neurobehavioral changes following proton exposure and impact an individual's sensitivity to proton radiation.

4. Studies supported by this grant were conducted by Dr. Catherine Davis as part of her newly-funded NSBRI Postdoctoral Fellowship to determine the degree to which radiation-induced deficits in neurobehavioral function differ as a function of basal dopaminergic function. Using inbred rats with inherent differences in dopamine (DA) function (Fischer 344 and Lewis rats), radiation-sensitive rats were found in the inbred Fischer rats, a strain with greater functioning DA system compared to Lewis rats but not yet in the Lewis strain, indicating again a possible involvement of the dopaminergic system in an individual's susceptibility to radiation-induced neurobehavioral damage to the central nervous system (CNS).

The results demonstrate the sensitivity of tests such as the rPVT for assessing the effects of head-only space radiation on cognitive neurobehavioral function. Such deficits could significantly impact routine performances in operational environments during long-duration exploratory missions, and also negatively affect post-mission adjustment upon return to Earth. These findings support the likely continued success of the rodent model for studying the cognitive, neurobehavioral, and CNS risks associated with living in the space radiation environment while providing an innovative experimental platform for exploring the bases of individual vulnerability to radiation-induced impairments and evaluating potential prophylactics, countermeasures, and treatments.

experiment_title: Sensitivity Modulation of Different T-Cells Activation Pathways by Microgravity (PADIAC)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Mammalian cells subjected to conditions of simulated microgravity on ground as well as to space flight conditions are showing alterations in their structure and function. Changes in proliferation, differentiation and genetic expression have been demonstrated in several types of cells. Among the mammalian cells, the cells of the immune system, in particular, are severely affected by the space environment. Especially T-lymphocytes are altered in their activation process. Changes in growth rate, cytokine production, locomotion, gene expression and protein kinase C (PKC) distribution have been observed on Space Shuttle flights. The main objectives of this proposal are to further investigate, using several activators, the genetic expression of the co-stimulatory transduction pathway mediated by the CD28, to assess whether the IL-1 receptor is involved in the inhibition of the activation, to see if the activation is also restored in space as it is in simulated microgravity using anti-CD3/IL-2 and to determine which genes are than expressed under these special conditions.

APPROACH:

PADIAC will utilize thirteen dedicated Type-1 Experiment Containers (EC). The experiment will be uploaded on Space Shuttle in passive thermal control unit to maintain the temperature above +25 degrees C to ensure good viability of the samples. Upon arrival to ISS, the ECs are installed in the Kubik incubator, prewarmed to +37 degrees C. Following a short pre-incubation period the experiment is started by adding activator. Samples are then fixed with RNAlaterTM at 2, 4 and 24-hour intervals after activation. Following fixation the cassettes are stowed, refrigerated, in the case of download within a few days of fixation. For longer on-orbit stowage (less than 2 weeks) the samples are maintained at -20 degrees C until download.

RESULTS:

The flight experiment was completed in 2011 and differences were found in immune response using either ConA/antiCD28, magnetic beads CD3/CD28 and CD3 or IL-2 activation methods. Both activation mechanisms of ConA/CD28 and CD3/CD28 activate the immune system. The absence of CD28 could replace induction of itself (IL2) and IL-2 could replace the need for CD28. Microgravity caused severe reduction of key immune gene expression of IL2, IL2ra, TNFa, Xcl2, EGR1, CCL20, GMCSF, and IFNg. Due to lack of sample and quality of RNA, we unfortunately were unable to use gene chip technology to find new pharmaceutical targets. No data submitted. Summarized and analyzed data may be available through publications. Omics data is available from GeneLab's Data Repository at https://genelab-data.ndc.nasa.gov/genelab/.

experiment_title: Retrospective Study of Serum Sclerostin Measurements in Bedrest Subjects
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Reduced mechanical loading, as in prolonged bed rest, immobilization or space flight, is invariably associated with bone loss. New investigations are needed to gain insight into the mechanisms underlying the musculoskeletal response to mechanical loading, thereby identifying novel targets for preventing musculoskeletal deterioration in situations of reduced mechanical loading, such as bed rest, immobilization, stroke, spinal cord injury, and age-related reductions in physical activity. Osteocytes are believed to play a key role in skeletal mechanosensing, modulating bone modeling, and remodeling by orchestrating the activity of osteoblasts and osteoclasts. However, little is known in humans as to how osteocytes respond to and regulate skeletal adaptation to mechanical unloading.

In mice, exposure to hindlimb tail suspension leads to increased osteocyte apoptosis in both trabecular and cortical bone. It has been postulated that osteocyte cell death is an initiator signal for osteoclast remodeling activity or that loaded osteocytes release an osteoclast-inhibiting factor. Furthermore, mature osteocytes are one of the only cells that express, postnatally, the protein sclerostin, a product of the gene SOST. Sclerostin protein has been shown, in vitro and in vivo, to be a strong inhibitor of bone formation, acting in part through the Wnt/B-catenin pathway to reduce osteoblast proliferation and differentiation. Consistent with the negative effect of sclerostin on bone mass, transgenic mice over expressing SOST have low bone mass, whereas SOST-null animals have high bone mass in line with the human conditions of Van Buchem’s disease and sclerosteosis, which are due to inactivating mutations in the SOST gene. Furthermore, the SOST/Sclerostin pathway has been implicated in the bone’s response to mechanical loading, such that increased skeletal loading reduces SOST/Sclerostin levels, and decreased mechanical loading leads to higher SOST/Sclerostin levels.

Specific Aims:

1. Determine whether skeletal unloading increases circulating levels of sclerostin by conducting assays in archived serum specimens of subjects exposed to 90 days of bed rest.
2. Determine association between serum sclerostin and standard measures of bone turnover markers (urine N-teleopeptide (NTX), serum osteocalcin and bone specific-alkaline phosphatase (BSAP).
3.Determine association between increase in serum sclerostin and BMD changes following bed rest (an analog for space flight).

APPROACH:
Seven healthy adult men underwent 90-day six-degree head down tilt bed rest at The University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) – NASA bed rest facility. Subjects were: a) between the ages of 25 and 55 years; b) required to pass a modified Air Force Class III flight physical within one year prior to the study; c) mentally fit for bed rest study as assessed by psychiatric interview and test; and d) not currently taking prescribed medication that would have interfered with physiological measurements, including bisphosphonate therapy. Serum and urine were collected prior to bed rest and during bed rest. The study protocol was approved by the NASA JSC Institutional Review Board, and all subjects gave informed consent prior to participation.

Areal bone mineral density (BMD) was measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA, Hologic Discovery). BMD of the whole body, lumbar spine, left and right hips, heel, and forearm was assessed at baseline and repeated at BR-60 and 5 days after the end of the bed rest period (BR+5). Serum sclerostin levels were assayed using the APLCO/Biomedica human sclerostin kit per manufacturer’s recommendations. Measurements were made on two pre-bed rest measurements and during bed rest days 28, 60, and 90 (BR-28, B-60, and BR-90). Assays were run in duplicate.

Markers of bone metabolism, formation and resorption were also assayed in urine and serum specimens, including serum parathyroid hormone (PTH), testosterone, leptin, 1,25 Vitamin D, markers of bone turnover (bone specific alkaline phosphatase, RANKL/OPG, and osteocalcin), and urinary calcium and phosphorus excretion normalized to creatinine, and 24 hour pooled urinary markers of bone turnover normalized to creatinine. All biochemical analyses were performed by personnel at the NASA Johnson Space Center Nutritional Biochemistry Laboratory with standard commercial techniques. For all serum and urine markers, the two pre-bed rest measurements samples were averaged to provide a single baseline value for each subject.

RESULTS:
Serum sclerostin increased after bed rest in all subjects. Specifically, serum sclerostin levels increased above BL at BR-28 and appeared to plateau in most subjects at BR-60. Sclerostin levels remained mildly elevated at BR-90, although this result did not reach statistical significance. In contrast, serum PTH levels declined at BR-28 and BR-60, remained reduced at BR-90, but did not reach statistical significance.

Urinary levels of bone resorption markers (NTX, DPD, PYD) increased significantly compared with BL at all time points. Urinary calcium excretion was also significantly increased throughout the study, whereas urinary phosphorus levels were elevated at BR-28 and BR-60, with a return to BL at BR-90. Serum bone formation markers (serum BSAP, osteocalcin), serum RANKL, OPG, and the RANKL/OPG ratio did not change. 25 (OH) vitamin D was above BL at all time points (P = 0.005), whereas 1,25 (OH)2 vitamin D was significantly lower than BL at BR-28 and tended also to be lower at BR-60 (P = 0.06) and BR-90 (P = 0.07).

Subjects had normal BMD because BL Z-scores at the distal radius, lumbar spine, total hip, and femoral neck were 0.2 ± 0.7, 0.6 ± 1.0, 0.2 ± 1.0, and 0.0 ± 1.3, respectively. BMD declined significantly at BR-60 and BR+5 at all weight-bearing skeletal sites, including the lumbar spine, hip, femoral neck, and calcaneus. There was no change in forearm BMD.

experiment_title: Mutagenic Effectiveness of Known Doses of Gamma Irradiation
experiment_description:
Objectives:

An experiment exploring the mutagenic effects of known doses of radiation in combination with microgravity on Neurospora crassa was first flown on the Gemini XI mission, in 1966. In Gemini XI, conidia were tested on both the surface of Millipore filters and in a colloidal suspension of sugar, and a 32P beta- ray radiation source was used. This experiment was to conduct a similar study on the genetic effects of space flight alone and in combination with known doses of radiation, on the surface of Millipore filters, using a 32Sr gamma-ray radiation source.

Approach:

A genetically marked two-compartment heterokaryon, heterozygous for two different genes that control sequential steps in purine biosynthesis, was used. The frequency of radiation-induced recessive lethal mutations, chromosome deletions, and overall survival were studied. A range of radiation exposures was given to determine the dose-response curves.

Results:

There was no difference between flight and ground control samples for survival, the overall induction of ad-3 mutations, or for point mutations or chromosome deletions. Gemini XI data show that space flight affected samples on Millipore filters in the same way as on Biosatellite II, with no effect on survival or mutation induction. Gemini Neurospora flown in suspension, however, had higher levels of survival and lower frequencies of mutation induction, due to a specific effect on point mutations and not on chromosome-deletion mutations. Through addition postflight experimentation, it was shown that anoxia, which may have occurred inflight, can produce a reduction in the frequencies of both point-mutations and chromosome-deletions. The effects of weightlessness on radiation-induced genetic damage are complex. Both antagonistic and synergistic effects have been found. The results depend on the assay system; in most cases however, the effects are small, twofold to fivefold differences being the usual order of magnitude.

experiment_title: Development of Methods/Technologies for Medication Stability and Shelf-life
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study analyzed nine expired medications that were returned from the International Space Station (ISS) in numbers sufficient for analysis. These medications included several of the most heavily used by the crewmembers: two sleep aids, two antihistamines/decongestants, three pain relievers, an antidiarrheal, and an alertness medication. There are no control samples available, which is a significant drawback. Notwithstanding, investigators suggested that analysis should be conducted using the HPLC/MS methods described in the United States Pharmacopeia (USP) for each of these medications to measure the amount of intact active ingredient in each medication, identify degradation products, and measure their amounts as well. Without ground controls, investigators cannot answer the question of differences in flight-aging compared to ground-aging. However, determination of the safety and efficacy of these nine heavily-used medications soon after storage on the ISS will provide useful information on the stability of these medications and may help determine the priority of future studies.

APPROACH:
Nine medications were chosen on the basis of their availability for study. Each medication was available at a single time point; analysis of the same medication at multiple time points was not possible. Because the samples examined in this study were obtained opportunistically from medical supplies, there were no control samples available (i.e. samples aged for a similar period of time on Earth); a significant limitation of this study.

RESULTS:
Only one medication met USP requirements five months after its expiration date. Four of the nine (44%) medications tested met USP requirements eight months post expiration. Another three medications (33%) met USP guidelines 2-3 months before expiration.

experiment_title: The Effects of Prolonged Space Flight on Head and Gaze Stability During Locomotion
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Newly returned astronauts have shown instability in walking and in making jump landings and have experienced oscillopsia (apparent bouncing of viewed objects). The mechanisms of these abnormalities are not known, although changes in muscle tone, muscle activation patterns and vestibular function could contribute. Instability of gaze could result from changes in the coordination of head and body movements. The objectives of this study were to investigate space flight-induced changes in locomotor control, including changes in the coordination of movements of the head, trunk and legs during walking, and the relation of those changes to the ability to maintain a stable gaze; changes in the ability to maintain spatial orientation while walking; and changes in motor strategies for absorbing impact during jump landings.

APPROACH:
Locomotor control was studied in 5 protocols. For 4 of the protocols, reflective markers affixed to appropriate places on the astronaut's head, spine, and limb joints were tracked by 4 video cameras. The position of each marker in space was determined with the aid of a video-based motion analysis system. In some of the studies, some subjects also wore shoes with foot switches beneath the heel and great toe.

In 3 of the protocols, the astronauts walked on a motorized treadmill at 6.4 km/h (4 mph) while wearing a safety harness attached to an overhead frame. (The protocol using the treadmill was denoted as DSO 614A and was performed on the following missions: STS-43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 53, 57, 58, 63, and 65). The treadmill tests were performed under 3 conditions: with the astronauts fixating on a visual target either 30 cm or 2 m in front of them, or alternating open eyes and closed eyes for 5 seconds at a time while trying to keep the eyes directed at the target. Eye closures were confirmed by electro-oculography. Data from about 10 days before flight and from 2 to 4 hours after landing were used for comparisons. Head-trunk coordination was studied in 23 astronauts (19 male, 4 female) who flew on 8- to 15-day missions. Fifteen were veterans of previous space flights. Recordings were made of the vertical movements of the trunk and the pitch movements of the head. Lower limb movements were studied in 7 astronauts (6 male, 1 female) on 8- or 9-day missions. Five were veterans of previous space flights. The angular displacement and angular velocity of the hip, knee and ankle in the front-to-back and vertical directions were determined from the video recordings, and the times of heel strike and toe off were determined from foot switch data or from toe velocity. Plots of angular velocity versus angular displacement were used to represent the periodic motion of each joint. Neuromuscular activation patterns were studied in 10 astronauts (7 male, 3 female) who flew on 8- to 15-day missions. Six were veterans of previous space flights. This protocol did not make use of the reflective markers and cameras; instead, electromyographic (EMG) recordings were made from electrodes placed on the skin over selected muscles of the lower limb. Foot switch data were also collected. The EMG recordings were normalized with regard to the level of activation and the temporal relation to heel strike, yielding reduced waveforms that represented the activity of each muscle throughout the gait cycle.

Spatial orientation while walking a path was studied in 7 astronauts (5 male, 2 female) who flew on 8- to 14-day missions (STS-64, 66, 67, 68); this protocol was referred to as DSO 614B. The astronauts walked clockwise and counterclockwise around a triangular path, either with their eyes open or with their vision blocked after they had looked at the path. The astronauts wore a helmet equipped with blackened goggles to block vision and headphones that played white noise to mask auditory spatial cues. Three reflective markers extended above the helmet, and their positions were used to compute the astronauts' walking direction and velocity. Data from 15 days before flight and from 2 hours after landing were used for comparisons.

Movements of the lower limb and the center of mass during jump landings were studied in 9 astronauts (8 male, 1 female) who flew on 7- to 14-day missions. The tests were performed 2 to 6 months and 9 to 15 days before launch and within 4 hours of landing. While wearing a safety harness and reflective markers, an astronaut jumped from a platform 30 cm (1 ft) high and landed on both feet. Jumps made with eyes open and fixated on a target were alternated with jumps made with eyes closed and directed toward the remembered target. The angles and angular velocities of the ankle, knee and hip joints were computed from the positions of the markers. The time of impact was determined from foot switch data or from toe velocity. The position of the astronaut's center of mass was estimated from the marker positions, and the velocity of the center of mass was calculated. A simple mathematical model for the vertical motion of the center of mass, in which a spring and a parallel damping mechanism represented the legs, was used to evaluate the stiffness and damping functions of the legs.

RESULTS:
In the preflight treadmill tests of head-trunk coordination, pitch head movements were smoothly coordinated to oppose the vertical movements of the trunk, thereby helping to maintain a stable gaze. The coherence between these wavelike movements decreased significantly after space flight, and the decrement in coherence was greater with the far visual target than with the near target. Both before and after space flight, the amplitude of the pitch head movements was greater with the near visual target, which would have larger apparent motion and would provide stronger feedback. After space flight, with near (or far) visual targets, the amplitude of pitch head movements was reduced in 6 (8) astronauts, unchanged in 13 (11), and increased in 4 (4) astronauts. The reductions occurred in novice astronauts, but not in veterans. Both before and after flight, when the eyes were closed the head was tilted forward and the amplitude of pitch head movements was reduced. The amplitude was restored almost immediately when the eyes were again opened.

In the treadmill studies of lower limb movement, variability in the gait cycle increased after space flight. Variability increased for the knee at the time of heel strike, for the ankle during the swing phase and for the hip at the moment of toe off. However, the increased variability in the motion of individual joints did not interfere with the basic pattern of lower limb coordination, and the stability of the system as a whole was retained. The basic temporal characteristics of the gait cycle were also retained: the stride time and the proportion of time spent standing during each step varied less than the variability of the treadmill speed. It was surprising that so little change was detected in the overall gait pattern, considering the wide-based, cautious, shuffling gait of several astronauts when they entered the testing room after flight. Use of the treadmill may have limited the gait abnormalities that could be detected by requiring a subject to keep the pace and restricting the width of the gait. Also, some astronauts chose not to walk on the treadmill after landing, perhaps feeling that their coordination was not yet sufficient for the task. Perhaps greater changes would have been detected in these astronauts' gait.

In the treadmill studies of neuromuscular activation, the symmetry of activation of the muscles of the 2 lower limbs was not affected by space flight. Few preflight-to-postflight differences occurred in the all-subject average of reduced waveforms for each muscle. However, significant functional increases and decreases were observed after space flight in the normalized mean amplitudes for various muscles around the times of toe off and heel strike. Also, between the preflight and postflight tests, co-contraction of the opposing muscles of the lower leg increased before toe off and decreased before heel strike, while co-contraction of the opposing thigh muscles increased before heel strike. In addition, many statistically significant preflight-to-postflight differences were found in the timing and duration of activation of specific muscles for individual subjects. The temporal relationship between the offset of the gastrocnemius and the onset of activation of the tibialis anterior at toe off was altered after space flight in 8 of the 10 subjects. In half of the subjects, the order of activation of these muscles was actually reversed. Also, the relative amplitude of activation of the tibialis anterior at toe off was reduced after flight. In the normal toe-off process, activity of the gastrocnemius with corresponding inhibition of the tibialis anterior pushes the toes back against the ground. Then, activity of the gastrocnemius ceases and the tibialis anterior is activated to lift the foot so that the toes will clear the ground as the foot swings forward. The changes that were found after space flight might explain the excessive scraping of the feet on the treadmill that was observed in postflight tests.

In the studies of spatial orientation while walking the triangular path, distance error was not significantly increased after flight. Astronauts tended to underestimate turns when walking with eyes closed, and the resulting directional error was larger after space flight than before. The astronauts walked the path more slowly after spaceflight, both with eyes open and eyes closed.

In the studies of jump landings, closing the eyes did not affect the astronauts' performance, perhaps because they had already judged the height. Some astronauts showed a preflight-to-postflight increase in lower limb compliance, with greater joint flexion and flexion rates. Some showed a decrease in compliance, and some showed no change. In the preflight jumps, after reaching its lowest point, the center of mass moved up and overshot the final rest position. After space flight, astronauts whose compliance had increased had much slower upward responses with little overshoot, while those whose compliance had decreased had faster upward responses with greater overshoot. The simple spring-and-damper model was able to predict the postflight alterations in the motion of the center of gravity by changing leg stiffness only; changes in damping did not appear to play a significant role.

These results are important for understanding how astronauts' abilities to manage an emergency egress, or even to walk on another planet, could be impaired after space flight The results show that space flight alters the coordination between vertical trunk movements and compensatory pitch head movements during walking. This alteration may partly account for the oscillopsia that was reported during the postflight treadmill tests. The postflight changes that were observed in the neuromuscular control of heel strike might affect the transmission of the jolt from the heel strike to the head, possibly exacerbating the postflight oscillopsia. Various head movement strategies were observed after flight. Astronauts who reduced the amplitude of their pitch head movements may have been trying to reduce confusing signals from the vestibular organs. It is also possible that the various strategies were not subject-specific but were part of an ongoing process of relearning motor strategies that are appropriate to Earth's gravity. The results indicate that veteran astronauts adapt more quickly upon returning to gravity, suggesting that preflight exposure to conflicting visual and vestibular inputs during locomotion could be used to train astronauts to rapidly reorder their motor control strategies to reduce postflight motor disturbances.

experiment_title: Dietary Sodium Effects on Bone and Calcium Metabolism
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
There is a predictable relationship between the amount of sodium in the diet and excretion of calcium in the urine.  It is not known whether the same relationship between sodium and calcium occurs in space or during bed rest. Urinary calcium increases during bed rest and space flight, a phenomenon that is thought to reflect increased resorption of bone and not the amount of dietary salt. We recently observed no increase in the excretion of urinary calcium during a 30-day bed rest study when subjects were fed sodium-restricted diets. The purpose of this research was to compare this 30-day study with restricted dietary salt to a 7-day bed rest study of volunteers fed normal salt diets.

APPROACH:
There were 8 men, aged 30-50 years in the 7-day and 11 in the 30-day study. The 30 day study was carried out 4 years before the 7 day study. Daily dietary sodium averaged 193 mm in the 7-day and 114 mmol in the 30-day study. Dietary calcium was the same at 20 mmol/d. Circulating levels of parathyroid hormone as well as indicators of the hormone action on kidney and bone were evaluated. The excretion of urinary calcium, sodium, and creatinine was monitored carefully. The renal excretion of urinary cyclic adenosine-monophosphate, an indicator of the action of parathyroid hormone on the kidney was measured. The excretion of hydroxyproline, a product of collagen metabolism in bone excreted as a reflection of the level of bone resorption in the urine, was also measured.

RESULTS:
Within the first 3 bed rest days, subjects fed normal sodium diets showed increases in fractional excretion of calcium, increased serum ionized calcium and decreases in circulating parathyroid hormone. In contrast, subjects fed restricted salt diets showed no early increase in ionized calcium or decrease in parathyroid hormone. Urinary hydroxyproline increased during the first few days of bed rest in subjects fed normal salt diets and remained elevated for one week, the duration of the study. This product of collagen metabolism did not increase in the 8 subjects in whom it was measured in the salt restricted study. We concluded that the level of dietary salt has a significant effect on the excretion of urinary calcium and on bone resorption during bed rest. The results suggest that low normal (restricted) dietary salt may reduce the early increase in urinary calcium during bed rest and possibly also, space flight.

experiment_title: Multisensory Interactions to Discriminate Gravity From Translational Acceleration
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES

Throughout the history of the manned space flight program, microgravity has produced vestibular-related symptoms that result in personal discomfort and a loss in crew performance. The symptoms subside within several days of microgravity exposure, suggesting that interactive multisensory mechanisms may be responsible for the initiation of symptoms and the subsequent adaptation. Specifically, the processing and detection of gravity and translational accelerations is one of the most fundamental issues for understanding vestibular sensorimotor control in normal gravity, as well as in altered gravity environments. In order to better understand the nature of multisensory signals in detecting gravity, this study will characterize how gravity and translational accelerations are encoded by vestibular neurons in the cerebellum of alert primates. Unless these multi-sensory interactions are better understood in normal gravity, our understanding of neurovestibular adaptation to altered gravity and the development of relevant countermeasures remains largely incomplete. The proposed study aims at filling an important gap in existing knowledge through state-of-the art electrophysiological and computational techniques.

The proposed study is also directly relevant to understanding complex processing and multisensory interactions in the brain. In addition to space flight, this knowledge is important for understanding brain function and computational neural networks.

RESULTS

This investigation is currently being conducted in ground-based studies sponsored by NASA's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Determining Muscle Strength in Space-Flown Caenorhabditis elegans
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
A major impediment to long-duration space travel is loss of muscle mass and strength during spaceflight. Surprisingly, the small worm Caenorhabditis elegans is a good, cost-effective model for studying the effects of spaceflight upon muscle. Our past experiments on Earth and on the International Space Station (ISS) have shown that the expression of key muscle genes that encode members of a muscle attachment complex is reduced in C. elegans during spaceflight. A key open question is if and how these changes in gene expression result in reduced muscle strength i n response to spaceflight. While reduced force production is documented for astronauts, it is yet to be demonstrated for C. elegans. Our proposed studies have important spin out implications for sarcopenia (an urgent public health problem on Earth) and may produce a terrestrial model for testing potential therapeutic interventions for muscle strength decline in flight.

APPROACH:
To address this critical knowledge gap, we developed a tin y new device that enables continuous measurement of worm muscle forces. Using this device, on Earth, we have shown that defects in muscle attachment complexes lead to decline in worm muscle strength. Motivated by these past flight data and ground results, we propose to (a) demonstrate the flight-readiness of our miniaturized device for quantitative characterization of muscle strength of C. elegans, (b) test our hypothesis, based on past flight data, that muscle strength decreases in flight as a result of altered muscle gene expression in the worm, and (c) quantify muscle strength loss in spaceflight across multiple worm generations. Successful measurements of muscle strength in flight will make C. elegans a much more complete and comprehensive genomic model for muscle physiology, enabling meaningful translation of discoveries made in C. elegans to astronauts.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Development of a Software and User Interface to Support Scenario Modeling of Astronaut Schedules to Aid in the Selection of Fatigue Countermeasures within the Behavioral Health and Performance Dashboard
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project integrated the Circadian Performance Simulation Software (CPSS) biomathematical model, developed by the Harvard Biomathematical Modeling Unit, with the Behavioral Health and Performance Dashboard Software tool (BHP-DS) to support scenario modeling of astronaut schedules to aid in the selection of fatigue countermeasures within the BHP-DS. Inputs were related to sleep, duty, and light exposure. The BHP-DS was developed to address the need to track a variety of astronaut behavioral health indicators so that behavioral and performance issues can be detected and mitigated at an early stage. It was not intended to be used to automatically establish a diagnosis but instead provided a dashboard of behavioral health indicators placed within the context of behavioral health stressors.

APPROACH:
Data was collected unobtrusively in the BHP-DS from multiple sources to monitor the subject’s behavioral health. All data used by the tool is encrypted and securely stored and accessible to approved NASA users, such as flight surgeons and operational psychologists. Algorithms are used to capture changes and meaningful feedback in behavioral trends related to specific mission stressors. The BHP-DS was developed to be modular in design to support the implementation of countermeasures developed by other research groups in the NASA and National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) community.

RESULTS:
Investigators accomplished the following objectives of this one-year project: (1) Developed engineering requirements for a software module and user interface to scenario modeling of astronaut schedules within the BHP-DS; (2) Developed user interface mockups; (3) Implemented the software within the BHP-DS platform; and (4) Developed a blueprint for future development.

experiment_title: Effects of Spaceflight on beta-Adrenoceptors in Rat Hindlimb Muscles
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Gravitational unloading has been observed to cause changes in the slow twitch muscle fibers of the antigravity soleus muscle. The density of beta-adrenoceptors (beta-AR) is greater in slow-twitch red muscle fibers than fast-twitch white muscle fibers. The density of beta-ARs in the rat soleus decreases in response to gravitational unloading which has lead to the hypothesis that the same metabolic adaptation would occur in the rat plantaris muscle.

Approach:

Plantaris muscles were taken from the right limb of rats approximately 5 hours after 14 days of spaceflight and were cut into 20 am consecutive cross sections. Quantitative autoradiographic analysis was performed determining the maximum binding capacity (Bmax) and the dislocation constant of beta-1 and beta-2 ARs. Qualitative histochemical analysis was performed, after staining for myosin adenosine triphosphatase. Fibers were categorized as slow, intermediate or fast. The activities of beta-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase (HAD) and succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) were measured spectrophotometrically.

Results:

The Bmax of beta-AR was significantly lower after flight and did not normalize after nine days of recovery. The dissociation constant remained unchanged, suggesting the changes in Bmax were caused by a change in the number of receptors. SDH activity was approximately 24 percent subnormal, but normalized after nine days of recovery. No significant responses were seen in HAD activity or in fiber type percentages of flight animals. The decrease in Bmax seems to be associated with a decrease in the inner membrane enzymes of the mitochondria rather than with the matrix enzyme HAD.

experiment_title: Midodrine as a Countermeasure Against Postflight Orthostatic Hypotension
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Following exposure to space flight, upright posture can result in an inability to maintain adequate arterial pressure and cerebral perfusion (orthostatic or postural hypotension). This may result in presyncope (lightheadedness) or syncope (loss of consciousness) during reentry or egress. A significant number of astronauts experience orthostatic hypotension and presyncope during upright posture. The severity of this problem increases with the length of the space flight mission, as seen in approximately 20% of short-duration and 83% of long-duration crewmembers. It is expected that orthostatic hypotension will be severe on exploration class missions.

To date, available countermeasures (LBNP, fluid loading, Florinef) have not eliminated postflight orthostatic hypotension. This study was designed to evaluate a new pharmacologic countermeasure for protection from postflight orthostatic hypotension. Investigators were studying the ability of the drug Midodrine to reduce the incidence and/or severity of orthostatic hypotension in astronauts returning to Earth. The subject pool included subjects who experienced presyncope as well as those who did not.

APPROACH:
Preflight:
A familiarization session and drug tolerance test was performed before flight. The familiarization session provided subjects with details of the drug tolerance test and the experimental protocol for preflight (L-10) and postflight (R+0) testing. Prior to the start of the drug tolerance test, an electrocardiogram (ECG) was obtained to determine if there was abnormal electrical activity of the heart. If no abnormal activity was detected, the drug tolerance test began. First, the baseline blood pressure was measured, followed by an ingestion of 10 mg of Midodrine. The subject’s blood pressure was monitored at regular intervals for four hours, to ensure that Midodrine did not cause a significant increase in the subject’s blood pressure. During this monitoring period, a record was kept of any subjective effects Midodrine may have caused.

Postflight:
Shortly after return to Earth, the subject ingested the Midodrine pill. Then, an Operational Tilt Test (MR001L) was performed in the Crew Transport Vehicle (CTV) to determine the crewmember’s orthostatic tolerance. The subject was instrumented with an electrocardiogram, a beat-to-beat finger blood pressure device, and an automatic blood pressure cuff. ECG measurements were made to determine aortic cross-sectional diameter and aortic flow while lying on a tilt table. Following this, the subject was brought upright by the tilt table to approximately 80 degrees for 10 minutes while the measurements continued. The tilt test was used to assess the effects of prolonged weightlessness on orthostatic tolerance during upright posture, as measured by supine and standing heart rate, blood pressure, stroke volume, cardiac output, and total peripheral resistance. After completion of the Tilt Test, blood pressure was monitored at regular intervals for an additional period of time. During this time the crewmember also completed a questionnaire.

It is critical that the postflight Operational Tilt Test was performed within 2.5 hours of pill ingestion. Arrangements were made to perform the postflight data collection on the CTV to accommodate this time interval.

RESULTS:
It was successfully shown that of the seven astronauts that participated, two had been presyncopal after previous missions and five had not. After taking Midodrine, the two previously presyncopal astronauts finished the tilt test and the five astronauts, who had not previously suffered from presyncopal symptoms after space flight, finished the tilt test and importantly, did not show signs of hypertension when supine or vertical.

experiment_title: Effects of Cosmic Particle Radiation on the Scalp
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Certain cellular components of the skin are known to be sensitive to conventional radiation, and there is evidence to suggest that these components might be altered by radiation from high-energy galactic cosmic ray particles. The objective of this study was to pursue the problem further by studying the scalps of mice flown on Apollo 17. However, while subscalp monitoring for cosmic ray particles allowed a check of correspondence between particle tracks in the dosimeters and any scalp lesions, the dosimeter itself is a foreign body which would be expected to induce cellular and tissue reactions.

Approach:

Two canisters were prepared with five pocket mice in each. One canister was used in the flight experiment; the other was used as a ground control, undergoing the same stress as the flight canister. Flight mice were implanted with plastic dosimeters underneath the scalp. The scalps of the four mice that survived the flight and two controls were fixed, embedded, and serially sectioned at 8 micrometers in the coronal plane. Stained sections were examined microscopically at 450x. A rectangular portion of skin was removed from the lower lumbar region of the back of one flight mouse to serve as an added control against any nonspecific trauma resulting from the dosimeter. Comparisons between the length of the dosimeter and total thickness of the 8 micrometer sections, and between dosimeter width and the dermal indentations along the dosimeter edges, suggested that an 8% scalp shrinkage had occurred during histological processing.

Results:

Only minor alterations were found in the scalp of the non-implanted control, while two epidermal lesions were identified in the flight backup. However, the absence of leukocytes served to distinguish this tissue reaction from reactions regarded as due to lesions in flight animals. The lesions detected only in the flight scalps were of a necrotic nature with regard to the epidermis and hair follicles, and acute inflammatory cells could be found in the dermis and the subcutaneous tissue as well. Similarities between lesions in the scalp and removed skin suggest that the area not exposed to the dosimeter had received comparable focal injuries during space flight. The number of scalp lesions and number of tracks in dosimeters varied notably, though, 13 lesions as opposed to 76 tracks. In explanation of this difference, it was suspected that lesions, if initiated by cosmic ray particles early in the flight, would have reached a state of advanced repair by recovery, while if such a trajectory was coincident with the dosimeter, it would be permanently recorded.
