experiment_title: Factors Contributing to Food Acceptability and Consumption, Mood, and Stress on Long-term Space Missions
experiment_description:
Objectives 

The three inter-related foci in this study explore factors that contribute to the long-term acceptability of a diet, in terms of satisfaction with and sufficient consumption of the foods, as well as associated moods and stress levels. Prolonged exposure to stress responses can have deleterious effects on overall astronaut health and consequently on mission success. One of the things that can contribute to both health and stress is diet and food preparation. Understanding the relation between preparation effort and the acceptability and consumption of the prepared food, as well as effects on moods and stress, will inform decisions on the amount of time and types of activities crewmembers should allot to meal preparation. The study had 3 specific aims:

1. To design procedures for preparing and consuming meals that maximize food acceptability and lead to increased consumption and positive mood, while decreasing stress.
2. To identify foods that trigger positive emotions and to evaluate the effect of such ‘trigger foods’ on the amount consumed, moods, and stress levels of individuals who are under stress.
3. To increase people’s appreciation of the variety in their diet (without increasing the number of menu items).

Methods

To determine whether preparing food and/or having the ability to choose the ingredients in the food would improve mood and reduce stress (aim 1), the investigators recruited 118 participants (36% male) and divided them into four treatment groups: choice/prepare, no choice/prepare, choice/no prepare, and no choice/no prepare. For each treatment group, subjects were given stress tasks to induce physiological and psychological stress. After the stress task, mood related measurements were taken, and participants were given menus (differing based on choice grouping) and then later food to eat (prepared based on prepare grouping). Physiological and psychological measures of stress were taken again after the meal.

To identify foods that trigger positive emotions and to evaluate the effect of such ‘trigger foods’ on the amount consumed, moods, and stress levels of individuals who are under stress (aim 2), the investigators recruited 100 participants, 67 females, who first completed an online questionnaire to indicate their comfort foods and a variety of comparison foods. Then, during two lab sessions a week apart from each other (and at least a week after the online questionnaire, counterbalanced in order), participants watched films that induced a negative effect. In one session, participants were served their comfort food. In the other, participants were served an equally liked non-comfort food, a neutral food, or no food. Short-term mood changes were measured to determine psychological effects of these foods, rather than biochemical effects on mood from particular food components (e.g., sugars or vitamins). 

To determine whether boredom with repeatedly eaten foods could be curbed by increasing appreciation for variety in one’s diet (aim 3), participants repeatedly consumed granola bars over a 2-week period. Half the participants were reminded to think about recently eaten foods, and half were reminded to think about music they had recently heard. 
The researchers also decided to recruit people to keep 28-day food diaries to determine the degree of food variety in the diets of free-living individuals. 

Results

Aim 1 test results showed that preparation group had little effect on reducing stress or improving mood. However, increases in heart rate and decreases in systolic blood pressure were observed for those in the No Prepare groups compared to the Prepare groups. Those in the No Choice groups showed a greater decrease in anxiety, anger, and systolic blood pressure after the meal than those in the Choice groups. After the meal, heart rate increased more for those in the Choice versus the No Choice groups. Stress and negative measures related to mood decreased post meal overall. 

Tests developed to satisfy aim 2 showed that consuming comfort food after the film was no more effective at improving mood than other foods or eating nothing after the film. 

Aim 3 results showed the first intervention of having participants think about foods they had eaten in the previous week significantly increased subsequent intake and self-reported satisfaction and decreased self-reported boredom. They also tested whether there was a difference in the curbing of boredom between a group that was asked to think of musical artists they had listened to recently and a group that was asked to think about recently eaten foods. There was no significant difference in the liking of granola bars between these two groups. There was however an observed behavioral difference in the willingness to continue eating granola bars. The participants asked to think of food they had recently eaten took significantly more granola bars home at the end of the study than did participants in the music group.

The ISS component of this study known as "Astro-Palate" was discontinued after completion of part A leaving parts B and C incomplete. 

Part A of Astro-Palate: The objective of this study was to determine the role of menu choice on meal satisfaction. This was conducted once relatively early and then again later in the flight.

Part B of Astro-Palate: The objective of this study was to determine the effects of eating situation on mood. Crewmembers completed questionnaires before and after the meals. This would have been done relatively earlier and then again later in the flight. The first subject arrived at the ISS in 2014. Other subjects had agreed to participate and were in varying stages of completing the pre-flight questionnaires.

Part C of Astro-Palate: Objectives: 1) to determine whether eating foods thought to be capable of improving mood will improve moods of astronauts in space when they are in a negative mood and 2) to determine whether eating such foods immediately prior to situations generating negative mood will ameliorate that mood. Crewmembers would have completed questionnaires before and after specific snacks and tasks.

experiment_title: Collecting Mir Source and Reclaimed Waters for Postflight Analysis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In this investigation, the water on the Mir space station was analyzed in detail to study the effectiveness of the Mir purification system. Potable water, water used to maintain hygiene, and water that accumulates from humidity condensate were analyzed to confirm that any potentially harmful contaminants were maintained at acceptably safe levels. The information gathered by this research supported the development and evaluation of water purification units, water quality standards, and in-flight water sampling hardware for the International Space Station. The experiment objectives were to:

  • Characterize the chemical composition of Mir recycled water, Russian ground-supplied water prior to launch and on orbit, and the Mir humidity condensate to support development and testing of the water recycling and monitoring systems for the ISS.
  • Determine and compare the chemical composition of Mir and Space Shuttle condensate.
  • Determine whether the potable water on board Mir meets the Joint U.S./Russian water quality specifications for ISS.

    This experiment has flown under the NASA Human Life Sciences Discipline during the Mir 18/NASA 1, Mir 19, Mir 20/STS-74, and Mir 21/NASA 2/STS-79 missions. In addition, this activity was performed under the Space Medicine Program during the Mir 22/NASA 3/STS-81, Mir 23/NASA 4/STS-84, Mir 23/NASA 5/STS-86, Mir 24/NASA 6/STS-89 and the Mir 25/NASA 7/STS-91 missions. Shuttle flights were used to return items and resupply the experiment.

    APPROACH:
    Recycled and stored water samples were collected periodically during each mission using U.S. developed water sampling hardware. In addition, raw unprocessed humidity condensate was collected using Russian-supplied hardware, while partially processed condensate was collected using U.S. supplied hardware. The partially processed condensate samples were collected as a result of ethylene glycol leaks on board the Mir, to assess the ability of the water processor system to remove this contaminant.

    RESULTS:
    In general, the recycled and stored water supplied to the Mir Space Station met NASA, Russian Space Agency (RSA), and/or U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) standards. Exceptions were found to include total organic carbon (TOC) and turbidity in the recycled water which routinely exceeded NASA standards. The TOC in some cases, exceeded Russian standards as well. Other parameters such as ethylene glycol, barium, nickel, chloroform, phenol, and dioctyl phthatate occasionally exceeded NASA, RSA or EPA standards. All but the TOC violations were transient.

    The humidity condensate exhibited steadily increasing levels of ethylene glycol throughout the missions. This is believed to reflect the increased levels of ethylene glycol in the Mir atmosphere following coolant loop leaks and maintenance activities. In one case, the presence of ethylene glycol in a condensate sample alerted the ground and crew to the presence of a previously undetected coolant loop leak.

    The chemical quality of the recycled and stored water, as determined through post-flight analysis met performance and potability requirements. The analysis of samples has provided important data for assessing the potability of recycled water. In addition, these data will be instrumental in developing appropriate water quality monitoring standards for ISS.

experiment_title: Spaceflight Cognitive Assessment Tool for the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test
experiment_description:
Objectives:
The purpose of the Spaceflight Cognitive Assessment Tool for the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) Phase III Test was to test an objective cognitive assessment tool in an environment comparable to a space station. This tool was called the Spaceflight Cognitive Assessment Tool (S-CAT) and was expected to assist in decisions regarding the cognitive health and capabilities of a crew. In addition to its monitoring functions, it could also assist in the case of accident, injury or off-nominal environmental exposure.

The two specific aims were to evaluate the use and sensitivity of the test during the LMLSTP study and to provide measures of cognitive functions that could assist in recommendations for the crew during the Phase III mission.

Three important operational issues regarding the use of the S-CAT were to be considered. First, subjects needed to be proficient at performing the test, so the amount of training and practice required to alleviate task-learning effects was to be determined. Based on previous testing experience, the S-CAT development team predicted that five to ten sessions would ensure that the subject learned the tasks well enough to work at the best performance level. Because the Phase III subjects did not have the time required for this recommendation, one familiarization and four sessions for training and baseline data collection sufficed. The second main issue concerned the best way to control the S-CAT data. Poor performance on the S-CAT would indicate a neurocognitive problem and possibly jeopardize the career of the subject. Thus, subjects could be reluctant to take the test or report the results. For LMLSTP Phase III, the best option was to trust, but not require, the crewmembers to report anomalies on the routine tests. The third issue was how often the S-CAT should be scheduled. Subjects needed to take the test often enough to keep up the skills required for it. The test would be administered if an event occurred that could impair cognitive function, and, for the scores to be meaningful, subjects must be proficient at taking the test.

Earlier experiments have indicated that the space environment might adversely affect human cognitive capabilities. Both short- and long-duration missions have provided some possible evidence of mild degradations in the crewmembers ability to remember tasks and recall information. In addition, off-nominal conditions have been shown to affect a person's ability to function. Experience in operations from the Space Station Mir indicated a need for cognitive and performance assessments.

The S-CAT was based on tests derived from the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics that were developed for the Department of Defense. The S-CAT consisted of several subtests. Code Substitution subtests tested memory and recall while a Running Memory subtest measured sustained concentration. A Math subtest measured verbal working memory and a Match-2-Sample subtest measured visual working memory. Due to the need for the test in a relatively short timeframe, the assessment tool was created from tests and methods already validated.

There were several constraints in the development of the S-CAT, which was intended to eventually be a part of ISS assessments. These constraints included the availability of computing equipment on the ISS, a limited amount of crew time to perform the test, and the need for results to be immediately fed back to the subject.

The S-CAT development team, which included clinical neuropsychologists and experts in the construction and use of automated psychological tests, developed a short and a long version of the S-CAT. The short version took approximately 15 minutes for a subject to complete and allowed monitoring of cognitive functions while providing initial diagnostic assistance in the event of an injury or toxin exposure. The long version of the test could be done in 35 minutes and was intended for enhanced diagnosis of the subject's condition.

Approach:
Four prime and four back-up Phase III LMLSTP subjects were proficient at taking the S-CAT and provided baseline data. First, subjects took a short familiarization about the use and purpose of the S-CAT. They each completed four sessions of the short version of the test and two sessions of the long version for baseline data collection. The same protocol planned for Space Station Mir and ISS missions was followed. Subjects were scheduled to take at least the short version of the test once per month during the mission for a total of three sessions. The subjects were responsible for scheduling and performing the test. The long version of the S-CAT was planned for a total of two times during the Phase III test, suggested at approximately days 45 and 75. After Phase III ended, the subjects were scheduled to be debriefed and possibly take the short version of the S-CAT one more time.

Taking the S-CAT repeatedly ensured that there would be good data from pretest and nominal operations over time for comparisons with any mishaps. Subjects would also maintain proficiency on the tests so that relearning effects would not affect the data and lead to a misdiagnosis of the cognitive condition. Although the LMLSTP subjects were given suggested test days of 30, 60 and 88 days of the mission, they were given the discretion to choose the exact days to complete the test. To address subject concern of reporting any low test scores, the subjects were given the freedom to decide whether to share the results. This approach mitigated the fear of detrimental judgment from management or the medical monitor, who did retain the right to request the results if warranted.

The hardware consisted of one DOS-based notebook computer and one desktop computer with a DOS-based operating system required to run the S-CAT. During the Phase III mission, the prime crew used their personal desktop computers in the test chamber, and the back-up crewmembers used a notebook computer stored in the test control room.

Results:
The long version of the S-CAT was troublesome due to some imperfections in the software. No meaningful baseline or in-test data were collected from the long version of the S-CAT. Significant improvements to the S-CAT have been made overall due to the resolution of these problems and other software-related issues.

The group training was not optimal. Each subject should have been trained in a private setting free from distractions. The first two pretest data collection sessions may not have produced the same quality of results as sessions that would have been performed in a more private environment. Direct observations and subject comments showed that the S-CAT needed to be performed in a quiet location without interruptions. The back-up crewmembers also had difficulty taking the test due to the constant distractions of on-going communications, problem solving and visitors in the control room.

For each subject, performance on the short version of the S-CAT leveled off, indicating proficiency, after the familiarization and two data collection sessions. It was inconclusive when the performance leveled off for the long version due to the software problems. The number of sessions required to achieve proficiency appeared to be fewer than the test developers originally predicted.

The S-CAT appeared to measure cognition reliably based on preliminary analysis of the data, and further assessment of the test was warranted with validation studies. No off-nominal events such as head trauma or exposure to toxins occurred during the mission, so evaluation of the comparison of such adverse conditions to normal conditions could not be made. In addition, control of the data and its release to the medical monitor by a subject was not tested. Conditions upon which a subject could have been concerned by adverse judgment did not occur. It was decided to allow the subjects to maintain control of their test results, unless an off-nominal event occurred. In that case, data could be used for medically-based diagnostic and management recommendations.

Neither the short version nor the long version of the S-CAT was taken on the days recommended, and some subjects did not complete either version for the recommended number of times. Those who did complete the test followed no schedule. When subjects were reminded to take the S-CAT, they did not necessarily fit it into their schedules, even though they attempted to complete the test. Futhermore, no meaningful data were collected from the S-CAT taken by the back-up LMLSTP subjects, although one or two of them attempted to take the short version once or twice.

Recommendations from nearly all subjects, as well as the history of manned space operations, indicated that the S-CAT sessions must be a requirement set in a timelined schedule and not simply recommended for suggested days. The test should also be scheduled during the normal workday so the subject is working at normal conditions rather than those under time and energy constraints. Following these recommendations should ensure that meaningful data can be collected from the S-CAT and, more importantly, that data is available for use in an event that is suspected of impairing cognition. Overall results showed that a computer-based cognitive assessment tool could be used on the Space Station Mir and on the ISS since such a tool was successfully developed and tested in the 91-day chamber study.

experiment_title: Rodent Tissue Repair: III. Skeletal Muscle
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Myofiber injury-repair was studied in the rat gastrocnemius following a crush injury to the lower leg prior to flight in order to understand if the regenerative responses of muscles are altered by the lack of gravitational forces during space flight. Skeletal muscle atrophy in actual or simulated weightlessness appears to be due to a combination of local and systemic factors' muscle tension and exogenous growth factors. If gravitational forces are necessary for optimal connective tissue organization and muscle repair, then muscle injuries in microgravity might require a special type of rehabilitation to prevent muscle fibrosis and/or movement dysfunction.

Approach:

Histochemical and immunohistochemical techniques were used to examine myofiber, vascular and connective tissue for alterations. Muscle tissues were sectioned at -20 °C in a cryostat at a thickness of 4 µm. Macrophages were localized using an alpha-naphthyl acetate esterase kit. Blood vessels and capillaries in the muscle sections were visualized using a histochemical procedure for the localization of dipeptidyl peptidase IV employing fast blue staining. Localizations of proteinases, proteins, and proteoglycans were performed by indirect immunohistochemical techniques using fluorescein-labeled second antibodies.

Results:

In general, the repair process was somewhat similar in all muscle samples with regard to the extracellular matrix organization and myofiber regeneration. Small and large myofibers were present within a newly organized extracellular matrix indicative of myogenesis and muscle regeneration. In the tail-suspended animals, a more complete repair was observed with no enlarged area of non-muscle cell of matrix material visible. In contrast, flight muscle samples were less well differentiated with more macrophages and blood vessels in the repair region, but small myofibers and proteoglycans were, nevertheless, in their usual configuration. Myofiber repair did vary in muscles from different groups, but for the most part resulted in functional muscle tissue. However, an increase in the vascularity of the repair site and in the number of macrophages in flight muscle might suggest the development of granulation tissue at the repair site of the flight animals, or that muscle regeneration was slowed down due to a variation in growth factors such as growth hormone and insulin.

experiment_title: Microgravity and Placental Development
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The role of gravity in proper placental development has not been previously studied, and could be necessary to successful mammalian reproduction. The objective of this experiment was to assess the effect of microgravity on placental growth and development of the rat, with the specific aim of 1) determining the morphology of the placenta and decidua and their organizational relationship immediately upon return from space, and 2) assessing the functional differentiation of trophoblast cells of the labyrinth and trophospongial regions of the placenta by comparing the expression of specific developmentally-expressed proteins.

Approach:

Between 3 and 6 hours following recovery, one uterine horn was removed from each of the flight and control group animals. After removing the fetuses from the horns, placenta were weighed and prepared for morphological evaluation and measurement of hormone expression. Expression of two forms of placental lactogen (PL) was measured using cDNA probes specific to the hormones.

Results:

Morphological studies showed that cross-sectional area of the total placenta, trophospongium and labyrinth, and placental wet weight were not different among flight and control groups. However, percent dry weight for the asynchronous control animals was less (p<0.05) than that for the other groups. Concentration of DNA in the placenta was also less in the asynchronous controls. Placental concentrations of RNA and protein were not different among flight and control groups. Hybridization with the cDNA probes showed that the quantity of PL-I, PL-II and the ratio PL-II:PL-I were not different among the groups. Space flight during gestation days 9-20 does not seem to influence placental growth, development and function.

experiment_title: The Effect of Increasing Mass upon Locomotion
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts perform locomotive exercise on the International Space Station (ISS) as a countermeasure to the physiological losses associated with space flight. The locomotive-related ground reaction forces may provide mechanical loading that is a sufficient stimulus for bone adaptation and thus reduce the bone loss that occurs. However, recent investigations have shown that the ground reaction forces developed during locomotion in microgravity are less than those occurring in normal gravity. Specifically, peak ground reaction forces measured in microgravity were less than those developed in normal gravity even when subjects were loaded at external load levels equal to or greater than their body weight.

The ground reaction force occurring between the foot and ground is equivalent to the resultant force applied to the body's center of mass. Since force is the product of mass and acceleration, an increase in body mass with a given acceleration should result in an increase in ground reaction force. The loading mechanisms used on the ISS to date, appear to be limited in allowing astronauts to achieve normal-gravity-like levels of peak ground reaction force. Thus, other approaches may be necessary to effectively create normal-gravity-like ground reaction force using the current treadmill onboard the ISS. Adding mass to the astronaut could result in an increased ground reaction force. The addition of mass to the subject, however, may also affect the kinematics, kinetics, and adaptations in normal locomotion.

Increasing the mass of the astronaut through a weighted vest offers a potentially economical and easily modifiable enhancement to current exercise countermeasures. The use of a harness capable of providing different levels of mass could save resources by reducing the need to develop new exercise devices. More importantly, the health and well-being of astronauts could be improved efficiently and inexpensively. Furthermore, exercise with body weight support and a weighted vest to increase overall mass may be useful during the rehabilitation process for individuals who are at risk for osteoporosis.

The goal of this study is to determine whether or not increasing subject mass can create more effective exercise countermeasures during long-term space flight and to better understand the motor accommodations made to gait. The primary purpose of this investigation is to determine how the manipulation of mass affects the ground reaction force during treadmill locomotion. The secondary purpose is to examine the kinetic adaptations to increased body mass during locomotion.

APPROACH:
Ten subjects (five men and five women) participated in this study. The sample was drawn from the test subject pool at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. The test subjects approximated the age range of the current astronaut population. In order to be eligible for the test subject pool, each subject had to be healthy and had passed a United States Air Force Class III equivalent physical. In addition, because the weighted vest had a maximum capacity of 38.1 kg (84 lbs), all subjects had to weigh less than 200 pounds. Prior to being accepted to the sample, each potential subject was screened to ensure that they were healthy and free from injury.

Vertical ground reaction force data were collected during the testing trials with a force-measuring treadmill (Kistler Gaitway, Amherst, NY) at 480 Hz. The treadmill was equipped with two force plates beneath the running tread arranged so one plate rested in the front and one in the rear of the locomotion area. Each plate contained four piezoelectric load cells that measure vertical ground reaction force and allow for a determination of the center of pressure during each sample.

Three-dimensional position data from reflective markers placed upon the subject were collected at 60 Hz with eight cameras (Smart Elite motion capture system, BTS Bioengineering Spa, Milanese, IT). Prior to each day of data collection, the motion capture system was calibrated to within 0.44 ± 0.03 mm of marker re-prediction accuracy. All three-dimensional data were expressed relative to an inertial reference frame that was established during calibration. A reference trial was collected after calibration but before the subject arrived at the lab to establish a treadmill reference frame. An electronic pulse was output by the force treadmill upon the initiation of data collection. The signal was recorded by the motion capture system and was used to synchronize the data during post processing.

Mass was added to each subject using a weighted exercise vest (X-Vest, Perform Better, Cranston, RI). The vest was worn over the shoulders and had top and bottom pockets on the front and back of the subject. Each pocket was fitted with slots in which up to twenty individual 1.1 kg masses could be placed. Slots for weight placement were located on the inside and outside inner surface of each pocket (10 on either surface). During AM (morning) trials, masses were added equally to the front and rear of the vest. The masses were always added to the inner-lower slots first, followed by inner-upper, outer-lower, and outer-upper slots. Within each pocket, weights were added to the center of each row of slots first, and then fanned outwards. Body weight was maintained with an overhead un-weighting system (H/P/Cosmos Airwalk, Nussdorf, Germany). The system provided a constant upward force via a pneumatic pump. The subjects wore a harness about their waist and thighs that were provided by the un-weighting system manufacturer.

Data were collected during five mass treatments at two speeds. Subjects walked at 1.34 km/hr (3 mph) and ran at 3.13 km/hr (7 mph). In addition to a control condition with no added mass (0% AM), mass was added while body weight was maintained. Added mass (AM) conditions included, 10% AM, 20% AM, 30% AM, and 40% AM. At each AM condition, subjects had their weight relieved with an unloading system so the net force between the subject and treadmill remained equal to 100% body weight during quiet standing. All trials at each speed were completed during a single data collection session for each subject. Prior to actual data collection, each subject participated in a familiarization session during which they had the opportunity to practice walking and running at each speed and treatment condition.

Subjects completed all added mass treatments at one speed before completing treatments at the other speed. The speed order was randomized for each subject by a coin flip prior to their first testing session. Treatment randomization occurred independently for each speed. In order to assure that there was a balance of increased mass conditions between subjects, a balanced Latin square random assignment was used. The design allowed for a balance of treatment orders so that no two testing sequences were the same for different subjects within each speed. Each subject was randomly assigned a sequence with only one subject completing each specific order. Trial order assignment occurred separately for each speed. The subjects wore the un-weighting harness during all conditions, including the control trial.

RESULTS:
Summary of Results During Walking

During walking, stride time increased as mass was added. Adding mass increased impact forces and loading rates. Peak propulsive forces decreased with additional mass, but impulse was not affected. Angular impulse at the hip during the stance phase was affected by the addition of mass during walking. Stance phase hip extension torques increased as mass was added, with the 30% AM condition having the largest angular impulse. Positive work at the hip increased and negative work decreased. Negative work at the ankle joint also decreased as mass was added. During the swing phase, knee extension torques decreased with the addition of mass. There were no differences at any joint in positive or negative work during the swing phase.

Summary of Results During Running

During running, contact time and stride time increased as mass was added. Peak impact forces and loading rates decreased, and impulse increased as mass was added. There were no effects of additional mass upon peak propulsive forces. During the stance phase, hip extension angular impulse and knee flexion impulse increased with additional mass. Positive work at the hip increased and negative work decreased. During the swing phase, hip extension and flexion angular impulse decreased as mass was added. Knee extension and ankle plantar flexion impulses also decreased as mass was added. Negative work at the knee decreased; otherwise, there were no added mass effects on any of the other work dependent variables.

The specific purpose of this investigation was to determine if adding mass to astronauts during locomotive exercise in microgravity would be beneficial to increasing the forces experienced by the musculoskeletal system. In both locomotive modes, hip musculature activity and positive work increased suggesting that the hip is the primary area of adaptation of joint torque. It is possible that increasing mass during locomotive exercise in microgravity may be beneficial to increasing impact forces and hip extensor activity during walking. During running, there may be adaptations in locomotive patterns to minimize increases in ground reaction forces.

experiment_title: Space Flight Effects on Fungal Growth, Metabolism, and Sensitivity to Antifungal Agents
experiment_description:
Objective:
From a basic biological research perspective, identification of gravity-dependent physiological processes may add significantly to our overall understanding of how the environment, and gravity in particular, affects the basic processes of life. Bacteria and yeast are some of the simplest forms of life, yet they exhibit physiological pathways that have been conserved through millions of years of evolution. In this way, microbes represent the ideal model for studying the most basic life processes. The simplicity of these organisms allows for targeting of specific bioprocesses without the complications of intercellular and system-level interactions. Gravity represents an under-utilized tool in the array of environmental parameters used to elicit metabolic responses. Gravity is unique in this array in that it is the one environmental constant under which all forms of life evolved. For this reason, researchers believed it would be especially intriguing to observe how microbes adapt to an environmental parameter, which their genetic programming had never encountered.

The hypothesis of this experiment was that microgravity increases gene expression, which could increase resistance to antifungal drugs. Two species of yeasts were used as a model to study gene expression and response to antifungal drugs as influenced by microgravity. Yeasts are unicellular eukaryotic microorganisms that are easily grown at various temperatures in well-contained systems. Compared to higher eukaryotes, their doubling time is very short (2 to 4 hours), thus several generations can be observed within a short period of time. In addition, their basic biological functions, biosynthetic pathways, and the genes associated with many functions have been identified and sequenced.

The specific aims for this experiment were:

  1. Evaluate VITEK® system for yeast identification and susceptibility testing of antifungal agents.
  2. Develop bioreactor system to function as a model for studying fungi and the effect of microgravity upon their fundamental processes.
  3. Evaluate Microarray technology for measuring gene expression as influenced by microgravity.

Approach:
Due to hardware commonality, this experiment was teamed with the experiment "Effects of Microgravity on Microbial Physiology (9307562)" on STS-107, and the experiments were jointly referred to as Microbial Physiology Flight Experiments (MPFE). For this experiment two yeast isolates were evaluated: Candida albicans (ATCC 90028) because it is always diploid with recombination of genetic material and a common opportunistic pathogen that is a component of the normal human flora; and brewer's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae (ATCC 9763), which is a haploid yeast that is used as a model to study eukaryotic organisms because its entire genome has been sequenced. The particular strains selected were ones that survived refrigeration well and provided reproducible data using the VITEK® system. The yeasts were tested with the antifungal drugs Cancidas, Fluconazole, and Amphotericin B.

Ground activities included performing identical studies using the same test isolates and the training hardware concurrently with the inflight experiment. Parallel Automated Microbiology System (AMS) evaluation of identical VITEK® Test Cards were done at the same time the inflight experiments were run. The Growth Control Assemblies (GCAs) were incubated for the same time in an incubator set at ambient Shuttle temperature. Additional GCAs were incubated in a bioreactor, a rotating growth vessel used on Earth to simulate microgravity. The GCAs allowed for the collection of messenger RNA that could be used to determine the total genomic expression patterns in microgravity and gravity.

Preflight activities included preparation and inoculation of the VITEK® Test Cards and GCAs followed by transfer to the Shuttle's refrigerator called the Thermoelectric Holding Module (TEHM). Two types of VITEK® Test Cards were used for this experiment. Yeast identification cards (VITEK® YBC) contained various growth media formulations and yeast susceptibility cards (unique formulation) contained various concentrations of the three antibiotics tested. (For a list of specific well components, see the AMS STS-107 hardware configuration.) Eight VITEK® Test Cards were placed into each VITEK® Card Tray. Two trays were used for this experiment containing a total of sixteen cards. In the first tray, all eight cards were identification cards. The first four cards were replicates in which each well was inoculated with 20 µl of a 6 x 108 cells/ml solution of C. albicans. The other four cards were replicates in which each well was inoculated with 20 µl of a 6 x 108 cells/ml solution of S. cerevisiae. Most of the wells contained a nitrogen base medium while a few contained a carbon base medium. In the second tray, all eight cards were yeast susceptibility cards. The first four cards of the second tray were replicates in which each well was inoculated with 20 µl of a 1 x 103 cells/ml solution of C. albicans. The other four cards were replicates in which each well was inoculated with 20 µl of a 1 x 103 cells/ml solution of S. cerevisiae. All wells of the second tray contained organisms in a RPMI, Roswell Park Memorial Institute (where it was developed), medium. One GCA contained 1 x 103 cells/ml of C. albicans and the other two contained 1 x 103 cells/ml of S. cerevisiae. The cells for the GCAs were in RPMI-1640 medium.

Flight day one (FD1) operations consisted of activation of the AMS and set up of the Laptop Experiment Computer System (LECS). The other MPFE experiment's VITEK® Test Trays were processed on flight days one through six. FD7 activities included the transfer of the first tray from the TEHM to the AMS. The three GCAs were removed from the TEHM and stored on the module wall to incubate at ambient temperature for two days. Cards and trays were incubated for 48 hours ± 4 hours in the AMS. The status of the AMS was checked and the filter was cleaned on FD8. On FD9, the first tray was removed from the AMS and transferred to the TEHM, and the second tray was transferred from the TEHM to the AMS. The clamps on the GCAs were removed allowing the RNAlater™ to mix into the solution thus preserving the genetic material for analysis. The GCAs were then transferred to the TEHM. The status of the AMS was checked and the filter was cleaned on FD10. On FD11, the second tray was removed from the AMS and returned to the TEHM and the AMS was deactivated.

Postflight activities were to include transfer of the VITEK® Card Trays with cards, GCAs, and data from the Shuttle to the investigators for analysis. The messenger RNA from the flight experiment, ground-based study, and the bioreactor GCAs was to be removed and applied to microarrays to determine which genes were expressed and to what degree.

Results:
Due to the STS-107 tragedy, this experiment was not completed.

experiment_title: Assessing the Impact of Communication Delay on Performance: An Examination of Autonomous Operations Utilizing Analog Environments
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study was conducted during NASA's Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO). It provided an opportunity to compare team performance across varying amounts of communication delays, using tasks that differ in criticality and novelty. This study examined how teams interact and perform tasks with and without communication delays. The tasks performed by the crew varied along two dimensions: 1) tasks that were either critical or not critical (criticality) and 2) tasks that were either novel or familiar (novelty). Tasks varied by criticality and novelty as it is assumed that highly novel and highly critical tasks are similar to tasks that a crew may encounter during a long-duration mission in which they have no prior training but must address. This feasibility study provided a preliminary understanding of what impact communication delay has on individual and team performance as well as insight into how teams perform and interact in high-fidelity, autonomous environments. Findings from this study were used for the second phase of this project, which took place on the International Space Station (ISS).

APPROACH:
Crewmembers in the Aquarius habitat and mission control personnel participated in performing tasks identified as highly novel and critical under three different scenarios: 1) response to smoke in the habitat involving no delay in communications; 2) response to a crewmember who had been stung by a lionfish involving a five minute one-way delay; and 3) response to a crack in the habitat window involving a 10 minute one-way delay. Participants included the four Aquarius crewmembers and three mission control personnel. Six of the seven participants provided complete data for each scenario, and the three mission control personnel participants provided assessments of individual and team performance.

RESULTS:
Levels of perceived autonomy in task performance appear to be associated with increased delays in communication. Reported quality of communication between crew and mission control declined significantly under conditions of the five minute one-way delay, but then appeared to increase during the ten minute delay scenario. Objective and subjective measures indicated a decline in task performance associated with difficulty in communications between the crew and mission control during the five minute one-way delay. Crewmembers that had become used to communicating under conditions of a 50 second one-way delay reported that a five-minute delay was equivalent to having no contact with mission control. However, performance appeared to improve during the ten minute one-way delay scenario, perhaps due to the debriefing conducted after the five minute delay scenario and team adaptation to the challenges of delayed communications.

This experiment was transitioned to the International Space Station (ISS). Please see experiment ID Comm_Delay for the inflight aspects of this study.

experiment_title: Urine Collection Device
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary benefits of an improved design for manual urine collection devices are twofold. The Urine Collection Device (UCD) will be used as a back-up to the waste collection system. In the event that it fails, the crewmembers currently use diapers and are required to cut the mission short. Secondly, current UCDs have proved unsuccessful at acceptably collecting voids from females, which is a serious disadvantage to scientific studies with potential female subjects. With the small number of subjects participating in microgravity experiments, loss of all female subjects in those requiring urine is unacceptable to the science community. Although this study aims to optimize UCD designs for both sexes, the priority is on finding an acceptable female adapter(s) given the problems with the current condition.

Male subjects have also experienced problems with the existing UCDs in the areas of leakage, fit, and urine remaining in the dead volume. Therefore, a secondary objective of this study will be to design and evaluate upgrades to the male interface.

The final designs were flown on all missions, which required urine collection samples, as either the primary method of collection or as a back-up to an automated urine collection system proposed for the International Space Station.

APPROACH:
Preflight, subjects received a familiarization session conducted by a certified crew trainer, where a model was used to demonstrate the correct position and steps to follow in the use of a UCD. Subjects were given a written list of "Tips for Correct Use", written step by step instructions, and a questionnaire to complete following testing. A test kit of urine collection devices was provided for home evaluation of the fit, size, and ease of operations. Following the crewmember's evaluation, there was a short debrief session, where feedback on the size and/or type preferred was disclosed.

KC-135 testing was a crewmember option following a successful ground test. A KC-135 preflight briefing was conducted, where the subject received all the items necessary to complete the flight test and a written protocol for KC-135 testing. A short debrief and questionnaire followed the flight.

In-flight, subjects destowed the kit and set up the contents in the waste collection system (WCS) area. Subjects voided into the bag, as trained, noting leaks and dead volume. They removed the adapter, inserted gauze to absorb the remaining drops, and inserted the entire UCD in Ziploc bag, provided. Gloves, wipes, or cloth were available for clean-up or as a precautionary measure. Sufficient supplies for three voids were included.

Subjects returned the urine to the WCS by squeezing the bag and squirting the contents into the WCS urinal funnel. The empty UCD (in Ziploc bag) was then disposed of in the wet trash. If the crewmember did not have the time or desire to empty the urine into the WCS, the sealed Ziploc bag was placed directly into the wet trash. If a Urine Containment Bag was manifested, used UCDs were stored inside.

experiment_title: Effects of Sub-Gravity on Cellular Phenomena of Developing Frog Eggs
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Developing frog eggs exhibit a marked sensitivity to disorientation with respect to the normal gravity vector. This study investigated the effect of weightlessness on the ability of the fertilized frog eggs to divide, differentiate, and develop normally. Although the original experiment plan called for fertilization of the eggs in space, the experiment was redesigned with fertilization occurring just before launch, due to difficulties in obtaining an acceptable degree of reliability in sustaining egg fertilizability over the expected launch pad hold-time by "freezing." Instead, maintenance at 43 °F would adequately inhibit the first division for fourteen to fifteen hours.

Approach:

Three days before launch, sixty female frogs were injected with gonadotrophin to induce ovulation, and two donor frogs were chosen to provide flight specimens. 12.5 hours before launch, stripped eggs were fertilized and divided into clusters of five. Ten eggs each were loaded into the first eight chambers to be fixed, and five eggs each were loaded into the remaining eight chambers. A coolant line around the modules was to maintain a temperature of 42.5 °F to prevent division on the launch pad, until a thermistor was switched to change the temperature to 70 °F at launch. The experiment design called for chamber actuations at Launch (L), L+1 hour, L+2 hours, L+3 (early cleavage), L+32 hours, L+40 hours (late gastrula), and L+68 hours, with the last two chambers remaining unfixed. Multiple temperature and centrifuged ground controls were microscopically compared to flight samples to detect any abnormalities.

Results:

The first cleavage, the one most sensitive to gravity, occurred before lift-off, due to a three-hour delay in the Biosatellite launch. Eggs fixed by the second actuation revealed that complete first cleavage was delayed beyond one hour post- launch. All actuations occurred as programmed, except for the last, which was commanded earlier due to the early call-down of the Biosatellite. No differences were observed in abnormalities between flight and ground control eggs; all fell well within the range of expected abnormal development; and the rate of development appeared unaffected. Data suggest that the fertilized eggs divided, differentiated, and developed normally in two days of weightlessness despite initiation of exposure at the middle of the two-celled stage. As with Gemini frog egg experiments, the effect of weightlessness on the initial dividing egg (before two-celled stage) remains yet to be studied.

experiment_title: Space Relevant Radiation-Induced Cardiovascular Disease Risk Thresholds: Effect of Gender on the Outcome
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
Our central hypothesis is that low-dose proton and HZE (high energy) particle IR-induced biological responses are long-lasting, IR type- and dose-dependent and may augment excess relative risk (ERR) estimates for the development of CV diseases during and after long-duration space missions. In addition, we hypothesize that gender differences could further modify radio-biologically effective (RBE) IR thresholds for CV risk estimates. Gene expression and epigenetic modifications in protein and microRNA (miRNA) in exosomes from the blood (e.g., plasma/serum) may be altered before the onset of the cardiac symptoms, which could be used as potential biomarkers to predict the CV disease risks. We will test our hypotheses with the following specific aims:

AIM 1. Determine the longitudinal effect of IR type, dose, and gender on cardiovascular physiology in wild type mice and ApoE null mice after full-body 5-ion simplified mixed field and gamma radiation.

AIM 2. Determine space-type IR mediated modulations in exosomal cargo in the blood, and determine whether these changes are associated with alterations in the heart function, structure, and vasculature before manifestation of clinical symptoms.

AIM 3. Utilize known and newly identified bio-markers in the blood to develop human-relevant point-of-care tests (POCT) for predicting and monitoring possible CV alterations before and during the space flights.

APPROACH:
To uncover qualitative differences and determine RBEs for biological damage of proton and HZE particles and mix field exposures compared to terrestrial IR and how this influences CV disease risk, we will compare the biological CV end-points of gamma-IR at 50 and 100 cGy to the end-points after exposure to space relevant doses of protons (5, 15 and 30 cGy, 500 MeV for 1H), iron (1, 5 and 10 cGy, 500 MeV/n for 56Fe) and mix field (10, 25, 50 cGy, where each dose will consist of 60% 1H at 500 MeV; 20% 2He at 250 MeV/n; 10% 12C at 290 MeV/n and 10% 56Fe at 500 MeV/n). At the time of initial IR exposures both male and female mice will be 8-9 months old. At various time-points after IR we will determine whether there may be a difference in the cardiac physiology, survival and function of CM and cardiac ECs. Blood (plasma/serum) will be collected for isolation of circulating exosomes for Next-Gen Sequencing (NGS) and proteomic studies. This will allow us to determine the lowest bio-effective IR dose that may induce alterations in heart function.

RESULTS:
We anticipate that the results of our proposed work may be beneficial for human space exploration and could (1) Determine single, low-dose 1H, 56Fe and mixed field dose-responses, radio-biologically effective IR thresholds in the heart and cardiac vasculature and whether gender differences could modify radio-biologically effective IR thresholds for CV risk estimates; 2) Determine whether space radiation leads to modifications in the circulating exosomal cargo contents and whether IR-induced exosomal cargo modulations are reflective of subclinical changes in the cells and organs of origin; 3) Ascertain if modulations of exosomal cargo may be representative of chronic oxidative stress and inflammation and could serve as early biomarkers of IR-induced CV disease initiation and progression; 4) integrate physiological CV endpoint data sets with gene expression and epigenetic data to identify bio-markers in bio-fluids that could be used for prediction of asymptomatic CV disease in the setting of space IR, which will include known early and intermediate bio-markers of cardiac damage, inflammation and oxidative stress, as well as currently unknown novel radiation-associated cardiac bio-markers.

experiment_title: Effects of Microgravity on Renal, Endocrine and Volume Regulatory Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES
Orthostatic intolerance remains an operational problem following space flight. In addition, there is growing evidence that cardiac dysrhythmias may pose a threat to the health of space travelers. At present, no effective countermeasures exist for orthostatic intolerance and for the probable increased risk of ventricular dysrhythmias.

In the last six years, investigators have addressed the subject of renal, endocrine and volume-regulating function during head-down tilt bed rest. They have found that simulated microgravity induces changes in the volume-regulating systems and electrolyte excretion, and leads to changes in cardiac electrical stability. They have also found that using their tilt-test protocol, the pre-bed rest tilt-test tolerance was predictive of post-bed rest tilt-test tolerance. Investigators proposed to conduct three double-blinded randomized trials to: 1) Investigate the use of a pre-bed rest tilt-test as a means to screen countermeasures against orthostatic intolerance, and investigate the influence of these countermeasures on the renal and endocrine responses to orthostatic stress. 2) Develop effective interventions for the treatment of orthostatic intolerance in women since from our previous studies this complication of space travel appear to have a gender difference. 3) Investigate the effectiveness of individualized countermeasures identified during a pre-bed rest tilt-test in reducing post-bed rest orthostatic intolerance, as well as their influence on the renal and endocrine responses to orthostatic stress. 4) Investigate the effects of different countermeasures in reducing cardiac electrical instability, and to study the effects of these countermeasures on baseline orthostatic tolerance. 5) Investigate the effects of different countermeasures in reducing cardiac electrical instability after simulated microgravity, and to study the effects of these countermeasures on orthostatic tolerance and on the renal and endocrine responses to simulated microgravity.

These studies have implications for the treatment and prevention of maladaptive hemodynamic responses experienced by astronauts particularly in women in flight and on return to Earth. They will provide an innovative way of testing "individualized countermeasures". Finally, the results of these studies may help us better understand the pathophysiology of alterations in volume homeostatic mechanisms in cardiovascular diseases such as congestive heart failure, dysrhythmias and hypertension.

APPROACH:
Healthy female and healthy male subjects were given a constant diet for 3 to 5 days, after which they underwent a tilt-stand test (pre-TST) and began 14 to 16 days of head-down tilt bed rest (HDTB), followed by a repeat tilt-stand test (post-TST).

RESULTS:
Instead of causing orthostatic intolerance, higher calf compliance before bed rest leads to recruitment of compensatory mechanisms for a better toleration of orthostatic stress. With the absence of orthostatic challenge during bed rest, the difference in calf hemodynamic parameters is attenuated between the tilt-tolerant and tilt-intolerant groups.

The frequency of orthostatic intolerance is higher in women than in men and is not modified by midodrine at the dose used. This increased susceptibility is likely secondary to intrinsic basal differences in the activity of volume-mediated parasympathetic and adrenergic systems and in venous tone. Thus, approaches to reduce orthostatic intolerance in women are likely to differ from those effective in men.

experiment_title: Cell Kenetic and Histomorphometric Analysis of Microgravitational Osteopenia
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The main hypothesis of this experiment was that space flight blocks osteoblast formation. However, it rapidly recovers upon return to Earth. The study attempted to gain a better understanding of the way that physiological processes adapt both to microgravity and a return to an Earth environment. In order to achieve this, four goals were established. First, DNA synthesis that leads to preosteoblast cell proliferation was studied through the use of a specific marker. This method would hopefully yield new results that could build on previous research. The second goal was to confirm previous findings that suggested the presence of post-spaceflight inhibition of osteoblast formation. A third goal was to determine whether the block to osteoblast formation is confined to specific areas of the skeleton. The fourth goal was to determine how long it takes for osteoblast formation to recover after space-flight.

Approach:

The incidence of osteoblast formation sites during a nine day flight as well as their rates of apposition at 4-6, 24, and 72 hours after space-flight were studied. Rat fibroblast-like osteoblast precursor cells from both maxillary molar periodontal ligaments (PDL) and mandibular condyle cells were analyzed using a nuclear morphometric assay. The PDL cells were placed in ~4M Hematoxylin and stained with eosin to obtain the relative number of preosteoblasts. The cell kinetics of osteoblast histogenesis at 4-6, 24, and 72 hours after flight were assessed to record the path of recovery of osteoblast production.

Results:

Analysis of fibroblast-like osteoblast precursor cells in rat periodontal ligament (PDL) yielded a statistically significant reduction in osteogenic precursor formation after a return from a microgravity environment. Production quickly returned to normal levels, and after twenty-four hours most cell populations were at pre-flight levels. These findings supported the hypothesis that microgravity inhibited osteoblast formation. However, analysis of the rat mandibular condyle cells showed that microgravity had not significantly affected osteoblast production. This was most likely due to the fact that the cells were growing rapidly, and thus the genetic need to produce new cells outweighed the effects of microgravity. Further study of adult mandibular condyle cells is needed and would be most relevant to human space-flight, particularly of growing individuals.

experiment_title: A Soluble Guanylyl Cyclase Mouse Knock-Out Model
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of the proposed study was to generate a soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) knockout mouse model to elucidate the role of sGC in the cardiovascular system under physiological and microgravity conditions. While the role for sGC in the vasculature was first identified 20 years ago, the precise understanding of the physiological significance of sGC-cGMP signaling in the myocardium remains incomplete. The exposure of astronauts to microgravity conditions in space results in cardiovascular alterations that are characterized by orthostatic intolerance and decreased exercised capacity, mainly after their return to Earth and gravity. However, the mechanisms of adaptation to microgravity conditions are unknown. As nitric oxide and sGC play a significant role in the cardiovascular system, we hypothesized that sGC plays a role in adaptation to microgravity. To investigate this hypothesis, we used a gene targeted mouse animal model with myocardium-specific and smooth muscle-specific disruption of gene expression to study the specific role of sGC in microgravity/gravity adaptation.

In specific aim 1, a mouse animal model with myocardium-specific and vascular smooth muscle-specific disruption of sGC beta 1 gene was developed. Following development, investigators aimed to characterize the effects of myocardial-specific and vascular smooth muscle-specific gene disruption on general appearance, embryonic development, histology of the heart and hemodynamic changes in knockout mice versus wild-type mice. In specific aim 2, investigators aimed to determine the role of sGC pathway deficiency on the development of orthostatic intolerance that occurs during re-adaptation to gravity using the established tail-suspended rodent model to stimulate the microgravity conditions. The time course of changes in cardiovascular function induced by re-adaptation to gravity in knockout mice versus wild type mice was studied. Finally, the cardiovascular responsiveness in knockout mice versus wild-type mice following de-suspension was assessed using vaso- and cardio-active agents. Comparisons between knockout mice and wild type mice in simulating weightlessness conditions will aid to identify sGC-dependent pathways necessary for adaptation to microgravity and re-adaptation to gravity.

APPROACH:
Investigators developed a mouse animal model with myocardium-specific and vascular smooth muscle-specific disruption of sGC gene. They used Lox-Beta 1 sGC targeted vector generated previous year to produce the gene-targeted mouse ES line. Targeted ES cells were introduced into mouse blastocysts and chimeric male mice were obtained. In order to identify animals with a transmission of the targeted ES cells into the germ line chimeric males were bred with wild type females. Homozygotes with Lox-targeted Beta1 sGC gene were obtained by crossing identified heterozygotic mice.

RESULTS:
Investigators developed Lox-Beta1 sGC targeted vector and used it to produce gene-targeted mouse Embryonic Stem cell (ES) line. Targeted ES cells were introduced into mouse blastocysts and chimeric male mice were obtained. To identify animals with transmission of the targeted ES cells into the germ line, chimeric males were bred with wild type C57Bl/6 females. Lox-targeted heterozygous mice were crossed to obtain homozygous mice with Lox-targeted Beta1 sGC gene. Presently, the investigator’s laboratory maintains the colony of homozygous mice of Beta1-sGC-Lox strain at the Animal Facility of the Institute of Molecular Medicine. The functional targeting of the sGC Beta1 gene in the strain Beta1-sGC-Lox (i.e. that the gene can be eliminated) was confirmed by mating of the Beta1-Lox strain with the Cre strain uniformly expressing Cre recombinase (EIIa-Cre).

experiment_title: Interaction of the Space Shuttle Launch and Entry Suit and Sustained Weightlessness on Egress Locomotion
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Two flight suits are currently worn by crewmembers during Space Shuttle launch and landing. The Launch and Entry Suit (LES) and Advanced Crew Escape Suit (ACES) are designed to protect crewmembers in the case of emergency but may increase thermal stress and limit their egress capabilities. A Liquid Cooling Garment (LCG) worn under the flight suit was designed to counteract the heat storage of the suit.

This study was conducted to assess egress performance of Space Shuttle crewmembers after space flight. Emergency egress performance was evaluated during a simulated egress in which an astronaut stands and then walks on a treadmill at 3.5 miles per hour for 5 minutes. Preflight testing was conducted in both unsuited and suited conditions. Postflight testing was conducted within two hours of landing in the suited condition only. To partially assess thermal load during the egress simulation, skin temperature was measured at four body locations: upper arm, chest, thigh, and calf.

The primary purpose of this of DSO was to assess the thermal loads experienced by Shuttle crewmembers during the performance of a simulated egress before and after space flight. Specifically, the investigators sought to:
1) Determine the additional heat stress imparted by the LES and ACES suits above normal unsuited conditions.
2) Determine whether there was a differential effect of suit choice (LES or ACES) on thermal stress during simulated egress.
3) Determine whether the LCG would successfully maintain a constant skin temperature from rest through the end of simulated emergency egress.
4) Assess any changes in thermal stress during egress from pre- to postflight.
5) Document skin temperature during deorbit burn, landing, and hatch opening immediately prior to egress.

APPROACH:
Crewmembers were tested twice: once three to six months prior to flight and once within two hours of landing. During the preflight testing, crewmembers were tested in both the unsuited (T-shirt and shorts) and suited (LES or ACES) conditions. On landing day (R+0), crewmembers were tested in the suited condition only. All subjects read and signed a statement of informed consent prior to participating in any data collection. The protocol for this study was approved by the JSC Institutional Review Board.

Preflight Testing
Unsuited Condition
In the first testing session, crewmembers performed the simulated unaided egress in the unsuited condition while wearing a T-shirt, shorts, and flight boots. Subjects stood in the center of the treadmill for approximately two minutes and donned the mouthpiece, pneumotach, and nose clips for the sampling of respiratory gases. Treadmill speed was increased to 3.5 miles per hour. Upon reaching 3.5 mph, the test began and the heart rate monitor was started. Subjects walked for five minutes at this speed.

Suited Condition
After unsuited testing was completed, crewmembers donned either the LES or ACES, depending on which suit they would use for flight, and repeated the above test. With the crewmember seated in a chair on the treadmill, the g-suit was inflated to the pressure anticipated to be used during landing and egress and the crewmember regulated the flow rate to the liquid cooling garment to maintain comfort. With the helmet visor closed, the crewmember pre-breathed 100% O2 for six minutes. The crewmember then stood, liquid cooling was discontinued, and he/she began walking as the treadmill speed was increased to 3.5 mph. Test time started when the treadmill speed reached 3.5 mph, at which time the heart watch was started. The crewmember continued walking at this speed until one of the following test termination criteria was attained: 1)subject request, 2) completion of five-minute walk, 3) inspired CO2 exceeded 6%, 4) medical monitor request, or 5) subject exhibited symptoms of CO2 toxicity (ie., unsteady gait).

Postflight Testing
While in orbit, crewmembers donned the skin temperature thermistors and the chest strap for the heart rate monitor. Crewmembers then donned their liquid cooling garments and either the LES or ACES. All crewmembers received self-controlled liquid cooling during re-entry and landing. Skin temperature data loggers recorded data in 15-second intervals for seven hours and 30 minutes prior to the completion of the simulated egress after landing. Time of major events, deorbit burn, landing, and hatch opening, were identified from Shuttle operations records. Data from these time points were collated and compared.

All postflight tests were conducted on the Crew Transport Vehicle (CTV) within two hours of landing. Crewmembers exited the Space Shuttle and were directed to the testing area at the rear of the CTV. Prior to testing, crewmembers self-adjusted cooling through the liquid cooling garment to personal comfort. Postflight testing was conducted in the same manner as the preflight suited condition, and the same termination criteria were applied. If on R+0 the crewmember chose to use a g-suit inflation pressure different from that used during preflight testing, the preflight suited testing condition was repeated three to six months after landing, and these data were substituted for the preflight data.

RESULTS:
In the comparison of LES and ACES, there is no significant difference between the two suits at the arm, chest, and thigh measurement sites, or in the mean skin temperature. ACES T-calf is significantly lower than LES T-calf during rest and through minute 2 of exercise. Both suits demonstrate a significant rise in skin temperature from rest to exercise, starting at minute 2, at the arm, chest, thigh, and mean skin temperature. ACES T-calf is also significantly greater than rest starting at minute 2 of exercise. LES T-calf during exercise is not different from T-calf at rest.

A comparison was also made for the skin temperatures at four stages of landing. Skin temperatures were compared at de-orbit (D/O) burn, landing/wheel stop, hatch opening, and orbiter exit. From D/O burn through Orbiter exit, all regions dropped in skin temperature. The arm and chest regions demonstrated the highest temperature from D/O burn through orbiter exit. The calf skin temperature was the lowest at D/O burn, while the thigh skin temperature was the lowest at landing through orbiter exit.

experiment_title: Envihab Bed Rest Standard Measures: Ocular Tests
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Ocular Test is one of eleven International Bedrest Standard Measures conducted on healthy subjects at the :envihab facility in Cologne, Germany. Ocular Tests consist of assessing Intraocular Pressure (IOP), an Ocular Ultrasound, and Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) and A-scan. The purpose of the standard measures project is to populate a repository with data that enables high-level monitoring of countermeasure effectiveness and meaningful interpretation of health and performance outcomes. These standard measures will support future, hypothesis-driven research that enables planetary missions by providing an optimized minimal set of measures captured from subjects. These measures will be available to other studies under data sharing agreements as well as undergo analysis to understand risk posture.

APPROACH:

Intraocular Pressure:

Intraocular pressure is the fluid pressure of the aqueous humor inside the anterior chamber of the eye. Tonometry will be performed on the right and left eye using a commercial tonometer. The operator will stabilize the subject's head and gently tap the tonometer tip to the clear surface of the open eye directly over pupil to obtain the measurement. Each measurement consists of six successive taps. The tonometer will automatically drop the highest and lowest values and report the mean of the remaining four values. The mean constitutes one measurement. If the variability between the four taps is too high, the device reports “deviation error” and the measurement will not be recorded. Three good measurements are required, and the measurements should fall within a range of 1.5 mmHg. Measurements will be continually taken until three measurements fall within 1.5 mmHg of one another.

Ocular Ultrasound:

The diameter of the optic nerve and nerve sheath will be analyzed using a Prosolv ultrasound. Other parameters that will be derived from the ocular ultrasound scan include assessment of the optic nerve tortuosity and increased optic sheath-to-optic nerve diameter. The ultrasound scan will also be used to identify changes in the globe morphology (flattening of the posterior globe and globe axial length). Optical Coherence Tomography and A-scan:

The retinal thickness, volume, and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness will be measured using optical coherence tomography (OCT) and a quantitative cross-sectional analysis method. Axial samples of A-scans will be obtained in each “scan pass.” All the A-scans will be combined into one image producing an image with a resolving power of about 10 microns vertically and 20 microns horizontally. However, OCT has a high sensitivity for detecting subtle changes to the RNFL of the optic nerve head. An anterior segment module will be used to measure corneal thickness, anterior scleral thickness, and anterior chamber angles. Subjects will be seated with their chin placed on a chin rest. Subjects will focus their eyes into the machine. The machine will scan the subject's eyes and an image and report will be generated and viewed by the ophthalmologist or optometrist.

The scheduled days of collection are as follows:

  • Three days prior to mission
  • The day mission ends
RESULTS:

The :envihab International Bedrest Standard Measures Test Battery is not a hypothesis-driven study, but rather a collection of data made available to future researchers and for trend analysis. As such, there are no specific hypotheses, outcome measures, or statistical analyses associated with the skeleton of the project. The questionnaire will capture a "snapshot" of optimized data that can be investigated by researchers in the future.

experiment_title: Photographic Documentation of Body Fluid Shift
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The known large shifts of fluid from lower to upper body assumed a fresh importance through the possibility that the central nervous system (CNS) or inner ear pressures might be altered and contribute to or even cause space motion sickness (SMS). There is currently no satisfactory way to measure shifts to the head and there is always a need for simpler procedures for other areas. The objective of this experiment was to gather data on the course and amount of fluid lost from the legs and gained by the head region to assess the role of fluid shift in SMS.

APPROACH:
A background grid with a standard STS 35mm Nikon camera, interior film, and flash were set up at known distances and angles and the subject placed his heel in a fixture at a known position. He sequentially rotated his leg 180° through five positions while pictures were made at each position. The head was photographed in three positions and without fixation. Data may be manually reduced by reconstruction of cross sections from the multiplane views and volumes calculated from these. Three photo views of the leg and head against a background grid were collected as early and as late as possible during flight. Photographs were collected on as many crewmembers as possible.

RESULTS:
Satisfactory in-flight and postflight pictures were made of all crewmembers. Results from the investigator’s analysis are currently unavailable.

experiment_title: The Actin Cytoskeleton: A Molecular Signature for Whole Blood Cell Cultures in the Bioreactor
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Studies of lymphocyte (T-cell) activation during space flight and in ground-based hypogravity model systems show a dramatic reduction in proliferative response to activating signals. The Biorack flight investigations demonstrate that this inhibition of T-cell activation is accompanied by dramatic alterations in the cytoskeletal response. Specifically, activation of human peripheral T-cells by bead-immobilized anti-TCR in microgravity culture fails to induce polarization of the Microtubule Organizing Center (MTOC) towards the cell-bead contact site. These results correlate with the inability of T-cells to express surface activation markers such as the receptor for IL-2 (CD25), an event that would certainly impair the proliferative response of T-cells. More recently the investigators have determined that exposure of the Jurkat T-cell line to hypergravity and microgravity culture can dramatically alter the state of the actin cytoskeleton and its response to stimulation. These findings have led to the following hypothesis: The actin cytoskeleton is a gravity sensitive element of cellular response and serves as a molecular signature for gravity sensitivity of cellular function.

A major goal of NASA’s cellular biotechnology program is to develop new technologies for the growth of three-dimensional mammalian tissues. Tissue engineering is an emerging field with enormous potential to restore, maintain, or enhance tissues and organs. Understanding of cellular, chemical, and physical responses of cells to stimuli is critical to successfully engineering tissue. A number of studies utilize microgravity culture and Bioreactor model systems for 3-D culture of cells, cell aggregates, and tissues, such as living skin equivalents, pancreatic islets, and engineered skeletal and cardiovascular tissues. While these studies are providing important data on the chemical and functional response of cells and tissues, little is known about the adaptation and response of important cellular cytoskeleton systems which play critical roles in signal transduction, functional response of cells, and tissue modeling.

The actin cytoskeleton plays a crucial role in signal transduction and activation response of human cells and is involved in many aspects of cellular function including orchestration of mechanical forces inside cells, signal transduction, and functional responses of cells. The principal aim of this proposal was to employ research at the cellular level to elucidate sensitivity of the actin cytoskeleton in human peripheral blood cells (T-cells, Neutrophils, and Monocytes) in the NASA developed HARV bioreactor, and in short-duration microgravity.

APPROACH:
Specific experiments will characterize the adaptation and response of the actin cytoskeleton in a number of primary human cells utilizing a novel technology that was developed to measure the polymerization state of the actin cytoskeleton in whole blood samples. The response of the actin cytoskeleton will be correlated with functional response of cellular subsets of whole blood samples (Neutrophils, T-cells, and Monocytes) cultured in (1) the HARV, (2) in short-duration microgravity on KC-135 parabolic flights, and (3) in unit gravity for control.

RESULTS:
In year one of this grant investigators developed a novel method for establishing whole blood cell cultures in the rotating HARV. A large number of experiments were devoted to evaluating various culture conditions and developing new methods for Autologous Plasma Supplementation of whole blood cultures. These investigations enabled them to develop superior culture environments for whole blood by increasing the buffering capacity of blood cultures in a simulated microgravity environment.

In year two and three of this grant they utilized the methods developed in year one to characterize the adaptation and response of circulating white blood cells to modeled microgravity, and their re-adaptation to 1-g upon return to static culture. In addition, they developed new methods for characterizing infection of human blood cells upon bacterial infection. These later investigations demonstrate the utility of this new method for identification of human blood infections and may be developed for advanced monitoring tool during long-duration space flight.

In summary, the investigations performed under this grant have provided deep insight into the adaptation and response of human circulating blood cells using the HARV model system. The technologies developed during this grant are providing new tools for monitoring immune cells and their functional responses in whole blood samples. The use of Actin signatures on long-duration space flight missions can provide early detection of cellular damage in flight crew prior to clinical manifestations.
