experiment_title: A Countermeasure for Space Motion Sickness
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Problems associated with space motion sickness and clear vision during space flight have no realistic solution given existing countermeasures. Preflight adaptation, while it appears to be effective, requires substantial investments in crew time, and crewmembers must experience some level of motion sickness if the preflight adaptation environment is a serious analog of flight. Inflight centrifugation may be the ultimate vestibular countermeasure, however, rapid implementation is impracticable, and like preflight adaptation protocols, crewmembers will experience motion sickness on both ground and flight centrifuges.

The purpose of this study is to investigate both the prevention of motion sickness and retinal slip through the use of stroboscopic vision. These investigations are intended to develop countermeasures to help crewmembers avoid disorientation, meet physical requirements for emergencies, treat motion sickness without side effects, and assure safe control of the spacecraft.

Specific Aims:

  • To study the effects of stroboscopic light on the motion sickness induced by performing visual tasks while wearing reversing prisms.
  • Research, develop, and build a set of goggles that will use polymer dispersed liquid crystal or ferroelectric liquid crystal display material as electronic shutters.
  • To study the effects of stroboscopic light on the motion sickness induced by using the goggles developed as a part of specific aim 2.
  • To evaluate the ability of stroboscopic vision due to liquid crystal goggles to prevent motion sickness in a range of experimental conditions, including parabolic flight and a slow rotation room.

    APPROACH:
    The research for this proposal is divided into four phases. The Phase I protocol requires a three-part research plan that will: (1) verify the effectiveness of stroboscopic vision in preventing motion sickness induced with left-right visual reversing prisms; (2) investigate the effect of flash rate and duration on prism- induced motion sickness; and (3) study the adaptation of motion sickness susceptibility under stroboscopic illumination.

    In Phase II, stroboscopic goggles using LCD electronic shutters will be constructed to replace the stroboscopic flash generator for use in environments where ordinary stroboscopic flash is not feasible.

    In Phase III the effect of these goggles will be verified; then tested in unique provocative environments; including both parabolic flight and tests within the Navy's Slow Rotation Room centrifuge.

    Finally, in Phase IV the probable mechanisms involved with stroboscopic presentation and the prevention of motion sickness and retinal slip will be investigated using the newly constructed stroboscopic goggles. These investigations are directly responsive to the goals of NSBRI's neurovestibular research program: To develop countermeasures that help crewmembers: avoid disorientation, meet the physical requirements for emergencies, treat motion sickness without side effects, and assure safe control of the spacecraft.

experiment_title: Human Lymphocyte Locomotion in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Understanding the movement of white blood cells (leukocytes) is a vital step for cancer researchers to determine how to help lemphocytes penetrate tissue to kill tumors. This is important because the lymphocytes fight cancers and all types of infection by moving into the diseased area. In the case of cancer, however; researchers have discovered that the closer a lymphocyte gets to a tumor, the more impaired its movement is.

The impact of long-term weightlessness on immunity has been revealed in extended manned space flights. This investigation (a) provided data which illuminates microgravity effects on locomotion and migration of human lymphocytes through an intercellular matrix, a function that is crucial to immunocompetence, (b) tested the adequacy of the Rotating Wall Vessel (RWV), a laboratory-based microgravity simulation environment developed by NASA, and (c) verified the Specimen Temperature Controller which is necessary to control the thermal environment of the living cells inflight. Analysis of in-flight data was performed in the Biotechnology Laboratory at Johnson Space Center.

APPROACH:
In single-phase microcarrier experiments, microcarriers were transferred to RWVs at a concentration of 200 microcarriers per 107 PBLs/100 ml c-RPMI culture volume. Controls were incubated at the same density in 24-well culture trays in stationary mode. In dual-phase microcarrier experiments, microcarriers were placed in RWVs at a concentration of 200 microcarriers/100 ml culture volume. Control cultures contained the same microcarrier-to-media density as their RWV counterparts. In a humidified, seven percent C02 incubator at 37° C, RWV cultures were rotated at 14 rpm, whereas control cultures were incubated in 24-well culture trays in stationary mode. At 24-hour intervals, four to six microcarriers were removed from the RWV and from control cultures and transferred to tubes containing one percent paraformaldehyde fixative, and the locomotion distance was measured.

Cell locomotion was defined as the distance between the microcarrier surface (single-phase microcarrier) or cell/collagen interface (dual-phase microcarrier) and the three leading-edge cells. This measurement was determined by fine focus microscopy using an inverted microscope with phase contrast (Nikon Diaphot, Japan). Using a predetermined calibration factor, this measurement was converted from fine focus units to locomotory distance in micrometers (gin).

RESULTS:
In the randomized gravity of the rotating-wall vessel culture system, peripheral blood lymphocytes did not locomote through Type I collagen, whereas static cultures supported normal movement. Although cells remained viable during the entire culture period, peripheral blood lymphocytes transferred to unit gravity (static culture) after 6 hours in the rotating-wall vessel culture system were slow to recover and locomote into collagen matrix. After 72 hours in the rotating-wall vessel culture system and an additional 72 hours in static culture, peripheral blood lymphocytes did not recover their ability to locomote. Loss of locomotory activity in rotating-wall vessel cultures appears to be related to changes in the activation state of the lymphocytes and the expression of adhesion molecules. Culture in the rotating-wall vessel system blunted the ability of peripheral blood lymphocytes to respond to polyclonal activation with phytohemagglutinin. Locomotory response remained intact when peripheral blood lymphocytes were activated by anti-CD3 antibody and interleukin-2 prior to introduction into the rotating-wall vessel culture system. Thus, in addition to the systemic stress factors that may affect immunity, isolated lymphocytes respond to gravitational changes by ceasing locomotion through model interstitium. These in vitro investigations suggest that microgravity induces non-stress-related changes in cell function that may be critical to immunity. Preliminary analysis of locomotion in true microgravity revealed a substantial inhibition of cellular movement in Type I collagen. Thus, the rotating-wall vessel culture system provides a model for analyzing the microgravity-induced inhibition of lymphocyte locomotion and the investigation of the mechanisms related to lymphocyte movement.

experiment_title: Microgravity Effects on Standardized Cognitive Performance Measures
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space travelers are subject to a variety of stresses during space flight. These include adapting to the microgravity environment, physical isolation, confinement, lack of privacy, fatigue and changing work/rest cycles. On Earth, both fatigue and changing work/rest cycle degrade cognitive performance and productivity. The purpose of this experiment was to determine the effects of microgravity upon cognitive skills critical to the success of operational tasks in space. Scientists have hypothesized that performance will deteriorate as a result of time in microgravity and that fatigue will increase concurrently.

APPROACH:
The subjects for the Microgravity Effects on Standardized Cognitive Performance Measures experiment were four crewmembers of the seven-person crew on Space Shuttle flight STS-78. A preflight orientation session provided subjects with background information and a demonstration of the cognitive test battery known as the NASA Performance Assessment Battery, or NASA-PAB. Data were collected from each subject during 37 experiment sessions: 24 preflight sessions, 9 inflight sessions performed approximately every other day, and 4 postflight sessions also performed every other day. A total of 1183 data sets were recorded for the experiment.

To evaluate any changes in cognitive performance and productivity, the investigators developed a test battery consisting of a questionnaire and several performance tests. Each test subject performed the battery at one sitting, meaning that no breaks were allowed once the test was started. A brief description of each performance test and its duration follows.

Mood Scale - This task consisted of 8 scales and involved pressing an arrow key to indicate the level of agreement with the mood description associated with each scale. The test took less than 1 minute to perform.
Fatigue Scale - This task required the subject to press a numbered key to indicate which statement best matches the subject's fatigue state. The task took less than 30 seconds to perform.
Tracking - One of the effects of microgravity is a disruption of visual-motor coordination. To investigate this effect, a tracking test was used. The test required the subject to maintain a target in the center of a horizontal line. The target was displaced by the computer program at a fixed difficulty rate, and the subject had to manipulate a control device to null the input disturbance.
Matrix Rotation Task - The functional deafferentation of the otolith organs that occurs in space, along with associated effects on the visual and cerebellar systems, raise serious questions about the individual's spatial oreintation. Thus, it is desirable to look for subtle effects on a subject's ability to perceive, remember and process spatial information. The Matrix Rotation task is used to evaluate the effects of microgravity on spatial information processing. The test used 100 basic patterns, each of which was a 5 x 5 matrix with five illuminated cells that had been selected at random. At the beginning of the trial, the subject saw a pattern. The subject studied the pattern and then pressed a response key. The pattern was immediately erased and a new one presented. The subject was asked to decide as quickly as possible if the new pattern was identical to the first pattern. The subject then pressed a designated key for "same" or another designated key for "different". As soon as the response was made, a third pattern appeared. Now, the subject had to compare the new pattern to the immediately preceding pattern, etc. For "same" responses, the two patterns were never presented in exactly the same orientation; the second pattern was always rotated either 90° to the left of 90° to the the right relative to the preceding pattern. Both reaction time and percentage-of-corrections-made were recorded. The self-paced test lasts about 1.5 minutes.
Sternberg Memory Search - The general Sternberg paradigm required subjects to respond as rapidly and accurately as possible to visually presented letters. At the beginning of the test, a set of letters drawn randomly from the alphabet was presented to the subject for memorization. Next, the screen was cleared and a series of single test letters were presented. If the presented letter matched one of the letters in the previously memorized positive set, the subject responded "same" (key press). If a different letter appeared (negative set), then the subject responded "different" (key press) indicating a non-matching letter was presented. The self-paced test lasts 2 minutes.
Continuous Recognition - One critical aspect of higher cognitive function is the ability to maintain attention and to carry out repetitive cognitive processes over some period of time. In many ways, such activities encompass those that were traditionally referred to as "vigilance". However, they add the dimension of active processing of information, rather than simple monitoring. One task that appears to capture the performance elements above is the Continuous Recognition Test. In this test, the subject saw two numbers, one above the other. The task was to remember the bottom number. When the next two numbers appeared, the task was to determine if the new top number was the same as the previous bottom number. However, before responding, the subject must note the new bottom number because as soon as a response was made, the numbers were replaced by a new pair. Thus, the subject must not only exercise very short-term memory, but, more importantly, must inhibit the response until the new button number ws committed to memory. The appropriate strategy was to develop a set pattern of observing, memorizing, observing, comparing and responding. This sequence was different from that required by most routine tasks in that it required constant attention allocation. Even brief lapses resulted in errors. The task could be made even more difficult by requiring the subject to remember and respond to numbers further removed (two or even three back) from the one immediately proceeding, thus imposing a much higher load on immediate memory. The self-paced test lasted about 2 minutes.
Performance Switching Task - Manikin and Mathematical Processing - Time-sharing was different from another required attention process that could be affected by microgravity. Astronauts must make rapid shifts in the attentional focus, as well as in the skills required to respond to a change in task demands. This externally-directed behavior cannot be made automatic in any true sense, since it must be flexible enough to respond to unusual demands. Thus, a test was needed to probe the subject's ability to shift attention and resource allocation in response to rapidly changing and unpredictable external demands.

In this procedure, the subject had to discrete tasks to perform. One was a spatially-based task, and the other was a mathematically-based test. Each of these appeared, trial by trial, simultaneously on the screen. However, an indicator appeared at the same time, directing the subject to the task that was "active" (i.e., must be responded to). The subject had to made an exclusive response to the active task, where reaction time and percent-correct data were obtained only for that task. The switching from task to task for each trial was random (within constraints). Therefore, the subject had to remember to watch the indicator on each trial, allocate the appropriate resources to respond to the trial, and then make the appropriate response. This paradigm provided a test of switching skills.

The two tests selected to exercise this paradigm were the manikin test and the mathematical processing test. As implemented in this microgravity experiment, a manikin "stick figure" was presented facing either forward or backward. In addition, the figure could be either upright or upside-down. The figure was also standing on a box and inside the box was either a rectangle or a circle. In the figure's two hands were a rectangle and a circle. The subject's task was to note which symbol was inside the box, and then to determine which of the manikin's hands was holding the designated symbol. The subject then presses the left or right of two keys corresponding to the manikin's left or right hand.

Exposing the astronauts to a series of manikins presented in a variety of orientations in microgravity, where the astronaut had the freedom to position his own body during work and sleep in non-traditional gravity orientations, was one of the more theoretically interesting tests of spatial processing using a human form. The effects of microgravity on whole-body orientation may give insight into whether this test was a perceptual measure of spatial transformation of mental images or involved pure spatial abilities requiring readaptation.

The Mathematical Processing test was based on similar tasks. It presented three single-digit numbers that must be added or subtracted. If the answer was greater than 5, one response was given. If the answer was less than 5, another response was required. This task had been reported to be a relatively pure index of mathematical functioning. The computer-paced test lasted 4 minutes.

Dual Tasking - Tracking and Sternberg Memory Search - One of the most critical and potentially sensitive higher cognitive functions that might be affected by microgravity is the ability of the subject to allocate attentional resources among several tasks. To investigate this, the task used the time-sharing paradigm which consisted of the Sternberg task and tracking task being presented simultaneously. In the implementation of the dual task, the tracking task was presented in the middle of the screen and the letters of the Sternberg task appeared in a fixed location directly about the center null point. The target of the compensatory tracking risk moved laterally. One memory set was used, consisting of 4 letters. Due to the nature of the dual task, the "fixed set" procedure was used, in which the same memory set letters were presented with several probe letters for each daily session. The test lasted 3 minutes.

RESULTS:
With only four subjects it is not possible to generalize results to a population of future space travelers. However, if one confines their analysis and interpretation to the four subjects tested in this 16-day mission, some tentative conclusions can be drawn. Generally, in-Qrbit subjects were able to respond to the tests without significant impairment. The mathematical processing task, a part of the Directed Attention Test, showed significantly degraded performance in two out of the four subjects. The Matrix test performance was degraded in one subject. The improvement seen in the Tracking test for one subject appeared to be the result of an improved tracking strategy developed in the last two practice sessions prior to launch.

experiment_title: Cellular and Molecular Mechanisms of Spaceflight-Induced Tissue Degeneration
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Our working hypothesis is that spaceflight factors (including radiation and microgravity) affect the growth and regenerative health of a broad range of mammalian tissues, including bone, muscle, and immune system, by causing indiscriminate slowing or arrest of normal cell proliferation. Specifically we hypothesize that there is a key regulatory cell-signaling pathway responsible for this space-induced arrest, namely the p53 signaling pathway, and that either radiation and/or microgravity can activate it. We have already tested this hypothesis with spaceflight tissues from STS-131, validating some of its key aspects such as p21 activation in osteoblasts, and are now utilizing mouse tissues from the recently completed Bion M1 30-day spaceflight to test the p53 hypothesis with long-term spaceflight tissue samples.

APPROACH:
We propose to determine if the p53 pathway is activated during 30-day spaceflight in bone tissues by:

1) Biochemically measuring total and phospho- p53, MDM2, p21, PI3Kinase, and ubiquitinated p53 levels in bone tissue.
2) Immunohistochemically identifying specific cell types in bone with active p53 and DNA damage.
3) Correlating p53 pathway and related cell cycle status to bone loss measurements by histomorphometry, microCT and transmission R-ray microscopy.

RESULTS:
In brief we have now determined that short-term spaceflight (15 days) induces significant bone loss in the pelvic-femoral body-weight load-center of C57B6 mice, and that the multiple cellular and tissue mechanisms of bone loss are activated, including ostoclast activation, osteocytic osteolysis activation and osteoblastic cell cycle arrest mediator induction. Specifically we found that the p53/p21 signaling pathway was altered by spaceflight with marked increases in the expression of CDKN1a/p21 in osteoblasts, and generalized suppression of p53. These results validate the hypothesis that cell cycle arrest in osteoprogenitors is activated by spaceflight through p21, but also shows that cells are not induced to undergo p53 mediated programmed cell death/apoptosis, as indicated by decreased p53 levels and unaltered cell death.

experiment_title: The Effect of Long-term Microgravity Exposure on Cardiac Autonomic Function by Analyzing 48-hours Electrocardiogram
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Biological clocks synchronize and modulate circadian rhythms of systemic organs. Disruption of circadian rhythm are not only associated with an enhanced risk of cardiac disease, but also induce variety of other disease, such as metabolic disorder. Biological clocks are known to be affected by external stimulation, such as light and darkness. However, it is uncertain what influence space environment has on the biological clock. Measurement of RR-interval variability can reflect the circadian rhythm on cardiac autonomic nerve function. The investigators conducted continuous 24-hour RR intervals measurement in ten subjects for on a previous project. The preliminary data showed a variety of changes on biological rhythms and some biological rhythm of subjects were prolonged for 24 hours or more after flight. Therefore, to clarify the change of an accurate biological clock from spaceflight influence, we will evaluate 48-hour HRV (Heart Rate Variablity) and 96-hours of inflight actigraph on the future subjects.

APPROACH:
Baseline Data Collection
Testing will be conducted once preflight (L-180 to L-30 days), and once postflight (R+15 to R+90 days) baseline data collection (BDC). BDC consists of 48 hours ECG monitoring and 96 hours actigraph monitoring.

Inflight Data Collection
The first inflight data collection will occur 21 days in space, the second in-flight data collection will occur R-1, approximately three weeks in space. The in-flight data collection consists of 48 hours ECG monitoring and 96 hours of actigraph monitoring. When there are restrictions of a schedule, the subject will wear the actiwatch for 168 hours. In-flight data collections will consist of the following: the crewmember will destow the Actigraph equipments and configure the Actigraph using Dock, USB cable, and personal computer (PC). Then, the crewmember will wear the Actigraph. After 48 hours of Actigraph recording, the crewmember will destow the Holter ECG equipment and insert the multimedia card and the battery into the Digital Holter Recorder. After attachment of the five lead electrodes on his or her chest, the electrode will be connected to the connecting cable of the Digital Holter recorder. The crewmember will verify ECG monitoring operation by battery power switch on. After the 24 hour ECG recording, the crew will exchange the ECG Holter. Forty eight hours of ECG monitoring will be recorded without any activity constraint. After the end of data collection, these equipments will be removed, and 48 hour ECG data and 96 hour (a maximum of 144 hour ) Actigraph data will be transferred to the PC using the MMC, Dock and USB cable. Both of the ECG and actigraphic data is down-linked by PC and MPS system. The crewmember will then stow the equipment in the orbit stowage configuration.

experiment_title: The role of mechanoperception in gravity responses of the model organism Drosophila melanogaster
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster offers unique opportunities for genetic and molecular studies of cellular processes common to all multicellular organisms. In order to learn more of the pathways activated by the force of gravity, we have isolated a series of Drosophila mutants that have altered behavioral responses to gravity. These and other Drosophila mutants will be used to explore the signaling pathways underlying one the most marked changes associated with exposure to microgravity - loss of muscle tissue. Specifically the studies will address the issue of whether mechanosensory neurons and associated central brain circuitry regulate muscles responses to altered gravitational force. These studies will provide unique information on the regulation of muscle metabolism in response to changes in gravity and significant insight into these adaptive processes.

APPROACH:

The experiments were performed in the model organism Drosophila melanogaster, a small fruit fly. The project grew out of our previous work to identify genes that contribute to responses to gravitational force. During the course of this funding, we have pursued molecular and behavioral studies of two of these genes, which we have named yuri gagarin (yuri) and jim lovell (lov) in honor of our NASA funding and two heroic space pioneers. A powerful technique has been developed within Drosophila that allows conditional inactivation of targeted neurons. This technique will be used to inactivate the neurons under study and to determine whether this loss of neural input alters the responses of the muscles to hypergravity. Quantitative PCR will be used to examine muscle responses. A selection of genes indicated by other studies to show altered expression in response to altered gravitational force will be examined.

RESULTS:

We have established that the yuri gene encodes a protein, Tropomyosin, that interacts with a key component of the muscle contraction apparatus and that yuri is required for attachment of the centriole (basal body) to the spermatid nucleus. We have also established that the Lov protein is expressed in a subset of chordotonal neurons associated with muscles involved in locomotion.

experiment_title: Second Generation Electronic Nose
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The JPL Electronic Nose program is developing a broad band air quality monitor which will facilitate crew health and safety in the Space Station. Successful completion will result in an incident monitor capable of real time air quality monitoring. This device, or a group of such devices deployed as distributed sensors, will monitor changes in air composition and return information on the identity and quantity of compounds causing the change. The monitor will determine whether the change involves contaminants on the target list, and the quantity of contaminant in concentrations related to Spacecraft Maximum Allowable Concentrations (SMACs). The JPL ENose is a low mass, low power device which requires little crew time for maintenance and calibration.

JPL's ENose is a miniature environmental monitoring instrument that detects and identifies a wide range of organic and inorganic molecules down to the parts-per-million level. The kinds of changes that the ENose is designed to detect are anomalous events such as leaks and spills. The monitoring device uses an array of electronically conducting, thin-film polymer-carbon composite sensors. The chemical sensors change resistance when exposed to vapors by swelling or shrinking when vapor molecules enter or leave the film. No one sensor is dedicated to identifying any one compound. The pattern developed by the change in resistance of the entire array of sensors is used to identify the compound, and the magnitude of the response pattern is used to quantify the compound. Deviations from a baseline of clean air, determined by recording the response of the array to air cleaned in an activated carbon filter, are identified and quantified using a software program designed for this use.

The need for a low power, autonomous air quality monitor is pressing for an enclosed space such as the crew quarters of the International Space Station (ISS). In such a space, the presence of contaminants is particularly threatening because the crew is entirely reliant on the air revitalization systems (ARS) for healthy air; the air is not easily replaced. Contaminants may enter the air through leaks and spills from equipment and experiments or from smoldering fires. This kind of incident is a threat to crew health because they are unexpected and can occur with a sudden, large increase in contaminant concentration that may be toxic. The earliest warning possible is necessary to avoid threat to crew health from such incidents. Ideally, monitors which provide early warning of danger to crew health in the breathing air would be interfaced to ISS controls for automatic cleanup, sealing off affected areas until the crew can clean it up, or alerting the crew.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Phase I was completed and resulted in a prototypic model ENose with the capability to detect 10 compounds at the 1 hour SMAC. This device was flown as an experiment on STS-95 in 1998. Results aren’t available for Phases II and III of this experiment.

experiment_title: Dynamics of Calcium Metabolism and Bone Tissue
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The effect of space flight on the skeletal system is one of the most critical issues that needs to be resolved to assure crew well-being during extended duration missions. Due to the absence of weight bearing loads and other factors, bone mineral is lost during space flight. There is significant evidence of the negative impact of microgravity on bone homeostasis. Negative calcium balance has been noted previously in extended duration space flights (84-day Skylab) as well as following bed rest (simulated microgravity). The negative balance has been corroborated with increased excretion of calcium in the urine and feces, as well as decreased calcium absorption.

In addition, the hydroxylated metabolites of vitamin D (e.g., calcidiol, 25(0H)D3 and calcitriol, 1,25(0H)2D3) have been shown to play an important role in calcium homeostasis, primarily at the level of intestinal absorption of dietary calcium. Vitamin D intake is particularly important during extended duration space flights due to the decreased in vivo production of vitamin D through skin exposure to ultraviolet light.

This study was designed to assess changes in several indices of bone and calcium homeostasis during extended-duration space flight and after return to earth. Specific objectives were to: a) determine the effects of microgravity and diet on calcium absorption/kinetics; b) determine the effect of microgravity on total and ionized serum calcium; c) evaluate bone/calcium homeostasis during space flight by measuring regulatory hormones such as parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcitonin, vitamin D metabolites, osteocalcin, and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase; d) determine changes in bone density following flight in order to assess the impact and recovery from flight; and e) determine the accretion of bone mass following extended duration space flight.

APPROACH:
Three astronaut subjects participated in this experiment. Calcium absorption and kinetics were determined before, during, and after the mission. Other related measurements included the monitoring of bone density, bone and calcium regulating hormones, and urinary markers of bone metabolism. Postflight studies were designed to examine the recovery of bone mineral loss during the mission, as well as re-adaptation of bone regulating hormones and calcium metabolism after space flight.

Baseline specimen collection was performed over three five-day periods before and after flight on all three subjects. Blood, urine, feces and saliva were collected from 150 to 145 days before launch (L-150 to L-145), L-60 to L-55, and L-35 to L-33. Postflight samples were collected in two sessions beginning immediately after landing until six days postflight (R+0-6) and R+9-15. Additional data were also collected on R+75 and R+115. Samples were analyzed for 43 Ca and 46 Ca calcium isotopes, vitamin D metabolites, and indices of bone metabolism, e.g., pyridinoline, hydroxyproline:creatinine ratio.

Inflight blood, urine and saliva collections were performed two times in flight on Mir 18 (mission day 12 (MD 12)) and MD 93, and on flight day 5 (FD 5) on STS-71. A fourth inflight session, planned for MD 70 was not performed. A total of 32 blood samples was collected aboard Mir and 25 samples on board the Shuttle. All blood samples were aliquoted and frozen at -20 degrees Celsius for postflight analysis except for blood ionized calcium and osmolality (pH), which were determined in "real time" with a portable clinical blood analyzer (PCBA.) Inflight urine samples were collected using void-by-void techniques. Urine collection devices (UCD) were configured such that: a) a known volume of lithium chloride was included as a volume marker, and b) syringe aliquots could be withdrawn and stored appropriately. Inflight urine samples were either frozen at -20 degrees Celsius or preserved with thimerosal or thymol. Overall, 51 urine samples were collected aboard Mir and 22 samples aboard STS-71. Prior to each calcium absorption and kinetics study, urine samples were collected as soon as possible postsleep. Crewmembers were instructed to avoid food and fluids at least 8 hours prior to urine collection and at least 15 minutes before saliva collection.

Calcium absorption and kinetics were examined using a double stable isotope method. After baseline blood, urine, saliva and stool (pre/post sessions only) collection, subjects ingested 125 mg calcium carbonate (43Ca) as soon after sleep as possible. This was followed 1 hour +/- 15 minutes later by an 8 mg intravenous injection of labeled calcium chloride (46Ca). Crewmembers were to be fasting and unexercised for at least 10 hours prior to testing. Blood was collected 24 hours +/- 1 hour after the 46Ca injection. The blood was allowed to clot at +4 degrees Celsius for a minimum of 1 hour to a maximum of 3 hours prior to centrifugation. The separated plasma was stored for calcium and bone regulatory hormone determinations (PTH, calcitonin, vitamin D metabolites, and osteocalcin) following return to earth. Calcium isotopic enrichments in biological samples were determined using thermal ionization mass spectrometry. Absorption data were determined using the ratio of the two isotopes.

All foods, fluids and medications consumed were recorded in flight using a Bar Code Reader and/or recorded in a log book. The intake of certain dietary elements, especially calcium and Vitamin D, was evaluated postflight as part of the calcium absorption and kinetics determinations. This enabled investigators to understand the impact of dietary calcium on bone loss. The type and duration of exercise were also logged using the Bar Code Reader.

Bone density measurements were made preflight and postflight using Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA). Whole body DEXA scans were used to calculate total body and regional bone mass. Any associated loss of bone mass during the study was observed by this same technique. Three sessions were scheduled preflight for baseline data. Postflight, bone density determinations were to be made during the first week after landing and at 3 months, 6 months, and once every 6 months until recovery (but no longer than three years). Calcium absorption/kinetics were determined at landing and monthly thereafter (concurrent with bone density determinations).

RESULTS:
Analysis of hormone levels in blood serum revealed that concentrations of intact PTH were reduced almost 30% during flight compared to preflight. Calcidiol (25-0H Vitamin D) decreased during winter training in Russia (compared to autumn in Houston), and decreased further during flight. Calcitriol ((1,25(0H)2 Vitamin D) concentrations were also reduced almost 30% during flight. Osteocalcin tended to decrease during winter, and was increased or unchanged during flight. Bone-specific alkaline phosphatase concentrations were an average of 39% lower on flight day 14 and 11% lower on flight day 110 than preflight values. Serum total calcium was unchanged, the ionized fraction increased slightly. Venous whole blood pH did not change.

Despite incomplete urine collections inflight and postflight, investigators concluded that urinary calcium excretion was higher during flight than before. Urinary collagen metabolite excretion (n-telopeptide and pyridinium crosslinks) was almost 40% greater than the preflight level. Calcium absorption decreased during (38+/-18% below preflight values on flight day 110) and after flight (56+/-9% below preflight on landing day, n=2; and 29+/-28% below preflight on return +6 days). Three months postflight calcium absorption had returned to 4+/-20% below preflight values. These data showed that inflight bone loss was associated with increased resorption and decreased formation. Calcium balance was further altered by decreased PTH activation of calcidiol, with subsequent decreased calcium absorption.

experiment_title: Morphometric and EM Analysis of Tibial Epiphyseal Plates From Cosmos 1887 Rats
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Studies have shown that bone formation ceases during space flight, that the matrix formed during flight does not mature normally, and consequently cannot mineralize normally. The cartilaginous epiphyses of the long bones of space rats have received less attention, even though some of the changes that are seen in bone (e.g. decreased length and decreased trabecular mass) must originate in the epiphyseal region. The objectives of the present study were to look for differences in plate parameters and cell and matrix ultrastructure, in proximal tibial epiphyseal plates of space-flown rats.

Approach:

Light and electron microscopy studies were carried out on decalcified tibial epiphyseal plates. Height and cell number per zone and plate, shape of plates, and size of collagen fibrils were determined. A series of micrographs were taken in each zone, and measurements of collagen fibril length and width were made using a digitizing tablet. Means per section were averaged to obtain means per animal and statistical analysis was performed.

Results:

Flight animals had more cells than synchronous controls in the proliferative zone, and less in the hypertrophic/calcification region. The total number of cells, however, was significantly higher in flight animals. No differences were found for perimeter or shape factor of growth plates, but area was significantly lower in flight animals in comparison to synchronous controls. Collagen fibrils in flight animals were shorter and wider than in synchronous controls. The time required for a cell to cycle through the growth plate is 2-3 days, so most of the cells and matrix present were formed after the animals had returned to 1 g, and probably represent stages of recovery from microgravity exposure.

experiment_title: Spaceflight Effects on Muscle Fibers
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Whether a muscle fiber employs an oxidative or glycolytic energy mechanism is not immutably fixed, but can be influenced by external factors. Since space flight drastically alters the stimulus patterns to which skeletal muscle is exposed, it is relevant to investigate the changes which take place, not only in the muscle fiber size, but also in the energy mechanism. Rather than sampling each muscle only at a few positions along its length, this experiment seeks a quantitative total ascertainment of fiber size, number, and type.

Approach:

Muscle fiber size and type distribution were studied in the extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscle of space-flown rats and controls, using histochemical preparation techniques and computer image analysis to quantify the spaceflight-induced changes in muscle fiber size, number, and energy metabolism. The computer program produces a scatter plot showing how the fibers are distributed in diameter and optical density.

Results:

Average fiber diameter was largest in the vivarium control animals and smallest in the flight animals. Flight muscles appeared to be shorter than those of other groups. If this length difference is not an artifact of dissection, it could be the result of chronic extension of the foot and/or toes during space flight. Fiber number showed no significant difference. The "slow" fiber percentage was quite variable, and no statistically significant fiber type conversion was noted. There were no major cytoarchitectural changes, and necrotic changes and "moth eaten" fibers were not seen. The grouped grand mean fiber diameters show 17% and 7% reductions for the flight and synchronous groups, respectively, when compared to the vivarium group, strongly supporting the contention that hypogravity aggravates the atrophic effects of hypokinesis. While reduced activity may be the major cause of fiber atrophy in space flight, other factors may contribute. For example, the stress of negotiating the microgravity environment could produce an ACTH-cortisol response, a possible contributor to reduced fiber size.

experiment_title: Skeletal Responses to Long-Duration Simulated Microgravity in Male and Female Rats
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
Long duration spaceflight can cause severe bone loss, particularly at the lumbar spine and hip. The rate of bone loss in crewmembers while on the space station can be profound, and a significant increase in estimated fracture risk remains even one year after returning to Earth. In addition to microgravity, the natural aging process leads to declines in bone mass and also increases in fracture risk, which suggests that the combination of the two could have compounding effects on bone structure and integrity. Changes in bone structure and strength have unknown consequences and important implications for the skeletal health of crewmembers. In recent ISS missions, crewmembers have maintained bone mass better, presumably due to improved resistance exercise protocols coupled with adequate energy intake and vitamin D; however, no predictors of bone geometry or strength were evaluated. As NASA is preparing to send astronauts to the ISS and beyond for missions exceeding one year, it is critical to characterize and understand bone loss and recovery for longer duration spaceflight.

The proposed project will take advantage of the unique tissue sharing opportunity for obtaining frozen specimens from a UC Davis experiment that entails 90-day rat unloading and reloading studies. Specifically, the aims of this project are: 1) Determine structural and gene expression changes in cortical and cancellous bone in growing rats (3 month old) during long-duration simulated microgravity exposure and recovery. 2) Determine whether skeletal responses to long-duration simulated microgravity differ in males compared to females (3 month old). 3) Determine age effects (9 mo old) on temporal changes in skeletal structure and gene expression during extended simulated microgravity followed by recovery. We predict that osteoclastogenic and oxidative stress-related factors relates directly to the extent of bone decrements.

APPROACH:
To accomplish our Aims, we will determine how responses to simulated weightlessness vary in young (3 month old) versus adult (9 month old) male rats as a function of time, using 3D imaging (microcomputed tomography), mechanical testing, and molecular gene expression analyses. We also will determine if bone loss and recovery differ between male and female rats.

experiment_title: Evaluation of Thermoregulation During Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Impaired thermoregulation may have significant impact during space flight operations such as extravehicular activities (EVA), entry, landing and egress. Impaired thermoregulation, as represented by an increase in core (intestinal) temperature in response to a given thermal load, has been consistently observed in subjects confined to bed rest or immersed in water (Greenleaf, 1980; Greenleaf, 1985; Fortney, 1987). Further, these changes were observed during exercise following these simulated microgravity exposures (Greenleaf, 1980; Greenleaf, 1985; Fortney, 1987). Similar changes were expected to occur during space flight.

This impairment of temperature regulation may be manifested as decreased exercise capacity and increased orthostatic intolerance; it may also be manifested as higher levels of core body temperature for a given level of work (oxygen consumption, Vo2) both during and after space flight. The higher core temperatures may be due to altered cutaneous vasodilatory reflex (delayed onset of vasodilatation and decreased skin perfusion for a given level of core temperature), increased sweating threshold, and decreased sweating sensitivity, while heat production might not be altered. The purpose of this preliminary experiment was to assess human core (intestinal) temperature and thermoregulatory responses to exercise after adaptation to long-duration spaceflight. Specific objectives of this experiment were to:

1) Determine whether overall thermoregulation is impaired during space flight by comparing core temperature (Tin) during two submaximal levels of aerobic exercise preflight, inflight, and postflight;

2) Determine whether the elevated core temperature is caused by altered heat production, as calculated by indirect calorimetry;

3) Determine whether the elevated core temperature is caused by impaired heat loss, as assessed by the skin blood flow/core temperature relationship (where changes in skin blood flow are measured pre- and postflight by laser Doppler flowmetry, and estimated during all tests by calculations of tissue conductance) and by the sweating response. Local sweat response/core temperature relationship was measured pre- and postflight using a dew point hygrometer, and total body sweat loss is estimated during all tests by measuring body weight loss.

It was anticipated that, for a given absolute level of work, body temperatures would increase to a greater degree due to (1) a smaller production and/or decreased efficiency of evaporation of sweat, and (2) decreased convective heat loss from the surface of the skin.

APPROACH:
This investigation examined body temperatures (skin and core), heat production (indirect calorimetry), and evaporative heat loss during 2 standard levels of exercise (40% and 65% of preflight VO2peak).

Submaximal Cycle Exercise Test (before and after flight) - Graded maximal cycle exercise testing was first conducted to volitional fatigue on 2 crewmembers in the supine position. These sessions occurred 2-3 days before the preflight submaximal exercise tests, repeated during the last 5 days of the mission, and 6 days after landing (R+6). The graded maximal cycle exercise test protocol consisted of:

  • 5 minutes of supine rest on the ergometer
  • 2 minutes of warm-up at 50 Watts (W)
  • 5 minutes of pedaling at 100 W
  • 5 minutes of pedaling at 125 W
  • 5 minutes of pedaling at 150 W

    After the 150-W segment of the protocol, exercise intensity was increased by 25 W-per-minute until the subject could no longer maintain the 75-rpm pedaling frequency. Cool down was conducted at 50 W for 3-5 minutes after maximal exercise. During each maximal test, oxygen (O2) uptake and carbon dioxide (CO2) production were measured and averaged over 30-s intervals using a gas analysis system. Heart rate was continuously monitored with a standard electrocardiogram (ECG). Blood pressure was measured during the last 30 seconds of each exercise level using manual sphygmomanometry. The highest level of O2 uptake, averaged over a 60-s period, was designated peak oxygen consumption (VO2peak). Exercise intensities requiring 40% and 65% of the preflight peak value were used during the submaximal tests.

    The supine submaximal cycle tests were conducted 145-146 days before flight (L-145) and on R+5. All testing was performed at room temperature (22.6-23.3°C; 56-64% humidity) and at the same time of day to mitigate circadian effects. Postflight sessions occurred during the summer (July, 1995), but the crewmembers were almost exclusively confined to air-conditioned buildings. The submaximal exercise tests consisted of a continuous protocol of the following:

  • 20 minutes of quiet rest
  • 20 minutes of exercise at 40% preflight VO2peak (50 or 60 W)
  • 20 minutes of exercise at 65% preflight VO2peak (100 or 110 W)
  • 10 minutes of quiet resting recovery

    Heart rates during submaximal exercise were monitored with a heart watch. Blood pressure was measured twice before exercise and every 10 minutes during exercise with a manual sphygmomanometer. Skin temperatures were measured continuously with four external skin thermistors (forearm, calf, thigh, chest) and recorded with a data logger. Core temperature was measured using a small ingestible telemetry thermal sensor pill that was ingested 6 hours before exercise. Temperature data was sampled every 30 seconds and stored in a receiver.

    Skin blood flow velocity was measured continuously with a laser Doppler skin blood flow monitor using an integrated probe attached to the forearm with a local skin-heating (38°C) collar. Local sweating rate at the upper quadrant of the chest was measured continuously with a dew point hygrometer sweat system. The dew point sensor was ventilated (500-800 ml· min-1) with ambient air from the room. Subjects towel dried after each exercise session and were weighed in the same dry gym shorts before and after exercise. All measurement devices were calibrated before each exercise session.

    Submaximal Exercise Test (during flight): No submaximal data was collected during flight due to the late arrival of the Spektr module and scheduling problems after the module arrived.

    RESULTS:
    These results should be viewed as preliminary results only, since the low number of subjects did not allow for statistical analysis of the data. However, the results do suggest that thermoregulation was impaired following long-duration space flight.

    Maximal Exercise: The preflight maximal exercise supine cycle VO2peak values for the subjects were 32.6 and 29.5 ml• kg-1• min-1 for Subjects 1 and 2, respectively. Due to the limited active muscle mass with this form of exercise, these supine cycle values were each approximately 20% lower than the measured upright treadmill VO2peak values. During flight, Subject 1 was reported to have performed approximately 70% of the standard prescribed Russian countermeasure program (which consists of approximately 2 hours each day of aerobic and resistive exercises), while Subject 2 was reported to have performed less than 70% of the prescribed countermeasures. Near the end of the mission, on flight day 112, Subject 1 had a cycle VO2peak of 27.2 ml• kg-1• min-1(reduced 17% from preflight); for Subject 2, the value was 20.8 ml• kg-1• min-1(reduced 29%). After flight, neither crewmember could complete the exercise protocol, stopping after 28-29 minutes. Postflight, cycle VO2peak on R+6 was further reduced to 23.5 ml• kg-1• min-1 for Subject 1 (reduced 28% from preflight). For Subject 2, no value was obtained because the medical monitor would not allow the postflight maximal exercise test to be performed because of the subject's delayed recovery from the mission.

    Submaximal Exercise: Both crewmembers were able to complete the preflight submaximal exercise protocol; final exercise heart rates were only 137 and 123 bpm for Subjects 1 and 2, respectively. On R+5, Subjects 1 and 2 could not complete 11 and 12 minutes of the 65% VO2peak level, respectively. In both cases, the medical monitor terminated the test shortly after the exercise heart rate exceeded the preflight response. In each case, the subject appeared fatigued and was having difficulty maintaining the pedaling frequency.

    Blood pressure responses to exercise were similar before and after flight. Oxygen uptake on R+5 was similar to preflight values, except at the last sampling time for Subject 1, where the lower value was most likely due to his difficulty maintaining the pedaling frequency. The Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER) value was higher at most sampling times on R+5.

    A consistent difference was not seen between pre- and postflight supine resting skin temperatures at any measurement site. Resting intestinal temperature was similar preflight and at R+5. During postflight exercise, the core temperature, (Tin, ingestible telemetry pill) at test termination was similar (37.8 degrees C for both subjects despite a 29% shorter exercise time and a 40% reduction in the total cumulative work (W• min-1).

    The sweating and skin blood flow responses for the two subjects were altered postflight. The slope of the sweating/Tin relationship (mg• min-1• cm-2• °C-1) was reduced from 4.5 preflight to 2.1 postflight for Subject 1 and from 11 to 3.6 for Subject 2. The slope of the skin blood flow/Tin relationship (percent change Perfusion Unit• °C-1) was also reduced from 346 preflight to 214 postflight for Subject 1 and from 214 to 143 for Subject 2. Tin thresholds for the onset of sweating and vasodilation were not altered in a consistent manner after flight. For sweating, Tin thresholds (°C) were 37.4 preflight and 37.6 postflight for Subject 1 and 36.6 and 36.6 for Subject 2. For skin blood flow, Tin thresholds were 37.3 preflight and 37.5 postflight for Subject 1 and 37.6 preflight and 37.7 postflight for Subject 2. Total body sweat (weight) loss during preflight exercise was 636 g vs. 272 g postflight for Subject 1 and 455 g vs. 45 g postflight for Subject 2. Subject 2 had just reached the sweating threshold postflight when the session was terminated. Body weight on R+5 was reduced in both crewmembers from the preflight value--for Subject 1 by 0.8 kg and for Subject 2 by 2.3 kg.

    In conclusion, these preliminary findings suggest alteration of heat loss responses in two crewmembers following a 115-day space flight. The sensitivity of the heat loss responses was reduced after long-duration space flight, resulting in a faster rate of increase in core temperature.

experiment_title: Genes that Predict the Loss of Bone during Weightlessness
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The amount of bone loss between individual astronauts is highly variable with some astronauts losing large amounts of bone while others are largely unaffected. This variability is accounted for, at least to a large extent, by genetic variations between individuals. Unfortunately, the specific genes that modulate this genetic sensitivity of bone loss in microgravity are unknown. To this end, we have recently completed a genetic study in which we identified specific regions on chromosomes (QTL or Quantitative Trait Loci) that either add to or reduce the propensity of an individual to lose bone when normal weightbearing is removed from the musculoskeleton. While providing critical information, these QTL still contain hundreds of genes, rather than a single one. The principal objective of this grant is to identify specific genes that modulate the magnitude of bone loss during unloading.

APPROACH:
Investigators propose to greatly reduce the number of candidate genes with bioinformatics tools and then experimentally test the shortlist of candidate genes using knockout mice available from the Jackson Laboratory’s (JAX) Genetic Resource Repository and the JAX Knock Out Mouse Project (KOMP) production center. The identification of single genes modulating bone loss during weightlessness can be used as a critical diagnostic tool for the identification of astronauts most in need of countermeasures as well as to unravel novel drug targets that preserve bone health in space.

RESULTS:
Investigators made significant progress towards the goal of identifying specific genes and pathways that determine the amount of unloading-induced bone loss based on an individual’s genetic make-up. A second approach explored how aging may influence this genetic relationship.

experiment_title: Effects of Microgravity on Gene Expression in the Brain
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The mammalian brain exposed to space flight experiences profound changes in neuronal activity. Immediate early genes (IEGs), such as c-fos and Fos-Related Antigens (FRA), are useful indicators of changes in neuronal activity and plasticity. Within minutes of exposure to neural stimulation, the mRNA levels of these genes increase. The corresponding proteins can be detected for hours (Fos) or days (FRA) afterwards. These proteins may act as messengers to regulate the transcription of target genes involved in the physiological responses and adaptation to mG or readaptation to 1 G. This experiment investigated whether changes in IEG expression, occurring during space flight, affect brain structures involved in the control of: a) somatic (postural and motor) functions; b) vegetative (cardiovascular, respiratory and gastrointestinal) functions; and c) the regulation of the sleep-waking cycle. These changes were investigated to see if they depend on alterations in neuronal activity induced by macular gravity signals and, if so, whether they could be related to or modified during different phases of the sleep-waking cycle.

Approach:

Flight rats used in this study were part of the integrated adult rat dissections performed on FD 2 and FD 14. Postflight, remaining animals were sacrificed at different days after landing (R+1 and R+13, respectively). Simulated Caged Control (SIM) and vivarium animals were sacrificed on a 48-hour and 96-hour delayed basis. All brain tissue, excepting the cerebellum, was used in this experiment. Adjacent sections of the same brain tissues were alternatively stained with either a Fos or a FRA antibody, to mark both short- and long-lived responses to changes in gravity stimulus. These were characterized by hypergravity followed by exposure to mG at FD 2 after launch, stabilization to mG at FD14, hypergravity followed by exposure to 1 G at R+1 after landing, stabilization to 1 G at R+13. Tissue was removed from the fixative, cryoprotected in 30% sucrose solutions in phosphate buffer (PB) at 4 °C, frozen, and sectioned into 40 micrometer sections with a cryostat. Immunocytochemistry was used to detect Fos and FRA proteins in the forebrain and brainstem. The distribution of labeled cells in each brain region was examined and quantified. The number of labeled cells was compared between flight and SIM groups.

Results:

Variable numbers of Fos- and FRA-positive cells were found during different space flight conditions in Medial (MVe) and Spinal Vestibular nuclei (SpVe), which contribute to the vestibulo-ocular and the vestibulo-collic reflex, and in Group F nuclei, which projects to the vestibulocerebellum. In particular, all these structures showed a small increase in Fos and FRA expression at FD2, due to exposure to hypergravity partially compensated by exposure to mG, while a prominent increase of this expression occurred at R+1, due to hypergravity followed by exposure to 1 G. Similar changes in Fos and FRA expression occurred in the Area Postrema, which appears to be involved in the development of motion sickness, in the Nucleus of the Solitary Tract (NST) and the related ventrolateral reticular structures, which intervene in the central and reflex regulation of cardiovascular and respiratory activities, and finally in the Central nucleus of the Amygdala.

An increased level of Fos expression occurred in the noradrenergic Locus Coeruleus nucleus (LC) of flight rats with respect to ground controls, without variations at different time points of the space flight. However, the number of FRA-positive cells selectively increased in the LC of flight animals sacrificed at FD 2 and more prominently at R+1. These differences were attributed to the fact that, while the Fos protein induced by the gravity force returns to basal levels within hours after stimulation, thus being undetected 24 h after launch or the reentry, FRAs persist for days after induction. Since activity of noradrenergic LC neurons has been shown to produce gene expression in several target structures, it is likely that the long-lasting induction of FRAs in the LC at FD 2 and more prominently at R+1 contributes to the molecular changes occurring in the vestibular and the related structures indicated above.

An increase in Fos expression was also observed in the spinal areas of both the Inferior Olive (IO) and the Lateral Reticular nucleus (LRt) at FD 2 and FD 14, i.e., during and after the launch. However, only few labeled cells were observed in these precerebellar nuclei at R+1 and R+13. This last finding was partly attributed to reduced somatosensory and motor activities occurring at these specific time points of the space flight.

In addition, the increase in gravity force at R+1 selectively increased the number of FRA-positive cells in the dorsomedial cell column of the IO (which corresponds to the vestibular area of this structure), while no such changes affected the Fos expression. This increase in gene expression could then be detected by using only a long-lasting (FRA) and not a short-lasting (Fos) marker of neuronal plasticity.

The results of this experiment indicate that the gravity force acts on specific vestibular nuclei and related structures controlling somatic and vegetative functions, and that the noradrenergic LC neurons, driven by the gravity force, may contribute to long-term molecular changes occurring in the brain during adaptation to mG and readaptation to 1 G. Changes in gene expression in forebrain structures, such as the cerebral cortex, were finally used to identify the different phases of the sleep-waking cycle and relate the molecular changes occurring during different time points of the space flight to the animal state.

experiment_title: Bacteria and Spores
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Cells are the fundamental building block for all living organisms. The word cells was first coined by physicist Robert Hooke during his examination of a cork slice under a microscope. Complex organisms such as plants and animals are made of many cells that work together. Microorganisms are single cell organisms that are too small to see with the naked eye. Microorganisms were first discovered with the invention of a microscope by the Dutch scientist Anton van Leeuwenhoek. Leeuwenhoek, who made microscopes to count threads in drapery material for his shop in Holland, first described microorganisms as animalcules or little animals. Improvements in microscopes have greatly increased the knowledge of microorganisms and have led to many advances in medicine. However, much is still to be learned about the biological processes of microorganisms. The objective of this experiment was to determine the effects of microgravity on the survival, growth rates, and mutations of certain bacteria and spores.

APPROACH:
Bacillus subtilis and Escherichia coli were selected from a group of eleven non-pathogenic bacteria species that were screened before the Skylab 2 flight for experiment suitability. Originally planned for one flight on Skylab 2, this experiment was performed a second time on Skylab 4 to collect additional data. B. subtilis and E. coli were grown from broth culture and added to a water solution containing polyvinyl alcohol (PVA). PVA kept the bacteria alive but dormant until the experiment was started. The PVA solution containing bacteria was transferred to a circular disk of filter paper. The PVA suspension polymerized, holding the bacteria forms suspended on the filter paper in a viable state. Each disk was covered with aluminum foil for storage until inoculation. Bacterial growth was initiated by the insertion of the filter disk into agar-filled Petri dishes. Nine of the Petri dishes were placed in an incubator at approximately 95 degrees F and six were incubated at ambient temperature of approximately 77 degrees F. The cultures were periodically observed and photographed by crew members. Bacteria Petri dishes were placed in a food chiller to stop colony growth and preserve the cells for postflight analysis. However, the loss of the Skylab heat shield during launch resulted in a 10 day period where the maximum ambient temperature that the bacteria inoculum discs were exposed to was approximately 120 degrees F. This high temperature may have affected the viability of the bacteria. Inoculation of the Petri dishes with the bacterial disc was performed, however, and the total incubation time was extended from 48 hours to 69 hours. On Skylab 4, Bacillus mycoides was substituted for E. coli because of the failure of E. coli to grow on Skylab 2.

RESULTS:
During Skylab 2, colonies of E. coli did not develop and 75 colonies of B. subtilis developed following inflight inoculation. Bacteria growth rate was slower than expected for the flight cultures, therefore, the incubation time was extended from 48 hours to 69 hours. In addition, the ground control colonies also experienced a slower than expected growth rate. This experiment was repeated on Skylab 4 with B. mycoides substituted for E. coli. However, B. mycoides, like E. coli, failed to grow colonies on Skylab 4. The slower-than-planned growth rate of both flight and ground control colonies was also observed on Skylab 4. In addition, it was observed that there was contamination in the Petri dishes. Overall, bacterial control cultures grew more colonies compared to the Skylab cultures. However, the colonies that grew on Skylab were larger, grew faster, and were more irregular than control colonies. On Skylab 2, B. subtilis colonies were 50 percent larger than control colonies. Individual cells grew larger in diameter, but did not significantly increase in number. In addition, Skylab grown bacteria appeared to be more sensitive to postflight antibiotic treatment.

experiment_title: Core Temperature and Circadian Rhythms in Humans During Long-Term Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The circadian timing system (CTS) has been shown to be involved in the coordinated daily variation of almost every physiological and psychological system evaluated thus far. Maintaining synchronized circadian rhythms is important to health and well-being. The investigators hypothesize that long-term space flights significantly affect the synchronization of the circadian rhythm in humans due to changes in body composition, reduced physical activity, and/or changes of heat transfer, thermoregulation, and non-24-hour light-dark cycle in space. Therefore, the investigators aim to investigate the changes of core temperature profiles in humans during long-term space flight. Typically, 36 hour rectal temperature profiles are used to determine any changes associated with the CTS. However, such long-lasting continuous rectal temperature recordings are quite inconvenient for the subjects being investigated, especially during daily exercise and hygiene activities. Therefore, we recently introduced the double sensor, a new non-invasive heatflux method for determining body core temperature. The double sensor is located at the forehead and at the sternum/chest and allows continuous body core temperature measurements for extended periods of time.

Data on circadian rhythm obtained with the double sensor pre- in-, and post-flight shall be correlated with melatonin, which is one of the best-studied hormones following a classical circadian pattern. The results derived from the study might be useful to:

  1. understand the time course and basic principles of the adaptations of the human autonomic nervous system in space,
  2. adjust more adequately physical exercise as well as rest- and work shifts, and
  3. foster adequate workplace illumination in the sense of occupational healthcare to humans in space.

APPROACH:
Pre- and post-flight data collections for circadian rhythms will include 36-hour body temperature monitoring sessions on L-180, L-60, L-30 and postflight on R+7, R+30, R+60. Temperature sensors will be placed on the head and chest and skin surface temperatures will be recorded continuously during 36-hour periods, starting in the evening on Day 1 until the morning of Day 3. Once preflight and once postflight a 24-hour urine collection is planned together with the last preflight and first postflight data recording. Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA) measurements is planned once preflight (as close to launch as possible) and once postflight (as close to landing as possible).

Inflight temperature recordings are proposed for FD 15, FD 30, and every 30 days after that until the end of mission (FD 60, FD 90, FD 120, FD 150). During each inflight session, the crewmember will be instrumented with the double-sensors (Thermolab hardware) during the pre-sleep period of Day 1, and body temperature will be recorded continuously for 36 hours until the morning of Day 3.

RESULTS:

experiment_title: Assessing and Mitigating the Impact of Transmission Delays on Teleoperations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this study was to examine coupled human-system performance in the presence of temporally varying communication delays between the human controller(s) and remotely operated robot(s), and to propose countermeasures for delay-induced performance decrements. This DRP will be conducted in support of the NASA Enabling Technology Development and Demonstration (ETDD) Program’s Human Exploration Telerobotics (HET) Project, in which ground-station operators will control robotic assets on board the International Space Station (ISS). Specifically, the DRP will concentrate on the element led by NASA ARC that is focused on ground-to-orbit control of the “Synchronized Position, Hold, Engage, and Reorient Experimental Satellites” (SPHERES) free-flying robots on the International Space Station (ISS).

The DRP will focus on the range of time delays encountered in the ground-based control of the robotic assets on the ISS, ranging from 20-50 ms (effectively for line-of-sight communication) up to 2-10 s for multiple satellite ground-station relayed (Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System, or TDRSS, and associated ground network) communication, and, in particular, as delay instantaneously varies because of real-time changes in communication paths and data buffering.

The aims of the proposed work were: 1) to employ human-in-the-loop (HITL) testing to empirically investigate the impact of variable communication delays, with latencies spanning from tens of milliseconds up to approximately five seconds, on coupled human-system performance for telerobotic systems; 2) to evaluate empirically the efficacy of existing time delay compensation schemes for this range of latencies for telerobotic tasks and control modes that have different required movement precision levels; and 3) to use the data resulting from these studies to identify the trade points between latency compensation schemes as a function of time delay and required task precision and then design and test strategies for gracefully switching between mitigation techniques as telerobot system time delays vary.

The guidelines, tools, mitigation techniques and performance metrics developed from this research will help provide a rational basis for the design of teleoperation tasks to be carried out in the presence of communication delays. These products will in turn assist subsequent task, technology design, and validation experiment decisions regarding acceptable or desirable delay compensation techniques and define at what point to engage more autonomous operational modes.

APPROACH:
Investigators conducted human-in-the-loop (HITL) performance experiments using visual display of a dynamic simulation representative of a variety of SPHERES operations requiring different movement precision under this range of time-delay conditions. Next, they examined HITL performance under these conditions employing mitigation techniques for short time delays such as prediction algorithms that generated compensatory in command signal lead and, for longer delays, predictive “feed-forward” graphical overlays that “look ahead” and provided a virtual view showing the future pose and location of the robot. The goal of the second of the studies was to understand the performance trades between these techniques in a wider variety of environmental and latency conditions than is usually achievable during in situ experimentation. Based on these empirical HITL results, investigators designed and tested a strategy for combining and gracefully switching between mitigation techniques as telerobot system time delays vary across the millisecond to second range.

To conduct the DRP studies, investigators built their experiment testbed derived from elements of the HET ground-to-orbit SPHERES task, encompassing ground operator user interfaces as well as computer-based simulations of the SPHERES robots and ground-ISS communication links. This strategy allowed them to run HITL tests that will reduce the operating environment to offer sufficient flexibility and control for human performance experiments, yet still maintain salient features of the HET tasks key for face-validity and applicability of the results. The results from the experimental studies will help define more focused and scientifically revealing experiments that could subsequently be conducted on the ISS.

RESULTS:
Movement time and trajectory data from all twenty participants, pooled across all experiment conditions, were significantly positively correlated, indicative of a speed-accuracy tradeoff in their performance. Analyses of Variance (ANOVAs) conducted separately on path length and movement time (transformed to correct for data skew) produced identical results. These ANOVAs showed a significant effect of rotation angle and an interaction between rotation angle and axis, but did not reveal a significant effect of the sequence of rotation axis. General features of the data indicate that the MDF, whether expressed in terms of movement time or path length, reaches a peak at or near 120 degrees for all axes and that the peak’s magnitude was significantly greater for rotation about the roll axis.

The results from this study indicate that the MDF, i.e., the effect of the control-display rotation, is not isotropic with respect to axis of rotation: roll produces a distinctly larger nonlinearity and peak magnitude. Investigators conjecture this is due to the displacement arising from the roll misalignment being projecting into the participant’s two key body reference axes, i.e., the lateral (left-right) axis and the vertical axis (usually aligned with gravity), which contrasts with pitch and yaw disturbances being projected into only one of these axes in the frontal plane.
