experiment_title: Development and Validation of Therapeutic Ultrasound for Bloodless Surgery in Clinical Simulation in an Analog Environment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As astronauts venture farther from Earth, the risks of medical crises increase. Ultrasound is a well-known imaging modality that has been successfully used on the International Space Station (ISS) to help mitigate these risks. In addition, there is potential to leverage advances in Earth-based clinical applications of high intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) to enable non-invasive surgical treatments during exploration missions. HIFU therapies have the potential to treat a wide range of indications that could occur in future exploration missions, including stopping internal bleeding with acoustic hemostasis, treating cancerous tumors that may arise quickly from exposure to radiation, palliation of pain, or even acting as an acoustic scalpel to treat serious internal injuries noninvasively, through the skin.

To realize the potential of using HIFU with flexible ultrasound system (FUS) guidance in space, a suitable test-bed phantom is needed to provide a training apparatus for astronauts and test the delivery of therapy to targeted anatomical sites. The goal of this project was to develop such phantom with anatomical and acoustical features relevant to clinical HIFU such as skin, ribs, inhomogeneous body wall, and tissue targets to simulate thermal and mechanical HIFU treatments.

APPROACH:
A HIFU transducer containing an imaging probe in its central opening was developed. A power source was built with the ability to deliver either short pulses at high powers for mechanical treatments or continuous output at moderate powers up to 700 W for thermal treatments. To represent fat and muscle in body wall, phantom layers were made from polyvinyl alcohol with irregular-shaped walls; the skin was represented by a silicone sheet; ribs were fabricated by 3D-printing based on a human anatomical model relevant to liver or kidney treatments. HIFU targets comprised optically transparent alginate or polyacrylamide gels that allows visualization of the lesion. These components were assembled in a water tank to provide coupling between layers and allow shifting of their relative positions. Free-field hydrophone measurements were performed for transducer characterization and shocked waveforms with peak positive/negative pressures of +100 / -20 MPa were measured; in situ fields behind ribs and body wall were then characterized both by hydrophone measurements and observations of lesion formation. When ribs were present, shocks formed at about half amplitude at the same power, and higher pressures were measured with ribs positioned closer to the transducer. The presence of a uniform body wall structure attenuated shock amplitudes by a smaller amount and was insensitive to axial position. Mechanically ablated lesions were visualized in target gels.

RESULTS:
Results showed that the presence of ribs and absorptive tissue-mimicking layers did not prevent shock formation at the focus and each layer simulated the impact on the beam focusing and shock formation similarly to the observations from in vivo and ex vivo experiments. Overall, with real-time lesion visualization, the developed low-maintenance HIFU phantom system compatible with FUS can serve as a training tool for researchers, engineers, and clinicians to facilitate faster acceptance of HIFU therapies for a number of applications to be used both in Earth-based and space-based conditions.

experiment_title: Whole Joint Health: Investigating Modeled Spaceflight Changes in Mice (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During extended space flight missions, astronauts are exposed to a microgravity environment. The disuse from unloading of the musculoskeletal system results in bone loss and could also degrade the soft connective tissues (i.e. cartilage, meniscus, ligaments), which are critical to the proper functionality of the joint. Degradation of the soft tissues is important because it leads to laxity and joint instability, which when combined with loss of bone strength, could amplify the risk of bone fracture and joint injury. The increased fracture and injury risks in astronauts could compromise a mission and hinder recovery upon returning to Earth.

Micro computed tomography (micro-CT) and computational modeling provide important information about bone strength changes in the femoral neck and proximal tibia in the Hind Limb Unloading (HLU) mouse animal model. Both space flight and HLU caused similar declines in bone volume, but different declines in bone strength and structural efficiency. The comparison between these two studies shows the deficiency in the current clinical assessments of bone health, which only measures bone density. The computational methods developed in these studies can be translated to assess humans as non-invasive clinical imaging improves. Developing these relationships between bone density and corresponding bone strength in the HLU model can provide information to help studies of humans on Earth undergoing disuse, such as during bed rest. This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Further develop the image analysis technology for assessing changes to mouse knee joint soft tissue with microCT, including cartilage, meniscus, ligaments, and tendons.
  2. Assess whole-joint changes in the knee, including bone and soft tissues, from both unloading and reloading using the established HLU model. This was accomplished with two studies:
    2a. Study the effects of HLU on integrated joint properties, mimicking the STS-135 Space Shuttle flight profile.
    2b. Study the effects of longer-term unloading followed by reloading on whole-joint structural and functional properties.

APPROACH:
Investigators performed finite element (FE) modeling at the proximal tibia skeletal site for mice undergoing 21-days of space flight on SPX-4. These mice were skeletally mature mice, which reduced any confounding effects of the animals still growing during the study. These findings were compared to results from mice flown on Space Shuttle Mission STS-135 for 13 days as well as the parallel HLU study which lasted 13-days.

RESULTS:
Analysis of the proximal tibia from skeletally mature mice flown on SPX-4, Rodent Research-1, found that approximately 21 days of space flight resulted in a decline in trabecular bone volume fraction (-45%) and total bone volume (-20% for combined cortical and trabecular bone) in the proximal tibia. FE modeling of this region found this corresponded to a decline in compressive structural stiffness (-28%) which corresponded to a 12% decline in bone structural efficiency. Separation of the cortical and trabecular bone compartments found the majority of loss in the bone strength was in the cortical compartment. These findings are consistent with those observed from FE Analysis of the mouse proximal tibia from STS-135 as well as the complementary Hind Limb Unloading study.

Results from the HLU study had similar overall trends that were observed in space flight. One major difference is that while both HLU and space flight caused a 17% decline in proximal tibia bone volume, HLU caused a 22% decline in bone strength, compared to the 34% decline from space flight.

The use of skeletally mature mice and having the mice sacrificed while in orbit reduce the confounding factors of reloading as well as skeletal growth of the animal during the study. Thus, the majority of the observed decline in bone can be attributed to the microgravity conditions, with some possible loss due to aging. Even in skeletally mature mice (32 weeks old), the 21 days of space flight caused a decline in proximal tibia structural efficiency. Using older mice could better model space flight related bone loss in astronauts, as the average astronaut has achieved skeletal maturity. The FE modeling provides a more detailed assessment of bone health compared to the traditional microCT analysis and should be considered in future assessments of bone quality.

experiment_title: Kinesthetic Compensation for Sensorimotor Rearrangement
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Laboratory studies were conducted to evaluate a newly proposed technique to allow users to control a computer screen cursor in the presence of large rotational sensorimotor rearrangements. This technique is called "kinesthetic cueing." Such rearrangements commonly occur when users teleoperate manipulators while remote cameras provide views of the worksite which are rotated with respect to the direction of command action. If the direction and position of the camera were sensed, consistent display and control actions can be achieved computationally. This remapping is, how-ever, not always possible and users of teleoperations systems often must train to work in rotated coordinate systems.

Development of portable, body-worn information appliances such as head-mounted see-through and partially occlusive displays has introduced a new environment in which rotated coordinate system can interfere with system usability. These portable systems often have Graphical User Interfaces for which the user inputs spatially continuous information with a cursor control device. Since these appliances are portable, the cursor control device must be hand-held or body mounted. The main question is whether kinesthetic information from holding or body mounting the cursor control device assists users who operate under conditions of rotational sensorimotor rearrangement.

Kinesthetic cueing will be provided to the experimental users by having them contact the cursor control device with the hand not controlling the cursor. This hand, usually the nondominant left hand, will be rotated to copy the rotation, i.e., mis-alignment angle, with which the operator must deal. Preserving its rotated position, it is then placed in contact with the cursor control device.

Early results of these three experiments will be provided to the developers of the Wireless Augmented Reality Prototype (WARP) Phase III, a head-mounted, wireless display system being designed at JPL. The design of WARP's cursor controller will be advanced by appropriate kinesthetic cueing. Benefits are also expected in the design of human interfaces for teleoperations.

APPROACH:
Informal observations suggest that the proposed technique works. Experiment 1 is intended to formally test the idea and determine whether the cueing hand needs to be the nondominant hand. If this technique can be successfully developed, it will solve two problems associated with training users to deal with sensorimotor rearrangements. First, it could reduce or eliminate the need for adaptation training. Secondly, it could remove concern about the perceptual after effects of adaptation. To examine this second possibility, Experiment 2 is specifically intended to measure the size of possible perceptual after effects experienced by users whose training to operate under conditions of sensorimotor rearrangement has been assisted by kinesthetic cueing. Finally, Experiment 3 will investigate the benefits of kinesthetic cueing with a variety of cursor input devices besides the graphics tablet used in Experiment 1. These will include trackpads, isometric joysticks, mice and tablet devices.

experiment_title: Oxidative Stress as a Mechanism for Altering Acute and Chronic Functional Changes in the CNS Exposed to Low Dose, Low Dose Rates, and Mixed Fields of Protons and HZE Nuclei
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The space radiation environment poses unique hazards that include solar particle events and galactic cosmic rays. These types of radiations have been shown to cause acute and long-lasting chemical changes referred to as oxidative stress that can alter the normal physiology of the central nervous system (CNS). The chemical species produced can cause a wide range of effects in cells within the CNS that largely depend on the types of pathways they activate and the types of damage they produce. Proper functioning of the CNS depends on many factors, but is known to require subpopulations of neural stem and precursor cells that participate in the repair of CNS injury resulting from irradiation. This proposal focused on analyzing the effects of space radiation on these critical populations of multipotent neural stem and precursor cells. Investigators have developed the technology to isolate and grow these cells in culture and will use a variety of techniques to analyze how cells exposed to space radiation change. They planned to monitor the time course of oxidative stress in these cells and how that depends on the dose, the dose rate and type of radiation applied. They will determine how radiation-induced oxidative stress impacts cellular proliferation, signaling between cells, cell fate and survival. Collectively their studies using both rodent and human neural stem and precursor cells will help NASA understand the acute and longer-lasting sequelae associated with the exposure of the CNS to the space radiation environment. These studies will facilitate efforts to more appropriately establish estimates of risk for radiation exposure to the CNS in space.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results below.

RESULTS:
Past data collected by the investigators has demonstrated that the radiation response of multipotent neural precursor cells to x-rays, protons, and HZE nuclei involves an acute and persistent oxidative stress that can last for months. The importance of neural precursor cells to the repair and remodeling of the irradiated CNS is underscored by the data showing that the radiation-induced depletion of these cells is linked to the inhibition of neurogenesis and the onset of cognitive impairment. Investigators believe oxidative injury is critical in this context, and plays a contributory if not causal role in determining neural precursor cell function, survival and fate. A summary of the study findings are listed below.
1. Mice genetically manipulated to overexpress human catalase in the mitochondria were found to exhibit higher basal levels of neurogenesis and after low dose exposure to 150 MeV protons. These data suggest that interventions targeted to reduce oxidative stress in the mitochondria are neuroprotective.
2. A great deal of work characterizing the response of cultured neural stem cells from both rodents and humans were performed. These data reveal a marked predisposition of neural stem cells to exhibit radiation-induced oxidative stress. The functional importance of radiation-induced oxidative stress in regulating adaptive responses was also shown, as treatment of cells with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine eliminated the protective effect of prior exposure on cell survival following exposure to a subsequent higher dose of protons. Collectively, these data provide further evidence in support of the ides that space relevant fluences of charged particles elicit significant levels of oxidative stress that impact survival and proliferation.
3. Work characterizing the effect of HZE particle irradiation on cultured neural stem cells and the irradiated rodent brain was performed. There was a marked and persistent increases in oxidative stress found months after exposure to very low fluences of 600 MeV iron ions. Oxidative stress measurement made in vivo found that low dose exposure caused marked changes in the level and activity of several key antioxidant enzymes two weeks after exposure that returned to background one month after irradiation. Importantly, exposure to 5 or 30 cGy of 600 MeV oxygen or titanium ions was found to elicit significant deficits in novel object recognition 12 weeks after exposure. These data link key changes in redox metabolism to functional changes in cognition, changes that have important implications for astronauts exposed to the space radiation environment.
4. Investigators were able to assess the metabolic activity of neural stem cells after low dose irradiation using non-invasive 2-photon spectroscopy.
5. This is a comprehensive study that has defined the radiobiological response and consequences of human neural stem cells exposed to low LET radiation.
6. A review of the redox stress biology of irradiated neural stem cells and stem cells from other organ systems.

In summary, investigators have obtained significant data over the course of their funding period demonstrating that low dose charged particle irradiation can elicit oxidative stress in multipotent neural stem and precursor cells, derived from both rodents and humans. Their data shows conclusively that prior exposure elicits adaptive responses that are capable of attenuating oxidative stress and survival. Collectively their data suggest that radiation-induced oxidative stress constitutes a biochemical mechanism of functional significance to neural stem cell biology and cognition.

experiment_title: Promoting Sensorimotor Response Generalizability
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this study is to develop an inflight treadmill training protocol that enhances adaptive generalization of locomotor function to facilitate rapid and robust recovery of functional mobility after long-duration space flight. Specifically, the investigator hopes to determine whether subjects exposed to a special inflight treadmill protocol will have greater proficiency in reassembling an appropriate, full-body postflight locomotor response. Will they recover locomotor function sooner than subjects not exposed to the inflight treadmill protocol? Data from this experiment are planned to be used to develop a countermeasure system.

APPROACH:
Locomotor function were assessed before and after space flight using two tests of gait function.

Test 1: The Integrated Treadmill Locomotion Test characterizes alterations in the integrated function of multiple sensorimotor subsystems. This test required subjects to walk on a motorized treadmill while researchers assessed changes in dynamic postural stability, head-trunk coordination, visual acuity and lower limb coordination strategies.

Subjects walked at 6.4 km/h on a motorized treadmill while performing a visual task consisting of identifying the position of the gap in the letter "C" that is presented centrally on a laptop computer positioned 4 meters in front at eye level. Each trial lasted approximately 30 seconds and was repeated four times. Subjects also walked at 6.4 km/h on the treadmill while performing the same visual task described above, but in this case, with the letter "C" presented centrally on a micro-display positioned 50 centimeters in front at eye level. Each of these trials lasted approximately 30 seconds and were repeated four times. While subjects were walking on the treadmill and performing the visual task, 3-dimensional full-body motion data were acquired using a video-based motion analysis system; gait cycle timing was measured using foot switches placed in the shoes and dynamic visual acuity was assessed by the visual task described above.

Test 2: The Functional Mobility Test provides a corresponding assessment of the functional and operational changes in locomotor function by testing a subject's ability to negotiate an obstacle course placed over a medium-density foam floor. Subjects walked at a preferred pace through an obstacle course set up on a base of 10 cm thick medium density foam. The foam provided an unstable surface that increases the challenge of the test. The 6.0 m x 4.0 m course consists of several pylons and obstacles made of foam. Subjects were instructed to walk through the course as fast as possible without touching any of the objects on the course. This task was repeated three times in the clockwise direction and 3 times in the counterclockwise direction. The dependent measures are time to complete the course and the number of obstacles touched or knocked down.

RESULTS:

Test 1: Integrated Treadmill Locomotion Test
Results showed that subjects exhibited postflight changes in head-trunk coordination, toe clearance and gait cycle timing during treadmill locomotion. Dynamic visual acuity was decreased postflight, followed by an improvement in performance during the postflight recovery period. An analysis of the relationship between inflight treadmill usage characteristics and postflight functional mobility performance revealed that subjects who exercised on the iRED with greater body loading had enhanced postflight (R+1) functional mobility performance.

Test 2: Functional Mobility Test
Results indicate that adaptation to space flight led to a 62% increase in time to traverse the obstacle course on one day after return, and recovery of function took an average of 11 days after return.

In conclusion, recovery of functional mobility after long-duration space flight is composed of two distinct but interrelated motor learning processes: 1) rapid on-line strategic change characterized by immediate onset after landing and 2) slower adaptive change requiring days to complete after landing.

Postflight (R+1) changes in gaze control produced decreases in dynamic visual acuity (DVA) during walking. For some subjects, the decrement was greater than the mean acuity decrement seen in a population of vestibularly-impaired patients (collected using a similar protocol). The population mean showed a consistent improvement in DVA performance during the two-week postflight recovery period. Post-flight neurological exams conducted by flight surgeons have rated gaze and ocular symptoms from mild to severe in over 50% of returning Shuttle astronauts. These observations are consistent with the decrements in visual acuity during locomotion described in this report. Future work should focus on the addition of a “field” test of dynamic visual acuity that could be incorporated in the postflight examinations. This research should focus on the development of a portable system that will provide passive body motion (i.e. seated subject on a motion base) while subjects perform tests of visual performance. Astronauts should be tested as soon as possible after landing to assess the early effects of gaze dysfunction related to sensorimotor adaptation. This will allow a better determination of the potential impacts of changes in visual acuity on landing performance.

This research led to conduct of ground-based studies focusing on developing adaptability training programs that include both gait and manual control training. In addition this research is investigating the retention capabilities of adaptability training, allowing this type of training to be conducted preflight and therefore reduce the requirement for an inflight training component, thus saving inflight crewtime and upmass hardware requirements. It will be useful to examine the relationship between other in-flight exercise modalities (cycle ergometer, upper body resistive exercise) and post-flight functional mobility performance to determine if a relationship exists. The current in-flight exercise data set includes only average data from US crewmembers over the entire duration of the mission. The exercise prescriptions to US crewmembers are graded over the duration of mission with the intensity (especially loading) and duration increased towards the end of the mission. Hence, the above analysis may be overly conservative in its estimates and should be extended with data over separate in-flight periods to confirm the relationships observed in the present study.

Results obtained from this research helped motivate the design of the Functional Task Test, a pre/postflight battery of tests used to assess performance of astronauts on functional tasks that are representative of critical mission tasks for lunar and Mars operations. The Functional Task Test will allow better definition of the linkage between physiological change and functional performance including across several physiological systems (sensorimotor, cardiovascular, muscle performance).

experiment_title: Response of Crown Gall Tissue to the Space Environment: Tumor Development and Anatomy
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The crown system has been suggested as a model to study the long-term effects of weightlessness on biological systems. Earlier studies show that tumors induced by inoculating cut surfaces of carrot disks with bacterium cells were significantly larger when gravity compensated on clinostats than those developed at 1 g. This study compared tumors developed in the space environment with Earth-based controls.

Approach:

Carrots were cross-sectioned and placed aseptically in flight canisters. The upper surfaces of the sections were inoculated with bacterial suspensions (1 x10-8 cells/ ml) of Agrobacterium tumefaciens. The inoculated disks in the canisters were incubated at 25°C for 72 hours to allow initiation of tumors. Canisters were exposed to the weightless conditions of the space environment and to the effects of the onboard centrifuge. Synchronous controls were maintained at both NASA-Ames and in the USSR. Tumors were excised from frozen tissue, weighed, and histologically examined.

Results:

Larger (statistically significant) crown gall tumors developed on flight-centrifuged disks than on those exposed only to microgravity. The reaction was opposite to that predicted from previous Earth-based gravity (non)compensated experiments. It is possible that more disks in the weightless treatment were nonresponsive to generation of galls than those on the centrifuge, but plots of individual tumor weights from each disk appear to eliminate this possibility. An increase in radius of the meristemic rings of growth centers in these teratoma type galls was observed, however, for tissues generated in the weightless (flight) and gravity- compensated (ground) conditions. In this respect, results obtained using a clinostat were similar to those observed in tissues developed in microgravity.

experiment_title: Morphometric Studies of Atrial Granules and Hepatocytes: I. Morphometric Study of the Liver
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The goal of the present study was to characterize the vacuoles, to obtain data with which to evaluate the gross and microscopic differences, and, if possible, to explain the increased liver weight of the flight group from microscopic morphometric findings. In addition to the use of general histological techniques, morphology of the hepatocyte nuclei and intracytoplasmic vacuoles was undertaken using light microscopic computer assisted image analysis.

Approach:

Light microscopic computer assisted morphometry was performed with an image analysis system of the hepatocyte nuclei and intracytoplasmic vacuoles of rat liver. Nuclei in 25 fields of view were measured in stained 4 µm embedded sections. Care was taken to include representative fields from all lobular regions. These were selected at random but were included only if scanning indicated that fixation was adequate. To ascertain the relationship between the increase in liver weight of flight animals and the results of this study, an assumption was made that the specific gravity of the vacuolar contents was similar to that of the other extranuclear components of the hepatocyte.

Results:

On that basis, calculations showed that the elevated vacuolar volume density in the flight group did not cause the increased liver weight in those animals, but that the non-nuclear, non-vacuolar parenchymal compartment did contribute significantly. Since only rare vacuoles were stained in all groups, severe glycogenic infiltration was regarded as the most likely cause of the pale appearance of the flight livers. Supporting this conclusion is the fact that glycogen would have been dissolved in the aqueous fluids used in processing, leaving empty spaces such as those seen in preparations. Regardless of the correctness of these assumptions, there is little doubt that changes in nuclear and vacuolar components were only minor contributors to the increased liver weight of the flight animals, while the remainder of the hepatocytic cytoplasm contributed the major portion of the increase.

experiment_title: Incapacitated EVA Crewmember Translation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:,
The objective of this DTO was to verify techniques to allow an extravehicular activity (EVA) crewmember to return an incapacitated EVA crewmember to the Shuttle airlock. The DTO evaluated several techniques to determine which techniques are the most efficient. The techniques were defined in this DTO. Some of the techniques used existing hardware; others required DTO hardware.

Incapacitated crewmember rescue techniques have been successfully demonstrated in the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL), but have not been successfully proven on orbit. A previous on orbit demonstration of crewmember translation techniques (STS-54) attempted to validate a technique for translating with an incapacitated crewmember. While the technique of holding onto the crewmember with one hand and translating with the other was successful in the NBL, it was not successful on orbit. This demonstrates that the NBL simulation is sufficiently different from the on orbit environment, and that the NBL results are not reliable for this purpose. A reliable verification of incapacitated crewmember rescue techniques is required to assure crew safety during EVA. APPROACH:
The demonstrations were conducted by one of the EVA crewmembers translating with the other crewmember simulating an incapacitated crewmember. The DTO was manifested on one or more Shuttle missions to allow the evaluation of several translation techniques. The evaluations were conducted in the Orbiter payload bay or on the International Space Station (ISS). The evaluations were conducted so that the results of the DTO will be applicable to ISS as well as Shuttle. Success was defined as the ability to translate the equivalent length of the payload bay (at a minimum) and into the airlock safely, i.e. without posing additional risk to the crew, Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU) or vehicle. Translation time was also evaluated based on a comparison between the DTO translation path and possible ISS translation paths.

experiment_title: Orbiting Frog Otolith Experiment: Comparison to Control Studies
experiment_description:
Objectives:

To obtain information concerning the response of the basic acceleration sensor mechanism (hair cells of the otolith organ) to weightlessness.

Approach:

Two bullfrogs were completely immersed in water. Action potentials were recorded from four vestibular nerve fibers corresponding to the gravity sensors of the inner ear. A centrifuge built into the experiment capsule subjected the sensors to a range of 10-3g during weightlessness and periodically up to 0.6g of stimulation.

Results:

During the first few days of weightlessness, the otolith showed 1) fluctuation of the activity at rest up to 20 times larger than on the ground, 2) a change of gain and mode of the responses to the centrifuge spin cycles; the mode changed from tonic to phasic and vice versa. Change 1 gradually disappeared in 4-5 days, the activity at rest returning to normal. Change 2 was maintained throughout the flight, not showing a trend toward normalization.

experiment_title: The Influence of Environmental Stress on Cell-Mediated Immune Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES
The human immune system is composed of multiple interacting elements including contributions from both the humoral and cell-mediated arms. These elements play unique roles and interact in various ways with each other in maintaining the optimum immune status and health of humans. Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) involving sensitized T-lymphocytes is important in defense against certain infectious agents (e.g., viruses and fungi), in surveillance against neoplastic cells, and in regulation of immune function. CMI function testing has traditionally been done by skin testing with cutaneous placement of recall antigens (delayed cutaneous hypersensitivity). By introducing an antigen to which an individual has been previously exposed, the capacity of T-lymphocytes to respond to an antigen in memory can be assessed.

Measurement of cutaneous delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) responses to a battery of commonly encountered antigens is a generally accepted and preferred means of assessing CMI function. In the past, such DTH testing suffered from lack of standardized testing techniques, number and characterization of reactions, doses employed, and interpretation of reactions and results. A commercially available system has solved these problems by providing simultaneous and reproducible application of seven standardized recall antigens as a means of measuring DTH in assessment of CMI. Because of its properties, widespread clinical acceptance, and ease of use, this system was adopted for this study.

This process of skin testing and evaluation of cell-mediated immune function has been used in other extreme environments such as Antarctic expeditions, tours of duty in submarines, and during both short- and long-duration space flights. All of these studies have shown that stress can have a negative impact on CMI function. The exact mechanisms underlying these changes are not yet fully understood.

APPROACH
In this investigation, repeated skin testing was utilized in order to determine the functional state of the chamber crews' CMI systems over time and compare to a control group of subjects not exposed to the environmental stress of isolation within the closed chamber.

There were two subject groups in this study: (1) the experimental (chamber) group, which consisted of the four chamber occupants, and (2) the control group, which consisted of four sex- and age-matched volunteers. All individuals completed a training session on the proper application of the skin test device and measurement of the results.

The following procedure was used for application of the testing device at each time point:
 

  1. The volar surface of a forearm was cleansed with an alcohol pad and allowed to dry.
  2. The test device was then placed against the forearm and firmly pressed into the skin. The prongs at the tip of each arm entered the skin and delivered the antigen.
  3. A rocking motion was used to ensure adequate delivery of the antigens and control.
  4. The test device was removed, and the area was allowed to dry for 5 minutes.
  5. A permanent marker was used to outline the skin area tested to allow later observation of the proper sites.
  6. After 48 hours, each antigen site was evaluated for induration, and calipers were used to measure the diameter of the induration along the vertical and horizontal axes.
  7. The number of antigens that reach at least 2 mm in diameter were considered positive. The sum total millimeters of induration and the number of positive antigens were recorded and used to determine a CMI score according to the formula: CMI Score = Sum of Mean Indurations/Number of Positive Antigens.

RESULTS
The chamber subjects had fewer responses to the seven antigens at the C-30 time point compared to the control subjects. By chamber day 45 (C+45), the chamber subjects showed hypoergic responses, and by chamber day 90 (C+90) all chamber subjects exhibited anergy to the seven challenge antigens. The chamber subjects had returned nearly to their prechamber baselines within 30 days of exiting the chamber. The control group subjects responded to more antigens at the C-30 time point and showed variable responses, but only minor changes throughout the study period.

Since the chamber subjects responded initially (C-30) to fewer antigens, the baseline value for the sum of the indurations in the chamber subjects is less than that for the control group. The chamber subjects showed a loss of reactivity to most of the antigens by chamber day C+45 and had no response to any of the antigens and thus no measurable indurations at chamber day C+90. By 30 days after exit from the chamber (E+30), the measured sum of indurations had returned to near baseline level in the chamber subjects. The control subjects showed a variable response throughout the study. One control subject exhibited a slightly attenuated response on chamber day C+45 while another showed increased responses at chamber days C+45 and C+90. On day E+30, all control subjects had values similar to pre-chamber baseline measurements.

The most interesting and meaningful results for both the control and chamber groups involved their average CMI scores. The average CMI score for the control subjects varied little throughout the entire study period (range 4.05 to 4.23). However, the chamber subjects as a group showed a profound decrement in their average CMI scores on chamber days C+45 and C+90 with no response to any of the seven challenge antigens noted in any of the four chamber subjects on chamber day C+90. The average CMI score of the chamber group had returned to near the baseline level at 30 days postchamber (E+30).

The chamber subjects had a nearly 49% decrease in their CMI scores during the chamber stay which was statistically different from the control data set at p = 0.002. The CMI scores of the chamber subjects were still decreased from control values by approximately 13% at time point E+30 (30 days after exiting the chamber), but the difference was not significant.

The primary aim of this study was to determine if isolation of human subjects within a closed chamber over a period of 91 days would adversely affect function of the cell-mediated arm of the immune system. The CMI scores were significantly decreased (-48.7% ± 10.1 SEM; p= 0.002; n = 8) for the chamber subjects during chamber isolation. The CMI scores were decreased below the control level (-13.1% ± 13.05 SEM) for the isolated chamber subjects at 30 days after exit from the chamber, but were not statistically different from the control values at this time point.

The short-term and long-term effects of decreased CMI in isolated human subjects are not known. Since CMI plays important roles in combating infectious agents (e.g., viruses and fungi), in surveillance against neoplastic cells, and in regulation of immune function, possible consequences include increased susceptibility to acute and chronic infections, increased cancer risk, and immune dysregulation. The level of these increased risks associated with decreased CMI function in conjunction with isolation and other still poorly understood environmental, physiological, and psychological factors is not known. Additional prospective and retrospective longitudinal studies are required to better understand underlying mechanisms and the level of risks associated with decreased CMI function in persons living in isolated environments. The role of exercise and the specific types, intensity levels, and duration in modulating the immune response during isolation requires further investigation.

experiment_title: Pathophysiology and Treatment of Spinal Pain Associated with Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this first back pain study was to determine whether the head-down tilt (HDT) bed rest model would elicit back pain and spinal lengthening similar to that in astronauts during space flight.

APPROACH:
Eight male subjects, aged 38±6 years with an average weight of 80.8±10.4 kg and height of 182.6±5.5 cm volunteered for a 21 day study. There was a 4-day control period, 16 days of HDT to simulate microgravity and 1 day of recovery standing upright. Subject heights were measured on 2 control days, the first 8 and last two days of bed rest. All subjects completed a pain questionnaire daily. The questionnaire asked the subjects to rate the back pain on a scale of 1-5, note any activity that eased or worsened the back pain and to describe sleep patterns.

RESULTS:
There was an increase of 2.1±0.5 cm by the 3rd day of HDT and no further increase. An increase in height during the night after a day of normal ambulation was less than the increase on the 3rd day of HDT. The intensity of back pain in the lower back increased to 2.5 (dull pain) and then decreased to basal levels by the 9th day.

Although spinal lengthening in space is twice that experienced during HDT, the type, level, distribution and time course of back pain during HDT was similar to that experienced during space flight. The pain subsided when the spinal lengthening stopped. Astronauts report dull back pain between days 1 and 6 of space flight and it is noted that a knees to chest position reduces the pain in astronauts as well as in volunteers in this study.

experiment_title: Adaptation of Rodent Vestibular Hair Cell Neurotransmission in Altered Gravity (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space motion sickness is the earliest impairment experienced by humans in altered gravity. It is an important problem, since it severely alters performance of affected astronauts. The investigators studied the early mechanisms that can affect the adaptation of mammalian vestibular hair cells in altered gravity. All specific aims focused on utricular hair cell neurotransmission in mice. The first aim provided an overview of synaptic transmission by looking at the vesicle recycling rates in utricle submitted to hypergravity over time. The second correlated aim attempted to understand the time-scale of molecular mechanisms that can sustain the modification of hair cell neurotransmission in hypergravity. Both aims provided a time-scale of the early modifications that can occur in primary gravity receptors undergoing altered stimulation. The last aim of this project was to study the functional capabilities of adult utricular hair cells whose development occurred under conditions of sensory deprivation. This last ground-based experiment used a mammalian "weightlessness" model, the tilted mouse. This last aim provided some insight about the risks of developing organisms in space. These objectives are directly relevant to different goals of the NSBRI Neurovestibular Adaptation team, since they can lead to the development of countermeasures to limit the risk of: 1) disorientation and inability to perform landing, egress, or other physical tasks, especially during/after g-level changes, and 2) possible chronic impairments of orientation or balance function due to microgravity. Centrifugation was used to submit mice to hypergravity. Their utricular maculae was studied using immunofluorescent staining, imaging, deconvolution and 3D reconstruction. A precise map of synaptic transmission, through vesicle recycling staining (AM 1-43), and the numbers of ribbons (Ribeye) and synaptic vesicles (Rab 3A, RIM 1) was provided for 2, 6 and 8 hours of hyperstimulation. The nitric oxide pathway and its relation to immediate early gene expression was also investigated in utricular hair cells during these time-exposures to hypergravity. Investigations of these same proteins and vesicle recycling in utricular hair cells of tilted mice will determine their functional capabilities. Thus, this project will help to understand the early and long-term effects of altered gravity on the function of its primary receptors, the utricular hair cells.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this experiment is not available.

RESULTS:
The “labeled multivesicular bodies” were, in fact, lipofuscin-like organelles. Even if the identification and quantification of these autofluorescent organelles in normal gravity conditions gave new insights on rodent vestibular hair cells, these lipofuscin-like organelles were no longer relevant to the first aim - to study the vesicle recycling rate of hair cells exposed to hypergravity for different time-exposures. In hypergravitational conditions, the investigators observed some discrepancies between experiments in the number of lipofuscin-like organelles in utricular hair cells, however they did not have enough time left to perform standardized experiments linking these differences to physiological state or gravity condition.

On the other hand, unlike the first year when they could not breed their animal model of vestibular sensory deprivation, the tilted mice, this year they had enough animals to precisely investigate their macular hair cells using morphological and molecular “tools” developed during the first year. They found that from their hair bundles, the mechanical sensors of head movements, to their afferents, transmitters of the sensory information, macular hair cells of the tilted mice display the morphological organization and molecular composition (actin filaments, calcium-binding protein, voltage-dependent channels and synaptic proteins) observed in control mice with a normal vestibular stimulation.

experiment_title: Metabolic Response to Exercise
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Both space flight and ground simulation of microgravity result in hemodynamic and biochemical changes in metabolites, enzymes and blood plasma hormones that correlate with deteriorated physical performance. Biochemical characterization of energy supply at rest does not provide full information on the body reserves, specifically the ability to maintain performance (i.e. during exercise). The study of the effects of graded exercise on these parameters during long-term bed rest has shown inadequate metabolic response to exercise and proved to be highly effective for assessment of applied countermeasures.

The primary objective of this experiment was to study directly the effect of long duration space flight on metabolic function during graded exercise on a bicycle ergometer, based on the levels of energy substrates and metabolites in the venous blood, enzyme activities and hormone levels regulating energy metabolism. This experiment was performed in conjunction with and to enhance another experiment entitled, “Aerobic Capacity using Graded Bicycle Ergometry” (3.2.1).

APPROACH:
A baseline blood sample was to be taken 10 minutes prior to aerobic exercise by bicycle ergometry. Crewmembers had a light breakfast before the test and recorded in detail food and fluid intakes. Aerobic exercise was to be performed as detailed in Experiment 3.2.1. Immediately following exercise and after a 20 minute rest period, repeat blood samples were supposed to have been drawn.

Blood samples were obtained preflight and were used for hematocrit measurement and determination of lactic acid, pyruvic acid, lactate dehydrogenase activity (LDH), and lipid content. Enzyme activities of ATPase, LDH, and glyceraldehyde-6-phosphate dehydrogenase were determined on sample erythrocytes. For comparison purposes these parameters were determined on other days when exercise was not performed.

RESULTS:
No results are available. This experiment was manifested on the Mir 18 mission. However, due to crew scheduling constraints, no data were obtained either preflight or inflight.

experiment_title: A Novel Biological Countermeasure and Mitigator of High LET-induced Cancer Progression
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This proposal addresses Radiation Carcinogenesis Cancer Specific Gap 8: Biological Countermeasures. While significant progress has been made since the NCRP report 132 in 2000, particle emission levels for fatal cancer risks are projected to be violated for a Mars mission under all possible scenarios, unless risk estimates are lowered considerably or the increased risk of potential fatal cancers is increased. It generally accepted that there appears to be no threshold below which radiation exposure can be viewed as harmless. With current permissive exposure limits, most astronauts would only be able to remain for about 6-8 months on deep space missions. Thus, if a goal of NASA is to have crews fly multiple times and on long missions, it is prudent to assume, even with new research to modify uncertainty reductions in fatal cancer risk projection models that it is appropriate to conduct research into the development of space radiation biological countermeasures. The investigator’s team work has been to investigate a family of plant titerpenoids (originally derived from Spanish moss) that have been synthesized and studied for radiation protection and mitigation experiments. Specifically they have conducted low and high LET IR experiments in human lung and colonic epithelial cell lines and in mouse models of lung and colon cancer susceptibility. Their cell culture studies during the first year of this project involved the use of bardoxolone methyl (BARD, also called CDDO-Me) and an analogue (CDDO-EA), both oral available non-toxic antioxidant inflammatory modulators (AIMs). BARD is a synthetic triterpenoid and there is a significant molecular understanding of its mode of action. They have already completed a series of investigations with low-LET and high-LET irradiation in both normal human lung and colonic epithelial cells and have published that single doses of 10-50nM BARD/CDDO-Me are effective radiation biological countermeasures, reducing double-strand DNA damage and anchorage-independent cancer progression. In mice they have also shown CDDO-EA may also have a mitigation effect by enhancing repair of DNA damage.

The specific aims were:

  1. To use the LA-1 lung cancer susceptible mouse model that develops significantly more invasive lung tumors when high-LET is provided in fractionated/protracted doses. The objective was to determine if pretreatment with nontoxic doses of CDDO-EA prior to acute or fractionated HZE irradiation reduces the number of invasive (e.g. more lethal) lung cancers. Investigators compared this to other priority HZE ions using fluences and energies that are representative of GCR including 28Si and 16O. They also planned to test a mouse model of colon cancer (CPC;APC).
  2. To test CDDO-EA as a biological countermeasure in mouse models exposed to SPE simulations.
  3. To test CDDO-EA as a radiation mitigator by providing it to mice within 30-60 minutes after irradiation (via IP and orally administered gavage). Investigators planned to compare SPE simulations (total body exposure 2 Gy protons) and two other ions (56Fe at 600 MeV/n, LET 175 at dose ranges between 0.1 Gy and 0.5 Gy and 28Si at 350-600 MeV/n LET 70 at doses between 0.2 and 0.8 Gy). They planned to test single acute versus fractionated doses of 56Fe and 28Si, having the expected outcomes (even with very short-term treatments).

APPROACH:
Criteria for approval by the FDA for BARD as a biological countermeasure can be met based on current data except for protection from high-LET irradiation in an animal model. Investigators have conducted experiments and now have robust results indicating that CDDO-EA partially protects induced invasive cancer from proton irradiation both single doses and provided as a simulated solar particle event. They also have experimental evidence that BARD can mitigate steps in cancer progression from gamma-irradiation (using colony formation assays) if provided 0.5-12 hours after IR via a novel mechanism of action that involve enhanced DNA damage repair and this work was published during the last review period. In summary, the main objective of this project was to investigate if CDDO-EA is a potent biological countermeasure and/or mitigator of SPE simulations and NASA priority HZE ions in mouse models that are predisposed to solid cancers. Since BARD is an anti-inflammatory modulator of oxidative damage, investigators believe BARD may also protect against HZE induced short-term and long-term neurodegenerative cognitive deficits and perhaps cardiovascular injury. They have already conducted a significant amount of research at the NSRL that support approaches to moving CDDO-EA forward as a lead space radiation biological countermeasure candidate.

RESULTS:
The summary of progress in the lung cancer mouse model:
• 2Gy SPE and 1 Gy fractionated Fe- irradiation decreases the lifespan of LA1 K-ras animals and results in an increase incidence of carcinoma.
• LA1 K-ras mice on CDDO-EA diet during fractionated Fe- irradiation exhibit a decreased incidence in invasive carcinoma in comparison to mice on control diet.
• LA1 K-ras mice on CDDO-EA diet during solar particle irradiation simulations exhibit a decreased incidence in invasive carcinoma in comparison to mice on control diet.
• LA1 K-ras mice fed CDDO-EA without irradiation show reduced tumor progression.

The summary of progress in the colon cancer mouse model:
• 2 Gy SPE - irradiation results in a 3-fold increase incidence of carcinoma.

experiment_title: Image Reversal In Space
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Image Reversal in Space (IRIS) experiment is an educational experiment developed by students at the International Space University. This experiment will study the effects of microgravity on the way people perceive two-dimensional and three-dimensional objects. The experiment and its software was designed by a multidisciplinary group of students, giving them valuable experience as they prepare to launch their own careers in space.

The IRIS experiment will measure how astronauts respond to a series of optical illusions and compare their reaction time for recognizing the different images to data recorded while the crew was on Earth.

There are many situations, known as illusions, which clearly demonstrate that our visual perception is less than entirely accurate. For example, when looking at a picture or a television screen, the brain assumes that we are seeing objects and spaces that have depth. As a result, we are accepting a set of signals or cues that create an illusion of three-dimensional space. The vast majority of human beings experience the same illusion, suggesting that its origin lies in the physiological mechanisms of perception.

A clear demonstration of the interpretive nature of visual perception comes from ambiguous figures (optical illusions), i.e., single images that can give rise to two or more distinct perceptions. These are two-dimensional images that are perceived as three-dimensional objects. Due to gravity constraints, some configurations are more often present than others. The IRIS experiment will investigate whether the perception of three-dimensional ambiguous figures is affected when the observer is in a reduced gravity environment.

APPROACH:
In order to conduct the IRIS experiment, a series of 20 to 25 obscured figures was displayed on one of the International Space Station (ISS) laptops using an interactive presentation. Some figures were three-dimensional while others were two-dimensional. For each figure, the astronaut-subject was asked to identify which form they see first, and then to indicate when they recognize the second form. The time delay between the occurrence of the first and the second form was calculated. The resulting data was uploaded for ground analysis by students.

Tests were performed pre-, in- and postflight. The same tests were also conducted on a population of subjects on Earth. The students hypothesized that there will be a significant difference in three-dimensional figures when observed both on Earth and in space, but not for two-dimensional figures.

RESULTS:
The processing of gravitational input is impaired in astronauts on long-duration missions. Their mental representation of the vertical dimensions is affected. Astronauts recover shortly after return to Earth.

experiment_title: Equivalent System Mass Impacts of Clothing on Wastes and Mission Cost
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Current and historical clothing system practice for space missions has been investigated. Terrestrial clothing system approaches have been evaluated for applicability. Future missions and clothing system options for those missions have been assessed. For all missions, including the crew exploration vehicle (CEV) and the Lunar surface access module (LSAM), there is an opportunity to reduce equivalent system mass (ESM) by changing the clothing fabrics used. Modern fabrics have generally higher performance than traditional fabrics like cotton typically used on STS and the International Space Station (ISS), in terms of mass, volume, useful life, water content, comfort, fire resistance, and fiber production. They can also allow clothing to be worn longer, reducing the rate of use. For vehicles with high volume equivalency, like the CEV, ESM can be reduced significantly by compressing the stowed clothing, both unused and used. There are some problems with this, particularly for long-duration missions, but modern fabrics would reduce these problems, and the benefits for these missions far outweigh the problems.

APPROACH:
Washer/dryer assessment was mostly based on a new design using largely-closed air and water loops to minimize ESM and impacts on the crew environment. The basic approach followed commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) practice, and is expected to be achievable by modifying COTS equipment, including COTS water purification approaches. Only minor changes to COTS designs are needed for operation in fractional gravity. Significant changes would be required to operate in weightlessness, but these changes do seem feasible, and some of them would also benefit operation in partial gravity. None of the identified changes for operation in weightlessness would necessarily hinder operation in fractional gravity. Thus, a single design with perhaps minor software changes does seem feasible for both weightlessness and fractional gravity. However, fractional gravity functionality would be needed several years earlier, and is easier to develop and so would provide a more gradual developmental pathway, and this might be preferred.

RESULTS:
A washer/dryer would be cost effective for the ISS, despite the high cost of power, cooling, and water regeneration, due to the long mission duration. One was not incorporated in the ISS design primarily because of development cost and risk. However, a washer/dryer would be more important for a long Lunar or Mars mission due to the expected high extravehicular activity (EVA) rates and increased delivery costs (location factors). Thus, development on ISS is justified by the need for clothes washing for the longer exploration missions, but could secondarily reduce ISS logistics loads.

A washer/dryer was also found to be cost effective for the longest Lunar missions evaluated – a 98-day Lunar outpost. The benefit of washing compared to shipped clothing was calculated to be a factor of two. If the base was occupied for multiple missions, the benefit would be greater. A washer might also be particularly beneficial for both Lunar and Mars surfaces because of the pervasive dust found at both locations. Dust control is likely to be both mandatory and difficult, and there may be differences between the two locations. Thus, a demonstration unit should be flown both on ISS and on the Moon, to validate the design both in weightlessness and in fractional gravity as well as to reduce operating costs at these locations. A washer/dryer could be incorporated in a volume equivalent to about half an ISS rack, smaller if subscale or if multiple loads were washed per day.

These two changes, in clothing materials and in reuse of clothing, are largely independent, and should both be pursued to reduce exploration mission costs. Because they can be implemented independently, they would have multiplicative effects. Use of modern clothing would reduce ESM, and also reduce the rate at which clothes would need to be washed, reducing the required size of washing/drying equipment.

experiment_title: Effects of Cosmic Particle Radiation on the Nasal Mucosa
experiment_description:
Objectives:

A totally unexpected result of the Apollo 17 flight was the appearance in all of the flight animals of profound alterations of the olfactory epithelium, while the epithelium of the control animals remained entirely normal. The alterations consisted of "disarrayed" olfactory epithelium, on the one hand, and of disseminated discrete lesions, on the other. This investigation was undertaken in an effort to elucidate possible causes of the alterations.

Approach:

Two canisters were prepared with five pocket mice in each. One canister was used in the flight experiment; the other was used as a ground control, undergoing the same stress as the flight canister. In addition, several control mice exposed to increased oxygen partial pressure in K02 tests during hardware verification were also examined. Histological sections were prepared from whole-head mounts and sectioned in the coronal plane. Camera lucida drawings were made at intervals of 80 micrometers to ascertain the topography of the olfactory and respiratory mucosa and record the location and character of lesions. Lesion dimensions were determined by an optical micrometer and shapes inferred from composites of 10 micrometer serial sections. Areas of olfactory and respiratory regions were calculated; volume and surface area covered by olfactory epithelium were also determined. By multiplying the dosimeter particle flux by the planar target area of the mucosa, it was possible to obtain an estimate of the number of HZE particles which passed through the mucosa.

Results:

The olfactory epithelium, but not the nasal respiratory epithelium, of the four mice that survived the flight showed both diffuse alterations and numerous disseminated focal lesions. The olfactory mucosa of the mouse that died inflight was also affected, but to a minor degree insofar as could be detected. A number of possible causes was considered: systemic or regional infection; inhaled particulate material (seed dust); by-products from the KO2 bed in aerosol or particulate form; gas contaminants originating in the flight package; volatile substances from the dead mouse; weightlessness; and cosmic particle radiation. Of these only the latter two seem likely as a result of control studies. It would be necessary to invoke the whole spectrum of radiation as causative if cosmic radiation were the cause. It was also noted that a Lunar Neutron Probe containing U235 was located in the locker next to the flight package; however, neutrons from this source have insufficient energy to penetrate the flight package.

experiment_title: Vestibular Experiments in Spacelab
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The neurovestibular system faces a special challenge in weightlessness and is involved in a complex adaptive process, which may be associated with space motion sickness. Nearly half of all space travelers experience symptoms resembling those of motion sickness. Susceptibility to space sickness appears highest during the first several days in space, and is generally limited to the first week. Symptoms range from nausea and headaches to severe vomiting. This neurovestibular adaptation is studied for the following reasons: 1) to develop methods for prediction, prevention and treatment of space motion sickness; 2) to reduce risk in an emergency egress in the event of an accident; and 3) to address the issues of human adaptation to very long duration flights.

The neurovestibular investigations were based on the sensory reinterpretation hypothesis, which provides a framework for interpreting many of the results. The sensory re-interpretation hypothesis holds that the following changes occur during spaceflight: 1) nerve signals from the otolith organs are reinterpreted as indicating head translation rather than tilt, 2) sensitivity to footward acceleration is reduced, and 3) the nervous system relies more on visual and tactile cues in the perception of orientation and control of posture.

APPROACH:
To explore the full range of neurovestibular adaptation, a series of human experiments was performed, each with a different combination of stimuli and responses. Each sub-experiment will be briefly described.

Visually induced roll/visual-vestibular interaction (rotating dome, rod and frame) The rotating dome experiment was designed to explore the conflicting visual, vestibular, and tactile sensory cues that occur in weightlessness. Visually induced self-motion and compensatory eye and head movements, stimulated by looking into the open end of a rolling drum, were measured. On Earth, gravity acting on human otolith organs inhibits the development of visually induced self-motion. In weightlessness, the strength of visually induced self-motion should increase because confirming vestibular signals are absent. This experiment was carried out with the head held stationary by a biteboard to eliminate stimulation of the vestibular organs and thereby understand their role in sensory input. The rod and frame test measured a subject’s dependence on a static visual field. Subjects indicated tilt of a perceived vertical marker. The experiment was performed before and after flight to determine if the increased dependence on static visual cues for orientation in space affects readaptation once back on Earth.

Vestibulo-ocular reflex (rotating chair): The rotating chair experiment was performed to determine how the vestibulo-ocular reflex is affected by otolith input. The vestibulo-ocular reflex provides a stable retinal (eye) image during head rotation by generating appropriate compensatory eye movements. Nerve impulses are conveyed from the semicircular canals and the otolith to the oculomotor nerve. When the otolith is no longer stimulated, as in microgravity, the vestibulo-ocular reflex is hypothesized to change.

To assess how this reflex is affected when it no longer receives input from the otolith, a rotating chair was used to stimulate the semicircular canals and study the nystagmus “dumping” (shortening of the time constant of nystagmus) produced by tilting the head face down after rotation. Eye movements were recorded while the subject was slowly spun in the rotating chair and afterward.

Awareness of position: The “position awareness” experiment was designed to examine the influence of weightlessness on the way subjects orient objects in the absence of a “real” vertical and the accuracy of cues from certain nerve receptors in determining perceived limb position. Subjects were instructed to view the location of several different targets placed on nearby walls. They were then blindfolded and asked to describe the position of their limbs and point to the target position from memory.

Considerable evidence indicates that knowledge of limb and body position may be altered by exposure to weightlessness. In this experiment, investigators attempted to separate two factors that might contribute to the apparent alteration in knowledge of limb and body position: (1) degradation of proprioceptive function, and (2) an inaccurate external spatial map. Subjects' ability to point at a target with a light pointer was measured twice: once during the continuous absence of vision, and once by closing the eyes only while pointing (to maintain a fresh image of the outside world).

Responses to linear acceleration (sled): The sled is a linear acceleration device, which was used for stimulating eye movement as well as subjective motion during horizontal linear acceleration. The purpose of these tests was to study the response of the linear acceleration sensors. It is hypothesized that weightlessness leads to an inhibition of otolith-derived spatial information, with the central nervous system (CNS) eventually learning to reinterpret otolith information as providing information on transient linear acceleration. This experiment was performed after landing to find out if the otolith input for linear acceleration is affected by spaceflight.

Postflight postural instability (rails, posture EMG/ muscle fatigue measurement): The rails experiment was designed to measure the degree of postural instability after flight by recording the astronauts’ ability to stand and walk on narrow and wide rails. The pre- and post-flight results were compared to determine if degradation of postural stability occurred. The EMG experiment studied the otolith-spinal reflex, which normally prepares one for a landing from a fall. Sometimes called “hop and drop”, the experiment required the subjects to be suspended from bungee cords; they hopped in an upward direction, then dropped toward the floor to simulate a fall. Electromyography (EMG) measurements were made during the activity.

Space motion sickness recording (head movement and symptom monitoring, head movement comparison test): In this investigation, space sickness symptoms were clinically characterized and their relationship to head movements; visual, tactile and proprioceptive cues; and the shift of body fluids toward the head was studied.

The crew was trained to log motion sickness symptoms according to a well-defined scale. Also, in-flight head movement data were obtained from one individual. Motion sickness susceptibility was measured using the head movement comparison test on the KC-135 before and after the mission.

RESULTS:
Visually induced roll/visual-vestibular interaction (rotating dome, rod and frame): Results suggested an increased weighting of visual cues and reduced weighting of gravireceptor (otolith) signals in weightlessness. After flight, all subjects showed an increase in postural instability, and a strong tendency to sway when the visual field rotated.

Vestibulo-ocular reflex (rotating chair): The rotating chair results showed no consistent vestibulo-ocular (VOR) gain changes in orbit. Although the strength of the angular VOR is known to decrease acutely in parabolic flight, a longer time constant was measured in subjects after 4 to 5 days of adaptation in weightlessness, suggesting a return of angular velocity storage. In half the rotating chair tests, the head was pitched forward 90 degrees immediately after stopping the chair rotation. In microgravity, the pitch movement produced rapid decreases in the perception of subjective rotation, but not in the VOR. The observed changes in the VOR and the perceptual indications of rotation may represent a sensory processing rearrangement induced by weightlessness.

Awareness of position: During the awareness of position tests, in-flight pointing accuracy was very poor, with a bias toward pointing low. Performance was always better when the eyes were closed only while pointing, and was unchanged before, during and after flight under these conditions. After the flight, all subjects made greater errors than before the flight, but in a similar direction. Recovery to the preflight level of performance was nearly complete by 7 days after landing. These results provide evidence that the primary adaptation in spaceflight is loss of the external spatial map and that complete postflight recovery requires several days.

Responses to linear acceleration (sled): After flight, erect posture with eyes closed was disturbed for several days. Somewhat greater visual field dependence after flight was observed for two of the crew. Postflight testing using the sled revealed increased variance in the detection of acceleration. The ability of the returned crew to use nonvisual lateral acceleration cues for a manual control task appeared enhanced over their preflight ability for a few days after their return to Earth.

Postflight postural instability (rails, posture EMG/ muscle fatigue measurement): An early otolith-spinal reflex, measured by EMG from the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles during sudden footward acceleration, was inhibited immediately upon entering weightlessness and declined further during the flight, but when measured shortly after return to Earth, was unchanged from preflight measurements.

Space motion sickness recording (head movement and symptom monitoring, head movement comparison test): Six short-duration tests of motion sickness susceptibility, conducted before flight, failed to predict sickness intensity in weightlessness.

experiment_title: Histochemistry of Hypothalamus
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous analysis of the anterior hypothalamus and the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland of rats flown on Cosmos biosatellites and Spacelab-3 revealed inhibition of the synthesis and excretion of growth hormone, and the system controlling these processes. This experiment was to assess spaceflight effects on the GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) and other enzymes in the system of the hypothalamus.

Approach:

The portion of the brain containing the thalamus and hypothalamus oriented in the anterior-posterior direction was dissected. Single tissue fragments, 0.2 to 1.0 µg in mass, were separated by micro-instruments from lyophilized sections (20 µm in thickness) of the arcuate nucleus and medial eminence hypothalamus. Quantitative histochemical analysis of glutamate decarboxylase and glutaminase, as well as determinations of the content of lipids and the defatted dry substance, were performed.

Results:

After spaceflight, glutaminase activity in the arcuate nucleus was decreased by 22.7%, and glutaminase activity in the medial eminence was decreased by 30.4%. The ratios of lipids and defatted dry substance in both structures remained unchanged. Since data indicated a high sensitivity of somatoliberan-containing neurons of the arcuate nucleus to glutamate, the possible participation of glutamate in the regulation of growth hormone secretion has been suggested.

experiment_title: Bed Rest Combined with 0.5% CO2 as a Spaceflight Analog to Study Neurocognitive Changes: Extent, Longevity, and Neural Bases
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Previous investigations have shown that exposure to microgravity can have significant effects on crewmembers’ posture control, locomotion, and manual control during and after flight. Additional studies provide evidence supporting the idea that the brain may experience structural and functional remodeling similar to the remodeling seen in bone and muscle. In other studies, exposure to microgravity has been shown to result in cortical reorganization of sensory and motor systems. However, the absence of supporting data in human subjects limits the understanding of whether the human brain is similarly effected following space flight, or even participation in space flight analogs.

The goal of this investigation is to quantify neurocognitive changes and associated neural structural and functional alterations occurring as a result of a 30 day head down tilt bed rest plus 0.5% CO2 environment, a well-established space flight analog. Within that context, the objectives of this study are to:

  1. Identify changes in brain structure, function, and network integrity as a function of 30 days head down tilt bed rest plus 0.5% CO2 and characterize the time course of the changes
  2. Specify relationships between structural and functional brain changes and performance and characterize their time course
  3. Identify predictors of individual differences in bed rest plus 0.5% CO2 responses

APPROACH:
This study will use advanced neuroimaging techniques with a battery of behavioral (cognitive, motor, and sensory) assessments to explore the relationships between neural changes and behavioral function. Twelve subjects are required. The subjects will undergo 30 days of head down tilt bed rest with elevated ambient (+0.05%) carbon dioxide. There are no control subjects.

There will be two data collections pre-bed rest at 12 days prior to bed rest (BR-12 days) and BR-7 days, two data collections post-bed rest at 6 days after bed rest (BR+6 days) and BR+13 days, and two data collections during bed rest at bed rest day 7 (BR7) and BR30. At each data collection, brain structural and functional images will be obtained. At the same time points, a broad ranging battery of cognitive, motor, and sensory tests will be performed. However, data collection on BR7 will not include standing tests. On BR30/BR+0, MRI scans are planned for BR30 with upright tests on BR+0. Therefore, balance and mobility tests will only be performed pre- and post-bed rest.

Neuroimaging tests will include both passive structural and functional scans and task-based functional MRI (fMRI) scans. A high-resolution structural MRI scan will provide volumetric measures of brain structures. An ultra-high resolution scan of the hippocampus will also be acquired. Resting state functional connectivity MRI (fcMRI) and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) scans will be obtained and used to study functional and structural network connectivity.

fMRI scans will be accomplished as subjects perform a variety of behavioral tests including cognitive tests, hand motor function tests, and vestibular function tests. Performance on the behavioral tests will be correlated with measures of brain structure, function, and network integrity.

Results of this study will be compared with results of other related studies, completed or in progress, by members of the investigative team.

RESULTS:
Results are not yet available for this investigation. However, this study may result in identification of the underlying neural mechanisms and operational risks of space flight induced changes in behavior using an established space flight analog. Further, it may determine whether a return to normative behavioral function following bed rest is associated with a restitution of brain structure and function or whether it is supported by substitution with compensatory brain processes.
