experiment_title: Skeletal Response
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone is a living organ that is continuously remodeling itself. When mechanical forces applied to the skeleton during normal activity in a 1-G environment are removed, bone mineral is lost because bone resorption is greater than bone formation. Bone resorption represents a danger not only because of the risk of fracture in demineralized bones, but also because the concomitant increased urinary calcium excretion might increase the risk for the formation of kidney stones.

The purpose of this experiment was to determine the effect of microgravity on the skeletal system during space flight. Studies conducted during the Gemini 4, 5, and 7, and Apollo 7 and 8 missions used x-ray densitometry to measure the amount of bone mineral present in the os calcis, radius, ulna, and phalanges. The studies revealed significant bone mineral losses in all areas measured. The degree of loss appeared excessive for such short periods in microgravity. Further evaluation of the data determined that bone mineral loses were lower than what was first measured. The overestimates were primarily due to problems inherent in the measurement techniques used. Scientists concluded that x-ray densitometry was unreliable for calculating bone mineral losses. It was not until a much more stable method of measuring bone mineral content, called photon absorptiometry, was developed that bone mineral studies continued during Apollo 14, 15, and 16.

Early reports of significant bone mineral losses in the 5- to 14-day Gemini and Apollo missions emphasized the need for correlating mineral losses observed in ground-based studies with those observed during microgravity. Ground-based studies designed to mimic the microgravity condition were used to estimate when changes were likely to occur during a mission. Bed rest served as an experimental model since the loss of bone mineral in bed rested and immobilized patients had been observed during periods of up to 36 weeks.

It was determined during these studies that the amount of initial mineral content in the os calcis could influence the rate of mineral loss. Bed rested subjects who exhibited a high mineral content at the beginning of bed rest showed the least mineral loss both in percentage and in quantity. Conversely, subjects who exhibited a low mineral content at the onset of bed rest showed a greater rate of mineral loss. The bed rest model was also used to determine what remedial measures might be used to both reduce bone mineral loss and predict bone mineral losses in the astronauts.

Thus, another goal of this study was to establish time courses for both the bed rest and flight situations so that better estimates could be obtained on the risk of prolonged space flight as translated from the ground-based bed rest studies.

APPROACH:
Bone scans using the photon absorptiometry technique were made on the crewmembers of Apollo 14 (10-day mission), Apollo 15 (12-day), and Apollo 16 (11-day) approximately one month, two weeks, and one week before flight. Each data collection session consisted of one x-ray and three bone scans of the left central os calcis, the right radius and the right ulna. Four postflight measurement sessions were conducted for each crewmember at various times. A series of control subject measurements was made in parallel with the crewmembers. Three subjects each were studied during Apollo 14 and Apollo 15, and four subjects were studied during Apollo 16.

A photon scanning device, called a rectilinear bone mineral scanner, was used during the experiment. The extremity to be measured was placed in tissue equivalent material (TEM) to compensate for the irregular thickness of tissue cover that surrounded the bone. The extremity, encased in the TEM, was placed between the photon source, Iodine-125 (125I), and a photon detector. The photon source and detector were aligned in direct opposition to each other so that a 3-millimeter source beam was directed into a 3-millimeter entrance on the detector. The absorptiometer scanned the section of bone in a series of sixteen straight, parallel lines covering the entire area. The scanner could be configured to accommodate either the upper or lower extremity. As the transmitted beam passed through the segment of bone, the detector on the opposite side measured the intensity of the radiation after it had passed through the TEM and the bone. Researchers were then able to calculate the amount of mineral content in the bone segment. The entire system was calibrated before and after each scan by making four passes over a Witt-Cameron standard.

Because of space restrictions in the quarantine facility and isolation restrictions, only a single scanner device could be used during the postflight period of Apollo 14. For this reason, arm and heel scans were performed separately using the same scanner in each of the two configurations. On the two subsequent missions, arm and heel studies were performed simultaneously both preflight and postflight, because quarantine was no longer required.

RESULTS:
Mineral losses were not observed in the os calcis, radius, or ulna in the Apollo 14 or Apollo 16 crewmembers. Only two Apollo 15 crewmembers lost mineral from the os calcis. Both crewmembers regained the bone mineral losses and were near baseline values by the end of two weeks. The magnitude of loss, when compared to the control subjects, was 5 to 6 percent. Mineral losses were not observed in radius or ulna mineral during the Apollo 15 flight.

A significant increase in fatty tissue was observed on the plantar side of the os calcis in one subject of Apollo 14 immediately postflight. This subject showed a 34 percent increase in fat equivalence when compared to immediate preflight measurements. This increase would have resulted in a 4.3 percent overestimation of bone mineral if the soft tissue contribution had not been measured. In contrast, the other two crewmembers showed between a 8.1 and 8.4 percent increase in fat equivalence with a potential 2.5 and 2.2 percent overestimation in bone mineral. No significant changes in the soft tissue composition were observed in the Apollo 15 or 16 crewmembers.

Researchers established a predictive model for bone mineral loss for the bed rested subjects. In this model, the ratio of initial bone mineral content to the initial 24-hour urinary hydroxyproline excretion was compared to observed losses. The greater the ratio, the slower and smaller the mineral losses and, conversely, the smaller the ratio, the faster and greater the mineral losses. The accurate measurement of baseline 24-hour urinary hydroxyproline excretion was therefore an essential requirement for these predictions. Unfortunately, no time course could be established for the microgravity state because of limited data. Researchers hoped that additional data collected during the Skylab missions would determine a time course of bone mineral losses that could be compared with the bed rest data. Therefore, bed rest studies could be established as a good model for the effects of weight unloading. Secondly, bed rest studies could serve as a predictive measure for longer space missions.

It was concluded that mineral losses from bone incident to periods of microgravity were comparable to that observed in bed rested subjects and that the magnitude was not severe. If these losses were allowed to continue unabated for a prolonged period of time, the consequences might be more serious because the losses were probably not confined to the bones described.

experiment_title: Study of the Digestive Transportation Function of the Small Intestine
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous experiments have revealed an increase in the acidic-peptic potential of the stomach and a decline of the functional capability of the pancreas. This experiment was to conduct a morphological and biochemical investigation of changes in the mucous membrane of the small intestine after spaceflight.

Approach:

The duodenum, jejunum, and ileum sections of the small intestine were removed from flight and control animals, and the mucosa was examined with an electron microscope. Enzymes involved in cavity and membrane digestion (carbohydrases, peptidases, monoglyceride lipase, alkaline phosphatase) were investigated biochemically.

Results:

The investigation of the functional status of the small intestine revealed complex changes of enzyme activities. In the system of protein membrane hydrolysis there was a shift of proximodistal gradient dipeptidase activity indicating the compensatory nature of the changes. Analysis of processes of lipid digestion revealed a number of alterations in their digestive pattern manifested as a significant decrease of nonglyceridelipase activity, and an increase of alkaline phosphatase activity in the proximal segment of the small intestine, again, reflecting the compensatory and adaptational nature of the alterations. In the carbohydrase enzymatic change no significant alterations were found. Changes of digestive/transport hydrolysis of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates were reversible and functional in nature. The adaptive nature of the rearrangements of membrane digestion is demonstrated by a self-regulatory activity of the digestive system in the distribution of enzyme activities.

experiment_title: Developmental and Physiological Processes Influencing Seed Production in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The investigator hypothesized that a plant may become limited in gas exchange due to the lack of convective air movement in microgravity. Since plants depend on convective air movement to aid the uptake of metabolically important gases, the lack of convection may affect these processes. Since the CHROMEX-03 plants were carbohydrate-poor, carbon dioxide transport to the plants may have been limited.

APPROACH:

Two Plant Growth Chambers (PGC) were used in the Plant Growth Unit, positions 3 and 4. Each chamber held 6 mouse-ear cress (Arabidopsis thaliana) plants, which were 14 days old at launch. The foam/agar plug nutrient system was used. A Warburg solution was added to the chamber to maintain carbon dioxide levels. The plants were flown for 10 days, and then recovered from the Shuttle for analysis. Measurements of pollen viability were made immediately after landing, and material was fixed for subsequent microscopy.

RESULTS:

The plants produced numerous flowers,which had a good appearance except for those in the latest developmental stages. Pollen viability was approximately 50% as assessed by fluorescein diacetate staining immediately after landing. Light microscope examination of the pollen showed a range of morphologies, from normal to collapsed, corresponding to the viability staining results. This amount of viable pollen should have been able to fertilize the flowers and initiate embryo development. However, no evidence of this was found, suggesting a pollen transfer problem. No differences between flight and ground material were observed in leaf or bract structure at the light microscope level.

experiment_title: NEXGEN Approaches to Chromatid Painting
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
There is every reason to believe that large and small scale chromosomal intra-changes (inversions) are just as important as inter-changes between chromosomes, e.g., translocations, the latter of which are well known to cause cancer. And yet, inversions, especially small ones, have been historically difficult, if not impossible to detect. Recently, KromaTiD Inc., using SBIR funding from NASA, successfully demonstrated a new platform technology to detect small chromosomal inversions using directional oligonucleotide probes called chromatid painting. In this study, the investigators propose to develop the next generation of whole chromatid paints using a much faster, more cost effective approach. If successful, this will facilitate the rapid development of additional chromatid paints, with the goal of ultimately covering the entire genome. These next generation chromatid paints will be of even higher resolution than currently possible, so they will greatly expand potential biodosimetric applications.

APPROACH:
The approach for this study is not available.

RESULTS:
KromaTiD Inc. previously completed a prototype of the methodology, i.e. a fluorescent chromatid paint to human chromosome three, and then demonstrated the predicted capability to detect inversions after exposure to ionizing radiation. Inversions were evidenced as fluorescent signal switches that appeared on the opposite chromatid of chromosome 3, opposite to their original position, allowing relative ease of scoring and suggesting that scoring might be automated completely in the future. The assay was then used to count the increased frequency of inversions that were produced after gamma radiation exposure, a proof of concept that the technology could be used for biodosimetry.

Subsequently, in collaboration with NASA space radiation investigators, the production of chromosome inversions caused by high linear energy transfer (LET), high energy ions (HZE) particles was described. Results showed a dramatic dose-dependent increase in the yields of inversions that were induced by high LET charged particles, similar to those encountered in deep space as compared to low LET gamma rays.

New directional genomic hybridization (dGH) chromatid paints to human chromosomes 1 and 2 were developed, and the previously created dGH chromosome 3 chromatid paint was recreated using a more efficient and less costly method. These paints have improved the performance of KromaTiD’s biodosimetry assays while reducing the cost per assay. This will allow the rapid development of increasingly sensitive biodosimetry inversion assays to be used in the analysis of radiation risk for astronauts.

experiment_title: Detection and Prevention of Neurobehavioral Vulnerability to Space Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Assessing the biological consequences of living in the space radiation environment represents one of the highest priority areas of NASA research. Of critical importance is the need for an assessment of the vulnerabilities of the central nervous system (CNS) leading to functional neurobehavioral changes during long-term space missions, and the development of effective countermeasures to such risks. This study addressed this need via the application of an innovative animal model to determine 1) the long-term effects of radiation exposure on cognitive neurobehavioral function; and 2) the likely mechanisms of damage to the CNS following radiation exposure (e.g., radiation-induced changes in neurotransmitter system function).

APPROACH:
To assess the likelihood of space radiation producing long-term functional changes in the CNS, neurobehavioral functions were measured in rodents via animal tests analogous to human 'vigilance' tests in humans. Cognitive neurobehavioral functions relevant to astronaut mission performance effectiveness were assessed with a rodent analog of the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) currently used in space analog environments and by astronauts aboard the International Space Station (ISS). Neurobehavioral functions examined included assessments of general motor function and speed, vigilance, inhibitory control ('impulsivity'), timing, motivation, and basic sensory function. Groups of animals were trained on the rodent version of the PVT (rPVT), following exposure to radiation and then re-tested periodically for up to 18 months post-exposure to assess potential long-term performance deficits. Likely mechanisms of damage to the CNS following radiation exposure were examined via pre-radiation behavioral pharmacology studies as well as post-radiation behavioral pharmacology studies and neurochemical assessments (Western blots) of proteins relevant to neurotransmitter function and inflammation.

RESULTS:
Results from the project have demonstrated that head-only exposure to space radiation (protons, 56Fe, 28Si) significantly impairs neurobehavioral function (e.g., decrease accuracy, increase impulsivity, increase lapses in attention) and slows motor function. These findings support the success of the rPVT as a rodent model for studying the risks of living in the space radiation environment due to changes in neurobehavioral function.

Specific findings from this study include:
1. Pre-exposure evaluations of a dopamine (DA) agonist and antagonist on fixed ratio/fixed interval performance were completed. Following radiation, retests on the rPVT performances revealed ~30% of the animals to be classified as radiation-sensitive. Post-exposure pharmacological challenges with a DA agonist and antagonist are underway to determine whether radiation-induced changes in the DA system are linked to pre-radiation DA system changes (i.e., whether pre-radiation DA system sensitivities may be predictive of subsequent radiation sensitivity).

2. Drug-induced yawning is being used as a sensitive metric for determining subtle changes in deiodinase 2 (D2) and deiodinase 3 (D3) activity in rodents. A rising and falling pattern of DA-induced yawning in rodents is induced by activation of the D3 receptor on the ascending limb, and by inhibition by the D2 receptor on the descending limb. This differential modulation by D3 and D2 antagonists results in D3-preferring antagonists producing selective rightward shifts of the ascending limb, and D2-preferring antagonists producing selective shifts of the descending limb. Following 25-100 cGy proton exposures, differential shifts in the ascending limbs of these curves have been observed, suggesting that D3 receptor activity and/or tissue levels are altered by radiation.

3. A study (part of Catherine Davis' NSBRI Postdoctoral Fellowship) determined the degree to which radiation-induced deficits in neurobehavioral function differ as a function of changes in cytokine protein expression. Brain tissue of both F344 and LEW rPVT-trained rats were found to have differential changes in frontal cortex cytokine levels; several neurotrophic and putative pro-cognitive cytokines were significantly elevated in the LEW rats, which could underlie the lack of radiation-induced rPVT deficits in this strain. Western blot analyses of several different proteins important for dopamine neurotransmission (e.g., dopamine transporter, D2 receptor, tyrosine hydroxylase) and cell survival (e.g., Akt, p-Akt, CREB), in addition to various cytokines (e.g., TNF-a, Il-1a, Il-6, GM-CSF, CNTF, VEGF) in the frontal and parietal cortices of the F344 and LEW rats were found to be differentially altered following proton exposure.

experiment_title: Microgravity Effects on the Function of Vascular Stem Cells
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The negative effects of space flight on cardiovascular health has been demonstrated and documented over many years. One of the body’s normal vascular repair mechanisms is the recruitment of adult stem cells from bone marrow to integrate into the vasculature. These recruited cells are involved in blood vessel wall repair and the formation of new blood vessels. This proposal seeks to study the effect of microgravity on adult stem cells. Of specific interest is how well these cells can differentiate into vascular cells under altered environmental conditions such as microgravity, and how well these cells function as healthy vascular cells once differentiated. Differentiation studies using a bioreactor will be conducted to expose the cells to microgravity conditions. Once differentiated, the cells will be exposed to several stimulatory environments that will demonstrate their functional ability. Molecular biology techniques, such as gene expression studies, will elucidate the effect of microgravity on these cells.

Studying adult stem cells is a means towards the goal to develop countermeasures for the negative effects of space flight on vascular health. This proposal addresses one of NASA's research interest, specifically, studies of the effect of gravity and the space environment on cellular and molecular processes. In this proposal, the cellular and molecular processes under investigation are stem cell differentiation and the corresponding molecular changes the stem cells undergo.

APPROACH:
To achieve our goal, we have established 2 specific aims, briefly, 1) Differentiate circulating stem cells into vascular endothelial (EC) and smooth muscle cells (SMC) under conditions of microgravity and normal gravity; 2) Assess the functional potential of the microgravity exposed differentiated cells. Our approach to achieving these goals involves first isolating blood derived stem cells, then culture under microgravity conditions in a rotating wall vessel bioreactor or static (normal gravity) in tissue culture polystyrene (TCPS) plates. Following dynamic and static culture, the cells are assessed for differentiation. Our assessments include both protein and gene expression changes, using western blot analysis and real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (rt-PCR), respectively. We are interested in the loss of stem cell protein and gene expression and upregulation of endothelial and smooth muscle cell protein and gene expression. For our second aim, our goal is to assess the changes in functional capacity of the differentiated cells, particularly the changes in function as a results of microgravity. To assess SMC function, we proposed to evaluate the ability of the differentiated cells to respond to contractile stimulation, migration, secrete extracellular matrix proteins, and modulate between synthetic and proliferative phenotypes. Our approach involves culture under stimulatory conditions where appropriate and assessments of SMC functions can be made. For endothelial cell functional analysis, we are interested in assessing the production and secretion of antithrombogenic factors, nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin (PGI2) by the differentiated endothelial cells. In addition, our approach involves assessing the hemocompatibility of the cells in terms of clotting and platelet activation when exposed to whole blood from human subjects.

RESULTS:

1. Goal: Optimizing bioreactor and experimental set-up and methodology with Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs)

The experimental set-up we proposed using a commercially available rotary cell culture system (RCCS) bioreactor (Synthecon) was optimized using HUVEC cells. Our goal was to optimize various bioreactor/experimental parameters such as microcarrier bead handling and protein coating, cell seeding density and culture parameters, bioreactor rotational speed, culture maintenance and sample extraction from bioreactor chambers, as well as overall training within the experimental system. Early project challenges such as low cell adhesion on microcarrier beads and cell detachment under dynamic conditions in the rotating wall vessel (RWV) were eventually overcome by changing our experimental design. Our results show successful cell attachment and faster proliferation of HUVECs under microgravity than under static conditions.

2. Goal: Isolation and culture of human endothelial progenitor cells and differentiation into endothelial cells

Once our bioreactor and experimental setup was optimized, we extended our work to the target cell population that is the focus of this work, human endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) derived from circulating blood. The human EPCs are a rare population of stem/progenitor cells that are isolated from the peripheral mononuclear cell (PBMNC) fraction of whole blood. PBMNCs were isolated from human blood obtained from donors as per Institutional Review Board (IRB) guidelines. Circulating progenitor cells contained within the PBMNC fraction of whole blood were differentiated into endothelial-like cells, as confirmed by the formation of colonies (within 2-6 weeks) with EC specific ‘cobble-stone’ morphology, and positive expression of EC specific proteins.

3. Goal: Study the effect of microgravity on the differentiated endothelial cells in culture

We assessed the ability of these cells to adapt to simulated microgravity conditions after short term culture and expansion. More specifically, the functionality of the differentiated ECs following exposure to simulated microgravity assessed conditions such as proliferation, release of soluble factors, changes in gene expression, and anti-thrombogenic potential was investigated. The results of the present study demonstrated that the populations of human blood EPC derived ECs when exposed to simulated microgravity proliferate faster, release higher amounts of soluble NO and lower amounts of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, when compared to their normal gravity cultured controls. This can be possibly attributed to the ability of the cells to sense simulated microgravity as a “stressful” condition and adapt by upregulating gene expression of hsp70. However these secretory as well as proliferative functions had no effect on the anti-thrombogenic functions of these cells. Their anti-coagulative and anti-thrombogenic ability as assessed by both upregulation of tPA as well their ability to delay plasma clotting, were impaired upon exposure to simulated microgravity. This study is the first step towards understanding the ability of these repair cells to regulate clotting mechanisms and cardiovascular health in space. Further studies to assess alternate and synergistic mechanisms involved in regulation of cardiovascular health as well as inflammatory dysfunction under microgravity are required to develop possible cell based countermeasures to prevent cardiovascular deconditioning due to space travel.

4. Goal: Expand to include porcine EPCs to further study the effect of microgravity on differentiation of the blood derived EPCs.

Due to the initial challenges we had faced with differentiating as well exposing human blood derived progenitor cells during the pre- differentation stage under simulated microgravity, our goal was to extend our work to an alternative cell source, porcine EPCs. Our lab has previously obtained porcine PBMNCs (under University of Florida IACUC approval) and differentiated these into cells with endothelial cell phenotype (PE-like cells). Circulating progenitor cells contained within the PBMNC fraction of porcine whole blood were exposed to simulated microgravity, using a RWV bioreactor. After exposing the circulating progenitor cells to 6, 12, and 18h of simulated microgravity, the cells were then cultured on fibronectin coated TCP under static conditions and their ability to differentiate into endothelial cells was assessed by the formation of colonies with EC specific ‘cobble-stone’ morphology and confirmed by immunohistocytochemical staining for CD31 as well as eNOS. Our results showed that longer exposure to simulated microgravity delayed the onset of differentiation of EPCs to PE-like cells.

Clotting behavior assessment showed that following the clotting rate for 6h-µg exposed cells are the clotting times for the 12h and 18h-µg exposed cells. Normal gravity cultured cells clotted the next while the last to clot was the plasma exposed to the EC control cells. Similarly, the whole blood clotting kinetics showed that the kinetic profile of whole blood when incubated with PE-like cells differentiated after exposure to simulated microgravity, showed faster clot formation than normal gravity controls. However, longer exposure times showed greater inhibition of clotting.

Collectively, the data shows that within the 3 time points of µg exposure, the longer exposure times showed greater inhibition of clotting, which may be attributed to the increased ability to release soluble anti-thrombogenic factors, NO and PGE2. While both the migration and proliferation of cells were inhibited by microgravity exposure, prolonged exposure of EPCs to microgravity resulted in decrease in the migration abilities of EPC derived EC and the proliferative capacity of the ECs seemed to recover on longer time of exposure. The initial decrease and subsequent increase in release of soluble factors such as NO and PGE2 reaffirmed the possibility of recovery mechanisms being involved on prolonged exposure to weightlessness. Finally the assessment of whole blood and plasma clotting, indicated that microgravity pre exposure at the progenitor stage caused inhibition, in the ability of PE-like cells to delay blood or plasma clotting while this effect was again nulled with increase in time of exposure of EPCs to microgravity. This data collectively provides some insight into the role of short term exposure to low shear stress environment due to simulated microgravity, on cardiovascular deconditioning during space travel.

experiment_title: Physiological Responses During Descent on the Space Shuttle
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary cardiovascular consequence of space flight and the most operationally important of all postflight physiological disturbances is orthostatic dysfunction. Impaired orthostatic function is indicated by significant tachycardia, drastic reductions in arterial pressure upon standing, lightheadedness, and visual disturbances. The most severe form of orthostatic dysfunction results in syncope or fainting. During entry, landing, and egress, these symptoms could impair the crew's performance of required cognitive and psychomotor activities. As a result, it was necessary to document the risk of orthostatic dysfunction and intolerance during the final phases of the mission. It was also essential to determine whether the risk of orthostatic impairments increased as the flight duration increased.

The hypotheses were:
(1) the probability that crewmembers will experience any type of orthostatic problem during entry, landing, standing upright in the Orbiter, and cabin egress is greater after long (> 3 months) flights than after short (< 16 days) flights

(2) as g-force increases during re-entry, heart rate (HR) and blood pressure (BP) will increase, even though the subjects will be in the recumbent position

(3) upon the initial standing after landing, arterial blood pressure will be maintained briefly by a compensatory increase in heart rate; maintenance of arterial pressure will begin to fail after standing in Earth's gravitational environment and at this time the heart cannot compensate and the crewmember may experience symptoms of orthostatic dysfunction.

The primary objective of this experiment was to begin a systematic collection of quantitative data on the acute cardiovascular response to re-exposure to gravity and to the orthostatic posture after long periods in weightlessness. The second objective was to compare the risk of orthostatic dysfunction and intolerance after long and short space flights. The third objective was to provide an assessment of the efficacy of the recumbent seat.

APPROACH:
This investigation involved monitoring of three crewmembers who returned to Earth aboard the Space Shuttle after a 115-day flight on the Mir Space Station. A recumbent seat was used for the first time aboard the Space Shuttle during entry and landing to provide some protection from orthostatic intolerance. Two astronauts, who were not participating as subjects and who were on the Shuttle, were trained to act as operators for the inflight portion of this experiment. These individuals configured the hardware, instrumented the subjects, and provided instructions for proper execution of protocol during re-entry. The subjects were instrumented with a commercial ambulatory blood pressure monitor to determine the heart rate (HR) and arterial blood pressure (BP) at pre-determined intervals during entry and landing. A cassette data recorder was used to record ECG, cuff pressure, Korotkoff sounds, and voice comments. Four single-axis accelerometers were worn to document changes in body posture and four skin temperature sensors were worn to obtain an estimate of mean surface temperature of each crewmember.

In a preflight session conducted six months prior to flight, HR, and systolic and diastolic BP were measured 3 times. These measurements were taken at three different postures: supine, seated, and standing, with and without the Launch and Entry Suit (LES) inflated to 1 pound per square inch (psi) above ambient pressure.

During inflight testing, data was compiled for the following times: a baseline measurement prior to onset of g-forces, at the onset of g-forces, at peak g-level during entry, at touchdown, and post-touchdown recumbent and standing measurements. All measurements were taken with the subject wearing the LES.

RESULTS:
This experiment focused on testing the three stated hypotheses. Cooperation between the U.S. and Russian team went smoothly, but there were several confounding factors that could not be controlled. This included: inconsistent g-suit usage which did not match the prescribed protocol; lack of participation in the post wheels stop and stand test by the cosmonauts (a true unassisted standing posture was never obtained); and inflight prescription and adherence to countermeasures, both operational and experimental, was not consistent among all three subjects in the Mir group.

There were no preflight or postflight anomalies, but inflight anomalies did occur because of deviations from the prescribed protocol.

The data was not optimal due to: a crew request for fewer samples (5-minute intervals between cuff inflations vs. the prescribed 2 min. intervals); non-continuous ECG, because of a crew failure to select the "Continuous ECG" option as stated in the protocol, on the programming menu of the ABPM (automatic blood pressure monitor); inconsistent compliance with g-suit inflation standards during entry and landing; non-participation in the postflight stand test in the Crew Transport Vehicle (CTV).

As a result of this, HR could not be assessed during the 2-5 minute intervals between cuff inflations, spectral analysis could not be performed because ECG data was non-continuous, and cardiovascular responses to orthostatic stress after 4 months in weightlessness in the two subjects who did not stand in the CTV could not be fully assessed.

Regarding each hypothesis, the following statements can be made:

(1) there is no higher incidence of orthostatic problems in the long-duration group, however, that is not conclusive due to the small sample size and the confounding factors

(2) HR and BP during re-entry showed a lower than expected, but small, increase above values found during normal preflight and intra-vehicular activities

(3) conclusive statements regarding the degree of orthostatic dysfunction or intolerance could not be made because of the lack of full participation in the postflight stand test by all 3 crewmembers.

Due to the confounding factors and small sample size, it is premature to make any definitive statements about the results. The data strongly suggest that the recumbent seat protected the crew from adverse cardiovascular stress during entry and landing, but did not provide protection from orthostatic stress upon egress from the seat. However, there is no statistical significance in any of the data and future investigations need to be conducted.

experiment_title: Crews Health:  Investigation on Reduced Operability
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The CHIRO program has been established to provide early data within a wide range of researches on human upper limb behaviour and performances. The aim of this particular aspect of the research is to monitor the impairment of muscle function in weightlessness, if any, and to clarify its physiopathology through an analysis of the different steps of electro-mechanical mechanisms of muscle contraction events. The observations relevant to this activity will be carried out during the grip maintenance of held objects, for example during grasping or lifting tasks, by comparing the performance of the weightless conditions to those recorded on ground, before and after the execution of the orbital flight.

APPROACH:
The main elements of the CHIRO payload are the Pinch Force Dynamometer (PFD) (Figure 1) and the HandGrip Dynamometer (HGD) (Figure 2). These elements are based on those developed for NASAs Human Research Facility (HRF). The HGD is a hand held device capable of measuring instantaneous hand strength (between 40 and 1000 Newtons) as a function of time for periods of up to 300 seconds. The principle components of the HGD are a transducer capable of measuring the handgrip force, instrumentation amplifier, and associated cables. Dynamic voltage representing instantaneous hand strength is taken from the output of the instrumentation amplifier and sent to a laptop computer or to a data acquisition system for data manipulation, display, correlation with other data sources, and/or storage.

The PFD is a hand held device capable of measuring instantaneous strength (between 0 and 270 Newtons) of the thumb and opposing finger or groupings of fingers as a function of time for periods of up to 300 sec. The principle components of the PFD are a pinch force transducer, instrumentation amplifier, and associated cables. Dynamic voltage representing instantaneous finger(s) pinch strength as a function of time will be taken from the output of the instrumentation amplifier and sent to a laptop computer or to a data acquisition system for data manipulation, display, correlation with other data sources, and/or storage.

In both instruments the measurement of the applied compression force is taken by using a beam load cell based on a full bridge strain gauge that is sensitive to the transverse shearing stress applied to the beam. Two protocols of experimentation will be carried out.

Protocol 1: In each session, the subject is tested on force isometric tracking. A sequence of force profiles are displayed on a computer monitor, and the subjects task is to reproduce them with his dominant hand quickly and accurately by using the Handgrip dynamometer. Each profile is presented for 10 s, allowing the subject to recognize and replicate it, and the screen is then blanked for 2 s, so that the hand can return to a common starting position (set at the beginning of the session). Each session also includes an isometric tracking task with the non-dominant hand. The subject is also instructed to keep a cursor centred on the screen by increasing or decreasing the force, which they exert on a pinch force dynamometer with their nondominant hand, while the cursor position is perturbed by a first-order instable element. This task is presented over 1.5 minutes, to collect a sufficient amount of data. The two tasks are also presented concurrently in each session. The subject is instructed to assign top priority to the task carried out with the dominant hand, and perform the concurrent tracking task to the extent possible; thus, a subsidiary-task paradigm according to dual-task terminology is used. Dual-task testing takes as long as the presentation of all the force profiles for no more than 10 minutes. Total session duration is therefore about 25 minutes including rest breaks, but excluding set-up and stowage time.

Protocol 2: After calibration of the set-up, the astronaut is asked to perform the following tasks. First, maximum grip and pinch forces that the astronaut is able to produce are recorded at 100Hz over a 30s time epoch. The PC immediately computes the mean and standard deviation (SD) of these force values (Fmax for grip and Fmax for pinch). Fmax values are used to scale the sine waves for the tracking task (so as to take into account possible changes in max force output during weightless exposure). Then, the astronaut is asked to perform the tracking tasks. The force tracked with either the grip or the pinch dynamometer varies sinusoidally. Sine waves of 2 different amplitudes (10 and 25% of Fmax, to avoid fatigue) and 7 different frequencies (0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1, 2, 4 Hz) are outputted according to a pseudo-random table previously stored in memory. The astronaut is asked to track the sine wave as fast and accurately as possible. The target force and the astronauts output force are displayed in real time on the PC display. The whole protocol is performed twice before launch (L-90 and L-30), 3 times in flight (Flight day (FD)2, FD5, FD8) and upon return to earth (R+0, R+1, R+5, R+10). Fmax for grip and pinch are compared statistically (ANOVA, paired t-tests) between pre-flight, in-flight and post flight conditions. As for the sine wave task, Fourier analyses are performed to compute gain and phase of the response output relative to the target force input.

RESULTS:
The upper limb is used for locomotion in a microgravity environment. Fatigue can impact the hand, musculo-skeletal degradation can be recognized in the upper limb. Specific protocols on the upper limb can facilitate the studies on learning mechanisms for the motor control. The results of such experiments can be transferred to the Earth, useful for treatment of subjects with local traumas or diseases of the Central Nervous System.

experiment_title: Integrated Stress Response in Space
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The long term objective of the proposed project is to evaluate the effects of "integrated stress response (ISR) in space" using bone metabolism as a model system. It is known that diverse environmental stresses including radiation, oxidative stress, nutrient limitation, and stress to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) induces ISR. ISR leads to a pro-survival pathway (rescue program) for alleviation of cellular injury or, conversely, an apoptotic pathway for removal of damaged cells. Unloading in space is a unique form of environmental stress, but its physiological responses in connection to ISR is poorly understood. There are no changes in the objective of the proposal.

To test the above hypothesis and examine a potential role of ISR-driven signaling under unloading, we are conducting the following three specific aims using a mouse hindlimb suspension model:

Aim 1: Evaluate phosphorylation of eIF2a and its kinases (e.g., PERK and GCN2) as well as translational efficiency in response to transient unloading
Aim 2: Evaluate gene regulatory mechanisms linked to oxidative stress and stress to the ER in response to continuous unloading
Aim 3: Examine the effects of administration of salubrinal (inhibitor of eIF2a phosphatase) on pro-survival signaling and bone metabolism

APPROACH:
The project will employ various molecular and cellular techniques including real-time polymerase chain reactions, Western blot analysis, enzymatic activity assays as well as bone histology. To test specific signaling, we will use pharmacological stimulators and inhibitors, and eIF2a-linked knockout mouse models.

RESULTS:
This study demonstrates that unloading-reduced bone mass is significantly restored by salubrinal. The result is consistent with salubrinal's stimulatory role on osteoblasts. The study provides evidence that salubrinal can be a potential therapeutic agent for preventing bone loss in disuse osteoporosis, which is encountered by astronauts under microgravity.

The result, obtained in this study period, was published in the following peer-reviewed journals:
Zhao, L., Tanjung, N., Swarnkar, G., Ledet, E., Yokota, H. (2012). Regulation of eIF2a phosphorylation in hindlimb-unloaded and STS-135 space-flown mice. Adv. Space Res. 50:576-583.
Zhao, L., Dodge, T., Ledet, E., Yokota, H. (2011). Knee loading stimulates bone formation in tail-suspended mouse hindlimb. Biol. Sci. Space 25:77-82.

experiment_title: Charged Particle Radiation-Induced Genetic Damage in Transgenic Mice
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Evaluations of risks involving alterations in the genome using whole animal systems are essential to missions in space. The lacZ transgenic mouse model is the only system available, to date, for the assessment of alterations in the genome in every tissue of the animal. In this model system, every cell of the animal contains multiple copies of an integrated but inert target transgene. Radiation-induced mutations can be measured and specific genetic alterations characterized using established protocols. Genetic alterations in tissues that are of high priority in NASA's Strategic Program Plans but are not accessible using conventional techniques, e.g., the central nervous system, can be evaluated using this model system. In addition, early (1-2 days) and late (up to 16 weeks) radiation responses in vivo can be examined in parallel by enumerating micronuclei in peripheral blood, evaluating chromosomal damage by using fluorescence in situ hybridization techniques, and induced gene expressions by using RT-PCR. Variation in genetic background has been shown to impact an individual's radiation sensitivities. The tumor suppressor p53 gene function has been shown to be radiation responsive and very important in the regulation of cell growth, proliferation, differentiation, and apoptotic signaling pathways in many tissues. LacZ transgenic mice with different p53 genotypes will be used to assess tissue-specific p53-dependent (or -independent) molecular and genetic mechanisms in radiation-induced damage resulting from exposure to particle beams in the energy range corresponding to space radiation. Shielding materials are being developed as countermeasures to protect astronauts against potential adverse radiation effects in long term manned space missions. This current project aims to establish the use of this transgenic mutation model system in the testing of currently available shielding material to examine the efficacy of each substance in radiation protection. The research objective for this project is to use lacZ transgenic mice that are either Tp53 wild type, hemizygous or nullizygous to examine the impact of Tp53 genetic status on radiation sensitivity.

The specific aims of this investigation include:

  1. Characterization of dose- and time-dependent radiation-induced responses in lacZ transgenic mice after exposure to low-LET proton radiation. It is hypothesized that the lacZ mutagenic potential of proton radiation is proton dose dependent and tissue specific. It is also hypothesized that the initial level of micronucleated (MN) in peripheral blood reticulocytes (RET) and chromosome aberrations in circulating lymphocytes will increase as a function of dose.
  2. Characterization of dose- and time-dependent radiation-induced responses in lacZ transgenic mice after 1 GeV iron particle irradiation. It is hypothesized that lacZ mutant frequencies (MF) will increase as a function of iron ion dose for each tissue, but the level of induction of MF is dependent on the specific tissues analyzed. It is also hypothesized that the initial level of MN in peripheral blood RET chromosome aberrations in circulating lymphocytes will increase as a function of dose.

For each of the above aims, the initial effects and long-term consequences of radiation exposure in tissues that are of high priority to NSBRI/NASA, namely the brain (CNS), spleen (highly proliferative tissue with stem cell populations), the hematopoietic system [immature polychromatic reticulocytes (RETs) and mature normochromatic erythrocytes (NCEs)] and lymphatic system will be examined. Using the same experimental animals, the transgene lacZ MF in brain and spleen, micronuclei in peripheral blood erythrocytes, and unstable chromosome aberrations in circulating lymphocytes, will be determined using conventional techniques. Comparisons of results from aims 1 and 2 will provide new information on the LET-dependence of lacZ mutations in tissues, MN-RET in peripheral blood, and chromosome aberrations in lymphocytes at early and late times after irradiation. In addition, the impact of Tp53 genetic background on tissue-specific responses will be revealed. Knowledge gained in this ground-based work is directed at understanding tissue and organ response to space radiation and will aid both in the estimation of risk to astronaut health and the design of appropriate countermeasures to ameliorate the negative effects in space flights.

APPROACH:
The approach for this investigation is not available.

RESULTS:
Significant progress has been made in examining the impact of Tp53 genetic background on radiation sensitivity in vivo. In this experiment, lacZ transgenic mice that are either Tp53 wild type (Tp53+/+), hemizygous (Tp53+/-) or nullizygous (Tp53-/-) were whole body exposed to either protons, X-rays or 1 GeV/n iron ions. The temporal regulation of cytogenetic damage to the hematopoietic system by measuring the level of micronucleated erythrocytes (%MN-RET) in the circulating red cells or stem cell population in the bone marrow was assessed. Using tissue samples derived from the same animals, the effect of radiation damage at the genome level by quantitating the mutations (MF) in the genomically integrated transgene in two tissues with contrasting proliferative capacities, namely the brain and the spleen was measured. The multi-prong approach has provided insight into the dynamic processing of space-relevant radiation effects in the whole animal.

Tp53 (-/-) and (+/-) animals, bred in-house at SRI International, were transported to Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) and exposed to graded doses of 1 GeV/n iron ions. The %MN-RET was measured in the peripheral blood in a time course after HZE radiation exposure. The earliest cells to appear in the peripheral blood are those that were in the G2/M phase in the bone marrow at the time of radiation exposure. It has been previously reported that the %MN-RET varies linearly as a function of dose and peaks at 48h after radiation exposure in the Tp53 (+/+) animals. New results show that %MN-RET in the peripheral blood shortly after radiation is dependent on Tp53 gene dosage. Animals lacking Tp53 gene function showed a delayed MN-RET output, independent of dose. At 48 hours after radiation, the level of %MN-RET appeared to vary linearly as a function of dose, saturating at doses >1 Gy, and was independent of Tp53 gene function. In addition to quantitating short term cytogenetic damage and processing by assessing the frequency of micronuclei in the peripheral blood, residual radiation effects in the bone marrow was evaluated by measuring MN and chromosomal aberrations (CA) in the bone marrow.

A variety of aberrations were observed including gaps, breaks, acentric fragments, dicentrics, centric rings, robertsonian translocations. In Tp53(+/+) animals, the frequency of CA were within the control range at lower dose levels (0.1 and 0.5 Gy) for all time points, whereas at the highest dose level (2 Gy) there was a 3-fold increase in CA at 1 and 8 weeks. The values returned to control levels at 16 weeks after irradiation. In Tp53(+/-), there was a dose-dependent increase in CA at 1 week. After 8 weeks, the CA frequencies were within the control range at all dose levels. In Tp53(-/-) animals, there was no increase in CA at all dose levels compared to controls at 1 and 8 weeks. These results suggest that Tp53 genetic background plays an important role in the determination of radiosensitivity of the stem cell populations and that most CA are readily removed during the recovery process in vivo.

Brain and spleen tissues were collected at 8 weeks post irradiation for mutant analysis. It has previously been reported that dose dependent increases in lacZ MF in the spleen tissues in Tp53(+/+) animals in response to iron ions. Evaluation of lacZ MF in the brain from the same animals during this current year showed that, in contrast to the dose-saturation effect at high doses seen in the spleen tissues, the MF in the brain appeared to increase linearly with dose. Results from spleen tissues harvested from the Tp53(-/-) animals showed that the lacZ MF was independent of the dose of iron ions, suggesting that damaged cells from the tissues in these animals were likely to be eliminated from the population and therefore, do not contribute to the long-term mutagenic potential for this tissue.

The effect of shielding animals with various thickness of polyethylene from 1 GeV/n iron ion exposure was examined. Transgenic mice were shielded with either 10 or 15 cm of polyethylene and exposed to either 0.1 or 1 Gy iron ions. Early cytogenetic damage was assessed by enumerating the level of circulating MN-RET shortly after exposure and lacZ MF was evaluated at a later time up to 8 weeks post exposure. No difference was observed between %MN-RET in animals with or without shielding at both dose levels. On the other hand, the lacZ MF in the brain and spleen with either 10 or 15-cm of shielding protected animals from radiation induced mutations in the reporter transgene. Results from these studies highlight the importance of endpoints considerations in the evaluation of the efficacy of potential radiation protectors.

This IMED Corporation Gemini PC-2 IV pump system was evaluated for suitability and operability in a continuous microgravity environment. Further testing in microgravity, with terrestrial correlation, will be required before man-rating the device.

experiment_title: Integrated plant experiments on Mir
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Long duration space flight missions will require a renewable source of food and an efficient method to process and recycle many waste materials. Plants provide an obvious solution to these problems. However, plant growth and reproduction in space have always been problematic. This experiment was designed to grow Super-Dwarf wheat on the Russian Mir space station through its entire life cycle.

Approach:

Hardware was transported to Mir and set up in July 1996. Seeds were planted on August 5, 1996. Plants were sampled at 21, 39, 52, and 63 days after planting. Samples were placed into a chemical fixative and placed into a desiccant bag. A second planting was made on December 6, 1996. CO2 and water vapor were measured and recorded. Several plants were sampled using the same procedure on December 24. After thirty-nine days of growth, the plants were harvested and transported back to Earth in the GN2 freezer aboard the space shuttle Atlantis.

Results:

Plants in the both batches appeared healthy and produced a considerable amount of biomass in comparison to previous experiments. The first planting produced about 280 heads by the time that the plants were harvested on December 6. However, the heads contained no seeds and the flower either had not formed pollen or had not released it. Further, the pollen grains contained only one or two nuclei and were probably sterile. Despite differences in growth rate, every plant appeared to have been arrested at the stage in growth just before pollen release. These defects could be a possible effect of elevated ethylene (C2H2) in the atmosphere of Mir and are consistent with the know effects of ethylene on plants. Both plantings were found to have elevated levels of calcium, boron, aluminum, and cadmium, while there were magnesium and phosphorous deficiencies in both sets of plants.

experiment_title: Enhancing Situation Awareness of Automated Procedures using Adaptive Multimodal Augmented Reality Displays [VITA]
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During the exploration class missions of the future, crews will no longer have the benefit of real-time or near real-time support from Mission Control and related teams on the ground due to the distance of the crew from the Earth. As a result, crews will have greater autonomy in every aspect of their missions and they are expected to depend more on automated systems to accomplish their tasks. This is an unfamiliar way of working that could put situation awareness (SA) at risk. Therefore, automated systems must include effective methods for promoting good situation awareness.

This study investigates the effects of a virtual task assistant on human performance of procedural work. The virtual task assistant combines procedure automation with augmented reality multi-modal user interfaces. The virtual task assistant will assist users in becoming familiar with planned procedures, in performing procedure actions, and in maintaining awareness of procedure actions taken by other crewmembers or automation. Human performance will be compared with and without the virtual task assistant with the goal of informing best methods for delivering and using such virtual task assistants.

This study has the following objectives:

1.   Determine the best methods to improve SA and improve crew autonomy when using a virtual task assistant to prepare for and perform manual maintenance.
2.   Determine best methods to improve SA and reduce workload when a virtual task assistant is used to handover maintenance tasks between users
3.   Determine best methods to improve SA and reduce workload when using a virtual task assistant to help manage concurrent manual and automated tasks.

APPROACH:
This ground-based investigation will utilize the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) located at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. Sixteen HERA Campaign 6 subjects, four per mission, will participate in three pre-mission sessions and one post-mission session as well as ten sessions during the mission.
Pre-mission:

In the first pre-mission session, subjects will provide demographic data and information about their background and experience. In the second session, subjects will receive a group introduction to the HoloLens and an overview of some of the tasks they will perform during the mission. In the third session, subjects will receive in-depth training on the HoloLens and the tasks they will perform during the mission.

In- Mission:
During their mission, subjects will be asked to perform two different procedural tasks.

The procedures necessary to complete the tasks are generated and delivered by the custom-designed software, Procedure Integrated Development Environment (PRIDE). PRIDE-Augmented and Virtual Reality (PRIDE-AVR) generates procedure-based cues by parsing text instructions into verbs and actions and distributing the parsed instruction as an action cue. PRIDE-AVR also extends system models in the PRIDE electronic procedure system to include AVR information (e.g., object location). Procedures include occasional interruptions for queries intended to establish the subject’s understanding of the task and provide a measure of SA.

The first task is a small rover construction and software testing task. The rover construction task will be performed over two sessions per week during the first four weeks of the mission. Subjects will follow specific sets of procedures involving the assembly of a rover during the first session and the testing (through computer programs) and disassembly of the rover during the second session each week. Individual subjects may be assigned to use HoloLens-based procedures in order to construct and test the rover or to use only tablet-based procedures to construct and test the rover. Other subjects may be assigned to a team of two without a HoloLens, where one subject will read procedures from a tablet device to a second subject performing the task. Different rovers will be constructed and tested, and subject groupings will change with each version of the rover. At the end of each session, subjects will complete a questionnaire (Bedford Workload Scale) to assess workload and ratings regarding aspects of using the HoloLens or tablet system. After all four weeks of rover tasks are complete, subjects will rate the procedure platforms and provide comments on the study.

The second task is a maintenance task on an inert generator that will be performed during the last two weeks of the mission. This is an individual task. Each subject will perform the task once using the HoloLens and once using the tablet-based procedure. At the end of each session, subjects will complete a questionnaire (Bedford Workload Scale) to assess workload and ratings regarding aspects of using the HoloLens or tablet system.

Post-mission:
Each subject will be individually debriefed on his or her in-mission experiences by the investigator.

RESULTS:
This investigation is still in progress. However, this investigation is expected to provide guidelines for designing effective human-automation systems and evaluate human-automation performance for exemplar procedure automation systems. In addition, it will also provide guidance for the application of multi-modal and adaptive displays and control to Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) design for long-duration operations.

experiment_title: How the Brain Constructs Stable Visual Representations: Cortical and Subcortical Mechanisms
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
When making our way through the environment our eyes are constantly moving, scanning the scene. Though images move on the retina, our perception of the world remains stable. What is the neural basis of this stability? Neurons in several cortical areas are capable of “remapping” visual representations in conjunction with eye movements. Recent experiments have suggested, surprisingly, that subcortical pathways can be recruited as well when the normal cortical pathways are interrupted. The aim of this study is to determine how subcortical pathways contribute to solving the problem of maintaining stable spatial representations.

APPROACH:
The investigators were focused on determining the brain circuits that contribute to creation of stable visual representations. These interests build upon illuminating studies done previously in the lab that focused on the transfer of visual information for the updating of an internal representation. The investigators asked whether updating of a visual representation across hemispheres depends on the forebrain commissures, the fiber bundle that connects the cortical hemispheres. Investigators tested the integrity of spatial updating in two ways. First, they used a behavioral test that required spatial information to be updated when the eyes move. Second, they analyzed the neural signal in the Laterial Intraparietal cortex (LIP), an area known to contain remapping signals. In both sets of experiments they examined the difference between a condition where the internal representation of the visual stimulus remained within a single hemisphere and a second condition where the internal representation must pass across to the opposite hemisphere. They hypothesized that when the internal representation of a visual stimulus remains within a single hemisphere, the behavioral task would be performed correctly and LIP neurons would have a normal remapped response. In contrast, when the representation of the stimulus has to move across hemispheres, they expected that the monkeys would be unable to perform the task and LIP neurons would not have a remapped response.

RESULTS:
A first, the monkeys’ performance confirmed their hypothesis. The monkeys were unable to complete the task when the visual information needed to pass across hemispheres. Surprisingly, recovery began almost at once. Both monkeys ultimately recovered to the point where they could correctly perform the task that required across-hemisphere remapping of visual information. Additionally, when thy recorded physiological activity in area LIP, they found neurons that fired both when the representation remained within a hemisphere and when the representation crossed hemispheres.

Three important discoveries were made. First, the investigators found that even in the absence of the forebrain commissures, neural activity in LIP is related to the monkey’s behavior during a task dependent on accurate spatial updating. These results suggest that LIP still plays a role in the behavior of the monkeys. After the removal of the forebrain commissures, the behavioral recovery might have been due entirely to subcortical mechanisms. Instead, it appears that information about the opposite visual field still reaches LIP, and this activity contributes to the overall behavior of the monkey.

Second, investigators determined that the remapping activity in the split brain animals is not due to representation of ipsilateral and contralateral visual fields in a single hemisphere. Investigators found that while in normal monkeys there is a small representation of ipsilateral space, that represenatation is absent when the forebrain commissures have been transected. This result indicates that a sub-cortical structure must be the source of the across hemifield remapping observed in the split brain animals.

Third, investigators determined that neurons in the superior colliculus (SC) in the intact monkey are capable of remapping when the visual information remains within or must pass across hemifields. The difference between the LIP and SC is the number of neurons that have remapping activity. In LIP, investigators found that approximately 70% of the neurons have remapping activity; this is compared to about 30% in the SC. Even thought the total numbers of neurons are different, theses structures are similar in their participation in across and within hemifield remapping. Neurons in both areas have potential access to visual information from large portions of the visual field. The across hemifield remapping observed in the SC may be the source of the across hemifield remapping that remains in the LIP of the split brain monkey.

experiment_title: Environmental Monitoring Air Quality
experiment_description:
Objectives:
The pollutants present in the atmosphere of a sealed environment represent the summation of many interacting dynamic processes. Those processes can be roughly separated into pollutant sources and pollutant sinks. This simple division, however, masks the complexity inherent in the behavior of each of the sources and sinks.

Air revitalization systems are necessarily thought of as sinks for air pollutants; however, there are examples where such systems have been the source of serious spacecraft pollution, or have converted relatively non-toxic pollutants to hazardous pollutants. Humans are generally regarded as pollutant sources; however, inhaled air is scrubbed of many pollutants by the human respiratory system before being exhaled into the vehicle atmosphere. Materials can be the source of offgassing of trace contaminants released from their molecular structures. On-the-other-hand, materials can provide surfaces for the condensation and absorption of less volatile air pollutants. The task of understanding and controlling the sources and utilizing the sinks to produce a healthy, respirable atmosphere in a sealed environment is not a simple one.

The primary objective of this investigation was to utilize the Air Revitalization System (ARS) to:
 

  • Maintain the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) chamber CO2 partial pressure below 5.3 mm Hg (0.7% or 7000 ppm) throughout the duration of the test
  • Control the O2 percent in the chamber between 20% and 22% throughout the duration of the test
  • Control trace gases below Spacecraft Maximum Allowable Concentration (SMAC) levels per JSC 20584
  • Control odors in the chamber to a level acceptable to the test subjects
  • Maintain humidity levels in the chamber between 25 and 70%

    Secondary objectives were:

  • Characterize air quality in the sealed chamber
  • Demonstrate that the Oxygen Generation System (OGS) can process recovered water, both from the Carbon Dioxide Reduction System (CRS) and the Water Recovery System (WRS)
  • Quantify the amount of expendables required for system operation.

    Tertiary Objectives were:

  • Characterize the Four-Bed Molecular Sieve (4BMS) CO2 product for major and trace gases
  • Evaluate performance of the subsystems and components in an integrated operation with humans in the loop
  • Measure chamber leak rates before and after sealed chamber test

    Approach:
    Air samples were acquired periodically in 500 ml, passivated canisters that had been evacuated, proofed for cleanliness, and spiked with three surrogate standards (C13-acetone, fluorobenzene-D5, and chlorobenzene-D5). The samples were analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) and GC/mass spectrometry (MS) in the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Toxicology Laboratory.

    During the Phase II test, formaldehyde was monitored using Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy of grab sample canister (GSC) contents. The major limitation of this method is that its detection limit is near 2 mg/m3, which is well above the long-term exposure limit for exposure to this irritant. For the Phase IIa and III tests, formaldehyde badge samples were obtained periodically, most often from chamber level 1, with nominal sampling durations of 24 hours. This improved the formaldehyde detection limit by approximately 100-fold. The diffusion-controlled, badge samples were analyzed by the chromotrophic acid colorimetric method in the JSC Toxicology Laboratory.

    During parts of the Phase IIa test, when formaldehyde became a crew health issue, the badge measurements were confirmed with two active sampling methods. In the first method, formaldehyde was trapped in impingers containing a 1% sodium bisulfite solution. The solution was subsequently analyzed by a chromotrophic acid colorimetric method. In the second method (EPA TO-11), formaldehyde was reacted with dinitrophenylhydrazine, which was coated onto silica gel beads in a tube. The tubes were extracted with acetonitrile, and the solution was analyzed by high-pressure liquid chromatography.

    Ammonia was monitored during Phases IIa and III with an Interscan Model 2900, which used an electrochemical cell to detect ammonia. The instrument was calibrated with a gas permeation source at 4 mg/m3.

    The mixture of pollutants present in the atmosphere was assessed according to methods applied to spacecraft atmospheres. The average toxicity index for each toxicological group (Tgrp) was calculated for groups of n toxicants found at their respective concentrations (Cn) for 30 to 90 days and causing similar toxic effects or targeting the same organ system (e.g. respiratory system irritants, cardiotoxicants, carcinogens, etc). The equation below was used with 180-day spacecraft maximum allowable concentrations (SMACs):

    Tgrp = C1/SMAC1 + C2/SMAC2 + .... + Cn /SMACn

    The atmosphere was considered acceptable if each Tgrp value was <1.0. Certain SMACs have been set lower because of the effects of space flight (e.g. immune effects, hematological effects, etc.), hence, for the Earth-based application in this study, a few SMACs may be lower than necessary to fully protect crew health.

    Results:
    Phase II 30-Day Test
    Even though the atmosphere throughout the test was acceptable for human respiration based on the T-value calculations from nine GSC samples, several atmospheric anomalies occurred during the test. On test day six, the carbon dioxide reduction system failed due to flooding of the methane/water separator. After replacement of the faulty, low-level water sensor, a methane leak was detected from one of the separator fittings and was replaced. This occurred over a period of approximately three days and caused unusually high levels of methane and, to a lesser extent, carbon dioxide in the sample taken on day 10. The methane concentration slowly decayed throughout the remaining 20 days of the test.

    The concentration of carbon monoxide was somewhat higher than that typically observed in space vehicles and the level of Freon® 113 was much higher than typically observed in space vehicles. The carbon monoxide concentrations increased from trace to approximately 4 mg/m3 by day 10 and stayed near that level until the end of the test. The Freon® 113 concentrations were relatively high before the test began (12 mg/m3) and increased through day 10 to about 20 mg/m3, after which they stabilized at about 10 mg/m3. This compound most likely originated from the pre-test cleaning of the electronic components of the hardware.

    Some of the low-molecular-weight alcohols exhibited interesting behavior. Ethanol and isopropanol concentrations varied from about 0.3 to 2 mg/m3 during the test. The variation was undoubtedly due to the use of these alcohols in hand wipes and sterilizing pads. This is in contrast to methanol, which maintained a steady state concentration of about 0.35 mg/m3 throughout the test. Methanol originates primarily from hardware offgassing and one would expect the continuous rate of production and the rate of removal to result in a nearly uniform concentration.

    As noted in the methods section, formaldehyde was measured during the 30-day test using FTIR spectroscopy on aliquots taken from the GSCs. This resulted in a method that was relatively insensitive to formaldehyde and led to concentrations that were consistently reported as less than the method detection limit. The method was replaced by a much more sensitive badge-sampling method.

    Phase IIa 60-Day Test
    The dynamics of air pollutants during the Phase IIa test were much different than during the Phase II testing. From an air-quality perspective, the 60-day test can be summarized as a learning experience about the importance of controlling materials offgassing.

    Steady-state concentrations were not achieved for methanol, acetaldehyde, or formaldehyde until the last few days of the study. Formaldehyde was of particular concern because the measured values increased to 0.25 mg/m3 by day 15, whereas the long-term SMAC is only 0.05 mg/m3.

    The accuracy of the badge method was confirmed by comparing it to an impinger method and an U. S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) method. The day 27 badge result from level 1 was 0.17 mg/m3, the coincident impinger sample was 0.17 mg/m3, and the average of four EPA-type samples was 0.18 mg/m3.

    A number of materials inside the chamber quickly underwent offgas testing to determine their rate of formaldehyde production. Most materials did not offgas detectable levels of formaldehyde; however, the poster murals were found to release measurable amounts of formaldehyde and were removed from the chamber on day 17. The airborne formaldehyde dropped from its high of 0.25 mg/m3 on day 15 to 0.16 mg/m3 on day 18.

    Three compounds, which came primarily from anthropogenic sources, showed very different concentration profiles. During this test the primary methane source was the human occupants; there was no evidence of a system leak such as that seen during the Phase II test. Methane concentrations increased steadily with time as the test progressed. Carbon monoxide also exhibited this behavior until day 30 when an abrupt drop in the concentration occurred. After this time, carbon monoxide was never found above a trace amount (about 0.5 mg/m3). Ammonia concentrations reached a steady state level of 0.14 mg/m3 by day 5 of the test and did not change from this level in the remaining 55 days.

    Phase III 90-Day Test
    Air pollutants were better controlled during most of this test than during the Phase IIa test. However, evidence was found that a new air contamination source was introduced late in the test, which caused a large increase in the concentration of respiratory irritants. Separate from this was a slight increase in formaldehyde toward the end of the test, but this was apparently caused by an anomaly in a catalyst bed rather than excessive offgassing of materials as found in the 60-day test. Another distinct difference between the 60-day test and the 90-day test was the accumulation of ammonia during the latter test.

    In conclusion, these findings underscore the need for comprehensive air quality analyses to determine whether preventative measures to limit pollution have been effective, to ascertain if the ARS is capable of dealing with the pollutant load on a sustained basis, to detect any new sources of air pollution, and to judge whether the air has been acceptable for crew health. These goals can be achieved only in a test chamber or space vehicle due to the complex interactions between the sources and sinks. Such interactions will only be made more complex as food preparation and waste processing systems are integrated into habitats.

    During the LMLSTP the analyses were retrospective, yet they still provided valuable insight into the dynamic changes that were occurring in the chamber. NASA is on the threshold of being able to analyze spacecraft air for trace pollutants on a near-real time basis, and this will further enhance the value of air quality assessments. Future research should focus on understanding the risks that specific air pollutants pose to crew health, and then developing analyzers capable of addressing those risks using a minimum of resources. That research must be conducted in realistic, ground-based environments before analytical hardware is flown in space vehicles, which one can only hope will be headed to Mars in the not-too-distant future.
