experiment_title: Microbiological Investigations of the Mir Space Station and Flight Crew
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Microorganisms are ubiquitous in spacecraft environments, as they are on Earth. Microbes pose several risks to humans in space including: infectious diseases, allergies, degradation of air quality (e.g., release of volatiles), release of toxins, degradation of critical materials, and systems failure (e.g., water reclamation system). Maintaining the health and performance of humans in closed microgravity environments while reusing reclaimed air and water is a daunting task. Determining medical and technological risks that are dependent on microbiological factors during long-term space flight is a vital problem in theory, as well as practice. In such a closed environment, humans will be a major source of microbes released into the spacecraft. Animals and plants, when present, will also be significant contributors to the overall bioburden. Suitable containment and purification technologies are essential. Studies of microbial ecology in spacecraft have been mostly limited to short (<30 days) duration missions in the US program. Similar studies have been conducted during long-duration missions in the Russian program. The Mir space station provided an opportunity for a relatively comprehensive US-Russian joint study of the crewmembers and the environment of the Mir.

The success of long-duration space missions will depend on our ability to mitigate the adverse effects of microorganisms. This will require a much better understanding of the microbiology of closed environments and the human-microbe-environment interactions than are currently available. This joint US-Russian investigation was an important first step in gaining this understanding.

The investigators hypothesized that during long-term space flight (>30 days) human microbiota and the microbial ecology of the Mir station will undergo quantitative and qualitative changes. The objectives of this study were to 1) characterize microbiota of crewmembers, air, surface, and water before, during, and after a long-duration mission aboard the Mir Space Station, 2) determine the exchange and distribution of microbes among crewmembers, and 3) assess the distribution and dynamics of crew microbiota throughout the Mir Space Station.

APPROACH:
Crew microbiology
Pre and postflight, microbial samples from the throat, nose, ear, hand, scapula, axilla, groin, feces, and urine were collected and examined for bacteria and fungi. Feces were also examined for ova and parasites. In-flight microbial samples from the throat, nose, ear, hand, scapula, axilla, and groin were collected with the Crew Microbiology Kit (CMK). Quantification and isolation of organisms was performed by, preparing serial dilutions of each sample and spread-plating those samples onto selective media. Any aerobic bacteria or fungi isolated were identified using a Vitek Automated Identification System, Biolog Automated Identification System, or classical means. Species that were not identified by these means were sent to a microbial reference laboratory for identification.

Air microbiology
Air samples were collected from the Shuttle middeck and flightdeck, pre, in, and postflight using the Microbial Air Sampler (MAS). In-flight air samples were also collected from and Mir with the MAS. Mir sampling locations included the area of the Commander's seat (Core Module), area of the dining table (Core Module), in the Commander's cabin (Core Module), and in the Kristall Module hatch. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section.

Surface microbiology
Surface samples were collected from the Shuttle pre, in, and post flight. Shuttle sample areas included the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System in the middeck, the left-most air return in the port side crawl-through, and the half-moon shaped air vent for the Commander's chair in the flight deck. In-flight surface samples were collected from the Shuttle and Mir with the Surface Sampler Kit (SSK). Mir sampling locations included the Commander's seat post #1 (Core Module), the dining table (Core Module), the Commander's cabin wall (Core Module), the right handle of the treadmill (Core Module), and the wall above the hatch in the Kristall Module. Once during the NASA 3 mission, a sample from the galley water dispenser needle was collected. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section.

Water microbiology
Water samples were collected from the Shuttle pre and postflight. Tank A was sampled preflight, and tanks A and B were sampled postflight. In-flight water samples from the Mir were collected and processed with the Water Experiment Kit (WEK). Mir sampling locations included the galley hot and coldwater ports, and the SVO-VZ port. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section.

Food packet microbiology
During the NASA 4 mission, a food packet was contaminated due to a puncture in the packaging material. A sample was obtained and processed similar to the procedure used for the shuttle surface sample.

'Free' surface sample
During NASA 6 and 7, crewmembers came in contact with 'free' surface condensate in various locations during housekeeping procedures. Representative samples were collected for evaluation of any potential risks that the crewmembers might be exposed to. The samples were collected using the Contingency Water Quality Kit (CWQK), this being assembled from hardware components contained within the Water Experiment Kit (WEK). The condensates were aspirated into a 60cc syringe, and then expelled into a 300 ml sample bag. These samples were returned to ground for complete analyses. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section.

RESULTS:
CREW MICROBIOLOGY
NASA 3/Mir 22
6 subjects were sampled pre and post flight, three of which were also sampled in-flight. No significant changes were apparent in the aerobic bacteria isolated from the pre-, in-, and postflight specimens. Staphylococcus aureus was the bacterial species used to follow microbial dissemination from crewmember to crewmember and throughout the Mir environment. Crewmembers 1 and 2 were the prime crewmembers that were replaced one week before flight; S. aureus was recovered only once from the nose on each of these crewmembers. Candida albicans was also recovered once from the throat of Crewmember 2. S. aureus was recovered from the throat of Crewmember 3 twice preflight and once postflight. This bacterium was also recovered from the nose of this crewmember at all preflight sampling sessions, three of four in-flight sessions, and two of three postflight sessions; the organism was occasionally isolated from this person's skin, urine, and feces samples. Candida albicans, an endogenous yeast, was isolated from the feces of Crewmember 3 once postflight. S. aureus was recovered from the throat, nose, hand, and axilla of Crewmember 4 at L-2 days. Enterobacter cloacae, Aeromonas hydrophila, and Enterobacter hormaechei were isolated from the throat of Crewmember 4 at L-2 days; E. cloacae were also isolated from the nose at this sampling time. Yeast was present in 5 of 9 samples collected from Crewmember 4 at R+0; Serratia liquefaciens was isolated from the hand at this collection period. Specimens from Crewmember 5 frequently had S. aureus isolated; is was present in the nose at 6 of 11 sampling periods. Once during flight, the organism was present in 4 of 7 samples. At R+0, it was recovered from 4 of 9 specimens, from 5 of 9 at R+7, and from 5 of 9 at R+11. At L-59, Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from the throat of Crewmember 5; Pseudomonas aeruginosa was isolated from the throat at L-2. S. aureus was not recovered from Crewmember 6.

NASA 4
One crewmember was sampled pre, in, and postflight. Opportunistic gram negative rods were recovered from the throat at several sampling times: Panteola agglomerans on FD19, Pastuerella multicoida, Serratia odifera, Serratia species, Enterobacter gergoviae on FD117, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa on landing day. Candida albicans, an endogenous yeast, was isolated from the throat 143 days before flight. Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from the nose at landing. Organisms recovered from the hand included Acinetobacter haemolyticus on L-9 and Enterococcus faecalis and Serratia marcescens on FD117. Candida albicans was recovered from the groin on FD117, and was present in the feces before and after flight. Enterococcus faecalis was present in low numbers in the urine on landing day and 5 days thereafter.

NASA 5/Mir 24
3 crewmembers were scheduled to be sampled pre, in, and postflight. The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on all crewmembers on FD15, FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135, was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. A number of opportunistic gram negative rods were recovered from 5 of 9 samples collected from Crewmember 1 at the L-10 sampling period. Staphylococcus aureus, a potential pathogen, was recovered from the nose of Crewmember 1 at all postflight sampling periods; this organism was also recovered from the throat at R+0.
Several opportunistic gram negative rods were recovered from 4 of 9 samples collected from Crewmember 2 at the L-11 day sampling period. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the nose of Crewmember 2 at all sampling periods; this organism was also recovered from the throat and groin at R+0. Candida species, an endogenous yeast, was isolated from the throat at all three postflight sampling periods.
Opportunistic gram negative rods were only occasional recovered from Crewmember 3. Klebsiella pnuemoniae was isolated from the groin at R+0 and from the nose at R+14 days. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the nose of Crewmember 3 at L-28 days; this organism was recovered from the throat and hand at R+14 days. Candida species, was isolated from the throat and feces during both preflight and postflight sampling periods.

NASA 6/Mir 25
3 subjects were sampled pre and postflight. The opportunistic bacteria Staphylococcus aureus as well as Candida albicans (a yeast) were recovered from the throat of Crewmember 1 during both of the preflight sampling times. Staphylococcus aureus was also recovered from the nose of this crewmember at all three sampling times. Enterobacter cloacae were isolated from the throat of Crewmember 1 at L-21; at L-14, Candida albicans was recovered from the feces. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the throat of Crewmember 2 on landing day and from the nose at the L-9 and R+0 sampling times; Candida albicans was isolated from the feces on L-9 and was too numerous to count in the throat at R+0. On landing day, Crewmember 2 exhibited a colony count of too numerous to count from the urine; the organism recover from this specimen was Staphylococcus species and was probably a contaminant. Enterobacter aerogenes was isolated from the throat and nose of Crewmember 3 on landing day. Candida albicans was recovered from this crewmember's throat at L-9 and R+0 (too numerous to count), and from the urine at R+0. Penicillium species (too numerous to count) and Candida parapsilosis were also present in the nose of Crewmember 3 on landing day. Staphylococcus aureus is frequently a resident of the nasal passages; Candida species are ubiquitous yeasts, being found as normal flora of the alimentary tract and mucocutaneous membranes.

NASA 7
One crewmember was sampled pre and postflight. The opportunistic bacteria Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the nose at all three sampling times. No clinical symptoms were experienced by the crewmember as a result of the presence of this organism. Staphylococcus aureus is frequently a resident of the nasal passages.

AIR MICROBIOLOGY
NASA 3 and STS-79
Fungal levels were often above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Enterococcus faecalis was isolated from the area of the dining table and in the Commander's cabin on FD52. On FD80, both bacterial and fungal levels in three of four Mir sampling locations greatly exceeded the US standard of 1000 CFU/m3 proposed for the International Space Station (ISS).
The highest bacterial level observed during any of the Shuttle sampling sessions was 319 CFU/m3, found in the middeck of STS-79 at R+0. The highest fungal level observed on the Shuttle was 550 CFU/m3 in the flight deck of STS-79 at R+0.

NASA 4 and STS-81
On board the Mir in the area near the commander's chair, the bacteria Aeromonas hydrophila and Comamonas testosteroni were recovered on FD53. Bacteria recovered from the area of the dining table included Staphylococcus aureus on FD80 and Pseudomonas putida on FD117; fungi isolated from this same area included Aspergillus niger and two species of the yeast Candida. The bacterium Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was isolated from the commander's cabin on FD19 and FD80; Sphingobacterium spiritovorum and Chryseobacterium meningosepticum were also recovered on FD80. Candida guilliermondii was recovered in the Kristall Module hatch on FD117; Sphingomonas paucimobilis and Candida fumata were isolated during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Fungal levels were above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3 in all sampling locations at all sampling times. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3 . This amount was only occasionally exceeded, e.g. in the area of the commander's seat on FD80, in the area of the dining table on FD117, and in the Kristall Module hatch on FD80 and FD117. Onboard the Shuttle, the fungal levels increased during the docked phases of STS-81.

NASA 5 and STS-84
The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on the Mir on FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135, was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. The in-flight recording of data from Mir samples collected on FD19 was received.
On board the Mir, Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the area of the dining table during the docked phase of STS-84; Sphingomonas paucimobilis and Candida famata were isolated from the area of the Kristall module during this same sampling session. On FD19, Mir bacterial levels slightly exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3 in 3 of the four sampling sites. Fungal levels were above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3 in all sampling locations at all sampling times. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3 . This amount was only occasionally exceeded, e.g. in the area of the commander's seat and in the Commander's cabin on FD19. Onboard the Shuttle, the fungal levels increased during the docked phase of STS-84.
 

NASA 6 and STS-86
On board the Mir, in the area of the dining table, the fungi Aspergillus niger was isolated on FD29. Bacillus cereus was recovered from this location of FD 54 and FD100; Staphylococcus aureus recovered on FD100. Fungi recovered from the area of the commander's cabin included Aspergillus niger on FD54. This same fungi was also recovered in the Kristall Module hatch on FD54. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Fungal levels were always above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3 . This amount was only exceeded once in the area of the Commander's seat on FD54 and once in the area of the dining table on FD29.
Onboard the Shuttle, the bacterial and fungal levels exceeded acceptability limits in the Middeck on FD5 of STS-86 during the docked phase. Aspergillus niger was recovered in low numbers from the Flight Deck during the pre-docked phase of STS-86.
 

NASA 7, STS-89, and STS-91
On board the Mir in the area near the commander's chair, the fungi Aspergillus niger was isolated; yeast recovered from this location included Rhodotorula rubra on FD43, Candida guilliermondii on FD 119, and an unidentified yeast on FD 135. Bacteria recovered from the area of the dining table included Pseudomonas fluorescens on FD119. Bacteria isolated from the commander's cabin included Serratia marcescens on FD78, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia on FD119, and Pasteurella haemolytica on FD135. Aspergillus niger was recovered in the Kristall Module hatch on FD135; The bacterium Serratia liquefaciens was recovered from all of the locations during multiple sampling periods; these included site 4 on FD 43, sites 1,2, and 4 on FD78, and from all sampling sites on FD 119. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Fungal levels were frequently above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3. This amount was only exceeded once in the Kristall Module hatch on FD43.
Onboard the shuttle, the fungus Aspergillus niger was isolated during the pre-docked phase of STS-89 in the Flight Deck. The yeast Candida guilliermondii was isolated during the docked phase of STS-91 in the Middeck; however, the bacterial and fungal levels never exceeded acceptability limits.

SURFACE MICROBIOLOGY
NASA 3 and STS-79
Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded both US and Russian standards; fungal levels exceeded the standards only once during the mission. S. aureus was isolated from the Commander's seat (post #1) on FD24. Yeasts were isolated from the dining table on FD24, FD52, and FD80 of the NASA 3 mission, as well as during the docked phase of STS-81. During the docked phase with STS-79 and on FD52, yeast was recovered from the wall in the Commander's cabin. In the Kristall Module hatch, yeast was isolated on FD109; Serratia liquefaciens was found during the docked phase of STS-81.
Both bacterial and fungal levels during all of the sampling sessions for STS-79 were within the US limits proposed for ISS. The yeast Cryptococcus albidus was isolated from the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System in the middeck at both preflight sampling periods of STS-79; an unidentified yeast was isolated from the same location during the docked phase with Mir. No yeast was recovered from any location after landing.

NASA 4 and STS-81
Mir bacterial levels frequently exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2, but exceeded the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS only once. Bacteria recovered from the commander's seat post #1 included Sphingomonas paucimobilis on FD19, Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria, Pseudomonas putida, and an unidentified gram negative rod on FD53, as well as an unidentified gram negative rod on FD80. Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was isolated at 4 of the 6 sampling periods from the dining table; other microorganisms recovered from this location were Rhodotorula rubra (a yeast) during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-81, Aspergillus niger on FD19, Aeromonas hydrophila on FD53, Candida parapsilosis on FD117, and Sphingomonas paucimobilis during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. From the commander's cabin wall, Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was again isolated at 4 of the 6 sampling periods; other microorganisms recovered from this location were Aeromonas caviae, Sphingomonas paucimobilis, and Vibrio alganolyticus on FD19, Sphingomonas paucimobilis on FD80, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and an unidentified gram negative rod on FD117, and Aspergillus niger during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. Bacteria isolated from the handle of the treadmill included Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria on FD53 and Chryseomonas luteola on FD80. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the Kristall Module hatch on FD117 and during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. Bacterium also recovered from this location were Serratia liquefaciens and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia during the during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-81, Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria on FD19, Aeromonas caviae on FD53, and Sphingomonas paucimobilis during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. On STS-81, both bacterial and fungal levels exceeded US limits at R+0 at the same air vent.

NASA 5 and STS-84
The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on the Mir on FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. The in-flight recording of data from Mir samples collected on FD19 was received. Mir bacterial levels frequently exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2, but never exceeded the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. On FD5, Sphingomonas paucimobilis was recovered from the dining table and Kristall module hatch; Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was recovered from the dining table and the commander's cabin wall. Staphylococcus aureus was also isolated on FD5 from the dining table and Kristall module hatch.

NASA 6 and STS-86
Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2 as well as above the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS once. Bacteria recovered from the commander's seat post #1 (site 1) included Vibrio alginolyticus on FD54. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia was isolated from the dining table (site 2) on FD28; an unidentified Gram negative rod was recovered from this location was on FD54. Rhodotorula glutinis, a yeast, was isolated from the handle of the treadmill (site 4) on FD100. The bacterium Pasteurella haemolytica was recovered from the Kristall Module hatch (site 5) on FD54.

NASA 7, STS-89, and STS-91
Mir bacterial levels frequently exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Bacteria recovered from the commander's seat post #1 included Serratia marcescens and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia on FD78, and Pasteurella haemolytica on FD135. The fungi Aspergillus niger was isolated from this site on FD43; yeast recovered from this location included Candida parapsilosis on FD78 and an unidentified yeast on FD135. Pseudomonas stutzeri and Serratia marcescens were isolated from the dining table on FD43; other microorganisms recovered from this location were Klebsiella pneumoniae and Rhodotorula rubra on FD78, and Serratia fonticola on FD119. From the commander's cabin wall, Serratia liquefaciens was recovered on FD43 and Aspergillus niger on FD78. Bacteria isolated from the handle of the treadmill included Sphingomonas paucimobilis on FD43; Aspergillus niger was recovered on FD43. Serratia liquefaciens and Aspergillus niger were recovered again from the Kristall Module hatch on FD43.
Onboard the Shuttle, Aspergillus niger, Candida parapsilosis, and Candida guilliermondii were recovered from the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System during the docked phase of STS-89. Yeast recovered from the left-most air return in the port side crawl-through included Candida guilliermondii during the docked phase of the STS-89. Acinetobacter lwofii was recovered from the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System during the sampling session performed 26 days before the launch of STS-91. Yeast recovered from the left-most air return in the port side crawl-through included Candida guilliermondii and Candida parapsilosis during the docked phase of STS-91. Acinetobacter lwofii was recovered from the half-moon shaped vent for the Commander's chair in the Flight Deck one day before the launch of STS-91.

WATER MICROBIOLOGY
NASA 3 and STS-79
All but one of the Mir hot water samples had no bacterial growth, indicating that the rigorous treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is well able to maintain the quality of water from this source at standards well below the US and Russian maximum limits. Burkholderia cepacia was the only bacterial contaminant recovered from the Shuttle potable water system; this organism is frequently recovered from this system. Tank B represents pre-treated water, and predictably contained many bacteria.

NASA 4 and STS-81
All Mir hot water samples were within the US acceptability limits set for the International Space Station. All but one of the Mir hot water samples had no bacterial growth, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. Cold and SVO-ZV samples predictably contained many bacteria.

NASA 5 and STS-84
The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on the Mir on FD15, FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135 was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. Pre and postflight samples from STS-84 were analyzed.
All Mir hot water samples were within the US acceptability limits set for the International Space Station. The one Mir hot water sample had a bacterial level of only 20 CFU/100 ml, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. Cold and SVO-ZV samples predictably contained many bacteria.

NASA 6 and STS-86
None of the Mir hot water samples had bacterial growth, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. SVO-ZV samples predictably contained a moderate number of bacteria.

NASA 7, STS-89, and STS-91
None of the Mir hot water samples had bacterial growth, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. Cold and SVO-ZV samples predictably contained many bacteria.
During the first water sampling session of the mission, the NASA 7 crewmember reported the presence of "brown specks" in the unprocessed sample. The crewmember was instructed to proceed with the sample processing and retain the sample collection bag for return to ground. All of the samples that were collected during the mission were returned to Earth. Analysis was based on the descriptions given by the crewmember during debrief, by visual inspection of the sample collection bags which were returned to ground, and by chemical analysis of the discolored water. Upon inspection of the bags, laboratory personnel did not observe any type of particulate present. However, in four of five bags that were returned, there was a small amount of discolored water in one of the two valve stems present on the bags. Chemical analysis showed that the water was found to contain sodium thiosulfate. Each sample bag contains a small amount of sodium thiosulfate, a chemical that is added to the bags before flight to neutralize the biocide (silver) used in the Russian water reclamation system. The cause of this observation noted by the crewmember has not been conclusively determined. One possible cause could have been inadequate temperature control of the Water Experiment Kit. It is known that elevated temperatures will cause a yellowish-brown discoloration of this compound.

FOOD PACKET
The microorganisms present seem to be of environmental origin, rather than contamination of the food.

'FREE' SURFACE CONDENSATE
NASA 6
A sample of 'free' surface condensate was collected on FD113 and returned to ground on STS-89 for complete analyses. Upon visual examination of the sample, the following observations were noted: the sample was cloudy with a brown particulate matter present. A wet mount preparation resulted in the rare observation of amoeba (Figure 1) and ciliated protozoa (Figure 2). Scanning Electron Microscopy revealed the presence of rod- and spirochete-form bacteria (Figure 3). Selected staining techniques resulted in no ova or parasites being observed. Culturing was performed using selective media for the detection of aerobes and fungi. A wide variety of bacteria were present in the samples. The bacteria isolated were of types that will grow in different environmental conditions and can tolerate a wide temperature range. Members of the Enterobacteriaceae family (organisms of enteric origin) that were isolated, such as the genera Serratia and Yersinia, can colonize sites in healthy hosts. The presence of these organisms is noteworthy in that they are opportunistic pathogens and can cause disease in immuno-compromised hosts. Other bacteria that were isolated, such as Flavobacterium meningosepticum, are rarely of clinical significance but may occasionally cause wound infections.

NASA 7
Two samples of 'free' surface condensate were collected on FD127 and returned to ground on STS-91 for complete analyses. Upon visual examination of each sample, the following observations were noted: the "slimy" sample was cloudy with a brown particulate matter present; the "fresh" sample was slightly cloudy with a white particulate matter present. A wet mount preparation resulted in the rare observation of dust mites and showed the presence of a few ciliated protozoa. Scanning Electron Microscopy revealed the presence of rod- and spirochete-form bacteria. Selected staining techniques resulted in no ova or parasites being observed. Culturing was performed using selective media for the detection of aerobes, anaerobes, fungi, Legionella spp., and mycobacteria. A wide variety of bacteria were present in both samples. The bacteria isolated were of types that will grow in different environmental conditions and can tolerate a wide temperature range. Members of the Enterobacteriaceae family (organisms of enteric origin) that were isolated, such as the genera Enterobacter, Citrobacter, Serratia and Yersinia, can colonize sites in healthy hosts. The presence of these organisms is noteworthy in that they are opportunistic pathogens and can cause disease in immuno-compromised hosts. Although a presumptive identification of Legionella spp. was reported, final pneumophila species identification was not confirmed. Other bacteria that were isolated, such as Comamonas spp., Flavobacterium meningosepticus and Pseudomonas fluorescens, are rarely of clinical significance but may occasionally cause wound infections.

CONCLUSIONS:
Overall, the microbiota of all crewmembers sampled was characteristic of healthy individuals. When present the fungal isolates recovered from specimens generally represented common environmental contaminants. No significant changes were found during spaceflight or upon return to earth relative to preflight results.

Amounts of microorganisms observed in the air and on surfaces of the Shuttle and Mir station were mostly within the acceptability limits set by the US for the ISS. The types of organisms recovered were consistent with previous findings from both Shuttle and Mir missions. Fungal levels of the air samples collected on the Mir were often above the limits set for this station; however, no major adverse health effects were seen in the crewmembers. The temporal fluctuations in levels of organisms probably reflect changes in environmental characteristics, such as temperature and humidity, at the time of sample collection.

The bacterial load of the Shuttle water samples were consistent with those seen on previous missions. All Mir galley hot water samples were within the standards set for both the Mir and the ISS. All isolates were consistent with findings from previous Shuttle and Mir missions.

The hardware designed for in-flight microbial monitoring performed nominally.

Collection and examination of 'free' surface condensate can prove to be a valuable tool in assessing the overall condition of the health of a closed environmental system such as a space station.

Although many potential pathogens were isolated from the surfaces, air and "free" surface condensate, it is interesting to note that the microbial flora of the crewmembers remained that of healthy individuals and that these microorganisms imposed no adverse health effects.

experiment_title: Effects of Microgravity in the Adductor Longus Muscle and Receptors in the Forebrain of Rats
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Although the effects of microgravity upon muscle tissue are far from being understood, previous studies have shown that "slow" muscle, mostly composed of type I fibers (e.g. soleus, adductor longus), carry the burden of the changes. This study places emphasis on some particular responses to weightlessness observed in the adductor longus muscle of rats, namely: 1) muscle fiber injury; 2) regenerative phenomena and 3) alterations of the neuromuscular junctions.

Quantitative autoradiographic analysis of receptors for GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) and acetylcholine in the forebrain of space-flown rats was undertaken as part of a joint U.S./U.S.S.R. study to determine the effects of microgravity on the central nervous system, and in particular on the sensory and motor portions of the forebrain. Changes in the binding of these receptors in tissue would provide evidence for possible changes in neural processing as a result of microgravity exposure.

Approach:

The motor endplate region was identified by acetylcholinesterase activity under the stereomicroscope and dissected; silver-gold ultrathin sections were stained with uranyl acetate-lead citrate, mounted in copper grids (100 mesh), and observed with an electron microscope. For light microscopy observations, fixed adductor samples were stained with hematoxylin and eosin. For N-CAM (neural cell adhesion molecule) immunocytochemistry, sections (25 micrometers) were mounted, rinsed, and incubated with anti-N- CAM rabbit antibodies.

Tritium-labeled diazepam and quinuclidinyl-benzilate (QNB) were used to visualize GABA (benzodiazepine) and muscarinic (cholinergic) receptors, respectively. The density of tritium-labeled radioligands bound to various regions of the forebrain were measured from autoradiograms. A video camera-based image analysis system was used to quantify densities of the autoradiograms. Within each brain, two different regions (superficial vs. deep or dorsal vs. ventral) were analyzed separately and, because of blocking variations in individual brains, together to determine differences among conditions.

Results:

N-CAM immunoreactivity was seen on the myofiber surface, satellite cells, and in regenerating myofibers reminiscent of myotubes. Light microscopy revealed myofiber atrophy, contraction bands and segmental necrosis accompanied by cellular infiltrates of macrophages, leukocytes, and mononuclear cells. The principal electron microscopic changes of the neuromuscular junctions consisted of a decrease or absence of synaptic vesicles, degeneration of axon terminals, increased numbers of microtubules, vacant axonal spaces, and axonal sprouting. These results indicate that major alterations such as myofibrillar disruption and necrosis, muscle regeneration and denervation and synaptic remodeling at the level of the neuromuscular junction may take place during space flight.

The absence of significant differences in GABA receptor binding between flight and control animals is not in itself conclusive due to the small number and anatomical variations among samples. The most significant finding in this study is the decrease in muscarinic cholinergic receptors in the stratum of flight rats, a down-regulation which conceivably might be a compensatory response to increased release of acetylcholine, or a possible result of decreased dopaminergic transmission stemming from a microgravity-induced reduction in spontaneous motor behavior. Future studies should perhaps address the importance of in-depth observations of the behavior of rats in space regarding motor activities to correlate with the changes in receptor binding sites.

experiment_title: Assessment of the Time Courses of Leg Muscle Strength and Performance Losses during Prolonged Spaceflight using MARES
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space flight induces significant loss of skeletal muscle mass and function in response to mechanical unloading of the neuro-musculoskeletal system. Contractile protein degradation, sarcomere rearrangement, reduced cross-sectional area, and consequent decrements in force production are all hallmarks of this response at the myofiber level. It is also well accepted that space flight induced myofiber alterations may be modulated or even triggered by a disruption in the interconnected “neuromuscular networks” which normally exist between myofiber and neural elements of the musculoskeletal system under terrestrial loading conditions. Activation of these neuromuscular networks for the antigravity muscles of the lower limbs and trunk is strongly influenced by load receptors in the soles of the feet and the muscles and joints of the lower extremities. This study seeks to characterize adaptive in-flight changes in lower limb muscle strength and neuromotor control performance using the Muscle Atrophy Research and Exercise System (MARES) in the Columbus module on the International Space Station (ISS).

APPROACH:
Investigators will use the MARES device to quantify the time course of changes in muscle strength and performance of crewmembers during six-month ISS missions. They will establish baseline strength and performance capabilities of each participating crewmember from two pre-flight test sessions, track changes from that baseline during three in-flight test sessions, and track recovery to baseline levels during five post-flight test sessions.

RESULTS:
This experiment is in progress. Results will be available at a later date.

experiment_title: Speech Monitoring Cognitive and Personality Alterations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Deep-space missions will expose crews to cosmic rays, which may damage brain structures including the basal ganglia and hippocampus. These subcortical structures are linked with cortical regions in circuits regulating motor control, cognition, and personality. As models for crews suffering neurological damage the investigators used climbers ascending Mount Everest and patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD). At altitudes above Everest Base Camp the low oxygen content can damage the principal basal ganglia output structure, the globus pallidus. The hippocampus also is sensitive to hypoxia. The ascent of Everest also resembles long-term space flight in that a small group in close contact for an extended period must make critical decisions in stressful, life-threatening situations.

PD, which affects basal ganglia function, impairs motor control but also causes deficits in cognition and language comprehension more severe than those in Everest climbers. Thus climbers and PD patients offer complementary Earthbound “space-analogs” for milder and more extreme forms of the dysfunction astronauts may suffer on long-term missions.

The rationale for using speech measures as cognitive indices is that the basal ganglia regulate sequences of speech motor acts as well as of cognitive operations. We can expect the corresponding circuits to show parallel declines in function due to hypoxia, PD, or radiological damage. One index we focus on is voice-onset time (VOT). Stop consonants in word-initial position are produced by first closing the lips or placing the tongue against the roof of the mouth. The obstruction then is abruptly released, yielding a “burst” with distinct acoustic properties. Speakers must also adjust the larynx to produce a vowel after the burst. For “voiced” stops like [b] the time between burst and vowel – the VOT – is less than ~30 milliseconds, while for “voiceless” stops like [p] it is greater than ~50 milliseconds. Hence VOT production requires precise control of the sequence of oral and laryngeal actions. PD patients show reduced differences between VOTs for voiced and voiceless stops. Such VOT convergence correlates with deficits in sentence comprehension.

APPROACH:
On Everest, investigators obtained measurements of VOT and other speech parameters, e.g., vowel duration, by using radios to record climbers reading words at different altitudes. Climbers carried picture booklets so that the investigators could administer, by radio, sentence-picture matching tests of language comprehension. To measure cognitive flexibility investigators gave the Odd-Man-Out test (OMO) and, in 2004, the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task. These required subjects to select stimuli using one of several possible criteria and then shift criteria following feedback. In 2003 the investigators added the Mini-Cog test battery developed by Stephen Kosslyn’s NSBRI group at Harvard. This battery, which tests cognitive capacities including verbal and spatial working memory, is implemented on Palm Pilot PDAs that climbers carry. In 2004 a group of climbers also took an implicit contextual learning test that reflects hippocampal function.

To test sentence comprehension, the investigators initial studies used the Rhode Island Test of Language Structure (RITLS), a sentence-picture matching test designed for use with hearing-impaired children. In 2002, the investigators replaced the RITLS with a test encompassing a better-controlled set of linguistic structures. In 2003 and 2004 they narrowed the range of structures tested to focus on those found the previous year to be most sensitive to hypoxia (while retaining some easier types for control purposes). The shortened test retains its sensitivity while being less time-consuming.

RESULTS:
Vowel duration and speech motor sequencing errors increase as climbers ascend, reflecting degraded basal ganglia activity. These metrics detect deficits in language comprehension and the ability to change plans in changing circumstances. Preliminary analyses also reveal memory deficits reflecting hippocampal damage. The speech metrics are unobtrusive and do not reveal the content of a verbal message; they could be derived automatically, allowing space crews to detect subtle motor and cognitive deficits and invoke countermeasures before performance is profoundly impaired.

experiment_title: Effect of Flight in Mission SL-3 on Cytokine Production by Rats
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Several lines of evidence suggest that there may be compromises of immune responses in humans or experimental animals exposed to weightless conditions during space flight, or maintained in hypodynamic, hypokinetic, antiorthostatic models simulating some aspects of weightlessness. Among those immune responses and defenses possibly altered in such conditions is the cytokine system. The present study was carried out to determine the effects of a period of weightlessness on interferon (IFN) and interleukin-3 (IL-3) production by rats.

Approach:

Spleens were removed from rats, separated into individual cells, suspended, and supplemented with antibiotics. Cultures were then stimulated with concanavalin A for 48 hours to induce IFN-gamma and IL-3. Supernatant fluids were harvested from the culture. Supernatant fluids were analyzed for IFN antiviral activity. Due to cross reaction of rat and mouse IFN, the assay was carried out on mouse L-929 cells using the Indiana strain of vesicular somatitis virus as the target. Assays used were either a plaque reduction or microplaque reduction, and the IFN titer corresponded to the reciprocal of the greatest dilution of the test sample that reduced virus plaques by 50%. IL-3 assays were carried out by determining the ability of the supernatants to support the growth of an IL-3-dependent cell line.

Results:

Spleens of all flown rats were substantially reduced in weight compared to controls. Spleen cells of seven of ten ground control rats produced moderate levels of IFN-g, while only one of ten flight rats whose IFN-g production was analyzed produced any IFN-g, and the level of production of that one rat was at the lower level of detection of the assay system. Decreased spleens size in flown rats may be due to altered activity of T-lymphocytes in the spleen which are responsible for IFN-g production. The drop in IFN-g production could been related to microgravity, or to stress during postflight transport. However, it is unknown if the IFN-g production decrease is permanent or transient in nature (i.e., would IFN-g production have returned to normal had the rats been allowed to recover further on the ground before sacrifice). Studies with antiorthostatic modeling have suggested that, in mice, ability to produce IFN recovers after return to normal caging. IL-3 production was not affected by space flight. Thus space flight only affects specific components of the immune response.

experiment_title: European Space Agency Nitric Oxide - 1
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Recent research has demonstrated that an elevation of expired nitric oxide (NO) is an early and accurate sign of airway inflammation especially in asthma but also after occupational dust inhalation. This experiment utilized improved techniques for analysis of NO in expired air. This was used to study physiological reactions in humans in microgravity.

Since dust never settles in microgravity, it is likely that there is an increased exposure of the human airways to inhaled particles in such an environment. The crewmembers performed a simple inhalation-exhalation procedure on a bi-weekly basis during their stay on the International Space Station (ISS).

APPROACH:
During orbital space flight, and in future space exploration missions, crewmembers are exposed to an increased risk of airway inflammation due to inhalation of free-floating dust and particles, and inhalation of dust particles. Analysis of exhaled nitric oxide (FENO) is a simple method to monitor inflamed airways. In preparation for possible future monitoring of lung health during long-term space missions, the effects of altered gravity per se on FENO was studied.

It was hypothesized that changes in gravity can influence FENO by altering lung gas exchange capacity and uptake of NO in the alveoli (tiny grape-like sacs in the lungs where the gas to blood exchange occurs). For this study, five healthy astronauts performed control FENO measurements on ground before space flight and then approximately every six weeks during their 23 to 28 week-long stays onboard the ISS during 2005-2008. A parallel ground based study with 10 subjects was completed for hypergravity (acceleration force greater than normal gravity) in a human centrifuge.

RESULTS:
Results show that during microgravity, FENO was significantly lower and fell to nearly half that of preflight value. In the centrifuge experiments, FENO was significantly elevated during exposure to two and three times the normal gravity. The findings of decreased exhaled NO in space and increased exhaled and estimated alveolar NO values in hypergravity suggest that gravity-induced changes in alveolar-to-lung capillary gas transfer greatly affect FENO, but there was no clear trend over time during the stays on the ISS or after landing. According to current models of NO transport, NO originates from conductive airways and alveoli, each source having a different impact on the exhaled amount. Additionally NO is taken up by blood in the alveolar compartment. Thus, a change in FENO may come from an alteration of the overall balance between production and blood recapture as well as by a change in the airway production. The principal observation was that exhaled NO is gravity dependent: its values were lowered in microgravity and elevated in seated humans during hypergravity

experiment_title: Sleep/Wake Activity Patterns of a Pig-Tailed Monkey During Nine Days of Weightlessness
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This portion of the primate experiment was to study the possible effects of the space environment on the sleep/wake cycle of a pig-tailed monkey. This study was to analyze time-lapse photographic records of the animal taken by the on- board camera inside the Biosatellite III capsule. Camera records were taken in conjunction with other physiological measurements on the animal just before and during the flight.

Approach:

The 16 mm cameras in the flight and simulated spacecraft were mounted above the left shoulder of the animal. A 24-hour clock and date indicator was placed in the photographic field by an auxiliary lens. Time-lapse pictures were taken at the rate of one frame every twenty minutes at zero, twenty and forty minutes after the hour. Data was obtained by analyzing each frame with an optical data analyzer, in which each frame was taken to represent the animal's state for a given twenty- minute period. Sleep/wake states were defined by the status of the eyes: open, closed, not discernible. Other activities, such as food and water consumption and telemetry data, supplemented the time-lapse data to indicate and verify the animal's sleep or awake state. In addition to the four controls, baseline data from five other monkeys subjected to simulated space flight up to thirty days were also analyzed.

Results:

The animal appeared to have began to adapt to space environment within thirty seconds after reaching orbit, when a rapid disappearance of anxiety and struggling could be observed. Lack of sleep in the preceding eighteen hours resulted in immediate sleep. Periods when the subject awoke briefly and drank water were noted, although absent from the time-lapse photographic record. The subject was generally awake during the light cycle, and with the exception of the last two days, the subject tended to remain on a consistent schedule regarding onset of "night" sleep. The sleep/wake cycle was generally 24-hour but a phase angle difference of two hours from the imposed day/night modes and rapid shifts in sleep/ wake states occurred. The subject remained asleep for longer periods of time as the flight progressed. Comparison with other circadian findings indicate that an internal desynchronosis occurred.

experiment_title: Contribution of the Vestibular and Sympathetic Nervous Systems to Space-Induced Bone Loss - Postdoctoral Fellowship
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Research has shown that genetic and pharmacologic approaches to sympathetic nerves contribute to the regulation of bone homeostasis. Osteoblasts express the beta-2 adrenergic receptor (ß2AR) and respond to catecholamines or pharmacological ßAR agonists with decreased proliferation and induction of RANKL expression, which leads to enhanced osteoclast formation and bone resorption. Propranolol, a ß1/ß2AR non-selective antagonist, inhibits these effects of sympathetic activation and protects from ovariectomy and unloading-induced bone loss in mice and rats. External factors also influence bone remodeling. In particular, gravity and inertial accelerations exert a range of mechanical stimulations on the skeleton that have an osteogenic effect demonstrated in birds, mice, rats, pigs, sheep and humans. In contrast, mechanical unloading as a consequence of bed-rest or microgravity conditions causes bone loss in humans and rodents, which is associated with suppressed bone formation and a mild increase in resorption.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine if vestibular lesion causes bone loss by activation of the sympathetic nervous system.
  2. Analyze the bone phenotype of mice devoid of vestibular gravity sensor.

APPROACH:
Investigators evaluated the effects of a bilateral vestibular lesion (VBX) on femoral bone mass using micro-CT analyses on two-month old mice. In addition, they used three-month old mice lacking otoliths (gravity sensors), in order to mimic the decrease in vestibular stimulation in space.

RESULTS:
The first step of this study consisted in evaluating the effect of a VBX on femoral bone mass. Using micro-CT analyses on two-month old mice, investigators demonstrated that VBX induces a significant decrease in femoral bone mass one month after the lesions. Histomorphometric analyses revealed that this bone loss was associated with a decrease in bone formation whereas bone resorption was not affected. The second step was to determine whether the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) mediates this VBX-induced bone loss. Using two-month old beta-2 adrenergic receptors Knockout (KO) mice, investigators detected no bone change in bone volume over total volume (BV/TV) one month after VBX. Moreover, daily propranolol treatment had no effect on WT-sham mice but completely blunted VBX-induced bone loss in WT-VBX mice. Finally the SNS involvement in the VBX-induced bone loss was further supported by the increase in Ucp1 gene expression in brown adipose tissue (a marker of the SNS activity). No change in BV/TV was observed one month after VBX in two-month old beta-2 adrenergic receptors osteoblasts-specific KO mice. These results suggest that VBX-induced sympathetic outflow to bone triggers bone loss via its effect on beta-2 adrenergic receptors expressing osteoblasts.

experiment_title: Determining the Dose Response Profile of the Headward Fluid Shift During Varying G-Levels
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Long-duration missions under weightless conditions have resulted in notable changes to the function and structure of the eyes in some astronauts. This phenomenon, Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), is hypothesized to develop in response to chronic exposure to the headward fluid shifts that occur in the spaceflight environment. The headward fluid shift increases congestion of the veins that drain the head, leading to impaired cerebrospinal and lymphatic fluid drainage from the head and changes to the eye. Countermeasures are being proposed to counteract these effects, however the amount of partial gravity required to re-establish footward fluid shift has not yet been identified. Parabolic flight provides a unique opportunity to evaluate the acute changes associated with varying levels of gravity (G-levels) and describe how important venous parameters change at levels less than normal Earth gravity.
This study has three specific aims:
(1) Determine the relationship between G-level and upper body venous hemodynamic parameters associated with a headward fluid shift, including internal jugular vein (IJV) pressure, flow pattern, and cross-sectional area.
(2) Assess if the relationship between G-level and upper body venous hemodynamic parameters is influenced by differences in anatomy between the left and right sides of the body.
(3) Determine whether the supine posture in normal gravity is an appropriate analog for weightlessness with respect to internal jugular vein hemodynamics.

APPROACH:
Internal jugular vein cross-sectional area, pressure, and flow pattern will be assessed in nine subjects across a range of G-levels and postures using ultrasound. Conditions will include: 1.0-G supine (preflight), 1.0-G seated (preflight), 0.0-G (parabolic flight), 0.25-G seated (parabolic flight), 0.50-G seated (parabolic flight), 0.75-G seated (parabolic flight), and 1.0-G seated (level flight). All participants will be between 25 and 55 years old, and between 157-183 cm tall. All IJV measurements will be collected bilaterally.
The aircraft will fly in parabolas that initially produce increased gravity (1.8-G, “hypergravity”), followed by ~20-50 second periods of partial gravity or weightlessness. After that, there will be another pull-up (hypergravity) to complete the parabola. The plane then will fly in normal horizontal flight for a few minutes before repeating the parabolic flight path again. Subjects will participate in two parabolic flights: one producing partial gravity and one producing weightlessness during each parabola. Each flight will include 31 parabolas, with the first parabola serving as a “practice” parabola to verify equipment operation. Then six sets of five parabolas will be performed. During the partial gravity flights, subjects will experience three different G-levels (0.25-G, 0.50-G, and 0.75-G) with at least 10 parabolas at each G-level. The order of the G-levels will not be randomly assigned within or across days of flight but will differ across days. During the flight(s) that produce weightlessness, the IJV parameters will be acquired for each subject across 10 parabolas. Accelerometer data (from an accelerometer affixed to an equipment rack) will be used to identify the respective partial-gravity and weightlessness epochs that participants experience during data collection. Baseline data will be collected at 1.00-G preflight in the supine and seated position and at 1.00-G seated during level flight.

RESULTS:
The investigators anticipate this research will expand the current knowledge base on the effects of IJV anatomy on hemodynamic variables believed to be associated with the risk of SANS and venous thrombosis during varying G-levels. Specifically, this research will fully describe the IJV pressure, cross-sectional area, and flow characterization during normal upright sitting in 1.00-G (normal Earth conditions), across a range of G-levels (including 0.00-G), and while supine as a 0.00-G analog. The investigators also seek to validate IJV hemodynamics during supine 1.00-G as an accurate model for IJV hemodynamics during weightlessness. Altogether, the results of this research will (1) inform the level of fluid shift required to reverse the hemodynamic effects of weightlessness, (2) guide the implementation of a SANS and/or venous thrombosis countermeasure during space flight, and (3) inform whether the gravitational levels on the Moon (0.16-G) and Mars (0.38-G) will be protective against these health risks.

OBJECTIVES:
The goal of the proposed work is determine the effects of space flight on growth, performance (productivity and time to maturation), metabolism, and genetic changes in radish plants (Raphanus sativus). We will measure the metabolic, physiological, and genetic responses of radishes grown on the ISS and identify the effect of the space environment on metabolite accumulation, flavor, enzyme activity, mineral uptake, and generation time. This knowledge will be essential for the transition from earth-bound cultivation of plants to growth conditions in space; the research is important for the establishment of human colonies on the Moon, Mars, and farther outposts.

experiment_title: Development of Vestibular Organs in Microgravity
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Many species sense gravity, and therefore linear acceleration, by way of otoliths (dense calcium carbonate crystals attached to hair cells and associated nerve fibers). As the mass moves with acceleration, a signal is sent through each hair cell to the central nervous system. The knowledge of the factors that control development of these otoliths (and their analogs in some species) is limited. Previous studies suggest that altered gravity does not substantially affect the volume of the otoliths or their analogs in adult animals. This study was designed to test the hypothesis that during development the mass of the otolith is regulated to achieve a desired weight; as such, one would expect to reference larger-than-normal otoliths in animals reared in microgravity.

Approach:

The statoconia (analogous to otoliths) of the pond snail, Biomphalaria glabrata, and the otoliths of the swordtail fish, Xiphophorus helleri, were the focus of this study. Thirty-five adult snails, four pre-mated adult female swordtail fish, and 50 to 200 juvenile swordtail fish were flown in the Closed Equilibrated Biological Aquatic System (CEBAS), which contained seven liters of water and 50 grams of the hornweed, Ceratophylum. The specimen container was videotaped for later analysis. Many of the snails mated in flight, and produced the juvenile snails used in the experimental analysis. The pregnant adult swordtail fish were selected at a stage that they would produce developing fry but not have any hatch by the end of the mission. On landing day, approximately half the juvenile snails were fixed; the other half were fixed five days postflight. Adult fish ovaries and juvenile fish were fixed in alcohol on landing day. Fixed snails were removed from their shell and sectioned at 1-2 micrometer; serial sections were examined by transmission electron microscopy.

Results:

Results were obtained from both the Neurolab flight (16-day) and a similar experiment of nine days duration, using the same organisms, flown on STS-89. Total statoconia volume in the snails varied considerably within both the flight and ground control groups. However, the difference in mean values for the two groups was significant at p < 0.05, with the average total volume greater in the flight group. In most of the groups of flight snails (divided into groups by shell diameter), the increase in statoconia volume increased as the animals developed another five days on Earth. Overall, the flight-reared snails had approximately 50 percent more statoconia than the ground controls. This indicated that rearing in microgravity causes the supporting cells to produce more statoconia, of approximately the same size as in ground-reared animals.

Otoliths of the embryonic fish from STS-90 (Neurolab) exhibited a greater growth, with increased body length in the flight-reared animals, compared to ground controls. Although there was a trend for larger otoliths in the flight-reared juvenile swordtails, this difference did not reach statistical significance. The embryos from STS-89 were much smaller that those retrieved after STS-90, since this was a shorter mission. In this case, the growth of otoliths of the ground-reared fish embryos was actually larger than that of the flight-reared animals. These results suggest a critical period, in the late embryonic stages, where rearing in microgravity produces larger otoliths.

experiment_title: Facilitating the Synergistic Side of Cultural Diversity in LDSE: Identification of Challenges and Development of Cultural Training
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Cultural diversity has been a staple of NASA missions since the 1970’s. However, the push for longer duration missions has increased the need to investigate the impact on cultural diversity and crew performance. Previous studies have indicated that culturally-based differences in values, beliefs, and preferences for cognition and action can have an impact on interdependent action. Cultural diversity can pose challenges for a number of transitions, actions, and interpersonal processes and emergent states in teams. However, almost all of these studies have been conducted outside the context of space flight. The little work that has been conducted within space flight has begun to suggest that the impact of culture on teams may be different in long-duration space environment (LDSE). This drives the question as to whether cultural diversity within space flight crews has the same impact on team performance as that reported within the wider literature on cross-cultural teams and what can be done to create synergy.

The investigators aim to leverage prior work on cultural diversity and teams in mission critical environments and retrospective data on team interaction in isolated and confined environments (ICE) and pair this with experimentation in ground analog studies to better understand the critical challenges created by cultural diversity in LDSE and use this information to create and test cultural training tools that can be used pre- and inflight.

This study has the following specific aims:


  1. Determine the critical issues surrounding culture and team performance in LDSE.
  2. Determine from a compositional standpoint if there an ‘ideal’ team profile in terms of cultural orientations to facilitate team performance and adaptability in LDSE.
  3. Determine what types of cultural training can be developed for use preflight and inflight.
  4. Determine what tools can be developed to facilitate practitioners in maximizing the potential synergy in culturally diverse teams operating in LDSE (e.g., pillars, guidelines, practices, tips).

APPROACH:
To study the impact of cultural diversity on crew interaction and performance over time, investigators plan to study participants in Russia’s Scientific International Research In a Unique terrestrial Station (SIRIUS). SIRIUS is a mock spacecraft habitat which provides an isolated and confinement environment. Subjects will participate in four-month missions in 2018, and an eight-month mission in 2019. The investigators also plan to participate in Russia’s ground-based Experimental Complex (NEK) chamber spanning two missions. In addition, investigators aim to reanalyze existing data collected within LDSE environments at NASA and reanalyze data previously collected on cultural diversity and teams for the Army. Investigators plan to use archived data and reanalyze that data to provide evidence for the model of cultural diversity and its impact on performance in LDSE.

Investigators will conduct interviews with approximately 10 subject matter experts (SMEs) such as astronauts, mission control personnel, flight surgeons, psychological support personnel, and analog researchers regarding their experience working with culturally diverse crews. Investigators plan to develop an evidence-based cross-level model which illustrates the individual and team level challenges and impact of cultural diversity on teams in LDSE. Using this information, investigators will develop and validate training tools for preflight and inflight use.

RESULTS:
This study builds on prior research to identify the critical challenges that cultural diversity imposes on crews in LDSE and how to mitigate those challenges through training. The investigation will result in evidence-based products, including guidelines, recommendations, and measurement tools. These products will aim to close the gaps in the understanding and measurement of shared mental models (SMMs) over time in long-duration space flight (LDSF) teams. Furthermore, this work will provide practical tools to allow for measurement of SMMs in LDSF teams to identify discrepancies among team member SMM and shifts in SMM. This knowledge and these products will serve to develop countermeasures for maintaining accurate and shared SMM over time within LDSF teams and with ground control.

experiment_title: Multianalyte Biosensor with Chips for Human and Environmental Monitoring
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The closed environments of space travel offer enhanced opportunities for transmission of pathogens and toxins. Ideally, food, water, air, and people need to be monitored in order to assure the continued health of the traveler. Rapid diagnostic systems are required, in particular, in cases of human illness to identify both the infection and the source. Investigators proposed to build a handheld, low-power biosensor capable of analyzing samples from virtually any aqueous medium for a customized array of targets. The sample was exposed to a sensing chip with an array of specific (antibody) and semi-selective binding molecules capable of recognizing multiple targets. The sample was followed by a fluorescent reagent capable of binding to any captured target. The identity of the target is determined by the location of the fluorescence on the chip. In the first year, the biosensor itself was miniaturized, while the second year focused on the design of chips that can be mass produced and included both a waveguide coated with the capture array and the reservoir of fluorescent reagent. In the third year, chips were adapted specifically for monitoring: (1) food and water, (2) air and surface samples collected using a small cyclone or swipe, respectively, and (3) human fluids such as nasal swabs and blood. Targets included bacteria, viruses, toxins and metabolic indicators.

experiment_title: Spaceflight Effects on Regeneration in Lower Vertebrates: Molecular-Biology and Cytochemistry Examinations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Tissue regeneration in Urodeles is an important, and well-established experimental model to study the effects of spaceflight factors, such as microgravity and radiation, on the long-term viability of biological organisms in space. Spaceflight experiments with the newt Pleurodeles waltl, aboard Foton-M3 in 2007, used new technical approaches to validate experiments on tissue regeneration in space. In these experiments we investigated newt lens, limb, and tail regeneration with respect to cell proliferation, apoptosis, morphology, and growth factor regulation. Results from space-flown newts were compared with a synchronous (1 g), and two aquarium controls. Progress of tissue regeneration was evaluated by comparison to basal controls operated 10 days prior to launch. Lens regeneration in space-flown animals was more uniform than synchronous controls and about 0.5 to 1 stage more advanced. In both groups lens regeneration was accompanied by the growth of the retinal radial glia cell population and by an increase of stress protein (HSP90) expression. In the growth zone of regenerating eyes, expression of FGFß, (a key cytokine in lens regeneration), increased simultaneously with cell mitotic activity in the lens regenerate.

APPROACH:

A total of 16 newts were flown in two separate habitats for 12 days on Foton-M3 in 2007. Prior to the flight all the animals underwent surgery to remove their lenses, toe, and tail tips for regeneration studies.

During flight (F) and synchronous control (SC) experiments we performed video recording, temperature, and radiation monitoring, as well as BrdU, nucleotide analog delivery, to detect cell proliferation occurring in space. Post-flight differential blood counts and histological analysis of the liver were conducted. In blood, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes were counted.

RESULTS:

Tissue expression HSP90 and FGFß were higher in space-flown animals than in synchronous controls. Forelimb toe regeneration proceeded to a comparable early stage of wound healing in both space-flown and synchronous control animals. At this stage no specific signs of toe formation could be detected. Tail regeneration in space-flown and synchronous control animals reached regeneration stage IV to V. Some tail size parameters, such as area, were also unchanged, while others, such as length, showed a decrease in spaceflight. In contrast, remarkable changes in tail tip morphology were found between synchronous, flight, and neutrally buoyant aquaria animals. Computer morphometric analysis showed that flight and aquarium-control tail regenerates were identical in shape, while synchronous controls developed distinct dorso-ventral asymmetry. The above results, together with findings from earlier flights, suggest that tissue regeneration in Urodeles exposed to spaceflight is altered in a tissue-specific manner, and can result in abnormally fast or slow regenerative tissue growth and differentiation.

experiment_title: Venous Congestion Countermeasure Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

During long-duration space flight, changes to ocular structures and visual function occur which is hypothesized to be the result of the chronic headward fluid shift that is induced by weightlessness. A variety of countermeasures aimed at reversing the headward fluid shift have been tested in ground-based studies. However, no countermeasure has been implemented during spaceflight because it is unknown which countermeasure, single or in combination with another, would be the most effective. Lower body negative pressure (LBNP), venoconstrictive thigh cuffs (VTC), and an impedance threshold device (ITD) breathing are countermeasures that partially reverse headward fluid shift. LBNP counteracts headward fluid shift by drawing the fluid from the upper body and shifting it into the legs. VTC reduces blood volume from the central circulation and ITD lowers intrathoracic pressure and augments venous return.

Although LBNP, VTC, and ITD have been shown previously to partially reverse the headward fluid shift, no single countermeasure has successfully reversed values to those observed in the upright position. LBNP, VTC, and ITD individually represent specific and unique physiological strategies to reduce headward fluid shift. When these countermeasures are combined, a flexible and sustained strategy can be developed to increase the magnitude and duration of effects.

The objectives of this three-part study were to determine if an individual countermeasure or a combination of countermeasures can reduce the headward fluid shift induced when moving from the upright to the supine posture, and determine the effectiveness of using a countermeasure during sleep. This experiment evaluated the following specific aims:

  1. Determine which countermeasure, individual or a combination, is most effective at reversing a seated-to-supine posture headward fluid shift and be able to sustain the reversal for 45 minutes.
  2. Determine if the effective countermeasure(s) in specific aim one, is also able to reverse the cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) shift.
  3. Determine if daily use of LBNP during sleep, up to eight hours per day, can prevent the headward fluid shift induced changes during three days of head-down tilt bed rest.
APPROACH:

For Aim 1, the effectiveness of the selected countermeasures, LBNP, VTC, and ITD, to reverse headward fluid shift was evaluated. Ten subjects visited NASA’s Johnson Space Center (JSC) Cardiovascular and Vision Laboratory three times for data collection. During each visit, subjects were studied in the seated and supine position (baseline) and in the supine position during individual countermeasure application, during recovery after the individual countermeasure is released, during combined countermeasures, and while maintaining one passive countermeasure after the combined countermeasure approach. Individual countermeasure application included: LBNP, VTC and ITD. Combined countermeasure and subsequent maintained conditions included: LBNP+VTC, maintaining VTC after LBNP+VTC, LBNP+ITD, maintaining ITD after LBNP+ITD, ITD+VTC, maintaining VTC after ITD+VTC, and LBNP+VTC+ITD, and maintaining VTC+ITD after LBNP+VTC+ITD.

Each data collection session consisted of a block of measurements implemented in the same order each time, lasting approximately 45 minutes. The measurement block began with five minutes of stabilization followed by ultrasound imagining of the bilateral internal jugular veins (cross-sectional area), cardiac ultrasound, otoacoustic emissions (OAE) measurements (non-invasive intracranial pressure), ocular ultrasound (left eye), bilateral internal jugular vein pressure (IJVP), intraocular pressure (IOP) measurement (right eye), and bilateral optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging. This block of measurements was taken during each condition (baseline, countermeasures and recovery/maintain conditions).

For Aim 2, co-investigators from the University of California San Diego and the University of Texas Health Science Center examined the effects of one countermeasure using quantitative magnetic resonance images (qMRI). Baseline data was collected in the supine position without the countermeasure, and then again with the countermeasure. The countermeasure was applied 10 minutes prior to the start of data collection. This approach was to help determine the effect countermeasures have on CSF, white matter and gray matter volume, aqueductal CSF pulsatility, and global cerebral perfusion. 

For Aim 3, co-investigators from the University of Texas Southwestern developed a LBNP device that was able be worn for eight hours during sleep. Subjects participated in a cross-over design study with a 3 day supine bedrest with no countermeasure, and then a 3-day supine bedrest with 8 hours of LBNP during sleep every night. The countermeasure was developed to be an easy-to-use sleep sac that can generate -20 mmHg LBNP that can be worn at night.

RESULTS:

Acute use of LBNP partially reversed the posture induced headward fluid shift by reducing IJV area and pressure, as well as non-invasive ICP. Most measures returned to supine baseline values after release of the individual countermeasures during the 45 min recovery phase, demonstrating that the countermeasures are maximally effective while actively applied. However, the use of combined countermeasures did not reverse the headward fluid shift to a greater degree than with LBNP as an individual countermeasure. LBNP, and to a lesser extent VTC and ITD, represents a promising mechanical countermeasure to reverse the headward fluid shift during spaceflight and warrants further investigation during longer-duration ground-based analog and spaceflight studies to determine effectiveness as a SANS countermeasure.
