experiment_title: Nutritional Intervention to Improve Muscle Protein Metabolism during Stress
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Debilitating injury or trauma is associated with muscle wasting and a progressive loss of functional capacity. An increased circulating level of the stress hormone cortisol likely facilitates this imbalance between muscle protein synthesis and breakdown. The hypercortisolemic response is generally proportional to the severity of an injury and has been shown to increase skeletal muscle proteolysis, particularly when combined with immobilization or bedrest. The metabolic changes that result in a loss of muscle tissue following injury can be broadly characterized as occurring as a result of two main physiological responses. These are changes in postabsorptive protein metabolism and alteration in the anabolic response to feeding. Several studies have characterized changes in postabsorptive protein metabolism in response to hypercortisolemia. In general, these studies demonstrate that in the postabsorptive state, cortisol increases whole body proteolysis, increases plasma insulin levels and raises plasma amino acid concentrations.

While physical interventions such as exercise may provide a potent anabolic stimulus, exercise may not be a feasible countermeasure in all situations, particularly those involving injury or trauma. Consequently, there is need to examine additional strategies, such as nutrition, that may arrest the catabolic process. Following severe injury or traumatic insult, the normal anabolic stimulus to feeding is disrupted. Even with tremendously elevated caloric intakes, some severely injured individuals fail to maintain lean body mass. Further, while chronic outcome measurements such as body-weight, strength and functional ability clearly demonstrate that protein catabolism exceeds muscle protein synthesis following injury, it is not clear if this disruption of physiological homeostasis can be blunted or offset by a nutritional intervention.

The researchers of this experiment have recently shown in healthy subjects that ingestion or infusion of essential amino acids (EAA) provides a potent anabolic stimulus. Further, preliminary data from their laboratory suggests that the anabolic response to EAA ingestion is substantially greater than a mixed meal or even an intact protein source.

The purpose of this study was to determine if the net muscle catabolism that accompanies hypercortisolemia could be ameliorated with a bolus ingestion of 15g of EAA. To compliment the protein kinetics data, the researchers chose two independent, primary endpoint measurements, muscle fractional synthetic rate (FSR) and net phenylalanine balance. The researchers hypothesized that EAA ingestion would be effective in stimulating muscle protein anabolism during acute hypercortisolemia.

APPROACH:
Twelve healthy male and female subjects (mean±SEM: 28±5yrs, 165±6cm, 70±2kg) were randomly assigned to one of two experimental conditions. In the amino acid group (AA; 2 male, 4 female), established stable isotope methodology was used to measure muscle protein kinetics before and after a bolus ingestion of 15g EAA. In the second group (C+AA; 2 male, 4 female) hypercortisolemia was induced and then the muscle protein kinetics was measured before and after ingestion of 15g EAA.

At 1100 hrs on day one of the protocol, subjects were admitted to the General Clinical Research Center (GCRC) at UTMB, given a standard meal and then allowed only water until the completion of the study. At 1200 hrs an 18-gauge, polyethylene catheter was inserted into a forearm vein for infusion of hydrocortisone sodium succinate (Infusion rate: 80µg·kg-1·hr-1), (Solu-Cortef, Upjohn Company, MI) or placebo (0.9% saline). The following morning at 0600 hrs, a second 18-gauge, polyethylene catheter was inserted into a peripheral forearm vein. After obtaining baseline blood samples, a primed (2µmol·kg-1) continuous infusion (0.05µmol·kg-1·min-1) of [ring-2H5] phenylalanine (d5-Phe) was started. At 0700, polyethylene catheters (3 Fr, 8 cm) were inserted into the femoral vein and femoral artery of one leg under local anesthesia. Arterial and venous blood samples were obtained at 10-20 minute intervals before and after the ingestion of the EAA drink for determination of amino acid kinetics and plasma concentrations of glucose, insulin and cortisol. The femoral artery catheter was also used for indocyanine green (ICG) infusion (IR=0.5 mg.min-1) for the spectrophotometric (» =805nm) determination of leg blood flow. Urine samples were collected over a 24hr period from the start of the cortisol/saline infusion (1200 Day one) for analysis of 24hr urinary cortisol levels. Muscle biopsies (50 mg) were taken from the lateral portion of the vastus lateralis approximately, 10-15 cm above the knee using a 5mm Bergstrom biopsy needle.

The composition of the EAA drink approximated the distribution of essential amino acids in skeletal muscle. An additional 0.186g of [ring-2H5] phenylalanine was added to the EAA drink to maintain blood isotopic enrichment. The amino acids were dissolved in 250ml of a non-caloric, non-caffeinated soft-drink and consumed as a bolus at 1100.

RESULTS:
Plasma cortisol levels were significantly elevated in the C+AA group (p<0.05). 24hr urinary cortisol levels were 67±15 and 773±136 mg.24hr-1 for the AA and C+AA groups respectively (P<0.05).

Following ingestion of 15g EAA, arterial and venous phenylalanine concentrations in the AA and C+AA groups increased significantly (P<0.05). However, the magnitude of the arterial and venous concentration change was significantly blunted by cortisol infusion {arterial peak values: 272.4±12.1 (AA) vs. 208.1±17.8 nmol Phe.ml-1 (C+AA)}(P<0.05). Further, hypercortisolemia resulted in arterial phenylalanine concentrations remaining elevated for a longer period of time post-EAA drink.

During the post-absorptive period, hypercortisolemia increased muscle intracellular phenylalanine concentrations. EAA ingestion further increased muscle intracellular phenylalanine concentrations, with the greatest increase occurring in the C+AA group.

During the postabsorptive period, phenylalanine rate of appearance (Ra), a reflection of leg muscle protein breakdown, was not significantly increased by acute hypercortisolemia. Hypercortisolemia did not alter phenylalanine rate of disappearance (Rd), a reflection of muscle protein synthesis, during the postabsorptive period. However, following EAA ingestion, Rd was blunted by hypercortisolemia, yet remained above postabsorptive levels for a greater period of time (P<0.05).

No differences in net phenylalanine balance (NB) were identified while subjects remained in the post-absorptive state. Both groups experienced a significant increase in net phenylalanine balance following ingestion of 15g EAA; however the response in the C+AA group was blunted but remained positive for a greater period of time.

Calculation of net phenylalanine uptake (NB area under the curve: above baseline NB=0) by the leg for the immediate 1hr and 3hr post-drink periods also reflect the blunted, yet prolonged period of positive net balance associated with hypercortisolemia.

Both groups experienced an increase in mixed muscle FSR in response to ingestion of 15g EAA (P<0.05). However, no between group differences were evident during the pre- or post-drink periods, or in absolute changes in FSR following EAA ingestion.

Postabsorptive plasma insulin concentrations were elevated in response to hypercortisolemia. Following EAA ingestion, insulin levels increased in both groups (P<0.05), but remained significantly higher in the C+AA group (P<0.05). Hypercortisolemia also increased plasma glucose concentrations (p<0.05).

The researchers found that while muscle phenylalanine kinetics was altered by acute hypercortisolemia, ingested EAA were still able to stimulate muscle protein synthesis and acutely reverse negative net phenylalanine balance. The present study was the first to investigate the time course and progression of the interaction between acute hypercortisolemia and protein metabolism in response to a bolus oral ingestion of an essential amino acid solution.

These data may reflect the very early stages of the catabolic process. Indeed, the increased circulating and muscle intracellular phenylalanine concentrations noted during the post-absorptive period raises the possibility that acute exposure to elevated cortisol levels primes the system by raising energy expenditure, increasing amino acid turnover and increasing amino acid movement between pools. The net loss of nitrogen from muscle may not actually occur unless hypercortisolemia is prolonged, combined with inactivity and/or combined with other mediators of the injury/trauma response.

Ingestion or infusion of essential amino acids provides a strong anabolic stimulus. Consistent with these previous data, a significant increase in mixed muscle FSR in both experimental conditions during the 4hr period following EAA ingestion was observed. Using the net balance approach to estimate the relationship between protein synthesis and breakdown, it is clear that hypercortisolemia acutely and transiently altered muscle phenylalanine kinetics immediately following EAA ingestion.

The mechanisms resulting in the altered phenylalanine concentrations and kinetics during hypercortisolemia are not entirely clear. Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid and is not synthesized or metabolized in the body, consequently changes in the rate of appearance or disappearance of plasma phenylalanine in the plasma reflects protein synthesis and breakdown. The fact there was an increase in arterial and venous phenylalanine concentration, yet only a trend towards an increase in muscle protein breakdown (Ra) during hypercortisolemia suggests that increased protein breakdown in non-muscle tissues may have contributed to the elevated plasma amino acid levels during the pre- and post-EAA drink periods. Certainly, the liver represents a large potential source of amino acids that could be rapidly released into the circulation given an appropriate signal. There are some data suggesting that the gut may provide a source of amino acids during periods of exercise-induced stress. Certainly, given the high protein turnover rate in the gut, even a slight imbalance between synthesis and breakdown could produce relatively large changes in plasma amino acid concentrations.

The infusion of cortisol to produce hypercortisolemia in healthy human subjects has broad ranging effects and ultimately influences a range of hormonal responses including the regulation of glucose metabolism. Consequently, it is possible that the altered phenylalanine kinetics observed during hypercortisolemia may have also been influenced by the concomitantly elevated plasma insulin levels both before and following ingestion of 15g EAA.

Results from the current study indicated that hypercortisolemia increased plasma glucose concentrations despite an accompanying increase in insulin levels. This elevation in plasma glucose levels was most likely due to a reduction in the rate of glucose disposal and not an increase in production. The suggestion that there was no increased requirement for glucose is congruent with the theory that acute exposure to hypercortisolemia primes the muscle for the subsequent use of glucose and amino acids for energy production if an additional stimulus presents (i.e., prolonged hypercortisolemia, inactivity, physical trauma).

In conclusion, the pattern of the anabolic response to amino acid ingestion is altered by hypercortisolemia. Nevertheless, dietary amino acids are still able to effectively stimulate muscle protein synthesis and reverse the negative net phenylalanine balance associated with hypercortisolemia and may provide an effective means of minimizing muscle loss during the first few days following debilitating injury.

experiment_title: The Effects of Microgravity on Neuromuscular Development
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous research has indicated that a critical period of weight bearing may exist for the development of the motor system in animals. If this is the case, there are striking implications for raising normal animals, including humans, in the microgravity environment of space. This experiment tested the hypothesis that gravity-associated weight bearing is required postnatally for normal neuromuscular development of motor neurons, neuromuscular junctions, and muscle fiber types of the antigravity soleus muscle, but not for that of the extensor digitorum longus (EDL), a nonweightbearing muscle.

Approach:

Rat pups, eight days old at launch, were exposed to microgravity during 16 days of their development. Because of high inflight mortality among the pups, specific studies of the development of soleus and EDL motor neurons and assessment of long-term recovery changes in the neuromuscular system could not be fully completed. The study focused on fiber-type differentiation and neuromuscular junction development. Muscle and spinal cord tissues of Neurolab rats were processed and analyzed to evaluate muscle fiber type differentiation, cytoplasm/nucleus ratios, neuromuscular junction development, and spinal motor properties. A ground-control simulation, consisting of a group of hindlimb-suspended pups with a schedule of four hours unloaded and two hours returned to the dam for nursing, was repeated 24 hours a day for nine days. Litter mates of the hindlimb-suspension control were removed from the dam on the same schedule as the unloaded rats and singly housed to provide isolation controls. The data from the ground controls were used to distinguish unloading effects from isolation effects on neuromuscular system development.

Results:

Exposure to space flight resulted in microgravity-induced unloading as well as reduced neonate-dam and neonate-neonate interactions. The inflight retardation of neonate body weight gain was recovered one month postflight. Fewer large soleus fibers postflight suggested stunted growth for some fibers. Higher cytoplasm/nuclear ratios indicated a persistent deficit in soleus myoblast function. Differentiation from embryonic to slow fiber type was transiently retarded and enhanced toward fast type. Space flight temporarily increased the susceptibility of developing soleus fibers to reloading damage. Elimination of multiple innervation was completed during space flight. The pattern of terminal branching of motor nerve endings was less complex, implying delayed maturation. Space flight retarded the growth of spinal motor neurons. Down-regulation of mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase activity and gene expression in lumbar spinal motor neurons indicated lower oxidative capacity in the flight rats. Lower levels of choline acetyltransferase and Cat-301 proteoglycan indicated delayed motor neuron maturation, regarding neurotransmitter synthesis and extracellular matrix organization. Overall, the results from the neonates emphasize the importance of weight bearing exercise for the normal development of the infant neuromuscular system.

experiment_title: Early Development of Fern Gametophytes in  Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Dormant spores of the fern Ceratopteris richardii were flown on Shuttle mission STS-93 to evaluate the effects of micro-g on their development and on their pattern of gene expression.

APPROACH:

Prior to flight the spores were sterilized and sown into one of two environments: (1) Microscope slides in a video-microscopy module; and (2) Petri dishes. All spores were then stored in darkness until use. Spore germination was initiated on orbit after exposure to light. For the spores on microscope slides, cell level changes were recorded through the clear spore coat of the spores by video microscopy. After their exposure to light, spores in petri dishes were frozen in orbit at four different time points during which on earth gravity fixes the polarity of their development. Spores were then stored frozen in Biological Research in Canister units until recovery on earth. The RNAs from these cells and from 1-g control cells were extracted and analyzed on earth after flight to assay changes in gene expression.

RESULTS:

Video microscopy results revealed that the germinated spores developed normally in microgravity, although the polarity of their development, which is guided by gravity on earth, was random in space. Differential Display-PCR analyses of RNA extracted from space-flown cells showed that there was about a 5% change in the pattern of gene expression between cells developing in micro-g compared to those developing on earth.

experiment_title: Robust Human-System Interface Design for Spaceflight-Induced Environments
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The next generation of human-rated space flight vehicles will expose astronauts to altered gravito-inertial forces and elevated vibration levels during launch and landing that can affect their ability to perform their assigned tasks. Furthermore, current plans call for crew action in critical tasks, including the override of flight automation in off-nominal conditions, while the crew may be exposed to four times normal gravity or more combined with vibration levels potentially higher than those experienced during Apollo and Shuttle. The risk associated with these dynamic phases of flight becomes even more acute when critical tasks are performed by de-conditioned crew returning after a long-duration space flight. Altered gravitational environments experienced in spacecraft impact human manual and gaze control and high-frequency vibration is also a serious challenge to visuomotor performance and gaze control. Unfortunately, the current quantitative knowledge of these effects is too limited to develop and validate operationally relevant predictive models of crew performance of sufficient reliability to support interface design or requirement verification. In particular, the interactions between increased gravity and vibration are poorly understood. The goal of the proposed research is to measure, analyze, and model human performance in display navigation and flight control tasks during centrifugation and vibration (in isolation and combination) to simulate ascent/descent conditions of space flight.

The proposed research will determine the impacts of transient and sustained acceleration on human sensorimotor performance. The benefit of this research for NASA is that it will fill a critical knowledge gap that is currently hampering the optimal design of astronaut and pilot displays and interfaces needed to maximize performance and safety and minimize human error. The benefit of this research for humanity above and beyond enabling safer and more productive space exploration is two-fold. First, the human performance databases (and models) generated will allow for better design of aircraft and other vehicles thereby ultimately facilitating the enhancement of safety for the traveling public by supporting improved cockpit/interface design and training. Second, the performance assessment technologies developed and validated in this project may have medical applications for enhancing diagnostic methods to identify sensorimotor deficits due to disease or injury.

APPROACH:
The proposed research aimed to measure performance (and associated workload) in operationally relevant display navigation and manual control tasks under simulated dynamic phases of flight and will compare the effectiveness of a variety of potential display and interface configurations. These data will enable investigators to identify and model the human capabilities and limitations in order to provide validated quantitative design guidelines for displays and controls to support crew-cockpit design engineers and operations/training development. This research will enable the development of validated spacecraft interface design guidelines and human-system verification tools with the ultimate goal of reducing mission risks and enhancing safety.

RESULTS:
Investigators measured the effects of elevated Gx-loads and vibration on human oculomotor, manual, and autonomic behavior to assess the impacts on vestibular, visual, and motor function and workload of induced environments representative of dynamic phases of flight. They found that gaze stabilization (via the Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex) is not the limiting factor for sensorimotor control with Gx loads up to 3.8Gx and vibration levels of 0.5g at up to 16 Hz. They found that retinal blur is typically about 0.25 degrees or less, indicating that the combined linear and translational Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex is nearly perfectly compensatory, even under challenging Gx-load and vibration conditions.

By comparing open-loop vs. closed-loop saccadic and reach performance, investigators found that:
1. 3.8-Gx loading significantly increases systematic errors for both saccades and manual reaches, compared to performance at 1 Gx.
2. Both saccadic and reaching accuracy and precision improved under closed-loop conditions as compared to open-loop conditions, indicating that oculomotor and manual control performance is visually limited under open-loop conditions (because of visual spatial uncertainty).
3. Vibration significantly decreases the precision of both saccades and reaches.
4. There is a significant correlation between the errors in eye and reach end points, indicating that at least some of the error is due to shared neural noise in visual localization for both oculomotor and manual control.

By comparing pursuit tracking performance in an upright (+1 Gz) vs. a supine (+1 Gx) posture, and under low (+1 Gx) vs. high (+3.8 Gx) G-loads, investigators found that visual motion processing is largely robust to altered G conditions with some exceptions:
1. The cardinal-oblique anisotropy (better performance for target motion along the cardinal directions than for those along the oblique direction) is insensitive to changes in the direction and magnitude of the G vector;
2. However, the horizontal-vertical asymmetry (typically higher direction gains for vertical than for horizontal target motion) is significantly flattened at 3.8 vs. 1 Gx, showing that this visual processing non-linearity is due to a different (possibly cortical) mechanism that is modulated by vestibular cues.

Elevated Gx-loads and vibration generate changes in Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) function, consistent with increased workload:
1. Both heart and breathing rates are significantly elevated during exposure to +3.8 Gx, as compared to +1.0 Gx.
2. There is a correlation between heart and breathing rate and response time showing that ANS effects are linked to task performance.
3. Heart and breathing are significant altered by vibration frequency, although dramatically differently for the two Gx levels.
4. This observed non-linear interaction between Gx-loading and vibration confirms why one must measure them in combination, as what was have done in this project.

experiment_title: Bioavailability of Scopolamine Dosage Forms and of a Combination Dosage Form with Dextroamphetamine after Oral Administration to Human Subjects
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space motion sickness (SMS) is one of the most common ailments experienced in space by astronauts. Although on ground, motion sickness is regarded as a nuisance or a discomfort, SMS occurs during mission-critical times in space and is suspected to hinder crew performance during launch and reentry. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Bioastronautics Critical Path document states that "the most overt change affecting an astronaut in space flight is the immediate response of the neurovestibular system to changes in gravity. Astronauts experience orientation illusions, posture and locomotion disturbances, vestibulo-occular function and gaze changes, space motion sickness, and possible structural changes affecting sensory-motor behavior and reorganization". SMS occurs most severely during gravity shifts (launch and reentry) and also during the first few days of (orbital) missions. Nearly 40% of in-flight medication use by US astronauts has been for the treatment of SMS. SMS symptoms include nausea and vomiting, both of which negatively affect drug concentration after oral administration and reaction time. Reaction time is a marker of cognitive performance.

Scopolamine (SCOP) is an alkaloid which has been used historically for many years as an anti-emetic, a medicine that prevents or controls nausea and vomiting, and a sedative. It is a muscarinic (a type of receptor in the parasympathetic nervous system that releases acetylcholine as its neurotransmitter) anticholinergic (a substance that opposes or blocks the action of acetylcholine) agent with anti-emetic and anti-vertigo activity resulting from suppression of vestibular labyrinthine input to the central nervous system (CNS). Earlier reports indicate that SCOP is efficacious for countering space motion sickness symptoms. Several sources report SCOP as being the most effective drug for suppressing nausea and vomiting caused by motion sickness. Many motion sickness drugs, including SCOP, have been reported to negatively affect concentration, cognition, and other cognitive behavioral measures. SCOP has a shorter half-life compared to other SMS medications used at the present time and therefore, side effects caused by the drug may resolve more rapidly.

Therapeutic effect of a drug is governed by its intrinsic activity and concentration at the site of action. Pharmacokinetics is the mathematical description of drug concentrations in the body (usually in blood or plasma) as a function of time after administration and the physiological variables that govern pharmacokinetic processes, absorption from the site of administration, distribution to the site of action and elimination from the body by metabolism and excretion. Pharmacodynamics, on the other hand, deals with the mathematical description of the onset, magnitude and duration of pharmacologic effect in relation to circulating drug concentration as a function of time. The therapeutic efficiency of a drug, therefore, is determined by the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of a dosage form. Earlier reports on SCOP pharmacokinetics indicate that the drug is rapidly eliminated from the body after administration with a systemic clearance of 65 ± 5.2 L/h and a moderate volume of distribution of 1.4 ± 0.3 L/kg. Oral and intranasal bioavailability of the drug is 10.7-48.2% and 83% after oral and intranasal administration, respectively.

There are no reports on the bioavailability or pharmacokinetics of the custom-dispensed combination dosage form of SCOP and dextroamphetamine (DEX), commonly referred to as SCOP-DEX. The KC-135 and currently the DC-9, affectionately referred to as the "vomit comet," are, or have been, operated by NASA's Reduced Gravity Office (RGO) as the primary simulation method of microgravity. They are flown in a series of parabolic maneuvers which cause brief periods of microgravity onboard and they are usually used for both astronaut reduced gravity training and equipment testing. Both the parabolic microgravity simulations of the KC-135/DC-9 and longer-term microgravity exposure, such as shuttle and International Space Station missions, induce SMS. Recent studies of SMS suppression on the KC-135 using SCOP-DEX have demonstrated an unexpected lack of efficacy prompting this investigation into the relative bioavailability of dosage forms of SCOP currently used by the NASA health care program. Further, KC-135 passengers who elect to take scopolamine to suppress or prevent motion sickness often have visual deficits which impede their performance.

A recent study comparing the efficacy of existing motion sickness medications indicated that SCOP was the most efficacious treatment for suppression of both nausea and the vomit reflex. Of the medications tested in the study, only SCOP was able to affect a prolongation in mean duration of rotation time in a vertical rotation chair. Additionally, accuracy of Delayed Match-to-Sample (DMTS) test, a short term memory and attention test, was found to be unaffected by SCOP whereas other medications negatively affected DMTS; this finding illustrates SCOP's lesser negative impact on cognitive performance when compared to other motion sickness medications.

Scopolamine pharmacokinetics
Bioavailability of 0.4 mg SCOP tablets in normal, nonsmoking male volunteers was reported to be 26.8 ± 5.1%. Plasma and renal clearance estimates in this study were 65.3 ± 5.2 L/h and 4.2 ± 1.4 L/h. Approximately 6% of intravenous and 1% of oral dose was reported to be eliminated unchanged in the urine.

SCOP is known to cross the blood-brain barrier and the placenta and to be reversibly bound to plasma proteins. SCOP is known to be metabolized in the liver mainly to conjugated forms. Oral bioavailability of SCOP has been shown to be increased by pretreatment with grapefruit juice due most likely to inhibition of gut metabolism and/or inhibition of gut transporter proteins caused by flavanoid-like compounds in grapefruit. No significant effect of grapefruit juice on elimination of SCOP was detected.

Dextroamphetamine pharmacokinetics
Dextroamphetamine is readily absorbed from the GI tract following oral administration with an onset of action generally within an hour of administration. Biological half-life of the drug was reported to be 11 h in adults with a systemic clearance of 0.31 L/h/kg. It is distributed throughout the body with high concentrations in the CNS. Elimination of the drug is affected by urinary pH: alkalinization of urine increases half-life and decreases clearance (18 h and 1.5 L/h/kg); acidification of urine decreases half-life and increases clearance (to 4 h and 2.6 L/h/kg).

Significance
Scopolamine is regularly used in the space program as a custom dispensed formulation, both by itself and in combination with dextroamphetamine, as a countermeasure for motion sickness; however, adequate pharmacotherapeutic evaluation of these formulations has not been conducted. It is important to characterize interactions between currently used countermeasures in order to optimize pharmacotherapeutics in space and on the ground. This study examines the pharmacotherapeutics of operational countermeasure formulations and interaction potential of two currently used medications for SMS; this study was conceived based on anecdotal reports of treatment failure by NASA RGO physicians. The results presented herein are also useful for the Space Medicine and Health Care Systems Office in selecting or optimizing treatment of SMS.

APPROACH:
Study design overview
The overall design consisted of 4 treatments administered separately in a randomized fashion to 12 healthy subjects. Treatments were separated by a minimum four-day washout period between doses. Serial biological samples were collected for 24 h post dose along with administration of the ANAM Readiness Evaluation System (ARES) test battery. ARES is a selection of Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric (ANAM) tasks presented on a handheld computer.

Subjects
Twelve healthy, non-smoking subjects of normal weight for body size between the ages of 21 and 48 years participated in the study. All subjects were screened and selected through the NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) Human Test Subject facility. Subjects were excluded if they reported: drug allergies to scopolamine or amphetamines, use of prescription or over-the-counter medications within 3 days of starting the study, use of antibiotics (especially furazolidone) or mono-amine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors within 14 days of starting the study, use of an investigational drug within 30 days of starting the study, tobacco smoking within the past year, blood donation or significant blood loss within 30 days of starting the study, significant gastrointestinal disorder, asthma, seizure disorders, glaucoma, history of urinary retention, history of alcohol or other drug abuse, pregnancy or suspected pregnancy, or lactation, or packed cell volume (Hematocrit®) values less than 41% for males and 37% for females.

Scopolamine dosage forms
All formulations were supplied by the flight medicine clinic at the JSC. The tablet manufacturers were Hope Pharmaceuticals & Eli Lilly & Company.

Treatments
A 0.8 mg dose of SCOP and a combination dose with 0.8 mg SCOP and 10 mg DEX were administered as tablets or in a gel cap on the morning of the study day after 8-10 h of overnight fasting. Subject numbers were assigned randomly.

Visual examination
Visual testing was administered by a nurse or laboratory personnel. All vision measurements were taken in the same windowless briefing room after having no less than five minutes of accommodation to the ambient lighting. Subjects identified their dominant eye after being taught a simple cover-uncover test. All vision measurements were taken on subjects' dominant eye, with the non-dominant eye covered by an eye patch. Visual acuity was measured using a Snellen chart held 38 cm from the dominant eye. Visual accommodation was determined using a Prince Rule, consisting of text of known font size on a card mounted on a slide rule. Subjects were instructed to hold the Prince Rule to their dominant eye with the text card adjacent to the eye, and to slowly slide the card out until the text is legible, but not yet clear. All three tests were administered immediately prior to dosing and immediately after ARES had been completed by the subject at 0.5, 1, 2, 8, and 24 hours post dose.

Sample collection
Blood and saliva samples were collected at 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 24h post dose. Urine samples were collected pre-dose and as PRN (pro re nata, a Latin term used in medicine that means "as necessary") voids for 24h post dose. Blood samples (7 ml) were collected into heparinized VacutainerTM tubes from an indwelling catheter (Intracath®, Becton and Dickinson) placed in the antecubital vein of the arm. Stimulated mixed saliva samples were collected using Salivettes® (Sarstedt Inc.). Blood and saliva samples were centrifuged at 3000 rpm, samples transferred to cryotubes and stored frozen at -70°C until analyzed. Urine samples were collected into labeled polycarbonate bottles, volumes measured, aliquots (10 ml) stored frozen at -70°C for future analysis, and the remainder discarded.

Sample analysis
SCOP and DEX concentrations were quantitated using a modified liquid chromatography quadrupole mass spectrometry (LC-MSMS) method. Plasma and saliva samples were processed by solid phase extraction followed by analysis by positive ion electrospray LC-MSMS; urine samples were diluted 1/100 fold before solid phase extraction.

Pharmacokinetic Analyses
Plasma and saliva concentration versus time profiles were plotted and PK parameters were calculated by area moment estimation using WinNonlin (software for pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and noncompartmental analysis). Relevant parameters were compared using both paired t-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA) to determine differences in PK parameters as a function of treatment.

RESULTS:
Significant differences were noticed between SCOP administration as a tablet and other formulations included in this study; most significant differences were observed with coadministration of SCOP and DEX.

SCOP Tablets (ST)
The pharmacokinetic parameter estimates of SCOP given orally are similar to those reported in the literature. Maximum concentration was 0.26 ± 0.04 ng/mL with time for maximum concentration at 0.71 ± 0.02 h after dosing; these data indicate a fairly rapid absorption rate after oral administration. Volume of distribution and clearance after oral administration are 47.6 ± 4.72 L/kg and 23.0 ± 4.58 L/h/kg, respectively, both of which were lower than those from earlier reports.

SCOP Gelcaps (SG)
Time to maximum SCOP concentration was significantly longer when given as gelcap formulation (1.04 h) than when given as a tablet; however, maximum concentrations for both formulations were not statistically different. No other pharmacokinetic parameter estimates were different from ST.

SCOP-DEX Tablets (SDT)
The area under the (concentration vs. time) curve (AUC) of SCOP was significantly lower when given with DEX than when given as SCOP tablet; bioavailability of SCOP from SDT was 75% of that from ST. In addition, both SCOP volume of distribution and clearance were higher with SDT (60.9 L/kg and 25.5 L/h/kg, respectively) than with ST (47.6 L/kg and 23.0 L/h/kg, respectively); however, this could be a result of lower bioavailability from SDT which leads to overestimation of clearance and volume of distribution parameters. This decrease in relative oral bioavailability may indicate a drug-drug interaction at absorption site.

SCOP-DEX in gelcap (SDG)
A trend similar to that with SDT was noticed after SDG administration. The AUC of SCOP was significantly lower with SDG; bioavailability of SCOP from SDG was only 78% of ST. The decreased relative oral bioavailability indicates the possibility of drug interaction between SCOP and DEX. Differences in clearance and volume of distribution of SCOP with SDG and ST were similar to those with SDT and ST. These results indicate that the effects of DEX on SCOP (SDT, SDG) pharmacokinetics and bioavailability are greater than those from gelcap (SG) formulation.

For pharmacodynamic analysis, linear regression analysis was performed between scores from ARES tests and circulating SCOP concentrations using both pooled data from all subjects and individual subject data. Simple reaction time throughput, a parameter that incorporates both accuracy and reaction time, was significantly (p<0.05) affected by SCOP concentrations from pooled data analysis. When the data were analyzed subject by subject, performance indices for several tests (reaction time and accuracy for simple reaction and memory related tasks) were found to be significantly affected by scopolamine concentrations. No uniform trend was observed in performance decrements; however, SCOP-related performance decrements were different among different subjects. Although DEX has been reported to enhance performance in humans, in this study, no significant differences in performance scores were observed between SCOP and SCOP-DEX treatments (p=0.69).

Visual acuity for some individuals, but not for all, was significantly affected by SCOP. Visual acuity for sensitive individuals was affected by even the lowest concentrations of SCOP. The relationship was sigmoidal, meaning that the effect of SCOP on visual acuity is linear, and therefore concentration dependent. In lower concentration ranges there is a minimal response, and in higher concentration ranges there is a maximum response.

experiment_title: Are Medications Involved in Vision and Intracranial Pressure Changes Seen in Spaceflight?
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It has recently been reported that intracranial pressure (ICP) and/or vision changes, have occurred in a number of long-duration astronauts. Some crewmembers have experienced changes in their vision after long-duration space flight on the International Space Station (ISS). These impairments include visual performance decrements, development of cotton-wool spots or choroidal folds, optic-disc edema, optic nerve sheath distention, and/or posterior globe flattening with varying degrees of severity and permanence. These changes are now used to define the visual impairment/intracranial pressure (VIIP) syndrome.

The reasons for these potentially debilitating medical issues are currently unknown. The potential role of administered medications has not yet been examined, but it is known that many medications can have side effects that are similar to VIIP symptoms. Some medications raise blood pressure, which can affect intracranial pressure. Many medications that act in the central nervous system can affect intracranial pressures and/or vision. About 40% of the medications in the ISS kit are known to cause side effects involving changes in blood pressure, intracranial pressure and/or vision. For this reason, investigators aimed to study the potential relationship between ISS medications and their risk of causing or exacerbating VIIP-like symptoms.

APPROACH:
This study employed a two-fold strategy to evaluate the role of medications in crewmembers' visual problems. First, the NASA Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA) and Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH) data repositories were queried for crew health information regarding in-flight use of medications by all crewmembers who received sufficient testing to be assigned a Clinical Practice Guideline (CPG) severity score. Use of medications was correlated in affected crew compared to the control group (CPG = 0) to assess the role of these medications in vision and ICP changes seen in space flight. Secondly, the FDA Adverse Event Reports were used a terrestrial source of data. These are publicly available and represent hundreds of thousands of cases in each quarterly data set. The quarterly reports were compiled into a database format and queried for data of interest. This resource represents a huge database; incorporating it into the study was an attempt to compensate for the extremely small sample number in the NASA data archive. For this data mining study, data associated with adverse events involving vision changes and intracranial pressure changes was examined.

RESULTS:
Medication use during space flight missions was similar to that during the Space Shuttle flights and in adult medicine, with the exception that usage of sleep aids was about 10 times higher during space flight missions.

experiment_title: Conversation Analysis to Measure and Manage Trust in Virtual Assistants
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Conversation analysis provides a promising, but relatively unexplored approach to measuring trust. The investigators propose a conversation analysis at the micro-, meso-, and macro-levels which includes, not just the words, but also pauses and facial expressions. Specifically, at the micro-level, conversation elements include, voice inflections, pauses between works and keystrokes, gaze shifts, and facial expressions. The meso-level analysis includes words exchanged during interactions with the virtual assistant along with other team interactions as they relate to the automation. At the macro level, conversational analysis considers interaction time, interaction effort, frequency of interaction, turn-taking, barging in tendency, and whether it is the person or the virtual assistant who initiates the interaction. Additionally, prior research into conversational analysis indicates there are novel ways of managing or calibrating trust through the presentation of information such as manipulating the tone and cadence of the system when using speech and through facial expressions. Such conversational affordances represent a promising, but relatively unexplored avenue for calibrating trust. The overall objectives of this research are to develop conversational indicators of trust and match these conversational indicators of trust with conversational affordances to calibrate trust.

The goal of this research is to develop conversation analysis to measure and mitigate inappropriate trust in virtual assistants. These trust measurements will guide system design, particularly the multimodal interactions and mode switching, as well as how to mitigate over trust and trust recovery. Investigators will use conversation analysis to measure trust at multiple timescales from real-time interactions to longitudinal monitoring of trust over a long-duration exploration mission.

This study has the following specific aims:

  1. Develop real-time conversational indicators of trust.
  2. Assess robustness of real-time conversational indicators of trust under long-duration mission stresses.
  3. Develop and evaluate conversational affordances for managing trust.

APPROACH:
The investigators are using three different experiments for measuring trust.

Total Organic Carbon Analyze (TOCA)
The data from the TOCA experiment performed on the International Space Station (ISS) will be used to develop an initial conversational indicator of trust. During the TOCA study, keystroke data (including time stamped entries and features used) was logged. This data can be used to determine the time crew spent interacting with the TOCA decision support user interface, frequency of the interaction, and if they accepted the systems recommendations. Additionally, the TOCA study recorded and transcribed crew communications with the ground and debriefs that occurred after their flight. Investigators will start with the meso-level analysis of the conversation. The meso-level examines the words spoken or typed, by both the virtual assistant, and other team members. These words will be analyzed quantitatively with text analytic approaches.

TOCA Microworld
The investigators aim to evaluate the sensitivity, diagnosticity, validity, reliability, intrusiveness and implementation of the real-time conversational indicators of trust using participants who will work with an intelligent virtual agent in the TOCA microworld. The focus of the microworld is to evaluate the appropriateness of using conversational indicators of trust, by determining that the investigators are only measuring changes in trust and no other constructs such as sleep deprivation, fatigue, situational awareness (SA) and workload. They will induce over and under trust by exposing participants to a sequence of trials where the TOCA aid performs well, then poorly, then well again.

The virtual agent will be designed to cause over and under trusting of the system by manipulating its reliability. The study will assess how well conversational affordances, such as the tone and cadence speech and the virtual agent’s facial expressions, signal uncertainty and confidence. This will provide information on how conversational affordances can be deployed during a mission to facilitate appropriate levels of trust.

Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA)
Due to the focus on measuring trust over an extended period of time using real-time conversational indicators, an analog study will be performed using HERA where, over time, errors will be introduced to the intelligent automated systems causing improper decision support. The errors will be introduced based on discrete events with frequency of errors, and type of error as controlled variables. The real-time conversational indicators of trust approach will be applied to determine changes in trust amongst the HERA crew and the conversation affordances will be used to calibrate trust. An analog, such as HERA, also provides an ideal scenario for understanding how external stressors affect trust calibration and the conversational analysis model. The HERA autonomous mission campaigns will be used to evaluate the impact of workload and sleep deprivation has on trust. Workload and sleep will be independent variables for which there will be two levels of workload (high and low) and two levels of sleep (deprived and satiated). Workload will be manipulated by adding secondary and tertiary tasks that HERA crew will have to complete while working with the virtual agent.

Sleep is of particular interest in that it has been shown that chronic sleep restriction is prevalent throughout the astronaut corps. Sleep restriction can lead to impaired cognitive abilities, which could increase an operator’s ability to use an informative process to develop trust in automated systems. Similarly, sleep deprivation can lead to riskier behavior which can influence both the cognitive and affective processes of trust. During each HERA Campaign the investigators will evaluate trust twice; once under typical sleep-deprived conditions and a second time after sleep satiation. Investigators will administer a baseline survey asking subjects to describe their sleep habits within the analog, and self-reported sleep need. In order to confirm each participant’s baseline sleep state, investigators will also ask participants to wear an activity monitor for one week prior to the first study. They will then ask participants to maintain a regular schedule with five days of eight hours of time in bed each night. Following this sleep satiation, investigators will ask participants to complete the task a second time at the same time of day in order to control for circadian phase. This approach will allow the team to look for any trends that provide insight into how sleep deprivation is affecting their trust calibration through measuring with the conversational analysis. Investigators will use the commercially available activity monitors within the habitat to monitor the number of hours of sleep the participants received.

RESULTS:
Results from the HERA campaigns will be used to make final adjustments to the conversational analysis and conversational affordances. The final results of this effort will be a validated approach to building trustable automation, i.e., automation that uses conversational metrics to unobtrusively determine crew’s trust and thus has the ability to use conversational affordances naturally promotes calibrated trust.

experiment_title: Cosmic Radiation and Effects Activation Monitor
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The increasing use of heavy space vehicles and payloads means that it is no longer adequate to predict radiation effects based on primary radiation alone. Pathlengtbs can readily approach and exceed I00 gm cm•2, which is of the order of the depth at which the maximum of cosmic-ray secondaries is produced in the atmosphere. While shielding can be beneficial against radiation belt and solar flare particles of energies up to a few hundred MeV, it can be detrimental when considering the energetic cosmic rays of several GeV. Effects of concern include biological dose to astronauts, where secondary neutrons and cosmic ray fragments are important, as well as induced radioactivity and secondary particle background in sensitive space borne instrumentation.

The Mir modules, and the forth coming International Space Station, represented opportunities to explore new radiation environments in order to obtain data on different shielding levels and the effects of radiation on larger spacecraft. The Cosmic Radiation Effects and Activation Monitor (CREAM) measures the Linear Energy Transfer (LET) effects within silicon and provides information relevant to single event upsets (SEUs) on avionics equipment.

Specific Aims:

  1. Monitor the energy disposition of spectra in silicon due to primary and secondary radiation as a function of time, orbital location and shielding.
  2. Obtain collateral data on mission integrated dose, particle influences, and induced radioactivity.
  3. Improve and test space environment and radiation shielding codes used to predict single event upset rates in electronics and background rates in sensors.

APPROACH:
The CREAM was used to collect data on cosmic ray energy loss spectra, neutron fluxes and induced radioactivity as a function of geomagnetic coordinates and detector location within the orbiter. Payload hardware consisted of the active cosmic ray monitor, a passive scintillation crystal canister, two neutron spectrometers and 10 passive detector packages. The active monitor was used to obtain real-time spectral data, while the passive monitors obtained data integrated over the mission duration. An additional control passive detector package was used for obtaining background data prior to launch.

The CREAM active monitor was a box containing sensors and associated electronics and solid-state memory. The active monitor was rotated between two passive package locations throughout the mission. CREAM used three different types of passive detectors. The first was a set of scintillation crystals packaged in an aluminum canister that remained in a central location within Mir throughout the mission.

There were also passive detector packages, which contained nickel and gold activation foils, neutron bubble dosimeters and thermoluminescent dosimeters. Eight of these packages were placed in four specific locations within Mir, while the remaining two remained in the central location within Mir. The third type of passive detector was the neutron spectrometer, which consisted of three identical sets of six gel-filled test tubes. The "test tubes," or neutron bubble detectors, were designed to measure specific energy thresholds of the neutron environment within Mir.

RESULTS:
The CREAM was flown on eight Shuttle flights between September 1991 and June 1998 and two NASA Mir missions covering the full range of inclinations as well as altitudes between 220 and 570 km, while a version has flown at supersonic altitudes on Concorde between 1988 and 1992 and at subsonic altitudes on a SAS Boeing 767 between May and August 1993.

Results show that cosmic-ray secondaries increase the fluxes of particles of linear energy transfer less than 200 MeV/(gm cm-2), while the activation of the crystals is enhanced by about a factor of three due to secondary neutrons.

Predictions of CREAM count rates during Shuttle flights show that n-Si interactions have less importance than at aircraft altitudes, and even for channels 5 to 9 contribute approximately 10-20% of the measured counts. However, the secondary particle environment (predominantly neutrons) generated by cosmic-ray interactions in the heavy spacecraft structure is the major source of activation in y-ray scintillators for low altitude Shuttle missions.

experiment_title: Somatosensory Suppression and Prevention of Post-Flight Re-Entry Disturbances of Posture and Locomotion
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The overall goal of this study was to develop procedures for alleviating post-flight disturbances of posture and locomotion experienced by astronauts. Research has shown that either non-mechanically supportive contact of the hand with an environmentally fixed surface or pressure cues from a mobile, hand-carried gyroscope stabilizes postural control in a normal 1g environment, a rotating environment, and parabolic flight. The strategy was to improve the effectiveness of the portable haptic device and to extend it to situations involving walking. The original plan was to investigate three avenues of potential improvement: 1) miniaturizing the sensory gyroscope, 2) comparing the gyroscope to a Tactor vest, and 3) providing subjects training with both devices.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this experiment is not available.

The investigators examined how the latency and pattern of postural stabilization are affected by touch contact of the hand with an environmentally fixed surface during quiet stance and whether position or velocity cues about body sway are keys to establishing stabilization. The results showed that natural finger contact forces encode body sway velocity, and that the sensed finger forces in turn control the position of the center of foot pressure with a very short latency. These results specified requirements for the motion sensing and stimulus delivery components of a mobile, synthetic system for tactile alleviation of post-flight disturbances of posture and locomotion. Year 2 and 3 work evaluated whether body sway and locomotion could be stabilized by a tactor vest device or a few tactors attached to the hand or other body part delivering synthetic tactile cues that provide naturally timed position and/or velocity cues. Investigators also evaluated the time course of postural stabilization and destabilization and whether immobilizing the arm is destabilizing.

experiment_title: Fetal and Neonatal Rat Bone and Joint Development Following In Utero Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The thrust of this study was altered by circumstances from the initial proposal to investigate the effects of prenatal exposure to space flight on rat limb development. Since no litters were born following inflight impregnation, the only specimens were produced by vivarium and postflight pregnancies. An effort was made to measure differences between groups of specimens attributable to maternal housing, diet, or stress, which must be compensated for in future mammalian embryology experiments in space.

Approach:

After separation into single limbs, with skin removed to mid-tibia, specimens were superficially examined and macrophotographed at 3x. With input from a microscope and camera, radiographic density was measured using an image analysis system consisting of a camera, a video-digitizer terminal and computer. Data were obtained on maturation of ossification centers, orientation of collagen fibers in the bone, tendon and ligament, joint surface texture and spatial relationships of bones and the hind limb. A comparison was also conducted between vivarium (standard) and flight-type (Soviet paste) diets.

Results:

No overt anatomical abnormalities were noted in domestic or Soviet specimens. Weights of offspring whose dams were fed Soviet diet did not differ significantly until after day fifteen from standard diet controls. In pups less than two days old, tendon and ligament insertions tended to merge with the perichondrium rather than penetrate into underlying cartilage or bone. The texture of the minuscule fibrocartilage was distinct from adjacent ligament, with prominent cell lacunae which could be indicators of states of mechanical stress. Because of unknown degrees of sensitivity of bone and joint maturation of Czech Wistars to such factors as litter size, gestation age, uterine position, or birth order, this data should be gathered for all specimens, in addition to the age and weight at sacrifice. Certainly, environmental parameters to which flight and synchronous control groups were exposed, such as noise, vibration, and possible hypoxia, should be measured during future studies. Computer reconstructions of knee and hip show promise as a means of investigating the etiology of congenital hip dislocation.
