experiment_title: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Metabolic Investigations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Exposure to microgravity is known to have profound effects on fluid homeostasis within the human body. The headward shift of fluids which occurs in microgravity results in an increased excretion of fluids and electrolytes. Fluid and electrolyte balance in the body is regulated by several systems, any or all of which are potentially responsible for the microgravity-induced changes in fluid balance. The kidneys play an important role in regulating fluid and excretion/retention, and changes in renal blood flow may prove to be an important factor in adapting to space flight. Many endocrine and circulatory factors contribute to fluid homeostasis, both in conjunction with and independently from the renal system. In addition, energy utilization and dietary intake of fluid and electrolytes may have profound effects on the body's ability to adapt to microgravity.

The hypotheses of this study were:

1. Loss of body water is complete by the third day of inflight and is maintained at a reduced level. This will be reflected by decreases in total body water (TBW), extracellular fluid volume (ECF), urine, and losses of electrolytes; as well as changes in peripheral venous pressure (PVP).

2. Plasma volume (PV) will decrease early in flight and is sustained at a lower level than preflight. This decrease in PV will affect neuroendocrine controls (e.g., plasma renin activity, epinephrine, and norepinephrine).

3. Enhanced excretion of sodium may be influenced by altered secretion of hormonal endocrine factors, e.g., atrial natriuretic factor.

4. The primary controlling factor for antidiurectic hormone (ADH) release is plasma osmolarity. As a result of exposure to microgravity, the effects of ADH on urine output may be counteracted by altered renal function.

5. Energy utilization during space flight remains similar to preflight levels even in the presence of reduced exercise.

The purpose of this study was to determine the effect of microgravity on:
1. TBW, ECF, PV
2. Body fluid distribution
3. Sodium/potassium balance (i.e., intake, serum concentrations, excretion)
4. Fluid/electrolyte regulatory hormones
5. Energy expenditure (EE)

APPROACH:
Flight Requirements and Procedures

Preflight, In Flight, and Postflight:

1. Participants drank enriched water, which contained naturally-occurring stable and nonradioactive isotopes after taking baseline urine and saliva samples.

Void-by-void urine samples and two saliva samples (at 3 hours and at 5-7 hours) were collected post isotope ingestion according to the timeline in the activity schedule. Samples of galley water were collected once every 24 hours in flight to monitor the isotope enrichment that occurs onboard. At L-3 days a dose of enriched water was ingested to increase the background of stable isotope concentrations. No samples were required on that day. On L-15 days through launch and at landing through R+6 days, participants (not the control subject) ate prepared meals which they had chosen from a menu.

A control subject was required for EE. Preflight activity included one training session at L-4 months, and saliva and urine collections according to the timeline in the activity schedule. There were no postflight requirements, and the only ingestion of enriched water was at L-3 days. In-flight, the control subject collected one saliva and one urine sample each flight day (FD) plus follow-up samples on test days.

2. Extracellular Fluid Volume (ECF):
ECF was determined through measurements of bromide dilution. Bromide is a stable compound that distributes throughout the extracellular space. The technique involved the collection of a 2 milliliter (ml) baseline blood sample, followed by ingestion of a specific amount of bromide. After three hours, a 2 ml blood sample was taken. Subjects were fasting and did not exercise for at least 12 hours prior to ingesting the bromide.

3. Blood/Serum Analyses:
Blood/serum was obtained via an indwelling catheter preflight, in-flight, and postflight for biochemical and hormonal analyses. Preflight and postflight, a 20-minute rest period was required after catheter insertion to restore resting catecholamine levels. Whenever possible, testing was coordinated with Medical Operations' activities to minimize crew time. In-flight catheter insertion, blood draws, analyses, and preparation of blood samples for storage was required.

4. Urine Collection:
All preflight and postflight urine samples were collected using void-by-void techniques. In-flight urine collection involved drawing syringe samples from a urine collection device (UCD), which contained lithium chloride inside as a marker. Specified syringes were frozen, and others were stowed along with UCD's in the urine sample containment bag.

5. Intake/Exercise Log:
Food/fluid/medications/exercise was recorded preflight and postflight according to the activity schedule. In-flight, the participants used bar code readers to record this information. Weighed (pre-proportioned) meals were provided from L-15 days through R+6 days.

6. Peripheral Venous Pressure (PVP):
A peripheral indication of central venous pressure was measured preflight and postflight using a strain gauge manometer. Inflight, the PVP measurements were taken using equipment in the Life Science Laboratory Equipment (LSLE) In-Flight Blood Collection System.

Preflight and Postflight Only:

1. Plasma Volume (PV):
PV was determined using a nonradioactive indicator dye (indocyanine green) injected through a catheter after the 2 ml baseline blood draw. One ml blood samples was drawn each minute for 10 minutes, then at 15 and 20 minutes. PV was performed simultaneously with ECF testing preflight and postflight.

2. Renal Clearance (RC) Tests:
Two indices of renal function, glomerular filtration rate (using inulin) and effective renal plasma flow (using para-aminohippuric acid [PAH]), were measured preflight and postflight. After a 2.5 ml baseline blood draw was taken via catheter, the insulin was infused at 0 minutes, and the PAH at 40 minutes. At minutes 90, 108, 126, 144, and 180, 1 ml blood samples were obtained.

3. Measurement of Body Weight (in conjunction with dietary intake monitoring):
Participants were weighed daily on calibrated scales preflight and postflight during L-15 days through L-0 and R+0 through R+6 days, in conjunction with the pre-proportioned diet.

Crew Training:
Training sessions were required for achieving proficiency in phlebotomy (i.e., venipuncture techniques), PVP, tracer handling, sample processing, and urine and saliva collection techniques, as well as blood sample analysis for specific in-flight portions of the investigation. Hardware training sessions covered the bar code reader and LSLE equipment.

RESULTS:
During flight, TBW decreased slightly and ECF did not appear to change compared to preflight. ECF and PV were slightly elevated after flight, most likely resulting from the pre-landing saline load. GFR was slightly elevated after flight, whereas the ERPF was lower. Body weight tended to be lower after flight. Hematocrit values during the flight were unchanged from preflight values. During flight, plasma concentrations of ANP and aldosterone were lower than preflight values. The plasma concentration of ADH didn’t change during flight. Plasma renin activity was elevated during flight and upon landing, and returned to normal on R+6.

The plasma concentration of ACTH didn’t change during the flight; however, there was a substantial increase in plasma ACTH at landing (R+0). Serum sodium concentration varied during flight, with a small elevation above preflight values on FD2 and a decline below those values on FD7. Serum potassium concentration increased slightly during flight, as a function of the flight duration. Serum chloride was unchanged on FD1, but increased on FD2 and FD7 and postflight. Urine volume during flight was below preflight values, and a return to preflight levels did not occur until several days after landing. Urine potassium excretion tended to be lower during flight and after landing. Urinary excretion of creatinine tended to decrease during flight. Urinary cortisol excretion was increased during flight, but quickly returned to normal after landing.

experiment_title: Microgravity, Sleep/Wake Immune Functions (SWIF) in Humans
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment was designed to study changes in the immune system coincident with sleep physiology during extended space flight and relate any found changes to preflight and postflight conditions. In particular, researchers wanted to determine if there are any long-term adverse effects of microgravity on the immune system that can be related to the sleep-wake cycle. Such disturbances in neuroendocrine system and immune system functions might have an impact on the risk for ill health, especially infectious disease. The study would contribute to our understanding of the role of the immune system in the sleeping-waking brain especially during and following spaceflight microgravity conditions.

In addition to the theoretical and space flight importance, there are important clinical implications to psychiatric and medical disorders. The associations of stress and depression with altered immune functions have been reported in medical literature. Stress, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep deregulation, and reduced slow wave sleep are related to major depressive disorders. Specifically, natural killer cell (NK cell) activity is reduced in sleep disturbed depressed patients. Furthermore, altered non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep physiology and immune function changes have been described in fibrositis/fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome that shares features of unrefreshing or non-restorative sleep, diffuse myalgia, multiple tender points, fatigue and depression. The outcome of the research would have important implications on the contributions of disordered sleep and immune functions for the pathogenesis of these illnesses.

APPROACH:
This investigation was conducted for the first time as part of the NASA-Mir Increment 4 mission. Three crewmembers completed measurements preflight, inflight and postflight. For each phase of the flight, the experiment was divided into segments called measurement "blocks". The inflight measurement blocks were scheduled early in the mission (mission day 37-49), in the middle (MD 79-91) and at the end (MD 110-122) of the mission. Preflight baseline data collection was performed once. Readaptation data was collected during two sessions postflight. The experiment protocols were repeated on the NASA 5/Mir 24 mission with two additional crewmembers.

During the preflight and postflight phases of the experiment, subjects answered questions before and after sleep periods on sleepiness, fatigue, pain and mood as well as performance. These questions were the main focus of a separate sleep study performed simultaneously with this investigation (see: "Human Circadian Rhythms and Sleep in Space" by Timothy H. Monk, Ph.D.)

In addition to the questionnaires, preflight baseline blood collection (BDC) involved 25 blood samples collected over a 24-hour wake/sleep cycle. Five daytime samples of 4-ml of blood were taken at 0800, 1000, 1200, 1400 and 1600 hours. A catheter was inserted before 2200 hours to allow for frequent blood sampling during sleep. Starting again at 2200 until 0700 half-hourly and again at 0800 hours, twenty 3-ml blood samples were taken in sterile, heparinized, pyrogen-free tubes connected to a 4-meter line and manifold located outside the bedroom. Samples were transported immediately to the laboratory for analysis. A total of 80 ml for each subject was collected.

The following immunologic assays were carried out: natural killer cells and T-cell subsets were stained and sorted using the two-color immunofluorescence technique with flow cytometry; plasma cortisol and human growth hormone (hGH) were determined by radioimmunoassay (RIA); plasma IL-1ß, IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1ra) and IL-2 and IL-2r concentrations were determined using enzyme-linked-immunosorbent-assay (ELISA). Cytokine biological activities were determined by reactions with D10 and CTLL cell lines; natural killer cell activity was tested by Chronium-51 release assay; IL-1ß mRNA from peripheral blood monocyte cells was studied by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (Rt-PCR). Plasma obtained from subjects was stored at -70 degrees C until use.

During flight, pre- and post sleep questionnaires were also completed. Blood samples were drawn on days 4 and 5 of the second and third blocks. Samples were drawn in the early afternoon (approximately 1400 hours) and prior to sleep. For each blood sample collection, two 3-milliliter (ml) blood samples were taken. One 3 ml sample was taken in a 5 ml plasma separator tube for centrifugation and storage at -20° C. One milliliter of the second 3 ml sample was injected into each of three 7 ml tubes prefilled with a cryopreservative. The procedure was repeated on the second day. Eight samples each of 6 mls for a total of 48 ml blood was collected from each subject in flight. Blood samples obtained during the mission were used to examine natural killer cells and plasma for lymphokines and endocrine substances. Immunologic and endocrine assays were carried out on samples returned to principal investigator.

Also on days 4 and 5 of the second and third blocks, subjects attached electroencephalography (EEG) electrodes and donned a Medilog Sleep Research Recorder (MSRR) skull cap prior to sleep. This piece of hardware was used to make standard sleep-wake physiologic assessments. The Medilog recorder was donned within two hours of sleep and removed within two hours after awakening. Data were recorded on magnetic tape and stored for return to Earth.

After flight, sleep tape recordings were scored without subject identification by a trained observer using standard criteria on a Medilog replay unit located at the principal investigator’s laboratory. Brain wave frequencies recorded on the MSRR tapes were analyzed to assess the relationship of brain waves delta (slow wave) sleep activity to immune functions. The method allowed for an objective, quantifiable, and reliable method for analyzing sleep EEG frequencies during sleep. Blood analyses and MSRR data were compared to test that changes in sleep, particularly between wakefulness and slow wave sleep, are indices of causal mechanisms that produce changes in the immune system.

RESULTS:
Immunologic and endocrine assays were carried out on blood samples collected preflight, inflight, and postflight to examine the relationship between sleep activity to immune functions. Preflight baseline data collection from all crewmembers were compared to a group of healthy male volunteers to determine if sleep/wake age-related immune and endocrine functions were present in the middle-aged male crewmembers during baseline conditions before flight on Mir versus young healthy males. Middle-aged crewmembers in preflight baseline conditions differed from young healthy males in the timing of the diurnal pattern of natural killer cell cytotoxicity, hGH and cortisol. They also secreted less hGH and more cortisol over a 24-hour period. These hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis endocrine differences in healthy middle-aged men were similar to those seen in healthy older men. While the dynamic structure of natural killer cell cytotoxicity differed, there was no overall mean difference from young males.

experiment_title: A Phantom and Test Bed to Enhance Kidney Stone Comminution by Therapeutic Ultrasound
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Kidney stones are common on Earth, and space travel only exacerbates the risk. Over 15 years of National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) funded research have developed burst wave lithotripsy (BWL), which comminutes stones faster and more completely than shock wave lithotripsy (SWL) in a bench top water bath. The University of Washington licensed the technology to a commercial partner, and NSBRI funded the BWL development for integration into NASA’s Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC)’s Flexible Ultrasound (FUS) system. However, neither SWL nor BWL comminutes stones as well in a confined space, such as the kidney, and both perform even less well when the stone is obstructing and surrounded by tissue. In addition, cavitation is acutely sensitive to carbon dioxide, which is 30 times more soluble than oxygen in water, and carbon dioxide levels can be elevated 20 times in NASA vehicles. Carbon dioxide dissolves bubble nuclei and quenches cavitation collapse, has been associated with visual impairment and intracranial pressure (VIIP), and suppresses kidney stone detection. This study sought to discover effective BWL exposures to counteract the effects of confinement and carbon dioxide.

APPROACH:
Five farm-bred pigs were implanted with ex vivo human calcium oxalate monohydrate kidney stones (approximately 4-mm diameter) that had been stored in water for at least a week and known to display the twinkling artifact in vitro via retrograde ureteroscopy. A baseline twinkling was collected at least 15 minutes before the anesthetic gas carrier was changed in four of the pigs from oxygen to elevated carbon dioxide in compressed air; the fifth pig was maintained on oxygen for more than one hour to serve as a control. The four treated pigs continued to breathe the increased carbon dioxide levels for two hours or until the oxygen saturation levels dropped below 45%, at which point the anesthetic gas carrier was switched back to oxygen. After about thirty minutes on oxygen, the pigs were again exposed to the elevated carbon dioxide levels until the oxygen saturation levels dropped below 45% at which time the pigs were once again returned to oxygen. Blood and urine samples were collected every thirty minutes and immediately before changing the anesthetic carrier gas.

RESULTS:
A mannequin phantom was developed for testing and as a continued training and research tool. Outputs were developed and measured to effectively comminute human kidney stones in the confinement of the kidney and ureter phantoms and in animal models breathing elevated carbon dioxide. Investigators developed and tested an ultrasound phantom and surrogate testing capabilities in the ground analog environment of an elevated CO2 atmosphere to enhance the utility of therapeutic ultrasound for kidney stone comminution. These validated outputs have been added to the BWL system integrated with NASA's flexible ultrasound system (FUS).

experiment_title: Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI of the Brain, Lungs and Plants Augmented with MRI Pulse Sequence Development--NNX07AP80G
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Investigators are developing a new diagnostic technology: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and spectroscopy of hyperpolarized noble gases. Large non-equilibrium nuclear spin polarizations can be created in the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe, using the technique of spin-exchange optical pumping. Such large polarizations greatly enhance the magnetic resonance detection of 3He and 129Xe, enabling high-resolution MRI studies of the lung and airways, as well as dissolved tissue-phase investigations of organs and tissues, such as the brain, using lipophilic 129Xe. An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional water proton MR method used in medical MRI. Low magnetic field MRI with hyperpolarized noble gases can allow investigators to use a small, light-weight, low-power devices. This capability provides potential for advances in both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. This ground-based investigation with hyperpolarized noble gas MR will affect biomedical research in two important ways: (1) by providing the potential to acquire novel information about physiological structure and function of the lung and the brain in space-flight and in terrestrial gravity, and (2) by developing a new diagnostic technology that has clinical applications for diagnosis of pathology.

An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional thermally polarized water proton MR method used in a medical MRI. As a result, at low magnetic fields (0.01 Tesla) the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is much larger than the SNR of conventional thermally polarized MR. Low field MR utilizing hyperpolarized noble gases should be practical in a small, light-weight, low-power device, providing the potential for both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. Specific magnetic and biological properties of hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe MRI include: (i) airway and lung gas space imaging (for diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), e.g. emphysema, asthma, and for studies of respiratory function); (ii) the imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis, and in research on brain function); and (iii) angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system). The recent progress made lays the foundation for the continued development of hyperpolarized xenon MRI for brain imaging. Specifically, imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis) and angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system), are now viable research goals. Because HP 129Xe is an MR signal source with properties very different from those generated from water-protons, it may yield structural and functional information not detectable by proton-based MRI methods. Thus brain imaging with hyperpolarized xenon should be of great benefit to the diagnosis and treatment monitoring of a number of neurological diseases.

APPROACH:
Investigators developed large volume hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe systems that take advantage of inexpensive, compact, and mechanically robust high-power diodelasers (in excess of 100 W of radiant energy), which have recently become available. By bringing together an optimized continuous flow optical pumping chamber with a storage and delivery system, a dedicated gas generation system was constructed to produce the large volumes of hyperpolarized gas necessary for this project.

RESULTS:
The overall goal of this proposal was to develop hyperpolarized noble gas magnetic resonance imaging (HP MRI) for the assessment of pulmonary and nervous system damage that may be incurred during human space flight. Hyperpolarized noble gas MRI is showing dramatic results for diagnostic imaging of the lungs, brain, and other parts of the body, some of which have been resistant to conventional proton MRI. Most notably, investigators have achieved high resolution dynamic images of the lungs and airways using hyperpolarized 3He, and have measured cerebral perfusion and functional activity in the brain using hyperpolarized 129Xe (HP 129Xe). The number of space flight-related pathologies which may benefit from this technique are vast and range from pulmonary dysfunction caused by microgravity to cognitive and neurobehavioral problems resulting from the stress and isolation of extended term space travel. This novel technology should also offer a rapid, sensitive method to detect treatment effects and thus may expedite the development of therapeutic strategies for treating space flight related injury, such as aerosol administration of drugs via the lungs, which may obviate the need for medicinal injections during space flight.

experiment_title: Model-based Support for Crew Activity Planning
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Investigators proposed to leverage previous research to provide a tool that will allow mission planners to easily construct a CPM-GOMS model of crew activities. The resulting model will enable predictions of the time required to complete common, routine tasks using parameters determined from the existing literature on human performance. The reduction in time to model will now make it feasible to model and simulate performance on several candidate task designs with varying interfaces. The reduction in time to model will now make it feasible to model and simulate performance on several candidate task designs with varying interfaces.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the Results below.

RESULTS:
Experiment 1- Multifunction Electronic Display System (MEDS ) : An experiment was run by the Intelligent Spacecraft Interface Systems (ISIS) lab at NASA Ames Research Center using the Space Shuttle Cockpit Simulator to examine the performance of novice and expert shuttle operators in handling single and multiple malfunctions. The experiment was used to test the hypothesis that reusable templates could predict performance of different participant populations in different workload conditions (low workload for single malfunction trials and high workload for multiple malfunction trials). Five former airlines captains with an average of 15,000 flight hours experience participated in the novice condition. Five current astronauts with a minimum of two years of training participated in the expert condition.

Each trial simulated the ascent phase of shuttle operations, starting from launch to Main Engine Cut-Off (MECO) and lasting 8 minutes and 30 seconds of simulated mission elapsed time. In the single malfunction condition, a main engine malfunction was inserted. In the multiple malfunction condition, a combination of helium system regulator failure, General Purpose Computer failure, and coolant system failure malfunctions were inserted. The Flight Data File procedure checklist, which lists all the steps required to recover from the malfunctions, was provided to the subjects during the simulation. Eye fixations were analyzed on regions of interest relevant to solving malfunctions.

Conclusions: The experiment tested the hypothesis that reusable templates could successfully predict performance of different participant populations in different experimental conditions. The phrase-reading template made generally good predictions of gaze durations for pilots and astronauts in the single malfunction condition, but there are some noticeable differences. The template represents the process of identifying visual information, but does not include the time to search for the information. The increased gaze time on the switch panel for the pilots relative to the model may represent some search, as the switch panel contains many similar-looking switches. The template also assumes that all information at a location is processed only once. The decreased gaze time on procedures for the astronauts relative to the template may represent the astronaut reading only a relevant subset of the procedure. Likewise, the increased gaze time on procedures for the pilots relative to the template may be due to the pilots reading parts of the procedure more than once. The phrase-reading template made very good predictions of astronaut gaze duration in the multiple malfunction condition, showing that the template generalizes across workload conditions.

For the screen touch template, there were not enough data points to evaluate generality across population or workload conditions. When creating the screen touch template, it was assumed that eye fixations were made before touching the screen. Close examination of the data suggests this may be incorrect and that some screen touches may be made without fixations.

Experiment 2 – new Cockpit Avionics Upgrade (CAU) : The phrase-reading and screen-touching templates were used to make predictions for an experiment comparing original CAU displays to new CAU in sessions with single or multiple malfunctions. The time for initial finding a malfunction page in the flight data file (FDF ) procedures was calculated as gazes at 3.5 (out of 7 possible) tabs plus a gaze to read the malfunction heading for a total of (3.5+1) x 470 = 2115 msec. The time for subsequently finding the correct place on the FDF page after looking at the screen was calculated as an orienting gaze to the FDF and a gaze to a finger keeping place on the page for a total of 2 x 470 = 940 msec. The time for reading information on the screen after looking at the FDF include an extra orienting gaze to the screen.

Conclusions: The model assumes the pilots are well-practiced in the procedures. The increased times of the pilots for the first switch throw of procedures may indicate task orientation that is not represented in the model. From analysis of pilot speech, the last switch throw of the single malfunction procedure is sometimes forgotten in the original CAU condition until a later time, and this forgetting is not part of the model. These initial and final increased times are not seen in performance with single malfunction procedures with newCAU, which may assist in task orienting and remembering. In multiple-malfunction procedures, newCAU appears to lessen the increase of initial time due to task orientation.

experiment_title: Phoenix Scout Lander: Countermeasures Testbed for Spaceflight Ground Controllers
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A multi-institutional team of investigators provided fatigue management education to the scientists and engineers working on the Mars Phoenix Lander project. This project was funded by NASA/JSC Behavioral Health and Performance (BHP) research program element and provided an operational opportunity, in a Mars Time Analog, to evaluate countermeasures in a real-time, field setting. Investigators sought to evaluate the acceptability, feasibility, and efficacy of a photic countermeasure used to treat fatigue, circadian misalignment, and sleep loss associated with the Phoenix Mars Lander mission.

The proposed research could have significant implications for both sleep disorders medicine and space life sciences. The results of the proposed research could lead to the development of a new treatment regimen for sleep disturbances of various etiologies during space flight missions, where crewmembers, mission controllers, and support personnel are scheduled to live on non-24 hour days, which could enable these individuals to avoid the decrements in alertness and performance associated with sleep deprivation.

APPROACH:
The Phoenix spacecraft landed on Mars on May 25, 2008 and the scientists and engineers supporting the Phoenix Mars Lander worked on a Mars sol schedule until August 11, 2008 when the official schedule reverted to an Earth schedule. A multi-institutional team of investigators provided fatigue management education to the scientists and engineers working on the Mars Phoenix Lander project. The investigators also recruited 19 subjects to participate in a research study to investigate the work hours, sleep, circadian rhythmicity, and performance of individuals living on a Mars sol schedule in an operational environment. Investigators sought to evaluate the acceptability, feasibility, and efficacy of countermeasures used to treat fatigue, circadian misalignment, and sleep loss associated with the Phoenix Mars Lander mission.

Investigators provided three educational sessions to the scientists, engineers, and support personnel working on the Phoenix Mars Lander project in the week prior to the mission. During those 1-hour sessions, the scientific team provided information on sleep, circadian rhythms, and appropriate countermeasures to facilitate entrainment to a Mars sol schedule and to maximize alertness and performance during work hours.

Investigators provided a blue light box to research subjects as well as instructions for when to seek and avoid light to facilitate entrainment to the Mars sol schedule. Ocular light exposure of a specific narrowband wavelength (±30 nm half-peak bandwidths) was encouraged using a light delivery system developed by Apollo Light Systems Inc., (American Fork, UT).

Research subjects continuously wore actigraphs on their wrists to monitor sleep and light exposure. They completed daily logs indicating work times and the fatigue countermeasures they used, and provided subjective evaluations of sleep and alertness. Subjects also accomplished daily performance testing and completed 48-hour urine collections about every two weeks to permit analysis of a melatonin conjugate to estimate circadian timing.

Subjects wore a Motionlogger on their wrists throughout the study period to provide sleep/wake activity and light exposure information. Each subject was given a personal digital assistant that contained two programs: a sleep-work log that was completed each day and a 5-minute version of the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) and Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS) that was completed twice per day. Subjects were requested to complete the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics (ANAM4) at the beginning and end of each work shift. The ANAM battery also included a mood scale.

RESULTS:
Nineteen subjects completed the study, although data collection was abbreviated in some subjects who traveled throughout the data collection period. The Mars Phoenix Lander project provided an operational opportunity, in a Mars Time Analog, to evaluate countermeasures in a real-time, field setting.

experiment_title: Intraocular Pressure
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Intraocular pressure (IOP) has been shown to be an objective and quantitative measure of fluid shifts toward the head in the 10-degree head-down tilt bed rest model of microgravity. However, insufficient numbers of measurements have been made in microgravity to correlate bed rest changes with changes that occur in weightlessness.

A study by Mader and Meehan (Mader et al., 1990) has quantified IOP changes that occurred with a 10-degree whole body head-down tilt over 48 hours. An immediate rise in IOP was documented upon assuming the head-down position. For the next 48 hours, variations in IOP were observed. Upon resuming the sitting position, there was a significant drop in IOP below the initial sitting values. The results of this study support the theory that distension of the retinal veins is a mechanism for the sudden changes in IOP that occur with changes in position. Assuming that head-down tilt is a valid model for fluid shifts in microgravity, the results from this study predict a similar sustained IOP increase in microgravity and a corresponding temporary drop in IOP (to below preflight values) upon return to Earth. Significant increases in IOP could result in visual impairment affecting crew performance and operations.

This study was designed to test the following hypothesis: Intraocular pressures will rise immediately upon entering microgravity due to fluid shifts toward the head, and will drop to below preflight levels upon return to 1-G. The objectives of this study were:

1. To establish a database of changes in intraocular pressures that can be used to evaluate crew health,
2. To validate 10-degree head-down tilt bed rest as a model for fluid shifts toward the head in microgravity,
3. To facilitate the interpretation of data by providing a quantitative measure of microgravity induced fluid shifts toward the head,
4. To validate the hand-held tonometer as an effective tool for diagnostic and scientific data collection that can be used in on orbit investigations.

APPROACH:
A series of measurements were taken (on one eye only) preflight at Launch-6 (L-6) weeks, L-4 weeks, and L-10 days (dates are approximate) using the Tono-Pen (a clinical instrument commonly used by non-physicians in an ophthalmologist's office for measuring IOP). All preflight measurements were taken with the subject in the seated position. During flight, measurements were taken as soon as possible on orbit, post-sleep on flight day (FD) 2 and on the final flight day post sleep. Additional measurements were desired on orbit (pre- and post sleep), but were optional. Postflight measurements were taken at return (R)+0 and during the postflight physical on R+3.

One drop of the short-activity topical anesthetic (proparacaine 0.5 percent) was instilled into the left eye and the subject instructed to look straight ahead. During flight, the drop of proparacaine was brought into contact with the lower conjunctival fornice to be absorbed onto the cornea by capillary action.

The operator performed the following steps:

1. Replaced the tonometer tip cover.
2. Instilled one drop of proparacaine into left eye.
3. Gently tapped the cornea 3-6 times until a beep is heard.
4. Recorded the data displayed on the Tono-Pen LCD screen.
5. Repeated the procedure 5 times.

Measurements were taken in the subject's left eye at each data collection point (in prior studies, there have been no significant differences between the measurements taken in 2 healthy eyes of an individual). The data collection sessions were approximately 5 minutes per subject; however, 15 minutes was scheduled to allow for the effects of the proparacaine to abate (the anesthetic deadens the eye for approximately 15 minutes). Neither the anesthetic nor the pressure measurement with the Tono-Pen caused discomfort to the eye when used properly.

RESULTS:
Acceptable data was acquired from 9 subjects on missions STS-31, 32, 34, 41, 52 and 53. Sufficient data was not collected on STS-33, 44, and 50. There was a mean increase in intraocular pressure during the first two days of space flight. This increase of approximately 20 percent above baseline values decreased during the remainder of the flight but was elevated above baselines on landing day.

experiment_title: Precise Assessment of Prevalence and Progression Rates of Lens Opacities in Astronauts as a Function of Radiation Exposure during Space Flight and Development of Improved Routine Clinical Assessment of Ocular Lens Status
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts appear to suffer from cataracts more than the general population. The onset of cataracts tends to happen at a younger age in those who have flown in space, and the tendency to develop cataracts is increased for astronauts who have been exposed to relatively higher doses of radiation throughout their flight careers. It has also been shown that there is an association between the development of cataracts and exposure to the high linear energy transfer (LET) radiation (including heavy ions and neutrons) that occurs in space, or within a higher orbital plane of Earth's atmosphere.

The objective of this study was to modify the current medical protocol used to assess the health of the eye's lens, as well as visual function, and then incorporate these modifications into a new periodic routine for vision assessment. The long term goal of this project was to improve ocular safety for astronauts during space flight.

APPROACH:
In an effort to more precisely define the magnitude of this risk and the relationship of space radiation to cataract progression, NASA funded this five year study to compare progression of cataract formation/development. The five institutions collaborating on this study were: Harvard University (Brigham and Women’s Hospital), NASA, Baylor College of Medicine, Space Center Eye Associates, and Wyle Laboratories.

The study was designed to measure the effect of deep space radiation on the lens of the eye, and to measure the changes in lens clarity that might develop as a result of exposure to radiation in deep space.

The study measured the status of the lens and visual function in the astronaut population (active and retired) and two control groups: military aviators (active and retired), and people without any military aviation background. The two control groups allowed comparison of cataract risks among space radiation-exposed astronauts and non-astronauts with and without controlling for a military aviator lifestyle. Included in this study are measurements of nutritional intake, ocular exposure to sunlight, and radiation exposure.

This investigation was designed to add validated measures of visual function to NASA’s Johnson Space Center’s (JSC's) current protocol, including a measure of visual acuity (logMAR) and cataract severity using a Nidek EAS 1000 Imaging System. Pupils were be dilated to maximal size using topical medications: 2.5% phenylephrine and 1.0% tropicamide. Imaging of the anterior and posterior lens and slit imaging of the nucleus were performed. The modified drop procedure currently used at JSC was evaluated for its performance in achieving maximum pupil dilation. Reverse dilation drops were used after the images were obtained.

From this digital lens data, a profile of the severity of each type of existing cataract was related to the type and duration of the astronaut's radiation exposure. These measurements will make it possible to predict the probability of cataract formation in astronauts if the anticipated radiation dose for a particular mission can be determined.

RESULTS:
A review of the evolution of methods of cataract documentation and classification, and a review of the current state-of-the-art digital measurements of early changes in cataract development, were conducted. A review of protocols used at the JSC for routine clinical assessment of the eye and lens has been conducted.

Participants included 171 consenting astronauts who flew at least one mission in space and a comparison group made up of three components: (a) 53 astronauts who had not flown in space, (b) 95 military aircrew personnel, and (c) 99 non-aircrew ground-based comparison subjects. Continuous measures of nuclear, cortical and PSC lens opacities were derived from Nidek EAS 1000 digitized images. Age, demographics, general health, nutritional intake and solar ocular exposure were measured at baseline. Astronauts who flew at least one mission were matched to comparison subjects using propensity scores based on demographic characteristics and medical history stratified by gender and smoking (ever/never).

The variability and median of cortical cataracts were significantly higher for exposed astronauts than for non-exposed astronauts and comparison subjects with similar ages (P=0.015). Galactic cosmic space radiation (GCR) may be linked to increased PSC area (P=0.056) and the number of PSC centers (P=0.095). Within the astronaut group, PSC size was greater in subjects with higher space radiation doses (P=0.016). No association was found between space radiation and nuclear cataracts. Cross-sectional data analysis revealed a small deleterious effect of space radiation for cortical cataracts and possibly for PSC cataracts. These results suggest increased cataract risks at smaller radiation doses than have been reported previously.

Because of high variability and skewness of opacity measures, nonparametric methods were used to test for association between rates of opacification and space radiation exposure. First, median regression was used to collapse longitudinal data into robust estimates of progression rates (opacity severity compare to time for each eye of each subject). To quantify and test for a radiation effect, median regression with the dependent variable being the maximum of the two slopes (OD and OS) per subject was then used, adjusting for the confounding variables of age, nutritional, and sun-exposure histories. Median regression showed evidence of an association between the rate of cortical progression in the worse eye with radiation dose and age. The estimated median progression rate from space radiation being 0.25 ± 0.13% lens area/Sv/year (P = 0.062). The investigators found no relationship between radiation exposure and progression of aggregate area of posterior subcapsular cataract or nuclear progression rates. However, longer follow-up may be needed to further understand any impact of space radiation on progression rates for posterior subcapsular cataracts and nuclear cataracts, and to characterize changes to visual acuity.

experiment_title: Time Perception in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Many spatial-temporal tasks require an explicit representation of both space and time. Ground-based research shows distance perception and time perception to be intimately linked. As a complement to previous studies on crew perception, this experiment will quantify subjective changes in time perception during and after long-duration exposure to microgravity.

The objectives of this study are to use crew judgements on specific time intervals pre-, in-, and postflight to determine:

  • If time duration is underestimated by astronauts in orbit
  • If an underestimation of time carries over to the early postflight period
  • If time re-adaptation to 1G is a gradual process

    Visual targets will be presented to subjects via laptop for evaluations based on 5, 12, and 38 second intervals. Crew will give their best estimates for the duration of time in which a blue square is displayed on the screen. Minutes, hours, and days will be evaluated using a questionnaire. A standard reaction time test is also used to assess alertness and fatigue. The visual target testing, questionnaire, and reaction time test will be repeated for 3 preflight, 6 inflight, and 3 postflight sessions for comparison.

  • Duration production and reproduction
  • Single tasks and dual tasks
  • Preflight and inflight measurements
  • Inflight measurements and various durations of microgravity exposure
  • Early and late postflight measurements

experiment_title: Personality and Biological Predictors of Resiliency to Chronic Stress among High-Achieving Adults
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In order to select candidate astronauts for high stress resilience, it is first necessary to identify traits that prognosticate resilience in high-achieving (astronaut-like) adults. Together, a combination of such traits would be compiled into a valid assessment tool to maximize accuracy. This study tested whether objective markers derived from innovative personality assessment and event-related potentials (ERPs; e.g., electroencephalography recorded during reaction time tasks) prognosticated stress resilience in high-achieving adults recruited from a naturally high-stress environment (e.g., Science, Technology, Engineering, and Medicine (STEM) graduate training programs).

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Test personality facets as predictors of resilience after accounting for cognitive ability, over-claiming response bias, and Big 5 traits.
  2. Evaluate contributions of neurophysiological markers for predicting resilience.

APPROACH:
207 high-achieving adults were recruited from graduate and post-graduate training programs to participate in a longitudinal stress study. The baseline assessment was approximately two hours and included several domains. 26 personality facets were assessed using a modified version of the Facet Inventory of the Five Factor Model, an empirically-designed self-report instrument. EEG was recorded while participants completed two speeded reaction time tasks designed to yield event-related potential (ERP) indices of error monitoring. Stimuli were presented briefly in order to increase likelihood of behavioral mistakes. Response locked (for error and correct response trials, respectively) and stimulus locked (N200 and P300 amplitudes) ERPs were created by averaging trials in the usual way. Cognitive ability, a standard marker of resiliency, was assessed using a standardized computer battery. Response bias was assessed using the Over-claiming Questionnaire (OCQ), which was designed to capture the tendency to report oneself as especially competent and knowledgeable. The baseline assessment also included stress (perceived stress scale, a Work-Life inventory) and behavioral health outcomes (mood, anxiety, and psychosocial functioning).

After the baseline assessment, participants were invited to repeat online assessments of stress and behavioral health outcomes monthly for five months. This allowed investigators to carefully monitor fluctuations in stress and link them to corresponding fluctuations in behavioral health outcomes. In this way, stress-related declines in each outcome could be modeled as a linear slope and resilience could be defined by baseline predictors associated with less decline in behavioral health during periods of high stress.

RESULTS:
As expected, level of ten behavioral health outcomes over five months could be predicted by personality facets assessed at baseline. Also as expected, increases in stress were associated with worsening behavioral health across five months. Importantly, certain baseline personality facets prognosticated the rate of stress-induced decline, especially for three key behavioral health outcomes. This prognostic validity of facets largely held when controlling for cognitive ability, response bias, and standard superordinate Big 5 traits. Neural traits recorded during repeated trials of speeded reaction time tasks (e.g., ERPs) did not prognosticate level of behavioral health outcomes, but prognosticated worsening behavioral health outcomes at high levels of stress for some traits. In other words, some personality facets and some ERPs appear to represent promising prognostic tools to identify resilient individuals for high stress situations, at least for some relevant behavioral health outcomes. On the other hand, stress resilience for other relevant behavioral health outcomes were poorly prognosticated by the candidate predicators included in this study.

experiment_title: Hyperpolarized Noble Gas Magnetic Resonance Imaging
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems that provide three-dimensional internal imaging of the body have been off-limits for use in spacecraft due to their large size and power requirements. A new technology utilizes hyperpolarized (HP) noble gases, such as xenon and helium to perform similar, but superior, non-invasive imaging of the body. The HP noble gas MRI does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional medical MRI machine, so it offers a potential for a more practical device that is both small in size, low on power demands and easy to use. HP noble gas MRI may be the ideal imaging tool for use in space. This three-year ground-based study evaluated HP noble gas MRI as a means to: 1) help acquire new information about the physiological structure and function of organs and systems of the body while they are affected by microgravity; 2) diagnose disease in microgravity environments; and 3) develop real-time treatments for space-related illnesses.

APPROACH:
From previous research, a very low-field MRI system using a signal generated from HP helium-3 and xenon-129 was built. This investigation began the phase of feasibility testing on this prototype unit as a diagnostic tool capable of imaging the function and structure of the lungs, heart and brain. The detailed protocol for testing was developed using a conventional commercial MRI scanner operating at 1.5 and 0.2 Tesla, a reliable and proven platform. The procedures were transferred for use on the prototype HP gas MRI and compared to those developed initially on a conventional MRI.

The HP noble gas imaging studies were conducted on the ground using both animal and human subjects. Imaging was aimed at determining lung structure, gas diffusion in the lung, cardiac perfusion, lipid membrane structure, blood flow, and general organ structure. Other specific goals were to: 1) develop small, distal lung airway imaging at resolutions below 1 mm; 2) measure regional ventilation and perfusion irregularities of the lung; 3) detect right to left shunt in subjects with foramen ovale, a condition that needs to be detected prior to EVA (space walks); and 4) test the imaging of lung ventilation and perfusion at very low magnetic fields (0.015 Tesla).

RESULTS:
In addition to the investigators’ lung studies, advances have been made in their effort to develop hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI for the assessment of brain structure and function. The three most significant advances in this area include: 1. The method of chemical shift imaging was validated in the laboratory, 2. Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI CSI was carried out in rat brain. 3. In vivo Functional Brain Imaging Using Hyperpolarized 129 Xe was demonstrated.

Previously, the investigators reported that the rigorous airway diameter quantification algorithm they developed has been tested on an anthropomorphic lung phantom, and presented the results. Five subjects who have had their airways scanned using HP 3He MRI have also been imaged with CT.

The algorithm computing the local ventilation coefficient of variation from HP 3He MRI images previously developed was applied to all ventilation data sets available. The resulting heterogeneity maps, viewed in the context of the ventilation maps, clearly demonstrate the capture of the ventilation heterogeneity characteristics.

The algorithms for mapping ventilation have been applied to four non-asthmatics and 13 asthmatic subjects. Statistical significant differences were observed in the heterogeneity scores as well as ventilation distribution standard deviation for various cases of comparison.

The results of this study support the idea that HP 3He MRI can serve as a diagnostic tool that can be regularly used to evaluate astronaut physiology, how that differs from their earth status, how it progresses with continued space flight, and how it alters in the presence of disease or impairment.

experiment_title: Spaceflight-Induced Changes in Non-Shivering Thermogenesis and Effects on Bone in Mice
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this project is to test the hypothesis that spaceflight will compromise the ability of mice to employ huddling and postural strategies to slow heat loss. To maintain body heat, flight animals will become more dependent on a mechanism, non-shivering thermogenesis, which is associated with bone loss. We anticipate that fat metabolism will be increased during spaceflight in response to increased sympathetic outflow (a negative regulator of bone formation). The proposed research will address the mechanism(s) by which the spaceflight environment impacts energy balance. At the completion of this study we expect to show that spaceflight results in increased non-shivering thermogenesis and increased fat oxidation in white adipose tissue. We have obtained and analyzed interscapular brown adipose tissue (BAT) from RR1. The results to date demonstrate upregulation of genes related to energy metabolism, supporting our hypothesis.

APPROACH:
Intraperitoneal white adipose tissue (WAT) is requested from mice flown on the International Space Station and their respective ground controls. We will isolate total cellular RNA from WAT and then measure mRNA levels for enzymes involved in fat metabolism. The results will establish whether the increased thermogenesis associated with activation of BAT has a functional outcome, specifically whether fat oxidation is increased in WAT.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Lignin Formation and Effects of Microgravity: a New Approach
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The focus of this experiment was to establish the effect of the microgravity environment on the ability of plants to form a reinforcement tissue known as compression wood. On Earth, woody plants produce this distinctive reinforcement tissue when their stems are bent contrary to their normal orientation. The compression wood formation helps restore the stem to its upright position, which contributes to the plants survival, but it has an adverse effect on wood quality and texture.

There were two main objectives of this study. The first one was to determine whether compression wood formation occurs in microgravity, and to establish the time-course of its [potential] induction at both 1g and in microgravity, respectively. The second objective was to develop methodology to determine the rate-limiting step(s) involved in formation of the monomeric lignin precursors from phenylalanine, including how the corresponding monolignols are transported to the plasma membrane and how the various metabolites and enzymes are organized at the subcellular level.

APPROACH:

This experiment flew on the STS-78 mission on the Space Shuttle Columbia, which was launched on June 22, 1996 for a 17-day mission. Conifer seedlings, Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) and Loblolly pine (Pinus taeda), were placed in the Plant Growth Unit (PGU) containing six Plant Growth Chambers (PGCs) in an orientation that favors compression wood formation in Earths gravity. Four plants were grown in each Plant Growth Chambers (PGC). A total of six PGCs were flown.

After two days on orbit, the crew opened the PGCs and bent the plants into a 45 degree orientation. The crew also performed a daily status check of PGU systems, and photographed the PGCs. During the flight, two of the chambers were opened for plant fixation, at which time the plants were harvested, sectioned, chemically fixed with 2.5% gluteraldehyde and 2% paraformaldehyde for postflight analysis. This harvesting occurred on days 10 and 13 of the mission. The remaining four chambers were harvested, sectioned and fixed with 2.5% gluteraldehyde and 2% paraformaldehyde upon recovery. Ground controls were conducted on a 24-hour delay in the Orbiter Environmental Simulator at environmental conditions (temperature, % relative humidity, and CO2) similar to those experienced by the flight samples.

After samples were returned to the investigators lab, electron and light microscopic study of the samples defined the time and place of compression wood formation and the extent to which it forms. Chemical and biochemical analysis complemented the study, enabling the investigator to measure the effects of microgravity and compression wood formation and define the regulatory enzymes and genes involved.

RESULTS:

This space flight experiment, while answering the question of whether compression wood formation occurred in microgravity, was not conducted without difficulty. Although the bending experiments were initiated in space, the Space Shuttle cabin temperatures were higher than any recorded previously (more than 29 degrees C). This condition had a deleterious effect on the growth of several specimens. The experiments had to be repeated several times postflight (under simulated flight conditions in the Orbiter Environmental Simulator) to confirm that the difficulties experienced were, in fact, due to high temperature.

From the specimens surviving in good condition, both sets of plants (i.e., microgravity and 1g) were essentially identical, all forming compression wood when orientated in a 45 degree orientation, and forming no compression wood when placed in a vertical orientation.

It was expected that compression wood would not be formed if the gravitational vector was removed as in microgravity. Thus, to account for its formation in space, either the small amount of gravity in microgravity is still large enough to ensure that the organisms can still respond to it, or, more likely, the effect of mechanical loading by harnessing overrides the gravitactic responses (i.e., due to overlapping signal transduction, perception and response mechanisms). Therefore, even in microgravity, the plants make appropriate corrections to alleviate the stress gradient introduced by bending, thereby forming compression wood.

It is now established that woody gymnosperm plants, such as Douglas fir, when placed in off-vertical configuration in microgravity, relative to the light source, respond by forming compression wood. This is proposed to be due to the influence of an internal stress gradient within the plant. It now needs to be established if woody angiosperms form comparable compression wood under these conditions. This finding would add to the steady growing body of knowledge associated with general phenylpropanoid metabolism and cell wall development. It also needs to be proven whether compression wood would occur if plants were able to realign their stems without the influence of harnessing, e.g., by phototropic responses over longer time periods (months, years.) This will be an important experiment to conduct on the International Space Station.

experiment_title: Cutaneous Hypersensitivity and Balance Control in Humans
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment studied the range of mechanisms that humans rely on to maintain balance while standing or walking. One of these mechanisms involves receptors in the sole of the foot, which for example, detect pressure changes as a person walks across the ground. Anecdotal evidence from crewmembers suggests that the tingling sensation some feel in their feet while in space and for short periods back on Earth may be the response of different sensory receptors in the skin that naturally compensate for the re-weighting of sensory information due to the decreased input from the vestibular, or inner ear, system in an environment of microgravity.

It is known that multiple sensory systems interact to develop a sense for body position and orientation within one’s environment. The removal or deficiency within one sensory system often leads to re-weighting, which results in a greater importance placed on the other reliable sources of input. The aim of this experiment was to understand the contributions that skin may play in providing information to establish orientation during and following a period of microgravity, when vestibular input is less reliable. The hope is to understand whether skin may be used to facilitate balance and orientation for the completion of tasks; a direct application would be extra vehicular activities. Equally important is how this information will help crew to regain stability as they transition back to a gravitational environment upon landing.

Information from the mechanoreceptors in the foot sole skin has a large impact on balance and postural control in the gravitational environment of Earth. Four different types of receptors provide information regarding skin contact, indentation pressure, slips and skin stretch to facilitate orientation of the body in the environment and for postural equilibrium. As we age, the fidelity of the information relayed by the sensors in the skin is decreased. With a reduction in skin information, there are deficits in balance control and an increased incidence of falls in the elderly. Current strategies to improve balance involve the augmentation of skin input through vibration devices.

Space flight provides a unique opportunity to further investigate the relationship between changes in balance control and skin contributions. During space flight, there are changes that occur with the postural control system due to the altered gravito-inertial (a process of mental rotation which involves three dimensions, rather than just one) environment. The specific changes that occur with skin have not been documented. The experiment aimed to use Von Frey monofilaments (a set of fine nylon hairs used to measure sensitivity of the skin) and vibration testing to determine changes in skin sensitivity postflight. Crewmembers indicated when sensations are present during the testing paradigm. Postflight values were compared to those obtained preflight. Values were correlated to changes observed in whole body postural control. It was hypothesized that skin sensitivity will be increased post space flight. It was also hypothesized that increases in the sensitivity of the skin will correlate with balance deficiencies related to vestibular information.

The research has the potential to impact:

1) investigators understanding of the mechanism by which skin contributes to balance control on Earth, and
2) future applications to further understand skin contributions to balance control in an altered gravito-inertial environment for space exploration.

To date, the majority of work examining skin contributions to balance control has explored the removal of skin information and the resultant postural instability. Devices to augment cutaneous input have been proposed as a means of re-establishing balance. Insight into balance challenges as a result of heightened skin input will enhance current theories concerning skin contribution to postural control.

APPROACH:
A vibration device and monofilaments (a single strand of manmade fiber similar to fishing line) were used to record the sensitivity of the receptors in eleven crewmembers. Researchers documented any changes in the skin sensitivity of each crewmember’s foot sole in order to identify which receptors may be influenced by a period of weightlessness. Coupled with tests that assess changes in crewmembers’ abilities to maintain their balance, these measures will help establish how increased skin sensitivity contributes to balance control.

In the 40 (±20) day period before flight, each subject was evaluated during a baseline data collection (BDC) session. Sensitivity of the sole was assessed at three specific locations using two methods: monofilament testing and by using a probe that delivers altered levels of force at specific frequencies to the sole of the foot. These tests were repeated after landing (on the day of landing and 2-4 days after landing). This experiment collected data before and after space flight, but not during the flight.

RESULTS:
Skin sensitivity of eleven astronauts (on missions ranging from 12-16 days) was measured pre- and postflight. Sensitivity was measured as vibration perception at the great toe, fifth metatarsal and heel. The frequencies targeted four classes of receptors: 3 and 25 Hz for slow-adapting (SA) receptors and 60 and 250 Hz for fast-adapting (FA) receptors.

This study demonstrated that there are changes in skin sensitivity following short-duration space flight. Skin sensitivity of the foot sole was altered from baseline in a population of astronauts aboard the Space Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS). Overall an increase in vibration threshold at low frequencies was found, indicating a decreased sensitivity to slow-adapting receptor input. Increased sensitivity to high-frequency vibration (250 Hz) was found for 6 out of 11 subjects indicating an increased sensitivity to velocity and high-frequency information. For detailed results refer to the publication cited below.

experiment_title: Effect of Sensorimotor Adaptation Following Long-Duration Spaceflight on Perception and Control of Vehicular Motion
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The central nervous system must resolve new patterns of sensory cues during movement in a novel gravitoinertial environment in order to maintain accurate spatial orientation awareness. Investigators hypothesize that adaptive change in how inertial cues from the vestibular system are integrated with other sensory information leads to perceptual disturbances and impaired manual control during transition to a new gravity environment. The primary goals of this investigation are to quantify postflight decrements in manual control performance during a rover simulation (both acute and recovery), and to examine the relationship between manual control errors and adaptive changes in sensorimotor function and motion perception.

APPROACH:
The simulator utilizes a Stewart-type motion base (CKAS, Australia), single-seat cabin with triple scene projection covering 150° horizontal by 50° vertical, and joystick controller. The rover simulation consists of a serial presentation of four discrete docking tasks that the crewmember attempts to complete within each session. Each task consists of 1) perspective-taking, using a map that defines the rover orientation and location relative to the docking target, 2) navigation toward the target around a Martian outpost as efficiently as possible, and 3) docking a side hatch of the rover to another rover or habitat hatch using a visually guided targeting system. At the completion of each task, a new perspective map will appear to initiate the next task in the series. The total time the crewmember can complete four docking tasks will determine the overall operator proficiency for the rover simulation.

RESULTS:

experiment_title: Apollo Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During the conduct of the early manned space flight program, the threat of an infectious disease occurrence in one or more crewmembers was always present. Although this threat is present during all phases of the preflight period, it is more critical, and potentially hazardous, during some phases than during others. Several potential dangers are associated with the occurrence of infectious diseases during a period immediately before launch. One or more crew members could be exposed to an infectious disease agent, become ill and not recuperate sufficiently by launch day; this occurrence could have resulted in launch delays. In addition, a crew member could be exposed to disease during the last days before launch and not exhibit symptoms during the preflight physical examinations. The probability would then exist for symptoms to become apparent during flight, where adequate medical treatment would be unavailable; this would also expose other crew members to infection. Furthermore, the loss of the capabilities of the ill crew member would impact the operations of the mission.

Though the risk of infection during the Gemini and Mercury missions was judged to be very low because of their short durations, some precautions (such as restricted access to the crew living quarters) were still taken to reduce the risk of crew members being exposed to disease. With the increased length of missions during the Apollo program, these health risks increased. Still, this type of plan was not implemented until the Apollo 14 mission. Previous attempts to implement the program were not completed due to operational problems or conflicts with the training schedules of the crew. However, with the exposure of a prime Apollo 13 crew member to rubella, the need for a more meticulously conceived and strictly enforced program was evident.

The Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program was finally implemented starting with the Apollo 14 mission. The objective of this program was to minimize or eliminate the possibility of adverse alterations in the health of the flight crews during the immediate preflight, inflight and postflight periods. The Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program covered four elements: Clinical Medicine, Immunology, Exposure Prevention, and Epidemiological Surveillance.

APPROACH:
Exposure Prevention

Minimizing or eliminating exposure to infectious diseases was the most important part of the preventive medicine program. Diseases could be transmitted by fomites (contaminated inanimate objects), contaminated consumables (such as air, food, and water) and personal contacts. Fomites probably represented the least important source of infectious diseases; however, precautions--such as use of separate headsets and microphones for each astronaut--was practiced.

Contaminated consumables presented a greater risk. To prevent transmission of an infectious disease through the air, a closely controlled living environment was provided during the pre-launch period. All areas in which the crew members worked or resided were equipped with high-efficiency bacterial filters in all the supply air ducts. This precluded exposure to microbial agents from adjacent non-medically controlled areas and individuals. Air handling systems were well balanced in a manner that provided higher atmospheric pressure in those areas inhabited by the crew members, as compared to the atmospheric pressure outside. This served to direct air leakage from windows, doors, floors and walls away from the crew.

Foods consumed by the astronauts were also a source of potentially infectious microorganisms. Because contamination of food could be accidental as well as intentional, no set pattern of food procurement was established. The procurement of food was handled by cooks in crew quarters and monitored by the medical team members. Portions of each lot of food purchased were subjected to microbiological evaluation. Food preparation areas were inspected daily for cleanliness and maintenance of satisfactory sanitary conditions.

Drinking water, another potential source of infectious disease agents, was subjected to daily microbiological evaluations. This ensured that the municipal water treatment procedures were satisfactory and that safe water was provided to the crew. Drinking water sources were limited to drinking fountains provided in the crew quarters and working spaces.

The most important measure taken in exposure prevention was the minimization of contact with other individuals during the critical preflight period. The areas the crew could visit were limited, as well as the number of persons who could come into contact with the crew. Crew members were also isolated from potential carriers, such as transient populations (launch site visitors), high incident groups (children), and uncontrolled contacts (maintenance personnel or those persons about whom no medical information was known). Children were the most common carriers of upper respiratory and gastrointestinal infections. Therefore, astronauts were isolated for 21 days prior to flight, even from their own children.

Clinical Medicine

Because it was important for all astronauts to remain in good health, the government provided a clinical medicine program for Apollo crew members and their families. The health program was initiated upon selection of the flight crew and continued as long as the astronauts were on flight status. The program provided both routine and emergency physical examinations. Complete virological, bacteriological, immunological, serological, and biochemical studies were conducted at Johnson Space Center to ensure rapid diagnosis and prompt treatment of any disease occurrence.

Immunology

Serological testing was conducted on the Apollo astronauts to determine immunity levels prior to immunizations. The serological tests were performed for tetanus, syphilis, typhoid, mumps, poliomyelitis, rubella, rubeola, and yellow fever. Tuberculin skin tests were also performed. Immunizations against diphtheria, tetanus, typhoid, influenza, poliomyelitis, smallpox, and yellow fever were given to the astronauts. Mumps, rubella, and rubeola immunizations were given if no serological response was obtained. The astronauts' families were immunized for diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, mumps, poliomyelitis, rubella, rubeola, and smallpox. Other immunizations were provided should the crew members or their families travel to endemic areas. Unfortunately, immunizations were not available for the illnesses most likely to occur--viral and bacterial infections of the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

Epidemiological Surveillance

The epidemiological surveillance program was designed to ensure that individuals who came into contact with the crew (primary contacts) were healthy, thus minimizing the risk of infectious disease transmission to the crew members. Three options were considered to help minimize crew exposure to infectious agents: 1) build housing facilities for the crew and their primary contacts; 2) modify existing housing for flight crews and primary contacts. or 3) provide strict isolation of the prime and backup crew members in the crew quarters and limit personal contacts to medically approved persons. Option 3 was selected; options 1 and 2 were determined to be cost prohibitive.

A medical surveillance program, initiated three months prior to launch, began with recording medical histories and other critical information of each primary contact. Each primary contact was then subjected to an extensive physical examination approximately 60 days prior to launch. Microbiological samples were obtained to determine carriers. Based on this information, certain individuals were approved for access to flight crew members during the 21-day pre-launch isolation period.

Each primary contact and all his family members were subjected to medical surveillance during the 21-day preflight period. Primary contacts were instructed to report to the medical examination facility whenever they or any of their family became ill or had been exposed to an infectious disease. Reports of illness events were also obtained from all schools attended by children of the crew members and primary contacts. Daily reports were solicited from each school of interest concerning the total number of absences, including absences of the children of any crew member and primary contact. Additional daily reports were obtained from public health authorities in the launch site area to determine trends and incidences of specific disease events within the population where primary contacts may have had exposure.

A computerized data processing system was developed to maintain complete and up-to-date records on all crew members and primary contacts, and their families. The system linked the medical analyses laboratories at Johnson Space Center with the Medical Surveillance Office at Kennedy Space Center, thus making information on these individuals readily available.

RESULTS:
The success of the Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program was evidenced by the absence of preflight, inflight and postflight illnesses during the Apollo 14 through 17 missions. Statistics recorded for missions prior to the Apollo 14 mission indicated that 57 percent of the prime crew members experienced some illness during the 21-day pre-launch period, as well as during flight. Monitoring the health of primary contact children proved valuable because, in approximately 30 percent of the cases of illness in primary contacts, similar illnesses had occurred previously in one or more of the family members, with the most common type of illness being upper respiratory tract infections.
