experiment_title: Bio-Assay of Body Fluids
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The space flight environment with its combination of stresses offers a unique challenge to the body’s biochemical control mechanisms. Astronauts returning from Gemini and Apollo flights demonstrated biochemical changes of sufficient magnitude and complexity to warrant detailed studies of the endocrine and metabolic systems. The Bio-Assay of Body Fluids (M073) experiment was designed to study homeostasis in the areas of (1) fluid and electrolyte balance, (2) regulation of calcium metabolism, (3) adrenal function, and (4) carbohydrate, fat, and protein utilization. The study was divided into two broad categories. One category included routine blood and urine studies similar to those used in clinical medical practice. The second category included a more thorough analyses to investigate the metabolic/endocrine responses to the space flight environment, including fluid and electrolyte control mechanisms.

APPROACH:
The nine astronauts who flew on Skylab 2, Skylab 3, and Skylab 4 all participated as test subjects. Metabolic monitoring of the astronauts began at least 21 days prior to each flight, continued throughout each flight, and proceeded for at least 17 days after flight. Following an overnight fast, blood samples were drawn. The blood volume required for preflight and postflight analyses was 25 ml and the inflight plasma averaged 3 ml. Sodium ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) was used as an anticoagulant for blood samples. Radioassay, fluorometric and gas chromatographic techniques were used for most hormonal analyses. Radioactive body compartment studies were conducted preflight and postflight. These included dilution studies of body water (tritium), extracellular fluid (35 sulfate), plasma volume (125 I-protein) and exchangeable potassium (42 K and 43 K) both preflight and postflight. Urine was collected on a void-by-void basis before and after each mission. Twenty-four hour urine collections on each subject were made throughout the flights as part of the Mineral Balance (M071) experiment. Because of limitations in return storage weight and volume, a 120 ml aliquot of each day's urine collection was collected, frozen, and returned to Earth. A measured quantity of lithium chloride, added to each 24-hour collection bag prior to flight, permitted urine volumes to be calculated based on lithium dilution. In addition, crewmembers measured the filled collection bag with a gage to provide an estimate of daily urine output. Data samples and results were shared among the three related investigations. Data on food and water consumption, body mass, and urine volume were telemetered nightly to the investigators.

RESULTS:
Analysis of postflight blood samples showed elevations in calcium and phosphorous were present throughout the three missions and remained higher than preflight control values for several days following flight. Cortisol and Angiotensin I were generally elevated, though not always significantly. Potassium and creatinine increased inflight and remained high immediately postflight. Plasma aldosterone, total protein, carbon dioxide, thyroid stimulating hormone, and thyroxine increased postflight. Inflight and postflight plasma measurements showed a decrease in sodium, chloride, osmolality, and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). Glucose, insulin, and aldosterone decreased inflight, but increased postflight. Postflight decreases were also seen in cholesterol, uric acid, magnesium, lactic dehydrogenase, and total bilirubin. Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and albumin were not changed at recovery, but were decreased on the third and fourteenth postflight days. All electrolytes in the 24-hour urine samples inflight and postflight were increased along with aldosterone, cortisol, and total 17-ketosteroids. Postflight increases were seen in epinephrine, norepinephrine, aldosterone, and cortisol. The data also showed a trend towards inflight decreases in antidiuretic hormone (ADH), epinephrine, norepinephrine and uric acid. The inflight norepinephrine levels were probably the reflection of the high levels of physical exercise undertaken by each crew member during the flight. Significant decreases in sodium, potassium, chloride, osmolality, phosphate, magnesium, uric acid, ADH, and total 17-hydroxycorticosteroids were observed postflight. This experiment examined the biochemical reactions of the body to the stress of space flight. The experiment was the first comprehensive and integrated study of endocrinology and metabolism during prolonged space flight. Significant biochemical changes were observed, but all disappeared shortly after returning to Earth. These changes for the most part indicated a successful adaptation of the body to the combined stresses of weightlessness. The transient nature of some changes, particularly in fluid and electrolyte metabolism, supported the conclusion that a new and stable condition of homeostasis had been achieved. In other areas, particularly those concerned with the metabolism of bone mineral, protein, and carbohydrates, unstable states appeared to persist. At the time, it was unclear in what form these changes would manifest themselves during flights of much longer duration.

experiment_title: The Role of Gap-Junction Communication and Oxidative Metabolism in the Biological Effects of Space Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this project is to investigate biochemical and molecular aspects of two inter-related fundamental biological processes, namely gap-junction intercellular communication and oxidative metabolism, in determining human cellular responses to exposures of very low to moderate fluences of protons (of energies such as found in the space environment) or high charge (Z) and high energy (E) particles (1 GeV/nucleon 56Fe ions). Gap junctions are found between most cells in the body, and the molecular signaling they mediate is crucial for normal development, physiology and response to disease. By allowing direct intercellular transfer of cytoplasmic molecules, they provide a powerful pathway for direct molecular signaling between cells. On the other hand, oxidative metabolism is primarily regulated by mitochondria, which mediate respiration and ATP synthesis in eukaryotic cells. They also participate in numerous indispensable metabolic pathways. It is hypothesized that exposure of human cells to high or low fluences of protons and/or HZE particles results in distinct molecular and biochemical changes not only in irradiated but also neighboring bystander cells. These events are modulated by oxidative metabolism and gap-junction coupling, which together induce persistent changes in mitochondria and in nuclear DNA in progeny of irradiated and affected bystander cells.

In Aim 1, it is proposed to define the aspect(s) of junctional communication leading to proton- and high charge/high energy (HZE) particle-induced toxic effects. Specifically, to examine the role of different connexin proteins in propagating death-inducing (growth delay, apoptosis) or pro-survival effects (proliferative capacity) among irradiated cells and also between irradiated and non-irradiated cells.

Aim 2 is to identify specific connexin channel permeabilities that correlate with intercellular propagation of toxic or protective effects in cultures exposed to HZE particles or protons. An emphasis will be to determine the nature of molecules communicated among irradiated cells and between irradiated and non-irradiated cells.

In Aim 3, mitochondrial function will be evaluated in cells exposed to low fluences of high energy charged particles. Specifically, mitochondrial protein import will be examined, mitochondrial protein synthesis, assembly of large protein complexes including respiratory complexes, and oxidative damage to mitochondrial proteins and DNA. The persistence of oxidative effects in the progeny of exposed cells and correlate the observed results with the overall cellular redox environment will be evaulated.

APPROACH:
Eight-week-old male Sprague-Dawley rats were exposed to 0 or 50 cGy from 1100 MeV/nucleon titanium ions at the NASA’s Space Radiation Laboratory located at the Brookhaven National Laboratory in Upton, NY. During the irradiation, the rats were placed in well-ventilated plastic restraining tubes that restricted the movement of the animal. The plastic tube was placed perpendicular to the beam and positioned so that the head of the rats was in the center of the beam. As such, the rat’s shoulders may have also received some radiation dose.

RESULTS:
The role of in vivo investigation of intercellular communication and oxidative metabolism in the biological responses to high charge (Z) and high energy (E) HZE particles has been extended. Twelve-week-old and 9-months-old male mice have been exposed to low (5 cGy) or moderate (50 cGy) mean absorbed doses of 1000 MeV/amu iron ions or 500 MeV/amu titanium ions delivered to the whole body. In young mice, the regulation of the MAF1 protein has been identified, a downstream effector of the TOR (target of rapamycin) pathway that regulates various cellular functions in response to environmental cues, is highly sensitive to space particulate radiations. Maf1 has been implicated in processes related to protein biosynthesis and RNA maturation. It is essential for the activity of the enzyme RNA polymerase III that regulates cell growth and cell cycle progression. Global analyses of post-translational modification of proteins in organs of control and irradiated young mice has been performed. Specifically, S-nitrosylation of proteins from mice exposed to 5 or 50 cGy of energetic titanium ions has been analyzed. S-nitrosylation is emerging as a fundamental mechanism that modulates the function of several proteins engaged in many signaling pathways. Our results showed that S-nitrosylation of proteins in space irradiated rodents is organ and radiation dose dependent. The S-nitrosylation level of brain proteins was significantly increased after whole body exposure to a mean absorbed dose of 5 cGy. Compared to control, 151 proteins were identified as newly S-nitrosylated 12 days after irradiation. A large fraction of the proteins (56%) were classified as enzymes. Pathway analysis showed that they are related to free radical scavenging, cellular assembly and organization.

In vitro studies in progeny of non-targeted bystander cells that were co-cultured with HZE-particle irradiated cells have been extended. Several biological endpoints, including chromosomal damage, gene expression and cellular senescence have been analyzed. It has been confirmed that stressful effects propagated from irradiated to bystander cells persist in their progeny. It has been shown that functional gap junction coupling between parental bystander and irradiated donor cells is a critical mediator of the observed stressful effects.

experiment_title: Telomeres and the One Year Mission - CIPHER
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
An astronaut’s individual genetic susceptibilities, the unique lifestyle stresses they encounter (e.g., nutritional, psychological, physical), and particular environmental exposures (e.g., microgravity, galactic cosmic rays) are all integrated and captured as changes in telomere length. Thus, the rate at which telomeres shorten provides a general measure of health that can be linked to aging as well as to risk of developing degenerative age-related pathologies, ranging from reduced immune function and dementia, to cardiovascular disease and cancer. Functional telomeres are also essential for maintaining genomic integrity and stability, as they protect chromosomal termini from inappropriate degradation and prevent natural DNA ends from being recognized as broken DNA, resulting in inappropriate triggering of DNA damage responses (DDRs).
The goal of this study is to establish temporal profiles of human telomere length dynamics (changes over time) and DNA damage responses of importance for the maintenance of human health and performance during long-duration deep space missions. This will be achieved by examining the potential of telomere length as a biomarker for individual astronaut’s health and identifying trends in adaptations to human health and performance during long-duration low-Earth orbit. The researchers will evaluate telomere length and DDRs as pioneered and validated in the NASA Twins Study (One Year Mission; Expedition 43), and the Telomeres 1 investigation, which involved 10 unrelated astronauts and age/sex matched ground controls. Telomeres 2 will evaluate telomere length dynamics and DDRs in crewmembers participating in various duration missions aboard the International Space Station (ISS) as part of the Complement of Integrated Protocols for Human Exploration Research (CIPHER), and in the concurrent ground analog component (prolonged isolation).
The specific aims of this study include:
(1) Establish temporal profiles of human telomere length dynamics in individual crewmembers participating in CIPHER onboard the ISS and participants in the concurrent ground analog component (prolonged isolation missions). As part of this specific aim, the researchers will evaluate telomere length dynamics and shifts in individual short/long telomere length distributions in bulk and stem/early progenitor cell populations. Telomerase activity will also be assessed.
(2) Establish temporal profiles of DNA damage responses for individual crewmembers participating in CIPHER onboard the ISS and participants in the concurrent ground analog component. As part of this specific aim, the researchers will evaluate genomic and telomeric DDRs, chromosomal damage and instability, telomere-specific oxidative damage, and alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) activation.

APPROACH:
This research will include crewmembers participating in = 2-month (n = 10), 6-month (n = 10), and 12-month-long (n = 10) missions aboard the ISS, and concurrent analog missions (n = 10). Blood samples will be collected 8 to 10 times per individual, depending on mission duration.
To address Aim 1, the researchers will use quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and telomere fluorescence in situ hybridization (Telo-FISH) to assess telomere length and create temporal profiles of individual participant’s average telomere length. Telo-FISH will serve to validate the qPCR telomere length results, and will facilitate evaluation of shifts in individual short and long telomere length distributions over time. Telomerase activity will be directly evaluated using qPCR-TRAP assay; protein levels of TERT and HIF-1A (indirect measures of telomerase activity) will also be assessed. Putative hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and progenitor cell populations will be monitored for evidence of stem cell enrichment resulting from ionizing radiation (IR) induced cell killing.
To address Aim 2, temporal profiles of individual participant’s DDRs will be established using strand-specific whole-chromosome directional genomic hybridization (dGH) for simultaneous detection of IR-induced chromosomal inversions and translocations. Together with strand-specific Telo-FISH and gamma-H2AX foci, a marker of double-strand breaks (DSBs), researchers will evaluate chromosomal damage and instability, telomere-specific oxidative damage (sister telomere loss), and evidence of ALT activation (heterogeneous telomere lengths).

RESULTS:
The researchers anticipate that results will serve to further support and validate the Twins Study and Telomeres investigations’ results regarding spaceflight-induced telomere elongation. Importantly, results will also offer mechanistic insight into how and why telomere lengthening occurs during spaceflight. Further, observed DDRs and chromosomal signatures consistent with inflight space radiation exposure will validate the utility of inversions as biomarkers of high-LET exposures. Taken together, results will improve our understanding of the potential health risks and consequences astronauts will face during and after long-duration spaceflight.

experiment_title: Evaluation of the MK I Rowing Machine
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The treadmill is presently the only Space Shuttle operational exercise device. Exclusive use of the treadmill for in-flight exercise has raised important scientific and operational concerns. Excessive noise and vibration of treadmill exercise will disrupt microgravity experiments and disturb sleeping crewmembers. In addition, treadmill exercise is mostly lower torso and aerobic in nature. It may not provide sufficient protection from muscle deterioration. Noise and vibration associated with the MK I are anticipated to be significantly less than the current treadmill. Ground-based studies have demonstrated that simulated rowing provides total body exercise including aerobic and anaerobic conditioning. In-flight simulated rowing is anticipated to produce a similar total response. Heart rate was recorded to determine the effectiveness of changes in the resistive settings of the device.

APPROACH:
Documentary 35 mm still photos were requested. Use of the Orbiter 8mm video camera using a wide angle lens and the multi-purpose was required. Footage of the hardware evaluation and the exercise session was requested for each participating crewmember. Full body scenes were also requested. If a camera is not available, one was added to the hardware list. It was recommended that the exercising crewmember consume eight ounces of fluid before and after the session to maintain hydration.

A familiarization session for the Rower, marker placement, and rowing capability were performed preflight. The in flight sessions were documented using a video camera. The camera was positioned perpendicular to the side of the exercising individual. Video marker tape was applied to the ankle, knee, shoulder, elbow, and wrist sites of the subject's side being monitored by the video camera.

Two crewmembers were requested. One crewmember changed the workloads on the Rower, and voice recorded comments about the hardware and perceived workloads. The other crewmember performed the exercise and contributed comments about the hardware. Hardware evaluation was accomplished by subjects exercising on the Rower at increasing workloads for 60 seconds followed by a continuous workload for 10 minutes at a comfortable level followed by a cool down stage at the lowest setting for two minutes. Heart rate was monitored using the heart watch to determine the efficacy of the changing workloads. The evaluation was performed at a stroke rate of 25 strokes/minute. Stroke rate was cued using a small electronic metronome having both audio and visual (light) cadence outputs.

experiment_title: Influence of Center of Gravity on Human Performance in Partial Gravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Apollo program demonstrated that suit center of gravity (CG) is an important variable affecting human performance in Lunar Extravehicular Activities (EVAs). This study assessed crew performance of representative planetary exploration tasks with a single EVA suit weight with six different CG locations.

APPROACH:
A reconfigurable back pack with repositionable weight modules was used to simulate Perfect, Low, Forward, High, Aft and NASA Baseline CG locations. All CG locations were based on the assumption of a 60 pound suit, a 135 pound Portable Life Support System (PLSS), and a standardized 6 foot 180 pound subject. These tests were conducted in NASA´s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory and during underwater missions in the NOAA Aquarius Habitat. Subjects were weighed out for lunar gravity. Twenty-one subjects performed a task-battery that included ambulation, kneel and recovery, fall and recovery, rock pick-up, rock transfer, inclined ambulation from 10-30 degrees, shoveling, and ladder climb. Subject performance was assessed using a modified Cooper- Harper scale to assess operator compensation required to achieve desired performance.

RESULTS:
Results suggest that CG location affects human performance. Subjects preferred Perfect, Low and Forward CG over High, Aft or Baseline (both High and Aft), which suggests that a conventional back pack PLSS may not be optimal and that alternative configurations should be considered.

experiment_title: Synaptic plasticity in mammalian vestibular maculae
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The nervous systems of animals, including man, have been found to exhibit a remarkable ability to adapt to changes in the ambient gravity environment. An understanding of these adaptations is critical to managing human exploration and survivability during long-term spaceflight. Previous studies have shown that a gravity-sensing structure within the inner ear, the utricle, exhibited quantitative changes in components of its constituent hair cells during microgravity exposures up to 14 days. This structure is known as one of the vestibular maculae, inner ear structures with important load sensing capabilities. The changes that were observed involved modification in the number of synaptic ribbons, which are organelles involved in the transfer of sensory signals from the hair cells to neurons that communicate with the central nervous system. Such changes represent a form of adaptation that is more generally characterized as synaptic plasticity. At present, however, it is not known whether these changes represented a transient effect of short-term spaceflight, or whether they are more permanent and reflect a chronic adaptive modification.

APPROACH:
The present study is designed to test whether the approximately 30-day exposure to microgravity proposed for the BION-M1 satellite mission results in chronic modification in synapse number within hair cells of the utricle. This will be achieved through transmission electron microscopy and quantitative analyses to estimate the density of synaptic ribbons in different hair cell types and in different regions of utricles from flight and control animals. In addition, we will utilize new methods of conical tomography to visualize these ribbon synapses in three dimensions. This enables us to test whether synaptic plasticity is manifested in changes in subpopulations of ultrastructural elements of the synaptic ribbon. These results will be critical to a more comprehensive understanding of the long-term exposure to spaceflight in mammalian gravity-sensing systems.

RESULTS:
The investigator team continues to collect and analyze ultrastructural data for additional tomograms and serial reconstructions. Two publications are in preparation, the first one reporting the synapse distribution data and the second on the ultrastructural findings from spaceflight specimens.

No data submitted. Summarized and analyzed data may be available through publications.

experiment_title: Female Reproductive Health: Space Flight Induced Ovarian and Estrogen Signaling Dysfunction, Adaptation, and Recovery
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Current evidence from three space shuttle missions (STS-131, STS-133, and STS-135) demonstrated that ovarian function is severely disrupted in female mice, rendering these adult female mice likely infertile. Both ovarian folliculogenesis and luteal function were disrupted as was uterine function likely as a result of the unbalanced ovarian steroid support. Our previous observations raised important fundamental questions on maintenance of female reproductive health that need to be addressed prior to conducting complex multigenerational studies in mammals under space flight conditions. The RR1 Biospecimens Collection can add greatly to our current knowledge base by addressing several important intermediate questions that were not addressable in the STS flights. These include an increase in exposure to space flight and collection of adult tissue prior to reentry. So these studies, will provide for the first time the ability to examine adult ovarian/uterine tissues following long term exposure to space flight without the confounding effects of stress of the reentry.

Aim 1 - Does space flight induced ovarian dysfunction represent an acute response to the transition to microgravity and space radiation?
Aim 2 - Does prolonged exposure to space flight allow recovery of normal ovarian function?

These samples will be examined using our standard molecular techniques, including quantitative RT-PCR, western blot as well as radioimmunoassays (RIA) for estrogen and progesterone. We will use steroid (estrogen/progesterone) content of the ovary as determined by RIA as a surrogate for establishing the functional ovarian status of the RR1 females at the time of their sacrifice. Additionally, key regulatory genes known to be markers of ovarian functional status, including those involved in estrogen and progesterone synthesis (i.e., aromatase, steroidogenic acute regulatory protein, P450 side chain cleave and steroid receptors, etc.) will be examined in ovarian and uterine tissues.

experiment_title: Use of a Molecular Marker of Learning and Memory to Assess Effects of 56Fe Irradiation on Hippocampus-dependent Cognition and Neurogenesis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Particulate irradiation in the space environment may pose a significant risk to space flight crews during a mission or upon return to Earth. This may involve the central nervous system, where low radiation doses can induce cognitive or behavioral impairments. Understanding the cellular and molecular basis of cognitive injury will facilitate the establishment of risk estimates and may provide a foundation for the establishment of effective countermeasures or treatments for such injury. Using an animal model, we will determine the extent to which low doses of 56Fe irradiation affect cognitive function and will determine if such changes are associated with the alteration of a gene that is associated with learning and memory, or with the production and maturation of newly born neurons.

APPROACH:
The overall goals of this project were to determine: (1) how low doses of 56Fe ions affected behavioral performance; (2) if specific cellular (e.g. neurogenesis) and molecular factors (immediate early gene Arc) might play a role in cognition; and (3) if those endpoints were affected by inflammatory changes. The experimental methods chosen to accomplish these goals provided a means by which the effects of low radiation doses could be quantified both in terms of behavioral performance as well as specific cellular and molecular endpoints that are associated with learning and memory.

The proposed measures of behavioral performance, which were also used to induce Arc expression, involved a fear conditioning paradigm with 2 versions: one that required the hippocampus (context version) and one that did not require the hippocampus (cued version). The version that required the hippocampus consisted of two types of behavioral paradigms. The first involved no tone shock pairing (-/-) and represented the ability of an animal to recognize an environment previously encountered. Animals that recognized that environment would explore it less, a behavior that is referred to as spatial habituation learning. The second paradigm involved tone shock pairing (+/+) and represented a Pavlovian type of response; that is, animals received a mild shock the first day, and when subsequently placed in the same environment, they would freeze more if they remembered having received an adverse stimulus in that environment the day before. For each version used, thirty minutes after the end of the final testing session on day 2, tissues were collected and prepared for microscopic analyses.

RESULTS:
Investigators completed all analyses related to behavior, neurogenesis, Arc protein expression, and measures of the endogenous inflammatory cells in the brain, the microglia. These endpoints were assessed after whole body irradiation with either 0, 0.25 Gy, 0.5 Gy or 1.0 Gy of 56Fe. All animals underwent cognitive testing 3 months after irradiation using a fear conditioning training- and testing-paradigm. The three-month time point was selected because that time has been previously used to show cognitive deficits after photon or HZE irradiation, as well as changes in Arc expression. Investigators quantified the effects of whole body 56Fe irradiation (600 MeV, 0.5 or 1 Gy) on hippocampus-dependent and hippocampus-independent cognitive performance and determined if those effects were associated with changes in Arc expression in the enclosed and free blades of the dentate gyrus. Whole body 56Fe irradiation impacted contextual but not cued fear freezing and the percentage of Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In mice tested for contextual freezing, there was a correlation between Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In addition, in mice irradiated with 0.5 Gy, contextual freezing in the absence of aversive stimuli correlated with the percentage of Arc-positive cells in the enclosed blade. In mice tested for cued freezing, there was no correlation between Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In contrast, cued freezing in the presence or absence of aversive stimuli correlated with Arc-positive cells in the free blade. These data indicate that there are blade dependent effects after particulate irradiation. More studies are required to address the physiologic significance of such findings.

One of the microenvironmental factors that may influence how irradiation affects cognition is inflammation. Investigators addressed this issue by irradiating animals deficient in a specific chemokine receptor: chemokine receptor-2 (CCR2). CCR2 mediates the recruitment of infiltrating and resident microglia to sites of CNS inflammation, and is upregulated by 56Fe irradiation. CCR2 knock out (KO) and wild-type mice were used to compare effects of 56Fe radiation (600 MeV, 0, 0.25 Gy) on hippocampal function using contextual fear conditioning involving tone shock pairing during training (+/+) and exposure to the same environment without tone shock pairings (-/-). In the -/- condition, irradiation increased freezing and hippocampal Arc protein levels in WT but not CCR2 KO mice, suggesting that a lack of CCR2 was associated with a poorer outcome. In contrast, in the +/+ condition, irradiation reduced freezing but there was no genotype difference. There were no significant correlations between the number of Arc-positive cells in the dentate gyrus and freezing in either genotype but in CCR2 KO mice, there was a trend towards a negative correlation between freezing and Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In the +/+ condition, BrdU alone and BrdU/NeuN were reduced in the free blade but not the enclosed blade of CCR2 KO. CCR2 status had no influence on total numbers of newly born activated microglia before or after irradiation, indicating that other mechanisms are involved in the genotype-dependent radiation response.

The investigators’ standard markers of neurogenesis, microglia, and the immediate early gene Arc have been shown to be good predictors of radiation response after relatively high doses of photons or heavy ions. However, in their current studies they were not particularly responsive to low dose irradiation with iron ions. Given those findings they wanted to look for other markers that might track with cognition and provide predictive value after low dose exposures. The formation of long-term memory relies on modulation of synaptic connections in response to neuronal input. This plasticity requires coordinated activity-dependent synthesis of specific mRNAs and proteins that facilitate molecular and structural changes at the synapse. Dendritic spines are bulbous membrane projections of mixed morphology, that form the postsynaptic specializations of the vast majority of excitatory synapses in the central nervous system (CNS) and their structure and density are important factors in synaptic function. Spine morphology can predict both spine stability and synaptic strength, and changes in dendritic spine density or structural reorganization of spines is thought to be important for cognitive processes such as learning and memory.

In their new study of dendritic spines, investigators irradiated young adult male C57BL6 mice with 0 or 0.5 Gy (whole body) of 56Fe ions. Within each radiation treatment group, animals were randomly assigned into cohorts that received cognitive testing using a no shock/no tone paradigm or no cognitive testing, i.e. caged controls. Half of the mice from each specific treatment group were used for the determination of dendritic spine density/morphology and the other half were used for measurement of Arc and other cellular markers. Dendritic spines were visualized using a well-established Golgi staining paradigm. In the CA1 and dentate gyrus of sham-irradiated mice, the behavioral testing enhanced the spine density as compared to behaviorally naïve mice. In contrast, behavioral testing did not affect spine density in irradiated mice. These intriguing data indicate that irradiated mice did not benefit from the environmental enrichment (i.e. behavioral testing) as sham-irradiated mice did.

Finally, investigators initiated and completed a mixed beam study to determine how the brain responds when it is confronted by two different types of irradiation. Mice either received a single whole body exposure of 1.0 Gy protons (n = 24), a single whole body dose of 0.05 Gy 56Fe (n = 24), a single whole body exposure of 1.0 Gy protons immediately before a single whole body dose of 0.5 Gy 56Fe (n = 24) or no irradiation (n =24). Two months following irradiation, all animals receives a daily i.p. injection of bromodeoxyuridine (100 mg/kg) for 7 days, and 1 month later mice were either cognitively tested for novel object recognition or acted as caged controls. Thirty minutes after the onset of the last session of the cognitive testing, animals were sacrificed and their brains bisected into the two hemispheres and then frozen. Tissues were either analyzed for cellular markers of neurogenesis, the immediate early gene Arc, or for molecular/biochemical assays for markers of inflammation/oxidative stress. No cellular, molecular, or biochemical changes were observed after either of the single doses or the combined treatment. This suggests either that the low doses used did not induce any significant alterations, or the specific endpoints chosen for study were not sensitive to minor changes induced by the relatively low doses used.

The data highlights the complexity of assessing how low doses of 56Fe affect hippocampal function. Those data suggest that even a relatively low dose of 56Fe can induce behavioral changes that involve the hippocampus, but the cellular/molecular/biochemical mechanisms responsible are still not yet known.

experiment_title: Development of Predictive Degradation Models and Determination of Bioequivalence of Pharmaceutical Preparations Contained in the Medical Kits on Board the International Space Station
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The environmental factors of space missions may cause accelerated physical-chemical degradation or alterations in the integrity of formulations stored onboard space missions for extended periods such as on the International Space Station (ISS) and exploration missions. The degradation of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) and adjuvants in addition to alterations of the chemical matrix of the formulation can decrease potency and bioavailability, and increase the risk of toxicity of degraded medications. Therefore, characterizing degradation profiles and developing predictive models of degradation using results from ground-based accelerated stability, bioavailability, and toxicity studies is important to ensure safe and effective pharmacotherapeutics for astronauts during extended duration space missions.

The overall goal of the proposed research is to develop and validate predictive degradation models for select pharmaceutical preparations contained in the ISS medical kits. A related objective is to examine whether or not integrity and performance of degraded formulations is compromised as indicated by bioequivalence in a ground-based animal model. The following specific aims will be pursued to accomplish the research goal:

  1. Establish a validated HPLC-MS/MS assay method that can be used for the identification and quantification of API and degradation products of the selected formulations.
  2. Characterize degradation profiles and API content of medications received from the ISS and compare with existing data from ISS payloads and irradiation studies.
  3. Conduct ground-based accelerated stability studies with a matching set of medications selected.
  4. Estimate bioequivalence between Earth-based control and Space X returned formulations in a small animal model (rat) to examine integrity and performance of medications stored onboard the ISS.

experiment_title: Pre- and Postflight Cardiac Assessment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space flight causes adaptive changes in cardiovascular function, and many astronauts have suffered postflight orthostatic tachycardia. However, previously available data about these changes have been inadequate and inconsistent. The objective of this study was to collect normative data about the effects of space flight on the volume, mass and function of the heart, and about the orthostatic response of the cardiovascular system.

APPROACH:
The heart rate and blood pressure of 32 astronauts were recorded while they were lying supine and then standing, before and after space flights of 4 to 5 days. At the same times, echocardiograms were recorded by 2-dimensional M-mode echocardiography. The total peripheral resistance index (TPRI), left ventricular end diastolic volume index (EDVI), left ventricular end systolic volume index (ESVI), left ventricular stroke volume index (SVI), myocardial mass index and ejection fraction were calculated, and the mean velocity of circumferential shortening of the myocardial fibers was estimated.

RESULTS:
The heart rate was greater on landing day than before the flight, and the EDVI and SVI in the supine position were less. (The mean EDVI was 11% less and the mean SVI was 17% less.) The mean EDVI, ESVI and SVI in the standing position were also less on landing day, but these changes were not statistically significant. Space flight caused no significant changes in the supine ESVI, the ejection fraction, the thickness of the left ventricular wall or the mass or contractility of the heart muscle. Before the flight, the TPRI increased significantly when astronauts stood up after lying supine. This orthostatic response was reduced on landing day, so that the TPRI failed to change significantly when the astronauts stood up, while the heart rate increased. The changes resolved within 7 to 10 days of landing. These results indicated that temporary changes in cardiovascular function may be expected even after short spaceflights of only 4 to 5 days. These changes included a decrease in the left ventricular end diastolic volume and stroke volume, with a compensatory increase in heart rate, as well as loss or reduction of the normal orthostatic response that maintains the blood pressure during postural changes.

experiment_title: Duty Standards Using Pre- and Post-Flight Capsule Egress and Suited Functional Performance Tasks in Simulated Reduced Gravity – Pilot
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Physiological adaptations to long-duration microgravity environments and deficits in perceptual and motor function during gravitational transitions are likely to result in reduced functional capacity after landing either on Earth or at an exploration destination, such as water-based Orion landings or Mars surface landings. All astronauts experience significant decrements in functional performance upon return from a microgravity environment. The losses in functional performance can largely be attributed to neurovestibular/sensorimotor deficits that can take days or weeks to recover from. Currently, there are no operational countermeasures, but crewmembers need to be capable of egressing their landing vehicle unassisted. This study aims to accelerate the operational planning and implementation of how to execute this testing in the dynamic, operational environments of Soyuz, Boeing, and SpaceX landing zones. Similar testing is planned for the CIPHER study on various missions.

The primary aim of this study is to allow the feasibility of the R+0/1 Egress Fitness CIPHER study tasks to be established before collecting data on the first CIPHER crew member. The investigators hypothesize that reductions in unassisted capsule egress and planetary EVA task performance will be observed after all mission durations. They also hypothesize that individual variability in planetary EVA task performance will depend on the task type and will be related to pre-flight fitness parameters, maintenance of in-flight muscle function, cardiorespiratory fitness, and sensorimotor function.

The overall objectives of the Egress Fitness study are twofold. The investigators seek to:

1.) Quantify post-landing time course changes in unassisted capsule egress and planetary EVA task performance, and

2.) Characterize the recovery to acceptable planetary EVA task performance as a function of EVA task type, time in space, time post-landing, and other potential determinants of performance (e.g., sleep, nutrition, exercise, sensorimotor performance).

APPROACH:
Data will be collected for spaceflight missions ranging from two months, six months, and up to one year in duration. Six subjects, ideally two crew from each landing vehicle, will undergo three pre-flight sessions: EVA Suit Fit Check, Partial Planetary EVA & Familiarization activities (EVAs), and Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress & Familiarization to quantify performance parameters in an operationally relevant environment. Post-flight sessions include the Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress on R+0 and Partial Planetary EVA on R+1.
Prior to the Partial Planetary EVA Circuit, crew members will be measured for proper fit and size in a MKIII or xEMU EVA suit. After the suit check there is no preferred order for the remaining sessions, unless they are scheduled on the same day. In such case, the Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress and Familiarization should be scheduled first. The Partial Planetary EVA Circuit consists of actions, movements, and component tasks sequenced to provide realistic post-landing EVA scenarios. The tasks are sequenced to allow individual evaluation on the performance of each specific sub-element on the overall EVA timeline. Tasks include translation tasks necessary for crew members to move from a lander to a habitat upon landing on Mars, as well as tasks that may be particularly influenced by spaceflight deconditioning. Prior to the start of the egress tasks, the crew member will don a heart rate monitor and lay in a recumbent position on a yoga mat. During the timed egress, the crew member will attain an upright position, deploy and secure the top hatch ladder, lift a backpack-style survival pack out of the capsule, walk up the ladder (simulating a top hatch egress) until the hip clears the hatch, then come back down. The crew member will then walk to a safe waypoint and doff the Heart Rate Monitor. When crew return in a Boeing or SpaceX vehicle, the Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress will be performed on R+0 at the rally airport. When crew return on a Soyuz vehicle, a partial Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress will be at the rally airport on R+0, and the full Unassisted Mock-up Capsule Egress will be conducted at the refueling airport on R+0. The Partial Planetary EVA Circuit will be on R+1 at JSC, as this requires the use of the Active Response Gravity Offload System (ARGOS), a permanent facility at JSC. The EVA tasks and gravity environment will be the same for both pre- and post-flight sessions.


RESULTS:
It is critical to understand what crews are capable of, and at which time points they will be able to perform which tasks. The research product will be a temporal profile of unassisted capsule egress and planetary EVA task performance pre-flight and at multiple post-landing intervals, the timing of which will be determined based on post-landing logistics and coordination with other investigations. By having participants perform unassisted capsule egress task and a partial planetary EVA soon after landing, the data from this study will verify methods of execution of these egress tests in the operational environment of Soyuz, and Boeing and SpaceX landings.

experiment_title: Psychophysics and Modeling of Spatial Orientation Perception (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Spatial orientation is achieved by integrating sensory information from different modalities in order to estimate both body orientation and self-motion. One aim of the study was to develop a comprehensive Bayesian model for spatial orientation perception. In order to develop the best possible model, the investigators conducted a thorough review of existing spatial orientation models. They focused on statistically optimal models of spatial orientation that were dynamic, meaning that the model input and output are continuous and vary over time. They concluded that the particle filter technique is best suited to modeling perception of spatial orientation because it is statistically optimal, the architecture is distributed rather than assuming particular feedback circuits, and most importantly, it is capable of implementing the non-linear system dynamics that are required for spatial orientation computations.

The second aim of the study was to measure visual and vestibular thresholds for detecting and discriminating spatial orientation stimuli. The investigators conducted three such experiments using a motion simulator with attached stereo visual display. They used a two-alternative-forced-choice procedure because this method minimizes potential sources of response noise and bias. Also, because all data were collected using a common method and apparatus, it is possible to make interesting comparisons across conditions.

APPROACH:
The methodologies for the study are embedded with the Results below.

RESULTS:
The first experiment investigated perception of heading, which is the direction of self-motion. Heading perception is fundamental to effective navigation and vehicle guidance, so it is important to understand the factors that influence the precision of visual and vestibular heading estimates. The investigators measured discrimination thresholds for heading azimuth and elevation in visual-only and vestibular-only conditions with observers oriented upright and side-down relative to gravity. Visual thresholds were significantly lower than vestibular, and upright thresholds were generally lower than side-down. Vestibular results revealed that observers are better at discriminating head-centric azimuth than elevation, regardless of body orientation. In other words, sensitivity to heading depends more upon the direction of self-motion relative to the head, than relative to gravity. Two follow-up experiments were conducted using the same subjects. The investigators found that performance on the three tasks was correlated and determined that the asymmetric vestibular sensitivity to heading stems from an underlying difference in sensitivity to linear acceleration along the interaural and dorsoventral axes of the head.

The second experiment investigated the question of whether or not vestibular cues to linear and angular self-motion interact during rotation about an earth-vertical axis. Linear and angular self-motion is signaled by the otoliths and canals, respectively. During rotation about an earth-horizontal axis (i.e. tilt), these signals must interact so that the brain correctly interprets the change in the otolith signal as due to a change in the direction of gravity. In contrast, the investigators found no evidence of canal-otolith interaction during rotation about an earth-vertical axis. Thresholds for detecting linear acceleration were not influenced by the speed of angular motion.

The third experiment investigated whether or not vestibular cues to linear self-motion facilitate the detection of visual object motion during self-motion. Linear self-motion gives rise to a distinctive globally consistent pattern of motion on the retina known as optic flow. Independently moving objects in the scene will generate visual motion signals that deviate from the global pattern. Thus, observers must parse the optic flow in order to judge object motion during self-motion. The investigators found that thresholds for discriminating object motion in optic flow patterns were reduced when vestibular signals consistent with the linear self-motion depicted by the optic flow were presented simultaneously. In other words, vestibular signals facilitate optic flow parsing.

The research described above contributes to a better understanding of spatial orientation in general. The modeling review provides unique insights that will be valuable for developing and evaluating models to predict and investigate situations where spatial disorientation is likely to occur. The results of the experiments provide a better understanding of visual and vestibular perception of spatial orientation stimuli which may be applied to the development of countermeasures like better cockpit display technology, and improved motion simulations. The psychophysical methods employed could be used to develop novel techniques for crew training and evaluation.

experiment_title: Nutritional Countermeasures to Radiation Exposure
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Information generated from this research project will easily extend to Earth medical research. Individuals exposed to radiation on Earth, either through their profession, or for diagnostic or therapeutic radiation procedures will benefit from the knowledge gained. The results, and the questions derived from them, should provide avenues for research to address the types of diets that might enhance the risk associated with professional exposure to radiation. It will also determine if there are dietary recommendations that would protect individuals from the increased risk occurring from radiation exposure when it is used for diagnostic techniques. Another area of potential application includes developing dietary recommendations that would benefit individuals undergoing radiotherapy as a cancer treatment by increasing the susceptibility of the cancer cells to the treatment, while helping to protect the normal cells.

APPROACH:
The overall goal of this research program was to develop nutrition countermeasures to radiation-induced colon tumorigenesis, using male Sprague Dawley rats as a model system. Superimposed on the background of irradiation with Fe-ions or no irradiation was the injection of a known colon specific carcinogen, azoxymethane (AOM) in order to simulate the potential exposure to environmental contaminants. The diet interventions tested were combinations of a lipid component (fish oil versus corn oil) and a fiber component (pectin vs cellulose).

RESULTS:
During the last year of the study investigators completed the live animal component of the project, finalized tumor characterization, and completed the remaining laboratory assays. There were several key findings. At the initiation stage of colon tumorigenesis fish oil supplementation results in less oxidative DNA damage to colon cells than does corn oil as evidence by lower levels of 8-OHdeoxyguanosine levels. Investigators previously demonstrated lower levels of methylation damage to colon DNA. One mechanism by which fish oil elicits this response is by producing a more reduced colonic environment, so that when there is an oxidative insult, the apoptosis of DNA damaged cells is initiated. These changes in redox state over time were tracked by measuring the ratio of reduced to oxidized glutathione. At the promotion stage of colon tumorigenesis (aberrant crypt formation) the combination of fish oil and pectin results in a lower number of aberrant crypts and a lower number of high multiplicity aberrant crypts (those considered most predictive of future tumor development).

Apoptosis also plays an important role at this stage of tumorigenesis with pectin resulting in a greater proportion of cells undergoing apoptosis than cellulose (P=0.02). Radiation-induced changes in gene expression profiles (measured by microarray from mRNA of exfoliated cells) were observed for proteins involved in signal transduction (insulin receptor, PPARgamma coactivator 1, and prostaglandin E receptor 1) and antioxidant function (coenzyme Q). At the final tumor stage (31 weeks after the 2nd carcinogen injection) rats fed corn oil were 2.2 times more likely to have a tumor than those fed fish oil (P=0.02). Collectively, these data show that a specific diet intervention can be an effective countermeasure against radiation-enhanced colon tumorigenesis.

experiment_title: The Impact of Modeled Microgravity and Prior Radiation Exposure on Cytomegalovirus Reactivation and Host Immune Evasion
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The reactivation of latent herpes viruses poses a significant risk to the health and safety of the crew during exploration class space flight missions. Of particular concern is cytomegalovirus (CMV), which infects 50-80% of the US population and is known to cause significant morbidity and mortality in immunocompromised patients. CMV DNA is frequently found in the body fluids of astronauts during space travel indicating that the space flight environment can initiate active CMV infections. As space flight also causes huge alterations in the normal functioning of the immune system, CMV reactivation in a potentially immunosuppressed crewmember could have disastrous consequences during long-duration exploration class missions. The effects of microgravity on CMV replication and its potential to evade the host immune system are unknown. In this study, investigators will utilize the rotating wall vessel (RWV) cell culture system to simulate microgravity on Earth allowing them to study the virulent and infectivity properties of CMV and how it interacts with host immune cells in the absence of gravity. The investigators hypothesized that modeled microgravity wiould evoke changes in cellular gene expression that will underpin CMV reactivation and increase virus replication and infectivity. They further postulated that modeled microgravity would impair the anti-CMV responses of host T-cells and NK-cells that will allow viral persistence and replication to occur.

This study had the following specific aims:

1. Determine the effects of modeled microgravity and radiation on CMV replication and the expression of genes associated with latency and lytic activity.

2. Determine the impact of modeled microgravity and radiation on the anti-CMV activity of host Tcells and NK-cells.

3. Determine the impact of modeled microgravity on the anti-CMV activity of host T-cells and NK-cells.

APPROACH:

The methodology to address Specific Aim 1: Investigators determined the effects of simulated microgravity and/or radiation on: (i) CMV infectivity and viral yield using human MRC5 cells and low-passage clinical and laboratory CMV strains; (ii) reactivation of CMV during monocyte to dendritic cell differentiation; and (iii) the molecular profile of CMV-infected cells before and after differentiation by measuring viral transcripts of the latency-control locus and of select lytic and latent genes using a human CMV gene array.

The methodology to address Specific Aim 2: Investigators determined the effects of simulated microgravity and/or acute radiation exposure on: (i) CMV--specific T-cell expansion and their recognition and functional responses to CMV viral antigens; (ii) the cytokine secretion profile of expanded CMV-specific CTLs; (iii) NK-cell phenotypic shifts and cytotoxic activity against standard and CMV-specific target cells in vitro; (iv) NK-cell expansion in response to CMV and CMV infection analogs; and (v) the ability of CMV-specific NK-cells and secretory products from CMV-specific T-cells to curtail CMV reactivation, replication and infectivity.

RESULTS:

Findings from Specific Aim 1

The researchers established a positive infection model for Kasumi-3 myeloid progenitor cells using a low fibroblast passaged, BAC-derived TB40/E clinical strain of CMV. The virus is cell associated as confirmed by both real-time PCR and confocal imaging. Cultures are separated into cell pellet and supernatant fractions via high sped centrifugation, 14,000 x g, and the viral copy number is highest in the cell pellet fraction; confocal imaging confirms internalization of the virus. Lytic infection has been confirmed by direct single color antibody staining using mouse anti-human mab810X-AlexaFluor-488(IE-1) and flow cytometry. Additionally, Kasumi-3 cells pre-treated to 12 days of simulated microgravity (SMG) are seemingly resistant to initial infection at the early 12-24 hour time point, with viral copy numbers being consistently lower than non-treated controls.

Findings from Specific Aim 2

All Kasumi-3 cells from the CMV infection experiments (with and without SMG) have been cryopreserved for future DNA extraction and gene expression assays by RT-PCR. The researchers expect that any increase in CMV reactivation due to SMG or otherwise will be preceded by an expression of lytic genes and a downregulation of latent genes. They also expect to see latent gene expression increase following primary infection to indicate that the virus has become latent. Downregulated IE-1 expression should occur concomitantly with this.

Findings from Specific Aim 3

In the process of understanding the mechanistic underpinnings of suppression in NK cell function seen in the International Space Station (ISS) study, the researchers have established an in vitro model using a rotary cell culture system to simulate microgravity in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Using this model, they were able to show that microgravity adversely affects immune cell viability (<90% viable) after a 12-hour exposure to microgravity. Researchers have also replicated the suppression in NK cell function seen in crewmembers. NK cells exposed to microgravity (SMG) killed fewer cancer cells compared to NK cells exposed to both 1g (static) and a rotational control (RC) (for shear stress). This suppression in function was evident despite absence of any phenotypic differences among the three groups (SMG, static, and RC). Microgravity reduced NK cell perforin expression but did not affect their conjugation rate to target cells. Furthermore, the researchers  used cytometry-by-time-of-flight to look at various functional and maturation markers, which hinted at reduced degranulation and cytokine production in NK cells exposed to microgravity. They confirmed this using flow cytometry, discovering that microgravity lowered degranulation of cytotoxic granules (reduced CD107a+ expression) and suppressed TNF-a and IFN-gamma expression in NK cells that were exposed to cancer cells.

No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

experiment_title: Biological Water Treatment Technology: Integrated Evaluation of Submerged Bioreactor Technology
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This Technology Development Project proposes to evaluate a submerged membrane bioreactor (MBR) design for treatment of wastewater for space flight applications. The combination of membrane separation technology and stirred tank bioreactor results in a water treatment system that is compact with high effluent quality, making it an attractive option for ALS water treatment applications. The retention of solids, including bacteria, within the reactor results in higher biomass concentration and concomitant improvement in biodegradation efficiency. The long solids retention time allows for the cultivation of slow-growing organisms (i.e., nitrifying organisms) and causes a general reduction in the growth of new microbial biomass, reducing problems associated with continual accumulation of microbial biomass (i.e., sludge) observed in other reactor designs. Initial trials with the MBR during FY2002 found complete degradation of the organic load (i.e., surfactants) within the wastewater analog with a 12.6 hour hydraulic retention time, indicating that a 12-L reactor could process the simulated wastewater stream (urine, graywater, and atmospheric humidity condensate) from a 2-person crew. However, no nitrification was observed during the 65-day test, and significant abiotic precipitation was problematic. Since the nominal reactor pH was approximately 8.5, FY2003 activities will determine if pH control will increase nitrification and reduce precipitation. Concurrent studies will involve diluting the urine stream to determine if high ammonia levels are inhibiting nitrification. Follow-up studies will be conducted to determine the level of pH control and influent dilution necessary to achieve optimal organic degradation and nitrification in the single-stage reactor. The first set of tests will determine if nitrification and denitrification processes can be supported in the same reactor by reducing aeration rates, thereby limiting costs associated with supplying oxygen to the system. The second set of tests will evaluate reactor performance and system stability in response to variation in surfactant loading rates simulating temporal fluctuation of crew hygiene inputs. This work will include the addition of the antibiotic amoxicillin to determine the fate and effect of the antibiotic in the reactor. Amoxicillin is a potential contaminant of concern in the system as it is approved for crew use and is excreted in the urine following oral application. Research within the second year will focus on optimizing simultaneous nitrification/dentrification in both gravity-dependent and -independent (i.e., “bubble-less” aeration via membranes) designs, while the final year will concentrate on long-term performance (6-12 month) with actual wastewater streams. A major component of the work within all three years will be analytical efforts to characterize the organic/inorganic chemistry and microbiology of the system. Chemical analyses will be performed to evaluate the kinetics and degradation pathway of major organic constituents (i.e., surfactants), and to quantify the fate and effect of trace organic contaminants (e.g., amoxicillin). Development of new analytical procedures has been, and will continue to be, an important component of this work. Microbiological characterization efforts will involve determining the spatial distribution of community members responsible for nitrification and denitrification, and evaluating the potential microbiological risks associated with the 1) survival and growth of human-associated microorganisms within the system, and 2) development of antibiotic resistant organisms in response to antibiotic addition.

experiment_title: Adaptation to Space Motion Sickness by Means of Prism Goggles Training
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Nearly a century before astronauts first flew into orbit, people who donned inverting lenses reported dizziness, disorientation, miss-reaching for objects, and great queasiness, especially during rapid head movements. In the 1980’s, a ground-based motion sickness study conducted for the U.S. Air Force demonstrated the similar symptoms when subjects wore an up-down reversing prism. It was observed, however, that eye-hand coordination improved significantly after only one hour.

The objective of this experiment was to determine if astronauts’ experiences with space motion sickness were similar, in certain respects, to the experiences of a prism-wearer on earth. If the experiences shared some similarity, and because adaptation to prism-wearing has been demonstrated, it was hoped that astronauts could be pre-adapted before space flight using up-down reversing prisms. Adaptation would occur prior to flight by means of training on earth.

APPROACH:
Subjects were assessed for susceptibility to motion sickness, using a Visual Motion Sickness Rating Scale (VMSRS) developed by the principal investigator, performing head movement/eye fixation tests for up to six minutes while wearing a pair of up-down reversing prism glasses.

During the experimental phase, the training battery consisted of the following tasks and the VMSRS, and was given to the subject in the order listed below:

  • One Leg Balance Test
  • VMSRS
  • Eye-Hand Coordination Test: stack 8 small cubes
  • VMSRS
  • Gross Motor Coordination Test: stack large cubes
  • VMSRS
  • Catch ball on pendulum
  • VMSRS
  • Head Movement/Eye Fixation 80 bpm
  • VMSRS
  • Calisthenics
  • VMSRS

    Subjects were asked to rate their perceptions of dizziness, queasiness, and body unsteadiness on a 5-point VMSRS scale ranging from #1 (“I feel fine”) to #5 (“I am extremely dizzy/queasy/unsteady”) several times during this sequence of tasks. No one was asked to proceed to the point of illness. If at any time a subject reported #3 (“I feel moderately dizzy or I feel moderately queasy”) rating assessment, testing would stop with the subject being judged susceptible.

    After these tasks, the subjects were interviewed individually. Each was asked to compare, in detail, their in-flight experiences with the prism goggles. The determination that an astronaut experienced motion sickness was made when the astronauts: (1) said they were ill, and their description of symptoms fit the motion sickness profile; (2) took medication to alleviate severe symptoms; or (3) vomited.

experiment_title: VIIP Simulations of Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF), Hemodynamics and Ocular Risk (VIIP SCHOLAR)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Exposure to microgravity induces physiological and pathophysiological alterations, including Visual Impairment/Intracranial Pressure (VIIP) syndrome. VIIP can result in permanent loss of visual acuity and is a major health concern for crewmembers. Although short-duration crewmembers experience VIIP, the most severe pathology is experienced by long-duration flight crewmembers. Out of 30 long-duration crewmembers, 21 exhibited signs of VIIP syndrome and 1 crewmember has persistent visual acuity changes more than five years after mission completion. Twenty percent have the most severe clinical classifications of VIIP. The pathophysiology of VIIP is poorly understood, however, evidence shows that alterations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and vascular flow dynamics/pressure are associated with VIIP.

Although a sophisticated modelling framework (MONSTR Sim) that can predict certain clinically observed features of VIIP exists, not all VIIP features are replicated. Therefore, there is a need to improve current models. This experiment will aim to improve these models by incorporating more sophisticated descriptions of key physiologic and pathophysiologic processes. Additionally, tools to evaluate the effectiveness of countermeasures will be developed as well as how effectiveness varies from one astronaut to another. The existing set of integrated computer models will be enhanced by (1) informing models with novel in vivo measurements, (2) modeling individual-specific CSF and blood flow dynamics/pressure in microgravity with and without countermeasures, and (3) modeling insults to optic nerve axons due to CSF and blood pressure changes in microgravity. This study has the following specific aims:

  1. Measure key physiologic parameters needed for modeling, including effects of intracranial pressure on optic nerve sheath diameter, optic nerve tortuosity, craniospinal volume, and cerebral blood flow.
  2. Incorporate “quasi-1D” effects into existing compartment models, allowing us to evaluate the effects of microgravity and countermeasures on CSF and blood flows/pressures.
  3. Extend finite element models of ocular biomechanics, specifically modeling (i) optic nerve kinking and (ii) compression of optic nerve fiber bundles in the lamina cribrosa; and relate kinking/compression to an index of axoplasmic insult/stasis.
  4. Carry out parametric studies integrating the above models to identify individual-specific factors that: (i) predispose for the development of VIIP and (ii) influence the efficacy of proposed countermeasures, both useful for risk profiling.
APPROACH:

For specific aim 1, 20 patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) will undergo Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) before and after intracranial pressure (ICP) reduction by lumbar puncture. There will be two types of MRIs, anatomical and dynamic. The anatomical MRI will be a T2 and T1-weighted MRI while the dynamic MRI will be an axial PCMRI of the C2-C3 region. The same measurements will be obtained for ten healthy control subjects who undergo six-degree head-down tilt (HDT) before the baseline MRI session. An existing ultrasound data set that measured ONS diameter before and after HDT and after application of the Braslet-M countermeasure will be reviewed to provide input parameters for modeling and model validation.

For specific aim 2, the integrated digital astronaut program (DAP) cardiovascular system (CVS) and central nervous system (CNS) models will have the passive compartment formulations replaced with two active compartments. This will capture the effects of Valsalva and high intensity resistive exercise. Capabilities that enhance the lumped parameter models’ ability to simulate the effects of mechanical countermeasures, specifically short radius centrifuge devices, lower body negative pressure (LBNP) systems, and local occlusion systems will be added. The lower extremity compartments of the DAP lumped model will be modified to accept changes in external pressures. The pressure formulation will be modified to accept a nonzero reference of atmospheric pressure, and appropriate retraining of the lower compartment resistances and associated regulatory mechanisms. Acute and potentially chronic effects of typical space flight countermeasures on the fluid distribution in the CVS and CNS will be evaluated using data from studies in Specific Aim 1, reviews of empirical data from published studies, Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis, and parameter systems optimization learning processes.

For specific aim 3, preliminary models will be extended by incorporating improved models of dural biomechanical properties, parametrically studying the effects of optic nerve axial tension, and modelling the stabilizing effect of the optic nerve fibers and the pia mater on the buckling process. Initially, the mechanical effects of the arachnoid trabeculae will not be included until a critical level of ICP can be determined. Existing data from the MONSTR Sim study and novel phase contrast micro-CT scans that measured both the microanatomy of the lamina cribrosa and optic nerve sheath at different levels of intraocular pressure (IOP) and ICP will be used to understand the interactions between optic nerve axons and lamina cribrosa. The scans will be of the porcine and human eyes to allow the direct determination of tissue deformation as IOP and ICP are changed. The datasets will be used to build two-level hierarchical finite element models of the lamina cribrosa.

For specific aim 4, the input factors that influence mechanical responses of optic nerve head (ONH) and optic nerve tissues to the countermeasure will be identified. Mean values and ranges for the input factors will be specified then a treatment variable will be identified. Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) software will be used to generate suitable combinations of input parameter values for each treatment variable. The fluid pressures acting on the eye will be computed using the lumped parameter model for each combination of input factor variables. The finite element models will be used to compute outcome measures of interest based on the information from the lumped parameter model.

RESULTS:

The experiment is in progress. Results will be available at a later date.

experiment_title: 24-Hour Pattern of Blood Pressure and Heart Rate in Weightlessness
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objecitve of this experiment is to measure the pattern of blood pressure and heart rate during a 24-hr period in astronauts. The combined data from two instruments used in this experiment enabled the team to unravel the underlying physiology of circadian cardiovascular control in weightlessness. The experiment did so by taking repeated automatic measurements of upper arm cuff pressure with the Bloodpressure Measurement Instrument, continuous measurements of finger blood pressure with the Portapres hardware, and heart rate.

APPROACH:
The total duration of each experimental session was 24 hr hours. During each session the following activities were executed: recordings with the Bloodpressure Measurement Instrument (BMI) and with the Portapres continuous finger blood pressure recorder.

The following periods are of very high importance for science: - from the beginning of lunch until 30 minutes after the end of lunch - from the beginning of dinner until 30 minutes after the end of dinner - from one hour before the cosmonaut goes to sleep until a minimum of one hour after the transition awake-sleep. The recording could last until the end of the sleep phase if the battery capacity allows it. - from wake up until one hour after wake up.

The cosmonaut shall do his normal work during the day of the experiment. The in-flight part of the experiment was conducted in the Russian module of ISS, and was repeated twice at the beginning and at the end of the flight. The overall experiment has two preflight baseline data collection sessions. The postflight part of the experiment recorded return to normal gravity circumstances. This part was also performed twice.

RESULTS:
This study has shown that astronauts on short-lasting space flight may be subject to strong psychological stimuli. In particular ‘official’ moments like press-conferences can induce surges of blood pressure and heart rate. The authors recorded in-flight 24-hour profiles of BP and HR in 2 ESA-astronauts by automatic upper arm cuff measurements; in one astronaut this was combined with continuous finger blood pressure monitoring, which allows additional estimation of cardiac output and vascular resistance. The initial hypothesis was that spaceflight would show the same day/night changes as had been observed earlier in ground based (Head Down Tilted – HDT) simulation studies. However, unlike the simulations, BP and HR were not very much changed in-flight from preflight. Only daytime diastolic pressures (both subjects) and nighttime HR (for one subject) were significantly lower in-flight than preflight. Actual space flight did not confirm the earlier HDT findings for BP-levels and for daytime to nighttime changes. Daytime BP-levels were definitely higher than was expected; strikingly, BP- and HR-surges during the working days in space were often related to stressful moments like live media events, but were not restricted to these moments. The authors hypothesize that the busy work schedule of short-stay astronauts adds to the general level of arousal that is apparent from the measurements. This study shows that extensive in-flight cardiovascular measurements are feasible, even in busy astronauts, while they are performing their normal duties. From these observations, researchers have learned to take the psychological aspects of spaceflight more into account when judging the adaptation to microgravity. (Karemaker et al., 2009).
