experiment_title: Toxicological Assessment of Air Contaminants
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In 1995, the Mir space station had been in operation for almost a decade. This presented a unique opportunity to quantify the air pollutants that had accumulated within the spacecraft over a long time period. Russian toxicologists and analytical chemists measured air pollutants periodically inside the Mir using AK-1 (Tenax) sorbent traps. However, their ground-based gas chromatography methods of quantifying pollutants were designed to quantify only a portion of the pollutants suspected to be present in Mir. Interest in the Mir atmosphere was heightened by reports that benzene was present in quantities averaging above 1 mg/m3 during the Mir 10 mission (the U.S. standard for safe levels of atmospheric benzene is 0.2 mg/m3).

The objective of the Toxicological Assessment of Air Contaminants experiment was to assess whether the Mir atmosphere met the U.S. toxicological standards for air quality. This objective was accomplished by obtaining valid samples of the Mir atmosphere during the Mir 17 - 20 missions, analyzing those samples in a ground-based laboratory, and applying toxicological assessment methods for mixtures to the analytical results. In addition to this general assessment of Mir air, spatial variations would be measured from various points within the Mir space station. A well-designed spacecraft should contain few "dead volumes" where air movement is low and pollutants can accumulate. Since the crew's duties require them to work in all Mir modules, it is important to know whether their exposure to pollutants depends on their specific location within the Mir. Temporal variations in the atmosphere were also quantified so that future sampling protocols could be designed to detect important variations in pollutant concentrations. A final objective was to compare three methods of air sampling according to the pollutant concentrations found in samples taken simultaneously during the Mir 19 mission.

APPROACH:
During Mir 17, air samples were collected using the solid sorbent air sampler (SSAS), which consisted of seven samples tubes containing 500 mg of Tenax sorbent each. This sorbent trapped contaminants found in the atmosphere for analysis on Earth. Seven samples were collected on seven different days during the mission with sampling times from 23.0 to 24.3 hours in length per tube. Upon return to the Johnson Space Center (JSC) laboratory, the SSAS tubes were thermally desorbed at 210 degrees Celsius into proofed (verified clean), 4-inch SUMMA-treated canisters. The canisters were filled with clean, humidified air to 14.7 psia. Samples were then analyzed in duplicate using gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) methods to identify and quantify compounds found on board the space station.

During Mir 18, 19 and 20, air samples were collected using the SSAS, grab sample canisters (GSC), Russian AK-1 sorbent system (Mir 19 and 20 only) and formaldehyde badges. Grab sample canisters and formaldehyde badges were added to supplement data during these missions, because the SSAS was not able to quantitatively trap highly volatile contaminants, such as carbon monoxide and formaldehyde.

Instantaneous air samples were taken using the GSCs. Grab samples were collected at the central control post, and periodically during Mir 19 at the core module post N1. Late in the Mir 18 mission, five grab samples were taken in a 30 minute time span from attached modules to assess spatial variations. GSC samples were analyzed by gas chromatography for highly volatile compounds such as carbon monoxide, hydrogen and methane, and by GC/MS to identify and quantify approximately 80 targeted compounds and an unknown number of non-targeted compounds. The quality of gas chromatography data was assured by the analysis of blanks, generation of calibration curves and data tracking with control charts. Calibration curves up to 440 ppb (parts per billion) were performed on the GC/MS for all target compounds. GC/MS facilitates the identification and quantification of many more contaminants than gas chromatography alone.

Two instantaneous Institute of Biomedical Problems (IBMP) AK-1 system samples were acquired during Mir 19 from the core module, presumably by using a calibrated bellow pump to aspirate 500 ml of air through a tube that had been inserted into the pump inlet. The tube remained sealed before and after sampling.

Time integrated air samples were taken by the solid sorbent air sampler (SSAS) over 24-hour periods by electronic pulsing of a diaphragm pump which drew air through a sorbent tube. One sorbent tube was used per sampling session, and the SSAS device was off most of the flight. Start and stop times were recorded on the instrument by a crewmember. SSAS sample analysis was similar to GSC sample analysis. The air flow through each SSAS tube was measured before and after flight to determine the volume of spacecraft air sampled during the sampling period on orbit. SSAS tubes were also cleaned and proofed before flight. After flight, selected tubes were sent to Johnson Space Center (JSC) where they were heated to 200 degrees Celsius and desorbed into canisters by passing ultra-pure nitrogen at 10.1 ml/min for 20 minutes through the tubes. The canister pressure was measured and the analyses were completed by following the GC/MS method for canisters.

Formaldehyde badges were used to measure the amount of atmospheric formaldehyde. After removing the face covering, the badges were attached to the cosmonaut's uniform with velcro. The badge was worn while the cosmonauts were active for periods of 11.5 to 13.2 hours (by a Mir 18 crewmember on nine days separated by 1 to 2 weeks) and for 11.9 to 13.0 hours (by a Mir 19 crewmember on four days separated by 1 to 2 months). When the sample period ended, the badge was removed and resealed for analysis at the JSC laboratory. The exposed badges, as well as negative and positive control badges, were analyzed by aqueous extraction of formaldehyde from the badges and quantification by a chromotrophic acid colorimetric procedure. The atmosphere concentration was calculated from the known uptake rate of the badges and the exposure time on orbit.

Grab sample canisters (GSC) were subjected to several steps before launch. A high vacuum manifold tested each canister valve and fitting for leaks, then each was cleaned and proofed to less than 5 ppb for each contaminant quantified by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS). Finally, each canister was evacuated to a pressure of 0.00010 torr or less. Each SSAS tube was cleaned with ultrapure nitrogen at 250 degrees Celsius and proofed to <5 ppb for each GC/MS analyte. The SSAS was dosed with fluorobenzene and bromofluoromethane to assess the recovery of compounds sampled during the flight. The flow through each tube was measured in triplicate using a small volume of clean, humidified air. The Russian AK-1 tubes were cleaned and repacked after each use. The Tenax gas chromotography sorbent was solvent rinsed and heat-treated at 300 degrees Celsius before being packed into 150 mm x 5 mm inner diameter tubes. After packing, the tubes were heated again and purged with a stream of inert gas. Preparation of the formaldehyde badges included quantification of their uptake rate by comparison with an impinger method and dosing two positive control badges which served as trip surrogates.

Toxicological assessment of air quality was based on grouping atmospheric compounds into toxicological effect categories, such as irritants, neurotoxins and carcinogens. For the air to be considered safe to breathe, the T-value in each toxicological category could not exceed 1. The T-value was defined for "n" contaminants in a toxicological effect group (teg) based on the measured concentration of each contaminant (Cn) in the group and the spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMACn) for each contaminant, as given by the equation:

T(teg) = C1/SMAC2 + &Cn/SMACn.

SMACs in this equation were selected for the crew's exposure time. Typically, the appropriate SMACs for Mir expeditions were for 180 days of exposure. Only compounds whose concentration reached at least 1/100 of their long term SMAC were considered. This mathematical paradigm may be precise; however, it is founded on an assumption of additivity of similar toxic effects, which has never been proven for the vast majority of toxic chemicals. The additive assumption is reasonable as long as the compounds are grouped appropriately and the concentrations of each are only a small fraction of the SMAC.

Mir 18 air samplers were returned by the Space Shuttle on STS-71, and Mir 19 air samplers were returned on the Soyuz vehicle. Samplers returned via the Shuttle were maintained under strict chain-of-custody procedures used by NASA. The chain-of-custody for the samplers returned through Russia was not as well established and there were problems getting the samplers to JSC for analysis.

RESULTS:
Mir 17 results showed that only dichlorofluoromethane and ethanol were found at concentrations at or above 10 mg/m3. Ethanol showed a consistent pattern of declining concentrations during the mission. Only trichlorofluoromethane and octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane were found consistently at concentrations near or above 1 mg/m3. These four contaminants are not particularly toxic. Benzene, a contaminant of particular concern, was found at 0.01 mg/m3 or below in each of the seven samples.

During the Mir 18, Mir 19 and Mir 20 missions, the measured concentrations of most contaminants were reasonably consistent, that is there were not large temporal variations unless a new source of air pollution occurred, such as a new module opening or experiment startup. Data collected during Mir 18 on June 12, 1995, also indicated that spatial variations in pollution levels were less than 20%. In general, the atmospheric contaminants of Mir were greater than those found in the Space Shuttle, but the Mir contaminant levels still meet U.S. standards for all toxicological categories except mucosal (eye, throat and upper airways) irritants. In particular, formaldehyde, a mucosal irritant and carcinogen, was consistently found in concentrations above the U.S. and Russian limits of 0.05 mg/m3. The T-value for mucosal irritants was 1.57, which is slightly above the acceptable limit of 1.0, with formaldehyde contributing 1.2 units of this value. Since the formaldehyde SMAC was set to reduce the risk of mucosal irritation to less than 1/100, it is unlikely that the crewmembers experienced any mucosal irritation as a result of formaldehyde exposure. Formaldehyde measurements also suggest that cosmonauts may be exposed to relatively high concentrations at certain times. Although formaldehyde was handled during some experiments conducted in the general time frame of the measurements, this activity could not be specifically correlated with the high measurements. All ground-based test data indicate that badges were a valid method to determine formaldehyde concentrations.

With only a few exceptions, the concentrations of individual contaminants did not vary more than 2 to 3 fold in samples taken with the GSCs. For example, some of the ranges of the major contaminants were chloromethane (0.07 to 0.11), methanol (0.14 to 0.41), trichlorofluoromethane (0.23 to 0.58), toluene (0.08 to 0.19), o-xylene (0.12 to 0.23), hydrogen (11 to 27), acetaldehyde (0.15 to 0.32), acetone (0.24 to 0.67), n-butanol (0.14 to 0.36), m&p-xylenes (0.14 to 0.24) and methane (520 to 690).

Major trace contaminants that showed greater than a 3-fold variation include dichlorodifluoromethane, ethanol, isopropanol, octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane, perfluorodimethylcyclohexanes, hexamethylcyclotrisiloxane, limonene and carbon monoxide. Some of these variations were due to periodic use of these chemicals for utility purposes such as hand cleaning (ethanol), lens cleaning (isopropanol) and personal hygiene (siloxanes). Others were probably associated with the opening of newly delivered modules or experiment startup (freons) or with food consumption (limonene). The reason for variability in carbon monoxide concentrations is unclear.

A GSC sample taken during Mir 18 on June 4, 1995, showed a large "spike" (32 mg/m3) of perfluorodimethylcyclohexanes (Freon 82) in the air. The concentration of Freon 82 decayed slowly, reaching a concentration of 3.5 mg/m3 on June 29, 1995.

The second GSC sample taken during Mir 20 on November 13, 1995, showed a measurable concentration (0.06 mg/m3) of acrolein (propenal). The SMAC for this irritant was so low (0.03 mg/m3) that for this single sample the 180-day SMAC was exceeded. A single T-value above the acceptance level of 1.0 does not suggest poor air quality when all other values were well below 1.0. The sample was paired with one taken 2 minutes earlier and the earlier sample was similar except that it showed significantly less acrolein, furan and carbon monoxide. All three contaminants are known to be associated with pyrolysis of organic materials.

Two anomalies occurred during Mir 19. The three earliest GSCs were returned from Mir via the Soyuz, which landed in Russia. Considerable delay occurred in getting these samples out of Russia and delivered to Houston. The second problem encountered was that the earliest GSC used for sampling in the dining area was lost due to a valve leak, which was discovered during in-processing in the JSC Toxicology Laboratory.

The 24-hour, time-integrated samples obtained by the solid sorbent air sampler (SSAS) during Mir 19 tended to smooth some of the variability in the trace contaminant concentrations. For example, except for a single outlying value for each contaminant, the following ranges were found:
dichlorodifluoromethane (1.5 to 2.7), ethanol (0.7 to 1.3), isopropanol (0.17 to 0.47) and hexamethylcyclotrisiloxane (0.25 to 0.60). All concentrations of octamethylcyclotetra-siloxane fell within the range of 0.49 to 0.93 mg/m3.

Perfluorodimethylcyclohexanes and limonene still showed some variability even in the integrated samples. Because pollutant concentrations measured from the SSAS showed total T-values less than 1.0, there was no need to calculate T-values for individual toxicants.

When the SSAS was returned to the NASA/JSC Toxicology Laboratory after Mir 18, it was found that the inlet was obstructed by a "milky" material. The flows had been reduced to approximately 1/3 their preflight values. Since the time when the obstruction occurred was unknown, the volume sampled by the SSAS could not be measured with sufficient precision to meet quality control criteria; therefore, the data were not available in reportable form.

The GSC and SSAS sampling methods showed important differences, but most differences could be understood in terms of limitations in the trapping efficiency of Tenax for volatile compounds. The concentrations determined on 5 marker contaminants from 3 sampling sessions appeared to be comparable between the GSC and SSAS methods.

The results from the IBMP AK-1 tubes were not useful in understanding the temporal variations in contaminant concentration because only two samples were available for analysis. Furthermore, the concentrations appeared to be comparable for some contaminants (e.g. acetone, trichlorofluoromethane, dichloromethane, 2-butanone, benzene and decamethylcyclopentasiloxane), while others varied over orders of magnitude (e.g. acetaldehyde and propenal). Results suggest that the AK-1 sampling method does not give comparable results to the GSC or SSAS methods. It must be emphasized that these are very limited data, and there are a number of possible explanations for these differences that may not involve inherent differences in the methods. Although the samples were paired for the purposes of comparison, even a few minutes difference in sample times could result in some variation in the atmosphere sampled. The AK-1 tubes were not verified as clean by the JSC laboratory that did the final analysis, but it seems unlikely that such large differences could be due to residual contamination. The most likely possibility seems to be that the seals on the ends of the AK-1 tubes may have leaked, permitting air contaminants from Mir and other locations to concentrate on the sorbent during transport and storage. The Russians have noted this sort of difficulty in the past. Well-controlled, ground-based testing with thoroughly characterized atmospheres is the best way to compare the GSC, SSAS and AK-1 air sampling methods.

In conclusion, data indicates that the Mir air quality meets U.S. standards for spacecraft; however, reference data from the formaldehyde badges indicates that sources of formaldehyde may need to be identified and controlled. The concentrations of most air contaminants were relatively stable during the missions; however, some activities resulted in spikes in pollutant concentrations on this stable background. Much more frequent sampling would be necessary to detect most of these spikes and identify their sources. Except for formaldehyde, the spikes detected so far have been well below concentrations that could pose a concern about air quality. Early concerns about atmospheric benzene were never confirmed.

experiment_title: The Role of Artificial Gravity in Promoting Tissue-Regenerative Matrix-Integrin-Kinase Cell Signaling
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
The broad working hypothesis is that in space the mechanical unloading caused by microgravity can affect the growth and regenerative health of a broad range of mammalian tissues. Conversely, we hypothesize that gravity on earth activates a key, complex cell-signaling pathway responsible for maintaining normal regenerative tissue growth, the extracellular matrix(ECM)-integrin-kinase signaling pathway. The work we proposed was centered on the specific hypothesis that somatic stem cells responsible for tissue regeneration may require the mechanical stimulation of gravity to proliferate and differentiate, and to regenerate tissues at normal rates, and that microgravity may slow down tissue regenerative processes. Specifically this experiment will investigate the role of gravity-generated forces in promoting tissue regeneration, and the molecular mechanisms by which gravity in stem cells is translated into proliferation and differentiation. Ground artificial gravity studies were expanded to microgravity during rapid turnaround spaceflight opportunities in the Space Tissue Loss (STL1) and (STL2) experiments with stem cell differentiation. This work was integrated in the ongoing grant research expanding the artificial gravity approach to the questions to also include microgravity.

Specifically, the following aims are proposed to broadly test the hypotheses:
1) Gravity-dependent mechanical loading regulates cell proliferation and differentiation in the in-vivo newt tail regeneration model
2) Gravity-dependent mechanical-load signaling in somatic stem cell progenitors regulates their proliferation and differentiation in-vitro

APPROACH:
The Space Tissue Loss 2 experiment on STS-135 studies microgravity effects on keratinocyte differentiation from embryonic stem cells. The choice of keratinocyte differentiation as a model to study the effects of microgravity versus 1g on stem cell differentiation addresses the key question in Aim 2 for a specific cell type, which was not possible with the mixed-lineage embryoid body model flown on STL1, and in addition addresses the important issue of wound closure by keratinocytes in microgravity. Between April and July 2011, development and ground verification of the spaceflight protocol for differentiation of mouse embryonic stem cells into keratinocytes was completed before the STL2 keratinocyte experiment was flown on the final space shuttle mission, STS-135.

RESULTS:
Results for Aim 1 are reported in the publication “Gravity Mechanical Load Modulates Tissue Growth and Regeneration in the Newt Pleurodeles waltl.” Results from the Foton M3 spaceflight experiment were analyzed in the context of this experiment as part of obtaining results for tissue regeneration going from unloaded condition in aquaria, and microgravity, as well as under normal load at 1g and hypergravity at 2g. In total these results offer a very complete picture of responses to varying regenerative responses to increasing load, and of the importance and necessity of gravity for normal tissue regenerative processes.

For Aim 2, the cell biology results clearly show a gravity-dependent switch between stem cells and their functional differentiated descendents, and suggest microgravity is a strong inhibitor of regenerative processes. The results of from these studies are being prepared for publication.

This proposal has a companion spaceflight component entitled, "The Effects of Microgravity on the Tissue Regenerative Potential of Stem Cells--Flight." The spaceflight experiments are relevant to Aim 2.

experiment_title: Personal CO2 Monitor
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Carbon dioxide (CO2) can cause health problems on Earth as well as in space, with enclosed environments raising the most concern. Many industries require their workers to enter enclosed environments, where environmental monitoring is critical to worker safety - mining, submarines, construction, inspection, and many other fields. The Personal CO2 Monitoring system may be applied to these fields, and with the addition of an alarm system may serve as a warning device for hazardous conditions. The wearable device is designed in such a way as to allow the CO2 sensing element to be replaced by another sensor, enabling a range of personal monitoring applications. The intentional focus on a very small form factor and comfortable body attachment method, make the device particularly well-suited for continuous wear.

Carbon dioxide is a particularly challenging gas to deal with in space. Humans produce CO2 through the natural breathing process, but too much CO2 in the air can cause headaches, dizziness, increased blood pressure, and much more severe symptoms. Human spacecraft must be designed with environmental control systems that remove CO2 from the air that their crews breathe, but the space environment can still lead to "pockets" of CO2 that are difficult to detect and remove. Additionally, recent research has indicated the space environment may make astronauts more sensitive to CO2, meaning symptoms may be more severe or may become apparent at lower concentrations than on Earth.

The objectives of this study are:

  1. To demonstrate the capability to unobtrusively collect individual crewmembers CO2 exposure.
  2. To evaluate wearability principles in microgravity.
  3. To demonstrate Modular Wearable Architecture Base Board, allowing rapid certification of future wearable devices.

APPROACH:
The Personal CO2 Monitor will demonstrate a new capability on the International Space Station (ISS) - continuous monitoring of the astronauts' immediate surroundings. The astronauts will attach specially designed CO2 sensors to their clothing and wear them continuously for days to weeks. The sensors will wirelessly send CO2 data to the astronauts' iPads, where mission controllers can download it for researchers. With this new individualized data, researchers will be able to gain a better understanding of the impact of CO2 on human health in space, impacting the ISS, and future spacecraft designs. In addition to monitoring CO2, the investigation also seeks to learn more about how to design wearable technology for human space flight. Devices that are to be put on the body for a long time must be comfortable. Without gravity and with the changes to the human body in space, designing comfortable wearable technology for astronauts is a challenge. Observation and feedback from astronauts on the "wearability" of the Personal CO2 Monitor in space will help engineers and designers create more appropriate wearable technology for future space missions.

RESULTS:
Results will be available at a later date.

experiment_title: Bone Cell Activity During Spaceflight and Recovery
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Microgravity associated with spaceflight has been shown in numerous experiments to be associated with marked skeletal changes, ranging from decrease in bone volume to alterations in biomechanical properties. However, little attention has been given to bone tissue recovery that follows spaceflight after return to Earth's gravity. In addition, how microgravity affects bone metabolism at the cell level has only been assessed by histological techniques: studies of osteoblastic cell number and differentiation in spaceflight animals have not been performed. This study investigated the effects of microgravity and subsequent recovery on trabecular bone morphology and compared histomorphometric parameters on caudal vertebrae with the behavior of vertebral osteoblastic cells in culture.

Approach:

Two groups of five rats were flown on SLS-2, one group was sacrificed after landing, the other after a recovery time equal to the flight (14 days). Histomorphometric measurements were made on caudal vertebrae, thoracic vertebrae and the left humeri. Lengths, volumes and wet weights were measured. Trabecular volume, thickness, and spacing was measured using vertebral bodies and humeral metaphyses. Osteoid thickness was measured. Osteoid, osteoblast and osteoclast surfaces were measured. Caudal vertebral bone cells were isolated and cultured. Cultures were evaluated for cell growth and phenotype. The proliferation rate was determined by cell number. Cell alkaline phosphatase activity (ALP) and osteocalcin production, two parameters of osteoblast differentiation, were determined in confluent cells isolated from the caudal vertebrae.

Results:

Humeral weight and length showed normal growth during the experiment and were unaffected by spaceflight or recovery from spaceflight. However, spaceflight resulted in inhibition of static indexes of bone formation in humeral proximal metaphyses and thoracic vertebral bodies. This was associated with a decrease in bone volume in humeral metaphyses. After 14 days of recovery on Earth, osteoblastic and osteoid surfaces returned toward normal and bone volume was normalized in humeri, whereas the static bone formation parameters were not restored on thoracic vertebrae. In addition, histological indexes of bone formation and osteoblastic cell growth in vitro were not affected by spaceflight in caudal vertebrae. The rat humeri and thoracic and caudal vertebrae exhibit different patterns of response to spaceflight and subsequent on-Earth recovery, which could be due, at least in part, to the different loading pattern of these bones, and to differences in bone turnover rate.

experiment_title: The Influence of Space Flight on Erythrokinetics in Man
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A consistent finding after exposure to microgravity has been a significant reduction in red blood cell mass. Erythropoietin was measured during the Spacelab 1 mission and was found to be decreased on the 8th day of flight and on landing. For SLS-1, erythrokinetics were studied before, during and after the exposure to microgravity. Measurements included plasma volume, red blood cell mass, red blood cell survival, iron kinetics, erythropoietin levels, ferritin levels and routine hematology parameters.

APPROACH:
Data were collected in the following sessions:
Preflight
Iron Kinetics, Red Blood Cell Mass and 51-Cr RBC T1/2, Hematology, Plasma Volume, Body Mass Measurement, Plasma Proteins
Inflight
Iron Kinetics, 51-Cr RBC T1/2, Hematology, Plasma Volume, Body Mass Measurement, Plasma Proteins
Postflight
Iron Kinetics, Red Blood Cell Mass and 51-Cr RBC T1/2, Hematology, Plasma Volume, Body Mass Measurement, Plasma Proteins

RESULTS:
During flight, each of the three subjects studied had a significant decrease in red blood cell mass and plasma volume. The decrease in plasma volume occurred during the first day of flight. Erythropoietin levels decreased during the first 24 hours and remained low throughout the mission. The rates at which labeled red blood cells were removed from the circulation were similar before and during spaceflight. The rate of dilution of the labeled cells by new red blood cells was markedly decreased during spaceflight when compared to the rate measured preflight. The rate of production of new red blood cells (measured with radioiron) within the bone marrow was similar after one day of spaceflight to the rate observed three months preflight and postflight. During spaceflight there was a reduction in the number of newly formed red blood cells in the circulation as indicated by reduced 59-Fe red blood cell incorporation and reduced reduced rate of change in the specific activity of older 51-Cr tagged red blood cells.

experiment_title: Spaceflight Effects on Mammalian Development
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The purpose of this study was to observe the in-flight activity of pregnant dams in order to obtain quantitative comparisons of the frequency and duration of definable species-typical behavior patterns in microgravity, with special attention to activities that can affect subsequent maternal behavior and fetal development. One objective was to observe post-flight activity of pregnant dams to assess the changes in activity profiles of flight dams as they re-adapt to the 1-g stresses, relative to the postures and established categories of maternal activities of the ground control animals. Another objective was to determine whether dams that have undergone surgeries and muscular deconditioning from microgravity exposure during pregnancy can give birth vaginally. The final objective was to quantitatively assess the vestibular and tactile function in flight pups for various postnatal days after normal delivery (or C-section delivery).

Approach:

Upon landing, each dam was videotaped for 1 minute and then transferred to surgery for unilateral hysterectomy (G20/21). Following three rounds of vestibular testing, each fetus was tested for tactile sensitivity. Between recovery day and gestational day 23, remaining flight dams were observed and videotaped to determine any quantitative changes in activity profiles as readaptation to 1 G proceeds Dams were allowed to deliver naturally. On recovery day 0, pups were tested for symmetrical and asymmetrical labyrinthine stimulation. On recovery day 1, pups were used for heart rate studies of vestibular responsivity to tilt and to tactile stimulation. On recovery day 2, pups were tested for head nystagmus responses to rotation. On recovery day 3, pups were tested for symmetrical and asymmetrical labyrinthine stimulation.

Results:

The flight dams observed on in-flight video records displayed seven more times rolling movement than controls, probably due to the increased number of surfaces available in microgravity. Immediately postflight, flight dams in general moved less. Flight dams had uncomplicated, and successful vaginal deliveries, and had similar size litters. However, flight dams had significantly more lordosis contractions probably related to spaceflight muscle atrophy. Pups had no difference in the success or latency of the righting response indicating the flight groups retained the ability to orientate themselves with respect to gravity. Flight pups tested on day 3, had a diminished water righting response, but flight pups tested on day 5 could not be distinguished from control animals. Flight pups showed the same response as controls during the rotary stimulus, but were less-likely to perform the post-rotary righting response.

experiment_title: Evaluation of Functional Skeletal Muscle Performance Following Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Muscular deconditioning after long exposure to microgravity could interfere with the safe completion of critical tasks during space flight or during emergency or routine landing or egress. The objective of this study was to evaluate changes in the strength of the arm muscles after space flight and to determine whether extravehicular activity during flight affects those changes.

APPROACH:
Before and after space flights of 9 to 14 days, the strength of the arm muscles of three astronauts who performed extravehicular activities during flight and one who did not was assessed. The muscles that act on the elbow and the muscles that turn the forearm and wrist were tested with LIDO isokinetic dynamometers. These dynamometers provide variable resistance so that movements continue at the same speed (i.e., they are isokinetic) regardless of the force applied. Both concentric and eccentric strength were measured. Concentric strength is the strength of a muscle as it contracts to move a body part, while eccentric strength is the strength of the muscle as it is gradually lengthened while resisting the motion of a body part.

RESULTS:
The astronauts who took part in extravehicular activity, as well as in the astronaut who did not, appeared to experience operationally relevant losses (>10%) of arm strength. However, the changes were not statistically significant. The effects of EVA on muscle performance require further study. Loss of muscle mass during space flight could increase the risk of injury during routine activities. According to rehabilitation standards, 40% of the astronauts were at increased risk of a back injury, and 20% were at increased risk of a leg injury. Because these standards are based on losses in a single muscle group, while space flight affects many major muscle groups, the risks may be even higher.

experiment_title: Chronic Recording of Otolith Nerves in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The goals of this study were to record the responses of primary afferents of the otolithic organs to document otolithic organ response dynamics in normal gravity and in microgravity. Studies of these aspects of the vestibular system and its efferent control can add to our knowledge of its function and may suggest future therapies for control of Earth-bound motion sickness.

APPROACH:

Experimental difficulties precluded obtaining useful inflight data as originally planned. However, fish were received within 8 hours of the Shuttle return to Earth and utricular nerve afferents recorded sequentially for 5 days postflight. For this, anesthetized, paralyzed toadfish underwent a small craniotomy to allow the implantation of glass micro-electrodes (2 M LiCl2), in the nerves innervating the utricle. Records of primary afferents in response to linear acceleration were taken. Position and motion of the fish were documented by linear and rotary potentiometers.

RESULTS:

Results from STS-95 were combined with those from Neurolab for a total of four experimental subjects. Control responses were obtained from three fish that did not fly. For flight subjects, the magnitude of response to an applied linear acceleration was on average three times greater than for controls within the first day postflight. By 30 hours post flight, responses had returned to normal and were statistically similar to controls. Directional selectivity appeared unaffected by exposure to microgravity. To examine for possible recording bias, all measured parameters were compared between control and post flight afferents; no statistical difference was found in the range and mean of afferent discharge rate and regularity of discharge between postflight and control fish. Thus the reduced gravitational vector and linear acceleration in orbit apparently resulted in an up-regulation of the sensitivity of utricular afferents. More tests must be done to determine whether a specific population of afferents demonstrated increased sensitivity or whether this finding is a general feature of all classes of cells. The original plan called for the implementation and perfection of a sieve electrode to allow for continuous recording of afferents during flight. Presently although experimental difficulties precluded the completion of the entire original plan, the perfection and utilization of the sieve electrode was achieved.

experiment_title: Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency-Education Payload Observation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency-Education Payload Observation (EPO) investigation is to use EPO materials in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station (ISS) to create educational videos, multimedia products and artistic goods that inspire the general public. These activities will enlighten the general public about microgravity research and human space flight. JAXA understands that the Japanese Experiment Module (JEM) on the ISS is useful not only for scientific investigations, but will also provide inspiration for writers, poets, teachers, and artists. The products will be distributed to the schools or exhibited in museums. The JAXA-EPO activities that will be conducted on various increments are as follows:

Life in the Universe: This experiment will investigate the effects of the space environment on board the ISS to the flown zooplankton eggs (Daphnia, water flea and Triops, tad pole shrimp) and plant seeds (Ipomoea nil, Japanese Morning Glory; Lotus japonicus, Bird's Foot Lotus; Arabidopsis thaliana, Thale Cress; Helianthus annuus, sunflower). The eggs and seeds remain on board the ISS inside the JEM. Photos are taken by the crew to document their conditions. The eggs and seeds are returned to Earth for distribution to schools and museums to enlighten children about science and space.

Space Poems Chain: This consists of a collection of poems composed by famous poets and the general public, recorded on a DVD, and stored on board the ISS in the JEM.

Microgravity Clay: The inspiration of space and the human space flight will be shown by clay figures. Videos and photos are taken by the crewmember to document the experiment. The dried figures are returned to Earth and used as art for a tribute to space flight.

Aquasphere: The motion of a water sphere will be recorded after external oscillations in microgravity environment with a HDTV camera.

Ink Ball: This demonstration will record and obtain the flow of ink on the water sphere.

Art with HDTV: Imagery will be obtained with HDTV, which will be returned to Earth for examination and used to create an intuitive image of the space environment.

Space Clothes: This will investigate the restriction of movement by clothes and obtain basic data. This line of clothing is threaded with anti-bacterial and deodorizing materials. The clothes are designed to absorb water, insulate the body and dry quickly. They are also flame-resistant and anti-static.

Educational Experiment: The Japanese astronaut will conduct simple activities (e.g. record the flight of a paper plane on the ISS) requested by Japanese children. The objectives are to enlighten the general public in human space flight.

Photographing the Moon: Images of the moon will be captured from the ISS. After they are returned to Earth, a musical score will be composed to match the images.

Spiral Top: The aim is to record the motion of a spinning top onboard the ISS.

Hiten (Dance): Ancient east Asian dances will be performed by crewmembers. These performances will be video recorded.

Try Zero-G: Simple experiments will be conducted for the Japanese people, primarily for children, to show the difference of the phenomenon between 0-G and 1-G.

Dewey’s Forest: This is intended to show how gravity controls the laws of nature and influences our ways of thinking. The project is a catalyst to rediscover human relationship with plants on the ground and the age old history of our gardens.

experiment_title: Toxicological Assessment of Airborne Volatile Organic Compounds
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts living for an extended period of time in a closed environment, such as the Mir Space Station, are continuously exposed to pollutants in respirable air. Pollutants originate from material off-gassing, human metabolism, systems and payload leaks, and utility chemicals. If pollutant concentrations reach high levels, crewmembers may experience health problems and scientific experiments could be confounded. This experiment was designed to sample the Mir Space Station air at various locations and times in order to estimate the effects of airborne pollutants on crew health. The following were objectives of this experiment:

  • Determine if Mir air meets U.S. standards for crew health during long-term exposure to trace contaminants
  • Sample air using several types of hardware to compare similarity of sampling methods
  • Sample Mir Space Station air at multiple locations simultaneously to assess spatial variations in the Mir complex
  • Measure ethylene concentrations to determine if plant growth experiments could be affected.
  • Assess the rate of pollutant mixing after hatch opening between shuttle and Mir.

    APPROACH:
    In-flight air sampling was performed on NASA-Mir 2-7. Instantaneous air samples were obtained using grab sample containers (GSCs), and 24 hour time-averaged air samples were obtained using solid sorbent air samplers (SSASs). Formaldehyde badges were used to measure formaldehyde concentrations throughout Mir.

    The GSCs and SSASs were tested preflight at the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Toxicology Laboratory to ensure that each sampler was clean and could perform as expected. Formaldehyde badges were tested, reconfigured to fit the NASA flight configuration, and packaged for use during flight.

    During flight, GSC and SSAS samples were taken approximately every thirty days. After each sampling session, the date, time, and location were recorded. Once during each mission, a spatial variation assessment was performed by sampling multiple modules simultaneously. The formaldehyde badges were worn by the crewmembers and also placed in the individual modules.

    Upon return to Earth, the GSC samples were analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) and a modified EPA TO-14 gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) method. The GC analysis was used to estimate ethylene concentrations. The SSAS samples were analyzed only via the GC/MS method. The filters were removed from the formaldehyde badges and extracted with formaldehyde-free water. The aqueous extracts were then analyzed for formaldehyde using a chromotropic acid-spectrophotometric method.

    RESULTS:
    The air quality on NASA-Mir 2-7 met, and exceeded, U.S. standards for human-rated spacecraft. However, the irritant group was slightly above a toxicity index of 1 during NASA-Mir 2, 6, and 7, and the carbon dioxide toxicity index was above 1 during NASA-Mir 2 and 3. The toxicity index was calculated for each toxicological group by summing the ratios of the measured concentrations to the space maximum allowable concentrations for each contaminant in a toxicological group. The high toxicity index of the irritant group was due in part to high concentrations of formaldehyde.

    As hypothesized, spatial variations of contaminants were small within the Mir complex for both SSAS and GSC samples. The variations were most likely caused by contaminants localized in the different modules. The rate of pollutant mixing after hatch opening between Shuttle and Mir could not be established because of too few samples. A comparison of the U.S. and Russian air sampling methods showed that the Russian AK-1 sorbent system samplers, on average, measured higher concentrations than did the U.S. samplers.

    During the course of this experiment, several opportunities arose that allowed scientists to study situations that had previously been unexamined. During NASA-Mir 4, a fire was caused by the solid fuel oxygen generator (SFOG); this presented an opportunity to study the contaminants released into the Mir atmosphere due to the fire, and also assess how well the life support system scrubs contaminants from the air. The life support system worked excellent and brought the pollutants associated with the fire back to baseline concentrations within 32 hours. During NASA-Mir 4 the investigators also had the opportunity to compare the results of the formaldehyde badges to those of the formaldehyde active sampler (FAS). Because of the difficulties involved with collecting inflight formaldehyde samples, conclusive results were not obtained. However, another opportunity arose to compare these two methods during the second phase of the Lunar Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP). The results of this test verified the validity of the badges when compared to other methods.

    During NASA-Mir 5, all sampling hardware was lost due to the decompression of the Spektr module. The focus of the experiment then changed to analyzing how well the humidity control system would scrub a large concentration of ethylene glycol from the air. It was hypothesized that ethylene glycol present in Mir air due to a leak would be removed quickly. However, ethylene glycol detector tubes were used to measure ethylene concentrations, and it took one month for the concentration to drop below the 180-day SMAC level. Additionally, ethylene concentrations measured by the GSCs during the other NASA-Mir missions were determined to be high enough to affect plant growth experiments.

    The final unscheduled event occurred during a low temperature catalytic oxidizer (LTCO) burn. Improper operation of the LTCO caused dangerously high levels of carbon monoxide (CO) to be released into the Mir atmosphere. The combustion products analyzer (CPA) recorded high levels of CO, but because the crew appeared to be doing well after the incident, the high levels were thought to have been caused by hydrogen interference. Because this was such a serious toxicological incident, many steps have been taken to prevent a reoccurrence. One step, which will be used on the International Space Station (ISS), is the use of a new CPA that has much less cross sensitivity to hydrogen.

experiment_title: Biomechanical Countermeasure for Disuse Osteopenia
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The osteoporosis which develops in microgravity is one of the greatest hurdles to an extended human presence in space. Earth-based animal and human studies have demonstrated that extremely low magnitude mechanical stimuli (LMMS), if imposed at a high frequency, is strongly anabolic to the skeleton, and can serve to inhibit the bone loss, which typically parallels disuse. This experiment is designed to evaluate the efficacy of this unique biomechanical countermeasure to inhibit the disuse-induced osteoporosis seen in long term bed-rest, the closest ground based equivalent of microgravity. To achieve this in a non-invasive, non-pharmacologic means would have tremendous impact not only in space, but would also address the bone loss which plagues over 20 million people world wide each year on earth.

Project Aims: 1) Show that application of low magnitude (0.3g), high frequency (30Hz) mechanical stimulation, will reduce the loss of bone seen with long term disuse 2) Show that application of low magnitude, high frequency mechanical stimulation will improve the postural control of subjects undergoing long term bed-rest 3) Determine if long term bed-rest affects the sensitivity of the lower extremities. Determine if the application of low magnitude, high frequency mechanical stimulation will inhibit the changes if they exist.

APPROACH:
This study is aimed at showing that LMMS can reduce the physiological changes seen in bone and postural control during long term bed rest. To perform these tests, control subjects undergoing 90 days of bed-rest will be tested at 0, 60, and 90 days of bed rest. Control groups will undergo mechanical stimulation for 10 minutes a day, 5 days a week for the duration of the study, with measurements taken at the same time points.

Stimulation is performed using an oscillating platform. The platform is designed to vibrate at a rate of 30 Hz, at an amplitude of 0.3 g, with doses of ten minutes each day. Typically, the subject stands on the platform, which is roughly the size and shape of a bathroom scale, for their daily treatment. However, in bed-rest as in space, the subjects do not have gravity pulling them to the plate. To overcome this, the plate will be hung on its side from a moving platform. This platform can be moved from room to room. The subject will put on a padded vest, which will then attach to the plate via two springs, one at each side of the plate. The springs will apply a force to the subject’s shoulders, coupling them to the plate. The magnitude of the applied force will be equal to 60% of the subject’s body weight. In previous work,at 60% body weight, a subject will undergo stimulation of 70-80% of the magnitude seen when standing on the plate under the effects of gravity. Balancing subject comfort and signal magnitude was the rational for settling at this number.

Postural Control: analysis of postural control was performed using a Kistler force plate. The force plate contains four piezoelectric load cells. The plate can detect forces in the vertical and both horizontal directions, as well as all three moments. When a subject stands on the plate, small shifts in posture result in changing forces applied to the plate. The location and magnitude of the resultant of these applied forces is recorded and defined as the Center of Pressure (COP). The subject stands barefoot on the plate with their hands at their sides. Foot placement is defined by a set of markings on the surface of the force plate, with the feet slightly spread and splayed outward at 10 degrees. The subject closes their eyes, and stand as still as they can with their head forward for 4 minutes. After 5 minutes of rest, the measurement is repeated with the subject’s eyes open. A marker is placed on a wall 2 meters from them at eye level, and they are instructed to focus on the marker for the duration of the measurement. The force plate output was recorded at 50 Hz using the Kistler Bioware software, used to convert the forces recorded by the force plate to COP.

Nerve sensitivity: the sensitivity of the foot is related to the balance of an individual. Those with diminished sensitivity have an increased risk of falling. To determine if the daily applications of LMMS will have an effect on the sensitivity of the feet and ankles, the following tests were performed:

a. Monofilament light touch sensitivity: A Weinstein Enhanced Sensory Test (WEST) foot monofilament set was used to perform this test. The device consists of a pen-sized stick with 5 plastic monofilaments attached perpendicularly, which can be rotated to select a single filament. The filaments are each of a different thickness. This test is performed with the subject lying in bed. The subject’s non-dominant foot is used, the subject is barefoot and eyes closed. The tester then lightly presses the filament against the skin on the foot of the subject, just enough so that a small indentation is made. The subject states where they feel the touch. The tester will not prompt the subject, if they don’t feel the touch, then it is counted as a failed identification. If the subject names an incorrect location, it is counted as a failure. The test is done randomly across different locations of the foot including the big toe, small toe, heal, ankle, and metatarsal heads. Before the test is performed, each location is touched with the thickest filament with the subject’s eyes open, so they know what sensation to expect. The test is performed with all 5 filaments, starting with the thickest, and working down.

b. Two Point Discrimination: The Touch-Test Two-Point Discriminator is used in this test, designed to determine the smallest distance that a subject can identify as two separate points. As with the monofilament test, this is performed first on the subject with their eyes open, so the subject is aware of how to perform the test. The test is performed again with the subject’s foot bare and eyes closed. The skin of the subject’s foot is lightly touched with the chosen size, until a slight indent in the skin is made. The subject then states if they feel one or two points. If they detect one, but two points are used, the next largest gap is chosen. If they detect two, the next smallest is chosen. This is repeated until the smallest gap that they can correctly detect 50% of the time is found. The next larger gap is given as the smallest detectable distance. This test is performed at 5 locations on the foot: the large toe, small toe, heel, first metatarsal head, and fourth metatarsal head.

c. Joint Pronation: The tester grips the subject’s large toe gently at the first joint, with one finger on each side. The tester grips the subject’s ankle to keep it from bending. The subject is told to relax, so that the tester can freely move the toe joint. When the subject has loosened their muscles, the tester will bend the toe joint in small, 5 degree angles. The subject states if they felt the toe move up or down. The toe is moved rapidly up and down at random in the same small angle changes 15 times. The number of incorrect answers is counted. If the subject delays more than a second before answering, it is counted as incorrect. This test is also performed with the ankle joint of the subjects if they fail more than 30% of the time at the toe. In this case, the tester will steady the leg of the subject at mid-calf, then grips the foot of the subject at the bony processes at each side of the foot below the large and small toe. The test protocols are identical, except that the ankle joint is rotated up or down at 5 degree intervals instead of the toe. For both cases, all motion is kept close to the middle range of motion of the joint, the joint will not be hyper- or hypo-extended.

d. Vibration Sensitivity: A vibration sensation exam was performed using two tuning forks. One fork has a natural frequency of 30 Hz, the second at 256 Hz. The tester strikes the fork to make it vibrate, while holding it at its neck. The base of the neck is held against the boney process below the large toe of the subject’s foot. This is repeated with the second fork, so that the subject has felt each with their eyes open. When this is done, the subject closes their eyes. The subject will then be stimulated with each fork five times with their eyes closed. The order of the forks will be random. The subject will be asked if it is the high or low frequency fork. The number of correct choices will be recorded. This will be repeated at the ankle as well.

Quantitative Ultrasound measures the properties of bone by passing an ultrasound signal through the bone, thus is a measurement of bone density. Measurements are performed on the non-dominant ankle of each subject. Depending on the density and structure of the bone, the magnitude of the signal that will be attenuated will change. Also, the velocity of the signal which exits the bone will be affected as well. By analyzing these two parameters, information on the quality of the bone can be ascertained. Measurements are performed using an ultrasound scanning device designed and built in our laboratory. The subject sits with their foot in a water bath to help couple the ultrasound signal. Ultrasound transducers scan the region of interest. CT Scans BMD of the lumbar spine (L1-4), right and left proximal femur (neck, trochanter, and Wards triangle, total proximal femur), and non-dominant radius (distal third) will be measured by CT scan. The method and location of the scans are designed to match those performed are part of the standard routine of examination of astronauts returning from space.

RESULTS:
Following one year of support, data have been collected from bedrest subjects (control), as the first stage in evaluating efficacy of a unique, non-pharmacologic countermeasure for disuse osteoporosis. This low magnitude (0.3g), high frequency (30Hz) mechanical signal has been shown to be anabolic to bone.

The team determined that application of mechanical stimulation can be achieved in a supine individual. By attaching a supine subject to the vibrating plate through a harness and spring system, coupling between the feet of the subject and the top surface of the plate is achieved. As the load applied to the shoulders of the subject increases, the magnitude of stimulation the subject undergoes increases. This was determined by attaching an accelerometer to a bite-bar to measure the acceleration of the subjects head. By comparing this to the acceleration of the surface of the plate, the percent transmission of the signal was calculated. With 60% of the subject’s body weight applied to their shoulders, the transmission is approximately 70-80% of that of a subject standing on the plate under the effects of gravity.

Foot sensitivity: The tests of the sensitivity of the foot showed that each subject had a typical sensitivity of a healthy individual. Comparisons will be made with those after extended bed-rest to determine if disuse causes a change in sensitivity.

Bone Density : Scans were performed on the non-dominant ankle by quantitative ultrasound. Broadband Ultrasound Attenuation (BUA) and Ultrasound Velocity (UV) were calculated from the raw data. Both are indicators of the structure and composition of the bone. The more dense the bone is, the more signal will be attenuated and slower the velocity will be. Thinner, less structured bone will attenuate signal less, and have an overall greater velocity.

Postural Control: Postural measurements at day zero were made on four control subjects. Postural data consists of Center of Pressure (CoP) information collected using a Kistler force plate. CoP is defined as the location of the ground reaction force under the feet of the subject. Figure 9 shows 4 minutes of CoP measurement for one of the subjects with their eyes closed. Data show that the subject sways mostly in the anterior/posterior direction. From the CoP recording, measurements of ML and AP sway magnitude and velocity, total path length, and frequency composition were made. These numbers give us information on the nature of the postural control of the subject. A subject with a larger sway magnitude and velocity will be a greater risk of falling than a subject who sways less. Day 0 measurements show all control subjects have postural control of a typical healthy adult.

Overall, this investigation collected data for four healthy controls. Follow-on bedrest studies were performed.
