experiment_title: Crew Task Simulation for Maintenance, Training, and Safety
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Ambitious space missions presented new challenges for space human factors as crews interact with and maintain complex equipment and automation. This demands that procedures for task design, rehearsal, and procedure refreshing be based on on-ground validated procedure instructions. This experiment investigated requirements for formulating, interpreting, and validating procedure instructions. Crew instructions should express clearly and unambiguously complex actions and their expected results. As NASA moves toward a "what to do" rather than a "how-to-do" approach, it is essential that textual instructions convey what is meant and correlate with equipment function and construction. Natural language instructions must coordinate with graphical simulations to provide both textual and visual guidance and context-sensitivity for procedures, especially when the equipment functions and features are accessible to the simulation. Current manuals and procedures need all alternatives to be made explicit, leading to documentation which must be laboriously prepared in advance. Any documentation for a complex procedure should "understand" the equipment and the human factors of the crew. One important aspect of "what-to-do" procedure documentation is that purposes and termination conditions of continuous processes are very frequently cited. These need to be generated from or interpreted by simulated actions. Although the focus in this project has been on ground-based procedure execution and validation, it is envisioned that future applications for spaceflight crews will use natural language to communicate with each other, the on-board automation, and to training and refresher simulations. The specific research goals were to use various user interfaces -- such as natural language instructions or virtual reality -- to control virtual crewmembers for procedure formulation, validation, inflight training, crew task allocation, and unusual procedure simulation. This project had its genesis in the confluence of prior research efforts for NASA, the Air Force, and the National Science Foundation (NSF). Having investigated computer graphics digital human models for quite some time, and having been familiar with their use for ergonomics and human factors applications, it is understood that some of the compelling problems today still add constrains to effective and widespread utilization of those models.

From prior NASA research spaceflight applications for human models, and the difficulties in modeling in-flight biomechanics, micro-gravity actions, and complex maintenance task manual manipulations were understood. This project was begun with the belief and expectation that digital human models could simulate spaceflight procedures to insure human competency to perform similar tasks in reality. Such simulations would insure good preflight designs, but required significant software investment and proper utilization by craft contractors. Indeed, some ergonomics human modeling tools do exist and are used in the design stages of a major project, but most of these are interactive systems and are not structured for flexible simulation: they are not particularly capable of taking instructions and executing them in a variety of design alternatives, and considerable operator expertise is required to set-up and run an analysis.

From prior Air Force research, extensive studies of instruction manuals were done for both aircraft maintenance and other mechanical applications. From this work an understanding was gained of the existing state-of-the-art in automated (electronic) instructions, and a priority ordering of problems that need to be addressed in order to produce better electronic instruction validation. The roles of validation and simulation are intertwined: a simulation may or may not succeed, and if not, the causes of failure must be established and understood. Failures may stem from or involve accommodation problems due to anthropometric variations, equipment design flaws, unforeseen procedure steps, impossible equipment access, misunderstanding or ignorance of equipment function, or inadequate or ambiguous instructions. Validation requires an integration of human modeling with equipment functional simulation, and a more automated analysis framework in which to probe the space of success and failure modes.

From prior NSF research the interrelationships between natural language and human animation was studied, and developed a Parameterized Action Representation (PAR) and an Actionary of digital definitions suitable for an action database. This work focused on how manual procedure instructions might be set on a computational basis appropriate to both natural language processing and computer animation on virtual human models. PAR describes actions with parameters such as agent, object, motion qualities, paths, preparatory specifications, termination conditions, and sub-actions so they can be re-used in a wide variety of spatial contexts, by various virtual actors, and with action modifiers.

APPROACH:
The approach for this experiment is not available.

RESULTS:
This NASA project sought to combine these observations, knowledge, and methodologies to serve the objective of designing better instruction delivery, simulation, and validation tools. This project has led to several specific accomplishments, which are summarized below.

Automated constrained human arm reach

This portion researched a novel way of computing real-time human arm reach actions for maintenance, operation, or scientific tasks in constrained physical environments. Such movements are essential for computer software that must automatically synthesize complex arm motions in confined spaces, such as glove box. Rather than rely on a human operator to guide the synthetic reach, the program can do the analysis itself, and do so in a fashion that:

1. Uses a simple spatial partition and spatial search algorithm to move the hand through space toward the goal,

2. Avoids arm and body contacts with the environment using the graphics hardware board to do fast collision detection,

3. Does not use the traditional configuration-space planning approach common in robotics, and

4. Uses arm strength data to favor more natural (less awkward) shoulder, elbow, and wrist postures during solution search.

This work is being extended to incorporate better empirical data (reported by others) to extend the reach chain beyond the shoulder joint to the whole upper body.

Shape Preserving object simplification

This addressed the very general question of converting geometric models from complex mega-polygon meshes into more compact representations that automatically preserved shape features such as pointed parts or sharp edges. The motivation for this arises from placing a simulated human (maintainer) in a complex modeling 3D environment. The numerous surfaces needed in a polygon model mostly arise from visual needs and local details that are possibly not very relevant to the accomplishment of a maintenance task. But some features, such as points and sharp edges, are important for safety. Semantically careless polygon decimation can eliminate some of these features and affect task accomplishment methods or viability. Although we have not been able to apply these results directly, the issues are nonetheless important for both equipment design and automatic human task simulation. In the former, the design features at the human manipulation level of detail are important, but make be overwhelmed by essential engineering detail. In the latter, fewer polygons means faster computation of reach and positioning tasks, since collision detection costs are highly dependent on the mesh size of the 3D model.

Interactive vibrotactile experience for confined arm reach

For maintenance and operational training, a virtual environment can provide visual feedback, but a human operator will not have the tactile benefit of feeling the mechanical constraints in a confined space such as an equipment bay or a glove box. Here, the question of whether a physical stimulus in a virtual reality experience could effectively substitute for a physical obstacle was explored. The physical component that is missing is the collision detection and response, so an array of vibrotactile devices (tactors) on the arm were used to simulate the "feel" of touching a real object though none is physically present. These small, inexpensive computer-controlled tactors deliver vibration to a small area of skin. Up to twenty-four of these were positioned on the arm and hand of a subject. In experiments, users were able to perform reaches to occluded targets in confined volumes faster with the vibrotactile display on their arm. Such a haptic array may help motor learning of complex tasks and provide valuable physical feedback (though not physical constraint) during initial task learning or later rehearsal. This could translate to reduced training time for complex assembly or disassembly tasks, with the added benefit that the human subject must actually perform the task without having the cost or expense of a physical model.

Deformable arm model with biomechanical tissue properties

A human arm model was created with biomechanical deformation parameters. Using a novel device to measure a local pressure/displacement function, the indentation of the arm tissue can be simulated when an external blunt (spherical) obstacle is applied. The purpose of such a model is to see whether the deformation of soft tissues can affect the reachable space of the arm, since all existing ergonomic digital human models have rigid surfaces. Reach analyses performed with rigid body collision detection are apt to be conservative (underestimating reachable space) with respect to what a real (deformable) arm model can reach. In informal experiments it was found that reach could be extended up to about 15% if deformation over small obstacles was considered. Results for larger obstacles (such as flat areas) will be closer to the predictions from rigid geometry models since volume-preserving tissue displacements limit the travel of the obstacle into the arm space. Accordingly, this research showed a local effect but not enough to continue with more detailed deformable arm models at this time. It is possible than these ideas can be profitable if applied to lower torso for whole body maintenance access problems or buttocks deformations for optimizing seat design, but to date it has not specifically addressed data acquisition methods for these body regions nor these particular applications.

The personality factor

As possibilities for crew simulation were investigated, it became clear that very important factors to consider in task accomplishment and success were an individual's personality and psychological state. This might even be the most important subjective issue for long duration flights: actually having the crew do what they need to do and not do what they should not do. Understanding how to include these considerations in task, workload, and mission simulations would presumably lead to better working conditions and overall mission success. This difficult aspect of human behavioral modeling was to look at a classification of plotlines from narrative stories. These plotlines could provide a "backbone" of human actions and reactions to support the selection of individual tasks. Plot action choices are highly dependent on an individual's personality, culture, and motivators. Work plans could then seek to include countermeasures to mitigate plotlines that might lead to negative crew consequences.

Parameterized Actions and the Actionary

This involved developing a parameterized action representation (PAR) and simulation system that creates a system in which domain experts, not simulation experts, can build a simulation to test maintenance procedures, habitability, or work schedules. Previous versions of the PAR system were based on Python and C++ under the IRIX operating system. In order to optimize the code and make it more accessible to a larger community, a Windows based operating system was used with a commonly-used free database called MySQL to store the database of available actions, the Actionary. PAR data is entered into MySQL through a graphical user interface (GUI) consisting of various windows. Through the main windows, the Object Edit and Action Edit windows, the user can create new objects, agents, and actions, as well as edit, and search through those already defined in the database. The programming of flexible base dialogs for repeated functionality among objects and actions (e.g., coordinate entry, object/action search dialogs) allows the user to quickly become accustomed to the interface, while the size of the program stays minimal. The object, agent, and action data are stored in a relational MySQL database in a normalized structure such as to speed up the retrieval of objects, agents, and actions. Also, because of the possibility of integrating this data into a mobile environment, the database model has been tuned to efficiently occupy a minimal storage space. This work has influenced future instruction delivery models for NASA, since the PAR allows re-use of stored instructional components and detail level-dependent delivery of instructional materials.

experiment_title: Concepts for Simplified Stowage
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Since the inception of long-duration human spaceflight, stowage management and accessibility has been reported as a major issue facing crews. Even with its relatively time in orbit, Skylab experienced stowage complications at the end of its functional life. The Mir crewmembers identified stowage as one of the primary issues that would face future space stations. Even with only three Expedition crews having provided feedback on the habitability of ISS, stowage has already been identified as an issue with every crew. The collection of feedback and crew comments collected over this history indicates that a simplified stowage system that provides optimized use of volume available, strategic organization, and easy crew access would eliminate many of the stowage problems encountered by the crew, as well as significantly increase crew productivity and safety. The project will first define and address the current on-orbit stowage situation as a method by which to scope to problem. Based on the recommendations provided by the team as a result of the assessment of the current situation, conceptual designs of a simplified stowage system will be developed. Following a heuristic usability assessment, prototypes of the concepts will be built for future testing. Referring back to the recommendations generated as part of this project, as well as previous spaceflight experience, the team will assess the strengths and weaknesses of the designs based on the prototypes. In addition, a formal usability test will be conducted. A final evaluation with the end user—the crewmembers—will be conducted to validate previous recommendations and gain additional feedback based on zero-gravity experience. Implementation of a stowage system that would maximize the usable dedicated stowage volume on ISS, as well as provide a more intuitive organizational scheme and better visual access to the crew, will improve crew efficiency and productivity on a daily basis. Develop human factors requirements and conceptual designs for stowage of cargo and hardware for long-duration space missions. Development of light-weight, flexible and reconfigurable stowage system that will maximize habitable volume and increase crew productivity.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this experiment is not available.

RESULTS:
Overall stowage analysis report has been completed for the existing space program as well as historical reference of both domestic and international space vehicles. Preliminary human factors requirements have been identified. Two case domains have been identified as candidates for concept development.

experiment_title: Crop Production Technology: Advanced Life Support
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The first opportunities for using plants in life support systems for space will likely involve a vegetable production unit (VPU) or “salad machine” to provide fresh vegetables and fruits to supplement the crew’s diet. Several crops were identified for initial testing, including: tomato, spinach, radish, chard, lettuce, cabbage, carrot, and green onion. To assess the challenges and potential yields in a typical space cabin environment, radish, lettuce and onion plants were grown at three temperatures (22, 25, and 28 C), three carbon dioxide concentrations (400, 1200, and 4000 ppm), and three light intensities (150, 300, and 450 micro mol m-2 s-1). A similar series of tests was carried out with dwarf tomato and dwarf pepper but only at 25 C. All the studies were repeated to provide statistical confidence, and samples were analyzed for taste and acceptability attributes by taste panels.

Related studies were carried out with radish and lettuce just at 25 C, 1200 ppm carbon dioxide, and several light intensities but in this case using light emitting diodes (LEDs). LEDs are solid state lamps that have a long operating life and hence are appealing for space applications. In addition, LEDs emit very little long wave radiation (heat) toward the plants, simplifying thermal management issues for space chambers. But the spectra of LEDs is very narrow compared to conventional fluorescent and high-intensity discharge lamps, and plant responses to these narrow spectra need study.

Findings from NASA sponsored testing with salad crops will provide valuable information to commercial controlled environment agriculture (CEA) operations, where optimizing light, carbon dioxide and temperature are important for maximizing yields. The routine use of recirculating hydroponic systems in NASA studies will also provide useful information for reducing nutrient discharge from commercial CEA systems into ground water and nearby aquatic systems. LED development continues at a rapid pace in the commercial world (e.g., traffic lights and car tail lights), and LEDs have already been tested in commercial CEA facilities in Japan. NASA’s continued testing with crops grown under LEDs will provide valuable information needed to develop acceptable combinations of spectra and intensity for competitive and profitable CEA systems around the world.

APPROACH:
Radish, lettuce, and green onion plants were grown hydroponically for 35 days at different combinations of temperature (22, 25, and 28 degrees C), carbon dioxide concentration (400, 1200, and 4000 ppm), and light intensity (150, 300, 450 umol m-2 s-1). Each test was repeated twice and harvest weights, texture, and color were assessed. A similar series of tests was conducted with dwarf tomato and dwarf pepper where plants were grown for 105 days at 400, 1200, and 4000 ppm carbon dioxide, 150, 300, and 450 umol m-2 s-1 light, but only at 25 degrees C temperature. For the tomato and pepper studies, fruits were also compared for sensory (taste) analysis. In general, increased light intensity increased growth for all species, but also increased the incidence of leaf tipburn injury in lettuce. Likewise, increasing the CO2 concentration to 1200 ppm from 400 ppm increased the growth for all species.

RESULTS:
Growth of lettuce and radish plants under red LEDs alone typically resulted in elongated stems and leaves, and occasional bleached (no chlorophyll) areas in radish leaves. Added blue light to the red prevented these effects and resulted in acceptable growth. Addition of green light to the red and blue increased growth in some cases but had no effect in others. But in all cases, the addition of green light provided a more balanced spectrum that allowed visual assessment of the health and development of the plants. When green light was provided alone, stomatal conductance of lettuce plants was reduced, suggesting a direct effect of the green light on the stomatal control mechanism.

experiment_title: Effects of Circadian Rhythms on Decompression Outcome
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Decompression sickness (DCS) can occur when the dissolved gases in blood and tissues exceed the ambient pressure of an individual following a pressure reduction. Astronauts performing space walks (extravehicular activity, EVA) are subjected to significant pressure decreases as they decompress from the space shuttle/station cabin pressure of 14.7 pounds per square inch absolute (psia) to that of the space suit at 4.3 psia. Decompression also occurs with deep-sea divers upon returning from the higher pressures beneath the ocean to surface pressure. DCS symptoms range from mild joint pain to severe neurological injury or even circulatory collapse. Most symptoms are attributed to the formation of gas bubbles in various tissues and venous blood. These bubbles may react with blood cells (platelets and neutrophils) and vascular endothelial membranes, causing an inflammatory-like response. The response is caused by mediator release (arachidonic acid metabolites) and other cellular injurious agents. These mediators can result in endothelial cell injury, vasoconstriction, alterations in vessel wall permeability, and tissue edema formation.

In this project, researchers examined the effects of the body’s endogenous circadian rhythms on the physiological consequences of decompression-induced venous bubble formation. Specific indices of inflammation and lung injury have been previously reported with DCS, even with mild to moderate levels of decompression. Based on these observations, the research team studied the effect of the circadian rhythms on the tolerance to decompression exposure and the underlying 24-hour bioperiodic dependencies. The overall objectives were to evaluate the quantitative evaluation of the physiological stress of decompression at different circadian times and to relate this to rhythms in cellular and biochemical variations over the 24-hour span. The measurement of these responses was hoped to elucidate some of the less understood risks associated with decompression illness, leading directly to operationally useful procedures.

The study included had five specific hypotheses:

  1. Changes in decompression-induced neutrophil and platelet counts are circadian rhythm dependent.
  2. The severity of decompression-induced changes in inflammatory mediators (leukotrienes and thromboxanes) correlates with specific stages of known circadian rhythms.
  3. The severity of DCS symptoms and lung injury correlate with circadian rhythms.
  4. Decompression-induced variables in Hypotheses 1-3 above are the result of venous bubble formation and blood interactions.
  5. Pharmacological inhibition of decompression-induced symptoms and inflammatory mediators is dose-responsive as a result of circadian rhythm dependencies.

APPROACH:
Circadian Rhythm Studies: Twelve groups of 12 adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (440 ± 35 gm) were studied in this series of experiments (n=144). For a minimum of 14 days, the rodents were acclimated to a 12-hour light/12-hour dark schedule and then selected for decompression exposure in reference to hours after lights on (HALO). The protocol called for the rats to be exposed to conditions that induce DCS at 6 different times, (i.e. at 4-hour intervals throughout a 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle). Data were collected at HALO 2, 6, 10, 14, 18 and 22. The animals were placed in the compression chamber and allowed 5 minutes to acclimate. If testing occurred in the animals’ dark cycle, the study was conducted in darkness with the decompression chamber covered to maintain the lighting conditions. The decompression exposures were selected to cause moderate to significant venous bubble formation in greater than 90% of the animals. Previous studies have demonstrated the utility of this model for decompression evaluation. The symptomology, however, was far less than usually reported with rodent experimentation where death or recovery endpoints were selected. The purpose of this study required less severe symptomology for outcome evaluation.

For decompression, the rats of 6 randomly selected groups (experimental) were placed in the decompression chamber, compressed to 683 kPa over 11 minutes (60 minutes exposure), then decompressed over 9.5 minutes back to ambient pressure, followed by a 60-minute observation period. The remaining 6 groups (controls) remained at atmospheric pressure for 60 minutes. Symptom scores were based on a normalized relative severity scale (minor = 1, to more severe (including death) = 4)).

At 60 minutes post decompression, the rats were anesthetized (halothane) for sample collection (urine, pleural fluid and arterial blood for differential cell counts, protein and mediator analysis) and pulmonary edema measurement. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was collected for protein, cell and eicosanoid analysis using enzyme immunoassays (EIA) and correlated as to the circadian staging.

Concentrations of thromboxane B2 (TXB2), 11-dehydrothromboxane B2 (11-DH-TXB2) and leukotriene E4 (LTE4) in the biological samples were determined by enzyme immunoassay. Plasma nitric oxide was analyzed using chemiluminescence. Pulmonary edema was determined using a blood-corrected wet/dry weight ratio method. Statistical evaluation consisted of analysis for time effect by analysis of variance (ANOVA) and cosinor using a single (24-hour) or multiple (24 + 12-hour) component cosine model.

Pharmacological Intervention Studies: Another aspect of this study was the investigation of the effects of inflammatory inhibitors to these mediators in decompression-exposed rats. Results of the decompression studies identified the extent of risk of DCS that is dependent on circadian rhythms or specific inflammatory mediators. From such data, the 2 biological times (with reference to circadian rhythms in risk) - one corresponding to the greatest and the second to the least susceptibility - were selected to conduct dose-response investigations of drug effect both on overt variables and on the release of inflammatory mediators (eicosanoids). Three agents were studied. The first was aspirin for determining the role of cyclo-oxygenase products of arachidonic acid metabolism, namely thromboxane A2 and its stable byproduct TXB. The second was zileuton, produced by Abbott labs, which is specific to the 5-lipoxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolic products, namely the leukotrienes. Zileuton actually blocks the 5-lipoxygenase enzyme rather than act as a leukotriene receptor antagonist. By selecting the appropriate cyclooxygenase and 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors above, and evaluating their dose response effects at different time points, it is anticipated that circadian rhythm dependent patterns will emerge and thereby enable a better assessment of risk and intervention possibilities with DCS. ß-agonist actions were studied with isoproterenol. Each drug was administered, either subcutaneously or by gavage, to the rats (468 ± 29 gm) prior to compression. Post decompression analysis is described above. Data were analyzed by ANOVA with Fisher’s post-hoc comparison for differences between means (p < 0.05 statistically significant).

RESULTS:
DCS-induced venous bubbles can lead to obstruction of blood vessels, alteration in vessel wall permeability and vasoconstriction. Apart from the mechanical obstruction induced by the bubbles, these effects are partially caused by biochemical processes such as release of arachidonic acid metabolites, including thromboxanes and leukotrienes, resulting from bubble-activated neutrophils and endothelial cell injury. Significant circadian rhythm dependencies in the tolerance to DCS were evident in most of the parameters studied. This was most apparent in measured variables comparing HALO 2 and 12 time points. Clear circadian rhythm dependencies were found in the inflammatory mediator levels and in the extravascular lung-water ratio levels post decompression. These observations concur with other studies examining the circadian rhythm-dependencies of inflammatory-like reactions to various different stresses.

Pharmacological intervention on the effects of inflammatory-like responses to DCS showed reductions. However, the hemodynamic and mechanical effects of the intravascular bubbles may also require specific intervention. Investigators concluded that DCS risk is affected by the circadian time structure and should be taken into consideration for properly assessing the underlying mechanisms of DCS, as well as the efficiency of preventive and intervention strategies.

experiment_title: Multidisciplinary Studies of Neural Plasticity in Space
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Ribbon synapses in the hair cells of the inner ear transmit information to the brain about linear acceleration forces acting on the body. This experiment was designed to build upon previous data collected on Spacelab Life Sciences 1 and 2 (SLS-1 and SLS-2), which showed that the ribbon synapses of gravity-sensor hair cells changed in number, kind, and distribution during space flight, a phenomenon known as neural plasticity. The three major points of interest in this study were 1) whether the ribbon synapses would rapidly increase in number upon initial exposure to weightlessness; 2) whether the changes observed early in flight would remain stable throughout the flight (expecting an initial overshoot as the body compensates for the new environment); and 3) whether different parts of the gravity sensors would show different synaptic counts.

Approach:

Flight rats used in this study were part of the integrated adult rat dissections performed on FD 2 and FD 14. Inner ear tissues were removed from four rats on FD 2, nine rats on FD 14, six rats 2 days postflight, and six rats 14 days postflight. In addition, tissues were taken from 10 basal controls on FD 2. Labyrinth dissection, microdissection, tissue preparation, and statistical analysis were performed as described in Ross 1993, 1994, 2000, except that the Neurolab study concentrated on the striolar macular area rather than on the posterior border. Only one of the four utricular maculae from FD 2 was in condition for transmission electron microscopy. To compensate for lost data, the saccular maculae were also examined.

Results:

Although findings from the utricular maculae must be considered anecdotal due to small sample size, the analysis provided several interesting results. The most important findings can be summarized as follows: 1) By FD 2, an upward change in the mean number of synaptic ribbons could already be observed in macular vestibular hair cells. 2) A decline from FD 2 values occurred in both kinds of hair cells by FD 14. 3) On both FD 2 and FD 14, increments in synaptic means were prominent in Type II hair cells and were significant compared to the basal. 4) Mean values of synapses for Type II hair cells of the striolar area were lower than those found previously in SLS-2. All these findings support previous evidence that changes in synaptic ribbons of utricular gravity sensor hair cells occur rapidly in weightlessness, and that the changes are more prominent in Type II hair cells. The decline seen in the striolar area by FD 14 is a new observation, suggesting a synaptic overshoot on FD 2.

A more interesting finding, perhaps, is that the striolar area of the saccular macula did not show the same changes in synapses observed in the utricular macula. The saccular macula has been studied in one basal, two FD 2, two FD 14 and one PFD 2 (postflight day 2) samples. Results indicate that the Type I synapses had decreased by FD 2, but were up again by FD 14 (FD 2 to FD 14, significant) and remained above FD 2 at PFD 2. Synapses in Type II cells remained relatively stable throughout the period of the experiment. It is noteworthy that the number of processes on Type II hair cells of the saccule were less numerous than those observed previously in the utricular macula.

Overall, the results provide the first evidence that maculae, and macular location (defined by variation in otoconial distribution, hair cell morphology, and vestibular afferent wiring) are related to the range of synaptic changes observed in weightlessness. The differences in saccular versus utricular macular results indicate that the two maculae have differing functional (and integrative) responses to translational and gravitational forces acting on the systems.

experiment_title: Subjective Vertical Analyzation and Visceral Receptors: On the Contribution of Visceral Receptors to the Sense of Subjective Vertical
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
On earth, the subjective sense of vertical is due to many sensory inputs, which are mainly related to the visual, vestibular and proprioceptive systems. These sensory systems utilise specialised sensors located respectively in the eye, in the inner ear, and in joints and muscles. Other sensory systems can also be pointed out in the detection of human orientation, although they usually play a minor role for the detection of the subjective vertical. More recently, a further contribution to the detection of subjective vertical was observed from visceral receptors sensitive to blood mass shifts, mainly located in the kidneys and in the thorax. Analyses of the subjective sense of vertical have in the past decades been carried out in equilibrium and orientation studies conducted under microgravity conditions. Nevertheless, due to their recent identification, specific data on the contribution of visceral receptors to the detection of subjective vertical in such a specific environment is still lacking. Theoretically, the ideal environment to analyse a single type of receptor is one where the contribution from all other sensory systems involved in performing the same sensory analysis can be cancelled. Therefore, the aim of this present experiment is the analysis of visceral receptor performance within an environment, which rules out possible bias due to visual and gravitational inputs. In fact, in this specific experiment, the weightless condition will eliminate contributions from all gravity sensitive sensors (i.e. from the vestibular and from part of the proprioceptive systems). Moreover, the visual orientation input will be manipulated in order to select detailed information from visceral sensors.

APPROACH:
The experiment will be carried out using three analysis sessions: pre-flight, in-flight and postflight. The analysis will be performed with an instrument called a Subjective Vertical Analyser (SVA), which will provide a completely darkened environment. The SVA is a tube shaped instrument, closed at its two extremities by two disks. The subject's disk will include a silicone-lined cutout for the subject's eyes. The second disk will have a rotating luminous rod and a fixed luminous frame to analyse the visual subjective vertical. An arrow firmly connected to the rod, which is on the other side of the disk, will indicate the degree of tilt. A handle will allow the operator to rotate the rod (and the connected arrow) according to the subject's indications. The internal part of the instrument will be completely dark. The astronaut will be tested first on earth while standing, and a recording under normal gravity conditions will be obtained by carrying out the experiment in complete darkness. During weightlessness, the astronaut will repeat the experiment and will not receive any more visual or vestibular cues, together with a reduced feedback from other body receptors. Manipulating the body fluid mass with the use of a Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) device - which is a standard method to shift fluids into the lower extremities of the body through suction - the role that the visceral receptors may play in finding the subjective vertical will be analysed. At the end of the experiment, the difference observed between the pre-flight and the in-flight sessions (without the use of LBNP) will indicate the global contribution to orientation of sensory organs sensitive to gravitational inputs. On the other hand, the difference observed between the two in-flight sessions, with and without the use of LBNP, will indicate the global contribution to orientation of visceral receptors sensitive to fluid mass shifts. Finally, further recordings (in- and post-flight) will be performed in order to detect hypothetical after-effects, due to the previous exposure to LBNP and to weightlessness.

RESULTS:
The results from this experiment indicated that subjects experienced only minor changes in their subjective visual vertical after a short duration of exposure to microgravity. Subjects did not have an increase of visual field dependence during flight or postflight in comparison to ground based recordings.

experiment_title: Nutrition Coupled with Traditional Resistance or Low-Load Blood Flow Restricted Exercise during Human Limb Suspension
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During periods of muscular inactivity such as with exposure to microgravity, bed rest, or unilateral lower limb suspension (ULLS), decrements in skeletal muscle size, strength, and endurance have been observed. During long-term space flight the aforementioned reductions in skeletal muscle function could negatively influence overall crew health and increase the risk of impaired performance on mission related tasks. Previous research has demonstrated that the most effective countermeasure to disuse induced muscle atrophy is traditional resistance exercise, which has been shown to maintain muscle size and strength during prolonged periods of bed rest. However, implementing traditional load resistance exercise during long-duration space flight is not without difficulty due to: a weightless environment, limited space for equipment, risk of crew injury, complexity and/or unreliability of exercise equipment to deliver high loads and a substantial risk to space craft’s structure. Therefore, if similar skeletal muscle benefits could be obtained with low load resistance training, this could be an attractive option, at least for circumstances in which high load exercise equipment is unavailable (confined space, severely limited upmass, equipment failure, etc).

Exercise is not the only factor that determines the adaptations observed in skeletal muscle during a period of disuse. Nutrient intake provides a potent metabolic stimulus independent of exercise and these factors can work synergistically. In this capacity, there is growing evidence to support nutrient timing (ingesting protein or amino acids and carbohydrate within approximately 30 minutes before or after a resistance training session) as an effective strategy to promote muscle growth. Previous studies in ambulatory subjects have shown that consuming a combination of amino acids and carbohydrates immediately before or after an exercise session stimulates muscle protein synthesis to a greater extent than when performing the same exercise when fasted. In studies focusing on disuse, timing essential amino acids with carbohydrate before (less than five minutes) or after (three hours) resistance training has recently shown to attenuate the loss of muscle mass and strength during 28 days of bed rest even when the body is in an overall energy deficit . Thus, there appears to be strong support for consuming a protein-carbohydrate source that is rich in essential amino acids before or after each resistance training session in order to optimize training adaptations and this strategy is effective even during energy restriction. Combining milk intake with resistance exercise training has also shown to increase muscle fiber size compared to fat-free soy milk and an isoenergetic carbohydrate supplement.

Specific Aims:

1. To determine the morphological and neurological alterations that occur in skeletal muscle following combined exercise and nutritional countermeasures during disuse (unloaded-left limb) and use (loaded-right limb).
2. To characterize local (calf and thigh) blood flow, tissue oxygen saturation, tissue pH, limb circumference, heart rate, systemic blood pressure, and stroke volume during low load, low load with low blood flow restriction (BFR), low load with moderate BFR, and high load resistance training.
3. To compare the effects of 30 days of traditional high load and low load with moderate BFR resistance training in the weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing limb on popliteal and femoral blood flow and diameter, and tissue oxygen saturation and pH at the calf and thigh.

APPROACH:
In this study, participants wore a thick-soled (10cm) shoe on the right foot and walked using crutches, thereby, allowing the left foot to be raised off the ground and unloaded from weight bearing activity. Participants were free to perform most normal ambulatory activities. During this time, both legs were exercised three days per week using one of two different exercise programs and participants were asked to consume milk before and after each training session. Subjects were randomized into one of two exercise training programs consisting of three sets of unilateral leg press and calf raise exercise to fatigue separated by a 90 second rest interval. One group performed traditional high load resistance exercise and a second group performed low-load resistance exercise with moderate BFR. BFR resistance exercise is a relatively new method of exercise that utilizes low-loads coupled with BFR to the working muscle (applied by inflating a blood pressure cuff around the limb). Recent studies have shown that this method may be as effective as traditional resistance exercise in inducing increases in muscle size, strength, and endurance, making it an attractive option in situations where high loads are not possible (lack of access to high load exercise equipment, rehab, aging, etc.). The intake of milk timed with the exercise was tested as a nutritional intervention in attempt to optimize exercise training adaptations. Timing protein intake with exercise is well known to enhance the effectiveness of resistance exercise in ambulatory subjects in 1-g. Milk was selected as a whole food source for this investigation because it is rich with proteins and calcium, which is optimal for both skeletal muscle and bone health.

Subjects must self-report that they are at least recreationally active and pass the standard physical (Air Force Class 3 equivalent). This study was divided into two phases: first, a characterization phase and second, a four week crutch walking paired with resistance training phase. During the characterization phase participants practiced crutch walking and resistance exercise and were educated on documenting serving sizes and recording dietary intake by a member of the research team. Each participant was provided with a food scale, a dietary log, and had communication ability with a research assistant to answer any questions pertaining to food content. With these resources, participants were asked to consume and document three to five days per week a euenergetic diet that is estimated from World Health Organization equations for age and gender. Additionally, participants worked with researchers on maintaining a macronutrient profile that is representative of the NASA requirements. During the characterization phase subjects also performed four resistance exercise sessions under four different conditions: low load, low load with low BFR, low load with moderate BRF, and high load resistance exercise. During these sessions several cardiovascular variables were measured rest and immediately after each set of exercise including, blood flow through the popliteal and femoral blood vessels (ultrasound), stroke volume (ultrasound), blood pressure (Finapres), heart rate (ECG), tissue oxygenation and pH (NIRS).

To characterize the cellular mechanism related to basal mTORC1 signaling, muscle biopsies were obtained on a subset of participants from vastus lateralis and lateral gastrocnemius in both unloaded and weight-bearing limbs. Muscle cross-sectional area (CSA), strength, central activation capacity, rate of force development, force steadiness, muscle endurance, and biopsies were obtained the week prior to starting unilateral lower-limb suspension (ULLS). Post-ULLS, muscle CSA was evaluated on either day 24 or 25 of ULLS. Strength, central activation capacity, rate of force development, force steadiness, muscle endurance were evaluated in a muscle function test battery performed on either day 25 or 26 of ULLS. Muscle biopsies were obtained on either day 27 or 28 of ULLS.

In the second phase of the study, subjects participated in a battery of muscle function, size, and strength tests that are indicators of muscle atrophy/hypertrophy before and after four weeks of ULLS combined with resistance training. These tests include MRI, 1 repetition maximum (1-RM), maximal power, interpolated twitch, isokinetic, isometric, and muscle biopsies. In addition, the previously mentioned cardiovascular parameters were measured pre, mid, and post ULLS.

This investigation measured local vascular responses, tissue oxygen saturation (StO2), and cardiovascular responses during supine unilateral leg press and heel raise exercise in four conditions: high load with no occlusion cuff (HL), low load with no occlusion cuff (LL), and low load with occlusion cuff pressure set at 1.3 times resting diastolic blood pressure (BFRDBP) or at 1.3 times resting systolic blood pressure (BFRSBP). Subjects (N=13) performed three sets of leg press and heel raise to fatigue with 90-seconds rest. Artery diameter, velocity time integral (VTI), and stroke volume (SV) were measured using Doppler ultrasound at rest and immediately after exercise. Heart rate (HR) was monitored using a 3-lead ECG. Finger blood pressure (BP) was acquired by photoplethysmography. StO2 was measured using near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS).

RESULTS:
Blood flow restricted resistance exercise resulted in exercise blood flow and tissue oxygen saturation compared to exercise without restricted blood flow. Systemic cardiovascular responses (i.e. HR, BP, SV, and cardiac output) were also altered with blood flow restricted exercise. We also demonstrated that 4 weeks of blood flow restricted exercise training maintained muscle function during normal ambulation similarly to high load resistance training. However, blood flow restricted exercise was not fully protective in an unloaded condition.

experiment_title: Fundamentals of Ion- Molecule/Surface Reactions and Instrument Development
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
By advancing mass spectrometric instrumentation and understanding of fundamental aspects of gas-phase ion/molecule and ion/surface reactions investigators contribute to NASA’s effort to characterize astrophysical and atmospheric environments. Progress has been made in ongoing research of (1) an anomalous heavy-atom kinetic isotope effect and (2) the development of a new instrument amenable to production of isotopically enriched species by this isotope effect and collection of this material by ion/surface collisions. These endeavors represent an effort to push the boundaries of fundamental physical science on this planet and beyond.

APPROACH:
Changes in charge can accompany ion/surface collisions and those associated with a change in polarity (positive to negative ions or vice versa) are an attractive method for ion structural characterization and isomer differentiation. The surface-induced charge inversion of nitrobenzene and other substituted aromatics was explored. Reactive collisions occurring between gaseous ions and surfaces depend on the chemical nature of the collision partners. These reactions can be used for selected chemical modifications of surfaces as well as for surface analysis.

RESULTS:
Progress has been made in ongoing research of a newly discovered anomalous heavy-atom kinetic isotope effect in the unimolecular dissociation of chloroalkane chloride complexes. Unexpected isotope abundances in the mass spectra of these species prompted much work on this striking phenomenon partly due to its unprecedented magnitude but also because of its extreme significance to atmospheric and environmental chemistry. Considerable advancements have been made in the understanding of the mechanism causing this isotope effect through numerous experiments. The effect is so great that it could potentially lead to molecular isotope separation method. Prompted by this potential, a device has recently been constructed with the goal of obtaining proof-of-principle data.

experiment_title: Muscle Size and Lipids
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Exposure to microgravity for extended periods causes atrophy in skeletal muscles, particularly in the lower extremities. The result may be a loss of strength that could impair crewmember performance during landing and/or egress. The purpose of this investigation was to noninvasively quantify changes in size, water, and lipid composition in antigravity (leg) muscles after space flight.

APPROACH:
Eight Space Shuttle crewmembers, five from a 7-day flight and three from a 9-day flight, participated in this study. The subjects underwent one preflight and two postflight tests on days L-30 or L-16 days and on R+2 and R+7. Testing involved obtaining an MRI scan of the leg (soleus and gastrocnemius) at The University of Texas-Houston Health Science Center, Hermann Hospital.

Test subjects were positioned supine inside the magnetic bore for approximately one hour. A 15 centimeter cage resonator was used for radio frequency transmission and signal reception. Multi-slice axial images of the leg were obtained to identify and locate various muscle groups. Image-guided localized proton spectroscopy of individual muscle groups used stimulated echo (STE) sequence. Spectral analysis was obtained with an echo time of 15 milliseconds (ms) and a mixing time of 7.8 ms. All MRI studies were performed on the soleus and gastrocnemius muscles. Water and lipid peak areas were computed to quantify concentrations. The proton sample was obtained from a standard placed within the field of view. Concentrations of tissue water and lipid in the soleus and gastrocnemius were expressed relative to a standard sample placed in the field of view. Changes in water and lipid content were measured, in addition to cross-sectional area (CSA), to distinguish changes in fluid versus tissue volumes. Multiple slices were measured by computerized planimetry.

The time in milliseconds required for protons to reach a resting state after maximal excitation is the relaxation time. Two types of relaxation time (T1 and T2) were used to detect changes in the water and lipid content of tissue. Skeletal-muscle volume was assessed in terms of CSA. Thirty to forty 3 to 5 millimeter slices were acquired in 256 x 128 or 256 x 246 matrices. Multiple slices were measured by computerized planimetry.

RESULTS:
CSA and volume of the total leg compartment, soleus, and gastrocnemius were evaluated to assess skeletal muscle atrophy. The volumes of all three compartments were significantly smaller (p <0.05) after both the 7 and 9-day Shuttle flights, relative to preflight, with a 5.8% loss in the soleus, 4.0% loss in the gastrocnemius, and a 4.3% loss in the total compartment. These decreases represent true skeletal muscle tissue atrophy, not fluid shift. No recovery was apparent by 7 days after landing.

Conclusions:
Results suggest that even 9 days of space flight may cause a significant decline in muscle CSA and volume. Increases in lipid/ water ratios suggest muscle tissue atrophy rather than a mere volume loss. MRS findings indicate that muscle fatty acid metabolism may be altered during space flight.

experiment_title: Synaptogenesis in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The effects of spaceflight on nervous system development and neuromuscular synapse formation were tested in a model genetic organism, Drosophila melanogaster. Specific objectives were: 1) To utilize the organism's genetic expression of a highly fluorescent mutant form of Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) to visualize singly identified motoneurons and muscle targets as well as all aspects of the nervous system development; and 2) To examine the critical developmental times of Drosophila embryos and larvae for the effects of microgravity during spaceflight.

APPROACH:

Both embryos and larvae at different stages in development were prepared, examined with fluorescent microscopy, and stored at 11 degrees C in order to arrest development. Specimens were housed on petri plates containing a culture medium in the incubator containment module (ICM) and launched on the STS-93 mission. The petri dishes were housed in seven Group Activation Packages (GAPs) within the ICM. At specific time points inflight, each GAP was heated to 25 degrees C to restart development for a set duration. Prior to landing and recovery, the GAPs were be cooled to 11 degrees C to halt development. Cell-specific Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) expression methodologies were used to analyze the data. This allows targeting errors and subtle defects to be detected in a large sample set.

RESULTS:

Preliminary results indicated that although the CGBA hardware operated successfully, there were unexpected temperature drifts above the planned temperature in two of the seven containers. While ground tests were completed for comparison to the in-flight samples, final data analysis has not been released.

experiment_title: Modification of Radiogenic Damage by Microgravity
experiment_description:
Objectives:

High-energy, high-atomic-number charged particle radiation (HZE) represents a significant health risk to humans during spaceflight. Although such radiation has been physically characterized during numerous manned spaceflights, limited attempts to explicitly correlate biological responses with naturally occurring HZE particles have been made. The purpose of this experiment is to induce controlled levels of DNA and chromosomal damage to somatic and germ-line cells and to determine whether exposure to microgravity perturbs cellular repair and tolerance mechanisms. Radiation-induced damage will be produced by the active radioisotope 45Calcium, which emits beta particles of energies of up to 250 keV.

Approach:

The approach is to irradiate healthy, growing nematode worms with §-particles from identical radioisotope sources inflight (0-g and 1-g control centrifuge) and, in parallel, on the ground. Before the mission, several strains of nematode larvae are freshly prepared and maintained in source cultures and placed in sample containers stowed at 5°C or ambient temperature in the Biorack. Some strains are transferred by syringe to unshielded and shielded radioactive tubes and either incubated in the 22°C incubator or in the Biorack 1-g centrifuge. After various exposure times, the larvae are frozen or returned to Earth at ambient temperature for fixation and histological examination.

Dose versus response curves are compared for somatic chromosome aberrations and germ-line mutations to determine whether there are modifications in the responses arising from altered gravity levels.

In addition, two containers house worm suspension tubes, without any radioisotopic source, and are exposed to ambient cosmic radiation in order to detect radiation-induced unc-22 mutants; unc-22 mutations were isolated from worms flown on Discovery during the IML-1/STS-42 mission, large deletions of chromatin were detected. Radiation-induced unc-22 mutant structure is LET (Linear Energy Transfer) dependent. Two additional containers contain a fem-3 (q20) mutant strain which allows comparisons at an independent chromosomal location.

Results:

Initial experimental results suggest that gravity level has little effect upon induced mutation frequency in relation to dose responses. As a result of ambient exposure, the samples contained fem-3 mutants, but, surprisingly, no unc-22 mutants were found. Fem-3 mutants exhibited molecular hybridization and one out of every twenty-six mutants had undergone a large structural change. Despite small sample sizes due to problems with sample recovery, experimental data was consistent with the results of the gravity-independent control.

experiment_title: Calcium Metabolism and Correlated Endocrine Measurements in Primates
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The problem of calcium loss from the body during space flight had been long recognized; however, little is known about the initiating mechanism of this loss. Two hypotheses have been suggested in explanation: 1) a primary increase in bone resorption due to decreased mechanical stress on the bone or 2) a primary renal calcium leak. This experiment was to measure the initial responses of the calcium homeostatic system in nonhuman primates subjected to the space flight environment.

Approach:

The basis for this study was the "tracer" technique, in which direct measurements of changes in bone resorption are possible through isotopically labeled calcium. Fifteen days prior to launch, flight and control subjects were started on a diet laced with the isotopically labeled calcium. Excretion samples were collected pre- and postflight, and amounts of labeled calcium were detected by means of irradiation. Single lateral x-rays were obtained for the right and left arms and legs of one flight, two synchronous, and one laboratory monkey to provide high contrast and good radiographic detail for bone. No serum samples were received for the flight experiment, so the planned endocrine studies were not done.

Results:

Results indicate that after five days of flight, the fraction of circulating calcium that comes from the bone was increased. A major point to be noted is that, even with a wide fluctuation in dietary calcium intake, urinary calcium output remained fairly constant over the two to three week period. Similar results have been noted in immobilized monkeys. However, the very low variation when expressed as calcium/creatinine suggests a technical explanation having to do with collection. Gross skeletal changes were not observed, but there was a suggestion of subtle changes as determined from the high-quality radiographs. Qualitative assessment of the films for cortical porosity suggests that one of the flight monkeys may have experienced a state of slightly increased bone turnover because of the presence of some intracortical striations in the radial and ulnar cortex. Data indicate that the methods used to study calcium metabolism during space flight were sufficient to answer the questions asked.

experiment_title: Spaceflight effects on renal and intestinal transporters associated with osteopenia and kidney stone formation and regulation of renal glucose and lipid metabolism
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Our hypotheses are that spaceflight will induce: 1) Major alterations in expression or modification of renal and intestinal transporters that regulate a) calcium and phosphate transport, b) uric acid transport, c) acid-base transport, and d) sodium and water transport, and play an important role in bone homeostasis and renal stone formation. These perturbations will be associated with major changes in the expression pattern of nuclear receptors, transcription factors, and G protein coupled receptors that regulate these transport functions; 2) Alterations in the hypoxia inducible factors (HIF-1a and HIF-2a) and their regulatory factors prolyl hydroxylases (PHDs) and factor inhibiting HIF-1a (FIH) will be associated with major changes in regulation of renal glucose and lipid metabolism (12-13).

APPROACH:
To test our hypothesis in kidneys and small intestine obtained from A) spaceflight mice and; B) age and sex matched ground controls fed the same diet as the spaceflight mice we will determine: 1) the mRNA and protein abundance of transport proteins that regulate calcium, phosphate, uric acid, acid-base, sodium and water transport, 2) mRNA expression pattern of nuclear receptors, transcription factors, and G protein coupled receptors that are associated with regulation of above transporters, 3) the renal expression of the hypoxia inducible factors (HIF-1a and HIF-2a) and their regulatory factors prolyl hydroxylases (PHDs) and factor inhibiting HIF-1a (FIH), and 4) renal lipid composition and determination of pathways that regulate lipid and glucose metabolism.

experiment_title: Physiological Effects of Iodinated Water on Thyroid Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Iodine has been used as a potable water treatment and storage bactericidal agent by NASA for over three decades beginning with the Apollo program, and was a critical factor for the achievement of human space flight. Iodine is currently used for Space Shuttle potable water microbial control and the U.S. component of the International Space Station (ISS). The ISS U.S. water system recycles water from urine and other wastewaters for human consumption and requires long-term storage. With the proposed iodine exposure levels and the crewmembers originating from many countries including regions of low iodine intake, concerns have been raised regarding the use of iodine in ISS potable water.

Iodine is a component of the two major thyroid hormones, thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). These hormones regulate many key biochemical processes. Major target organs are the developing brain, muscle, heart, pituitary, and kidney. Most ingested iodine is reduced in the gut to iodide, which is absorbed almost completely. Once in circulation, iodide is removed primarily by the thyroid gland and kidney. The thyroid selectively concentrates iodide with the excess excreted into the urine. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), produced in the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland, regulates the release of thyroid hormones from the thyroid gland into the blood. TSH secretion from the pituitary gland increases when the levels of circulating thyroid hormones decrease. The thyroid responds to the ingestion of elevated quantities of iodine by a transient decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis, termed the acute Wolff-Chaikoff effect.

An investigation was undertaken during three ground-based, closed-chamber tests to examine thyroid function and hormone levels in chamber subjects who consumed potable water containing iodine. The purpose of this study was to document the thyroid functional biochemical measurements (n=12), urine iodine levels (n=8), and any clinical signs or symptoms of thyroid dysfunction in the 12 crewmembers who participated in the chamber studies.

APPROACH:

The chamber tests, in order of occurrence, were 30 days, Phase II; 60 days, Phase IIa; and 91 days, Phase III. Each chamber test had four crewmembers. Each crewmember was considered to be in good health and had normal thyroid function. In all three chamber tests, after the water recycling process was completed, 3.5 to 5.2 mg iodine/L was added to the water as the disinfectant. In Phase II (30 days) and Phase IIa (60 days), thyroid hormonal status (TSH and thyroid hormone levels) was assessed both in the pre- and postchamber period. In Phase III, the 91-day study, TSH, thyroid hormones, and urinary iodine levels were measured before and several times in chamber (first measurement at the 30-day mark). These were followed up with several more measurements in the postchamber period upon the subjects' exit from the chamber at the completion of the study. Subjects were monitored until all indices of iodine/thyroid status had returned to prechamber levels.

For the Phase III study (91 days), due to changes in TSH levels at the 30-day mark, iodine was removed from the potable water before consumption. This was accomplished by installing an iodine-removal device and a microbial filter (0.2 µm) at the point of use of the water on chamber day 35. This device removed the iodine (I2 and I-) from the drinking water but did not affect the iodine levels in the remainder of the water used, i.e., for hygiene activities. Urinary iodine levels were spot-checked to determine iodine exposure.

RESULTS:

While individual water consumption was not determined for Phases II and IIa crewmembers, analysis of diet records and the systematic evaluation of water usage indicates the crewmembers consumed from 4 to 10 mg total iodine/day. For Phase IIa (60 days), drinking water contained approximately 2 to 4 mg I/L and subjects excreted approximately 4.5 to 14 mg/day. Intake measurements were only completed twice during the study. The actual individual water iodine intakes and urinary losses were quantified for the Phase III, 91-day test. The total iodine in the water varied from approximately 3 to 8 mg/L with an average level for the first 35 days around 5 mg total iodine/L. Urinary iodine levels reflect recent iodine consumption. In all subjects, urinary iodine levels increased about 10-fold during the first 30 days of the Phase III chamber study, with iodine consumption levels ranging from 8 to 20 mg/day. Urinary excretion means for subjects ranged from 9.4 to 16.9 mg I/day. The variation in iodine intake between crewmembers was related to the individual volume of potable water consumed. Following installation of the iodine removal device at the galley sink, the total iodine levels measured less than 0.05 mg/L in the drinking water but remained in full concentration in the shower and wash water. Urinary iodine levels decreased 5- to 10-fold after cessation of the water iodine exposure but remained above baseline values. By the end of the 91-day study, 56 days after cessation of drinking water iodine, the urinary values continued to remain above baseline values in three of the four subjects. In three of the crewmembers, urine iodine levels fell to an average of 0.283 mg/24 hrs by three days after test completion.

Although mean TSH levels remained within normal range throughout the studies, there was a statistically significant increase in TSH levels in the Phase II and III studies. For the Phase II study, the values returned to baseline levels in all subjects within two weeks after the subjects exited the chamber. In the 60-day Phase IIa study, although not a statistically significant change, serum TSH in three of the four subjects had increased by the end of the study. One subject, who had a baseline TSH value close to the upper limit, had a decreased TSH value below the baseline value at the end of the chamber study. This subject had the highest iodine consumption and urinary levels of the four subjects in the Phase IIa test. At day 62 postchamber, this subject had a very high TSH level and was referred for medical evaluation by an endocrinologist. There were no other biochemical or clinical signs of thyroid disease, and the TSH returned to near baseline value several months later.

In the 91-day study, the mean serum TSH level in the four test subjects increased significantly above baseline values 30 days after entering the chamber. After the iodine was removed from the drinking water on day 35 (concentration < 0.05 mg/L), the TSH values gradually decreased but did not completely return to baseline during the subsequent 56 days in the chamber.

For one subject in the Phase III study, the TSH remained higher than the baseline value but within the normal reference range throughout the chamber study period, with no decrease in the level after removal of iodine from the drinking water. After one year, the TSH levels returned to prechamber baseline levels. All other measures of thyroid function remained within normal ranges. The consulting endocrinologist diagnosed the crewmember with iodine-induced subclinical hyperthyroidism.

During the Phase III study, urinary iodine levels remained at approximately 1 mg/day after iodine removal from drinking water at day 35, but returned to baseline levels within three days of exiting the chamber. One potential source of iodine contamination involved the methods for urine collection and measurement. A study was completed and found that this was not the cause of the persistence of urinary iodine levels above baseline. Other potential sources of iodine contamination were discussed and considered, however, no plausible explanation was identified.

The results from the three chamber tests demonstrated that the levels of iodine in the potable water system proposed for the ISS were too high. Since these studies were concluded, the Food and Nutrition Board has established an upper limit for iodine intakes from all sources as 1.1 mg/day. The subjects in the chamber studies exceeded this level and consequently, for two subjects, TSH levels were significantly changed by the end of the chamber test. Since food consumption provides about 0.25 mg/day, the requirement was set at a maximum of 0.25 mg of iodine/L in ISS water supplied by the United States. This would limit water consumption to a maximum of 3 L/day to maintain daily intake levels from all sources at less than the limit established by NASA of less than 1.0 mg/day of iodine. Consequently, there remains concern that the maximum level of 0.25 mg/L of iodine in the spacecraft water will not provide sufficient microbial control, thus increasing the risk to ISS crewmembers.

experiment_title: Effect of Sex on Orthostatic Intolerance and Cardiovascular Responses during Lunar Descent and Ascent
experiment_description:
Objectives
The Artemis missions to the Moon have initiated the development of the Human Landing System (HLS) to transport astronauts to and from the lunar surface. The risk of orthostatic intolerance (OI) and the cardiovascular responses experienced during lunar descent and ascent are important considerations in the development of the HLS. OI is characterized by a group of signs and symptoms that occur after assuming an upright posture, including lightheadedness, dizziness, visual changes, increased heart rate, sudden drops in systolic or diastolic blood pressure, and significant cardiac arrhythmias. Given that OI is a concern during re-exposure to normal gravity (1-G) even after short duration exposures to weightlessness and that crew may be in a standing posture in the vehicle during decent to and accent from the lunar surface, G-loads during the dynamic phases of the Artemis mission may be problematic for some individuals. OI when standing is apparent after just days of exposure to weightlessness and spaceflight analogs, and thus it is expected that OI may be a concern even during lunar descent. Furthermore, it is unlikely that the partial gravity exposure during stays on the lunar surface will be protective against OI during ascent from the surface.

There were no reports of symptoms consistent with OI during the Apollo missions. However, all the Apollo crewmembers were male with a history high performance aircraft experience, and almost all the commanders demonstrated high heart rates during sustained G-levels ranging from 0.4- to 0.6-G over ~9 min during lunar descent and ascent. The G-levels to which the Artemis astronauts will be exposed have not been defined, but it is likely that the G-levels will be greater and/or the exposures will be longer than those experienced by Apollo astronauts based upon the flight plan required to reach Gateway, which will be at a higher orbit than the Apollo Command and Service Module. Further, the proportion of women in the astronaut corps has been increasing and it has been publicly stated that the first Artemis mission to the lunar surface will include at least one woman; thus the effect of sex on the cardiovascular responses to acceleration should be considered with regard to lunar descent and ascent. In general, women have lower orthostatic tolerance and are more susceptible to post-spaceflight orthostatic intolerance when re-exposed to 1-G. However, it is unclear whether women also would be less able to the tolerate lower levels of acceleration that likely will be experienced during descent to and ascent from the lunar surface.

Lower body compression garments are one of the countermeasures that have been used to protect against OI after exposure to weightlessness. Specifically, NASA has developed the Orion Orthostatic Intolerance Garment (OIG) for the Artemis missions, but the suit's efficacy has not been demonstrated in women and men during long exposures (20 minutes) to simulated G-levels (0.5-, 0.75, 1.0-G) that astronauts may experience during lunar descent and ascent during the Artemis missions.

This study has the following aims

1. To determine whether there are differences between hypovolemic men and women in orthostatic tolerance (assessed by tilt time) and cardiovascular responses during 20 minutes of exposure to a range of gravity levels (0.50-, 0.75-, and 1.00-G) simulated by different angles of head-up tilt that Artemis astronauts might experience during descent to and ascent from the lunar surface.
2. To determine whether the Orion Orthostatic Intolerance Garment (OIG) will protect men and women against orthostatic intolerance (assessed by tilt time) and reduce the cardiovascular responses caused by exposure to the range gravity levels (0.50-, 0.75-, and 1.00-G) simulated by different angles of head-up tilt that Artemis astronauts might experience during descent to and ascent from the lunar surface.

Approach
19 men and 19 women will be recruited to complete this study. The participants will be similar to the astronaut population along important characteristics such as age, body mass index, and physical fitness. To complete the study, subjects will participate in two phases of testing.

Phase I will evaluate differences in OI between the sexes (Aim 1). During the first of two laboratory visits (1A), test operators will obtain anthropometric measurements to be used in the design and construction of an individualized Orion OIG, familiarize the subjects to the tilt test procedures, and measure the subject’s baseline plasma volume (carbon monoxide rebreathing method) and tolerance to 80° head-up tilt (1.00-G). During the second of two laboratory visits (2A), plasma volume will be measured prior to inducing hypovolemia through administration of a furosemide infusion (20 mg). Once hypovolemia is achieved, participants will be exposed to three 20-minute sessions of head-up tilt tests at 30° (0.50-G), 50° (0.75-G), and 80° (1-G) in a randomized order counterbalanced across subjects. During each tilt test, measurements that will be obtained while supine and during head-up tilt include brachial blood pressure, beat-to-beat finger blood pressure, and heart rate (ECG) and ultrasound parameters required to calculate stroke volume, cardiac output and total peripheral resistance. Hematocrit, hemoglobin, and carboxyhemoglobin will be measured from blood samples and used to calculate red blood cell volume, total blood volume, and plasma volume. Blood samples will be collected prior to each tilt test to calculate changes in plasma volume across the test day.

Phase II also will consist of two laboratory visits. During the first visit (2A), subjects will don the OIG constructed from the anthropometric measures obtained in visit 1A to ensure correct sizing. During the second visit (2B), plasma volume will be measured using the same carbon monoxide rebreathing method prior to inducing hypovolemia through administration of furosemide infusion. After hypovolemia is achieved, subjects will don the OIG, and will be assessed for orthostatic tolerance with compression garments using the same tilt test protocol as in phase I, with G-levels presented in the same order in which they were in visit 1B to avoid any potential confounding effects of order when comparing tilt results within subjects.

Results
It is expected that females will be more susceptible to OI and demonstrate a greater heart rate response when hypovolemic than males at 1-G (Phase I) and that differences between sexes (tolerance time and cardiovascular responses) will be less as simulated G-levels decrease. The findings from this phase of the study will provide additional detail to the HLS acceleration limits during the dynamic flight phases when astronauts are standing but not wearing compression garments. However, it is expected that all subjects will be able to tolerate the entire tilt duration when hypovolemic and using lower body compression garments (Phase II). The findings from this phase of the study will provide additional detail to the HLS acceleration limits during the dynamic flight phases when astronauts are standing, but wearing compression garments, particularly with regard to the duration of tolerance.
