experiment_title: Measurement of Body Composition for Nutritional Assessment in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Long-term space flight increases the risk of reduced human performance due to loss of body cell mass resulting from the combined effects of microgravity and energy imbalance. Although countermeasures have been proposed, there are no valid means of monitoring these body composition changes in flight or monitoring the effectiveness of countermeasures prior to return to Earth (1-G). As missions increase from weeks to years in length, the need for inflight methods to monitor the nutritional status of astronauts becomes critical to health maintenance. To address this limitation, investigators undertook a systematic validation of hardware for measuring body composition during space flight. Investigators completed ground-based studies to validate bioimpedance spectroscopy (BIS) to measure the compartmentalization of total body water between intra- and extracellular spaces under conditions of 1-G. Ground-based studies were then completed using a head-down-tilt model to validate BIS in simulated microgravity. Next, a study attempting to validate the ability of BIS was undertaken to detect and quantitate changes in body cell mass due to short-term negative nitrogen balance and negative energy balance. The methods to be used during this validation were measurement of total body water by deuterium dilution and extracellular water by bromide dilution.

Hypothesis I. Bioelectrical spectroscopy will provide an accurate measurement of water compartmentalization in humans under simulated microgravity environments.
Aims:
1) Correlate bioelectrical spectroscopy with deuterium oxide (Total Body Water) and bromide dilution (Extracellular water) during simulated microgravity (head-down-tilt).
2) Develop equations to calculate intra- and extracellular water volumes under conditions of simulated microgravity.

Hypothesis II. Bioelectrical spectroscopy will provide an accurate measurement of water compartmentalization in humans during simulated microgravity and short-term under nutrition.
Aims:
1) Determine if simulated microgravity alters the calibration of bioimpedance for body water analysis
2) Optimize electrode placement to minimize interindividual variation in water redistribution to the trunk during under nutrition.

Hypothesis III. Bioelectrical spectroscopy will accurately and precisely measure changes in leg and arm muscle volume.
Aim:
1) Validate bioimpedance spectroscopy of peripheral segments against nuclear magnetic imaging of muscle volume.

The goal of this study was to validate bioelectric spectroscopy as a form of body composition analysis for space flight. If this method has acceptable precision and accuracy, it would allow for body composition analysis during space flights, rather than waiting for return to Earth. Astronauts would be allowed to design individualized treatment programs, including strength training or increased fluid intake, to resolve their specific health problems while still in space. This is particularly important during long space flights or during residency on a space station. Under these conditions, resolution of health problems should not, and can not, wait months or years.

APPROACH:
Two human studies were performed. To simplify the report, these are referred to as Study I and Study II. The subject pool included 39 Caucasians, 6 Hispanics, and one African-American. Subjects were of normal weight, were weight stable in the previous month (<2 kg change), and were not taking any medications known to affect body composition. Subjects ranged in age from 19 - 45 years and had no medical contraindications to the protocol. Women participated during the seven days between the end of menstruation and before ovulation. Women on oral contraception were not excluded from participation. All subjects gave written informed consent before participation.

Study I
Day 1: Subjects reported to the University of Wisconsin General Clinical Research Center (GCRC) by 08:00 following an overnight fast. A pregnancy test was administered to all female subjects, but none required exclusion due to pregnancy. Weight and height were measured. A catheter with heparin lock was inserted and baseline blood was collected (10 mL). Subjects were orally dosed with a 100 mL mixture of deuterium oxide (4 g) and sodium bromide (NaBr)(10 mg/kg body weight) in tap water to drink. More blood (10 mL) was drawn twice during the morning (3 and 4 hours after consuming the tracers). Electrodes were placed and multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance measured. Electrode placement was marked with waterproof ink. At approximately 13:00, subjects were given a liquid meal (Ensure™). They received a volume of supplement that provides approximately one third of daily energy needs (e.g. 1/3th of basal energy expenditure (BEE) x 1.2). After this ambulatory period, the subjects assumed the 6º head-down-tilt (HDT) position for the duration of the study. Blood was drawn, and weight and bioelectric impedance were measured four hours after assuming HDT. At approximately 17:00, subjects received a no added salt, low residue diet with an energy content at 1.2 x BEE and a protein content of 15% of kcal. Subjects consumed 30 mL/kg fluids per each day of the study. Caffeine and alcohol consumption were not allowed.

Day 2: Subjects remained in HDT and received the study diet. At 08:00, measurements of body water were repeated. This included collection of blood three times, assessment of bioelectric impedance two times, measurement of weight two times, and consumption of the 100 mL deuterium oxide/NaBr mixture for tracer dilution analysis.

Day 3: Subjects remained in HDT and received the study diet. At 08:00, measurements of body water were repeated. This included collection of blood three times, assessment of bioelectric impedance two times, measurement of weight two times, and consumption of the 100 mL deuterium oxide/NaBr mixture. Subjects were given a full lunch and rehydration fluids before leaving. Staff ensured subjects could tolerate standing up before they were allowed to leave the GCRC.

Study II
Day 1: Subjects reported to the GCRC by 18:00. A pregnancy test was administered to all female subjects, but none tested positive. Height and weight in hospital gown was measured. Subjects underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the calf and upper arm. Bioelectric impedance analysis of these same limbs was conducted. Electrode placement was marked with waterproof ink. At 22:00, subjects assumed the 6° head-down-tilt position in bed, which continued for the remainder of the study. A blood-drawing catheter with heparin lock was inserted. Subjects did not receive food until after the next morning’s study period was over (at approximately 12:00 noon). All urine was collected.

Day 2: At 19:45, subjects had 10 mL blood drawn. An oral dose was administered to subjects with a 100 mL mixture of deuterium oxide (4 g) and NaBr (10 mg/kg body weight) in tap water. Additional blood was drawn twice during the morning. Weight, whole body, and segmental multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance were measured. Electrode placement was marked with waterproof ink. At approximately 12:00 noon, subjects began receiving the study diet. This diet was a clear liquid, low calorie regimen designed to induce the negative nitrogen balance and glycogen depletion necessary for intracellular volume to decrease. Subjects received 800 kcal as carbohydrate with no additional kcal from either protein or fat. A multivitamin/mineral pill was given so that micronutrient needs were met. This diet continued for the duration of the study (approximately 32 hours). Blood was drawn daily to ensure electrolyte levels were maintained.

Day 3: Subjects remained in HDT and received the study diet. Blood was drawn to ensure electrolyte levels were maintained.

Day 4: Subjects remained in HDT. At 08:00, subjects repeated tracer dilution tests. This involved collection of blood three times, assessment of bioelectrical impedance two times, measurement of weight twice, and consumption of the deuterium oxide/NaBr mixture. No food or beverage was allowed until the 4-hour collection period had been completed. At 8 pm that night, subjects were transported on a gurney to have a second MRI of their upper arm and calf. A repeat bioelectric spectroscopy scan of these limbs was taken. Subjects were given a full dinner and rehydration fluids before leaving. Subjects were discharged when they demonstrated orthostatic tolerance.

Body Water Assessment:
Analysis of total body water (TBW), extracellular water (ECW), and intracellular water (ICW) was completed using tracer-dilution methods. For all assessments, baseline blood samples were collected for deuterium and bromide analysis. Subjects were then dosed with 10 mg/kg NaBr and 40 g of 10 atom% deuterium solution. Blood samples were collected four hours after dosing. All urine output during the 4-hour tracer equilibration time was collected and pooled so that urinary losses of deuterium and bromide could be directly measured.

TBW was calculated from deuterium dilution as described by Schoeller (1999). Deuterium enrichment of plasma and urine samples was quantified using isotope ratio mass spectrometry. Corrections were made for lost dosage of deuterium in urine and water vapor, as well as non-aqueous hydrogen exchange. ECW was quantified using the equations and techniques of Miller et al. (1989), with the addition of a correction of 0.987 for the concentration of water in serum ultrafiltrate. The bromide concentration of plasma was assessed using Miller’s anion-exchange high-pressure chromatography technique. Corrections were made for lost dosage of bromide in urine. Urine samples were cleaned using solid-phase cation-extraction filters, diluted threefold, and then analyzed using the same anion-exchange high-pressure chromatography technique used for blood. ICW was calculated as the difference between TBW and ECW.

Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis:
Electrode placement was proximal as described by Scheltinga et al (1991). This was used instead of typical wrist/ankle electrode placement because the proximal placement is less sensitive to temperature and orthostatic effects. After cleaning the electrode site with isopropopol alcohol, electrode patches (7.6 x 1.9 cm) with self-adhesive conducting gel were attached to the dorsal surface of the right foot and right hand for current injection. Detector electrodes were attached to the dorsal surface of the right leg with the proximal edge 1 cm distal to the center of the knee cap and on the dorsal surface of the right forearm with the proximal edge 1 cm distal to the mid-crease of the antecubital fossa.

Muscle Volume Modeling:
Selection of arm and leg segments to model: A 13.3 cm section of the upper right arm and a 16.1 cm section of the right leg were modeled using both magnetic resonance imaging and bioelectrical impedance spectroscopy. For the arm segment, the elbow was bent at a 90-degree angle and a straight edge was applied to the underside of the forearm. A ruler edge was applied to the backside of the upper arm so that it bisected the straight edge at a 90-degree angle. A line was drawn 10 cm up from the tip of the ventral side of the elbow. The arm was straightened then abducted so that it was parallel to the floor, and the mark was extended to circumscribe the arm in a circle that was perpendicular to the floor. Another circumscribing line was drawn 13.3 cm proximal to the first line. For the leg segment, a mark was drawn 2 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity. While subjects were standing, the mark was extended to circumscribe the leg in a circle that was parallel to the floor. Another circumscribing line was drawn 16.1 cm distal to the first line.

Magnetic resonance imaging procedure: Gel beads (containing oil) were applied to the dorsal side of the leg and the ventral side of the upper arm at the sites of the circumscribing lines to allow for detection of desired limb regions. T1 weighted scans (TE=25, TR=600, NEX=1.0) were conducted to differentiate between muscle, fat, bone, and air. Using the gel beads as a guide, twenty-three 7mm thick leg slices and one 7 mm thick arm slices were selected for analysis. The slices were processed using the custom 3-D modeling package of an Advantage Windows workstation (software version 2.0.20). In brief, thresholds were manually set to eliminate air, bone, and subcutaneous fat from the scans. Then, the software integrated the slices to produce a muscle volume estimate for the entire set of slices. The muscle volume modeling procedure was conducted in a blind fashion on three separate occasions. For outlying points the procedure was repeated a fourth time. The average of volumes (excluding outliers) was used as the criterion measure of muscle volume for further statistical analysis.

Bioelectrical Impedance Spectroscopy (BIS) procedure: The areas of the arm and leg containing the circumscribing lines were cleaned with isopropyl alcohol. Then 0.5 cm wide electrode tape for current detection was wrapped around the arm and leg directly on the circumscribing lines. Current injection electrodes were placed 8 cm away from the electrode tape. BIS scans of the arm and leg segments were completed in triplicate.

RESULTS:
Generation of BIS Water Space Prediction Equations The primary focus of this research project was to develop a method to measure body composition that could be used during space flight. This technique is Bioelectrical Impedance Spectroscopy (BIS). The instrument has a volume of less than 0.02 cubic meters, weighs less than 2 kg, and consumes little power. These studies demonstrate that the instrument could measure ECW, ICW and TBW with an accuracy of 1.2 kg for ECW, 2.2 kg for ICW, and 2.4 kg for TBW. Accuracy of this instrument was not altered by simulated microgravity. More importantly, BIS was able to follow the changes in ECW and ICW that occur when a person moves from standing to HDT and that it can measure these changes with a relative precision (SD) of 2 to 3% in a single individual. Thus, BIS can provide inflight technology for monitoring body fluid shifts. The ability to independently measure ECW and ICW means that the BIS can be used to monitor loss of extracellular fluids that often occurs in microgravity. The ability to measure ICW provides the clinical capacity to monitor changes in nutritional status. Finally, BIS was found to provide clinical capacity to measure changes in peripheral muscle volume. This is limited to peripheral muscles, however, because BIS requires that the object be presented as a cylinder in order to make an absolute measure of volume. It is also notable that BIS should be able to distinguish between muscle volume changes resulting from changes in ECW or ICW and thus distinguish between movement of extracellular water and loss of muscle fiber volume.

Investigators found that BIS was not as effective at detecting a sudden decrease in intracellular volume that is concentrated in the trunk. This could be circumvented through the use of segmental analysis, but this increases the complexity of the measurement and decreases the precision. It is likely that some of the problem lay in the choice of a somewhat unphysiologic model in which investigators severely restricted the subjects with regard to protein and energy for 48h. This is likely to produce a relatively specific loss of liver volume due to protein breakdown and glycogen utilization. Investigators are collaborating with a French investigator to access the accuracy and precision of BIS to monitor microgravity induced changes in ICW using a chronic 90-day, HDT, bed rest model that is likely to provide a more physiologic alteration of body composition.

Nutritional Deficiencies
The BIS instrument now offers the clinical capacity to study and diagnose clinical deficiencies during space flight. Until now, measurement of body composition could only be performed before launch and after reentry. The BIS technology provides a means to distinguish between the various causes of weight loss and to test countermeasures in space flight. Fluid loss secondary to exposure to microgravity is primarily due to extracellular fluid loss. BIS is very accurate at measuring ECW and thus determining what percentage of weight loss is due to simple diuresis. BIS can also be employed in real time to monitor the effectiveness of countermeasures, such as lower body negative pressure and saline ingestion.

In contrast, chronic, mild undernutrition will induce a loss of body protein and or body fat. The former will be accompanied by a loss of ICW while the latter will not, because fat in anhydrous. BIS can be used for differential diagnosis of fat loss or body cell mass loss and this information can be used to make prescriptions for dietary change.

Human Performance
The BIS instrument also provides clinical capacity for the study and diagnosis of loss of muscle mass during space flight. Loss of muscle mass usually results in loss of strength, which can be detrimental upon the return to gravity. This ability enables investigators and medical personnel to monitor the effectiveness of exercise countermeasures on muscle mass.

experiment_title: Adaptation in Artificial Gravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Many of the space flight-related deleterious physical effects on the human body associated with space flight are caused by a lack of gravity. For years, researchers have sought to design artificial gravity for use during space flight to reduce or eliminate inherent physiological risks, such as degeneration of the skeletal, muscular, cardiovascular, and sensorimotor systems. One practical method of providing artificial gravity during space flight is to design a rotating chamber that generates a centrifugal force on the astronaut's body. An understanding of the limits of the ability of the human to adapt and function within a rotating environment is needed to design an effective rotating artificial gravity chamber.

The goals of this experiment were threefold: 1) to determine whether individuals can be trained to move between stationary and rotating environments without exhibiting errors in arm movement control, 2) to enhance the ability to use tools and move objects in rotating environments, and 3) to determine whether mechanical disturbance of movement pathways can be used to preadapt astronauts to the centrifugal forces that they would encounter in a space vehicle rotating to generate artificial gravity.

APPROACH:
The corresponding aims of this study were: 1) to measure the acquisition of dual adaptation of arm movements to rotating and non-rotating environments, 2) to measure disruption and restoration of object transport accuracy as a function of background gravitoinertial force level, and 3) to determine whether adaptations to mechanical and to centrifugal disturbances of reaching movements show transfer and can be substituted for one another. The study was conducted in a slow rotation room that was manipulated by robotic action.

RESULTS:
Specific Aim 1
The investigators found that when subjects are initially exposed to a rotating room the Coriolis forces generated when they attempt a reaching movement causes large errors in the endpoint and path of the movement. The dominant models of movement control had predicited there would be no endpoint errors. Similar errors occur for other types of movements – leg movements, head movements, whole body movements. They found that 10-20 reaching movements in a rotating environment is sufficient to restore accurate reaching movements to a visual target. Earlier work had suggested that many orders of magnitude more movements would be required. The magnitude of initial reaching errors increases monotonically from room speeds of 5 to 30 rpm, and there is rapid, complete adaptation at all speeds.

It was shown that adaptation is extraordinarily rapid if subjects are given a spatial goal or target to attain rather than just make random arm movements. Investigators also found that if subjects in a rotating environment stand passively, they do not show post-rotation postural aftereffects. However, if they voluntarily sway they rapidly adapt to the Coriolis forces generated by their movements and show large aftereffects post-rotation. The key to postural adaptation is - as with the arm – having spatial goals.

Subjects who have adapted to one speed of rotation can be switched to other rates of rotation and maintain good accuracy. Once they are exposed to a new rotation speed their first reach is in error and subsequent reaches are again accurate. It is as if the first reach serves as a probe keying the CNS to the rotation rate and allowing corrective adjustments to be made.

Specific Aim 2
When subjects make reaching movements during passive body rotation that the way in which they adapt depends on the presence or absence of contact cues on the hand. If subjects reach with their hand free, then normal movement paths and accuracy will be regained within 20 movements. However, if the adapted subjects then reach while holding an object, renewed errors will result. By contrast, if subjects initially adapt while reaching and holding an object, they do not overcompensate when reaching without it. This means the CNS identifies some of the Coriolis forces during the initial reaches as having arisen from the object and some from the arm itself. The component of adaptation is tuned out when the subject reaches without the object. This decomposition of contacting and non-contacting forces on the arm must underlie context specific adaptation of tool use and self-calibration.

Specific Aim 3
The investigators studied adaptation to Coriolis force perturbations of reaching movements in a rotating environment when subjects reached freely to targets or when they reached to them while grasping a robotic manipulandum that was deactivated. After adaptation was achieved they then looked for transfer to when they reached grasping the deactivated robotic manipulandum or when they reached with the free hand. Subjects who initially reached holding the manipulandum showed little transfer to the free hand. This means they attributed the perturbation during the initial movements to the manipulandum not to properties of the environment or of the hand. Subjects who initially reached with the free hand showed retention of adaptation when reaching while holding the manipulandum. Such asymmetric transfer emphasizes the critical role of contact cues on the hand in determining the characteristics of adaptation, whether it is hand or tool dependent. Further experiments are necessary to determine if contact cues can be simulated – and in some conditions masked – to allow predictable manipulations of the adaptive state. This is key if robotic manipulanda are to be useful for pre-adapting astronauts to the Coriolis forces associated with rotation.

experiment_title: Effect of Spaceflight on Level and Function of Immune Cells: I. Immunology Studies
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The purpose of the immunology studies was to continue the systematic attempt to define the range of immunological parameters affected by space flight. The experiments were designed to allow repetition and expansion of studies from a previous flight (Cosmos 1887), with the addition of an antiorthostatic suspension study for direct comparison with space flight effects.

Approach:

The first portion of this experiment involved the ability of cells to respond to colony stimulating factor-granulocyte/monocyte (CSF-GM). For colony stimulating factor assays, 1x105 bone marrow cells were suspended with 10% fetal bovine serum and antibiotics containing 3% agar. The second set of studies involved the expression of cell surface markers (T-cell markers, B-cell markers, natural killer cell markers and interleukin-2 receptors) of both spleen and bone marrow cells. Populations stained with fluorescein-labeled antibodies were analyzed using a flow cytometer. In addition, natural killer cell levels were also examined.

Results:

Bone marrow cells from flight and tail suspended (TS) rats had reduced response to CSF-GM, demonstrating that response to a recombinant DNA-derived cytokine affecting both monocyte and granulocyte cell populations in bone marrow was compromised by space flight. Spleen cells from flown rats showed increased percentages of pan leukocyte, helper-T, and suppressor-cytotoxic-T-cells, while TS samples had a different pattern of markers. In bone marrow lymphocytic cell population, the percentage of anti-asialo GM-1 bearing, interleukin-2 receptor bearing, pan-T, and helper-T cells was increased after flight, while TS samples again had a different pattern. This shows that suspension is useful for modeling space flight effects of functional immune responses, but not adequate for modeling space flight effects on cell population distribution. Additionally, specific natural killer cell subpopulations were depressed after space flight, while others were not, indicating lack of a general blunting of natural killer cell responses.

experiment_title: Gastrointestinal Absorption and Pharmacokinetics in Astronauts
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Weightlessness during space flight induces a wide range of physiological and biochemical changes in crewmembers, such as disruption of gastrointestinal (GI) function and physiology, changes in liver function, alterations in organ blood flow, and hormonal and metabolic perturbations. Any of these changes can influence the pharmacokinetic behavior and pharmacodynamic consequences of medications administered to crewmembers during space flight. As mission durations increase, the effects of spaceflight-induced physiologic changes and the resulting pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic deviations will also increase. These effects must be countered in order to maintain optimum health and performance during flight, as well as to initiate re-adaptation to gravity upon return to Earth.

Comparison of results from the "Pharmacokinetics of Acetaminophen (DSO 458)" experiment (7 subjects - Tylenol tablets) and the "Gastrointestinal Function During Extended Duration Space Flight (DSO 622)" experiment (4 subjects - Tylenol syrup) indicated that absorption and bioavailability of oral liquid dosage may be better and more reliable than that of an equivalent solid dosage form. Medication uptake may also improve in a fed state during which a low fiber breakfast was ingested, than during a fasted state, lasting 8 to 10 hours, as a means of compensating for the expected GI decrements during space flight.

Additionally, unusually high breath levels of hydrogen (Shuttle data) and methane (Mir data) were observed, in addition to the reported regular use of countermeasure (lactobacillus) by the Russian program, which indicated changes in GI microbes. This warranted the need to examine the microbial physiology of the GI tract. Decreased GI motility--as indicated from the limited results from the Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project and the Shuttle-Mir Science Program experiment "Gastrointestinal Function During Extended Duration Space Flight (DSO 622)"--will affect drug absorption and bioavailability of oral medications and thus compromise therapeutic effectiveness during space flights. This effect will be compounded by anticipated changes in the hepatic metabolism of drugs and other xenobiotics.

The purpose of this experiment was to determine changes in the GI function and physiology and examine the pharmacokinetics of orally administered pharmaceutical probe acetaminophen. Estimating clinically significant organ functional changes and resultant pharmacokinetic consequences will lead to the design and development of effective pharmacologic countermeasures and therapeutic adjustments.

APPROACH:
This investigation was comprised of three tests: lactulose and acetaminophen test, glucose breath hydrogen test, and 3-C Urea Helicobacter test. Each of these tests was to be conducted both before and after flight; no data collection was scheduled during flight. During pre- and postflight sessions, a specified breakfast was to be provided, followed by an oral ingestion of acetaminophen. Timed breath and saliva samples were collected, as were void-by-void urine samples. Food, fluid, exercise and medications were monitored during the urine and saliva collections. The rate of acetaminophen absorption and metabolism would be determined by analysis of the urine samples and timed saliva samples.

Lactulose and Acetaminophen Tests: Participants were asked to avoid eating foods that are likely to generate hydrogen (such as cabbage, beans, dairy products) for twenty-four hours before the test. After approximately an 8-hour fast (sleep period), a saliva sample, a urine sample, and two consecutive breath samples, 5 minutes apart, were collected from the subjects. The subjects then ate a low fiber breakfast, followed by ingestion of 650 mg of acetaminophen (650 mg). After acetaminophen ingestion, participants drank orange juice (or an agreed-upon fluid) containing 20 g of lactulose.

Subjects were to record intake of food, fluids, medications, and exercise during the 24-hour protocol period. They were not to eat or exercise for 4 hours following ingestion of medication; however, drinking water was allowed. After ingesting the acetaminophen and drinking the lactulose/orange juice mixture, the following samples were collected from the subjects:

1) 12 additional saliva samples
2) 16 additional breath samples (per the prescribe schedule)
3) Urine voids for 24 hours (as separate samples)

Glucose Breath Hydrogen Test: After an overnight fast, a breath sample was collected. Participants then consumed a dose of glucose dissolved in water. Breath samples were collected every 15 minutes for 120 minutes after dose consumption.

Urea Helicobacter Test: After overnight fasting, a baseline breath sample was obtained. Subjects then consumed a liquid test meal containing 13-C urea. Breath samples were collected every 10 minutes for 30 minutes post-ingestion.

A ground-based protocol of DSO 632 was also performed. Recent data collected on GI function (DSO 632) in astronauts indicates five out of the six subjects tested exhibited active colonization of H. pylori in their stomach. H. pylori is a bacterial pathogen suspected to promote incidence of gastric and duodenal ulcer disease. The objective of this addendum was to screen and establish population data for the incidence of H. pylori in the local Johnson Space Center (JSC) population in reference to the astronaut population. The investigators aimed to screen a total of 50 subjects from ground support personnel and from astronaut core (about 30 and 20 each, respectively). The investigators wanted to screen astronauts that have flown before and those who have not flown. Crewmembers from international partners were also encouraged to participate in the screening. Subjects could self administer at their convenience. This simple, safe and noninvasive breath test known as Breath Tek -UBiT, is a clinical test administered by health care providers to diagnose pathology associated with H. pylori incidence. The test was administered in the morning after an overnight fast. The total time required for the implementation of this protocol was 30 minutes for briefing before the test (at subjects' convenience) and approximately 20 minutes for the test itself. Test protocol includes collection of two breath samples, one before and another 15 minutes after consumption of a test beverage provided by the vendor. Samples were analyzed using vendor-provided instrumentation. A GI symptoms checklist was provided to subjects having results in the positive range to assess any incidence of pathology associated with H. pylori. A copy of the test results was provided to the subjects along with instructions for action if positive test results were observed.

RESULTS:
Results indicated significant changes in GI motility and absorption of APAP during both short and long-duration space flights; difference between early, mid and late flight days (n=2) was not significant suggesting that the GI functional changes manifest early in flight and remain consistent throughout the mission.

Results for the ground-based portion of this study aren't available.

experiment_title: Constant Force Resistive Exercise Unit Evaluation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Exposing humans to weightlessness during space flight induces significant structural and functional changes in the musculoskeletal system. These changes are manifested as muscle atrophy and bone degradation accompanied by neuromuscular changes including muscle fatigue and weakness, abnormal reflex behavior, and diminished neuromuscular efficiency. Recommendations to remedy the negative effects of microgravity on muscles and bones suggest that astronauts perform strengthening exercises while in space. Such resistive exercises provide a load that is otherwise absent in space, presumably preserving musculoskeletal function. Many principles must be considered while designing an exercise device as a countermeasure for muscle atrophy due to disuse. Most importantly, load capabilities, constant force resistive output, and eccentric and concentric exercise capabilities should be the primary design goals of any resistive exercise device.

The proposed experiment contributed to the development of practical and useful exercise countermeasures by introducing and evaluating a novel resistive exercise machine, the Constant Force Resistance Exercise Unit (CFREU). Unlike past countermeasure devices, the CFREU has been designed to exercise muscle groups at a constant force concentrically and eccentrically throughout an entire range of motion during exercise. The objective of this experiment was to evaluate the CFREU for ease of use, reliability, and life cycle in an International Space Station (ISS) analog setting. Wireless physiological monitoring information was also collected during exercise.

APPROACH:
Prior to the mission, participants received a 1.5-hour training session on the CFREU mechanics, maintenance, and exercise protocols. During the mission, participants performed a prescribed exercise protocol using the CFREU within the Aquarius habitat on selected days, and upon completion of each session, participants recorded results in an exercise log. Crewmembers exercised in teams of two, over a one-hour time period. Thirty minutes of exercise was performed by each crewmember; while one was exercising, the other acted as a "spotter". The spotter was also responsible for ensuring that a video recorder was set up and each exercise session recorded. During each exercise session, one of the two participants wore a VitalSense physiological monitoring system. This experiment evaluated the ease of use, overall mechanical performance, and maintenance issues related to the CFREU.

RESULTS:
NEEMO 6 Crewmember feedback was overwhelmingly positive; a highlight of the mission. Crewmembers suggested reducing the size further than it is, with a few design changes. Hardware performance was not optimal. The crewmembers noticed increased friction in the system that developed over the mission duration, which restricted them to performing exercises at >15lbs.

experiment_title: Development and Use of Human 3-Dimensional Tissue Culture Models for the Study of Space Radiation Effects on the Central Nervous System
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Human space exploration involves exposure to types of radiation not normally encountered on earth. The effect of these particles on the human central nervous system (CNS) is of particular concern since impairment of cognitive function could not only compromise missions but cause later effects on the quality of life. Studies in animals have shown that space radiation particles can have adverse effects on cognition and behavior. The effect on neurogenesis has also been documented and proposed to be a cause of cognitive loss. Information regarding the effects of space radiation on the CNS is, however, still in its infancy due to the difficulty of extrapolating data from animals and cell lines to the intact human being.

The primary objective of this investigation was to increase the understanding of the effects of space radiation on the human central nervous system with an emphasis on neurodegeneration. There were two primary goals:

  1. Develop 3-dimensional tissue models for neural tissue, achieving a more accurate representation of human neural tissue by incorporating human neuron, astrocytes, and endothelial cells into the model.
  2. Apply the 3-dimensional models to develop assays to support projected studies of the effects of space radiation on neurodegeneration.

APPROACH:
The study began with the development of the human brain tissue model. At least 3 human cell types were acquired for each of the components of the model: neurons, astrocytes and endothelial cells. This ensured the best possible model and provided back-up cells. Then, a multistep protocol was developed for the generation and differentiation of normal human neurons from stem cells. Expression of neuronal markers and degeneration markers in 3D monocultures was successfully detected. The strategy for constructing tissue models was to embed neurons and astrocytes into protein gel matrices after they had been differentiated into the respective cell type and then induce morphological or “end stage” differentiation while they were in the matrix.

Endothelial cells were added, given the right factors, and allowed to grow into the matrix and form blood vessels as in vivo during angiogenesis. Different media types and different pairings of cell types were tested. As a result, it was found that the requirement of endothelial cells was not entirely compatible with that of neurons and astrocytes. Endothelial cells, which line the vessels and are in contact with blood in vivo require serum for vessel formation. Neurons and astrocytes, normally behind the blood brain barrier (BBB), require serum-free conditions to differentiate in matrices. However, a prototype neurovascular unit using the above protocol was created by reducing the serum concentration and relying on trophic support from astrocytes for the maintenance of vessels. At this stage, it was determined that tissue models were developed enough to be incorporated into assays that assess tight junctions and provide an additional relevant endpoint.

Assay development was directed towards determination of the effects of space radiation on the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB).

Assays to determine the function of the endothelial barrier were developed. For the first assay, trans-endothelial resistance measurement was achieved by using equipment that measures electric cell-substrate impedance sensing (ECIS). Resistance monitoring of monolayers was easy and continuous. This assay is useful for determining parameters such as the time course of the effects of radiation. A second assay was developed using tissue inserts to determine the rate of labeled molecules permeation through the cell layer on the insert. This provides a direct measurement of the passage of molecules of varying sizes through the endothelial cell layer. This assay does not utilize the neurovascular unit but can still include a cell mixture of endothelial cells and astrocytes or pericytes. Endothelial cells are plated on one side of the membrane and the other cell types are plated on the other side of the membrane. Thus it represents the human blood-brain-barrier more closely than endothelial cells alone. 2 additional assays were developed for localization of the junction proteins that seal the BBB using immunolabeling of these molecules: the first examining the junction proteins in normal monolayers and the second, examining the junction proteins in the 3-D human tissue models. Further assays include endpoints more directly applied to human neuro-degenerative diseases. One such endpoint is the metabolization and localization of the protein involved in Alzheimer’s disease – the amyloid precursor protein (APP).

RESULTS:
The primary goal of this investigation has been achieved. Human 3-D tissue models have been developed sufficiently for use in novel assays to determine degenerative markers. Other assays were developed for use in future studies that address a pivotal part of the brain involved heavily in many neuro-degenerative disorders – the brain blood capillaries. Work going forward includes improving the longevity of these models and substituting neurons from stem cells for the neuroblastoma used in the prototype model.

experiment_title: Morphological Analysis of Pituitary Somatotrophs of SLS-1 and SLS-2 Rats
experiment_description:
Objectives:

In order to gain a better understanding of the mechanisms involved in metabolic disorders in response to microgravity, it is important to study the somatotrophic function of the pituitary gland controlling growth and anabolic processes in mammals. Previous inflight experiments have shown a progressive minimization of endocrine regulatory function and inhibition of GH production and secretion with increased flight time. The objective of this study was to determine the histological and cytokaryometric changes in the somatotroph cells of rats flown on SLS-2.

Approach:

Pituitary glands were fixed in Bouin's fixative and embedded in paraffin. Horizontal 4 millimeter thick sections were stained with paraldehyde fuchsin and Halmi's mixture to identify both basophilic cells and somatotrophs. The major ingredient of Halmi's mixture selectively stains pituitary somatotroph cells. Cytokaryometric examination of somatotroph cells was performed. In the pituitary of each flight and control rat, 100 somatotroph cells and their nuclei located along capillaries and between capillaries in glandular areas were outlined. Diameters and volumes of the cells and their nuclei were measured and statistically treated by means of routine morphometric methods. Somatotrophic cell status was determined from cytokaryometric data and visual evaluation of growth hormone in the cytoplasm.

Results:

Pituitary glands of rats sacrificed five hours after spaceflight had a greater GH concentration than those of the controls. The pericapillary somatotroph cells had a high GH concentration but no change in cell size, while intervascular glandular somatotroph cells had a low GH concentration and a smaller cell size. Both populations exhibited drastically reduced and dense maculae. These observations indicate that spaceflight diminishes the function of somatotroph cells. During readaptation to 1 g, the secretory and biosynthetic function of the cells recovered and their activity returned to normal.

experiment_title: Haughton Mars Immune Assessment (HMIA)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective for this activity was to use the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Haughton Mars Project (HMP), a ground based model for planetary surface exploration, to validate immune system monitoring assays designed to support a proposed immunology Supplemental Medical Objective (SMO). Immune system abnormal regulation has been demonstrated to occur during space flight and has the potential to cause serious health risks to crewmembers participating in exploration class missions. This may be caused by mission-associated factors, other than the direct influences of microgravity or radiation, such as stress, confinement or an altered microbial environment. These mission-associated factors may be simulated to reasonable accuracy in ground-based spaceflight analogs such as the HMP. Data from other ground-based models for space flight (extended bed rest, closed chamber confinement, etc.) have confirmed their value for human physiology studies.

The HMP consists of simulated Mars exploration missions performed at the Haughton meteorite impact crater. The Haughton crater is located on Devon Island, in the province of Nunavut, in the high Canadian Arctic. The remote location, harsh polar desert environment, local impact-related and other Mars-like geological features make the Haughton crater one of the closest analogs on Earth to the true Mars environment. While there are significant differences between Devon Island and Mars, many aspects of field exploration activities conducted at Haughton present challenges that are relevant to human planetary exploration. At Haughton crater, a full-size prototype Mars habitat was recently constructed by the Mars Society under the auspices of the NASA Haughton-Mars Project and based on the NASA reference-mission projections for the possible size and capabilities of a Mars habitat capable of supporting human life. HMP participants conduct field exploration while adhering to specific sets of 'true Mars' conditions to ensure the quality of the spaceflight analog situation:

  • Relatively long travel to and from Devon Island.
  • Disruption of circadian rhythms (24 hour daylight).
  • Harsh polar desert conditions.
  • Removal from familiar surroundings.
  • Possible mission-simulation confined to the prototype habitat.
  • Performance of Mars-relevant surface exploration and field activities.
  • Performance of simulated spacesuited Extra-Vehicular Activities (EVA's) (including timed pre-breathe activities, etc.)
  • Performance of Mars-relevant Intra-Vehicular Activities (IVA's) (data analysis, reporting, EVA planning, repairs, etc.)
  • Reliance on remote telemedicine and communications equipment (including artificially-inserted 4 to 20-minute communication delays).

These conditions and factors combined make the HMP a well suited opportunity for simulated Mars exploration and research. In addition, the conditions to which the crewmembers were subjected made the HMP an excellent opportunity to evaluate monitoring strategies and potential countermeasures for spaceflight human factor concerns. The data generated from this activity directly addressed (in a ground-based spaceflight analog) the following questions identified by the NASA-Johnson Space Center (JSC) Critical Path Roadmap as a research priority for space flight:

7.01 Are there assays of immune function that reliably predict immune compromise?

7.03 Do factors associated with flight (stress, environment, microgravity, nutritional status, radiation) affect humoral or cell-mediated immune function, non-specific immunity, mucosal immunity, or immune surveillance capabilities of crewmembers in a manner that exposes them to unacceptable medical risk (disease, allergy, delayed wound healing)?

7.29 Are there surrogate marker assays that can be adapted to space travel that will quantitate the degree of immunodeficiency for antibody, T-cell, phagocyte, and complement function?

In addition, the data derived from this study identified the most relevant assays for routine monitoring of the immune system and provided a system to monitor the effectiveness of immune countermeasures development. There are currently no standardized immune monitoring assays. This data was a necessary and critical prerequisite for initiating studies designed assess immune countermeasures and to answer the following Critical Path questions:

7.22 Are there countermeasures for space flight-associated defects in antibody, T-cell, phagocyte, and complement systems?

7.23 Are there countermeasures for infections developed in space travel, especially latent virus infections?

APPROACH:
The Haughton Mars Immune Assessment (HMIA) was designed to assess the immune function, cellular distribution, and viral reactivation status of HMP crewmembers in a fashion mirroring a space flight experiment (pre, mid, and post-mission assessments). A unique obstacle for this study was the multinational distribution of the subjects over North America with respect to both pre and post-mission sample collection. All mid-mission sample collection and processing occurred on location at Devon Island during the 2002 field season. For pre- and post-mission sampling, arrangements were made with individual local clinics that possessed both phlebotomy capabilities and the availability of the appropriate sample collection tubes. The protocol was designed to tolerate 24 hour shipping delays of specimens with minimal loss of data, despite the requirement for live cells. When possible, immediate testing is preferred for live cell assays.

ASSAY LIST
The assays selected for the HMIA were designed to comprehensively assess both the functional capabilities and the activation status of the immune system and correlate that data with latent viral Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) reactivation. EBV reactivation is a demonstrable adverse clinical outcome that can be quantitatively measured. The assays were designed so that samples may be processed remotely and transported without cold storage, making these assays compatible with current spaceflight experiment requirements. The following is a list of the assays used to monitor immune status:

Immune System
Peripheral blood immune cell subsets
Cell-specific activation status
Th1/Th2 cell cytokine production profiles
Plasma cytokine levels

Viral reactivation
EBV-specific humoral responses
EBV-direct plasma viral DNA via PCR

FIELD SAMPLE PROCESSING ACTIVITIES
The field activities required to be performed on Devon Island consisted of cell culture and sample processing to render all sample types stable for storage and transport to JSC for subsequent analysis. The individual field requirements per assay are as follows:

Blood collection: On Devon Island, a phlebotomy station was set up in the main laboratory tent. Samples were collected from each subject by venipuncture using sterile techniques and butterfly type collection equipment.

Leukocyte subset analysis: Whole blood was treated with a newly developed preservative that maintains the antigenic structure of the cell surface molecules. Samples may be stored at room temperature for up to two weeks. There are several markers that are incompatible with this preservative. For those markers, actual fluorescent antibody staining for flow cytometry analysis was performed on Devon Island and samples were preserved for later analysis.

Plasma cytokine levels/ plasma EBV humoral responses/ EBV Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) by Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR): A micro-centrifuge was transported to Devon Island and used to purify plasma from Ethylene diamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) whole blood samples.

Cytokine production profile cultures: Heparinized whole blood was mixed with media and the appropriate mixture of mitogens and a reagent to halt extracellular transport of proteins. The cultures were then incubated for 5 hours (T cell) or 24 hours (Monocyte) to allow full activation. A portable lightweight field incubator developed by the Cell and Molecular Research (CMR) laboratory was used for these activities. Following culture the supernatant was removed and the activated cells were preserved using a leukocyte preservative.

RESULTS:
The protocol developed for immune sample processing in remote field locations functioned properly. Samples were processed on Devon Island, and stabilized for subsequent analysis at the Johnson Space Center in Houston. The data indicated that some phenotype, immune function and stress hormone changes occurred in the HMP field participants that were largely distinct from pre-mission baseline and post-mission recovery data. These immune changes appear similar to those observed in astronauts following space flight.

The immune system changes described during the HMP field deployment validate the use of the HMP as a ground-based space flight/planetary exploration analog for some aspects of human physiology. The sample processing protocol developed for this study may have applications for immune studies in remote terrestrial field locations. Elements of this protocol could possibly be adapted for future in-flight immunology studies conducted during space missions.

Ten subjects participated during the HMP 2002 field season. One pre, mid, and post-mission sample was collected for each subject. Pre-mission samples collection ranged from 36 days prior to launch of the mission (L-36) to L-4. In-mission samples were collected between Mission Day 4 (MD 4) to MD 18. Post-mission samples were collected from 47 days after the end of the mission (Recovery (R)+47) to R+110. One subject did not provide a post-mission sample.

experiment_title: Incidence of Latent Virus Shedding During Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Latent virus reactivation may be an important threat to crew health during extended space missions as crewmembers live and work in a closed environment. Infectious disease risks associated with latent viruses are not mitigated by a quarantine period before space flight or by prophylactic treatment, as are most bacterial, fungal, viral, and parasitic agents. Herpesviruses are the most readily recognized of the latent viruses and are the leading infectious cause of blindness in the United States. The establishment of latency and the subsequent reactivation are not well understood, but decrements in the immune system are known to increase the incidence and duration of viral reactivation and shedding of some latent viruses. An increasing body of evidence indicates that the physical and psychological stressors associated with space flight cause anomalies in the human immune response. The hypothesis tested for this experiment was that space flight would increase the incidence and duration of herpesvirus reactivation and shedding in saliva.

The specific goals of this experiment were to:

  1. Collect saliva, urine, and serum specimens from crewmembers at appropriate intervals before, during (saliva only), and after space flight.
  2. Analyze for herpesvirus DNA in saliva and urine and determine serum antibody titers.
  3. Quantify shedding frequency and duration during flight and compare them with ground-based control values.
  4. Determine if shedding patterns of individual herpesviruses during flight differ from ground-based values.
  5. Develop ground-based models to supplement space flight studies.

Data from this study will support and expand information on latent virus reactivation during space flight. Information gained from the experiment performed during Space Shuttle missions will be indispensable for development of countermeasures for long-duration missions. These data will be essential for the overall infectious disease risk assessment associated with space flight.

APPROACH:
Saliva and urine samples were collected from crewmembers before, during (saliva only), and was scheduled to be collected after space flight. Preflight activities included saliva collection from L-180 to L-150 every other day and blood and urine collection at L-51. Inflight activities included daily saliva collection from FD2 to FD16. After flight, blood and urine were scheduled to be collected at R+0 and saliva was scheduled for daily collection from R+0 to R+14. The saliva and urine samples were analyzed using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to detect the presence of four important herpesviruses (herpes simplex type-1 and type-2, cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus). The PCR technique allows both symptomatic and asymptomatic shedding to be detected. Serum levels of antibody to the four herpesviruses studied were determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).

RESULTS:
Due to the STS-107 tragedy, this experiment was not completed. However, the Detailed Supplementary Objective (DSO) 493 "Monitoring Latent Virus Reactivation and Shedding in Astronauts" followed a similar protocol.

experiment_title: Hypovolemia as a Model of Space Flight: Cardiovascular Exercise Effects and Countermeasures
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Reduced exercise capacity, orthostatic tolerance, and plasma volume are common observances following space flight and bed rest. The Johnson Space Center Cardiovascular Laboratory (CVL) investigated the relationship between orthostatic hypotension and plasma volume by pharmacologically inducing hypovolemia in normal subjects. The Exercise Physiology Laboratory (EXL) sought to extend this information to understanding the factors involved in decreased exercise capacity. Following orthostatic testing in normal and hypovolemic conditions, a subset of the subjects recruited performed a graded cycle exercise test to volitional fatigue to determine peak oxygen consumption (VO2pk).

The CVL was responsible for the overall administration of the project, and the EXL was responsible for the additional measurements and analyses. Specifically, the CVL recruited and instructed subjects, scheduled the testing, and was responsible for measurement of plasma/blood volume and orthostatic tolerance. The EXL was responsible for administering the test of exercise capacity using a cycle ergometer protocol similar to that used for International Space Station (ISS) and Space Shuttle (STS) astronauts. In addition to the ISS and Flight Analog Project standard measures during the cycle ergometer test, the CVL obtained echocardiographic measures of cardiac function and plasma catecholamines, and the EXL measured blood lactate concentrations and peripheral muscle metabolism by near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS).

Oxygen consumption, heart rate, rating of perceived exertion, and blood pressure were measured per standard laboratory protocols. Additionally, echocardiographic measures of stroke volume, systolic and diastolic function, blood lactate, plasma catecholamines, and peripheral muscle metabolism by NIRS was measured. Data from these testing sessions assist in understanding the factors associated with reduced exercise capacity after space flight; served as a basis of comparison for responses to similar tests after space flight and bed rest; and aided in the continued development of NIRS as a non-invasive metabolic measurement system for space flight and extravehicular activities.

The primary purpose of this study was to determine the specific effects of decreased plasma volume, independent of deconditioning, on aerobic exercise capacity (VO2pk), cardiac function, and peripheral muscle metabolism. The investigators also sought to collect pilot data regarding two pharmacological interventions that are being considered for the treatment of post-flight orthostatic hypotension that may similarly protect VO2pk. The secondary purpose of this project was to validate the use of a National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) funded sensor as a surrogate measure of oxygen consumption in an analogue of space flight and as non-invasive method to determine anaerobic threshold.

Specific Aims were:

(1) To determine whether central cardiac and peripheral skeletal indices of exercise performance are related to reduced VO2pk and anaerobic threshold in subjects whose plasma volume is reduced.

(2) To determine whether near infrared spectroscopy can be used to non-invasively, unobtrusively measure oxygen consumption during cycle ergometer exercise in normal and hypovolemic conditions.

APPROACH:
Subjects gave written informed consent prior to participation. Twelve healthy subjects (8 men and 4 women), passed a modified Air Force Class III physical examination, and volunteered to participate in this study. Subjects received written and verbal explanations of the testing procedures and provided written documentation of informed consent prior to participation. Study protocols and procedures were reviewed and approved by the NASA Johnson Space Center Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects.

Following a familiarization session, subjects participated in testing in both the normovolemic and hypovolemic conditions in cross-over design. For the seven days prior to the normovolemia testing day, subjects were encouraged to drink fluids ad libitum and consume a normal diet supplemented with 2 g of sodium each day. To induce hypovolemia, subjects received a single dose of furosemide and consumed a low salt diet provided by the investigators. The order of the conditions was not randomly assigned initially due to the constraints of a companion study, but the investigators attempted to balance the order of the test conditions. Seven of the 12 subjects completed testing in the normovolemic condition first.

Hypovolemia

Subjects received a single dose of furosemide through a catheter in an antecubital vein. Blood pressure and urine output were monitored during and after the infusion until they had stabilized, typically one to two hours. Following the infusion, the catheter was removed and subjects consumed a controlled, low-sodium, caffeine-free diet for 30 hours.

The diet was developed by dieticians at Memorial Hermann Hospital General Clinical Research Center (Houston, TX), and the food was prepared by the Space Food Systems Laboratory at Johnson Space Center. The diet was limited to 600 calories and 250 mg sodium per day. Subjects were allowed to drink sodium-free bottled water ad libitum.

Plasma Volume

Plasma volume was measured using the carbon monoxide rebreathing technique, as previously described. In short, an intravenous catheter was inserted into an antecubital vein. After 20 minutes of supine rest, a 3 mL baseline blood sample was collected. Thereafter, subjects breathed 100% oxygen for two minutes using a closed breathing circuit with a two-way non-rebreathing valve. Sixty mL of carbon monoxide were then added to the system and rebreathed for 10 minutes, followed by the collections of a second blood sample.

Graded Exercise Test

Subjects reported to the laboratory in comfortable exercise clothes which allowed access to the chest for echocardiographic measures and 12-lead ECG and to the thigh for near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) measurements. Subjects performed the exercise test in the upright posture to simulate orthostatic characteristics of normal gravity exercise following space flight exposure. Prior to the start of the test, subjects were instrumented with electrodes for the monitoring of 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and heart rate. Also, a small non-invasive NIRS sensor was adhered to the skin overlying the mid-point of vastus lateralis, and a catheter was inserted into the antecubital vein by a registered nurse to obtain resting, exercise, and immediate post-exercise blood samples.

During the cycle ergometer test, heart rate, metabolic rate, and NIRS were continuously measured. Stroke volume and cardiac output were measured halfway through each stage. Blood pressure, Rating of Perceive Exertion (Borg Scale, 6-20), and blood lactate were obtained near the end of each stage. Blood also was drawn from the catheter during exercise to determine plasma catecholamines, blood glucose, serum electrolytes, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and carboxy-hemoglobin at exercise stages corresponding to approximately 75% of VO2pk, estimated from RPE reported in the previous exercise stage. Based upon data previously collected in the investigator’s laboratory using the same testing protocol, the investigators estimated that the 75% VO2pk exercise stage would correspond to the exercise stage following that which a subject reported a RPE of 11 or greater. The exercise stage in which blood was drawn was determined in the first exercise test irrespective of whether the subject was normo- or hypovolemic.

RESULTS:
The primary finding of this study was that plasma volume loss to levels similar to those reported following short-duration Space Shuttle missions does not result in a decrease in VO2pk as great as that previously observed following space flight. In this study, VO2pk during a graded exercise test on a cycle ergometer, using a protocol similar to that used in previous space flight investigation conducted at JSC, was eight percent lower during pharmacologically-induced hypovolemia, but this is only one half to one third that which has been reported after Space Shuttle missions. Additionally, submaximal stroke volume and cardiac output were lower during hypovolemia, as has been observed after space flight, but other symptoms of deconditioning such as elevated submaximal heart rate, respiratory exchange, and ventilation rate, were not evident.

experiment_title: Non-Thermal Sanitation By Atmospheric Pressure Plasma
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
ORBITEC's Non-Thermal Sanitation by Atmospheric Pressure Plasma technology sanitizes fresh fruits and vegetables without the use of consumable chemicals and without significantly raising the temperature of the food, so food taste and quality are not affected. Atmospheric pressure plasma is well known to be highly effective in promoting oxidation, enhancing molecular dissociation, and producing free radicals and other types of high energies. It has recently attracted much attention in the food industry due to its potential for being a non-thermal and highly effective sanitation method. The proposed technology will support surface sanitation of delivered fresh fruit and vegetables, and freshly prepared foods in a space-based habitat. It can function in reduced gravity and pressure environments, and is efficient in terms of waste and resource use. During this Phase 2 effort, designs of the primary operating components of the system were refined and incorporated into a plasma processing chamber prototype capable of treating one to two servings of fresh food at a time. The antimicrobial performance of the prototype was tested with a number of fruits/vegetables and different inoculums. The prototype was also be evaluated for the effect of plasma treatment on food quality.

APPROACH:,
The methodology isn’t available for this study.

RESULTS:
Terrestrially, non-thermal plasma sanitation technology can reduce the number of cases of food-borne illness due to contaminations by sanitizing food at the point of use, such as a restaurant, or at a food processing facility. This technology can be used in place of chlorinated water, which can leave a residue and is not entirely effective, and irradiation, which generally has a poor public perception.

experiment_title: Epigenetic and Protein Expression Pattern Profiling of Caenorhabditis elegans Exposed to Time-Varying Gravitational Fields: a Multi-Generational Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
We hypothesize that long term temporal changes in the gravity vector will result in animal adaptation via epigenetic mechanisms that are passed onto subsequent generations. We further hypothesize that the gravity-influenced epigenetic profile can be restored to the consensus wild-type (i.e., Earth born) upon introduction to stable 1x g conditions. We propose to utilize C. elegans as a model organism to address this hypothesis by performing the following experiments. 1) Determine C. elegans behavioral responses (i.e., changes in migration dynamics, animal body posture, metabolism, etc.) due to temporal changes in the gravity vector. The gravity vector will be controlled by placing the animals inside a rotating CubeSat microscope developed by our group. The frequency, direction and duration of rotation will be varied to elicit the most dramatic behavioral responses. Habituation time will be evaluated, and also changes in lifespan. 2) Identify gravity responsive genes by utilizing the vast collection of fluorescent strains of C. elegans available to researchers. We will monitor gene expression by fluorescence microscopy from the embryonic stage through adulthood during changes in the gravity vector. Genes of interest include those associated with muscle development, cell apoptosis, and neuronal development. 3) Profile the epigenetic marks on C. elegans exposed to long periods of continuous gravity vector changes that range from 1/4 of an animal's lifespan to three generations. We will examine the epigenetic consequence of restoring constant 1xg conditions over successive generations. The three Specific Aims can be conducted with the same animal strains, and thus allows the opportunity to correlate the findings across different experiments.

APPROACH:
For simulated microgravity experiments, we designed and constructed a clinorotation device with integrated microscope, and a fluidic sample system. As clinorotation necessarily involves a fluid environment, C. elegans were maintained in liquid CeMM (C. elegans Maintenance Media); control animals were maintained on agar plates with a bacterial food source (OP50 strain). Stock cultures were maintained on agar plates at 16C.

Five histone modifications were targeted, based on previous publications: H3K4Me3, H3K27Me3, H3K9Me3, H3K36Me and H4K20Me. ChIP was performed in duplicate, in varying environmental conditions (i.e., agar, liquid, clinorotation settings or generational). Bioinformatics software packages such as: MACS, Homer, IGV, DiffBind and SICER were utilized to identify changes in gene expression, as well mine public genome/protein databases. RNA sequencing was used to validate epigenomic data.

We used the method of Chromatin ImmunoPrecipitation (ChIP) followed by high throughput Next Generation Sequencing on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 to identify DNA sequences enriched in specific histone modifications. C. elegans embryos were harvested from stock cultures by bleaching and centrifugation. Embryos were transferred to different environment and grown up to roughly synchronized late L4-young adult stage of development (6 days for CeMM cultures). Animals were also maintained for multiple generations, estimated by the amount of time (days).

RESULTS:
This project provided insight to the major Decadal Identifier AH16: Studies on transmission across generations of structural and functional changes induced by exposure to space during development. Our initial hypothesis that exposure to simulated microgravity will change gene expression levels, and that these changes will persist through multiple generations was confirmed primarily by RNA sequencing. We find that C. elegans embryos raised during clinorotation (F1 generation) elicits the transcription of new genes that were are not expressed in the parent (P0, ground control), and many of these genes are non-coding (nc)RNAs with unknown function. These new genes are still expressed in generations F2 through F4 raised in ground conditions, demonstrating a powerful epigenetic memory of the microgravity environment. It is important to note that these ncRNAs are not typically included in “standard” gene hybridization arrays (e.g., Affymetrix), but are identified using next-generation sequencing (NGS) methods. Future flight experiments should favor NGS over hybridization arrays because this will enable a complete representation of the transcriptome. Our RNA expression profiles show that upon return to ground conditions, about 1500 genes are differentially expressed for two generations; by the third generation on ground this number drops sharply to 104 genes. Thus, for the case of C. elegans and clinorotation, the exposure to altered gravity persists for about three generations.

We compared our simulated microgravity results with similar flight experiments involving C. elegans in the NASA GeneLab database (four flight experiments + our clinorotation). The largest differentially expressed gene overlap between all the experiments was with the CERISE 4 spaceflight experiment and our clinorotation data. These results support the use of clinorotation as a ground- based analog that captures some aspects of true space microgravity, quantitated through gene expression profiling. It might be expected that CERISE 4 and CERISE 8 should be the most similar, but the experiments differed in that 9,000 animals were used in CERISE 4, while only 30-50 were used for CERISE 8. A low number of animals will produce highly variable DNA microarray results, which may have been the case for the CERISE experiments.

Additional results will be made available by NASA's GeneLab.

experiment_title: Homeostasis and Biological Rhythms in the Rat During Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Homeostatic regulation of various physiological and behavioral systems may be altered as a function of the ambient gravitational environment of the organism. Changes in homeostasis have been observed in these and other systems as a result of chronic exposure to a hyperdynamic environment induced by centrifugation. Life science research capabilities are now being extended into the realm of the hypodynamic environment by research capabilities aboard spacecraft. This study examined the regulation of body temperature and heart rate in rats with biotelemetry implants.

Approach:

Four rats were implanted preflight with a biotelemetry transmitter capable of sensing and transmitting information on heart rate and deep body temperature. The telemetry data from the animals was monitored during the period which Spacelab was activated (approximately from eight hours after launch to six hours prior to re-entry). The average 24-hour waveforms of body temperature in preflight and flight conditions were examined. Four ground control animals were similarly implanted and monitored.

Results:

Microgravity altered the steady state regulation of heart rate and body temperature. During the preflight conditions, the animals demonstrated no net change in phase relationship with the mean period 23.9 ± 0.2 over the course of the pre- flight study; while inflight, the phase of all the animals consistently delayed such that the average period of the temperature rhythm inflight was 24.4 ± 0.3 hours. A longer flight will be necessary to identify whether or not the animals are freerunning with a period independent 24-hours or rather simply showing an internal phase angle shift which had not reached a steady state during the seven-day flight. Heart rate phase rhythm was stable in both conditions with a mean period of 23.9 ± 0.2 in either. The heart rate itself was, however, depressed inflight, the possible result of a reduced load on the cardiovascular system in space or a resetting of some other component within this regulatory system. Data suggest that normal expression of the circadian timing system is extensively modified in microgravity.

experiment_title: Exercise Countermeasure to Prevent Ocular Structural and Functional Changes in a Terrestrial Model of SANS
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Optic disc edema develops in approximately 16% of astronauts during long-duration spaceflight and is of high concern to the NASA medical community because of potentially irreversible vision loss during exploration-class spaceflight missions. Currently there is not a reliable method to predict which crewmembers will develop disc edema; however, recently, a novel ground-based spaceflight analog, consisting of strict 6° head-down tilt (HDT) bed rest, was developed that reproduced disc edema in healthy test subjects that can be used to test novel pathophysiological hypotheses and possible Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) countermeasures.

The goal of this experiment is to identify underlying mechanisms of optic disc edema in a ground-based analog and test an operationally relevant countermeasure (CM) to prevent it from developing.
To meet this goal, the experiment will address two specific aims.
Aim 1: Determine if donning veno-occlusive thigh cuffs (VTC) during and for 120 minutes after daily aerobic exercise can be used to (a) reverse headward fluid shift from bed rest for a sustained period of time and (b) to prevent ocular structural and functional changes from developing at the end of bed rest
Aim 2: Determine the role altered vasculature in the development of optic disc edema in the spaceflight analog.

APPROACH:
This study is part of a larger study that will test multiple countermeasures. The larger study will include 48 human subjects separated into four groups (12 subjects per group): one control groups defined by NASA and three countermeasure treatment groups. The control group will remain in strict 6° HDT bedrest with no countermeasures. The three countermeasure treatment groups include (1) daily exposure to exercise with VTCs during HDT, (2) strict HDT bed rest with six hours of 25 mmHg LBNP, daily, during strict HDT bedrest, and (3) six hours of upright (seated) posture, daily, during the strict HDT bedrest portion of the study. The experiment described here will focus on the effects of exercise plus VTCs.

To address Aim 1, the researchers will determine femoral artery conductance before and up to 120 minutes after cessation of aerobic exercise before, during, and after bed rest. Femoral vein cross sectional area, internal jugular pressure, and vein cross sectional area will be used to quantify the amount of blood trapped in the periphery versus above the level of the heart. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging will be used to identify structural and functional changes to the optic nerve and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) of the retina. Total retinal thickness (TRT) will quantify the effectiveness of the CMs applied in this study. Minimum rim thickness (MRW) and RNFL thickness measurements will allow for direct comparison of change in TRT between subjects participating in this study, previous bed rest campaigns, and astronauts who have flown on the ISS. Full-field flash electroretinography (ERG) and pattern ERG (PERG) will be used to directly measure the electrical activity within the eye in order to detect subtle abnormalities in visual function that may not otherwise be captured by current clinical metrics.

To address Aim 2, OCT angiography (OCTA) will be applied over the optic nerve head in subjects before, during, and after bed rest to identify subtle changes in ocular vasculature which may precede or result from the development of optic disc edema. OCTA images of the retinal and choroidal vasculature will be used to create detailed visualizations of the foveal avascular zone (FAZ) and perfusion and vessel density maps, and to monitor the thickness of the choriocapillaris. Intravenous fluorescein angiography (IVFA) will be used to assess retinal vasculature and blood-retinal barrier status immediately after the conclusion of bed rest to determine if the optic disc edema that presents in spaceflight analog subjects disrupts the retinal-blood barrier. Both IVFA and OCTA will be used to evaluate perfusion density and microvasculature integrity around the optic nerve.

RESULTS:
This experiment will apply a novel countermeasure approach to prevent the development of optic disc edema in a ground-based spaceflight analog and identify alterations in microvascular blood flow around the optic nerve, macula, and choroid using OCTA and IVFA. The researchers for this experiment anticipate wearing VTC during and after daily aerobic exercise as a countermeasure will reverse the headward fluid shift that arises from HDT bed rest. As a result, fewer subjects receiving the countermeasure treatment will develop disc edema, and the increase in total retinal thickness will be less compared to the control group. There will also be mitigated loss of electrical optic nerve function and vascular leakage on IVFA in the treatment compared to the control groups.
