experiment_title: Mechanisms of Musculoskeletal-Induced Nucleation in Altitude Decompression Stress II
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Musculoskeletal activity has the potential to both improve and compromise decompression safety, depending on the intensity, sequence and level of tissue supersaturation. Exercise enhances inert gas elimination during oxygen breathing prior to decompression, but it may also promote bubble nuclei formation, which can lead to gas phase separation and growth resulting in increased decompression sickness (DCS) risk. The timing, sequence and intensity of musculoskeletal activity may be critical to the net effect, but there are limited data available. This study will help determine the cost/benefit relationship of exercise, describe underlying mechanisms of nucleation in exercise prebreathe protocols and quantify variable risk in gravity and microgravity environments when musculoskeletal effort can differ substantially. Data gathered during prebreathe reduction program (PRP) studies combined multiple variables (prebreathe exercise and microgravity simulation) to produce a procedure now used by astronauts preparing for extravehicular activity (the PRP Phase II protocol). The PRP results will serve as control data for this NASA/Duke multi-center study to investigate the influence of individual variables (exercise and ambulation) on bubble formation and the subsequent risk of decompression sickness.

APPROACH:
Four separate experiments would replicate the PRP Phase II protocol, each with a different exception. A minimum of 25 and a maximum of 50 subjects would be tested. A Fisher’s exact test would be used to compare the results of the test and control groups. Each experiment will be stopped when pre-defined accept/reject criteria are met. Experiment I – Subjects would be ambulatory during both preflight and at altitude instead of non-ambulatory throughout. Experiment 2 - Subjects would remain non-ambulatory during the preflight period and ambulatory at altitude. Experiment 2 would use the same statistical design, as experiment I. Experiment 3 – Subjects would be ambulatory during the preflight period and non-ambulatory at altitude. Experiment 4 - The order of heavy and light exercise would be reversed, with the light exercise occurring first. For experiment 4, all subjects will be non-ambulatory during the pre-extravehicular activity (EVA) and simulated EVA phases to match the phase II control group. Venous blood will be collected via needlestick at three points to investigate whether the concentration of microparticles is associated with the presence of venous gas emboli (VGE) or DCS.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress.

EXPECTED RESULTS: It is anticipated these experiments will show that for exercise prebreathe protocols, decompression stress is related to musculoskeletal nucleation, and that nucleation can be controlled to reduce decompression stress. Specifically, ambulation during the altitude exposure results in increased decompression stress, but that ambulation prior to altitude exposure does not. Additionally, the results will show that reversing the order of light and heavy exercise will result in higher decompression stress, suggesting that light exercise facilitates the removal of heavy exercise induced nucleation. These results will demonstrate that the degree, sequence and level of supersaturation under which musculoskeletal activity is performed are important in controlling nuclei generation and subsequent decompression stress. Finally, there will be a correlation in the microparticle concentration observed prior to the decompression and the occurrence of decompression stress during the simulated EVA.

experiment_title: Dyads and Triads at 140 Million Miles: Factors Affecting Interpersonal Relations in Long-Duration Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Psychosocial dynamics within the context of spaceflight have been shown to have a large impact on crew performance and well-being. The increased social support provided by crewmembers along with increased social interdependence has the potential to cause differential levels of interpersonal and/or intimate relationships among subsets of the crew. The valance of such relationships within a team must be viewed at both the dyadic level and at the team level. Given the potential for variation in the type and intensity of interpersonal relationships within the crew, this aspect of crew dynamics and its impact on the behavioral health and performance of the crew is a critical research gap.

Interpersonal relations within teams have been conceptualized to include (a) role-based behaviors, such as team members relating to others as role occupants, (b) close or friendship relations, and (c) intimate or romantic relations. Although positive interpersonal relations are critical to effective team functioning, variations in the strength and type of relationship ties can lead to breakdowns such as the formation of subgroups and cliques.

The primary product of this experiment will be a comprehensive and validated countermeasure designed to mitigate adverse effects of alterations in interpersonal relationships and sustain individual and team well-being in future long duration missions.

Specific aims of this multi-faceted program include:
  1. Determine the risks to team functioning and performance impacts resulting from development, maintenance, and breakdown of different types of interpersonal relationships (e.g., conflict) within a team along with key contributors of resilience to shifts in these team dynamics.
  2. Develop, test, and validate an individual- and team- based training and intervention recommendations (and/or other countermeasures) to prevent adverse effects resulting from such shifts in team dynamics.

APPROACH:
To achieve the specific aims outlined above, this experiment has been broken down into three studies.

Study 1 will examine the disparities in interpersonal relationships among crewmembers based on data obtained from prior analog missions relating to subgroup formation and its impact on crew wellbeing. The research team’s current database consists of 640 crew communication transcripts representing 188 mission days, 16 HERA missions (Campaign 1 [7-days]; Campaign 2 [14-days]; and Campaign 3 [30-days]), and 64 crewmembers.

This portion of the study will employ a unique and innovative approach to examine interpersonal dynamics among crew members by applying and adapting a linguistic analysis technique called Language Style Matching (LSM). This technique is an interactive assessment of verbal coordination that provides a measure of synchrony (or closeness) in social interaction by examining the extent to which two or more persons in conversation match each other’s speech style. This is accomplished by examining the relative use of nine function-word categories (e.g., personal pronouns, adverbs) that can be drawn from the current transcript data. By utilizing the validated LSM measure, as well as adapting this measure to examine affective-word categories (e.g., positive emotion, negative emotion, anger), the research team will create a proxy measure to evaluate closeness between crewmembers.

Study 2 will focus on factors that promote and inhibit subgroup formation within a laboratory setting. Prior research has suggested that whereas factors such as increased familiarity among two or more team members may led to subgroup formation, introducing a cross-cutting variable may inhibit subgroup formation. This creates a divergent strategy in which subgroups are broken up into other subgroups that do not align with the original subgrouping. An alternative is a convergent strategy in which the attempt is made to merge the subgroups into one larger group, thus helping to promote team-level interdependence. The research team will utilize a 3 x 2 between-subjects design using 4-person teams to represent the different strategies (divergent, convergent, control) and levels of familiarity within the team (high and low). In addition to measuring the effectiveness of these types of strategies, demographic data, personality measures, process measures, and outcome measures will also be collected.

Study 3 will also be conducted in a laboratory setting and will investigate the efficacy of two aspects of the Detect, Integrate and React (DIR) countermeasure. First, the PI team will examine the direct effectiveness of the DIR countermeasure on the core competencies they train (e.g., interpersonal sensitivity, perspective taking). Second, we want to examine the effectiveness of the training on team-level outcomes in a team-based setting. To accomplish this, the laboratory study will be carried out in three phases: Phase 1 (DIR Training), Phase 2 (DIR testing), and Phase 3 (Team-based Task). For data collection, researchers will recruit 4-person teams. Phases 1 and 2 will be completed at the individual level and Phase 3 will be completed collectively as a team.

RESULTS:
This research is currently ongoing, results will be made available at a later date.

experiment_title: Timed Feeding and Resistance Training to Prevent Muscle Atrophy
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Muscle mass and strength, important components of health-related fitness, are significantly reduced during space flight due to a combination of factors, including the elimination of gravity and dietary deficits. Resistance training (RT) is an exercise modality that offers the hope of mitigating or reversing muscle loss induced by weightlessness. Recent studies suggest that the timing of an essential amino acid supplement around a bout of RT may augment the effect of exercise on muscle protein balance. The present study evaluated the effect of an integrated nutrition and RT approach as a countermeasure against deleterious effects of space flight on muscle health using bed rest as a model of weightlessness.


The hypotheses of this study were:
a) The combination of timed feeding (TF) of an essential amino acid (AA) supplement with RT (TFRT) is more effective than RT or TF alone as a countermeasure against bed rest induced muscle loss.
b) TFRT accelerates recovery from 28 days of bed rest compared to RT or TF alone over 14 days following strict bed rest.
c) TFRT works at least in part by modulating muscle levels of anabolic growth factors and cytokines (insulin-like growth factor-1, transforming growth factor-beta, and interleukin-15), and catabolic cytokines (interleukin -1beta, interleukin -6, myostatin, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha).

APPROACH:
The investigators examined the effect of these countermeasures on body composition, strength, and insulin levels in 31 men (ages 31-55 yr) during BR (28 days) followed by active recovery (14 days). Subjects were randomly assigned to essential AA supplementation (AA group, n = 7); RT with AA given 3 h after training (RT group, n = 12); or RT with AA given 5 min before training (AART group, n = 12)

RESULTS:
Energy intake was reduced by 8 +/- 6%. Mid-thigh muscle area declined with BR for the AA > RT > AART groups: -11%, -3%, -4% (P = 0.05). Similarly, greatest losses in lower body muscle strength were seen in the AA group (-22%). These were attenuated in the exercising groups [RT (-8%) and AART (-6%; P < 0.05)]. Fat mass and mid-thigh intramuscular fat increased after BR in the AA group (+3% and +14%, respectively), and decreased in the RT (-5% and -4%) and AART groups (-1 and -5%; P = 0.05). Muscle mass and strength returned toward baseline after recovery, but the AA group showed the lowest regains. Combined resistance training with AA supplementation pre- or post-exercise attenuated the losses in muscle mass and strength by approximately two-thirds compared with AA supplement alone during BR and energy deficit. These data support the efficacy of combined AA and RT as a countermeasure against muscle wasting due to low gravity.

experiment_title: Bioreactor Technology Transfer
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The NASA-NIH Center for Three-Dimensional Tissue Culture supports a number of scientists who work on projects related mainly to cell-cell interactions, cell differentiation, and the pathogenesis of infectious diseases. Many mainstream medical research studies have important implications for human space exploration and the Center helps promote the transfer of technology and interests between NASA and NIH. Intramural and extramural scientists launch pilot projects involving the RWV Bioreactor as extensions of their main research projects. Based on preliminary results, a research group can apply for a small grant proposal for a study involving the RWV. Additionally, many in-house projects are ongoing at the Center.

Below are the current projects at the NASA/NIH Center: 1) understanding the role of microgravity on the immune function of lymphoid tissue and cells, 2) studying the role of extracellular matrix and growth factors on differentiation of embryonic stem cells, 3) isolating and characterizing breast cancer stem cells, and 4) attempting to propogate Noroviruses in vitro.

The goal of the Center is to maintain a core facility at NIH for use of the NASA Rotating Wall Vessel (RWV) Bioreactor and related three-dimensional tissue culture systems for studying the basic mechanisms of normal and pathological intercellular interactions in multi-cellular systems, and how these interactions can be influenced by modeled microgravity. Investigators provide biological material or instruct the Center staff on experiment design, dissection and culture techniques. The investigator provides mentorship and is available for questions beyond staff expertise. The Center researchers prepare and culture the cells or tissues, and perform the primary analysis, including gathering data on tissue metabolism and tissue cytoarchitecture. The Center’s staff also provides services such as immunocytochemistry, ELISA, confocal microscopy, electron microscopy, and flow cytometry. The primary investigator performs specialized analyses specific to their project. Successful pilot projects can then apply for funding, which keeps the staff of the Center available for new pilot projects, and promotes technology transfer by recruiting scientists to work on three-dimensional tissue culture full time. Because of NASA funding, and because of the possibility that results obtained in suspension culture may relate to health problems of astronauts, or present unique opportunities for studying physiology in microgravity, there are possibilities of flight experiments for PIs of NASA/NIH projects.

APPROACH:
The Center provides researchers an opportunity to develop new model systems for biomedical research and provides access to the RWV, which allows cellular growth, aggregation, and development of in vivo-like structures. This vessel allows the culture of cells under minimal shear forces in a well-oxygenated medium under conditions that mimic microgravity. RWVs and experienced staff are available for testing tissues, primary cell cultures, and cell lines under these conditions that facilitate cell-cell interactions and promote differentiation. NASA funding for equipment has enabled investigators to procure state-of-the-art microscopes to determine structure and function relationships between cells of developed tissues. The design of the Center allows investigators to assess potential benefits of the RWV for their specific aims without having to commit major resources, which greatly increases the number of investigators who will explore the RWV as a tissue culture opportunity and apply their knowledge and experience to space research. Results from projects at the Center benefit space research, since the RWV models some aspects of microgravity, but since they stem from basic medical research, they have many terrestrial benefits as well.

RESULTS:
1. Study of immune dysfunction of human lymphoid tissue in microgravity.
Investigators found in previous studies that human lymphoid tissues and cells cultured in RWVs and onboard the ISS remain metabolically active, however, they demonstrate impaired antibody and cytokine responses to recall antigens and polyclonal activators. They found that cells activated in microgravity (modeled or true) did not increase glucose consumption, increase antibody production, or increase cytokine/chemokine secretion in response to polyclonal challenge compared to their static ground-based counterparts. However, if cells were challenged with activators prior to exposure to either modeled or true microgravity their glucose consumption and antibody and cytokine responses did increase. The consistent results between modeled and true microgravity suggest that RWVs provide a useful model of some aspects of microgravity. Current studies are now focused on understanding the mechanisms of immune dysfunction in ground-based experiments with the RWV, looking at the roles of both T and B cells in the immune dysfunction. Investigators are using various flow cytometry assays to track activation and differentiation of T and B cells in ex vivo tonsil cultures and cell culture suspensions of lymphocytes, as well as evaluating antibody and cytokine/chemokine/growth factor secretion using multiplexed bead assay for analysis of cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors. Previous experiments on board the ISS have also helped to optimize culture conditions within the TCM (tissue culture modeule) culture system to ensure better science with future experiments. The investigators were able to develop better mixing and bubble removal procedures in microgravity as well as promote interactive science between the flight crew and the ground team. Continued studies will help to develop a complete protocol for future tissue culture investigations in ISS.

2. Effects of extracellular signals on the differentiation of embryonic stem cells (ESC) in three-dimensional static and dynamic culture systems.
Studies have shown that both soluble factors and the type of ECM seem to be critical in directing differentiation and the formation of tissue-like structures. In addition, the composition of the ECM as well as the physical properties (rigidity, etc) of the ECM may influence cell morphology, proliferation, and differentiation. The cell shape acquired by the ESCs, which is mediated by the cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, may be related to proliferation and lineage specific differentiation. The investigators were able to stimulate ESC into cardiomyocyte lineages without addition of any growth factors and future studies are planned to further enhance this differentiation. New studies were directed toward differentiation into lymphoid lineages using conditioned medium from human tonsil cultures, stromal cells derived from tonsillar tissue, and decellularized tissue. Preliminary experiments did not demonstrate any advanced differentiation into lymphoid cells but further analysis is concentrating on earlier differentiation stages such as CD34. Investigators hope to couple these differentiation studies with HIV experiments. To use stem cells in an HIV therapy application, it would be important to know the susceptibility to HIV infection of the embryonic stem cell, and at which stage of differentiation is it most and least susceptible. The HIV receptors and co-receptors being expressed by the stem cell at those stages, as well as production of certain HIV-inhibitory chemokines, could be important weapons against HIV infection and exploiting the function of those proteins could be used in therapy.

3. Isolation and Characterization of Breast Cancer Stem Cells Using Three-Dimensional Tissue Culture Conditions.
Investigators developed protocols for culturing human breast tissue in microgravity conditions. Tissue blocks were inoculated into RWV bioreactor in culture medium. Tissue samples were collected during the culture experiment so that viability and proliferation activity of epithelial cells could be examined. Results demonstrated that cultured tissues blocks showed high viability and potential proliferation of cells up to one month after the initiation of the culture, documented by mitotic figure density. To test for proliferation, investigators labeled samples for the proliferation marker Ki-67. To confirm the epithelial origin of proliferating cells, samples were labeled for epithelial (wide spectrum cytokeratin antibody) markers. Together these results demonstrated high proliferative activity of the epithelial cells surrounding ducts. In conclusion, the data indicate that culturing of human breast tissues under microgravity increase fraction of epithelial cells with high proliferative activity. Thus there is a possibility that the origin of this proliferation is stem cells.

4. Growth of Noroviruses in the RWV Bioreactor.
Previous studies with cultures of INT-407 cells inoculated with a stool filtrate containing Norwalk virus, a Genogroup I (GI) norovirus showed suggestions of cytopathic effect on cells and investigators detected viral RNA by RT-PCR for up to two weeks post-inoculation. A new report using this cell line reported infection using a pool of stool filtrates was used as the inoculum (containing one GI and two GII norovirus strains). Investigators decided to revisit the INT-407 cell line in order to confirm this new report with their improved detection methods. INT-407 cells were cultured for several weeks on microcarrier beads and on a new mucosal substrate in bioreactors and then inoculated with Norwalk virus (GI) and infection will be determined by quantitative RT-PCR. In addition small and large intestine biopsies were placed in three-dimensional culture and infected with the GI virus and evaluated for infection.

experiment_title: Genome and Epigenome Analysis of Circulating Free DNA and RNA-based Liquid Biopsy
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Unlike conventional bulk DNA profiling from blood which mainly observes blood cells, cell-free DNA (cfDNA) and cyanine RNA (cRNA) profiling detects cellular status of internal body without invasive operation. This is because cfDNA and cRNA represent genetic and epigenetic information released from cells in tissue. When cells are damaged or targeted by immune system, the original cellular DNA and RNA are thought to be released into circulating blood flow. Therefore, cfDNA and cRNA profiling can be used as “liquid biopsy” to assess cellular status and integrity of tissue inside the body.

Investigators will compare cfDNA and cRNA profile among samples collected on the earth and during space flight. The results should provide key information including (i) low-frequency gene mutation events in internal tissue cells, (ii) cellular origin of cfDNA which represents sites of cellular damage or excessive tissue turnover by alteration of stem cell activity or cell death, and (iii) cRNA expression profile to screen gene-specific biomarker of stress response. Direct sequencing of cfDNA by ultra-high-throughput sequencing could detect mutations in DNA. DNA mutation rate will be a reliable indicator of genetic damage by space radiation in the human body under normal DNA repair function. Investigators will also perform detection and quantification of epigenetic modification (methylation) of cfDNA. Since methylation pattern of DNA is specific for cell types, this information will be used to identify the cellular origin of cfDNA. cRNA expression profile indicates cellular pathways that respond against environmental stress. If there are any genes specifically up or down-regulated during flight, these genes could be important to enhance environmental tolerance. Such genes may be targets for drug development or specific biomarker candidates.

APPROACH:
In this study, investigators plan to perform whole-genome profiling of blood-circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) and RNA (cRNA) to screen biomarkers for human stress response against space environment. They will collect blood samples from crewmembers preflight, in-flight, and postflight to screen for these biomarkers.

RESULTS:
Results for this investigation are unavailable. This is an international experiment. NASA does not currently have an agreement with international space partners to archive their data in the LSDA.

experiment_title: Mineralization in Teeth and Jaws, as Judged Radiographically, in the Rats of the Cosmos 782 Experiment
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This study presents data on the mineralization of the teeth in rats subjected to prolonged space flight. Although the pitfalls inherent in quantitative radiologic studies were kept in mind, there was an advantage in knowing the resorption in the spongy bone and the ambiguous result on dense bone in the same animals. Special efforts were made to standardize the regions of tooth structure measured, in the hope that masses of tissue in low experimental reactivity might not obscure more highly reactive sites.

Approach:

Heads were divided sagittally and x-rayed. Optical densities were measured on the films with a densitometer calibrated in American Standard Diffuse Density units. Limitations were principally: 1) that readings would be taken at some reasonable distance from the apex (region of tooth formation) to reach the mineralized band of structure and 2) that readings would not be over the tip of the tooth since the greatest part of the tooth was in fact closed in thin bone. While the density readings followed a logarithmic scale, the light transmission values were on an arithmetic percentage scale.

Results:

Although enamel values in the flight animals, both at recovery and 25 days postflight, seemed lower than controls, the difference was not significant. Other findings suggest a small amount of mineral loss may have occurred during the experimental period. Mineral repletion was not observed during the recovery period. The thin bone of the mandibular body was slightly reduced in both synchronous and flight rats, but rose to the level of vivarium controls after the recovery period. Changes of similar direction were found in the heavy bone underlying the molar teeth, suggesting that the stimulus of chewing was reduced in these groups, with restoration of a firmer diet during the recovery period increasing masticatory activity and improving bone structure.

experiment_title: Lunar Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) Architecture
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
For the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP), the retrofit of an existing 6-meter (20-foot) vacuum chamber, renamed the Life Support Systems Integration Facility (LSSIF), was challenged to provide for a human’s basic needs, in addition to those that would be required given the unique nature of the environment and test objectives.

APPROACH:
Located within a building at the Johnson Space Center, only a limited volume was available within the geometry of the chamber, which was already divided into three levels. Each floor provided approximately 29.1 square meters (314 square feet gross area) and 226.5 cubic meters (approximately 8000 cubic feet gross volume) for crew functions and equipment. Required was an overall plan to divide each of the levels into functional spaces, several serving as dual- or triple-use areas. The lower level was dedicated to most of the crew’s public and group activities, the second level housed systems equipment, stowage, and occasional exercise equipment, and the upper level provided for crew privacy.

Of importance was that the interior configuration and outfitting would need to address the safety of the crew. The design addressed potential mechanical and electrical hazards and endeavored to eliminate them. Fire safety and warning systems were employed. A lift was required on the upper level to allow for the safe exit of a crewmember in the event of an emergency. A considerable challenge confronting the team charged with the interior configuration was the materials from which the vacuum chamber had been constructed. Metal was the construction material of choice – an acoustics challenge to be sure. The selection of all interior surfaces and materials had several critical criteria that had to be met: they should be nonflammable, should produce minimal outgassing (within acceptable limits to the life support system), should be easy to maintain and clean using cleansers compatible with the recycling systems, depending upon use could not be porous, and would support acoustics abatement when possible.

RESULTS:
The “20’-Chamber” design for the LMLSTP was to provide for basic needs and to allow the outfitting of a number of crew functions: external/internal communications,general meeting capability, personal hygiene, health care, food preparation and associated stowage, dining, exercise, sleep, crew privacy, general stowage, cleaning of clothing, recreation, trash management, and installation of equipment required to support the tests.

experiment_title: Effects of Spaceflight on Muscles and Nerves
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The purpose of this experiment was to determine the influence of gravity on anatomical, cellular and molecular aspects of neuromuscular development. It's specific aims were to: 1) assess the effects of microgravity on the formation of individual muscles following cleavage by comparing muscles that developed in microgravity to those which developed under the influence of the normal gravity on earth; 2) ascertain the effects of microgravity on the placement of the large nerves that course through muscles leading to innervation; 3) use isoform-specific DNA probes to study levels of myosin heavy chain (MHC) fibers, myosin light chain (MLC) fibers and actin from experimental (microgravity) and control (earth-bound) embryos to ascertain whether gravity plays a role in the molecular development of contractile proteins.

Approach:

The muscle and the nerves of the thigh were delineated using immunohistochemistry antibody staining of fixed and frozen cross-sections of the entire thigh. Tissues were double-labeled with MF20, an anti-myosin antibody which binds to embryonic, fetal and adult skeletal muscle cells and TUJ-1, an antibody against a neuron-specific tubulin isoform. Slides were used to compare muscle size, placement of divisions among muscles, and locations of major nerve branches between control and experiment thighs. In situ hybridization with riboprobes provided a sensitive method for examining the localization (cellular distribution) of transcripts. Serial sections of tissues were cut and hybridized with anti-sense riboprobes generated to be non-isotopic. Probes were generated to be complementary to the mRNA of MHC slow, MLC 1f, MLC 2f and gamma-actin. Sections were compared to those from embryos developed in normal gravity.

Results:

From the data of this experiment, it was discovered that the general shape of the thigh muscle was similar between the flight and control animals. However, in the flight subjects there were sections within muscles that appeared to be separated from the rest of the muscles. Results also showed a lack of connective tissue formation in the space between the muscles in the flight group. Three distinct proteins of the muscle responded to microgravity. The fetuses of the flight group displayed less alpha-skeletal actin RNA than the control. Alpha-skeletal actin RNA appeared in similar levels in the pups of both flight and control groups. MLC RNA and MHC were found in a greater amount in the fetuses of the flight group than the control. However, the amount of MHC decreased from fetuses to pups in flight animals while the amount of MHC increased from the fetuses to pups in control animals.

experiment_title: Viral Reactivation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Seven or more herpesviruses commonly establish infections in humans. Herpes simplex type-1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex type-2 (HSV-2), cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), varicella-zoster virus (VZV), human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6) and human herpesvirus-7 (HHV-7) are some examples of the double stranded DNA viruses that may establish a life-long latent infection in a host organism. Latent viruses are subject to intermittent reactivation. For example, replication of the reactivated herpesvirus genome may give rise to both infectious and noninfectious (defective) virus particles. Since one or more of the herpesviruses infects nearly 100% of the adult population, they are prime candidates for studying the effects of space flight on latent viral reactivation in astronauts.

Latent virus reactivation may be an important threat to crew health during extended space missions where crewmembers live and work in a closed environment for 3 months or more. Exposure to infectious agents such as bacteria, fungi, viruses and parasites can be controlled by preflight quarantine as opposed to latent virus reactivation, an infection that originates inside the host organism. The establishment of viral latency and the subsequent reactivation are not well understood, but changes in the immune system are known to increase the incidence and duration of viral reactivation and shedding. Increasing scientific data indicates that the physical and psychological stressors associated with space flight cause alterations in the human immune response. Therefore, the objectives of this experiment were to evaluate the effects of long-duration habitation in space on latent virus reactivation, indicative of perturbations to the intricate host-parasite relationships. In this experiment, scientists tested the hypothesis that stressors associated with space flight will alter the host-parasite relationship in crewmembers inhabiting the Mir space station during extended stays, increasing both the incidence and the duration of herpesvirus reactivation and shedding.

APPROACH:
The approach to this experiment was to assess viral reactivation by the collection of serum and saliva samples. The original plan for sample collection included both the Mir 18 and 19 crew. The inflight and postflight sampling sessions on Mir 18 were not completed due to a cancellation of this experiment. Preflight saliva samples were obtained, but no blood samples were collected. However, contingency saliva sampling was performed on one crewmember during the flight. Preflight, inflight, and postflight saliva samples were collected from two crewmembers of the Mir 19 mission. Detection of the herpesvirus reactivation and shedding was conducted by saliva sample collection, DNA extraction from saliva, Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) amplification of herpesvirus DNA, and analysis of PCR products by gel electrophoresis.

DNA extraction from saliva
Saliva was collected and transferred to microcentrifuge tubes for extraction. DNA was extracted using a modification of the RNAzol method. Genomic/viral DNA was isolated simultaneously by adding 0.75 ml of Tris-saturated phenol (pH 6.6) RNAzol solution to 250 microliters saliva and briefly vortexing. After incubating on ice for 15 minutes, the tubes were centrifuged for 15 minutes at 12,000 x g and stored at -20 degrees Celsius overnight. The tubes were then centrifuged for 30 minutes at 16,000 x g and the supernatant removed. The DNA was then washed once with 7% ethanol and resuspended in 20 microliters DEPC-treated water. The suitability of extraction was evaluated by gel electrophoresis without nucleic acid quantitation.

PCR Amplification of Herpesvirus DNA
The oligonucleotide primers selected for this investigation amplified a highly conserved region of the DNA polymerase gene from the herpesvirus group. These primers allowed amplification of DNA to be directed to selected nucleotide fragments of the DNA polymerase genes for HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV and EBV . DNA was amplified in a total volume of 25 ml or a reaction mixture consisting of 50 mM KCl, 10mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.3), 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.01% gelatin, 5% dimethylsulfoxide, 200 micromolar deoxynucleoside triphosphates, 20 pmol of each oligonucleotide primer, 0.625 U Taq polymerase, and 2 ml purified DNA solution. The reactions were performed in an automated thermocycler. The cycle, repeated 40 times, consisted of 15 seconds of denaturation at 96 degrees Celsius, 15 seconds of annealing at 60 degrees Celsius, and 15 seconds of elongation at 72 degrees Celsius. All samples were run with simultaneous positive control and negative (reagent) control. Measures to control contamination included the use of latex gloves, aerosol-resistant pipette tips, and two separate laboratories for preamplification and postamplification procedures.

Analysis of PCR Products
Ten microliters of the reaction mixture was run on a 2% Nusieve GTG agarose gel containing 1 microgram of ethidium bromide per ml in 1x TBE buffer. The gels were then placed under UV light for visualization of the amplified products and photographed.

Results:
The cancellation of this experiment on Mir 18 resulted in a limited sample collection. Inflight and postflight samples were not collected from the Mir 18 crewmembers. Preflight samples were collected from three crewmembers and five inflight samples were collected from one crewmember as contingency samples. Therefore, the only samples analyzed were those collected from the crewmember that participated in the inflight collection. The samples collected from the other crewmembers are archived for future analysis. All of the preflight samples were negative for the presence of herpesvirus DNA. However, two of the five inflight samples were positive for the presence of herpesvirus DNA. Since these data were very limited, no conclusions were made concerning the effects of microgravity on the host-parasite relationship. However, the methodology and sample handling logistics were successful.

Two cosmonauts, both backup crewmembers for Mir 18, participated in the viral reactivation study on the Mir 19 mission. Thus, the preflight saliva specimens collected to establish baseline shedding patterns were collected prior to the Mir 18 mission. Saliva specimens were collected before, during, and after the flight. The samples were analyzed for the presence of Herpes simplex type-1 (HSV 1) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). All specimens were negative for HSV 1. Unfortunately, preflight saliva specimens were insufficient in number and frequency to establish a sound baseline for either crewmember. However, preflight shedding of EBV in the saliva was detected in over half of the total specimens. EBV DNA were detected in the saliva of crewmember A before, during, and after the flight. At least six episodes of shedding of EBV were observed during the mission. Inflight saliva specimens were collected beginning at about FD 25 and ending on FD 75. Shedding was also observed on R+14 and R+24. Crewmember B shedded EBV much less frequently during the mission than crewmember A. EBV DNA was observed in saliva from crewmember B on only two occasions during the mission. The conclusions made from this experiment were: (1) PCR methodology was capable of detecting latent viral DNA in saliva specimens collected and stored on the ground and on Mir, (2) neither crewmember appeared to be shedding HSV 1, (3) both crewmembers shed EBV before, during and after the mission, (4) shedding patterns of EBV of the two crewmembers were highly different during the inflight phase, (5) the technical feasibility of the approach was clearly demonstrated. The low number of subjects prevented any major conclusions from being drawn related to host-parasite relationships during space flight.

experiment_title: Carotid Baroreflex Function during Prolonged Exercise
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts are often required to work (exercise) at moderate to high intensities for extended periods while performing extra-vehicular activities (EVA). Although the physiologic responses associated with prolonged exercise have been documented, the mechanisms involved in blood pressure regulation under these conditions have not been fully elucidated. An understanding of this issue is pertinent to the ability of humans to perform work in microgravity and complies with the emphasis of NASA's Space and Physiology and Countermeasures Program.

Prolonged exercise and a constant workload is known to result in a progressive decrease in mean arterial pressure (MAP) concomitant with a decrease in stroke volume and a compensatory increase in heart rate (HR). The continuous decrease in MAP during exercise, which is related to the thermoregulatory redistribution of circulating blood volume to the cutaneous circulation, raises the question as to whether there is a loss of baroreflex regulation of arterial blood pressure. The researchers proposed that with prolongation of the exercise to 60 minutes, progressive increases in central command reflect a progressive upward resetting of the carotid baroreflex (CBR) such that the operating point of the CBR is shifted to a pressure below the threshold of the reflex rendering it ineffectual in correcting the downward drift in MAP. In order to test this hypothesis, several experiments were designed to uncouple the global hemodynamic response to prolonged exercise from the central command mediated response via continuous maintenance of cardiac filling volume by intravenous infusion of a dextran solution and whole body surface cooling to counteract thermoregulatory cutaneous vasodilation.

As the type of work (exercise) performed by the astronauts is inherently arm and upper-body dependent, the researchers also examined the physiologic responses to prolonged leg cycling and arm ergometry exercise in the supine positions with and without lower body negative pressure (-10 torr) to mimic spaceflight-related decreases in cardiac filling volumes.

APPROACH:

Experiment 1
Subjects performed two 1-hour bouts of leg cycling exercise with 1) no intervention and 2) continuous infusion of a dextran solution to maintain central venous pressure constant at the 10-min pressure.

Experiment 2
Carotid baroreflex (CBR) stimulus-response relationships were compared in seven subjects using the neck pressure-neck suction technique during dynamic exercise that ranged in intensity from 50 to 100% of maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max). Leg (L) exercise alone was performed at 50 and 75% VO2max, and L exercise combined with arm (A) exercise (L + A) was performed at 75 and 100% VO2max.

Ancillary Investigations to Experiments 1 and 2

Ancillary Study 1
Subjects performed four bouts of exercise: exercise with no intervention (CON); exercise with bilateral thigh cuffs inflated to 90 mm Hg (CUFF); exercise with application of lower-body positive pressure (LBPP) to 45 torr (PP); and exercise with 90 mm Hg thigh cuff inflation and 45 torr LBPP (CUFF+PP). Ventilatory responses and pulmonary gas exchange variables were collected breath-by-breath with concomitant measurement of leg intramuscular pressure.

Ancillary Study 2
Subjects performed 3.5 min of static one-legged exercise (20 % maximal voluntary contraction) and 7 min dynamic cycling (20 % maximal oxygen uptake) under two conditions: control (no intervention) and with the application of medical anti-shock (MAS) trousers inflated to 100 mmHg (to activate the exercise pressor reflex). Carotid baroreflex function was determined at rest and during exercise using a rapid neck pressure/neck suction technique.

Ancillary Study 3
Carotid baroreflex (CBR) function was evaluated at rest and during 20 min of arm cycling at 50% peak oxygen uptake using 5-s periods of neck pressure and neck suction.

Experiment 3: Part 1
Arterial (aortic + carotid) baroreflex control of HR was quantified using ramped changes in MAP induced by bolus injection of phenylephrine (PE) and sodium nitroprusside (SN). To assess aortic-cardiac responses, neck pressure (NP) and suction (NS) were applied during PE and SN administration, respectively, to counter alterations in CSP thereby isolating the aortic baroreflex. Graded levels of NP and NS were delivered to the carotid sinus using a customized neck collar device to assess the carotid-cardiac baroreflex, independent of drug infusion. The operating characteristics of each reflex were determined from the logistic function of the elicited HR response to the induced change in MAP.

Experiment 3: Part 2
Arterial and aortic baroreflex (ABR) functions were assessed utilizing hypo- and hyper-tensive challenges induced by graded bolus injections of sodium nitroprusside (SN) and phenylephrine (PE), respectively. Carotid baroreflex (CBR) sensitivity was determined using ramped 5-s pulses of both pressure and suction delivered to the carotid sinus via a neck chamber collar, independent of drug administration.

Experiment 3: Part 3
Acute hypotension was induced nonpharmacologically in subjects, half of which were of high fitness (HF) and the other half were of average fitness (AF), by releasing a unilateral arterial thigh cuff after 9 min of resting ischemia under two conditions: control, which used aortic and carotid baroreflex (ABR and CBR, respectively) deactivation; and suction, which used ABR deactivation alone.

RESULTS:
Experiment 1
Volume infusion resulted in a significant reduction in the decrement in mean arterial pressure seen in the control exercise bout (6.7+/-1.8 vs. 11.6+/-1.3 mmHg, respectively). However, indexes of central command such as heart rate and ratings of perceived exertion rose to a similar extent during both exercise conditions. In addition, the carotid-cardiac baroreflex stimulus-response relationship, as measured by using the neck pressure-neck suction technique, was reset from rest to 10 min of exercise and was further reset from 10 to 50 min of exercise in both exercise conditions, with the operating point being shifted toward the reflex threshold. It was concluded that the progressive resetting of the carotid baroreflex and the shift of the reflex operating point render the carotid-cardiac reflex ineffectual in counteracting the continued decrement in mean arterial pressure that occurs during the prolonged exercise.

Experiment 2
Oxygen consumption and heart rate (HR) increased in direct relation with the increases in exercise intensity. The threshold and saturation pressures of the carotid-cardiac reflex at 100% VO2max were >75% VO2max, which were in turn >50% VO2max (P < 0.05), without a change in the maximal reflex gain (Gmax). In addition, the HR response value at threshold and saturation at 75% VO2max was >50% VO2max (P < 0.05) and 100% VO2max was >75% VO2max (P < 0.07). Similar changes were observed for the carotid-vasomotor reflex. In addition, as exercise intensity increased, the operating point (the prestimulus blood pressure) of the CBR was significantly relocated further from the centering point (Gmax) of the stimulus-response curve and was at threshold during 100% VO2max. These findings identify the continuous classic rightward and upward resetting of the CBR, without a change in Gmax, during increases in dynamic exercise intensity to maximal effort.

Ancillary Investigations to Experiments 1 and 2

Ancillary Study 1
Ventilation (VE) was significantly elevated from CON during PP and CUFF+PP at workloads corresponding to > or = 60% CON peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) and during CUFF at workloads > or = 80% CON VO2peak, P < 0.05. The VO2 at which ventilatory threshold occurred was significantly reduced from CON (2.17+/-0.28 L x min(-1)) to 1.60+/-0.19 L x min(-1), 1.45+/-0.15 L x min(-1), and 1.15+/-0.11 L x min(-1) during CUFF, PP, and CUFF+PP, respectively. The slope of the linear regression describing the VE/CO2 output relationship was increased from CON by approximately 22% during CUFF, 40% during PP, and 41% during CUFF+PP.

Ancillary Study 2
During exercise, the application of MAS trousers (MAS condition) increased mean arterial pressure (MAP), plasma noradrenaline concentration (dynamic exercise only) and perceived exertion (dynamic exercise only) when compared to control (P < 0.05). No effect of the MAS condition was evident at rest. The MAS condition had no effect on heart rate (HR), plasma lactate and adrenaline concentrations or oxygen uptake at rest and during exercise. The carotid baroreflex stimulus-response curve was reset upward on the response arm and rightward to a higher operating pressure by control exercise without alterations in gain. Activation of the exercise pressor reflex by MAS trousers further reset carotid baroreflex control of MAP, as indicated by the upward and rightward relocation of the curve. However, carotid baroreflex control of HR was only shifted rightward to higher operating pressures by MAS trousers. The sensitivity of the carotid baroreflex was unaltered by exercise pressor reflex activation.

Ancillary Study 3
From rest to steady-state arm cycling, mean arterial pressure (MAP) was significantly increased from 90.0 +/- 2.7 to 118.7 +/- 3.6 mmHg and MSNA burst frequency (microneurography at the peroneal nerve) was elevated by 51 +/- 14% (P < 0.01). However, despite the marked increases in MAP and MSNA during exercise, CBR responses elicited by the application of various levels of neck pressure and neck suction ranging from +45 to -80 Torr were not significantly different from those at rest. Furthermore, estimated baroreflex sensitivity for the control of MSNA at rest was the same as during exercise (P = 0.74) across the range of neck chamber pressures. Thus CBR control of sympathetic nerve activity appears to be preserved during moderate-intensity dynamic exercise.

Experiment 3: Part 1
The arterial pressures at which the threshold was located on the stimulus-response curves determined for the arterial, aortic and carotid baroreflexes were not significantly different (72+/-4, 67+/-3, and 72+/-4 mm Hg, respectively, P > 0.05). Similarly, the MAP at which the saturation of the reflex responses were elicited did not differ among the baroreflex arcs examined (98+/-3, 99+/-2, and 102+/-3 mm Hg, respectively). These data suggest that the baroreceptor populations studied operate over the same range of arterial pressures. This finding indicates each baroreflex functions as both an important anti-hypotensive and anti-hypertensive mechanism.

Experiment 3: Part 2
During vasoactive drug injection, mean arterial pressure (MAP) was similarly altered in average fit (AF) and high fit (HF) groups. However, the heart rate (HR) response range of the arterial baroreflex was significantly attenuated (P < 0.05) in HF (31+/-4 beats x min(-1)) compared with AF individuals (46+/-4 beats x min(-1)). When sustained neck suction and pressure were applied to counteract altered carotid sinus pressure during SN and PE administration, isolating the ABR response, the response range remained diminished (P < 0.05) in the HF population (24+/-3 beats x min(-1)) compared with the AF group (41+/-4 beats x min(-1)). During CBR perturbation, the HF (14+/-1 beats-min(-1)) and AF (16+/-1 beats-min(-1)) response ranges were similar. The arterial baroreflex response range was significantly less than the simple sum of the CBR and ABR (HF, 38+/-3 beats x min(-1) and AF, 57+/-4 beats x min(-1)) in both fitness groups.
CONCLUSIONS: These data confirm that reductions in arterial-cardiac reflex sensitivity are mediated by diminished ABR function. More importantly, these data suggest that the integrative relationship between the ABR and CBR contributing to arterial baroreflex control of HR is inhibitory in nature and not altered by exercise training.

Experiment 3: Part 3
The application of neck suction to counteract changes in carotid sinus transmural pressure during cuff release significantly attenuated the MSNA response (which increased 134 +/- 32 U/14 s) compared with control (which increased 195 +/- 43 U/14 s) and caused a greater decrease in MAP (19 +/- 2 vs. 15 +/- 2 mmHg; P < 0.05). Furthermore, during both trials, the HF subjects exhibited a greater decrease in MAP compared with AF subjects despite an augmented baroreflex control of MSNA. These data indicate that the CBR contributes importantly to the MSNA response during acute systemic hypotension.

experiment_title: Physiological Parameters that Predict Orthostatic Intolerance After Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this experiment was to predict orthostatic intolerance due to the space environment after return from spaceflight. Orthostatic intolerance is defined as the inability to stand for 10 minutes in the usual flight-medical test directly after return from Space.

APPROACH:
The AORTA experiment was not executed in space, but rather measured parameters of the astronauts before and after the flight. To make this prediction the astronauts/cosmonauts were tested before their spaceflight in an elaborate (3 hr) test protocol on a computerized tilt table, while (non-invasively) measuring blood pressure, ECG and brain blood flow (by ultrasound) as main physiological parameters. This protocol was designed to categorize the cardiovascular reaction pattern of a person and act as predictor for the outcome of the test. As test outcome, the normal stand test that is part of the medical check-up immediately after return was used. Astronauts were asked to stand relaxed, leaning against a wall or some other fixed object for a maximum of 10 minutes. Orthostatic intolerance is defined as the inability to stand for 10 minutes. The upright time before this test should be minimal, since hormonal re-adaptation to 1 G starts immediately after resumption of upright Earth-bound life.

In five cosmonauts, finger arterial pressure noninvasively in supine and upright positions was measuread. Preflight measurements were repeated using venous occlusion thigh cuffs to impede venous return and "trap" an increased blood volume in the lower extremities; postflight sessions were between 1 and 3 days after return from 10- to 11-day spaceflight. BaroReflex Sensitivity (BRS) was determined by spectral analysis and by PRVXBRS, a time-domain BRS computation method.

RESULTS:
Blood pressure (BP)-levels in space were not very much changed from preflight; the circadian BP-rhythm seemed dampened. Only daytime diastolic pressures (both subjects) and nighttime HR (one subject) were significantly lower in Space. However, compared to the effect of a control tilt manoeuvre on the ground, even lower BP values might have been expected. Striking were the BP- and HR-surges during the working days in Space, often related to stressful moments like live appearances on public TV. Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) dropped during the night, unlike HDT. Thus, actual spaceflight refuted our earlier findings in HDT both for BP-levels and for daytime to nighttime changes.

experiment_title: International Space Station (ISS) Urine Monitoring System (UMS) Test Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Science teams using the International Space Station (ISS) Human Research Facility (HRF) identified a need for an automated void volume measurement and sample acquisition system for long-term ISS science applications. A similar system has been used on Shuttle and, prior to installation on ISS, the design of the ISS UMS) was required to first undergo integrated test operations in microgravity on a Shuttle flight.

The ISS UMS is an upgrade to the previous Shuttle UMS that is capable of:

  1. collecting and accurately measuring void volume,
  2. separating urine from air, and
  3. allowing acquisition of individual, uncontaminated urine samples.

Although ISS UMS is a design upgrade, all existing Shuttle and ISS Waste Collector Subsystem (WCS) interfaces remain unchanged. ISS UMS was designed to operate in conjunction with the airflow of the WCS of both the Shuttle and ISS. The hardware consisted of two modules, the Avionics Module (AM) and the Mechanical Module (MM). The AM includes electrical components and the primary crew interfaces, a color-coded keypad and Liquid Crystal Diode (LCD) screen. The MM contains a liquid/air separator, a motor, solenoid valves, fluid plumbing and the sample acquisition port. While deployed for the Shuttle test flight, the MM was targeted to reside in the Orbiter Side hatch, next to the Waste Management Compartment (WMC). The AM was capable of being temp-stowed in any location convenient to the WMC. Similarly, the eventual location on ISS was targeted to be the Node 3 Waste & Hygiene Compartment (WHC).

It was expected that the innovative design features within the ISS UMS would result in very accurate and repeatable micturition measurements suited for science applications on ISS. The objectives were to:

  1. Functionally test the effectiveness of the ISS UMS hardware in solving the following operational issues of the previous shuttle UMS; liquid carry-over between cycles, inaccurate void volume measurements, and cross-contamination in void samples
  2. Obtain crew insight as to the effectiveness and ease of use of the new design
  3. Validate extensive 1g development testing and provide a basis for the development of future urine analysis capability upgrades

APPROACH:
Inflight the crew de-stowed and set up the hardware and performed an initial air purge, followed by a validation sequence. The crew utilized the UMS for nominal use and performed void collections and sampling. After testing, the hardware was disassembled and stowed.

RESULTS:
Successful verification of ISS UMS hardware will result in eventual installation on ISS for science applications. A safe, very accurate and reliable means of obtaining representative urine samples and total void volume measurements from ISS crewmembers is essential to human research. The ISS UMS measurements are a vital component in calculating bone calcium loss and other metabolic changes that occur as a function of microgravity exposure duration and microgravity countermeasure evaluations.

experiment_title: Micro-Machined Drift Tubes for Ion Mobility Spectrometry: Studies Toward a Microbial Analyzer for Manned Spacecraft
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this research program was to provide capabilities for the detection and identification of microorganisms on manned spacecraft through chemotaxonomy with chemical instrumentation. Essential engineering considerations include small size, low weight, and low power. The requirements for performance include automated operation, response toward microorganisms relevant to spacecraft, and suitability for sampling air, water, and certain materials. The chemical instrument is based on pyrolysis of microorganisms with vapor characterization by gas chromatography/mobility spectrometry and technology upgrades were made with micro-machined mobility spectrometry and small gas chromatographs. These new micro-scale drift tubes have been operated under high field radio frequency (RF) regimes without ion shutters and aperture grids yielding low detection limits and high mechanical integrity. A research program to meet the goal of small size with high bio-analytical performance was planned with four stages of effort including: refinement of existing instrumentation, creation of a library from the determination of microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi) by pyrolysis-gas chromatography/micro-machined mobility spectrometry, preparation of methodology for data processing, and creation of procedures for automated interpretation of data.

APPROACH:
Advances were made using drift tubes barely the size of a quarter coin to detect the volatile organic compounds that are formed as thermal decomposition products from pyrolysis of microorganisms. The drift tube was joined to newly available, low mass, temperature programmable gas chromatographs and small Curie Point pyrolysis units. The combined pyrolysis-gas chromatograph/micro-mobility spectrometer and resultant experiments permit a clear assessment of this technology for potential service on spacecraft. All studies were completed in the laboratory where experience and technology of micro-drift tubes have been matured and where all aspects of this project (separations, mobility spectrometry, bacterial measurements by mass spectrometry as a validation technique, and chemometric analysis of data) exist.

RESULTS:
Micro-fabricated drift tubes for differential mobility spectrometry (DMS) were used as detectors for gas chromatography (GC) separations of vapors from pyrolysis (Py) of bacteria and provided response through gas phase ion chemistry at ambient pressure. Topographical plots of ion intensity, compensation voltage, and retention time were obtained simultaneously for positive and negative ions from py-GC-DMS analysis of bacteria. Thus, each Py-GC-DMS experiment included selectivity from chemical reactions in air through reagent ions H+(H2O)n and O2-(H2O)n. Chemical information was available throughout the span of elution temperatures from 35 to 200 degrees Celsius extended here over previous designs with improved temperature control of the DMS analyzer. Nine bacteria, amongst which were representatives of Gram-positive (e.g., M. luteus), Gram-positive spore formers (e.g., B. subtilis) and Gram-negative (e.g., K. pneumoniae) species, were analyzed by Py-GC/DMS and plots of intensity versus retention time were extracted from topographic plots at six different compensation voltages. These chromatograms contained chemical information from differential mobility analysis of ions in the elution profile and their distinctive patterns were used with backpropagation neural networks to categorize bacteria. Adjusted values (AV) for identification of bacteria were dependent on the compensation voltage used and average AV were up to 75 percent for vegetative cells and up to 78 percent for spores. Assignments of peak identity in the Py-GC-DMS plots were supported by parallel experiments using Py-GC with electron impact mass selective detection.

experiment_title: A Novel Membrane Microbial Fuel Cell for Energy and Resource Recovery from Solid Organic Wastes
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Membrane Microbial Fuel Cell (MMFC) is an innovative approach that could produce modest amounts of electricity while removing contaminants from the water and breaking down organic waste into water and other harmless compounds. The MMFC marries membrane technology with biotechnology. Bacteria catalytically oxidize the organic material in the MMFC to produce electrons that flow in an external circuit. Unlike a standard fuel cell, which operates at high temperature, the microbially catalyzed reactions in an MMFC occur at room temperature. Thus, the MMFC processes organic waste and wastewater in a way that helps produce pure water, generates electricity, and avoids extreme conditions in the spacecraft.

Although the MMFC is a very new approach, the potential advantages are enormous: processing organic waste to produce pure water and electricity with small size and no extreme conditions. Thus, the MMFC addresses several aspects of wastewater and solid waste in the AHST Critical Path Roadmap. To determine if and how this technology can be brought into practice, the investigators established the following objectives for the proposed study: a. Develop a bench-scale MMFC for laboratory testing b. Testing the MMFC with simple substrates to begin assessing its performance c. Establish the ecology and electrochemistry principles underlying the performance of an MMFC

APPROACH:
As a simple prototype MMFC, investigators constructed an HFMC in two steps. First, they sputter-coated 20 hollow-fiber membranes with metal to create a conductive layer on the membrane surface. The conductive layer was 60-nm-thick 60/40 Au/Pd and was applied using a Denton Vacuum Desk III. The membranes were fixed in place with cardboard to avoid fiber twisting, and, after coating one side, they rotated the cardboard to coat the other side. The resistance of the individual hollow-fiber membranes after sputter-coating was only 9 ohms/cm. Since each fiber was 7 cm long, the resistance of the individual fibers was approximately 60 ohms.

Second, they assembled sputter-coated membranes into a bundle wrapped inside a graphite foam, which serves as the porous graphite electrode. They attached the Au/Pd-coated fibers to plastic tubing with polyurethane adhesive. While they left one end of the fibers open to allow pressurized oxygen to flow into the fibers, they completely sealed the other end with polyurethane adhesive. They wrapped the bundle of 20 fibers with conductive graphite foam and sealed the two ends of the conductive graphite foam using polyurethane adhesive.

RESULTS:
During Phase I Pilot Study, the investigators accomplished the following tasks:
1. Created a simple MMFC by using a hollow-fiber membrane cathode (HFMC), in which the MFC cathode is attached directly onto a hollow-fiber membrane that supplied O2 for the cathode reaction.
2. Preformed kinetic characterization in single- and double-compartment MFC.
3. Compared the rate of degradation of common fermentation byproducts (acetate, butyrate, propionate, ethanol, and H2) in a dual-compartment MFC.

Investigators made an experimental MMFC in which the cathode and anode are immersed in the liquid media without separating them with a membrane. This MMFC generated electricity successfully (188 mA) and maintained the current for weeks. The design is unique and potential advantageous, because the MMFC design allows MFC electrodes to be placed directly into wastewater without the need of specialized compartments, simplifying the overall design. The simple MMFC design also demonstrates the concept investigators proposed for integrating the membrane and electrode in an MFC.

Investigators tested the MFC with acetate, which is one of the simplest organic contaminants in ALS wastewater and a simple substrate that MFC bacteria can use. Their fundamental studies make it possible for them to identify critical operational parameters. Although initial startup of an MFC took about 60 days with anaerobic digester sludge as inoculum, once suitable bacteria accumulated, starting up a new electrode was a rapid process that occurred over only about a week.

Investigators assessed the dual-substrate limitation effects on the bacterial kinetics. The current output of MFC depended strongly on the working electrode potential, especially at potentials lower than -0.1 mV against the Ag/AgCl electrode. When the current output was plotted against the potential, the current showed the classic Monod like saturation response. Substrate concentration and the electrode potential controlled the output current. A high substrate concentration produces more current; however, one goal of MFC is to remove the substrate. Thus, the result illustrate one of the tradeoffs in MFC. The Monod-Tessier model appears to capture overall behavior of the current generation better than the Monod-Monod model. Investigators plan to conduct more comprehensive studies on how the substrate concentration, biofilm density and structure, and the electrode potential together limit the current output response, because these are the factors that can be controlled via MFC design and operator.

Investigators tested the ability of MFC to remove typical fermentation byproducts acetate, propionate, butyrate, and H2. The fraction of electron of the substrates consumed (i.e. Coulombic efficiency) increased with the acclimation of bacteria. While acetate and ethanol were consumed fairly rapidly, butyrate and H2 consumption was slow. The presence of butyrate and H2 increased the current production in respect to the decay; however, their contribution to the overall current was small. The current production of propionate was much more favorable compared to butyrate, and further improvement in the current production was observed for ethanol and acetate. While the saturation type response was observed for propionate, saturation was not observed for acetate, indicating that the bacteria for the acetate biofilm were limited more by the anode potential than by the donor. The results indicate that fermentation, which converts complex mixtures of organic materials to simpler byproducts, such as ethanol and acetate, is essential for good MFC performance.

MFC can generate electricity from many of simple alcohols, acids, and amino acid. More complex organic materials such as glucuronate can be fermented to ethanol, acetate, and lactic acids. A next crucial step will be to identify conditions required to directly utilize or ferment other major ALS wastewater constituents, such as Igepon and creatine, in an MFC.

The pH of the reactor was crucial operational variable for system performance. In general higher pH improved the system performance, and the pH dependencies were different for types of substrate utilized. While acetate had a most stringent pH requirement for maximum performance (pH > 7.3), propionate and ethanol was able to tolerate pH below 7 without significant loss in the current density. Wastewater that has a high pH value, such as those in Early Planetary Base Wastewater Ersatz, should be favorable for MFC performance.

experiment_title: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Responses to Standing Before and After Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
On landing day, some astronauts become presyncopal, which means that their blood pressure drops, their heart rate increases, and they feel faint. These responses may occur because some of their physiological responses for maintaining blood pressure, such as releases of norepinephrine, epinephrine, and renin are inadequate in some way. The objective of this study was to define differences in the physiological responses to space flight of astronauts who did or did not become presyncopal on landing day.

APPROACH:
Studies were performed on 40 astronauts at (although only 29 were included in the analysis) L-30 and L-10, on R+0 after space flights of up to 16 days, and R+3 and R+10. An enhanced stand test was performed that included an echocardiographic measurement of the aortic cross-sectional area, ultrasonic (continuous-wave Doppler) measurement of aortic flow, beat-to-beat measurement of arterial pressure, and an electrocardiogram while the astronauts were lying supine and then while they were standing. During the supine and the standing parts of the stand test, the astronauts gave blood samples for analyses of plasma norepinephrine and epinephrine levels and renin activity. The cerebral vascular resistance and the mean flow velocity in the middle cerebral artery were also measured in the supine and standing positions with a transcranial Doppler device. Plasma volume was measured by the carbon monoxide re-breathing technique.

RESULTS:
Eight astronauts could not complete their stand tests on landing day because they became presyncopal. These astronauts had significantly lower norepinephrine levels when standing than the astronauts who did not become presyncopal. The increase in their norepinephrine levels during the stand test was smaller than it had been before the flight, and smaller than the increase produced by the stand test in the nonpresyncopal astronauts. These results indicate that the sympathetic nerves failed to release sufficient norepinephrine to increase the peripheral vascular resistance and avoid presyncopal symptoms.

Three days after landing, the presyncopal group had recovered their ability to raise norepinephrine levels when standing. The astronauts who became presyncopal on landing day showed significant differences before the flight from those who did not become presyncopal. They had lower blood pressures, lower peripheral vascular resistance, and higher heart rates, although all values were within normal limits. Most of these differences were still present three days after landing.

The results suggest that adaptation to microgravity alters the reflexes that maintain blood pressure so that about one-fourth of astronauts have inadequate norepinephrine responses to orthostatic drops in blood pressure. It appears that these astronauts may have some difference in venous compliance or vascular responsiveness even before the flight. It may therefore be possible to identify before launch a subset of astronauts who are more susceptible to postflight presyncope and are more likely to benefit from countermeasures.

OBJECTIVES:

experiment_title: Simulated Microgravity and Radiation-Induced Bone Degeneration: Oxidative Stress- and p53-Dependent Mechanisms
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

To determine the risks and mechanisms of tissue degeneration in the spaceflight environment, we will examine the combined effects of radiation and simulated weightlessness on bone. We will focus our studies on two important pathways, p53 and oxidative and nitrative stress-related species, in bone marrow progenitor populations because there is abundant evidence that the biological effects of weightlessness and those of radiation share these mechanism. Experiments will be conducted using the rodent hindlimb unloading model, the best validated animal model for simulating weightlessness, followed by irradiation. In Aim 1, we will test the hypothesis that simulated weightlessness of mice modulates the response of bone and bone marrow to radiation, both acutely and during tissue regeneration. In Aim 2 we will identify the target marrow-derived stem, progenitor and differentiated cell populations sensitive to the combined stimuli of simulated weightlessness and radiation. In Aim 3, we will explore the relevance of specific ROS/RNS and p53-dependent mechanisms for mediating cellular responses to combined simulated weightlessness and radiation. The results of these studies are expected to provide important information for the development of countermeasures both to help prevent degeneration of connective tissues such as bone during spaceflight and to improve subsequent tissue regeneration.

APPROACH:

Experiments will be conducted using the rodent hindlimb unloading model, the best validated animal model for simulating weightlessness, followed by irradiation. In Aim 1, we will test the hypothesis that simulated weightlessness of mice modulates the response of bone and bone marrow to radiation, both acutely and during tissue regeneration. In Aim 2 we will identify the target marrow-derived stem, progenitor and differentiated cell populations sensitive to the combined stimuli of simulated weightlessness and radiation. In Aim 3, we will explore the relevance of specific ROS/RNS and p53-dependent mechanisms for mediating cellular responses to combined simulated weightlessness and radiation.

RESULTS:

We were the first to report in the scientific literature on the influence of simulated weightlessness and radiation on mineralized tissue. Our published results show that total body irradiation of adult male mice with doses of iron as low as 0.10 Gy and doses of photons (Cesium-137) as low as 1.0 Gy can cause significant loss of mineralized tissue within the spongy areas of bone. This bone loss is very rapid (within 3 to 7 days), and appears to be caused by an increase in the activity of bone resorbing osteoclasts. The importance of the osteoclasts for radiation-induced bone loss is further supported by our findings that radiation can increase the number of osteoclasts in cultured cells.

One of our surprising findings is that radiation-induced bone loss is restricted to high turnover rate cancellous tissue, in contrast to unloading-induced bone loss, which manifests in both cortical bone tissue (outer shell) as well as cancellous tissue. As a consequence, the mechanical properties of the spine are largely preserved after low dose, total body irradiation alone and are likely to be preserved for most bones, at least in the short term.

Simulated weightlessness at the time of radiation exposure appears to impair skeletal remodeling even during a prolonged period of recovery. Furthermore, relatively low doses of space radiation can exert system-wide and persistent change. All of our experiments have been conducted using adult, male mice of a single strain (C57Bl/6J). Differences in biological responses to treatments can occur simply due to age, gender, strain, as well as species, and therefore further studies are needed to help assess human risk. Nonetheless, our findings suggest space radiation, alone and combined with musculoskeletal disuse, may pose a long-term risk to the skeletal health of astronauts.
