experiment_title: Exosomes and Secretory Factors as Mediators of Non-targeted Effects of HZE Particles
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This is a proposal devoted to understanding the mechanism of radiation-induced non-targeted effects, and in particular, how they lead to genomic instability in bystander cells (those not directly traversed by a radiation track). Once a bystander cell has become unstable, it is susceptible to mutations induced by endogenous and exogenous stressors, which in turn creates a permissive environment for acquisition of oncogenic mutations. Non-targeted effects (NTE) are a crucial mechanism contributing to solid tumor carcinogenesis in the space environment, yet in many respects they remain poorly understood. Investigators hypothesize that NTE signaling leads to reliance on low-fidelity repair pathways in bystander cells; that the NTE signal is transmitted by exosomes, soluble secretory proteins, or both; and that the NTE signal affects repair through changes in the proteome and transcriptome. To test these hypotheses, investigators propose three specific aims.

Aim 1 is to determine effects of radiation quality, dose, and dose rate on genomic instability in bystander cells, as measured by use of low-fidelity repair pathways. Experiments will focus on range of energies for intermediate Z particles. Experiments will use human bronchial epithelial cells, believed to be the target for lung carcinogenesis and bladder cancer cells, used as a positive control because they are known to generate strong non-targeted effect signals.
Aim 2 is to determine the non-targeted effect signaling mechanism, with a focus on exosomes and secreted soluble proteins as candidates.
Aim 3 is to investigate the exact mechanism by which NTE signaling produces genome instability in bystander cells.

APPROACH:
Human cells will be irradiated and co-cultured with I-SceI-expressing reporter cells at intervals up to 21 days post-irradiation. Assays will be developed to measure the relative efficiency of the CRISPR/Cas9-induced inversion in a number of candidate cell lines.

RESULTS:
This study is in progress. However, preliminary results are available.

Establishment of a new assay system for repair fidelity, based on mis-joining of double-strand breaks in endogenous genes (rather than the artificial reporter genes used in earlier work):
The assay uses the CRISPR/Cas9 nuclease to induce a paracentric inversion involving the EML4 and ALK genes. This is the most commonly occurring rearrangement in lung cancer patients and is particularly frequent in never-smokers, the population of most interest to NASA. A sensitive and quantitative qPCR assay was established to measure the relative efficiency of the CRISPR/Cas9-induced inversion in a number of candidate cell lines. Three of these cell lines were chosen for radiation studies: near-normal human bronchial epithelial cells (HBEC3-KT); HZE radiation-transformed HBEC3-KT cells (HBECK3KT-F25F); and, as a positive control, the human bladder cancer cells (DsR-7F4) used in previous work by the investigators.

Irradiation of a panel of human cell lines in the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) 15C run:
To define radiation quality effects, 16-O, 28-Si, and 48-Ti ions were used at energies calculated to provide linear energy transfer (LET) values of 100 and 200 keV/µm. These represent a range of species that might be encountered within a shielded crew habitat. Irradiation was performed at doses ranging from 0.2 to 1.0 Gy. Initial results showed that radiation led to a modest, dose-dependent reduction in cell growth rate, as expected. At day seven post-irradiation, the directly irradiated and bystander cell populations were challenged with CRISPR/Cas9 nuclease to induce targeted strand breaks in the EML4 and ALK loci. Molecular analysis of the relative frequency of inversions in different treatment groups is in progress.

Establishment of methods for analysis of radiation-induced exosomes, including light scattering and electron microscopy to determine the size distribution, immunoblotting, and mass spectrometry to identify exosomal proteins, and fluorescence labeling to allow visualization of uptake in bystander cells:
Irradiated cell conditioned medium was also collected from 48-Ti-irradiated cells in the NSRL (15A and 15C runs). This conditioned medium will be used to prepare exosomes for proteomic analysis.

experiment_title: Characterization of the Tumor Spectrum Arising in HZE Ion Irradiated Outbred Mice
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment had two key objectives. The first was to compare the spectrum of tumor types that arises in a genetically diverse mouse population irradiated with HZE ions to the spectra arising in similar unirradiated or gamma-ray irradiated populations. The second objective was to identify genetic differences between individual outbred mice that make them susceptible or resistant to the induction of specific types of tumors by radiation and then to determine if the same genetic factors that control sensitivity to gamma-ray induced tumors also control sensitivity to HZE ion induced tumors.

APPROACH:
To accomplish these objectives investigators irradiated mice from an outbred, heterogeneous stock, HS/NPT, with HZE ions or gamma-rays and monitored them along with unirradiated control mice for tumor development. Tumors that arise in the mice were classified by histological examination and the tumor spectra was compared between the three groups. The investigators identified the genetic differences, known as QTL or quantitative trait loci, underlying susceptibility to HZE ion-induced and gamma-ray-induced tumorigenesis and determined their overlap by analyzing single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) throughout the genomes of tumor bearing and unaffected mice for association with specific tumor types. This work addressed the solicitation's emphasis on studies of the individual basis of space radiation risk assessment including the use of genetically diverse populations of mice to represent human heterogeneity that will elucidate the spectrum of tumor types caused by HZE nuclei as well as possible differences compared to gamma-rays.

RESULTS:
Carcinogenesis
To determine whether tumors that arise following HZE ion exposure are more malignant than their counterparts arising in unirradiated or gamma-ray irradiated mice, the investigators characterized two measures of malignancy: tumor latencies (analyzed by Kaplan-Meir survival procedures) and metastatic events. As expected, tumors arising in both HZE ion and gamma-ray irradiated mice showed significantly decreased latencies. However, HZE ions did not produce tumors with decreased latencies when compared to tumors in gamma-ray irradiated mice. Pulmonary metastases were observed in cases of hepatocellular carcinoma, Harderian gland adenocarcinoma, osteosarcoma, and ovarian granulosa cell tumor. Metastases were no more frequent in irradiated animals than in controls and there was no significant difference in metastatic incidence between HZE ion irradiated mice and gamma-ray irradiated mice.

Ocular Effects
The cataract data was analyzed in conjunction with the SNP genotyping data to identify quantitative trait loci (QTL) that control susceptibility to radiogenic cataracts. The mapping phenotype was days to grade two cataract and genome wide scans were performed using the DOQTL program which was modified for use with Cox regression. Significance at 80% and 95% confidence was determined by permutation. Several QTL were identified at 95% confidence and one, on chromosome 13, was narrow enough that a strong candidate gene emerged.

Cognitive Effects
Approximately 1,850 mice were irradiated and behaviorally tested in two cohorts of 600 and 1,200 mice, respectively. Statistical analysis for behavioral and genetic analyses, the investigators detected a significant cohort effect. This might be due to the fact that urine was collected 24 hours following sham-irradiation or irradiation for NMR analysis as part of the second cohort but this additional procedure was not part of the experience of the first cohort of mice. Investigators assessed whether the NMR data was related to or could predict behavioral or cognitive outcome measures three months later but they did not detect evidence for that. They also did not detect an effect of irradiation on the NMR data. Based on the cohort effect described earlier, investigators analyzed the data separately and focused the main analysis on first cohort of about 600 mice.

The genetic data consists of approximately 77K genetic markers across the genome. Among these, about 40K markers were deemed as informative, i.e., they had a minor allele frequency above 5%. As described below, the utilization of this set of informative markers increased the robustness and reproducibility of the results. However, The investigators recognize that the low frequency alleles could also be informative in some cases and/or have a strong effect on some phenotypes.

The QTL analysis is based on more than 40 behavioral and cognitive phenotypes for radiobiological outcome measures of interest related to performance in the hippocampus-dependent contextual and hippocampus-independent cued fear conditioning tasks. This large collection of related phenotypes and genotypes required the adoption of a data reduction technique that 1) summarizes the essential features of the behavioral and cognitive measures and 2) enhances the ability to detect significant genotype-phenotype associations.

For the behavioral and cognitive measurements, based on the observation that many of the measurements display significant correlations, the investigators employed an analysis strategy based on a Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Results show that the first five principal components (PCs) contain more than 65% of the variability of the data and each of the remaining individual PCs contain little additional variance. As predicated by the PCA, all the principal components are linearly independent. Moreover, by examining the “loadings” or the projections of the original behavioral and cognitive measures on the PCs, it is apparent that related behavioral and cognitive phenotypes map onto distinct PCs. This observation verifies that of the original. Additionally, it appears that distinct behavioral and cognitive domains map into distinct principal components, as quantified by the “loadings,” or the level of association between the original approximately 40 behavioral measurements and the reduced five PCs. What is striking is that for example PC1 contains cognitive measures of hippocampus-dependent fear memory (contextual fear memory, i.e., a fear memory in the same environment or context as where the aversive stimulus was experienced during training), while PC3 contains cognitive measures of hippocampus-independent fear memory (cued fear memory, i.e., fear memory in a novel environment). PC2 contains cognitive measures in response to the aversive stimulus during training, while PC5 contains cognitive measures of performance at baseline prior to training (prior to an aversive stimulus) and during the training (i.e., learning). Finally, PC4 contains cognitive measures) during training (i.e., learning).

experiment_title: Effects of Microgravity on the Body Wall Muscles in Rodents
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Numerous studies on rodent skeletal muscles exposed to orbital space flight have documented histological changes associated with muscle deconditioning. This experiment examined the effects of a 16-day space flight mission on the size of muscle fibers in the rectus abdominis, external oblique, and transversus abdominis muscles of adult male Fisher rats.

Approach:

Five male Fischer 344 rats were individually housed in orbit in the RAHF, in contrast to the one previous space flight investigation of the same muscles, where the rats were group-housed pregnant females. Ground controls consisted of rats similarly kept in the RAHF and another five rats maintained in standard vivarium cages to determine cage effects. Rats were euthanized approximately 24 hours after Shuttle landing and the cross-sectional area of the muscle fibers was used as a measure of muscle atrophy or hypertrophy.

Results:

The transversus, which is presumed to be the primary expiratory muscle and consequently works against internal hydrostatic pressures that are not likely to change much between 1 G and weightlessness, did not change in size. However, both the rectus abdominis (a spinal flexor) and the external oblique (a rotator of the torso), which resist gravity in the 1 G environment, showed significant signs of atrophy after extended exposure to microgravity. The atrophy of the external oblique was diametrically opposite to hypertrophy of the same muscle observed in group-housed rodents previously exposed to space flight. Although the two missions differed in several factors, such as the gender of the rats and mission duration, we believe that housing of the animals was the key factor that accounted for the different responses of the external oblique. Previous research has shown that group-housed rats in space flight exhibited seven times more rotations of their torsos than matched ground controls. Thus unloading of the musculoskeletal system may not be achieved in weightlessness when animals have the freedom to interact with each other. No cage effects between RAHF- and vivarium-housed rats was observed.

experiment_title: Long-term Test of the JPL ENose in Crew Habitat on Orbit
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The JPL Electronic Nose (ENose) is a full-time, continuously operating event monitor designed to detect air contamination from spills and leaks in the crew habitat in the International Space Station. It fills the long-standing gap between onboard alarms and complex analytical instruments. ENose provides rapid, early identification and quantification of atmospheric changes caused by chemical species to which it has been trained. ENose can also be used to monitor cleanup processes after a leak or a spill.

Electronic noses have been applied to environmental monitoring and quality control in many fields such as food processing, industrial environmental monitoring and medical diagnosis. What is unique about the JPL E-Nose is not only the small size and power requirement, but the ability to quantify gases and mixtures of gases at very low levels, even lower than the Spacecraft Maximum Allowable Concentration (SMAC), which are the quantities of specific compounds that can be breathed safely by crewmembers for a specific length of time. Most compounds SMAC values are very minute, in the single to tens of parts-per-million regime. Also E-Nose can detect levels at smaller concentrations than the human nose. For example the E-Nose can detect ammonia at 1 part-per-million; whereas, the human nose detects ammonia at 50 parts-per-million. This piece of hardware is self-automated in that it processes the information with its own computer system which controls the device, collects and analyzes data.

The need for a low power, autonomous air quality monitor is pressing for an enclosed space such as the International Space Station. In such a space, the presence of contaminants is particularly threatening. The crew is entirely reliant on the air revitalization systems (ARS) for healthy air; the air is not easily replaced. Contaminants may enter the air through leaks and spills from equipment and experiments or from smoldering fires. This kind of incident is a threat to crew health because they are unexpected and can occur with a sudden, large increase in concentration that may be toxic. The earliest warning possible is necessary to avoid threat to crew health incidents. E-Nose has this capability of contributing to a safe environment for the crew by monitoring the station for multiple specific contaminants.

APPROACH:
The JPL Electronic Nose (ENose) is an array-based sensing system which contains 32 conductometric sensors. The Second Generation ENose was trained to detect, identify and quantify 21 chemical species, the majority of which are organic solvents or commonly used organic compounds, which might be released through a leak or a spill in a spacecraft crew cabin. It was extensively ground-tested, and includes data analysis software which will identify and quantify the release of a target chemical within 40 minutes of detection.

Past ENose investigations have focused on organic compounds such as common solvents and a few selected inorganic compounds, ammonia, water and hydrazine. For the new ENose to be performed on the ISS, two inorganic species have now been added to the analyte set, mercury and sulfur dioxide. To accommodate these inorganic species, the sensor array will incorporate a hybrid sensor approach, including both new sensing materials and new sensing platforms made up of microhotplate sensor substrates. Materials approaches to these analytes have been determined using models of sensor-analyte response developed under this program. Predictive models will also be used to complement array training for additional software analyses including chemical family identification and identification of unknown analytes. Analysis of data taken by the sensor array will be included on the ENose control computer, and event analysis will be available within 40 minutes of event onset.

On ISS crewmembers retrieved the ENose from stowage and installed it on an EXPRESS Rack with a bracket assembly and/or Velcro; connected the power cable and the data cable. ENose was powered on and the crewmember verified the following: LED illumination; display operation; clear air inlet and outlets. ENose is autonomous with possible occasional crew commanding and periodic status checks (once or twice per month). Crewmembers had periodic attended events if ENose detects a potential spill or leak. When ENose is relocated, the crewmember was required to reset the IP address.

RESULTS:
The ENose event monitor, by identifying and quantifying trained-for chemical species, fills the gap between an alarm (which provides no ID or quantification) and high-end analytical instruments. ENose has demonstrated a wide dynamic range, ranging from fractional ppm to 10,000 ppm. Its array based sensing mechanism means that it can be trained to detect new chemical species, and training data can be uplinked to add new species to its on-board data library. ENose runs continuously (30 to 360 data points/hr) and autonomously; it requires only minimal crew interaction and requires no consumables. The ENose is low mass (less than 4 kg), small volume (less than 4 liters) and low power (less than 20 W), in addition to being microgravity-insensitive, robust, and rugged. It is capable of analyzing volatile aerosols as well as vapors.

Future applications of the JPL ENose may also include environments other than the spacecraft crew cabin and similar enclosed environments. Such applications may include integration with larger devices such as analytical instruments, and with environmental monitoring and control systems.

experiment_title: Effects of Anti-orthostatic Suspension on Innate Immunity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The overall objective of this work is to determine a model of altered inflammation and wound healing, reflecting the possible conditions experienced by individuals in zero gravity. The significance of such a model would be to allow definition of possible molecular and cellular mechanisms, and to serve as a basis for development of therapies to promote effective inflammation and wound healing.

A specific aim of this grant was to assess the effects of hind limb unloading (HU) on wound healing. Previous studies have shown that HU induces liver injury as a result of increased portal endotoxemia, and the current work extends these studies to the evaluation of the inflammatory response associated with wound healing. The investigators have chosen as a model superficial abrasion of the corneal epithelium. This model allows accurate documentation of re-epithelialization and the attendant inflammatory response, including neutrophil, dendritic cell, and Langerhan cell mobilization.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
There are several important finding in these studies that raise potentially critical questions regarding negative effects of space flight on wound healing. They involve wound healing in the skin and wound healing in the cornea.

Wound healing in the skin: A commonly used experimental model to study wound healing is to place surgical sponges under the skin for a period of time and then determine the extent to which the tissue attempts to heal the wound. There are several ways to measure this response and the investigators chose to determine the amount of collagen produced since collagen is the most important component of a successfully healed wound in adults. They found that there was a greater than 50% reduction in the amount of collagen in 7 and 10 day old wounds from animals exposed to hindlimb unloading (a model developed by NASA scientists that simulates important physiologic aspects the stresses imposed by zero gravity conditions of space flight). These results are consistent with published studies of rats flown in a shuttle flight.

Wound healing in the cornea: A common concern among astronauts is foreign body injury to the surface of the eye. Normal healing of these types of wounds is critical to the maintenance of excellent vision. Since the investigators found that healing in the skin was reduced, they were concerned that healing in the cornea may also me impaired. Mice subjected to hind limb unloading for three weeks were given a superficial injury to the cornea. This involved scraping a small portion of epithelium off of the corneal surface, a common type of superficial injury. These wounds normally heal within 18-24 hours, but there was a significant delay in the healing in the animals exposed to hind limb unloading. Healing time needed to re-grow the epithelium so that the wound was covered was extended by 40 – 50%. What was more troubling, though, was the fact that complete healing (determined by the thickness of the epithelium) was not complete even after 11 days. Normally full thickness is complete within 4 days. Additional concern was raised by another observation. That was that the inflammatory white blood cells that normally come into the wound to protect it from infection were also significantly delayed and reduced in number in the animal exposed to hind limb unloading. From these observations, the investigators are very concerned that if the hind limb unloading model in animals reflects the conditions in space flight, astronauts will be at risk for abnormal healing of superficial surface injuries to the eyes.

Possible mechanism of reduced wound healing in the skin and eyes: The investigators found that hind limb unloading causes an increase in bacterial toxin (“endotoxin”) to appear in the blood flowing into the liver. The liver responds to this toxin in several ways. 1) The liver clears the blood of the endotoxin. Investigators could not find endotoxin in the blood that was coming out of the liver. 2) The liver is activated by the endotoxin. They found that the livers began to synthesize new proteins that are released into the blood that is coming out of the liver and distributed throughout the body. Some of these proteins have the ability to alter the inflammatory and healing responses. Of concern is that these proteins may play important roles in the reduced healing in the skin and eyes described above. 3) The liver is injured by the endotoxin. They found inflammatory cells in the livers and measures of cell death. The importance of endotoxin is shown by the fact that a strain of mice that are genetically unable to respond to endotoxin did not synthesize new proteins or show evidence of liver injury.

Summary of important findings: Hind limb unloading, a NASA model simulating important physiologic stressors of space flight resulted in significant reductions in wound healing in the skin and the cornea. In addition, there was significant reduction in the influx of white blood cells that normally protect the wound from infection. Also, there were increases in endotoxin in the blood flowing from the intestines into the liver with evidence of liver injury and release of proteins that may have the ability to reduce wound healing.

experiment_title: Evaluation of Maximal Oxygen Uptake and Submaximal Estimates of VO2max Before, During, and After Long Duration International Space Station Missions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Evaluation of Maximal Oxygen Uptake (VO2max) and Submaximal Estimates of VO2max Before, During, and After Long Duration International Space Station Missions will document the characteristics of maximum oxygen uptake (VO2max) during flight and to assess the validity of the current methods of tracking aerobic capacity change during and following International Space Station (ISS) missions.

VO2max is the standard measure of aerobic capacity and is directly related to the physical working capacity of an individual. The VO2max of an individual is affected by uptake of oxygen in the lungs, extraction of oxygen from the arterial circulation by working muscles and by cardiac output. Aerobic deconditioning causes a lowering of VO2max which results in a diminished capacity to perform strenuous physical tasks. Heart rate data previously collected during cycle exercise tests onboard the ISS indicate that VO2max is likely lowered during and following flight; however, actual measurements of VO2max have not been made during long-duration space flight.

The European Space Agency (ESA) provided Portable Pulmonary Function System (PPFS), which was used to measure the oxygen uptake, cardiac output, heart rate, and blood pressure responses of the astronaut participants when performing a cycle exercise test at submaximal, maximal, and peak levels. The maximal exercise tests conducted during flight occurred during portions of the ISS orbit suitable for real-time downlink of single lead electrocardiograph data.

APPROACH:
Maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) is a more accurate method of determining a crewmember's aerobic capacity than the current estimation method. Along with adding cardiac output measurements to the current estimations method will improve the accuracy of estimating a crewmember's aerobic capacity. Therefore, the following preflight and in-flight protocols have been established.

During baseline data collections, the subjects underwent a peak cycle test. During this test, a standard commercial off the shelf metabolic gas analysis system was used. The early preflight test results were used to define the exercise protocol used for subsequent pre- and postflight testing conducted during baseline data collection. During these tests, the crewmember performed a modified exercise protocol consisting of 5 minute stages at workloads eliciting 25, 50, and 75% of their preflight aerobic capacity test, followed by a 25 watt increase in workload every minute until the subject reached their maximum exercise capacity. During these tests heart rate (ECG), blood pressure, workload, perception of effort, metabolic gas exchange, and cardiac output were measured using the PPFS hardware.

The In-flight protocol was conducted on flight day 15 and every 30 days. Prior to performing the exercise test, the PPFS’s gas analyzer and respiratory volume measurement components were calibrated. During the test, the crewmember exercised on the cycle ergometer, inhaling cabin air and expiring through a mouthpiece; the nostrils were occluded with a nose clip. Expired breath was collected for metabolic gas analysis. Blood pressure was measured at automatically designated time intervals throughout the protocol. Cardiac output measurements were performed using a non-invasive rebreathing technique prior to exercise and during the last minute of the first three exercise stages. The electrical signals of the heart were measured using electrodes placed on the skin. Once the protocol has been completed, the PPFS was powered down and the sub-instruments were disconnected and stowed.

RESULTS:
The main findings of this study were that VO2peak decreased early in-flight then gradually increased during flight but never returned to preflight levels. VO2peak was lower on R+1 and R+10 than preflight but recovered by R+30. Peak heart rate was not different from preflight at any time during or following flight. A sustained decrease in VO2peak during and/or early postflight was not a universal finding in this study, since seven astronauts were able to attain their preflight VO2peak levels either at some time during flight or on R+1. Four of these astronauts performed in-flight exercise at higher intensities compared with those who experienced a decline in VO2peak, and three had low aerobic capacities before flight. These data indicate that, while VO2peak may be difficult to maintain during long-duration ISS missions, aerobic deconditioning is not an inevitable consequence of long-duration space flight.

experiment_title: Hematology, Cytological Composition of Bone Marrow and Standard Blood Parameters
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Exposure to microgravity has numerous effects upon human physiology. The effects of the space flight environment upon blood are not well understood. The extent of the hematological analysis of cosmonauts has been blood tests during flight, or for the most part, after their return to Earth. Only one postflight bone marrow draw has ever been performed on a human subject. Other bone marrow studies have been limited to myelograms of rats sacrificed after the Cosmos biosatellite missions. Rhesus monkeys have the same hemopoietic type (myeloid) as humans, and therefore are useful in the study of cytological components of bone marrow after microgravity exposure. This experiment measured hematological parameters in Rhesus monkeys after a 14 day space flight.

Approach:

Under ketamine anesthesia, bone marrow samples were drawn from the proximal metaphysis of the humerus twice before flight and several times after landing. Bone marrow hemopoiesis was measured as cell counts and cytological composition in 1 ml of marrow. A minimum of 500 cells were counted in the myelogram. Blood tests were performed to measure erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hematocrit, hemoglobin, erythrocytes, reticulocytes, and total and differential leukocytes. Proliferative, maturing, and mature pools of neutrophils, and early and mature erythrokaryocytes were measured. The ratio of early erythroblasts to total erythrokaryocytes was used to determine the rate of erythropoiesis. After the postflight ground control studies at R+17 and R+45, hematological tests were performed according to the flight protocols.

Results:

Data were collected from three Bion missions: Bion 9, 10, and 11. Preflight, animals received antibiotic treatment following bioimplantation. This may have impacted preflight blood data. Postflight data were compared with data collected at the last stage of preparation before flight. After both the flight and the R+45 control study, stress reactions were manifested through increased neutrophils and decreased lymphocyte and eosinophils in the blood. These stress reactions are due to such factors as decreased motor activity (restraint) and examinations, as well as microgravity exposure. Space flight led to diminished erythropoiesis and granulocytopoiesis in the bone marrow, indicated by a reduced reticulocyte count in the blood and a reduced population of early erythroid elements and proliferative neutrophils in the bone marrow, observed at R+1. Upon return to 1G, stimulated erythropoiesis and granulocytopoiesis were indicated by a greater number of dividing neutrophils, eosinophils, early generations of erythrokaryocytes, and a higher reticulocyte count in the blood. Decreased lymphoid population in the bone marrow was only observed after space flight, not after the ground control studies.

experiment_title: The Effects of Weightlessness on Human Single Muscle Fiber Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Investigations on previous space flights have documented that microgravity produces significant muscle atrophy, particularly in the anti-gravity muscles, such as those in the calf. However, a comprehensive description of microgravity-induced changes in human skeletal muscle structure and function and the underlying cellular mechanisms contributing to the altered function have not been established. Consequently, the overall objective of this project was to study the effects of microgravity on skeletal muscle function and to establish the cellular causes of the reduced functional capacity of skeletal muscle.

Specific objectives were the following:
1. To determine the extent to which microgravity alters human performance and skeletal muscle function.
2. To study the effects of microgravity on single fiber function, including the physiological and biochemical properties of the individual slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibers of human skeletal muscles.
3. To elucidate the cellular mechanisms of the observed microgravity-induced alterations in single fiber function.
4. To assess the role of an altered cellular capacity in eliciting the microgravity-induced reduction in both skeletal muscle and whole body performance and physical work capacity.

APPROACH:
To determine the effects of microgravity on maximal aerobic work capacity (VO2 max), maximal heart rate, VO2 max, calf muscle functions, and calf muscle performance were monitored during different tests. In addition, a muscle biopsy sample was obtained from the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles of the calf, both preflight and immediately postflight.
Test for maximal oxygen consumption (VO2 max): The subject exercised on a bicycle ergometer with gradually increasing workloads. During the test the subject rode with a mouthpiece and noseclip in place for measurement and analysis of the expired oxygen and carbon dioxide. Preflight and most postflight tests were performed up to a 100% volitional maximum. Inflight and immediately postflight, tests were performed at 85% of this level.
Calf muscle testing: The Torque-Velocity Dynamometer (TVD) was used to evaluate functional capacity of the calf muscle group. During the tests, the astronaut was supine with the right leg secured to the TVD. Three different protocols were tested: isometric, isokinetic and fatigue test. They are described as follows:
1. Isometric: The test subject was asked to apply the maximal force onto the TVD, while the footplate was in a fixed position. The test was repeated three times with different angles of the footplate: 80 degrees, 90 degrees, and 100 degrees.
2. Isokinetic: This test was employed at six different velocities (30, 60, 120, 180, 240 and 300 degrees per second), starting with the slow speed. The footplate was moving and the subject was asked to apply as much force as possible onto the moving surface.
3. Fatigue test: Thirty contractions were completed at 180 degrees per second. The subject was asked to perform with maximal effort and then attempt to maintain that effort.
4. Muscle biopsy: A small section of muscle (about 50 mg) was taken from the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles with a special biopsy needle. The sample was taken from the left leg preflight and right leg postflight. Muscle samples were analyzed by single fiber physiology to look at their contractile characteristics and biochemistry, by histochemistry to look at the fiber composition and size and the capillary density, and by electron microscopy to look at fiber microtrauma.

In addition to the above tests, VO2 max was tested three times during the flight; on Flight Days 3/4, 8/9 and 13/14. VO2 max tests were preceded and followed by a pulmonary function test (Experiment 284030). Calf muscle function testing was performed on Flight Days 2/3, 7/8 and 12/13 following the motor control tests of Experiment 284036 on the right leg. The fatigue test portion of the test was only performed during the Flight Day 2/3 and 12/13 sessions. Postflight testing included another muscle biopsy sample on landing day, calf muscle function testing on R+2, 4, 8, 15 and 30, and VO2 max testing on R+1, 5, 9, 16 and 31 (R is the day of landing).

RESULTS:
The 17 day LMS space flight resulted in significant decline in the whole body aerobic capacity of the crew, and in the functional performance of individual slow- and fast-twitch fibers. The fiber atrophy and decline in function (force and power) was greatest in the slow type I fibers of the antigravity soleus muscle. Considerable subject variability occurred for example, subject 0 showed a 40% decline in peak power of the soleus type I fiber, while this parameter was reduced by only 12% in subject A. The reason for the different responsiveness of the crew to microgravity is unknown, but could relate to the degree of exercise countermeasure performed.

Cell atrophy was the primary cause of the decline in fiber force and power as the force per cross-sectional area showed only minimal changes. In the slow type I fibers of the soleus, 2 of the 4 crew members showed a significant drop in peak power. All 4 subjects showed an increased shortening speed, and this partially protected against the loss of power. The increased velocity appears to have resulted from a selective loss of filamentous actin. This increased the actin-myosin filament spacing which in turn allowed a faster cross-bridge cycling rate and increased fiber speed. The structural rearrangement of the filaments represents an important adaptation to preserve cell power. One expects that this strategy is considerable more efficient than switching the myosin phenotype from the slow to the fast isozyme. The latter strategy occurs in rats flown in space, and results in a faster but less efficient muscle.

The reduced force and power of the individual fibers of the soleus and gastrocnemius did not result in a compromised calf muscle function. This suggests that the cellular changes were either too small to be detected by the TVD or that the crew compensated for the decline in cell function by altering their motor unit recruitment pattern.

experiment_title: Gravity and Skeletal Growth: III. Nuclear Volume Analysis of Osteoblast Histogenesis in Periodontal Ligament Cells of Cosmos 1887 Rats
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Bone is a mechanically sensitive tissue that is particularly responsive to gravitational forces. An understanding of changes in bone mass is important since it functions not only as structural support, but also as a metabolic source of calcium. The periodontal ligament (PDL), a well defined cell kinetic model for assessing the proliferation and differentiation of the cells associated with osteoblast histogenesis, was used to study the effect on osteoblast production.

Approach:

PDL, the osteogenic interface between tooth and bone, was morphometrically analyzed. 3 µm sections of methyl methacrylate embedded maxillary halves were stained with hematoxylin and eosin. Only PDL samples with a resorbing (scalloped with occasional osteoclasts) or resting (no morphological evidence of active resorption or formation) alveolar bone margin were selected for analysis. Nuclear volume analysis of cells in the PDL midroot area was performed and statistically considered.

Results:

Compared to synchronous controls, this flight treatment resulted in a 40% decrease in less differentiated osteoblast progenitor cells, a 42% increase in preosteoblasts (immediate precursors to osteoblasts), and increased numbers of PDL fibroblast-like cells within 25 µm of the bone surface. These results are consistent with a post-flight osteogenic response in PDL adjacent to previously resting or resorbing alveolar bone surfaces. This osteogenic response occurred despite physiological stress in the flight animals that resulted in a highly significant (p >=0.001) increase in adrenal weight. The data suggest that following space flight there is a strong and rapid recovery mechanism for osteoblast differentiation that is not suppressed by physiological stress.

experiment_title: Integrated Biotreatment Technology for Nitrogen-Rich Wastewaters in Advanced Life Support Systems
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this project was to develop a functional, closed-loop water recovery system for Space Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS) operations. To do so, technologies are required to treat blended urine and humidity condensate wastewaters that contain high concentrations of reduced nitrogen (~ 1.6 g/L as N). Removing this N via conventional treatment means is both resource and cost intensive. This project was proposed to develop, test, and optimize a novel, less resource-intensive, microgravity-compatible, high-capacity nitrogen removal technology termed the oxygen-limited autotrophic nitrification-denitrification (OLAND) process. The OLAND process offers the advantages of effective nitrogen removal to dinitrogen gas (N2), no reliance on external electron donors, and low biomass generation. The novel application for this project involves applying OLAND using a hollow fiber membrane bioreactor (HFMBR), which provides ample support for biofilm growth, permits bubbleless gas addition, enables very high volumetric removal rates, and combines the successfully demonstrated OLAND technology within a HFMBR configuration that permits increased process control. It was originally anticipated that at least 90% of the total Kjeldahl nitrogen in the wastewater will be converted to N2 with the remaining exiting as nitrate-N; this can be removed downstream via biological or physico-chemical polishing.

APPROACH:
An OLAND-HFMBR was constructed and assessed using organic carbon-free synthetic wastewater. Because the extent of oxygenation is a key parameter for controlling the metabolic processes that occur in a wastewater treatment system, the first part of the research investigated oxygen transfer characteristics of the HFMBR in clean water conditions and with actively growing biofilm. A mechanistic model for oxygen concentration and flux as a function of length along the non-porous membrane fibers that comprise the HFMBR was developed based on material properties and physical dimensions. This model reflects the diffusion mechanism of non-porous membranes; namely that oxygen follows a sorption-dissolution-diffusion mechanism. This is in contrast to microporous membranes in which oxygen is in the gas phase in the fiber pores up to the membrane surface, resulting in higher biofilm pore liquid dissolved oxygen concentrations. Compared to off-gas oxygen analysis from the HFMBR while in operation with biofilm growing, the model overpredicted mass transfer by a factor of approximately 1.3. This was in contrast to empirical mass transfer coefficient-based methods, which were determined using either bulk aqueous phase dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration or the DO concentration at the membrane-liquid interface, measured with oxygen microsensors. The mass transfer coefficient determined with the DO measured at the interface was the best predictor of actual oxygen transfer under biofilm conditions, while the bulk liquid coefficient underpredicted by a factor of 3. The mechanistic model exhibited sensitivity to parameters such as the initial lumen oxygen concentration (at the entry to the fiber) and the diffusion coefficient and partitioning coefficients of oxygen in the silicone membrane material. The mechanistic model has several advantages over empirical-based methods. Namely, it does not require experimental determination of KL, it is relatively simple to solve without the use of advanced mathematical software, and it is based upon selection of the membrane-biofilm interfacial DO concentration. The last of these is of particular importance when designing and operating HFMBR systems with redox (aerobic/anoxic/anaerobic) stratification, because the DO concentration will determine the nature of the microenvironments, the microorganisms present, and the metabolisms that occur.

During the second phase of the research, the coupling of two autotrophic metabolisms, partial nitrification to nitrite (nitritation) and anaerobic ammonium oxidation, was demonstrated in a single HFMBR. The system successfully treated a high-strength nitrogen wastewater intended to mimic a urine stream from such sources as extended space missions. For the last 250 days of operation, operating with an average oxygen to ammonia flux (JO2/JNH4+) of 3.0 resulted in an average nitrogen removal of 74%, with no external organic carbon added. Control of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) presented a challenge that was addressed by maintaining the JO2/JNH4+ below the stoichiometric threshold for complete nitrification to nitrate (4.57 g O2 / g NH4+). Of particular concern for application of this technology for space flight, we found that the DO-limiting condition resulted in formation of harmful gaseous emissions of nitrogen oxides (NO, N2O), which could not be prevented by short-term control strategies. Controlling JO2/JNH4+ prevented NOB proliferation long enough to allow an anaerobic ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AnaerAOB) population to develop and be retained for >250 days. Addition of a supplemental nutrient solution may have contributed to the growth of AnaerAOB by overcoming a possible micronutrient deficiency. Disappearance of the gaseous nitrogen oxide emissions coincided with the onset of anaerobic ammonium oxidation, demonstrating a benefit of coupling these two autotrophic metabolisms in one reactor. Obvious differences in biofilm density were evident across the biofilm depth, with a region of low density in the middle of the biofilm, suggesting that low cell density or exocellular polymeric substances were primarily present in this region. Microbial community analysis using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) did not reveal consistent trends with respect to length along the fibers, but radial stratification of aerobic ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AerAOB), NOB, and AnaerAOB were visible in biofilm section samples. AerAOB were largely found in the first 25% of the biofilm near the membrane, AnaerAOB were found in the outer 30%, and NOB were found most often in the mid-depth region of the biofilm. This community structure demonstrates the importance of oxygen availability as a determinant of how microbial groups spatially distribute within an HFMBR biofilm.

RESULTS:
The combination of these two aspects of the research, predictive oxygen transfer capability and the effect of oxygen control on performance and populations, provides a foundation for future application of HFMBR technology to a broad range of earth-based and planetary or long-term space flight wastewater treatment scenarios. However, the onset of hazardous nitrogen oxide gases during the long acclimation phase of the reactor (removed later when anaerobic ammonia oxidation was initiated) presents a challenge when considering how one would apply this technology to long term space flight or planetary base stations. Nevertheless, the successful demonstration of this technology in a ground-based research project paves the way for further testing and validation in simulated microgravity environments on the ground as well as testing and demonstration of a prototype unit in space. Furthermore, the results are pertinent to significant applications on Earth, where use of anaerobic treatment technologies for sustainable waste management is increasing in frequency. Such applications generate strong ammonia-ladened waste streams that may benefit from being treated by an OLAND-HFMBR application.

experiment_title: ISS Microbial Observatory (Microbial Tracking-1A)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As recommended by the National Research Council Decadal Survey, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) proposes to establish an International Space Station–Microbial Observatory (ISS-MO) to generate a microbial census of the space station’s surfaces and atmosphere using advanced molecular microbial community analysis techniques, supported by traditional culture-based methods and modern bioinformatics computational modeling.

The proposed ISS-MO establishment leads into a long-term, multigenerational study of microbial population dynamics. The ISS-MO project’s methodology serves as the foundation for an extensive microbial census, offering significant insight into spaceflight-induced changes in the populations of beneficial and potentially harmful microbes. Additionally, it provides NASA with both a mechanistic understanding of these changes (e.g., cataloging population changes and mapping/linking these to environmental niche and genomic changes), as well as insight into practical countermeasures for mitigating risks to humans and environmental systems. The ISS-MO team uses existing ISS sample collection technologies to generate an initial microbial census. Following their return to Earth, samples from the various ISS modules are analyzed using standardized technologies from the Mars Program-funded projects.

The proposed ISS-MO project includes the delivery of a database that compiles the genomic sequences and genetic information for all the microbes encountered within the ISS habitat. Using this data, NASA can more accurately and confidently assess the status of microbes associated with closed habitation and crew health maintenance. In addition to providing microbial profiles, the ISS- MO team identifies which microbial taxa pose particular threats to crew health. Furthermore, specific ISS-MO project aims shall enable scientists to resolve applicable NASA-Human Research Program integrated research plan risks.

APPROACH:
Surface and air samples were collected and analyzed. The sampling was performed on 8 specific locations inside the US modules for surfaces, and 6 locations for the air. Surface sampling procedures involved the use of polyester wipes, swabs, contact slides (two types), and adhesive tapes; a gelatin filter was used to sample the air. In this study, traditional cultivation, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) assay, and propidium monoazide-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PMA-qPCR) method were employed to quantify the microbial populations. In addition, the next- generation sequencing analyses were used to elucidate the microbial diversity and clarify difference between the microbiomes of ISS and Earth cleanrooms.

RESULTS:
The statistical analysis of these microbiomes showed that three bacterial phyla dominated both in ISS and Earth cleanrooms, but varied in their abundances. While members of Actinobacteria were predominant on ISS, Proteobacteria, the least abundant on ISS, dominated the Earth cleanrooms. Alpha diversity estimators indicated a significant drop in diversity associated with PMA treated samples. On average, PMA treated samples had 48% fewer operational taxonomic unit (OTU) than their respective untreated samples (paired T-test P= 0.004). This consistent reduction in microbial diversity of PMA samples was also true for Faith’s diversity, Chao1, and Shannon diversity measures, and was also constant with the depletion of many taxa identified by differential abundance analysis. To better characterize the shared community composition among samples, beta-diversity metrics analysis were conducted. A significant difference was noticed between ISS and cleanroom samples, i.e., samples from the same site are highly similar microbiome composition regardless of PMA treatment. At the OTU level, the microbial community composition is strongly associated with sampling site, and the reduced overall diversity of PMA treatment does not dramatically impact the composition relative to sample origin. Results of the study indicate significant differences between ISS and Earth cleanroom microbiomes in terms of community structure and composition.

experiment_title: Vitamin D Supplement Evaluation of Dosing Requirements
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Vitamin D is critical for space travelers because they lack ultraviolet light exposure and have an insufficient dietary supply of vitamin D. Despite the provision of vitamin D supplements to International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers, vitamin D status is consistently lower after flight than before flight, and in several crewmembers, levels have decreased to concentrations considered clinically significant. Vitamin D has long been known to play a role in calcium metabolism, and more recently its non-calcitropic functions (functions not related to calcium metabolism, e.g., effects related to the incidence of cancer or diabetes) have been recognized. According to the results of several recent studies, functionally relevant measures indicate that the lower limit of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (a marker of vitamin D status) should be raised from the current standard of 25 nmol/L to 80 nmol/L. The mean preflight serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D for U.S. ISS crewmembers to date is 63 ± 16 nmol/L, and after a four to six-month space flight mission it typically decreases 25-30% despite a supplementation of 400 International Units per day (IU/d). The suboptimal pre- and postflight vitamin D status is an issue that needs to be addressed so NASA can better define the appropriate amount of supplemental vitamin D to serve as a countermeasure against vitamin D deficiency in crewmembers. This is very important for long-duration crewmembers, and is critical for exploration class missions.

The investigators recently completed a ground-based investigation titled, "Efficacy of Vitamin D Supplementation in an Antarctic Ground Analog of Space Flight," which evaluated vitamin D supplementation efficacy during the winter months in Antarctica, when UV-B radiation levels are essentially zero. A supplement of 2,000 IU/d raised serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D to acceptable levels, but as with any time a daily supplement or change in routine is required, compliance can be an issue.

In this study, investigators studied whether a weekly or monthly dose of vitamin D could be substituted for a daily dose. Data from this study will help investigators provide long-duration space flight crewmembers a safe, effective, and evidence-based recommendation for vitamin D supplementation to achieve and maintain optimal vitamin D status before, during, and after flight.

Approach:
This study was conducted at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, TX. Subject participation and sample collection occurred between June 2008 and September 2009. The protocol was approved by the Johnson Space Center Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects. The procedures followed were in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration of 1975 as revised in 1983. The subjects provided written informed consent before they participated in the study.

Subjects were randomly assigned to one of 4 groups: no supplement (placebo), 2,000 IU per day, 10,000 IU per week, and 50,000 IU per week for 4 weeks and then monthly for the next 2 months. The placebo group consisted of 4 subjects taking a daily placebo, 4 subjects taking a weekly placebo, and 4 subjects taking a weekly placebo for 4 weeks and then monthly for the next 2 months. There was one exception to randomization: subjects whose screening serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was greater than 85 nmol/L were assigned to the placebo group. Ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation exposure was recorded using polysulfone film badges. Subjects were asked to wear the badges the day before the 0-day and 60-day blood draws.

Materials
Vitamin D3 capsules (2,000 IU, 10,000 IU, 50,000 IU, and placebo) were manufactured by Tishon Corp. (Westbury, NY). All doses (and placebos) were identical in appearance. Three samples from each dose were analyzed for actual vitamin D3 content before the study began. The 2,000-IU and 10,000-IU capsules (and daily and weekly placebo doses) were repackaged into blister-sealed pouches to most efficiently track compliance. The 50,000-IU capsules (and corresponding placebo group) were administered in a supervised manner for each dose and therefore were not supplied to the subjects in blister packs. Ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation exposure was recorded using polysulfone film badges. Subjects were asked to wear the badges the day before the 0-day and 60-day blood draws.

Study Design
The supplementation period was 3 months. In the first week of each study month, subjects came to the Human Test Subject Facility at the Johnson Space Center for a fasted blood draw and 24-hour urine sample (baseline, 0 days). Immediately after the fasted blood draw, subjects were administered a placebo or a 2,000-, 10,000-, or 50,000-IU pill of vitamin D3. Blood was collected again 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours after this initial dose. A fasted blood draw and 24-hour urine sample was collected again from all subjects after 30, 60, and 90 days. On day 60, subjects came in for a fasted blood draw and were administered their respective vitamin D dose (or placebo) and blood was collected 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours later.

Vitamin D Intake Assessment
At the monthly blood draws (0, 30, 60, and 90 days), subjects completed a 7-day recall food questionnaire for the 6 days before the blood draw and supplement provision, and the 24 hours after supplement provision. The questionnaire was developed for this study, and was designed to include foods known to contain vitamin D. Supplement use was also recorded. Questionnaires were analyzed and vitamin D intake was calculated using the Nutrition Data System for Research developed by the Nutrition Coordinating Center, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN.

Sample Collection and Processing
All baseline (time 0) blood samples were collected in the morning after an 8-hour fast. Blood was allowed to clot, and then it was centrifuged and serum was separated into individual aliquot cryotubes. Serum calcium, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and liver enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase) were measured within 4 days of collection for each blood draw. Other samples were frozen at minus 70 degrees?Celsius and batched until the end of the study so that all samples were analyzed together.

RESULTS:
The data provides evidence that vitamin D doses of 2,000 IU daily, 10,000 IU once weekly, or 50,000 IU (weekly then) monthly dosing regimens used in this study were similarly effective at raising circulating vitamin D status over the course of 90 days. Even though the mean urinary calcium response at 30, 60, and 90 days was not different between groups, more subjects in the 50,000-IU group had urinary calcium concentrations higher than the upper end of the normal range at some point during the study.

The investigators found no overt signs of chronic vitamin D toxicity with the doses and study duration used, but the increased rate of elevated urinary calcium should not be ignored, especially for high-risk groups for which vitamin D supplementation is recommended. For space travelers, Antarctic winter crews, submariners, and others where medical facilities are limited, and travel to medical facilities is prohibitive at best, the ease of less frequent supplementation does not seem worth any increased risk of renal stone formation.

experiment_title: Nanoscale Test Strips for Multiplexed Blood Analysis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of the nanoscale test strips, or nanostrips, is to provide rapid, low-cost, powerful multiplexed analyses in a diminutive form so that whole body health checks can be performed on a single drop of blood. The approach is conceptually similar to pH or urinalysis test strips which allow multiplexed measurements in a linear format. The main difference is that we are proposing test strips at the nanoscale, shrunk in size over a billion-fold in volume, allowing multiple sensing elements to be included in a tiny area. In Phase I, we fabricated, tested, and demonstrated functional parathyroid hormone and vitamin D nanostrips for bone metabolism. Furthermore, we developed thrombin aptamer and immune IgG antibody nanostrips. For Phase II, we will develop a breadth of nanostrips designed to address key space-flight medical needs. These will be for assessment of bone metabolism, immune response, cardiac status, liver metabolism, and lipid profiles. We plan to enhance our technology capabilities by developing a Rapid Nanostrip Assay Capability, mix-and-run assay capability, in-house aptamer production, advanced lyophilization technology, and nanostrip accelerated stability tests. The nanostrips will be read out in a time-of-flight flow-based manner utilizing our rHEALTH sensor.

experiment_title: Physiological and Anatomical Rodent Experiment 1
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous to PARE 01, the only studies comparing unweighting through microgravity and unweighting through hindlimb suspension were performed on adult rats. These studies have shown that posterior hindlimb muscles, the function of which depend on opposing the pull of gravity, are the most responsive to unweighting. Another effect found in unweighting studies has been the increased response of insulin to glucose transport. This experiment was designed to test the validity of using tail suspension methods as models for studying microgravity unweighting effects on developing rats. Several muscle parameters were compared between rats subjected to space flight and rats subjected to hindlimb suspension. A main objective was to determine whether microgravity causes an increase in glucose uptake in the presence or absence of insulin.

Approach:

Flight rats and ground control rats were 26 days old at the beginning of the experiment. Rats were flown for 5.4 days and muscles were removed within 3 hours of landing. Body weights and muscle weights were measured for flight and control rats. Protein analysis for total protein content and concentration was performed on the soleus, gastrocnemius, plantaris, tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum. The soleus and extensor digitorum were used for glucose uptake studies. The extensor digitorum served as a control to the soleus because it is not affected by loading or systemic effects. The uptake of 2-deoxyglucose was measured in the presence and absence of insulin.

Results:

Despite similar food and water consumption, flight rats gained more weight than the control rats. Comparisons of muscle sizes normalized to body mass showed that flight and suspension reduced muscle mass of the soleus by 38 percent and 33 percent respectively. Smaller differences were seen in masses of plantaris and gastrocnemius muscles and no differences were seen in anterior muscles. Protein content of the soleus muscles from flight rats was reduced by 20 percent and was characterized by a lower concentration. Protein content from the soleus muscles of suspended rats was reduced by 23 percent. In the absence of insulin, there was no difference in the rate of uptake of 2-deoxyglucose in the soleus or the extensor digitorum. However, in the presence of insulin, the uptake of 2-deoxyglucose was significantly higher in flight and suspended rats than in control rats. This increase may be due to an increase in insulin binding capacity due to unloading effects.

experiment_title: Sensorimotor Adaptation Following Exposure to Ambiguous Inertial Motion Cues
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The central nervous system must resolve the ambiguity of inertial motion sensory cues in order to derive accurate spatial orientation awareness. The investigators general hypothesis is that the central nervous system utilizes both multi-sensory integration and frequency segregation as neural strategies to resolve the ambiguity of tilt and translation stimuli. Movement in an altered gravity environment, such as weightlessness without a stable gravity reference, results in new patterns of sensory cues. Adaptive changes in how inertial cues from the otolith system are integrated with other sensory information lead to perceptual and postural disturbances upon return to Earth's gravity. The primary goals of this ground-based study were to explore physiological mechanisms and operational implications of disorientation and tilt-translation disturbances reported by crewmembers during and following re-entry, and to evaluate a tactile prosthesis as a countermeasure for improving control of whole-body orientation during passive tilt and translation motion paradigms.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Aim 1 was to examine the effects of stimulus frequency (0.01 - 0.6 Hz) on adaptive changes in eye movements, motion perception, and cognition during combined tilt and translation motion profiles. The investigators hypothesized that adaptation of otolith-mediated responses would be greatest in the mid-frequency range where there is a tilt-translation crossover. Their findings emphasized differences in the neural processing to distinguish tilt and translation between eye movements and motion perception. Specifically, during dynamic linear stimuli in the absence of canal and visual input, a change in stimulus frequency alone elicits similar changes in the amplitude of both self motion perception and eye movements. However, in contrast to the eye movements, the phase of both perceived tilt and translation motion is not altered by stimulus frequency over this limited range. Their findings also suggest that the frequency at which there was a crossover of perceived tilt and translation gains appeared to vary across different motion paradigms (e.g., near 0.3 Hz during off-vertical axis rotation and near 0.15 Hz during sled translation).

Adaptation experiments conducted below this cross-over frequency using the 'vision-aligned' paradigm have resulted in modest changes to both eye movements and motion perception, consistent with their first hypothesis. Adaptation experiments conducted around this cross-over frequency range using the 'GIF-aligned' paradigm demonstrated a significant effect of stimulus frequency on both motion sickness and spatial cognitive performance.

Aim 2 was to examine changes in control errors during a closed-loop nulling task before and after tilt-translation adaptation.They hypothesized that the ability to control tilt orientation would be compromised following tilt-translation adaptation, with increased control errors corresponding to changes in self-motion perception. Roll tilt nulling was implemented using the both step and pseudorandom stimuli in darkness. These findings suggest that these types of manual control tasks are sensitive to underlying changes in sensorimotor physiology, and specifically to changes in the brain's interpretation of linear acceleration stimuli.

Aim 3 was to evaluate how a tactile prosthesis might improve control performance. A simple four electromechanical tactor system was developed that provided six threshold levels of orientation information. They also examined the influence of vibrotactile feedback during computerized posturography. A significant reduction in RMS error (p <0.05) was observed using this simple tactile prosthesis, both during manual and balance control tasks. These results are promising in that a fairly simple device with as few as four tactors may prove useful to significantly improve landing performance.

Aim 4 was to examine how spatial awareness is impaired with changing gravitational cues during parabolic flight, and the extent to which vibrotactile feedback of orientation can be used to help improve spatial awareness. The findings suggest that tactile cueing may improve navigation in operational environments, such as extravehicular activities on a lunar surface. This type of sensory feedback may also prove beneficial as a navigation aid in patient populations, providing non-visual, non-auditory feedback of orientation or desired direction heading.

experiment_title: Effect of Spaceflight on Development of Immune Responses
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The objectives of this experiment are as follows: 1) to evaluate the influence of spaceflight on the maternal-fetal interface, 2) to evaluate the influence of spaceflight on the development of immune system cells, 3) to evaluate the influence of spaceflight on the development of functional activities of immune system cells, 4) to evaluate the influence of spaceflight on the development of immunoregulation, 5) to evaluate the influence of spaceflight on the development of immune responsiveness to cytokines, and 6) to evaluate the influence of spaceflight on the ability to resist microbial infection.

Approach:

Total antibody titer and percent antibody isotype were determined in the plasma of the mother and progeny animals. Flow cytometric analysis of the percentages of leukocyte populations were performed on spleen, blood, and bone marrow tissues. Splenocytes and thymocytes were stimulated with the T cell mitogen concanavalin-A (ConA) to evaluate blastogenic potential in progeny animals. Profiles of a broad spectrum of splenic and thymic cytokine activities were conducted at the genetic level as revealed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Bone marrow cells were incubated in the presence of macrophage-colony stimulating factor (M-CSF) to stimulate the differentiation of these cells into macrophages. Splenic macrophages harvested from progeny animals were analyzed for their ability to phagocytize pathogenic bacteria.

Results:

The response of bone marrow cells to M-CSF, leukocyte blastogenesis and cytokine production were altered in cells obtained from flight dams. Contrastingly, the response of bone marrow cells to M-CSF as well as leukocyte blastogenesis were not altered in cells taken from fetuses and pups from flown animals. Leukocyte subset analysis showed that flown dams, fetuses, and pups were altered. Cytokine production was reduced in flight pups, while immunoglobulin levels were not altered in offspring after space flight. This data indicates that there may be differential regulation in the development of immune responses.

experiment_title: Studies of Vestibular Neurons in Normal, Hyper- and Hypogravity
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Two types of neurons were studied in this experiment: horizontal (lateral) semicircular canal afferents and type I or type II vestibular nuclei neurons found in the medial vestibular nucleus. The purpose of this study was to gain an understanding of neural adaptation of the semicircular canals to microgravity and to compare results to the previous study performed on Cosmos 2044.

Approach:

Monkeys were implanted with electrodes to monitor neuronal activity. Recordings were made during pre and postflight studies from 118 semicircular canal afferents and 27 vestibular nucleus neurons from 7 rhesus monkeys. Five of these monkeys were ground controls and 2 were flight subjects. 137 pulse rotation protocols were executed. Usable data was obtained from 127 horizontal afferents concerning spontaneous discharge. Rotation protocols for the semicircular canals included tests of spontaneous discharge, a pulse rotation test, a sum of sines test and a sinewave test. Rotation protocols for the vestibular nuclei neurons included spontaneous sinusoidal discharge test, oscillation at 0.2, 0.5 and 1.0 hertz, pulse constant velocity of 60 degrees per second and a sum of sines stimulus covering the bandwidth from 0.02 hertz to 1.0 hertz.

Results:

The mean spontaneous rate varied from 128 spikes per second during preflight tests to 92 spikes per second during postflight tests, for a change of 28%. The best filtered neural adaptation operator (k) and the gain of pulse response were decreased during postflight compared to preflight. This contrasts with results obtained from Cosmos 2044. The best filtered gain and k values for the sum of sines were slightly elevated post flight. For periodic stimuli (pulse and sine waves) no change was found in gain and neural adaptation post flight. This is different from results found in 2044 but may be attributable to differences in experimental procedures.

experiment_title: Increasing Cognition Administration Order Flexibility
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The study will provide regression estimates that adjust for the effects of both administration order such as practice effects and difficulty of stimulus sets which vary between batteries. These can be used to make all Cognition administration regimens comparable. This study will also show whether practice effects differ depending on the interval between Cognition administrations, which will inform pre- and in-flight testing schedules.

This study has the following specific aims:

  1. Disentangle practice effects and stimulus set difficulty effects to make Cognition administration more flexible.
  2. Investigate the effects of administration rate of the Cognition test battery on practice effects.

APPROACH:
Investigators will study 30 high-functioning subjects that perform all 15 versions of the 10 tests of the Cognition test battery. Subjects will perform the battery at an interval of five days between consecutive tests, while the other half will perform the battery at an interval of ten days between consecutive tests. This will inform any differences in practice effects depending on administration intervals. The test version administration order will be random but balanced, such as each version will appear in each position exactly once. Investigators will also administer a standard measure of social functioning during the familiarization session to investigate how the Emotion Recognition Test (ERT) relates to non-cognitive measures of social functioning.

experiment_title: Effects of Charged Particles on the Uterus
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In NASA space missions about 15% of astronauts are women, and women made up half of the 2013 NASA Astronaut Class. However, risks of uterine exposure to galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events during space missions remain completely unknown. Normal uterine structure and function is required for a healthy pregnancy and optimal development and subsequent health of the offspring. Uterine function in adults is largely regulated by ovarian steroid hormones secreted from the growing pool of follicles. Preliminary data generated under a NASA pilot grant showed that Iron (56Fe) charged particle radiation induces apoptosis and destroys ovarian follicles in mice. Radiotherapy for the treatment of cancer in the pelvic region has been shown to damage uterine cells, reduce blood circulation to the uterus, and increase the risk for miscarriage, low-birth weight, and premature birth. In addition, pelvic irradiation for cancer treatment is associated with higher risk of uterine cancer. Female atomic bomb survivors have increased risk of uterine leiomyoma (fibroid). This experiment hypothesizes that high charge and energy (HZE) particles (Iron or Oxygen) typical of space radiation alter uterine function and contribute to the pathogenesis of uterine leiomyoma and cancer. This proposal will provide preliminary findings for further detailed studies and formulation for necessary remedies associated with risk of uterine exposure.

APPROACH:
To test the hypotheses, three month old female mice will be irradiated with charged iron or oxygen particles. In situ detection of uterine cell morphology, DNA double strand break, apoptosis, pregnancy outcome, and uterine pathogenicity will be determined.

RESULTS:
Results for this experiment are currently not available.
