experiment_title: Design and Evaluation of Automated Electronic Checklists for Robotics Operations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The investigators aimed to develop a prototype electronic procedure system and use it to study how the automated features of this system should be implemented to enhance situation awareness (SA), operator workload, and task execution in the context of robotic arm operation. Future long-duration, long-distance mission crews will have to operate more independently from the ground and rely more on automated spacecraft systems to support them while executing mission tasks. NASA has relatively little experience designing systems to support this concept of operations so the overall goal was to provide to NASA design guidelines for implementing these automation features in electronic procedures and empirical evidence that demonstrates how the operator and task performance are affected. Investigators used well defined International Space Station (ISS) robotic arm operations as their proxy for future arm or rover operations. They included capabilities in the electronic procedures that are not currently available, such as automatic multi-step execution or verification and control of current robot system states (e.g., arm configuration, camera control).

The primary objective of this project was to provide empirical evidence supporting design guidelines for automated electronic checklists for robotics operations. While planning to use the ISS robotic arm operations as their proxy for general arm or rover operations but they will develop scenarios that test a crew’s ability to operate more autonomously than in ISS operations.

This study had the following two specific aims:

  1. Develop a prototype display for robotics operations that integrated the electronic procedures with the displays for performing robotic tasks. The design process began with a hierarchical task analysis approach to drive out functional and information requirements for the display. Additionally, critical system states were identified using “Object-Process Methodology,” a task modeling approach that extends the task analysis to a computable level. We augmented our prototype design with the capability for automated execution of procedural steps. This prototype was integrated into the MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) ISS robotic workstation simulation that has previously been used in several National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) projects.
  2. Perform a human-in-the-loop study that provided empirical evidence about the effects of the prototype system architecture, including varying levels of automation, on task performance, operator situation awareness, and mental workload. The study investigated how the allocation of procedural step execution between human operator and automation affects situation awareness (SA), mental workload, and task performance. Shifting more procedure steps to the automation may ease workload and speed task completion, but may also degrade the operator’s SA and ability to detect and resolve errant conditions. The experiment scenario included interrupting events that required switching between different procedures.

APPROACH:
Initial efforts focused on developing a prototype electronic procedure system with new automated capabilities and integrating this capability into the robotic workstation simulator. First, informed by actual robotic arm procedures conducted on the ISS, investigators defined and developed a set of robotic task scenarios that includes system setup, support of a series of simulated spacewalk activities, and system shutdown. Within these scenarios, the possibility for a variety of failures and associated failure recovery steps were designed and built into the simulation so that they can test responses to non-normal situations. Investigators used tools including Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) and Object-Process Methodology (OPM) to break down each task goal into its components and necessary actions and to define system states throughout the flow of the simulated robotic arm operation.

Secondly, investigators used the HTA and OPM analyses to design the computer code that creates the simulated integrated control panel and procedure checklist system. In doing so, they created a new type of human-machine electronic procedure interface that integrates automation and system information into an electronic display. By integrating a functional electronic control panel, procedure, and checklist into their simulator, they created a system that presents information equivalent to two separate systems and laptops that are currently used on the ISS during robotic operations. This, in turn, reduces the required number of displays and equipment, an important feature for future space missions that will have strict mass and power constraints.

Following the development of the prototype automated electronic procedure system, investigators completed a human-in-the-loop experiment to investigate how the allocation of procedural step execution between the human operator and automation, or level of automation, would affect task performance, situation awareness, and mental workload. The key independent variable in the experiment was the level of automation used during task completion. The simulator was capable of allocating the automation to perform all or a subset of the procedural steps including state selection, identification verification, and confirmation. Three levels of automation were tested--Full Auto, Full Manual, and Auto Set/ Manual Verify. If the automation was tasked with doing all of the procedure steps, then the system is in Full Auto mode in which we expected low subject mental workload and high performance but also low situation awareness. In Full Manual mode, all steps were allocated to the human operator, and we expected high situation awareness but also high workload and possibly lower task performance. In the intermediate automation allocation, Auto Set/ Manual Verify, the automation was tasked with setting the states while the human operator verified the state change. In this intermediate automation level, investigators expected high task performance and situation awareness, and intermediate workload.

RESULTS:
Results are largely consistent with the investigators' initial hypotheses, that Full Automation mode results in faster task completion times with practically no errors and low subject mental workload, measured objectively with a visual secondary task and subjectively using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). The reduction in completion time comes primarily from the automatic selection of cameras and entry of arm parameters for Space Station Remote Manipulator System (SSRMS) movement performed by the automation, rather than manually. The elimination of manual control tasks reduces the visual demands of the task and frees attentional resources for monitoring system state and task progress. This behavior was observed in the improvement of the operator’s ability to detect system events and states in the Full Manual condition. However, the use of automation also degraded the operator’s ability to comprehend of current system state and predict future states compared to Full Manual mode. The intermediate automation mode, Auto Set/Manual Verify, was generally preferred by the subjects as the best compromise to speed up task completion while maintain their situation awareness of the task and also resulted in the best overall performance across time, workload, and awareness.

experiment_title: Assessment of Sleep Dynamics in a Simulated Space Station Environment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
 

Based on prior experience, it is believed that the unique environmental conditions and work-rest schedules aboard orbital spacecraft result in sleep decrements and fatigue in astronauts. Potential disturbances of circadian rhythmicity in the space flight environment and consequent decrements in performance efficiency and in the well being of astronauts are major concerns of NASA. In addition to changes in environmental factors, such as the absence of a gravity vector and ultra-shortened light-dark cycles, other factors that contribute to the development of sleep disturbances and fatigue during space flights include the abnormal length of working periods (high work load effect), continuous deviation of the sleep-wake cycle duration from 24 hours ("migrating day"), and cyclic noise disturbances. In addition to these physiological and sleep disturbances, in order to meet operational demands, crewmembers have been assigned shift-work schedules during certain dual-shift missions. Sleep deficits, biological asynchrony with work-rest activities, and sleep-promoting medications have been documented to impact alertness and induce fatigue. This presents a very high risk for shuttle and ground-operations of the space program and particularly to crew health and safety.

To augment sleep quality, pharmacological agents are often prescribed during flight in addition to preflight entrainment. However, a systematic evaluation of the effectiveness of light treatment on the maintenance of in flight work-rest demands is missing due to a lack of methods and technologies that are both sufficiently sensitive and flight-suitable. To fill this gap, the present study was conducted to evaluate objective and subjective data collection methods for sleep quality and contributing variables in a ground-based analog environment in human subjects confined to a closed chamber during as part of Phase IIa and Phase III Lunar Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP). Information gained from this study will be useful in the identification and validation of sensitive, non-obtrusive techniques for evaluating sleep and circadian rhythms during space flight.

APPROACH:
 

Methods for estimating sleep variables and circadian rhythms in a simulated work-rest environment that mimics the schedule of International Space Station (ISS) crew activities were investigated. Eight healthy subjects, three females and five males, stayed for 60 days (Phase IIa) and 91 days (Phase III) in a closed life support test facility at the Johnson Space Center. Each phase consisted of one pre-chamber data collection session, four (Phase IIa) or six (Phase III) in-chamber sessions, and one post-chamber session. Each session was 48 hours long during which time the subjects wore an activity and ambient light monitor (Actillume) on the wrist of the non-dominant arm, completed sleep logs twice daily, and collected timed saliva and void-by-void urine samples.

The activity data recorded by the Actillume were autoscored for sleep, while the illumination data were analyzed for patterns of light exposure. An electronic sleep/wake questionnaire was completed upon wake-up and before bedtime using the Ames Interactive Reporting Log (AIRLOG). AIRLOG is a tool developed exclusively for research in aviation and ground transportation environments; the instrument was developed by NASA Ames Research Center and includes separate components that relate to the events of the day preceding the sleep period, the quality of sleep period, and the ensuing wake time. These data were analyzed to estimate subjective changes in sleep duration, latency, efficiency, and quality during chamber stay.

Saliva samples were collected every two hours while subjects were awake using salivettes. Void-by-void urine samples were also collected during the 48-hour period. All saliva and urine samples were processed and stored at -40° C until analysis. Samples were analyzed using commercial radioimmunoassay kits to determine levels of melatonin and melatonin sulfate.

Sleep variables (latency, duration and efficiency) were estimated from the Actillume data (objective) and from sleep logs (subjective); acrophases for salivary melatonin and urinary melatonin sulfate were determined from concentration versus time profiles.

Data Analysis

Illumination data from the Actillume were analyzed for patterns and intensity of light exposure using vendor provided Action-3 software. Activity data were analyzed with Action-3 software using both the manual and autoscore options in the software to estimate objective sleep variables. Data from the AIRLOG were analyzed to estimate subjective sleep quality, efficiency, and latency. Salivary melatonin concentrations were determined using commercially available direct radioimmunoassay kit (ALPCO). Urine aliquots were assayed to determine 6-hydroxymelatonin sulfate levels. Cosinor and cross-correlation methods were used to analyze salivary melatonin and urinary melatonin sulfate measurement data with respect to time. Cosinor analysis was based on least-squares fit of the cosine function to a series of observations. This technique allowed characterization of the mesor (the 48-hour time-series mean), acrophase (peak time, referenced to local midnight) and amplitude (half of the peak-to- trough variability). Phase shifts were calculated from the entire 48-hour session by subtracting the baseline acrophase from the in-chamber acrophase.

RESULTS
 

Objective measurements of sleep variables by Actillume showed no statistically significant differences between baseline (pre- and post-chamber) and in-chamber periods. These data suggest that crewmembers adjusted with the Space Station analog work-rest activities. Light intensity during waking periods in the chamber was lower (50-100 lux) compared to baseline readings (1000-1500 lux.) Similar readings of light intensity have been observed on two earlier space flight missions as well. Self-assessment of sleep variables (sleep latency, number of awakenings, sleep duration and sleep efficiency) by AIRLOG showed no changes between chamber stay and baseline. In addition, sleep quality scores did not reflect any sleep decrements during chamber stays. A comparison of the sleep variables data from the objective and subjective scores indicated that subjective assessment scores of sleep by the crewmembers were higher than the respective objective measures derived from actigraphy. This observation confirms the general notion among sleep researchers that perception of sleep decrements is always less than actual deficits. In addition, the number of awakenings recorded by actigraphy was higher than those from the subjective sleep log scores. Results from this study indicate that the methods tested here are suitable for in-flight assessment of sleep during long-duration flights. Non-obtrusive wrist-actigraphy appears to be a valuable diagnostic method for the assessment of sleep decrements in astronauts.

Urine melatonin sulfate is well known to be a good index for determining circadian rhythmicity. Earlier reports have suggested that salivary melatonin rhythm is an accurate predictor of circadian rhythmicity. Cosinor analysis of salivary melatonin and urinary melatonin sulfate excretion rates from the present study yielded valuable information on the applicability of salivary data for the assessment of circadian rhythms. When circadian variables derived from both markers are in agreement, acrophase estimates calculated from time profiles of both markers and an accepted measure of circadian shifts, are also in agreement. Salivary melatonin acrophase was delayed during the chamber stay by 2.7 hours and compared well with the urinary melatonin sulfate acrophase, which was delayed 3.0 hours. The chamber light conditions were similar to those of ISS and may be responsible for the melatonin acrophase delays noted during the chamber study. Regression analysis of these data indicated that good correlation exists between estimates from the two sets of data (r = 0.79). However, the correlation between delayed salivary melatonin rhythm and sleep duration, although weak (r =0.42) suggests that the desynchronized melatonin rhythm and sleep period may have affected the sleep quality in the chamber crewmembers as depicted by reduced sleep duration. These results suggest that salivary melatonin rhythms may be successfully employed for estimating circadian rhythms and related sleep decrements in astronauts during space missions.

experiment_title: MRI Pulse Sequence Development
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Investigators are developing a new diagnostic technology: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and spectroscopy of hyperpolarized noble gases. Large non-equilibrium nuclear spin polarizations can be created in the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe, using the technique of spin-exchange optical pumping. Such large polarizations greatly enhance the magnetic resonance detection of 3He and 129Xe, enabling high-resolution MRI studies of the lung and airways, as well as dissolved tissue-phase investigations of organs and tissues, such as the brain, using lipophilic 129Xe.

An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional water proton MR method used in medical MRI. Low magnetic field MRI with hyperpolarized noble gases can allow us to use a small, light-weight, low-power devices. This capability provides potential for advances in both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems.

The proposed ground-based investigations with hyperpolarized noble gas MR will affect biomedical research in two important ways: (1) by providing the potential to acquire novel information about physiological structure and function of the lung and the brain in space-flight and in terrestrial gravity, and (2) by developing a new diagnostic technology that has clinical applications for diagnosis of pathology.

APPROACH:
Investigators developed large volume hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe systems that take advantage of inexpensive, compact, and mechanically robust high-power diodelasers (in excess of 100 W of radiant energy), which have recently become available. By bringing together an optimized continuous flow optical pumping chamber with a storage and delivery system, a dedicated gas generation system was constructed to produce the large volumes of hyperpolarized gas necessary for this project.

RESULTS:
Adjustment of the TR (repeat time) parameter on the scans has been discovered to enable decreasing the static ventilation scan time from 10-13 seconds, down to 5-8 seconds. This gain cuts down on the time subjects need to hold their breath, which can be very helpful for patients with pulmonary diseases, vastly reducing their discomfort.

A model-based approach has been developed to measure the diameters of airways captured with the dynamic imaging protocols. The rigor of this approach virtually eliminates the dependence on the unreliable human detection of airway edges, and the resultant randomness by which diameter endpoints are selected.

experiment_title: Effects of Microgravity on Tobacco Hornworm (Manduca Sexta) During Metamorphosis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Metamorphosis in biological species provides a unique condition for studying the role of gravity in development. Formation of new organs in a previously existing organism requires a highly active period of turnover of amino acids and proteins, and of changes in the endocrine profile. Furthermore, metamorphosis offers the advantage of studying a self contained biological system.

The tobacco hornworm provides a suitable species to study the effect of an altered gravitational environment on invertebrate development. This species has been one of the most thoroughly investigated organisms in a variety of aspects of insect biology. Manduca sexta pharate adults can provide significant amounts of relevant material, for investigating metabolic aspects of adult development. During the wandering stage, which occurs immediately following cessation of larval feeding, the larvae burrow into the soil to form a pupation chamber. Despite burrowing down 25 to 30 cm, the larvae reorient themselves to a slightly heads-up vertical position. Since light and temperature are not factors in this process, they must sense the gravity vector.

Ground based studies on altered orientation of tobacco hornworm (Manduca sexta) pupae, relative to gravitational field, showed changes of some amino acids, rate of adult development, and flight muscles. These parameters are dependent on ecdysone levels, which are elevated when the insects reorient into a heads-up vertical position. This study was undertaken to examine the effects of microgravity on tobacco hornworm ecdysone release and subsequent development. It was hypothesized that the virtual absence of gravity might have an adverse effect on the "open" circulation system by reducing flow of the hemolymph through the body, which would also reduce the appearance of ecdysteroid.

APPROACH:

Larvae that were one or two days into the wandering stage were shipped to KSC. They were washed with sterile water upon arrival. Under aseptic conditions, insects were selected after pupation, as early in development as possible. The pupae were wrapped in tissue and placed in individual Lexan tubes. The tubes were closed with sterile cotton and attached to petri dishes with Velcro.

Fifty-four pupae were loaded into three BRIC-100 canisters ( 18 in each canister) and placed in a Shuttle Middeck locker. The experiment was launched aboard the STS-77 mission on May 19, 1996. Ground controls were conducted on a 24-hour delay in the Orbiter Environmental Simulator (OES) with conditions (temperature, % relative humidity, and carbon dioxide levels) similar to those experienced by samples during flight.

The BRIC -07 experiment was totally passive with no crew interaction or inflight manipulations. After 10 days on orbit, the Shuttle landed at the Kennedy Space Center on May 29, 1996. The canisters were recovered approximately four hours after landing and ground controls were "recovered" from the OES 24 hours later.

Measurements included: 1) development of all insects during flight, 2) analysis of hemolymph, obtained from half the insects postflight, for ecdysteroid, amino acid, urea, ammonia and trehalose concentrations, 3) continuing development of the remaining insects to adult (moths), and 4) analysis of flight muscle protein content of the adults. All samples were shipped to the University of Arizona the day after landing for further analysis.

RESULTS:

Spaceflight caused development to be slowed by about 15%. Flight pupae lost less weight than controls, which is consistent with slower development. The flight insects required 6% longer time to become moths even though only about half of their adult development occurred during space flight. Postflight, the rate of development was normal. Spaceflight caused a decrease in total amino acids as a result of a decrease in the concentrations of isoleucine, urea, cysteine, methionine, aspartic acid, threonine and glutamic acid+glutamine. Insects subjected to weightlessness and allowed to complete development postflight showed an 11% lower protein content and a 10% smaller protein concentration of their flight muscle, indicating that muscle growth was diminished. The concentration of trehalose in the hemolymph was not affected by space flight. The timing of this flight study was subsequent to the peak period of ecdysone release. Despite the very low levels of ecdysone in these insects, a trend towards less ecdysone was detected in flight insects. The investigators speculate that without gravity, flow of the hemolymph away from the head region was slower, thereby reducing ecdysone availability and slowing development.

experiment_title: Advanced Water Recovery Systems
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This task provides for technology development for water recovery systems. The task encompassed both biological and physical/chemical system development. Together these technology areas provide technology development for both near and long-term International Space Station (ISS) requirements as well as technology development for future extended duration missions. The primary focus was on microgravity-compatibile technologies and ISS-similar wastewater streams; however, early definition of more complex wastewater streams was planned. Included in the biological system development is continued evaluation of bench-scale biological water processors and testing of microgravity-compatible nitrification systems. Physical-chemical system development includes development of high-recovery membrane filtration systems and optimization of postprocessing systems.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is not available.

RESULTS:
An AWRS technology development project continued to study the minimum size anoxic reactor to treat a given flight crew's wastewater for a specific time period. AWRS Development Facility Anoxic Biological Water Processor test stands operated with nitrification and denitrification bioreactors successfully. Good removal of total organic carbon (TOC) has been achieved through the test points to date, although performance of the nitrifier has been below expectations.

Post Processing System (PPS) phase II testing, which was to provide data which can be used to accurately size a photolytic subassembly, was successfully completed. The PPS test stand was then reconfigured for Phase III testing, which was to compare the performance of an optimized PPS versus a system approximating the JSC Integrated Water Recovery System Test post processor. PPS Phase III testing was successfully concluded. During the course of the Phase III testing, the PPS test stand was successfully operated for 68 days of near-continuous batch operation and processed over 700 liters of influent. In the area of physical/chemical systems, the Cascade Distillation Subsystem (CDS) project was initiated. This project developed and demonstrated an advanced wastewater processing subsystem that is based on centrifugal vacuum distillation with a team comprised of commercial, government, and academic partners. The CDS utilizes an innovative and proven multi-stage thermodynamic process to efficiently produce purified water, and its rotary centrifugal design provides gas/liquid phase separation and liquid transport (pumping) under microgravity conditions.

CDS breadboard testing was completed and a milestone was achieved with the completion of the CDS prototype design review. In the area of AWRS Development Facility enhancements, a second generation Waste Water Collection and Transportation System (WWCTS) was completed. The WWCTS is for the collection and transport of human waste water for the evaluation of water processing systems.

experiment_title: Morphological and Functional Adaptations of Muscle Fibers Myo-tendonous Junction to Hypokinesia and Hypogravity
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous studies have shown that both space flight and simulated microgravity (hind limb suspension) induce ultrastructural changes in the myotendinous junction (MTJ) of the soleus in the rat. The MTJ is a specialized region of skeletal muscle fibers where the muscle-tendon interface is increased by folding of the muscle fiber plasma membrane. The increased surface area results in reduced stress to the plasma membrane during contraction. A chronic change in muscle use and/or loading leads to a structural remodeling of the MTJ. Previously, only one histological study has examined the muscle-tendon interface in non-human primates. This experiment will examine the effects of space flight on the soleus MTJ ultrastructure in the rhesus.

Approach:

Biopsies were taken from the distal MTJ region in the soleus muscles of flight and vivarium control monkeys after the 14-day space flight. Since the MTJ morphology would not significantly differ after a 14-day period, no growth control biopsies were used. Biopsies were fixed in a graded series of glutaraldehyde solution in 0.4 M cacodylate buffer at pH 7.4, then postfixed in a 2% osmium tetroxide solution. The fixed samples were dehydrated, then embedded in epoxy resin and cut into longitudinal ultra-thin sections (70 nm) through the muscle-tendon interface. The sections were mounted on copper grids and stained with uranyl and lead citrate for electron microscopy.

Results:

Structural remodeling occurred at the MTJs after a 14-day space flight, in a similar manner as observed in rat soleus MTJs during the SLS-2 mission. Soleus MTJs of the flight monkeys appeared more shredded than vivarium control MTJs, due to deeper and larger invaginations of the plasma membrane. As observed in rats, the larger, deeper invaginations of the sarcolemma seemed to increase the myotendinous interface. Signs of membrane and basal lamina remodeling were also observed. Granular and vesicular globules observed at the MTJs are likely due to muscle fiber degenerative material. An alteration of contractile material and myofilament anchoring structures was suggested by the presence of numerous vacuoles and caveolae along the lateral sides of the muscle fiber processes. Unlike in the rat soleus MTJ, the contractile apparatus in the rhesus monkey appeared to be less affected by a 14-day space flight. The only misalignment observed was that of adjacent Z disks in the parajunctional region. The structural remodeling described appears to be influenced both by weightlessness and constrained movement during flight.

experiment_title: Low Latency Teleoperation Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA’s Human Architecture Team (HAT) has been studying the feasibility of human exploration missions to the moons of Mars as an intermediate step toward the eventual Mars surface missions. Human missions to Mars’ moons would result in the development and operation of new technologies, systems, and ops concepts, many of which will be required for an eventual Mars surface missions, without the added complexity and risk associated with a Mars descent, ascent, and long-duration surface systems and operations.

The opportunity to perform low-latency teleoperation (LLT) of robotic Mars surface system could provide significant benefits not only for scientific exploration purposes, but also in the scouting and preparation of landing sites in advance of human surface missions. Although the Mars moons of Phobos and Deimos differ significantly from each other in respect to latitudes, duration, and frequency with which line-of-sight to Mars is achievable, both moons offer frequent and operationally useful period of time and latitudes within which low-latency teleoperations of Mars surface assets could be performed such as the selection of landing sites or use of communication relays. Low-latency teleoperations may also include collection and launch of Mars samples into Mars orbit for retrieval and return as part of a human mission to Mars’ moons.

APPROACH:
This study will be part of a larger multi-engineering study to test all types of robotic teleoperation scenarios across a variety of latency time conditions using ground analogs. This pilot study will the first in a possible series of later studies to determine how latency times could affect human performance on teleoperation tasks. Since this is the first study of its kind for low latency teleoperation, the outcome of this study will give investigators a first glimpse into what they can learn from this experimental protocol, and estimates of the variability within and between subjects that would be useful for planning later studies. This study will take place in three locations with approximately 26 subjects. The first four subjects will be onboard NEEMO 20 located in Florida, the next six subjects will be located at Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Building 16’s TRAC lab, and the last 16 subjects will be located onboard the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facility.

Before testing begins, participants will be given a 10 minute familiarization (FAM) session. The aim of this session is to get the participant “warmed up” for the tasks to come plus give them some training along the way on the simulation itself. Each session will have a predefined set of parameters for the simulation run with a unique starting position and attitude. The five time latency states will be chosen and position the robotic arm in Zone 3 (1 meter away from the target) for the beginning of the test session. The participant will perform five different tasks to fully complete the test session at approximately five minutes each. If the participant hits the target within the task time allotted or earlier, the simulation will note this and prompt the participant to move on to the next test session. However, if the participant does not make the target in the allotted task time, the simulation will automatically stop the test session and prompt the participant to move on to the next test session. After a subject completes a session, the investigator will record his objective results in Snap Shooter before proceeding to the next session.

RESULTS:

experiment_title: Sleep Wake Actigraphy and Light Exposure on ISS12
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
An inadequate quantity or quality of sleep may impair an astronaut’s ability to maintain a high level of cognitive performance and vigilance while operating and monitoring sophisticated instrumentation during space flight. One astronaut and one cosmonaut took part in a one-year International Space Station (ISS) mission. Given that the duration of this mission was essentially twice as long as the nominal ISS missions, investigators wanted to study is how the mind and body, including sleep and the circadian system, responded or adapted to that much time in space. This study estimated sleep and circadian alignment throughout the mission via actigraphy, photometry, and sleep logs. Wrist actigraphy and photometry provided a simple, objective, and noninvasive means of collecting data about the sleep/wake state as well as more specific information about various aspects of sleep. The actigraphy and photometry data were analyzed in conjunction with subjective sleep log information to evaluate multiple parameters related to sleep quality such as timing, length, latency, efficiency, continuity, and number of awakenings.

The objectives of this study were to test the following hypotheses:

  1. Long duration (one-year) space flight will result in disruption of sleep, as measured by wrist actigraphy, during a one-year ISS mission;
  2. Sleep disruption will be associated with light exposure that is inappropriately timed and/or of insufficient intensity to entrain crewmembers to the scheduled sleep-wake cycle;
  3. Sleep disruption and/or circadian rhythm misalignment will lead to subjective dissatisfaction with sleep and daytime alertness; and
  4. Long-duration (one-year) space flight will result in reduced sleep and sleep quality, as reported by sleep-wake diaries.

APPROACH:
Participants wore a small light-weight activity and light recording device called an Actiwatch Spectrum continuously throughout four terrestrial data collection intervals and throughout their space flight mission. Actigraphy and photometry data were collected for two weeks and occurred approximately one year and six months prior to launch (pre-flight L-365, L-180) and from eleven days prior to launch (pre-flight L-11) until launch day (L-0). Inflight, crewmembers donned the Spectrum as soon as possible when arriving on the ISS and doffed it before landing. Participants were given a Spectrum as soon as possible after the landing and post-flight data were collected for two weeks (R+0 through R+14). Terrestrial and inflight data were collected in one-minute epochs. There were no restrictions on participant behavior or countermeasure use during any of these data collection sessions. Data were downloaded following each terrestrial data collection sessions and monthly on the ISS.

Additionally, crewmembers were instructed to complete a daily sleep log within 15 minutes of awakening during all data collection intervals with the exception of ISS flights where crewmembers were scheduled to complete the log approximately every three weeks. The sleep log contained subjective ratings of alertness and fatigue, subjective quantification of sleep, and documentation of sleep disturbances and medication usage. Through a data sharing agreement, the investigators used medication logs from the crewmembers’ post-flight interviews with crew surgeons in order to compare with medications reported on the daily log.

Sleep duration was estimated in one-minute epochs from actigraphy data using Actiware Software. A modified sleep efficiency was calculated as total sleep divided by the time between actigraph-defined start sleep and end sleep times. Subjective sleep quality and alertness were measured on the 100 mm visual analog scales contained in the sleep log. Subjective sleep quality was assessed with the question “How did you sleep last night?” anchored at 0 with “poorly” and with “great” at 100. Alertness (daytime fatigue) was assessed with “How do you feel right now?” anchored at 0 with “sleepy” and with “alert” at 100. The number of days on which sleep medication was taken and the reasons for sleep disturbances were tabulated from the sleep log. At the end of the pre-flight scheduled L-360 and scheduled L-180 data collection and following the post-flight data collection, the crewmember performed a 30-minute debrief with investigators to share data with the crewmember and a structured interview format was used to illicit additional information on his or her sleep.

RESULTS:
On the one-year mission, there was considerable variation in sleep between the two crewmembers. On average, the mean nightly sleep duration of the two crewmembers on ISS12 was one hour more than the mean nightly sleep duration on the 2004-2011 shorter ISS missions. Several factors may have affected nightly sleep duration including less shifting of the sleep-wake cycle and thus, reduction in circadian misaligned days from 20% on the 2004-2011 missions to 3% on the one-year mission. During space flight, objective sleep efficiency was significantly correlated with reported sleep quality and alertness.

experiment_title: Flow and Distribution of Fluid Phases through Porous Plant Growth Media in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA's Advanced Life Support program believes that particulate solid substrates are best suited to meet its short and long-term needs for plant growth during space flight. Due to mass, volume and power constraints, root modules are characterized by small volumes of growth media and high root density. These conditions leave little margin for error in control of water, air and nutrition. Results from plant growth experiments utilizing particulate growth media during space flight have demonstrated the difficulties associated with providing reliable reproducible air and water (and thus nutrients) supply to plant roots. This is attributed to the general lack of understanding of fundamental transport processes occurring in the growth media. The quantitative characterization of physical processes associated with the flow of wetting and non-wetting phase(s) in particulate plant growth media in microgravity is essential for the successful design and control of plant production systems during space flight. It has recently become evident that the macroscopic dynamic behavior of the temporal and spatial under-saturation levels in particulate media strongly depends on the physical behavior of the fluid at the microscopic (pore-scale) level. Ultimately, the stability and break-up of liquid-bridges, -columns, and -films, dynamic rearrangement of particles, contact angle dynamics and hysteresis, phase discontinuities, capillary fingering and entrapment of the non-wetting phase together with the time-dependent complex geometry of porous media will determine the saturation levels and its stability on macroscopic (integral) scales. However, it is not yet obvious if and how much some of these micro-scale phenomena are gravity dependent.

APPROACH:
The investigators proposed a comprehensive program of research that will employ some new advanced experimental, numerical and analytical techniques for examining flow and distribution of fluids in plant growth media. For example, Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) will provide a visual record of wetting front dynamics and gas diffusion in porous media. New mathematical models that account for adsorption and liquid films, discontinuous phases, effect of vibration, solitary ganglion, pore network behavior, fingering, capillary instabilities, air entrapment, medium anisotropy and heterogeneity, and the hyperbolic nature of moisture distribution will be evaluated. Upscaling procedures will be employed to describe microscale phenomenon on scales relevant to root modules. Hydraulic conductivity and water retention characteristics will be experimentally verified under simulated microgravity conditions using terrestrial zero-g simulators. The final conceptual model of water and air transport will be verified in 1 g by forward and inverse simulation on the root module scale using flight compatible measurement techniques. The research will result in a model and experimental methods that are ready for final validation in microgravity.

RESULTS:
Key findings:
1. Characterization of porous plant growth media – optimal set points for water delivery in any g environment strongly depend on growth-media hydraulic properties. Although baked ceramic aggregates have been used in space flight for over 10 years, the team conducted the first rigorous characterization of physical and hydraulic properties. This work has enhanced the understanding of aggregate dual porosity, pore size distribution, water conducting porosity, air entrapment, and air entry that allows critical examination of water delivery set points that have been used in space flight. Water retention remains a key physical property of interest with recent KC-135 measurements providing some of the very limited microgravity datasets to date.

2. Small volumes and susceptibility to heterogeneous fluid distributions - limitations on mass and size of flight-sized root modules accentuate the impact of inherently irregular wetting patterns in particulate media and the role of root volume. Wetting front irregularities may span the entire root module depth used for space flight promoting entrapment and discontinuous phase formation. Root proliferation modifies media properties, especially with high root density where an entirely new porous medium is created with different physical and hydraulic properties. Consequently, water management based on macroscopic criteria (set points) may be constantly changing.

3. Micro- and reduced gravity effects on water transport - water moves within porous media under the influence of pressure, gravity and surface/capillary forces. Surface/capillary forces dominate in micro- or low gravity environments when both water and air phases are present. Wetting front irregularities or surface forces that cause water and air to segregate into wet and dry clusters are difficult to control or predict. Irregularities in pore size distribution and expansion of capillary length scales enhance phase entrapment in 0g. Once these clusters become established during initial infiltration they may be hard to remove in 0g due to the combination of water-primed pathways and dominance of capillary forces. Additionally infiltration into pre-wetted porous media occurs faster in 0g.

4. Water content sensing and control - matric potential or water content sensors have been used to control and schedule water delivery to plant growth media. Limited sensing volume of most sensors used in root modules (<1 cm3) combined with discontinuous phases (#2 and 3 above) may result in “accurate” readings on the mesoscale (several pores or particles), but an inaccurate assessment of water content in the bulk volume of growth media.

experiment_title: Cyber Partners: Harnessing Group Dynamics to Boost Motivation for More Efficient Exercise
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts may have difficulty adhering to exercise regimens at vigorous intensity levels during long space missions. Keeping up with exercise prescriptions is important for aerobic and musculoskeletal health during space missions and afterwards. A key impediment to maintaining intense levels of exercise is motivation. However, finding ways to motivate astronauts to be physically active at the levels necessary to lessen the effects of bone and muscle loss and aerobic capacity has not been explored. Typically individuals become bored with training regimens over time or find them less enjoyable if they do not have strategies to maintain their motivation. Although traditional group exercise leads to higher exercise adherence than individual exercise programs, structured group exercise programs are not possible for astronauts during space missions. Exercise video games have been marketed as a way to increase people’s motivation and enjoyment to exercise by being entertaining, engaging and providing a means by which to interact with other players. Although many exercise games involve competition among players, few take advantage of group dynamics to motivate play and there has been little attempt to analyze what game features and interpersonal interactions would best motivate users to continue exercising with these games. Using individuals closely matched in age and fitness to current astronauts, this research was designed to determine whether recently documented motivation gains in task groups can be harnessed to improve motivation in interactive exercise games using virtual, software-generated (SG) partners. Exercising with an SG partner offers a number of advantages such as availability, flexibility, and autonomy over a live human partner.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Develop software to create SG exercise partners and interface with exercise equipment (cycle ergometer) similar to equipment available on the International Space Station (ISS).
  2. Test various design features of an SG partner within designed exercise video games to determine the most effective features for enhancing motivation to exercise, enjoyment, confidence, and connectedness.
  3. Test whether exercising with an SG partner over a 24 weeks, compared to exercising alone, leads to better aerobic capacity and muscle strength, adherence to exercise regimen, enhanced exercise enjoyment, self-efficacy, and sense of social connectedness.

APPROACH:
To address the second aim, investigators tested an SG partner in one of three modes against an individual control condition: (a) co-acting mode, where the subject cycled with the SG partner but whose performance was independent of the partner (i.e., they were not teammates), (b) conjunctive-teammate mode, where scores were based on the slower performer, and (c) choice mode where subject could choose co-acting mode or conjunctive teammate mode for all trials. The experiment routines consisted of (a) 30 minutes of continuous aerobic exercise on a cycle ergometer at or above 75% of maximum heart rate and (b) high-intensity interval training involving four repetitions of four minutes at or above 90% heart rate (HR) max. Investigators tested an additional 38 chronic exercisers. Subjects were allowed to adjust the power output (watts) during workouts. The main outcome variable was average watts cycled above target prescribed watts.

To address the third aim, investigators tested an SG exercise partner in one of two modes: (a) conjunctive-teammate mode and (b) conjunctive teammate who is not always superior (NAS) and is sometimes surpassed by the subject, plus (c) individual control condition. Subjects exercised six days a week for 24 weeks, using the following aerobic routines: (a) 30 minutes of continuous aerobic exercise on a stationary cycle at or above 75% HR max, (b) 4x4 minute intervals at or above 90% HR max with three minutes of active rest, (c) 6x2 minute intervals at varying intensities with two minutes of active rest, and (d) 30 second sprint intervals at maximal effort with 20 seconds of active rest.

In addition, investigators first tested whether the Conjunctive or NAS groups adhered more to the protocol than Controls. Conjunctive and NAS conditions averaged 15 more days completing the protocol than the Controls. However, group differences were not statistically different. In terms of the primary dependent measure, effort analyses are based on the continuous and four minute interval sessions. Subjects were not allowed to increase their intensity on the two minute intervals. Similarly, the dependent measure for the 30 second sprints was number of intervals completed, which all subjects completed. During Week 20, NAS subjects increased their effort more (M = 8.9 watts) compared to Controls (M = 1.5 watts) and Conjunctive subjects (M = 3.9 watts) on the four minute interval workout.

RESULTS:
In regards to target prescribed watts, results showed no condition main effects from baseline; however, during the four minute interval sessions conjunctive trended toward greater exercise effort than control and coactive conditions. The four minute intervals likely represent the most motivationally demanding workout at 90% HR max. Increases in effort above target watts positively correlated with enjoyment, self-efficacy, and team perceptions during the four minute intervals. No relationships were found with less intense continuous exercise. Although this study did not find significances between group increases in performance effort, participants significantly increased their effort with the exercise video game (i.e., simulated bike paths).

Throughout the duration of the study, NAS subjects always outperformed Controls on the four minute intervals. All groups had large significant increases in VO2max from baseline to midpoint, then values leveled off from midpoint to final. Social connectedness rose significantly from midpoint to final, and those with an SG partner increased their teams' perceptions from midpoint to final. Subjects in NAS and Conjunctive conditions had higher self-efficacy beliefs than Controls after one week with the SG partner. Enjoyment remained stable, above response scale midpoint, across 24 weeks.

experiment_title: HZE Radiation: Modulation Of Genetic Effects By RNA Interference Of NHEJ--NAG9-1516
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
For extended missions in space, astronauts will be exposed to a radiation environment unlike any on the earth's surface. Galactic cosmic rays include a particularly worrisome component of energetic iron nuclei which are high atomic number, high energy (HZE) charged particles with linear energy transfer (LET) similar to alpha particles but with very different track structures. While the relative biological effectiveness (RBE) of a particular radiation roughly depends on the LET, the very different track structures for these two radiations may well modulate this RBE even if they have identical average LETs. Further, this "radiation quality" for the exposures actually relevant for astronauts will be modified by interactions with materials in the spacecraft, including their own bodies.

Basic to virtually all relevant biological effects of ionizing radiation is the underlying damage produced in DNA, and the subsequent cellular processing of such damage. The damage can be qualitatively different for different kinds of radiations, and the genetics of the biological systems exposed can greatly affect damage processing and ultimate outcome the biological effect of concern. The accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) is critical for the maintenance of genomic integrity and function. Incorrect repair of such lesions results in chromosome rearrangements and mutations that can lead to cancer and heritable defects in the progeny of irradiated parents. It is important, therefore, to understand cellular responses to DNA damage and to elucidate the mechanisms and phenotypic consequences of DSB misrepair.

APPROACH:
The general aim in this proposal is to examine connections between cellular radiosensitivity phenotypes relevant for carcinogenesis, namely chromosome aberration formation, mutagenesis and telomere fusions, and deficiencies in various components of the non-homologous end joining system, using RNA interference to systematically knockdown gene products known to be involved, either singly or in combination.

RESULTS:
In 2002, it proposed to utilize the relatively new technique of RNA interference (RNAi) to deplete levels of various components of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) double-strand break (DSB) repair system, and to study the effects on HZE radiation-induced chromosomal rearrangements and gene mutation. This was supported with a one-year of awarded support. The suggestion from reviewers and NASA program officers was that before the project could be considered for further funding, it would be necessary to demonstrate that the proposed studies involving siRNA knockdown of various proteins would be feasible. During this year (June 1, 2003 - May 31, 2004) considerable additional data has been collectedsupporting the ability to conduct theses studies.

The accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) is critical for the maintenance of genomic integrity and function. Incorrect repair of such lesions results in chromosomal rearrangements and mutations that can lead to cancer and heritable defects in the progeny of irradiated parents. Focus has been on the consequent phenotypic effects of faulty repair by examining connections between cellular radiosensitivity phenotypes relevant for carcinogenesis after exposure to IR, and deficiencies in various components of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) system. Deficiencies of individual components of the DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PK) holoenzyme (Ku86 and the catalytic subunit, DNA-PKcs) were produced, both singly and in combination, using RNA interference (RNAi) in human lymphoblastoid cell lines. Exposure of cells exhibiting reduced protein expression to either gamma-rays or 1GeV/nu Fe particles demonstrated differential effects on telomere dysfunction and mutation frequency, as well as differential effects between radiation qualities. The initial results are reported in the article "Suppression of DNA-PK by RNAi has different quantitative effects on telomere dysfunction and mutagenesis in human lymphoblasts treated with gamma-rays or HZE particles" by Qinming Zhang, Eli S. Williams, Kristin F. Askin, Yuanlin Peng, Joel S. Bedford, Howard L. Liber and Susan M. Bailey, currently in press (2005) in Radiation Research (NASA supplement).

experiment_title: Orthostatic Function During Entry, Landing and Egress
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Several cardiovascular parameters were measured during entry, landing, and egress in order to develop and assess countermeasures designed to improve orthostatic tolerance upon return to Earth.

APPROACH:
Heart rate and rhythm, blood pressure, cardiac output and peripheral resistance were monitored during entry and landing of the Shuttle, and during crewmember egress from the Shuttle.

RESULTS:
Systolic and diastolic blood pressure increased during space flight and were highest when gravity reached its peak during entry and at touchdown. Systolic blood pressure decreased significantly when the astronauts first stood up from their seats after landing. Heart rate increased at the time of peak gravity during entry and at touchdown, and it rose even higher when the astronauts first stood up. The increase in heart rate varied, but was generally substantial.

experiment_title: The Effect of Skeletal Unloading on Bone Formation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Skeletal unloading results in an inhibition of bone formation associated with a decrease in osteoblast number, impaired mineralization of bone, and altered proliferation and differentiation of osteoprogenitor cells. Although such changes are likely to be mediated by multiple factors, resistance to the skeletal growth promoting action of insulin like growth factor-I (IGF-I) appears to play an important role. IGF-I mRNA and protein levels rise during skeletal unloading, but the ability of IGF-I to stimulate proliferation of bone cells in vivo and in vitro when taken from unloaded bone is markedly impaired. This resistance to IGF-I is associated with a failure of IGF-I to activate its receptor and the subsequent IGF-I signaling pathways. BMSC from unloaded bone show a reduction in integrin expression, and inhibition of integrin signaling reproduces the findings of IGF-I resistance.

Specific Aims: 1. Determine the point(s) at which skeletal unloading blocks IGF-I stimulated bone formation. a. Determine whether skeletal unloading alters the mesenchymal pool committed to osteoblast differentiation. b. Determine whether skeletal unloading alters the ability of IGF-I to bind to and activate the IGF-I receptor (IGF-IR) in those cells committed to osteoblast differentiation c. Determine the relative contributions of the ras/MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways to the proliferative response to IGF-I. d. Determine whether skeletal unloading alters the protein levels and/or activation of the components of the pathway(s) mediating the proliferative response to IGF-I. e. Determine whether skeletal unloading alters the nuclear translocation of ERK, PI3K, and Akt and cellular levels of cyclin D1, p21cip, and p27kip 2. Determine the ability of skeletal unloading to block the response of BMSC to other growth factors such as EGF, PDGF and FGF with respect to: a. Proliferation b. Growth factor receptor number, binding, and activation c. Activation of the ras/MAPK and/or PI3K/Akt pathways 3. Determine the interaction between IGF-I and integrin signaling as affected by skeletal unloading in the regulation of osteoprogenitor cell proliferation. a. Determine the mRNA and protein levels of the various integrins in osteoprogenitor cells from normally loaded and unloaded bone b. Determine which integrins potentiate IGF-I responsiveness with respect to proliferation and activation of the IGF-IR and the ras/MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways c. Determine whether the effect of integrins on IGF-IR activation requires direct interaction with the IGF-IR d. Determine whether correction of integrin levels, if altered by skeletal unloading, will restore IGF-I responsiveness with respect to proliferation and activation of IGF-I signaling pathways.

APPROACH:
The methodologies are embedded in the Objectives above and the Results below.

RESULTS:
1) Determine the points at which skeletal unloading blocks IGF-I stimulation bone formation.
Skeletal unloading does not alter the binding of IGF-I to its receptor. Investigators used an analog of IGF-I, namely des IGF-I, which does not bind to IGF-binding proteins and demonstrated that like IGF-I itself binding to the bone marrow stromal cells (BMSC) from loaded and unloaded bones is equivalent. The down stream events such as activation of the MAPK pathway and the subsequent proliferative response to IGF-I are impaired in BMSC from unloaded bones, but this follows the failure to activate the IGF-I receptor. We have shown that skeletal unloading reduces the expression of a number of integrins, and the use of the integrin inhibitor echistatin reproduces the effects of skeletal unloading on IGF-I responsiveness. Thus, the investigators believe that the loss of bone during skeletal unloading is due to IGF-I resistance caused by the failure of integrins to enable IGF-I to activate its receptor. In contrast when the animals are reloaded, they are able to restore IGF-I responsiveness, integrin expression, and accelerated bone formation.

2) Determine the ability of skeletal unloading to block the response of BMSC to other growth factors.
Investigators examined in depth the effect of skeletal unloading on the resistance to PDGF. To their surprise, BMSC from unloaded bones respond quite well to PDGF with respect to activation of the PDGF receptor (via phosphorylation) and proliferation. Furthermore, the integrin antagonist echistatin, which blocks the response of BMSC to IGF-I, fails to block the response of BMSC to PDGF. Thus, the resistance to IGF-I caused by skeletal unloading appears to be specific to IGF-I and is not generalized to all other growth factors.

3) Determine the interaction between IGF-I and integrin signaling as affected by skeletal unloading.
As noted above the investigators found that the expression of a number of integrins is reduced in the BMSC from unloaded bones. They are having some difficulty showing that the protein levels are reduced because of the lack of good antibodies to rat integrins. However they have developed methods to selectively knockout specific integrins to determine which if any are critical for BMSC response to IGF-I. These experiments are being performed in both rat BMSC and a human osteoblast cell line for which better integrin antibodies are available. Using this latter cell line, the investigators have had success in showing that at least one of the integrins of interest binds directly to the IGF-I receptor, as shown by co-immunoprecipitation. Furthermore, they have developed an in vitro model using pulsatile fluid flow to test whether integrins per se can activate the IGF-IR when load is applied in the absence of IGF-I. The results show that load can activate the IGF-IR, which appears to be dependent on selected integrins and the matrix containing selected integrin ligands on which the cells are plated.

experiment_title: Effects of Micro-G on Gene Expression in Higher Plants
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Although various effects of microgravity at the whole plant, organ, tissue, and cellular levels have been observed, little is known about the molecular mechanisms involved. This experiment studied the effects of microgravity on the expression of auxin-regulated GH3 and SAUR genes in transgenic tomato, tobacco and Arabidopsis seedlings that express the auxin-inducible GH3 gene promoter-GUS and SAUR gene promoter-GUS fusion genes.

This was the second flight of this experiment and there were four objectives. The first objective was to determine how the expression of the auxin- and gravistimulation-inducible genes (e.g. GH3 and SAUR genes) is altered under the microgravity environment. The second objective was to identify the effects of microgravity on auxin transport/distribution and/or tissue's sensitivity to auxin in higher plants. Identification of the genes whose expression is significantly altered in microgravity grown plants (in addition to the auxin inducible genes) was the third objective. The fourth was to determine the functions of the genes whose expression is altered in plants grown in microgravity.

This experiment provided information about how expression of the auxin- and gravistimulation-inducible genes is altered at microgravity as compared to the ground controls. It also provided some insights into the effects of microgravity on auxin transport/distribution and/or tissue's sensitivity to auxin in higher plants. Molecular cloning and characterization of gravity-regulated genes is a crucial step to elucidate the mechanisms of gravity effects on growth, development, and metabolic processes in higher plants.

APPROACH:

The BRIC-10 experiment flew on the STS-85 mission which lasted approximately 12 days. It was launched aboard Discovery on August 19, 1997. The experiment was placed in two BRIC-60 canisters, each containing eleven 60 mm petri plates. Transgenic tomato, tobacco and Arabidopsis seedlings were grown on the petri plates, which contained five layers of filter paper and one layer of nylon membrane to support seedlings and nutrient media. At 5 dayts into the flight (MET 5/02:10) one of the BRIC-60 canisters was frozen in the LSLE GN2 Freezer. Ground controls were conducted on a 24-hour delay in the Orbiter Environmental Simulator at environmental conditions (temperature, % relative humidity, and CO2) similar to those experienced by the flight samples.

Upon recovery, the flight samples frozen in space were treated in the following fashion: forty representative seedlings were fixed in a solution containing 5% formaldehyde for microscopic analysis; ten seedlings were photographed; and the remainder were returned to the investigator's lab on dry ice for RNA isolation and screening for the genes of interest.

The flight samples which were not frozen in space were treated in the following fashion: three to four representative seedlings from each petri dish were photographed with a camera coupled to a microscope; forty seedlings from each petri dish were incubated in x-gluc solution for histochemical staining of the GUS activity at 37C for 12 to 24 hours, and after staining, the seedlings were photographed. All seedlings stained with x-gluc solution were stored in water with sodium azide for further analysis at the investigator's lab. Thirty seedlings from each petri dish were fixed in 5% formaldehyde solution for microscopic analysis. Between sixty and one hundred and fifty seedlings (50 seedlings per assay, 3 replicates) from each petri dish were frozen at -70C for quantitative assay of GUS activity.

RESULTS:

The results of this study indicate that the expression of both the GH3 promoter-GUS and SAUR promoter-GUS fusion genes was significantly enhanced (2 to 3-fold increases) in space-grown seedlings when compared with the ground control seedlings. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS fusion gene in tobacco plants was dependent on the developmental stage, initially with an activation in cotyledons, followed by activation in elongating regions of hypocotyls and roots of the space-grown seedlings. As seedlings developed, the expression of the gene was reduced in cotyledons but further enhanced in root elongating regions. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS gene was relatively higher in vascular tissues and much lower in other tissue types. The expression of the SAUR promoter-GUS gene in the elongating region of hypocotyls in the space-grown seedlings was also significantly higher than in the ground controls. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS and SAUR promoter-GUS genes in space-grown plants strongly suggests that micro-gravity affects auxin transport/distribution or tissue's sensitivity to auxin.

The space-grown seedlings from the BRIC-9 experiment had shorter roots and more and longer root hairs. Increased auxin concentration or tissue's sensitivity to auxin in elongating regions of roots as indicated by activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS gene, suggests that auxin is involved in the micro-gravity mediated reduction in root growth and increases in root hair elongation.

We have isolated mRNA from both the space-grown and ground control seedlings of Arabidopsis. A cDNA library has been constructed and we are currently in the process of screening genes whose expression is altered in space-grown seedlings. Once the genes of interest are recovered, the investigators will perform sequence analysis, Northern blot analysis and other analysis.

experiment_title: Prevalence of Hypertension in LSAH Participants
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Blood pressure is the force of the blood pushing against the walls of arteries. It is measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg), and given in two numbers. The higher number indicates systolic pressure, which is the amount of force exerted on the walls of arteries within and leading from the heart when it contracts (i.e., during systole). The lower number is the diastolic pressure, which is the force existing between contractions (i.e., during diastole).

Normal blood pressure is usually considered to be 120/80 mmHg; measurements above 140/90 mmHg are considered to be hypertensive. Hypertension, or high blood pressure, simply refers to the increased tension or pressure in the arteries. Hypertension is a major risk factor for heart attack, heart failure, stroke, and kidney failure. Most hypertensive people have no symptoms.

For most people, there is no single known cause of high blood pressure. This type of high blood pressure is called primary or essential hypertension. Essential hypertension can't be cured, although in most cases it can be controlled. In some cases, high blood pressure can be traced to a known cause like tumors of the adrenal gland, chronic kidney disease, hormone abnormalities, use of birth control pills, or pregnancy. This is called secondary hypertension, and is usually cured if the underlying cause passes or is corrected.

The goal of this study was to examine hypertension among the astronaut and comparison populations.

APPROACH:
According to data from the third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey conducted from 1988-1991 (NHANES III), 20.4% of the US adult population is hypertensive (defined as systolic pressure of at least 140 mmHg or diastolic pressure of at least 90 mmHg).

RESULTS:
Annual examination data for active and inactive NASA astronauts between 1959-1999 show 5.5% of them (21 of 291) have been diagnosed with hypertension. In comparison, data from the annual examinations of comparison participants over a similar time period show 13.9% (121 of 870) had corresponding hypertension diagnoses. As physical fitness is a requirement for astronauts, they are expected to show a lower rate of hypertension as compared to the general population. The comparison participants had more than double the hypertension rate of the astronauts, but still had a lower rate than the general population. This lower rate of hypertension may be an effect of being a healthy working population.

Cross-sectional data of LSAH participants by age group show that most of them have average systolic pressure around or below 120 mmHg. Up to age 49, male comparisons show the same trend of systolic pressure measurements, although with slightly higher values, with that of the male astronauts. Male comparison participants aged 50 and older showed a higher increase of their systolic pressure as compared to male astronauts aged 50 and older. The diastolic pressure measurements for the male comparisons do not show a corresponding upward trend. Although the highest average measurement from the oldest age group of male comparisons is still below the hypertensive value of 140 mm Hg, this trend follows one observed in the general population. Data from NHANES III show that the highest increase in hypertension prevalence occurs between the 40-49 and 50-59 years age group for men. The small sample size of female participants does not allow for age group comparisons beyond the 40-44 age group.

experiment_title: Denitrification Composter to Stabilize Space-Mission Trash
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Treatment of space solid wastes, or trash, is a critical issue for mid to long duration space habitation or transportation. Solid wastes are not stable because they are wet (40 – 90 percent moisture) and contain levels of soluble organic compounds that can contribute to the growth of undesirable microorganisms with concomitant production of noxious gases and foul-smelling odors. The purpose of the proposed research project is to determine the feasibility of using a denitrifying composter to stabilize trash from space-habitation (STS, ISS, and ALS) life support activities. The method of approach starts with design of the denitrification composter, with design criteria derived from experimental variables investigators wish to manipulate and variables to be held constant. Key environmental and bioprocess parameters for evaluation are nitrate concentration and rate of addition, oxygen concentration, mixing duration and frequency, and inoculum. Parameters to be held constant are pH, temperature, moisture, C:N, solid waste feed material, size reduction, gas recirculation rate, trash addition rate, and mode of operation. Important performance parameters to be measured are: minimization of undesired products – N2O, NH3, and volatile organic compounds; maximization of desired outcomes – BOD5 removal, and CO2 production. The project’s overall goal was to determine if nitrate can be used as an electron acceptor to replace oxygen during composting of simulated space-mission food wastes to stabilize this solid waste.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results.

RESULTS:
A pre-existing aerobic composter was adapted and engineering evaluation tests were performed to ensure that the key design criteria were met. Two composter runs of baseline operation with a known solid waste feed were conducted under aerobic versus denitrification conditions using a given set of environmental and process conditions. Investigators then determined the effects of oxygen on composting of simulated space-mission trash (aerobic versus denitrifying conditions versus a combination of these). They assessed the need for an inoculum and developed both thermophilic and mesophilic denitrifying mixed cultures, if needed. These were tested in denitrifying composter runs. The effects of nitrate addition rate on N2O production was determined in sequentially replicated composter experiments as were the effects of mixing duration and frequency on nitrate distribution and on production of volatile fatty acids (VFAs).

experiment_title: Just-in-Time Simulation Platform
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Long-duration space flight and exploration missions will require complex operations and demanding tasks. A better system for creation of intelligent simulations will be needed to prepare future crews for the rigors ahead. The software system proposed will create a method for authoring intelligent 3D simulations for training and operations support without the need for high-level programming. An authoring tool of this type will allow NASA subject matter experts to capture their knowledge and build a simulation from it, or allow developers to create scenario-based simulations for troubleshooting and repair. This tool will also be more cost effective than hardware. A specific and immediate use will be for extravehicular activity (EVA) training, particularly when an EVA or intravehicular activity (IVA) task needs to designed during a mission and the simulation delivered just prior to execution.

After a successful tool test is complete, training materials and user-guide documentation will be completed. This will allow PLANET LLC to train a number of NASA personnel on the system, and prepare the software for commercial release.
