experiment_title: Predicting and Assessing Postural Reentry Disturbances
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study investigated a technique for predicting the severity of re-entry disturbances of posture and locomotion experienced by astronauts in space flight relevant environments and developing techniques for attenuating them. We are concerned not only with return to earth from orbital flight but also transfer to other force environments astronauts may encounter in the future, such as moon gravity, a rotating artificial gravity vehicle, or Mar’s gravity. The investigators developed a hold and release (H&R) paradigm and mathematical model for quantifying multi-link postural performance, investigating the influence of flight-related factors and understanding neuromotor mechanisms. The linear model they developed of upright posture as a four link inverted pendulum in a regime of small oscillations, a H&R experimental paradigm for producing transient postural oscillations, and data showing that the model fits the postural responses to H&R. The fitted parameters discriminate normal subjects and vestibular loss patients. This approach provides a way of quantifying astronauts’ postural changes following re-entry, in terms of the latency of EMG responses, and characteristic stiffness and damping of the ankles, knees and hips. It may also provide a means of assessing the efficacy of countermeasures while astronauts are still in-flight.

Specific Aims:

  • Measure postural responses to the hold and release technique in parabolic flight during conditions of weightlessness with the aid of a hold-down device and during high force levels
  • Measure postural responses to the hold and release technique before and after adaptation to artificially increased or decreased body weight
  • Measure postural responses to the hold and release technique before, during, and after exposure to increased gravitioinertial force level in a rotating room

    APPROACH:
    The methodologies for this study are embedded in the Results section below.

    RESULTS:
    Hold & Release in Parabolic flight:
    The aim of the study was to quantify recovery from simulated falls in altered force backgrounds and to investigate the mechanisms of recovery, using the H&R paradigm. The investigators tested three healthy men and two healthy women ranging in age from 26 to 60. The experiment was conducted during the 0g and 1.8g phases of parabolic flight as well as during 1 g straight and level flight and 1 g on the ground pre- and post-flight. 0g trials were conducted with 50% body weight bungee cord loading. Subjects were tested both with their eyes open and closed in all force backgrounds. During testing, subjects stood feet side by side with the soles of their shoes anchored to a force plate attached to the deck of the aircraft. Loss of balance was elicited using the H&R paradigm. A horizontal force was applied to the subject’s sternum, which he or she actively resisted. Removing the force caused subjects to sway forward, and they had to react to prevent falling. The exact time of release of the holding force was measured with a load cell. Motion of the head, shoulder, waist, knee and ankle were monitored with an OPTOTRAK, and surface EMGs were collected from tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, biceps femoris, and rectus femoris muscles.

    The kinetic and kinematic data showed the characteristic features of the H&R paradigm: center of foot pressure initially remains unchanged after release as body momentum develops and then the gastrocnemius and biceps femoris muscles are activated and produce torques that move the center of pressure in front of the center of mass thus arresting the forward momentum of the body. The earliest EMG response was a simultaneous activation of gastrocnemius and biceps femoris at 50-60 ms in 1g. This initial reaction was significantly longer in 0g and shorter in 1.8g, but vision did not affect it. A second synergy involved tibialis anterior and rectus femoris, and it occurred later than 200 ms in 1g. The onset latency of the secondary reaction was significantly reduced in the presence of vision but was not affected by g level. The latencies of both synergies differed in the sequential 1g test periods. That is, latencies were longer in 1g in flight than 1g pre-flight and got longer still in 1g post-flight. The rate of body sway prior to EMG responses was not correlated with g level. This study shows that the H&R paradigm is feasible for postural evaluations in hypo-g and hyper-g force backgrounds as well as in 1g. G-related modulation of the earliest corrective EMG responses could be due to altered vestibulo-spinal modulation of muscle spindle gain, as a function of background force level. Later EMG responses to induced falls are under the control of vision.

    Hold & Release During Galvanic Stimulation
    To assess vestibular influences on recovery of balance during sudden falls, the investigators measured the postural responses of five healthy subjects to a hold and release perturbation coupled with galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS). Two electrode pairs were located with the anterior electrode of each pair over the mastoid process and the posterior electrode over the trapezius muscle on the same side. Bilateral unipolar GVS was generated when a holding force against the sternum was released and the subject began moving forward, by individually driving left and right electrode pairs as cathode-anode or vice versa at 1 ma for 12 seconds or 2 ma for 6 seconds. The investigators computed the frequency and damping parameters of a multi-link inverted pendulum model of the body which best fit the transient postural oscillations after release for each subject. These parameters did not differ significantly across conditions indicating that GVS did not modify the preset overall strategy of postural recovery. The intensity and polarity of GVS significantly biased both the postural lean during the oscillatory period and the resting postural stance after recovery, deviating them forward for cathodal-anodal stimulation and backward for anodal-cathodal. Because the GVS affected postural bias but not dynamics, it is likely that GVS either biased signals from otolith regular fibers or provided erroneous velocity signals leading to vestibulospinal compensations complementing the segmental stiffness and damping mechanism. The residuals of the multi-link fit, i.e., the frequency spectra of the actual body sway ripples about the modeled sway, were different across conditions, which also suggest that GVS affects the descending velocity and acceleration drive of the vestibulo-spinal pathway. This finding is consistent with recent theoretical analyses of the influence of GVS on the semicircular canals and otolith organs of the inner ear.

    Response to Hold & Release in Patients with Bilateral Vestibular hypofunction
    The investigators measured the postural responses of six bilateral vestibular hypofunction patients and 19 control subjects to a hold and release test paradigm that induced a brief sudden forward pivot about the ankles. A linear four link inverted pendulum model was used to fit the resulting recovery of balance that was achieved without stepping. EMG latencies of the initial muscle responses to brake the forward tilt of the body did not differ across subject groups. Both subject groups exhibited linear time invariant behavior throughout the recovery period after release maintaining constant stiffness and damping. Both groups also exhibited significantly greater damping, energy dissipation, when light touch of the hand at mechanically non-supportive force levels or sights of the surroundings were permitted. The patients showed significantly less accurate control of the hip sway component than the normal subjects. The findings indicate that for both normal subjects and vestibular deficient subjects the pattern of response to be initiated at release is preset based on the body configuration and hold force prior to release and is executed as a unit.

    The H&R paradigm reveals adaptation of long latency reflexes during exposure to a rotating artificial gravity environment.
    The aim of this study was to quantify recovery from simulated falls in altered force backgrounds and to investigate the mechanisms of recovery, using the H&R paradigm. The investigators tested 16 healthy men and women pre-, per-, and post- 10rpm rotation in the center of the Brandeis slow rotation room. Subjects were divided into two groups: one group had an extra load equivalent to 25% of their body weight strapped to their waist, the other did not. Subjects voluntarily rocked back and forth about their ankles in 30 second trials, 3cm sway amplitude, for 3 pre-rotation, 20 per-rotation, and 10 post rotation trials. Loss of balance was elicited with the H&R perturbation paradigm in 3 pre-rotation trials and 3 trials immediately post-rotation. An OptoTrak system was used to measure postural sway and response to H&R.

    Pre-rotation subjects successfully swayed fore and aft. During per-rotation trials they initially swayed in a deviated path, of approximately 20 degrees, reflecting the influence of Coriolis forces on the body. With additional trials, subjects swayed in a progressively more fore-aft pattern. Adaptation was fastest for the loaded subjects. Post-rotation subjects initially swayed in a mirror image path to that initially seen during rotation. The aftereffect was largest for the subjects with additional load. A comparison of pre- and post-rotation H&R trials indicated that the postural recovery response is not anti-parallel to the direction of the induced fall. Instead, it is in the same direction as the voluntary sway aftereffects, indicating a remapping of both voluntary sway and also of reflexive responses to postural perturbations. After 10 post-rotation sway trials, sway patterns returned to pre-rotation patterns.

experiment_title: IntraVenous Fluid GENeration for Exploration Missions (IVGEN)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Over four hundred medical conditions have been identified that may present and require treatment during long-duration space exploration. Of the conditions, approximately 25 percent may require medical fluids during the course of treatment. Some of the conditions that may require IV fluid treatment include major bone fracture, burns, and acute anemia. NASA is currently developing hardware that can produce IV solution using spacecraft cabin water (also called the feedstock.)

The IntraVenous Fluid GENeration for Exploration Missions (IVGEN) experiment was designed to demonstrate a water purification and pharmaceutical mixing system that can make intravenous (IV) fluid in microgravity. IVGEN utilized a deionizing resin bed to remove contaminants from cabin water to a purity level that meets the standards of the United States Pharmacopeia (USP), which is chartered by the United States Food and Drug Administration to function as the governing body for pharmaceuticals in the United States. The water was then introduced into an IV bag where the fluid was mixed with USP grade crystalline salt to produce USP normal saline. Inline conductivity sensors quantified the feedstock water quality, output water purity, and normal saline mixing uniformity.

APPROACH:
The resin bed was made from 0.5 mm diameter beads packed into a cylinder including bubble-trapping hardware upstream from the filter to insure that no failures occurred from trapping bubbles within the filter to insure optimal performance. The hardware quantified system performance using flow and pressure transducers. If the hardware were to experience performance degradation, these transducers would allow the fluid physicists to identify and fix the problem.

IVGEN operated inside the Microgravity Sciences Glovebox (MSG) laboratory and utilized cameras and video recording devices to observe system performance. IVGEN required MSG resources such as electrical power, video capability, and data collection/transmission. IVGEN also required access to pressurized nitrogen to pressurize the accumulator. The experiment protocol required that one 1.5 liter bag of IV fluid be returned in refrigerated stowage for ground-based analysis. IVGEN also required the return of a second 1.5 liter bag of IV fluid, but it remained ambient. Each IVGEN run took approximately 1.5 hours, but did not require crew interaction for the duration of the session.

Astronauts installed IVGEN inside the MSG per procedures. The astronaut transferred ISS potable water from the Water Processing Assembly (WPA) to the IVGEN accumulator. When that was completed, the astronaut pressurized the IVGEN accumulator with nitrogen. The pressure forced water through the IVGEN system, beginning with a bubble trap to eliminate unwanted air, and a conductivity sensor to quantify the quality of the incoming water. Following the conductivity sensor, the water passed through the packed resin bed, through another bubble trap to remove any air that may have been present in the filter, and then into the mixing bag. The mixing bag contained the salt required to make a saline solution, as well as a sterile magnetic stir bar. After the bag had been filled with 1.5 liters of water, the stir bar mixed the solution. Following mixing, the fluid passed out of the mixing bag, through a conductivity sensor to measure uniformity, and into a final collection bag. After all of the solution was in the collection bag, it was disconnected from the system, sealed, and appropriately stowed.

RESULTS:
On-orbit results indicated that all of the experimental success criteria were met with the exception of the salt concentration. Problems with a large air bubble in the first bag of purified water resulted in a slightly concentrated saline solution of 117 percent of the target value of 0.9 g/L. The second bag had an inadequate amount of salt premeasured into the mixing bag resulting in a slightly deficient salt concentration of 93.8 percent of the target value. The USP permits a range from 95 to 105 percent of the target value.

experiment_title: Effects of Zero-Gravity Exposure on Biochemical and Metabolic Properties of Skeletal Muscle
experiment_description:
Objectives:

1) To determine impairments in the functional capacities of skeletal muscle due to microgravity by measuring and comparing the following parameters (under precise loading conditions):
a) Muscle Strength
b) Muscle Power
c) Muscle Performance
d) Ability of muscle to sustain work

2) To focus analyses of muscle performance directly at the whole muscle level rather than at the whole animal level.

3) To continue studies on the effects of spaceflight on biochemical, metabolic, and functional properties of skeletal muscle.

4) To relate contractile and work properties of muscle to biochemical and metabolic properties.

Approach:

Flight and flight control animals were anesthetized and prepared for a series of muscle contractile tests. Preparation for the contractile tests included dissection of the left hindlimb and exposure of the sciatic nerve. Afterwards, the distal tendon of the soleus muscle was dissected, freed from the surrounding tissue and attached via a hook directly to an ergometer as the rodent was immobilized on a stereotaxic frame. Rodents received electrical stimulation via a miniplug that was implanted in the cranial region of each animal.

Contractile tests measured the following: force output and twitch contraction times; force/velocity relationships, force/frequency relationships, maximum work and power output; and fatigability (isometric vs. isotonic). After the completion of these measurements, the stimulated (left) and non-stimulated, contralateral sides (right) hindlimb muscles (Soleus, Plantaris, Medial Gastrocnemius, Vastus Intermedius, Vastus Lateralis, and Tibialis Anterior) were removed and sent to the investigator' laboratory for biochemical, histochemical, immunohistochemical, mRNA and RNA analysis.

These analyses will be discussed in more detail in the appropriate sections devoted to collection and processing of biological specimens:Muscle contractile properties (shortening speed),pattern of activation (stimulation frequency/force response), maximum muscle strength (force output), work and power generating capacity, and work and power sustaining capacity (muscular endurance).

Results:

Spaceflight, even short duration, produces important changes in contractile properties of antigravity skeletal muscles. These changes are mediated by alterations in myosin heavy chain phenotype and reductions in muscle mass. In some cases, the alterations in myosin heavy chain isoform content seemed to be uncoupled from those occurring at the protein level. This apparent uncoupling between mRNA and protein expression demonstrates that the effects of microgravity must be better understood at the transcriptional, translational, and post-translational level.

Individual results:

1) Muscle mass/or weight: Soleus, Vastus Intermedius (VI), and Plantaris (the extensor muscles) had a significant decrease in mass. The Tibialis Anterior (TA) (a flexor muscle) did not.

2) Contractile Properties of antigravity skeletal muscle (soleus muscle)
TPT and RT1/2: were 25% faster in flight than in flight controls (Speed-Related Contractile Properties)
Vmax: 20% faster in the flight than in the flight controls (Force-Velocity Relationship)

3) Myosin Heavy Chain Isoform Content:
Soleus: Significant increase in percentage of hybrid fibers and decrease in percentage of slow fibers
Vastus Intermedius: Same trend as with Soleus, but not quite as dramatic
Plantaris: Did not show trend as Soleus or Vastus Intermedius
Tibialis Anterior: Did not show same trend as Soleus or Vastus Intermedius
Slow type I fiber: Displayed no decrease in relative content
Fast type IIa fiber: Its relative content was affected in the Vastus Intermedius
Fast type IIb fiber: Unaffected by microgravity

4) Myosin Heavy Chain mRNA Isoform Content:
total RNA was unaffected by 14 days of spaceflight.

experiment_title: Haptics Feedback Control in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It is expected that the future of human space exploration will rely heavily on advanced telerobotic systems to support human presence and activity in harsh environments. So far, all testing of the technology has been performed on the ground, and never with a microgravity adapted crewmember. Ground testing has shown that proprioceptive feedback – the awareness of the position of the body’s limbs and the applied forces when performing a task – is important for the control and the performance of remote operated telerobotic systems. It is known that the kinesthetic feedback for humans in space is altered, and little is known about haptic (i.e. force) proprioception alterations when subjected to a microgravity environment. Therefore, a series of tasks will be performed by microgravity-adapted crewmembers using a telerobotic system with proprioceptive feedback that utilizes haptic display technology. Haptic displays are mechatronic devices that provide force stimuli to crew during control to stimulate force proprioception, similar to a force-feedback joystick. Such force stimuli are then either simulated (as is the case for this experiment) or can also directly result from measured forces from a telerobotic system that interacts with its environment.

It is the objective of the Haptics-1 experiment to perform an in-orbit engineering parameter calibration and identification for one joint of a future exoskeleton haptic device and to perform a first extensive set of force feedback control performance measurements with crew operating force reflective controllers in microgravity.

In particular, the following results are expected from the experiment:
(1) The first, complete set of mechatronic engineering parameters identified for enabling safe interaction in microgravity with high performance haptic devices;
(2) The first detailed evaluation of haptic feedback perceptional changes under micro-gravity during position and force control tasks;
(3) The first extensive human factors data set identified for haptic interaction after long exposure to microgravity environments (more than 3 months)
(4) Validation of a new Graphical User Interface (GUI) guided procedures approach for robotics control software (used for real-time experiment control & monitoring from a touch-screen tablet); and
(5) Validation of mechatronic safety concept for haptic controllers in close human contact for safety relevant applications.

APPROACH:
The purpose of this experiment is to gather information about haptic feedback in microgravity, in order to allow more efficient preparation of technologies necessary for such future applications. For this purpose, a single degree of freedom haptic force control joystick will be provided, together with a touchscreen tablet, for performing a suite of parameter identification and control experiments with human-in-the-loop characteristic.

The Haptics-1 experiment consists of two sessions made up of seven independent protocols each that will be carried out by each crew participating in the experiment. The two sessions will be distinguished by two mounting configurations of the force control joystick, i.e. wall-mounted and body-mounted.

Two inflight data collection sessions are planned for each crew; one as a wall-mounted configuration and the other as a body-mounted configuration. Each session consists of seven individual small protocols that can be performed in random order. The Tablet PC GUI keeps track of status of execution per crew. The inflight portion of the experiment should be performed no earlier than three months after arrival in orbit to ensure that the crew is fully adapted to the microgravity environment.

Data collection will be done by the payload hardware itself. Prior to the sessions, the crew will set-up the equipment from its storage location in either the wall-mounted or body-mounted configuration. Then, the crew will follow the guided procedures on the Tablet PC screen. They can select each of the seven protocols and perform them until the minimum number of trials has been performed by that crew. The software logs the crew ID and the number of trials executed per protocol.

The seven protocols that make up one session are:
(1) System self-test
(2) Human admittance identification (human-in-the-loop)
(3) Human position control bandwidth identification (human-in-the-loop)
(4) Human force control bandwidth identification (human-in-the-loop)
(5) Torque discrimination task (human-in-the-loop)
(6) Stiffness discrimination task (human-in-the-loop)
(7) Crisp contact perception choice task (human-in-the-loop)

experiment_title: Recovery of IGF-1 Signaling in Bone by Skeletal Reloading (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Prolonged space flight causes osteopenia due to decreased bone formation secondary to impaired osteoblast proliferation and increased osteoblast apoptosis. Hindlimb unloading by tail suspension, a model for skeletal unloading of space flight, causes osteoblast precursor and skeletal tissue resistance to the effects of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1). The nature of this resistance is characterized by decreased activation of the IGF-1 receptor and downstream signaling pathways. Osteoblast precursors isolated from unloaded bones demonstrate decreased expression of integrins, putative mechanosensors that bind extracellular matrix proteins, and in vitro treatment of normal osteoblasts with echistatin, an integrin antagonist, recreates the phenomena of unloading-induced IGF-1 resistance. Additionally, mechanical stimulation of human osteoblasts activates the IGF-1 receptor and augments the receptor response to IGF-1. These effects are abrogated by echistatin treatment. These findings suggest that integrin receptors have a role in mechanical regulation of IGF-1 receptor in osteoblasts.

Investigators hypothesized is that interaction of integrin and IGF-1 receptor signaling cascades is required for IGF-1 activation of its receptor and intact IGF-1 signaling in osteoblasts. Mechanical loading stimulates the formation of an integrin/IGF-1 receptor complex, thus, enhancing IGF-1 signaling and enabling mechanically induced osteoblast proliferation and bone formation. To test the hypothesis, investigators proposed the following specific aims:

  1. Determine the means by which skeletal reloading regulates skeletal response to IGF-1. Tail suspended rats treated with IGF-1 will be skeletally reloaded to preserve bone mass and osteoblast IGF-1 signaling. Integrity of IGF-1 signaling will be correlated with the interaction between integrins and the IGF-1 receptor.
  2. Determine the mechanism for regulation of the osteoblast IGF-1 receptor by integrins in response to mechanical loading by pulsatile fluid flow. Formation of the integrin and IGF-1 receptor complex in human osteoblasts will be stimulated by fluid flow loading in order to determine the components within the complex and their function.

    APPROACH:
    The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

    RESULTS:
    At the completion of this project investigatores established the critical regulatory role of integrins in IGF-1 signaling of osteoblasts. Mechanical stimulation of human osteosarcoma (HOS) cells activates the IGF-1R including the proliferative MAPK signal pathway and the anti-apoptotic Akt signal pathway in a ligand independent manner. The sensitivity of HOS cells and its IGF-1R to mechanical stimulation requires and is influenced by integrin receptor signaling. This is illustrated impaired activation of IGF-1R induced by echistatin and augmented activation of IGF-1R by stimulation of integrin receptors with exposure to their ligands. The results of siRNA knockdown experiments indicate that both integrin beta1 and beta3 are required for normal activation of the IGF-1R by treatment with either ligand or mechanical stimulation. The integrin regulation of IGF-1 signaling in osteoblasts allows osteoblasts to sense and respond to mechanical load, providing a link between mechanical loading, bone formation, and skeletal integrity.

    The feasibility of intermittent cyclic skeletal loading and IGF-1 infusion to prevent unloading-induced bone loss was evaluated. Tail suspended rats treated with intermittent short duration cyclic loading totaling only 42 minutes over 2 weeks had significantly blunted unloading induced trabecular bone loss. The mechanism of the enhanced response of the unloaded bones to cyclic loading is due to augmentation of bone formation rather than reduction in osteoclast activity and these responses were not affected by IGF-1 treatment. However, within the cortical bone compartment, the intermittent loading induced stimulation of periosteal bone formation was further augmented by treatment with IGF-1. These findings demonstrate the complex nature of the skeletal response to mechanical loading in that in cancellous bone, the threshold for mechanical stimulation induced bone formation in the unloaded state is lower than that required to prevent unloading induced osteoclast mediated bone loss and IGF-1 has a limited role in modulating the response of cancellous bone to mechanical loading but works synergistically with mechanical loading in cortical bone at the periosteal bone surface. The complexity of these differing skeletal responses to mechanical and pharmacologic treatments and the interactions between the integrin and IGF-1 signaling cascades in osteoblasts will need to be considered in the design of potential targets for countermeasure treatments to preserve the effects of mechanical loading and prevent the bone loss of space flight.

experiment_title: Light Flash Observations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During the Apollo missions 12-17 and Skylab missions 2-4, the crews observed and recorded the frequency and character of light flashes through their eyes. After approximately 17 minutes of dark adaptation, tiny dots and thin streaks of white light were seen at frequencies of approximately three events per minute by crewmembers when on translunar coast (TLC) or transearth coast (TEC) or over the polar part of Skylab orbits. When near the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), where the proton flux was over 1000 times greater than in other parts of the orbit, the frequency increased to approximately nine events per minute for Skylab altitudes of 443 km.

Nearly 20 years ago, it was hypothesized that astronauts were likely to see flashes of light from cosmic ray particles when they were outside the shielding provided by the Earth’s magnetic field. The site of action of these particles, and whether cosmic particles actually caused the light flash phenomenon, were topics of conjecture in 1970, when this phenomenon was first reported. The causes for luminous phosphenes included ionizing radiation, mechanical pressure, electrical currents, magnetic fields, stimulation of the cerebral cortex, or pathological conditions of the Central Nervous System (CNS). In 1970, these phenomena were believed to be caused by ionizing heavy nuclei such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, which transversed the spacecraft and the body when outside the Earth’s magnetic shielding. The conjecture that the major mechanism for these visual phenomena was Cerenkov radiation was controversial.

Simulation studies were used to determine whether carbon, nitrogen, oxygen or other ions with equivalent ionizing characteristics could cause the same phenomena seen by astronauts. The exact mechanism in which the retina was stimulated by ionizing particles traveling at velocities below those necessary for emission of Cerenkov light was unclear. Experiments in which nitrogen ions were stopped in the cerebral cortex showed that the brain and optic nerve were not stimulated. Several mechanisms existed by which cosmic particles could produce visual sensations. They were: 1) electrical excitation resulting in near-ultraviolet (UV) radiation in the vicinity of the retina, 2) ionization by cosmic ray particles through the retina, 3) local ionization by the products from a nonelastic collision of the high-velocity proton and carbon, nitrogen, or oxygen, or 4) a shock wave phenomenon from charged particles passing through the tissue matrix.

The purpose of the experiment was to ascertain quantitatively the frequency, character, latitudinal dependence, and identity of cosmic particles that caused the light flash phenomenon during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. The ultimate objective was the assessment of radiation hazards of long-term Earth-orbiting and interplanetary missions.

APPROACH:
Special features of the experiment included measurement of the characteristics of the cosmic-particle environment in the vicinity of the eye, measurement of dark adaptation, and continuous onboard accumulation of the light flash observations from astronauts and particle detectors throughout one complete 90-minute orbit.

Two revolutions of the Earth were devoted to this experiment. During revolution 110, the silicon telescope-spectrometer was deployed to measure the trajectory, atomic charge Z, and velocity of cosmic particles with a stopping power of 10 kilo-electron volts per micrometer or greater. During revolution 111, two crewmembers donned special masks in order to become completely dark-adapted. After approximately 10 minutes, the two observers reached dark adaptation and made continuous observations of visual sensations. At each event, a push-button signal from the observing astronaut was recorded on the digital tape and the verbal description was recorded on the onboard tape recorder. The third crewmember operated the experiment control unit, which received data from silicon detectors and silver chloride AgCl(Cd) crystals. The crystals were used to register particle tracks in four sectors of orbit, those corresponding to the northern latitudes, equatorial latitudes, the SAA, and the southern latitudes. After the flight, the digital tapes, voice tapes, detector boxes, and masks were returned to the investigators.

The digital tapes were transcribed, and each event was related to the orbital position of the spacecraft. Events from the silicon detectors, pushbuttons and control unit were read from the digital tape by a specially constructed microprocessor. The push-button events and time marks were related to the verbal reports. The energy and trajectory information were inadequate because of a paucity of recorded events.

The AgCl(Cd) crystals were transported to the University of Frankfurt, Germany, where they had been produced and calibrated. The crystals were analyzed for the abundance of tracks produced by protons, alpha particles, or heavier ions.

The characteristics of the cosmic particle environment inside the spacecraft were determined by converting the spectrum and abundance of particles outside the spacecraft to the number of particles with various stopping powers and residual ranges, using aluminum shielding data for 512 sectors of solid angle around the spacecraft.

RESULTS:
There were 82 visual events reported by two crewmembers during a 90-minute orbit at an altitude of 225 kilometers (km).

The results of the light flash experiment indicated that the abundance of ions that caused the light flash phenomena was minimal between latitudes 30° N and 30° S. The frequency of light flashes between latitudes 30° N/50° N and 30° S/50° S was 25 times higher than noted in the equatorial latitudes. Increased flash phenomena were not reported through the SAA, as was expected after reviewing a Skylab 4 report of increased activity through the SAA. However, at the 225-km altitude of Apollo-Soyuz, the proton flux was much less than that of the Skylab 4 altitude of 443 kilometers. Also, the shielding of the Apollo spacecraft was greater than that of Skylab. This distribution of flashes was correlated with the distribution of cosmic particles with stopping power greater that 15 kilo-electron volts per micrometer in the eye.

The frequency of reported light flash events was strongly dependent on latitude. At the points of closest approach to the geomagnetic poles, the observed events occurred at one to two per minute; however no events occurred near the equator. These observations were consistent with the change in abundance of cosmic particles with latitude that was also noted during the Skylab 4 mission. The increased rate of visual events near the south geomagnetic pole can be explained by increased dark adaptation of the crewmembers. The observed event rate correlated with a cosmic particle abundance for heavy particles with energy losses > 5 kilo-electron volts per micrometer.

The AgCl(Cd) detector results suggested that 60 events of 15 kilo-electron volts per micrometer or greater would be observed during three-minute intervals in the northernmost portions of the orbit. The highest observed event rate at high latitudes was only 14 events per three minutes near the south magnetic pole. This rate implied a 23-percent efficiency for the detector. However, near the equator, where only a few events were observed, the detectors recorded the equivalent average of 73 events per four cm2/minute. An explanation of this inconsistency was that the fading time from the heavy ions was long relative to the orbit sectors. Thus, identification of the heavy particle environment in each sector could not be expected. Also, particles interacting in the crystals hours before the experiment might have been included in the event.

Assuming the complete retina target area of four cm2, the efficiency of visualizing the events was 36 percent for the northernmost sector. In the SAA sector, the detector efficiency diminished to eight percent. Thus, the AgCl(Cd) detector data did not correlate well with either the observed event rate or the calculated abundances.

There were no reports of high frequency throughout the SAA, as was expected from a previous Skylab 4 report of markedly increased flash activity. At the 225-km altitude of Apollo-Soyuz, the proton flux of particles was 14 times less than at the 443-km altitude of Skylab 4. Also, the aluminum shielding of the Apollo command module was much greater than that of Skylab.

The more favored hypothesis for the events seen in the SAA, particularly at higher altitudes, was the mechanism of proton nonelastic nuclear collision with carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen in tissues of the retina. This mechanism was similar to that proposed for neutron interactions, which also cause discrete flashes. If the average cross-section for interactions such as (p, p’, 3a) on carbon, nitrogen, or oxygen was assumed to be approximately 450 millibars in the proton energy range of 175 million electron volts (MeV) or less, only one event per three minutes would occur during Apollo-Soyuz altitude of 225 km. Under the reduced shielding conditions of Skylab 4, 51 times more protons would interact with the eye tissues of one observer, or 26 events might be observed during a three-minute interval. The average rate was 28 events per three minutes on Skylab 4. Thus, the nuclear collision hypothesis for the origin of light flashes in the SAA had some validity.

experiment_title: Individualized Behavioral Health Monitoring Tool
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Given the extended duration of future missions and the isolated, extreme and confined environments, there is the possibility that behavioral conditions and mental disorders (DSM-IV-TR) will develop. The overarching goal of this project was to deliver an Individualized Behavioral Health Monitoring Tool that unobtrusively integrates all available behavioral measures collected during a mission to provide a dashboard of behavioral health indicators. These indicators were placed within the context of quantitatively-tracked mission stressors to provide meaningful feedback allowing behavioral issues to be detected and mitigated at an early stage. The result of this project will be a system prototype that can be deployed in space analog environments (e.g., Mars 520 study, Antarctica) for validation testing and ultimately deployed in long-duration space exploration missions. Phase II is expected to achieve: (1) an Individualized Behavioral Health Monitor software interface; (2) a data integration system; (3) a trend and change detection algorithm; and (4) a countermeasure selection aid.

POTENTIAL NASA COMMERCIAL APPLICATIONS: The Individualized Behavioral Health Monitoring Tool is expected to meet the specific requirements of long-duration exploration missions and provide feedback to astronauts, operational psychologists, and flight surgeons about behavioral health status as well as aid in the selection of countermeasures. experiment_title: Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI of the Brain, Lungs and Plants Augmented with MRI Pulse Sequence Development
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional water proton MR method used in medical MRI. Low magnetic field MRI with hyperpolarized noble gases can allow investigators to use a small, light-weight, low-power devices. This capability provides potential for advances in both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. This ground-based investigation with hyperpolarized noble gas MR will affect biomedical research in two important ways: (1) by providing the potential to acquire novel information about physiological structure and function of the lung and the brain in space-flight and in terrestrial gravity, and (2) by developing a new diagnostic technology that has clinical applications for diagnosis of pathology.

An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional thermally polarized water proton MR method used in a medical MRI. As a result, at low magnetic fields (0.01 Tesla) the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is much larger than the SNR of conventional thermally polarized MR. Low field MR utilizing hyperpolarized noble gases should be practical in a small, light-weight, low-power device, providing the potential for both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. Specific magnetic and biological properties of hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe MRI include: (i) airway and lung gas space imaging (for diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), e.g. emphysema, asthma, and for studies of respiratory function); (ii) the imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis, and in research on brain function); and (iii) angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system). The recent progress made lays the foundation for the continued development of hyperpolarized xenon MRI for brain imaging. Specifically, imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis) and angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system), are now viable research goals. Because HP 129Xe is an MR signal source with properties very different from those generated from water-protons, it may yield structural and functional information not detectable by proton-based MRI methods. Thus brain imaging with hyperpolarized xenon should be of great benefit to the diagnosis and treatment monitoring of a number of neurological diseases.

APPROACH:
Investigators are developing a new diagnostic technology: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and spectroscopy of hyperpolarized noble gases. Large non-equilibrium nuclear spin polarizations can be created in the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe, using the technique of spin-exchange optical pumping. Such large polarizations greatly enhance the magnetic resonance detection of 3He and 129Xe, enabling high-resolution MRI studies of the lung and airways, as well as dissolved tissue-phase investigations of organs and tissues, such as the brain, using lipophilic 129Xe.

RESULTS:
The overall goal of this proposal was to develop hyperpolarized noble gas magnetic resonance imaging (HP MRI) for the assessment of pulmonary and nervous system damage that may be incurred during human space flight. Hyperpolarized noble gas MRI is showing dramatic results for diagnostic imaging of the lungs, brain, and other parts of the body, some of which have been resistant to conventional proton MRI. Most notably, investigators have achieved high resolution dynamic images of the lungs and airways using hyperpolarized 3He, and have measured cerebral perfusion and functional activity in the brain using hyperpolarized 129Xe (HP 129Xe). The number of space flight-related pathologies which may benefit from this technique are vast and range from pulmonary dysfunction caused by microgravity to cognitive and neurobehavioral problems resulting from the stress and isolation of extended term space travel. This novel technology should also offer a rapid, sensitive method to detect treatment effects and thus may expedite the development of therapeutic strategies for treating space flight related injury, such as aerosol administration of drugs via the lungs, which may obviate the need for medicinal injections during space flight.

experiment_title: Organ Dose Measurement Using the Phantom Torso
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary risk to long-duration space flight crewmembers is radiation-induced cancers. One of the main obstacles in assessing radiation risk in manned space flight is related to the estimation of organ level radiation dose-equivalent. Currently both experimental and operational methods for assessing radiation dose are limited to the measurement of surface (skin) dose. Organ level dose is approximated only by calculations using the radiation environment model and the appropriate radiation transport models. These estimates may be overly conservative because of their known limits of accuracy. The accuracy problem is two-fold: separate models are required for the spacecraft shielding distribution and anatomical male or female models, and the incident radiation models are inaccurate. The inaccuracy comes from the fact that they do not account for anisotropy and do not include the production of secondary particles within the spacecraft and the human body. This study proposed to provide the necessary depth-dose-equivalent measurements using a fully instrumented Phantom Torso (with head). The Phantom Torso was to be assembled on orbit, and the sensors activated. Depth-dose-equivalent measurements were to be taken as a function of spacecraft altitude, attitude, location and time. Measurements internal to the Phantom Torso would be supported by other radiation measurement instrumentation.

APPROACH:
The radiation data for this experiment were collected via three main pieces of hardware: a Phantom Torso, Tissue Equivalent Proportional Counter (TEPC), and Charged Particle Directional Spectrometer (CPDS). The Phantom Torso mimicked a human torso in size and shape, and contained over 300 passive dosimeters and three active dosimeters.

Space Shuttle flight 5A.1 carried the Tissue Equivalent Proportional Counter (TEPC), Charged Particle Directional Spectrometer (CPDS), and associated hardware to the International Space Station (ISS). Crewmembers deployed the experiment hardware in empty rack space in the U.S. Lab. The Phantom Torso and remaining experiment hardware was carried to the International Space Station (ISS) by Shuttle flight 6A.

The experiment was designed as follows. After the Phantom Torso was set-up, all of the experiment hardware would be activated. All three pieces of hardware (Phantom Torso, CPDS, and TEPC) were designed to continuously collect data without crew intervention. Data from the CPDS, TEPC, and Phantom Torso (each active dosimeter) were to be downloaded separately and sequentially to the onboard computer every 7 to 10 days. Data would then be downlinked to the ground at the earliest convenience. Deactivation, disassembly, and stowage of experiment hardware would take place as late as possible before departure from the ISS.

RESULTS:
The results of the Torso experiment show that models of space radiation transport developed by the NASA Langley Research Center and the NASA Johnson Space Center are in good agreement with the measured organ doses. The largest differences observed are less that 15% between measurements and calculations. The majority of organ biological doses (80%) on station were from GCRs because trapped protons were well attenuated by the spacecraft and skin and because of the higher biological effectiveness of the GCR. The average quality factor (a measure of the impact of space radiation compared to X-rays) was shown to have a value of about 2.6 on ISS.

NASA uses a risk assessment model that employs orbital inclination, altitude, phase in the solar cycle, vehicle shielding, and body shielding when calculating the risk from radiation. Data from the Phantom Torso experiment indicated the prediction of radiation dose and dose equivalent by the model to have an accuracy of ±25%. Torso results also indicate the need to improve the measurements on secondary neutrons in space flight.

experiment_title: Effects of Spaceflight on Plasma and Glandular Concentrations of Pituitary Hormones
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The important role played by hormones in regulation of metabolic parameters affected by space flight suggests that altered endocrine function may have contributed to other observed metabolic changes. The aims of the present study were to clarify the effects of space flight on pituitary function by measuring plasma and glandular concentrations of pituitary hormones and, where feasible, evaluating the status of the appropriate target tissue.

Approach:

At the conclusion of the flight all rats were weighed and inspected. Anterior and posterior-intermediate lobes were collected, weighed, and individually frozen for assays. Plasma and pituitary growth hormone (GH), and prolactin were immunoassayed using GH and prolactin purified in-house as standards. Thyrotropin was assayed by a double antibody method, and luteinizing and follicle stimulating hormones by procedures employing NIAMDD (National Institute of
Arthritis, Metabolism and Digestive Diseases) rat standards. Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) was immunoassayed using the 3rd International Standard (porcine). Vasopressin was measured by a radioimmunoassay procedure and melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH) by the bioassay method.

Results:

Although of modest extent, some perturbations of endocrine function were found in this investigation. The low plasma GH titers of flight animals either reflects the unusual sampling conditions at recovery or the effects of weightlessness. The larger adrenals of flight rats suggests they were secreting increased quantities of corticosterone over a significant part of the flight, which may have contributed to the smaller flight body weights by its protein catabolic effect. The adrenal hypertrophy of flight rats suggests these animals were secreting more ACTH and corticosterone during flight. There were no changes in either pituitary or plasma MSH suggesting that either the type or degree of stress was not adequate to stimulate MSH secretion.

experiment_title: Arabidopsis as a Model for the Study of DNA Double Strand Break (DSB) Repair and DSB Induction by Space Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Ionizing radiation (IR) induces oxidative damage, which affects all cellular components. However, the most significant form of damage induced by ionized radiation (IR), in terms of cell death, mutagenesis, carcinogenesis, and effects on the cell cycle, is clustered DNA damage, often resulting in the formation of DNA double strand breaks. The DNA damage induced by high mass, high energy (HZE) space radiation is thought to be more complex than that induced by gamma radiation, as HZE particles generate a denser trail of ionization events in their wake. The investigators proposed to determine whether the same DNA repair pathways required for resistance to gamma radiation are also required for resistance to HZE particles. Because of the importance of double strand break (DSB) repair in prevention of carcinogenic “loss of heterozygosity” events, they have focused on DSB repair pathways. However, they are also interested in signal transduction pathways involved in the detection of IR induced damage- these pathways are important initiators of responses to IR, including cell cycle arrest, induction of repair, and induction of cell death. Thus the investigators are studying the effects of mutations in the nonhomologous end joining genes DNA ligase IV (LigIV), and Ku80, the endonuclease XPF, and the damage response genes ATM, ATR, and SOG. All of these genes are known to affect gamma resistance in mammals, fungi, and plants. Because knockouts in these genes are lethal in mammals (and, in some cases, in fungi), the investigators used the plant Arabidopsis as a model system. They used the NSRL facility at Brookhaven to compare the sensitivity of these lines to gamma versus 1GeV Fe particles.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this experiment isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Effects of gamma versus HZE on plant growth: The investigators irradiated Arabidopsis seeds of various genotypes and wild-type backgrounds in doses ranging from 25 to 200 Gy. Approximately 40 seeds were then sown on agar plates and the plates digitally imaged eight days later. They used the application NIH Image to trace the roots and enter the length into Excel for statistical analyses.

In no case did irradiation prohibit germination- at these doses Arabidopsis embryos do not die. Germination is driven by cell expansion, not cell division, but elongation of the root to lengths greater than approx. 1.5 mm requires cell division. At the highest doses of Fe ions (200 Gy), cell expansion as well as cell division was inhibited. Approximately twice this dose of gamma would be required to induce this effect on cell elongation.

In order to contrast sensitivity in a quantitative fashion, the investigators interpolated their dose-response curves to estimate the dose required to inhibit root growth at eight days by 50 percent. Most mutants that are sensitive to gamma radiation are also sensitive to HZE. In almost all cases, the biological effectiveness of HZE was about three-fold that of gamma radiation, suggesting the all of the mutations tested play similarly important roles in resistance to the effects of both types of radiation on root growth. The RBE numbers, however, need additional statistical analysis to determine their significance. The checkpoint genes ATR and ATM differed widely in their effects on resistance to HZE. Plants defective in ATR were relatively resistant to HZE versus gamma (RBE = 2.7, rather than 3.7), while ATM knockouts were relatively sensitive (RBE = 4.5). Correct interpretation of this result would depend on whether growth inhibition in these mutants is due to the prolonged imposition of a checkpoint, or to the failure of a checkpoint and resulting cell death. The LOH data suggests that the relatively HZE-resistant growth of ATR versus ATM may be due to the loss of the ATR-imposed checkpoint, resulting in enhanced loss of heterozygosity in the prematurely dividing cells.

The investigators also found that the sog mutation, a defect in a transcription factor required for checkpoint response to gamma radiation in the apical meristem, has little effect on root meristem response to either gamma or HZE.

experiment_title: Glial Cell Reaction from Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The goal of the project is to determine the effects of space flight on glial cell proliferation and reactive gliosis in the adult nervous system.
Gliosis and glial cell proliferation are a common reaction to injury of the CNS. The goal of this experiment is to determine if space flight, notably lift-off, produces subclinical damage to the brain, presumably as a result of compression by the forces associated with launch.

Approach:

Brains from rats used in the Physiological Anatomical Rodent Experiment 3 (PARE.03) were requested through the NASA tissue sharing program. These animals had received subcutaneous injections of tritiated thymidine (1 uCi/g) at R+0, R+24, and R+72; the brain had been removed and stored frozen as part of the tissue sharing program.

Results:

A total of 18 brains (9 flight and 9 control) were received. Unfortunately, these brains had been badly damaged during the initial dissection and freezing and their condition on receipt in this laboratory was poor; the best description of the brains is that they were flattened so that they resemble quarters. This has made processing difficult because achieving the goals of this project requires that we be able to identify anatomical landmarks in the brain. These landmarks have been completely distorted. Nevertheless, we initially determined using one of the control brains that we could detect successfully the radioactivity in the brains; however, subsequent analysis of experimental brains was unsuccessful due to their poor preservation.

experiment_title: Neuronal Development Under Conditions of Space Flight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Considerable development of the hippocampus occurs in rats after birth. Therefore, the hippocampus, which is required for spatial learning, is more likely to be affected by microgravity exposure at a young age. This experiment examined the hypothesis that exposure of rat neonates to microgravity will result in altered activity that will lead to altered development. This study evaluated the cognitive mapping abilities of rats that spent part of their early development in a microgravity environment. Another objective of this experiment was to analyze neuronal morphology and determine the synaptic functional plasticity in the developing nervous system of rat neonates raised in microgravity. Finally an analysis of the distribution of specific protein components of the nervous system was conducted, with particular emphasis on the cytoskeletal synaptic proteins, in rat neonates raised in microgravity.

Approach:

Litters of male and female Sprague-Dawley rat pups were launched into space aboard the NASA Space Shuttle Columbia on either post-natal day 8 (P8) or 14 (P14), and remained in space for 16 days. These animals were designated as flight (FLT) groups. Two age-matched control groups remained on Earth: those in standard vivarium housing (VIV) and those in identical housing to that aboard the Shuttle (SIM, Simulated Caged Control). Upon return to Earth, all animals were tested in three different tasks, the Morris water maze (MWM), a modified version of the radial arm maze (RAM), and an open field apparatus (OFA), to measure general activity and exploratory activity. Performance and search strategies were evaluated in each of these tasks using an automated tracking system (Poly-Track, San Diego Instruments). The analysis of the hippocampus included a determination of dendritic extents, a quantitative analysis of the synaptic structure and spinal architecture, an analysis of isoform expression of specific cytoskeletal and synaptic proteins, and a determination of the onset of long-term potentiation.

Results:

There were remarkably few differences between the FLT groups and their earth-bound controls in these tasks. FLT animals learned the MWM and RAM as quickly as controls. Evaluation of search patterns suggested subtle differences in patterns of exploration and in the strategies used to solve the tasks, but these differences normalized rapidly. Together, these data suggest that development in an environment without gravity has minimal long-term impact on cognitive mapping. Any differences due to development in microgravity quickly reversed after return to Earth normal gravity.

experiment_title: Cardiovascular Regulation in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The D-2 experiment, Cardiovascular Regulation in Microgravity, flown on Spacelab, was designed to test the general hypothesis that human cardiovascular adaptation to microgravity is rapid and effective but associated with significant dysfunction on return to Earth. The principal specific objectives were to (1) contribute to better understanding of the control of body fluid volumes at microgravity by characterizing the responses to rapid expansion of intravascular volume before, during, and after space flight, and (2) to define the mechanisms underlying post-flight orthostatic hypotension.

APPROACH:
Responses to rapid intravenous fluid loading
Preflight measurements were obtained, supine and sitting, in the four D-2 payload crewmembers at six and nine months before flight and in-flight on mission day 5. A system for warming saline to 37 degrees Celsius and an air-free intravenous infusion system was developed through a collaborative effort involving the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center and NASA Johnson Space Center. The isotonic saline solution, 22 ml/kg, was delivered over 20 minutes by air pressure from two inflatable bladders compressing a plastic saline bag. The driving pressure was generated by a hand-held inflation bulb and displayed by an aneroid manometer. Mean delivery in microgravity was 95.9% of the intended volume which ranged from 1595 to 1919 ml. Finger arterial pressure was monitored. Cardiac output was measured by the foreign gas rebreathing technique.

Mechanisms of post-flight orthostatic intolerance
The stand test had a scheduled duration of 10 minutes with detailed cardiovascular measurements at rest supine, after five minutes standing, and during the last minute of the test. An electrocardiogram and Finapres arterial pressure were recorded continuously. Cardiac output was measured with the acetylene rebreathing technique. Leg volume was measured at rest and during standing using a stocking plethysmograph.

RESULTS:
Studies of the four D-2 payload crewmembers before and immediately after flight were an essential part of a detailed study of orthostatic intolerance that also involved crewmembers from the flights of the Spacelab life sciences missions SLS-1 and SLS-2, in 1991 and 1993 respectively. Combined, 14 crewmembers, 11 men and 3 women, were examined preflight and within four hours of landing after flights of 9 to 14 days.

Preflight, all crewmembers were able to complete the ten-minute stand test. Post-flight, nine of the fourteen (64%) were unable to finish. Pre- and post-flight supine haemodynamics were similar in both groups except slightly (p < 0.05) higher systolic and mean arterial pressures in the finishers. Post-flight, finishers and non-finishers had equally large postural decreases in stroke volume during standing, and also similar degrees of leg pooling. Non-finishers had a greater (but not significantly so) heart rate increase. Cardiac outputs during standing were also similar. The salient difference between finishers and non-finishers was a greater vasoconstrictor response among the finishers with a mean total peripheral resistance during standing (p <0.01).

The cardiovascular effects of fluid load on-orbit were significantly different from the preflight supine data and closely approached, but did not consistently reach, the preflight sitting response levels. The stroke volume data from microgravity were virtually identical to preflight measurements in the sitting position.

At the time of this experiment, the exact mechanism(s) underlying the inadequate vasoconstrictor response early after return to 1-G were yet to be defined. Maximal oxygen uptake was reduced post-flight but maintained at preflight levels after five to eight days in space, which was consistent with grossly intact cardiovascular regulatory mechanisms at microgravity.

Responses to a graded intravenous infusion of the alpha-adrenergic agonist phenylephrine were measured as changes in leg and total peripheral resistance; responses noted two days after return to 1-G were not different from preflight. However, a series of stand tests performed early after return from space demonstrated lower plasma norepinephrine levels in non-finishers than in finishers.

The results from D-2, SLS-1, and SLS-2 provided the base for a new series of detailed and specific studies of cardiovascular control mechanisms planned for Neurolab, a Spacelab flight, flown in 1998, and for a series of long duration flights in the Russian space station Mir.

experiment_title: Effect of Weightlessness on Tissue Regeneration in Rodents
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Little is currently known about the effects of microgravity on tissue repair. In the era of a long-term human presence in space, the probability of minor injury requiring on orbit treatment will increase. This experiment aims to evaluate the effects of spaceflight on the histological and tensiometric properties of full-thickness abdominal incisional skin wounds in the rat. A second objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of basic fibroblast growth factor (FGF) and platelet-derived growth factor (bb-homodimer, PDGF) in promoting granulation tissue formation and collagen deposition.

Approach:

Before flight, both flight and control rats received abdominal implants of polyvinyl acetal sponge disks containing either recombinant human bFGF, recombinant PDGF-BB, or a placebo. After flight, animals received an injection of hypothalamic-releasing hormones. After sacrifice, the sponges were removed and prepared for biochemical and histological analysis of DNA, protein, and collagen content. Histological organization, amount of visible collagen, and the resolution of hemorrhage at the infiltrating interface were also examined.

Results:

Histological analysis showed that both bFGF and PDGF showed positive effects in the ground control rats, but only immediate-release bFGF and delayed-release PDGF had significant, positive effects in the flight rats. This may be due to the 2-day launch delay of the shuttle mission, which caused the growth factor to be released earlier during flight than planned. Although cellular influx into the tissue space of placebo-treated sponges was unaffected by spaceflight, there was a significantly blunted response to either bFGF or PDGF-BB in flight animals. Microgravity significantly reduced wound collagen concentration regardless of the treatment group. The collagen concentration of granulation tissue in flight animals treated with bFGF was significantly less than in those treated with PDGF, but not significantly less than in the placebo treated group. These results show that a highly standardized wound repair process in young rats is significantly altered by spaceflight.

experiment_title: Multisensory Real-Time Space Telerobotics
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As humans prepare for exploration class missions in space, the use of remote telerobotics controls to accomplish desired tasks is expected to increase significantly. Future telerobotics tasks carried out from on orbit are estimated to take up to eight hours to complete. Enhanced telerobotic control systems may be helpful in improving perceptual functions of the crew and overcoming the sensorimotor perturbations caused by microgravity while completing these tasks.

The investigator hypothesizes that real-time telerobotics operations in microgravity can be improved by offering enhanced sources of sensory information to the astronaut operator by combining visual, auditory, and somatosensory stimuli.

The aims of the Multisensory Real-Time Telerobotics experiment are to:

  1. Analyze and refine a real-time space telerobotics control station for future space telerobotics missions in microgravity
  2. Determine if enhanced sensory experiences combining visual, auditory, and somatosensory stimuli (vestibular, proprioceptive, cutaneous) reduce mental and physical fatigue and improve performance in humans when compared to restricted sensory experiences in microgravity
  3. Understand how multisensory integration combining visual, auditory, and somatosensory stimuli (vestibular, proprioceptive, cutaneous) proceeds in the human brain in microgravity

APPROACH:
In this study, right-handed astronaut subjects onboard the International Space Station (ISS) will interact with a telerobotics control station that will be used to control a prototype rover located at a lunar analog in Lazarote, Spain. Hand controllers will be used to accomplish rover navigation and manipulation tasks. Neurophysiological, physiological, and performance data will be collected.

There will be one preflight baseline data collection to take place between launch minus 180 (L-180) days and L-30 days. In addition to demographic data, baseline neurophysiological and physical load data will be collected.

There will be one inflight session between flight day 15 (FD15) and flight day 180 (FD180). During the session, the investigator will continually evaluate cognitive and physical responses as well as performance. The telerobotics control station to be used consists of a laptop computer to provide visual information to the astronaut subject from the remote site, a joystick controller to provide navigational control of the rover and control of rover head movements (for visual inspection of the landscape), a hand force feedback controller to control the rover’s robotic arm and gripper, and ear plug monitors to provide sounds that link directly to and are streamed from the remote location. As the astronaut subject utilizes the control station to operate the rover, a second laptop will be recording research data. Cognitive response and cognitive load will be determined from electroencephalographic (EEG) activity recorded by an EEG headset system worn by the subject. Physical response and physical load will be determined by measuring metabolic response using a physical activity monitor. Performance measures including efficacy, efficiency, and safety will be determined from video recordings of performed telerobotics tasks.

RESULTS:

experiment_title: Test and Evaluation of Liquid Cooling Garments
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This research evaluated the physiological functioning and subjective comfort of subjects while donned in five liquid cooling garments. The goal was to identify the optimal features of each of the garments to maintain core temperature and comfort under intensive physical exertion.

APPROACH:
Four males and two females between the ages of 22 and 46 participated in this study. The garments evaluated were the Minnesota Advanced Cooling Suit (MACS-Delphi), Russian Orlan, NASA Liquid Cooling and Ventilation Garment (LCVG), MACS-Delphi without hood, and Russian Orlan without hood. Subjects were tested on different days in two different environmental chamber temperature/humidity conditions. Each session consisted of stages of treadmill walking/running (250W to 700W at different stages) and rest. Skin and core temperatures, energy expenditure, heart rate, evaporative/nonevaporative sweat rate, and ratings of thermal comfort and heat sensation, overall and on specific body areas were measured throughout each session.

RESULTS:
There were significant differences among garments in femoralis temperature (p<0.001), and calf temperature (p<0.05); the LCVG was lowest in temperature on these areas. In general, the findings showed few consistent differences among the garments. The MACS-Delphi was better able to maintain subjects within a skin and core temperature comfort zone than was evident in the other garments as indicated by a lesser fluctuation in temperatures across physical exertion levels. The LCVG provided the greatest amount of cooling, in some conditions this resulted in body overcooling as noted in declines in skin temperature below a comfort level. Subjective ratings of thermal comfort were higher in the MACS-Delphi. Physiological findings comparing garments with and without the hood were inconclusive; however, subjects rated both the MACS-Delphi and the Orlan with hood as higher in overall thermal comfort.

experiment_title: A Comprehensive Characterization of Microorganisms and Allergens in Spacecraft Environment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Classical Microbial Risk Assessment focuses on key components such as hazard identification and characterization, dose-response, and exposure. Thus, the determination of risk from infectious disease during long-duration missions is composed of several factors including the concentration and the characteristics of the infectious agent. Therefore, a thorough knowledge of the microorganisms on board a spacecraft is essential in mitigating infectious disease risk to the crew. While preventive measures are taken to minimize the transfer of potential pathogens to spacecraft, several medically significant organisms have been isolated from both the Mir and International Space Station (ISS). Historically, the method for isolation and identification of microorganisms from spacecraft environmental samples depended upon their growth on culture media. While extensive, culture media may still only isolate a small percentage of the viable bacteria from a consortium. Current operational monitoring care of ISS surface, air, and potable water using culture-based techniques to date has shown 1) relatively low microbial concentrations, 2) common environmental isolates, 3) several opportunistic pathogens, 4) occasional spike in microbial concentration level, often associated with unexpected moisture on surfaces, and 5) occasional fluctuation in potable water that could be associated with biofilm buildup.

The Surface, Water, and Air Biocharacterization (SWAB) Flight Experiment was designed with the general aim of developing advanced collection and analysis techniques to better understand the microbial ecology and potential health risks in spacecraft, specifically focusing on the application of molecular identification techniques. The specific aims of this experiment were:

  • Collection of preflight and in-flight surface, air and water samples using methods that would allow for long-term storage of samples
  • Extraction of DNA from environmental samples that may be used to perform molecular analyses
  • Analysis of samples using Denaturing Gradient Gel Electrophoresis (DGGE)
  • Development of real-time PCR assays to detect specific molecular targets for specific medically significant organisms

    APPROACH:
    Air, surface and water samples were collected on board the ISS, approximately 48 hours before docked operations with all launch vehicles. Collection of all samples into a liquid simplified handling and enabled advanced analysis. To preserve a representative sample for microbial quantification, the samples were refrigerated after collection and destowed as soon as possible from the returning space shuttle.

    Surface samples were taken at a variety of locations, including air supply surfaces, food locker surfaces, and water dispenser surfaces. A surface sampling tube containing a Dacron swab and phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) was removed from the SWAB kit. The swab was used to swab a 25 cm squared surface area. The swab was then returned to the vial and marked with the date and location where the sample was collected using a Sharpie marker. Upon return to Earth, the swab and buffer were sonicated to facilitate microbial detachment into the liquid.

    Potable water samples were collected directly into 1 liter Teflon bags currently approved for in-flight use. ISS water sampling sites included the US Potable Water Dispenser (PWD) that distributes water for potable use. Surface samples were collected using a modified damp swab and liquid vial produced by Charm Sciences. Air samples were collected using gelatin filters incorporated into the Sartorius MD 8 Air Port System.

    Denaturing Gradient Gel Electrophoresis (DGGE):
    DNA samples were analyzed for relative concentration and identity of ribosomal sequences using a combination of PCR, Denaturing Gradient Gel Electrophoresis (DGGE), and 16S ribosomal analysis for identification. 16S-ribosomal DNA was extracted from the consortium and amplified using a universal primer set. This amplified mixture of various ribosomal sequences was separated using DGGE to determine the number of bacterial species present in a sample. The isolated DNA was eluted from the gels and sequenced for identification. Identification was determined by comparison of the sequences with the National Center for Biotechnology Information database.

    Real Time PCR:
    All samples except potable water were analyzed for specific fungal species using PCR primers for medically significant or indicative fungi, including Aspergillus fumigates and Stachybotrys chartarum. A relative moldiness index (RMI) multiplex technique developed by the Environmental Protection Agency was also utilized to provide a thorough fungal characterization. Samples were also analyzed for the presence of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV).

    Whole Genome Analysis:
    ISS water samples were analyzed by whole genome sequencing performed at the University of Houston Institute for Molecular Design using technology developed by Illumina, Inc.

    RESULTS:
    Preflight sampling was completed for air, surface, and water samples. In-flight sample collection was completed for a total of eight air, surface, and water sample collection sessions. In-flight hardware performed well, and the surface sampling device received positive feedback from the crew for its ease of use.

    Denaturing Gradient Gel Electrophoresis (DGGE)
    The DGGE technique was found to be less sensitive than culture-based methods. One million cells need to be present to detect a PCR band on an agarose gel. In addition, DGGE has a greater incidence of Gram-negative bacteria on surface samples when compared to culture methods. Subsequent experiments suggested that primer bias or contamination was not the cause.

    Real Time PCR
    To determine the utility of QPCR for monitoring and the potential presence of two toxigenic fungi, preflight and in flight samples were analyzed using QPCR analysis developed for the detection of Aspergillus fumigates and Stachybotrys chartarum at the University of Nevada Las Vegas. These fungi were not detected. The use of QPCR was further investigated in a collaborative effort with colleagues from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). In this study, dust from four ISS vacuum bags and two HEPA filters used from 2007 to 2009 were returned to the ground for QPCR-based molecular analysis. An environmental relative moldiness index (ERMI) multiplex technique developed by the EPA was also utilized to provide a thorough fungal characterization. The most common species measured was P. chrysogenum followed by Aureobasidium pullulans. Of the 36 species in the standard ERMI analysis, 17 were detected at some concentration. Results were comparable to what would be found in a home.

    Finally, QPCR technology was tested by analyzing 336 environmental samples (both pre- and in flight) from spacecraft surfaces (266), water (5) and air (70) for the presence of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV). These latent viruses may be carried asymptomatically by the crew and have the potential to be “reactivated” into live, infectious viruses. This reactivation has been associated with stress and suppressed immune function. Analyses revealed no CMV in any samples. VZV was detected in 6 air samples and 5 surface samples. EBV was detected in 2 air samples and 10 surface samples.
