experiment_title: Metabolism of Red Blood Cells
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Previous space flight studies revealed that exposure to microgravity causes changes in red blood cells (erythrocytes), which are manifested in changes in erythrocyte mass, a decreased osmotic stability and alterations in metabolic parameters. Changes in erythrocyte shape and plasma membrane parameters were observed during and after previous space flights in humans and animals, and can cause a deterioration in erythrocyte function. The purpose of this investigation was to determine and evaluate the dynamics of the changes in erythrocyte function during and after space flight. In particular, the parameters of (1) energy metabolism, (2) oxidation-reduction system, and (3) condition of plasma membrane were evaluated.

APPROACH:
The biochemical characteristics of erythrocytes were studied before flight (at L-60 and L-30), during flight (Mission Day (MD) 14, MD 90 and MD 108), and postflight on R+0 and R+9 (days after landing) on three astronauts. Before and after flight the studies were performed using intact and frozen erythrocytes and whole blood, whereas during flight only frozen erythrocyte samples were collected. The erythrocytes were obtained from venous blood stabilized with EDTA, which was centrifuged and then frozen at -20 degrees Celsius until analysis.

To analyze the changes in energy metabolism, oxidation-reduction system, and the condition of the plasma membrane, a series of parameters was determined:

  • Energy metabolism was determined by content of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), glycolysis rate, activity of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and hexokinase (HK).

  • The oxidation-reduction system was determined by the content of reduced glutathione and glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity.

  • The condition of plasma membrane was evaluated based on parameters describing the lipid and phospholipid composition and the activity of the transport ATPases for sodium ions (Na+), potassium ions (K+), calcium ions (Ca++), and magnesium ions (Mg++).

    The metabolic indices were assayed using spectrophotomeric techniques. Lipid and phospholipid composition were studied with thin-layer chromatography, and the extraction was performed by the method of Bligh and Dyer. The transport ATPase activity was based on the decrease in inorganic phosphate content associated with ATP dephosphorylation in the incubation medium at +38 degrees Celsius.

    RESULTS:
    Glutathione levels and ATPase activity could not be determined for the samples taken on MD 14. Also, hexokinase activity was not determined for samples taken on MD 90, MD 108 and postflight on R+0 and R+9 due to an insufficient amount of cell material.

    The analyzed data showed that, starting from MD 14, the ATP level decreased, mainly in one subject, and the activity of glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase decreased in all three subjects. This effect, as well as a decline in the intracellular ATP content, may indicate a decrease in cellular resistance. This suggestion is also confirmed by data about plasma membrane characteristics. In particular, the activity for Na+, K+, Ca++ ATPases were declined, which may have been caused by changes in the membrane’s physical and chemical properties and in the composition of its main components, the lipids and proteins.

    The study of lipid and phospholipid composition of the membranes revealed significant changes in the cholesterol content, which was increased in all crewmembers inflight and postflight, starting on MD 14 and was still elevated on R+9 in all three crewmembers. While the phospholipid content of the membrane remained practically at the same level, the elevated cholesterol content indicated a change in the membrane’s phase state -- an increase in the membrane’s rigidity and a possible reduction of its deformability.

    Postflight, the ATP level and the glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity were increased in all three crewmembers compared to inflight data. Also, the Na+, K+, and Ca++ ATPase activity was increased. Elevated lactate levels measured on R+0 indicated the prevalence of anaerobic processes.

    On R+9 virtually all parameters were within the normal range except for cholesterol content and reduced glutathione content in two subjects. The membrane cholesterol levels of these two subjects remained elevated and the glutathione content was significantly decreased.

    Overall, the results of this investigation showed significant inflight changes in erythrocyte metabolism and membrane condition for all subjects. The observed destabilization of the cell membrane may have resulted from changes in the blood plasma, caused by shifts in hormone levels, electrolyte balance and lipid metabolism. But direct effects of space flight on the quality of erythrocytes cannot be excluded.

experiment_title: Space Adaptation Effects on Immune System Impacts Reproductive Function and Mammary Gland Development Across Generations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
Space travel results in adaptation to unique conditions that include exposure to low doses of cosmic radiation and microgravity, and heightened stress. Adapting to these physiological and psychological stressors can alter hormone and immune functions, disrupting normal development of hormone-sensitive organs and negatively impacting reproductive health. Studies investigating mammary gland development in young adult mice will help define how adaptations to space travel can influence these fundamental processes. The ductal network of the mammary gland contains a number of different cell types including epithelial cells, adipocytes, immune cells, vascular endothelial cells, and fibroblasts. Signaling between these cell types is highly sensitive to environmental perturbations. In addition, both hormone and immune responses have been shown to play a critical role in ductal network branching of the developing mammary gland. A combination of novel assays will be used to understand how space exposures impact immune function adversely affecting mammary gland development, stem cell populations, and the reproductive ability of mice. We will test whether space adaptation-induced epigenetic changes in the oocytes of mice correlate with reproductive ability. We hypothesize that the space environment weakens the immune system, and alters hormone balance resulting in alterations in number and function of mammary stem cells and development of the mammary gland. Additionally, we hypothesize that epigenetic changes as a result of space exposure will affect reproductive capability as compared to mice on Earth. We further propose that the sensitivity to these effects is dependent on the genetic background of exposed mice. These studies will aid in defining how alterations in immune function from adaptation to space travel and subsequent re-adaptation on Earth, results in defects in organ development, reproductive ability, and epigenetic changes affecting the fitness of subsequent generations.

Definition stage, ground-based experiments to prepare for in-flight space studies. Hypothesis for ground-based study: We will test the hypothesis that the genetically driven sensitivity of the immune system affects mammary gland development post fractionated Low LET (low energy transfer) radiation exposures. In space flight, mice are subject to chronic low-dose radiation exposures. This low dose of radiation exposure may have a significant impact on endocrine function and immune response and influence organ development. Prior to in-flight experiments it would be useful to perform ground-based studies using fractionated X-ray exposures to streamline procedures and to obtain information regarding how genetic background and associated immune system response impacts mammary gland development following radiation exposures. To answer this, we propose to test our hypothesis with the following specific aims in these modified ground-based studies:

AIM 1: To determine how low-dose fractionated radiation affects immune function in young adult mice and its consequences on mammary organ development.

AIM 1.1: To examine acute effects of immune response to low-dose fractionated radiation on mammary gland development.

AIM 1.2: To investigate how genetic background modulates the biological effects of fractionated radiation.

APPROACH:
The preliminary portion of this study involves ground-based work to optimize protocols and define whether very low doses of fractionated radiation exposures, given to mimic the low constant radiation in space, will influence mammary gland development and genetics role in this effect. For this study we will sacrifice two genetically diverse strains of mice (C57BL/6 radiosensitive and BALB/c radiosensitive) and perform analysis of endpoints identical to that described for the ISS experiments. Initially we will just expose mice to radiation, but in subsequent experiments we will also expose mice to LPS prior to radiation as will be done in space. These studies will help to optimize assays and timepoints for in flight experiments. For ground-based radiation only work we have performed one study using 36 mice and a second study we are in the midst of using 24 mice (in both cases ½ of each of these mice are of a different genetic background). Our next phase will involve a smaller experiment exposing 24 mice to two doses LPS (12 mice each dose) to confirm optimal dose +/- radiation and its dependence on the mouse strain.

Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulates the innate immune response and will allow us to test the immune system function following the low dose radiation or aboard ISS. Once these preliminary ground-based studies are complete, we will be ready for the next phase of the work aboard ISS. The ISS study entails two different phases, one centering on understanding acute effects of adaptation to space environment, whereby animals will be sacrificed in space and relevant organs and blood sent back for processing. The second phase of the study will focus on understanding re-adaptation effects, and for these studies animals will be sent back and studied for a period before sacrificing a fraction of the animals to test as in AIM 1. Additionally the effects on reproduction and potential epigenetic effects on sperm and egg will be studied by mating some of the mice upon re-adaptation to earth. Overall ~240 mice will be used in this study.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Defining the Role of the Receptor Like Kinase FERONIA in Plant Architecture Development Under Mechanical Load
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The principal objective of this research proposal is to understand how mechanical loads imposed by gravity are translated into developmental programs that maintain structural integrity of the plant body.

APPROACH:
Specifically, we will investigate the role of the plasma membrane receptor-like kinase FERONIA in this process, as we have recently discovered that FERONIA is crucial to normal mechanical signaling and mechanical development of the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana (Mouse Ear Cress). We will employ fluorescence microscopy, growth kinematics, molecular biology, and genomic approaches to investigate the impact of variable gravity conditions on plant architecture development and to define how FERONIA interacts with mechanical signal transduction pathways.

RESULTS:
Cellular perception of mechanical stress is of fundamental importance to living systems. In plants, environmental mechanical stresses shape plant architecture from the cellular level to the level of organ formation. We have previously identified a receptor-like kinase, FERONIA, as a key regulator of mechanical Ca2+ signaling and control element of root growth responses to environmental mechanical stresses and turgor-driven cellular expansion. We have now further found that FER is also an important regulator of seedling shoot responses to mechanical perturbation. Whether FER functions as a true mechanosensor remains to be established, but current evidence suggests that FER is directly involved in the early phases of mechanical signal transduction. We have developed computer-vision-assisted assays to monitor how mechanical signaling affects the mechanical properties of cell walls in living, intact organs at subcellular spatial and second temporal resolution.

experiment_title: Evaluation of Microbial Capture Device in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Currently, the NASA imposed water quality requirements provide maximum contaminant limits for physical parameters, inorganic compounds, organic compounds, and microbiological constituents. These requirements, most specifically the microbiological requirement of one colony-forming unit (CFU)/100 milliliters (ml), mandate that sources of contamination in potable water be minimized and controlled. Data collected during Shuttle, Apollo, and Skylab missions imply that a closed system could become significantly contaminated by both bacteria and fungi from long-term habitation.

Paramount to controlling the introduction of contaminants into the potable water system is the ability to accurately and consistently monitor the quality of spacecraft potable water. The collection and in-flight microbiological analysis of Shuttle potable water is necessary to evaluate the operation of hardware and the growth of microorganisms in a 0-g environment.

Flight evaluations of this hardware are required since there is no information concerning the complete integration of microbial potable water testing procedures in a 0-g environment. Although KC-135 testing has demonstrated the fluid transfer capabilities of the Microbial Capture Device (MCD), concern still exists over the ability of the bacteria to adhere to the MCD in 0-g.

The findings from this investigation will help determine and direct the need for redesign of water sampling hardware and microbial procedures for future routine application on long-duration missions.

APPROACH:
The Water Microbiology Kit (WMK) is a compact series of consumables that allows for the enumeration of water borne microbes. The proposed method for testing microbial quality of spacecraft water supplies is a traditional technique involving membrane filtration. This method has been adapted for space flight by the use of an off-the-shelf filter unit developed by Millipore Corporation for the field analysis of water. The Millipore Field Monitor, or what is called the microbial capture device (MCD) is a sealed filter unit that allows for filtration of any volume of liquid across a 0.45 µm cellulose acetate filter. The filter sits on top of an absorbent pad that allows for the addition of microbial growth medium to the pad, presenting nutrients for growth of the trapped microbes. Samples include ground supplied controls and flight collected galley water.

RESULTS:
STS-70: The kit was used successfully. Water containing bacteria grew in zero gravity as well as on the ground. Sterile water was processed successfully on orbit without contamination. The galley water contained bacteria, thus allowing a performance check of direct enumeration in flight. Two problems were encountered in flight, (1) separation of the luer fitting from the MCD and (2) the in ability to process the expected amount of water (only 50-70% of the expected sample volume was pulled across the filter). The first problem has been corrected by manufacture of a custom MCD fitting. The second problem appears to be associated with the syringe pump, The syringe pump has been altered, but not tested in flight.

STS-94: DT0-677 was successfully completed on this mission. The objective of DT0-677 was to test the ability of the hardware to transfer fluid from the sample bag across the MCD to the waste bag. On a previous flight (STS-70) only 50-70 % of the expected volume was transferred. After STS-70 the syringe pump was modified to enhance fluid transfer in microgravity. DT0-677 on STS-94 confirmed the successful modification of the syringe pump in that 95-102% of the expected volume was transferred.

experiment_title: Sporesat Mission: Investigating biophysical mechanisms of plant gravisensing using a lab-on-a-chip approach
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

SporeSat is a Small Complete Mission based on a Mission of Opportunity-2 nanosatellite designed for real time measurement of calcium signaling and maintenance of variable gravity treatments during flight. The impetus for SporeSat is to gain a deeper knowledge of the molecular and biophysical mechanisms for plant gravity sensing by studying the activation of cell gravity-sensing and electrophysiological signaling in the single-cell model system, Ceratopteris richardii, using a novel ‘lab-on-a-chip’ microsensor technology platform called a CEL-C advanced bioCD.

Science Objectives: 1) Determine gravity thresholds for Ca2+ channel activation in wild-type spores; 2) Observe Ca2+ current response of gene knockout mutants.

Technology Objectives: 1) Design and fabricate the CEL-C advanced bioCD; 2) Integrate bioCD with data acquisition hardware and ground-based validation experiments; 3) Develop and integrate centrifuge hardware; 4) Operate bioCD in space-relevant environment; 5) Conduct spaceflight experiments.

APPROACH:

In 2013, SporeSat was adapted into a 2 flight mission strategy with flight 1 focused on the technology objectives and flight 2 focused on the scientific objectives. In April 2014, SporeSat-1 was deployed from a SpaceX Falcon 9 launched from Cape Canaveral as part of CRS-3. SporeSat-1 was successfully commanded and science data downloaded.

RESULTS:

The SporeSat mission operations team at Santa Clara University in collaboration with NASA Ames successfully commanded the spacecraft, initiated the experiment, and downloaded the science data, which is currently being analyzed. During the mission the two rotational bioCDs rotated as expected, calcium ISE recordings we obtained from all three bioCDs and temperature data from the RTDs on the bioCDs was obtained. However, the OLED light source failed and one of the three bioCDs overheated (40C) above its target set point (29C).

experiment_title: Specimen Mass Measurement
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objectives of the Specimen Mass Measurement experiment were to demonstrate the accuracy of mass measurement under weightless conditions, to validate the use of the Specimen Mass Measurement Device (SMMD) in measuring solids as well as fluids, and to support Skylab experiments M071and M073 which required mass determination. Experiment M071 was a metabolic balance study on changes in mineral and nitrogen balances and their effect on the musculoskeletal system. Experiment M073 involved analyzing urine samples to investigate biochemical changes caused by exposure to weightlessness. The SMMD supported these experiments by providing accurate mass measurements of food residues and fecal deposits.

APPROACH:
The Specimen Mass Measurement experiment consisted of preflight and inflight calibrations, tests for repeatability, and mass measurements that supported Skylab experiments M071 and M073. The SMMD was calibrated a number of times during the preflight period with calibration weights that were later used for inflight calibrations. The preflight and inflight calibration data were compared and then used to calculate a correction factor for the gravitational force that influenced the preflight measurements. Five calibrations were performed on each of the Skylab 2 and 3 missions, and six on Skylab 4 mission. The special test designed to verify the repeatability of the SMMD measurements was performed twice on Skylab 3 mission.

The protocols for experiment M071 and M073 incorporated the SMMD to produce raw data pertaining to food residue and fecal weights. Two SMMD's, each with a capacity of one kilogram, were used for these measurements. One was used for the food wrappers and the other was used for the fecal samples and vomitus. The procedure for weighing residual food called for the wrapper or container to be measured with the residual food inside. These weights were later compared to preflight weights for the food samples to determine the amount of nutrients remaining in the wrapper or the container. The procedure for weighing fecal and vomitus samples involved collecting the specimen in a plastic bag and then weighing it. After weighing, the samples were placed in a drying oven before being stored.

The sample measured had to be securely fastened to the device because of the sensitivity of the device to external movement. A perforated elastic sheet held the specimen in place during operation. For the food samples, the SMMD readout (period of oscillations) was recorded and voice transmitted to Earth where mass was calculated and then transmitted back to the crew. For the vomitus and fecal samples, an on-board graphic conversion was used to convert the SMMD readout to mass, which allowed for proper setting of the fecal drying timers. All samples returned to Earth for analysis included records of oscillation periods.

RESULTS:
The SMMD proved to be an instrument worthy of measuring food residue and fecal weights.

experiment_title: Healing Response of Injured Rodent Knee Ligaments to Hindlimb Unweighting and the Therapeutic Efficacy of Growth Hormone
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Short-term and long-term exposure to either microgravity or hindlimb unloading has proven to suppress connective tissue formation in a variety of tissue types. In the growing rodent, hindlimb unloading causes a significant reduction in new bone formation and in knee ligament strength. Additionally, microgravity and hindlimb unloading also dramatically suppress immune function and endocrine function, specifically the reduction of growth hormone secretion in rodents, non-human primates, and humans. In essence, spaceflight has been shown to induce musculoskeletal weakness and reduce the release of various anabolic hormones responsible for growth promoting processes. Normal dense fibrous connective tissue regeneration is significantly impacted by tissue load histories and responds to growth promoting hormones and various cytokines. The rodent model for knee ligament injury and repair has been well characterized and has been used to study wound healing mechanisms by serving as a test physiological system for implementing countermeasures. The primary objective of this study was to use the rodent knee ligament injury repair model to study the impact hindlimb unloading has on the wound healing processes. The investigators hypothesized that hindlimb unloading would (1) diminish the ability of knee ligaments to repair a surgical lesion, and (2) compromise the mechanical and biochemical properties of the ligaments, thus producing inferior material at the site of the ligament lesion. Growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) are potent stimulators of protein synthesis. The investigators have given recombinant human GH (rhGH) and IGF-1 to promote wound healing during hindlimb unloading in the second half of the study. This study focused on critical regenerative pathways of the injured knee ligaments after three weeks and seven weeks post-surgery. Collagen metabolism, tissue cytokine gene expression, collagen fibril organization, and tissue material properties in surgically oblated and non-surgical sham ligaments have been thoroughly examined

This study will provide essential insight on injury response to microgravity. Clinicians can use the data from this study to determine the time course effects of unweighting on the healing response of knee ligaments. Information generated from this study will aid in the development of appropriate countermeasures for astronauts who acquire soft tissue injuries during chronic exposure to microgravity. Secondly, since GH secretion is compromised in animals and human astronauts during acute and chronic spaceflight, the assessment of the therapeutic efficacy of rhGH on soft tissue recovery as a hormonal countermeasure during hindlimb unloading has intrigue. rhGH and IGF-I will be investigated as a potential anabolic modulator to decrease the wound healing duration in a simulated microgravity environment. This therapy may prove useful not only in the spaceflight environment, but could be targeted to site specific tissues to decrease the time needed for regeneration and provide a rapid healing response during normal orthopaedic surgery. APPROACH:
The methodology for this study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
The surgeries and hindlimb unweighting experimental protocol has proven to be a successful animal model to study unloading on MCL wound healing. Hindlimb unweighting has a profound effect on ligament strength, matrix organization and the rate of ligament repair during wound healing. The integrity of the ligament is compromised during hindlimb unloading and the addition of time (3 weeks + an additional 4 weeks = Total 7 weeks) as a component to aid in healing actually further delays the wound repair process in the MCL. IGF-1 showed a significant effect in ultimate strength, stress and modulus in ambulatory animals, which was significantly less in the hindlimb unloaded animals. The combination of GH+IGF-1 revealed a significant effect in hindlimb unloaded animals, which was not present in ambulatory animals. The strength gains in the IGF-1 treated wounded ligaments can be attributed to increases in collagen gene expression (Collagen type I and III) mature collagen cross-link formation, collagen organization and decreased tissue cellularity. IGF-1 and GH+IGF-1 treated HLS+lesion groups similarly increased MCL tissue strength, collagen gene expression and tissue cellularity decreased. Together, these data suggest that IGF-1 alone or in a combination with rhGH may be a viable countermeasure to facilitate improved MCL wound healing.

experiment_title: Monitoring of Sweat Calcium Using Skin Patches
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone loss can occur during bed rest due to lack of limb use, and exercise has been researched as a potential countermeasure. Calcium loss in sweat from this normal exercise program has been a concern, especially if the exercise occurs at normal room temperature.

In previous bed rest studies, early changes in bone mass have been detected by measuring calcium. Past subjects have undergone a negative calcium balance due to a rapid increase in calcium excretion through the urine and feces. Most studies did not measure calcium loss in sweat, because researchers assumed that the loss had a negligible effect on calcium balance. This assumption was not tested often, partly because an accurate measurement of sweat calcium was difficult. However, one previous study showed that calcium loss through sweat was much greater during one hour of running on a treadmill at room temperature than for the entire remainder of the day. The mean value of the calcium loss was 47 mg per hour while running and 0.8 mg per hour for the rest of the day. Another earlier study also supported the conclusion that sweat calcium loss was greater during strenuous exercise than for sedentary activities. Thus, loss of calcium in sweat could indeed prove to be a significant factor in total body calcium loss, especially when the countermeasures for bone density loss are applied. Since bone density and calcium balance are important factors in health, countermeasures against their degradation need to be optimized and a simple, reliable method of calcium sweat detection should be determined.

This bed rest study had two main purposes. First, researchers tested a non-invasive sweat collection method for its ability to monitor sweat calcium loss. Second, changes in skin calcium loss were measured with and without a resistive exercise countermeasure performed at a lower environmental temperature.

APPROACH:
The subjects of this bed rest study consisted of six females (five white and 1 black) and ten males (nine white and one black). The subjects ages ranged from 22 to 48 years, and weight ranged from 60 to 97 kg. Heights ranged from 157 to 185 cm.

Subjects were divided into three groups. One group was assigned resistive exercise with a workload that increased progressively throughout the bed rest study. A second group did not exercise, but ingested a drug called alendronate (brand name of Fosamax®), which is used to strengthen bone. The third group did not exercise or ingest a drug; these subjects served as controls.

To collect sweat from the subjects, skin patches (Osteopatch®), were attached to the skin on the back, lower chest, and upper part of the arm. Initial studies involved placing two patches, one on each side of the body, on each area for a total of six patches. Later the number was reduced from two patches to one per body region. Data from the patches were collected from four different time periods: a baseline ambulatory time before bed rest and at 6, 12 and 17 weeks of bed rest. Patches were worn for 24 hours on two consecutive days.

The subjects that were assigned resistive exercise performed the exercise six days a week with no exercise performed on Sunday. The two consecutive days for exercise sweat collection occurred within this six-day period so that both days contained exercise. For this group of subjects, sweat was collected on rest days, as well as exercise days. Since there were not two consecutive days without exercise, this sweat collection occurred on two successive Sundays. The bed rest room temperature was 23 to 26°C. The room temperature during exercise was 18°C or less to minimize sweat loss.

The skin patch used to collect sweat had an absorbing area of 14 cm2 and absorbed the solid components of sweat while the fluid evaporated out. The skin was cleaned with an alcohol swab and allowed to dry before the patch was applied. After 24 hours of wear, the patch was removed and the absorption pad portion was refrigerated until analysis. During elution, the pad was placed at the top of a tube and dried for 30 minutes to remove all fluid. One milliliter of distilled water was then added to the pad. After an hour, the tube was centrifuged for ten minutes at 3000 rpm to collect the liquid at the bottom of the tube while the patch remained secured at the top. Calcium concentration was determined from the collected liquid.

RESULTS:
Baseline data, which were taken from 12 subjects, each with six different patches duplicating the three body areas, show no differences between the duplicate body measurements. Significant differences in calcium excretion were found between back versus arm sweat and back versus chest sweat. However no significant differences were found between chest versus arm calcium excretion in sweat. No significant differences were found between the two different but consecutive days. In addition, no interaction or change in the relationships between the three regions was found over the consecutive days. The most variability in the results, 58%, was attributed to body region site with only 0.3% variability attributed to the day and 10% to site by day interaction. The range of inter-individual variability during the baseline collection varied from 18 to 32% for the three regions, with arms at 20% variability, chest at 18% variability and back at 24% variability combined over the days. The inter-individual variability for the two days combined over sites was 20% and 29%.

For seven subjects who did not exercise, data collection occurred over the four time periods. No significant differences were observed between their baseline and the other collections, which occurred at 6, 12 and 17 weeks of bed rest. Some of these subjects ingested the alendronate and others were in the control group.

During the bed rest timeframe, data from five exercise subjects were taken on exercise days and on rest days. No significant differences were observed between the rest days and the exercise days or between the two consecutive exercise days for the same subject.

Total body sweat calcium for the twelve subjects during baseline data collection was averaged for the three sites and was 35 ± 4 mg/day. The mean value for the arm was 33 mg/day. The chest mean value was 35 mg/day and the back was 37 mg/day.

The patch collection method was shown to be reliable for the measurement of sweat calcium loss. This conclusion was supported by the lack of large variations among repeated measurements by day and by site. The small difference between the back calcium excretion and the arm and chest excretion agreed with another published study that found a higher evaporation rate from the back. In this investigation, dermal calcium excretion was not studied during profuse sweating, so no conclusions could be drawn about the use of the skin patch in that circumstance.

No significant differences were found between exercise and rest day values of sweat calcium loss for bed rest subjects that performed resistive exercise with a lower room temperature. In addition, no significant differences were found between baseline and bed rest calcium loss values; this room temperature was also controlled, but was not kept as low as it was during the exercise condition. Calcium excretion in sweat has been shown in other studies to increase significantly when aerobic exercise was performed at standard room temperature. In this study, no effect was observed on sweat calcium due to exercise. This observation was due to the cool environment in which the exercise was performed and also, possibly, to the fact that the exercise in this study was resistive rather than aerobic.

This bed rest study showed that the skin patch could be used to determine the amount of calcium excreted in human sweat for up to 24 hours in normal sweating conditions. Any changes in sweat calcium from bed rest, with or without exercise in a cool environment, did not significantly affect total body calcium balance.

experiment_title: Mir Audible Noise Measurement
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Besides weightlessness, there are many stress factors that bombard astronauts and cosmonauts inhabiting long-duration vehicles. With increased stress levels, stress sensitivity increases. One of the goals of the ISS discipline is to minimize the environmental stress factors as much as possible. This experiment measures the acoustical signatures in the exercise area, workstations, and habitation modules within the Mir space station. Questionnaires are also filled out by the crew to ensure completeness. With this information, protective steps can be implemented and sound dampening measures incorporated into the International Space Station (ISS).

1. To ensure the Mir environment does not exceed the acoustic emission requirements.
2. To account for where acoustic mitigation may be required to assure crew protection.

APPROACH:
The MANM hardware (sound level meter, one-third-octave filter, microphone, acoustic dosimeter, audio recorder, and headphones) was taken to the Mir and positioned in 10 locations within the designated modules. Sound levels were measured in the core module (3 locations), Kvant-2 (3 locations), Kvant (1 location), Spektr (2 locations), and the docking module (1 location). Crewmembers noted the location using the audio recorder and took sound level measurements. Sound level measurements were taken about the center frequencies of 63, 125, 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, and 8000 Hz. Questionnaires were also completed during flight to document the crewmembers' subjective acceptability of the measured noise levels.

RESULTS:
All ten planned locations were measured, and all desired sound level meter data were captured with the exception of the higher frequency spectral data for the Kvant-2 airlock. The lowest sound pressure levels in Mir existed at this location and dropped below the sound level meter range chosen.

The NC 50 curve was exceeded at all measurement locations except in the Kvant-2 airlock compartment. Mir science and exercise activities during the docked period of STS-74 were low; transfer operations predominated during this period. Sound level meter data, dosimeter measurements, and questionnaire responses are understandably different due to the varying lengths and places of noise exposure.

Overall, the crew's subjective impressions of the Mir acoustic environment were favorable. However, the limited time of exposure and lack of science and exercise activities during the docked period may have skewed the responses. While the NC 50 curve is exceeded, the sound pressure levels at all locations were lower than anticipated based on past data documentation.

experiment_title: NSCOR: The Contribution of Non-targeted Effects in HZE Cancer Risk
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Clear mechanistic understanding of the biological processes elicited by high linear energy transfer (LET) radiation increased cancer risk will reduce the uncertainties in assessing the risk of space flight. Classic targeted radiation effects such as cell kill and mutation are proportional to dose and their LET dependence is described by relative biological effectiveness (RBE). However recent data suggests that high LET radiation affects multicellular processes that promote cancer. The investigators propose that radiation carcinogenesis results from two classes of ionizing radiation effect: targeted effects that alter genomic sequence and non-targeted effects (NTE) that alter phenotype and multicellular interactions. Since NTE are not proportional to dose, new approaches are required to assess the impact of NTE, which alter gene expression, cell signaling, genomic stability, and cell phenotypes, on carcinogenesis. It is unknown to what extent NTE contribute to the significantly greater carcinogenic effect of high LET radiation. Investigators hypothesize that NTE promotes epithelial cancer.

APPROACH:
This project used experimental studies and modeling to define the efficiency and physiological context in which high LET radiation exposure increases epithelial cancer risk. Investigators hypothesized that NTEs both contribute to radiation carcinogenesis. Targeted effects includes DNA damage responses and changes in genomic sequence that is the result of interaction between ionizing irradiation and DNA. NTE alter the phenotype and multicellular interactions that can contribute to cancer. The hypothesis proposed that the greater carcinogenic risk from high LET irradiation is due to NTE promotion of targeted radiation effects. The NSCOR was composed of three projects at New York University (NYU), University of California San Francisco (UCSF), and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL).

RESULTS:
The goal of Project 1 was to determine the contribution of NTE as a function of radiation quality on breast cancer. Investigators used a radiation chimera mammary model to discern the effects of radiation-induced microenvironment from DNA damage and potential mutation. In this model they first surgically cleared the mammary gland of endogenous epithelium. Then the mouse was irradiated and the fat-pad subsequently orthotopically transplanted with un-irradiated, non-malignant epithelial cells primed for malignant transformation by Trp53 deletion that were evaluated for tumors for 600 days.

To compare the contribution of targeted and NTE, investigators irradiated mice after Trp53 null outgrowth was established (i.e., epithelium was exposed, i.e., targeted and NTE) and the other group was irradiated before transplantation (i.e., NTE only, epithelium was not exposed). Tumors in mice irradiated with densely ionizing 600 MeV/amu Fe charged particles or sparsely ionizing gamma-ray radiation were compared to those in contemporaneous sham-irradiated controls. Irradiation of the in situ mammary outgrowth with either radiation quality decreased Trp53 null tumor latency and increased tumor frequency a year after. Mammary tumor latency arising from non-irradiated Trp53 null outgrowths in irradiated hosts was also decreased indicating that this effect was mediated by the microenvironment. Tumors arising from densely ionizing irradiated outgrowths gave rise to aggressive tumors with increased growth rate compared to sham-irradiated mice. Importantly, increased tumor aggressiveness was also observed in tumors arising from irradiated hosts, suggesting that this effect was mediated by NTE. Only densely ionizing radiation affected tumor markers of differentiation in both models. The data from these studies supports the conclusion that tumor aggressiveness is indirectly promoted by NTE and that NTE elicited by HZE particles results in more aggressive tumors. The RNA of these tumors has been sequenced. Notably, preliminary analysis using unsupervised clustering separated tumors arising from irradiated epithelium in irradiated hosts (i.e., targeted) from those that arose in irradiated mice.

Investigators also evaluated the effect of age in the radiation chimera-experiment; mice were irradiated at 10 months, simulating the average age for astronauts. Notably high LET exposure of aged mice is much more efficient inducing tumorigenesis than low LET. Cancer incidence in humans increases exponentially with age, with 75% of newly diagnosed cases occurring in susceptible populations aged 55 years or older. The aging process has been shown to be associated with increased levels of chronic inflammation, which are thought to contribute to many age-associated diseases, including cancer, and increased serum levels of IL-6 have been reported in older individuals. Interestingly, A-bomb survivors have significant increases in serum IL-6 levels that are still detectable five decades after exposure. These findings suggested the possibility that radiation carcinogenesis, at least in part, is mediated by induction of a pro-inflammatory environment similar to the aging process.

To test this, mice were irradiated at 10 months of age, comparable to the middle age of astronauts during space flight missions to test the hypothesis that NTE overlap with the biology that increases cancer incidence in aged versus young people. The inguinal mammary glands of 200 mice were cleared at three weeks of age and the mice housed under standard conditions. Hosts were irradiated at 10 months of age with 10, 50, or 100 cGy gamma-radiation or 350 MeV/amu Ar or Si, or 600 MeV/amu Fe at a fluence of 1 particle per 102 mm, and transplanted three days later with Trp53 null epithelium. Tumorigenesis was monitored for 600 days. As expected due to decreased ovarian hormones in aged mice, fewer mammary outgrowths were obtained in aged mice; outgrowth efficiency is greater than 90% in young mice mammary but approximately 50% in aged mice. This limited the ability to compare dose or particles individually. However, investigators were able to compare tumors arising in sham-irradiated mice to gamma-irradiated hosts or HZE-irradiated hosts. Age and radiation NTE were not epistatic as both low- and high-LET irradiation of aged hosts significantly increased tumor incidence and tumor growth rate. Moreover, this experiment revealed a strong radiation quality effect in which HZE NTE was considerably more effective than gamma-radiation.

Expression profiling of these tumors indicate that the top ranked (p> 0.00001) processes that distinguish tumors from aged mice irradiated with HZE particles from age-matched, sham-irradiated tumors were inflammation (70 genes), immune cell trafficking (79 genes), and cancer (271 genes). Among the 20 most significant upstream regulators ranked by z-score (p <0.05), the majority are pro-inflammatory factors such as IL-1ß, TNFalpha, and IL6. Consistent with previous findings, TGFß1 is predicted by IPA to also be a significant regulator in cancers from both HZE and gamma-irradiated host. Investigators speculate that gamma- and HZE-irradiated microenvironments might evoke common mediators, but their magnitude or persistence might be different. Among the top-ranked upregulated molecules are COX2 and granzyme H. They validated this signature using relative COX2 transcript abundance and protein expression, which support high levels of COX-2 in tumors arising in HZE-irradiated mice.

Together these data lead investigators to postulate that a high degree of immunosuppressive inflammation promotes these aggressive tumors. To test this idea, investigators used immunostaining to evaluate lymphoid and myeloid cellular subsets within tumors. Most strikingly, tumors arising in HZE-irradiated aged hosts have significantly (p <0.05) more myeloid derived suppressor cells (MDSC) and Treg cells compared to tumors arising in age-matched, sham-irradiated hosts. Treg frequency inversely correlates with tumor growth rate and MDSC is positively correlated with Cox2 staining, leading to the new hypothesis that HZE radiation exposure in mid-life is strongly immunosuppressive.

Project 2, directed by Dr. Allan Balmain at UCSF, had the ultimate goal of identifying the genetics associated with susceptibility to cancer risk from high LET radiation. The strategies employed were based on systems genetics approaches to identify germ line polymorphisms and somatic genetic changes associated with tumor development. This project focuses heavily on genetic analysis of radiation-induced tumors.

Interestingly the irradiated tumor spectrum of both Trp53 deltaP and Trp53+/- mice in the FVB/N background falls into three main tumor types: thymic lymphomas, mammary tumors, and skin carcinomas. It should be noted that lymphomas are often observed post-radiation in mice of compromised Trp53 function, particularly after exposure to high radiation doses (4 Gy). After exposure to a low dose (50cGy) of either low or high LET radiation, investigators observed increased frequency of mammary tumors and skin carcinomas in both genotypes. Although the tumor spectrum is similar between mice exposed to high or low LET radiation, there was an increased incidence of mammary tumors following high LET radiation.

The tumor spectrum in 129/Sv Trp53+/- mice was markedly different from FVB/N. Regardless of radiation quality there was a high incidence of thymic lymphomas. A wide range of tumors of varying types with no distinguishable pattern but no skin carcinomas were observed. A small number of mammary tumors developed following high LET radiation (n=3), whilst none were observed in the gamma-irradiated group. These differences further illustrate the influence of background strain upon tumor latency, susceptibility, and spectrum following exposure to high or low LET radiation. These data demonstrate that FVB/N mice are particularly susceptible to radiation-induced mammary tumor development. High LET radiation was also more potent at inducing a higher incidence of mammary tumors with a shorter latency compared to gamma-radiation (p= 0.0004 CoxPH).

Little is known about the mechanisms by which high LET induces carcinogenesis. Exposing mice of abrogated Trp53 function to either high or low LET radiation provided investigators with a unique opportunity to compare and contrast the genetic aberrations and potential radiation-quality specific signatures in tumors. Next generation sequencing offers a powerful tool to gain a deeper understanding of the complex mutational processes driving radiation-induced tumorigenesis.

Project 3, led by Dr. S. V. Costes and Dr. Mao, undertook to use computational modeling of experimental data. Linear-quadratic models have been used for decades to interpret cell survival after exposure to ionizing radiation. However, parameters for these models change with LET, forcing investigators to measure experimentally cell survival for any LET of interest. In contrast to the current paradigm, investigators hypothesize that double strand breaks (DSBs) are moved into repair domains and consequently merge into clusters. Overall, this work suggests that microdosimetric properties of ion tracks at the sub-micron level are sufficient to explain both RIF data and survival curves for any LET, similarly to the Local Effect Model assumption.

experiment_title: Regulation of Blood Volume During Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Human adaptation to space flight is accompanied by a loss of red blood cell mass (RBCM), a loss of plasma volume (PV), and a decrease in total blood volume. This leads to a decrease in gravity-dependent space below the heart. In this study, rats were examined to determine whether similar hemodynamic changes occur, making them a suitable subject for study. SLS-1 marked the first time PV and RBCM were measured before and after flight. SLS-2 allowed for repeat determinations and the first opportunity for inflight assessment of erythropoiesis. An additional inflight experiment tested the ability of the rat bone marrow to respond to a bolus of erythropoietin, the major hormone controlling erythropoiesis in animals and humans.

Approach:

Seven days prior to launch PV and RBCM were determined by isotopic dilution of 125I labeled albumin and 51Cr labeled red blood cells respectively. On flight day 6, five rats (group A) were given 125I labeled albumin and 59Fe injections. Samples were taken ten minutes later to determine PV. Samples to determine 59Fe incorporation into RBCs were taken 24 hours later and on landing day (9 days later). The remaining 10 rats (groups B and C) were given 59Fe injections on flight day 9. Group B was also given a 200-U injection of erythropoietin at this time. Upon landing, RBCM and PV were measured for all flight rats and ground controls. 59Fe incorporation into red blood cells was also determined.

Results:

RBCM showed an increase in both the spaceflight animals and ground control animals, but less of an increase in flight animals. When this increase was normalized for growth (flight animals had a lower growth rate than ground controls), a decrease was seen in the flight animals' RBCM. Plasma volume increased in both flight and ground control animals. The PV increase was greater in ground control animals although not statistically different. 59Fe incorporation was lower in flight animals but again not statistically different. Animals that received erythropoietin injections had higher levels of iron incorporation. Incorporation was not statistically significant, indicating erythropoiesis is stimulated normally under conditions of microgravity.

experiment_title: Examining the Effects of Spaceflight on GSK3 Activation in Murine Muscle
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It is well established that spaceflight leads to muscle and bone loss, and the promising future of long-term spaceflight missions heightens the need to develop interventions that maintain musculoskeletal health. On earth, the deleterious effects observed on muscle and bone with spaceflight mimics the effects observed with human aging (ie. osteoporosis and sarcopenia). Therefore, examining the cellular mechanisms that contribute to muscle and bone loss will help in directing the development of mitigation strategies not only for spaceflight but also for aging on earth. Glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) is an enzyme that has been implicated in several other musculoskeletal conditions. Thus, our proposed research seeks to examine the effects of spaceflight on GSK3 activity in murine soleus muscle and bone while correlating it with markers of muscle proteolysis, oxidative metabolism, and bone mineral density, structure and strength. The specific aims and corresponding hypotheses of our proposal are listed below. For our muscle analyses, we propose to examine the effects of spaceflight on the soleus muscle, given that this muscle is primarily affected by microgravity.

Aim 1: Examining GSK3 activation in muscle and bone samples collected from male C57BL/6 mice from the RR9 mission
Aim 2: Examining GSK3 activation in muscle samples collected from female C57BL/6 from the RR1 mission

APPROACH:
Aim 1 Experimental groups: RR9 male C57BL/6 mice (3-4 month old) were flown onboard the SpaceX Dragon capsule to the International Space Station. The flight group (FLT) mice were in orbit for 33 days. A second set of Vivarium (Viv) and Ground control (GCrerun) experiments were conducted 9 months after the FLT experiment. Our analyses will compare the following groups: FLT, Viv and GCrerun. To control for any variation between cohorts, we will first make comparisons between cohort control 1 (CC1), which was run alongside the FLT group, and cohort control 2 (CC2), which was run alongside Viv and GCrerun. In the event of a significant difference (p < 0.05) between CC2 and CC1, then GCrerun and Viv will be normalized using a calculated factor (CC2/CC1) prior to running a one-way ANOVA with FLT. Based on our previous studies (1-3), we estimate a minimum of 4-10 samples per group across all measures in muscle and bone. According to the Life Sciences Data Archive the right soleus (RNA later), right and left tibias are available for request.

Aim 2 Experimental groups: RR1 female C57BL/6 (3-4 month old) mice were flown onboard the SpaceX4 Dragon capsule to the International Space Station. The flight group (FLT) mice were in orbit for 35 days. A Vivarium control and Ground control were housed on earth at the same time. Similar to Aim 1, we estimate a minimum of number of 4-10 samples per group across all measures in muscle. According to the Life Sciences Data Archive the left and right soleus are both available and stored in RNA later. For the purposes of our experiments we are only requesting right soleus muscles from each experimental group (n = 9-10 per group).

GSK3 activation will be assessed via an enzyme-linked GSK3 activity assay developed in our lab, as well as Western blotting for serine phosphorylation. Increased serine phosphorylation of GSK3 inactivates the kinase and thus an reduction in serine phosphorylation may be indicative of enhanced GSK3 activity. These assays will be completed on muscle (soleus and tibialis anterior) and bone (femur) samples.

Measures of muscle oxidative phenotype will be assessed via Western blotting for proteins that are abundant in oxidative fiber types including: myosin heavy chain I, PGC-1alpha, and other mitochondrial markers. Western blotting will also be conducted to examine muscle proteuloysis, specifically the ubiquitin proteasomal degradation pathway with total ubiquitinylation and the expression of E3 ligases MuRF1 and Atrogin-1. These assays will be completed on muscle (soleus and tibialis anterior) samples.

We will examine bone structure of right tibia's of male mice from the RR9 mission using µCT. Trabecular structural measurements assessed using 3D analyses will include: percent bone volume (BV/TV), trabecular thickness (Tb.Th), trabecular number (Tb.N), trabecular separation (Tb.Sp). Cortical structural measurements using 2D analyses will include: cortical area fraction (Ct.Ar/Tt.Ar), cortical thickness (Ct.Th), periosteal perimeter (Ps.Pm), endocortical perimeter (Ec.Pm), and medullary area (Ma.Ar).

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: In vivo Testing Confirms a Blunting of the Human Cell-Mediated Immune Mechanism During Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Changes in cellular immune potential during or following space flight have been reported in both the U.S. and Russian space programs. These changes were usually discovered using in vitro testing performed after flight, with various findings related to alterations in cellular responses. Direct in-flight, in vivo testing was used in this study to demonstrate the cell-mediated immune (CMI) system response during space flight.

APPROACH:
The delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) response of 10 Space Shuttle astronauts to 7 common recall antigens was measured using the Multitest CMI test system to administer antigens of tetanus, diphtheria, Streptococcus, Proteus, old tuberculin, Candida, and Trichophyton to the forearm after 2, 4, or 8 days of flight. This approach was used because DTH accompanies many manifestations of CMI and because skin reactions have often provided a model for the elucidation of effector mechanisms in CMI. Readings were conducted 48 hours after antigen administration. Data were evaluated in three ways: (a) the number of positive responses of the 7 possible, (b) the individual mean diameter (mm) of the positive response, and (c) the total sum, in mm, of all the positive reactions (reaction score).

RESULTS:
The mean number of reactions was reduced from 4.5 before flight to 3.0 during flight, and the mean reaction score was reduced from 21.4 mm before flight to 13.7 mm during flight. The data suggest the CMI system was still being degraded by space flight conditions on day 4 of flight, and between day 5 and day 10 the depression maximized and the system began to stabilize at the new level.

experiment_title: Analysis of the Skylab Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A well-defined Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program was first introduced into the space program on the Apollo 14 mission. The program was initiated following a number of prime crew illnesses and crew exposure to persons with infectious illnesses during mission critical periods. As a result of these incidences, it was recognized throughout the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) that crew illness could cause loss in valuable crew training time, postponement of missions, or could even compromise crew safety and mission success.

The purpose of the Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program was, therefore, to minimize the possibility of adverse alterations in the health of flight crewmen during the preflight, in-flight, and postflight periods.

APPROACH:
A 21-day isolation period was established for the Skylab crew prior to the launch of each mission. The 21-day period was chosen as it covered the incubation period for a majority of infectious disease organisms. A 7-day postflight isolation period was also imposed to protect the crew from any increased susceptibility to infectious diseases because of the lengthy mission. Reducing the possibility of a crewman being exposed to an infectious disease agent was accomplished by:

1) Establishing a primary work area for the crewmen during isolation periods
2) Establishing isolated crew housing at both the Kennedy and Johnson Space Centers (KSC and JSC) with methods to prevent crew exposure to infectious disease agents
3) Establishing a medical program for those persons who were required to work with the crewmen during the isolation periods, and
4) Establishing a Medical Surveillance Office as a coordination center for the operational aspects of the program.

Personnel who would come into direct contact (within 2 meters) of the crew were known as class A primary contacts; these persons were required to wear surgical masks when in the presence of the crew. Persons who worked in primary work areas, but were not in direct contact with crewmembers were called class B primary contacts.

For each primary work area identified, the area was inspected and procedures were established to minimize the possibility of crew exposure to pathogenic microorganisms. Positive air pressures and 80 percent ASHRAM (American Society of Heating, Refrigeration, and Air-Conditioning Engineers) air filters were used in the principal training area. A security guard and a nurse were stationed at the door of the primary work areas on the days that crewmen would be in the area. Only properly badged primary contacts were allowed to enter the area on these days.

Crew housing at JSC consisted of four mobile homes. Two were placed inside a large building; a third mobile home adjacent to the building served as the food service center. All food and drink consumed by the crew during the isolation period was specially prepared Skylab food (quality control had been designed into the food program, so no additional controls were needed). A fourth mobile home was available for isolation should any crewman become ill. Housing at KSC was provided in existing crew quarters and high efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters were used in these living quarters to reduce airborne pathogens. Measures were taken to prevent crew exposure to illness while traveling between primary work areas. Non-primary contacts were kept at least 100 feet away from the crew. Biorespirators were kept near the crew at all times in the event of an emergency.

All primary contacts were given thorough examinations to ascertain their freedom from infectious diseases. Immunizations were given to those persons who were not immune to certain infectious diseases. Based on the results of the medical examinations, these persons were either approved or disapproved as primary contacts. Class A primary contacts (such as food handlers or personnel needing close direct or indirect contact with the crews) underwent further examinations later in the program. All primary contacts were instructed to report any illness or contact to an infectious illness to the Medical Surveillance Office. A primary contact found to have an infectious illness was temporarily withdrawn from the program and the primary work area. Re-admittance to the program occurred only after a medical examination indicated the infection was no longer present.

A report form was completed by the clinical staff for each occurrence of illness and forwarded to the Medical Surveillance Office. The report was coded for the type of illness using predetermined operational definitions of infectious illness. Medical surveillance continued throughout each mission to provide epidemiological support data for any crew illness occurring during the mission.

RESULTS:
The list of approved primary contacts changed throughout the Skylab program, as names were added or deleted as required; the total number of primary contacts ranged from 620 to 709 throughout the program. The majority of the primary contacts were located at JSC. During the Skylab preflight phase, a modified Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program was initiated at the Marshall Space Flight Center, where additional training was being conducted. The primary contacts reported both illnesses and contact with sick persons to the Medical Surveillance Office.

The majority of illness reports and reports of contacts with illness originated from JSC. A total of 197 illnesses were reported to the Medical Surveillance Office during the Skylab program; 88 percent were reported from JSC. A total of 73 contacts with illness were reported during Skylab 2 and 4; Skylab 3 contacts with illness were not reported because of an error in the recording of the reports.

The rate of illness reported by the primary contacts declined from Skylab 2 to Skylab 4. During Skylab 2, the rate of illness reporting was 10.7 illnesses per 1000 primary contacts per week. During Skylab 3 the rate declined to 8.4, and during Skylab 4 to 6.7. The drop in illness rate is especially dramatic since the lowest rates occurred during the winter season when most respiratory infections were expected.

Active surveillance of class A primary contacts produced only 23 referrals to the clinic from a total of 3483 examinations. The small number of possible illnesses that were discovered suggests that active surveillance indirectly influenced the primary contacts to report their illnesses voluntarily. In addition, the presence of a nurse at the entrance of the primary work area may have indirectly protected the crew from infectious agents.

The most frequently reported illness by primary contacts was the upper respiratory infection. Syndromes other than the upper respiratory infection were relatively low and equally distributed in number. All of the percentages were below 10 percent with the exception of the reported presence of fever, which reached 14 percent during Skylab 3 and 11 percent during Skylab 4.

Exposure to persons with upper respiratory infections was the most frequently reported contact with illness. Fifty-seven percent were reported for Skylab 2 and 67 percent for Skylab 4. Skylab 3 contacts with illness were not reported due to an error in recording reports. However, the reporting trend appeared to decrease in rate in the same manner as illness reporting. A greater percentage of contacts with upper and lower enteric illness were reported for Skylab 4 than for Skylab 2. None of the Skylab 4 reports involved skin infections, while 18 percent of the Skylab 2 reports involved contact with skin infections. During the Skylab 3 and 4 missions, a minor skin infection, or rash, occurred on two of the crewmen of each mission. It is doubtful that either of the latter could have been prevented by measures taken in the health stabilization program, since each problem appears to have occurred for reasons other than preflight exposure.

The results indicate that the Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program successfully accomplished the goal of reducing the number of illness exposures to flight crewmen.

experiment_title: Critical Mission Tasks Assessment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Exercise Countermeasures Project (ECP) is conducting Critical Mission Tasks assessment to determine the level of muscle strength, bone strength, aerobic capacity, and neurovestibular function that must be maintained throughout a mission so that crewmembers may safely accomplish their mission objectives. Critical Mission Tasks are defined as nominal and off-nominal key tasks which may be physically challenging for the crew to perform but important for mission safety or success. From the ECP perspective, the information gained will help to determine whether an exercise countermeasure capability is required for lunar missions, and if so, for what duration of lunar stay. Furthermore, this information will help to determine to what extent lunar extravehicular activity (EVA) can serve as an effective exercise countermeasure.

The primary objectives are:

Objective 1 (Phase I)
Identify the most physically challenging critical mission tasks that must be completed to ensure mission success.

Objective 2 (Phase II)
Quantify the physiological performance demands associated with the critical mission tasks.

Objective 3 (Phase III)
Correlate the critical mission tasks performance demands with exercise performance.

APPROACH:
It is expected that the critical mission tasks will require a submaximal level of exertion. Most assessments will require between 10 to 20 subjects who have completed the JSC Human Test Subject Physical Exam (equivalent to Air Force Class III). To the greatest extent possible, subjects will be recruited that fall in the age range representative of the astronaut population, that collectively span the range of body size and mass from 5th percentile Japanese female to 95th percentile American male, and that achieve a ratio of 50% males to 50% females.

During task assessments requiring significant cardiovascular exertion, subjects will wear a Polar Heart Rate Monitor to ensure that their heart rate does not exceed 85% of age-predicted maximum heart rate for more than one minute. In anticipation of a Level III medical monitoring requirement, an Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS)-certified physician will be available within 15 minutes of notification via the emergency dispatch system.

Raw and processed data will be archived in the Critical Mission Task (CMT) Principal Investigator Data Services (PIDS) database currently being developed by the Glenn Research Center (GRC). The data contained in the database will be a collection of physiological parameters collected through trials conducted at various labs. A record of this study will be maintained in the Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA) along with the other ECP-sponsored studies.

RESULTS:
This experiment was discontinued. Results will not be available.

experiment_title: Vestibular Modulation of the Circadian Timing System in Altered Gravity Environments
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Circadian Timing System (CTS) is essential for the generation and internal temporal coordination of biochemical, physiological, and behavioral rhythms, as well as for synchronizing these physiological oscillations with the external 24-hour environment. When CTS function is disrupted, an organism's ability to respond appropriately to a physiological stressor is inhibited. Patients with CTS dysfunction often suffer from sleep-wake, affective and neuroendocrine disorders. In addition, CTS dysfunction can severely compromise an individual's long-term health. The vestibular system is responsible for perception, orientation and equilibrium within the three dimensional environment. Over the last 10 years a wider functional role has been demonstrated for the vestibular system. The vestibular system can modulate cardiovascular and respiratory function and has a role in anxiety disorders and spatial navigation. The study’s objectives are aimed at understanding how the vestibular system mediates CTS responses to changes in gravity. Vestibular mediated alterations in the period of the pacemaker would affect the ability of the CTS to synchronize with the external environment. Any influence of the vestibular system on photic responsiveness of the CTS would have important implications for both astronauts in altered gravity environments as well as individuals with vestibular and/or circadian disorders.

The overall objective of this study was to determine if the changes in circadian function induced by exposure to a hyperdynamic environment (i.e. 2G) are mediated by input from the vestibular sensory receptors located in the inner ear, specifically the macular receptors. In order to accomplish this objective, this task elucidated the physiological and molecular influence of the vestibular sensors on the regulation of the endogenous circadian period in +G environments.

APPROACH:
Vestibular function is critical to sensorimotor systems that provide an organism with the means to maintain postural equilibrium, sensory orientation and spatial perception. In addition, our recent evidence has shown that the vestibular system plays a role in neurobiological and physiological regulatory systems, including the circadian timing system. Therefore, this program contrasted the responses of the CTS of normal mice (PWT) with those of a genetic mutant, the head tilt, or het, mouse. This mouse has a spontaneous, homozygous mutation on chromosome 17 that results in a lack of otoconia within the macular gravity receptors. The auditory and rest of the labyrinth appears normal. Het mice appear to have normal hearing and respond normally to cranial rotation.

The period of the circadian clock is affected by light intensity. Therefore, the period of the body temperature and activity rhythms of het and PWT mice were determined under three lighting conditions: constant darkness (DD), constant dim light (LLD) and constant bright light (LLB).

RESULTS:
In DD, the period of the Tb rhythm was significantly longer (p<0.001) in het than in PWT mice. In contrast, the daily mean Tb and Tb circadian rhythm amplitude did not differ between het and PWT mice. Similar to Tb, in DD, the het mice demonstrated a significantly longer (p<0.001) circadian period of ACT as compared to PWT mice. Again, mean daily ACT and ACT circadian rhythm amplitude, in DD, were similar between the het and PWT mice.

In LLB, the het mice demonstrated a significantly shorter (p<0.01) circadian period of Tb compared to the PWT mice. The circadian period of Tb was significantly longer (p<0.01) in LLB than in DD for both the het and PWT groups. However, increasing ambient illuminance (0 µmoles s-1 m-2 to 0.5 µmoles s-1 m-2) had a significantly greater (p<0.01) period-lengthening effect in the PWT group than in the het group. Similar to Tb, in LLB, the circadian period of ACT was also significantly longer (p<0.01) in LLB than in DD for both the het and PWT groups. Also similar to Tb, the increased light intensity (DD to LLB) had a significantly greater (p<0.01) period-lengthening effect on ACT in the PWT group compared to the het group. In LLD only the PWT mice demonstrated a significant change (p<0.01) in the circadian period of Tb and ACT.

Similar to DD, mean daily Tb, Tb circadian amplitude, daily mean ACT and ACT circadian amplitude did not differ between groups in either LLB or LLD. The PWT and het mice groups demonstrated quantitatively equivalent negative light masking (i.e., suppression) of ACT when comparing data from DD and LLB. Here, negative light masking was assessed as a % drop in mean ACT levels in LL as compared to DD. Moreover, the het and PWT mice demonstrated ACT alpha (activity) to rho (rest) ratios in DD, in LLB and in LLD similar to that observed in LD, i.e., greater activity consolidation in the het mice. The magnitude of the decrease in the ACT alpha/rho ratio between DD and both LLB and LLD was similar between het and PWT mice, however. Collectively, these observations suggest that enhanced negative light masking does not explain the changes in activity consolidation seen in the het mice. Prior to release into constant darkness, under a 24-hour LD cycle (LD 12:12) daily mean Tb and Tb circadian rhythm phase and amplitude did not differ between het and PWT mice. Daily mean ACT and ACT circadian rhythm phase and amplitude also did not differ between het and PWT mice. Despite equivalent mean ACT levels, however, the distribution of activity between subjective night and day was different between het and PWT mice. Specifically, during LD, the het mice were significantly less active during the subjective day (16.5+5.1%) than PWT mice (31+6%), suggesting possible differences in behavioral state control, e.g., increased sleep in het mice.

The present study demonstrates that mice lacking otoconia, and hence the perception of inertial and gravity accelerations, exhibit alterations in the period of the intrinsic circadian pacemaker and the period-lengthening response to changes in tonic light intensity. These results support the proposal that inputs from the vestibular system can modulate the CTS and represent the first neurobehavioral evidence for a vestibular-CTS interrelationship. As such, these data suggest multi-sensory regulation of the CTS as well as a possible novel vestibular etiology for a host of circadian-related disorders. As an example, because the intrinsic period of the circadian pacemaker is a determinant of the phase angle of entrainment, vestibular-mediated alterations in the period of the pacemaker could affect the ability of the CTS to synchronize with the external environment, i.e., entrainment. CTS dysfunction has also been implicated in sleep-wake, psychiatric, and aging-related disorders, e.g., familial advanced sleep phase syndrome, whose sufferers possess a mutation in a key clock gene, per2, which alters the intrinsic period of the circadian pacemaker. More generalized circadian dysfunction, with or without an altered period basis, has been demonstrated to decrease homeostatic capacity and linked with increased cancer incidence.

In summary, the results of the present study: 1) provide the first neurobehavioral evidence for a vestibular-CTS interrelationship; 2) contribute to our understanding of the regulation of the intrinsic circadian period; 3) suggest a novel afferent role for the macular gravity receptors in transducing activity-based non-photic stimuli; 4) may have important implications for space-bound individuals; and, perhaps most importantly, and 5) have practical implications for understanding the pathophysiology of, and developing treatments for, circadian and circadian sleep-wake disorders with vestibular etiologies.
