experiment_title: In-flight Sleep Analysis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Early in the space program, attention was directed to the possibility of monitoring brain function during space flight. The in flight sleep analysis experiment conducted on Gemini 7 was the first attempt to record electroencephalograms (EEG) during orbital flight. The primary purpose of the experiment was to obtain objective and precise information concerning the number, duration, and depth of sleep periods in flight on one test subject. The EEG would measure any deviations from the normal sleep pattern and pinpoint any factors that may interfere with sleep in an orbiting spacecraft. This was important since several astronauts on previous flights had reported difficulty sleeping. In addition, the experiment was also to determine the effects, if any, of weightlessness on the electrical activity of the brain.

APPROACH:
Multi-channel EEG data were recorded preflight on subjects A and B of Gemini 7 during all stages of sleep and during the waking state. These recordings were used as baseline for comparison with simulation recordings and the in flight records. During flight, EEG measurements were collected only from subject A.

Prior to the day of launch, the helmet liner of test subject A was perforated at four electrode sites. The helmet liner was fitted to the subject's head, and perforations in the liner were used to mark the electrode sites. This procedure assured an exact correspondence between the helmet liner perforations and the electrodes attached to the scalp. Four electrodes, filled with electrode paste, were attached to the scalp sites using adhesive. The impedance of each electrode was tested with reference to the other three electrodes using an impedance tester. All electrodes were found to have an impedance of less than 1000 ohms.

Preliminary studies of 200 control subjects showed that four stages of sleep (i.e., stage 1 sleep, stage 2 sleep, stage 3 sleep and stage 4 sleep) could be differentiated and identified from a single pair of electrodes placed on the scalp. Placing the electrodes along the midline of the head was found to attain the fewest possible artifacts from muscle activity. Thus, researchers chose the midline-center and midline-occipital sites as the primary sites for EEG channel 1 electrode placement. Weight and space limitations permitted only one more EEG recording channel. A duplicate of the first electrode pair was used (channel 2) but displaced a few centimeters to the left of the midline. Such electrode placements would reveal essentially the same information as the midline pair. This choice was made (rather than obtaining data from another area) to provide for the possibility that one or more of the electrodes of one pair might be dislodged or become defective.

The recording system consisted of two miniature-transistorized amplifiers, carried by the subject in the pockets of his underwear, and a small biomedical tape recorder inside the spacecraft. The tape recorder, running at slow speed, was capable of recording 100 hours of data continuously.

EEG recording was to be continuous throughout the first 4 days of the Gemini 7 flight. During these 4 days, subject A was to keep his helmet on unless significant discomfort or other factors necessitated its removal.

RESULTS:
The electrodes dislodged from the subject A's scalp before 100 hours had elapsed, but 54 hours and 43 minutes of interpretable EEG data were obtained. Most of the data were of excellent quality from the standpoint of visual interpretation. The astronaut was alert and active during the major part (77.5%) of the recording. Temporary interruptions in the interpretability of the EEG data were produced by periods of rhythmic chewing motions during meals and while chewing gum.

Two periods of sleep occurred during the recording. The EEG patterns during sleep were distinctive and, since the astronaut was quiet, no artifact obscured the recording. Each minute of sleep was classified according to the four sleep stages, and was plotted graphically against time. An attempt was made to correlate the transient arousals from sleep with various environmental factors, such as suit and cabin temperature variations, cabin pressure variations, and the night-day light shifts inside the spacecraft. In spite of the astronauts' report that they were able to exclude sunlight from the spacecraft completely, the shadow history was the only fact showing a suggestive relationship with arousal. Of the total one-minute epochs in the two sleep periods, 26.4% contained some arousal-type EEG activity (eyes-open and resting). Of the sleep minutes recorded while the spacecraft was in sunlight, 35.2% showed some arousal, whereas only 9.3% minutes showed arousal while the spacecraft was in the Earth's shadow.

During the first in flight sleep period, subject A was awakened after 2 hours 45 minutes, but the first part of the characteristic cyclic alterations in sleep levels could be seen. The sleep period contained significant fluctuations between light sleep and arousal, with occasional brief episodes of stage 3 for the first 80 minutes. At that time, stage 4 sleep was reached. However, in less than 15 minutes abrupt arousal occurred, and sleep was terminated.

On the second day (33 hours and 10 minutes after liftoff), the subject again closed his eyes and immediately showed evidence of drowsiness. Within 34 minutes he was in the deepest level of sleep (stage 4). During this long period of sleep, there were cyclic alterations in sleep level similar to those that occurred during a full night of sleep under normal conditions. Generally, after the first period of stage 4 sleep has been obtained, each successive swing toward deeper sleep only reaches successively lighter levels of sleep. However, during the second night of sleep, the subject A attained and maintained stage 4 sleep for 20 minutes or more at three different times after the first episode. This increase in the number of stage 4 periods was speculated to be a manifestation of sleep deprivation during the first 24 hours of flight.

After approximately 7 hours of sleep, a partial arousal from stage 4 occurred. After a brief period (12 minutes) of fluctuation between sleep stages 2 and 3, the subject remained in a condition fluctuating between drowsiness and stage 1 sleep until a condition of full arousal was reached approximately 1.5 hours later. Periods of rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep could not be determined with certainty from the data because of the absence of electro-oculogram (EOG) measurements and because REM sleep is very similar in character to stage 1 sleep. However, for relatively long periods during sleep that occurred on the second day, two patterns were recorded that resembled a mixture of certain characteristics of stage 1 and stage 2 sleep. The patterns resembled some of the activity observed in REM sleep.

The experiment clearly demonstrated the feasibility of recording EEG during space flight. Although the technique employed and the experiment hardware were both elementary, it was possible to obtain precise information regarding the duration, depth, and number of sleep periods in flight. Researchers hoped that the potential of EEG as an analytical tool to study brain function would be continued on future flights.

experiment_title: Intuitive Ultrasound Catalog for Autonomous Medical Care
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The diagnosis and management of acute health problems in space is problematic; there is no radiological capability aboard the International Space Station (ISS) however, an ultrasound system is operational. Terrestrial investigations suggest expanded clinical applications of ultrasound which could be used to diagnose over 75 percent of space medical conditions. This proposal used an outcomes oriented approach to develop an intuitive ultrasound image catalog, coupled with just-in-time training methods, to allow non-experts to acquire and interpret advanced ultrasound examinations.

The Specific Aims were:
1. Develop an intuitive ultrasound image cataloging system which incorporates ground acquired ultrasound whole body images. The catalog will acquire ground based crew-member images to use for medical diagnosis in space.
2. A mathematical coupling model will be developed based on existing ground/in-flight ultrasound data which will allow microgravity associated morphometric and topographic changes to be predicted.
3. Assess the ability of non-physician crew medical officers (CMO) analogs to acquire and interpret complex ultrasound examinations autonomously or with remote guidance.

The constraints of space flight require the development of novel strategies for crewmember health problems including ultrasound. Evidence based trials have demonstrated the accuracy of ultrasound in aerospace relevant clinical conditions when performed and interpreted by experts. ISS experiments have shown that just-in-time trained astronaut crew-members, augmented by on-board proficiency enhancement, can acquire complex, diagnostic quality ultrasound images. Expanding just-in-time ultrasound training to autonomous ultrasound operation, coupled with enhanced on-site interpretative capabilities, significantly expands diagnostic capabilities during exploratory class space missions. The majority of the training algorithms in this proposal is readily transferable to terrestrial medicine and provides a significant, clinically relevant advance in space medical capabilities with profound Earth-based ramifications.

experiment_title: Quantification of In-flight Physical Changes - Anthropometry and Neutral Body Posture (NBP)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA suit engineers and the Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Project Office have identified that suit fit in microgravity could become an issue, as evidenced during a recent incident on-board the International Space Station (ISS). It has also been noted that crewmembers often need to adjust their suit sizing once they are in orbit. This adjustment could be due to microgravity effects on anthropometry and postural changes, and is necessary to ensure optimal crew performance, fit, and comfort in space. To date, the only data collected in space to determine the effects of microgravity on physical human changes have been during Skylab, STS-57, and a recent Human Research Program (HRP) study on seated height changes due to spinal elongation, Spinal Elongation (Young, 2011). Skylab and the STS-57 studies found that there is a distinct neutral body posture (NBP) based on photographs. Additionally, Skylab studies found that crewmembers could experience a stature growth of up to 3 percent. The Spinal Elongation study in 2011 identified that the crewmembers could experience about a 6 percent growth in seated height and a 3 percent stature growth when exposed to a microgravity environment. The results prove that not all anthropometric measurements have the same microgravity percent growth factor. In order for the EVA Project Office and the suit engineers to properly update the sizing protocol for microgravity, they need additional anthropometric data from space. Hence, this study was recommended by the ISS and sponsored and funded by the EVA Project Office to gather additional in-flight anthropometric measurements, such as lengths, depths, breadths, and circumferences to determine the changes to body shape and size due to microgravity effects. It was anticipated that by recording the potential changes to body shape and size, a better suit sizing protocol could be developed for ISS and other space missions. In essence, this study aimed to help NASA quantify the impacts of microgravity on anthropometry to ensure optimal crew performance, fit, and comfort. Additional in-flight physical changes due to NBP and the effects of spaceflight on NBP during extended exposure to microgravity also needed to be quantified. This study used simplistic data collection techniques as well as digital still and video data to perform photogrammetric analyses and determine the changes that occur to the body shape, size, and NBP while exposed to a microgravity environment.

The objectives were:
1. To initiate an activity to gather and document microgravity effects on body measurements: lengths, breadths, widths, circumferences, and joint angles of subjects exposed to microgravity in an unsuited condition.

2. To determine if/how the NBP is influenced by the above factors.

3. This was the first time these proposed measures were collected in space. It was anticipated that body measurements would change due to microgravity and fluid shifts. The goal of this study was to gather preliminary data to better understand the magnitude and variability of these changes. This data is important for NASA to be able to determine the changes that may occur during long-duration space flight and once obtained, NASA engineers may be able to apply these changes to suit fit, suit sizing, work station design, etc. for current and near future missions. These changes will help NASA to prevent potential crew injury during extended on-orbit missions.

APPROACH:
Pre and Postflight Baseline Data Summary:
The data collection methods entailed the collection of anthropometric data using photographic imagery, a tape measure to measure lengths, heights, depths, circumference data for all appropriate body segments, and a body weight measurement from the astronauts for pre- and post-flight conditions. Pre- and post-flight anthropometric measurements were collected using two methods, standard anthropometric measuring techniques (anthropometer and tape measure) and stereo-photogrammetric method.

Pre- and post-flight data collection sessions took place at JSC in the ISS U.S. Lab mock-up facility in B9, in the morning. Pre-flight data collection occurred for one session at L-6 months. Post-flight data collection occurred for one session within R+30 days. Each single pre- and post-flight data session was 60 minutes long, and measurements were collected using a standard anthropometer and tape measure three times; for photographic imagery, two pictures per posture were collected using the same procedures as the in-flight data session.

Inflight Operations:
In-flight measurements were collected using a tape measure for circumferences, still digital cameras on-board ISS to capture photographs, and the Space Linear Acceleration Mass Measurement Device (SLAMMD) for body mass measurements. In addition, the tape measure could also be used to measure segment lengths for comparison to data from the photogrammetric method in-flight, time permitting. During in-flight data collection sessions, circumference measurements, photographic imagery, and video imagery were collected twice during three 140-minute sessions (215 minutes with operator time) on FD 15, 80, and R-30 (reserve sessions on FD 45, 105, 135). The process included setup of the cameras, subject preparation (placing body markers on the subject), collecting two photographs of each of three postures, measuring circumferences with a tape measure, and NBP video. A camera calibration activity was also conducted prior to each Body Measures data collection session. Body mass measurements were taken during three 50-minute sessions.

experiment_title: Use of Fludrocortisone or Salt Load to Expand Plasma Volume in Ambulatory Subjects
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It is known that a fall in blood pressure occurs after space flight on return to Earth's gravity. This is associated with a reduced volume of plasma, an adaptation made for the weightless environment, and currently restored by the ingestion of large volumes of water and salt tablets on landing. Earlier work revealed that the synthetic corticosteroid, flurocortisone, clinically useful in patients with low blood pressure, could expand plasma volume in subjects exposed to the bed rest model for space flight. The purpose of this study was to compare the effectiveness of salt ingestion with the administration of a synthetic corticosteroid to prevent orthostatic hypotension.

APPROACH:
A previous study (HR77) had tested 4 subjects with fludrocortisone (Florinef) and 4 subjects with a saline load after 7 days of – 6o bed rest. Florineff restored plasma volume to pre-bedrest levels, but a saline load did not. The response in ambulatory subjects was opposite to this post bed rest response. This study plans to repeat the earlier study in the same subjects, reversing the protocol (giving Florinef to subjects who were treated with a saline load before and giving a saline load to subjects treated with Florinef earlier). A second group of tests was done at night to understand if the lack of effect of a salt load in some astronauts was related to a difference in the regulation of salt excretion during the evening. The saline load was 8 g NaCl, (1 g/tablet) given with 960 ml water and the dose of Florinef was 0.2 mg every 8 hrs for 3 doses.

RESULTS:
Four of 5 subjects in the saline group experienced syncope and could not complete 15 minutes of standing after bed rest, while 5 of the 6 subjects given Florinef showed no syncope. After 7 days of bed rest, the increase in heart rate was similar in Florinef and saline treated subjects (to 24 bpm) and greater than the heart rate response before bed rest (to 13 bpm, p<0.05). However the saline load failed to maintain mean arterial pressure during standing post-bedrest, while Florinef treatment did maintain blood pressure. Plasma volume decreased approximately 12% after 7 days bed rest. Following treatments, Florinef returned plasma volume to within 4% of baseline whereas saline failed to restore plasma volume. Urine volume increased during 2 hours of standing after the saline load and decreased after Florinef compared with the pre-bed rest response. Urine Na and the Na/K ratio was similar before and after bed rest following the salt load, but urine Na was decreased and the Na/K ratio reduced after bed rest following Florinef.

Conclusions: Acute treatment with Florinef appears to have distinct advantages over the administration of a saline load as a countermeasure for post-bed rest orthostatic intolerance. Florinef restored plasma volume, maintained mean arterial pressure, and reduced the renal excretion of Na and the Na/K ratio whereas a saline load did not.

To determine the effects of microgravity on developmentally programmed expression of Troponin T and I isoforms known to regulate cardiac and skeletal muscle contraction.

Approach:

This experiment was performed twice, once during Mir 18 (returning on STS-71) and once during Mir 19 (returning on STS-74). Fertilized eggs were carried to the Mir space station aboard a Russian Progress (227) supply vessel, and placed in an incubator supplied by the Institute for Biomedical Problems. Results:

During both runs of the experiment, internal incubator temperature was higher than nominal throughout the experiment, and most of the quail embryos failed to develop as expected, resulting in low science return. During Mir 19, ten embryos developed past 7 days and four embryos developed to an appropriate age. Analysis of the effects of microgravity on isoform expression are still underway.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Previous studies have shown that long-duration exposure to microgravity causes bone loss. In the absence of gravity, bone mass decreases in the load-bearing regions of the skeleton. This space condition mimics osteoporosis, a medical condition characterized by brittle bones. By learning more about the process of bone mineral loss and recovery, researchers hope to be able to implement effective countermeasures in space, and develop more effective treatments for those who suffer from bone disorders on earth.

In the absence of effective countermeasures, crewmembers will lose significant amounts of bone mineral, manifested as a decrease in bone mineral density assessed by dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA). Bone loss will show significant intra and inter-subject variability. Recovery of bone may take several months or more, and may be incomplete in some individuals. The degree and rate of bone recovery will depend in part on the amount of bone lost during flight, as well as on postflight muscular fitness.

Space flight without appropriate or effective countermeasures will also cause significant loss in muscle mass and strength, similar to losses experienced during horizontal 1-g bed rest. These muscle losses will be manifested as degraded performance or as decrements from preflight strength tests. Readaptation to the 1-g environment will result in rapid recovery of muscle mass and strength. Recovery will be complete by 6 months after return from microgravity.

Changes in the metabolism of bone can be assessed indirectly by measuring serum and urinary markers of bone metabolism and bone related hormones. Long-duration flight can be expected to increase total and ionized serum calcium, as well as urinary excretion of calcium. Levels of bone markers and bone related hormones indicate the altered metabolic activity of bone resulting from flight; postflight levels indicate the readaptation of the skeletal system to 1-G.

This investigation measured the space flight induced losses in bone mineral density and lean body mass of long-duration crewmembers and will determine the rate and extent of recovery after returning to earth. Preflight and postflight blood and urine samples were obtained to measure hormones involved in bone formation and resorption and other indicators of bone metabolism. Muscle strength testing was performed in conjunction with bone density measurements to study the relationship between muscular fitness and changes in bone density. Bone density and muscle strength measurements were obtained periodically for up to three years postflight to gain important information regarding the rate of bone recovery after return to earth's gravity.

The objectives of this study were to:

  1. Determine the regional losses in bone mineral density and lean body mass of the crewmembers of each of the four Phase 1B Shuttle-Mir flights
  2. Determine the regional rate and extent of recovery of the bone mineral and lean tissue in the same crewmembers
  3. Determine the muscle strength of the lower extremities and back before and after flight and relate this data to the bone loss during flight and to the degree and rate of bone recovery postflight
  4. Determine the levels of serum and urinary markers of bone metabolism before and after flight.

APPROACH:
To measure bone density, DEXA scans were obtained pre- and postflight using a Hologic QDR 2000 whole body densitometer (United States) or QDR 1000W densitometer (Russia). Bone mineral density data were obtained from scans of the whole body, lumbar spine, proximal femur (hip) and calcaneus (heel). Whole body and regional measurements of lean tissue mass (LTM) were obtained from the whole body scans.

Strength testing was performed pre- and postflight using a LIDO isokinetic dynamometer. Peak torque was measured for muscle groups in the legs and back. Testing time points were the same as for DEXA scans.

Serum and urinary markers of bone metabolism were measured pre- and postflight. Urine was collected over a 24-hour period; serum was collected by a fasting blood draw. Urine markers included total calcium, pyridinium cross-links, n-telopeptide, hydroxyproline, and creatinine. Serum markers included total and ionized calcium, pH, calcitonin, PTH, osteocalcin, total and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D. Testing time points were 30 and 7 days before launch, the day of landing, and 7, 14 and 180 days after landing.

PRELIMINARY RESULTS:
Preliminary DEXA findings on the seven crewmembers whose data have been analyzed to date (including six astronauts and one cosmonaut) indicate that the regional bone changes are similar to those documented in the 18 cosmonauts studied previously, both in terms of degree and in terms of "between-subject" and "within-subject" heterogeneity. Muscle strength results will be correlated with the bone density results during the 3-year recovery period. Recovery DEXA data are too limited to report at this time; these results and corresponding muscle strength changes will be reported at a later date. There are no preliminary bone marker findings at this time.

experiment_title: Body Mass Changes in NASA/Mir Astronauts
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
International Space Station (ISS) Phase I, more commonly known as Phase I, served as a precursor to the ISS experience. In this program, the existing resources of the US Shuttle orbiters and the Russian Space Station Mir were used to test the challenges facing the international partners in the areas of cooperation, data gathering, and logistics. As part of Phase I, seven NASA astronauts served as Mir crewmembers between March 1995 and June 1998. Physiological data gathered on these NASA astronauts can give insight on the effects of long-term weightlessness on individuals, which in turn is important for future ISS considerations.

APPROACH:
Changes in body weight during periods of prolonged weightlessness were examined for six of the seven US astronauts who have flown on Mir. The data present mean body weight and standard deviations (SD) at four intervals: the annual examination in the year prior to flight (Preflight Annual), inflight on approximately Flight Day 90 (FD 90), the third day after return to Earth (R+3), and the annual examination in the year after flight (Postflight Annual).

RESULTS:
Mean weight was 77.2 kg at the preflight annual examination, 73.8 kg at FD 90, 77.3 kg at R+3, and 78.1 kg at the postflight annual examination. There was a downward shift in mean weight inflight, with return to preflight mean weight occurring by R+3. However, inflight mean weight was not statistically significantly different from the preflight and postflight mean weights.

Another way to look at this type of data is to calculate and examine the percent change between preflight and inflight values. Data are inflight data, comparing weight on FD 30, FD 60, and FD 90 to weight at preflight annual examination. Percent of change is calculated by the difference between the preflight annual examination weight and the inflight weight divided by the preflight weight multiplied by 100. The resulting negative value indicates that weight decreased early in the mission (-3.5% by FD 30) and then remained relatively constant at the next two inflight intervals (-4.0% by FD 60 and -4.25% by FD 90).

The method of measurement is different for inflight and on ground, which may contribute to the differences in weight reported here. These results suggest that during periods of prolonged weightlessness, astronauts may experience weight loss early in the mission. Inflight weight appears to stabilize at the new level, and return to preflight levels after return to Earth. Further research into nutritional status during long duration spaceflight may reveal the causes and consequences of this temporal weight loss.

experiment_title: Circadian Disruption in the Space Environment
experiment_description:
OJECTIVES:
In any long duration space flight rhythmicity or lack of it in the space environment will be of paramount concern to the health of the personnel. It is therefore important to learn what are the biological effects of the environments to which human space travelers are likely to be exposed. Some of these biological effects will be the result of disruption of circadian organization of the kind that produces the temporary malaise of "jet lag" and the more serious pathologies of long -term shift work. Circadian disruption in the space environment will be severe and long-lasting but it may be possible to mitigate its effects if we understand its physiology.

This study was directed at understanding the physiology of long-term circadian disruption (dysphasia) using a unique transgenic rat as a model system. This model enabled the investigators independently to assess rhythmicity of the master circadian oscillator in the brain, other brain oscillators, and the damped circadian oscillators that are found in almost every organ and tissue, and to infer whether normal synchrony is maintained in a variety of environments.

experiment_title: In-flight Use of Florinef to Improve Orthostatic Intolerance Postflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Hypovolemia may be one cause of the orthostatic intolerance that is common after space flight. Space flight is known to cause a shift in fluid away from the lower body and a decrease in body fluid. These effects are also produced by head-down tilt bed rest. Fludrocortisone (Florinef) is a drug that increases plasma volume by causing the kidneys to retain sodium. It has shown some ability to restore plasma volume and orthostatic tolerance after bed rest. However, the absorption of a drug may be altered in microgravity, and a dosage regimen that is effective on the ground may not be effective in space. The objective of this study was to test the use of fludrocortisone during space flight to expand plasma volume and improve postflight orthostatic tolerance, comparing three dosage regimens.

APPROACH:
There were 25 male astronauts who were randomized into 2 groups: placebo (n = 18) and fludrocortisone (n = 7), and participated in stand tests 10 days before launch and 2-4 hours after landing. Three regimens of fludrocortisone were used: (1) 0.2 mg twice daily (B.I.D.) for the last 5 days of flight,(2) 0.1 mg twice a day for the last 5 days of flight, or (3) a single dose of 0.3 mg taken 7 hours before landing. Supine blood volume, supine and standing heart rate and arterial pressure, as well as plasma catecholamines were measured before and after flight.

RESULTS:
Only limited conclusions could be made because participation in the protocols was incomplete, and were also limited by subjective evaluation of the medication. The first two protocols (five-day regimens) were not well-tolerated by the crew, being found to cause unacceptable side effects such as congestion, head fullness, and headache. The third regimen (single-dose) did not restore plasma volume and did not seem to improve orthostatic tolerance on landing day.

None of the protocols restored blood volume. The percent change in plasma and red blood cell volumes from preflight to postflight was not significantly different in the fludrocortisone vs. non-fludrocortisone group. Fludrocortisone subjects did not have greater orthostatic tolerance than control subjects on landing day.

On landing day, 2 of 18 in the placebo group and 1 of 7 in the fludrocortisone group became presyncopal (chi2 = 0.015, p = 0.90). Plasma volumes were significantly decreased after flight in the placebo group, but not in the fludrocortisone group. During postflight stand tests, standing plasma norepinephrine was significantly less in the fludrocortisone group compared with the placebo group.

The conclusion therefore, was that treatment with a single dose of fludrocortisone results in protection of plasma volume but no protection of orthostatic tolerance. Fludrocortisone was, therefore, not recommended as a countermeasure for spaceflight-induced orthostatic intolerance.

experiment_title: Effects of Micro-G on Gene Expression in Higher Plants
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Although various effects of microgravity at the whole plant, organ, tissue, and cellular levels have been observed, little is known about the molecular mechanisms involved. This experiment studied the effects of microgravity on the expression of auxin-regulated genes in transgenic tomato and tobacco seedlings that express the auxin-inducible GH3 gene promoter-GUS and SAUR gene promoter-GUS fusion genes.

The objective of this experiment was to use transgenic plants that express GH3 promoter-GUS and SAUR promoter-GUS fusion genes to study the effects of microgravity on expression of auxin- and gravistimulation-inducible genes, GH3 and SAUR, at the organ and tissue levels.

This experiment provided information about how expression of the auxin- and gravistimulation-inducible genes is altered in microgravity as compared to the ground controls. It also provided some insights into the effects of microgravity on auxin transport/distribution and/or tissue's sensitivity to auxin in higher plants.

APPROACH:

The BRIC-09 experiment flew on the STS-80 mission that lasted approximately 18 days. The experiment was placed in five BRIC-60 canisters, each containing eleven 60 mm petri plates. Transgenic tomato and tobacco seedlings were grown on the petri plates, which contained five layers of filter paper and one layer of nylon membrane to support seedlings and nutrient media. No inflight manipulation was performed. Ground controls were conducted on a 24-hour delay in the Orbiter Environment Simulator at environmental conditions (temperature, % relative humidity, and CO2) similar to those experienced by the samples during flight.

Upon recovery, three to four representative seedlings from each petri dish were photographed with a camera coupled with a microscope. Forty seedlings from each petri dish were incubated in x-gluc solution for histochemical staining of the GUS activity at 37 degrees C for 12 to 24 hours, and after staining, the seedlings were photographed. All seedlings stained with x-gluc solution were stored in water with sodium azide for further analysis at the investigator's lab. Thirty seedlings from each petri dish were fixed in 5% glutaraldehyde solution for microscopic analysis. One hundred and fifty seedlings (50 seedlings per assay, 3 replicates) from each petri dish were frozen at minus 70 degree C for quantitative assay of GUS activity.

RESULTS:

The results of this study indicate that the expression of both the GH3 promoter-GUS and SAUR promoter-GUS fusion genes was significantly enhanced (2 to 3-fold increases) in space-grown seedlings when compared with the ground control seedlings. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS fusion gene in tobacco plants was dependent on the developmental stage, initially with an activation in cotyledons, followed by an activation in elongating regions of hypocotyls and roots of the space-grown seedlings. As seedlings developed, the expression of the gene was reduced in cotyledons but further enhanced in root elongating regions. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS gene was relatively higher in vascular tissues and much lower in other tissue types. The expression of the SAUR promoter-GUS gene in the elongating region of hypocotyls in the space-grown seedlings was also significantly higher than in the ground controls. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS and SAUR promoter-GUS genes in space-grown plants strongly suggests that micro-gravity affects auxin transport/distribution or tissue's sensitivity to auxin.

The space-grown seedlings from the BRIC-9 experiment had shorter roots and more and longer root hairs. Increased auxin concentration or tissue's sensitivity to auxin in elongating regions of roots, as indicated by activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS gene, suggests that auxin is involved in the microgravity mediated reduction in root growth and increases in root hair elongation.

experiment_title: Bioluminescent Monitoring of Opportunistic Pathogens in the Spacecraft Environment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The specific research objective of this proposal was to insert a quorum sensing gene (luxI) into bacteriophage to intrinsically generate autoinducer molecules upon target cell infection and subsequent amplification of lux-based bioluminescent signaling mechanisms. Using quorum sensing molecules as a means of detection allows for sensing of biological agents at very low level concentrations. As opposed to chemical detection systems, where typical toxic thresholds of part-per-billion to part-per-million still equate to >1014 molecules available for detection, a quorum sensing biological detection system may be capable of sensing down to one individual biological agent. This technology provides a unique mechanism to provide a measurable amount of bioluminescence from these low event numbers by using the production of autoinducer molecules to produce amplification of individual targeted biological agents, thus avoiding dependence upon target cell growth. The sensors are capable of functioning as a network of autonomous detectors for continuous on-line, near real-time monitoring in a low-power, low-mass, low-maintenance, redundant framework.

APPROACH:
To assist in the detection of E. coli, a recombinant bacteriophage reporter was developed that uses quorum sensing (luxI/luxR) signaling and luxCDABE-based bioluminescent bioreporter sensing to specifically and autonomously respond to serotype E. coli. The bacteriophage reporter, derived from phage PP01, was tested in artificially contaminated foodstuffs including apple juice, tap water, ground beef, and spinach leaves.

RESULTS:
Testing of these reporter phage systems indicates detection limits approaching 10e4 CFU/ml without sample preincubation and down to 10 CFU/ml with sample preincubation for E. coli O157:H7 within a 96-well plate assay format. Testing in artificially contaminated apple juice demonstrated detection limits down to 10e4 CFU/ml in less than 8 hours.

For general E. coli detection using strain XL1-Blue as a target, identification in pure culture occurred within 1.5 – 5 hours at high cell densities (10e8 – 10e5 CFU/ml) and at lower cell densities (<10 CFU/ml) with requisite preincubation within a total assay time of approximately 10 hours. When tested against artificially contaminated lettuce, the assay detected original inoculums between 10e8 – 10e5 CFU/ml within 2.6 – 12 hours, respectively.

While the overall assay limits fall short of the 1 – 10 CFU/ml detection limits typically desired in food matrices, their limits of detection are close to that of existing immunoassays and fluorescent-phage based assays, and the sensitivity of these assays may be increased through additional genetic modifications of the phage (i.e., linkage of luxI to multiple phage promoters) or through better sample concentration techniques (i.e., immunomagnetic separation). Since no ancillary reagents or manipulations are required other than incubation and light measurement, these assays remain highly amenable to automated high-throughput monitoring using any number of available photomultiplier-based luminescent readers, including miniaturization in a BBIC format. Phage-based sensing also ensures only the detection of live cells, thereby overcoming the false positive detection of dead cells often inherent in other assaying methods such as ELISA and PCR. Further manipulations of phage reporter genetic mechanisms and advances in miniaturized electronic optics will clearly impact future monitoring and detection strategies in the food industry.

experiment_title: Biochemistry and Endocrinology Results
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
One medical objective of the Apollo program was to continue the investigation of biomedical changes incident to space flight and to detect, document and understand changes occurring during space flight. On the Apollo 7 through 17 missions, the objective of the endocrine, electrolyte and fluid volume changes study was to evaluate the biochemical changes in Apollo crewmembers. The areas studied were balance of fluid and electrolytes, regulation of calcium metabolism, adaptation to the environment, and regulation of metabolic processes. These studies, like others of the Apollo program, were designed mainly to ensure crew heath and well-being.

During the Apollo Soyuz Test Project (ASTP), the Biochemistry and Endocrinology investigation continued the studies begun during earlier programs. In combination with information from other medical disciplines, data from this investigation allowed for objective assessment of the individual crewmember's health. Preflight data provided baseline information for the detection and identification of postflight physiological changes that may have occurred as a result of exposure to the space environment. The results of the biochemistry and endocrinology studies were not only helpful in the diagnosis of abnormalities, but also provided rationale for accurate remedial procedures.

APPROACH:
Blood samples and 24-hour urine samples were collected pre- and postflight; no samples were collected inflight. Both sample types were collected 30, 15 and 5 days before flight (L-30, 15 and 5). Postflight, blood samples were drawn as soon after recovery as possible (on R+0) as well as 28 days after recovery (R+28). The preflight blood samples were taken in the morning after bladder emptying and prior to food intake. The crew consumed diets of their choosing pre- and postflight, but followed the ASTP diet inflight. Fluids were available when desired.

The blood samples (plasma or serum) were analyzed for glucose, cholesterol, serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT), serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase (SGPT), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), uric acid, alkaline phosphatase, calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg), inorganic phosphate, bilirubin total, creatinine, creatine phosphokinase, lactic dehydrogenase (LDH), osmolality, sodium (Na), potassium (K), chloride (Cl), triglycerides, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), angiotensin I, aldosterone, and cortisol. A limited amount of plasma was available from the immunology studies on days R+1, 8, and 13 and were analyzed for cortisol and aldosterone.

The 24-hour urine samples were analyzed for specific gravity, osmolality, Na, K, Cl, Ca, Mg, inorganic phosphate, uric acid, creatinine, aldosterone, antidiuretic hormone (ADH), cortisol, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and amino acids.

Body fluid compartments were determined on subjects B and C on L-15 days and immediately postflight. These compartments included plasma volume (iodine 125 method), total body water (tritium method), extracellular fluid (sulfur-35 method), and total body exchangeable potassium (potassium 42 method).

Because of the crew's inhalation of toxic fumes during reentry, and concern for the crew's health, the postflight protocol deviated from the originally approved schedule. Additional testing was conducted to try to identify the components of the inhaled gases which affected the crewmen. This was done by analyzing postflight blood samples for the presence of hydrazine and 1-methylhydrazine. Also, the effects of the toxic gas (nitrogen dioxide) inhalation were evaluated by measurements of various forms of urinary hydroxylysine.

RESULTS:
Results from the ASTP crewmembers were similar to findings from previous space flight crews who flew missions of comparable duration. The results of the blood biochemistry analysis showed postflight decreases below preflight values for glucose in subjects B and C, for cholesterol in subjects A and B, and for uric acid in subjects A and C. Increases above preflight values were observed in SGOT, SGPT, BUN, alkaline phosphatase, creatinine, LDH, and angiotensin I.

The component isoenzymes of LDH were examined to ascertain the effect of the toxic gas inhalation on the normal isoenzyme distribution. The LDH isoenzyme values show nearly equal distribution of the total LDH increase through all five bands on R+0. By day R+28, the elevation was shifted more toward LDH isoenzyme 1 for subjects A and B. Subject C's results were still more elevated in bands 2, 4, and 5. However, the changes observed in the LDH isoenzyme patterns of the ASTP crewmen did not reflect damage in tissue other than lung.

The postflight 24-hour urine sample analysis showed a decrease in Na, K, and Cl in all three crewmen. Hydrogen ion, cortisol, and aldosterone were all elevated after flight. The body compartments results showed decreases in plasma volume, total body water, extracellular fluid, and total body exchangeable K. The postflight urine results and the body compartment results indicated that body fluids and electrolytes were decreased on return to normal gravity and that a process of conservation by the body had been initiated. This process was shown in particular by the results of angiotensin I and aldosterone measurements.

Collagen Breakdown and Nitrogen Dioxide Inhalation

Measurements of urinary hydroxylysine glycosides indicated that considerable collagen degradation occurred during the reentry phase of the mission. Nitrogen dioxide, a recognized pulmonary irritant, was inhaled during reentry. (Nitrogen dioxide, a reddish brown gas, available commercially, under pressure, as a brown liquid, is in fact an equilibrium mixture of nitrogen dioxide and the colorless nitrogen tetroxide). The first hours after splashdown were marked by crew complaints of tightness of the chest, retrosternal burning sensations, the inability to inhale deeply, and nonproductive coughing. Oxygen was administered to each crewman. Since the crew showed clinical and roentgenographic signs of diffuse chemical pneumonitis, it was likely that collagen degradation occurred in the pulmonary parenchyma.

Similar changes of the urinary excretion of hydroxylysine were not observed in the various astronauts who participated in Apollo or Skylab missions, even though many lasted considerably longer that the Apollo-Soyuz mission. The well-known properties of nitrogen dioxide and it's ability to affect enzymatic activities, cell membrane structures, and structural proteins of the pulmonary parenchyma suggest that the increased urinary excretion of hydroxylysine metabolites might have been related to the acute pulmonary lesions caused by the inhalation of the toxic gas.

Identification of Toxic Gas Components

Attempts to identify the components of the gas inhaled during entry were done by analyzing blood samples for hydrazine and 1-methylhydrazine. Test results were negative. The absence of these compounds was also confirmed by the lack of consistent change in serum cholesterol and triglycerides.

experiment_title: Investigation of Microgravity Effects on Physiology, Global Gene Expression, and Biofilm Phenotypes of the Caries-Causing Bacterium Streptococcus mutans
experiment_description:
https://genelab-data.ndc.nasa.gov/genelab/OBJECTIVES:
Although preventable by fluoridation of water and various dental procedures, dental caries remains one of the most prevalent chronic diseases in the world. The oral bacterium Streptococcus mutans is considered the major etiological agent of dental caries, and displays a remarkable ability to persist as part of dental plaque biofilm on the tooth surface. Traditionally, the approach to maintaining astronaut oral health during space flight missions has been routed in rigorous preventative dentistry. However, in the face of future long-term space flight missions, research and discovery of new methods for maintaining oral hygiene and dental health under a microgravity environment will be required. Recent studies have shown that simulated microgravity exposure can cause increased mandibular and alveolar bone loss and decreased saliva flow, but little research has been dedicated to studying the effects of space flight and microgravity on virulence attributes of oral pathogens such as S. mutans. Therefore, the overall hypothesis of this New Space Biology Investigation proposal is that S. mutans physiology, biofilm formation and/or expression of virulence phenotypes will be altered in response to simulated microgravity conditions, and will be tested in two specific aims: (1) Gene expression profiles and cell physiology of S. mutans will be compared when grown in rotating wall vessels to simulate microgravity and “normal” (1×g) gravity conditions, using RNAseq and metabolomics approaches, respectively; (2) S. mutans biofilm formation on hydroxyapatite (HA) and related virulence phenotypes will be compared when grown under simulated microgravity and normal gravity conditions. The outcomes of this pilot study will serve as a springboard to development of a full Ground-Based Research proposal, focusing on understanding the regulatory mechanisms behind microgravity-specific changes in gene expression, physiology or virulence phenotypes, in the hopes of targeting these for development of future anti-caries therapies that could be easily adapted to space flight.

APPROACH:
For the experiments in both aims, microgravity conditions were simulated using rotating wall vessels (RWV), bioreactors that maintain cells in a sustained low-shear, low-turbulence growth environment. When the RWV vessel is rotated on an axis perpendicular to the gravitational vector, cells or small spheres within the vessel will remain suspended in solution. Conversely, when rotated on an axis parallel to the gravitational vector, “normal” (1 ×g) gravity conditions are obtained, whereby cells or particles will sediment at the bottom of the vessel. All experiments in this project utilized Rotary Cell Culture Systems designed to rotate High Aspect Ratio Vessels (HARVs) in both perpendicular axis and parallel axis orientations. To minimize the effects of possible carry-over contamination and clogging from build-up of physical debris i.e. hydroxyapatite (HA) powder, disposable HARVs were used in these studies. Growth media used in these studies was either Brain Heart Infusion Broth (BHI, containing 11 mM glucose) or semi-defined biofilm media (BM, containing 11 mM glucose and 10 mM sucrose), as indicated. S. mutans strain UA159 was used for all experiments.

For Aim 1, an “-omics” approach was utilized to study the effects of microgravity on the global transcriptome and metabolism of S. mutans. Both end-point (where separate HARVs were grown undisturbed to defined time points) and continuous (where the same HARV was sampled throughout the experiment) growth curves were performed to determine if major growth differences would be observed between the S. mutans normal gravity and simulated microgravity HARV cultures. End-point HARV S. mutans cultures (both simulated micro-gravity and normal gravity, n=3 independent experiments each) were harvested at 4, 8, and 24 hours growth in BM, and cell pellets and culture supernatants were harvested and stored at -80 C for metabolomics analysis by Metabolon, Inc. Metabolite profiles were obtained from cell pellets and supernatants using untargeted, metabolic profiling on three different platforms [liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS/MS) with and without electrospray ionization (ESI), and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS)]. Duplicate cell pellets from each 8 hour HARV (both simulated micro-gravity and normal gravity, n=3 independent experiments each) were also stored at – 80 C for RNA isolation and DNase treatment. RNA samples were then submitted for analysis, which included an mRNA enrichment step and generation of a library of cDNA template molecules of known strand origin using the Illumina TruSeq Total mRNA Sample Preparation Kit. All sequencing and subsequent data analysis (alignment of reads, differential expression analysis, and statistics) was performed by SeqWright using the Illumina HiSeq Platform. Select genes of interest that exhibited significant expression changes in response to microgravity were also validated in our research lab by performing quantitative real-time PCR on cDNA from the original RNA samples.

For Aim 2, a variety of S. mutans virulence and biofilm-specific phenotypes were evaluated in HARVs (simulated microgravity and normal gravity growth, n=2-4 independent experiments each). These included: (1) ability to form mono-species biofilm on HA powder (determined by CFU/ml of planktonic and HA-associated bacteria); (2) ability to form mono-species (GFP-expressing S. mutans) and dual-species (GFP-expressing S. mutans – RFP-expressing S. gordonii) biofilms on microcarrier beads (determined by CFU/ml and confocal microscopy); (3) quantitative competence assays performed in BHI + 5% horse serum (used to induce natural competence) and in BM media; and (4) oxidative stress assays performed on cells harvested from HARV cultures grown in BM for 4, 8, and 16 hours (determined by %survival in response to challenge with 5 mM hydrogen peroxide).

RESULTS:
The results from our experiments suggest that S. mutans undergoes changes in metabolism, physiology, and global gene expression during stationary-phase simulated microgravity growth that impact cell aggregation and oxidative stress resistance. Defining the exact regulatory circuits and contributions of these differentially regulated genes to the ability of S. mutans to survive and adapt to LSMMG and spaceflight environments will help in the development of treatment and control strategies to combat the caries potential of this pathogen. Furthermore, these studies may provide insight into the response of S. mutans to low-fluid shear encountered in the oral cavity. Our future research efforts will focus on assessing S. mutans biofilm formation during simulated microgravity growth using culture conditions more closely mimicking the oral cavity (i.e., artificial saliva media and periodic pulsing of sucrose addition), as well as growth of S. mutans as part of a mixed-species biofilm consortium.

For Aim 1, detailed analyses of S. mutans HARV growth, and the metabolomics and RNAseq results are complete. There were not major differences in S. mutans growth observed between normal gravity and simulated microgravity end-point HARV cultures, although they did display macroscopic differences in cell-cell aggregation structures at early stationary phase (8 hrs growth). For the continuous HARV cultures, the simulated microgravity culture appeared to enter stationary phase slightly earlier than the normal gravity HARV culture. In the metabolomics experiment, 286 and 250 biochemicals were detected in the cell pellets and supernatants, respectively. However, it appears that only subtle differences in the metabolite profiles were observed between the normal gravity and microgravity conditions at each of the 4, 8, and 24-hour time points. These results also indicated that time had much more of a significant impact on global metabolism than growth under the different gravity conditions. For RNA-seq differential expression (DE) analysis, 155 genes were significantly up-regulated = 2-fold and 94 genes were significantly down-regulated = 2-fold in the microgravity growth condition relative to the normal gravity condition. A subset of these genes was chosen to validate the dataset by qPCR, and these tested genes follow the same pattern of DE changes as observed in the RNA-seq data. These DE genes have been assigned to functional groups using gene annotations and DAVID tools, and the metabolic gene expression changes have been analyzed using a “paint-omics” and pathway enrichment type tool via BioCyc.

For Aim 2, detailed analysis of the results is complete. It has been determined that competence (ability to uptake exogenous DNA) was not affected by simulated microgravity growth in both BHI and BM media at the time point tested. However, some competence genes were differentially regulated in the RNA-seq analysis, which was performed in BM at a later time point of growth (8 hours). Cells isolated from simulated microgravity HARV cultures were more sensitive to H202-killing at stationary phase (16 hrs growth), but not at the earlier time points. HA biofilm experiments revealed that HA-associated biofilm cells were not altered by simulated microgravity growth (as measured by CFU), but increased CFU were observed in the corresponding planktonic bacteria during simulated microgravity growth in HARVs. A similar result was also observed when S. mutans biofilms were grown on microcarrier beads in microgravity HARVs. S. mutans and S. gordonii were capable of forming dual-species biofilms when grown on microcarrier beads in normal gravity and microgravity HARVs. Confocal microscopy data indicates that similar biofilm structures formed under each HARV growth condition.

experiment_title: Plant Growth at Sub-Ambient Atmospheric Pressures with Control of the Partial Pressures of Constituent Gases
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The development of an Advanced Life Support System for Lunar/Mars bases, and space-flight, including orbital-based missions, will incorporate the use of physicochemical and biological components, in which there will be a role for plant growth systems for air and water revitalization and food production. Some environmental conditions to which plants will be exposed are certain to differ from those on Earth (NASA, Advanced Life Support Program: Advanced Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions), and such conditions have not been extensively tested before with higher plants. A central goal of this research is for the targeted crop species to successfully complete their life cycles at sub-ambient pressure. The objectives of the proposed research are: 1. To characterize plant growth, gas exchange (respiration and photosynthesis), constituent gases (oxygen, carbon dioxide, ethylene and other trace gases), and water reclamation (transpirate) under environmental conditions that may apply to an Advanced Life Support System.
Investigators will determine the effectiveness of plant performance at low total gas pressures. In some experiments low pressure will be combined with high partial pressures of CO2, with or without O2 enrichment. They will test the hypothesis that at low gas pressure, the detrimental effects on cellular respiration of a low partial pressure of O2 will be offset by increased gaseous diffusion, and also by the beneficial effects of high CO2. With newer, leak-tight design, low-pressure plant growth system — ethylene (C2H4), a plant hormone, and water vapor, a byproduct of transpiration — can reach unacceptable levels and need to be controlled.

2. To model the dynamics of carbon dioxide exchange in a closed microecosystem such as an Advanced Life Support System. Investigators will utilize modeling principles to determine the steady state and transient control parameters of carbon dioxide exchange by plants in an Advanced Life Support System. Modeling will include release of CO2 by plants in dark respiration, and transient changes in CO2 concentration as a result of increased metabolic activity by plants (in response to light or temperature) or by crew during exercise.

The growth and gas exchange of plants in long-term experiments at different concentrations of O2, CO2, N2, and trace gasses, as well as total gas pressure, have not been extensively characterized. Such data is extremely useful in determining the overall design requirements for Advanced Life Support Systems. This information is also relevant to nutrient cycling, sustainability and closed-system microenvironments on Earth. 1. To characterize plant growth, gas exchange (respiration and photosynthesis), constituent gases (oxygen, carbon dioxide, ethylene and other trace gases, and water reclamation (transpirate) under environmental conditions that may apply to an Advanced Life Support System.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
Engineering Developments for the Texas A&M Low Pressure Plant Growth System
The Low Pressure Plant Growth (LPPG) system at Texas A&M University was upgraded to improve performance and enhance data collection. The GCX gas chromatograph was replaced with individual gas sensors for O2 and CO2 in each chamber. Although functional, the GCX had several disadvantages when incorporated with the LPPG:
The sampling time is five minutes per chamber so that a complete sampling circuit of the six chambers took thirty minutes. This limited the ability to control gas concentrations to tight specifications and limited the accuracy of in situ gas exchange measurements. The GCX removed a small amount of gas (140 mL) for each sample and violated the design goal of maintaining a closed system. The sampling subsystem of the GCX was limited by design to six chambers. The GCX had ongoing maintenance issues and reliability concerns. Much of the work done by the factory field installer had to be reworked by the engineering staff to function as intended. Unfortunately, when the GCX is not functioning correctly the entire LPPG system is shutdown. When one or more of the four columns in the GCX failed and required replacement, the engineering team decided to accelerate incorporation of new gas sensors rather than spend $5,000 per column to repair the GCX, which we wanted to eliminate from the LPPG system anyway. Thus, the engineering focus for the second half of the year was to incorporate the sensors identified under the previous grant into the LPPG system at Texas A&M University. This new system is currently designated as the Generation IV Low Pressure Plant Growth (LPPG) system.

Generation IV LPPG Hardware Development
The Generation IV LPPG utilizes individual PIC16F877 microcontrollers (Microchip Technologies, Scottsdale, AZ) for pressure and gas composition control and data acquisition for each growth chamber. This is the same MCU that was used in the Generation III LPPG and it has proven to be highly serviceable. A newer MCU from Microchip, the 18F452, shares the same pin configuration with the 16F877 and could be used to upgrade if additional program memory was needed.

The selected O2 sensor is a motion stable, weak acid electrolyte oxygen sensor (MAX-250, Maxtec Inc, Salt Lake City, Utah). This sensor provides a stable signal over an oxygen concentration range of 0 – 100% (0 – 101 kPa partial pressure of O2), will operate for 900,000 hours, utilizes a non-caustic electrolyte, and is unaffected by acid gases including CO, CO2, and NOx. Testing of these sensors in two LPPG chambers has shown them to be reliable over the range of total pressure and O2 partial pressures used in our plant growth experiments. The sensor output is approximately 10 mV DC at ambient O2 partial pressure (20.9 kPa) and must be amplified prior to sending it to an available analog to digital conversion (ADC) channel on the MCU. A similar sensor from a different manufacturer (P8R-11-37-D7, Analytical Industries, Pomona, CA) is under evaluation as a replacement for the Maxtec sensor. The Analytical Industries sensor provides an output of about 20 mV at ambient O2 pressures and may improve the resolution on the O2 measurements.

The CO2 sensor selected utilizes a silicon based non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) technology to optically determine the CO2 concentration (model GMM222, Vaisala). The sensor response is converted to a 1 – 5 VDC signal, which is proportional to the CO2 concentration, and sent to another of the available ADC channels on the MCU. An additional vacuum rated instrumentation conductor fitting was needed for each chamber to incorporate the new sensors. Temperature and relative humidity (RH) will be measured with a HT-761 transmitter from Ohmic Instruments, Co. (Easton, MD). This instrument provides two 0 to 1 VDC outputs, proportional to temperature over the range 0 to 100oC and 0 to 100% RH, respectively. Temperature measurement is to a precision of ± 0.3oC and RH is measured to a precision of ± 2%. The conditions in the LPPG chambers are typically between 25 and 35oC and 60 to 80% RH.

An additional hardware upgrade between the Generation III LPPG and the Generation IV system was the addition of nine mass flow controllers (MFCs) so that each chamber has a dedicated set for O2, N2, and CO2. With the dedicated MFCs, the response is greatly improved and O2 and CO2 levels are held much closer to the setpoint. Also, the CO2 flow meters were calibrated to a much lower maximum flow (7 mL per minute) which greatly reduced the amount of overshoot in the gas addition. The improved control of the Generation IV system and ability of each chamber to be fully independent has greatly expanded our capabilities. New printed circuit boards (PCBs) were designed to provide access to the MCU analog input pins to read the new sensors and to provide the appropriate power to the RH/Temperature sensor.

Generation IV LPPG Software Development
There were only minor software modifications needed from the Generation III LPPG program to accommodate the Generation IV LPPG hardware. The MCU program is written in C and programmed into the MCU using Microchip development tools. In preparation for incorporation of the new sensors, the microcontroller (MCU) program was modified to access the additional analog inputs and to set up a secondary timing circuit to control when the sensors are read. Both the O2 and CO2 sensors have a reported response time to of about 30 seconds to reach 97% of the final reading. The only other significant modification of the program was relocation of the calibration equations from the MCU to the LabVIEW interface program. That allows investigators to recalibrate without having to reprogram the MCUs. The research team has determined to work exclusively in units of partial pressure for CO2 and O2. These units are equivalent to mass by the ideal gas law (PV=nRT) and eliminate any confusion about the environmental conditions surrounding the plants. Partial pressure is also the driving force in gas exchange in the plants.

Plant Biology Studies at the Texas A&M Low Pressure Plant Growth System
There are advantages in growing plants under hypobaric (reduced atmospheric pressure) conditions in biomass production for extraterrestrial base or space flight environments. Elevated levels of the plant hormone, ethylene, occur in enclosed crop production systems and in space-flight environments leading to adverse plant growth and sterility. Objectives of this research were to characterize the influence of hypobaria on growth and ethylene evolution of lettuce (Lactuca sativa L. cv. Buttercrunch).

As reported in the Engineering Section, considerable time was spent on reconfiguring the LPPG system from its reliance on the process GCX gas chromatograph to direct sensor monitoring of the partial pressures of CO2 and O2. Because of the difficulty in changing over the system from the GCX, investigators have been limited to shorter 7-8 day duration studies. They plan on doing longer-term studies under low pressure (25 kPa) and ambient (101 kPa) total pressure.

Investigators are finding that plants can be grown under low pressure and that dark respiration and ethylene levels are much higher under ambient than low total pressure with lettuce production. The night (dark respiration) levels were greater under ambient than low pressure. The O2 levels increased under both ambient and low pressure. There was a faster draw-down, which had a higher dark respiration and subsequent CO2 substrate level. This suggests a higher net assimilation rate of the ambient pressure plants. A minimum CO2 of 100 Pa was maintained during the light cycle. The dark respiration of 101 kPa (ambient) is greater (larger slope) than low pressure plants.

Growth was comparable in lettuce grown under low (25 kPa) and ambient (101 kPa) total gas pressures. However, tip burn occurred under ambient, but not low pressure, in part because of adverse ethylene levels (He et al., 2005). Under ambient pressure, there were higher CO2 assimilation rates and dark respiration rates (higher night consumption of metabolites) compared to low pressure. This could lead to greater growth (biomass production) of low pressure plants during longer crop production cycles.

experiment_title: Surveyor 3 Streptococcus Mitis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Surveyor 3 spacecraft was launched in April 1967 and was exposed on the lunar surface for 31 months before the Apollo 12 mission. The Apollo 12 Lunar Module landed approximately 160 meters from the Surveyor 3 spacecraft.

APPROACH:
In November 1969, the Apollo 12 crew retrieved several pieces of the Surveyor, including the TV camera and associated electrical cables, the sample scoop, and two pieces of aluminum tubing. These items were returned to Earth and analyzed to determine how they were affected by exposure to the lunar environment.

A particularly important aspect of the Surveyor 3 analysis was the search for living material on the spacecraft. Surveyor was not sterilized prior to launch, and scientists wanted to know if terrestrial microorganisms had survived for two and a half years in space.

RESULTS:
One research group found a small amount of the bacterium Streptococcus mitis in a piece of foam from inside the TV camera. Culture plates from Surveyor 3 camera foam samples(1 cc volume of polyurethane foam)were prepared, and samples sent to the US Communicable Disease Center at Atlanta, Georgia, which confirmed it as Streptococcus mitis, a common harmless bacteria from the nose, mouth and throat in humans. The NASA researchers believed that these bacteria had survived in this location since before launch. They only found evidence for living material in one of 33 samples from various parts of Surveyor that they cultured. This was attributed to the camera not being sterilized on Earth prior to its launch two and a half years previously and this is still the conclusion accepted by NASA for these findings. The 50-100 organisms survived launch, space vacuum, 3 years of radiation exposure, deep-freeze at an average temperature of only 20 degrees above absolute zero, and no nutrient, water or energy source. The United States landed 5 Surveyors on the Moon; Surveyor 3 was the only one of the Surveyors visited by any of the six Apollo landings. No other life forms were found in soil samples retrieved by the Apollo missions or by two Soviet unmanned sampling missions, although amino acids - not necessarily of biological origin - were found in soil retrieved by the Apollo astronauts.

Another research group found no evidence of life inside a section of electrical cable. Some people associated with the curation of the Surveyor 3 materials have suggested that the one positive detection of life may be the result of accidental contamination of the material after it was returned to Earth. Other explanations include that a breach of sterile procedure took place at just the right time to produce a false positive result. One of the implements being used to scrape samples off the Surveyor parts could have been laid down on a non-sterile laboratory bench, and then was used to collect surface samples for culturing. It is, therefore, quite possible that the microorganisms were transferred to the camera after its return to Earth. Furthermore, the Surveyor 3 camera was returned from the Moon in a nylon duffel bag, and was not in the type of sealed airtight metal container used to return lunar samples in the early Apollo missions. It is therefore possible that it was contaminated by the astronauts and the environment in the Apollo 12 capsule itself. The bacterial test is now non-repeatable because the parts were subsequently taken out of quarantine and fully re-exposed to terrestrial conditions (the Surveyor 3 camera is now on display in the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.). This subject was covered in the 2008 Discovery Channel documentary series, When We Left Earth.

experiment_title: Extended Duration Orbiter Treadmill Evaluation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The newly designed Extended Duration Orbiter (EDO) treadmill and restraint system required an in-flight hardware evaluation. Improvements in the size of the running surface and the restraint system allowed for greater comfort during exercise. The speed of the treadmill was adjusted using a power driven governor. The subject load device/restraint system was also adjustable. The main objectives of this experiment were: (1) Evaluate EDO treadmill for ease of setup and use, physical comfort at different restraint loads, noise, ease of stowage, and subject restraint system; and (2) Compare 0-g heart rate responses to 1-g workload responses using a Heart Watch.

APPROACH:
Documentary 35 mm still photos were requested. Periodic 8mm video footage during exercise sessions was also requested. The scenes required included: LIOH door movement, crewmember's harness system, body posture, and arm position. A total of five crewmembers were required to evaluate this hardware on missions of any duration. A familiarization session for the treadmill and bungee restraint system was performed preflight. Exercise training sessions using a prototype passive treadmill was performed two times preflight to acclimate the crewmembers to the running style on a passive treadmill and comfort level of the restraint system. A final preflight exercise session was performed using a heart rate monitor to log 1-g responses.

In flight, the treadmill was unstowed and configured for exercise. Subjects stretched prior to exercise and donned a Heart Watch. Exercise protocols were provided for individual workloads based on 1-g responses. Three 20 minute exercise sessions using the restraint system at 1/2, 3/4, and 1-g loads were performed. Post exercise, crewmembers recorded comments about the hardware.

experiment_title: Understanding Full-Body Gaze Control During Locomotion
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Control of locomotion requires precise interaction between several sensorimotor subsystems. Exposure to the microgravity environment of space flight leads to postflight adaptive alterations in these multiple subsystems leading to postural and gait disturbances along with decrement in visual acuity during body motion. Countermeasures designed to mitigate these postflight gait alterations need to be assessed with a new generation of functional tests that evaluate the interaction of various elements central to locomotor control. Traditionally, gaze stabilization has been studied almost exclusively as a problem of eye-head-trunk coordination. However, coordination between the eye-head and trunk are not the only mechanism aiding gaze stabilization particularly during locomotion. Therefore the first goal of this study was to develop new techniques to evaluate the multiple, interdependent, full- body sensorimotor subsystems that aid gaze stabilization during locomotion. The second goal was to develop new tests to evaluate changes in dynamic visual acuity during body movement. To address the first goal, two experiments were performed.

APPROACH:
To address the first goal, two experiments were performed. In the first study (Study 1) investigators evaluated how alteration in gaze tasking changes full-body locomotor control strategies. Subjects (n=9) performed two discreet gaze stabilization tasks while walking at 6.4 km/hr on a motorized treadmill: 1) focusing on a central point target; 2) reading numeral characters; both presented at 2m in front at eye level. The second study (Study 2) investigated the potential of adaptive remodeling of the full-body gaze control systems following exposure to visual-vestibular conflict. Subjects (n=14) walked (6.4 km/h) on the treadmill before and after they were exposed to 0.5X minifying lenses worn for 30 minutes during self-generated sinusoidal vertical head rotations performed while seated. In both studies the investigators measured: temporal parameters of gait, full body sagittal plane segmental kinematics of the head, trunk, thigh, shank and foot, accelerations along the vertical axis at the head and the shank, and the vertical forces acting on the support surface.

RESULTS:
In both studies the investigators measured: temporal parameters of gait, full body sagittal plane segmental kinematics of the head, trunk, thigh, shank and foot, accelerations along the vertical axis at the head and the shank, and the vertical forces acting on the support surface. Results showed that while reading numeral characters as compared to the central point target: 1) compensatory head pitch movements increased, 2) the peak acceleration measured at the head was significantly reduced, 3) the knee joint total movement was on greater during the period from the heel strike event to the peak knee flexion event in stance phase of the gait cycle. Results also indicate that following exposure to visual-vestibular conflict known to adaptively modify the VOR subjects predominantly: 1) decreased the amplitude of head movement with respect to space; 2) increased the amount of knee and ankle flexion during the initial stance phase of the gait cycle. These responses serve to aid gaze stabilization during locomotion. Taken together, results from Studies 1 and 2 provide evidence that the full body contributes to gaze stabilization during locomotion, and that different functional elements are responsive to changes in visual task constraints and are subject to adaptive alterations following exposure to visual-vestibular conflict. These studies successfully validated new integrated methodologies designed to assess locomotor function for countermeasure evaluation and validation. To address the second goal of this study the investigators developed a new test to measure dynamic visual acuity during treadmill walking. Upon their return to earth, astronauts experience the effects of vestibular adaptation to microgravity. The postflight change in vestibular information processing affects postural and locomotor stability and leads to reduced visual acuity during body movement due to alterations in gaze control. These changes in acuity have significant operational implications. The inability to see clearly during body motion can impair the ability to operate spacecraft, conduct EVAs and perform an emergency egress soon after landing following a long-duration space flight. However, it is likely that time spent in microgravity affects canal and otolith function differently. As a result, the isolated rotational stimuli used in traditional tests of canal function may fail to identify vestibular deficits after space flight. In a gaze control task, the relative contributions of the canal and otolith organs are modulated with viewing distance. The ability to stabilize gaze during a perturbation, on visual targets placed at different distances from the head may therefore provide independent insight into the function of these systems. The newly developed dynamic visual acuity test allows the investigators to measure changes both in static and dynamic visual acuity for both near (0.5 m) and far (4 m) visual target positions. This test was evaluated in both normal subjects and in patients with bilateral vestibular impairment. Results show a significant ability to reliably differentiate normal from clinical behavior.

Taken together, results from Studies 1 and 2 provide evidence that the full body contributes to gaze stabilization during locomotion, and that different functional elements are responsive to changes in visual task constraints and are subject to adaptive alterations following exposure to visual-vestibular conflict. These studies also successfully validate new integrated methodologies designed to assess locomotor function for countermeasure evaluation and validation.
