experiment_title: Human Otolith Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
If an individual observes a dim line of light in darkness, while seated upright under ordinary conditions, he or she is able to set a line in the dark to the horizontal with great accuracy. This confirms that in the absence of visual cues, the ability of the observer to estimate the vertical and horizontal is dependent upon the influence of primary and secondary gravitational cues. In microgravity, primary gravitational cues are lost and the body’s otolith organs lose their normal stimulus.

Microgravity thus offered a unique opportunity to investigate the role of secondary gravitational cues to orient a person to this environment. During space flight, astronauts are cued to their position inside the spacecraft, even with eyes closed, by virtue of tactile cues. The first step in exploring the loss of primary gravitational cues in space flight was to estimate horizontality with reference to the spacecraft in the absence of visual and primary gravitational cues. Egocentric visual localization of the horizontal (EVLH) was the test chosen to measure space perception in the absence of adequate visual cues.

Researchers then assessed the possible effect of prolonged microgravity on otolith function by measuring ocular counterrolling (CR). The CR test was based upon the observation that when a normal person is tilted to the right or to the left, the eyes tend to rotate in the opposite direction. If proper technique is used, the amount of counterroll is a specific and valid measure of otolith function. The object of the test was to determine whether prolonged physiological deafferentation of the otolith apparatus altered its basic sensitivity.

APPROACH:
Both portions of this experiment were performed on subjects A and B during the Gemini 5 (8-day) mission and subjects C and D of the Gemini 7 (14-day) mission. Due to space limitations, the CR test was limited to preflight and postflight measurements. Subjects A and B were tested for CR and EVLH sixteen days before flight. Subjects C and D were similarly tested on two different occasions, nineteen and six weeks preflight. Inflight testing of EVLH was performed on seven occasions during Gemini 5 and fourteen occasions during Gemini 7. Subjects A and B were examined approximately 6 and 5 hours, respectively, after recovery at sea. Subjects C and D were examined approximately 6 and 4.5 hours respectively, after recovery at sea.

Preflight and postflight, the EVLH test was performed as follows. Immediately before performing the test, one drop of 1 percent pilocarpine hydrochloride ophthalmic solution was placed in the subject’s eye that would not be used to make visual orientation judgments. The ophthalmic solution was used to constrict the pupil, thereby restricting the amount of light that could enter the eye. The subject was then placed in a CR device that could be tilted back and forth. A binocular vision tester measured the subject’s interpupillary distance and was held stationary by inserting the biteboard into the subject’s mouth. The researcher initially offset the line target presented to one eye only (the other eye observed a completely dark field). By turning a knob on the vision tester, the subject rotated the target clockwise or counterclockwise until it appeared to be aligned parallel to the gravitational horizontal. This procedure was repeated in each test session until eight settings had been made in the upright position.

Inflight, the subject prepared for EVLH testing inflight by covering the left eyepiece (subjects B and D) or right eyepiece (subjects A and C), and turning on the luminous target before the other eye. The choice of which eyepiece to cover was dependent on which seat the test subject was stationed. The target appeared against a completely dark background was initially was offset at random by the observer. The subject was to adjust the target until it appeared horizontal with respect to the immediate spacecraft environment. The subject, when satisfied with each setting, closed his eyes and removed his hand from the adjustment knob. The observer then recorded the setting and offset the target. This procedure was repeated five times each day. The vision tester was then handed to the other subject and the same procedure was followed. Finally, readings for each subject were voice-recorded. The Gemini 5 subjects were requested to maintain an erect position by alignment with the seat headrest. During Gemini 7, the method of testing EVLH inflight was identical, but a head brace was included as part of the experiment equipment.

Following the EVLH test, the subject remained upright in the tilt device. At this time the preflight and postflight ocular CR measurements were accomplished. The vision tester and its biteboard were removed, and preparations were made to photographically record the eye position associated with a given body tilt position. The CR biteboard was inserted in the subject’s mouth. The eye position was adjusted to coincide with the optic axis of the camera system when the subject fixated the center of the flashing red ring of light. Six photographic recordings were made at this position; then the subject was slowly tilted in his lateral plane to four other positions (plus/minus 25 degrees, and plus/minus 50 degrees) and the same photographic procedure was repeated.

During the EVLH and CR tests, blood pressure, heart rate, and electrocardiogram (ECG) were also monitored.

RESULTS:
Preflight ocular CR responses for both crews of Gemini 5 and Gemini 7 were within normal ranges, but the values for the Gemini 5 crewmembers were considered low. Comparison of the preflight data between the two flights revealed significant differences between the Gemini 5 and Gemini 7 crewmembers with regard to the basic magnitude of otolith response. Postflight data for all four subjects revealed that the CR response was not significantly different from the comparable data collected preflight. That was indicative that no significant change in otolithic sensitivity occurred as a result of space flight, or at least no change persisted long enough to be recorded several hours after recovery.

The EVLH data recorded for each subject confirmed the observation (made repeatedly in parabolic flight experiments) that a coordinate space sense existed even in a weightless environment if contact cues were adequate. However, it was noted that the apparent location of the horizontal within the space craft did not necessarily agree with its physical correlate in the spacecraft (a line parallel to the pitch axis of the vehicle). For example, data taken from crewmember A were indicative of greater than 30 degree deviation from the absolute horizontal. These data were indicative that, with closed eyes, cues furnished by contact with the spacecraft did not facilitate correct perception of the cabin axes. Furthermore, the uniformity of the settings by this crewmember throughout the flight was suggestive that learning did not occur in the absence of any knowledge of the accuracy of these estimates.

The EVLH judgments of Gemini 5 crewmember concerning the location of the gravitational horizontal for an upright position were quite accurate and stable prior to flight. On the day of recovery, the pattern of response was similar to that of preflight, but was less accurate and less consistent. Although the seas were relatively calm, the researchers believed the fact that judgments were made on an unstable platform could have be responsible for these differences. The EVLH judgments of Gemini 7 subjects in an upright position under normal gravitational conditions were unstable preflight. In approximately one-half of the settings, deviations greater than 5 degrees were recorded, and one setting exceeded 10 degrees. On the day of landing, the response pattern was similar to preflight data even though the judgments were made under unstable, though relatively calm, sea conditions. (During the Gemini Program, crews landed and were recovered at sea, and were transported to shore aboard a ship.)

Inflight, subject B of Gemini 5 produced accurate and consistent visual estimation. Subject A, although no less consistent than subject B, made judgments that were significantly (<30 degree) deviant from the absolute horizontal of the spacecraft environment. The uniformity of subject A’s settings throughout the flight suggested, furthermore, that learning did not occur in the absence of any knowledge of the accuracy of these estimates. The EVLH judgments of both crewmembers of Gemini 7 throughout the flight showed no trends with respect to longitudinal changes in the stability or absolute position of horizontal within the spacecraft. For the most part, EVLH judgments for the Gemini 7 crewmembers were relatively accurate and more stable than under normal gravitational conditions. These data showed that relatively accurate and consistent nonvisual orientation was possible throughout prolonged periods of microgravity exposure so long as secondary cues were adequate.

Further experimentation involving inflight serial EVLH measurements were planned in conjunction with the Apollo flights to increase the knowledge of the role of secondary cues in orientation and the possible interindividual differences.

experiment_title: Combined Blood Investigations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary objective of this investigation was to measure selected hormone and electrolyte components of the blood early in space flight. The blood components selected reflect the status of fluid and electrolyte metabolism. Measurement of these variables may help investigators determine whether responses predicted by the fluid redistribution hypothesis occur. According to this hypothesis, losses of body fluid and electrolytes result from the headward shift of fluid brought about by exposure of the human body to weightlessness. Estimation of early changes previously was not possible because of inflight scheduling priorities and constraints. The most dramatic changes in the adaptive response to weightlessness are believed to occur in the first hours of a mission.

APPROACH:
The Inflight Blood Collection System was used to collect samples by venipuncture from 6 subjects on 2 missions 1 or 3 times before flight; on mission days 2, 4, and 6 during flight; and within 2 hours (R+0) and 3 days (R+3) after landing. The concentrations of electrolytes and other blood components were determined using established clinical laboratory procedures such as spectrophotometry and radioimmunoassay.

RESULTS:
The earliest inflight blood collection time of 31 hours may not have been early enough. High levels of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) may have been related to space motion sickness. Angiotensin I levels increased while aldosterone was suppressed at the inflight times measured. Cortisol secretion appeared to have been stimulated by high levels of adrenocorticotropic hormone. Most hormones increased at landing. Serum sodium decreased slightly during flight, and potassium decreased in the first 4 days but increased on flight days 6 and 7. The results, especially those for hormone levels, indicated that the fluid redistribution hypothesis does not explain changes in the regulation of body fluid and electrolytes during weightlessness. Renal function and other factors involved in fluid and electrolyte regulation, such as atrial natriuretic factor and prostaglandin E, need to be measured during flight.

experiment_title: Behavior and Performance Project
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Physiological and behavioral adaptations to a change in environmental conditions are primarily dependent upon the subject's sympathetic/parasympathetic nervous system balance, stress tolerance level, and health status. In order to determine the effects of microgravity on physiology, scientists devised eye-head-hand/foot coordination exercises to be performed by two monkeys during the 14-day Bion 11 space flight.

Approach:

In Program I, each monkey was required to touch a lighted stimulus presented on a panel in front of it with its left hand. The stimulus could appear in the center of the panel, called the trigger stimulus, or in one of four peripheral locations. After touching the trigger stimulus, a peripheral stimulus would appear in a positive sign or a differential sign. If a positive sign appeared and the monkey touched the stimulus, it was rewarded with a small quantity of juice. If the differential stimulus appeared, the monkey would be required to stop. Failing to touch the positive stimulus or procrastinating would cause a delay in the appearance of the next stimulus. By the same token, touching the differential stimulus would invoke a delay. Program II was similar to Program I with the exception that the monkey responded to the stimuli by pushing a foot peal. In response to the trigger stimulus, the monkey would push the pedal in three successive movements. After completing that task, another stimulus would appear, instructing the monkey to hold down the pedal for 2 seconds. If both activities were completed successfully, the monkey was rewarded with juice. Program I occurred twice a day every flight day, whereas Program II occurred at 9 am every flight day and 1 pm every odd flight day.

Results:

Following the flight, adaptability to microgravity was determined in terms of stimulus recognition, response time, and performance success rate. For the first 2 days of flight, monkey #484 developed motion sickness and could not perform the exercises. After FD3, Monkey #484 had greater accuracy in responding to stimuli 2 and 4 (those closest to the center). Monkey #357, on the other hand, demonstrated higher accuracy and swiftness in responding to the peripheral stimuli. Although both monkeys were able to complete Program II on the ground, they both failed to complete it in space. This could be attributed to their inability to visualize their foot movements. With the exception of monkey #484's brief bout with motion sickness, microgravity had no affect on the monkey's performance as compared to pre- and postflight data.

experiment_title: HZE-induced Skin Carcinoma: An in-vivo-like Multicellular Epithelial Model System for Analysis of Radiation Quality Effects and DSB Repair Processes
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Skin as a model system to study radiation-induced human epithelial cancers: Skin is one of the most complex organs of the body, consisting of multiple cell types, including epithelial keratinocytes and connective tissue (i.e. fibroblasts). Keratinocytes form a stratified squamous epithelium and are composed of one basal cell layer and several differentiated cell layers. Proliferation is limited to the basal layer, whereas differentiating cells withdraw from the cell cycle and express various differentiation markers, dependent on the stage of their differentiation. Because radiation-induced neoplasms in skin derive primarily from epithelial cells, radiobiological studies on keratinocyte monolayers (2D) provide a good first approximation for assessing cancer development processes triggered by ionizing radiation, but also by other environmental mutagens.

APPROACH:
There is considerable evidence that ionizing radiation causes non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), and the risk for NMSC in astronauts is increased. To further assess the cancer risk for humans from space radiation, an in-vivo-like multicellular skin model system was used. Multiple different endpoints as surrogate markers for skin cancer were assessed. Persistent chromosomal damage, altered cell proliferation, and evasion from apoptosis were studied in 2D monolayer cultures of normal primary and of initiated human keratinocytes exposed to a variety of charged nuclei (Aim 1). In addition, to more realistically recapitulate the complex architecture of a tissue, an in-vivo-like skin model system, composed of fibroblasts and keratinocytes, was used to ascertain the risk of space radiation-induced cancer development processes in 3D (i.e. persistent chromosomal damage, altered cell proliferation, evasion from apoptosis, and differentiation) (Aim 2). Lastly, a surface transplantation assay of exposed 3D reconstructed human epithelia onto immunodeficient mice was carried out to test for intermediate and late events in cancer progression (cell invasion and metastasis, respectively) (Aim 3). Investigators hypothesized that, in basal cells, unfaithful DNA DSB repair will lead to persistent chromosomal damage, promoting altered cell growth and escape from tissue homeostasis. They believe that the proposed approach is highly relevant for assessing the risk of skin cancer in astronauts and for modeling space radiation-induced tumor development in other epithelial tissues.

RESULTS:
The cytokinesis-block micronucleus (MN) assay was used to assess the genotoxicity of low doses of different types of space radiation. Normal human primary keratinocytes and immortalized keratinocytes grown in 2D monolayers each were exposed to graded doses of 0.3 or 1.0 GeV/n silicon ions or similar energies of iron ions. The frequencies of induced MN were determined and compared to gamma-ray data. RBEmax values ranged from 2.0 to 3.9 for primary keratinocytes and from 2.4 to 6.3 for immortalized keratinocytes. At low radiation doses = 0.4 Gy, 0.3 GeV/n iron ions were the most effective at inducing MN in normal keratinocytes. An “over-kill effect” was observed for 0.3 GeV/n iron ions at higher doses, wherein 1.0 GeV/n iron ions were most efficient in inducing MN. In immortalized keratinocytes, 0.3 GeV/n iron ions produced MN with greater frequency than 1.0 GeV/n iron ions, except at the highest dose tested. MN formation was higher in immortalized keratinocytes than in normal keratinocytes for all doses and radiation qualities investigated.

MN induction was also assessed in human keratinocytes cultured in 3D to simulate the complex architecture of human skin. RBE values for MN formation in 3D were reduced for normal keratinocytes exposed to iron ions, but were elevated for immortalized keratinocytes. Overall, MN induction was significantly lower in keratinocytes cultured in 3D than in 2D. Together, the results suggest that tissue architecture and immortalization status modulate the genotoxic response to space radiation, perhaps via alterations in DNA repair fidelity.

Investigators also established a surface transplantation assay, which allowed them to extend their studies of the biological responses of human skin equivalents up to several months post radiation exposure. To do so, male NOD.SCID mice (obtained from Jackson Laboratory) were subjected to the skin grafting procedure at approximately 8 weeks of age and sent to BNL 4 weeks post-surgery. Cohorts of 6 mice each were exposed to 1 Gy of 300 or 1000 MeV/n Fe ions, or to 1 Gy of 137Cs gamma-rays for comparison purposes. Six mice were sham irradiated. All mice remained at BNL until necropsy at 8 weeks post radiation exposure. Tissue sections of the human skin grafts and of the undisturbed mouse skin were fixed in 10% buffered formaldehyde for 48 hours, followed by transfer and storage in 70% ethanol until processed and embedded in paraffin. Sections of 3 µm each were assessed by H&E staining for tissue architecture, by FISH using mouse and human COT1 DNA for tissue origin, and by IHC for markers of radiation exposure (53BP1 (i.e. genomic instability), Ki-67 (i.e. cell proliferation), and involucrin (i.e. keratinocyte differentiation).

Preliminary results show that 53BP1 foci are elevated and persistent in basal keratinocytes of human skin equivalents after radiation exposure. Keratinocytes with locally accumulated nuclear staining for 53BP1 are negative for Ki-67, indicative of a reinforced irreversible growth arrest of cells with persistent genomic instability. Investigators speculate that cellular senescence is accelerated in human basal cells following high LET radiation exposure to limit the proliferation of damaged cells that are at risk for neoplastic transformation, similar to the observations reported by others using low LET IR.

experiment_title: Resistance Exercise as a Countermeasure to Disuse-induced Bone Loss
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During spaceflight, skeletal unloading results in loss of bone mineral density (BMD). This occurs primarily in the spine and lower body regions. This loss of skeletal mass could prove hazardous to astronauts on flights of long duration.

APPROACH:
In this study, intense resistance exercise was used to test whether a training regimen would prevent the loss of BMD that accompanies disuse. Nine subjects (5 men, 4 women) participated in a supine maximal resistance exercise training program during 17 wk of horizontal bed rest. These subjects were compared with 18 control subjects (13 men, 5 women) who followed the same bed rest protocol without exercise. Determination of treatment effect was based on measures of BMD, bone metabolism markers, and calcium balance obtained before, during, and after bed rest.

Effects on bone and muscle of a load-progression regimen modeled after those used by resistance-trained athletes using the HEM. Subjects exercised 6 days per week during bedrest, alternating days of lower- and upper body work. Maximum-effort sets were designed in order for subjects to perform an 11-, 8-, or 5-repetition maximum (RM) (+ 1 repetition), to assure progression in training loads throughout the study.

RESULTS:
Exercisers and controls had significantly (P < 0.05) different means, represented by the respective following percent changes: lumbar spine BMD, +3% vs. -1%; total hip BMD, +1% vs. -3%; calcaneus BMD, +1% vs. -9%; pelvis BMD, -0.5% vs. -3%; total body BMD, 0% vs. -1%; bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, +64% vs. 0%; alkaline phosphatase, +31% vs. +5%; osteocalcin, +43% vs. +10%; 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D, +12% vs. -15%; parathyroid hormone intact molecule, +18% vs. -25%; and serum and ionized calcium, -1% vs. +1%. The difference in net calcium balance was also significant (+21 mg/day vs. -199 mg/day, exercise vs. control). The gastrocnemius and soleus muscle volumes decreased significantly in the exercise group, but the loss was significantly less than observed in the control group. The results indicate that resistance exercise had a positive treatment effect and thus might be useful as a countermeasure to prevent the deleterious skeletal changes associated with long-duration spaceflight.

Resistance exercise was effective in ameliorating bone loss (as measured by BMD) in the lumbar spine, total hip, heel, total body, and pelvis. Regional BMD was similar after BR to baseline levels in the EX subjects, except for lumbar spine, which was increased (+3.4%). Variations in response to EX in the trochanter region were noted. Biochemical markers in CTRL subjects indicated that bone resorption was increased with no change in bone formation, suggesting an uncoupling of bone remodeling. Both bone formation and resorption were increased in EX subjects, suggesting that bone remodeling was increased with less uncoupling. Changes in serum iCa, vitamin D metabolites and iPTH in CTRL but not EX subjects were consistent with the hormonal response to disuse-mediated increases in calcium release from bone (PTH is decreased, subsequently decreasing the hydroxylation of 25OHD to diOHD). Calcium balance was preserved in EX subjects and significantly negative in CTRL subjects, suggesting that resistance exercise is effective in preventing hypercalciuria with implications for renal stone risk. At the end of BR, 1 RM strength (isotonic protocol) was increased while lower body muscle mass, volume, and isokinetic strength were relatively unaffected by EX. These findings support the concept of specificity of isotonic training for the EX protocol. The authors conclude that increasing resistance exercise in the inflight exercise prescription is warranted as are further investigations of the efficacy of RE alone or with other countermeasure approaches in ameliorating microgravity-induced bone and muscle loss.

experiment_title: Evaluation of Skeletal Muscle Performance and Characteristics
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Traditional muscle deconditioning is characterized by atrophy and decreases in metabolic enzymes. Previous studies have demonstrated post-flight or post-bed rest decreases in muscle tone and other alterations in neuromuscular functions. Different degrees of altered performance (strength, endurance, and coordination) appear in different muscle groups and may be related to these changes after exposure to real or simulated microgravity. Altered integrated muscle performances (walking, running, standing, etc.) have been noted after exposure to real or simulated microgravity. All changes have been reported from a series of separate flight and simulation studies on different subjects and species over "flights" of different duration using a variety of in-flight exercise countermeasures. Muscle deconditioning may be better understood by examining multiple individuals doing the same countermeasures and tests during a single space flight. The objective of this experiment was to increase the understanding of muscle deconditioning and to evaluate the effects of the inflight countermeasures on muscle performance and characteristics. Based upon previous research, the investigators evaluated the following hypotheses.

Muscle performance will change in a non uniform manner during flight and will slowly readapt to before flight levels upon return to 1-g. These non uniform changes include:

  • Legs, arms, back and neck muscles will decondition to different levels
  • Extensors muscle characteristics will have greater changes than flexors
  • Different types of contractions will have disproportionate changes after flight
  • The major mechanisms for muscle deconditioning will be neural and changes in other muscle characteristics. These changes will slowly readapt to before flight levels upon return to 1-g.
  • There will be a significant decreases in integrated muscle performance (treadmill and cycle exercise) during the flight and will slowly readapt to before flight levels upon return to 1-g.
  • The decreases in integrated muscle performance will be due to the changes in the individual muscle performance and their underlying mechanisms.

    APPROACH:
    Skeletal muscle characteristics and performance were measured before and after flight on the three Mir 18 crewmembers. Muscle tone was the reflex muscle stiffness measured with a reflex myotonometer on the gastrocnemius. Strength velocities characteristics were assessed with the LIDO (LIDO Active Multi-Joint Isokinetic Dynamometer). Subjects contracted muscles of the ankle, knee, and back at maximal levels against a lever arm that is moving in the same direction as the muscle contraction (concentric contraction), and in the opposite direction as the muscle contraction (eccentric). No back data was collected at the flight surgeons' request. Voluntary Isometric contractions were assessed with the LIDO. Subjects contracted muscles of the ankle, knee, and neck on LIDO at maximal levels against a stationary lever arm. EMGs were recorded on select muscle groups. Fatiguability was assessed with a hand dynamometer (hand). Hand endurance was assessed at current and relative strength levels. The crewmember will be asked to hold a 50% of current strength for as long as possible. The absolute endurance was assessed with a series of contractions (3 s contraction, 2 s relaxation) at 75% of preflight strength. The test stopped when the target force was not met. Evoked isometric contractions (tendometria) assessed the single, double and tetanic twitches of the soleus/gastroc muscles in one subject. Sport (treadmill) testing was done using the Russian protocol. Metabolic and physical (running speed) parameters were recorded. EMG data of select muscles were recorded.

    RESULTS:
    Although time constraints canceled 50% of data collection sessions (SPORT had 75% canceled) and sample size was too small to make general inferences for all long duration space flights, valuable results were still obtained. Results showed that subjects who completed a greater percentage of the prescribed exercise were closer to before flight levels of performance for postural muscles (Quadriceps, Tricep Surae, Hamstrings, Neck Extensors), than those who completed less of the prescribed countermeasure program. Muscles used to maintain position during flight (tibialis anterior) maintained isometric but not isokinetic strength. The magnitude of the decreases in isokinetic strength, appear to be related to joint speed. Regardless of maintenance or loss of strength all muscles lost efficiency (more electrical activity needed to produce force after flight). The decrease in efficiency may be a function of contraction speed. Relative endurance (relative to 50% current level of strength) increased or was maintained after long duration flight. However, the absolute endurance (same work rate before and after flight) decreased dramatically. This decrease in absolute endurance may impact future EVAs. Evoked (tetanic) Contractions of Subject C. The decrease in the maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) was 4 times greater than that observed from the tetanic (evoked) contraction. This suggests that muscle potential for force developement was a small reason for the decrease in performance. Decreases in neural factors probably account for this difference. The large decrease in the single twitch force is thought to be related to decreased muscle tone (stiffness).

    Twenty-five percent of the large decrease in ankle strength (MVC) in subject C was due to the muscles inability to produce force (tetanic). Slower rates of force development and relaxation and the larger IEMG activity suggests that the remaining (75%) decrease in force in this subject had a strong neural component. The treadmill (SPORT) results showed decreases in peak running speed while maintaining metabolic demand, which suggests a decrease in running economy that may be linked to the decrease in muscle performance and vestibular problems. The larger decreases in NME at the high joint speeds may also be a contributing factor.

experiment_title: Artificial Gravity and Light as Countermeasures for Circadian Dysfunction in Altered Gravity Environments
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study will characterize disturbances of sleep in rhesus monkeys. The rhesus is a well established model for human physiology in many disciplines and is showing promise as a model of human sleep disturbances. This study will directly relate to issues of sleep and circadian rhythm disturbance as a result of occupational factors such as shift work or other irregular schedules and jet lag.

The Circadian Timing System (CTS) is an important temporal organizer controlling both the physiology and behavior of organisms. The CTS has been shown to be sensitive to altered force environments (AFE) in both the microgravity of space flight and in hypergravity produced by centrifugation. Evidence from several species shows that AFE produces changes in the period of the circadian clock (tau). Evidence from rodents also shows that AFE can phase-shift and synchronize the circadian pacemaker. Further, sensitivity to light exposure, the most potent synchronizer of the CTS, appears to be impaired in AFE, as shown by both molecular and physiological evidence. Thus, circadian regulation in AFE may result from interactions of G and light inputs to the CTS. It is important to understand how AFE alters the CTS response to light exposure to ensure that countermeasures for CTS dysfunction such as timed bright light are equally effective in AFE.

APPROACH:
The investigators used AFE produced by centrifugation to determine if the phase-shifting responses to light were impaired in AFE. Countermeasures for circadian dysfunction may differ from those suitable at 1G. They tested a light countermeasure for circadian dysfunction, with defined spectral content, duration and schedule, to determine how its efficacy was affected by AFE. Timed AFE exposure by centrifugation is a proposed countermeasure for changes in cardiovascular, skeletal, muscle and other systems in space flight. Pulses of AFE, however, can entrain and phase shift the CTS in rats, which possess similarities in CTS inputs to rhesus and humans. Of concern is that the use of a timed AFE countermeasure could potentially compromise CTS function, or even conflict with circadian countermeasures, by inappropriately phase-shifting the CTS. It is important to understand how acute AFE exposure at different times of day alters circadian phase and period in a diurnal primate. Impaired phase shifting by light would impact adjustment to new schedules as well as entrainment to either 24-hour or non-24-hour days. Conversely, if AFE is capable of phase shifting or entraining the primate CTS, AFE could also serve as a countermeasure for circadian dysfunction.

RESULTS:
This research program has made significant progress in examination of the mechanisms underlying the response of the CTS of primates to altered gravity. The investigators initiated new studies on the interaction of altered gravity and light sensitivity on the CTS. They have examined changes in circadian rhythms, sleep and performance to controlled lighting environments, with and without the perturbation of hypergravity produced by centrifugation. Several improvements have been made to the telemetry system and to the centrifuge housing and data collection system. In addition they have collaborated on a revision of the Psychomotor Test System for performance metrics, which also serves as enrichment by providing an operant task to the animals. In studies of blue light as a potential circadian countermeasure the investigators have seen that the effects of blue light on sleep and alerting depend on the time of day of presentation. They used non-24-hour light dark cycles of alternating 3-hour light and 3-hour dark periods (LD and DL 3:3) to present light and dark at all times of the 24-hour day. Increased sleep was seen following blue light presentation during the day and a phase-dependent alerting effect was seen following blue light exposure early in the subjective night. Blue light was tested as a substitute for white light in a conventional 24-hour day of 12-hour light and 12-hour dark (LD 12:12) to provide a worst-case test of augmented blue wavelengths, known to have the maximum effect on circadian timing. In this study, total sleep time and individual sleep stages did not differ significantly in blue light with the exception of increased rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. However, phase advances in sleep and brain temperature rhythms were seen in blue light, indicating phase re-alignment (advance) during the 24-hour day. Investigators have completed a renovation of their centrifuge facility for suitability with larger rhesus and can now evaluate how these changes interact with those induced by an altered gravitational field.

experiment_title: Chronobiology of Pocket Mice
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The objective of this experiment was to study the circadian system of a mammal during space flight. Specifically, it was intended to discover whether the periods of circadian rhythms of body temperature and animal movement of the pocket mouse would be affected under conditions of prolonged weightlessness. Free ranging mice were to be maintained in space in a closely controlled environment for 30-56 days under constant dark and constant temperature conditions. Pocket mice were chosen as subjects in part because of their ability to hoard food and survive without water. Their concentrated feces permit continuous isolation for several weeks uninterrupted by cage cleaning. Also the pocket mouse has a well defined marker of circadian phenomenon (torpor), in which its metabolic rate drops dramatically while at rest or in response to environmental stress. This is reflected as a drop in body temperature.

Approach:

Body temperature as a function of time is the primary data required from the mice, and a small block oscillator type transmitter was developed for the experiment. Subjects were selected on a number of criteria, including: expression of torpor, precision of circadian period of body temperature, body weight (10 grams), stability, food consumption, and general "housekeeping" behavior. Twenty-eight pocket mice were implanted with biotelemetry devices a little over a month before launch. Baseline data was collected at the launch site in a specially designed holding unit, and flight and backup CPE packages were loaded with six animals each. Scientific analysis and evaluation of the experiment were derived from a master magnetic tape of all data retrieved from the CPE units and as necessary an examination of mission voice tapes. Average daily activity records referenced the time or arousal from torpor and were correlated with body temperature measurements.

Results:

The quality of the data was excellent with data loss well below the specified 5% limit, and the flight hardware operated flawlessly for thirty hours after launch. Fairly regular bursts of activity at approximately sixty- to ninety-minute intervals were apparent in animals prior to launch and correlated with a rise in body temperature. Following launch, the tendency for bursts of activity persisted, but the pattern was more random. Analysis of activity data collected inflight demonstrated a good correlation with body temperature data, but the short inflight recording precluded any significant conclusions regarding patterns of activity. Attempts were made to average the daily activity record referenced to time of entry into torpor and other arbitrary phase markers, but the bursts of energy tended to average and meaningful patterns were not apparent. It was concluded that had the experiment been completed, the additional activity data would have been quite useful in accomplishing the stated objectives.

experiment_title: Rodent Research 6 (RR6)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Rodent Research 6 (RR-6) science investigation was sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration and the Center for Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) in partnership with Norvartis and NanoMedical Systems to evaluate the impact of a new treatment drug (fomoteral or FMT) designed to mitigate muscle atrophy caused by exposure to microgravity, and to test a new subcutaneous delivery system for the drug using nanochannel implants.

This flight had two aims:
1. To study the efficacy of constant FMT release in vivo in microgravity.
2. To analyze sample and data and assess side effects associated with constant FMT delivery in microgravity.

Exposure to microgravity during spaceflight results in significant and rapid effects on the musculoskeletal system, similar to what occurs in certain muscle wasting diseases on Earth that are triggered by, for example, prolonged immobilization, cancer, and aging. Studying accelerated muscle wasting in space could provide insight into disease mechanisms, confirm potential new drug targets, and enable the preclinical evaluation of a candidate therapeutic targeted to such disease. This research also improves understanding of nanochannel delivery systems, also known as drug release chips). Results of this investigation are also expected to increase our understanding of ground-based diseases, disorders and injuries affecting millions of people globally and aid in the development of new therapeutics and strategies to treat such conditions.

experiment_title: Microbial Risk Assessment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this study was to utilize a systematic approach toward evaluation of current data, identify gaps in knowledge, develop confidence levels, identify risks, and determine acceptable and unacceptable risks. The study used quantitative microbial risk assessment approaches that have been applied to great success in the food and potable water industries. The application of these methods to the latest data sets obtained in space travel allowed the most appropriate data sets to be assessed for health assessment.

APPROACH:
The objective of this study was to develop and apply the quantitative microbial risk assessment (QMRA) framework at the International Space Station (ISS). Specifically, QMRA was used to translate ISS microbial water monitoring data to flight crew health impact in order to direct water monitoring practices and inform health risk reduction strategies. QMRA is a four-step paradigm – including (1) hazard identification; (2) dose-response assessment; (3) exposure assessment; and, (4) risk characterization – that is used to evaluate human health risks resulting from environmental exposure to pathogens. For this project, the framework was reviewed and modified for its applicability to address flight crew health risks associated with exposure to potable water at the ISS. The research plan was divided into four (4) phases. Phase 1 involved the initial evaluation of the QMRA process with the objective of identifying critical areas where QMRA can be effectively applied to the space flight scenario as well as areas where data are needed. Potable water monitoring data for microorganisms were reviewed and potential waterborne pathogens at the ISS were identified and characterized.

Phase 2 specifically addressed the dose-response step of the QMRA process. Using microbial water monitoring data obtained at the ISS, dose-response relationships that represent the flight crew (host) and microorganism (potential pathogen) interaction were developed. This Phase of the project identified Pseudomonas as an appropriate model microorganism to address potable water quality at the ISS. Pseudomonas was chosen as a microbe of interest because of its occurrence in ISS water, the availability of dose-response data derived from human volunteer studies and published in the peer-reviewed literature, and its association with a wide range of human health effects. Pseudomonas offers unique challenges because it is ubiquitous in the environment, is an opportunistic pathogen, is resistant to different types of disinfectants, is capable of forming biofilms, and has the ability to grow in unusual environments. In addition, in some ways Pseudomonas is representative of several members of the heterotrophic plate count (HPC) bacteria, which are routinely detected in ISS potable water. Furthermore, Pseudomonas is transmitted through water through a variety of different exposure routes, which is a necessary consideration when addressing flight crew exposures to water at the ISS.

Phase 3 focused on the exposure assessment aspect of the QMRA. Several pertinent questions related to exposure were initially identified and included: (1) What factors affect the occurrence of pathogenic microbes at ISS?; (2) What factors affect the likelihood of flight crew exposure to waterborne microbes at ISS?; (3) What factors affect the extent of flight crew exposure to waterborne microbes at ISS?; (4) In what ways are flight crew exposed to waterborne microbes at the ISS?; (5) How important are certain exposure factors to flight crew health risks?; and, (6) How do estimated risks associated with ISS potable water compare to health risks in terrestrial water environments? Previous QMRAs involving the terrestrial water environment have shown that it is the exposure assessment step that contributes the greatest source of variability and uncertainty in the QMRA. Typically, exposure-related input parameters are either unknown or they represent a wide-range of plausible values. This Phase identified key aspects of the ISS environment that introduce different challenges related to exposure, which can subsequently impact health risks.

Phase 4 integrated all of the information learned from the first three Phases to complete a risk characterization of flight crew exposure to identified hazards in ISS potable water. The approach was both qualitative and quantitative, with the overall objective to predict flight crew health outcomes from exposure to water at the ISS. Infection risk ranges estimated in Phase 3 for Pseudomonas, Salmonella, and E. coli were evaluated for practical implications.

RESULTS:
Results for this experiment will be available once the investigators have published their findings.

experiment_title: PharmaSat: Effect of Microgravity upon Yeast Susceptibility to Antifungal Drugs
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The PharmaSat experiment was designed to measure the effect of microgravity upon yeast resistance to the antimicrobial agent - voriconazole. Voriconazole is a stable and broad spectrum antimicrobial that targets the fungal cytochrome p450 sterol 14-demethylase enzyme (CYP51) Previous experimentation in microgravity and under modeled microgravity conditions suggest that in these environments, resistance to azoles is increased. Voriconazole has excellent stability under ambient conditions and exhibits a broad spectrum of activity and is being evaluated in vitro as a potential antifungal counter-measure in space. The PharmaSat experimental design uses a recognized laboratory testing method for antimicrobial resistance. The experiment investigated three concentrations of voriconazole (a low concentration, a concentration at the minimal inhibitory concentration, MIC and a high dose, plus a no-drug control) for their effect on yeast growth cell and viability. Saccharomyces cerevisiae was used as a model microorganism and has been the subject of previous space-flight studies, and is used as a standard to evaluate resistance to antifungal agents. Growth was measured by two independent methods - optical density (OD) and Alamar Blue reduction as a metabolic indicator. Statistical analysis of the data used longitudinal data, a more robust approach than traditional end-point-based analysis. The underlying hypothesis for this experiment was “yeast growing in microgravity has altered resistance to azole antifungal agents”. The experiment was conducted in a 59-well Fluidic Card with 48 biology wells in four independently plumbed banks with 11 reference wells in the center bank. Gas- permeable membranes on both sides of the wells allowed for air exchange and 1µm Nylon filter membranes retained the yeast cells inside the wells The experiment used a complex fluidic system capable of two fluid exchanges, dilution of the antifungal agent and replenishing evaporative losses by using 2 pumps, 9 reservoir bags and 14 valves.

APPROACH:

The nanosatelite was deployed ~20 min after launch and radio contact was established during the first orbit. The satellite orbit became stabilized in ~24 hours. Its orbital trajectory put PharmaSat in sunlight ~ 67% and darkness ~ 33% of each 97-min orbit. After stabilization (gravity < 10-3 g), at t = 47 hr after orbital deployment, the temperature of the fluidic card was set to 27 °C. After allowing 3.6 hr for temperature stabilization, S. cerevisiae growth was initiated (in all 48 wells of the microfluidic plate) by introducing RPMI1640 cell culture medium containing the viability dye - Alamar blue. Each 12-well bank of wells was activated in sequence. Two concentrations (0.1 and 0.2 OD600) of the yeast were utilized. In each bank one set of six wells were loaded with yeast at the lower optical density, while the remaining 6 wells of each bank were loaded with yeast at the higher OD (0.2). This strategy insured that if insufficient organisms survived the stasis period in the lower OD groups of wells, the higher OD wells would provide an ~2X higher initial population to begin growth. Since antifungal tests are more reliable at lower cell densities, the successful growth of all 24 wells at the lower OD cultures led us to choose those data for our initial ground/flight comparisons.

Voriconazole, a stable antifungal agent was introduced after the yeast had initiated growth. Based on initial growth rates, voriconazole was introduced by pumping ~ 12 hr after initial growth medium introduction. Ground controls for this experiment consisted of an identical satellite system at NASA Ames, housed in a thermal chamber with temperatures set to those reported by the satellite. This Ground Control, with S. cerevisiae loaded from the same flight cultures was conducted as a “delayed synchronous” (~1 day) ground control experiment to compare ground and space results.

After allowing for initial growth (re-activation of the yeast cultures), growth medium + voriconazole was pumped into the four 12-well banks at 0.25X, 1X, and 4X the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). The MIC of voriconazole for S. cerevisiae was 0.5 µg/mL in ground studies. This allowed each of the four conditions tested with multiple independent microwells at both concentrations.

RESULTS:

Yeast cultures showed a longer “lag time” (time to the mid-point of mid-logarithmic growth), growth time (time in exponential growth) and doubling time in space samples than ground controls. All values were significant except for cell division for the growth time measurement. It may be the case that the yeast grow more slowly in space because the transport of nutrients to the cells and/or the transport of waste products away from the cells is slower, being driven solely by diffusion, than on Earth where convection can play a role in mass transport. Overall, the PharmaSat experiment was a success. Cell growth and metabolic activity was observed in all wells, and an antifungal effect was observed in both ground and spaceflight samples. All equipment functioned nominally. Biological results showed: 1) differences in the growth rates between flight and ground samples, 2) antifungal activity was observed in both cultures, 3) no significant differences between the spaceflight and ground cultures were observed with the low and MIC concentrations but a large difference was observed at the high antifungal concentration.

experiment_title: Identification of Aerobic Fitness Standards for Exploration Mission Tasks
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The physical demands of exploration mission tasks, like any job, can vary depending on the task and environment. During the original Apollo missions certain tasks like photography needed little effort whereas construction and shoveling type tasks required increased physical exertion. Planned missions to terrestrial surfaces (e.g., asteroid, the moon, and Mars), where crewmembers will spend an extended period of time in a microgravity setting, may result in a plausible scenario in which at some point within the mission critical tasks may become physically challenging enough that a decrease in performance and safety results. Therefore, it is critical to understand the relationship between the ability to complete specific mission critical tasks and aerobic exercise capacity. To mitigate the risk of an unacceptable scenario in which crewmembers are unable to perform critical mission tasks due to inadequate aerobic exercise capacity, a set of easily administered predictor tests must be developed and used to evaluate both countermeasure effectiveness and ultimately, whether a crewmember is ready and capable of performing various physiologically demanding tasks. Therefore, the overall goal of this proposed work is twofold: develop a thorough understanding of the physiological parameters associated with the ability to complete simulated mission critical tasks, and develop a battery of predictor tests that will provide critical information regarding a crewmember’s readiness and capability to perform these tasks.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine values and ranges for aerobic fitness variables that can individually or in aggregate (a) map to the level of success for a given mission critical task and (b) provide an aerobic fitness standard.
  2. Using the information obtained from Specific Aim 1, design predictor testing protocols that can be performed with in-flight hardware and astronaut time constraints.

APPROACH:
Project 1
Investigators studied a group of 45 men and women who completed a series of mission critical tasks; a surface traverse task and a hill climb task. Participants performed each mission task at a low and moderate intensity designed to elicit specific metabolic responses similar to what is expected for ambulation in Lunar and Martian gravities, respectively. Aerobic fitness was characterized via cycling and rowing VO2peak, ventilatory threshold (VT), and critical power. Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis were used to determine the cutoff thresholds for each aerobic fitness parameter that accurately predicted task performance.

Project 2
Fifteen participants volunteered for this study. VO2peak and peak power output (PPO) were determined on cycle and rowing ergometers. Critical power (CP) was determined by a three minute all-out rowing test. Subjects then performed an emergency capsule egress on a mock-up of NASA’s Orion space capsule. Peak metabolic data were compared between the cycling and rowing tests. Pearson’s Correlation was used to identify relationships between egress time and VO2peak, PPO, and CP.

RESULTS:
Project 1
The low and moderate intensity traverse tests estimated a VO2 response of 23±1 ml kg-1 min-1 and 29±1 ml kg-1 min-1. VO2peak, VT, and critical power all showed high sensitivity and specificity for identifying individuals who could not complete the mission tasks. Therefore, minimum fitness thresholds for each task at each intensity were determined for each of the submaximal and maximal fitness variables. In summary, investigators identified aerobic fitness thresholds below which task performance was impaired for both low and moderate intensity mission critical tasks. Specifically, cycling VO2peak, VT, and rowing CP could each be used to predict task failure.

Project 2
VO2peak, VCO2peak, and minute ventilation were not different between cycling and rowing tests. Cycling elicited a greater PPO than the rowing test. Egress time was negatively correlated to cycling and rowing VO2peak (r=-0.61) and cycling and rowing PPO (r=-0.56 and r=-0.74, respectively), but not CP. Conclusions: Our data suggest that rowing PPO/kg was a strong predictor of egress time. Although individuals with higher PPO/kg were able to finish the task in less time, even sedentary individuals with low fitness levels (VO2peak<20 ml/kg/min) were able to complete the egress within two minutes. This suggests that if minimum fitness is maintained, completing the emergency egress should be successful.

experiment_title: Microfluidic Device-Based Capture and Concentration of Microbial Contaminants in Recycled Water
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As the duration of space mission’s increase, recycling of metabolic and hygienic wastes becomes a necessity. Thus, the microbiological quality of recycled water is of critical importance to astronaut health and environmental quality during such missions. Accidental or catastrophic failures of the recycling process can introduce opportunistic organisms, pathogens, and organisms that cause biofouling of water distribution lines. It is critically important that water quality monitoring systems are able to capture, concentrate, and detect these contaminants effectively and efficiently. An efficient microbial capture and concentration device is needed for concentrating the sample prior to detection. The overall objective of this project was to design, fabricate, test, and optimize a prototype microfluidic device that can capture and concentrate microbial contaminants based on electrostatic trapping and electrophoretic motion principles. The microfluidic device was designed to concentrate microbial contaminants from 120L/day of recycled water on a continuous basis. The salient feature of the device is that the final concentrated volume will be 1 mL which will facilitate integration with any current or future contaminant detection technologies. In this pilot study proposal, investigators proposed to demonstrate bacterial capture and concentration by the microfluidic device and detection by culture and PCR-based detection and characterization. This interdisciplinary project involving engineering and microbiology delineated the design and performance characteristics of the microfluidic device. In addition to the benefits to NASA, the proposed technology has value in terrestrial and homeland security applications as well.

APPROACH:
Reclaimed and bottled water samples at pH values ranging from 5.2-6.5 were seeded with bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella, and Pseudomonas) and viruses (MS-2 and Echovirus). Negative control and capture experiments were performed simultaneously using two identical devices. Culture based methods were utilized to characterize the capture efficiency as a function of the species type, time, flow rate, and applied electric field.

RESULTS:
Funding from the NASA Phase 1 Pilot Study project was used to design and demonstrate the applicability of a microfluidic device-based capture and concentration of microbial contaminants in recycled water. During the initial phases of this project investigators developed a basic understanding of the electrophoretic mobilities of selected bacteria under conditions that were realistic within recycled and drinking water distribution systems. Electrophoretic mobility and zeta potential measurements of bacterial cells in municipal drinking water can lead to enhanced understanding of bacterial surface interactions and adhesion to surfaces in realistic environmental conditions. During the second half of this project a large number of laboratory experiments were performed to design, fabricate, and test the efficacy of a microfluidic-device based microbial capture system. These studies have led to the development of a microfluidic device based on electrophoretic transport and electrostatic trapping of charged particles for continuous capture and concentration of pathogens from water. Reclaimed and bottled water samples at pH values ranging from 5.2–6.5 were seeded with bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella, Pseudomonas) and viruses (MS-2 and Echovirus) and used in device testing. Both culture based methods and real-time PCR analysis were utilized to characterize the capture efficiency as a function of time, flow-rate, and applied electric field. Based on differences between the capture and negative control data, capture efficiencies of 90% to 99% were achieved for E. coli, Salmonella, Pseudomonas, and MS-2, while the capture efficiency for Echovirus was around 75%. Overall, the device exhibits 16.67 fold sample volume reduction within an hour at 6 mL/hr. This results in a concentration factor of 15 at 90% capture efficiency. Scaling of the device to sample 5 L/hour can be achieved by stacking 835 identical micro-channels. The device can thus function either as a filtration unit or as a sample concentrator to enable the application of real-time detection sensor technologies. The ability to continuously sample water without chemical additives facilitates the use of this device for NASA applications within enclosed environments. The successful completion of this project constitutes the first step in the development of a continuous, microbial capture and concentration system from large volumes of potable water. A key driving force in the device design was to achieve reduced mass, and reduce power and volume requirements.

experiment_title: Streptococcus Pneumoniae Expression of Genes in Space (SPEGIS)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

To investigate the alteration of virulence of Streptococcus pneumoniae ATCC 6304 after growth in spaceflight compared to cultures grown on earth. This bacterium was investigated on a previous flight (STS-118, SPEGIS I) for alterations in gene and protein expression and is an opportunistic respiratory pathogen. It has been isolated previously from a crewmember’s nasopharynx preflight indicating that this normally commensal bacterium could become a risk during flight.

APPROACH:

Streptococcus pneumoniae ATCC 6304 was cultured in spaceflight or in parallel ground controls using Group Activation Pack (GAP) hardware. MDRV flew on STS-123 (March, 2008). The Flight FPAs in GAP8 were activated on MET day 11. The Ground Control (GC) samples were activated one hour later. FPAs were received ~2.5 hrs after landing. The culture media from each sample was collected and aliquots diluted for serial dilution and plate counting on Blood Agar plates. There was minimal growth in the Flight samples. The optical density at 600nm of flight cultures with high initial loading was similar with the ground control with low loading, which showed a slightly higher value. Because of similarity of optical density which is indicative of bacterial cell numbers, the Flight high load and Ground Control low pools were selected for the post-flight mouse virulence study.

RESULTS:

There was an obvious and clear difference in mouse virulence between the flight and ground control cultures in terms of LD50 (16-fold lower for the flight grown cultures). However, the LD50 of these suboptimal cultures were much higher (FLT 35-fold; GC 566-fold) than that observed for strain ATCC 6304 under optimal culture conditions (37C). The differences between flight and ground cultures may reflect virulence differences arising from changes in bacterial gene expression or altered physiology/metabolism in the space environment. Alternatively, the differences observed could arise from the differential growth temperature between the flight and ground controls. This seems unlikely as the ground cultures were at a higher temperature closer to the growth optimal where maximal virulence is observed. However, this remains to be fully established with additional flight experimentation and ground controls.

experiment_title: Habitability Assessment:  Habitat Utilization Analysis from Human Factors Perspective
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of the habitability assessment project is to evaluate the Aquarius from the human factors and habitability perspective as an isolated, confined analog for the International Space Station (ISS), determine the human factors and habitability requirements for such an isolated and confined analog, and identify potential enhancement for the next generation habitat via use of naturalistic data capture, habitability questionnaire, and Space Operations Issues Reporting Tool (SOIRT).

By identifying how participants use the Aquarius habitat, conclusions can be drawn about which habitability attributes cause specific interactions and behaviors facilitating a systematic design to achieve desired human performance. In addition, the inclusion of objective data may provide inputs to other analysis of work/rest schedules.

Finally, naturalistic data collection has been under investigation as a means to opportunistically gather data during NASA training and actual International Space Station (ISS) missions. Inclusion of this method of data collection served as a test case to identify pros and cons and associated technological challenges.

APPROACH:
Crewmembers filled out a habitability survey, including questions regarding acceptability of the Aquarius habitat such as its interior layout, physical environment (e.g., noise, humidity), tasks, and individual experience/comments. This survey was required to be completed only once for the duration of each mission.

Crewmembers also filled out an issue reporting form, called SOIRT, to note any design or activity based issues and/or enhancements. This form was filled out on an as-needed basis throughout each mission.

The NEEMO 5 project also involved taping live feed from cameras, positioned with a view to the central common areas in the Aquarius. Taping took place during pre-defined periods of the 14-day mission. A heads-up signal was given at bedtime the night prior to taping, to remind the crewmember of the taped monitoring the following day. A second heads-up was given upon wake-up the following day, and a third at the end of the taping. The videos, which showed how crewmembers chose to use common spaces in Aquarius during the course of the day, were analyzed by computer to extract objective data. Once the data was extracted and analyzed, the videotapes were destroyed.

After the mission, the videotapes were reviewed and the amount of time each area was used by the crew at various times during the length of the mission was calculated. In addition, qualitative and descriptive analysis of the types of behaviors in each area was performed with the purpose of identifying any behaviors not typical of a certain area. If a participant used an area in a way different than expected, a subsequent analysis of the features of that area may result in conclusions of certain features that cause certain behaviors.

Finally, questionnaire data was analyzed to look for common pros and cons of the habitat across NEEMO/Aquarius crews, as well as consistency across different analogs used for space missions. This will help identify the functional needs and human factors requirements for living and working in an isolated, confined environment.

RESULTS:
From analysis of the video, several habitability issues related to the Aquarius habitat became apparent:

  • Workstations were poorly placed and interfered with the flow of traffic in and out of the Main Lock. Particularly, the two workstations located near the entrances were problematic both for people trying to pass through, as well as for people working at them who were interrupted in their work. When more than one person was at either of the two workstations, sitting on the step ladder or standing and looking over the shoulder of the other person, traffic flow was obstructed even more. In at least one instance, the stepladder was left behind after two crewmembers were working together, and another crewmember passing through had to step over it.

  • Another habitability issue revealed by the video analysis was the inappropriate size of the table. Used for eating, working, meetings, and group teleconferences with ground, the table sometimes needed to accommodate up to six people at once. Even for four people, as was more often the case, the table was far too small and it was obvious from the video that the crewmembers were uncomfortable. Often during group meetings some of them would have to sit on the step ladder or stand. Given its frequency of use, the table should be larger to comfortably seat all members of the crew to improve comfort, work, and social interaction. From the videos it also became evident that the food storage was poorly sited. Multiple instances were recorded where crewmembers were seen reaching across the small galley, blocking traffic or standing precariously on the stepladder to reach the storage areas. This also occurred frequently near and during meal times when most of the crewmembers were in and moving about the Main Lock.

  • Also noted during these periods was the fact that the refrigerator and microwave/storage areas were located too far from each other, as lots of back and forth traffic occurred between them. Given the narrow passage, it was readily apparent that traffic within the Main Lock could be much ameliorated simply by moving these two areas closer together.

    In conclusion, video analysis provided useful ideas as to how an enclosed habitat might be improved. As with the common human factors method of link analysis (e.g. Thelwell, 2004), simply noting which areas are accessed frequently together can provided insight into how to rearrange the habitat to improve efficiency and even reduce risk of injury. While web cast video had its technological problems, such as erratic skips, lags, graininess, blocked views, and lighting inconsistencies, it did provide useful overall information for practical recommendations. Systematic research, however, would require a higher standard of data collection. Perhaps in the future, notes regarding crew activity could be added by those recording the video to aid those tasked to analyze it later. This feature was sometimes present in the NEEMO 5 video; however, it was not present often enough to prove useful to the researchers. Also, video size and quality should be closely monitored to ensure that a larger percent of the captured video is analyzable.

    Naturalistic data capture by webcast video was found to be effective for getting the broad picture of habitat use by the NEEMO 5 crew. While there is obviously room for improvement, predominantly with the technology, there are some major benefits to be taken from this type of effort, as Adams (2002) reported previously. This type of work is crucial for designing and optimizing a habitat to support crew behavior as it will occur, especially since many of the findings were not captured in crew debriefings. This may be due to the unconscious influence of environmental performance shaping factors; however, more research is needed to support this claim. The inclusion of automation, such as sensors and location tracking, in future studies would make recording and analyzing certain metrics far easier and improve accuracy (e.g., entries and exits, frequency of use). The significant input that this type of research provides for generating optimal habitat designs and guidelines should not be neglected in any future long duration spaceflight effort.

experiment_title: (NSCORT) for Advanced Life Support at Purdue/Howard/AAMU - Integrated Systems Group
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Throughout the life of ALS NASA Specialized Center of Research and Training (NSCORT), the systems group researchers matured from learning and exploratory mode, which can be mainly characterized by proof-of-concept studies to build a viable toolbox of systems analysis methodologies suitable for ALS analysis, e.g. SimOpt (SIMulation based OPTimization), Markov Theory and Model Predictive Control, towards well-structured and coordinated efforts to improve their readiness level for repeated use in answering questions that matters to NASA and ALS community at large.

As systems group was undergoing through its voyage within ALS NSCORT, the systems group’s analysis and modeling scope has been expanded to all ALS technologies and to adopt lifecycle management view to study 15-20 year Mars Base ALS system evolution which recognizes the fact that Mars Base ALS system will not stay as it was deployed at the very first mission. Unfortunately, the plans and resources had to be revised per early termination notice as NASA was undergoing through major re-organization and re-prioritization to maximize the return on NASA’s investment in ALS NSCORT by focusing on completing the matured on going tasks and retiring the new initiatives such as, the proof-of-concept study that has been initiated in collaboration with Envision Center at Purdue University on visualizing the evolution of Mars Base and its ALS system.

A simulation was developed to assist decision-making in choosing control policies in a closed environment. This closed environment consists of a simplified representation of the water subsystem based on the documentation by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). The water requirement (consumption) and generation are based on the crewmembers’ demographics, activity schedules as well as intensity of each activity. The overall goal of this project was to develop methodologies to ensure crewmembers survive while on space missions.

APPROACH:
The health of this system is the result of the intricate interaction between the crewmembers as well as the water subsystem. The primary measure of the health of the system is the “state” representation of the system. This representation is a conglomeration of various hourly assessments of different aspects of the system. These aspects include the deterministic as well as the stochastic nature of the system. Due to the potentially vast number of possible states in the entire state space, state reduction techniques as well as assessments for infeasible states are applied for state reduction. A reward system is designed for allocating reward/penalty values to system states that satisfy predetermined conditions. Due to the strong stochastic characteristics and the “memoryless” property of the system, the transition of system state can be modeled as a Markov process.

Due to the incomplete knowledge of the new system (that is not yet in existence) and its dynamics, process-control strategies need to be developed in such a way that they are comprehensive enough to manage the system given any kind of system behavior, anticipated or otherwise. However, before strategies can be developed, system states need to be captured. In order to explore the possible system states, a Controlled Random Walk (CRW) algorithm is developed to visit more system states in less amount of time, compared to traditional techniques such as the Pure Random Walk and the Round Robin Walk.

Transition probabilities are obtained through the simulation of the Markovian model. Capturing “true” state transition probabilities has been a challenge to researchers. In this research, a methodology is developed to minimize the number of data points (or simulation hours) while obtaining the transition probabilities that are closest to the system’s steady state probabilities by observing the percentage increase of states visits as well as probabilities convergence based on discrete consecutive time periods. The Kullback-Leibler Divergence distance is used as the foundation of the measurement. It is then modified in order to be used in this research study. A reference index is also defined based on this measure to study the “distance” between each probability distribution from the index. These probabilities, together with the reward values are formulated into appropriate mathematical representation and are solved by applying the Policy Iteration (PI) algorithm. The outcome from PI is an indication of the “best” policy to be applied when the system is in a given state.

RESULTS:
The simulation was done in three stages: Data Collection/State space exploration, System Evaluation with Dynamic Policy and System Evaluation with Fixed Policy. The Data Collection stage was performed through 800,000 ticks (simulation hours) of simulation time. Every set of 100,000 ticks consists of 5 sets of 20,000 ticks, each with a re-initialized starting condition. This is done to prevent the system from being “stuck” in a state or a loop of states. The proposed Controlled Random Walk technique is used during the data collection. Best policies are obtained through every set of 100,000 ticks, yielding eight sets of best policies. Every set of best policies are applied to a test system for evaluation. Results show that outcomes from applying these best policies are statistically better than using fixed policies, or using random policies.

As mentioned above, comprehensive process-control strategies are to be developed for various system states. The system might visit certain states that have not been visited before during data collection. These states will not have a corresponding “best” policy as they are “new” to the control system. In order to counter that problem, machine-learning technique is used. The See 5.0 algorithm (previously ID3) is used to generate a complete decision tree based on every set of best policies obtained from the PI. With the outcome from the See 5.0 algorithm, an action is available for use in the system given any state that the system visits. The outcomes of See 5.0 algorithm are evaluated against the outcomes from the PI using an independent test system. Results from non-parametric tests show that there is no statistical difference between the two, indicating that while policies obtained from See 5.0 perform as good as optimal policies from PI, See 5.0 also provides a complete decision tree, covering the entire state space.

experiment_title: Rodent Research 2 (RR2)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Rodent Research 2 study was sponsored by the Center for Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS), who collaborated with Novartis (lead scientist, Samuel Cadena) to characterize changes in the musculoskeletal tissues of mice exposed to varied lengths of spaceflight exposure.

The primary objective of the study was to evaluate molecular changes in hind limb tissues of mice and correlate these with changes in structure, morphology, materials properties, and function of muscle and bone. The secondary objective was to examine other organ systems for molecular and morphological changes as a function of duration of spaceflight exposure in order to further characterize the potential use of mice in space to model human cardiovascular, immunological, ocular, metabolic and neurological diseases and disorders.

Specifically, this flight study had three aims:
1. To evaluate muscle atrophy and bone loss under microgravity conditions and to identify molecular pathways and targets that could be used to develop novel therapeutics for muscle disease.
2. To quantify changes in various molecular markers from several tissues including whole blood, brain, heart, lungs, kidney/adrenal glands, liver, spleen, and small intestines.
3: To characterize the magnitude and time-course of bone loss during spaceflight exposure for future commercial bone drug testing.

APPROACH:
To evaluate structural and molecular changes over time, twenty wild-type female C57BL/6J mice were divided into four groups of five, which were processed identically: anesthetization and a scan using a bone densitometer, exsanguination via cardiac puncture, right and left hind limb removal, left eye removal, and preservation of the carcasses by freezing. The mice were processed over four dissection sessions throughout the mission after one week (Group 1), fifteen days (Group 2), twenty-seven days (Group 3), and fifty-four days (Group 4) of microgravity exposure after launch.

The ground control experiments were conducted on a four-day delay from the on-orbit experiment. The mice were housed in the environmental simulators and planned and non-planned events (such as unexpected power losses) were replicated for ground controls. Ground control procedures followed strict timelines from on-orbit time logs. The same kits and hardware were also used on the ground, whenever necessary, to replicate the flight operations. The major difference between the on-orbit and ground control animals was that the ground control procedures were conducted on a standard laboratory work bench instead of a simulation of the Microgravity Sciences Glovebox. Also, the on-orbit habitats were warmer by approximately 2 degrees Celsius.

Following on-orbit operations, the tissues were returned to Earth for evaluation.
