experiment_title: Circadian Entrainment, Sleep-Wake Regulation and Neurobehavioral Performance during Extended Duration Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Since the finding that appropriately scheduled light/dark exposure is a powerful means of resetting the human circadian pacemaker, bright light has been used in various clinical settings to induce physiologic adaptation in individuals suffering from circadian rhythm disorders (e.g. night shift workers, people with Advanced and Delayed Sleep Phase Syndromes). The investigators found that appropriately timed exposure to bright light can produce rapid physiologic adaptation of the circadian pacemaker to a single week of night work and facilitate rapid entrainment to a rotating work schedule, as well as enhance the alertness of night workers during their work shifts. Advanced and Delayed Sleep Phase Syndromes (ASPS and DSPS, respectively) are characterized by a marked difficulty in maintaining appropriate timing of sleep during the desired hours, and there is evidence suggesting that circadian misalignment may underlie the pathophysiology of this condition. Data from clinical studies suggest that evening exposure to bright light or early morning exposure to bright light are successful in the treatment of ASPS and DSPS, respectively. Since the current study was designed to evaluate the effectiveness of blue-enriched light exposure over white light as a countermeasure for circadian misalignment during exploration class mission to mars, it had implications for the development of effective and energy-efficient methods for treatment of circadian rhythm disorders. Optimizing the wavelength of light holds the potential for producing shorter, more efficient light treatment regimens. Shorter treatment regimens would not only increase compliance in clinical populations, but would make light treatment more practical in industrial/work settings.

APPROACH:
Seven healthy subjects participated in a 71-day inpatient protocol consisting of three baseline days (16:8 h wake: sleep) followed by 60 experimental days (24.65 h, 16.43:8.22 h). Light intensity during the experimental days was ~ 100 lux (n=2) and ~50 lux (n = 5) at 137 cm height in the horizontal angle. Circadian phase was measured by the Dim Light Melatonin Onset (DLMO) measured six times under dim light (~ 1.8 lux at 137 cm height in the horizontal angle ) and postural control (before and after the experimental days, and on experimental Days 6, 20, 34, and 48) and during several segments on the experimental days. The critical manipulation in the study was the timing of sleep on the first experimental day was shifted 12 hours compared to baseline; equivalent to a slam shift. To assess entrainment, phase angle was calculated from the difference between DLMO and scheduled bedtime.

RESULTS:
The results showed that the average phase angle for subjects on the first 24.65 hour day was 12.5 + .26 hours for the 50 lux group and 8.96 + .96 hours for the 100 lux group, which is indicative of acute circadian misalignment. The average phase angle on the sixth experimental day was 5.8 + 1.6h for the 50 lux group and 7 + 3.7 h for the 100 lux group, showing that subjects continued to be misaligned. The average phase angle on the fifteenth experimental day was 1.5 + .46. Thereafter they stabilized. The average phase angle was 2.4 + .31 hours on experimental day 34 and 2.2 + .26 hours on experimental day 48 (p>.05).

It is important to note the following: First, the results showed that crewmembers would be most vulnerable to the detrimental effects of circadian misalignment during the first two weeks of a mission. This is important, because the duration of short-term mission such as those to the ISS and the moon are approximately two weeks long. Second, the data reveal that light intensities that are similar to the lighting conditions during space flight are insufficient to induce rapid entrainment during a short-term mission. Therefore, it was critical to develop countermeasures that would facilitate sleep and circadian adaptation rapidly.

experiment_title: Cartilage in Space
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Exposure to microgravity can affect cells and tissues at a variety of levels. Musculoskeletal changes (e.g. significant bone and muscle loss) occur even when astronauts exercise regularly, but the mechanisms are not yet understood. Tissue engineering, a new field that enables tissue equivalents to be created from isolated cells in combination with biomaterials and bioreactors, potentially can provide a basis for systematic, controlled in vitro studies of tissue growth and function. We previously developed methods to create three dimensional cartilaginous tissue based on cartilage cells (chondrocytes), synthetic polyglycolic acid (PGA) scaffolds, and bioreactors. The scaffold induces cell differentiation and biodegrades at a defined rate, whereas the bioreactor maintains controlled in vitro culture conditions that permit tissue growth and development. In the present experiment, tissue engineering was studied in space using cartilage as a model musculoskeletal tissue. Cartilage was selected because of its resilience and low metabolic requirements. Previous microgravity experiments involving mammalian cells focused on the cells themselves in monolayers and lasted for six to twenty eight days. In the present experiment, engineered cartilage grown for three months on Earth followed by four months on the Mir Space Station was compared with that grown for seven months on Earth. The objectives were to: (1) examine cell viability and differentiated function in a long-term flight study, and (2) to assess the effects of the space environment on tissue growth and function.

APPROACH:
Pre-flight (M.I.T.): Cell-polymer tissue “constructs” based on bovine calf articular chondrocytes and polymer scaffolds (5 million cells per 5 mm diameter, 2 mm thick PGA disc) were prepared according to previously established methods and cultured on Earth in NASA developed rotating bioreactors (Synthecon, Houston, TX). In particular, constructs were cultured in a 110 mL Slow Turning Lateral Vessel (STLV), configured as the annular space between two cylinders, the inner of which was covered with a silicone membrane and served as an internal gas exchanger. The vessel, filled with culture medium and eleven constructs was rotated as a solid body around its central axis at 15 – 28 rpm. The constructs within maintained freely suspended by adjusting vessel rotation speed to establish a dynamic equilibrium between the acting forces, such that culture on Earth simulated some aspects of actual microgravity. Fluid was exchanged batch-wise, at a rate of 50 % every 3-4 days.

Flight and ground control studies (astronaut John Blaha, JSC team): After three months of culture on Earth, constructs were divided into two groups and transferred into two NASA-provided rotating, perfused bioreactors (Biotechnology system, BTS) for an additional four months of cultivation on either Mir or on Earth. In particular, one BTS containing ten constructs was transferred to the Priroda module of Mir via the US space shuttle STS-79 (9/16/96 launch), operated in microgravity, and brought back to Earth via STS-81 (1/22/97 landing). A second BTS with ten constructs was operated on Earth (at NASA-JSC) served as a ground control.

Post-flight (M.I.T.): At the time of launch (i.e. after three months of culture) and after additional cultivation on either Mir or Earth (i.e. after seven months of culture), constructs were compared to native bovine calf articular cartilage with respect to: morphology (weight, histological and ultrastructural appearance), cell viability (trypan blue exclusion, intracellular esterase activity), biosynthesis rates(macromolecular incorporation of radiolabeled tracers), biochemical composition (DNA, glycosaminoglycan (GAG), total and type II collagen), and mechanical properties (aggregate modulus and hydraulic permeability in radially confined compression).

RESULTS:
Construct shape: Constructs grown on Mir tended to become more spherical whereas those grown on Earth tended to maintain their initial discoid shape (Figure 2a). These findings might be related to differences in cultivation conditions, i.e. videotapes showed that constructs floated freely on Mir but settled and collided with the vessel wall on Earth.

Cell viability: Cells isolated from post-flight constructs were alive and metabolically active, as demonstrated by attachment to Petri dishes, proliferation, and enzymatic conversion of a tracer substrate. Cell viability post-flight was 95 – 99 %. Rates of macromolecular incorporation of radiolabeled tracers in Mir-grown constructs (post-flight) and Earth-grown controls were comparable.

Construct structure: Constructs grown on Mir and on Earth appeared histologically cartilaginous throughout their entire cross-sections (5 - 8 mm thick), with the exception of fibrous outer capsules (0.15- 0.45 mm thick), as assessed using histological staining for GAG and immunostaining for collagen type II. Earth-grown constructs appeared to have a more organized extracellular matrix with more uniform collagen orientation than their Mir-grown counterparts, but collagen fiber diameters were similar in the two groups.

Construct composition and function: At the time of launch and after additional culture on Mir and on Earth, constructs contained thirteen, fourteen, and nineteen million cells, respectively. On Earth, construct wet weights increased 1.7-fold between three and seven months, which could be attributed to increasing amounts of collagen and GAG. On Mir, construct wet weights increased 1.3- fold over the same time interval, due to deposition of collagen and unspecified components.

experiment_title: 6 Degree Headdown Tilt with Balance Traction to Emulate Spinal Lengthening Experienced by Astronauts during Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of ARCbedrest117 was to develop a balanced traction to elongate the spine to the degree experienced by astronauts. The effects of traction on the spine exposed to the 6o head down tilt (HDT) model is compared to effects on the spine with traction and horizontal bed rest (HBR).  The second part of this study (ARCbedrest129) was designed to determine the electrical activity and intramuscular pressures of the muscles along the lumbar spine while upright and while in 6o HDT or HBR position.

APPROACH:
Healthy volunteers were tested in the MRI before and after 3 days exposure to a balanced traction device that placed a load on the spine by suspending a load corresponding to 5% of the body weight from each leg with a cable-pulley system.  The volunteer was at bed rest in the 6 degree HDT or in HBR position.  Activity was not restricted.  HDT with traction was compared with HBR with traction. The second part of the study conducted a few days after #117 estimated the electrical activity of lumbar spine muscle through surface electrodes for specified hours of normal activity.  Through a catheter inserted into the muscle on either side of the lumbar spine, the pressures were recorded during upright and then at three time intervals during of HDT or HBR.  Electrical activity was recorded concurrent with intramuscular pressure.  Subjects were randomized into 2 groups of three.  Group 1 underwent HBR followed by HDT in balanced traction.  Group II underwent HDT in balanced traction followed by HBR.  There was a two-week recovery period between the two forms of 3d-bed rest.
 


RESULTS:
Repeated measures ANOVA indicated that total body length increased more (mean±SE) during HDT with balanced traction (22±8 mm) than during HBR (16±4 mm).  Spine length between L5 and C7 also increased more during HDT with traction  (25±8 and 14±9 mm).  Ultrasonography showed increases in lumbar disc height during HDT and HBR (2.9±0.8 mm vs. 3.3±0.6 mm), but there were no differences among groups.  Seventy percent of the increase in disc height occurred during the first 5 hours of bed rest.  Within the first hour of standing, there was a 10 mm decrease in body height, about 80% of the normal diurnal variation in our subjects.  The intensity of pain in the back, abdomen and head was greater during HDT with traction than during HBR with traction.  Reflexes were normal in both groups.  Intramuscular pressure in erector spinae muscles that averaged 8.4±0.7 mm Hg did not change during the study and was similar in HBR and HDT.  Ankle joint torque during plantar- and dorsi-flexion did not change during the study and was similar in HBR and HDT with balanced traction.

Conclusions: Results suggest that HDT with balanced traction may combine the advantages of both models to simulate total body and spinal lengthening, as well as back pain associated with microgravity. 

Note: Both studies were carried out on the same group of subjects.  The measurements of intra muscular pressure in ARCbedrest129 were reported separately, but the protocols for each study were the same.  Therefore, it is more complete to have both ARCbedrest117  and ARCbedrest129  reported together as the first part and the second part of the study as described.

experiment_title: Simulated Microgravity and Radiation-Induced Bone Degeneration: Oxidative Stress- and p53-Dependent Mechanisms
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
To determine the risks and mechanisms of tissue degeneration in the space flight environment, investigators examined the combined effects of radiation and simulated weightlessness on bone. They focused their studies on two important pathways, p53 and oxidative and nitrative stress-related species, in bone marrow progenitor populations because there is abundant evidence that the biological effects of weightlessness and those of radiation share these mechanism. Experiments were conducted using the rodent hindlimb unloading model, the best validated animal model for simulating weightlessness, followed by irradiation. In Aim 1, they tested the hypothesis that simulated weightlessness of mice modulates the response of bone and bone marrow to radiation, both acutely and during tissue regeneration. In Aim 2 they sought to identify the target marrow-derived stem, progenitor and differentiated cell populations sensitive to the combined stimuli of simulated weightlessness and radiation. In Aim 3, they explored the relevance of specific ROS/RNS and p53-dependent mechanisms for mediating cellular responses to combined simulated weightlessness and radiation. The results of these studies are expected to provide important information for the development of countermeasures both to help prevent degeneration of connective tissues such as bone during spaceflight and to improve subsequent tissue regeneration.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
Key questions are whether or not low doses and unique types of radiation that astronauts are exposed to in space are detrimental to mineralized tissue, and if space radiation worsens the bone loss that occurs due to unloading of muscles and bones in the reduced gravity environment of space. First, investigators conducted relatively extensive dose-response and time course experiments using radiation such as high energy Fe-56 (iron), which is encountered in space. Results show that total body irradiation of adult male mice with doses of iron as low as 0.10 Gy and doses of photons (Cesium-137) as low as 1.0 Gy can cause significant loss of mineralized tissue within the spongy areas of bone. This bone loss is very rapid (within 3 to 7 days), and appears to be caused by an increase in the activity of bone resorbing osteoclasts. The importance of the osteoclasts for radiation-induced bone loss is further supported by our findings that radiation can increase the number of osteoclasts in cultured cells.

When unloading to simulate weightlessness and radiation are combined, changes emerge over time, which are greater than each treatment alone can exert. Mechanical tests are arguably the gold standard for assessing the main function of bone, which is to support the body at rest and in motion. Unloading and radiation each alone have modest effects to lower the yield force in the lumbar spine, defined as the force applied that causes failure, here in compression. However, when unloading and radiation are combined, there is a significant reduction in yield force. This combined effect was accompanied by compromised structural integrity of cancellous tissue in the long bones (tibiae) as well as in the spine. One of our surprising findings is that radiation-induced bone loss is restricted to high turnover rate cancellous tissue, in contrast to unloading-induced bone loss, which manifests in both cortical bone tissue (outer shell) as well as cancellous tissue. As a consequence, the mechanical properties of the spine are largely preserved after low dose, total body irradiation alone and are likely to be preserved for most bones, at least in the short term.

Investigators also obtained several lines of evidence in support of the hypothesis that cells responsible for bone formation, osteoblasts and their stem cells and progenitors that reside in bone marrow, may contribute to bone loss caused by radiation. Irradiation can reduce the activity of osteoblasts in cancellous bone. In the short term, the combination of unloading and iron has a greater acute effect (-60%) to reduce the number of stem/progenitors in the marrow for osteoblasts than either treatment alone (-20%, -25% respectively). These results suggest bone marrow stem and progenitor cells for the bone-forming osteoblasts may be more sensitive to adverse effects of radiation under conditions of disuse in space, than occurs under normal conditions on Earth.

These findings raise the possibility that radiation may damage stem cells or progenitors for osteoblasts so that recovery of skeletal tissue from the space environment also is impaired. In the short term (1 mo), investigators found that recovery of the spine from disuse in irradiated mice (0.5Gy iron) was similar to controls. Reasoning that if low dose radiation damages stem and osteoprogenitor cells, adverse effects may manifest much later in life as the mice age. To test this possibility, mice were unloaded then exposed to iron, then released to ambulate normally for six months. Investigators found that bone structural changes in mice that had been unloaded (but not irradiated) were consistent with the adaptive changes that occur in astronauts one year after prolonged space flight. In contrast, irradiation of unloaded mice with a low dose of iron (0.5Gy) impaired adaptive recovery. These results support these hypothesis that low dose, iron radiation impairs adaptive remodeling of bone due to the damage inflicted upon stem and osteoprogenitor cells that reside within the marrow.

The question of whether or not weightlessness and/or radiation exert chronic, system-wide effects is an important one. The results show exposure to space radiation causes persistent oxidative damage to bone marrow proteins in unloaded mice at lower doses of radiation than in normally loaded controls. Investigators propose weightlessness interferes with the ability of cells in bone and marrow to protect from oxidative damage, which leads to persistent oxidative stress, osteoclast-mediated resorption, damage to stem and osteoprogenitors and impaired adaptive remodeling. Although other explanations are possible for their findings, given the well-established effect of radiation to cause oxidative and DNA damage to stem cells and inflammation, we will test this hypothesis in future efforts to improve understanding of space flight.

The importance of these findings is that simulated weightlessness at the time of radiation exposure appears to impair skeletal remodeling even during a prolonged period of recovery. Furthermore, relatively low doses of space radiation can exert system-wide and persistent change. All of the experiments have been conducted using adult, male mice of a single strain (C57Bl/6J). Differences in biological responses to treatments can occur simply due to age, gender, strain, as well as species, and therefore further studies are needed to help assess human risk. Nonetheless, the findings suggest space radiation, alone and combined with musculoskeletal disuse, may pose a long-term risk to the skeletal health of astronauts.

experiment_title: Effects of Microgravity on Lymphatic Structure and Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project combines aspects of two proposals that were selected for funding: “Effects of microgravity on lymphatic proliferation and transport efficiency in the gastrointestinal system of C57/BL6 mice” (#14-14SF_Step2-0079) and “Tissue Sharing (B7): Effects of Microgravity Adaptations on Cephalic Lymphatic Function and Associated Edema Development and Immune Dysfunction” (#14-14SF_Step2-0092). Both of these proposals have at their basis the idea that long-term space flight inhibits lymphatic function, which will impair the transport of immune cells, fluids, and macromolecules from the interstitium. This lymphatic inhibition could affect many aspects of astronaut health, especially upper body edema, CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) pressure regulation, visual acuity loss, gastrointestinal dysfunction/ inflammation and immune impairment due to diminished transport of fluid, large molecules and immune cell transport to and from the nodes.

The visual acuity disturbances from space flight are thought to be related to the increases in intracranial pressure because of the space flight induced cephalic fluid shift. Cephalic lymphatic function has been intimately linked to the regulation of CSF pressure via the lymphatic removal of CSF through the cribriform plate. The cribriform plate and associated lymphatic network moves lymph derived from CSF towards the cervical lymph nodes en route to the veins of the neck. This provides part of a multi-faceted CSF pressure regulatory mechanism as well as a modulator of neurological immunity. We will study the role of the cephalic lymphatic network in CSF pressure dysfunction and the assessment of correlative immunological components.

Space flight is also known to cause alterations in the development and function of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. This is associated with lymphostasis, gut edema, reduced fat deposition in the mesentery and visceral organs, and reduced size of immune associated organs, similar to what is seen in intestinal lymphangiectasia. All of these symptoms are also found in patients with GI inflammation. Intestinal inflammation has not been studied in human subjects during space flight, but we have seen that simulated space flight resulted in the development of intestinal inflammation in animal models. However, this has not been measured in the same space-flown animal model. The role of GI lymphatic dysfunction, which is likely a causative factor in many of these pathologies has NEVER been systematically assessed.

APPROACH:
Thus we propose that space flight induced lymphatic dysfunction is responsible for the development of edema and inflammation in multiple tissues, specifically producing dysfunction in CSF pressure regulation and GI function. The previous applications both proposed to test this general hypothesis using very similar experimental protocols applied to the head/neck and GI tissues respectively for #14-14SF_Step2-0092 and #14-14SF_Step2-0079. In the combined grant we propose 3 modified Aims to test this general hypothesis: Aim 1--To analyze changes in the structure and functional implications of the pre and postnodal cephalic lymphatic architecture due to spaceflight-induced adaptations (old Aim 1 of #14-14SF_Step2-0092); Aim 2--To evaluate space flight adaptations of the network structure of lymphatic vessels of the cribriform plexus and the GI tract. Increases in lymphangiogenesis are commonly associated with inflammation and lymph transport insufficiency. We will determine alterations in lymph vessel number, size, and distribution in these tissues. We will also determine if there are alterations in the formation of lymphatic valves, which are an important structural component of lymphatic vessels (old Aim2 of #14-14SF_Step2-0092 combined with old Aim 1 of #14-14SF_Step2-0079); Aim 3--To analyze changes in lymph node structure that could alter the delivery of important immunological components to and from the nodes (cephalic for the head and neck tissue and mesenteric node for the GI tissue) leading to immune dysregulation and modulation of nodal lymph flow. We will also determine if there are shifts in the cell populations that reside in the lymph nodes, and around the prenodal lymph vessels (old Aim 3 of #14-14SF_Step2-0092 combined with Aim 2 of #14-14SF_Step2-0079). Cunent changes to the source of the tissue and preservation techniques will however preclude histological (Haemotoxilin and Eosin staining).

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Human Factors Analysis Support Tool
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Designing complex systems, such as those used by NASA, requires a coordinated effort among a variety of engineering teams. In order to be successful, the human-computer interactions in these systems need to follow a principle-based design process. In Phase II, TiER1 and Alion proposed to continue development on HFE-AT, renaming it and creating a Human Factors Analysis Support Tool (H-FAST), which provided human factors guidance and support to engineering design teams. This tool was used throughout the design lifecycle, and provided inputs to engineers and program managers to help them identify and avoid potential human factors problems early in the design process. It also provided detailed guidance regarding human factors evaluations, and it stored data and provided feedback on the results of these evaluations. H-FAST will improve the engineering design process by providing engineers with easy access to detailed human factors methods, relevant research, and subject matter expert contact information. This will empower engineers to create more usable systems, thus reducing the number of design iterations and resulting in higher-quality products.

APPROACH:,
The methodology isn’t available.

RESULTS:
H-FAST will provide a tool to support the engineering design process at NASA JSC. As such, it will be populated with human factors requirements and guidelines related to the design of systems for space exploration. The design patterns and methods will be chosen to support particular design issues related to NASA JSC missions. H-FAST will also provide a modular framework that can be customized to a variety of NASA engineering projects. By including relevant requirements, guidelines, methods, and design patterns, NASA project managers will be able to customize H-FAST for their particular application. Investigators expect that H-FAST can be used to support space vehicle design projects; ground systems, such as mission control center designs; and flight deck design projects at NASA Ames and Langley.

experiment_title: The Evaluation of Concentric and Eccentric Skeletal Muscle Contractions Following Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Loss of muscle strength and endurance after long exposure to microgravity can interfere with the safe completion of critical tasks during space flight, emergency or routine landing, or during egress. Decreases in leg strength have been documented after Skylab missions as well as after Russian space flights. The objectives of this study were to assess pre flight-to-postflight changes in muscle strength and endurance and to evaluate the effect of in flight exercise on these changes. Changes in muscle performance after missions of shorter or longer duration were compared.

APPROACH:
Muscle performance was tested before and after space flight in 19 astronauts (3 women, 16 men), 10 from 5-day missions and 9 from missions lasting 9 to 11 days. LIDO isokinetic dynamometers were used to measure muscle performance in the back and abdomen and at the knee, ankle, shoulder, and elbow. These dynamometers provide variable resistance so that movements will continue at the same speed (i.e., they are isokinetic) regardless of the force applied. Both concentric and eccentric strength were measured. Concentric strength is the strength of a muscle as it contracts to move a body part, while eccentric strength is the strength of the muscle as it is gradually lengthened while resisting the motion of a body part. Endurance was tested during 25 repetitions of concentric knee flexion and extension.

The eccentric torque maximum was 400 foot pounds. Subjects abstained from food for 2 hours before testing, from caffeine 4 hours before, and from exercise 12 hours before. The dynamometers were calibrated externally and internally (electronically) before each test session. Joint configurations and ranges of motion were recorded for each subject and reproduced for each test session. Testing of the limbs was unilateral with the dominant limb, unless contraindicated. Verbal instructions were consistent and given before each joint test. No verbal encouragement was given during the tests.

Mean results from tests conducted approximately 1, 2, and 3 weeks before launch were compared to results from landing day and from 7 days after landing. Only 17 subjects were tested on landing day. Losses greater than about 9% were considered to be operationally relevant.

Four of the astronauts also performed in flight exercise as part of DSO 476, using a treadmill with a tether system to simulate gravity. They followed continuous or interval exercise protocols with target heart rates intended to correspond to 60% to 85% of preflight maximum oxygen consumption. The percentages of change in their strength and endurance test results were compared with those of 5 astronauts who did not exercise during the flight.

RESULTS:
From before the flight to landing day, large decreases in the strength of the back and abdomen occurred. Strength had decreased by 23% in the concentric tests of the back, 14% in the eccentric tests of the back, and 10% in the concentric tests of the abdomen. The loss in back strength was greater after flights of 9 to 11 days (concentric, 28%; eccentric, 17%) than after flights of 5 days (concentric, 18%; eccentric, 11%). Eccentric abdominal and concentric back strength had recovered significantly 7 days after landing. A significant (12%) decrease in concentric strength of the quadriceps muscle of the thigh was also seen on landing day. No significant loss of strength was seen in the hamstring muscles or in the tests at the ankle, shoulder or elbow, except for a few minor losses that were not considered operationally relevant.

The four astronauts who exercised during flight actually gained eccentric strength of the gastrocnemius muscle of the calf. Although the exercising astronauts lost concentric strength in the quadriceps, the percent change was significantly less than for the four nonexercising astronauts. For the other results of the knee and ankle tests, decreases in strength were generally smaller in those who exercised; although, the differences between exercisers and nonexercisers were not statistically significant. Treadmill exercise did not prevent losses of strength in the back or abdomen. Decrements exhibited by muscles of the five astronauts who did not exercise during flight indicated that muscles are less able to maintain endurance and resist fatigue after space flight. The astronauts who exercised had no loss of endurance.

There was no change in endurance after 5-day flights, but the endurance of the quadriceps decreased after flights of 9 to 11 days. Endurance recovered within 7 days of landing.

These results showed that space flight results in losses of skeletal muscle strength and endurance, and that the losses are greater after flights of longer duration. Strength was lost primarily in the antigravity muscles of the legs and torso. Exercise may prevent losses of muscle strength and endurance.

experiment_title: Effects of Cosmic Particle Radiation on the Calvarium, Brain, and Meninges
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The stopping point region of a cosmic ray particle, the Bragg peak, has the greatest potential for injury of the brain or other tissue because it is here that the particle's LET reaches a maximum. Because an acute inflammatory reaction was observed in two monkeys within a few days after balloon flights, the decision was made to process the mice as soon as they were recovered. It was realized, however, that a considerable proportion of the acute inflammatory cells would disappear, if evoked earlier in the mission; the lifetime of these cells in tissue is no more than five days.

Approach:

Two canisters were prepared with five pocket mice in each. Heads of flight mice and seventeen control mice that had been "tracked" in the trajectories of cosmic ray particles were serially sectioned, from anterior to posterior, in the coronal plane at 10 micrometers, yielding 1,200 sections per animal. In the event that, during the search, a lesion was found in the brain of a flight animal, the "tracked" section from the same level of the brain of a control mouse was examined to see if the lesion and "tracked" hole would correspond. To ascertain whether differences existed in the numbers of mitotic figures in the ependyma and in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampal formation, an enumeration of metaphase figures in these regions were counted.

Results:

A concentrated search was made of the flight brains and meninges for lesions of cosmic ray origin but no evidence of injury was found. In one flight mouse, however, were sizable congregations of polymorphonuclear leukocytes in the region of the inferior sagittal sinus. Judging from findings in the "tracked" control mouse, a heavy or very heavy particle having a declination angle of 47.1 degrees through the cerebrum passed within 0.4 mm of this sinus. Mitosis in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampal formation was considerably reduced in comparison with that in control animals. Several variables may have caused negative findings in the flight brains, including size of the brain, limitations imposed by dosimeters, and the attenuation of particles of high LET by spacecraft or animal canister shielding. Since the animals were exposed primarily to HZE cosmic ray particles at the lower end of the light LET spectrum, the lack of observable changes cannot be taken as evidence that the brain will suffer no damage from the heavier HZE particles on prolonged manned missions.

experiment_title: A Multipurpose Fruit and Vegetable Processing System for Advanced Life Support
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The research data on concentrating tomato juice using new generation membranes is valuable for the food industry. Only one Japanese company is currently employing this technique in a food plant located in California. Data s study from this should prove useful for those food processors who are seeking optimization of the process.

APPROACH:
The following tasks were identified in the proposal:
1) Year 1 (January 1, 2003-December 31, 2003): a. Select varieties of tomatoes and other vegetables suitable for processing b. Develop conceptual design for the MFVP c. Develop computer-aided simulations of each operation to assist in design d. Build bench-scale components of the MFVP and conduct preliminary trials for technical feasibility e. Select optimum design parameters f. Select membranes for water cleaning and product recovery.

2) Year 2 (January 1, 2004 – December 31, 2004) a. Construct MFVP from components b. Select membrane systems for concentration of tomato juice c. Conduct trials with MFVP to determine operational feasibility d. Determine ESM and other operational variables e. Conduct optimization trials.
3) Year 3 (January 1, 2005 – December 31, 2005) a. Conduct experimental trials to determine safety, quality and acceptability of foods processed in MFVP b. Develop final modifications as indicated from the experimental data c. Write final project report.

The development of the fruit and vegetable processor represents the first attempt to miniaturize and integrate the array of unit operations required for preparation and processing of fruits and vegetables such as tomato. Additionally, the developers integrate the ESM metric evaluation throughout the development process as the primary project management tool.

RESULTS:
During the one-year no-cost extension, investigators completed the fabrication of the multipurpose fruit and vegetable food processor (MFVP) and the remaining trials with its components. In addition, they conducted a comprehensive study to obtain data on using electrolyzed water for cleaning-in-place (CIP) of the MFVP. CIP with electrolyzed water is an attractive option for cleaning as it does not require detergents (caustic solution) or disinfectants (chlorine). Therefore it could be more suitable for application in a controlled environment system. Electrolyzed water is generated from salt mixed in water. Investigators conducted trials with a stainless steel test-bed containing various components used in the MFVP. The cleaning and disinfection of the components after inoculation was validated with microbial testing. Specifically, the effectiveness of electrolyzed oxidizing water (EOW) and electrolyzed reducing water (ERW) used in clean-in-place (CIP) applications for MFVP were studied using 38 mm (1.5 in) diameter stainless steel (SS316L) pipes fouled with apple juice. Data were compared with industrial CIP cleaner (chlorinated NaOH) and antimicrobial solution (mixture of peroxyacetic acid and hydrogen peroxide). Cleanliness of stainless steel (SS) pipe surfaces was quantified by a hygiene monitoring test and aerobic plate count. Data were obtained to determine the removal of organic debris and microorganisms at 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes of washing using electrolyzed water and industrial cleaning chemicals. Electrolyzed water showed potential use in CIP applications, it is easy to use and less hazardous compared to the industrial cleaning chemicals. experiment_title: Atmospheric Analyses During Space Flight: Enhanced Total Hydrocarbon Analyzer
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Crew health considerations create a requirement to measure volatile organic compound (VOC) concentrations in normal and contingency operations. Furthermore, spacecraft atmospheres are partially closed environmental systems, and the crew is thus exposed to atmospheric contaminants for the duration of their mission. The effects of continuous exposure may be different from the usual eight hour per day occupational exposures. Finally, the projected infrequent missions to International Space Station (ISS) make reliance on archival air quality samples impractical. Instead, air quality were monitored by onboard analyzers.

The objectives of this study were:
1. Develop and test an instrument that will determine normative concentrations of VOCs in spacecraft cabin atmospheres.
2. Verify satisfactory hardware performance (particularly heating and cooling) by conducting VOC measurements and comparing the measurements with those obtained through archival sampling.

APPROACH:
The Enhanced Total Hydrocarbon Analyzer (ETHA) was removed from its locker and located in the middeck in an orientation that allowed its nozzle to collect cabin air at least 4 inches away from walls and other equipment. The air sample needed to be as close to what the crew is breathing as possible. Suggested location for deploy was on the starboard wall of the middeck or on the sleep station near the forward lockers.

Preferred configuration: The ETHA was powered continuously (taking periodic samples) throughout the mission. Remote samples were collected three times during the mission. Air cylinder samples were also collected three times during the mission. If continuous power was not available, a minimum of three four-hour data collection sessions was required.

experiment_title: Center for Research on Cardiac, Vascular, and Acute Effects of Space Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Recent evidence strongly suggests that humans will face increased risks for adverse effects on heart and blood vessels from radiation exposure during space travel; however, these risks are not well defined. The Center for Research on Cardiac and Vascular Effects of Space Radiation comprises teams from four institutions with experts in the fields of space radiation, cardiovascular radiation injury, and modern techniques of molecular analysis. The goal is to characterize the cardiovascular risks of space radiation. Studies involve mouse, rat, and rabbit models of exposure to protons and oxygen ions. Animals were monitored for up to 12 months after radiation exposure, comparable to many years observation in humans. Heart function was measured non-invasively at regular intervals with high-resolution ultrasound. Heart and abdominal aorta were obtained at different time points after irradiation to investigate pathological changes, including cell death, adverse tissue remodeling, and inflammatory cell infiltration. Plasma and urine samples were collected to assess clinical markers of cardiac injury and changes in metabolic profiles using proteomics and metabolomics approaches. We also examine the microvasculature in the heart and retina, since low-dose ionizing radiation may cause changes in the microvasculature that could alter heart and eye function. Mathematical modeling will be used to assess in vivo and ex vivo obtained reconstructions of the microvascular bed in the heart and retina. Lastly, we will test whether gamma-tocotrienol, a safe dietary antioxidant and the strongest natural product radiation protector yet discovered, will reduce the effects of low-dose oxygen ions on heart and blood vessels. Altogether, these studies use innovative methods to characterize acute and degenerative cardiovascular effects of space radiation, and will help develop safe and effective countermeasures to protect humans against these effects.

APPROACH:
The Center for Space Radiation Research (CSRR) pursues the following Specific Aims: 1) Define acute effects of low-dose proton irradiation on the hematopoietic system, skin, heart, and retina; 2) Examine acute effects of low-dose protons in combination with modeled microgravity; 3) Evaluate acute effects of protons on the adaptive immune response; 4) Determine effects of heavy ion and proton irradiation on cardiac and vascular function and structure; 5) Identify acute and chronic biomarkers of cardiovascular dysfunction after particle irradiation; 6) Elucidate the role of metabolic and epigenetic changes in the cardiovascular response to radiation; 7) Determine effects of radiation dose and quality on endothelial cell functional phenotype; and 8) Test whether gamma-tocotrienol protects against acute and cardiovascular effects of particle irradiation.

This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: The Role of the Bone Marrow Microenvironment in Space Radiation-Induced Leukemogenesis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) comprise less than 0.1% of the bone marrow (BM) of adults, yet they produce all blood cells that are responsible for constant maintenance and immune protection of the body. In addition to the requirement for high cell output, the concentration of the different blood cell lineages produced are precisely controlled to allow not only preservation of normal homeostasis, but also the prompt response to specific stimuli and demands. Previous studies have suggested that exposure to galactic cosmic radiation (GCR) and solar particle event (SPE) radiation that occur or may potentially occur during space flight may increase the likelihood of carcinogenesis, with leukemia being one of the most frequent radiogenic cancers, and the ones with the smallest latency period. The investigators hypothesize that GCR and SPE radiation can have a deleterious impact not only at the level of the mature immune cells and their committed progenitors, as is currently thought, but at the earlier developmental stage of the HSC. Genetic lesions induced by this exposure can lead directly to leukemic transformation, and may also cause these cells to generate a functionally compromised immune system lacking the ability to effectively fight challenges such as pre-leukemic transformations and viral/bacterial infections. As such, investigators hypothesize that astronauts would be doubly at risk, due to both the potential for induction of leukemia by SPE/GCR radiation, and the reduced ability of the astronauts’ immune systems to identify and eliminate malignant cells or pathogens in the body.

APPROACH:
In ground-based studies performed at NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) and Wake Forest, investigators spent four years assessing the risk of leukemogenesis from space radiation by examining the effects of simulated SPE/GCR exposures on human hematopoiesis, testing the hypothesis that the quality and quantity of cells being produced can be altered not only from direct exposure of HSC themselves, but also via indirect, biological bystander effects arising from exposure of MSC within the critical hematopoietic niche. Human HSC and MSC were immunomagnetically-sorted with antibodies to CD34 and Stro-1 respectively and exposed to: A) sham irradiation; B) 1 Gy of 137Cs gamma-irradiation (LET = 0.91 keV/µm); C) 1 Gy of 50 MeV protons (primary SPE energy; LET = 1.26 keV/µm); D) 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions (model GCR radiation; LET = 151 keV/µm); or E) 1 Gy of 50 MeV protons followed 15 minutes later by 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions at NSRL. Immediately following irradiation, aliquots of HSC and MSC were cultured for chromosomal aberration (CA) analyses and DNA/RNA isolations, one aliquot of HSC was immediately assessed for functionality/ differentiative potential using the highly sensitive and quantitative, luminescence-based Hemogenix HALO® assay, and the remainder of the cells were placed in an MSC-based HSC maintenance/expansion culture system, testing four different combinations: 1) unirradiated HSC plated over unirradiated MSC; 2) unirradiated HSC plated over irradiated MSC; 3) irradiated HSC plated over unirradiated MSC; and 4) irradiated HSC plated over irradiated MSC. Hematopoietic cells were then collected after seven days, and methylcellulose or HALO® assays were used to assess the impact of irradiation of the HSC, the MSC, or both cell types on hematopoietic colony-forming potential.

RESULTS:
Direct Effects on Human HSC: Methylcellulose and HALO® assay data showed that gamma-rays and 50 MeV protons exerted fairly similar effects on HSC function, both reducing by 50–80% the ability of HSC to form both more primitive (HPP-CFC and CFU-GEMM) colonies, as well as more differentiated myeloid (CFU-GM), erythroid (BFU-E), megakaryo-cyte/platelet (CFC-Mk), and lymphoid (CFC-T and CFC-B) colony types. The marked deleterious effect of protons on the ability of human HSC to give rise to cells of the T and B lymphoid lineages is of particular note, given the body of published work showing that astronauts, even on fairly short missions, exhibit pronounced immune alterations. In contrast to the result seen with gamma-rays and 50 MeV protons, 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions had much less pronounced effect on HSC colony-forming potential, exerting no significant effect on their ability to give rise to the most primitive HPP-CFC colonies, but reducing the colony-forming potential in the remaining lineages by 20–40%, depending upon the specific colony type. Exposing sequentially to protons then iron ions, however, proved to be highly deleterious to HSC function, reducing the ability of HSC to produce all colony types by 80–90%. This decrease was, in all cases statistically different than the effects seen with either iron ions alone or protons alone.

Indirect/Biological Bystander Effects on Hematopoiesis following Exposure of the Niche to SPE/GCR: Irradiation of MSC with gamma-rays or protons produced similar effects on the most primitive HSC, reducing HPP-CFC output 30–40%. Importantly, irradiation of both HSC and MSC produced a negative additive effect on the most primitive HSC, reducing HPP-CFC output ~75%. The results with 56Fe ions were far more unexpected, as irradiation of MSC alone reduced HPP-CFC output 30%, yet co-culture of both irradiated HSC and MSC somehow restored the HPP-CFC potential.

Additive Negative Effects on Hematopoiesis Following Sequential Exposure to SPE then GCR Radiation: Perhaps the most remarkable results came from the sequential treatment with protons and iron ions. While sequential treatment reduced HPP-CFC output 70%, treating the MSC with this sequential dosing regimen actually increased HPP-CFC output of the co-culture roughly 20%. Unexpectedly, however, co-culturing HSC and MSC that had both been sequentially exposed to both ions resulted in an 80% reduction in HPP-CFC output. Very similar results were obtained when the investigators examined the next most primitive colony type, CFU-GEMM, and more differentiated myeloid CFU-GM. Striking results were also obtained when they examined the effect proton and iron ion irradiation of the MSC had upon co-cultured HSC’s ability to generate megakaryocyte and lymphoid (CFC-T and CFC-B) colonies.

Alterations to Human Hematopoiesis Assessed in vivo: The investigators conditioned NOD/SCID/IL-2rgamma null (NSG) mice by administering 2 sequential doses of busulfan spaced 24 hours apart. Conditioned NSG mice were then transplanted with 2x10(5) human HSC that had been exposed to one of the following irradiation schemes (n=9 per group) at the NSRL: 1) sham irradiation; 2) 1 Gy of 137Cs gamma-irradiation; 3) 1 Gy of 50 MeV protons; 4) 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions; or 5) 1Gy of 50 MeV protons followed immediately by 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions. Mice were then sacrificed at 4–6 months post-transplant, their spleen and bone marrow harvested, and analyzed by multicolor flow cytometry to ascertain the levels of human hematopoietic engraftment and assess whether exposure to SPE/GCR altered the engraftment potential and/or differentiative capacity of the HSC. In addition to affecting overall levels of engraftment, treatment with protons, 56Fe ions, or sequential exposures also led to pronounced skewing of the differentiative potential of the human HSC, as shown by the relative lineage distribution of the engrafted human cells in the bone marrow and spleens of the transplanted mice. Commitment to the erythroid lineage was significantly impaired following exposure of human HSC to all radiation types tested, and there was a significant expansion of both the T and B lineages. In addition to this lineage skewing, 5 of the 14 recipients of 56Fe ion-irradiated human HSC (obtained from 2 different healthy donors) exhibited dramatic splenomegaly, with one mouse’s spleen reaching ~30X the normal size. To ascertain the cause of splenomegaly, spleens were analyzed by histopathology and immunophenotyping. The spleen exhibited an abnormal morphology, populated largely by cells with a rounded, highly monotonous appearance consistent with lymphoid cells. Immuno-histochemistry with human-specific anti-bodies confirmed that the vast majority of the cells populating the spleen were human, and they expressed CD3 and CD7. Many of these cells also expressed terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), a marker frequently associated clinically with human lymphocytic leukemias. The absence of any staining in an untransplanted NSG mouse spleen stained with the same panel of antibodies verified their specificity. The observed histopathology and immunophenotyping led a team of clinical hematopathologists to concur that human T-ALL developed in these mice.

No datasets exist for this experiment. A final report was archived.

experiment_title: Radiation Protection and Instrumentation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The solar and cosmic radiation found in space has long been recognized as a possible danger in space travel. Apollo missions, for the first time, placed men outside the Earth's geomagnetic shield, subjecting them to potentially hazardous particulate radiation of an intensity and frequency not encountered in Earth's environment. During a complete Apollo mission, astronauts were exposed to widely varying radiation sources, such as the Van Allen belts, solar surface eruptions, cosmic rays, neutrons, and subatomic particles created in high-energy collisions of primary particles with spacecraft materials. The primary objective was to limit exposure to these sources, and also to measure the dose from each source.

A secondary objective was to protect the astronauts and ground crews against sources of man made radiation, such as the radioisotope thermal generator used to conduct the lunar surface experiments, and some radioluminescent sources on the spacecraft.

The Apollo radiation protection program focused on avoiding the harmful radiation effects encountered in space by limiting the radiation dose to the lowest level judged consistent with achieving beneficial goals.

APPROACH:
Van Allen Belt Radiation
The simple solution to protection against the radiation found within the Van Allen belts was to (1) stay below the belts (556 km) when in Earth orbit, and (2) to traverse the belts rapidly on the way to outer space. The inclination of a spacecraft determines the number of passes made per day through the South Atlantic Anomaly region of the Van Allen belts, and thus determines the radiation dose. Particles within the Van Allen belts, because they are spiraling around the Earth's magnetic lines of force, display directionality that varies in angular relationship to the trajectory of the spacecraft. The Van Allen belt dosimeters used on Apollo had relatively omnidirectional radiation sensors so that the radiation flux would be measured accurately.

Solar Particle Radiation
It is difficult to forecast individual eruptions on the solar surface, which made planning for the Apollo missions difficult. In the event of a solar surface eruption during the Apollo missions, NASA planned to estimate the particle dose, given either visual or radiofrequency confirmation of an eruption from the Solar Particle Alert Network (SPAN), a NASA-sponsored network which provided continuous data on solar flare activity. In the heavy, well-shielded Command Module, even one of the largest solar particle events would not have caused any impairment to the astronauts. However, radiation doses to astronauts in the thinly shielded Lunar Module during an event like this would have been extremely serious. To monitor particle activity, the Apollo missions were equipped with a nuclear particle detection system, designed to have a relatively narrow acceptance angle. This device measured the isotropic proton and alpha particles derived from solar particle events.

Cosmic Rays
Cosmic ray fluxes consist of completely ionized atomic nuclei originating outside the solar system. They are accelerated to very high energies and provide an average dose rate of 1.0 millirad per hour in cislunar space, and 0.6 millirads per hour on the lunar surface. During Apollo, the effect of high-energy cosmic rays on humans was not a concern unless exposures were of duration of a few years.

Neutrons
Neutrons created by cosmic ray collisions with lunar materials were a potential hazard to Apollo astronauts. Furthermore, the astronauts might have encountered neutron exposure from the radioisotope thermal generator used to power the Apollo lunar surface experiments. Two methods for neutron dose assessment, initiated on the Apollo 11 mission, were used: whole body counting and neutron resonant foil.

Other Radiation Measurements
To allow accurate determination of overall radiation exposure of the astronauts, each carried a personal radiation dosimeter (PRD) and three passive dosimeters. As the mission progressed, the PRD provided a visual readout of the accumulated dose to each astronaut. Each of the three passive dosimeters was placed in the astronaut's garment at various locations (ankle, chest, and thigh) to determine radiation doses for various body portions. A radiation survey meter allowed astronauts to determine radiation levels in any desired location in their compartment. This allowed the astronauts to find a habitable low dose region of the spacecraft in the event of a radiation emergency.

RESULTS:
Radiation was not an operational problem during the Apollo missions. Doses received by the astronauts were significantly lower than the yearly average of 5 rem set by the US Atomic Energy Commission for workers who used radioactive materials in factories across the United States.

Average radiation doses for all astronauts on a particular mission were computed for each of the Apollo missions, and ranged from skin doses of 0.16 to 1.14 rads. The maximum dose limit was 400 rads to the skin for each of the Apollo missions, so actual radiation levels were well below the limit. Individual readings varied 20 percent because the astronauts were in different parts of the spacecraft, which had different shielding effectiveness, and because of their different duties and movements. Doses to blood forming organs were 40 percent lower than doses measured at the body surface.

The main reason the doses were low is that no major solar particle events occurred during the Apollo missions. One small event was detected by a radiation detector outside the Apollo 12 spacecraft, but no increase in radiation dose to the astronauts inside the spacecraft was detected. One possible effect of cosmic ray radiation was the light flash phenomenon observed during Apollo 11 and subsequent flights; although ionizing radiation can produce visual phosphenes, a correlation was not established between cosmic rays and the observation of the light flashes. (Further information on the light flashes can be found in this archive.)

In terms of sources of man-made radiation aboard the Apollo spacecraft, there were two key problems that were resolved. First, the leakage of radioactive materials from radioluminescent sources was eliminated by a change in encapsulating material. Emission of soft x-ray radiation from radioluminescent sources was resolved by applying a layer of plastic to the panels.

Although the Apollo missions did not encounter any major space radiation event, procedures for handling any contingency were in place so that space radiation events would be recognized and dealt with immediately for the safety of the crew and mission objectives. The possible deterent to manned spaceflight by large radiation doses was avoided during the Apollo program.

experiment_title: Dietary Fat Consumption of U.S. General Population and LSAH Participants
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Nationwide, heart disease is the leading cause of death in both men and women. Many clinical studies have shown a correlation between nutrition and cardiovascular health. Much of this research has been focused on dietary fats and oils, which can promote either good health or disease depending on their quality and quantity. So choosing quality fats and oils should help improve personal cardiovascular disease risk and help decrease national cardiovascular disease rates.

The three main types of fats are called saturated, monounsaturated, and polyunsaturated. Excessive consumption of saturated fats is one of the major risk factors for heart disease. Substituting either monounsaturated or polyunsaturated fats for saturated fats may help lower the blood cholesterol level and has been shown to have a protective effect on the cardiovascular system. This investigation compared the quality and quantity of dietary fat intake of the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participants (astronauts and a group of comparison participants) with the U.S. general population.

APPROACH:
Dietary fat consumption data was taken from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 1988-94 (NHANES III) and compared with data from the 1998 LSAH Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ).

RESULTS:
According to the NHANES data, the average adult consumes approximately 33.6% of total calories from dietary fats, 11.6% from saturated fat, 12.5% from monounsaturated fat, and 6.9% from polyunsaturated fat. These data show that Americans are consuming an excessive amount of the most harmful fats and a deficient amount of the most beneficial fats. On average, comparison participants (N=512) consumed the same percentage of dietary fats as the general population, while astronauts (N=134) reported a slightly lower figure (33.6% and 31.9% respectively). Both groups showed lower saturated fat consumption as compared to the general population, but neither group consumed enough of the beneficial fats. LSAH participants also reported more frequent use of polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats and oils.

experiment_title: The Relation between Mutagenesis and Genomic Instability after Particle Exposure In Vivo
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts in the space environment are at risk for a variety of health-related concerns from exposure to accelerated ions that can pass through the spacecraft hull and interact with astronauts’ cells within the body. These particles are released from the sun in solar particle events (SPE) and exist as part of the galactic cosmic ray (GCR) background radiation, although the types of ions and their energies can differ widely in SPE and GCR. A significant concern for astronaut health is an increased risk of cancer, which is linked to a variety of radiation exposures. The underlying cause of cancer, regardless of its source, is mutations in critical genes and ongoing gains, losses, and rearrangement of chromosomes. Collectively, these ongoing changes in the cell are termed genomic instability. The goal of this study was to determine how frequently different types of accelerated ions found in the GCR cause mutations and genomic instability and to describe what these changes look like. To better extrapolate the results to potential harms to astronauts from space radiation, the investigators used a mouse model for the study. This ensured that the cell types of interest found in the spleen and kidney will be exposed to accelerated ions in their normal tissue environment. A second goal of the study was to determine if mutant cells induced by space radiation exhibit signs of genomic instability, which are ongoing changes to the genome and common in many types of cancer.

APPROACH:
Investigators used an in vivo system, in which mice were exposed to a specific ion at three or more doses, because this best mimics what will happen to astronaut tissues. The mice have a genetic marker that allows mutant cells to be selected directly from cells isolated from exposed tissues. Although the mutant cells are then grown in culture to obtain material for molecular and sometimes cytogenetic analyses to determine the types of mutational events induced by exposure, mutation formation occurred in cells in the normal tissue environment within the mouse. Investigators isolated and examined mutant cells from the kidney (epithelial cells) and the spleen (blood T cells).

RESULTS:
Most work was performed with the kidney epithelial cells. In all cases, the investigators observed increased numbers of mutant cells per tissue after exposure to the ions, and in some cases (Ti and Fe ions) at doses equivalent to approximately one to two particles per cell nucleus. Simply stated, a single particle passing through a cell is the lowest possible exposure, aside from no exposure. For Fe, Ti, O, and Si ions, investigators observed a linear increase in mutations as a function of dose. The only exception was for Ti ions at the highest dose tested because no increase was observed relative to the next lower dose. For protons, no increase was observed at the lower doses tested (0.5 to 3.0 Gy), with a dramatic rise in mutations at 4 and 5 Gy. Average exposures in space for a Mars trip will be approximately 0.2 to 0.4 Gy, but could be higher if a major solar flare occurs, which would release large amounts of protons.

The mutant cells investigators selected were due to mutations that affected mouse chromosome 8. Thus, they focused molecular and cytogenetic studies on this chromosome and identified three types of radiation signature mutations, which are rare in spontaneous mutant cells isolated from unexposed mouse kidneys and relatively common in mutant cells induced by accelerated ion exposure. These are 1) large deletions in which a large piece of chromosome 8 is lost, 2) loss of portions of chromosome 8 that are not linked to loss of the target gene (discontinuous), and 3) translocations in which a portion of chromosome 8 is fused to a piece of another chromosome.

The selection assay only selected for mutational events affecting chromosome 8: To search for evidence of genomic instability, investigators also examined other chromosomes in the space radiation induced kidney cells for evidence of additional mutations. Although they found mutations affecting other chromosomes in both spontaneous mutants and mutants from the exposed kidneys, these genomic mutations were both quantitatively more frequent and qualitatively distinct in the mutant cells isolated from the irradiated kidneys. A detailed analysis of mutant cells isolated from Fe ion exposed kidneys demonstrated that these cells had very extensive genomic damage, similar to what would be expected in cancer cells. The goal for future research will be to determine if signature mutations and more extensive genomic damage will be observed in cancers induced by space radiation exposure in the kidney. If so, investigators will have identified markers that distinguish space radiation induced cancers from those that occur spontaneously, and in doing so will have established an absolute link between mutations and cancers induced by the space environment.

Investigators also examined space radiation mutagenesis in T cells from the spleen. T cells can give rise to leukemias and lymphomas, which are distinct from cancers that occur in epithelial tissues. These cells are more difficult to grow than kidney epithelial cells, so they restricted their analysis to chromosome 8. They identified radiation signature mutations (large deletions and discontinuous mutations), though unlike the kidney cells they did not observe these mutations at the highest doses tested. They believe that this absence occurred because the T cells are more sensitive to radiation exposure and high doses killed most of the mutant cells that were also induced. Interestingly, the kinetics of radiation signature mutation was similar to that reported by another group for space radiation-induced leukemias, suggesting a link between mutations and blood-derived cancers.

In sum, the investigators showed that space radiation will induce signature mutations that can be used to qualitatively and quantitatively distinguish spontaneous mutations from those induced by exposure in two distinct cell types, kidney epithelial and spleen T cells. Further, they showed that the induced mutant kidney cells had extensive mutations throughout the genome, which was surprising because mutations on chromosome 8 were the only ones required for the mutant cells to be isolated. Because of the known link between mutation and cancer, our work will be useful to estimate cancer risk in astronauts from prolonged space trips.

experiment_title: Behavior of Postnatal Rats After Space Flight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This study makes use of neonatal mammals in order to study the effects of microgravity on the development of the nervous system. Altering gravity during development provides a noninvasive technique by which the influence of motor activity on the development of the nervous system may be studied. Neonates offer a unique and valuable model for experimentation because they possess critical periods of development during which an organism's development is most sensitive to environmental changes.

Approach:

The flight experiment consisted of six groups of ten neonates. The groups were housed in six nursing facilities that were contained within three Animal Enclosure Modules (AEM) and flown in shuttle middeck lockers. After landing, the P8 and P15 litters were studied for fourteen days. Swimming ability was measured daily by placing the animal in an aquarium and videotaping them for two minutes. Strokes that propelled the animal forward were counted and hindlimb angles were measured using the Peak5 Motion Measurement System. The free walking capabilities of the animals were also measured by videotaping their walking and analyzing their step cycle with the Peak System. Finally, surface righting ability was quantified using frame by frame analysis.

Results:

Results demonstrate that the development of the nervous system in microgravity is altered for both nonweightbearing activities, such as swimming, as well as for weight-bearing activities. Although microgravity has more of an effect on those functions that require weight-bearing. These results clearly show that environmental factors, such as gravity, affect the development of the nervous system. The data further supports the hypothesis that developing organisms have sets of overlapping critical periods.

experiment_title: Measurements of Dose as a Function of Shielding Thickness
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Shuttle flights are only about two weeks in duration and thus the cumulative radiation exposure is relatively small. However, with long stays on the Mir station, the International Space Station, and planned human exploration, flight duration will be very long. The radiation risk, consequently, will be significantly higher. The risk can be reduced by increasing the shielding thickness and judicious choice of shielding material. Increasing the shielding mass increases the launch cost significantly. For a fixed level of radiation risk (protection), uncertainties in the biological dose equivalent leads to nearly exponential increase in the shielding thickness and thus cost. Uncertainties in the radiation transport through matter models are much too large to accurately predict the biological dose equivalent under arbitrary depths. Thus it is crucial to reduce these uncertainties and develop new shielding design strategies.

The objectives of this experiment were: (1) measure the shielding depth dependence of absorbed dose, dose equivalent, and linear energy transfer spectra for galactic cosmic radiation and trapped protons, (2) validate and improve model(s) of radiation transport through shielding material, and (3) assess the relative efficacy of polyethylene, carbon, and aluminum in providing shielding protection. This study is important for long term stay in low-Earth orbit and for human exploration studies program.

APPROACH:
As soon as possible after attaining orbit, crewmembers destowed the hardware and mounted on velcro placements. They connected the DC power cable to the hardware and activated, noting the Mission Elapsed Time to the nearest second. Near the end of the flight, any time after completion of the last set of passes through the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), crewmembers deactivated and stowed the hardware.

experiment_title: Chemoprevention of Radiation-Induced Neoplasms
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The major long-term risk associated with the types of low-dose radiation exposure that could possibly be encountered during prolonged space missions is radiation-induced cancers which probably won't appear until later in life. Protons and heavy ions as well as their secondaries are the major types of radiation likely to occur in the space environment.

Chemopreventatives offer potential pharmaceutical countermeasures to reduce the increased cancer risks; however, no studies have tested chemopreventatives in studies relevant to proton or heavy ion-induced cancer. Surging scientific and public interest in applying chemoprevention strategies to people in the general population that have been identified to carry even slight increases in the genetic risk of developing cancer is fueling the identification of exciting new chemopreventive agents. Appropriate animal models provide a powerful tool for examining the effects of proton and heavy ion radiation at doses relevant to space as well as for directly evaluating the effectiveness of particularly promising chemopreventatives against cancers that occur following such exposures.

This project is a collaborative effort to characterize the carcinogenic risks associated with exposure to radiation which is relevant to the space environment and to develop countermeasures to minimize the long term effects of radiation exposure. In this study, a model of breast cancer, a tissue with known links between cancer development and radiation, will be used. The study will further characterize countermeasures to this radiation-induced cancer using the prototype breast cancer chemopreventive tamoxifen to establish a proof of principle in the chemoprevention of cancer caused by protons and heavy ions.

experiment_title: Genotyping (ACE 20)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The response of human physiology to space flight showed remarkable interindividual variability. However, the potential role of differential gene expression in this process had yet to be investigated. To that end, two candidate genes which may exert an influence in the observed physiological alterations associated with space flight, bed rest and artificial gravity paradigms were studied. Each subject provided a 10 ml sterile 0.9% saline mouthwash sample, from which DNA was extracted for assessment of two specific genetic polymorphisms: the I/D allelic variants of the Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (ACE) gene, which may influence cardiovascular performance, and the Guanosine-Cytosine nucleotide substitution at position 174 of the IL-6 gene, which influenced bone remodeling. Data from this test was correlated with Centrifuge Tolerance screening test results as well as primary results from the main experiment.

APPROACH:
The ACE I/D Polymorphism: The angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) gene found on chromosome 17 contains a restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP). The I and D allelic variants of this gene are respectively associated with the inclusion or deletion of a 287 base pair 'Alu' repeat sequence in intron 16. The D allele is associated with higher ACE levels in plasma and tissue. Within the renin-angiotensin system, ACE catalyses the cleavage of the octapeptide angiotensin II from the nonapeptide angiotensin I. This appears to be the rate-limiting step in the production of angiotensin II. The D allele is therefore also associated with higher serum and tissue concentrations of angiotensin II. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor, acts on hypothalamic centers to stimulate thirst, augments mineralocorticoid secretion, stimulates vasopressin release and is known to facilitate norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve terminals. Furthermore there is evidence of genotype dependent effects on left ventricular remodeling and vascular reactivity both of which may be implicated in etiology of postflight orthostatic hypotension. In addition to its actions in the renin-angiotensin system ACE also plays a role within the kallekrein-kinin system, inactivating a number of vasodilatory kinins. It is expected to see a genotype dependent effect in bed rest, flight and centrifuge paradigms with the DD genotype being associated with superior orthostatic tolerance. The importance of the renin-angiotensin system in the chronic maintenance of intravascular volume and blood pressure.

IL-6 174 G>C Polymorphism: Comparisons of monozygotic and dizygotic twins suggest that up to 80% of the variance in bone mineral density was influenced by genetic factors. While chronic regular exercise was known to be associated with preservation of bone density the early response to exercise involves a bone remodelling process in which both resorption and deposition were simultaneously and dramatically increased. As little as 30 minutes of brisk treadmill walking in young males led to an increase in markers of resorption but not of deposition. The cytokine IL-6 has been implicated in driving bone resorption in systemic inflammatory conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease and appears to play a role in the regulation of osteoclast and osteoblast function. A common polymorphism was present in the IL-6 gene promoter region. At this locus a single Guanosine-Cytosine nucleotide substitution at position 174 is associated with variations in levels of circulating IL-6. Evidence has been presented suggesting that genotype dependent increases in IL-6 mediate exercise-related bone resorption. This may go some way to explaining why exercise countermeasures are not uniformly successful in preventing microgravity induced bone loss.

RESULTS
This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during the Artificial Gravity Bed Rest Study.

The original intent of this experiment was not able to be accomplished during the Artificial Gravity study. The published results changed significantly and reporting was focused primarily on the gender differences in cardiovascular tolerance to the Short Radius Centrifugation (SRC).

Six men and five women were assessed during the centrifuge tolerance test or loading protocol, for 60 minutes at 2.5G. This is equivalent to 1G at the subject’s feet. Among the male population five out of the six completed the trail successfully. For the females, four out of five tests were terminated early because of pre-syncope. The true cause of this difference requires further investigation. LSDA does not expect to receive results from this study however, more information can be found through the publication listed.
